en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods (Śiva), Śeṣa, all the deities, the Manus, and the lords of sages—
I bow to that Sovereign Lord whom Sarasvatī, Śrī, Girijā, and the other goddesses revere.
(1) I worship that Unborn One, the Great and Primordial, who assumes gross bodies composed of the three qualities and in whose pores of the skin the entire universe resides;
who, intent on creation, having united with his own subtle power, brought forth the eternal subtle form within his heart. (2)

3. Devoted to meditation, gods, humans, and demigods—saintly yogis firmly established in yoga—meditate upon Him who, though existing, is not seen by even a few people throughout many births, even in their dreams, despite their austerities. Obeisance to that Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond the three modes of nature, infallible, and from whom [the universe arises]. I meditate with devotion upon Him who consists of His own will, who is beyond the three qualities (*guṇas*), changeless, and effortless; who, for the sole purpose of being the object of meditation, assumes a form of incomparable beauty and eternal youth. I bow to Kṛṣṇa, who transcends all attributes, the Supreme Brahman, the Infallible One.
The primordial deities, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, became manifest. Om, salutations to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men.
Then one should utter the victory-hymn to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa.
(1) The divine Vyāsa milked this most ancient nectar—the wish-fulfilling cow of Bhāratī—having made the collection of the Vedas its calf.
O simple ones, drink, drink this most beautiful Purāṇa, the Brahmavaivarta, this inexhaustible and desired milk! (2)
In the Naimiṣa forest in Bhārata, the sages headed by Śaunaka, having performed their daily and occasional rites, were seated upon grass mats. In the meantime, Sauti arrived there by chance.
Seeing him bowed down and well-disciplined, they offered him a seat.
Having honored that guest with devotion, Śaunaka, the bull among sages—himself peaceful and a knower of the Purāṇas—joyfully inquired after the welfare of the tranquil sage. (2–3)
Free from the fatigue of the journey, seated firmly upon his seat,
smiling, knowing all principles, the ancient among the ancients—
[he heard] that supreme Purāṇa, endowed with the narrations of Kṛṣṇa and in accord with the Vedas. 4.
He is auspiciousness itself, worthy of auspiciousness, the source of auspiciousness, and the abode of auspiciousness;
he is the seed of all auspiciousness, the perpetual bestower of auspiciousness,
the destroyer of all inauspiciousness, and the supreme bringer of all prosperity.
It bestows devotion to Hari, eternally grants happiness, and delivers one from worldly existence;
it imparts the knowledge of reality and increases one's wife, sons, and grandsons.
(7) Being well-pleased, he questioned him with great humility in the assembly of sages.
Just as the king of the twice-born shines among the stars in the sky.
Śaunaka said:
Where is your destination, and from where do you come? May it be well with you.

What a day of merit this is for us today through the sight of you! (9) We ourselves are terrified by the Kali age, devoid of superior knowledge, and submerged in worldly existence while longing for liberation; it is for that reason that you have come here. (10)
You are a virtuous and highly fortunate master of the Purāṇas,
well-versed in all the Purāṇas, an ocean of great compassion,
from whom eternal and unwavering devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa arises. (11)
Therefore, O illustrious one, let that Purāṇa which increases knowledge be told—
[that Purāṇa] which is most weighty, which directly cuts away the root of karma,
and which acts as a pair of shears for severing the fetters of those bound to saṃsāra.
O Sauti, for living beings whose minds are scorched by the forest fire of worldly existence, this work— showering a rain of nectar, bestowing happiness and bliss— is eternally [a source of comfort].
In it, there is first of all the description of the Supreme Brahman, who is the seed of all.
Even though he was intent on creation, there follows the supreme glorification of that creation (verse 15).
[The inquiry concerns] the nature of the Supreme Self, whether it possesses form or is formless;
what is the form of that Brahman, what is its meditation, and what is its contemplation? (verse 16).

What indeed do the Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon, or likewise the peaceful yogins? Whose doctrine is considered primary, as set forth secretly in the Veda? And what is the nature of Prakṛti, wherein it is described as a calf? (17)
Wherein there is the definition of the *guṇas* and the determination of the principles beginning with Mahat;
wherein there is the description of Goloka, the description of Vaikuṇṭha, the description of Śivaloka, and other descriptions of heaven. (18–19)
O Sauti, where there is a description of the *aṃśas* and *kalās*,
who are the *prakṛtas*, what is *prakṛti*, who is the *ātman* beyond *prakṛti*,
and for which gods or divine women birth is hidden? (20)

The origin of the oceans, the mountains, and even the rivers; what are the portions of *prakṛti*, what are its parts, and what are the sub-divisions of those parts? Furthermore, their conduct, meditation, auspicious worship, hymns of praise, and so forth. (21–22)

In it is the description of Durgā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and Sāvitrī; therein also is the most extraordinary account of Rādhikā, which is like nectar, as well as the ripening of the karma of living beings and the description of the hells. (23)
Wherever there is the destruction of karmas and liberation from them;
whatever place belongs to which living beings and where their merit and demerit reside;
and from what karma of living beings [they arise] in whichever wombs. (24–25)
Since whatever disease may arise here for living beings is caused by their own karma,
therefore explain to them the means of liberation from that karma.
[25] Mentally, Tulasī, Kālī, Gaṅgā, Pṛthvī, and Vasundharā—
O Sauti, that in which there is the auspicious narration of these [rivers], as well as of others;
wherein there is a description of Śāligrāma stones and of various gifts;
and wherein there is an unprecedented exposition of dharma and adharma.
In it is the life story of Gaṇeśvara, including his birth and deeds;
therein is a description of the armor, hymns, and mantras that are profound and secret;
and there is an unprecedented narrative, unheard of before, most wonderful of all. (29)

Having taken all of this to heart, you should now speak concerning that place where the birth of Kṛṣṇa— the Supreme Soul, the most perfect one— occurred in the holy land of Bhārata, amidst the delusion of the world. (30–31)
O Sage, in whose meritorious house was this son of merit born? Which blessed, venerable, and virtuous woman gave birth to him? Having appeared from that house, where has he gone and for what reason?
Having gone there, what did he do, and how did he return?
By whose request did he perform the removal of the earth's burden?
And having constructed the bridge, what else did he do before returning again to Goloka?
Thus, this is another ancient narrative, difficult to find even in the Vedas;
it is hard for even sages to comprehend, yet it is the cause of the purification of the mind.
Whatever—whether auspicious or inauspicious—I have asked concerning my own knowledge and so forth, or even what was not asked, [has been told].
"You ought to explain that to me which instantly generates dispassion.
He who provides an exposition—whether asked by a disciple or unasked—is a true guru, the best among the virtuous, and one who is impartial toward the worthy and the unworthy. (36–37)
Sauti said:
"All is well for us from the sight of your lotus-like feet.
Having come from Siddhakṣetra, I am now going to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa. (38)
Having seen the assembly of Brahmins, he has come here to offer salutations;
and having seen the Naimiṣa forest, which bestows merit even in Bhārata, he has come.
But he who, upon seeing a god, a Brahmin, or a guru, does not bow down out of haste— [he incurs sin]. (39)
He goes to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Hari constantly wanders upon the earth in the form of a brāhmaṇa;
a meritorious person, through his virtue, should bow before that brāhmaṇa who is the very form of Hari.
O Blessed One, that which was asked by you has been understood—all that is desired. The Brahmavaivarta is the most excellent among the Purāṇas, the very essence of them all.
It is the dispeller of confusion regarding the Purāṇas, the Upapurāṇas, and the Vedas. (42)
It bestows devotion to Hari and increases the knowledge of all essential truths;
it grants the desires of those who possess longing and grants liberation to those seeking release;
it bestows devotion upon the Vaiṣṇavas and is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
The Brahma-khaṇḍa is the seed of all, a description of the Supreme Brahman;
virtuous Vaiṣṇava yogis meditate upon that which is higher than the highest.
O Śaunaka, the Vaiṣṇavas, the yogis, and the virtuous are not distinct from one another.
Through the ripening of their own ignorance, living beings gradually become [ordinary] people;
through association with the virtuous, they become virtuous; through association with yogis, they become yogis;
through association with Vaiṣṇavas, they gradually become supreme practitioners of yoga. 46–47.
Wherein is the origin of the gods, the goddesses, and all living beings;
thereafter, in the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, is the auspicious life-story of the goddesses,
the ripening of the karma of living beings, and the description of the Śāligrāma.
And therein is the description of their armor, hymns, mantras, and worship;
the definition of primordial nature (prakṛti), the description of its constituent parts and portions, the glorification of their fame, and their power have been set forth. (Verses 49–50)
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious destination awaits the doers of good and evil deeds,
as well as the description of the hells and the liberation from diseases— after that,
in the Gaṇeśa-khaṇḍa, his birth is fully proclaimed. (51)
This is an exceedingly unprecedented account, difficult to find even through the Vedas;
it is the exposition of all essential truths within the dialogue between Gaṇeśa and Bhṛgu, and the description of the secret armor, hymns, mantras, and tantras. (52–53)
And thereafter, the Śrīkṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa was proclaimed;
[it describes] the birth and deeds of Śrīkṛṣṇa in the meritorious field of Bhārata,
the removal of the earth's burden, and the auspicious wonders of his divine play.
And the construction of the bridge for the virtuous has been described in the Janmakhaṇḍa.
This supreme Purāṇa, O Brahmin, has been narrated to you;
it consists of four sections and provides a comprehensive exposition of all dharmas.

The Purāṇa named Brahmavaivarta grants the desires of all, bestows prosperity, fulfills every hope, and yields the fruits of all cherished goals. It is the very essence among the Purāṇas and is solely equal to the Vedas. (57)
O Śaunaka, because the entirety of Brahman was revealed therein by Kṛṣṇa,
those who know the past call it the Brahmavaivarta;
and this sūtra of the Purāṇa was formerly given to Brahmā.
In the stainless Goloka, by Kṛṣṇa the Supreme Soul,
it was given to Dharma at the great holy site of Puṣkara;
and by Dharma, out of affection, it was given to his son Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada gave it to Vyāsadeva on the bank of the Jāhnavī;
Vyāsa, having composed that vast and great Purāṇa-sūtra,
gave it to me at Siddhakṣetra, a delightful and meritorious region.
O Brahmin, listen to all of this that has been told by me.
This Purāṇa consists of eighteen thousand verses as composed by Vyāsa. Now, hear what fruit a man obtains from listening to the entirety of the Purāṇa.
One certainly obtains that fruit by listening to this chapter.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Table of Contents," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Śaunaka said:
"O Sauti, what unprecedented, most wonderful, and desired thing have you heard?
Tell us everything, including the unsurpassed Brahmakhaṇḍa.
Sauti said:
I bow to the lotus feet of my guru Vyāsa, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Having prostrated before Hari, the gods, and the twice-born, I shall declare the eternal dharmas.
That unsurpassed Brahmakhaṇḍa which was heard from the mouth of Vyāsa [shall now be told].
O twice-born one, at the time of primordial dissolution, there existed only a mass of light— the destroyer of the blinding darkness of ignorance, the illuminator of the path of knowledge,
eternal, immeasurable, possessing the splendor of ten million suns, and the cause of the universe. (3–4)
And within that great, blazing light of the Lord, who consists of His own will,
there is the enchanting triple world;
above those, O twice-born one, is Goloka, which is eternal like the Lord Himself.
It is three million yojanas in length and breadth, circular in shape,
consisting of the nature of light, and composed of supreme, magnificent jewel-ground.
It is invisible to yogis in their dreams, yet visible and accessible to the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Held by the Lord through his yoga, that excellent [abode] is situated in the intermediate space;
it is free from mental anguish, physical disease, old age, death, sorrow, and fear,
and is adorned with countless palaces constructed of precious gems.
In the creation, [he saw] Kṛṣṇa accompanied by his attendants and surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses.
Fifty koṭis of yojanas below that, to the south and to the north,
are Vaikuṇṭha and Śivaloka, which are equal in extent and exceedingly beautiful.
Vaikuṇṭha is ten million yojanas in extent and is circular in shape.
At the time of dissolution it is void, and at the time of creation it is endowed with Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
It is accompanied by four-armed attendants and is free from old age, death, and other such afflictions.
And on the left is the world of Śiva, extending for ten million yojanas;
it is empty during the dissolution and filled with Śiva and his attendants during the creation.
Within Goloka is a light that is exceedingly beautiful.
It is eternally most gladdening and the cause of supreme bliss;
yogis constantly meditate upon it through yoga with the eye of knowledge.
That very thing is the generator of bliss, formless, and higher than the highest. (14)
Within that light was a form exceedingly beautiful to behold:
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like red lotuses, its stainless face graced by the splendor of the full autumnal moon. (15–16)
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, the delightful abode of grace,
two-armed, with a flute in his hand, smiling, clad in yellow garments,
adorned with a multitude of ornaments of excellent gems, and affectionate toward his devotees. (11)
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with musk and saffron;
his chest shining with the Śrīvatsa mark and resplendent with the Kaustubha gem;
blazing with a crown and diadem fashioned from the finest essence of precious jewels.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and adorned with a forest garland—
He is that very Supreme Brahman, the eternal Blessed Lord,
consisting of His own will, the seed of all, the support of all, and higher than the highest. (20)
[He is] eternally in the bloom of youth, always assuming the dress of a cowherd;
rich with the splendor of ten million full moons, bestowing grace upon his devotees;
effortless, changeless, the most perfect, and all-pervading. (21–22)
Standing in the center of the circle of the rāsa dance, the peaceful and excellent Lord of the rāsa;
auspicious, worthy of auspiciousness, the embodiment of auspiciousness, and the bestower of auspiciousness;
the seed of supreme bliss, the true, imperishable, and immutable one. (23)
The Lord of all accomplishments, the embodiment of all success, and the bestower of perfection;
the Sovereign beyond primordial nature, devoid of qualities, possessing an eternal form;
the Primordial Person, unmanifest, invoked by many, and praised by many. (24–25)
The peaceful Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon that which is true, independent, one, and the very nature of the Supreme Self—that peaceful ultimate refuge.
Bearing such a supreme form, he is indeed the one Blessed Lord alone. (26)
He beheld the entire universe as empty, together with the quarters and the sky.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Brahman," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
Having seen the entire universe as consisting of emptiness and Goloka as terrifying— frightful, devoid of living beings, devoid of water, windless, enveloped in darkness,
and stripped of trees, mountains, oceans, and the like, appearing in a distorted form— (1).

O twice-born one, having mentally surveyed everything as being devoid of liberation, devoid of elements, devoid of crops, and devoid of grass, the Lord— who consists of his own will— began by himself, alone and without companion,
to create the world according to his desire. (2–3)
At the beginning of creation,
the three qualities (guṇas), which are the embodied forms of the cause of existence, manifested from the right side of the Person.
From that [emanated] the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
Form, taste, smell, touch, and sound— these were their names.
Thereafter, the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself appeared,
dark-complexioned, youthful, clad in yellow garments, wearing a forest garland, and four-armed.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with a smiling lotus-face, richly adorned with jewel ornaments, bearing the Śārṅga bow, and decorated with the Kaustubha gem;
having the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, the abode of Śrī, the ordainer of Śrī, and the source of Śrī’s manifestation. (7)
Hara, who possesses a face like the moon of autumn, polished by its radiance, and who is as beautiful as a lovely flower;
he, whose form and loveliness were made exquisite by the splendor of Kāmadeva, stood before Śrī Kṛṣṇa and praised him with palms joined in reverence. (8–9)
Nārāyaṇa said:
He is the most excellent boon, the bestower of boons, worthy of boons, and the cause of all boons;
he is the cause of causes, and his action is the cause of that very action. (10)
I bow to the ascetic who bestows the fruit of austerity, the eternal Lord of ascetics, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, delighting in his own Self, and captivating to the mind;
who is free from desire, yet assumes forms at will, destroys desire, and is the cause of desire. (11)
He is everything, the Lord of all, the supreme seed-form of all;
He is the embodiment of the Vedas, born from the Vedas, the bestower of the fruits proclaimed by the Vedas, and the fruit itself;
He is the knower of the Vedas, the ordainer thereof, and the foremost among those who know all the Vedas.

Having spoken thus, filled with devotion, he dwelt by the command of the Supreme Soul upon a beautiful jeweled throne before Him. Whoever recites this hymn composed by Nārāyaṇa with a well-concentrated mind—
Whoever recites this constantly at the three junctions of the day, for him no sin exists.
(15) One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring a wife obtains a beloved spouse.
One who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom; one whose wealth is lost regains his wealth. (16)
One who is seized by calamity in prison is liberated by this hymn;
and a sick person, being self-controlled, is certainly freed from disease upon hearing it.
Sauti said:
Thereafter, he manifested from his own left side:
pure like white crystal, five-faced, and clad in the directions as his garment;
possessing the luster of molten gold, the excellent one bore a mass of matted locks. (18)
With a slightly smiling, serene countenance, three eyes, and the moon as his crest-jewel;
bearing a trident and a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), with a rosary in his hand, he is the Supreme One.
He is the Lord of all accomplishments, the perfected Siddha, the Guru of the lords of yogis. (19–20)
The Lord who is death unto death, Śiva who is both death and the conqueror of death;
the bliss of knowledge, the possessor of great knowledge, the supreme bestower of great knowledge.
(21) He is captivating, his face visible with the luster of the full moon and polished like nectar.
The foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, stood before Śrī Kṛṣṇa and offered praise with palms joined in reverence;
his entire body was marked with horripilation, his eyes filled with tears, and his voice was exceedingly faltering. (22–23)

Mahādeva said: I bow to that unconquered one, who is the very nature of victory, the giver of victory, the Lord of victory, the cause of victory, and the most excellent among all givers of victory. (24)
The universe, the Lord of the lords of the universe, the Sovereign of the universe, the cause of the universe;
the support of the universe, the one in whom the universe rests, the cause of the cause of the universe;
the cause of the protection of the universe, the destroyer of the universe, the supreme source born of the universe. (25)
"The seed of fruit, the support of fruit, the fruit itself, and the giver of that fruit;
the very nature of splendor, the giver of splendor, the best among all who possess splendor.
Having spoken thus and bowed to him, [he seated him] upon an excellent jewel-throne.
Having addressed Nārāyaṇa, he dwelt there by his command.
(27) Whoever recites this hymn composed by Śambhu while self-restrained shall attain all perfections and victory at every step. (28)
A friend, wealth, and power increase continuously;
the enemy's army perishes, as do sorrows and misfortunes.
(29) Thus ends the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Stotra composed by Śambhu in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Sauti said: Thereafter, there appeared from the lotus of Kṛṣṇa’s navel an excellent being, an ancient ascetic of great austerity, holding a water-pot in his hand. (30)
Clad in white, with white teeth and white hair, he is four-faced;
the Lord of Yogins, the Lord of artisans, the progenitor and teacher of all.
He is the bestower of the fruits of austerities and the giver of all prosperity. (31)
He is the creator, the ordainer, and the performer of all deeds;

he is the destroyer and the sustainer of the four Vedas. He is the knower of the source of the Vedas, peaceful, the beloved of Sarasvatī, of virtuous character, and a treasure-house of compassion. (32–33)
Standing before Śrī Kṛṣṇa with palms joined in reverence, his entire body covered in horripilation and his neck bowed low in devotion, he offered praise to Him. (34) Brahmā said:
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, who transcends all qualities, the one Govinda, the imperishable, the unmanifest, the undecaying, the manifest, who assumes the guise of a cowherd;
who is of youthful age, peaceful, the beloved of the gopīs, and captivating to the mind. (35)
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, more beautiful than ten million Cupids,
situated within the circle of the rāsa dance on the outskirts of the Vṛndāvana forest—
the Lord of the rāsa, the abode of the rāsa, and eager for the joy of the rāsa. (36–37)

Having spoken thus and bowed to him, he conversed with Nārāyaṇa and Īśa on their excellent jewel-throne and dwelt there by their command. (38) Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this hymn composed by Brahmā—
His sins perish, and his bad dreams become good dreams.
(39) Devotion to Govinda arises, which increases one’s prosperity, sons, and grandsons.
Infamy comes to an end, and true fame increases for a long time. (40)
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa composed by Brahmā in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Sauti said:
Thereafter, [the goddess] manifested from the chest of the Supreme Self.
A certain person, smiling, white-complexioned, and wearing matted locks;
the witness of all, the omniscient one, the equal toward all and all their actions, truly compassionate, and free from violence and anger. (41–42)
One who is endowed with the knowledge of Dharma becomes a practitioner of Dharma, most righteous, and a giver of Dharma.
He alone is the Dharma of those who possess it; he is the Supreme Self, the source of all fruits.
(43) Standing before Śrī Kṛṣṇa and prostrating like a staff upon the ground—
He praised the Supreme Self, the Lord of all, the granter of all desires.
Śrī Dharma said:
[I praise] Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, the Lord.
Govinda, supreme bliss, the one, the imperishable, the infallible;
the Lord of the cowherds and the Lord of the cowherd-maidens, the protector of the cows, the all-pervading one;
the Master of the cattle, dwelling in the cow-pen, and bearing the tail of a calf. 45–46.
"Standing in the midst of the cows, cowherds, and gopīs, [I am] the Pradhāna, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Having uttered this, he rose upon an excellent jewel-throne;
having addressed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, he sat down.
These twenty-four names have emerged from the mouth of Dharma;
whoever recites them upon rising in the morning shall be happy and victorious in all things.
At the time of death, he will certainly attain the goal of the name of Hari.
In the end, he goes to the abode of Hari; service to Hari will certainly become his constant lot.
Eternal dharma accrues to him, and he shall have no delight in unrighteousness.
The fruit of the four aims of life will forever remain within his grasp.
Upon seeing him, all sins flee out of fear,
and even terrors and miseries vanish like serpents before Vainateya (Garuḍa).
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa composed by Dharma in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
Sauti said:
A single maiden appeared from the left side of Dharma;
she was the personified form of Virtue itself, like a second Lakṣmī in visible form. (53)
Thereafter, from the face of the Supreme Self, there appeared a single goddess, white in complexion, holding a lute and a book;
she was enriched with the splendor of ten million full moons, and her eyes were like autumn lotuses. (54)
Clad in garments as pure as fire, adorned with jewel ornaments, smiling, possessing beautiful teeth, dark-complexioned, and the most beautiful among beauties;
she is the supreme mother of the Vedas, the scriptures, and the learned. (55–56)
She is the goddess presiding over speech, the beloved deity of poets;
Sarasvatī, whose nature is pure sattva and whose form is peaceful, stood before Govinda and first sang joyfully. (57)
She danced upon her lute, chanting the praises of his names and virtues;
with palms joined in reverence, she offered hymns of praise for all the deeds performed by Hari throughout every kalpa and every yuga. (58–59)
Sarasvatī said:
[He is] situated in the center of the circle of the rāsa dance, eager for the joy of the rāsa;
seated upon a jeweled throne, and adorned with ornaments of gems. (60)

I bow to the Lord of the Rāsa, the bestower of the Rāsa, the supreme Lord of the Queen of the Rāsa, the presiding deity of the Rāsa, who delights in the Rāsa; I bow to Him who wanders in the Rāsa-dance, though He is weary from the exertion of the Rāsa. (61)
Having bowed to Him— the beloved of the gopīs who were eager for the *rāsa* dance, who is peaceful and captivating—
and having spoken thus with a joyful countenance,
that virtuous woman, full of longing, sat upon an excellent jewel-encrusted throne.
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this hymn composed by Vāṇī,
shall always be intelligent, wealthy, learned, and possessed of sons.
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa composed by Sarasvatī in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
Sauti said:
From the mind of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, there appeared a single goddess, fair-complexioned and adorned with jewel ornaments. (65)

Clad in yellow garments, smiling, and in the bloom of youth, she is the presiding deity of all sovereignty and the bestower of the fruits of all prosperity. She is the Fortune of Heaven in heaven and the Royal Fortune among kings. (66)
Standing before Hari, that virtuous woman, bowing down with her neck bent low in devotion, praised the Supreme Self, the Lord. (67) Mahālakṣmī said:
"I bow to Him whose nature is truth, the Lord of truth, the seed of truth, the eternal,
the support of truth, the knower of truth, and the root of truth. Having spoken thus and bowed to Śrī Hari, she sat upon a comfortable seat.

Then, after that, there appeared she who possesses the luster of molten gold, illuminating the quarters with her radiance— the Goddess who is the presiding deity of all, the Sovereign Mūlaprakṛti, the Supreme Self of the Buddha. (69–70)
She possesses the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to ten million suns;
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and her eyes are like autumn lotuses.
She is clothed in red garments and adorned with jeweled ornaments.
Sleep, thirst, hunger, craving, compassion, faith, forgiveness, and so forth—
of all these powers, the presiding deity is Īśa.
She is the terrifying one, the hundred-armed Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress.
She is the supreme mother of the worlds, the very form of the power of the Self.
[She holds] the trident, the spear, the Śārṅga bow, the sword, and arrows;
the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the rosary, and the water-pot.
Bearing the vajra, the goad, the noose, the *bhuśuṇḍī*, the staff, and the *tomara*—
as well as the Nārāyaṇa weapon, the Brahmā weapon, the Raudra, the Pāśupata,
the Pārjanya, the Vāruṇa, the Āgneya, and the Gāndharva— the virtuous lady shone.
Standing before Kṛṣṇa, she, filled with joy, praised him.
Prakṛti said:
"I am Prakṛti, the sovereign, the ruler of all, and the embodiment of all."
The entire world is of the nature of power (śakti) and possesses power;
it was created by you and is not independent. You alone are the Lord of the worlds, the refuge, the protector, the creator, the destroyer, and again the ordainer.
I bow to you, who are the creator for creating and the destroyer for destroying, the ordinance ordained by the Ordainer;
I bow to you, whose nature is supreme bliss, preceded by bliss.
And in the time of a single blink of an eye, the fall of Brahmā occurs. (79)
O Lord, who is capable of describing his incomparable power—
he who, by the mere play of a frown, can create ten million Viṣṇus and all the gods throughout the worlds, headed by Brahmā? (80)
O Goddess, how many like me could even you create with ease?
I bow with joy to that most perfect and adorable Lord,
O All-pervading One, of whom the great Virāṭ is but a fractional part and who is the refuge of all the worlds.
I bow to that Supreme Lord, the Self, who is preceded by bliss (Ānandapūrva),
whom even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others are unable to praise;
I, along with the Vedas, Speech, and myself, bow to Him who is beyond primordial nature (Prakṛti).
"Even the Vedas, the best among the learned, are not capable of praising him;
who is able to praise that desireless one who is beyond all marks? I bow to him.
Having spoken thus, that Durgā [sat] upon an excellent jeweled throne.
Having bowed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they dwelt there, and the lords of the gods offered praise to her.
Thus is the hymn composed by Durgā for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
whoever recites it at the time of worship shall be victorious everywhere and happy in every way.
Durgā never leaves his house at any time;
he shines with glory in the ocean of existence and, in the end, goes to the city of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Hymn to Durgā," in the Description of Creation within the Dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka, in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sauti said: Thereafter, there appeared before the tip of Kṛṣṇa’s tongue a single, enchanting goddess, resembling pure crystal. (1)
Clad in white garments and adorned with all ornaments,
holding a rosary, she is celebrated as Sāvitrī.
Standing before him, she praised the supreme, eternal Brahman.
With her hands joined in reverence, that virtuous woman, her neck bowed in devotion, spoke.
Sāvitrī said:
"I bow to you, the seed of all, the eternal light of Brahman."
"Higher than the highest, dark-complexioned, changeless, and stainless"—
having spoken thus, the goddess, the mother of the Vedas, bowed again to Śrī Hari and sat upon an excellent jeweled throne with a smile. (4–5)
Thereafter, from the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa,
there appeared a single male being born of his mind, resembling molten gold;
he churns the minds of all lovers with his five arrows.
Therefore, the wise call him Manmatha (the Mind-agitator).
From the left side of that man, Kāma, there arose an excellent woman,
exceedingly graceful and the enchantress of all.
Seeing that virtuous lady smiling, delight arose in everyone;
therefore, the wise call her by the name "Rati.
Having praised Hari, he dwelt with her before the presence of Hari.
And upon his jeweled lion-throne sits the five-arrowed one, the wielder of the bow;
he bears five arrows—slaying, paralyzing, causing yawning, drying up, and likewise intoxicating. (10–11)
Kāma discharged all his arrows for the sake of testing them;
by the will of the Lord, they all immediately became filled with desire.
Upon seeing Rati, the seed of Brahmā fell.
There the great yogi remained, covering himself with a cloth out of shame.
Having burnt the cloth, the Lord of the Gods rose up as a blazing fire, ten million palm trees in height, with a crest of flames, intensely radiant. (13–14)
Seeing that increase, Kṛṣṇa, by his own divine play,
emitted water from his mouth along with the breath of his exhalation;
O twice-born one, that water from the drop of his mouth flooded the entire multitude of worlds.
There, a certain drop of water extinguished the fire.
From that time forward, fire would go to extinction by means of water.
Then, a single Person appeared as its presiding deity.

A single man rose from those waters; he is known as Varuṇa, the presiding deity of the waters and the lord of all aquatic creatures. (18) A certain maiden appeared from the left side of that Fire-god.
The wise call her Svāhā, the wife of Agni.
From the left side of the Lord of Waters, a maiden was born;
she is renowned as Varuṇānī, the virtuous beloved of Varuṇa. (19–20)
From the breath of the Lord, there arose the glorious Wind;
he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all beings, and exhalation is produced as its fruit.
From the left side of that Wind, a maiden was born.
She is the wife of Vāyu, and that goddess is celebrated as Vāyavī.
By the arrow of Kāma, Kṛṣṇa’s semen was discharged;
out of shame in the assembly of the gods, he released it into the water. (22–23)
At the end of a thousand years, he indeed assumed the form of an infant;
from him was born the great Virāj, who is the very support of the multitude of all worlds.
In a single pore of his hair resides the entire universe.
He is even vaster than the vast; there is nothing greater than He. (25) He alone is the sixteenth part of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
He should be known as Mahāviṣṇu, the eternal support of all. (26)
As he lay upon the great ocean like a lotus leaf upon the water,
those two Daityas, born from the wax of his ears, came into being.
Rising up from the water, they prepared to slay Brahmā.
And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa struck those two on their hindquarters.
The entire earth became completely covered with that fat;
all the worlds are situated right there, and she is the goddess Vasundharā.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Creation," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Śaunaka said:
Are the cows, the cowherds, and the cowherd-maidens in Goloka eternal, or are they merely created?
"You ought to explain that to me for the purpose of dispelling my doubt.
Sauti said:
"In every initial creation they are fashioned, and at every dissolution they remain [in their state]."
O twice-born one, I have related to you this account of the primordial creation.
In every beginning of creation and in its arrangement, Nārāyaṇa and Maheśvara are manifested;
in every dissolution, they remain manifest, as does that Prakṛti.
"O twice-born one, at the very beginning, the history of the Brahmakalpa has been told.
I shall now relate the two kalpas of Vārāha and Pādma; you shall hear them.
O sage, the kalpas are of three kinds: Brāhma, Vārāha, and Pādma."
Just as the four ages have been described in sequence—
Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— this constitutes the cycle of the four ages (caturyuga).
A divine age (divya-yuga) is recorded as consisting of three hundred and sixty such ages.
A Manvantara consists of seventy-one divine Yugas.
When fourteen Manus have passed, that constitutes one day of Brahmā.
And three hundred and sixty such days constitute one year of Brahmā.
One hundred and eight years have been determined as the lifespan of Brahmā.
This [lifespan] is but a single blink of an eye for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, those who know time have determined that one kalpa is equal to the entire lifespan of Brahmā.
Those minor cycles, such as the periods of dissolution and so forth, are remembered as being more numerous.
According to that view, Mārkaṇḍeya is one whose life lasts for seven kalpas;
and that [period] is proclaimed to be a single day of Brahmā.
And the lifespan of the sage [Brahmā] was determined to be seven days by Vidhi (Brahmā).
Three kalpas—the Brāhma, Vārāha, and Pādma—have been described.
Listen as I relate how the creation occurred during those three kalpas. || 11–12 ||
And in the Brāhma Kalpa, having created the earth, that Creator brought forth creation;
and by the command of the Lord, it was formed from the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
In the Vārāha Kalpa, he raised her up after she had been submerged and lost in the netherworld (rasātala).
Through the agency of Viṣṇu in his Boar form, and with great effort,
the Creator fashioned the creation within the lotus of Viṣṇu’s navel—
the three worlds ending with the world of Brahmā, excluding the three eternal worlds.
This enumeration of time has been declared in the description of creation. What further description of creation do you wish to hear? (16) Śaunaka said:
What did the Blessed One, the Lord of the Sātvatas, do after this?
Having created these [beings], what did he do next? You should explain that to me.
Sauti said:
Beyond this, however, in Goloka, the great Lord, the Master of Goloka, having created these [beings], went to the most beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala;
together with them, the Blessed One appeared exceedingly lovely. (18)
In the midst of beautiful *kalpa* trees, it was exceedingly captivating;
very extensive, perfectly level, very smooth, and circular in shape.
It was exquisitely prepared with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
It was strewn with curds, parched grain flour, rice, and dūrvā grass;
it was tied with knots of silk thread and adorned with fresh sandalwood sprouts; and it was encircled by clusters of banana tree trunks. (20–21)
With thirty million pavilions fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems,
illuminated by jewel-lamps and perfumed with flowers, incense, and other offerings;
surrounded by a multitude of articles of enjoyment suitable for the erotic sentiment.
It was exceedingly beautified by those who were adorned with most graceful ornaments and garments.
Having gone there together with them, the Lord of the World dwelt there;
and upon seeing the *rāsa* dance, O best of sages, they were filled with wonder. (23–24)
A certain maiden appeared from the left side of Kṛṣṇa;
having run forward and brought flowers, she offered water for the feet (arghya) at the feet of the Lord.
Having joined the Rāsa dance in Goloka, she ran before Hari.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, she is called Rādhā by those who know the ancient lore.
She is the presiding deity of the life-breaths of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
she manifested from his vital breaths, being even dearer than those very breaths. (26–27)
The goddess was sixteen years of age, endowed with fresh youth;
she wore garments as pure as fire, was smiling, and exceedingly beautiful.
With limbs most tender, she was graceful and the most beautiful among the beautiful. (28)
Afflicted by the weight of her large hips, with full hips and breasts, that excellent woman surpassed the bandhujīva flower with her beautiful red lips;
she was enchanting, with a lovely row of teeth that outshone a string of pearls. (29–30)
Her auspicious face was polished with the splendor of ten million full moons of autumn;
she possessed the beautiful eyes of an autumn lotus and the lovely womanly charm of a beautiful lady;
her enchanting nose surpassed even the beak of the king of birds. 31.
Her two cheeks, which surpassed golden bowls in beauty, were adorned with beautiful earrings decorated with jeweled ornaments;
she was further graced by drops of saffron mixed with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk. || 32–33 ||
Her beautiful cheeks were adorned with dots of vermilion; she was captivating,
possessing a well-groomed mass of hair decorated with garlands of jasmine,
and bearing a lovely, fragrant braid.
Bearing a pair of feet that eclipsed the luster of land-lotuses, she moved with a gait that put to shame both the swan and the khañjana bird;
she wore a beautiful forest garland fashioned from the finest precious gems. (35–36)
A necklace fashioned of diamonds, jeweled armlets and bracelets,
a most enchanting noose crafted from the finest essence of precious gems,
and [a pair of] anklets adorned with the tinkling sound of priceless jewels. (37)
Bearing that beautiful [form], richly adorned with various kinds of wonders,
she addressed Govinda and sat upon an excellent jeweled lion-throne,
smiling as she gazed at her husband’s lotus-face. (38–39)
And from her pores, immediately there appeared a multitude of cowherd girls, equal to her in form and attire;
numbering in the hundreds of millions and billions, they were eternally fixed in the bloom of youth.
O sage, the multitude of cowherd girls was counted by those skilled in calculation in Goloka; and from the pores of Kṛṣṇa’s skin, the multitude of cowherds immediately manifested,
identical to him in form and attire.
42–43. A charming and captivating host of cowherds, numbering thirty crores, was mentioned in the Vedas by those skilled in calculation.
That multitude suddenly manifested from the pores of Kṛṣṇa’s skin.
There was a herd of cows of various colors, eternally possessed of stable youth.
There were bulls, Surabhis, and auspicious calves of many kinds;
indeed, there were many exceedingly graceful, dark-hued wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus).
Among them, Kṛṣṇa gave one bull, as powerful as ten million lions and as captivating as a vehicle, to Śiva.
From the darkness of the nails of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, a beautiful row of swans emerged.
Suddenly she appeared, accompanied by a male and female child. Kṛṣṇa gave one royal swan, possessed of great strength and prowess, as a vehicle to Brahmā, the ascetic.
From the opening of the left ear of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
there appeared a captivating host of white horses.
And from among them, one white horse was [given] for the sake of Dharma as a mount.
And the Lord of the cowherd women, with great affection, gave [them] in the assembly of the gods.
From the cavity of the right ear of that Person, in the assembly of the gods,
there appeared a row of lions of great strength and prowess.
Kṛṣṇa gave one of them to Prakṛti with the highest respect,
along with a garland of priceless jewels and whatever boon she desired.
Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yogis, by means of his yoga, fashioned five chariots.
Constructed from pure sapphire and ruby, it is mind-swift and enchanting.
It is one hundred thousand yojanas in height and one hundred yojanas at its base.
It possesses a hundred thousand wheels, is driven by the wind, and is endowed with a hundred thousand pleasure-pavilions.
It was worthy of the erotic sentiment, furnished with countless articles of enjoyment and couches,
adorned with hundreds of thousands of jewel-lamps and horses,
and resplendent with various wonderful paintings and excellent jeweled pitchers.
Richly adorned with jewel-mirrors and ornaments, beautified by white chowries (56);
decorated with variegated garments pure as fire and embellished with nets of pearls;
resplendent with necklaces of the finest gems, pearls, rubies, and diamonds (57).
It was beautifully adorned with countless, exquisite lotuses made of artificial materials from the finest essence of reddish-pink gems;
among them, the best of the twice-born gave one to Nārāyaṇa.
Having given one to Rādhikā, he kept the remainder for himself. Thereafter, a single tawny man appeared from the secret region of Kṛṣṇa's body, together with hosts of tawny attendants.
Because they were manifested from the secret [place], they are known as Guhyakas.
He who was the male became Kubera, the Lord of Wealth and Sovereign of the Guhyakas;
and there was one daughter on the left side of Kubera.
That goddess, the wife of Kubera, was the most beautiful and enchanting of all lovely women.
Then, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Brahma-rākṣasas,
and deformed Vetālas emerged from her secret parts.
All of them bear the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; they wear forest garlands, are clothed in yellow garments, and are dark-complexioned with four arms.
They wear crowns and earrings, and are adorned with jewel ornaments.
O sage, the attendants manifested from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa;
he gave four-armed attendants to Nārāyaṇa,
Guhyakas to Guhyakeśa, and Bhūtas and others to Śaṅkara.
The excellent male servants, dark-complexioned and two-armed,

held prayer beads in their hands and constantly meditated with joy upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. The female servants were likewise appointed, and they diligently brought the water for the guest-offering (arghya).
And all the Vaiṣṇavas, devoted solely to Kṛṣṇa, appeared;

with all their limbs marked by horripilation, their eyes filled with tears, and their voices choked with emotion, they manifested from his lotus feet, their minds fixed on his lotus feet alone. (68–69)
From the right eye of Kṛṣṇa there emerged terrifying beings, three-eyed, with the crescent moon upon their heads, bearing tridents and battle-axes;
they were naked, possessed of massive bodies, and resembled blazing crests of fire. (70)
Those Bhairavas are highly fortunate and equal to Śiva in splendor.
Known as Ruru, Saṃhāra, and Kāla, and terrifying with their dark wrath, they are remembered as the eight Bhairavas, including Mahābhairava and Khaṭvāṅga. (71–72)
From the left eye of Kṛṣṇa there emerged a terrifying being, bearing a trident, a sharp-edged spear, a tiger-skin garment, and a mace;
he was naked, possessed of a massive body, had three eyes, and bore the moon upon his crest. (73)
He is the Lord, the highly fortunate sovereign of the guardians of the quarters.
And thousands of ḍākinīs, yoginīs, and kṣetrapālas manifested from the interior of the opening of Kṛṣṇa’s nostrils.
"Surās, numbering thirty million, excellent and possessing divine forms,
suddenly manifested from the back of the Person.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Creation," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said: Then Kṛṣṇa respectfully presented Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī to Nārāyaṇa, along with the king of jewels and a garland. 1.

He respectfully gave Sāvitrī to Brahmā as his consort, and Mūrti to Dharma; he gave Rati, rich in beauty, to Kāma, and Manoramā to Kubera. And whatever other [daughters] there were, he gave them to others from whom they had sprung.
To each of them Kṛṣṇa gave that very same virtuous and beautiful woman.
Then, having summoned Śaṅkara, the teacher of yogins and Lord of All, he spoke these pleasant words: "You should accept this one who rides upon the lion."
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nīlalohita, laughing yet fearful, bowed down and spoke to the Lord Acyuta, the Master of life. (5) Śrī Maheśvara said:
Now I no longer accept nature as an ordinary person does—
nature which is obstructed solely by devotion to you, which stands in opposition to the path of service,
and which is the bolted door to the gateway of yoga, covered over by the knowledge of reality.
It takes the form of the destruction of the desire for liberation, yet it possesses desire and increases that very desire.
Its true nature is concealed by asceticism; it is a casket of great delusion and a firm shackle within the terrible prison of worldly existence.
O Lord, I do not desire a wife who constantly generates delusion, who cuts off right understanding,
whose essence is perpetual sensual enjoyment, and who increases the craving for sense objects;
grant me my desired boon instead.
That true Lord grants to each person whatever they desire.
(10) My longing for service within the sphere of devotion to you increases incessantly;
indeed, no satiety arises from chanting His name or from serving at His feet. (11)
Constantly singing the virtues of your name— the abode of true auspiciousness— with my five mouths,
I wander through both sleep and waking;
and for ten million times ten million kalpas, I remain intent on meditating upon that form.
May my mind be fixed on yoga and austerity, directed solely toward the desire for enjoyment of You;
and may it find constant delight in serving, worshipping, saluting, and chanting Your names, as well as in finding detachment when these cease. (13–14)
Remembering, chanting the name, hearing of Your qualities, and reciting [mantras]; meditating upon Your beautiful form, serving Your feet, and bowing down;
offering oneself and constantly partaking of the food offering (naivedya). 15.
"O Lord of boons, grant me this boon characterized by the ninefold devotion (navadhā-bhakti).
O All-pervading One, those who know the liberated and the unliberated speak of six kinds of liberation: sārṣṭi, sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya, sāmya, and līnatā. (16–17)
Atomicity (aṇimā), levity (laghimā), attainment (prāpti), efficacy (prākāmya), magnificence (mahimā), lordship (īśitva), mastery (vaśitva), and the fulfillment of all desires (sarvakāmāvasāyitā);
omniscience, hearing from afar, and entry into another's body. 18.
Mastery of speech, the state of being a wish-fulfilling tree, the power to create and destroy, immortality, and preeminence over all—these are recorded as the eighteen perfections (siddhis).
All yogas, austerities, gifts, and vows [are contained therein]. (19–20)
Fame, renown, truthful speech, religious duties, and fasting; wandering to all sacred fords, bathing, and the worship of other deities;
the sight of divine images, and circumambulating the seven continents seven times—(these are not equal to the merit of seeing the Lord). 21.
It is a bath in all the oceans and a vision of all the heavens;
it is the state of Brahmā, the state of Rudra, and the supreme station of Viṣṇu. Are these states, which are thus indescribable, truly desirable? (22–23)
"O Lord of All, all these things that have been mentioned do not equal even a sixteenth part of a fraction of devotion to You.
Having heard these words of Śarva, Kṛṣṇa [addressed] him, the teacher of yogins.
Laughing, he spoke these words, which are true and bestow all happiness. The Blessed Lord said:
O Lord of All, O Śarva, O best among those who know everything, perform service unto Me.
For a full hundred billion kalpas, day and night,
you have been the supreme among ascetics, as well as among the Siddhas, Yogins,
the wise, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the gods, O Lord of Gods. (26–27)
"Obtain immortality and become a great conqueror of death;
by my boon, receive all perfections, the Vedas, and omniscience.
O child, you shall behold the fall of countless Brahmās with ease."

From this day forward, O Śiva, through your knowledge, splendor, age, supreme status, fame, and majesty, become my equal. You shall be superior even to my own life-breaths; there is no devotee other than you who is dearer to me.
There is no one dearer to me than you; you are the supreme essence of my very soul.
Those most sinful ones, devoid of knowledge and lacking consciousness, who revile you, shall be cooked in the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
And at the end of hundreds of millions of kalpas, O Śiva, you shall attain auspiciousness. You ought to fulfill my word so that it may not be in vain;
for I will not now do what has issued from your own mouth.
And you shall fulfill both my word and your own word;
having taken up Prakṛti, O Śambhu, for a thousand divine years,
you will undoubtedly experience great happiness and passion.
"You are not merely an ascetic; you are a lord, great like me.
For he who is a householder, an ascetic, and a yogi at the proper time is indeed composed of his own will.
And as for the suffering in union with a wife that was described by you, O Śiva—" (35–36)
A wicked woman brings suffering to her husband, whereas a devoted wife does not.
She who is born into a great family, noble by birth and a protector of the lineage, out of affection provides care for her husband as if he were a virtuous son. (37)
For women of noble family, the husband is their kinsman, their sustainer, and their deity.
Whether he has fallen from grace or not, whether he is wretched or a lord, for one born of an ignoble lineage who is tainted by her parents’ bad character, [he alone remains her refuge]. (38–39)
Surely those virtuous women who constantly disparage their husbands and look upon another man as superior to us two shall enjoy others and find constant fault with their own lords. Yet,
that virtuous woman who beholds her husband as superior to both of us shall rejoice for ten million kalpas together with her lord in Goloka.
O Śiva, that auspicious Prakṛti shall become Śaivī and Vaiṣṇavī;
by my command, you shall take that virtuous woman for the sake of your manifestation.
Your Liṅga, joined with Prakṛti as its womb, shall be fashioned from the clay of the sacred ford.
Having worshipped a thousand [deities] at a sacred ford with devotion through the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra),
he who is self-restrained, pure, and has conquered his senses, and who gives a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
rejoices with me in Goloka for ten million kalpas.
Whoever worships a hundred thousand [images] at a sacred ford according to the rules, providing excellent sacrificial fees, shall not fall from Goloka; he shall become equal to us two.
Even with clay, ashes, balls of cow dung, or even with sand at a sacred ford, [one attains this].

Having fashioned a *liṅga* and worshipped it even once, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas. Through the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, one becomes possessed of progeny, land, wisdom, sons, and wealth; likewise, one becomes endowed with knowledge, liberation, and virtue.
The worship of the Śiva-liṅga is the true place; that very spot is my sacred ford (tīrtha).
Even a sinner who dies there goes to the world of Śiva.
For those who utter, "Mahādeva, Mahādeva, Mahādeva," [that very place becomes their salvation].
Later, driven by great terror and longing to hear his name, I departed.
That man who gives up his life after uttering the word "Śiva" is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births and attains final liberation. (48–49)
The word *śiva* is auspicious and denotes liberation;
because [liberation] originates from him, he is celebrated as Śiva.
When one is submerged in an ocean of grief due to the loss of wealth and kinsmen, [he provides refuge].

By uttering the word "Śiva," a person shall obtain all that is auspicious (śiva). The syllable *śi* exists as the destroyer of sin (*pāpaghna*), and the syllable *va* likewise bestows liberation (*muktiprada*). Because he destroys the sins of men and grants them liberation, he is celebrated as Śiva.
"Whoever has the name 'Śiva' proceed upon their tongue,
the sin accumulated over ten million births is certainly destroyed for them.
Having spoken thus to the wielder of the trident, Kṛṣṇa gave him the mantra of the wish-fulfilling tree.
He who rides upon a lion declared that the knowledge of reality conquers death.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Now remain here, my child, in my presence in Goloka."

In due time, you shall worship Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness and the path to auspiciousness. O fair-faced one, having manifested within the splendors of all the gods and having destroyed all the Daityas, you shall become honored by all.
Then, in a particular kalpa, when the Satya Yuga prevails,
you shall become the daughter of Dakṣa, Suśīlā, the wife of Śambhu.
Thereafter, having cast off your body at the sacrifice due to the censure of your husband—
And she shall become Pārvatī in Menā, the wife of the Mountain;
for a thousand divine years you shall sport with Śambhu,
and thereafter you shall obtain this entire [world] for all time.
O Goddess of the Suras, when you are worshipped during all the great festivals at the proper time, you shall be honored every year during the autumnal rites;
you are the village deity worshipped in both villages and cities.

By my command, and according to the various tantras composed by Śiva, I shall prescribe the ritual of worship for you— who are known by the beautiful distinction of names such as Bhavatī and Bhavitrī—
along with a protective armor (kavaca) accompanied by hymns of praise.
And they shall become great attendants of you alone;
having attained perfection in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, they shall partake of the fruits [of their merit],
O Mother, those who shall worship you in the sacred field of Bhārata.
"Their fame, renown, and sovereignty over righteousness shall increase.
Having spoken thus, he gave her that eleven-syllable mantra,
the unsurpassed king of mantras, together with the seed-syllable of desire.

Out of compassion for his devotee, he performed meditation according to the prescribed rite and bestowed upon him the ten-syllable mantra, enriched with the glorious seed-syllables of Māyā and Kāma. He granted him the power conducive to creation and all-encompassing success that fulfills every desire.

The All-pervading Lord gave him that knowledge of the most excellent reality distinguished by those [qualities]. Having bestowed upon him the thirteen-syllable mantra, O twice-born one, the Lord of the World likewise gave it to Śaṅkara along with the armor and the hymn.
Having given that mantra and the very same knowledge of accomplishment to Dharmarāja,
and likewise to Kāma, Vahni, Kubera, and Vāyu—
having thus bestowed the supreme mantra and so forth upon Kubera and the others.
He, who is indeed the Creator himself, proclaimed the procedure for the sake of creation.
The Blessed Lord said: "Having performed my own divine austerity for a thousand years," ||| 70 ||
"O illustrious Vidhi, perform a supreme creation of various kinds.
Having spoken thus to Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa gave him a beautiful garland and departed for the forest of Vṛndāvana together with the gopīs and the gopas.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Creation," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
Then Brahmā, having performed penance, attained the perfection he desired.
In the beginning, he created the earth from the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
He created eight principal mountains that were exceedingly beautiful; as for the minor ones, they are innumerable—what more need be said? Now listen to the names of the principal ones.
He created Sumeru, Kailāsa, Malaya, and Himālaya;
likewise Udaya, Asta, Suvela, and Gandhamādana.
He created the seven oceans and the rivers—of how many kinds are the rivers?
Behold the trees, the villages, the cities, and that which is called the ocean.
[Observe] the oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water,
each twice as large as the one preceding it, measuring a hundred thousand *yojanas*.
And [he described] the seven continents and their lands within that lotus-shaped orb of the earth,
as well as the seven sub-continents and the seven boundary mountains. O Brahmin, learn now the names of the continents as they were established by the Creator in the past.

On the eight peaks of Meru, the Lord created eight captivating cities for the recreation of the eight world-protectors (lokapālas), namely Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Plakṣa, Krauñca, Nyagrodha, Pauṣkara, and [the eighth]. || 7–8 ||
Having constructed the city of Ananta at its base, the Lord of the worlds created seven heavens above; hear their names:
Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and the most enchanting Svarloka.
O Śaunaka, [he saw] Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka;
at the summit of the peak, Brahmaloka, which is free from old age and other such afflictions;
and above that, Dhruvaloka, which is beautiful in every respect.
Below that, O Sage, the Lord of the World fashioned the seven netherworlds (pātālas),
which are progressively richer in enjoyments than heaven, situated one below the other:
Atala, Vitala, Sutala, and Talātala.
Below that are Mahātala, Pātāla, and Rasātala.
Together with the seven islands, the seven celestial realms, and those known as the seven netherworlds—
by means of these worlds, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is presided over by Brahmā alone.

And thus, O Śaunaka, this entire multitude of innumerable universes is indeed artificial; it exists within the pores of the hairs of Mahāviṣṇu. In every universe, there are the world-protectors, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
All the gods, beginning with Nara, exist through the illusory power (māyā) of Kṛṣṇa.
Even the Lord of the worlds is not capable of counting the multitude of universes;
neither Śaṅkara, nor Dharma, nor Viṣṇu—what then of the other gods? (16–17)
Although he is capable of counting, he is nevertheless unable to count them;
likewise, although he is able to count the entire universe, the ether, and the directions on all sides, as well as all things both artificial and those situated within the universe. (18)
O best of Brahmins, they are impermanent and perishable like a dream.
Vaikuṇṭha, Śivaloka, and Goloka— which is superior to those two—
are eternal, transcendent of the universe, and like the self, space, and the directions.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Creation," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
Having fashioned the entire universe, Brahmā [placed it] in Sāvitrī, the most excellent of women.
And he infused his virility into her, just as a lustful man does into a woman in love. Having carried that most difficult-to-bear embryo for a hundred divine years,
she gave birth and brought forth the four Vedas, who were truly enchanting.
And various collections of treatises, such as logic and grammar;
thirty-six divine *rāgiṇīs*, exceedingly beautiful;
and six lovely *rāgas* accompanied by various rhythmic measures (*tāla*).
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, which is fond of strife;
the year, month, and season; the lunar day (tithi), the danda, kṣaṇa, and so forth;
the day, night, the weekdays, the twilights, and the dawn.
Puṣṭi, Devasenā, Medhā, Vijayā, and Jayā;
the six Kṛttikās, the Yogas, the Karaṇas, and Tapodhana;
and the virtuous Devasenā, the great Ṣaṣṭhī, the beloved wife of Kārttikeya.
Among the *mātṛkās*, she is the foremost; she is the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) of children.
These three *kalpas*—the Brāhma, the Pādma, and the Vārāha—are traditionally known.
[The dissolution is] constant (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and that which occurs at the end of two *parārdhas*, the primordial (*prākṛta*).
Having brought forth the fourfold dissolution, Time, the Daughter of Death, and all the hosts of diseases, she gave them her breast. Then,
from the back of the Creator, Adharma was born.
From his left side, Alakṣmī was born, who was exceedingly passionate.
From the region of his navel, Viśvakarman was born, the preceptor of artisans.
And the eight great Vasus, endowed with immense strength and prowess, were born. (10–11)
Then, from the elements and the mind, four boys appeared, five years of age and blazing with the splendor of Brahman:
Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana as the third. (12)
The blessed Sanatkumāra, the fourth among the best of the wise,
manifested from [his] mouth as a youth with the luster of gold,
possessing a divine form, glorious, equipped with weapons, handsome, and young. (13–14)
Among the Kṣatriyas, he was the seed-form, known by the name Svāyambhuva Manu.
She who was his wife was Śatarūpā, rich in beauty, a digit of Kamalā.
Accompanied by his wife, Manu remained there, fulfilling the command of the Creator.
The illustrious Creator himself spoke to those sons who were filled with joy:
"O twice-born one, create beings who are great devotees of the Lord.
Having said, "We shall not," they departed to perform austerities, being solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
For that reason, Vidhātṛ, the lord of the worlds, became enraged.
And as Vidhātṛ was possessed by anger and blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
O Lord, the eleven Rudras manifested from his forehead.
Kālāgnirudra is proclaimed as their sole destroyer;
he is remembered as the *tāmasa* among all the Viśvas.
Brahmā himself is *rājasa*, while Śiva and Viṣṇu are *sāttvika*.

Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, is beyond the material qualities and transcends primordial nature (prakṛti). While fools speak of Śiva as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), he is in truth the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, whose essential form is pure goodness (śuddhasattva) and who is stainless. (21)
Listen to the names of the Rudras as they are declared in the Vedas:
Mahān, Mahātman, Matimān, Bhīṣaṇa, and Bhayaṃkara;
Ṛtudhvaja, Ūrdhvakeśa, Piṅgalākṣa, Ruci, and Śuci. (22–23)
Pulastya was born from the right ear, and Pulaha from the left ear;
likewise, Atri from the right eye and Kratu himself from the left eye.
Araṇi was born from the nostrils, and Ruci from the mouth.
Bhṛgu was born from the left side, and Dakṣa from the right side.
From Chāyā’s navel Kardama was born, and likewise Pañcaśikha;
from her chest came Voḍhu, and from the region of her throat, Nārada.
Marīci emerged from the region of the shoulders, and Apāntaratama from the throat;
Vasiṣṭha from the region of the tongue, and Pracetas from the lower lip;
Haṃsa from the left side of the abdomen, and Yati himself from the right side of the abdomen. (27)
In order to carry out the creation, that Creator issued a command to his sons.
Having heard his father’s words, Nārada spoke to him.
Nārada said:
"O Grandfather, first bring Sanaka and the others who are my elder brothers;
O Lord of the World, after having them join us with wives, speak to us.
How is it that while our father is engaged in asceticism, we are destined for the cycle of worldly existence?"
Alas! Oh, how the Lord’s intellect has turned toward the contrary!
To which son has the penance—which is superior even to nectar—now been given?
And to whom do you give the realm, which is as dangerous as poison and worse than poison? (30–31)
O Father, for one who falls into the ocean of existence, which is exceedingly deep and terrible,
there is no atonement even after ten million kalpas have passed.
[Yet] the seed of liberation for all is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He who bestows everything, who grants devotion, who grants servitude, who is truth, and who consists of compassion;
(33) who is the sole refuge of devotees, who is affectionate toward his devotees, and who is utterly pure;
who is dear to his devotees, the lord of his devotees, and the one who bestows grace upon his devotees. (34)

Abandoning the Supreme Lord—who is to be propitiated by devotion and attained through devotion—what deluded person would fix their mind upon sense objects, which are the cause of destruction? And what person, having abandoned the service of Kṛṣṇa—which is dearer than nectar—[would seek anything else]? 35.
What fool consumes the poison known as the sense-objects?
(36) They are as evanescent as a dream, trivial, unreal, and the cause of death;
they are like the tip of a lamp’s flame, which is very attractive to moths. (37)
"Just as the meat on a fishhook provides a momentary pleasure to the fish upon its capture,
so too, O dear one, are sense objects the cause of death for those addicted to them.
Having spoken thus before Brahmā, Nārada fell silent.
Having prostrated before his father, he stood there like a blazing crest of fire.
O twice-born one, Brahmā, overcome with anger, cursed his son;
with trembling limbs, a blood-red face, and quivering lips, he spoke. (39–40)
Brahmā said:
"O Nārada, by my curse your knowledge shall be lost;
you shall become a wild animal, a prey to women, and a lecher. (41)
He was the charming husband and life-cherished beloved of fifty women who were endowed with perpetual youth and rich in beauty;
he was a knower of the science of love (śṛṅgāraśāstra) and intensely devoted to great passion.
He was the teacher of teachers to those skilled in various kinds of amorous arts;
he was the most melodious among the Gandharvas, possessing a beautiful voice and being an excellent singer.
He was proficient in the composition of lute-playing and possessed perpetual youth.
"You shall become wise, sweet-spoken, peaceful, virtuous, handsome, and intelligent;
of this there is no doubt. And you shall be known by the name Upabarhaṇa.
