for two divine lakhs of years in the secluded forest
Furthermore, by my curse, he shall become the son of a maidservant and devoted to that [low state].
But, O child, through association with Vaiṣṇavas and by eating the remnants of the food of Vaiṣṇavas,
you shall again, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, become my own son.
"I shall grant you again that divine, ancient knowledge.
Now become lost; fall down certainly as my son.
Having said "Brahman" to his son, O Brahmin, the Lord of the Universe ceased speaking.
Nārada wept and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to his father.
Nārada said:
"O Destroyer, O Father, O Father, O Teacher of the World, restrain your anger!"
"Alas! This anger of the Creator, the Lord of Ascetics, toward me is unprecedented.
A wise man should curse or even abandon a son who walks the wrong path;
O learned one, how can you deign to curse your own ascetic son?"
May my birth be in those wombs which are devoted to Brahman;
may devotion to Hari never forsake me—grant me this boon.
Even if one is the son of the Creator of the worlds, if there is no devotion at the feet of Hari, [what is the use? (52)
And he who is even superior to a pig is the lowest on the earth of Bhārata.
But one born from a pig-womb who remembers his past lives and is endowed with devotion to Hari shall attain a preeminent birth; by that deed, he goes to Goloka.

The earth is purified by the touch of Vaiṣṇavas and others who drink the desired honey-wine of devotion to the lotus feet of Govinda. O Grandfather, even sacred fords long for the touch of Vaiṣṇavas. (55)

For the sake of washing away the sins and sinful natures of even themselves, men in Bhārata were liberated by the mere instruction of the mantra; oh, along with ten million other men from former times, they attained liberation through Hari! (56–57)
Merely by receiving this mantra, those who have been liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes become pure;
they utterly eradicate their prior karma.
[They should likewise entrust it to] sons, wives, disciples, servants, and kinsmen.
He who shows the true path shall certainly attain a good rebirth. But that teacher who, having been trusted by his disciples, shows them a false path,
shall remain in Kumbhīpāka for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Who is his guru, who is his father, who is his master, and who is his son—
he who is unable to bestow devotion at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa?
O Four-faced One, I have been cursed by you despite being innocent.
"You are worthy of being cursed by me; for even the wise strike back at one who strikes them.
(62) "By my curse, let that mantra of Manu, along with its armor, hymns, and rites of worship, certainly become lost throughout all the worlds. (63)
"O Father, remain unworthy of worship among all beings for three kalpas.
When those three kalpas have passed, you shall become the most worthy of worship.
For now, O observer of noble vows, you shall receive a share of the sacrifice as well as in other rites."
"Let my worship be singular, and may you be honored by the gods and others.
Having spoken thus before his father, Nārada fell silent;
Brahmā remained in the assembly with a heart deeply distressed.
O Śaunaka, by means of that very bed, the Gandharva Nārada became the son of a slave-girl through his father’s curse;
thereafter, he once again became the great ṛṣi Nārada.
"Having obtained knowledge from my father, I shall speak further later; for now [I must depart].
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Curse of Brahmā by Nārada," in the *Brahma-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
Then Brahmā commanded those sons of his for the sake of creation.
O best of Brahmins, they all carried out the creation, with the exception of Nārada.
From the mind of Marīci was born Kaśyapa, the progenitor of beings.
From the eye of Atri, the Moon was born in the Ocean of Milk.
From the mind of Pracetas, Gautama was also born.
And from the mind of Pulastya, Maitrāvaruṇa was born as his son.
From Manu and Śatarūpā, three daughters were born:
Ākūti, Devahūti, and Prasūti; they were all devoted wives.
Two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, were also born, both of whom were charming.
Uttānapāda’s son was Dhruva, who was supremely righteous.
He gave Ākūti to Ruci and Prasūtikā to Dakṣa;
he gave Devahūtī to Kardama, whose son was Kapila himself.
From Prasūti, sixty daughters were born through the seed of Dakṣa.
He gave eight of them to Dharma; eleven are recorded as having been given to Rudra;
he gave one, Satī, to Śiva; and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Dakṣa gave twenty-seven maidens to Candra.
O brāhmaṇa, hear from me the names of his lawful wives:
Śānti, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Kṣamā, Śraddhā, Mati, and Smṛti. (8–9)
Śānti’s son was Santoṣa, and Puṣṭi’s son was Mahān.
Dhṛti’s son was Dhairya, and it is remembered that Tuṣṭi’s sons were Harṣa and Darpa.
Kṣamā’s son was Sahiṣṇu, and Śraddhā’s son was Dhārmika.
From Māriṣā was born a great son named Jñāna, who possessed the memory of his former births;
and from his first wife, Mūrti, were born the two ṛṣis Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
These sons of Dharma, O Śaunaka, were most righteous. (11–12)
Listen attentively to me as I recite the names of the wives of Rudra:
Kalā, Kalāvatī, Kāṣṭhā, Kālikā, Kalahapriyā, Kandālī, Bhīṣaṇā, Rāsnā, Pramocā, Bhūṣaṇā, and Śukī. (13)
These women had many sons who became attendants of Śiva. That Satī cast off her body at the sacrifice due to the censure of her husband;
having been born again as the daughter of the Mountain, she obtained Śaṅkara as her husband.

O righteous one, hear the names of Kaśyapa’s beloved wives: Aditi, the mother of the gods; Diti, likewise the mother of the Daityas; Kadrū, the mother of the serpents; and Vinatā, the mother of birds. (16)
Surabhi is certainly the mother of cows and of buffalo;
Saramā is the mother of four-footed creatures such as dogs and other animals;
Danu is the progenitor of the Dānavas; and there are others such as these. (17–18)
O sage, Indra and the twelve Ādityas, headed by Upendra,
are the gods said to be the sons of Aditi, endowed with great strength and prowess.
O Brahmin, Jayanta was born as the son of Indra by Śacī.
To the daughter of Savarṇā, the wife of Viśvakarmā,
were born two sons, Śanaiścara and Yama, as well as a daughter, Kālin-dī.
Furthermore, from the seed of Upendra, Maṅgala was born upon the Earth.
Śaunaka said: O Sauti, how did that auspicious Upendra come to be born upon the earth as a powerful being? You should explain this to me. (22)
Sauti said:
Beholding the form of Upendra, the Earth, afflicted by desire, assumed the guise of a beautiful woman—unblemished and in the full bloom of youth. (23)
In the secluded and beautiful Malaya forest, amidst lovely sandalwood sprouts, he lay—
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with jewel ornaments,
virtuous, peaceful, smiling, and desirable. (24)
Smiling, she suddenly appeared upon his bed;
the fair-faced woman gave him a most beautiful garland of jasmine,
as well as fragrant sandalwood paste mixed with lovely musk and saffron.
Upendra, perceiving her mind to be that of a woman afflicted by desire,
engaged in various forms of amorous dalliance with her. Then Satī, clinging closely to contact with his body, fell into a swoon.
When Hari had performed the act of impregnation, she was as if dead or asleep;
he [beheld] her, the fair-hipped one, clinging to him, unconscious from the bliss of sexual union, with her broad hips relaxed, smiling, and possessing full breasts. (28–29)
Having placed her for a moment upon his chest, he kissed her lip;
then, leaving her there in that secluded place, Puruṣottama departed.
O Sage, as Urvaśī was walking along the path, he awakened her.
She asked about the events, and the Earth told her.
Being weak and unable to restrain her seed,
she, terrified at the mine of coral, deposited her seed there.
By that [act], the prince became coral-colored;
the great son of Nārāyaṇa was like the sun in splendor.
Medhā was the beloved of Maṅgala, and his [son] was the great Ghaṇṭeśvara.
The wound-inflictor (Vr̥tra) became exceedingly radiant and equal to Viṣṇu.
From Diti were born the two of great strength, Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, as well as a daughter, Siṃhikā, O Brāhmaṇa, and her son, Saiṃhikeya (Rāhu). || 34-35 ||

Nirṛti was Siṃhikā, and by her Rāhu, the son of Nirṛti, was born. Hiraṇyākṣa was killed by the Boar (Varāha) while still young and childless. Prahlāda, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, was the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu.

Virocana was his son, and his son was Bali himself. Bali’s son was a great yogi, a man of knowledge, and a servant of Śaṅkara. Thus the lineage of Diti has been told; now learn from me the lineage of Kadrū.
Ananta, Vāsuki, Kālīya, Dhanañjaya, Karkoṭaka, Takṣaka, Padma, Airāvata,
Mahāpadma, Śaṅku, Śaṅkha, and Saṃvaraṇa as well. (39)
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Durdharṣa, Durjaya, Durmukha, Bala,
Gokṣa, Gokārmuka, Virūpa, and others, O Śaunaka—
there were no foremost leaders among them, as numerous as the various species of serpents. (40–41)
The maiden was a goddess born from a portion of Kamalā;
she was the most excellent among ascetics, auspicious and possessed of great splendor.
And her husband, Jaratkāru, was born of the lineage of Nārāyaṇa. (42)
Āstīka was his son, who was equal to Viṣṇu in splendor.
By the mere mention of these names, men have no fear of serpents.
The lineage of Kadrū has been recounted; now hear from me that of Vinatā.
Vainateya and Aruṇa were his two sons, whose prowess was equal to that of Viṣṇu.
From them, in due course, arose all the species of birds;
and these cows and buffaloes, with Surabhi as their foremost, likewise came into being.
All the dog-like beings were indeed the offspring of Saramā.
The Dānavas are the descendants of Danu, as are other common species.
The lineage of Kaśyapa has been described; now learn from me the narrative concerning the Moon.
Listen attentively to the names of the wives of the Moon, and to their most extraordinary and ancient history as found in the Purāṇas:
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and likewise Rohiṇī. (48)
Mṛgaśīrṣā, Ārdrā, and the virtuous Punarvasu are likewise to be honored;
so too Puṣyā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhikā. (49–50)
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, as well as Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā are recorded [as such];
Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and likewise the auspicious Śatabhiṣak;
Pūrvābhādrapadā, Uttarābhādrapadā, ending with Revatī—these are dear to the Moon (Candra). 51.

Among them, the fortunate Rohiṇī was the most excellent and full of passion; through her constant state of erotic sentiment, she brought the Moon under her control. Once approached by Rohiṇī, the Moon did not go to any other beloved woman.

All the sisters, full of respect, spoke to their father about the supreme torment caused by his co-wife, which was life-threatening. Dakṣa, greatly incensed, cursed Candra with the utterance of mantras.

Quickly, by his father-in-law’s curse, he became seized by consumption (yakṣman). Wasting away day by day from consumption and filled with grief as half his body decayed, he went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
Seeing Candra afflicted and having come for refuge, Śaṅkara,
an ocean of compassion, granted him fearlessness out of pity.
Having freed him from consumption, he gave him a place upon his own cheek.
Becoming immortal and fearless, he remained upon the crest of Śiva.
Having placed him upon his crest, Śiva became Candraśekhara (the Moon-crested).
Among the gods and in all the worlds, there is no cage of refuge other than Śiva.
Seeing their husband released, the daughters of Dakṣa wept again;
they went for refuge to their father Dakṣa, the best among the radiant ones.
Having approached him, they wailed aloud, striking their own bodies again and again.
The miserable daughters of Dakṣa spoke to that dejected one, the lord of the distressed,
the son of Brahmā:
"We ourselves indeed urged you for the sake of obtaining the good fortune of our husband."
"O father, may we have good fortune; our virtuous lord has departed.
O father, while the eye remained, the world was seen as consisting of darkness; now it is understood that for women, the husband alone is indeed the eye. (62–63)
For women, the husband alone is their refuge; the husband is their life and their wealth.
He is the cause of virtue, prosperity, pleasure, and liberation, and a bridge across the ocean of worldly existence.
For women, the husband is Nārāyaṇa; his vow and his duty are eternal.
All the actions of those women who are averse to their husbands are in vain;
likewise, bathing at all sacred fords, the sacrificial fees at all sacrifices, all meritorious gifts, vows, and observances [are fruitless]. (65–66)
Worship of the gods, fasting,
and all forms of austerity do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to the feet of the Master.
He is dear to all kinsmen and to women as a son.
He alone is the master’s portion and a husband superior to a hundred sons.
She who is born of an evil lineage always hates her master;
she whose mind is fickle and wicked, constantly fixed upon another man. (68–69)
Whether he has fallen from his status, is diseased, wicked, impoverished, or devoid of virtue—
whether he be young or old— a virtuous wife should serve him and never abandon him.
She who hates her husband or would forsake him, regardless of whether he possesses virtues or lacks them, [is not a virtuous wife].
She is cooked in the Kālasūtra hell as long as the moon and sun endure;
she is devoured day and night by worms resembling dogs.
She eats the flesh of dead corpses and drinks urine out of thirst.
She becomes a vulture for thousands of millions of lifetimes, a pig for a hundred births, and a beast of prey for a hundred births; thereafter, she becomes a killer of her kinsmen.
Then, if by virtue of her prior karma she should obtain human births, [she remains bound by that same fate].
She will certainly become a widow, destitute of wealth, and afflicted by disease.
O son of Brahmā, grant us the gift of a beloved husband who fulfills our desires;
for you are equal to the Creator and capable of creating the world anew.
Having heard the words of the maidens, Dakṣa went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Upon seeing him, Śambhu rose and bowed;
Dakṣa, having offered him his blessing, spoke to that ocean of compassion. (76)
The invincible one abandoned his anger upon seeing Śiva prostrate before him.
Dakṣa said:
"O Śambhu, give me back my son-in-law, who is as dear to me as my own life."
"O son-in-law,
if you do not give me my son-in-law Candra, who is most dear to the lives of my sons,
I shall cast a terrible curse upon you; by what means will you be released?"
Having heard the words of Dakṣa, the storehouse of compassion,
the refuge-enclosure of Brahman, spoke these words to him that were sweeter than nectar.
Śiva said:
"Even if you were to reduce me to ashes or even if you were to cast a curse upon me,
I am not capable of giving up the moon who has come to me for refuge.
Having heard these words of Śiva, Dakṣa prepared to curse him.

Śiva remembered Govinda, the one who effects liberation from calamity. (82) In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa, assuming the form of an old brāhmaṇa, arrived before them; the two of them bowed to him in due order. (83)
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon them, O twice-born one, that eternal Brahmajyotis,
the most perfect Supreme Lord, first spoke to Śaṅkara.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Śarva, among all kinsmen, there is none dearer than one's own self.
O Lord of the Gods, protect yourself and give up the moon to Dakṣa.
You alone are the best of ascetics, peaceful, and the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas.
He was impartial toward all living beings, free from violence and anger;
he was capable, yet free from wrath, invincible, radiant, and the son of Brahmā.
The disciplined one feared the invincible, yet the invincible feared no one at all.
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, Śaṅkara himself smiled and spoke that which is the essence of policy, the seed of policy, and higher than the highest. Śaṅkara said:
"I shall grant you austerity, splendor, all perfections, and prosperity;
yet I am not capable of giving up my own life to one who has come for refuge.
He who gives away one who has approached him for refuge out of fear alone [is guilty of a great sin]. (89)
And that Dharma, having uttered a most terrible curse, departs after abandoning him.
O Lord of the World, I am capable of renouncing everything, but not my own duty (svadharma).
He who is devoid of his own duty is excluded from all things.
And he who always protects the Dharma, the Dharma protects him in turn.
O Lord, you know the Dharma; why then do you speak to me through your own power of illusion?
You are the mother of all, the creator, and the destroyer by way of transformation.
"For one whose devotion to you is firm, from what source could fear arise?
(93) Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, the Blessed Lord Hari, who knows the nature of all things, drew the moon out from the moon and gave it to Dakṣa. (94)
The half-moon set out for the peak of Śiva, free from disease.
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) seized the supreme moon given by Viṣṇu;
and seeing him afflicted by consumption, Dakṣa praised Mādhava.
In one fortnight Hari himself inflicted a full wound upon him, and in the other fortnight he healed it.
O twice-born one, Kṛṣṇa, having granted them a boon, went to his own abode;
and Dakṣa, taking the moon, gave it back to the daughters once more.
Having obtained them, Candra sported with them day and night;
from that time forth, trembling, he looked upon all of them with equal regard.
Thus, O Sage, the entire account of the sequence of creation has been briefly told.
And it was heard from the mouth of the Guru in Puṣkara, in the assembly of sages.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
Bhrigu’s sons were Cyavana and Śukra, the best among the wise.
Kratu’s wife, Kriyā, gave birth to the Vālakhilyas. Aṅgiras had three sons who were the most excellent of sages.
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, and Śambara as well, O Śaunaka.
Vasiṣṭha’s son was Śakti; Śakti’s son was Parāśara.
Parāśara’s son was the illustrious Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Hari.
Vyāsa’s son Śuka, who was a portion of Śiva, was the best among the wise.
Viśvaśravas was the son of Pulastya, whose son was the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
Śaunaka said:
"Aha! The speech of the ancient sages is exceedingly difficult to comprehend;
not a single word regarding the origin of the Lord of Wealth was understood [before].
Now, this birth of the Lord of Wealth has been told by you, O Ishvara. (5)
Furthermore, why do you speak of my birth in such a way, with the sequence of events reversed?
Sauti said:
"In ancient times, these guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) were born from the Supreme Lord."
Furthermore, due to a Brahmin’s curse,
that son of Viśvāvasu [Utaṅka] and Utaṅka himself diligently entreated the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) for ten million gold pieces as a sacrificial fee to give to their preceptor, Pracetasa.
The Lord of Wealth, becoming dispassionate, prepared to give that [wealth] to him;
O Brahmin, he reduced it to ashes, and he obtained rebirth.
Through that [rebirth], he became the son of Viśravas, Kubera, the lord of wealth.
Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa;
Vātsya was the son of Pulaha, and Śāṇḍilya was the son of Ruci.
Sāvarṇi was born from Gautama, and he indeed was the most eminent of sages.
Kāśyapa was born from Kaśyapa, Bharadvāja from Bṛhaspati;
Vātsya himself from Pulaha, and likewise Sāvarṇi from Gautama.
Śāṇḍilya, the son of Ruci, was a sage, the best among the radiant.
There were five lineages (gotras), and these would be their principal ancestors.
O Śaunaka, other Brāhmaṇa castes arose from the mouth of Brahmā; they reside in various regions and are devoid of [specific] lineages.
The foremost Kṣatriyas are remembered as being from the Moon, the Sun, and Manu;
other Kṣatriya lineages likewise arose from the region of Brahmā’s arms.
The Vaiśyas arose from the region of his thighs, and the Śūdra castes from his feet. (15)
From the intermixture of these [castes], there arose various mixed castes:
Gopas, Nāpitas, Bhillas, as well as Modakas and Kūbaras;
Tambūlis, Svarṇakāras, and indeed various merchant classes (vaṇig-jātayaḥ). || 16–17 ||
O best of Brahmins, such as these are proclaimed to be the true Śūdras.
From a Śūdra woman and a Vaiśya man is born a Karaṇa; from a Vaiśya woman and a twice-born (Brāhmaṇa) man is born an Ambaṣṭha.
And he (Viśvāmitra), having deposited his seed upon a Śūdra woman, produced Viśvakarman.
From that, these nine sons were born as craftsmen:

the garland-maker (mālākāra), the conch-shell worker (śaṅkhakāra), the laborer (karmakāra), the weaver (kuvindaka), the potter (kumbhakāra), and the brazier (kāṃsyakāra); these six were the best among artisans. (19–20)
The author of the Sūtras, the painter, and likewise the goldsmith—these have fallen due to the curse of a Brahmin; they are unworthy of sacrificial offerings and are of mixed caste.
Śaunaka said:
How did that god Viśvakarman perform the act of bestowing virility?
How did those three fall upon a Śūdra woman, the lowest of castes?
And for what reason did the curse of a Brahmin fall upon them?
"O best among those who know the Purāṇas, you ought to explain that to us.
Sauti said:
"Ghṛtācī, out of desire, assumed a charming form according to her wish."
Viśvakarman saw her as she was walking on the path at Puṣkara (24).
Upon beholding her as she approached, his mind blossomed with grace;
his heart stolen by desire, he begged her for love (25).

Richly adorned with jewel ornaments, her every limb was tender; she appeared as if sixteen years of age, possessing eternal and stable youth. Oppressed by the weight of her broad hips, she enchanted the minds of sages. (26)
With a side-glance of intense passion, she was restless and tormented by desire.
Seeing her firm hips, whose garment had been blown away by the wind, and her pair of exceedingly high, firm, and perfectly round breasts... (27–28)

Her face is graced with a beautiful smile and is more lovely than the autumn moon; it is enchanting, with upper and lower lips as red as ripe bimba fruit, marked by a dot of vermilion and a dot of musk. (29)

To his beloved Śāntā, whose cheeks were perpetually radiant with costly jeweled earrings, he— being an expert in the science of love— spoke words that were beautiful to the ear and intent on increasing the fire of passion. (30–31)
Viśvakarman said:
"O Lalitā, where are you going, my beloved who is dearer to me than life? O beautiful one, stay for a moment, O auspicious lady, having taken away my very breaths. (32)
Having searched for you alone, I wander the surface of the earth.
Desiring to give up my own life in the sacrificial fire if I do not see you, I heard from the mouth of Rambhā that you had gone to the world of Kāma. (33)
"I myself have come today, stationed upon this very path.
Oh, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, in a charming flower garden made fragrant by a sweet and gentle breeze! (34–35)
"O beautiful one, a union with me, your youthful lover, shall be virtuous—a meeting of the clever with the clever.
You alone shall possess enduring youth and live for a long time. (36)
She was amorous, soft-limbed, and the most beautiful among the beautiful.
By the very boon of Mṛtyuñjaya, the Daughter of Death was conquered by me. Having gone to the abode of Kubera, wealth was obtained from Kubera. (37–38)
From Varuṇa he obtained a jewel-garland, and from Vāyu the ornament of the best of women;
from the highly powerful Agni he received a pair of garments purified by fire;
and from Kāmadeva he received the science of love, which brings delight to women.
Whatever art of love-making was difficult to obtain, I received it from the Moon.
(40) A necklace of jewels, a pair of garments, and all manner of ornaments—I resolved in my heart to give these to you, and at that very moment they were obtained. (41)
"Having placed those [garments] in my house, I have come here seeking you. Now that our union has ceased, I shall give them to you this very moment.
O Sage, having heard these words of the lustful man, Ghṛtācī smiled.
She quickly gave a reply that was both wise and charming.
Ghṛtācī said:
"O auspicious one, I now accept what you have spoken."
But, O one afflicted by love, I shall speak a word for the occasion:
"I am going to the temple of Kāmadeva, having dressed up for his sake. On the day and for the purpose for which we go, so too do their women. (44–45)
Today I am the wife of Kāma and now the wife of your guru.
This which was spoken by you has been recited from the god of love (Kāmadeva).
A guru who bestows knowledge and bestows mantras is a hundred thousand times superior to a father.
There is no other teacher equal to one's mother, who possesses a thousandfold greater weight;
it is declared in the Śruti that the wife of the teacher is to be honored with a hundredfold the respect shown to the teacher himself.
O wise one, just as the mother is to be honored, so too is she to be honored a hundred times more than the father.
Whatever fault is heard in the sacred tradition regarding the union with one's mother’s daughter, a hundred thousand times greater than that is the fault in approaching the wife of a guru.
Furthermore, that woman whom a man addresses simply by the word "Mother"— [the fault in approaching her is likewise immense]. (49)
Truth is equal to a mother; it is the witness even for the virtuous.
(50) For he who is united with her goes to the Kālasūtra hell;
there he dwells in that terrible place as long as the moon and sun endure. (51)
In union with one's mother, the fault is fourfold;
and with the wife of one's guru, it is indeed a hundred thousandfold.
Such a person surely falls into the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
No expiation for that sinner has been heard of in the Vedas.
[It is] shaped like a potter’s wheel, sharp-edged like a sword, filled with fat, urine, and excrement, and extremely difficult to cross. (53–54)
Filled with worms like a trident, heated and flowing like fire—
that is proclaimed as the *kumbhīpāka* hell, the place of recreation for sinners,
corresponding to the magnitude of the fault committed by men in approaching the wife of their guru. (55)
If the teacher’s wife there should indeed be desirous of him,
then today I shall go to that lover’s temple;
having assumed his guise, I will go for your sake on the following day.
Having heard the words of Ghṛtācī, Viśvakarman became enraged at her;
he cursed her, saying, "Go to the womb of a Śūdra upon the surface of the earth!
(58). Hearing those words, Ghṛtācī cursed him back with a most terrible curse.
"May you obtain birth in this world, and may you fall from heaven," Ghṛtācī said to Kāru, and she went to the abode of Kāma. Having engaged in amorous play with Kāma, she related that story.
O Śaunaka, through the power of her desire, she took birth in the city of Prayāga as the wife of a cowherd named Madana;
born with the memory of her former life, that ascetic woman remained devoted to penance.
The most virtuous woman did not choose a boon, but instead set her mind upon asceticism.
Resembling molten gold through her penance,
she performed austerities for a hundred divine years on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having given birth to nine sons by Vīrya and Surakāru,
she returned once more to her own world and became Ghṛtācī.
Śaunaka said:

How did that ascetic woman, who had recently given birth to nine sons, maintain her vigor? And for how many days after giving birth did she remain there? Sauti said: 65. How did that ascetic woman, who had recently given birth to nine sons, maintain her vigor? And for how many days after giving birth did she remain there?

But Viśvakarman, having heard that curse, filled with rage and his mind overwhelmed by grief, went to the abode of Brahmā. Having bowed to and praised Brahmā, he related that story to him.
By the command of Brahmā, he was born on earth as the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman.
Having been that very same Brāhmaṇa, he became a Kārū on earth;
indeed, he practiced various crafts for kings and householders.
And he constantly caused all kinds of crafts to be made by everyone from everywhere—
crafts that were diverse, manifold, wonderful, and most enchanting.
Once, however, having performed a craft for the king at Prayāga, ||| 69 || [he departed].
He went to the Gaṅgā to bathe, and there he saw a beautiful woman— Ghṛtācī, a young woman of fresh beauty who was performing ascetic penance.
And that twice-born man, himself remembering his former births, recognized her as one who remembered her own past lives.
Upon seeing her, he suddenly became filled with desire and his mind was stolen away.
