"O most enchanting Ghṛtācī, ah! Do you not remember me here now? O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, I am indeed Viśvakarman.
I shall grant you release from the curse; come to me, O beautiful one. (73)
"Because of you, this god of love burns my heart intensely.
(74) Having heard the words of the twice-born, Ghṛtācī, assuming a new form, spoke these sweet, peaceful, and highly prudent words. (75)
The Gopikā said: On that day I was beloved by Kāma, but now I am a poor ascetic;
how could I be united with you on the banks of the Gaṅgā in Bhārata? (76)
O Viśvakarman, this Bhārata is a meritorious field of action;
whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is performed here, its fruit is experienced elsewhere.
A righteous person, having obtained birth for the sake of liberation through the fruit of austerity, [attains that goal].
Bound by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, one performs actions while deluded. To whomsoever the sovereign Māyā of Nārāyaṇa becomes fully pleased,
to him Śrī Kṛṣṇa grants devotion and his desired mantra.

That fool who, though born in Bhārata, is deluded and attached to sense objects, abandons Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All—he is bewildered by the māyā of Viṣṇu. (80) O Goddess, I remember everything; indeed, I am one who remembers my past births from of old.
"I was Ghṛtācī, a celestial courtesan, but now I am a cowherd girl.
I am performing penance on the most merit-bestowing bank of the Gaṅgā for the sake of liberation.
This place is not for dalliance; remain steadfast, O lustful one! (81–82)
Any sin committed elsewhere is destroyed by the Gaṅgā;
however, a sin committed on the bank of the Gaṅgā becomes multiplied a hundred thousandfold instantly.
That [sin] is destroyed only through penance at the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa.
If, having acted thus out of desire, he should then turn back—
having heard the words of Ghṛtācī, Viśvakarman, assuming the form of the wind,
took her and went to Malaya, the abode of sandalwood trees. (84–85)
In the delightful valley of Malaya, upon a charming bed of flowers,
which was constantly perfumed by the breeze carrying the scent of blossoms and sandalwood,
he enjoyed amorous union with her in that secluded forest.
For twelve full years, she was not aware of day or night.
The fetus of that passionate woman became fully developed and exceedingly difficult to bear.
There, in that very place, she gave birth to nine beautiful sons.
O Śaunaka, [he appointed] those who had mastered their crafts through training and were endowed with knowledge; those who were previously experienced, capable, strong, and discerning;
as well as garland-makers, smiths, shell-workers, and weavers. (89)
To the potters, the weavers, and likewise the goldsmiths and painters,
they both granted boons and established them upon the earth; then,
casting off their human bodies, they departed for their own abode.
O best of the twice-born, due to the theft of gold from Brahmins,
the goldsmith immediately became fallen through the curse of a Brahmin and his own deed.
Likewise, the author of the Sūtras fell to the earth by the curse of the twice-born.
And for that reason, he did not promptly provide the sacrificial wood;
because of that transgression regarding the variegated paintings,
the painter immediately fell by the curse of the Brahmins and through their wrath.

A certain distinguished merchant, through association with a goldsmith, fell due to the fault of stealing gold and other such acts, as well as by the curse of a Brahmin. Furthermore, [another] was born from the seed of a painter upon a Śūdra woman who was unchaste. 95.
Due to the fault of old age, he fell and became one who builds watchtowers (aṭṭālikākāra).
From the seed of a watchtower-builder in the wife of a potter,
there was immediately born a Koṭaka, who fell and became a house-builder.

By means of the potter’s seed, a crooked oil-presser immediately came into being upon the wife of a weaver, fallen to the earth. By means of the Kṣatriya’s seed, [a son was born] upon the wife of a prince.
And Tīvara also became fallen due to the fault of old age.
From the seed of Tīvara, however, upon the wife of an oil-presser, there was born a Dasyu who is proclaimed as a Leṭa; he too was fallen. (99–100)
Letas begot six sons upon Tīvarakanyā:
Malla, Mantra, Mātara, Bhaṇḍa, Kola, and Kalandara.
Born of a Brāhmaṇī through the seed of a Śūdra, he was fallen due to the fault of adultery.
Immediately he became a Caṇḍāla, the lowest of all and impure.
And by [union with] a fierce Caṇḍālī, he became a leather-worker.
And from a Caṇḍāla by a leather-worker woman, a flesh-cutter was born.

The Māṃsacchedya is proclaimed as being born from a Koñca woman by a Tīvra man; however, O Śaunaka, the Kaivarta man begets a Kartāra upon a Koñca woman, and a Sadya upon a Caṇḍāla girl through the seed of a Leṭa. 104.
Thus those two sons, Haḍḍi and Ḍimba, were both wicked.
In due course, from the seed of a Caṇḍāla upon the daughter of Haḍḍi, five sons were born who were likewise wicked and forest-dwellers.
O Śaunaka, from the daughter of Leṭāttīvara on the banks of the Gaṅgā, there was a boy who was immediately born; he is celebrated as Gaṅgāputra.
From the seed of Veṣadhārī, [he was born] in the daughter of Gaṅgāputra.
And the son known as Yuṅgī became a wearer of disguises.
From a Vaiśya and the daughter of a Tīvara, Sadya was born;
from a Śuṇḍī woman and a Vaiśya, Pauṇḍraka was born.
From a Kṣatriya and a Karaṇa woman, a Rājaputra was born;
from a Karaṇa and a Rājaputrī, however, one known as an Āgārī was proclaimed. Indeed, from a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya woman, a Kaivarta is proclaimed.
In the Kali age, due to contact with a fisherman (dhīvara), the Tīvarī woman fell to the earth. From the fisherman and the Tīvarī woman, a son was born who is known as the Rajaka.
And from the Rajakī woman and the Tīvarī man, one named Koyālī was indeed born.
From a barber and the daughter of a cowherd was born Sarvasvī, his wife.
From a Kṣatriya was born the powerful hunter Vyādha, a slayer of wild animals. From a Tīvara and the daughter of a vintner were born seven sons.
In the Kali age, due to contact with bones, they always became robbers.
On the first day of her fertile period, by means of the seed of a sage, Kutsita was born from the womb of a Brāhmaṇī; for that reason, he is celebrated as Kūḍara.

In that case, the impurity is equal to that of a Brahmin; however, one who has fallen from his status due to the fourfold defects becomes the lowest on the face of the earth through immediate association with a Koṭaka.
[This applies] when one dies on the first day after a Kṣatriya’s seed was placed in a Vaiśya woman.
A son was born who was a great bandit, powerful and a wielder of the bow;
even when restrained by a kṣatriya, he acted beyond the bounds of speech.
Because of that, such a son is proclaimed as one "born of his [evil] nature" (jātya) and "beyond speech" (vāgatīta). (117–118)
Through the Kṣatriya’s virility upon a Śūdra woman, and due to the fault of the [untimely] season,
there arose sinful and powerful Mleccha tribes who were difficult to restrain, cruel, fearless, and invincible in battle. (119) Their ears remained unpierced.

Devoid of purity and proper conduct, difficult to subdue, and abandoned by dharma—thus the Jola caste arose from a Mleccha and the daughter of a weaver. From a Jola and the daughter of a weaver, the Śarāṅka is proclaimed to have been born. (120–121)
Due to the fault of the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*), many unrecorded castes have arisen.
O twice-born one, who is capable of stating their names and numbers?
A *Vaidya* is born from a Brahmin woman by the Aśvinīkumāras.
Through the power of the physician, many people were born of a Śūdra woman;
they were knowledgeable of the qualities of village life and devoted to mantras and medicinal herbs.
From them, those who were snake-catchers on earth were born of a Śūdra woman. (123–124)
Śaunaka said:
How did the son of the Sun, the offspring of the Aśvins, deposit his seed in the wife of a Brāhmaṇa? Alas, by what lack of discernment did he perform this act of impregnation? (129)
Sauti said: On his journey to the sacred fords, the son of the Sun, being lustful yet composed, beheld a brahmin woman in a secluded flower garden. 126.

Though that powerful god was strenuously restrained by her with force, upon seeing her who was exceedingly beautiful, he discharged his seed. She quickly cast off the embryo in a charming flower garden. (127)
Immediately a son was born, resembling molten gold.
Accompanied by her son, she went to her husband's house, always feeling ashamed.
She related to her husband the divine calamity that had occurred on the road.
Out of anger, the Brahmin abandoned both that son and his beloved wife;
through yoga, she became a river known as the Godāvarī. He diligently taught his son the science of medicine.
That son of the Sun himself became a master of various arts and mantras;
and as a Brahmin, he constantly engaged in the calculation of the stars for wages,
and having abandoned the Vedic dharma, he became an astrologer on earth.
A greedy Brahmin accepted gifts from Shudras;
in the receiving of gifts for the deceased, he became a foremost taker.
A certain man arose from the sacrificial pit during a Brahma-sacrifice.
That Sūta was remembered as a speaker of Dharma and my own ancestor;
Brahmā, the storehouse of compassion, taught him the Purāṇa.
Sūta, the narrator of the Purāṇas, was born from the sacrificial fire-pit (yajñakuṇḍa).
From a Vaiśya woman, by the seed of a Sūta, one son was born.
He was a Bhaṭṭa, eloquent, and a reciter of praises for all.
Thus has this brief determination of castes on earth been told to you.

Due to the fault of the intermixture of castes, there are many other castes as well. I shall declare the truth concerning the relationship that exists among all these castes in every respect, as it was spoken by Brahmā and declared in the Vedas of old.
The father is celebrated as *tāta*, *janaka*, and *janmadātā*.
The mother is *ambā*, *mātā*, *jananī*, *janayitrī*, and *prasū*. The grandfather is the father of the father; his father is the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*).
From this point forward, those of the same lineage (sagotra) are declared to be kinsmen (jñāti).

The maternal grandfather, the father of the mother, and the great-grandfather of the mother; the progenitor of the maternal grandfather and his father, known as the "Great-Grandfather" (vṛddhapūrvaka); [these are the maternal relatives]. 140–141.

The paternal grandmother is the mother of one's father; she is his mother-in-law and is to be known as the paternal great-grandmother. Her mother-in-law is to be understood as the paternal great-great-grandmother. The maternal grandmother is the mother of one's mother; she is equal to a mother and is to be honored. (142)
The wife of the paternal great-grandfather is to be known as the *pramātāmahī*;
likewise, the wife of the paternal grandfather is to be known as the *vṛddhamātāmahī*.
The brother of one’s father is the *pitṛvya* (paternal uncle), and the brother of one’s mother is the *mātula* (maternal uncle). (143–144)
The paternal aunt (*pitṛṣvasṛ*), the maternal grandmother’s sister (*pitur-mātṛṣvasṛ*), and the mother’s sister (*mātuḥ-svasṛ*) are so designated.

Furthermore, *sūnu*, *tanaya*, *putra*, *dāyāda*, and *ātmaja*—meaning "born of oneself"—denote a son; they signify one who shares in the inheritance and is born of the seed in the masculine gender. (145)
A daughter born of a wife is proclaimed as *janyā*, *duhitā*, *kanyā*, and *ātmajā*. A son’s wife is to be known as *putrapatnī* and *vadhū*; the husband of a daughter is the *jāmātṛ*.
The words *pati*, *priya*, *bhartṛ*, *svāmī*, and *kānta* are used for a husband. (146–147)
The husband’s brother is called *devara*; the husband’s sister is *nanāndā*.
The husband’s father is *śvaśura*, and the husband’s mother is *śvaśrū*.
A wife is proclaimed by the names *bhāryā*, *jāyā*, *priyā*, *kāntā*, *strī*, and *patnī*. (148)

The brother of a wife is called *śyālaka*, and the sister of a wife is called *śyālikā*. (149) Likewise, the mother of a wife is known as *śvaśrū*, and her father is remembered as *śvaśura*. A brother born of the same womb is a *sodara* brother, and a sister born of the same womb is remembered as a *sagarbhā* sister. (150)
The sister’s son (bhaginīja) is the same as the nephew (bhāgineya); the brother’s son (bhrātṛja) is the same as the brother’s son (bhrātṛputraka).

The father-in-law (āvutta) is the lover of the sister (bhaginīkānta) and also the husband of the sister (bhaginīpati). Furthermore, the brother-in-law (śyālīpati) is the same as the brother (bhrātṛ), due to the singular nature of the term for father-in-law (śvaśura).
O Sage, the father-in-law should be known as equal to the father who gave one birth.
The giver of food, the protector from fear, the savior of the wife, the giver of knowledge, and the giver of birth—these five are the fathers of men. (192–193)
The wife of one who gives food, a sister, a teacher’s wife, a mother, her co-wife, a daughter, and likewise a son’s beloved wife;
the mother of one’s mother, the mother of one’s father, and likewise a father-in-law’s sister. (154)
The paternal uncle’s wife, the maternal aunt, and the mothers—these are fourteen [types of women].
(155) The grandson is [the son] of the son, and the great-grandson is [the son] of that grandson;
those who are his sons and so forth, belonging to the lineage and born of the family, are proclaimed as such. (156)
The daughter’s son, the son of a daughter, their sons and other such relatives;
the sons of a sister and others—these men are remembered as *bāndhavas* (kinsmen).
The sons of a brother’s son and so forth are, moreover, remembered as *jñātis* (agnates). 157.
O Sage, the preceptor’s son, as well as his brother, are to be supported as supreme kinsmen;
the preceptor’s daughter is to be supported like a sister and is equal to one's own mother.
Furthermore, the preceptor’s son and brother are to be supported by a son as very affectionate kinsmen.
The father-in-law of a son is considered a brother by marriage and a kinsman;
likewise, the relationship with the father-in-law of a daughter is proclaimed to be the same.
Furthermore, the father-in-law of a daughter is her brother and a very affectionate relative. (160)
The teacher, the father-in-law, and the brother are proclaimed to be equal to a preceptor.
He with whom one shares kinship is celebrated as a friend.
A friend should be known as one who bestows happiness; one who causes suffering is called an enemy. (161–162)
By fate, a kinsman may cause suffering, while one who is unrelated may bestow happiness.
O best of Brahmins, there are three kinds of relationships for men on this earth:
those born of learning, those born of birth, and those proclaimed to be born of affection. (163)
A friend born of affection should be known as a true kinsman; such a bond is very difficult to find.
A friend’s mother and a friend’s wife are undoubtedly equal to one’s own mother.
For men, a friend’s brother and a friend’s father are equal to one’s own brother and father. (164–165)
The Lotus-born One has stated that the fourth [category] is the connection of names:
*jāra*, *upapati*, and *bandhu* are used for one who performs sexual enjoyment with a wicked woman;
*upapatnī*, *navajā*, *preyasī*, and *cittahāriṇī* are used for a beloved mistress. (166)
The paramour is equal to the husband, and the wife is equal to [the paramour];
such a relationship, occurring even across different countries, is censured everywhere. It is un-Vedic, condemned, and was established by Viśvāmitra. (167–168)
And the abandonment of one's wife by great men is prescribed in different regions;
it brings ill repute to men, and especially to women. However, for those of great luster, it is not a fault in every age that exists. (169–170)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Relationship of Birth," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Śaunaka said:
What did that twice-born man do specifically after abandoning his wife?
"O highly fortunate one, what are the names of the Aśvins, and from whose lineage are they born? Sūta said:
"There was a great sage named Sutapas, a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan."
On the Himālaya, he performed austerities for a hundred thousand years for Kṛṣṇa.
A great ascetic and radiant one, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
he suddenly beheld for a moment the light of Kṛṣṇa in the sky.
He chose as his boon a self untainted and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
he did not beg for liberation, but rather for service and unwavering devotion.
Then a voice from the sky spoke: "Take a wife."
"O twice-born one, when my enjoyment has ceased, I shall grant you service and devotion.
Brahmā himself gave him the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs;
and with her, O best of sages, Kalyāṇamitra became united.
By the mere recollection of whom there shall be no fear of the thunderbolt;
by recollecting him, one will surely obtain not merely a kinsman, but one who is worthy of being seen.
Having abandoned his mother, the Kalyāṇamitrā, the Great Sage [departed].
And he cursed the son of the Sun: "May you be deprived of a share in the sacrifice!
O lowest of gods, may your brother also be worthy of worship!
May you be afflicted by disease, have paralyzed limbs, and be devoid of fame! (8–9)
Having spoken thus, Sutapas set out for home with his son;
and Sūrya, accompanied by the two Aśvins, proceeded to his presence.
Sūrya, the lord of the three worlds, [came] because of his two sons who were afflicted by disease.
O Śaunaka, he indeed praised the Lord of Sages, who was performing great penance.
Sūrya said:
"Forgive me, O Blessed One, O Brahmin, O form of Viṣṇu, in age after age."
O Bhāradvāja, lord of sages, forgive the offense of my son.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, constantly enjoy fruits, flowers, water, and other offerings given by brāhmaṇas. (12–13)
The gods are eternally invoked by Brahmins and are always worshipped among all beings.
There is no god higher than the Brahmin; Hari himself is present in the form of the Brahmin.
When a Brahmin is fully satisfied, Nārāyaṇa himself is satisfied.
When Nārāyaṇa is satisfied, all the deities are satisfied.
(15) There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, nor is there a god higher than Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, there is no Vaiṣṇava greater than Śaṅkara, and no earth more patient than her. (16)
There is no dharma higher than truth; there is no woman more virtuous than Pārvatī.
There is nothing more powerful than fate, and no one dearer than a son.
There is no enemy equal to disease, and none more worthy of worship than the guru. (17)
There is no kinsman equal to a mother, nor is there a friend superior to a father. (18) There is no austerity greater than the Ekādaśī vow, and none higher than fasting.
Knowledge is the supreme jewel among all wealth; indeed, it is the highest treasure beyond that. (19)
"A brahmin is superior to all stages of life; there is no teacher equal to a brahmin.
He who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—thus spoke the Lotus-born One.
Having heard these words of the Sun, Bhāradvāja bowed down to him.
And by the fruit of his asceticism, he made those two sons free from disease.
"Furthermore, your two sons shall also become partakers of the sacrifice.
Having spoken thus to him, the sage Sutapas bowed to the Maker of Day.
Terrified and intent on serving Hari, he went to the Gaṅgā;
accompanied by his two sons, Sūrya went to his own abode.
By the blessings of the twice-born, those two became worthy of worship and partakers of the sacrificial offerings.
That man who recites this hymn composed by Sūrya shall become victorious everywhere through the grace of the Brahmins' feet. (24) He who,
having risen in the morning, recites "Salutations to the Brahmins," [shall attain all his desires].
He has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, they are all contained within the ocean;
and whatever sacred fords exist in the ocean, they are all present in the feet of the Brahmins.
As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of a brahmin,
for that long the ancestors drink water from lotus-leaf cups.
Whoever drinks the meritorious water from a brahmin’s feet with devotion [attains great merit].

O twice-born one, if a person suffering from a great disease should drink the water from the feet of a brāhmaṇa with devotion for one month, he has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices; he is liberated from every ailment. (28–29)

Whether he be ignorant or possessed of knowledge, that twice-born man who is purified by the twilight devotions is indeed equal to Viṣṇu, provided he is not averse to Hari. One should neither strike nor curse a Brahmin, even if he is striking or cursing [others].
He who is a devotee of Hari is remembered as one hundred times more worthy of honor than cows.
O twice-born one, he who eats the water from the feet and the food offering (naivedya) of a brāhmaṇa,
and who constantly partakes of the food offering, shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He who never eats on the eleventh lunar day and constantly worships Kṛṣṇa—
by obtaining the water from his feet, even a dry place shall certainly become a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
He who always eats the remnants of the meal, the food offered as *naivedya*.
He is purified by Kṛṣṇadeva and is liberated while living on this earth.
"Food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu is excrement, and milk is urine," so said the Lotus-born One regarding those born into the families of the twice-born. (34–35)
Brahmā and the sons of Brahmā are all devoted to Viṣṇu;
how then can a brāhmaṇa born in their lineage be averse to Hari?
Or [how could he be so] due to association with his parents, maternal grandfather, and others, or even with his guru? (36)
Those Brahmins who are averse to Kṛṣṇa due to their faults are as good as dead while still alive. (37) Who is his guru? Who is his father? Who is his son? Who is his friend?
Who is his king? Who is his kinsman—he who would not offer his mind to Hari? (38)
O Brahmin, a Vaiṣṇava is indeed superior to a non-Vaiṣṇava twice-born man;
even a dog-eater (caṇḍāla) who is liberated along with his kin is better than a Brāhmaṇa who goes to hell.
A twice-born man who neglects the twilight prayers, who is constantly impure, or who is averse to Kṛṣṇa [falls into such a state].
He alone is a semblance of a Brahmin, like a snake devoid of venom.
But he into whose ear the Viṣṇu-mantra has entered from the mouth of the Guru—him the Lord of Rites (Brahmā) should call a Vaiṣṇava, supremely pure, and liberated while living. (40–41)

The Vaiṣṇava goes to the abode of Hari together with hundreds of his maternal grandfathers and others, as well as with ten million ancestors of his own lineage. Just as there are four castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—so too [is this lineage]. (42)
There is indeed one independent birth in the universe called Vaiṣṇava.
The Vaiṣṇavas constantly meditate upon the lotus feet of Govinda, and Govinda likewise constantly meditates upon them in their presence. (43–44)
Having appointed Sudarśana for the protection of his devotees, He nevertheless does not remain free from anxiety in the presence of His devotees.

(45) Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Praise of Viṣṇu, Vaiṣṇavas, and Brāhmaṇas," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka. (11)
Śaunaka said:
In the course of the lineage of the sages, various stories have arisen;
through this censure, prompted by the context and out of curiosity, they have been heard by me. (1)
Did they indeed create progeny, or were there any who remained perpetual celibates?
What did that Nārada do due to his conflict with his father? What befell the son because of his opposition to his father’s curse? (2)
"Or was it by his father's curse, O Sauti? Let that auspicious account be told.
Sauti said: "Haṃsa, Yati, Cāraṇi, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha—"
O Śaunaka, there were Apāntaratamas, Sanaka, and others;
besides these, there were many other sons of Brahmā who were constantly engaged in worldly life, possessed offspring, and were obedient to the commands of their guru. (4–5)
Due to the curse of his son, even Brahmā himself, the Lord of Creatures, became unworthy of worship.
For that very reason, the wise do not practice the mantras of Brahmā.
And Nārada, due to the curse of his preceptor, became a Gandharva.
I shall relate that account in great detail; listen to it.
(7) There was a king of the Gandharvas, the greatest among all Gandharvas, endowed with supreme sovereignty, yet he was childless due to his past karma. (8)
By the command of his guru, at Puṣkara, that wretched man of distressed mind performed penance for Śambhu with supreme concentration.
[He recited] the armor-verse (kavaca), the hymn (stotra), and the twelve-syllable mantra of Śiva.

And Vasiṣṭha, that ocean of compassion, gave [the mantra] to the king of the Gandharvas. O Sage, tormented by the grief for his son, he remained without food at Puṣkara and chanted the supreme, divine mantra for a hundred years.
At the conclusion of a hundred years, he beheld Śiva before him, illuminating the ten directions and blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
the Lord, eternal, whose very nature is great light. (12)
With a gentle smile and a serene countenance, he bestows grace upon his devotees.
He is the very form of austerity, the seed of austerity, the fruit that grants the rewards of ascetic practice,
and the giver of all prosperity to the devotee who has sought refuge.
Holding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, seated upon a bull,
naked, resembling pure crystal, three-eyed, with the moon as his crest-jewel,
and bearing a mass of matted locks endowed with the luster of molten gold— the excellent one. (15)
He who has a blue throat, the omniscient one, with a serpent as his sacred thread;
the destroyer of all, Time, the supreme conqueror of death, the Lord who resembles ten million suns at midday in the summer heat. (16–17)
Seeing him— who bestows the knowledge of reality, who is peaceful, who grants liberation, and who grants devotion to Hari—
the Gandharva suddenly prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and praised the Supreme Lord with the hymn given by Vasiṣṭha.
"Choose a boon," Śiva, the ocean of compassion, said to him.
He requested devotion to Hari and a son who was a supreme Vaiṣṇava.
Having heard the words of the Gandharva, the moon-crested Lord spoke again.
The Lord of the distressed, the friend of the wretched, spoke to the eternal one:
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"You have achieved your purpose through this one boon; anything else would be like chewing what has already been chewed."
"O King of Gandharvas, who is it that you choose? For who could be satiated by such supreme auspiciousness?
O child, he whose devotion to Hari is very firm and all-auspicious is capable of protecting and creating the entire universe with ease."
Having delivered ten million ancestors of his own lineage and a hundred ancestors of his maternal grandfather—
these men— he certainly goes to Goloka. So too, he delivers those with the three kinds of sins accumulated over ten million births.

Having destroyed the enjoyment of merit, one will certainly attain service to Hari. (24) So long as the mind is not fixed on Kṛṣṇa, men possess only so much a wife, a son, desired sovereignty, happiness, and suffering. (29)

When the mind is fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, the sword of devotion—which is difficult to surpass—indeed cuts through the roots of the trees of karma for men. Ah! This occurs for those fortunate ones who have sons who are supreme Vaiṣṇavas. (26)
They effortlessly uplift even ten million generations of their kin.
(27) Alas! A man who has achieved his purpose desires a boon for the sake of a single son; yet what is the use of a second boon? For men, there is no satiety in auspiciousness. (28)
"The wealth accumulated by us Vaiṣṇavas is indeed very difficult to obtain;
yet we are not eager to give even devotion and service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O child, choose another boon that is desired in your heart. (29)
"Obtain the state of Indra, immortality, or even the rare state of Brahmā!
I shall easily grant you all—every perfection, great yoga, knowledge, the conquest of death, and so forth. Therefore, certainly abandon service to Hari. (30–31)
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, with his throat, lips, and palate parched, the distressed Gandharva spoke to the Lord of the Distressed, the bestower of all prosperity. (32) The Gandharva said:
That state of being Brahman, by the mere movement of whose eyelashes the fall of Brahmā occurs—
that Brahmanhood is like a dream, and a devotee of Kṛṣṇa does not desire it.
O Śiva, [he likewise desires] neither the status of Indra nor immortality, nor the attainment of supernatural powers, yoga, and so forth.
Knowledge such as the conquest of death and the like is certainly not desired by the devotee;
nor do Vaiṣṇavas desire even the states of *sālokya*, *sārṣṭi*, *sāmīpya*, and *sāyujya* with Śrī Hari, nor indeed liberation (*nirvāṇa-mokṣa*) therein. (34, 39)
May there be constant and firm devotion to Him there; the service of Hari is very difficult to attain.
In both sleep and wakefulness, the devotees desire this and that supreme boon.
O Kalpataru, grant me the boon of that service which is the son of Vaiṣṇava.
Having obtained you, even the lowest of men receives a boon when you are pleased.
O Śambhu, if you will not grant this boon to me, a man of evil deeds,
I shall indeed cut off my own head and offer it into the fire.

Having heard the words of the Gandharva, the treasure-house of compassion, the Lord of devotees who bestows grace upon his followers, spoke to him. Śrī Śaṅkara said: 39. [The Lord of devotees, who bestows grace upon his followers, spoke to that devotee who was distressed. Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Devotion to Hari, service to Hari, and a son who is a supreme Vaiṣṇava—
one who is long-lived, virtuous, eternally stable in youth,
wise, most handsome, devoted to his guru, and a master of his senses. (40)
"Obtain this boon, the most excellent of the Gandharva kings; do not grieve.
Having spoken thus, O Sage, Śaṅkara departed from there for his own abode.
The Gandharva king, being satisfied, returned to his own palace.
All the people were delighted in mind, their tasks accomplished.
Nārada took birth from his wife in Bhārata;
that aged woman gave birth to a son on Mount Gandhamādana.
The venerable preceptor Vasiṣṭha gave the boy a name as was appropriate on an auspicious day— a name that was itself auspicious.
The prefix *upa* signifies "superiority" (*adhika*), and the word *barhaṇa* is masculine when denoting one who is worthy of honor (*pūjya*).
"Because he was superior even to those worthy of worship, he was therefore named Upabarhaṇa.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of Nārada’s Birth," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:

And at the festival for his son, the King of the Gandharvas, filled with joy, bestowed jewels and various kinds of wealth upon the Brahmins. Upabarhaṇa, however, in due course [received] the mantra of Hari, which is very difficult to obtain.
Having obtained [him] from Vasiṣṭha, he performed difficult austerities.
(2) Once, on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī, the wives of Gandharvas beheld him as he had reached youth, and at that very moment they fell into a swoon. (3)
Having performed intense austerity and renounced their lives through yoga,
those fifty became the daughters of Citraratha;
they chose the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa as their husband.
By their father’s command, the lustful women joyfully gave garlands to him.
Having accepted them, that youthful Gandharva, possessed of firm youth,
being full of desire, took his pleasure in secret for three hundred thousand divine years.
Having ruled the kingdom for a very long time even after that,
O Sage, he went to the abode of Brahmā along with them night and day, singing the songs of Hari.
Seeing Rambhā’s firm breasts as she danced upon her shapely thighs, he [gazed].
The great-souled Gandharva stumbled;
he suddenly abandoned his music and fell into a swoon upon the floor of the assembly.
The gods laughed aloud, and Brahmā, out of anger, cursed him. (8–9)
"Go to the womb of a Śūdra and cast off this Gāndharva body.
Indeed, through association with Vaiṣṇavas at the proper time, you shall become my son.
O son, without adversity, the greatness of men can never manifest."
"May happiness and suffering arise for all of them in due order.
Having spoken thus, that Creator departed from Puṣkara to his home;
at that time, the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa abandoned that body.
Having pierced the six chakras— namely the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and the one called Ājñā—
as well as the Iḍā, Suṣumnā, Medhā, Piṅgalā, and the life-taking [nāḍī], || 13 ||
The bestower of all-knowledge, as well as the restrainer of the mind;
the pure and the restrained, as well as the mover of the vital breath;
the drier of fire, and likewise the nourisher of strength. (14–15)
Moving through the intellect, causing the expansion of knowledge,
taking away the life of all, and bestowing life once again—
having pierced these sixteen channels as well as the *haṃsa* itself.
Having brought [the mind] together with the intellect to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) through yoga,
he remained for a moment and united the self within the Self alone.
O Śaunaka, that lord of yogis, possessing the memory of his former births, attained Brahman.
Placing the three-stringed lute, so difficult to obtain, upon his left shoulder,
and holding a rosary of pure crystal in his right hand,
he meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, the essence of the Vedas, higher than the highest. (19)
The two syllables "Kṛṣṇa" are the supreme seed of liberation.
Placing the position of the head in the east and the two feet in the west, one lies upon a bed of *darbha* grass like a person lying down. (20–21)
Upon seeing him, the Gandharva king, together with his wife,
instantly attained Brahman through yoga while mentally remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
His wives and all his kinsmen, having lamented, wept bitterly.
Afflicted by grief and deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, they proceeded in due order.
Among the fifty women was the chief queen, a virtuous and most excellent lady named Mālavatī, who was his dearest beloved. (23–24)
She wept loudly and intensely, placing her beloved upon her breast;
and afflicted with grief, she spoke thus, addressing her beloved.
Mālavatī said: "O Lord, O best of lovers, O clever one, O sovereign of connoisseurs!"
Grant me your sight, O kinsman, for I am submerged in an ocean of grief.
[I dwell] in the beautiful and delightful sandalwood grove,
on the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā River, in a charming flower garden.
In the vicinity of Mount Candana, within a beautiful sandalwood forest, upon a bed of flowers and sandalwood, scented by the breeze of sandalwood;
on a delightful portion of Mount Gandhamādana, on the bank of a river. (28)
In the sound of the male cuckoo, amidst the clusters of *mālatī* flowers,
in the divine Śrīvana on Śrīśaila frequented by Śrīnivāsa—
in that auspicious, pure lotus-foot of Śrī, fashioned by Acyuta, and endowed with glory. (29–30)
The various sports that were formerly performed by you and me together in secret during the spring season— my mind is indeed pained by the memory of them, even though I was with a wicked-hearted man.
And formerly, I was sprinkled by you with words as sweet as nectar.
Because of that, the Supreme Self is constantly and most terribly tormented.
(32) Association with the virtuous is more difficult to attain than even Vaikuṇṭha; alas, separation from them is even harder to endure than death. (33)

Therefore, the severance of those [relationships] causes supreme and virtuous grief; even more than that, the grief of separation from kinsmen is most cruel. Indeed, the loss of one's offspring exceeds even death.
For there is no greater calamity than separation from one's husband;
whether at rest, while eating, bathing, sleeping, or even waking, there is the fresh sorrow of being parted from her lord day after day. (35–36)
A woman forgets all sorrow merely through union with her husband;
I see no other kinsman whom, upon seeing, she might forget her husband. I see no relative superior to this, apart from her lord. (37)
"Thus spoke the Lotus-born regarding virtuous women born of noble families.
'O lords of the quarters, O guardians of the directions, O Dharma, O Prajāpati, O Lord of the Mountain, O Beloved of Kamalā! Grant me the gift of a husband. (38–39)
Having spoken thus, that daughter of Citraratha, afflicted by the pain of separation,
fell into a swoon right there in the impenetrable, dense forest. Remaining unconscious there, she held her beloved to her breast.
Throughout the full day and night, she was protected by all the gods.
Having regained consciousness at dawn, she lamented intensely and repeatedly;
then that virtuous woman, addressing Hari there once more, spoke as follows.
Mālāvatī said: "O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the worlds, O Lord, I am not outside the world. You alone are the protector of the worlds; why do you not protect me, O Master? (43)
"This man is my husband and I am his wife"—this [notion] is due to your Māyā.
You alone are the source, the husband of all, and the cause of everything.
By [my own] past action I was a Gandharva, my beloved; and by that same action, I am now his beloved.
Where has he gone at the end of his enjoyment of the fruits of his karma, and where has he left me, his beloved?
O Lord, who is whose husband or son, and who is whose beloved?
The Creator unites and separates beings according to their karma.
In union there is supreme bliss, and in separation there is danger to life;
this is certain for the fool in this world, but not for one who delights in the Self.
Truly, sense objects, worldly enjoyments, and kinsmen on earth are perishable.
When one renounces of one’s own accord, it leads to happiness; when one is made to renounce by others, it leads to suffering.
Therefore, the virtuous, having themselves renounced even their most desired supreme sovereignty, constantly meditate upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, which are free from all calamity.
"Wherever there are wise and virtuous people, who among the women on earth is truly possessed of wisdom?
Therefore, it behoves you to grant my desire to me, for I am utterly deluded.
I have no longing for immortality, nor for the state of Indra, nor even for the path to liberation."
"Grant me this beloved, supreme boon which brings about the four goals of human existence. O Lord of the World, among all the classes of women in the universe,
no one has ever been given such a husband by the Creator."

To him were granted all virtues and various forms; indeed, O Hari, all excellent qualities were bestowed upon him, with the sole exception of immortality. In beauty, virtue, splendor, and prowess, he was peerless.
Through wisdom, tranquility, and contentment, my Lord is equal to Hari.
(54) Devoted to Hari, he is like Hari; in depth he is like the ocean;
he is radiant like the sun, and likewise pure like fire. (55)
He was as beautiful as the moon, as handsome as Kandarpa,
equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, and likewise a poet equal to Kavi in poetic art;
his speech was conversant with all the śāstras, and his genius was like that of Bhṛgu.
He was as wealthy as Kubera, a great donor like Manu;
in righteousness he was equal to Dharma, and in his devotion to truth he excelled Satyavrata. In asceticism he was like Kumāra, and in his conduct he was equal to Brahmā. (57–58)
Equal to Śakra in sovereignty and as patient as the earth—
how is it that my life-breaths do not depart from such a beloved one who has died? O gods who partake in sacrifices, you are capable of consuming clarified butter on this earth!
"In an instant, by my own effortless play, I shall deprive you of your share in the sacrifice.
O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of the world, I am not outside this universe!
Quickly restore my beloved to life; otherwise, I shall curse you! (60–61)
"O Prajāpati, due to the curse of your son, you shall be unworthy of worship on the surface of the earth. Now, in this world, I shall bring about your own lack of qualification.
O Śambhu, by means of a curse, I shall cause the loss of your knowledge."
I shall indeed cause the neglect of dharma through mere play;
I shall cast the office of Yama far away, of this there is no doubt.
I shall curse True Time and the most cruel Daughter of Death.
"I curse you all to remain right here now, free from old age and disease;
for neither by disease nor by old age has death come to my husband.
Having spoken thus, she went to the bank of the Kauśikī river specifically to curse them.
The great virtuous Mālāvatī placed the corpse upon her breast.
Seeing her prepared to curse [him], Brahmā, preceded by the gods,
went for refuge to Viṣṇu on the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having bathed there, Brahmā praised the Supreme Self, the Lord Viṣṇu, who is beloved by the world; he spoke thus like one struck with fear:
Brahmā said:
She is the wife of Upabarhaṇa and the daughter of Citraratha;
O Mādhava, protect her so that she does not long for the gods for the sake of a husband.
The virtuous remember her, and the holy sages joyfully recite her name.
In dreams and in waking alike, in all undertakings, [we call upon] Mādhava.
O You who are solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge, the wretched, and the distressed—protect us, protect us, O Hṛṣīkeśa! We go to You for refuge.
"O Lord, my worship has now been thwarted by the curse of my son;
moreover, the virtuous Mālatī has deprived me of my authority.
O Lord, previously you granted me supreme authority over the entire universe. (72)
"O Lord, such [knowledge] as this shall indeed now depart from me.
Mahādeva said:
"The great knowledge given by you is secret and difficult for all to obtain."
In former times at Puṣkara, by the fruit of ascetic penance performed for a hundred manvantaras,
whether it be sovereignty, wealth, learning, or even valor—
none of these are worth even a sixteenth part of knowledge that is the supreme reality.
My jewel of the knowledge of reality—which is entirely unknown, completely secret, and exceedingly difficult to attain—is departing from this woman due to a curse.
Oh, how great is the power of a devoted wife, surpassing all other powers! (76)
"O Hari, O Hari! Protect me, protect me, who am being consumed by the fire of *tejas*!
Dharma said:
"Dharma alone is the eternal jewel, the jewel superior to all jewels."
"O Lord, such a dharma as was given by you in the past will surely depart in this manner, O Supreme Lord;
for through the fruit of penance performed during seven *manvantaras*, the dharma that was attained has now departed due to the curse of a woman. (78–79)
The gods said:
"O Mādhava, we were made by you alone the partakers of sacrifice and consumers of clarified butter; all of that now perishes because of the curse of a woman. (80)
Having spoken thus, they all remained there, restrained and afflicted by fear. In the meantime, suddenly an incorporeal voice arose: "Go to his presence; Janārdana is there in the form of a brahmin."
"He will come later for the sake of peace and for your protection.
Having heard those words, the gods, their minds joyful and faces uplifted,
went to the place where Mālāvatī was, to the bank of the Kauśikī, O lords.
The gods beheld that very lady, the virtuous Mālāvatī,
radiant with ornaments of the finest jewels and like a portion of Kamalā herself;
she was clad in garments purified by fire and adorned with a dot of vermilion.
Peaceful and illuminating the quarters with her radiance like the light of the autumn moon,
she blazed with the supreme splendor long accumulated through the great dharma of service to her husband,
like the most excellent flame of a well-kindled fire. (85–86)
And she is performing a yogic posture, seated upon the chest of a corpse;
she bears her Lord’s beautiful lute in her right hand,
holding a rosary of pure crystal between the tips of her index finger and thumb.
Bearing the *yogamudrā* out of devotion and love for her beloved, she possessed the luster of a beautiful campaka flower, with lips like the *bimba* fruit and adorned with a necklace of jewels;
she appeared as if sixteen years of age, eternally fixed in the bloom of youth. (88–89)
Afflicted by the weight of her broad hips, with full buttocks and breasts,
she gazed again and again upon the corpse of the Lord with auspicious eyes.
Seeing her in such a state, those gods were filled with wonder.
And there, for a moment, those who were righteous and fearful of unrighteousness remained silent.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of Mālāvatī," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:

Having stayed there for a moment, the gods, led by Brahmā and Īśāna— who bestow supreme auspiciousness— went to the presence of Mālāvatī. Seeing the gods, the devoted Mālāvatī prostrated herself before them.
O sage, having placed her beloved husband down in the presence of the gods, she wept.
In the meantime, a certain most charming young brahmin arrived there at the assembly of the gods.
Carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in white garments, and bearing a radiant tilaka;
with a long book in hand, he was exceedingly peaceful and possessed a gentle smile.
His entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, and he blazed with the splendor of Brahmanic power.
Having conversed with the gods who were there, amazed by Viṣṇu’s illusory power (māyā),
he dwelt in the midst of that assembly like the moon among the stars.
Then the wise one spoke to all the gods and to Mālatī.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
How is it that all the gods, led by Brahmā and Īśāna, as well as the Creator himself, the progenitor of the worlds, [were born] through what specific action? 7.
"Śambhu himself, the all-pervading Lord and destroyer of the entire universe, is present here!
Oh, Dharma is indeed the witness of the three worlds and of all actions!
How is it that the Sun, the Moon, and the Fire-god are here?"
How is it that Time and the Daughter of Death are here, or how are Yama and the others present?
O sinless Mālāvatī, who is this utterly withered corpse upon your lap?
And how is it that there is a male corpse at the very root of a living woman?
Having spoken thus to them and to her, the brahmin ceased on the floor of the assembly.
Mālāvatī, having bowed down to that wise man, spoke to him.
Mālāvatī said: "With joy, I salute Janārdana in the form of a brahmin."
The gods are pleased and Hari is pleased by the water and flowers of one who [offers them].
O Lord, give your attention to the petition of this woman afflicted by grief;
for the compassionate always extend equal mercy toward the worthy among the virtuous. (12–13)

"I am the wife of Upabarhaṇa and the daughter of Citraratha, O best of brahmins; all [the gods] address me as Mālavatī. For a divine pair of lakṣas of yugas, I have dwelt in various delightful and enchanting places. (14)
She played at will together with this husband of hers.
O best of Brahmins, you, being wise, know according to all the scriptures how much affection virtuous women have for their beloveds. (15–16)
Suddenly, due to the curse of Brahmā, my husband gave up his life-breaths.
I shall lament before the gods so that my husband may return to life.
Everyone on the surface of the earth is preoccupied with accomplishing their own tasks.
They do not know existence or non-existence; they are solely intent upon their own self-interest.
(18) Happiness, suffering, fear, grief, and the distress of men arise from their actions.
So too do sovereignty, supreme bliss, birth, death, and liberation. (19)
The gods are the bestowers of the fruits of all actions;
they are the creators of the trees of karma, and they sever their roots with ease.
Indeed, there is no kinsman superior to the gods, and no one more powerful than the gods.
For there is no one more compassionate than a god, nor any giver greater than he.
I entreat all the gods for the gift of a husband that I desire—
one who is like the celestial trees that bestow the fruits of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
"If the gods grant me the gift of my beloved as I desire, then it shall be well;
otherwise, I will certainly inflict the death of their wives upon them, and I shall cast a terrible and unavoidable curse upon them all. (23)

"Whose curse can be difficult to avert? By what austerity can the curse of a chaste woman be warded off? Having spoken thus in the assembly of the gods, the virtuous Mālatī, afflicted with grief, fell silent.
O Śaunaka, best of the twice-born, he then spoke to her.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Mālatī, it is true that the gods are the givers of the fruits of actions;
for men, these do not appear immediately nor even after a very long time, just as grain [appears] for a farmer. (25)
When a householder sows grain in the field through the agency of a farmer,
its sprout shall appear in due time, and in due time it shall even bear fruit as a tree.
In due time it becomes fully ripe, and in due time the householder receives it.
In this way, one should infer that the fruit of action comes after a long time.
Sown in the cycle of existence by the illusory power of Viṣṇu, the householder plants seeds;
in due time they become sprouts and trees, and in due time he obtains their fruit. (28–29)
The meritorious person performs penance for a very long time on this ground of merit;
and the gods are the givers of the fruits thereof—this is the truth, there is no doubt.
[They bestow these fruits] into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇas, which is an excellent field, truly free from salt.

Whoever offers oblations with devotion certainly attains that very thing. Neither strength, nor beauty, nor sovereignty, nor wealth, nor a son, nor even a wife, nor a beloved husband—what can exist without austerity? (32)
He who indeed serves Prakṛti with devotion in birth after birth shall obtain a beautiful, beloved, humble, and virtuous wife;
as well as stable prosperity, sons, grandsons, land, wealth, and progeny.
And by the very grace of Prakṛti, the devotee shall effortlessly obtain Śiva—
the one whose nature is auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, the cause of auspiciousness,
the great-souled one consisting of knowledge and bliss, the supreme, and the transcendent conqueror of death. || 34–35 ||
Indeed, the man who serves that Lord with devotion in birth after birth obtains a virtuous wife;
and the woman likewise obtains a virtuous husband.
He also attains learning, wisdom, skill in poetry, sons, grandsons, and supreme prosperity.
By the boon of the excellent Hara, he shall obtain strength, wealth, and valor.
Indeed, the man who worships Brahmā shall also obtain progeny and prosperity;
by the boon of Brahmā, he attains knowledge, sovereignty, and bliss. (37–38)
The man who worships with devotion the Lord of the Poor, the Sun-god,
will certainly obtain knowledge, health, bliss, wealth, and a son.
He who worships Gaṇeśvara, the eternal God of gods—
To him who worships with devotion, birth after birth, the Lord of All, who is worthy of the highest worship—
there shall be the destruction of obstacles at all times, both in dreams and while awake.
He shall obtain supreme bliss, sovereignty, sons, grandsons, wealth, and progeny.

And by that boon, he obtains knowledge, wisdom, and skill in poetry—he who indeed worships Viṣṇu, the beloved of Lakṣmī and lord of the gods. If he seeks a boon, he shall obtain everything; otherwise, liberation is certain.
By serving Śānta, the Protector, a person shall obtain truth, truth indeed.
Having served Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, what fool would seek any other boon—[neglecting] all austerity, all dharma, and unsurpassed fame and glory? (43–44)
He has been mocked by the Creator and deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
That Māyā is the consort of Nārāyaṇa and Īśāna, the sovereign source of all nature (sarvaprakṛti). She bestows grace upon whomsoever she grants the mantra of Viṣṇu.
The righteous person who devotes themselves to Dharma will certainly attain all dharmas.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, they go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Whichever deity one worships with devotion, that very deity one first attains. (46–47)
In due time, he shall attain the supreme abode of Viṣṇu together with Him.

Indeed, he who worships Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa), beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the seed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, and higher than the highest—[attains that goal]. 48.
The imperishable, supreme Brahman, the eternal Blessed One;
possessed of form and yet formless, the light consisting of His own will, the all-pervading Lord;
the support of all, the Lord of all, the Sovereign of supreme bliss. (49–50)
He is of the nature of an unattached witness and has a form that manifests for the grace of devotees.
Indeed, that wise one who is liberated while living does not seek any boon;
he considers even the fourfold state of liberation, beginning with *sālokya*, to be trivial.

He regards the state of Brahmā or immortality, as well as liberation—which [he considers] to be as insignificant as chaff—as being like a clod of earth; he likewise considers sovereignty to be perishable. He views even the status of Indra, the status of Manu, or long life itself in the same way. (52–93)
Perceiving it with the intellect to be as utterly trivial as a bubble on the water, one does not take it into account.
Whether in a dream or in the waking state, one constantly desires service;
without such service, one should not seek the supreme abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having attained firm devotion to His lotus feet, he is eternally fulfilled.
Always remaining steadfast, he constantly serves the Supreme Brahman, the most perfect reality.
He [delivers] ten million ancestors of his own lineage, as well as a hundred of his maternal grandfather’s.
Having effortlessly first delivered a hundred ancestors of his father-in-law,
a devotee of Kṛṣṇa shall deliver even more than a hundred— male and female servants, his mother, his wife, and his sons— and he will certainly go to Goloka.
A person possessed of desire shall dwell in the womb for as long as there is the torment of Yama;
likewise, a householder seeking worldly enjoyments remains so only as long as he does not serve Kṛṣṇa.
But he into whose ear the mantra of Viṣṇu enters from the mouth of the Guru [is liberated]. 59–98.
Yama, out of fear, immediately distances himself from that drawing;
Brahmā, however, should beforehand prepare the madhuparka and other offerings for him [thinking]:
"Oh, he will bypass my world and proceed by this path!"
Indeed, there is no atonement for him even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. And his sins, committed over ten million births, being terrified,
flee away leaving him behind, just as serpents flee from Vainateya.
Whatever ancient karma has been performed by him, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
Kṛṣṇa constantly cuts it away with his sharp-edged discus.
Leaving him behind, old age and death depart out of fear of that discus.
Otherwise, Sudarśana shatters her into a hundred pieces;
then, casting off his human body, he goes fearlessly to Goloka.
Having gone there and assumed a divine form, he serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa forever.
As long as Kṛṣṇa remains in Goloka, so long shall the devotee dwell there eternally;
the servant considers even the lifespan of Brahmā to be perishable, lasting but a mere moment.

(66) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Viṣṇu and Mālāvatī," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka. (14)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O virtuous lady, by what disease has your beloved now died?
As a physician, I know the treatment for every ailment. (1)
If death occurs within seven days of a disease, it is equal to being dead;
yet by means of great knowledge, I revive that living soul with ease.
Having brought King Death, Yama, Time, and Disease before you, [I shall restore him].

I am capable of binding and delivering [the disease], just as a hunter binds and delivers a beast. (3) Since I know the cause of every disease that afflicts the bodies of embodied beings, O beautiful one, I know how the disease may not circulate within their bodies. (4)
Since the wicked and inauspicious seed of disease does not spread from it, I know the means for that in accordance with the principles of the scriptures.
Or, one who abandons the body through yoga or through exhaustion [is also successful]. (5)
"I know that means of his livelihood through the practice of yoga.
(6) Having heard the words of the Brahmin, the virtuous Mālāvatī, flourishing in prosperity, spoke to him with a smile, her heart full of affection and great joy. (7)
Mālāvatī said:
"Oh, what a marvelous speech has been heard from the mouth of a child!
Though he appears very young in age, he possesses the supreme knowledge of those who know yoga. (8)
"And the vow made by you to restore my beloved to life—
since that virtuous word cannot be reversed, my husband was restored to life at that very moment. Afterwards, the best among those who know the Vedas shall restore my beloved."

Whatever I ask out of doubt, you ought to explain that to me. While my beloved lord was alive and in the presence of that formidable one within the assembly, I was indeed not able to question you while my master was present.
These gods, beginning with Brahmā, are present here in this assembly;
you are the foremost among those who know the Vedas, and there is no one who is my master.
If a husband protects his wife, no one is capable of violating her. (12)
If he does not issue a command, there is no protector whatsoever on earth.
(13) Thus, we have no power over the gods, nor over Śakra, Brahmā, or Rudra.
One must understand that both womanhood and manhood exist; the husband is the master and the agent for women. (14)
The master is the doer, the taker, the ruler, the nourisher, and the protector;
he is the beloved deity and the one to be worshipped, for there is no teacher higher than the master. A maiden born of a noble family remains under the control of her husband.

Yamarāja indeed composed the *Jñānārṇava*, the great tantra; the venerable sage Cyavana composed the *Jīvadāna*; and the yogi Janaka composed the *Vaidyasandehabhañjana*. (18–19)
Jābāla, the son of Candra, composed the *Sarvasāra-tantrasāra*.
The sage Jājali composed the *Vedāṅgasāra-tantra*. Paila composed the *Nidāna*, and Karatha composed the supreme *Sarvadhara-tantra*.
And the pitcher-born sage composed the *Dvaidhanirṇaya-tantra*.
These sixteen treatises are the seeds of the science of medicine;

A devotee of Śiva and a yogi, yet cruel and deformed in appearance;

Weak digestion is its progenitor; there are three progenitors of weak digestion:

Likewise, [diseases] are born of wind, born of bile, and born of phlegm.
The varieties of fever are threefold, and the fourth is born from the three *doṣas*.

There are also anemia (*pāṇḍu*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), swelling (*śotha*), splenic enlargement (*plīhā*), colic (*śūlaka*), fever-dysentery (*jvarātisāra*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), cough (*kāsa*), ulcers (*vraṇa*), and chlorosis (*halīmaka*). (30–31)
Dysuria, abdominal tumors arising from blood disorders, abnormal urinary excretion (viṣameha), constipation, scrotal enlargement, goiter, vertigo,

These are the sons of Mṛtyukanyā (the Daughter of Death), and Old Age is her daughter;

Eye-wash, water, physical exercise, and massaging the soles of the feet with oil [are recommended].
Oil applied to the ears and the head destroys old age and disease.
(36) Old age does not approach that man who wanders about in the spring, maintains a small fire, and enjoys the company of young women at the proper time. (37)
One who bathes in naturally cool water, uses sandalwood paste, and resorts to the breeze during the summer heat does not succumb to old age;
likewise, one who bathes in warm water during the rainy season and does not resort to thick rainwater [is likewise preserved]. || 38 ||
At the proper time, one who is composed in diet—old age does not approach him.
He does not take [food] that is harsh like autumn; he should avoid wandering there.
One who bathes after digging [a well], who is composed in diet—old age does not approach him. (39–40)
Bathing after eating during the winter season and tending the sacred fire, as well as consuming fresh, warm food—old age does not approach such a person.
In the cold season, he partakes of fine garments, fire, and fresh, warm food. (41)
Old age does not approach him who bathes in warm water;
nor does old age approach him who consumes fresh meat, new grain, the milk of a young woman, and ghee. (42–43)
He eats excellent food when hungry and drinks water when thirsty;
he constantly consumes betel leaf, and old age does not approach him.
[He also partakes of] curd, *haiyaṅgavīna* butter, fresh butter, and likewise molasses. 44.
Old age does not approach that self-controlled man who always eats [moderately].

She who is the wife of a priest for a Śūdra, and she who, though being a chaste wife, is devoid of her menses—

There is constant and certain friendship between sins and diseases.
Sin is certainly the seed of disease, old age, and obstacles.

One who is engaged in the practice of his own duty, initiated, and a servant of Hari;

Having by chance heard a great censure of Śrī Viṣṇu, the wise man is liberated from all sins through remembrance [of Him] and attains rare merit.
Whoever, whether intentionally or unintentionally, utters a censure of Viṣṇu...
That lowest of men who listens to or laughs [at such matters] in the midst of an assembly shall be cooked in Kumbhīpāka for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.

And a living being goes to hell; it is certain that this has been heard in that very place.
Furthermore, three kinds of reviling Viṣṇu were described by Brahmā in the past: [reviling him] behind his back, or not respecting him at all. 48.

for him there is no atonement here until the end of a hundred Brahmās.
That lowest of men who reviles his guru or reviles his father [is likewise without atonement].
He goes to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Viṣṇu is the teacher of all, the progenitor, the bestower of knowledge,
the nourisher, the protector, the savior from fear, and the giver of boons throughout the three worlds.
And having heard these words of the three, O best of Brahmins,
he laughed and spoke again to those gods with sweet speech.
The Brahmin said:

"Alas! What insult to Viṣṇu has been committed? O gods, upholders of righteousness, Hari has not come here!"—thus was empty, celestial speech uttered by me. "O lords, speak auspiciously for the sake of dharma. (53)
Being partial in the assembly, they killed Śatapūruṣa.
And you, who are full of devotion, say that Viṣṇu is eternally present everywhere;
if so, how did he go to Śvetadvīpa for the sake of a boon? (54–55)
If it is certain that there is no difference between the part and the whole,
then how is it that the virtuous abandon a mere fraction and devote themselves to the Supreme Fullness—
which is difficult to propitiate even over ten million lifetimes and unattainable even for the wicked? (56)
The hope of men is powerful; they desire to serve Kṛṣṇa.
Do the lowly or the great wish to attain the supreme state?
He desires to grasp the moon with his two arms, just as Vāmana did.
He who is Viṣṇu, the pervader of all, the dweller in the White Island (Śvetadvīpa)—
you, Brahmā, Śiva, Dharma, the guardians of the quarters, the lords of the directions,
and the worlds of the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, along with all things moving and unmoving.
Thus, how many kinds of universes exist eternally?
And who is capable of counting the universes and the gods?
Kṛṣṇa, whose form is the grace bestowed upon his devotees, is the Lord of them all.
Above all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) is Vaikuṇṭha, the desired realm of truth.
Above that is Goloka, fifty crores of yojanas away.
In Vaikuṇṭha resides the eternal Lord with four arms, the beloved of Lakṣmī.
Surrounded by his attendants Sunanda, Nandaka, Kumuda, and others,
the eternal Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Rādhā, appears in Goloka with two arms,
accompanied by cowherd women and his subordinate attendants, who likewise have two arms. (63–64)
He is the most perfectly complete Brahman and the Self of all embodied beings;
composed of His own will, He always sports in Vṛndāvana at Rāsa.
That light is circular in form, with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Virtuous yogis constantly meditate upon that which is free from all affliction—
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, two-armed, clad in yellow garments,
the enchanting abode of the playful beauty of ten million Cupids. (66–67)
The virtuous Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon the Lord, who has the eyes of a youth, who is eternally peaceful, and who smiles; they serve Him, whose form is truth.
And you too are Vaiṣṇavas; tell me, from whose lineage are you descended?

"Of which Lord of Sages am I the disciple?"— thus you have asked me again and again. O hosts of gods, listen to these words and this knowledge of him, from whose lineage I am born and of whom I was a young disciple.
"O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, quickly restore the Gandharva to life!
When the truth has been discerned, who is a fool? What is the use of a war of words?
Having spoken thus, Janārdana, in the form of a Brahmin, remained there as a boy.
He ceased speaking in the midst of the assembly and laughed aloud, O Śaunaka.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Praise of Viṣṇu," in the dialogue between Viṣṇu and the hosts of gods within the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:

Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, the gods, led by Brahmā and Īśāna, went together with the brāhmaṇa to the root of a *mālatī* tree. Brahmā then poured water from his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) upon the body of the corpse.
He assumed the beautiful form of that mind’s movement.
Śiva himself, as Jñānānanda, bestowed the gift of knowledge upon him;
Dharma himself gave the knowledge of dharma, and the Brāhmaṇa gave the gift of life.
By the mere sight of Vahni, the fire of his stomach was kindled;
by the mere sight of Kāma, he certainly became the possessor of all desires.
This occurred through the presiding presence of that Vāyu, whose nature is the vital breath of the universe.
The movement of the breath and of the vital energies (prāṇas) indeed occurred;
by the mere act of presiding over everything, the power of sight arose.
Speech came through the manifestation of voice, and beauty through the manifestation of Śrī.
Nevertheless, the corpse did not rise; it remained just as it lay, like one who is inert.
It attained a distinguished awakening, yet without the presiding presence of the Self.
At the word of Brahmā, the virtuous woman praised the Supreme Lord.
Having bathed quickly in the river water and put on two washed garments,
Mālāvatī said:
"I bow to that Supreme Self, the cause of all causes."
Without whom all living beings on the surface of the earth would be corpses; who is untainted, the witness of all, and present in all their actions;
yet who, though existing everywhere and at all times, is not seen by anyone.
By whom Prakṛti was created— she who is the support of all, higher than the highest,
the mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, and whose nature consists of the three guṇas;
by whose service the creator of the world, Brahmā himself, is constrained.

Viṣṇu is the protector of the worlds, and Śaṅkara himself is their destroyer. All the gods, as well as the sages, the Manus, the Siddhas, the Yogins, and the virtuous, constantly meditate upon Him who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is with form and without form, supreme, consisting of His own will, and all-pervading;
the best, the most worthy of worship, the giver of boons, the one deserving of boons, and the cause of all boons;
the fruit of austerity, the seed of austerity, and the bestower of the fruits of austerities. (14)
He is the very nature of self-discipline (*svayaṃtapas*), possessing all forms and existing everywhere;
he is the support of all and the seed of all, the action itself and the fruit of those actions;
he is the giver of their fruits, that seed which is also the cause of their destruction. (15–16)
He is the very embodiment of splendor and the form that manifests for the grace of his devotees.
Without a physical form, meditation upon service is not possible for devotees.
That splendor of his is circular in shape, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
And there his form was exceedingly lovely and heart-stealing:
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like autumn lotuses, a face like the full moon of autumn, and endowed with a gentle smile. (18–19)
Possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids, a charming abode of grace, with all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments;
two-armed, holding a flute in his hand, and clothed in yellow silk garments. (20)
Somewhere in a secluded forest, [he beholds] the youthful, peaceful, and infinite Lord who is the beloved of Rādhā; surrounded by the cowherd girls in one place, and in another,
situated in the midst of the rāsa dance, attended by Rādhā.
In a certain place within the beautiful Vṛndāvana forest, which excels even the Śataśṛṅga mountain, he was dressed in the garb of a cowherd and surrounded by cowherd boys;
there he stood in the form of a child, tending a multitude of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus).
In Goloka, on the banks of the Virajā, in the forest of Pārijāta trees,
he was sounding his flute sweetly, the cause of the enchantment of the gopīs;
and in the stainless Vaikuṇṭha, in some place, he appeared with four arms.
He is the beloved of Lakṣmī, served by four-armed attendants;
and in some places, for the protection of the worlds,
he exists in his own partial form as Viṣṇu in Śvetadvīpa, attended by Padmā.
In one place, by a portion of His own part, He is the form of Brahmā who consists of the cosmic egg;
by His own part, He is the nature of Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness, whose form is Śiva;
and by a sixteenth part of Himself, He is the support of all, higher than the highest. (27–28)

He himself is the Great Virāṭ form, within whose body hairs the entire flood of the universe resides; and by his own partial expansion (*svāṃśakalā*), for the sake of protecting the worlds, he assumes various incarnations—the eternal seed of them all. (29)

I am unable to praise that Lord, the Supreme Self, who dwells somewhere within the hearts of the virtuous yogis, who is the life-force of all living beings, and who is the all-pervading, attribute-less One— [I,] a weak woman. (30–31)
Beyond perception and devoid of effort, the essence and supreme beyond speech and mind— He whom the infinite Ananta is unable to praise even with a thousand mouths,
nor the five-faced, the four-faced, the elephant-faced, or the six-faced [Śiva]. (32)
He whom Māyā, deluded by whose own power, is unable to praise;
he whom even Śrī, Sarasvatī, and the Vedas—having become stupefied—are unable to praise;
who indeed is the learned knower of the Vedas capable of praising him? (33–34)
"What can I praise that Supreme Being, who is free from desire, while I am a woman afflicted by grief?
Having spoken thus, that Gandharva woman ceased speaking and wept;
trembling with fear, she bowed down again and again before the ocean of compassion.
And Kṛṣṇa, together with the Śaktis, established his presence there.
Within that husband of hers, the formless Supreme Soul,
having quickly risen, taken up his lute, bathed, and put on two garments— 35–37.
He prostrated before the host of gods and the Brahmin standing in front of him. The drums resounded, the gods rained down flowers,
and seeing [the flowers] above the couple, they bestowed the highest blessing.
The Gandharva danced and sang for a moment before the gods.
By the boon of the gods, he regained his life;
and filled with joy, he departed together with his wife, father, and mother.
The Gandharva Upabarhaṇa, moreover, gave a celestial city to the Gandharvas;
and Mālāvatī bestowed ten million jewels and various riches upon the Brahmins, while that virtuous woman fed them.
He caused him to study the Vedas and performed auspicious rites;
he held various great festivals, for the name of Hari alone is auspicious.
Then the gods departed to their own abodes, and Hari himself, in the form of a brahmin, remained.
All this has been told to you, O Śaunaka, as well as this king of hymns. That Vaiṣṇava person who recites this meritorious hymn at the time of worship attains devotion to Hari and service to Hari.

He who desires boons, being faithful and possessing supreme conviction, shall certainly obtain the fruit of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth obtains wealth. (45–46)
One desiring a wife obtains a wife; one desiring a son obtains a son;
one desiring merit obtains merit; and one desiring fame obtains fame.
One who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom, and one deprived of subjects regains his subjects. (47)
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one who is bound shall be released from bondage.
One who is afraid shall be freed from fear, and one whose wealth is lost shall regain it.
Even one seized by robbers in a vast forest, beset by predatory beasts, [shall be delivered].
One who has been consumed by a forest fire shall be liberated, as shall one submerged in the ocean.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Composition of the Hymn to the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣastotra) in the Bestowal of Life upon the Gandharva," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:

Having given wealth to the brahmins, Mālāvatī was filled with joy; for the sake of her husband, she prepared various kinds of attire for herself. She performed service and worship for her lord as was appropriate for the occasion.
She took great delight with him for a very long time in joy.

Then, in private, that woman of excellent vows herself reminded him of the hymn to the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣastotra*), the ritual worship (*pūjā*), the armor-verse (*kavaca*), and the mantra, which he had forgotten. (2–3)

Formerly, at Puṣkara, Vasiṣṭha, the ocean of compassion, bestowed upon the Gandharva Mālatī the hymn of praise, worship, and other rites for Hari, as well as a single mantra; however, he forgot the hymn and the armor-vidyā (kavaca). ||4||
In private, he enlightened the king of the Gandharvas regarding the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
Thus, in that hermitage which resembled the palace of Kubera, the Gandharva Paramānanda ruled his kingdom together with his kinsmen.
Having arrived with women who had gone there as they were, and with others as well,
his own master reached that place with supreme joy.
Śaunaka said:
What was the hymn, the armor, and the procedure for mantra-worship of Viṣṇu given to those two in ancient times?
You ought to tell us that distinguished [teaching],
as well as the twelve-syllable mantra and the armor and other [protections] of the Wielder of the Trident.

O Sauti, tell me that as well: what was given by Vasiṣṭha to the King of the Gandharvas in the past? I have a great curiosity to hear it—that hymn of praise to Śaṅkara, the armor, and the mantra that destroys all misfortune.
Sauti said: Listen to that very hymn, the mantra, and the armor (kavaca) with which Mālatī praised the Supreme Lord. (11)
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Lord of the Rāsa-maṇḍala, svāhā!
He bestowed this sixteen-syllable mantra, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru).
In ancient times, it was given by Brahmā to Kumāra at Puṣkara in the presence of Hari.
Formerly, Kṛṣṇa bestowed upon Śaṅkara in Goloka the eternal meditation on Viṣṇu as declared in the Vedas, which is difficult for all to attain. All offerings,
including the most excellent food offerings (naivedya) and so forth, should be presented with the root mantra.
I heard from my father’s own mouth that this armor is exceedingly well-guarded.
O brāhmaṇa, it was certainly given to my father by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) long ago on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
It was given to the wielder of the trident by Brahmā in the Rāsa-maṇḍala of Goloka.
Out of compassion for Dharma, the beloved of Gopikā performed this most wonderful [act].
Brahmā said: O highly fortunate beloved of Rādhā, this armor (kavaca) which has been revealed—

O Lord, out of compassion, please tell me that which is named the Purifier of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍapāvana). O Maheśa, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, through your grace I shall bestow it upon my sons, endowed with devotion, as well as myself, Dharma, and [my other] devotee.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Brahmā and Śiva; I shall declare this supreme armor (*kavaca*) which bestows righteousness. I shall give it to you both; it must be kept secret and is exceedingly difficult to obtain. 19.
This [weapon], which is equal to my very life, must not be given to just anyone;
for whatever splendor exists in my body, that same splendor is also in this armor.
Wearing this, perform the act of creation and become the sustainer of the three worlds.
"O Śambhu, become my destroyer; O Bhava, become equal to me.
O Dharma, having assumed this form, become a witness to all actions.
By my boon, may you all become the bestowers of the fruits of ascetic penances. || 21-22 ||
Hari himself is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this armor (*kavaca*) which purifies the entire universe;
the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, and I, the Lord of the World, am the deity.
Its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (23)
O Creator, by reciting this armor-mantra three hundred thousand times, it bestows perfection;
whoever possesses this perfected armor becomes equal to me in splendor, in the yoga of accomplishment, in knowledge, and in prowess. (24–25)

May the Praṇava protect my head, and may "Obeisance to Rāmeśvara" protect my forehead; may "Obeisance to Rādheśvara" protect the pair of my eyes. May Kṛṣṇa protect the pair of my ears, and may "O Hare" protect my very life-breath.
The tongue is protected by the wife of Fire (Svāhā) and the word "Kṛṣṇāya" on all sides. May the six-syllabled mantra, "Śrīkṛṣṇāya Svāhā," protect the throat.
"Hrīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Namaḥ" protects the face, and that preceded by "Klīṃ" protects the two arms.
Homage to the Lord of the cowherd maidens; may the eight-syllable mantra of the shoulders protect me.
Homage to the Lord of the cowherd girls for the row of teeth and the pair of lips. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of the circle of the rāsa dance, svāhā!
May this sixteen-syllable mantra protect his own chest:
*aiṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā*. May it always protect the pair of ears.
