And may the mantra *oṃ viṣṇave svāhā*, together with the syllable *vaṭ*, protect the cheek. (30–31)
"Oṃ, obeisances to Hari"—may this protect my back and feet at all times.
"Oṃ, svāhā to the upholder of Govardhana"—may this protect my entire body.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect me in the east, and Mādhava protect me in the southeast.
May the Lord of the Gopīs protect me in the south; may the Son of Nanda protect me in the southwest (nairṛtyā).

May Govinda protect me in the west (vāruṇī); may the Lord of Rādhikā protect me in the northwest (vāyavī). May the Lord of the Rāsa dance protect me in the north; may Acyuta himself protect me in the northeast (aiśānī). (33–34)
"May the supreme Nārāyaṇa himself protect you constantly and from all sides.
Thus, O Brāhmaṇa, this most wonderful armor has been narrated to you;
it is equal to my own life, and it is now granted to you.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit from wearing this armor alone,
provided one has worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste. (36)
Having bathed and paid homage to him, the wise man should wear the armor (*kavaca*).
By the grace of this armor, a person becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). O twice-born one, if one has mastered the armor, he would indeed become Viṣṇu himself.
Sauti said:
O Śaunaka, listen now to the armor (kavaca) and hymn (stotra) of Śiva, which was bestowed by Vasiṣṭha upon the Gandharva, as well as the mantra. (39)
"Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Śiva; svāhā"—this is the mantra that was formerly bestowed out of compassion by the Lord Vasiṣṭha upon Datta at Puṣkara.
This mantra was formerly given to Rāvaṇa by Brahmā.
In former times, Śambhu himself [bestowed this] upon Bāṇa and likewise upon Durvāsas.
Everything, including the most excellent food offerings and the like, should be given with the root mantra.
One should perform the daily meditation and other rites as prescribed in the Vedas, which are approved by all.
Oṃ, salutations to Mahādeva.
Bāṇāsura said:
O Maheśvara, O illustrious one, that armor which has been revealed—
"O Lord, please graciously tell me that which is called the *saṃsārapāvana* [purifier of worldly existence].
Maheśvara said:
"Listen, my child; I shall speak of the most wonderful armor (*kavaca*)."
I shall bestow upon you this secret armor, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
(44) It was given in former times to Durvāsas for the sake of victory over the three worlds.
(45) This very armor of mine, whoever possesses it with devotion—that wise person—shall be protected.
O Blessed One, by the mere effortless gesture of his hand, he is able to conquer the three worlds.
Prajāpati is the seer of this armor that purifies the cycle of existence;
the meter is Gāyatrī, and I, Maheśvara, am its deity.
Its application is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By merely reciting it five hundred thousand times, this armor (*kavaca*) becomes a bestower of perfection. Whoever possesses this perfected armor shall become equal to me upon the earth.
By his splendor, by the yoga of perfection, by austerity, and by valor;
may Śambhu protect my head, and may Maheśvara protect my face. May Nīlakaṇṭha protect the row of my teeth, and Hara himself protect my lower lip.
May the moon-crested Lord protect my throat; may the bull-vehicled Lord protect my shoulders;
may the blue-throated Lord protect my chest; may the sky-clad Lord protect my back;
and may the Lord of the Universe protect every limb in all directions at all times. (50)
"May Sthāṇu protect me constantly, both in sleep and in waking.
Thus, O Bāṇa, this most wonderful armor has been told to you;
it must not be given to just anyone, but should be guarded with great effort.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas),
that fruit he surely obtains simply by wearing this armor (kavaca).
That person of very dull intellect who would worship me without knowing this armor—
Even if recited a hundred lakhs of times, the mantra does not grant success.
Sauti said:
O Śaunaka, this armor (kavaca) has been declared; now hear the hymn (stotra).
In former times, Vasiṣṭha bestowed this king of mantras, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree.
Oṃ namo śivāya.
Bāṇāsura said:
I bow to Nīlalohita, the essence of the gods and the Lord of the gods;
the master of yogis, the seed of yoga, and the teacher of teachers for yogis.
I bow to the eternal one, whose bliss is knowledge, whose form is knowledge, and who is the seed of knowledge.
The bestower of the fruits of austerities, the giver of all prosperity;

the embodiment of austerity, the seed of austerity, the treasure-trove of the wealth of austerity—the excellent one, the most worthy of choice, the granter of boons, praised by the foremost hosts of Siddhas. (57–58)
The cause of enjoyment and liberation, the one who ferries across the ocean of hell; he who is easily pleased, whose face is serene, an ocean of the essence of compassion;
resembling snow, sandalwood, the kunda flower, the moon, the kumuda lily, and the lotus.
He is the very nature of the light of Brahman, whose form consists of grace toward devotees.
Assuming many forms through the diversity of sense objects, He is the Lord who takes the form of water, the form of fire, and the form of space. (60–61)
He who is the form of wind, the form of the moon, and the form of the sun; the great Lord, capable of bestowing his own abode upon the self by his mere effortless play;
the Lord who is the life of his devotees and who is ever-anxious to show grace to his devotees.
The Vedas are not able to praise him; how then can I praise that Lord?
He is the all-pervading Ishana, beyond the reach of speech and mind—wearing a tiger-skin garment, seated upon a bull, and clad in the directions as his raiment.
"Bearing a trident and a sharp-edged spear, smiling, with the moon as his crest-ornament"—
having spoken thus, Bāṇa, ever self-restrained,
and Durvāsas, the lord of sages, both bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara by means of this king of hymns.

O Sage, this most wonderful great hymn to the Wielder of the Trident was formerly given by Vasiṣṭha to the Gandharva; and it has been told. That man who recites this highly meritorious hymn with devotion—

One who listens for one year, being self-restrained, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and bowing to Śaṅkara, the Guru, certainly obtains the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas); even one who is childless obtains a son. (67–68)

He who listens for one year, even if afflicted by leprosy or great colic, is certainly liberated from disease; such is the word of Vyāsa as it has been heard. Even he who is bound in prison and finds no peace at all [is freed].
Having heard this hymn for one month, one is certainly released from bondage.
He who listens with devotion for one month shall regain a kingdom if he has been deprived of it;
and having listened for one month while self-restrained, one who has lost his wealth shall recover it. (70–71)
If one who is afflicted by consumption listens for one year with faith,
he will certainly be freed from the disease through the grace of Śaṅkara.
O twice-born, he who always listens to this king of hymns with devotion—
O Śaunaka, there is nothing in the three worlds that is impossible for him to achieve.
At some time in the land of Bhārata, he shall never suffer separation from his kinsmen;
he attains stable and supreme sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. (73–74)
He who listens for one month with great devotion and self-restraint—if he is without a wife, he obtains a well-disciplined and most virtuous wife;
and even one who is a great fool or dull-witted, if he listens for one month— [attains wisdom]. (75)
One obtains wisdom and knowledge merely through the instruction of the guru.
He who listens with devotion for one month, though suffering from the pain of karma and being poor,
will certainly attain wealth by the grace of Śaṅkara.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world and having established a fame that is very difficult to attain, as well as practicing various kinds of dharma, he goes at the end to the abode of Śaṅkara;
becoming a preeminent attendant, he serves Śaṅkara there.
Whoever hears this unsurpassed hymn daily at the three junctions of the day.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn to Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
And the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa, together with Mālāvatī,
rejoiced with them in the secluded forest for the remainder of his time;
the king of the Gandharvas delighted himself along with his sons, wives, and others.
He indeed performed various kinds of great and most meritorious sacrifices.
The king enjoyed his sovereignty in a palace resembling the abode of Kubera,
and he took delight with Suśīlā, who possessed enduring youth.
And at the proper time, on the enchanting bank of the Gaṅgā, the Gandharva king,
together with his wife, cast off his life-breaths and joyfully went to Vaikuṇṭha.
By the grace of Śiva and through the service of Viṣṇu performed by his son, he became a devotee of Śiva.
He became a dark-complexioned, four-armed servant of Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha. Having honored his parents, O brāhmaṇa, the gandharva Upabarhaṇa gave various kinds of wealth to the brāhmaṇas.

In due time, O Śaunaka, that wise man, having voluntarily cast off his life-breaths due to a Brahmin’s curse, was born from the womb of a *vṛṣalī* through the seed of a Brahmin. Mālāvatī [was born] in the sacrificial fire-pit at Puṣkara on the land of Bhārata.

Having fulfilled her desired wish, that virtuous woman gave up her life. She was born as the wife of King Sṛñjaya, a descendant of the lineage of Manu; she was a holy, auspicious, and excellent woman who remembered her former births.

"Upabarhaṇa, the Gandharva, shall be my husband"—with this desire, that beautiful Sundarī, the most excellent of lovely women, remained full of longing. Śaunaka said: *Note: The repetition of "sundarī" at the end of the verse is likely a scribal error or a stylistic emphasis.*
"How was it that the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa was born from the wife of a Śūdra through the virility of a Brāhmaṇa? You ought to tell me the manner in which this occurred.
Sauti said:
In the region of Kānyakubja, there was a king named Drumila.

His wife was Kalāvatī, who was both barren and devoted to her husband. Due to her husband's fault, she remained childless; nevertheless, at the command of her lord, she [remained] with him in due time.
In that terrible forest, she approached the sage Nārada Kāśyapa,
who was meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Having dressed herself in fine attire, she stood before the sage at the conclusion of his meditation.
With a splendor equal to the sun at midday in the summer heat,
he was scorching such that they were unable to approach him even from afar.
And at the conclusion of his meditation, that best of sages, the supreme devotee of Kṛṣṇa—
He saw before him, at a distance, Sundarī, whose youth was permanent;
she possessed the luster of a beautiful campaka flower, her eyes were like autumn lotuses, her face was like the full moon of autumn, and she was adorned with jewel ornaments. (16–17)
Oppressed by the weight of her large hips, with full buttocks and breasts,
adorned with a yellow garment, smiling, and with reddened eyes—
she was infatuated by the form of the sage and tormented by the arrows of Kama. (18)
Displaying her breasts and hips with a mind intent on sexual union,
richly adorned with a dot of vermilion and radiant with beautiful kohl,
and graced by the splendor of red lac upon her feet— she was, by her very form, like Urvaśī herself. (19–20)
Seeing her in that desolate place, the sage asked: "Who are you, O lovely woman?
Whose wife are you, and how have you come to be here? Speak the truth, O unchaste woman!
Hearing the words of the sage, Kalāvatī trembled.
Having placed Śrī Hari in her heart, she spoke with humility.
Kalāvatī said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am a cowherd woman, the wife of Drumila."

"Desiring a son, I have come to you at my husband's command. Bestow your seed upon me; for a woman who has approached you must not be neglected. Indeed, this is not a fault for those of great power, just as fire consumes everything."
Hearing the words of the *vṛṣalī*, the best of sages became enraged.
With his lower lip quivering from anger, he spoke these words, which were both righteous and true.
(25) Kāśyapa said:
"She who desires to give her own fortune, worthy of enjoyment, to another—
she certainly abandons that fool, as it is said, 'This is the doctrine of the Vedas' (Vedavāda).
You, however, O Drumilā, shall never again become worthy of such enjoyment."
Having been abandoned by one who is himself dispassionate, she does not take you back again.
(27) That Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, who takes a Śūdra woman as his wife, truly becomes a Caṇḍāla; he is not fit for the rites among the twice-born. (28)
The Lotus-born One declared that he alone possesses the right to perform ancestral *śrāddha* rites, sacrifices, the touching of the sacred stone, and the worship of the gods; yet,
by causing others to fall [into hell], he himself goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
[Offering water] for one's maternal grandfathers and ten ancestors before and ten descendants after oneself—
this libation is merely urine, and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is immediately excrement.
Upon touching a Śālagrāma stone [containing such], one must fast for three nights.
His chosen deity accepts neither that food offering nor that water;
and for those Brahmins who have renounced the world, that food is like excrement.
Indeed, he is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell until the very end of the reign of Śakra.
"O unchaste woman, you have spoken the truth along with twenty-one men.
That lowest of Brahmins who eats the leavings of Śūdras is equal to one who eats from a lower lip; so it was declared by Aṅgiras. (33–34)
If a Śūdra, weak in knowledge, takes a Brāhmaṇī wife,
he is cooked in the Kālasūtra hell for as long as fourteen Indras [reign];
and for a period delimited by eighteen Indras in the Kālasūtra.
There, the Brāhmaṇī woman is certainly cooked, being devoured by worms.
Then, having obtained birth in the womb of a Caṇḍāla, the Brāhmaṇī becomes a Śūdra afflicted with leprosy, abandoned by her kinsmen. (36–37)
Having spoken thus, O Śaunaka, the best of sages fell silent;
meanwhile, the Vṛṣalī stood before him with her throat, lips, and palate parched.
In that interval, Menakā was traveling along that very path.
Upon seeing her thigh and breast, the sage’s semen fell.
Having drunk it there for a moment with joy after her ritual bath at the end of her season,
the low-caste woman bowed to the sage and, greatly delighted, went into the presence of her husband.
Having gone and bowed to Drumila, the beloved wife related the entire account concerning the cause of her pregnancy to her charming husband.
Upon hearing Kalāvatī’s words, his face and eyes became radiant with joy.
He spoke sweetly to his beloved, words that bring happiness in the end.
Drumila said:
"The seed of a high-souled Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa has indeed been placed within your womb."
The child shall become a Vaiṣṇava, and you too, O virtuous lady, shall be fortunate.
Since a Vaiṣṇava has been born from your womb, and by his power,
O virtuous one, a hundred and ten generations of men on both sides shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.
And those two, by means of a celestial chariot of Viṣṇu fashioned from excellent jewels,
went to the city of Vaikuṇṭha, which removes birth, death, and old age.
"O lady of auspicious countenance, go to the house of a certain brāhmaṇa."
"O blessed lady, you shall come to my presence later at the city of Hari.
Having spoken thus, the king of the cowherds bathed, performed the libations,
worshipped his chosen deity, and gave wealth to the Brahmins.
With joy, he gave to the Brahmins four hundred thousand horses, one hundred thousand elephants, and a hundred rutting lordly elephants;
[he also gave] five hundred thousand [horses] like Uccaiḥśravas and a thousand chariots.
With joy, he gave three hundred thousand carts to the Brahmins; with joy,
he gave twelve hundred thousand cows, three hundred thousand buffaloes,
and three hundred thousand royal swans to the Brahmins.
O Sage, he joyfully gave to the Brāhmaṇas a hundred thousand pigeons, a hundred parrots, and a hundred thousand male and female servants;
as well as a thousand villages and ten thousand cities.
With joy, he gave mountains of grain and rice to the Brahmins;
he joyfully gave a hundred crores of gold pieces, a thousand of jewels,
and ten million jars of coins to the Brahmins.
He gave away countless ornaments made of radiant gold.
With joy, he bestowed that woman, adorned with jewel-encrusted decorations, upon the brāhmaṇas.
Having given away his kingdom, the great king remained mindful of Hari both internally and externally.
The cowherd, moving as fast as thought, went to Badarī filled with joy.
Having performed a month of penance there on the enchanting bank of the Gaṅgā,
he gave up his life-breaths through yoga, suddenly beheld by the great sages.
And he, joined by Viṣṇu’s celestial chariot fashioned from the finest jewels and accompanied by the messengers of Viṣṇu, went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha.
There he attained the state of servitude to Hari; he became a servant of Hari.
"And hear the account of Kalāvatī," [said he], O Śaunaka.
When her husband had departed, Kalāvatī wept aloud;
desiring to cast off her life-breaths into the fire, she was saved by a Brāhmaṇa.
Having addressed her as "Mother," the Brāhmaṇa took her with him, filled with joy,
and in an instant went to his own home, which was filled with jewels.
That virtuous woman, in the house of the Brāhmaṇa, gave birth to an excellent son.
Resplendent with the luster of molten gold and blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
all the women stationed there beheld that auspicious boy,
who surpassed the midday sun of summer by his divine radiance.
In form he surpassed Kāmadeva; his beautiful face was more radiant than the moon.
His face was like the full autumn moon, his eyes like autumn lotuses;
his hands, feet, and other limbs were well-proportioned, his cheeks were lovely, and he was enchanting to the mind. (63)
Seeing the incomparable, radiant lotus-foot marked with the signs of the lotus and the wheel, or seeing the incomparable pair of hands, weeping and reaching for her breast,
the women joyfully returned to their own hermitage upon beholding the child. (64–65)
Accompanied by his son and wife, the Brahmin danced with great joy.
There, that boy grew like the moon in the bright fortnight;
and the Brahmin nurtured her, along with her son, as if she were his own daughter.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Birth of Upabarhaṇa," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
In the course of time, he gradually became a boy of five years.
Remembering his former births, endowed with knowledge, and always recollecting his previous mantras;
he constantly sings of the fame, names, qualities, and so forth of Kṛṣṇa.
For a moment he weeps, his body bristling with horripilation through the act of dancing. (1–2)
Wherever he hears a verse concerning Kṛṣṇa,
the boy remains right there, listening to the Purāṇa related to Him;
his entire body is grey with dust, and he desires offerings of dust as his oblation.
Having fashioned an image out of dust, one should worship Hari with dust. (4) O Sage, if a mother calls her son for his morning meal, he should reply to his mother, "I am worshipping Hari. (5)
Śaunaka said: What was the name given to this child at his birth? Whether derived from his character or as a conventional designation, you ought to tell me that.
Sauti said:
At a time when nothing remained but the aftermath of a drought, he became a child;
because he was given [by] Nara at the time of his birth, he is named Nārada. (7)
The child gave human knowledge to the children;
because he was a great sage with the memory of his past lives, he was named Nārada.
O Sage, by the very power of Nārada, he became a child.
By that very boon of the Lord of Sages, he is named Nārada.
Śaunaka said:
"The name 'Śiśu' has been understood both through its etymology and in its proper sense."
"How indeed did Nārada become the auspicious name of the Lord of Sages?
Sauti said:
"To the sonless Brahmin, the sage Nara, the son of Dharma..."
He gave [the child] to Kaśyapa as a son; therefore, he is named Nārada.
Śaunaka said:
O Sauti, I have now heard the etymology of the child’s name.
"How was he, the son of Brahmā named Nārada, born from a Śūdra womb?
Sauti said:
"In another kalpa, many men were born from the throat of Brahmā."
He gave him to the men, and because of that [giving] from his throat (*kaṇṭha*), he was remembered as Nārada.
Then a boy emerged from the region of the throat through Nārada;
therefore Brahmā gave him the auspicious name "Nārada. (13–14)
Now, listen attentively to the account of the child.
What further purpose is served by the secret of the reproach?
(15) The cowherd boy grew day by day in the house of the brahmin.
He protected her along with her son, just as a brahmin protects his own daughter. In the meantime, O brahmins, five-year-old children of great splendor arrived at the brahmin’s house. (16–17)

Having secretly taken [the sage], who was like the midday sun of summer, the householder brahmin offered them the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors, and bowed down to those four eminent sages at the proper time as they accepted fruits, roots, and other offerings. 18. 19.
They ate what was offered by the brahmin, and the child ate the remains.
The fourth sage joyfully gave him the mantra of Kṛṣṇa;
by the command of his mother, he became a servant to those twice-born ones.
Once, while traveling on a path at night, a mother of young children was bitten by a snake and died; yet, remembering Hari at that very moment,
that virtuous woman immediately went to Vaikuṇṭha by means of Viṣṇu’s vehicle.
Accompanied by the attendants of Viṣṇu and [mounted upon] that which was fashioned from excellent jewels,
the boy set out in the morning from the brahmin’s house along with the twice-born.
And those compassionate brāhmaṇas imparted the knowledge of reality to him.
The sons of Brahmā, having abandoned the child, indeed departed for their own abode.
The great sage of a child remained on the enchanting bank of the Gaṅgā;
having bathed there, he chanted the Viṣṇu-mantra bestowed by the brāhmaṇa.
It removes hunger, thirst, disease, and grief, and is difficult to find even in the Vedas.
(25) Having assumed a yogic posture at the foot of an aśvattha tree in a formidable great forest, the boy remained there for a very long time. (26)
Śaunaka said: What mantra did the boy receive from the wise Kumāra? You ought to tell me that supreme mantra of Śrī Hari which was given to him. (27)
Sauti said: In ancient times, Kṛṣṇa mercifully bestowed upon Brahmā in Goloka this twenty-two-syllable mantra, which is very difficult to obtain even within the Vedas. (28)
And Brahmā gave that [mantra] with devotion to the wise Kumāra;
and that mantra was given by Kumāra to the child, O twice-born one:
"Oṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Rāsa-maṇḍala."
The mantra "Śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā" is a wish-fulfilling tree;
so too are the previously mentioned *Mahāpuruṣa-stotra* and the *Kavaca*. Furthermore, the meditation appropriate for this [mantra] is exactly that which is declared in the Sāmaveda. (30–31)
And within that form of a circle of fire, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns—
which is desired in meditation by yogis, hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), and gods—
the Vaiṣṇavas indeed meditate upon His form in close proximity within it.
Exceedingly desirable, indescribable, and captivating;
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like autumn lotuses, a face like the full moon of autumn, and lips surpassing the ripe bimba fruit. (33–34)
Charming with a row of teeth that puts to shame a string of pearls, smiling, and with his hand resting upon the support of the flute;
possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids, he is a captivating abode of grace. (39)
Adorned with the splendor of a hundred thousand moons, his body endowed with full majesty;
(36) either assuming the triple-bend posture or joined with two arms, clad in yellow garments;
adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets. (37)
His cheeks were adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings;
he had a crest of peacock feathers and was decorated with a garland of jewels. He was further beautified by a forest garland of *mālatī* flowers that reached down to his knees.
His entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, and he bestowed grace upon his devotees.
His chest was brilliantly illuminated by the great Kaustubha jewel, and he was constantly gazed upon by the cowherd women with eyes full of bashfulness. (39–40)
He was constantly surrounded by women endowed with eternal youth and adorned with ornaments, seated upon the chest of Rādhā;
he who is worshipped, saluted, and praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other gods.

One should meditate upon that Lord of all, the Supreme Self and Sovereign— the youthful beloved of Rādhikā, whose form is peaceful, who is higher than the highest, untainted, the witness-form, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature. (42–43)
O Sage Śaunaka, this meditation, hymn, and armor has been told to you;
it is the true application of mantras, for the mantra is indeed a wish-fulfilling tree.
At that moment, O Śaunaka, the boy remained there absorbed in meditation.
For a thousand divine years, he remained without food and became lean of belly;
yet, by the power of his perfected mantras, he became strong and well-nourished.
While in meditation, the boy beheld a divine world and a divine child.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with jewel ornaments, youthful in age, dark-complexioned, dressed as a cowherd, and smiling;
surrounded by cowherds and cowherd women, he was clothed in yellow garments. (47)

Having beheld for a long time that Supreme Being, who has two arms, holds a flute in His hand, is anointed with sandalwood paste, and is being praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others— the peaceful son of the cowherd girl himself became peaceful. 48–49.
Afflicted by grief and unable to bear the sight of it, he desisted;
and not seeing the young child, the boy wept at the foot of the *aśvattha* tree. Then, a voice from the sky spoke to the weeping boy: [50]
It is true, endowed with awakening, beneficial, and measured in its syllables.
That very form which was shown once is not [seen] again now;
it is difficult to perceive even for those whose impurities are ripened, and for those who are bad yogis.
"When this present form has passed away and the divine form has been attained,
you shall again behold Govinda, Hari, the remover of birth and death.
Having heard this, the boy, filled with joy, fell silent.
In due time, at a sacred ford, he cast off his body while remembering Kṛṣṇa in his heart.
In heaven, the kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
And the great sage Nārada became liberated from the curse.
Having cast off his body, that living soul dissolved into the form of Brahman.
Though eternal, he had been concealed due to the difference in time from his former state.
Manifestation and concealment occur at will for those who possess eternal bodies.
"O Śaunaka, for those who are devoted [to Him], there is no birth, death, old age, or disease.
(57) Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation from Nārada’s Curse," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
When many kalpas had passed, during the Creator’s act of creation once again,
he was born from the throat together with the sages headed by Marīci.
He was also born from the region of the throat of the Ordainer named Nārada.
For that reason, he became renowned as the lord of sages, Nārada.
That bull among sages, who was the son of the creator Cetas,
was given the name Pracetas by his grandfather.
He who was the son of Dhātṛ was born suddenly from the right side [of his mother];
because he performed all rites (*dakṣa*) well, he is celebrated as Dakṣa.
In the Vedas, the word *kardama* clearly occurs in the sense of "shadow" (*chāyā*).
From Kardama was born Bāla; therefore he is celebrated as Kardama.
Marīci is clearly mentioned in the Vedas as a variety of splendor.
Born instantly with exceeding brilliance, he is celebrated as Marīci.
And by the boy, a multitude of sacrifices was performed in another birth;
even though he is the son of Brahmā, he is called by the name "Kratu. Furthermore, the boy was born from the primary limb of the Creator.
Although Aṅgiras is also a term denoting great splendor, he was proclaimed as such by him [Bhṛgu].
O Śaunaka, the name Bhṛgu applies to one who possesses exceeding splendor;
because he was born instantly with exceeding splendor, he was therefore proclaimed as Bhṛgu.
Though but a child, he was immediately born with a ruddy complexion and exceeding splendor;
blazing with his upward-directed asceticism, he was therefore celebrated as Aruṇi.
By means of yoga, the swans—those self-controlled beings—are certainly brought under his power by that yogin.
The child became a supreme lord of yogis; therefore he was proclaimed as Haṃsī.
Indeed, the child immediately became self-controlled and a disciple.
Because he was exceedingly dear to the Creator (Brahmā), he was celebrated as Vaśiṣṭha.

He whose effort is constant and who is devoted to austerities like a child is proclaimed a *yati*; by him all actions are restrained. He abides in austerities, in the Vedas, and in the day, even when it is manifest. (13)

And because he was clearly a mass of austerities (*tapas*), the boy was Pulaha. And because he possessed a mass of austerities belonging to his previous births, and because he was the very embodiment of a collection of penances, the boy was Pulastya. (14)
In Prakṛti, which consists of the three guṇas, Viṣṇu likewise manifests in three ways.
He whose devotion toward these two is equal is called the child Atri.
On his head, there are five matted locks in the form of tongues of fire.
He who was born from the splendor of his asceticism is remembered as Pañcaśikha.
In another birth, he performed austerities in a remote region;
because of that, the child became celebrated by the name Apāntaratamas.
He himself attains austerity, and he causes others to carry it out—that is, to reach its fulfillment. Because he is capable of carrying out austerity, he is celebrated as "the Carrier" (Vāha).
O Sage, by the splendor of his austerity, the boy is ever radiant.
His mind delighted in ascetic practices; for that reason he is celebrated as Ruci.
Those eleven who were born from the Creator at the time of his anger became the Rudras because they were made to weep (rudana) by him for that cause. (19–20)
Śaunaka said:
I have a doubt that one among the Rudras is the boy Maheśa;
you, who know the truth of the Purāṇas, ought to dispel this uncertainty.
Sauti said:
Viṣṇu, characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), is the protector; Brahmā, characterized by the quality of passion (rajas), is the creator;
and those Rudras, characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas), are difficult to restrain and terrifying. || 22 ||
Among them, Kālāgnirudra is the single destroyer who is a portion of Śaṅkara;
he is of the nature of pure *sattva*, and as Śiva, he bestows auspiciousness upon the virtuous. The others are portions of Kṛṣṇa, while Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara are his two parts.
"O twice-born one, how can you forget what was said at the time of Rudra’s manifestation—that these two are equal in their essential nature to the Most Perfect One?
All are deluded by Māyā; even the minds of sages are subject to error. (24–25)
Sanaka, Sananda, the third Sanātana,
and the venerable Sanatkumāra were the fourth son of Brahmā.
When Brahmā spoke to these first-born sons in order to create, they did not consent.
O sage, by him Dhātṛ was provoked to anger, as were the Rudras born of his wrath.
Sanaka and Sananda— those two who signify bliss—
were the two boys who were always most filled with devotion and were made joyful.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is eternal, perpetual, and Himself the most perfect;
His devotee is equal to Him, and for that reason, Bāla is truly Sanātana.
The word *sanat* signifies "eternal," while *kumāra* denotes a child. (29)
Therefore, the Lotus-born One spoke this to Sanatkumāra:
"O Sage, the instruction regarding Brahmā and his sons has been told;
now listen in due order to the narrative of Nārada."

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of the Sons of Brahmā," in the *Brahmakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
The Creator, having appointed all the boys according to the rules of creation, [proceeded].
O Śaunaka, Brahmā urged Nārada to carry out the work of creation.
Then Brahmā spoke to Nārada, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, words that were beneficial, truthful, the essence of the Vedas, and bringing happiness in the end. (1–2)
Brahmā said: "Come, my child, O best of your lineage, O Nārada, dear as life to me! You are the one who causes the destruction of the darkness of ignorance by the flame of the lamp of knowledge. (3)
He is the progenitor of even those venerable ancestors and the supreme teacher;
the giver of knowledge and the giver of mantra are two who are superior to the father and equal to him.
O son, I am your progenitor, the giver of knowledge, and your protector.
"By my command and out of love for me, take a wife.
He alone is a disciple and he alone is a son who obeys the command of his guru;
there is no well-being for that fool who disregards the word of his guru."

He is wise, he is a man of knowledge, he is secure, and he is meritorious—he who honors his guru; for him there is well-being at every step. (7) Among all the stages of life, the meritorious householder is the foremost.
A home filled with wife, sons, and grandsons is the fruit of ascetic practice (8).
In former times, the ancestors and at the time of the lunar day, the deities—
all come to the householder like cows to a watering place (9).
Householders always perform the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and desire-driven (*kāmya*) rites.
This brings merit and happiness in this world, as well as enjoyment in heaven in the hereafter.
Such a householder is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and a protector of his own duty (*svadharma*).
He is indeed illustrious, meritorious, famous, wealthy, and happy.
For he who possesses fame and renown truly lives forever even after death;
whereas one devoid of fame and renown is dead even while living.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Nārada, the best of sages,
spoke with humility, being terrified and with his throat, lips, and palate parched.
Nārada said:
Once, due to a conflict of words between both the father and the son,
a great and disgraceful loss befell them through the power of fate.
And by your curse, I obtained the status of a Gāndharva and a Śaudra.
"O Creator, by my curse you shall be born and perform actions; remain unworthy of honor in this world. My curse has been released at the proper time;
O Ordainer, perpetual enmity leads only to fault and never to virtue. (15–16)

He who causes firm devotion to be established in the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the father, the guru, the kinsman, the son, and the sovereign lord. Even if children should wander onto an evil path out of ignorance, [he is their protector]. (17)
That father, a treasury of compassion, turns them back [from that path].
(18) Since that father has caused his son to abandon devotion for Kṛṣṇa’s feet, would he ever set him to kill another person? (19)
For taking a wife leads only to suffering and not to happiness;
it is an obstacle to the practices of austerity, heaven, devotion, and liberation.
O Brahmin, there are three kinds of women for householders of deluded mind. (20)
The virtuous wife is to be enjoyed, yet all those unchaste women are intent on their own self-interest.
Out of fear of the next world, for the sake of her own reputation here, and out of passion and affection, the virtuous wife performs service to her husband constantly. (21–22)
Desiring enjoyment, she is constantly devoted to her lover solely out of passion and affection;
she serves her beloved not for a moment without sensual pleasure, [offering] excellent garments, ornaments, enjoyments, and very palatable food. (23)
As long as she gains [wealth], that beloved woman remains under one's control;
yet a woman who is a charcoal-fire to her family, unchaste and the destroyer of the lineage, performs service to her master out of deceit and not out of devotion. (24–25)
Constantly longing for union with a man and afflicted in mind by passion, she sought a new lover after each one, desiring her paramour more than food.
O dear one, that unchaste woman even desired to kill her own husband for the sake of her paramour.
The life of that fool who places his trust in her is fruitless.
(27) All women—superior, inferior, and middling—have been described;
those who delight in their own self alone know their minds, not the learned. (28)
The heart is like the edge of a razor, the face is a festival of autumn lotuses, and the speech is as sweet as nectar for the sake of achieving one's own ends;
yet in anger it is like poison, and when trusted, it brings about total destruction. (29)
Their intention is difficult to discern; their actions are solely secret. They are always lacking in discipline, possessing excessive and supreme recklessness.
There is an abundance of faults, an abundance of deceit, and constant illusion that is hard to overcome. (30–31)
O Teacher of the World, the desire of a man is always eightfold;
his appetite is eternally twofold, and his cruelty fourfold. His anger is sixfold, and his resolve is likewise certain [to be so]. (32)
Since these multitudes of defects exist here, O Grandfather, what reliance can there be on it?

What sport, what pleasure can there be for a man in this abode of excrement, urine, and filth? Vital energy is destroyed by sexual union, and one's reputation perishes through talk during the day. (33–34)
Excessive affection leads to the loss of wealth; excessive attachment leads to the decay of the body; in literary pursuits, manliness is lost; in quarreling, honor is destroyed;
and in placing trust, O Brahmin, there is total ruin—what happiness, then, can there be in women? (35)

Indeed, as long as a man is wealthy, radiant, prosperous, and devoted to his duties, he alone is capable of winning over a woman. A woman, however, looks with disfavour upon one who is diseased, penniless, or old. (36)
Out of fear of social convention, he gives him only a small amount of food.
(37) Thus, O Brahmin, everything has been told to you regarding the traditional teaching concerning the Self.
You know everything, O omniscient one; you are a lord who delights in the Self. (38)
"O Lord, show me favor; grant me leave now.
I pray for devotion to Kṛṣṇa from you, who are beyond even the wish-fulfilling tree.
Having spoken thus, Nārada there took hold of his father’s lotus feet.
He requested permission from his father to go forth for auspicious asceticism.
With palms joined in reverence and his neck bowed low in devotion,
he circumambulated Brahmā, prostrated before him, and prepared to depart.
O Sage, seeing his son departing,
the Creator of the worlds wept loudly with an unrestrained throat, like a great deer;
holding him by the hand, he embraced him and kissed him again and again.
Having held him for a long time against his chest, he placed him upon his lap.
Brahmā, the Lord who delights in his own Self, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis, was unable to endure the separation;
for the severance of ties is difficult for men to bear.
O Śaunaka, distressed by grief and deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu through the separation from his son, the cowardly king began to speak, addressing his son.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Brahmā said:
"Go, my child, for the sake of penance; what use have I for the activities of worldly existence?
I shall go to Goloka to seek out the Lord Kṛṣṇa. || 1 ||
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
Sanatkumāra, who is free from passion, was the fourth son.
Furthermore, Yatī, Haṃsī, Āruṇi, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha.
All my sons are ascetics; what use have I for the activities of worldly existence?
My sons are Vacaḥkara, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Ruci, Atri, Kardama, Pracetas, Kratu, and Manu.
Vasiṣṭha is eternally self-controlled regarding all things and his sons;
others are undiscerning and incurable—what use have I for the activities of worldly existence?
Listen, my child, I shall speak auspicious words as declared in the Vedas.
Supreme in its lineage of transmission, it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
(6) All wise men desire these—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—which are established in the Vedas and praised by the sages in assemblies. (7)
For dharma is that which is ordained by the Vedas, while adharma is its opposite.
At the outset, a Brahmin, having donned the sacred thread, becomes happy and prosperous;
then, having thoroughly studied the Vedas, he bestows the teacher’s fee.

Then, he should marry a woman born of a distinguished family who is well-disciplined. (9) She is a virtuous woman of noble birth who is devoted to the service of her husband; a man of good character should never take a woman who is ill-behaved.
In a mine of rubies, how could a glass gem be born?
(10) O Nārada, she who is born of an ignoble lineage due to the fault of her parents is ill-behaved, wicked, and independent in all her actions. (11)
"O child, not all women are wicked; some are portions of Lakṣmī.
Some are portions of celestial courtesans, while unchaste women are born of ignoble lineages.
Furthermore, a virtuous wife serves and praises even a master who is devoid of merit."
An unchaste woman does not serve her beloved and she reviles his virtuous qualities. (13) A virtuous man should carefully take a maiden born of a noble lineage as his wife;
having procreated sons upon her, he should, when old, depart for ascetic practice. (14)
It would be better to dwell in fire, or in the mouth of a serpent, or upon a thorn,
than to dwell with these [misfortunes] or with a woman of ill countenance who causes such suffering.
(15) You have studied the Veda from me, and you must now pay me the teacher’s fee.
"O son, give [this gift] here; take a wife.
My child, O sinless one, perform the marriage with Mālatī, who is born of a noble family and was your former wife, on an auspicious day, O blessed one. (16–17)
Having obtained birth here in the house of Śṛñjaya, born of the lineage of Manu,
she performs penance in Bhārata for your sake;
take also this supreme jewel-garland, a portion of Kamalā herself.
In Bhārata, the fruit of people’s asceticism shall not be in vain.
First, one should be a householder; after that, a forest-dweller;
then an ascetic for the sake of liberation—this is the sequence heard in the Śruti. (19–20)
For Vaiṣṇavas, the worship of Hari and austerity are both heard of in the Vedas.
(21) O son, remain at home as a Vaiṣṇava and perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa’s feet;
for him who has Hari within and without, what is the need for austerity? (22)
O sinless one, for him who perceives Hari neither within nor without, what is the use of austerity?
Hari is to be propitiated through austerity; no other means exists.
Service rendered to Kṛṣṇa wherever it may be performed is the supreme austerity.
"My dear child, remaining at home, worship Hari according to my very words.
Become a householder, O best of sages; for householders there is happiness at all times.
The enjoyment of pleasure with a beloved woman is considered equal to the enjoyments of heaven. (24–29)
Those seeking liberation desire even the sight or the touch of him.
The pleasure of touching women is superior to the pleasure of all other touches;
O Sage, the sight and touch of one's son is more pleasant than that.
Because she is dearer than all else, the beloved wife is proclaimed as "kāntā" (the lovely one). A wife has her purpose in her son; the son is dearer than a hundred wives.
There is no kinsman superior to a son; there is no one dearer than a son. (27–28)
One should seek victory over all others, but defeat from one’s own son. For even wealth is not as dear to oneself as a son;
therefore, one should entrust one’s most precious treasure to a beloved son.
Having spoken thus, O Śaunaka, that Brahmā became silent.
Then Nārada, the best among the wise, spoke these words to his father.
Nārada said:

Having personally realized the meaning of all things, how could that compassionate father set his own son upon an evil path regarding the vision of the Vedas? All of saṃsāra is as impermanent as a bubble on the water.
O Brahmin, just as a line drawn on water is false, so too is the triple world.
Let that human birth, so difficult to obtain, never be fruitless—provided that one does not abandon service to Hari and allows the mind to wander among sense objects. (32–33)

Who is dear to whom, or who is whose son or kinsman, in this ocean of existence? Union is brought about by the waves of karma, and separation is their cessation. He indeed who causes one to perform wholesome deeds is a friend, a father, and a teacher.
"Indeed, how could he who would produce evil thoughts be considered a father?
Thus, O dear one, has the seed of the Vedas been declared according to tradition. Nevertheless, you must certainly carry out my command. (35-36)
"O Blessed One, first I shall go to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
having heard the discourse on Nārāyaṇa, I will take a wife.
Having spoken thus, the sage fell silent before his father.
At that very moment, a rain of flowers fell upon him.
Having stood before his father for a moment, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke again these words which bestow auspiciousness. (38–39)
Śrī Nārada said: Grant me the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which is the desire of my heart, as well as the knowledge concerning Him and the description of His qualities. (40)
"After that, out of affection for you, I shall take a wife;
for when one's heart's desire is fulfilled, a man is happy to perform his duties.
Having heard these words of Nārada, the Lotus-born One was delighted.
The best among those who know wisdom spoke this once again to his son.
Brahmā said:
"A discerning man should not accept the mantra of his husband nor the mantra of his father."
Furthermore, for those dwelling in secluded hermitages, the mantra does not bestow happiness.
(43) A mantra is obtained through the *niṣeka* rite; likewise, a guru and a wife are obtained.
Knowledge, happiness, fear, and suffering are not acquired by men according to their own will. (44)
"Maheśvara was our ancient and primordial preceptor.
Go, my child, to Śiva—the peaceful one, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the teacher of the wise.
From that very ancient one, you shall obtain the mantra and knowledge. (45)

"Having heard the story of Nārāyaṇa, come quickly to my home," said the Creator of the worlds, O Śaunaka, and then he became silent. Having bowed with devotion to his father, the sage departed for the world of Śiva.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pleasures and Miseries of Saṃsāra as Spoken by Brahmā and Nārada," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
In an instant, that foremost of brāhmaṇas, filled with joy, went to the enchanting abode of Śambhu.
One hundred thousand yojanas above Dhruva lies that great, magnificent realm, fashioned from a multitude of precious jewels.
(1) Supported by Śambhu through the power of yoga in the supportless void, it is wondrous and filled with various abodes;
auspicious and complete, it is beheld by the best of sages, those excellent practitioners whose intentions are most meritorious. (2)
O Sage, the city of the Sun and Moon is devoid of rays and is entirely surrounded by fires;
it is encircled by walls that are exceedingly high, immeasurable in number, and blazing with flames.
That excellent city, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas, is always filled with three crores of palaces made of the finest jewels.
It was adorned with various, diverse, and manifold enchanting designs fashioned from the finest diamonds;

it was endowed with mirrors made of rubies, pearls, and gems—O twice-born Śaunaka, such a place had never been seen even in dreams by Viśvakarman, and it was constantly frequented by people who serve Śiva alone until the end of the kalpa. || 4–9 ||
It was attended by Siddhas numbering one hundred and thirty-one million, joined by their own retinues;
it was accompanied by three hundred thousand formidable Bhairavas and surrounded by four hundred thousand sacred fields (kṣetras).
It was constantly encircled by celestial trees, preeminent among them being the Mandāra trees, all in full bloom.
It was resplendent with beautiful wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadhenus*), just as the sky is graced by flocks of cranes.
Seeing this, the sage felt wonder in his mind: "What is not marvelous here, in the presence of the teacher of the gods and yogis?
This supreme world is distinct from the three worlds; it is excellent, removing the pain of terrible death, disease, and old age. (7–8)
From afar, he beheld Śiva seated in the center of the assembly hall—peaceful, bestowing auspiciousness, and captivating;
three-eyed with lotus-like eyes, five-faced with the moon as his crest, bearing the Gaṅgā, and crowned by the stainless moon;
the omnipresent Lord wearing matted locks with the luster of molten gold, naked, radiant, infinite, and imperishable. (9)

Joyfully chanting the name "Kṛṣṇa" with a rosary of lotus seeds from the Mandākinī river—[I bow] to him who has a beautiful blue throat, who is adorned by the lord of serpents, who is worshipped by the lords of yogis, the lords of perfected beings, and the lords of sages;
the Lord of Siddhas, the cause of the accomplishment of all perfections, the conqueror of death, and the one who brings about the end of Time and Yama. (10–11)
Approaching the presence of the wielder of the trident— the one whose face is enchanting with a serene smile, the bestower of boons upon those who are the refuge of the universe,
the granter of boons, ever-quickly pleased, free from the disease of worldly existence, beloved by devotees, and the sole kinsman of those devoted to him—
this sage, his body marked by horripilation, bowed his head in salutation.
Striking his three-stringed lute, he, possessing a beautiful voice, sang again and praised Kṛṣṇa with sweet melody.

Then the Lord, seeing the preeminent chief of sages, the son of Brahmā, the most excellent among the knowers of the Vedas, smiling, rose from his seat with joy along with the lords of yogis, the perfected masters, and the great seers. (13–14)
And with great haste, he offered that sage an embrace, blessings, a seat, and so forth;
O Śaunaka, he then questioned that ascetic, whose wealth is penance, regarding the purpose of his auspicious arrival.
Furthermore, Śambhu sat upon a beautiful throne of excellent jewels together with his foremost attendants.

O twice-born one, Nārada, the son of the Novāsa lineage, having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord with devotion. Having offered praise with the beautiful and auspicious hymn composed by the king of the Gandharvas,
and having prostrated once more, he dwelt to the left of Bhava at Bhava’s command.
Right there, he made his petition to Śiva, the fulfiller of one's own desires, regarding the longing of his heart.
Hearing those words of the sage, the treasure-house of mercy quickly promised and said, "So be it.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Nārada’s Arrival at Kailāsa," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said: The celestial sage requested from Hara the hymn of praise to Hari, the armor-mantra, the supreme ritual for worship, as well as meditation and knowledge. (1)

Maheśvara gave him the hymn of praise, the armor, the mantra, the meditation, as well as the ritual procedure for worship and his previous knowledge. Having obtained everything, the best of sages had his desires completely fulfilled.
Bowing with devotion, he spoke to his guru, who was affectionate toward those who prostrate before him.
Nārada said:
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the daily ritual (*āhnika*) of the brāhmaṇas."
For it is from this that the constant protection of one's own duty arises perpetually.
Śrī Maheśvara said:
Having arisen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, [one should meditate] upon the lotus situated at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
In that subtle, thousand-petalled [lotus], which is pure, stainless, and free from weariness—having abandoned the night’s dwelling—one should contemplate the Guru right there:
joyful, with hands in the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā), smiling, and affectionate toward his disciples. (5–6)

One should always contemplate the supreme one, whose face is serene, who is tranquil and perpetually content, and who is the very embodiment of Brahman itself. Having thus meditated upon and worshipped the Guru within the pure, white lotus of the heart—
One should contemplate the deity desired by the gods upon a broad, thousand-petalled lotus (8).
One should contemplate whatever meditation and whatever form belong to whichever deity;
having received their permission, one should perform what is appropriate for the occasion (9).
First, having meditated upon and bowed to the Guru, and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
one should thereafter receive his permission, meditate upon the chosen deity, and perform worship.
The deity, the procedure for mantra-worship, and the recitation are all revealed by the Guru.
The Guru has not been seen by the gods; therefore, the Guru is superior to the gods.
(11) The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the god Maheśvara.
The Guru is Prakṛti, Īśa, and the others; the Guru is the moon, fire, and the sun. (12)
The teacher is Vāyu and Varuṇa; the teacher is mother, father, and friend.
The teacher alone is the Supreme Brahman; there is nothing more worthy of worship than the teacher.
Even when one’s chosen deity is angry, the teacher is capable of providing protection.
When the guru is angry, all the gods are powerless to protect [one].
(14) For him whose guru is perpetually pleased, there is victory at every step;
for him whose guru is angry, there is total ruin at all times. (15)

That fool who, through delusion, worships [another] without first worshipping the Guru as God, that sinner incurs the sin of a hundred murders of Brahmins; of this there is no doubt. Thus did the Blessed Lord Hari himself declare in the Sāmaveda.
Therefore, the Guru is even more worthy of worship than one’s chosen deity.
O Sage, having meditated upon and praised his own chosen Guru, the practitioner, having reached a pure place, should joyfully discharge his excrement and urine. (17–18)
Water, a place near water, a location with holes, a place frequented by living beings,
the vicinity of a temple, the root of a tree, a path,
(19) a place where a plough has turned the soil, a field of crops, and a cow-pen.
The interior of a river or a cave, a flower garden, and a marshy place;
the interior of a village and the like, as well as the vicinity of men's houses; a stake, a bridge, a thicket of reeds, a cremation ground, and the proximity of fire. (20–21)
A playground, a great forest, the area beneath a bedstead,
a place provided with the shade of trees that is devoid of living creatures within,
a spot of durvā grass, a spot of kuśa grass, and likewise an anthill. (22)

Having abandoned all these places— including land for planting trees, areas prepared for specific purposes, and those devoid of the sun’s heat— one should avoid voiding excrement or urine after having dug a hole. (23–24)
One should void feces and urine facing north during the day;
at night, facing west; and during the two twilights, facing south.
Remaining silent, one should exhale breath so that no odor spreads.
Having discarded [the earth] and covered it with soil, the wise man should perform purification.
Having performed purification with clods of earth, he should thereafter perform purification with water.
Listen now to the proper measure of that water combined with earth. (26–27)

One should apply a single application of clay to the penis, four to the left hand, and two to both hands; this is declared to be the purification after urination. If it occurs after sexual intercourse, the purification for urination is doubled.
After sexual intercourse, or after urination, purification is fourfold:
one application [of earth] on the penis, three on the anus, ten on the left hand, and seven on both hands; thus the foot [of the body] is purified by the sixth [application].
This very same rule for purification after voiding feces applies to Brahmin householders;
for widows, however, purification is proclaimed to be twofold.
For ascetics, Vaiṣṇavas, celestial sages, and celibate students, [the rule is as follows].
The purification for householders is proclaimed to be fourfold.
As long as a twice-born man, a Śūdra, or a woman has not been initiated [with the sacred thread], their purification is proclaimed to consist in the removal of odor and stains. (32–33)
Purity for the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, as well as for twice-born householders, is the same;
however, it is proclaimed to be double for Vaiṣṇavas and other sages.
One who desires purity must not perform purification that is either deficient or excessive.
An expiation should be performed when a prescribed rule has been transgressed.
(35) Listen attentively from me regarding purity, those observances, and the penance:
even a Brahmin who is pure in ritual cleansing becomes impure through a transgression. (36)
One should not offer earth dug up by anthills or rats, nor earth from within water, nor that which remains after cleansing, nor that taken from a house, nor that which involves hardship;
especially not earth dug up by a plow or containing living creatures within it.
Likewise, [earth] arising from the roots of *kuśa* grass, as well as that arising from the roots of *dūrvā* grass;
that brought from the root of an *aśvattha* tree, and likewise that from a bed;
and also from a crossroads, from cow-pens, and likewise from the hoofprints of cattle. (38–39)
One should avoid the soil of grain fields, cultivated plots, and gardens.
Whether he has bathed or not, a Brahmin becomes pure through ritual cleanliness (*śauca*).
One who is devoid of purity is perpetually impure and unfit for all religious rites.
Having performed this purification, the wise Brahmin should wash his face comfortably.
First, having effected the cleansing of the mouth with sixteen mouthfuls of water, he should thereafter scrub his teeth with a tooth-stick. (41–42)
Furthermore, one should perform the purification of the mouth with sixteen mouthfuls of water.
Listen, O Nārada, to the rules regarding the tooth-cleansing twigs,
as they were prescribed by Hari in the Sāmaveda within the sequence of daily rites (āhnika).
Apāmārga, sindhuvāra, mango, and karavīraka;
khadira and śirīṣa, jasmine, punnāga, and śāla; aśoka and arjuna, as well as milky trees and kadambaka. (44–45)
One should avoid the Jambūka, Bakula, Tokma, and the excellent Palāśa;
likewise, the Badarī, Pāribhadra, Mandāra, and Śālmali.
One should also completely avoid trees that are thorny as well as creepers and the like.
One should completely avoid the *pippala*, the *priyāla*, the *tintiḍīka*, and the *tālaka* (47).
One should also avoid the *kharjūra*, the *nārikela*, and the *tāla*. Furthermore, one who neglects the cleansing of the teeth is devoid of all forms of purity (48).

One devoid of purity is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts. Having performed purification, being pure, and having put on two washed garments, a Brahmin should wash his feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then carry out the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥ-saṃdhyā).
Thus, the twice-born born of a noble family performs the twilight ritual at the three junctions of the day.
He who practices this at the three junctions has effectively bathed in all sacred fords;
yet one who is devoid of the three twilight rituals is unworthy to perform any rites.

Whatever rite one performs during the day, he shall not partake of its fruit—[he] who does not attend to the morning [prayer] and who does not perform worship at the evening [prayer]. He is to be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (52)
By neglecting the morning twilight devotion, as well as the midday and evening ones,
a twice-born man incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and the sin of killing himself every day.
That twice-born man who is devoid of the eleventh lunar day and he who is devoid of the twilight devotions [incurs the same].
Indeed, the husband of a *vṛṣalī* shall go to the Kālasūtra hell for an eon.
Having thus performed the morning twilight devotion (*prātaḥ-sandhyā*) to his chosen preceptor, the god Ravi,
Brahmā, Īśa, Viṣṇu, Māyā, Padmā, and Sarasvatī—

Having prostrated before the guru, and having touched clarified butter, a mirror, honey, and gold, the best of practitioners should perform his bath and other rites at the proper time. When he performs his bath in a lotus pond or a step-well, [he should do so according to the following]. (56–57)
Having first removed five lumps [of earth],
the wise practitioner should perform his bath in a river, a stream, a cave, or at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
O Sage, having bathed, he should then make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and thereafter bathe once more.

The resolve of householders desiring to please Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas is indeed the destroyer of committed sins. Having made this resolve, the brāhmaṇa should smear clay upon his body.
With this mantra declared in the Veda, a person should perform the purification of the body:
"O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!
O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. (61)
"You were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.
Having ascended my limbs, release me from all sin.
O highly fortunate one, grant me merit; give me permission to bathe."
Having spoken thus, O ascetic, one should place one's hand in water reaching to the navel and, preceded by the recitation of mantras,
fashion an auspicious circular mandala measuring four cubits;
there, having placed the hand, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas).
And I shall name to you all those various holy fords (tīrthas):
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! 65–66.
The Nalinī, Nandinī, Sītā, and the great river Mālinī; the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths and originates from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu;
the Padmāvatī, Bhogavatī, Svarṇarekhā, and Kauśikī.
Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Subhagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivā, Amṛtā;
Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, and likewise Lokaprasādhinī;
Kṣemā, Vaiṣṇavī, Śāntā, Śāntidā, Gomatī, and Satī. (68–69)
Sāvitrī, Tulasī, Durgā, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī; Rādhā, who is dearer than the life-breath of Kṛṣṇa, Lopāmudrā, Aditi, Rati; Ahalyā, Aditi, Saṃjñā, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Arundhatī. (70)

The wise one, having become greatly purified by bathing again and again, should apply the *tilaka* mark on the roots of the arms, the forehead, the region of the throat, and the chest, while recollecting Śatarūpā, Devahūtī, and the others. (71–72)
Bathing, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, and rites for the deities and ancestors—
all these go to naught if there is no sectarian mark (tilaka) upon the forehead.
A Brahmin, having applied the tilaka, should perform the twilight prayers (sandhyā) and the libations (tarpaṇa).
Having paid homage to the gods with devotion, one should go home filled with joy.
Having carefully washed one's feet and put on two clean garments, the wise man should enter the house; thus indeed has Hari spoken. (74–75)
If one who has bathed enters the house without washing his feet,
his bathing and the other four acts— recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth— are rendered fruitless.
Having put on a smooth, clean garment, the householder should enter the home.
When Lakṣmī becomes angry, she departs from the house after uttering a most terrible curse.
And that Brahmin who washes his feet above the knees becomes a Cāṇḍāla for as long as he does not behold the Gaṅgā.
O Brahmin, having sat upon his seat, purified himself, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the practitioner,
being self-restrained and filled with devotion, should perform the worship according to the Vedic injunctions—
whether it be at a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a mantra, an image, in water, or on land. (79)

O Nārada, the worship of Hari is highly praised when performed upon the back of a cow, before a guru, or before a brahmin; indeed, worship is commended before all these, as well as before a Śālagrāma stone,
which is the very abode of all the gods.

He who performs his ablution with the water of the Śālagrāma alone has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices. That man who daily drinks the water of the Śālagrāma with devotion [attains the same].

He becomes liberated while living and, at the end, goes to the abode of Kṛṣṇa. O Nārada, wherever the discus of the Śālagrāma stone resides, there the Blessed Lord dwells with His discus; it is certain that all sacred fords are present there.
In that regard, whichever embodied soul dies there by the power of fate— whether through knowledge or ignorance—
he goes to the abode of Śrī Hari by means of a vehicle fashioned from jewels.
(85) Without the Śālagrāma, who else could properly worship Hari elsewhere?
Having performed the worship of Hari there, one obtains the full fruit.
(86) The substratum for worship has been described; now hear the sequence of worship.
I shall describe the highly esteemed worship of Hari according to the scriptures. (87)
A certain Vaiṣṇava constantly offers beautiful and pure articles of worship, including the sixteen services, to Hari with devotion;
another offers twelve items, and yet another offers five.
For those whose devotion and capacity for worship are indeed rooted in their own power,
[there are] a seat, clothing, water for the feet, an offering of honor, water for sipping,
flowers, sandalwood paste, incense, a lamp, and excellent food offerings. (89–90)
Fragrance, garlands, and a beautiful, well-characterized bed;
water, food, and betel, along with common articles—these indeed should be given.
Excluding fragrance, food, the bed, and betel, there are twelve such items.
These five— water for the feet, water for the guest-offering (arghya), food offerings (naivedya), and flowers—
the best of practitioners should offer all of these with the root mantra.
And the root mantra taught by the guru is recommended for all ritual acts.
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and thereafter the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma),
one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the limbs and sub-limbs, followed by the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
Having completed the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa), one should then designate the vessel for the offering water (arghyapātra).
Having fashioned a triangular maṇḍala, one should worship Kūrma there.
Then, having filled a conch with water, the twice-born should place it therein.
Having worshipped the water according to the rules, he should then invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas).
One should wash the articles of worship again with that water.
Then, having taken a flower and assumed a pure yogic posture,
one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa with undistracted mind through the meditation imparted by the Guru.
Having meditated, the practitioner should offer all the items beginning with water for the feet (pādya) using the root mantra.
He should worship Hari, including the deities of the limbs and sub-limbs as prescribed in the Tantra.
Having recited the root mantra according to his capacity, he should dismiss the deity and the mantra.
Having presented various offerings and offered praise, one should recite the armor-mantra (*kavaca*). Then, having performed the circumambulation, one should prostrate on the ground with the head.
Having indeed performed the worship of the deity, the wise person should perform the sacrifice.

O Sage, having offered the *bali* oblation accompanied by the fires of the *Śrauta* and *Smārta* rites, and having performed the daily *śrāddha* and given gifts according to his ability and wealth, he, being perfected, may enjoy himself; this is the sequence heard in the *Śruti*. 101–102.
Thus I have related to you everything concerning this supreme Sūtra declared in the Vedas regarding the daily rites (*āhnika*) of the Brahmins. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Daily Rites," in the *Brahmakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada.
Nārada said:
O Lord, what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born householders, as well as for renunciants, Vaiṣṇavas, widows, and celibate students? 1.
"What is to be done and what is not to be done? What is unfit for enjoyment and what indeed is fit for enjoyment? Tell me all this, O Omniscient One, Lord of All, Cause of All.
Maheśvara said:
One was an ascetic, a brahmin, and a sage who had long been without food;
another subsisted on air, while yet another fed on fruits;
and one was a householder living with his wife, eating food at the proper time.
O Brahmin, whatever the desire and whatever the various inclinations of people may be—(4)—food fit for oblation is always recommended for Brāhmaṇa householders;
however, that which has been tasted by Nārāyaṇa is desired, while that which has not been offered is unfit to be eaten. (5)
Food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu is excrement, and water is urine;
on the day of Hari, food is said to be entirely feces and urine.
The Brāhmaṇa who intentionally eats food on the day of Hari [incurs this fate].
He too shall undoubtedly experience the sin produced by the three worlds.
O Nārada, food must not be eaten, must not be eaten,
must not be eaten by householders and Brāhmaṇas when the day of Hari has arrived.
A householder who is a devotee of Śiva or Śakti, yet is a Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge,
goes to the Kālasūtra hell after eating on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī).
There he remains, being devoured by worms as numerous as grains of rice.
Having consumed feces and urine, [one remains so] for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
furthermore, he who eats on the day of Janmāṣṭamī, on the day of Rāmanavamī of Hari, or on Śivarātri, is a sinner of double the measure. (10–11)
One who is unable to observe a fast should consume fruits, roots, or water;
otherwise, if his body perishes, he becomes a self-killer.
He should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) only once, as well as the *naivedya* offered to Viṣṇu.
He shall incur no transgression and obtain the fruit of fasting.
A householder and a Brahmin who remain without food on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) in Bhārata reside in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
O Nārada, this has been stated for householders who follow Śiva and Śakti;
it is especially so for Vaiṣṇavas, ascetics, and celibate students.
He who always eats the *naivedya* (food offering) of Śrī Viṣṇu is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
For one who constantly performs a hundred fasts, there shall be the fruit of liberation while living (jīvanmukta). All sacred fords (tīrthas) and all deities desire contact with such a person;
even their conversation and sight destroy all sins.
In certain regions, flattened rice (*pṛthuka*) that has been steamed twice and purified is not highly recommended for consumption by Brahmins, nor for offering in ritual oblations (verse 18). Indeed,
it is forbidden as food for ascetics (*yati*), widows, and those observing celibacy (*brahmacārin*).
And just as with betel, O Brahmin, this matter is not certain:
for widows, ascetics, celibate students, and those practicing austerities, O best of Brahmins, betel is certainly equivalent to beef. (19–20)
Listen, O Nārada, to that which is unfit to be eaten by all Brāhmaṇas,
as it was declared by Hari in the Sāmaveda within the sequence of daily observances (Āhnika):
drinking milk from a copper vessel and eating ghee while in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa).
Milk mixed with salt is equivalent to the immediate consumption of cow-flesh.
Coconut water kept in a vessel of bell-metal or a copper vessel is light [to digest]. Sugarcane juice kept in a copper vessel is equal to *surā* liquor; of this there is no doubt. (22–23)

That twice-born man who, having risen, drinks water with his left hand should be known as a drinker of liquor, excluded from all religious duties. He who constantly eats food that has not been offered to Hari, as well as the remnants of what he himself has eaten, [is likewise fallen].
O Sage, water remaining after being drunk is like beef;
in Kārttika, the fruit of the vaṅgaṇa plant is remembered as beef. In Māgha, the radish is so regarded, and likewise the kalambī in Śayana (Phālguna). (25–26)
White-colored *tāla* (palmyra), *masūra* (lentils), and fish—
these must be avoided everywhere by all Brāhmaṇas in every land.
Having eaten fish out of desire, one should dwell for three days observing a fast.
Then, having performed the expiation, the Brāhmaṇa attains purity.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), the kūṣmāṇḍa fruit is indeed unfit for consumption as it causes the loss of wealth;
on the second lunar day, one should remember Hari while eating bṛhatī.

Paṭola is unfit for consumption and is the supreme cause of increasing one's enemies. On the third and fourth lunar days, radish causes the destruction of wealth. And on the fifth day, eating wood-apple (bilva) is a cause of blemish.
Eating a neem tree on the sixth lunar day causes one to fall into the animal realm;
likewise, eating a palmyra fruit on the seventh lunar day increases the diseases of men and leads to the destruction of the body.
Eating coconut on the eighth day causes the destruction of the intellect;
on the ninth day, the gourd (tumbī); on the tenth, beef; and on the eleventh, the kalambikā plant. Likewise, on the twelfth day, one should avoid the legume (śimbī) as well as the pūtikā.
On the thirteenth day, eggplant (vārttākī) must not be eaten, for it causes the destruction of one’s sons.
On the fourteenth day, eating black gram (māṣa) is a supreme cause of great sin.
Likewise, O Sage, meat must not be eaten by householders on the fifteenth day.
For householders, consecrated meat may be eaten on other days;
likewise, O Nārada, mustard oil and refined oil are recommended for morning ablutions, at a *śrāddha* ceremony, during the *pārvaṇa* rite, and on the day of a religious vow.

On the new moon, the full moon, the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, on Sundays, during śrāddha ceremonies, and on the day of a religious vow, oil from sesame seeds used by women is inauspicious;
as are meat, red leafy vegetables, and eating from a bell-metal vessel. (37–38)
Sleeping and the consumption of consecrated tortoise meat are forbidden;
for all castes, sexual intercourse with one's own wife during the day is forbidden. At night, curd may be eaten, and sleeping during the two twilights of the day is prohibited. (39)
Sexual intercourse with a woman during her menses is a cause for rebirth in hell.

(40) The food of a menstruating woman, the food of a hero, the food of an unchaste woman, the food of a Śūdra, the food of a priest, and likewise the food from a Śūdra’s funeral feast—these must not be eaten. (41)

O Brahminical Sage, the food of one who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* is unfit to be eaten; O Brahmin, the food of usurers, the food of astrologers, and the food of those who do not offer the first portion (*agrādānin*) to the twice-born, as well as the food of a physician, are not to be consumed. (42)
Oil should not be taken and food should not be eaten on the days of Hasta, Citrā, and Svāti (43).
On the Mūla and Mṛga constellations in the month of Bhādrapada, meat is equal to beef.
Shaving should be avoided by the twice-born on the new moon day and under the Kṛttikā constellation (44).
If one performs the rite of shaving after engaging in sexual intercourse and then offers libations to the gods and ancestors,
that water becomes blood and the giver shall go to hell.
[45] One should know what is to be done and what is not to be done, what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten.
Everything has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Edible and Non-Edible Foods," in the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka within the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, concerning the instruction of Śiva to Nārada.
Nārada said:
"O Lord of the World, O Teacher of the World, by your grace I have heard everything.
Now, please describe the nature of Brahman and the definition of Brahman.
O Lord, O Sovereign, is Brahman with form or is it without form?"
Is it qualified, or is it indeed unqualified?
Is it visible or invisible, and is it smeared upon embodied beings or not?
Furthermore, what is its definition as set forth in the scriptures or in the Veda? (2–3)
Is Prakṛti distinct from Brahman, or is she of the very nature of Brahman?
What is the essential definition of Prakṛti as heard in the Śruti?
And between these two, which is supreme in the process of creation? 4.
"O Omniscient One, having reflected upon everything with your mind, tell me for certain.
Having heard Nārada's words, the five-faced Lord laughed and began to provide a description of the Supreme Brahman.
Mahādeva said: "O child, O Nārada, whatever supreme and secret knowledge you have asked about is indeed very difficult to obtain, even within the Vedas and the Purāṇas."
"I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śeṣa, Dharma, and the Great Virāṭ;
O Sage, everything has been described by us through the Vedas, as well as that which is characterized by distinctions, the visible, and the perceptible. (8)

O best among the knowers of the Vedas, that has been described by us in the Veda. Furthermore, listen to what Hari said when he was questioned by Dharma and Brahmā in Vaikuṇṭha in the past; I shall relate it to you.
It is the essence of all principles, an eye for those blinded by ignorance;
it is the most excellent lamp that destroys the darkness of the delusion of duality.
It is the nature of the Supreme Self, the eternal Supreme Brahman. (11)
