Abiding within the entire body as the witness-nature of the bodily actions—[I am] the five vital breaths, Viṣṇu himself; the mind, Brahmā Prajāpati;
I am the nature of all knowledge, and Śakti, the sovereign Prakṛti.

We are all dependent upon the Self; while it remains, we remain, and when it has departed, we depart, like attendants following a supreme king. The individual soul (*jīva*) is its reflection, for it indeed experiences the fruits of all actions.
Just as the orb of the sun and the moon [is reflected] in jars filled with water,
when those jars are broken, the reflection of the sun and moon dissolves;
so too, at the time of dissolution, that individual soul (jīva) merges into Brahman.
O child, at the end of existence, you rest in that one supreme Brahman alone;
we, as well as this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, have dissolved into that very same place.
And that [Brahman] is of the nature of light and is indeed circular in form.
Possessing a splendor equal to ten million times ten million suns at midday in the summer heat, it is as vast as the sky, all-pervading, and imperishable;
it is easily perceived by yogis, like the orb of the moon. (18–19)
There, the yogis proclaim the supreme, eternal Brahman;
day and night they meditate upon that Truth, which is the source of all auspiciousness—the desireless, formless Lord, the Supreme Self. (20)
Consisting of His own will, independent, and the cause of all causes;
having the nature of supreme bliss and being the cause of supreme bliss;
the Supreme, the Primal, the Person, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Right there, Prakṛti is dissolved, possessing the nature of all seeds.
O Sage, just as the power of burning resides in fire, as radiance in the sun, as whiteness in milk, and as coldness in water; so it is. (22–23)
Just as sound is always in the sky and fragrance is always in the earth,
so indeed is Brahman devoid of qualities, and so too is Prakṛti devoid of qualities.
When that Brahman is intent on creation, it is traditionally called Puruṣa by way of its partial manifestation.
That very [Self], when possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*), my child, is known as the primordial subject (*prākṛta-viṣayin*).
For she, consisting of the three *guṇas*, is indeed recorded there as the supreme shadow-form (*parā-chāyāmayī*).
Just as a potter is always capable of making a jar out of clay, so too [is he].
Likewise, O Sage, by its very nature that Brahman is capable of creating the universe,
just as a goldsmith is capable of fashioning an earring from gold;
so too is the Lord capable of performing creation here together with her (Prakṛti).
The clay created by the potter is not eternal, yet the clay itself is indeed eternal and ancient.
That gold created by the goldsmith is likewise not eternal, yet the gold itself is indeed eternal.
That Supreme Brahman is eternal, and Prakṛti is traditionally held to be eternal as well.

Indeed, some say that both [the material cause and the efficient cause] possess equal primacy. For instance, a potter and a goldsmith are not able to produce clay or gold respectively; each is capable only of producing what is appropriate for him to bring forth. (30–31)
"Therefore, O Nārada, some say that Brahman is indeed the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti);
thus they maintain the certainty of the eternity of both.
Others say that Brahman is himself both the primordial nature and the person (puruṣa)."
And some say that primordial nature (prakṛti) is distinct from Brahman.
That Brahman is the supreme abode, the cause of all causes.
O Brahman, this definition of Brahman has been heard somewhat in the Śruti.
Brahman and the Self are both untainted and the form of the witness for all;
they are all-pervading, the beginning of all, and their characteristics are heard in the Śruti.
That Brahman’s power is Prakṛti, whose nature is the seed of all.
Since that Brahman, which possesses power, is this very nature (prakṛti),
yogis always meditate upon that Brahman as being of the form of light.
However, my devotees who follow Viṣṇu and possess subtle intellect do not accept that [view].
Whose wonder would that splendor not be, that they meditate upon the Supreme Person without [any other] cause?
For how could an effect ever arise on this earth without a cause?
Therefore, the Vaiṣṇavas indeed meditate there upon His enchanting form.
And for that Person who consists of His own will, the embodied Self,
there is always a place known as Goloka, which is eternal, concealed, and shaped like a circle of light with a radiance equal to ten million suns. (39–40)
It is four-sided and enchanting, measuring one hundred billion yojanas;
it is constructed from the finest essence of jewels and is always surrounded by gopīs.
It is clearly visible and circular in shape, like the orb of the moon.

Inlaid with various jewels, it is supported by His will alone. Fifty crores of yojanas above eternal Vaikuṇṭha, it is filled with cows, cowherds, and gopīs, and is endowed with desire-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
O Sage, it was filled with wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu), adorned with the circle of the rāsa dance, sheltered by the forest of Vṛndāvana, and encircled by the Virajā river;
it possessed a hundred peaks made of gold, brilliantly radiant, glorious, and desirable. 44.1–2.
[It was surrounded] by hundreds of thousands of most enchanting hermitages.
[There was] a most enchanting hermitage provided with a hundred mansions, equipped with walls and moats, and endowed with groves of *pārijāta* trees. (45–46)
It was resplendent with the Kaustubha, the jewel of Indra, and supremely radiant;
it possessed exceedingly beautiful staircases constructed from the finest diamonds, and doors made of the essence of the best jewels, fitted with mirrors. (47)
The hermitage was well-constructed, enriched with various wonderful and diverse decorations;
it possessed sixteen doors and was brilliantly illuminated by jewel-lamps.
There stood a beautiful jeweled throne fashioned from precious gems.
The supreme Lord dwells within that which is richly adorned with various wonderful and diverse [forms]:
a youth in his prime, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, a child, whose eyes emit the brilliance of the midday sun in autumn. (50)
His face possesses the auspicious radiance of the full moon on an autumnal night;
he surpasses the god of love in the playful grace of ten million Cupids.
Endowed with the splendor of ten million moons, his well-proportioned body is graced with beauty. (51–52)
Smiling, flute in hand, most praiseworthy and auspicious;
resplendent with a pair of most excellent yellow garments;
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste and shining with the Kaustubha gem.
Adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers reaching down to his knees and a forest garland (*vanamālā*), he is endowed with the triple-bend posture (*tribhaṅga*) and decorated with jewels and rubies.
He has a crest of peacock feathers and is radiant with a crown of excellent gems. (54–55)
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets;
beautifully graced on the cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings;
and possessing most enchanting teeth whose luster resembles a string of pearls. (56)
With lips like a ripe bimba fruit and a nose beautiful for its elevation,
he was gazed upon by the cowherd girls who surrounded him on all sides—
women endowed with perpetual youth, smiling, and full of reverence. (57–58)
And she was adorned with supreme ornaments fashioned from excellent jewels;
she was joyfully saluted by the lords of the gods, the lords of sages, other sages, and the lords of men, as well as by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Ananta, Dharma, and the rest. (59)

O Sage, the Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon Him who is dear to His devotees, the Lord of devotees, the bestower of grace upon devotees, the Lord of the Rāsa dance, the connoisseur of aesthetic delight, and who dwells upon the breast of Rādhā— Him who is both of such a form and yet formless. (60–61)
We must constantly meditate upon the Supreme Lord, our Īśvara—
the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the Blessed One, the eternal,
who consists of His own will, is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), is free from worldly effort, and is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). (62)
He is the support of all, the seed of all, the omniscient, and indeed everything itself;
he is the Lord of all, the one to be worshipped by all, the bestower who grants all perfections.
He alone is the primordial Blessed One, manifest in two arms in Goloka.
Clad in the dress of a cowherd and surrounded by his cowherd attendants,
the most perfect and glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhikā,
is remembered as the inner self of all, omnipresent, and manifest everywhere. (69)
The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies "all," and the syllable *na* signifies "self. Since he is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, he is therefore celebrated as Kṛṣṇa.
Furthermore, *kṛṣi* signifies "all," and *na* signifies "the beginning. (66)
He is the primordial person, all-pervading; therefore, Kṛṣṇa is so proclaimed.
That very Lord, as a partial manifestation, is four-armed in Vaikuṇṭha, surrounded by those four-armed attendants, the Lord of Kamalā.
He alone, as Viṣṇu, is the protector and the Lord of the worlds;
in Śvetadvīpa, he is the four-armed husband of the Daughter of the Ocean.
All this, which is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, has been told to you.
"O Śaunaka, having said, 'He is to be meditated upon by us, served, saluted, and desired,' Śaṅkara then ceased speaking.
And Nārada praised him with a hymn composed by the king of the Gandharvas. || 70-71 ||
Satisfied by the sage’s hymn of praise, the Lord Ādi-Acyuta granted him the boon he desired: the knowledge of Mṛtyuñjaya.
The lord of sages, his face and eyes beaming with joy, bowed down deeply before Him.
By his command, he went to the meritorious hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Brahmā, Vaikuṇṭha, and Other Realms, and the Departure of Nārada," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Sauti said:
Then the divine seer Nārada beheld that wondrous hermitage belonging to the sage Nārāyaṇa itself, endowed with the Badarī forest;
it was strewn with the fruits of various trees and resounded with the songs of male cuckoos. (1)
It was surrounded by lordly śarabhas, lordly lions, and throngs of tigers;
yet, through the power of that lord of sages, it was free from the fear of violence.
That great forest was inaccessible [to others] and more enchanting even than heaven. (2–3)

He beheld that charming lord of sages in the midst of the assembly hall— a place surrounded by thirty million hermitages of the lords of perfected ones and lords of seers, filled with sandalwood forests and groves of *pārijāta* trees.
And seeing the teacher of yogis seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
chanting the supreme Brahman— Kṛṣṇa, the Self, the Lord—
the son of Brahmā, Śaunaka, bowed down to him. (5–6)
Rising suddenly, he embraced him and bestowed the highest blessing.
Out of affection, he inquired after his welfare and performed the rites of honoring a guest.
He seated Nārada upon a beautiful jeweled throne.

Dwelling on a delightful seat, freed from the fatigue of the journey, he spoke to that best of sages, the blessed and eternal one: "Having studied all the Vedas, which are very difficult to master even in my father’s presence... (8–9)
Having attained knowledge from the lords of yogis and indeed the mantra from the omnipresent Śaṅkara,
my mind— fickle and difficult to restrain— is still not satisfied.
And yet, your lotus feet have been beheld by me through the impulsion of my mind.
"And now I desire to obtain some particular knowledge,
wherein the narration of Kṛṣṇa’s qualities— which removes birth, death, and old age— is found.
O Lord, [even] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as the lords of the gods and the deities themselves..."
Whom do the sages and wise men contemplate?
From whom does creation arise, and wherein is it dissolved?
Who indeed is Viṣṇu, the Lord of all and the creator of all causes? (13–14)
"O Lord of the world, what is the form and what is the activity of that Īśvara?
Having reflected upon all this with your mind, you ought to explain it.
Having heard these words of Nārada, the blessed Ṛṣi smiled.
He began to relate the meritorious narrative that purifies the worlds.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Nārada’s Inquiry Regarding Nārāyaṇa," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: One should meditate upon the lotus feet of the Blessed Lord, [while visualizing] Lambodara, Hari, Umāpati, Īśa, Śeṣa, Brahmā and the other hosts of gods, the Manus, the lords of sages, Vāṇī, Śivā, the triple-pathed river Gaṅgā, Kamalā, and the others. (1)

Indeed, he who desires to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra— which is exceedingly deep and terrible, and whose limbs are writhing, encircled by forest fires and serpents— should contemplate the lotus-feet of the Blessed One as his servitude. (2) The earth, exhausted from the fame of lifting Govardhana, was supported by him with the very tip of his tusk, remaining moist.

One should meditate upon the lotus feet of the primordial Lord, who sustains all things within the pores of his hair. (3) One whose body is torn asunder by the fear and grief of birth, death, and other such states, should meditate upon the lotus feet of the Lord Hari, the Creator, whose fame has issued from the mouths of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and who is the progenitor of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas. (4)

One should meditate upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One, the Lord of the *rāsa* dance, the lover of the connoisseurs of rasa, who is like a bee to the lotus-faces of the cowherd women; he who sports in Vṛndāvana as Viṣṇu in the guise of a cowherd.
O child, who on earth is capable of describing the deeds of that Creator of the worlds, which occur within the blink of an eye?
And you too, O sage Nārada, perform meditation with supreme reverence upon the lotus feet of Hari.
We, you, the Manus, the lords of sages, and the foremost among the gods are but infinitesimal portions of His portions;
even the great Virāṭ is but a specific manifestation of His portion. (6–7)
The thousand-headed one bears the entire universe, which is equal in size to a mustard seed, upon his head.
Just as Śeṣa is to Kūrma, and a mosquito is to an elephant, so too is Kūrma but a minute fraction of a fraction of a part of Kṛṣṇa.
The stainless glory of the omnipresent Lord of Goloka is not clearly manifest anywhere in the Vedas or the Purāṇas.
Even those headed by Brahmā are not capable of describing him; worship that Lord of All, who is the foremost of the lotus-born.
(9) In all the worlds, there are indeed eternally the creators, Viṣṇus, and Rudras belonging to the Abode of the Universe;
yet even the Vedas and the gods do not know the number of them. Worship that Supreme Lord. (10)
The Ordainer of destiny brings about creation by establishing Prakṛti, who is eternal and the mother of the universe.
Brahmā and all others born of Prakṛti worship Śrī Prakṛti, the bestower of devotion.
Prakṛti is not different from the nature of Brahman; it is through her that the Eternal One performs creation.
All forms of fortune in the worlds are but a portion of her, and by her all are utterly deluded.
She is Nārāyaṇī, the supreme and eternal power of the Supreme Person, the Self and the Lord;
for even He, though possessed of power, is truly unable to create without her. (12–13)
"Go, my child, and perform the marriage now; you have been enjoined to carry out your father's command.
By obeying the instructions of your guru, you shall be honored everywhere and ever victorious.
Indeed, he who honors his own wife with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste [attains these blessings]."
His nature is satisfied just as Kṛṣṇa is when engaged in the worship of the twice-born.
And she exists in the form of a woman throughout all universes by her power of illusion (māyā);
she becomes utterly dejected by the insult of women. (15–16)
By him who has honored a divine woman who is virtuous and possesses a husband and sons, Nature—the bestower of all auspiciousness—has been honored.
She is the one Root-Nature, whose essence is the perfect Brahman. (17)
In the process of creation, she is fivefold; she is the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu.
She who is the presiding goddess over the vital breath (prāṇa) of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, and who is the most beloved of them all, is celebrated as Rādhā. (18–19)
Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, who is the embodiment of all prosperity;
Sarasvatī, the goddess presiding over passion, who is also to be worshipped;
and Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, the beloved of Brahmā, whose form is worthy of worship. (20)
Durgā is the beloved of Śaṅkara, whose son is Gaṇeśvara.

(21) Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise and the Nature of the Blessed Lord," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sauti and Śaunaka.
Thus the first section, the Brahma-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa* is complete.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara.
Salutations to Śrī Mahāsarasvatī.
Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī and Narasiṃha.
Now begins the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa.
Nārada said:

Ganesha’s mother, Durga, Radha, Lakshmi, Sarasvati, and Savitri—these five are remembered as Prakriti in the process of creation. By whom did she manifest, and who is she, that most excellent among the wise? (1)
Or rather, tell me what its characteristics are, and how it became fivefold. What is the conduct of them all, and how is the ritual of worship desired?
Where is the descent of each, and you should explain that to me. (2–3)
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O child, who indeed would be capable of describing the characteristics of Prakṛti?
Nevertheless, I shall say something that I have heard from the mouth of Dharma."
The syllable *pra* denotes excellence, and *kṛti* denotes creation.
That Goddess who is supreme (*prakṛṣṭā*) within creation (*sṛṣṭau*) is proclaimed as *Prakṛti*.
In the Veda, the word *pra* also occurs in the sense of the quality of supreme goodness (*prakṛṣṭasattva*).
The letter *kṛ* is remembered as being in *rajas*, and the sound *ti* is said to be in *tamas*.
That which has the nature of the three *guṇas*, which is endowed with all powers,
and which is primary in the act of creation, is therefore called *prakṛti*.
In the first [verse], the word *prakṛti* occurs; it is a term denoting creation. That Goddess who is the primordial source of creation is celebrated as *Prakṛti*.
Through yoga, in the process of creation, that Self became twofold in form.
The male is known as the right half of the body, and the female (prakṛti) is remembered as the left half.
She is of the nature of Brahman, eternal and everlasting Māyā;
just as the Self exists, just as power exists, and just as the power of burning is inherent in fire.

Therefore, O Nārada, the lord of yogis perceives no distinction between male and female; he eternally beholds everything as consisting of Brahman, as Brahman. This occurs through the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is composed of His own free will, and by His desire to create.
She, the Sovereign Primordial Nature (mūlaprakṛti), suddenly manifested.
By her command, she became fivefold for the sake of the work of creation through differentiation;
or else, out of regard for her devotees, she assumed a form to bestow grace upon them.
She who is Gaṇeśa’s mother, Durgā, whose form is Śiva and who is beloved by Śiva;
she who is Nārāyaṇī, the Māyā of Viṣṇu, and whose nature is the perfect Brahman;
she who is eternally worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, by sages, and by the Manus. (14)
She is the sovereign goddess of all, eternal and of the nature of Brahman;
she bestows fame, auspiciousness, dharma, prosperity, truth, and merit;
she grants liberation and joy, and destroys grief, suffering, and affliction. (16–19)
She is solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge and those who are miserable and distressed.
She is the supreme deity presiding over that [power], whose nature is splendor.
And she is the eternal power of the Lord, whose nature consists of all potencies.
Siddheśvarī, she whose form is perfection, the giver of success, the sovereign of the attainment of success;
(18) intellect, sleep, hunger, thirst, shadow, lassitude, compassion, memory;
birth, patience, peace, splendor, delusion, and consciousness; (19)
Satisfaction, nourishment, as well as fortune, conduct, and likewise the Mother—
she is the embodiment of all powers belonging to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
Her qualities, as described in the Śruti according to tradition, have been stated here very briefly.
The quality (guṇa) of the Infinite One is infinite; now behold another [aspect].
She who is Padmā, whose nature is pure being (śuddhasattva), is the goddess presiding over that [Infinite One], whose nature is all prosperity. (21–22)
She was beloved, self-controlled, exceedingly tranquil, virtuous, and the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
Though she had been abandoned by her husband due to greed, delusion, lust, anger, pride, and ego, she remained devoted to him; she was the foremost of all women and a faithful wife.
She was as dear to the Blessed One as his own life, a worthy recipient of his love, and sweet-spoken.
(24) In Vaikuṇṭha, she was Mahālakṣmī, the essence of all crops and the embodiment of every means of sustenance, devoted solely to the service of her husband. (25)
In heaven there is the splendor of heaven, and among kings the splendor of royalty;
likewise, in the homes of mortal householders there is the splendor of the home—appearing as beauty and enchanting to the mind in all living beings and material things. (26)
She is the form of joy for the meritorious and the form of splendor among kings;
she is the form of trade for merchants and the instigator of quarrels for sinners.
She is composed of compassion, the mother of her devotees, and the bestower of grace upon her devotees.
O Sage, the fickle riches of devotees are indeed fickle; and for their protection, there is that Goddess without whom the entire world, both living and dead, [would perish].
This second Śakti has been described as declared in the Vedas and is universally acclaimed. (29)
She is worthy of all worship and worthy of all homage; hear now of another [goddess] from me.
She is the presiding deity of speech, intellect, learning, and knowledge, and she is the goddess Sarasvatī, whose very nature is all forms of learning. 30–31.
She bestows upon the virtuous excellent intellect, poetic talent, wisdom, intuition, and memory;
she provides the conceptualization of the meanings of various types of philosophical systems;
her nature is the understanding of commentaries, and she shatters all doubts. (32)
She is the one who performs reflection, the author of the scriptures, and whose nature is Śakti.
She is the form of the cause of all music, its composition, and its rhythmic timing.
And she is the form of the knowledge of objects and speech for all living beings in every universe. (33–34)
Without whom the flood of the universe would always be mute and like one dead;
she who holds the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*) and is peaceful, bearing a lute and a book;
she whose nature is pure being (*śuddhasattva*), who is of excellent character, and the beloved of Śrī Hari. (39)
Resembling snow, sandalwood, the kunda flower, the moon, and the white and blue lotus;
chanting the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with a rosary of jewels;
she is the very embodiment of austerity, the bestower of the fruits of austerities, and the ascetic herself. (36–37)
She is the very nature of perfected knowledge and is the eternal bestower of all accomplishments.
Now, understand from me another [aspect] of her, according to tradition and as it is:
she is the mother of the four Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the meters. (38–39)
She is the expert in the mantras of the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana) and the tantras;

she takes the form of the twice-born castes and the like, and she is the ascetic woman whose nature is the recitation of prayers (japa). She is the embodiment of the splendor of Brahmanical power and the performer of all purificatory rites (saṃskāra).
Sāvitrī is of a purifying nature; she is Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā.
Even sacred fords long for contact with her or even a sight of her for the sake of purification.
She resembles pure crystal and has the nature of pure sattva.
She is of the nature of supreme bliss, supreme and eternal;
she is the very essence of the Supreme Brahman and the bestower of the state of Nirvāṇa.
She is the Power consisting of the splendor of Brahman, the presiding deity thereof. (43)

O Nārada, by the dust of whose feet the entire world is purified—this fourth goddess has been described; now I shall describe the fifth to you. She who is the presiding deity of love and life, whose very nature is the five vital breaths (prāṇas). (44–45)
She is dearer than life itself, the first of all, beautiful, and most excellent;
endowed with every auspicious fortune, she is proud and possessed of dignity;
she is the very form of the left half of [Śiva’s] body and is equal to him in her virtues and splendor. 46.
She is both supreme and subordinate, the mother of all, the primordial and eternal one.
She is the embodiment of supreme bliss, the blessed, the venerable, and the worshiped;
she is the presiding deity of the Rāsa dance of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (47–48)
Born from the circle of the *rāsa*, adorned by the circle of the *rāsa*,
the Mistress of the *rāsa*, full of divine relish, she dwells in the abode of the *rāsa*.
(49) The Goddess who resides in Goloka, she who assumes the guise of a cowherd girl (*gopī*).
She is the form of supreme bliss, and she is the embodiment of contentment and patience.
She is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), formless, untainted, and the very nature of the Self.
She is effortless, free from ego, and her form consists of grace toward her devotees.
That vision is to be known by the wise through meditation in accordance with the Vedas;
it has been seen by thousands of lords of the gods and eminent sages.
Clad in garments as pure as fire and adorned with jeweled ornaments—
Adorned with the splendor of ten million rays of light, she possesses auspicious beauty and embodies devotion.
She bestows the singular service of a servant to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and all forms of prosperity. Furthermore, during the Vārāha incarnation, she was the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu. (53–54)
The earth was purified by the touch of her lotus feet;
she, who was unseen even by Brahmā and the other gods, was seen everywhere in Bhārata.
Born from the essence of the jewels among women, she rested upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa.
O Sage, even the flickering lightning in thick, fresh clouds is thus [insignificant] compared to her.
In the past, Brahmā practiced austerities for sixty thousand years for the sake of beholding the toenails of her lotus feet and for the purification of his own self. (56–57)
She would not have been seen even in a dream, so what to speak of being perceived directly?
By that very same austerity, she was beheld extensively in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
That fifth goddess who was described is celebrated as Rādhā.

In the form of parts (*aṃśa*), in the form of digits (*kalā*), and arising from portions of those digits (*kalāṃśāṃśa*), the form of every woman throughout the universe is derived from *prakṛti*. These five classes of goddesses are proclaimed to be the most perfectly complete (*paripūrṇatama*).
Listen as I describe those forms which consist of the primary portions:
Gaṅgā, the purifier of the worlds, is the very embodiment of the primary portion;
she is born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, eternal, and in the form of liquid. (61)
She is like blazing fuel for the burning away of the sins of the wicked;
she bestows liberation through sight, touch, bathing, and drinking;
and she is the very form of the excellent staircase for ascending to the realm of Goloka.
She is the purifier of sacred fords and the supreme among rivers;
she takes the form of a string of pearls from the matted locks on Śambhu’s head, which resemble Mount Meru.
She instantly brings about the perfection of asceticism for those practicing penance in Bhārata.
Resembling a conch, a lotus, and milk, she is the very embodiment of pure being;
stainless, free from ego, virtuous, and the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
Tulasī, the consort of Viṣṇu, is the essential nature of the primary constituent (pradhāna). (65–66)
O Sage, she who is the ornament of Viṣṇu, who dwells at the feet of Viṣṇu,
who instantly accomplishes penance, resolve, worship, and so forth,
who is the very essence of flowers, and who is eternally pure and bestows merit— (67) — [she is Śrī].
She bestows immediate liberation through both sight and touch.
In the Kali age, she takes the form of fire for the purpose of burning the fuel of impurities;
by the touch of her lotus feet, the earth is instantly purified.
That which people desire to touch or behold for the purification of their souls at sacred pilgrimage sites;
that without which every action in the worlds is fruitless;
she who grants liberation to those seeking release and fulfills all desires for those possessed by longing.
In Bhārata, she exists in the form of trees as the Kalpavṛkṣa itself;
she is the supreme deity for the protection of the people of Bhārata and their worship.
She is the embodiment of the primary portion [of Prakṛti], and in her mind, she is the daughter of Kaśyapa.
She is the beloved disciple of Śaṅkara and is highly proficient in great knowledge. She is the sister of Ananta, the Lord of the Nāgas, and is herself worshipped by the Nāgas.
She is Nāgeśvarī, the Mother of the Nāgas, the beautiful one who is borne by the Nāgas.
She is accompanied by hosts of lordly nāgas, adorned with ornaments of nāgas,
saluted by the lordly nāgas, a perfected yoginī dwelling among the nāgas;
she is a devotee of Viṣṇu, possesses the form of Viṣṇu, and is solely intent on the worship of Viṣṇu.
She is the very embodiment of austerity, the bestower of the fruits of penance, and the ascetic par excellence.
She performed divine penance for three hundred thousand years for the sake of Hari.
Among female ascetics in Bhārata, she is the most venerable, and among male ascetics as well.
She is the presiding goddess of all mantras, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
She is the supreme embodiment of Brahman, intent upon the meditation on Brahman.
She is the wife of the sage Jaratkāru, a devoted wife to Kṛṣṇa and Śambhu.
O Nārada, she who was Devasenā, the mother of the eminent ascetic Muni Āstīka, whose nature consists of the primary portion [of Prakṛti],
is that most worshipful Mātṛkā, who is celebrated as Ṣaṣṭhī.
She who provides protection for children at every moment,
the ascetic one devoted to Viṣṇu and the beloved wife of Kārttikeya,
is celebrated as Ṣaṣṭhī because she is a sixth-part manifestation of Prakṛti. 80–81.
She is the bestower of sons and grandsons, and the eternal nurse of the worlds;
beautiful, youthful, and charming, she is always by her husband’s side.
In the presence of children she is most excellent, yet as a yoginī she assumes the form of an old woman.
The worship of that [deity] on the sixth day is performed continuously throughout the twelve months;
there is also worship in the lying-in chamber for the infant on the sixth day after birth,
and on the twenty-first day as well, worship is performed for the sake of auspiciousness.

She is eternally restrained, yet she is also the eternal one who fulfills desires; she is the supreme mother, the embodiment of compassion, and the constant protector. She dwells in water, on land, and in the atmosphere, appearing to children even within their dreams.

The Goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā, whose essential nature is a portion of Pradhāna, is born from the mouth of Prakṛti and is the eternal bestower of all auspiciousness. In the process of creation she is the form of auspiciousness, and in the process of dissolution she takes the form of wrath. (86–87)
Therefore, she is celebrated by the wise as Maṅgalacaṇḍī;
worshipped with devotion through the five types of offerings by women on every Tuesday and in every universe. (88)
She bestows sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, fame, and auspiciousness;
she destroys grief, feverish distress, sin, affliction, suffering, and poverty.
When fully gratified, she grants all desires to all women. (89–90)
The Great Goddess, lotus-eyed Kālī, who is the very nature of the constituent of Pradhāna, is capable of destroying the entire universe in an instant when enraged;
she was born from the forehead of Durgā in the battle against Śumbha and Niśumbha.
She is the very embodiment of half a digit of Durgā, equal to her in virtues and splendor.
Her divine and beautiful form is graced by the radiance of ten million suns.
She is the foremost of all powers, the most excellent, the powerful, and the supreme. (92–93)
The Goddess who bestows all perfections is the supreme Yoginī of perfection;
she is devoted to Kṛṣṇa and equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor, valor, and virtues;
through constant contemplation of Kṛṣṇa, she is eternally of the color of Kṛṣṇa. (94)
She is capable of destroying the entire universe with a mere breath;
her battle with the Daityas is but a sport for the protection of the worlds.
When well-worshipped, she is capable of bestowing virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
Praised by Brahmā and the others, as well as by sages, Manus, and men;

she whose essential nature consists of the primary constituent (pradhāna), she who is Primordial Matter (prakṛti) and the Earth (vasundharā); she who is the support of all things and the progenitor of all crops. (96–97)
She is the mine of jewels, the womb of jewels, and the foundation of all sources of jewels.
She is eternally worshipped and saluted by the lords of creatures and by the creatures themselves.
She is the form upon which everyone depends for livelihood and she bestows all prosperity.
Without her, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings would be without support.
O Lord of Sages, learn now of those various powers (kalās) which belong to Prakṛti;
I shall describe to you all those who are the wives of each respective one. (99–100)
The goddess Svāhā, the wife of Agni, is worshipped in the three worlds;
without her, the gods are not able to accept the offered oblation.
Dakṣiṇā, the wife of sacrifice, and Dīkṣā are everywhere honored.
Without her, every ritual action among all beings is fruitless.
She is Svadhā, the wife of the ancestors, worshipped by sages, Manu, and men;
and without her, the ancestral offering is fruitless. (102–103)
Svastidevī, the consort of Vāyu, is worshipped among all people;
without her, both receiving and giving are fruitless.
Puṣṭi, the consort of Gaṇapati, is worshipped upon the surface of the earth.
Without her, both men and women are utterly ruined.
She is Anantapatnī (the Consort of the Infinite One) and Tuṣṭi (Contentment), who is always worshipped and saluted.
Without her, all people everywhere remain dissatisfied. (105–106)
Sampatti, the wife of Īśāna, was honored by gods and men;
without her, all people in all worlds would be impoverished.
Dhṛti, the wife of Kapila, is likewise honored everywhere by everyone. (107)
All the worlds would become restless without her;
she is the wife of Yama, the virtuous and well-behaved Kṣamā, honored by all.
All the Rudras and all the worlds are utterly distraught without her. (108–109)
She is the presiding goddess of play, the virtuous Rati, the consort of Kāma;
without her, all the worlds would be devoid of sport and curiosity.
She is the virtuous Satī, the consort of Satya, who is honored as liberation (Mukti) and beloved by the worlds.
Without her, the world would always be devoid of kinship;
she is Compassion, the virtuous wife of Delusion, honored and beloved by the universe.
Without her, all people everywhere would be cruel. (111–112)
She is the wife of merit, the foundation, of meritorious form, and honored;
O Sage, without her the entire world is like one dead while living.
She is the wife of virtuous action, fame, blessed, venerable, and worshiped. (113)
Without her, the entire world is devoid of glory, like one who is dead;
she is Action (Kriyā), the wife of Udyoga, honored and associated with all.
Without her, O Nārada, the entire world is as if utterly destroyed.
That unrighteous wife is a falsehood, yet she is honored by all deceivers;
without her, the entire world created by the Ordainer would be destroyed. She who was invisible in the Kṛta age and exists in a subtle form in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, she was withdrawn out of shame, appearing only as half a body;
but in the Kali age, she becomes exceedingly bold and, for the sake of pervading everywhere,
wanders from house to house together with her brother, Deceit.
Peace and modesty are the two honored wives of good character, O Nārada, without whom the entire world is as if intoxicated. Knowledge has three wives: intellect, understanding, and memory.
Without her, the entire world is always deluded, like one who is dead.
She is the embodiment of Dharma’s wife, radiant in form and captivating to the mind;
she is the Supreme Self of the multitude of universes, without whom [the universe] would be without support. (120–121)
Everywhere she is Lakṣmī, whose form is splendor, existing as a personified being;
she is Śrī by nature and Mūrti by form, venerable, fortunate, and worshipped.
She is the consort of Kālāgnirudra and the sleep of the perfected yogins.
All worlds are completely enveloped by the power of illusion during the nights.
Time has three wives: the two twilights, night, and the days;
without these, it is impossible even for the Creator to calculate [time].
Hunger and thirst are the two wives of greed; they are auspicious, worthy of honor, and revered.
By these two, the world is pervaded, agitated, and even brought to reflection.
Splendor and burning power are likewise the two wives of fire.
Without these two, the Creator would indeed not be capable of creating the world.
O Kālakanyā, O Death and Old Age, beloved consorts of Fever!
When the Creator had fashioned the moon, the world was utterly destroyed by her.
Sleep is his daughter Tandrā, and Pleasure is another, Priyā, who is fond of happiness;
by these two, O son of Vidhi, the entire world is pervaded within the ordinance of Vidhi.
And Vairāgya has two wives, Śraddhā and Bhakti, who are honored.
By these two, O Sage, this entire world is eternally liberated while living.
Aditi, the mother of the gods; Surabhi, the progenitor of cows;
Diti, the mother of the Daityas; Kadrū, Vinatā, and Danu. 129–130.
These portions of Prakṛti have been employed in the process of creation.
There are many other portions as well; hear from me about some of them:
Rohiṇī, the wife of the Moon, and Saṃjñā, the beloved of the Sun.
Śatarūpā was the wife of Manu, and Śacī is the consort of Indra;
Tārā is the wife of Bṛhaspati, and Arundhatī belongs to Vasiṣṭha; Ahalyā was the wife of Gautama, and Anasūyā was the beloved of Atri. (132–133)
Devahūti was the offspring of Kardama and the wife of Dakṣa;
Menakā, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, was the mother of Ambikā.
Likewise, Lopāmudrā and Hūti were the wives of Kubera.
Varuṇānī, Yamī, Vindhyāvalī the wife of Bali,
Kuntī, Damayantī, Yaśodā, the virtuous Devakī,
Gāndhārī, Draupadī, Sāvitrī, and Satyavatī, the beloved of Satyavān. (135–136)
The virtuous Kalāvatī, mother of Rādhā and beloved of Vṛṣabhānu;
likewise Mandodarī, Kausalyā, Subhadrā, and Kaikayī;
as well as Revatī, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, and Lakṣmaṇā.
Mitravindā, the daughter of Agnijit, as well as Jāmbavatī;
Lakṣmaṇā, Rukmiṇī, and Sītā, who is proclaimed to be Lakṣmī herself;
Kalā, Yojanagandhā, and the great chaste mother of Vyāsa. || 138–139 ||
The daughter of Bāṇa, Uṣā, and her friend Citralekhā; Prabhāvatī, Bhānumatī, and the virtuous Māyāvatī;
Reṇukā, the mother of Bhṛgu, and Rohiṇī, the mother of Balarāma. 140.
Ekānaṃśā is Durgā, the virtuous sister of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (141) There are many such portions of Prakṛti herself in Bhārata; all those who are village goddesses are likewise portions of Prakṛti. (142)
In every universe, women are born from a minute fraction of a fraction [of Prakṛti].
By insulting women, one insults Prakṛti itself.
By that man who honors a virtuous Brāhmaṇa woman who has sons and a husband, [Prakṛti is honored]. (143)

By him, Prakṛti was honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste. And by him who honors an eight-year-old maiden with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste, Prakṛti of the Brahmin is honored. (144–145)
All women, whether superior, inferior, or middling, are born of *prakṛti*.
Those who possess a portion of *sattva* should be known as the best; they are well-behaved and devoted to their husbands.
The middling ones are portions of *rajas*, and they are proclaimed to be objects of enjoyment.
They enjoy pleasures and are always intent on their own purposes.
(147) The lowest [class] consists of portions of Tamas; they are born of unknown lineage, foul-mouthed, unchaste, deceitful, independent, and fond of quarreling. (148)

Those who are unchaste women on earth and the hosts of apsarases in heaven are proclaimed to be portions of *prakṛti* and of *tamas*. Thus has been described the entire fivefold division of *prakṛti*.
All of them were worshipped on earth in the sacred field of Bhārata. First, Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress, was worshipped by Suratha;
second, she was worshipped by Rāmacandra, who desired the slaying of Rāvaṇa. (150–151)
After that, the Mother of the worlds, who is worshipped in the three realms,
was first born as the wife of Dakṣa in order to slay the Daityas and Dānavas;
subsequently, she cast off her body due to the censure of her husband at the sacrifice.
She was born from the wife of Himavat and obtained Paśupati as her husband.
O Nārada, Gaṇeśa himself and Skanda, who was born from a portion of Viṣṇu, later became her two sons. 153–154.
Lakṣmī was first worshipped by King Maṅgala;
thereafter, she was worshipped in the three worlds by gods, sages, and humans.
Sāvitrī, moreover, was first worshipped with devotion. (155)
Thereafter, in the three worlds, the goddess Sarasvatī was first worshipped by gods, sages, and humans;
thereafter, in the three worlds, [she was worshipped] by gods, sages, and humans. (156–157)
First, Rādhā was worshiped by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, on the full moon day of Kārttika in the Rāsa-maṇḍala of Goloka,
along with the gopīs, the gopas, the girls, and the boys. (158)

Following her were herds of cows and hosts of gods; then she was always worshipped and saluted with devotion by Brahmā and the other deities, as well as by sages and Manus, with flowers, incense, and other offerings, through the illusory power of Hari. (199–200)
On earth, she was first worshipped by Suyajña at the holy site of Bhārata, as instructed by Śaṅkara;
thereafter, by the command of the Supreme Self, she [was established] throughout the three worlds. (161)

Worshipped with devotion by sages and gods with flowers, incense, and other offerings, those various arts that have arisen well are also worshipped in Bhārata. And the village goddesses are worshipped in the village and in the city, O Sage. (162–163)
Thus has the entire auspicious conduct of Prakṛti been told to you, according to the scriptures and its defining characteristics. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature and Divisions of Prakṛti," in the second section (Prakṛtikhaṇḍa) of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
O Lord, I have heard the entire account of the goddesses in brief;
for the sake of further enlightenment, you ought to recount it in detail. (1)
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me how she, the primordial power of creation, manifested during the process of creation; or how she became fivefold;
and which beings arose through that three-guṇa portion of yours.
O Vyāsa, I now desire to hear their life stories;
describe their births, their meditation, the supreme ritual for their worship,
their hymn of praise, their armor, their sovereignty, their heroism, and their auspiciousness.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The eternal Self and the sky are eternal, as are time and the directions;
Gokula is eternal for all beings, and Goloka itself is eternal. (5)
Vaikuṇṭha is a single portion of that [Brahman], its hanging part, which is eternal.
Likewise, Prakṛti is eternal, merged in Brahman, and everlasting.
Just as burning power resides in fire, beauty in the moon, and radiance in the lotus, so does splendor reside in the sun.

That primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternally joined with the Self and is not distinct from it. (7) Just as a goldsmith is unable to fashion an earring without gold, so indeed a potter is not capable of making a jar without clay. (8)
Indeed, Brahmā is not capable of creating the creation without her;
she is the embodiment of all powers, and by means of her, he is always possessed of power. The root *śak* denotes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and *tiḥ* denotes valor (*parākrama*).
That which bestows their essential nature upon those two is proclaimed as Śakti.
The word *bhaga* denotes prosperity, intelligence, perfection, and fame;
therefore, Śakti is eternally *bhagavatī* (possessing *bhaga*) and has the form of *bhaga*.
The Lord is always said to be the Self joined with that [power].
And that Kṛṣṇa consists of His own will; He is both with form and without form. Yogins always meditate upon Him as formless, consisting of radiant light.
They speak of him as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the Lord;
the invisible one, the seer of all, the omniscient, the cause of all;
the giver of all, the end of all forms, the formless, the nourisher of all. (13–14)
Those devotees of Viṣṇu, who perceive the subtle, do not believe that; they ask, "Whose splendor is this? regarding that which exists apart from any [other] luminous being.
They declare that the Supreme Brahman, the truly radiant one, resides in the center of the circle of light.
Consisting of His own will, possessing every form, and the cause of all causes;
bearing an exceedingly beautiful and most captivating form;
youthful in age, peaceful, the beloved of all, and higher than the highest. (16–17)
He has the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, the singular dark beauty of the rāsa dance, and eyes that possess the captivating splendor of a multitude of autumnal midday lotuses;
he is enchanting with rows of teeth as pure and brilliant as the finest pearls. 18.
With a crest of peacock feathers and adorned with garlands of jasmine, he has a beautiful nose and is ever smiling, bestowing grace upon his devotees;
he is resplendent in a single yellow garment as pure as blazing fire. (19–20)
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, adorned with jewel ornaments;
the support of all, the Lord of all, the pervasive one endowed with all powers;
the bestower of all sovereignty, the All, the independent one, the source of all auspiciousness. (21)
The Vaishnavas constantly meditate upon this supreme, eternal Lord, who is most perfectly accomplished, the bestower of perfection, and the cause of all success;
he is the ultimate remover of birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and fear.
He whose blink of an eye is measured by the lifespan of Brahmā is that Self, the Supreme Brahman, who is designated as Kṛṣṇa.
The word "kṛṣi" signifies devotion to Him, and "na" denotes the one who performs service to Him. (24)
He who bestows devotion and servitude is celebrated as Kṛṣṇa.
The syllable *kṛṣ* signifies "all," and the syllable *na* signifies "seed.
That Supreme Brahman, the seed of all, is designated by the name Kṛṣṇa. (25)

O Nārada, even when an incalculable number of Brahmās have passed away in the course of time, there is no destruction of his qualities; he is equal to them in virtue. That Kṛṣṇa alone, at the beginning of every creation, desires to bring forth the universe.
Then the Lord, intent on creation and impelled by a portion of Time,
who consists of his own will, became twofold in form by his own will.
The female form arose from the left half, while the right half is known as the male.
The eternal one, the great lover and the support of desire, beheld her—
exceedingly beautiful, resembling a lovely campaka flower,
and supreme, with a pair of hips like the orb of the full moon. (30)
She was beautiful with hips resembling the trunks of lovely plantain trees;
she was delightful with a pair of breasts shaped like auspicious *śrīphala* fruits; she was well-proportioned, exquisitely graceful, slender-waisted, and captivating. (31–32)
Exceedingly beautiful, peaceful, smiling, and with arched eyes;
wearing garments as pure as fire and adorned with jeweled ornaments;
she was constantly and joyfully drinking [him] in with her two eyes, which were like those of a cakora bird. (33)
Kṛṣṇa’s beautiful face mocks ten million moons.
(34) She bears a drop of musk together with a drop of sandalwood paste below it, and likewise a dot of vermilion in the middle of her forehead. (35)
Bearing a mass of beautiful braided hair adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers,
and wearing a necklace of the finest essence of jewels, she was a woman who kindled desire in her lover;
she possessed a full splendor graced by the radiance of ten million moons.
Seeing that royal swan in her gait, who put the *khañjana* bird to shame,
the Lord of the Rāsa dance performed the rāsa-play with her in secret amidst the exultations of the rāsa within the rāsa-maṇḍala. (37–38)
Adorned with various kinds of erotic grace, like the god of love incarnate,
he enjoyed blissful union with her for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Then the Father of the World became exhausted within her womb.
And at an auspicious moment, Nityānanda bestowed his virility upon her;
O observer of noble vows, at the conclusion of the sexual union,
perspiration born of fatigue issued from every limb of that exhausted woman due to the splendor of Hari.
Exhausted by great sexual passion, she indeed let out a sigh;
that sigh became the wind that supports everything, and all the water produced by her exhaustion became the entire cosmic egg (Viśvagolaka).
That wind of her sigh, moreover, became the support of all things.

The breath of exhalation became the beloved wife of the Wind-god, emerging from his left side; she was the consort of that embodied Wind, and their sons were the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of all living beings. (43–44)
Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna indeed became his sons, as did the five downward-moving breaths (adhaḥprāṇas). And from the deity of the heat-water (gharmatoya) was born the great Varuṇa.
From his left side, his wife Varuṇānī was born.
Then she, the power of Kṛṣṇa, bore a fetus from Kṛṣṇa;
for as long as a hundred manvantaras, she blazed with the splendor of Brahman.
She is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath, dearer to Him than His own life;
she is eternally the companion of Kṛṣṇa, ever residing upon the surface of Kṛṣṇa’s chest.
After a period of a hundred manvantaras had passed, that most beautiful woman appeared.
Having seen that supreme egg, which was golden-hued, well-formed, and the abode and support of the universe,
the Goddess, with a grieving heart,
cast that egg into the waters of the cosmic sphere (golaka) out of anger.
Seeing that abandonment, Kṛṣṇa raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
and the Lord of Gods immediately cursed the Goddess as was fitting:
"O you of wrathful nature, O most cruel one, since offspring has been abandoned by you..."
"From this day forward, you shall certainly remain childless.
And whatever celestial women shall exist who are partial incarnations of you, they all shall likewise be childless, equal to you, and eternally youthful. (52–53)
In that interval, from the tip of the Goddess’s tongue,
there suddenly appeared a single maiden, white-complexioned and enchanting,
dressed in yellow garments and holding a lute and a book. (54)
Adorned with an abundance of jewel ornaments, she is the presiding deity of all scriptures. (59) Then, after some time, she indeed became twofold in form:
Kamalā as the left half of her body, and Rādhikā as the right half. (56)
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa indeed became twofold in form:
his right half was two-armed, and his left half was four-armed.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke these words: "Become his beloved."
"In this very matter, the proud Rādhā will certainly not find well-being.
Having thus bestowed Lakṣmī upon Nārāyaṇa, he was indeed satisfied;
and the Lord of the World departed for Vaikuṇṭha together with those two.
And since those two were born from a portion of Rādhā, they were childless;
and from the body of Nārāyaṇa there arose four-armed attendants who were equal to Hari in splendor, age, beauty, and virtues. (60)
And from the body of Kamalā, there arose ten million female servants equal to her.
Then, O Sage, from the pores of the Lord of Goloka,
there emerged gopas in numbers beyond counting, equal to him in age and splendor.
By virtue of their beauty, excellent qualities, attire,
and prowess, all the attendants of the Lord became as dear to him as his own life.
From the pores of Rādhā’s body, the cowherd girls were born.
All of them were equal to Rādhā, none could be compared to another, and they were sweet-spoken.
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments, they possessed eternal and stable youth.
Yet all of them remained perpetually childless due to the curse of a man.
In that interval, O Brahmin, from the body of Kṛṣṇa there suddenly appeared that eternal Durgā, the illusory power of Viṣṇu,
the goddess who is the sovereign Nārāyaṇī and the embodiment of all powers. (66)
She is the presiding goddess of the intellect of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;
she is the seed-form of all goddesses, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti.
She is the most perfect, whose nature is splendor, and who consists of the three guṇas. (67–68)
She possesses the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to ten million suns;
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and she is endowed with a thousand arms.
Bearing a multitude of various weapons and missiles, she is three-eyed.
Clad in garments as pure as fire and adorned with jewel ornaments— she,
by whose infinitesimal portion all women came into being, and by whose power of illusion all the worlds situated within the entire universe are deluded. (70–71)
She is the bestower of all sovereignty upon householders who possess desires;
she is Vaiṣṇavī, the giver of devotion to Kṛṣṇa for the Vaiṣṇavas;
she is the giver of liberation to those seeking release, and the bestower of happiness upon those who are happy. (72)
In the heavens she is the Fortune of Heaven; in houses, she is the Fortune of the Home.
Among ascetics she is austerity, and among kings she is Sovereignty (Śrī).
She who exists in fire as the power of burning and in the sun as radiance—[she is that same Śrī].

She whose nature is splendor, who is most beautiful in the moon and in lotuses; she who is the embodiment of all powers within Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self—by whom the Self possesses power, and by whom indeed the world possesses power. (79)
Without her, the entire world remains as if dead while yet living;
and she, O Nārada, is the eternal seed-form of the tree of worldly existence, and its form as stability, its form as intellect, and its form as fruit. (76–77)
She, whose form consists of hunger, thirst, compassion, faith, sleep, drowsiness, forgiveness, fortitude,
peace, modesty, contentment, nourishment, delusion, splendor, and so forth,
having praised the Lord of All, stood before Him. (78)
The Lord of Rādhikā gave her a jeweled lion-throne. In the meantime, O Sage, a four-faced man emerged from the navel-lotus of Padmanābha along with his wife.
Holding a water-pot, glorious, an ascetic and the best among the wise,
the four-faced one, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, praised him.
She was possessed of beautiful teeth, lovely, most excellent, and radiant like a hundred moons.
Wearing garments as pure as fire and adorned with jewel ornaments, she—
praised indeed as the cause of all— sat joyfully with her Lord before Kṛṣṇa upon a beautiful jeweled throne. (82–83)
In that interval, Kṛṣṇa became manifest in two forms:
the left half was Mahādeva, and the right was the Lord of the Gopīs.
He resembled pure crystal and possessed the brilliance of a hundred million suns.
Hara wields the trident and the paṭṭiśa, and wears a tiger skin;
he is the Supreme One, possessing the luster of molten gold and bearing a mass of matted locks.
His limbs are adorned with ashes, he is smiling, and he has the moon as his crest-jewel. (86)
Naked, blue-throated, and adorned with ornaments of serpents,
he held a well-refined garland of jewels in his right hand;
with his five faces, he was chanting the eternal Brahma-light.
[He meditated upon] Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is truth, the Supreme Self, the Lord,
the cause of all causes, the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious,
the supreme remover of birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and fear. 88–89.

Having praised that Death of deaths, he who was born under the name Mṛtyuñjaya sat upon a beautiful jeweled throne in front of Hari. (90) Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Origin of the God and the Goddess," in the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then that cosmic egg remained in those waters for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Thereafter, at its own time, it suddenly became twofold in form. (1)
In the midst of that [water] was a single infant, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns;
for a moment he cried out piteously, that child being tormented by hunger,
abandoned by his father and mother, and without refuge in the middle of the water.
He who is the lord of many world-systems, yet perceives what is above as if he were without a protector—
he is the deity named Mahāvirāṭ, the grossest of the gross.
Just as an atom is subtler than the subtle, so too is he greater than the gross.

This Mahāviṣṇu, the lord of the gods, is a sixteenth part of the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self; he is the support of innumerable universes, and within each and every pore of his skin reside all the worlds in their entirety. (5)
Even today, Kṛṣṇa is indeed not able to state their number.
Just as there is never a number for the dust particles of the entire universe,
so too no number exists for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
In this manner, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others exist in every universe.

That which extends from the netherworld (pātāla) up to the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is proclaimed as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). Above that is Vaikuṇṭha, which lies entirely outside the cosmic egg.
And he is eternal and of the nature of truth, just like Nārāyaṇa.
Fifty crores of yojanas above that is Goloka;
it is eternal and of the nature of truth, and this [Goloka] is just like Kṛṣṇa.
The earth, measuring seven continents and joined by seven oceans,
contains forty-nine subcontinents and is endowed with innumerable forests.
Above, there are the seven celestial worlds, including the world of Brahmā.
And likewise the seven netherworlds (pātālas) below, as well as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Above the earth are Bhūrloka, and beyond that Bhuvarloka;
after that is Svarloka, then Maharloka, and then Jana[loka]. (12–13)
Beyond that is the world of heat (Tapoloka), and beyond that is Satyaloka.
Beyond that is Brahmaloka, fashioned from molten gold.
Thus, everything—both external and internal—is artificial.
Upon its destruction, O Nārada, there is the destruction of all things indeed.
The entire collection of the universe is impermanent, like a bubble on the water.
Eternal, true, and forever uncreated are Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha. (16–19)
And in every single pore of his, a cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is certainly established.
Even Kṛṣṇa does not know their number—what then to say of anyone else?
Within each and every cosmic egg, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
O son, the number of gods everywhere is three crores;

likewise the lords of the quarters, the guardians of the directions, the lunar mansions, the planets and so forth, the four castes on earth, and below them the nagas, along with all things moving and unmoving. (18–19)
Then, in the course of time, that Virāj, looking upward again and again,
saw no other infant and nothing else at all; being empty and utterly alone,
he fell into anxiety, and overcome by hunger, he wept repeatedly.
Having attained that knowledge, he then meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
Thereupon, right there, he beheld the eternal Brahman-light—
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, two-armed, and clad in yellow garments.
Smiling, with the flute in his hand, and bestowing grace upon his devotees,
the Child laughed joyfully upon seeing his father, the Lord.
The Lord of boons, being pleased, granted him a boon appropriate for the occasion.
"O child, remain until the dissolution, equal to me, endowed with knowledge, free from hunger and thirst,
dwelling within the countless cosmic eggs;
be free from desire and fear, the bestower of boons to all, and the most excellent."
"Free from disease, death, old age, sorrow, affliction, and the like.
Having spoken thus, he whispered the six-syllabled great mantra—
the supreme limb of the Vedas— three times into his right ear.

Having bestowed the supreme mantra— which begins with the syllable *praṇava*, ends with the dative case, consists of the two syllables "Kṛṣṇa," and concludes with the fire-flame (*svāhā*), and which is desired as the remover of all obstacles—
the Lord then ordained his food.
Listen to that, O son of Brahmā; understand it, for I shall tell it to you.
(28) A devotee of Viṣṇu should indeed offer the *naivedya* in every universe.
Of the worldly Viṣṇu, there is one sixteenth part, while fifteen parts belong to this [Supreme] One. (29)
For the Self, which is devoid of qualities and most perfectly full,
there is no need whatsoever for the food offering of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever person offers whatever food offering to whichever deity, [that is for that deity].
He eats all of that, yet it becomes whole again through the glance of Lakṣmī.
Having granted him that excellent mantra, the Lord spoke to him once more: "What other boon do you desire? Tell me that, and I shall grant it to you. (31–32)
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, the great Virāṭ spoke to him; there, the child, though lacking teeth, spoke words appropriate to the occasion. Mahāvirāṭ said:
May unwavering devotion to your lotus feet be my boon—lasting throughout my entire life, whether for a single moment or for a very long time.
He who in this world is endowed with devotion to you is eternally liberated while living. (34)

One who is devoid of devotion to you is a fool; though living, he is indeed dead. Of what use is the muttering of mantras, austerity, sacrifice, or ritual worship? Of what avail are vows, fasting, or the frequenting of sacred pilgrimage sites? (35–36)
The life of a man devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa is in vain;
for he does not even regard as his own self that very soul by which he lives.
As long as the self remains within the body, it shall be endowed with power.
After he has departed, the powers do not go along, for they are not independent.
You and he, O illustrious one, are the Self of all, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
you are composed of your own will, the first of all, the eternal Brahman, the light.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the boy fell silent there.
Kṛṣṇa then uttered a reply that was sweet and beautiful to the ear.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Abide for a very long time, remaining perfectly stable; as I am, so may you become.
Even when the countless Brahmās pass away, no destruction shall befall you.
And by a portion of yourself, O son, become the Virāṭ in every cosmic egg."

And in the lotus of your navel, Brahmā shall become the creator of the universe. Furthermore, from a portion of Śiva, the eleven Rudras shall arise upon the forehead of Brahmā for the purpose of carrying out the process of creation.
Among them, Kālāgnirudra shall be the one who effects the dissolution of the universe;
and Viṣṇu, as the enjoyer of objects, shall exist through a minute portion [of my power].
By my boon, you shall always be endowed with devotion to me.
"By means of meditation, you will certainly behold me, the desirable one, eternally;
and likewise my mother, the desirable one, situated upon my chest. Having said, "I am going to the world; stay, my child," he vanished.
Having gone to heaven, he spoke to Brahmā and Śaṅkara—
the creator capable of creating and the destroyer— at that very moment.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Go, my child, to create the creation; become one born from the navel-lotus of the Great Virāṭ. Listen, O Creator, regarding the small Virāṭ within the hair-pore.
Go, my child, O Mahādeva; become one born from the forehead of Brahmā."
"And by a portion of yourself, O illustrious one, perform penance for a very long time.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds, the son of Brahmā, ceased speaking;
and having bowed to him, Brahmā departed, as did Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness.
Within the pore of the Great Virāṭ, in the cosmic egg, the sphere, and the water,
he became the Virāṭ-kṣudra (the small Virāṭ) by means of a portion of the Virāṭ;
he was dark-complexioned, youthful, clad in yellow garments, reclining upon a bed of water.
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, Janārdana assumed his universal form (viśvarūpa).
From the lotus at his navel, Brahmā was born, originating from that lotus. Having come into being, he wandered for a million aeons around the stalk of the lotus.

The lotus-born Grandfather reached no end to the rod of Padmanābha; he fell into anxiety regarding the lotus born from his navel. Returning once more to his own abode, he meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having meditated upon that subtle [reality] with his divine eye,
he beheld him lying upon a bed of water within the mass of the cosmic egg;
and that Supreme Lord, in whose single pore of skin the entire cosmic egg resides.
Having praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is accompanied by the cowherds and cowherdesses in Goloka, he obtained a boon from him and subsequently performed the work of creation.
The mind-born sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others, came into being.
Then the eleven Rudras are remembered as having emerged from the skull of Śiva.
And Viṣṇu became the protector at the left side of Kṣudra;
he is the four-armed Lord who makes his abode on Śvetadvīpa.
And in the navel-lotus of the Subtle One (Kṣudra), Brahmā created the universe:
heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld—the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving.
Thus, the entire universe exists within every single pore.
For every universe, there are the minor Virāṭs, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
Thus, my dear child, has this auspicious glorification of Kṛṣṇa been told—bestowing happiness, granting liberation, and being the very essence. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Universal Egg," in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
"By your grace, I have heard everything unprecedented and as sweet as nectar."
Now, O Lord, describe the expansion of the *prakṛtis*.
By whom was the worship of which performed? How was it manifested in the mortal world?
O Sage, by whom was which one worshipped, and by whom was which one praised?
The armor, the hymn of praise, the meditation, the power, and the auspicious conduct; by whom and to whom was the boon granted? You should explain that to me. (3) Nārāyaṇa said:

Ganesha’s mother, Durga, Radha, Lakshmi, Sarasvati, and Savitri—these five are remembered as Prakriti in the process of creation. She was worshipful and renowned, and her power was most wonderful. (4)
And their conduct is like nectar, the cause of all auspiciousness.
(5) O Brahmin, I shall tell you everything regarding the portions of Prakṛti, their arts, and their auspicious conduct; listen attentively. (6)
Vāṇī, Vasundharā, Gaṅgā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Maṅgalā, Caṇḍikā, Tulasī, Mānasī, Nidrā, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Dakṣiṇā—
these are equal to me in splendor, as well as in beauty and virtue. (7–8)
I shall relate their beautiful and merit-bestowing conduct in brief, as well as the beautiful account of the ripening of their past actions;
and likewise, the vast and great life-story of Durgā and Rādhā.
I shall explain that later; listen now to it briefly and in due order.
First is the worship of Sarasvatī, established by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by whose grace, O best of sages, even a fool becomes a scholar. (10–11)

When the goddess appeared from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa’s wife, she, a lustful woman capable of assuming any form at will, desired Kṛṣṇa out of passion. And he, the omniscient one, perceiving her intention, [addressed] the mother of all.
He spoke to her words that were beneficial, true, and bringing happiness in the end.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O virtuous lady, worship Nārāyaṇa, who is a portion of Me and possesses four arms."
A youth, beautiful and endowed with all virtues, equal to me;
a granter of desires to those longing women, fulfilling their every wish; possessing the loveliness of ten million Kandarpas, he surpassed the God of Love in his playfulness. (14–15)
"O beloved, if you wish to remain here after making me your lover, [know that] Rādhā is more powerful than you; no good will come to you.
For whoever is stronger than another is capable of protecting anyone other than himself. (16)
How can one bring others to perfection if one is oneself not self-mastered? (17) I am the Lord of all and the teacher of all, yet I am unable to win over Rādhā.
She is equal to me in splendor, and equal to me in beauty and in virtue. (18)
She is the goddess presiding over the vital breaths; who is capable of abandoning those very breaths?
And where, or for whom, is there anyone dearer than life itself?
(19) O blessed lady, go to Vaikuṇṭha; it shall be well with you.
Making that husband your lord, rejoice for a very long time in happiness.
Indeed, free from greed, delusion, lust, anger, and violence, you shall be equal to Lakṣmī in splendor, beauty, and virtue. (20–21)
Together with her, you shall spend your time happily in love;
your husband will treat both of you with equal respect.
Filled with joy, he will offer you great honor throughout all the worlds.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, O beautiful one, during the commencement of studies,
humans, Manus, gods, lords of sages, those seeking liberation,
the virtuous, yogins, siddhas, nāgas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras [all gather]. (23–24)
By my boon, they shall perform [the rites] in every kalpa according to the prescribed rule,
endowed with devotion, having indeed offered the sixteen types of service (upacāra),
according to the procedure declared in the Kāṇva Śākhā, through meditation and hymn of praise.
Those who have conquered their senses and are self-restrained will place a golden pill, anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste, inside a book or even a jar;
they will then take that armor upon their neck or their right arm. (26–27)
"And the learned shall recite [this] at the time of worship, once the deity has been worshipped.

Ananta, Dharma, the lords of sages such as Sanaka and others,

Sarasvatī was eternally worshipped by all these worlds. (29–30)
Nārada said:
[Tell me] the procedure for worship, hymns of praise, meditation, and the desired armor;
as well as the food offerings used in worship, flowers, sandalwood paste, and so forth. (31)
"Speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas; my curiosity to hear it increases constantly at this moment. What is this that is so beautiful to the ear? (32) Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Sarasvatī, the Mother of the World, as set forth in the Kāṇva Śākhā, together with the ritual injunctions. [This should be performed] on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, or on the day one begins one's formal studies. (33)
Having practiced self-restraint on the preceding day, one should remain disciplined and pure there.
Having bathed and performed the daily rites, one should devoutly establish a water-pot and worship the six deities with offerings of food and other gifts.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā,
and being self-restrained, he should then worship his chosen deity in front [of the vessel],
after the wise practitioner has meditated upon it with the meditation that will be described, within the external jar.
Having meditated thus, the observer of the vow should again worship her with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Whatever food offerings (naivedya) are prescribed in the Veda for use in worship, I shall now describe some of them according to what has been studied and according to tradition. (37–38)
Fresh butter, curd, milk, parched grain, sesame balls,
sugarcane, sugarcane juice, white-colored ripe molasses,
honey, the svastika design, sugar, and unbroken grains of white rice. (39)
Parched rice from unhusked white grain, white sweetmeats (modaka),
along with sacrificial side-dishes (vyañjana) prepared with ghee and rock salt,
as well as cakes made from the flour of barley and wheat, seasoned with ghee. (40–41)
Flour-cakes, even those of the *svastika* variety, and ripe *rambhā* fruits;
milk-rice with ghee, and sweetmeats comparable to nectar;
coconut, its water, its kernel, and fresh ginger. (42)
A ripe mango fruit, a beautiful bilva fruit, and a jujube fruit;
a ripe fruit produced in the proper season and place, white and well-prepared;
fragrant white flowers, and white sandalwood rich in scent.
A new white garment, a most enchanting conch shell,
a garland of white flowers, ornaments such as pearls and diamonds,
whatever is seen or heard that is praised in meditation and beautiful to the ear— [all these should be employed]. 44.
Understand that, O highly fortunate one, which is the cause for shattering delusion:
Sarasvatī, white in color, smiling, and most enchanting; her form endowed with full splendor, graced by the radiance of ten million moons. (45–46)
Wearing garments as pure as fire, smiling and most enchanting,
adorned with excellent ornaments inlaid with the finest gems,
she was well-worshipped by the hosts of gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (47)
I worship with devotion her who is worshipped by the lords of sages and by men of discernment.

Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the armor (kavaca) that grants all desires;

It was spoken by Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Rāsa, the all-pervading Master of the Rāsa, in the forest of Vṛndāvana in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance itself:
"It is most secret, supreme, and equal to the wish-fulfilling tree. (63)
It is endowed with collections of wondrous mantras never heard before.

Śātātapa, Saṃvarta, Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara,

Oṃ Hrīṃ, Svāhā to Sarasvatī; may she protect my head from all sides.

Oṃ! May the goddess presiding over passion always protect all my limbs.

Svāhā to her who dwells on the tips of the poets’ tongues; may she protect me in the northwest.

Oṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in all scriptures; may she protect me always in the northeast.
Oṃ, svāhā to her who is worshipped by all; may she protect me always above. Aiṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in the book; may she protect me always below.
Oṃ, svāhā to her whose form is the seed-syllable of the book; may she protect me from all sides.
(85) Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you this entire collection of mantras.

Formerly, on Mount Gandhamādana, this was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
Out of affection for you, I have related it; it must not be told to anyone.
Having duly honored the Guru with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste, [one should listen].
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, the wise one should wear the armor (*kavaca*).
By merely reciting it five hundred thousand times, the armor becomes perfected.
If one possesses the perfected armor, he shall become equal to Bṛhaspati.
One shall become a great orator, a lord of poets, and a conqueror of the three worlds;
by the power of this armor, one is able to conquer everything.
O Sage, this armor, as declared in the Kāṇva recension, has been told to you.
The hymn of praise, the ritual of worship, meditation, and likewise salutation.

Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen to the hymn of praise to the Goddess of Speech, which grants all desires—
the very hymn with which the great sage Yājñavalkya formerly propitiated her.
Due to his teacher’s curse, that sage had indeed become one whose knowledge was destroyed.
Then, afflicted by grief, he went to the merit-bestowing abode of Ravi.
Having reached Koṇārka, where the Sun was within the range of his vision,
he praised the Sun with penance and wept again and again out of sorrow.
The Lord Sūrya taught him the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
He said, "Praise Vāgdevī with devotion for the sake of memory.
Having spoken thus to him, that protector of the distressed vanished from sight.
Having bathed, the sage, with his neck bowed low in devotion, offered praise:
Yājñavalkya said:
"O Mother of the World, have mercy upon me, whose splendor has thus been destroyed."
I am deprived of memory due to the curse of my guru, bereft of knowledge, and distressed.
O Goddess presiding over learning, grant me knowledge, grant me memory, and grant me wisdom!
Grant me stability, poetic skill, and the power to awaken my disciples.
And [grant] the power to compose treatises, a well-established good disciple,
eloquence in the assembly of the virtuous, and auspicious capacity for critical inquiry;
restore everything that has been lost through the power of fate, making it new again and again.

Just as the Blessed One produces a sprout through his yogic power (yogamāyā), so be it. Salutations again and again to that Vāṇī, who is the supreme light, whose nature is Brahman, who is eternal, and who is the presiding deity of all knowledge.

Salutations again and again to that Sarasvatī, the presiding deity of knowledge, without whom the entire world is perpetually as if dead while living; salutations again and again to her, without whom the entire world is always like one who is mute or insane. (11)
Salutations again and again to Vāṇī, the goddess who presides over speech.
Salutations again and again to Akṣarā, the goddess who presides over phonemes, who resembles snow, sandalwood, the kunda flower, the moon, the kumuda lily, and the lotus. 12–13.
And that which is the very locus of the visarga, the bindu, and the mātrās—in this way you are praised by the virtuous; salutations again and again to you, the mother of the Bhārata!
Without whom one is unable to perform the calculation of numbers here.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess whose nature is time and number.

Salutations again and again to her whose nature is the power of memory, the power of knowledge, and the power of intellect; and salutations to her who is the power of intuition and creative imagination.
