Having heard the Purāṇa-sūtra, that Vyāsa, born from a portion of Kṛṣṇa, attained stainless knowledge which is the cause of destroying negligence. He served you and meditated upon you for a hundred years at Puṣkara.
Then, having received a boon from you, he indeed became the lord of poets (Kavīndra).

For a thousand divine years, he meditated upon you at Puṣkara.

he spoke the science of grammar and its meaning to the Lord of the Gods (Sureśvara). And those disciples who were taught by him, and those lords of sages by whom it was studied— ‖ 28 ‖
And they proceed, O Goddess of the Gods, having fully reflected upon you.
You are praised and worshipped by the lords of sages and men,
as well as by the lords of the Daityas and the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
"Even one with a thousand mouths, five faces, or four faces would become stupefied;

Whoever, with self-restraint, recites this hymn to Vāṇī composed by Yājñavalkya,
shall become a lord of poets, a great orator, and equal to Bṛhaspati.
Even one who is a great fool or of dull intellect, if he recites it for one year, [shall attain the same].
"He shall certainly become wise, intelligent, and a true poet.

by the curse of Gaṅgā, she became a river in Bhārata through a portion [of herself] due to a quarrel.
She is the bestower of merit, the mother of merit, and the very embodiment of holy pilgrimage sites.
O Sage, this state is to be cultivated by the meritorious; it belongs to the meritorious.

Those men on earth who have gone to the waters of the Sarasvatī at Jñāna attain a long-lasting residence in Vaikuṇṭha in the assembly of Hari.
Even one who has committed sins in Bhārata, by merely bathing there effortlessly, [is purified].
One is liberated from all sins and shall dwell for a long time in the world of Viṣṇu.
[This occurs] on the fourteenth day, the full moon, the Akṣaya day, at the end of the day (the new moon),
during an eclipse, at the Vyatīpāta yoga, or on any other auspicious day.
He who bathes even incidentally, whether with indifference or with faith,

And he who recites the Sarasvatī mantra for one month [attains the same].
He shall become a great fool and a lord among poets; of this there is no doubt.
(8) That man who, having bathed daily in the waters of the Sarasvatī, shaves his head, that human being does not enter a womb again. (9)
Thus has been told this brief glorification of the qualities of Bhāratī, which bestows happiness, liberation, and essence. What more do you wish to hear?
Sauti said:
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, Nārada, the best of sages,

(11) Nārada said:

How did the goddess Sarasvatī, through the curse of Gaṅgā and by means of a mere quarrel, become a merit-bestowing river in Bhārata even in her partial incarnation? My curiosity increases at hearing this essence of the Vedas.

We are never satiated with the nectar of your stories; by what could one ever be satiated in matters of the highest good? How did she curse Gaṅgā, who is honored by all, who is peaceful, whose nature is pure goodness (*sattva*), and who always bestows merit upon men? (13–14)
"You ought to explain to me that cause of the dispute between those two radiant women, which is so beautiful to hear and extremely rare even among the Purāṇas.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Nārada, I shall tell you this ancient tale,
by the mere remembrance of which one is liberated from all sins.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Gaṅgā— these three are the wives of Hari as well.
Out of love, they all remain constantly in the presence of Hari.
Once, Gaṅgā cast a glance at the face of Viṣṇu—smiling, full of desire, and with repeated sidelong glances. (17–18)
The All-pervading Lord, beholding her face, laughed joyfully for a moment.
Seeing that, Lakṣmī showed forbearance, but Sarasvatī did not;
rather, Padmā, whose nature is goodness (*sattva*), spoke to her with a smile.
Overcome by anger, that speech did not become calm.
With blood-red face and blood-red eyes, trembling with the force of her rage and her lower lip constantly quivering, she spoke to Gaṅgā, her husband. (20–21)
Sarasvatī said:
"A virtuous and most excellent man maintains an attitude of equanimity toward all the wives of his husband, whereas for a wicked man, it is the opposite. (22)
O Gadādhara, I have learned that your extraordinary good fortune resides in Gaṅgā, and it is equal in Kamalā; O Lord, there is nothing at all in me.
Furthermore, the affection between Gaṅgā and Padmā is highly esteemed.
Because of that, the beloved of Hari committed this reversal:
"What is the use of life for me, unfortunate as I am, right here now?
The life of her who is deprived of her husband's love is fruitless. (24–25)
"Those wise men who claim that you, the Lord of All, are of the nature of *sattva*—they are fools; they do not know the Vedas, nor do they understand your true intent.
Having heard these words of Sarasvatī and seeing her filled with anger, [he spoke].
Having reflected thus in his mind, he went out from the assembly hall.
(27) When Nārāyaṇa had departed, Gaṅgā, presided over by Passion, spoke these words in anger—words unbearable to hear. (28)
O shameless and lustful woman, why do you display pride toward your master? Do you wish to proclaim his excessive good fortune?
Today, in the presence of Hari, I shall cause you to suffer the loss of your honor.
"What will your lover do for you, O beloved of my lover?
Having spoken thus, Padmā, the virtuous one residing in the Middle Country, restrained Gaṅgā as she was raising her hair in a desire to seize it.
The virtuous Vāṇī, filled with great anger, cursed that Padmā:
"Without a doubt, you shall become a tree and a river, since, having seen something contrary [to my will], you did not speak out. (32)
You stand in the midst of the assembly like a tree, like a river.
Having heard the curse, that goddess neither cursed nor became angry;
she remained right there in distress, holding her speech in her hand.
Seeing her so excessively arrogant, Gaṅgā, her face quivering with anger, spoke to that lotus-eyed goddess Padmā. Gaṅgā said:
"Abandon that most terrible one; what will she do to me, O Padma?
This goddess, the presiding deity of speech, is fond of quarreling.
Whatever her fitness may be, and whatever her power indeed—"
"O Sudurmukhā, let her do so and engage in debate with me.
Let her announce what my own strength is and what my power is. For let everyone truly know the majesty and prowess of both of us. (37–38)
Having spoken thus, that goddess pronounced a curse upon Vāṇī:
"May she who cursed you out of anger become a river;
may she go down to the mortal world, to where the sinners dwell. (39)
"In the Kali age, you will undoubtedly receive a share of their sin.
Having heard these words, Sarasvatī cursed her:
"You yourself shall go to the earth, and you shall receive the sin of a sinner."
In the meantime, the Blessed One arrived there,
four-armed and accompanied by four four-armed attendants;
holding Sarasvatī by the hand, he placed her upon his chest.
The omniscient one awakened the ancient, all-encompassing knowledge.
Having heard their secret concerning the curse and the quarrel,
the omnipresent Lord spoke these timely words to those who were distressed.
The Blessed Lord said: "O auspicious Lakṣmī, go with a portion of yourself to the house of Dharmadhvaja;
you shall become his daughter on earth, born not from a womb. (49)
Right there, through the fault of fate, you shall attain the state of a tree;
having become the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa, who is indeed a portion of myself— an Asura—
you will thereafter become my wife, without a doubt.

O fair-faced one, go quickly to Bhārata as a river by a portion of yourself; you shall be known by the name Tulasī, the purifier of the three worlds, and due to the curse of Bhāratī, become Padmāvatī in Bhārata. (47–48)
O Gaṅgā, you shall later go there with a portion of yourself as the purifier of the universe,
for the burning away of the sins of embodied beings in Bhārata due to the curse of Bhāratī;
you were brought there by that most difficult penance of Bhagīratha.
"By name Bhāgīrathī, you shall become purified upon the surface of the earth.
O Goddess of the Suras, by my command, become the wife of the ocean, who is a portion of myself,
and the wife of King Śantanu, who is a minute fraction of me."
"O Bhāratī, by a portion [of yourself] go to Bhārata due to the curse of the Gaṅgā;
experience the fruit of this quarrel together with your two co-wives, O Acyutā, and you yourself become the beloved wife of Brahmā in the abode of Brahmā. (52)
"Let Gaṅgā go to the abode of Śiva; let Padmā remain here.
She is peaceful, free from anger, my devotee, and of my own nature.
She is a great virtuous woman, highly fortunate, well-behaved, and a follower of dharma. (93–94)
By a portion of that [divine power], in every universe there are women who are entirely righteous, devoted to their husbands,
peaceful in nature, and of excellent character.
There are three wives, three brothers-in-law, and three servants who are kinsmen.
Surely these are contrary to the Vedas, for they do not bestow auspiciousness.
(56) For those householders in whose home the woman acts like a man, and the man is under the control of the woman, their birth is indeed fruitless and inauspicious at every step. (57)
He whose wife is foul-mouthed, foul in her conduct, and fond of quarreling must go to the forest; for the great forest is better than one's home.
Furthermore, there is the attainment of people, places, and ancient cities.
There, as well as in their own homes, that [pleasure] is not easily obtained by them at all times. Indeed, it is better to dwell in fire or to find comfort in the presence of predatory beasts;
even more painful than those for men is certainly the proximity of a wicked woman.

O fair-faced one, for men, the flame of disease or the flame of poison is better than the flame from the mouths of wicked women; it exceeds even death [in its harm]. (61) Furthermore, the life of a man conquered by a woman in this world is certainly fruitless.
Whatever action one performs during the day, one shall not partake of its fruit.
Such a person is censured everywhere in this world and shall go to hell in the next;
he who is devoid of fame and renown is indeed dead even while living. (62–63)
For many co-wives, a happy state does not exist in one place.
A man with a single wife is happy; one with many wives is never so.
Go, Gaṅgā, to the abode of Śiva; go, Sarasvatī, to the abode of Brahmā.
Let the lotus-dwelling Lakṣmī, who is of excellent character, abide here within my body.
For him whose wife is easy to manage, virtuous, and devoted to her husband,
there is the happiness of heaven in this world, and both merit and liberation in the next.
"He whose wife is devoted to her husband is liberated, pure, and happy;
whereas he whose husband is ill-behaved is as good as dead while living, impure, and miserable.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the Lord of the worlds became silent.
The goddesses wept most bitterly, embracing one another;
and having all observed this, they spoke in turn to the Lord, trembling with both grief and fear, their eyes filled with tears. (68–69)
Sarasvatī said:
"O Lord, grant an expiation that purifies the birth of this wicked woman.
Abandoned by their virtuous husbands, where can such women live? (70)
"I shall certainly cast off my body through yoga in Bhārata;
it is certain that one who has reached such great height ought to fall.
Ganga said:
"O Lord of the World, for what offense have I been abandoned by you?
I shall give up my life; let him who kills an innocent woman receive the fruit of that act.
May he who abandons an innocent wife in this world [suffer the same fate]. (72)
"He goes to hell for an eon; what [fault] of yours is there, O Lord of All?
Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord, you are the very embodiment of goodness (sattva); how, alas, can there be anger in you?"
Grant us your grace, for forgiveness from the Lord is supreme.
(74) If I shall go to Bhārata with a portion of my self due to the curse of Sarasvatī, how long will my stay there be, and when shall I behold your feet? (75)
"Sinners will transfer their sin to me through bathing and immersion;
by what means shall I be liberated from that and come to your abode?
[I shall do so] as a digit in the form of Tulasī, the virtuous daughter of Dharmadhvaja."
"O Acyuta, having become what, shall I ever obtain your lotus feet?
I shall become a tree and its presiding deity;
tell me, O ocean of mercy, when will you deliver me? (77-78)
If Gaṅgā should go to Bhārata due to the curse of Sarasvatī,
when, freed from that curse and from sin, will she attain you?
If Vāṇī should go to Bhārata by the curse of Gaṅgā...
"When shall she, released from the curse, attain your state?
O Lord, you speak of going to that speech, to the abode of Brahmā, to the Gaṅgā, or to the temple of Śiva; therefore, forgive those words of yours."
Having spoken thus, Kamalā took hold of her beloved’s feet and bowed;
encircling them with her beautiful hair, she wept again and again.
Then Padmanābha, placing that radiance upon his own chest, spoke to her.
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, he bestows grace upon his devotees.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Queen of the Gods, I shall carry out your word and my own word as well."
And I shall bring about equality; listen now to that very sequence:
let Sarasvatī go to Bhārata in the form of a river by means of one part;
let half a portion remain in the abode of Brahmā, while she herself shall abide in my own home. (84–85)
"Led by Bhagīratha, that Gaṅgā shall go to Bhārata;
let her remain in my own abode to purify the three worlds. There she alone shall attain the difficult-to-attain crest of the Moon-crested Lord. (86)
Therefore, though already pure by nature, she shall become exceedingly pure.
O lotus-born one, go to Bhārata with a sixteenth part of a sixteenth part of yourself, taking the form of the river Padmāvatī and the Tulasī tree. (87–88)
When five thousand years of the Kali age have passed, your liberation shall occur;
you rivers will come once again to my abode.
For all embodied beings, even calamity can become the cause of prosperity.
In this world, for whom can there be greatness without adversity?
(90) But for the virtuous who worship my mantra, by bathing and immersing themselves [in this lake], there shall be your liberation from the sin caused by touching a sinner. (91)
O beautiful one, whatever innumerable sacred fords (tīrthas) exist upon the earth shall become purified by the touch and sight of my devotees; indeed, O virtuous lady,
my devotees who worship my mantra wander throughout Bhārata.
To purify Bhārata and the most sacred earth,
wherever my devotees reside and wash their feet, that place shall certainly become a great tīrtha and supremely pure. (93–94)
The killer of a woman, the killer of a cow, the ungrateful, the killer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
by the touch and sight of my devotee, they become purified and liberated while still alive (jīvanmukta).
Even one who neglects the Ekādaśī fast, omits the Sandhyā prayers, or is an atheist [is likewise purified].
One who drives an ox-cart becomes purified by the touch and sight of my devotee.
(96) A sword-seller, an ink-seller, a washerman, and one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras—such a person becomes purified by the touch and sight of my devotee. (97)
A betrayer of trust, a slayer of friends, a giver of false testimony,
and a misappropriator of deposits— such a person becomes purified by the touch and sight of my devotee.
(98) One burdened by debt, a usurer, one born of an adulterer, and the husband of an unchaste woman— [are likewise purified].
Even the son of a prostitute is purified by the touch and sight of my devotee.
(99) Even a Śūdra cook, a Devala, or a village priest who has not received initiation becomes pure through the touch and sight of my devotee. (100)

Even one who has killed an *aśvattha* tree, or one who reviles my devotees, or one who eats food that has not been offered—such a person is purified by the sight of my devotee. [Likewise, one who has slain] mother, father, wife, brother, son, or daughter... 101.
O Nārada, he who does not support his guru’s family, his sister, a kinsman of low lineage,
and likewise his mother-in-law and father-in-law,
is a perpetrator of great sins; yet he is purified by the sight and touch of my devotee.
One who steals the property of the gods, one who steals the property of Brahmins,
a seller of lac, iron, and mercury, as well as one who sells his own daughter—
these are great sinners (mahāpātakin), as are those who burn the corpses of Śūdras. (104)
"May these [beings] become purified by the touch and sight of my devotees.
Lakṣmī said:
"O you who bestow grace upon your devotees, tell me the characteristics of those devotees."
By the mere sight or touch of whom even the lowest of men are instantly purified—
[those who are] devoid of devotion to Hari, possessed of great egoism,
devoted to self-praise, rogues, deceitful, and indeed revilers of the virtuous. (106–107)
All sacred fords are purified by bathing and immersion in them;
by the dust of their feet the earth is sanctified, and by the water used for washing their feet. Even the gods long for the sight and touch of them in Bhārata-varṣa.
The supreme gain for all is the company of Vaiṣṇavas. (109) For holy places are not merely made of water, nor are gods made of clay or stone;
those [latter] purify only after a long time, whereas devotees of Viṣṇu purify in an instant—how wonderful! (110)
Sauti said: Having heard the words of Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Lakṣmī, smiling, began to explain the hidden truth to the best of sages. 111.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, the characteristics of devotees—which are hidden in the Vedas and Purāṇas, which are meritorious in nature, destroyers of sin, bestowers of happiness, and granters of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—[shall now be told]. (112)
The essence must be kept secret and should not be spoken of to the wicked.
Listen as I tell you of you, who are pure and equal to my own life-breath.
That supreme Viṣṇu-mantra which enters the ear from the mouth of a Guru—
They declare that he who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences is the most excellent of men and a vessel of purity.
By the mere birth of such a person, a hundred ancestors before him are purified;
whether situated in heaven or in hell, they attain liberation at that very moment. (114–115)
By whomever birth has been obtained, or in whatever beings,
those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and purified go at the time of death to the abode of Hari.
One who is endowed with devotion to me, intent on my worship, and possessed of my qualities—
He is constantly praising my virtues and is perpetually absorbed in me.
(117) Merely by hearing of my qualities, he becomes filled with bliss and his hair stands on end;
with a faltering voice and tearful eyes, he even forgets his own self. (118)

They do not desire happiness, liberation, or the fourfold states such as *sālokya*; nor do they desire the state of Brahmā, immortality, or even the sovereignty of Indra, the status of Manu, or divinity—so difficult to attain—all for the sake of my service. (119)
He does not desire even in a dream the enjoyment of the kingdom of heaven and other such things. (120) The cosmic eggs perish, as do the gods beginning with Brahmā;
yet my devotee, endowed with auspicious devotion, is never destroyed. (121)
"Devotees wander throughout Bhārata after having obtained this most difficult birth;
they too go [to the supreme state] after purifying the earth by making my abode a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha). 122. All this has been told; O Padmā, do as is appropriate."
Having received that command, they did so, and Hari remained upon his comfortable throne.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sarasvatī," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:

Indeed, that Sarasvatī came to the field of merit in Bhārata; by the curse of Gaṅgā, she herself remained in a portion at the abode of Hari. Having gone to Bhārata as Bhāratī, she is Brāhmī, the beloved of Brahmā. (1)
She is the goddess presiding over speech, and for that reason she is celebrated as Vāṇī.
Since she is seen pervading the entire universe like [the reflection of] Hari in lakes within a stream,
she is therefore called by the name Sarasvatī.
And that river Sarasvatī is a sacred ford (tīrtha), exceedingly purifying;
she is like a blazing fire for the burning away of the sins of the wicked.
Afterwards, the auspicious Bhāgīrathī was brought to the earth by Bhagīratha.
O Nārada, she arrived there by means of a portion [of herself] due to the curse of Vāṇī.
At that very moment, the omnipresent Lord Śiva bore her upon his head at the request of the Earth,
who was unable to withstand the force.
Padmā departed as a partial incarnation (kalā), and she became the river Padmāvatī;
due to the curse of Bhāratī, she herself remained at the abode of Hari.
Then, by another partial incarnation, she took birth in Bhārata.
The daughter of Dharmadhvaja was Lakṣmī, who became renowned as Tulasī.
(8) Formerly, due to the curse of Sarasvatī, and subsequently due to the curse of Hari, she became a tree by means of a portion of herself, the purifier of the universe. (9)
Having remained in Bhārata for five thousand years of Kali,
they abandoned their river-forms and went to the abode of Śrī Hari.
All those holy places (tīrthas), with the exception of Kāśī and Vṛndāvana, [did so].
By the command of Hari, they shall go together with them to Vaikuṇṭha. Śālagrāma, the form of Hari, and Jagannātha in Bhārata departed for the abode of Hari at the end of ten thousand cycles of Kali.
The Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas, the conch-sounds, the ancestral rites (śrāddha), and the libations (tarpaṇa),
as well as the rituals prescribed in the Vedas, all proceeded together with them.
So too did the worship of Hari, the name of Hari, and the chanting of His glories and virtues.
The Vedāṅgas and the Śāstras likewise went along with them.
Purity, truth, righteousness, the Vedas, and the village deities, as well as vows, austerity, and fasting, all went along with them as well. (14–15)

All will be devoted to left-handed practices (vāmācāra) and possessed of falsehood and deceit; thereafter, worship will be devoid of Tulasī. Furthermore, all will be bereft of Ekādaśī and abandoned by dharma.
Beyond that, they will become averse to devotion to Hari;
thereafter, they will all be deceitful, cruel, hypocritical, possessed of great egoism, thieves, and violent. (17–18)
From this time forward, there will be no distinction between men and women, nor marriage, nor legal adjudication, nor the distinction between property and its owner;
all people, in every household, will be under the sway of women and will become unchaste. (19)
They constantly strike their master with threats and reproaches.
The mistress of the house and the wife are like mistresses, while the husband is the lowest of servants.
The daughters-in-law, the mother-in-law, and the father-in-law are equal to maidservants and slaves. (20–21)
In one's home, kinsmen by birth and maternal relatives are powerful;
even conversation with those related through learning does not take place.
Just as people are familiarized, so too are the kinsmen of a man. (22)
Men are incapable of performing any rites without the command of women.

(23) The determination of conduct for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras is based on birth; likewise, the twilight devotions and the sacred thread are undoubtedly lost when one's inner disposition is corrupted. (24)

In the Kali age, even the four social orders will adopt the conduct of barbarians; abandoning their own scriptures, they will study the scriptures of barbarians. The lineages of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will become servants of Śūdras. (25)
There will be cooks, washermen, and ox-drivers;
all people will be devoid of truth, and the earth will be devoid of crops. Trees will be devoid of fruit, and women will be devoid of offspring. (26)
Likewise, cows devoid of milk; milk from which butter has been extracted;
a husband and wife lacking affection; householders deprived of happiness; kings bereft of majesty; and subjects oppressed by taxes. (27–28)
Rivers, streams, ponds, caves, and the like are devoid of water;
likewise, the four castes are devoid of righteousness and merit.
Beyond that, not even a single meritorious person remains among hundreds of thousands.
Men, women, and children will become contemptible and deformed in appearance;
thereafter, there will be evil rumors and wicked paths.
Furthermore, some villages and cities will become terrifying and devoid of people. (30–31)
In villages and cities alike, there will be forests consisting of nothing but small huts and men;
all people living in those forests will be oppressed by taxes.
Crops will grow even in ponds and rivers;
fields that are currently excellent in terms of their value will become devoid of grain.
The lowly will become eminent and wealthy, endowed with strength and pride.
In the Kali age, those born of noble lineages will become degraded;

rogues will be speakers of falsehood, while the deceitful will indeed be regarded as speakers of truth. Sinners will be considered meritorious, and the uncultured will be treated as if they were truly refined.
Those who have conquered their senses and those who are licentious; unchaste women and devoted wives; ascetics and sinners; devotees of Viṣṇu and non-devotees of Viṣṇu;
those who are violent and those endowed with compassion; thieves and murderers of men. (36–37)
These rogues, wearing the garb of monks, will revile and mock [the true practitioners]. Skilled in serving spirits and other such beings, they will bring joy to the people.
These deceivers, weak in knowledge, will become objects of worship. (38)
In the Kali Yuga, men and women everywhere will be stunted in stature and afflicted by diseases;
they will have short lifespans and be burdened with old age even in their youth.
At sixteen years of age they will have grey hair, and at twenty they will appear as great elders.

A young woman of eight years who has reached puberty and becomes pregnant gives birth at the end of a year; she is possessed of old age by her sixteenth year. Among thousands, some such women are even barren in the Kali Yuga. (41)
All four castes who sell their daughters;
those intent on taking lovers of their mothers, wives, and daughters-in-law;
and those who live by taking lovers of their daughters and sisters. (42–43)
In the Kali age, there will be sellers of the names of Hari;
having themselves bestowed gifts for the sake of increasing their own fame,
they will later, after reflecting in their minds, transgress those very vows.
He will transgress everything—the conduct of the gods, the conduct of Brahman, the conduct of the teacher’s household, and whether it was given by himself or given by another.
Some will violate virgins; some will violate their mothers-in-law. (45–46)

In the Kali age, there will be some who approach their wives, some who go everywhere [without restraint], some who approach their sisters, some who approach the wives of their co-wives, and some who approach the wives of their brothers. 47.
They will commit forbidden sexual acts in every household;
abandoning their own wives, they will roam about everywhere. In the Kali age, there will be no settled rule regarding wives or husbands.
Regarding subjects, possessions, and especially villages, all will be speakers of falsehood; all will be greedy for wealth through theft;
they will be mutual destroyers, and all will be slayers of men.
The lineages of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will become sinful.
They will engage in the trade of lac, iron, juices, and salt.
Members of the Brahmin caste will drive oxen, and they will burn the corpses of Śūdras.
All of them ate the food of Śūdras, and all were devoted to Vṛṣalīs;
they abandoned the five festival days and ate on the nights of the new moon; they were devoid of the sacrificial thread and lacked both the twilight prayers and ritual purity. (53–54)
Adulteresses, usurers, childless women, procuresses,
and menstruating women will become cooks in the kitchens of Brahmins.
There will be no discernment regarding food, and especially none regarding [the purity of] wombs.
In the Kali age, all the hermitages and the people will be Mlecchas.
Thus, when the Kali has fully set in, everything will consist of Mlecchas;
trees will be the size of a hand, and humans will be the size of a thumb.
The son of the Brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas will be Kalkī;
he is a portion of a digit of Nārāyaṇa, a lord who is the strongest among the strong. With a long sword and riding upon a long horse, he will appear.
He will make the earth devoid of Mlecchas within three nights;
having made the earth free of Mlecchas, he will disappear.
And the earth will become kingless and exceedingly fierce.
The gross measure [of time] is six nights; the earth will be drenched by the downpours of rain, becoming empty of people, empty of trees, and empty of houses. And then, O Sage, twelve suns will rise.
The earth will attain dryness through their combined heat.
When the unassailable Kali age has passed and the Kṛta age has fully commenced,
Dharma, endowed with austerity and truth, will become complete.
On this earth, there were ascetic Brahmins who were most righteous and learned in the Vedas;
in every household, there were women who were devoted to their husbands and most virtuous;
and all the kings and Kṣatriyas were devoted to the Brahmins and remained true to their own duties.
The Vaiśyas were powerful, most righteous, and always devoted to meritorious deeds;
they were intent on trade, devoted to the Brahmins, and virtuous.
The Śūdras were of meritorious character, most righteous, and served the Brahmins. (65–66)
The lineages of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas were all devoted to the sacrifice of Viṣṇu;
they were all intent on the mantras of Viṣṇu, devotees of Viṣṇu, and followers of Viṣṇu.
They were knowers of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, knowers of dharma, and approached their wives only during the proper season.
For there is no trace of unrighteousness when the Kṛta Yuga is full of dharma.
Dharma is said to have three feet in the Tretā, and two feet in the Dvāpara.
When the Kali age has set in, it consists of only one foot; after that, there is the total disappearance [of dharma].
O Brahmin, just as there are seven days of the week and sixteen lunar days (tithis) are remembered;
just as there are twelve months and indeed six seasons;
two fortnights and two solstices; and a day consists of four watches (praharas). 70.

A night consists of four watches, and a month likewise consists of thirty days; know that a year is of five kinds. Learn from me the calculation of time: just as they come and go, so too does the cycle of the four ages (yugas).
When three hundred and sixty years of men have passed, along with a day and night of the gods, one *yuga* of the gods is known to those who understand the calculation of time. (73)
A Manvantara consists of seventy-one divine Yugas;
the lifespan of an Indra is proclaimed to be equal to a Manvantara.
When twenty-eight Indras have passed, one day and night of Brahmā has elapsed.
When one hundred and eight years have passed, the downfall of the Creator occurs;

this should be known as the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya), wherein the earth is no longer perceived, all worlds are submerged in water, and [the gods] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva [perish]. || 75–76 ||
All the living sages are dissolved into Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest.
Therein alone is primordial nature (prakṛti) dissolved; therefore, this is called the dissolution of nature (prākṛtika-laya).
O sage, when this natural dissolution has passed and at the fall of Brahmā—
The time of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, is but a mere blink of an eye.
In this way, all entire universes perish;
yet Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha remain, as does Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with his attendants.
The dissolution (*pralaya*) in which the entire universe is submerged in water lasts for only the duration of a single blink of an eye;
immediately following that blink, creation occurs again in its proper sequence.
(80) Thus, how many kinds of creation are there, or how many kinds of dissolution as well?
O Nārada, what man knows the number of times he has gone and returned? What man knows the number of creations, of parts, and of cosmic eggs?
And within the egg of Brahmā, what man knows the number of those beginning with Brahmā himself?
He alone is the Lord of all the cosmic eggs;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond material nature, is the Supreme Self of all.
Brahmā and the other gods are His portions, and the Great Virāṭ is a portion of Him. (83)
And a portion of Him is Virāṭ, and a small portion of him is known as Prakṛti.
He, Kṛṣṇa, has become twofold: two-armed and four-armed;
the four-armed one resides in Vaikuṇṭha, while He Himself is two-armed in Goloka.
Everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is composed of *prakṛti*.
Whatever has been created from *prakṛti* is entirely perishable.
Know that the one source of creation is the Truth, eternal and everlasting. (86)

The Supreme Brahman consists of His own will; He is untainted, beyond attributes, supreme, without limiting adjuncts, formless, yet possessing a form for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees—exceedingly beautiful and resembling a fresh rain cloud. (87–88)
He has two arms, holds a flute in his hand, wears the dress of a cowherd, and is a youth;
he is the omniscient Lord, the Supreme Self, and the one to be served by all.
The Creator Brahmā, born from the lotus and whose nature is knowledge, fashions the cosmic egg.
He is Śiva, the conqueror of death, the destroyer, and the knower of all principles (tattvas).
Through his knowledge and through his austerity, he is equal to the Great Lord;
he is endowed with great majesty, omniscient, and eternally self-existent.
All-pervading, the protector of all, the giver of all prosperity—
Viṣṇu, the glorious Lord of all, by whose knowledge one becomes the master of the universe.
And Mahāmāyā is Prakṛti, the sovereign mistress endowed with all powers.
Through the knowledge of whom, through whose austerity, through devotion to whom, and through service to whom [is this attained]?
(93) Sāvitrī is the mother of the Vedas and the presiding deity of the Vedas;
she is to be worshipped by the twice-born who know the Vedas, and [all is attained] through service to her and to sacrifice. (94)
She is the presiding goddess of all sciences, who was worshipped by the wise in ancient times; through her service, through her austerity, and through her knowledge, Sarasvatī [bestows grace],
and through her service and her austerity, she is the giver of all prosperity.
She is Mahālakṣmī, the eternal presiding deity of wealth and crops;
(96) by whose service and by whose austerity she is worshipped throughout all the worlds.
She is the presiding deity of all villages, the bestower of all prosperity. (97)
The sovereign of all, worthy of worship by all, she who obtained the Lord of All as her husband; praised by all, omniscient, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune;
born from the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa, the presiding deity of love for Kṛṣṇa. 98.
Through her love and service to Kṛṣṇa, Rādhikā attained a life dearer than Kṛṣṇa’s own,
as well as a form and fortune superior to all, along with honor, dignity,
the station upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest, and the status of his consort. (99–100)

Formerly, on the mountain Śataśṛṅga, she performed austerities for a thousand divine yugas, abstaining from food and becoming exceedingly emaciated. Seeing her— emaciated, breathless, and resembling a digit of the moon— [the gods were moved].
The all-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa, placing her upon his chest, wept out of compassion. He granted her a supreme boon, the most difficult for anyone to obtain:
"Dwell upon my chest; may you have devotion unto me. (102–103)

By good fortune, by honor, by love, and indeed by respect, you are the best to me; out of supreme affection, you are the eldest among all women. You are the most excellent and the most venerable, praised and honored by me.
"O beloved of my life, I am forever to be won over by you and yet to be constrained by you.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds then restored her consciousness and made that beloved of his life free from any rival wife.

O Sage, whatever goddesses were worshipped by whom, and whatever kind of austerity they performed, such was the fruit obtained by them. Having practiced penance for a thousand divine years on the Himalayas, [they attained their respective goals].
And Durgā, having meditated upon that state, became worthy of worship by all. Sarasvatī, having performed penance on Mount Gandhamādana for a hundred thousand divine years, became venerable to all.

Having performed penance at Puṣkara for a hundred divine yugas, Lakṣmī became the bestower of all prosperity through her service to him. Having performed penance on Malaya, Sāvitrī became worthy of worship by the twice-born.
And having meditated upon that state for sixty thousand divine years,
O Lord, Śaṅkara formerly performed austerities for a hundred *manvantaras*,
and Brahmā likewise did so with devotion for a hundred *manvantaras*.
Having performed austerities for a hundred *manvantaras*, Viṣṇu indeed became the protector; having performed austerities for a hundred *manvantaras*, Dharma indeed became worthy of worship.
And Śeṣa, O Nārada, performed austerities with devotion for one *manvantara*.
For a Manvantara, Sūrya, Śakra, Candra, and likewise Guru,
as well as Vāyu, performed penance with devotion for a hundred divine Yugas;
he thus became the life-force of all, the one worthy of worship by all, and the support of all.
Thus, by the austerity of Kṛṣṇa, all the gods were honored;
likewise, the sages, men, kings, and brahmins were honored.
In this way, I have related to you the entire Purāṇa as well as the Āgama.
"What more do you wish to hear regarding that which has been understood from the mouth of the Guru?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Yugas, the Intervals of Manvantaras, and the Qualities of the Lords," in the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
In the mere twinkling of an eye of Hari, there is indeed the fall of Brahmā.
Upon his fall, the dissolution of nature (prākṛtika-pralaya) is proclaimed. And regarding this natural dissolution, it is said that the earth is not perceived there.
"All things were submerged in water; everyone was dissolved in Hari.
Where did the earth remain when it had vanished?
And how did it manifest once again at the time of the creation's ordainment? (2–3)
How did that blessed, venerable, all-supporting Jayā come to be?
Tell me the full account of her birth, which is a cause of auspiciousness.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

The Śruti declares that in every initial creation, the birth of all beings is from Kṛṣṇa; likewise, their manifestation and disappearance occur in all dissolutions. (5) Listen now to the account of the birth of Vasudhā, the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
It destroys obstacles, is supreme, destroys great sin, and increases merit.
(6) "Aha! Some say that the earth became blessed by the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha"—hear now the opinion that contradicts this. (7)
In the past, those two, gratified by his prowess in battle, said to Viṣṇu:
"Slay us both when the earth is covered with water.
And clearly, this shall come to pass within the span of their lives.
Then, after their death, there arose fat (*medas*);
because it was said by those [sages] that she became renowned as "Medinī" (the Earth), hear their reasoning:
since she was previously washed by water and emaciated, she was subsequently nourished by fat (*medas*). (9–10)
And I shall relate that birth, which is meaningful and universally esteemed;
it was heard of old, declared by the Vedas, and taught by the mouth of Dharma at Puṣkara,
concerning the great Virāṭ body clearly situated in the water for a long time.
In time, that impurity certainly became pervasive throughout his entire body.
It entered into all the pores of those hairs,
and from that, O Sage, after a long period, the earth came into being.
She remained firm within the pits for each individual hair;
she appeared and disappeared again and again, moving back and forth.
At the time of creation, she manifested, emerging from that water.
And at the time of dissolution, having become concealed and remaining within the waters,
the earth— possessing mountains and forests,
joined by the seven oceans, and consisting of the seven continents— exists in every universe. (15)
Joined with the Himālaya and Meru mountains, and with the planets, the moon, and the sun;
likewise praised by the gods and the worlds, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
endowed with sacred pilgrimage sites, and joined with the meritorious land of Bhārata.

Consisting of golden ground and endowed with all types of fortresses, there are seven netherworlds (pātālas) beneath that; above them is the world of Brahmā, and right there also is the world of Dhruva. Indeed, the entire universe is contained therein.
Thus, indeed, all the various worlds on earth have been fashioned.
Above them are Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha, which are eternal and transcend the universe. All other worlds, whether artificial or natural, are subject to destruction.
O Brahmin, at the time of the primordial dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*) and upon the passing away of Brahmā,
he was created by Kṛṣṇa through his own self for the creation of the Mahāvirāṭ and other beings.
He remains eternally present during that dissolution along with Kaṣṭhā, Ākāśa, and Īśvara.
That goddess, the presiding deity of the earth, was worshipped by the gods,
the Manus, the sages, the brahmins, the gandharvas, and others during the Vārāha incarnation.
She is celebrated in the Vedas as the wife of Viṣṇu in his boar form.
His son was to be known as Maṅgala, and Suyaśas was the son of Maṅgala.
Nārada said:
"In what form was the Earth worshipped by the gods during the Vārāha-kalpa?"

And by the Boar, Vārāhī was [established] as the refuge of all through all [means]. O Lord, tell me the procedure for her worship, the sequence of her extraction from below, the auspiciousness even of the auspicious, and the birth of Vyāsa. (25–26)
Nārāyaṇa said:
In the Vārāha [Kalpa], Varāha was praised by Brahmā in the past;
having slain Hiraṇyākṣa, he lifted the earth from the netherworld (rasātala). || 27 ||
He placed her upon the water like a lotus leaf upon the ocean;
there, Brahmā fashioned the entire enchanting universe.
Seeing the Goddess upon that [lotus] and filled with desire, Hari, the lover, [beheld her].
The Lord, in the form of a boar, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
having prepared a delightful bed and a most enchanting image,
sported in secret day and night for a divine year.
From the touch of that blissful enjoyment, Sundarī fell into a swoon;
for even the union of the clever with the clever bestows happiness.
Due to the embrace of her body, Viṣṇu was not aware of day or night.
At the end of the rainy season, having regained his consciousness, the lustful one abandoned the amorous woman.
Indeed, he effortlessly assumed his former form as a boar;
and having meditated upon the virtuous Earth, he worshipped her with devotion. (32–33)
Having worshipped her with incense, lamps, food offerings, vermilion, ointments, garments, flowers, and oblations, Hari spoke to her. Mahāvarāha said:
O auspicious one, may you become the support of all, honored by all for the sake of well-being—

by sages, mantras, gods, siddhas, humans, and others— at the time of drawing water, releasing water, and at the commencement and entry into a house. (39) At the time of drawing water, releasing water, and at the commencement and entry into a house.

At the commencement of the construction of ponds and lakes, and during auspicious agricultural work, the gods and others will perform your worship with great zeal. Those fools who do not perform it shall go to hell. (36–37)
Vasudhā said:
"O Blessed One, at your command, I bear everything—the entire universe with its mobile and immobile beings—by mere sport, in the form of a boar. (38)
A pearl-oyster shell, an image of Hari, a Śiva-liṅga, a stone,
a conch, a lamp, a gem, a ruby, a diamond, a jewel,
a sacred thread, a flower, a book, and a Tulasī leaf. (39)
"I am unable to carry these—a rosary, a garland of flowers, camphor, gold, yellow pigment, sandalwood, and likewise water from the Śālagrāma—and I am distressed; O Blessed One, please listen. (40–41)
The Blessed Lord said:
O beautiful one, those fools who shall offer these substances to you will go to the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred divine years.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the Blessed One became silent.
By that embryo, the radiant planet Maṅgala was formed.
And by the command of Hari, they all performed worship to the Earth.
They meditated according to the path taught by Kaṇva and praised her with hymns.
They offered the food offering (naivedya) and other gifts with the root mantra.
Thus praised and honored, she became renowned throughout the three worlds.
Nārada said: What is her meditation, or what is her hymn of praise? Tell me, what is her root?
I have a great curiosity to hear that which is hidden within all the Purāṇas. (46)
Nārāyaṇa said:
In the beginning, the goddess Earth was well-worshipped by Varāha;
after that by Brahmā, and subsequently in ancient times by Pṛthu. (47)
Then, O Nārada, listen as I shall speak of the meditation, the hymn of praise, and the mantra, [as taught] by all the lords of sages, the Manus, Nārada, and others. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vāṃ vasudhāyai svāhā.
In ancient times, she was worshipped by Viṣṇu with this very mantra:

[she who] possesses the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, whose radiance is equal to a hundred moons, whose every limb is anointed with sandalwood paste, and who is adorned with all ornaments. (49–50)

I worship her who is praised by all, who is the support of jewels, whose womb is filled with jewels, who is endowed with a mine of gems, who wears garments as pure as fire, and who smiles with a gentle smile.
By this meditation, that Goddess shall indeed be worshipped by everyone.
"Listen, O best of brahmins, to this hymn of praise as it is recited in the Kaṇva Śākhā.
Viṣṇu said:
"You are the wife of the Sacrificial Boar; victory to you, O bringer of victory!"
Victorious one, unconquered one, support of victory, whose nature is victory, bestower of victory;
O Goddess, support of all, seed of all, endowed with all powers, granter of all desires, O Steadfast One, grant me all that is desired.
O you who are the abode of all crops, rich in all crops, the giver of all crops;
O time that takes away all crops, O earth whose very soul is all crops!
O auspicious one, the support of auspiciousness, the source of auspiciousness, the bestower of auspiciousness! 55.

O Auspicious One, for the sake of auspiciousness and as a portion of auspiciousness, grant me supreme auspiciousness. O Earth, you who are the sovereign treasure of all lands, the ultimate refuge of the protectors of the earth,
and the very embodiment of the pride of those who rule the land— O Vasundharā, grant me land!
Whoever recites this hymn of great merit after having fully worshipped her will become a lord of kings for ten million births. By reciting it, a person obtains the merit produced by the gift of land.
One is liberated from the sin arising from the misappropriation of what was given; there is no doubt in this matter.
(59) He will certainly be liberated from the sin of digging up water-wells or the earth;
he will certainly be liberated from the sin arising from [digging] a bad pit in another's well. (60)
One is liberated from the sin born of faith in another; there is no doubt in this matter.
Likewise, from the sin of discharging semen upon the ground or from the sin of placing lamps and such [inappropriately], the wise man is freed from that evil by reciting this hymn, O Sage.
One obtains the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices; there is no doubt about this.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Earth," in the *Pṛthivyupākhyāna* (The Narrative of the Earth) within the *Nārada-Nārāyaṇa-saṃvāda* (Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa), in the second section (*Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārada said:
The merit produced by the gift of land and the sin resulting from its seizure;
likewise, the sin of performing a *śrāddha* on another's land, as well as that born of digging a well in a bad spot;
and also the sin arising from the digging of the earth and the sowing of seeds in water-waves.
I wish to hear with effort about the sin resulting from the placement of lamps and such;
or whatever other sin arises from the earth that follows from my question—O best among those who know the Vedas, tell me the remedy for whatever exists. (2–3)
Nārāyaṇa said:
He who gives even a piece of land measuring a vitasti in Bhārata to a brahmin purified by the twilight prayers shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu. 4.

He who gives land abounding in all kinds of crops to a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are particles of dust in that land. He who gives a village, land, or grain, and he who takes them away— [the latter incurs great sin]. 5.
Both, liberated from all sins, become residents of Vaikuṇṭha.
And that virtuous person who at that time approves of the gift of land goes to Vaikuṇṭha, accompanied by his friends and kinsmen.
Whoever should seize the property granted for the sake of Brahman— whether given by himself or by another—
shall remain in the Kālasūtra hell as long as the moon and sun endure.
His sons, grandsons, and descendants shall be deprived of land and struck down by misfortune.

Deprived of happiness, he shall become poor, and in the end he goes to the Raurava hell. (9) He who, having cleared a path for cattle, gives grain [to them], remains in the Kumbhīpāka hell for a hundred divine years. (10)

He who provides a cow-pen, a pond, a path, or grain for a traveler shall remain upon the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras. He who bathes in another’s well without first removing five lumps of earth [from the bank] [incurs the same fate].

He indeed goes to hell and does not obtain the fruit of his bath. He who, driven by lust, discharges semen upon the ground in a secluded place remains in the Raurava hell for as many years as there are particles of fine dust [in that spot]. (12–13)
And that man who causes the water in a well to be churned up like waves goes to the realm of the worm-bites, and his stay there lasts for four *yugas*.
That fool who constructs a well in another's abandoned well [goes to the same state].

And the man who gives away that lotus pond when it has fallen into ruin—[he reaps] all the fruit for another; he shall go to the Taptasūrmī hell, where he remains tormented for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. (15)
And having removed the mud from another's pond, a man should cast it out;
for as many years as there are particles of dust [in that mud], he shall dwell in the world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, a man who does not offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father, the sustainer of his prosperity...
The fool who performs a *śrāddha* [offering] goes certainly to hell.
(18) He who places a lamp on the ground will be blind for seven births;
and by placing a conch shell on the ground, he shall suffer from leprosy in another life. (19)
He who places pearls, rubies, diamonds, gold,
and likewise gems upon the ground shall remain poor for seven births;
so too he who offers a stone Śivaliṅga for worship upon the earth.
For as long as a hundred *manvantaras*, he remains as a worm-eater. He who offers a hymn, a mantra, water from a stone, or a *tulasī* leaf upon the ground shall remain in hell for an entire *yuga*.

That fool who offers a rosary, a garland of flowers, camphor, or yellow pigment upon the ground certainly goes to hell. O Sage, [the same applies to] sandalwood, a rudrākṣa, or the root of kuśa grass.
Having placed [these] on the ground, one shall dwell in hell for the duration of a manvantara.
He who places a book or a sacred thread on the ground shall not have a birth in a future life within the womb of a Brahmin.
He certainly incurs a sin here equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
A sacred thread (yajñasūtra) provided with knots should be honored by all social classes.
But he who, having performed a sacrifice, does not sprinkle the ground with milk [incurs such sin].
He goes to the heated iron pillar, tormented throughout all his births.
Indeed, he who digs the earth during an earthquake or an eclipse becomes a great sinner and will certainly be deprived of his limbs in another birth. (27–28)
Because all beings dwell (*bhavana*) upon her, she is proclaimed as *Bhūmi*.

She who possesses wealth (*vasu*), jewels (*ratna*), and the earth (*dhara*), is called *Vasudhā* and *Vasundharā*. And because she was born from the thigh (*ūru*) of Hari, she is celebrated as *Urvī*.
She is Dharā, Dhatri, and Dharaṇī because she supports all beings. She is Ijyā because she sustains the sacrifice, and Kṣoṇī because she is diminished at the time of dissolution;
she goes to destruction in the Great Dissolution (Mahālaya), and for that reason she is celebrated as Kṣiti.

This earth is *Kāśyapī* because it belongs to Kaśyapa by virtue of its immovable nature; it is *Viśvambharā* because it supports the universe; and it is *Anantā* because of its infinite form, O Sage. It is *Pṛthvī* because it is the daughter of Pṛthu, and it is *Mahī* because of its vastness. (32–33)

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Earth," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
I have heard the narrative of the Earth, which is exceedingly beautiful.

O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell now the legend of the Gaṅgā. The supreme Goddess Sureśvarī, who is herself Viṣṇu’s own form and the virtuous Viṣṇupadī, descended from the curse of Bhāratī onto the land of Bhārata.
"How and in which age was she formerly requested and impelled by whom?
I wish to hear that sequence, which destroys sins, bestows merit, and is auspicious.
Nārāyaṇa said:
The illustrious Sagara, born of the solar dynasty, was the sovereign lord of kings.
He had two beautiful wives, Vaidarbhī and Śaivyā.
He was the embodiment of truth, beloved of truth, truthful in speech, and devoted to truth.
He was a knower of the investigation of truth and dharma, and he was born during the supreme Kṛtayuga.
He had one daughter and one son who was exceedingly charming;
known as Asamañja, he increased the lineage through Śaibyā. (5–6)
Another woman, desiring a son, propitiated Śaṅkara;
by the boon of Śiva, she became pregnant.
When a hundred years had passed, she gave birth to a mere lump of flesh.
Having seen that and meditated upon Śiva, she wept aloud again and again.
Then Śambhu, assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa,
approached her and divided this lump of food into sixty thousand portions.
All the sons became possessed of great strength and supreme prowess,
their bodies radiant with a splendor like that of the sun at midday in summer;
yet, by the wrathful gaze of the sage Kapila, they were reduced to ashes.
Upon hearing that, the king wept and met his death out of grief.
Asamañja performed incomparable penance for the purpose of bringing down the Gaṅgā.
Having practiced penance for a hundred thousand years, he died according to the course of time.
His son was Dilīpa; having performed austerities for a hundred thousand years for the sake of bringing the Gaṅgā, that king went to the other world.
His son was Aṃśumān, who likewise [performed penance] for the sake of bringing the Gaṅgā.
Having performed austerities for a hundred thousand years, he died according to the course of time.
His son was Bhagīratha, a highly fortunate and wise devotee of Viṣṇu,
a Vaiṣṇava who was devoted to Viṣṇu, virtuous, and free from old age and death.
Having performed austerities for a hundred thousand years for the sake of bringing the Gaṅgā,
he beheld Kṛṣṇa with a joyful countenance, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns—
two-armed, holding a flute in His hand, youthful, and dressed as a cowherd. (16)
The Supreme Self, the Lord, whose form consists of grace toward his devotees;
the Supreme Brahman, composed of His own will, the most perfect, the all-pervading;
praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, and accompanied by hosts of sages. (17–18)
Untainted, in the form of a witness, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature;
with a slight smile and a serene countenance, bestowing grace upon his devotees;
pure as fire, seated upon a parrot-throne, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (19)
Having seen this, the king praised him and bowed down again and again. Having effortlessly obtained his desired boon, which would save his lineage,
Gaṅgā arrived there upon the Supreme Soul’s mere remembrance.
Having bowed to her, he set out with his hands joined in reverence before her.
There, seeing her—who was performing a most enchanting, divine hymn of praise, her body bristling with horripilation—the Blessed One spoke to her. (22)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Sovereign Goddess, go quickly to Bhārata by virtue of the curse of Bhāratī;
by my command, purify all the sons of Sagara.
Purified by the wind of your touch, they shall go to my abode;
bearing divine forms and traveling in celestial chariots, they shall become my attendants, free from all ailment for all time. (24–25)
Having completely severed the experience of karma performed birth after birth—
whether it be various kinds of great or small sins committed by men in Bhārata—
it is heard in the Śruti that they are destroyed by the touch of the wind from the Gaṅgā.

Touching the Goddess is ten times more meritorious than seeing her. It is heard in the Śruti that by the mere act of bathing in the Mausalasnāna on an ordinary day, the sins accumulated over ten million births of men are destroyed.
Whatever sins there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others,
even those accumulated over various births and committed intentionally—
all these perish for men through the ritual bath at the Mausala-tīrtha.
Even the Vedas do not describe the merit born from bathing on a Puṇyāha day.
O Goddess, some say that its fruit is exactly as stated in the scriptures;
yet Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all others do not truly know it.
Listen, O beautiful one, to the formal resolve for the ordinary daily bath;
its merit is ten times greater than that of the *mausala* bath.
Furthermore, on the day of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*), the merit is thirty times greater still.
On the new moon day as well, the merit is equal to that; during the southern transit of the sun, it is double. From that, the merit for men is tenfold during the northern transit.
And on the full moon day of the Cāturmāsya, the merit is indeed infinite.
And on Akṣayā, the result is equal to that; this is not described in the Veda. Bathing and giving gifts during these [occasions] yield the fruit of incalculable merit.
On an ordinary day, bathing yields a hundredfold fruit through meditation.
O Goddess of the gods, likewise during the Manvantaras and at the beginnings of the Yugas;
on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, as well as on Bhīṣmāṣṭamī;
and similarly on the lunar day of Aśokāṣṭamī, and on the ninth day of Hari.
Twice that merit, which is difficult for you to attain, is found at Nandā;
and on the tenth day, which removes ten sins, the fruit is exceedingly great.
At Vāruṇī, it is equal to Nandā, and at Mahatpūrva, it is four times that.
Then, when there is one who has performed two great [deeds] before him, the merit is fourfold;
and from an ordinary bath, the merit becomes ten millionfold.
During eclipses of the moon and sun, it is remembered as being ten times that.
Even during the meritorious time of Ardhodaya, the fruit is a hundredfold;
however, for all Vaiṣṇavas, every resolve is the opposite [of this calculation].
Indeed, Vaiṣṇavas are free from attachment to fruits and are liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
They always desire love and devotion for me in all their actions.
(42) All the Vedas declare that he into whose ear the supreme Viṣṇu-mantra has entered from the mouth of a guru is a Vaiṣṇava who is liberated while living. (43)

One hundred ancestors on the paternal side, one hundred on the maternal side, and one hundred on the maternal grandfather’s side; as well as the mother, the mother’s mother, the sister, the brother, the sister’s son, and the maternal uncle. (44)
One’s mother-in-law, one’s father-in-law, the wife of a teacher, the son of a teacher,
the teacher himself, the giver of knowledge, a friend, a companion,
a servant, a disciple, as well as a maidservant and one’s subjects, when they are in the vicinity of one’s own hermitage— (45–46)
By the mere reception of the mantra, he shall uplift himself along with others;
by the mere reception of the mantra, a person becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
By his very touch, even a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) on the earth in Bhārata becomes purified.
By the mere dust of his feet, the earth is instantly purified.
This place where his water for washing the feet stands shall certainly become a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu is excrement, and water is urine. 48–49.

Indeed, the Vaiṣṇavas always eat [only] what has been offered as *naivedya*. Those men who constantly consume food offered to Viṣṇu—oh, by the mere touch of them, all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) become purified! (50)
Those men who constantly partake of the meritorious water from Viṣṇu’s feet—sins flee from them like serpents from Garuḍa;
by the mere sight of them, the three worlds are purified. (51–52)

Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus constantly protects them. Those men whose bodies are marked by horripilation from hearing my qualities, who are faltering in speech and have eyes filled with tears—they are indeed the best of Vaiṣṇavas. (53)
Those men for whom there is constant love for me even greater than for their own sons,
and who have entrusted their homes and all else to me— they are indeed the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, everything moving and unmoving is from me.
Those who know that "I alone am the Lord of all" are the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
(55) Those who know that "the countless millions of cosmic eggs, along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, dissolve into me at the time of dissolution" are the best of Vaiṣṇavas. (56)
He is the supreme embodiment of light, whose form consists of grace toward His devotees;
He is composed of His own will, devoid of material qualities, free from worldly desire, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
All things pertaining to nature have emerged from Me and are withdrawn back into Me.
"O Goddess, those men who know this are indeed the most excellent Vaiṣṇavas.
Having spoken thus before them, the Lord of Gods ceased speaking.
Then the River of the Three Paths (Gaṅgā), her neck bowed low with devotion, spoke to him.
Gaṅgā said: "O Lord, O King of Kings, although I previously went to Bhārata due to the curse of Bhāratī, I shall go now by your command and through my own ascetic power. (60)
"Whatever sins sinful men may heap upon me, by what means, O Lord, shall they be destroyed? Tell me that method.
For how long will my stay there in Bhārata be limited? (61)
O Lord of All, O Viṣṇu, when shall I go to Your supreme abode?
Whatever other desire I may have, You know it all, O Knower of All.
O Inner Self of All, O Omniscient One, O Lord, tell me the means to attain that.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Gaṅgā, O Queen of the Gods, I know all that you desire.
This Lord Rudra shall become your husband in the form of the salt ocean. (64)
The ocean is indeed a portion of me, and you are Lakṣmī herself in embodied form.
On this earth, the union of the wise with the wise is full of merit.
As for all the rivers that exist in Bhārata, beginning with the Bhāratī—
Your good fortune lies in them alone, as does that of the Salt Ocean in the solar region.
From this day forward, O Goddess of gods, for five thousand years of Kali,
your residence on the earth shall be in Bhārata by virtue of a curse.
"You shall eternally enjoy secret dalliance with the Ocean.
You alone, O Goddess, are the connoisseur united with the Lord of Connoisseurs (Śiva).
They gratify you with the hymn composed by Bhagīratha."
All the people residing in Bhārata will worship you with devotion. Having meditated upon you through the meditation taught by Kauthuma, they shall offer worship.
Whoever praises you and bows down to you daily shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whoever should say "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," even if accompanied by hundreds of people,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. Whatever sin shall belong to those thousands of sinners through bathing and other acts [there], [that too is removed].

Indeed, at the mere sight of my devotee, [that sin] perishes right then and there. Even that evil which belongs to thousands of sinners through the touch of their corpses is destroyed by the bathing of one who worships my mantra. (72–73)
"O auspicious Gaṅgā, wherever there may be the chanting of the qualities of my name,
you shall establish your presence right there for the sake of liberation from sin,
together with the most excellent rivers such as the Sarasvatī and others. (74)
That very place shall instantly become a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) where my virtues are proclaimed;
by the mere touch of its dust, even a sinner becomes purified.
For as many years as there are particles of dust, he shall dwell eternally in Vaikuṇṭha.
But those who, through knowledge and devotion toward you, cast off their lives while preceded by the remembrance of my name, go to the abode of Hari;
they shall become the foremost attendants of Hari for a long time. (77)
Those men shall witness the countless natural dissolution.
By the great merit of the deceased, one should place that corpse upon you;
he goes to Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the bones remain upon you.
Then, having manifested a bodily array and fed him his own ritual food,
I grant him a form identical to my own and make him an attendant.
But if an ignorant person should give up their life through contact with my water, [he too shall attain the same].
To him I grant the state of having the same form (sārūpya) and I make him an attendant (pārṣada).
Or, if he should give up his life elsewhere while preceded by the remembrance of your name,
to him I grant the state of residing in the same world (sālokya), which lasts until the end of countless dissolutions (pralaya).
Or else, one may give up one's life elsewhere while preceded by the recollection of My name;
to him I grant residence in the same world [as Mine] for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Whether death occurs at a sacred ford or not a sacred ford, there is no distinction whatsoever.
For he is indeed capable of purifying the three worlds with ease, for those who worship my mantra and constantly partake of the offered oblations (naivedya).
And by means of a vehicle made of the essence of the finest jewels, he proceeds to that world.
O auspicious lady, those who are kinsmen of My devotees are all of meritorious intellect;
they go by means of a jeweled vehicle to Goloka, which is very difficult to attain.
This applies to whoever dies anywhere, whether with knowledge or without knowledge, O virtuous one. (86)
"And they are liberated while living and purified merely by the proximity of a devotee.
Having said this to her, Śrī Hari spoke to Bhagīratha:
"Praise this Gaṅgā with devotion and perform worship now."
Bhagīratha praised and worshipped her with devotion,
again and again, through meditation and by means of the hymn proclaimed by Kauthuma.
Then he prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and the Lord.
Having caused Bhagīratha to behold Gaṅgā, Hari vanished;
Nārada said:
"By what hymn, by what meditation, and by what sequence of worship [is He to be attained]?"
The king performed worship; speak, O best among those who know the Vedas!
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having bathed, performed his daily rites, and put on two clean garments...
Having washed his feet and sipped water, the man, self-restrained and filled with devotion,
should worship Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā;
thus purified, he becomes qualified for the worship.
A person should worship Gaṇeśa for the destruction of obstacles, the Sun for the removal of sin, Agni for one's own purification, Viṣṇu for liberation,
Śiva for knowledge, and Śivā on that day for the increase of intelligence. (94)
Having worshipped thus, the wise man attains this; otherwise, he obtains the opposite.
O Nārada, listen now to that meditation (dhyāna) according to its true nature as taught by Kauthuma, which destroys all sins. 95–96.
She has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, the Gaṅgā who destroys all sins;
she is born from the body of Kṛṣṇa, equal to Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Satī;
she wears garments as pure as fire and is adorned with jewel ornaments.
Her body is graced by the splendor of a hundred autumnal full moons;
her face is bright with a gentle smile; she possesses eternal, stable youth;
she is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, peaceful, and endowed with perfect good fortune.
She bore a heavy braid of hair adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers, graced with a dot of vermilion alongside dots of sandalwood paste;
and upon her cheek was a musk-leaf design accompanied by various colorful patterns. (100)
Her excellent pair of lips was as beautiful as a single ripe bimba fruit;
her row of teeth was enchanting, graced by the luster of a string of pearls;
her face possessed lovely eyes, and she was delightful with her side-long glances. (101–102)
She possessed a pair of firm breasts shaped like *śrīphala* fruits;
she had broad hips that were very firm, adorned like the trunks of plantain trees;
and she bore upon her two lotus-feet the splendor of land-lotuses.
Adorned with jewel ornaments, smeared with saffron and lac-dye,
reddened by drops of nectar from the *mandāra* flowers on the crowns of the lords of the gods,
and always attended by the offerings (*arghya*) presented by the gods, *siddhas*, and great sages; (104–105)
It is joined by rows of bees that are the crowns of ascetics;
it bestows liberation upon those seeking release and grants the enjoyment of heaven to those possessed of desire.
It is excellent, most worthy of praise, the giver of boons, and ever-attentive to the grace of its devotees. (106)
"I worship the virtuous Viṣṇupadī, who bestows the station of Śrī Viṣṇu. Having thus meditated upon the auspicious river that flows through the three paths with this meditation,
O Brahmin, one should offer and worship her with the sixteen types of offerings.
A seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, bathing materials, and unguents;
incense, a lamp, food offerings, betel, and cool water;
clothing, ornaments, garlands, fragrance, and water for sipping—109.
A captivating and excellent bed—these sixteen things are to be given.
Having offered them with devotion, one should bow down and praise her with palms joined in reverence.
By worshipping in this manner, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Listen, O Nārada, I shall recite the hymn spoken by Kauthuma, the dialogue between Viṣṇu and Brahmā; it destroys sin and bestows great merit. (112) Śrī Brahmā said:
"I desire to hear, O Lord of Gods, O Consort of Lakṣmī, salutations to You, O Master!
[Please recite] the hymn to the Gaṅgā (Viṣṇupadī), which destroys sins and is the cause of merit.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I bow down to that Gaṅgā, who arose from the melting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s limbs as he was enraptured by the song of Śiva, and who was born from the melting of Rādhā’s limbs;
she who, at the beginning of the creation of worlds, [dwells] in Goloka within the circle of the Rāsa dance. (114)

In the presence of Śaṅkara, I bow down to that Gaṅgā. || 115 || In the auspicious Rādhā-mahotsava, crowded with cowherds and cowherdesses, I bow down to that Gaṅgā who appeared on the full moon day of Kārttika. || 115 ||
I bow to that Gaṅgā which, ten million *yojanas* in width, is then increased a hundred-thousandfold in length, and which completely encircles Goloka;
she who is sixty million *yojanas* in width and four times that in length. (117)
I bow to that Gaṅgā which, twenty lakhs of yojanas in width, is four times that in length, and which encircles Vaikuṇṭha. I bow to that Gaṅgā which encircles the world of Brahmā. 118–119.
I bow to that Gaṅgā which is thirty lakhs of yojanas in width and five times that in length, which encircles the world of Śiva;
she who is six yojanas wide and ten times that in length.

I bow to that Gaṅgā who is the Mandākinī in the world of Indra; I bow to that Gaṅgā which is one hundred thousand yojanas in width and seven times that in length, and which encircles the world of Dhruva.
I bow to that Gaṅgā, which is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in width and six times that in length, and which encircles the world of the Moon;
she who is sixty thousand *yojanas* in width and ten times that in length. (123)

I bow to that Gaṅgā which, having a width of one hundred thousand yojanas and a length six times that, encircles the world of the Sun (Sūryaloka). I bow to that Gaṅgā which encircles the world of Truth (Satyaloka). 124–125.

I bow to that Gaṅgā which is ten lakhs of yojanas in length and five times that in width, which encircles the world of heat (Tapoloka). And she who is one thousand yojanas in length and seven times that in width.
I bow to that Gaṅgā which, having a width of a thousand yojanas and a length seven times that, encircles Janaloka. I bow to that Gaṅgā which encircles Kailāsa. (127–128)
I bow to that Gaṅgā which, in Pātāla, is Bhogavatī, ten yojanas wide and ten times that in length;
thereafter she diminishes until nowhere is she more than one krośa in width. (129)
I bow to that Gaṅgā who, on earth, is the Cālakanandā;
I bow to that Gaṅgā who is white as milk in the Satya age, resembles the moon in the Tretā age, and has the luster of sandalwood in the Dvāpara age. (130–131)
In the Kali age, her radiance is like water and exists nowhere else on the surface of the earth;
in heaven, it is eternally like milk. I bow to that Gaṅgā, whose incomparable power has been heard in the Purāṇas and in the Śruti.

I bow down to that Gaṅgā, who bestows merit and removes sin. O Grandfather, the touch of even a single drop of her water would burn away the sins of the wicked, such as the killing of a Brahmin, accumulated over ten million births. (133–134)
Thus, O Brahman, have these twenty-one verses concerning the Gaṅgā been told;
they are in the form of a supreme hymn, destructive of sins and a seed of merit.
Whoever indeed recites them daily with devotion, having first worshipped the Goddess of the Gods, [attains the highest state].
One constantly obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice; there is no doubt in this matter.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one bereft of a wife obtains a beloved spouse.
The sick are freed from disease, and the bound are released from their bonds. (136–137)
One of obscure fame becomes renowned; a fool becomes a scholar.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this auspicious hymn to the Gaṅgā, may their evil dreams become auspicious, and they shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (138–139)
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, having praised Gaṅgā with this hymn, Bhagīratha took her and went to the place where the Sāgaras had perished. || 140 ||
They went swiftly to Vaikuṇṭha by means of the wind touched by the Gaṅgā.
She was brought down by Bhagīratha; therefore she is known as Bhāgīrathī.
Thus has this entire, excellent narrative of the Gaṅgā been told.
It bestows merit, it bestows liberation, and it is the essence; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa had become overwhelmed by the song of Śiva and had entered a state of melting devotion...
When Rādhā had fled away, what indeed happened?
And as for those people who were stationed there, what effort did they make?
O Lord, you ought to tell me all of this here in great detail. (143–144)
Nārāyaṇa said:
On the full moon day of Kārttika, during the great festival of Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa, having fully worshipped that Rādhā, dwelt in the circle of the Rāsa dance. 145.
Having worshipped her who had been worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā and all the other sages, headed by Sanaka, spoke with devoted minds. In that interval, O Kṛṣṇa, Sarasvatī sang a song.
She sang with beautiful melodies and played the lute most enchantingly.
(147) Pleased, Brahmā gave her a garland rich with great jewels, as well as a crest-jewel of supreme essence, difficult to find in all the universes. (148)
Kṛṣṇa [received] the Kaustubha jewel, the most excellent and supreme of all gems;
and Rādhikā [received] the finest necklace, inlaid with priceless jewels.
And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa [received] a captivating forest garland.
Adorned with priceless jewels, Lakṣmī wears makara-shaped earrings.
The divine Viṣṇu-māyā is the sovereign Mūla-prakṛti;
she is Durgā, Nārāyaṇī, and Īśānī—the devotion to Viṣṇu that is so very difficult to attain. (150–151)
"May there be a mind devoted to Dharma, and may there be Dharma and vast fame.
May there be fire-pure garments, fire, and wind, and jeweled anklets.
In the meantime, Śambhu was repeatedly urged by Brahmā.
He sang the song of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, filled with the joy of the rāsa dance.
(153) All the gods fell into a swoon like painted dolls; regaining consciousness in an instant, they beheld the circle of the rāsa dance. (154)
The entire land was flooded with water, and likewise Hari had abandoned Rādhā.
All the cowherds, cowherd women, gods, and twice-born brahmins wept most bitterly.
Through meditation, the Creator (Brahmā) understood all of this that had transpired.
And Śrī Kṛṣṇa departed together with Rādhā, saying, "Let [the world] flow away.
Then Brahmā and all the others praised the Supreme Lord:
"O All-pervading One, show us Your own form; grant us our desired boon. || 156–157 ||
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice arose there;
everyone heard it, perfectly clear, sweet, and auspicious:
"I am the Self of all, and this is my power, whose form consists of grace toward devotees."
"O gods, what use have I or she for this body?
All the Manus, all human beings, and the Vaiṣṇava sages, purified by my mantra, shall come to see me at my abode. (159–160)
"O lords of the gods, if you are all so eager to behold my form, Śambhu shall do so right there; in that way, my word will be fulfilled.
O Brahmā, you yourself are the Creator; O Teacher of the World, give the command. (161)
And he composed a most beautiful specialized scripture (*śāstra*) that is an auxiliary of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*),
endowed with collections of unprecedented mantras that grant all desired fruits,
