as well as hymns (*stotra*), armor-protective charms (*kavaca*), meditations (*dhyāna*), and the sequential procedures for worship (*pūjāvidhi*). || 162–163 ||
Having composed my mantra, armor, and hymn, guard them with diligence,
so that people may turn away from whatever he shall do.
Among hundreds and thousands, there might be but one who is a devotee of my mantra.
Those various people, purified by mantras, shall come to my abode;
otherwise, all the inhabitants of Goloka will cease to exist,
and the entire universe of Brahmā will become fruitless.
And beings of five kinds are joined to the Creator in every birth:
some dwell upon the earth, some dwell in heaven, some dwell below, and some dwell in the world of Brahmā. (167)
Whether they be Vaiṣṇavas or inhabitants of my own world, let Mahādeva make this very firm promise in the assembly of the gods; then you shall immediately behold his form. (168–169)
Having spoken thus, the Eternal One (Sanātana) ceased speaking in the sky.
Seeing that, the Lord of the World joyfully spoke to Śiva.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the Lord of Knowledge, the best among the wise, [replied].
Holding the water of the Gaṅgā in his hand, he accepted those words:
"In order to carry out the command of Kṛṣṇa, I shall compose this supreme scripture, the essence of the Vedas, joined with the Māyās of Viṣṇu and other mantras. (171–172)

"O Brahmin, when Śaṅkara had thus spoken in the assembly of the gods in Goloka: 'If a person, having touched the waters of the Gaṅgā, should speak falsely, he shall go to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā. (173)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa appeared together with Rādhā, intent upon her.
Seeing him, they were filled with joy; having offered praises to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and overflowing with supreme bliss, they celebrated the festival once again.
In due time, that blessed Śambhu composed the *Śāstradīpa*.
Thus has everything been told—this which is most secret and very difficult to obtain.
And she, who is the Gaṅgā born of Goloka, exists in this way as a liquid form.
Born from the bodies of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, she bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Installed in various places by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, she is the supreme embodiment of Kṛṣṇa himself, worshipped throughout the entire universe. (177–178)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Gaṅgā," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
When five thousand years of the Kali age had passed, that Sovereign Goddess of the gods—
"Where has that illustrious lady gone? You should explain that to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"By the will of the Lord, Bhāratī came to Bhārata [the land] due to her curse."
And at the end of the curse, that Sarasvatī returned once more to that Vaikuṇṭha;
O Nārada, having abandoned Bhāratavarṣa,
Padmāvatī likewise went to that abode of Hari at the conclusion of her curse from the Gaṅgā.
"O Brahman, these three—Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī—are the beloved wives of Hari;
when Tulasī is added, they are declared to be four in the Śruti.
Nārada said:

O best of sages, by what cause did that Gaṅgā, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, who was born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, come to reside in the water-pot of the Creator and then rest upon the head of Śaṅkara? (5)
"Aha! In what manner did this happen? You should explain that to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"In ancient times, in Goloka, that Gaṅgā existed in the form of liquid."
Born from the limbs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, she is a portion of them and identical in nature to them.
She is the presiding form of the liquid element, possessing a beauty unparalleled on earth;
endowed with fresh youth, she is adorned with jewel ornaments.
Her face is like a lotus at midday in autumn; she is smiling and exceedingly beautiful.
She possesses the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon.
Her light is smooth and intensely tender, and her nature is that of pure sattva.
Her hips were exceedingly plump and firm, and her pair of buttocks was excellent;
her pair of breasts was full, elevated, very firm, and perfectly round.
Her pair of eyes was most beautiful, with lovely side-glances and a charming curvature. (10–11)
Her curly mass of hair was adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
it was made beautiful by a dot of vermilion along with dots of sandalwood paste.
Her charming pair of cheeks was marked with decorative patterns of musk. (12)
Her beautiful lower lip has the form of a *bandhūka* flower;
she is radiant with a row of teeth resembling the seeds of a ripe pomegranate;
and she wears two garments purified by fire, fastened with a waist-knot. (13–14)
Her desire fulfilled, she stood by the side of Kṛṣṇa, deeply bashful;
with her two eyes, which resembled lotus petals and were devoid of blinking, she gazed constantly and joyfully upon the face of the Lord. (15)
With a blossoming face, longing for the joy of a new union,
she fainted at the sight of the Lord’s form, her body marked with horripilation. In that interval, Rādhikā was present there.
Accompanied by thirty million *gopīs*, she possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons.
With her face like a red lotus and eyes like red lotuses due to her wrath,
she has the hue of a white *campaka* flower and the gait of an elephant in rut.
Adorned with various ornaments inlaid with priceless gems,
she wears a priceless necklace set with rubies that is pure as fire,
and she bears a pair of yellow-hued garments secured with a waist-knot. (19–20)

Descending from her celestial chariot inlaid with the finest of jewels, she placed her lotus feet— tender, beautifully adorned, and graced by the luster of land-lotuses— down, while they were being honored with the *arghya* offering presented by Kṛṣṇa. (21)
And she was being served by her female companions with the breeze of white chowries;
[she wore] a tilaka-mark made from a drop of musk, combined with sandalwood and moon-cream, possessing the luster of a blazing lamp, and beautiful, reddened with vermilion. (22–23)
And she bears, in the middle of her forehead and below the parting of her hair,
a beautiful, curved [jewel] shining brightly, adorned with garlands of *pārijāta* flowers and the like; and,
being herself trembling, she causes her mass of lovely braided hair to quiver.
Trembling with anger, she shook her lip, which was joined to a most beautiful nose.
Having gone there, she stood by the side of Kṛṣṇa upon an excellent jeweled throne.
And the assembly hall of the Lord was filled with throngs of female companions.
And seeing her, the infallible Kṛṣṇa rose up with reverence;
having addressed her with sweet words, he smiled and was filled with eagerness.
The cowherds, bowing their necks and deeply alarmed, prostrated themselves before him.
They praised him with devotion, and he in turn praised the Supreme Lord.
Rising up suddenly, Gaṅgā addressed him;
filled with fear, she inquired after his welfare with great humility. (28–29)
Standing in a state of prostration, terrified, with her throat, lips, and palate parched,
she took refuge through meditation in the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, situated within the lotus of her heart, granted fearlessness to her who was afraid.
And by means of that most excellent Lord of All, she became firm in mind.
Then Gaṅgā beheld Rādhā seated upon a throne above—
exceedingly affectionate, pleasant to behold, and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
He beheld the primordial and eternal first creation of countless Brahmās,
like a twelve-year-old girl in the bloom of fresh youth,
peerless in the entire universe for her beauty and her virtues. (33)
She who is peaceful, lovely, infinite, and devoid of beginning or end; she who is the eternal reality, auspicious, most blessed, fortunate, and endowed with the good fortune of her Lord;
she who is beautiful with beauty, the most excellent among all beautiful women. (34–39)
With half her body dark, equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor, age, and brilliance,
she was Mahālakṣmī, worshipped by the Lord of Mahālakṣmī;
she eclipsed the radiant assembly hall of the Lord with her own luster.
Accepting the betel-roll given by her friend, which was difficult for others to obtain— [I salute] that Ramā,
the mother of all, the fortunate one, the venerable, the proud one,
the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s very life, and his dearest beloved. (37–38)
Having beheld the Queen of the Rāsa, the Queen of the Gods did not reach satiety;
with eyes free from blinking, she drank her in.
In the meantime, that Rādhā spoke to the Lord of the World.
O Sage, with sweet speech, peaceful, humble, and smiling,
Rādhikā said:
"O Lord of my life, who is this auspicious woman, smiling as she gazes at your lotus-like face?"
Constantly gazing at his side with longing and bloodshot eyes, she fell into a swoon at his beauty, her body covered in horripilation;
veiling her face with her garment, she looked at him again and again. (41–42)
And you too, having gazed upon me with desire, always smile;
while I am alive in Goloka, such wicked conduct has occurred.
You yourself repeatedly commit such evil deeds.
"I grant you forgiveness out of affection, for the female species is tender-hearted.
Take this beloved, cherished woman and go from Goloka, O lecher!
Otherwise, O Lord of the Gods, no good shall come to you."
"I saw you united with Virajā in the sandalwood forest.
Alas, I previously offered my forgiveness at the word of my friends;
yet you formerly vanished at the mere sound of my voice."
Having cast off her body, she became the river Virajā;
extending ten million yojanas in width and four times that in length,
she exists even today as the embodiment of your virtuous fame.
And when I had gone home, she went back to his presence and cried out loudly, "O Virajā! O Virajā! as she remembered him. Then, that perfected yoginī arose from the water through her yogic power.
Adorned with ornaments and embodied in form, she granted you her sight.
Then, having embraced her, you performed the act of bestowing seed;
from that, the seven oceans indeed came into being within her.
You were seen in the campaka grove accompanied by Śobhā;
at the mere sound of my voice, you instantly vanished.
Śobhā, abandoning her body, entered the lunar orb.
Then her body indeed became radiant with luster.
Having been divided by you, it was given with a grieving heart:
a portion for the jewel, a portion for the gold, and a portion for the excellent intellect.
A little from the lotus-faces of women, a little for the king, a little from the finest garments, and also a little from silver objects;
a little from the paste of sandalwood, and also a little from the waters. (55)
Something from the young shoots, something also from the flowers;
something from the fruits and from the well-ripened grains; and something from the consecrated dwellings of kings and gods. (56–57)
You were seen in the forest of Vṛndāvana joined with Prabhā;
immediately upon my mere utterance of your name, you vanished.
Prabhā, abandoning her body, entered the solar orb.
Then her body indeed became intense heat;
for previously, while weeping, it had been given away by you with affection,
having been divided and given from your eyes out of shame and fear of him.
He gave something to the sacrificial fire, and something also to the kings;
something to the multitudes of men, and something also to the gods;
something to the hosts of bandits, and something also to the serpents.
Having given something to the Brahmins, the sages, and the ascetics;
and having given something to women endowed with good fortune and to those who are illustrious—to all of them he gave that, and then first prepared himself to weep. (62–63)
You were indeed seen in the circle of the Rāsa dance accompanied by Śānti and Gopī;
in the springtime, upon a bed of flowers, adorned with garlands and anointed with sandalwood paste,
you were present in a palace constructed of jewels, illuminated by jewel-lamps.
Richly adorned with jewel-ornaments, together with her who was likewise decorated with jewels— O Lord,
in former times you ate the well-scented betel leaf offered by her after she had eaten,
and she ate the betel leaf offered by you.
Immediately upon the mere sound of my name, you caused her disappearance.
O Lord, Śānti abandoned her body and merged into you out of fear.
Thereupon, her body became preeminent in its qualities.

O Lord, in the past you gave a portion with love while weeping to Viṣṇu, who is the enjoyer of all objects and whose nature is *sattva*; and you gave a portion in the past to Lakṣmī, whose essential nature is pure *sattva*. (68–69)
And something for the Vaiṣṇavas who worship your mantra, and something for the ascetics, for the sake of Dharma, and for those most righteous; for indeed,
you were previously seen by me together with the secret Kṣamā.
Well-dressed, wearing garlands, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood,
he was comfortably absorbed in passion upon a couch adorned with flowers and sandalwood, together with her who was likewise bedecked with jewels and smeared with beautiful sandalwood paste.
He was immediately embraced by sleep due to the pleasure of our new union.
He and you were awakened by me; please remember this.
I have taken your yellow garment and your enchanting flute.
The forest garland, the Kaustubha gem, and the priceless jeweled earrings were later given out of love at the request of Your friends;
yet, O Lord, You have remained dark-complexioned even until this day because of that shame. (74–75)
Forgiveness, having abandoned her body out of shame, went to the earth.
Then her body became the most excellent of virtues;
for it was previously given by you with love and with tears, after having been duly apportioned.
Something was given to Viṣṇu, and something to the Vaiṣṇavas;
something to the most righteous for the sake of Dharma, and something to the weak;
something also to the ascetics, to the gods, and to the learned. (77–78)
"All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
O Lord, I know that your virtues are of vast extent.
Having spoken thus, Rādhā, whose eyes were like red lotuses, [remained silent].
She began to speak to Gaṅgā, who stood with her face bowed down, modest and virtuous.
Having understood the secret through yoga, Gaṅgā—she who is indeed a perfected yoginī—vanished from the midst of the assembly and entered her own waters. (80–81)
Having realized through yoga that she was present everywhere, the Siddhayoginī began to drink from her mouthful;
having known the secret of the Gaṅgā through yoga, she indeed became a Siddhayoginī. (82)
She went to the supreme refuge of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet.
(83) Rādhā beheld Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise the world of Brahmā and other realms everywhere; yet she did not see the Gaṅgā at all. (84)
It was entirely devoid of water, consisting of dried-up mud and globules of clay;
it was filled with multitudes of aquatic creatures and the corpses of the dead.
[85] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Ananta, Dharma, Indra, the Moon, and the Sun—
All the Manus, human beings, gods, Siddhas, and ascetics,
their throats, lips, and palates parched, arrived at Goloka;
they all bowed down to Govinda, the Lord of all, who transcends primordial nature (prakṛti).
The bestower of boons, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the most eminent, the cause of all boons;
the Lord of boons, worthy of boons, the foremost of all, the Sovereign;
(88) devoid of desire, formless, untainted, and without support.
He is devoid of qualities, devoid of exertion, devoid of expansion, and stainless;
He consists of His own will, possesses form, and has a body for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees;
He is the true nature of reality, the Lord of truth, the witness-form, and the eternal. (89–90)
Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord, the Highest, the Supreme Soul, the Ruler, they all praised Him with their necks bowed in devotion;
their voices were choked with emotion, their eyes filled with tears, and their bodies were marked with horripilation. (91)
Having all together praised the Lord of All, the Supreme Hari—
the light-filled Supreme Brahman, the cause of all causes—
seated upon a variegated lion-throne inlaid with priceless jewels.
Being served by cowherds with the breeze of white chowries,
looking upon the dancing and singing of the cowherd girls with a joyful smile,
and surrounded by hundreds of millions of cowherds in elegant attire. (94)
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments,
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, a youth wearing yellow garments,
appearing like a twelve-year-old child in the form of a cowherd.
His body was endowed with full splendor, graced by the radiance of ten million moons;
surrounded by his own brilliance, it was most beautiful and captivating. His form possessed the grace, charm, and loveliness of ten million Cupids.
And he was constantly being beheld by the cowherd girls,
who were smiling and adorned with ornaments fashioned from great jewels, as they joyfully drank in the moon-like face of the Lord with their eyes. (98–99)

The gods beheld Him everywhere in the Rāsa dance—Him who was the most beloved, dearer even than His own life, seated upon the chest of Rādhā; who had consumed the fragrant betel-leaf offered by Her; and who was the most perfect Supreme Being. (100)

The sages, men, perfected ones, and ascetics through their penance—all with delighted minds—were struck with supreme wonder. Having deliberated among themselves, they spoke to that four-faced one: [101]
In order to inform the Lord of the World of his desired intention,
Brahmā— having heard those words— approached the supreme Kṛṣṇa, who was standing to the right of Viṣṇu and to the left of Vāmadeva.

Filled with supreme bliss and having the form of supreme bliss, the Creator beheld everything within the circle of Rāsa as consisting of Kṛṣṇa; everything was dressed in identical attire, seated together upon their respective thrones. (104–105)
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, adorned with a forest garland, with a crest of peacock feathers, and resplendent with the Kaustubha gem;
exceedingly lovely, beautiful, and possessing a peaceful form. (106)
In terms of his qualities, ornaments, form, splendor, age, radiance,
clothing, fame, appearance, and beautiful physique— he was entirely perfect in every respect and endowed with all sovereign powers. (107–108)
Seeing him for a moment as pure splendor and for a moment as a mass of beauty, one is unable to declare whether he is the served or the server;
yet in another single moment, he is seen as the supreme Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā. (109)
For a moment, he envisioned [the Lord] seated upon an individual throne together with her;
Kṛṣṇa assuming the form of Rādhā, and his consort assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Unable to conceive of it otherwise, the Creator imagined him in both female and male form. (110–111)
Then Dhātṛ, having bowed down many times with devotion, offered praise with a mind fixed in meditation upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa residing within the heart-lotus.
Thereafter, by His permission, he opened his eyes once more.
He saw Kṛṣṇa alone, seated upon Rādhā’s breast,
surrounded by his own attendants and adorned by the circle of gopīs.
Upon seeing him, they bowed again and praised him once more.
Having understood their intention, the Lord of the Gods spoke to them—
he who is the soul of all, the lord of all sacrifices, the lord of all, and the creator of all.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Come, O Brahmin; come, O Lord of Kamalā!
Come here, O Mahādeva; may there be eternal well-being for you all.
You highly fortunate ones have arrived for the purpose of bringing the Gaṅgā."
"The Gaṅgā has come for refuge out of fear to my lotus-feet. Seeing her desiring to protect Rādhā from my presence, cast her outside and make her fearless. (117–118)
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-born Brahmā, smiling,
praised Rādhā— who is worshiped by all and honored by Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
with his four faces, bowing his neck in devotion. (119)
The four-faced Creator spoke of the four Vedas.
"O Lord, Gaṅgā was indeed produced from your body in the circle of the Rāsa dance;
she became liquid through the voice of the charming Śaṅkara."
Your beloved daughter, who is a portion of Kṛṣṇa and a portion of yourself, is like your own child;
having received his mantra, let her perform your worship.
In Vaikuṇṭha, the four-armed Lord shall become her husband.
And from the digit (kalā) that has descended to the earth comes the ocean of salt water.
O Goddess of gods, you are of the nature of that Rādhā who resides in Goloka and likewise pervades all places; you are her very self, and your daughter is always [one with] you.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, she accepted them with a smile.
She emerged from the tip of the nail of Kṛṣṇa’s big toe;
there, composed and tranquil, she stood in their midst.

The presiding deity of that water rose from the waters and remained there. That water had been placed by Brahmā partly in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and partly the Moon-crested Lord (Candraśekhara) bore upon his head as the crescent moon.
The lotus-born Brahmā bestowed the Rādhikā-mantra upon Gaṅgā,
as well as her hymn of praise, armor-verse (kavaca), the ritual procedure for worship, and the method of meditation;
indeed, all of that, along with the sequence for the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), was declared in the Sāmaveda.
Having fully honored her, the virtuous Gaṅgā departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
O Sage, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī— the purifier of the universe—
these four are indeed the wives of Nārāyaṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa, smiling, spoke to Brahmā concerning the events of all time, which are difficult for those lacking insight to comprehend. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Accept the Gaṅgā, O Brahmā, O Viṣṇu, O Maheśvara!
Listen to the account of Time; behold what has passed.
You, as well as the other gods, sages, and Manus—"

The perfected ones and the ascetics, whoever have gathered here, they all live in Goloka, which is free from the wheel of time. When the entire universe is submerged in water during the dissolution into primordial nature (prākṛta-laya), [they remain there]. || 133-134 ||
"Brahmā and all others who reside in other universes have now dissolved into me.
O Lotus-born One, behold everything except Vaikuṇṭha as submerged in water.
Go and once again create the supreme creation, beginning with the world of Brahmā."

"First create the universe together with its cosmic egg, and afterwards Gaṅgā shall follow. Having thus created Brahmā and the others once more among the various worlds, I shall perform the creation again; go quickly with the gods."

"With the closing of His eyes, the fall of Brahmā occurs; how many such creators have already passed away, and how many will yet come to be? Having spoken thus, O Sage, the Lord of Rādhikā departed for His inner apartments.
The gods went and diligently created creation once again.
Gaṅgā remained in Goloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in the world of Śiva; likewise, she remained in Brahmā’s world and elsewhere, wherever she had previously resided. (139–140)
Right there, by the command of the Supreme Self, that Gaṅgā went;
having emerged from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, she is therefore remembered as the Viṣṇupadī.
Thus has this entire, excellent narrative of Gaṅgā been told.
"It bestows happiness, it bestows liberation, and it is the essence; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Gaṅgā," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
"Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī, the purifier of the worlds—these four are indeed the beloveds of Nārāyaṇa. (1) "Gaṅgā went to Vaikuṇṭha; this very thing was heard by me."
"How did she become his wife? Tell me, O Keśava.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Gangā went to Vaikuṇṭha, and after her, Brahmā followed."
Having gone there, he prostrated before the Lord of the Universe along with her and spoke.
Brahmā said:
"That goddess who was born from the sin of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa took the form of liquid."
This goddess who presides over that [place] is peerless in beauty on earth;
she is endowed with fresh youth, virtuous, beautiful, and excellent.
She is the very embodiment of pure sattva, free from anger and egoism. (4–5)
Since she was born from his very limbs, she does not choose anyone other than him;
even so, the proud Rādhā, the most excellent and highly effulgent one, has intentionally risen up to protect her out of fear. (6)
I entered the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
Seeing all of Goloka completely parched, I then went to Goloka,
where Kṛṣṇa was, in order to obtain news of everything.
The inner soul of all, having known our entire intention,
brought forth the Gaṅgā from the tip of his big toe;
and having given her the mantra of Rādhikā, he filled Goloka.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Rādhā and taken her with me, O All-pervading One, I have come here.
Accept this Queen of the Gods through the Gāndharva form of marriage.
You are the Lord of the Gods, a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, and the source of all rasa; [accept] this passionate woman.
This virtuous woman is a jewel among women, just as he is a jewel among men;
the union of the wise with the wise shall be full of merit.
And he who, out of pride, does not accept a maiden who has presented herself— ||| 12 ||
If he abandons her, Mahālakṣmī departs in anger; of this there is no doubt.
Even he who is a wise man does not despise Prakṛti.
All men are products of Prakṛti; women are the very digits of Prakṛti.
You alone are the primordial Lord, devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). Kṛṣṇa, though two-armed, becomes four-armed through half of his body;
and in ancient times, the supreme Rādhikā was born from the left side of Kṛṣṇa’s body. (15)
She herself [arose] from his right side, and Kamalā from his left side, just as she did.
Therefore, she indeed chooses you, since she was born from your own body.
For man and woman are truly one body, just like Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Having spoken thus, Dhātṛ handed her over and departed;
Hari himself then took her as his wife by the Gāndharva rite.
Having prepared a bed conducive to pleasure, anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste, he remained there.
There the Lord of Ramā sports joyfully together with Gaṅgā.
Because she went to the earth (gām) and has returned again to her own abode,
and because she emerged from the foot of Viṣṇu, Gaṅgā is known as Viṣṇupadī.
That goddess fell into a swoon from the mere touch of her first union;
she, a connoisseur of pleasure joined with the Lord of Connoisseurs, was lost in the bliss of their amorous enjoyment.
Seeing this, Vāṇī became sorrowful, though she was free from the jealousy of a co-wife.
The river Gaṅgā was constantly jealous of Sarasvatī, yet Gaṅgā did not [envy] Sarasvatī. O Sage, the Lord of Ramā had three wives together with Gaṅgā; later, with Tulasī, he came to have four.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Gaṅgā," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
How did she become the virtuous beloved of Nārāyaṇa?
Where was Tulasī born, and who was she in her previous birth?
(1) In whose lineage was she born, and whose daughter was that ascetic woman?
By what austerity did she attain that which is beyond primordial nature? (2)
Nirvikalpa (beyond conceptual construction), devoid of effort, and the very nature of the witness of all;
Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the Lord;
the one to be worshipped by all, the Master of all, the omniscient, and the cause of all. 3.
The support of all, possessing every form, and the protector of all—
how did such a goddess come to attain the state of a tree?
And how did that ascetic lady become seized by an asura?
"My mind is doubtful and restless; it impels me again and again.
You, who shatter all doubts, ought to dispel this uncertainty.
Nārāyaṇa said:
And Manu Dakṣasāvarṇi shall be meritorious, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure;
he will be illustrious and renowned, born from a portion of Viṣṇu.
His son, Dharmasāvarṇi, will be most righteous, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure.
His son was Viṣṇusāvarṇi, a Vaiṣṇava who had conquered his senses.
His son was Devasāvarṇi, devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
His son was Rājasāvarṇi, devoted to Mahāviṣṇu.
And his son was Vṛṣadhvaja, who was devoted to Vṛṣadhvaja;
in whose hermitage Śambhu himself resided for three divine ages.
And Śiva’s affection for that king was even greater than for his own son.
He did not acknowledge Nārāyaṇa, nor Lakṣmī, nor Sarasvatī.
He caused the worship of all the gods to be abandoned;
the king, out of pride, even gave up the worship of Mahālakṣmī in the month of Bhādrapada.
In the month of Māgha, he caused the worship of Sarasvatī to be abandoned;
he censured sacrifice and the worship of Viṣṇu, and performed neither of them.
No deity whatsoever cursed the lord of the earth because of his devotion to Śiva.
"O King, may you be deprived of your glory," thus did Divākara curse him.
Taking up his trident, Śaṅkara himself restrained the Sun;
then the Lord of Day, together with his father, sought refuge with Brahmā. (14–15)
Śiva, with the trident in his hand, went to the world of Brahmā in a rage;
Brahmā, placing Sūrya before him, went to Vaikuṇṭha out of fear. Even there, Śaṅkara took up the trident and held Sūrya.
Brahmā, Kaśyapa, and Mārtaṇḍa were terrified, their throats parched;
out of fear, they all went for refuge to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of All. Having approached him, they bowed their heads in prostration and praised him again and again. (17–18)
All of them, out of fear, made a petition to Hari regarding the cause of their terror. O Sage, Nārāyaṇa, out of compassion, granted them freedom from fear, saying:
"Be steadfast, O frightened ones; what fear can there be for you while I am present?"
"Those who, filled with fear in times of calamity, remember me wherever they may be—having gone there, I protect them with the discus in hand, acting with haste.
I am the Lord of the worlds, their protector and their eternal creator. (21)
Having created [the world] in the form of Brahmā, I am the destroyer in the form of Śiva. "I am Śiva, you are also I, and I am the Sun, consisting of the three qualities.
Having assumed various forms, I perform the activities of creation and so forth. (22–23)
"Go, may it be well with you; whence can there be fear?
From this day forward, by my boon from Śaṅkara, you shall have no fear.
That Blessed One is quickly pleased, the protector of those who seek refuge, and the goal of the virtuous. (24)

The Lord of devotees is dependent upon His devotees; He is the soul of His devotees and is affectionate toward them. O Brahman, Sudarśana and Śiva are dearer to Me than My own life-breaths; in all the universes, there is no one more radiant than these two.

Mahādeva is capable of effortlessly creating ten million suns and even ten million Brahmas; what, then, is impossible for the wielder of the trident? For one who meditates upon me day and night, there is no external knowledge whatsoever.
Know that my host is praised with devotion by the five-faced one (Śiva).
I alone contemplate that auspiciousness day and night.
In whatever way people surrender unto me, in that very same way do I honor them. (28–29)
The Blessed One is the very nature of Śiva, the presiding deity of Śiva;
because one becomes Śiva through him, the wise know him as Śiva. (30) In the meantime, Śaṅkara himself arrived there.
With a trident in hand, mounted upon his bull, and with eyes like red lotuses,
he quickly descended from the bull with his neck bowed in devotion and prostrated with devotion before that peaceful one, the beloved of Lakṣmī, who is higher than the highest. (31–32)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with jewel ornaments, wearing a crown and earrings, bearing a discus and a forest garland;
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, beautiful, and four-armed. (33)
He was served by four-armed attendants with the breeze of white chowries;
his entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with yellow garments, and he was consuming betel nut offered by Lakṣmī, O Nārada. (34–35)
He was listening with a smile and joy to the dancing and singing of the Vidyādharīs;
he is the Lord, the Supreme Self, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon his devotees.
Mahādeva bowed to him, and he (the Lord) bowed to Brahmā.
Sūrya bowed with devotion to the moon-crested Lord, trembling with awe.
Kaśyapa, with great devotion, offered praise and bowed down.
Having praised the Lord of All, Śiva sat upon a comfortable seat.
Candraśekhara was seated comfortably on a pleasant throne, at rest,
served by the attendants of Viṣṇu with the breeze of white chowries;
free from anger due to his union with the quality of purity (sattva), he was serene, smiling with joy.
To that supreme, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, who was being praised by the five-faced [Śiva] in the assembly of the gods, he—
whose soul was serene—
spoke these words which were as sweet as nectar and most enchanting.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Śivā, your question regarding Śiva is exceedingly laughable;
yet, even so, I shall answer it for your peace, whether it concerns worldly or Vedic matters."
To you, the bestower of the fruits of austerities, the giver of all prosperity,
who are yourself worthy of inquiry regarding both prosperity and austerity—
to you, the omniscient presiding deity of knowledge, why do I ask about knowledge in vain?
"O Hari, you are capable of resolving questions regarding calamities even when no disaster has occurred;
O Lord of Speech, you alone are capable of resolving questions concerning the scriptures that have their own refuge.
Why have you come here with such speed?"—thus spoke the Lord of Ramā. (44–45)
Śrī Mahādeva said: "The Sun cursed my devotee Vṛṣadhvaja, who is dearer to me than my own life; this is the reason for my arrival and my anger. (46)
Out of grief from affection for his son, he was prepared to destroy the sun;
he sought refuge with Brahmā, and both that sun and Brahmā have sought refuge in you.
Those who have sought refuge in you, whether through meditation or even by word alone—
Free from calamity and devoid of fear, they have conquered old age and death.
O sirs, what can I say of the fruit for those who have directly sought refuge?
The remembrance of Hari always bestows fearlessness and grants all auspiciousness. (48–49)
"O Lord of the World, tell me what will become of me, your devotee,
now that this fool has been slain by Śrī on account of the Sun’s curse?
The Blessed One said:
By the power of destiny, twenty-one yugas have passed;
go quickly to the king’s palace in half a ghaṭikā at Vaikuṇṭha.
Vṛṣadhvaja has died due to Time, which is most terrible and impossible to ward off.
And his son Haṃsadhvaja died, having been struck down by Śrī. His two illustrious sons, Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja—both supreme Vaiṣṇavas—had their fortune destroyed by the curse of Sūrya. (52–53)
Both Kamala and Tapasa shall be deprived of their kingdom and fallen from their prosperity;
yet Lakṣmī shall be born as a portion of the wives of those two.
Then, endowed with wealth, those two shall become the best of kings.
"O Śambhu, your servant is dead; you may go, and all of you may depart.
Having spoken thus, he, together with Lakṣmī, entered the inner chamber from the assembly hall.
The gods, filled with joy, departed for their own supreme abodes with great delight.
And Śiva, most perfect, went quickly for the sake of penance.

(57) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Tulasī," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, having propitiated Lakṣmī and those two [deities] with fierce austerity,
they each obtained their desired and cherished boons.
By the very boon of Mahālakṣmī, those two became lords of the earth.
The two were wealthy and possessed sons, Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja.
And the wife of Kuśadhvaja was the virtuous queen Mālāvatī;
in due time, she gave birth to a daughter, a virtuous girl who was a portion of Kamalā.
And she, through her connection with the earth, became endowed with knowledge;
having clearly uttered the sound of the Vedas, she rose up in the lying-in chamber.
As soon as she was born, that girl produced the sound of the Vedas.
Therefore, the wise call her Vedavatī.
As soon as she was born, she bathed and went to the forest for asceticism;
though restrained with great effort by all, she remained devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
For one entire Manvantara, that ascetic woman performed most rigorous penance at Puṣkara with ease;
yet she remained well-nourished, not emaciated, and endowed with fresh youth.
And suddenly she heard an incorporeal voice in the sky:
"In another birth, Hari himself shall become your husband;
O beautiful one, you shall obtain as a lord a husband who is difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to propitiate."

Having heard this, she became enraged and performed penance once more on Mount Gandhamādana, in an exceedingly secluded place. Having practiced austerities there for a very long time, she dwelt there, trusting in [her success].
There she beheld before her Rāvaṇa, who was difficult to resist.
Having seen him, out of devotion to a guest, she indeed offered him water for his feet,
as well as very sweet fruits and roots and also very cool water.
Having eaten that, the most wicked man dwelt in her presence and asked her, "Who are you, O auspicious lady?
And he gazed upon her, the woman of excellent limbs, with full and elevated breasts.
His face like an autumn lotus, smiling, with beautiful teeth and virtuous—
afflicted by the arrows of desire, the wretched man fell into a swoon.
Drawing her toward him with his hand, he prepared to engage in sexual union.
That virtuous woman, with a glance of anger, rendered him paralyzed.
He became motionless, unable even to speak with his hands or feet;
he mentally praised the goddess Padmāṃśā, the lotus-eyed one.
Satisfied by that hymn of praise, she released him from his natural form.
And she cursed him: "On my account, you shall perish along with your kinsmen;
look, I release you now that I have been touched by you out of lust. (17–18)
Having spoken thus, she indeed abandoned her body through yoga.
Having cast her into the Gaṅgā, Rāvaṇa went to his own home.
"Aha! What a wonder has been seen; what have I done now?"

Having reflected and recollected this, she lamented again and again. (20) And in the course of time, that virtuous woman became the daughter of Janaka, renowned as Queen Sītā, for whose sake Rāvaṇa was slain. (21)
And that great ascetic woman, through the power of her penance in a previous birth,
obtained Rāma— the most perfect Hari— as her husband;
having attained him and propitiated her Lord, the Master of the Universe, by means of her austerity.
That beautiful Ramā sported with Rāma for a very long time.
Remembering her former births, she recalled the sequence of her past austerities;
through that happiness, she abandoned all suffering and obtained bliss. (23–24)

Having obtained him— who was exceedingly delicate, in the full bloom of youth, virtuous, refined, tranquil, and possessed of unsurpassed and lovely form— the chaste woman for a very long time displayed manifold kinds of splendor. (25)
He obtained that which was pleasing and beautiful to women, exactly as he desired.
Then, in order to fulfill his father’s word, that best of the Raghus, who was true to his promise, departed for the forest; and subsequently, by the power of time, [he was overcome].
He stayed near the ocean with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
There, Hari beheld Agni in the form of a brahmin.
Seeing Rāma distressed, he too became sorrowful.
He who was devoted to truth spoke a few words that were true and desired by the virtuous.
Vahni said:
"O Blessed One, let these words be heard, which have been brought forth by time."
This very time for the abduction of Sītā has arrived for you alone.
Destiny is indeed difficult to avert, and there is no power superior to destiny.
Having entrusted me, who gave birth to you, to my care like a shadow, protect me now by my side.
"I shall give Sītā back to you at the time of the trial;
I was sent by the gods, and I am not the Brahmin Agni.
Having heard those words, Rāma did not reveal it even to Lakṣmaṇa.
With a grieving heart, he accepted her of his own free will.
By means of yoga, Vahni created a Māyā-Sītā, just like Sītā;
O Nārada, he gave her to Rāma, for she possessed qualities and beauty equal to hers.

Taking Sītā with him and forbidding Lakṣmaṇa from speaking of the secret, he departed; Lakṣmaṇa did not even know of it, so what need is there to mention anyone else? In the meantime, Rāma saw a golden deer.
Sītā urged him toward that end with great effort.
Having left Lakṣmaṇa in the forest for the protection of Jānakī,
Rāma went there himself and pierced him with an arrow to slay him.
Then, uttering the word "Lakṣmaṇa," the illusory deer suddenly gave up its life-breaths before him, remembering Hari;
casting off its deer-form and assuming a divine form.
He went to Vaikuṇṭha by means of a vehicle fashioned from jewels.
At the great gate of Vaikuṇṭha were two powerful gatekeepers, servants of the Lord, named Jaya and Vijaya. || 39-40 ||
Having attained a demonic body due to the curse of Sanaka and the others, he first went to that very gate of the two doorkeepers. Then, she heard his distressed voice crying out, "Lakṣmaṇa! 41.
Sītā urged Lakṣmaṇa to go into the presence of Rāma. When Lakṣmaṇa had departed, the irresistible Rāvaṇa took Sītā and went to Laṅkā itself with ease.
Rāma was despondent upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa in the forest;
having quickly returned to his own hermitage, he did not find Sītā there at all.
Having fallen into a swoon for a long time, he lamented again most bitterly.
He wandered again through the dense forest in search of him. Then,
having obtained news of him from a vulture on the riverbank,
the monkey Hanumān made an ally of a monkey and bridged the ocean.
Having gone to Laṅkā, that best of the Raghus slew Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen by means of an arrow, and he recovered the sorrowful Sītā;
he then quickly caused her to undergo the trial by fire.
At that time, the Fire-god presented the real Jānakī there.
Then the Shadow (Chāyā), filled with humility, spoke to both Agni and Rāma:
"I shall do it; tell me the means by which I may do so."
Vahni said:
"O Goddess, go to Puṣkara, which bestows great merit;
by performing penance right there, you will become the very embodiment of celestial splendor. (50)
Having heard those words, she performed penance at Puṣkara for three hundred thousand divine years; indeed, she became Lakṣmī in heaven.
And by that time, through her asceticism, she was born from the sacrificial fire-pit.

In the Kṛta Yuga she was Vedavatī, the auspicious daughter of Kuśadhvaja; in the Tretā Yuga she became Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and the wife of Rāma, who was the beloved Draupadī, daughter of Drupada, among the Pāṇḍavas.
The goddess Draupadī, the daughter of Drupada, was her shadow;
she is said to be "three-year-old" (trihāyaṇī) as she exists throughout the three ages.
Nārada said:
"O bull among sages, how did she come to have five beloved ones?
O Great Lord, please dispel this doubt in my mind.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, in Laṅkā, Sītā indeed attained Rāma;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, yet that shadow-form was greatly distressed.
Having performed austerities by the command of Rāma and Agni, she requested a boon from Śaṅkara.
Afflicted by desire and distracted for her husband, she entreated him again and again:
"Grant me a husband, grant me a husband, grant me a husband, O Three-eyed One!
Grant me a husband, grant me a husband," thus the devoted wife spoke five times.
Having heard her prayer, Śiva, the Lord of Rasikas, smiled and granted her a boon, saying:
"O beloved, you shall have five husbands.
By that [boon], she became the beloved wife of the five Pāṇḍavas.
Thus everything that was relevant has been told; now listen to the actual matter.
Then, having reached Sītā, the enchanting one, in Laṅkā, Rāma gave that Laṅkā to Vibhīṣaṇa and went back again to Ayodhyā.
Having ruled the kingdom in Bhārata for eleven thousand years,
he went to Vaikuṇṭha together with all the worlds.
Vedavatī, who was a portion of Kamalā, entered into Kamalā.
This meritorious narrative has been told; it bestows merit and destroys sin.
(63) She upon whose tip of the tongue the four Vedas themselves are ever present in embodied form is known as Vedavatī. (64)
The narrative of Kuśadhvaja’s daughter has been told to you in brief.
Now listen as I relate to you the narrative of Dharmadhvaja’s daughter.

(65) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Introduction of Vedavatī" within the "Episode of Tulasī," in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*. (14)
Nārāyaṇa said:
The wife of Dharmadhvaja was renowned as Mādhavī;
she indeed took delight with the king out of passion on Mount Gandhamādana.
Having prepared a bed made delightful for pleasure, anointed with flowers and sandalwood,
her entire body sprinkled with sandalwood paste by the breeze scented with flowers and sandalwood—
she who was a jewel among women, possessed of exceedingly beautiful limbs, and adorned with jeweled ornaments. (2)
The passionate woman, the most excellent of connoisseurs, was united with the Lord of Connoisseurs. (3) There was no cessation from amorous play for those two who were experts in the arts of love;
though a hundred divine years passed day and night, they did not perceive it. (4)
Then, having reached her during her menses, he desisted from sexual union;
yet that beautiful woman, full of desire, did not attain even slight satisfaction.
That virtuous woman immediately conceived a fetus that lasted for a hundred divine years.
And she, Śrīgarbhā, became endowed with splendor day by day. On an auspicious moment, on an auspicious day, joined with an auspicious conjunction,
in an auspicious ascendant and an auspicious division, and associated with the house of an auspicious lord.
And on the full moon day of Kārtika, on a Saturday, O Lotus-born One,
she gave birth to Padminī, a most enchanting girl who was a portion of Padmā,
and whose pair of lotus-feet shone with rubies.
The sovereign queen of kings, Lakṣmī, beautiful in every limb;
endowed with the marks of royal fortune, the presiding deity of royal prosperity; her face like the full moon of autumn, her eyes like autumnal lotuses. (9–10)
And beholding her in the house, smiling, with lips like a ripe bimba fruit, with the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet reddish, with a deep navel, and enchanting;
below that, marked with the three folds [of the waist], and possessing rounded, shapely hips. (11)
In the cold season, her entire body was pleasantly warm; in the summer, she was pleasantly cool.
She was dark-complexioned, with beautiful hair, radiant, and well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
With the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, she was the singular beauty among all beauties. (12–13)
Seeing her, both men and women were unable to offer her any comparison;
therefore, those who know the ancient lore call her by the name Tulasī.
And by the mere act of touching the ground, she became as worthy as the very nature of a virtuous woman.
Forbidden by all, she went to the Badarī forest for asceticism.
There, having resolved that "Nārāyaṇa shall be my lord," she performed supreme penance for a hundred thousand divine years. (15–16)
In summer she practiced the penance of the five fires, and in winter she remained in water;
that Sundarī stood in the open air, enduring the downpour of rain day and night.
For twenty thousand years, she subsisted on fruits and water.
For three million years, that ascetic woman subsisted on leaves;
for forty thousand years, she, with her slender waist, subsisted on air;
thereafter, for ten thousand years, she remained without food.

Seeing her standing on one leg, devoid of any distinguishing marks, the Lotus-born One went to the supreme Badarikāśrama to grant her a boon. Upon seeing the four-faced one whose vehicle is a swan, she prostrated before him.
The Creator of the world, the Ordainer of all worlds, spoke to her.
Brahmā said:
"Choose a boon, O Tulasī, whatever is desired in your heart."
"Devotion to Hari, or even liberation, or even the state of being free from old age and death.
Tulasī said:
"Listen, dear one, I shall tell you what is desired in my heart."
What shame do I feel now even before the Omniscient One?
(23) Formerly, I was the Gopī Tulasī in Goloka; I was Kṛṣṇa’s beloved, his servant, a portion of Him, His friend, and His dear one. (24)
The Queen of the Rāsa, having arrived at the circle of the rāsa dance, saw me— clinging to Govinda, insatiable, and unconscious;
filled with wrath, she rebuked Govinda and cursed me.

"O Grandfather, Govinda spoke thus to me: 'By performing austerities in the land of Bhārata, by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, you shall obtain a human womb and become a four-armed portion of mine. (26–27)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods vanished;
out of fear of the Goddess, he abandoned his body and obtained birth upon the earth.
I [saw] my beloved Nārāyaṇa, peaceful and of beautiful form.
"Now I wish to obtain a boon; grant it to me in this way.
Brahmā said:
"There is a cowherd named Sudāmā, born from the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
A portion of Him, exceedingly effulgent, took birth in Bhārata.
At present, due to a curse from Rādhikā, he has arisen from the lineage of Danu,
renowned in the three worlds as Śaṅkhacūḍa, and is intent upon nothing else.
Having seen you previously in Goloka, his mind was agitated by desire;
yet, due to the power of Rādhikā, he was unable to transgress her bounds.
Remembering his past lives, he performed austerities and obtained you through a boon.
"O beautiful one, you too, being a rememberer of your past lives, know everything. O noble and auspicious lady, now become his wife;
afterwards, you shall obtain the peaceful Nārāyaṇa as your husband."

By the power of Nārāyaṇa’s curse alone, through the turn of fate, you shall assume the form of a tree; purified and the sanctifier of the universe, you shall become the foremost of all flowers and superior even to the life-breath of Viṣṇu. (35)
And without you, the worship of all would become fruitless.
(36) In Vṛndāvana, you shall take the form of a tree named Vṛndāvanī;
with your leaves, the gopīs and gopas will worship Mādhava. (37)
"By my boon, you shall sport at will with Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd, eternally in the form of the presiding goddess of the trees.
Having heard these words, she smiled, her heart filled with joy.
She bowed down to the Creator and spoke something to him.
Tulasi said:
"Just as I have a longing for the two-armed Kṛṣṇa, the dark and beautiful one..."
I tell you the truth, O dear one, and it is not so regarding the Four-Armed One (Viṣṇu).
I am unsatisfied with Govinda because, by fate, my erotic passion was interrupted;
therefore, at the very word of Govinda, I pray for the Four-Armed One.
"By His grace, O Rādhā, dispel my fear; I shall certainly obtain Govinda once again, who is so very difficult to attain. (42) Brahmā said:

"Accept the mantra of Rādhikā; I shall indeed give you the sixteen-syllable one. By my boon, you shall become as dear to her as her own life-breath, and Rādhikā will recognize the secret amorous union of you two."
"You shall become as fortunate as Rādhā to Govinda.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the World gave the Goddess that sixteen-syllable mantra, as well as the supreme hymn and armor (kavaca). || 44–45 ||
Having bestowed all the rules for worship, the sequence of the preliminary rites (puraścaryā),
and the supreme auspicious blessing, he indeed attained invisibility.
And she, by the instruction of Brahmā, [resided] in the holy hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
She recited the supreme mantra that had been dear to her in a previous birth;
for twelve divine years she performed worship,
and that goddess became perfected and granted her a response.

When her asceticism and mantras were perfected, the goddess, having obtained the boon she desired, abandoned the exhaustion of her penance; with a serene mind, she enjoyed that which is exceedingly difficult for all beings to attain, O fortunate one. (49)
When the fruit was accomplished for men, both suffering and supreme happiness were experienced;
having eaten and drunk and being fully satisfied, she lay down upon that delightful couch, which was anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste. (50–51)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon Tulasī," in the *Tulasī-upākhyāna* within the *Nārada-Nārāyaṇa-saṃvāda* of the second book, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Tulasī was completely satisfied; with a joyful heart, she fell asleep.
Endowed with fresh youth and praising [him], that excellent woman—
[attracted] by the five-arrowed one who discharged five arrows toward her—
was consumed by the flower-armed god, though she was already anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste. (1–2)
With all her limbs covered in horripilation, trembling and with reddened eyes,
she at one moment became parched and at another fell into a swoon;
for a moment she was filled with agitation, and at another she experienced a blissful drowsiness.
For a moment she encountered fire; for a moment she fell into heedlessness.
For a moment she regained consciousness; for a moment she fell into despondency.
For a moment she rose from her bed; for a moment she went near him. (4–5)
Wandering about for a moment out of agitation, and again dwelling for a moment,
she fell asleep once more for a brief instant due to her distress;
yet even that bed of flowers and sandalwood became exceedingly thorny to her.
Poisonous food, delicious fruit, and divine water; (7) a formless dwelling, fine clothing, and fire;
likewise, vermilion leaf-designs and wounds—these bring about suffering. (8)
In her state of lassitude, Satī beheld for a moment a well-attired man—handsome, youthful, smiling, and the lord of connoisseurs;
his entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments. (9)
Seeing Mālyavān approaching, gazing at his lotus-like face,
speaking of amorous matters, repeatedly kissing his lower lip,
reclining upon a bed of flowers, and embracing his body— (10–11)
But as Vasantaka was once again departing and returning, she said to him, "O beloved, where are you going? O lord of my life, stay!
Having regained her senses once more, she lamented again and again.
Thus, O Nārada, she remained right there in that penance grove;
while the great yogi Śaṅkhacūḍa, having obtained the enchanting mantra of Kṛṣṇa from Jaigīṣavya, attained perfection at Puṣkara.
Constantly reciting this armor-mantra, which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things,
he obtained from Brahmā and Īśvara the boon that was desired in his heart.
By the command of Brahmā, he indeed went to Badarī.
O Sage, Tulasī saw Śaṅkhacūḍa approaching—
endowed with fresh youth, possessing a splendor equal to that of Kāmadeva,
having the hue of a white campaka flower, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (16–17)

With a face like the full moon of autumn and eyes like autumn lotuses, he is seated in a celestial chariot fashioned from a multitude of great jewels; he is captivating, and his cheeks shine, adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings. (18–19)
Adorned with a garland rich with *pārijāta* flowers, smiling beautifully,
joined with musk and saffron, and radiant with a fragrant tilaka—
seeing him in her presence, she covered her face with her garment. (20)

Gazing at him again and again with a smile and sidelong glances, she became downcast-faced, abashed by her first union; the amorous woman was tormented by the arrow of Kāma and her body was covered in horripilation. (21–22)
And Śaṅkhacūḍa beheld a certain maiden in the penance grove, constantly drinking in his lotus-face with her two eyes;
she was seated upon a bed of flowers and sandalwood, dwelling there clothed in a garment. (23)
Constantly gazing at his face, she was ever-smiling and most enchanting;
she possessed full and firm hips and plump, elevated breasts, and she bore a row of teeth graced by the luster of strings of pearls. (24–25)
With lips like a ripe bimba fruit and a beautiful nose, she was a most excellent beauty;
possessing the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon, she was surrounded by her own splendor, pleasant to behold, and enchanting. (26)
[She was] eternally radiant in the region below her parting of the hair with drops of musk together with a drop of sandalwood paste and a dot of vermilion;
she possessed a deep, sunken navel, and below that, she was marked by the three folds of skin.
She bears lotus-feet with palms as red as the surface of a lotus, adorned with moon-like nails,
and graced by the splendor of land-lotuses; her feet are of a lovely,
slightly reddish hue, possessing a luster like that of liquid lac.
It was resplendent with land-lotuses and water-born lotuses, shining with rubies;
it was illuminated by the rays of moon-like nails that put the autumnal moon to shame,
and it was beautifully adorned with a pavement inlaid with priceless gems.
Adorned with the resonance of tinkling anklets set with the finest of jewels, she bore a mass of braided hair entwined with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
[her forehead] was graced by a makara-shaped ornament fashioned from priceless gems. (32–33)
She is resplendent with the exquisite beauty of a pair of variegated earrings;
her chest is radiant in the space between her breasts with the splendor of necklaces of supreme gems and pearls;
she is adorned with ornaments such as jeweled bracelets, armlets, and conch-shell bangles.
Seeing that graceful, charming, well-behaved, and virtuous woman with beautiful teeth, her fingers adorned with rows of divine jeweled rings,
he stayed near her and spoke sweetly to her.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: Who are you, and whose daughter are you, O blessed one, worthy of honor among excellent women? Who are you, O lovely one, auspicious lady, bestower of all prosperity? (37)

O you who sport in the stream of celestial enjoyments and other delights, O you who take the form of a necklace; O you who are the essence of the wife of worldly existence, O charming support of *māyā*;
O you who are distinct from the world, yet subtle, and the cause of delusion even for sages.
"O beautiful one, abandon your silence and speak with me, your servant.
Having heard these words, that lovely-eyed woman, filled with desire, spoke with longing to him who was likewise filled with desire, smiling and with a downcast face. (39-40)
Tulasī said:
"I am the daughter of Dharmadhvaja, and I am performing penance in this ascetic grove.
As an ascetic, I dwell here; who are you? Go as you please. (41)
"One born of noble family does not question a woman of good birth who is alone in private; this is exactly what has been heard in the Śruti.
A libertine born of an ignoble family is devoid of the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras."
He who has not heard the meaning of the scriptures desires a woman;
he desires her who is sweet at first sight but deadly in the end for a man—
she whose form is like a jar of poison, yet whose mouth is constantly like nectar.
In her heart, she was like the edge of a razor, yet she spoke ever so sweetly;
she was constantly and always intent on the accomplishment of her own purpose.
For the sake of her mission, she remained under the control of her master, though otherwise she was forever independent.
Who among the wise would ever place their trust in those whose inner nature is impure despite their serene faces and eyes,
and whose conduct is not described in the Śruti or the Purāṇas—
just as an unwise man might? (46–47)

Among them, who indeed was not an enemy, seeing that they were always longing in their hearts for some ever-new man well-adorned, while outwardly they strove with effort to manifest their own virtue as chaste wives? 48.
She was ever-desirous, beautiful, the support of passion, and captivating;
she concealed her inner longing for sexual union with outward pretense;
she devoured her lover in secret while appearing exceedingly modest in public. (49–50)
She was proud, angry at the absence of sexual union, and the source of quarrels;
she was terrified of excessive indulgence and distressed by too little sexual intercourse.
In her mind, she longed for well-prepared food and cool water. (51)

[She saw] her son, who was handsome, charming, beloved, young, and always virtuous; [she saw him] showing supreme affection toward his wife, who was skilled in the arts of love; [she saw] her most beloved husband, dearer to her than life itself, and expert in sexual enjoyment. (52–53)
She who looks upon an old man, equal to an enemy, or one incapable of sexual union;
she who constantly quarrels with him and is exceedingly wrathful;
she who consumes him through her service as a plowman consumes the dust of a cow—[these women are to be avoided]. 54.
She is always the very embodiment of wicked violence, the constant refuge of all faults;
she is eternally of the nature of deceit and the perpetual abode of every defect.
She is the form of delusion that even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others find difficult to abandon. (55–56)
It is the bolt on the path of austerity, the door-leaf of the gate of liberation;
it is separated from devotion to Hari, the casket of all illusion, and in the prison of saṃsāra, it is eternally the form of a shackle. (57–58)
She was like a magical illusion and the very embodiment of a false speaker;
she bore external beauty while her middle body was utterly loathsome—a vessel filled with various excrement, urine, and pus, and joined with filth. (59)
Foul-smelling, possessed of defects, smeared with blood, and unrefined;
a deceptive form created by the Creator in ancient times for the sake of deceivers,
appearing as poison to those seeking liberation, yet always invisible to them.
Having spoken thus to him, O Nārada, Tulasī ceased;
and Śaṅkhacūḍa, smiling, began to speak.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said:
O Goddess, what has been spoken by you is not entirely false; listen to me as I explain that some is true and some is false.
The Creator fashioned two kinds of female forms, both of which enchant all beings. (63)
He created the forms of action, both real and unreal, as well as the praiseworthy and the blameworthy;
and having first fashioned the primordial form of the thread of creation, he manifested Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Rādhikā, and the rest. (64–65)
That which is the essential form of these [energies], known as the female form, is considered real;
it is praiseworthy, consists of glory, and is the cause of all auspiciousness. Śatarūpā, Devahūtī, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Dakṣiṇā [are its manifestations].
Chāyāvatī, Rohiṇī, Varuṇānī, and Śacī;
likewise the wife of Kubera and Vāyu, as well as Aditi and Diti;
Lopāmudrā, Anasūyā, Kaiṭabhī, and Tulasī. (67–68)
Ahalyā, Arundhatī, Menā, Tārā, Mandodarī, and another;
Damayantī, Vedavatī, Gaṅgā, and likewise Yamunā;
Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kālikā, and Vasundharā. (69)
The sixth is Maṅgalacaṇḍī, whose form is indeed Dharmakāminī.
[70] Svasti, Śraddhā, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, and likewise the supreme Śānti;
Nidrā, Tandrā, Kṣut, Pipāsā, Sandhyā, Rātri, and the Days. [71]
That which has arisen as the female form— possessing prosperity, conduct, fame, and the splendor of the beauty of action— is supreme in every age. Furthermore,
that which is of the nature of a magical spell (*kṛtyā*), as well as the celestial courtesans and so forth, [is likewise supreme].
That [form] which is dominated by *sattva* is pure by its very nature;
it is the most excellent among all things, the form of a virtuous woman (*sādhvī*), and is highly praised. (73–74)
The wise declare that to be real;
it is remembered as being of two kinds in its activities—consisting of *rajas* and consisting of *tamas*.
Due to the absence of a location, the absence of duration, and the absence of a middle state, [it is unreal].
O beautiful one, through physical hardship, illness, association with the virtuous,
frequent attendance at assemblies, and even through fear of enemies and kings,
the state of being a chaste woman arises from this very [practice] regarding that which is of the nature of passion (rajas). (76–77)
The wise declare this to be the form of the middle [quality];
the learned know that which is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*), difficult to restrain, and base, to be the lowest.
One born of noble lineage and a scholar does not inquire after another’s wife.
Whether in a secluded place or even among the wicked, I shall speak these words to you, O woman:
"I am now coming into your presence by the command of Brahmā;
O beautiful one, I shall take you as my wife through the Gāndharva rite. || 79–80 ||
I am indeed Śaṅkhacūḍa, the one who puts the gods to flight;
I am Sudāmā, born of the lineage of Danu, in the city of Hari throughout the universe.
Among the eight cowherds, as well as among the cows, the gopīs, and the attendants, I am he. (81)
Now I am the lord of the Dānavas due to the curse of Rādhikā;
by the power of the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, I remember my past lives.
O Tulasī, you too remember your past lives, for you were formerly united with Hari.
"You alone were born on the earth of Bhārata from the anger of Rādhikā.
Desiring to enjoy you, I am not capable of it due to the fear of Rādhā.
Having spoken thus, O great sage, that man fell silent.
Smiling and delighted, Tulasī began to speak. Tulasī said:
"Such is this wise man, praised among all the wise in the universe."
A beloved woman always desires such a lover as this according to her heart's desire.
(86) Now, by you, I have truly been defeated through your discernment.
That man who is conquered by a woman is censured and considered impure. (87)
The ancestors, the gods, and kinsmen censure a person who is enslaved by women.
A father and even a brother reproach one who is enslaved by women in thought and speech.
A Brahmin is purified in ten days following both a birth and a death.

A Kṣatriya becomes pure in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra in a month, according to the Vedas. One born of mixed castes is impure for as long as it takes to perform the cremation of his mother; likewise, one who is dominated by women is purified at the time of her cremation.
His ancestors do not accept the offering of rice-balls or water libations at his will;
the gods do not accept his flowers, water, and so forth at his will.
Of what use to him are knowledge, austerity, recitation, fire-offerings, or worship? (91)
"What is the use of learning, fame, or women for one whose mind has been stolen?
(92) You were tested by me for the sake of knowing the power of your learning.
Having performed this test of her beloved, a loving woman chooses her husband. (93)
To one who is unworthy, devoid of virtue, aged, and likewise ignorant;
to one who is poor, foolish, diseased, and contemptible;
and to one who is excessively prone to anger and exceedingly foul-mouthed. (94)
To one who is lame, physically deformed, blind, or deaf;
to one who is dull-witted, mute, impotent, or sinful—he who gives his own daughter to such a person incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. (95–96)
By giving one’s daughter to a Vaiṣṇava who is peaceful, virtuous, young, and learned, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices. He who,
having raised a girl, sells her— if he does so— [incurs great sin].
Through greed for wealth, he goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
There, that sinner eats the urine and excrement of young girls;
bitten by worms and crows, he remains there for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.
At the end of that [life], he certainly obtains birth in the womb of a disease;
he sells loads of meat and carries them indeed day and night.
Having spoken thus, Tulasī ceased speaking in the penance grove.
In the meantime, Brahmā approached them;
O Nārada, Tulasī and Śaṅkhacūḍa bowed their heads to him.
The Lord of Gods sat there and spoke for their benefit.
"O Śaṅkhacūḍa, what are you doing conversing with her?
Take her as your wife by the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
You are a jewel among men, and she is a virtuous jewel among women. || 103 ||
The union of the wise with the wise shall be virtuous.
O King, who would renounce that rare happiness which is free from conflict?
He who abandons the happiness of non-conflict is a beast; of this there is no doubt. (104–105)
O virtuous lady, why do you neglect such a beloved husband,
who is endowed with every virtue and is the subduer of gods, asuras, and dānavas—
just as Lakṣmī is to the Lord of Lakṣmī, or as Rādhikā is to Kṛṣṇa? (106)
Just as Sāvitrī was to me and Bhavānī to Śiva; just as Dharā was to Varāha and Menā to Himālaya; just as Aditi was to Kaśyapa and Sūryā to Vivasvat, and as Damayantī was to Nala. (107–108)
As Rohiṇī was to the Moon, as Rati was devotedly faithful to Kāma, as Diti was to Kaśyapa, and as Arundhatī was to Vasiṣṭha;
as Ahalyā was to Gautama, and Devahūti to Kardama. (109)
Just as Tārā was to Bṛhaspati, as Śatarūpā was to Manu;
as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is to the sacrifice, as Svāhā is to the consumer of oblations (Agni);
as Śacī is to Mahendra, and as Puṣṭi is to Gaṇeśvara. || 110–111 ||

O beautiful one, just as Devasenā is to Skanda and Mūrti is to Dharma, and just as Satī is [devoted] to Śiva, so may you be the beloved wife of Saubhāgya and Śaṅkhacūḍa. O lovely lady, remain with this handsome man for a very long time.
Constantly wander from place to place according to your desire. Afterwards, when Śaṅkhacūḍa has been slain, you shall again attain Govinda in Goloka as the four-armed Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.
Having thus pronounced this benediction, Brahmā departed for his own abode;
and the Dānava took her as his wife by the Gāndharva rite of marriage. In heaven, there was the sounding of drums and a rain of flowers fell.
He took delight with Rāmā in the enchanting bedchamber.
Tulasī, having attained her first union, fell into a swoon;
the virtuous woman was immersed in the ocean of the bliss of sexual enjoyment in that secluded place.
The science of love (*kāmaśāstra*), which consists of sixty-four arts and provides sixty-four kinds of pleasure, has been described according to the desires of connoisseurs;
it captivates women through the union of major and minor limbs. (118)
The Lord of Connoisseurs (Rasikeśvara) made all of that a source of pleasure and erotic delight.
In an exceedingly beautiful place, devoid of all living beings,
upon a bed of flowers and sandalwood, with the breeze of flowers and sandalwood— || 119–120 ||
In a flower garden by the riverbank, anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste—
having taken hold of a passionate woman, a beautiful lady anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste,
adorned with every ornament and exceedingly captivating.
There was no cessation of their amorous play; for those two who were cognizant of such dalliance,
the virtuous Tulasī playfully captivated the mind of her husband, while he, who knew the nuances of passion, captivated the consciousness of that connoisseur of love.
She removed the sandalwood paste from her chest and the tilaka from her arms;
he, for his part, took from her the leaf-designs of vermilion powder.
With joy, he placed those [designs] upon her chest and gave her nail-marks.

She placed it on his left side, marked by the ornament of her hand; the king then gave a bite with his teeth upon the bud of her lip, and she, in turn, bestowed fourfold that mark upon the pair of his cheeks. (123–125)
When their lovemaking had ceased, the two of them rose from each other and there they dressed themselves in the manner they had desired in their hearts.
She applied a forehead mark (*tilaka*) to him with sandalwood paste mixed with saffron.
She applied anointment to all her beautiful and lovely limbs;
she took well-perfumed betel, two garments purified by fire, and a most splendid garland of *pārijāta* flowers. (128–129)
"This supreme ring, fashioned from priceless jewels, beautiful and made of the finest gem, is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Having repeatedly uttered these words, 'I am your slave,' [she gave it to him]. (130)
She bowed with supreme devotion to her lord, who was endowed with excellent qualities.
Smiling, she drank in his lotus-like face again and again with her eyes,
which were beautiful, devoid of blinking, and cast sidelong glances.
Drawing her toward him, he placed his beloved upon his chest;
with a smile, he beheld her lotus-like face veiled by her garment,
and he kissed her firm cheek and her bimba-red lips once again.
He gave her a pair of garments which had been brought from Varuṇa;
he gave her the jewel-garland brought from him, renowned throughout the three worlds;
and he gave her a pair of anklets which had been taken from Svāhā.
A pair of armlets for Chāyā, earrings for Rohiṇī, jeweled rings for Rati, and excellent ornaments;
as well as a beautiful and wonderful conch shell given by Viśvakarman. (135–136)
Having given her a row of various seats, a bed that was very difficult to obtain,
and ornaments, he indeed granted her exemption from taxes;
and having fashioned for her a mass of braided hair adorned with garlands.
A most beautiful leaf-design on her cheek, resembling a letter of victory,
adorned with three crescent moon-marks made of fragrant sandalwood paste,
and surrounded on all sides by various wonderful dots of saffron. (138–139)
She gave him a vermilion tilaka in the shape of a blazing lamp, and with joy she applied the bright red dye of lac to his toenails, which surpassed land-lotuses in their beauty. (140)
He repeatedly placed his passion-filled lotus-foot upon his own chest;
(141) and having uttered again and again, "O Goddess, I am your servant," he took her onto his chest by means of a vehicle fashioned of jewels. (142)
Leaving the penance grove, the king went to another place—
in the Malaya mountains, the abode of the gods, on mountain after mountain, forest after forest,
in spot after spot that was exceedingly beautiful, and in most secluded flower gardens. (143)
In every cave, on the beautiful banks of the Sindhu river, in the forest;
on the banks of the Puṣpabhadrā river, enchanting with its cool breezes;
on every divine sandbank, by every river and every stream. (144–145)
In the springtime, resounding with the sweet humming of bees,
amidst fragrant breezes in the Nandana, Gandhamādana,
Devodyāna, Devavana, and the wondrous sandalwood groves— 146.
In the month of Mādhava, amidst groves of *campaka*, *ketakī*, and *mādhavī* flowers;
amidst *kunda*, *mālatī*, and forests of night-lotuses and day-lotuses;
and in every single *kalpavṛkṣa* tree within the groves of *pārijāta* trees.
In a secluded place on a golden site, on the auspicious Golden Mountain,
in the forest of Kāñcī, in the Kiñcanaka grove, in a golden garment, in a mine of gold, and upon a couch of flowers and sandalwood where the songs of male cuckoos are heard. (149)

Accompanied by flowers and sandalwood, and by the breeze scented with flowers and sandalwood, that lover dallied out of desire with Rāmā, the woman who desired him; yet the lord of the Dānavas was not satiated, nor did she ever reach satiety. (150–151)
Like a fire fed by oblations, the passion of those two increased.
Then, having returned with her to his own hermitage,
the Dānava made a delightful pleasure-garden and sported there once more.
Thus the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa,
the mighty lord of the kings of kings, enjoyed his kingdom for the full duration of one Manvantara,
constantly presiding over the gods, the asuras, and the dānavas. (153–154)
He was the subduer of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Rākṣasas.
The gods, their authority destroyed, wandered about like beggars;
he forcibly took away from them their domain, including their worship, fire-offerings, and other rites. (155)
Their base, their purpose, their weapons, missiles, ornaments, and so forth—all the gods were devoid of effort, like painted puppets;
dejected, they all went to the assembly of Brahmā. (196–157)
They related the account and wept repeatedly and profusely.
Then Brahmā, together with the gods, went to the abode of Śaṅkara.
There, the Creator related everything to the Moon-crested Lord.
Brahmā and Śiva, together with them, went to Vaikuṇṭha—
the supreme abode, most difficult to attain, which removes old age and death—
and reached the excellent gateway of Hari’s hermitages.
He saw the gatekeepers seated upon jeweled lion-thrones,
adorned with yellow garments and decorated with ornaments of precious gems;
all of them wore forest garlands and possessed dark, beautiful forms.
Brahmā described to them— the four-armed ones bearing the conch, discus,
mace, and lotus, smiling, with lotus-like faces, lotus-like eyes, and captivating forms—
the account concerning their departure. (162–163)
They granted him permission, and by their command he entered.
Thus, having observed the sixteen gates,
the lotus-born Lord Brahmā passed them along with them and entered the assembly hall of Hari.

She was surrounded by celestial sages and four-armed attendants who were all of the nature of Nārāyaṇa and adorned with the Kaustubha gem; she was square in shape, yet as enchanting as the orb of the full moon.
Constructed from the essence of the finest jewels, beautifully adorned with the finest diamonds, and inlaid with priceless gems, it was fashioned at the will of Hari;
rich with clusters of ruby garlands and embellished with strings of pearls. (167)
Adorned with circular forms by millions of jewel-mirrors (168),
variegated with diverse painted lines and embellished with various colorful designs,
it was fashioned with artificial lotuses made of the finest rubies (169).
It was provided with hundreds of steps fashioned from syamantaka gems, adorned with beautiful sandalwood sprouts tied with knots of silk thread,
and encircled by pillars of sapphire, making it most enchanting. (170)
It was provided with clusters of jars filled with the seven precious gems, and it shone with networks of garlands made from *pārijāta* flowers;
it was further adorned with fragrant liquid sandalwood mixed with musk and saffron. (171–172)
It was exquisitely refined everywhere, perfumed by fragrant breezes,
and captivating with the musical performances of throngs of Vidyādharīs;
it extended for a thousand yojanas and was filled with attendants.
Brahmā, together with Śaṅkara and the gods, beheld Śrī Hari dwelling in their midst,
like Indra surrounded by stars,
seated upon a variegated lion-throne fashioned from priceless jewels. (174–179)
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with a forest garland,
holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and possessing four arms;
dark-complexioned like a fresh rain-cloud, beautiful and most enchanting.
Adorned with all ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels, his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, he holds a play-lotus;
with a smile and great joy, he gazes upon the dancing and singing before him. (177–178)
Peaceful, beloved of Sarasvatī, with his lotus feet supported by Lakṣmī;
having consumed the fragrant betel offered by his devotees;
