served with supreme devotion by Gaṅgā with white chowries. (179)
And being praised by all, whose necks were bowed in devotion—
having thus beheld that most excellent, omnipresent Lord who is the Supreme Perfected One,
Brahmā and all the gods then prostrated themselves and offered hymns of praise. (180–181)
With all their limbs marked by horripilation, eyes filled with tears, and voices choked with emotion,
the devotees, out of supreme devotion, were both fearful and humble, with their necks bowed.
Then even the Creator of the worlds joined his palms in reverence.
He related the account with humility before Hari.
Having heard those words, Hari— the omniscient one who knows the nature of all things—
smiled and spoke to Brahmā concerning a charming secret.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Lotus-born One, I know the entire account of Śaṅkhacūḍa, as well as that of my devotee, the cowherd of great splendor, from long ago. (185)
O gods, listen to all of that ancient history—
the account of Goloka itself, which destroys sins and is a cause of merit.
There was a cowherd named Sudāmā, who was my foremost attendant.

He attained the womb of a demoness due to the most terrible curse of Rādhā. Once, leaving behind the proud Rādhā—who is dearer to me than life itself—I went from my own abode to the circle of Vṛndāvana. (187–188)
Having learned from the mouth of her servant that I was with Virajā, she subsequently arrived there in a rage and saw me;
and having recognized Virajā as being in the form of a river and myself as having become invisible, [she departed]. (189)
Enraged, she returned to her own abode along with her friends.
Previously, upon seeing me in the palace accompanied by Sudāman, the goddess had severely rebuked me, even though I remained silent and composed. (190–191)
But he, being very great and possessing a beautiful form, became enraged at her;
and in my presence, he rebuked her with anger.
Hearing that, she was filled with wrath, her eyes becoming like red lotuses.
Terrified, she issued the command to expel me from my assembly;
a hundred thousand companions, blazing with irresistible splendor, rose up.
She quickly cast him out as he continued to prattle on again and again.
Having heard those words of his, she became enraged and cursed him with these harsh words: "Go, you wretch, to the womb of a demoness!
As he was departing, cursing her, and weeping, he bowed down to her.
But she, being pleased, weeping out of compassion, restrained him again and again, saying, "O child, stay! Do not go! Where are you going? After she had spoken thus, she departed, filled with wonder.
All the gopīs and the gopas wept, being deeply distressed.
They all, as well as Rādhikā, were then consoled by me:
"After fulfilling the curse for half a moment, she will return. (198)
"O Sudāmā, come here! she said, having been restrained [by her husband].
"Half a moment in Goloka would become an entire Manvantara on earth; such is the certain word of the Creator of the worlds. (199-200)
That very Śaṅkhacūḍa, the most powerful lord of yogīs and expert in all forms of illusion, will go back to that very place. Take my trident and go quickly to Bhārata.

May Śiva bring about the destruction of my demon with his trident. That Dānava constantly wears upon his neck my very armor, the most auspicious of all auspicious things; it is for that reason that he is eternally victorious in battle.

When Brahmā is stationed there at the throat, no one indeed is capable of causing harm. I myself shall assume the form of a Brahmin and offer a petition; at that time, the violation of my wife’s virtue will occur. (204)
At that very time, you granted him the boon, "This shall be his death.
I shall certainly deposit my seed within the womb of his wife;
at that very instant, his death will occur—of this there is no doubt. (205–206)
"Afterwards, having cast off her body, she shall become my beloved.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds gave the trident to Hara;
and having given the trident, Hari joyfully went quickly into his inner abode.
And the gods, led by Brahmā and Rudra, went to Bhārata.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Episode of Tulasī," in the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O great sage, having commissioned Śiva for the destruction of the Dānava, Brahmā quickly went to his own abode,
to his proper place at the base of a charming banyan tree on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river. (1)
There Mahādeva remained for the sake of rescuing the gods;
having appointed Puṣpadanta, the desired lord of the Gandharvas, as his messenger,
he joyfully dispatched him quickly to the presence of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
By the command of Īśvara, he went quickly to that excellent city,
which was superior to the city of Mahendra and greater than the abode of Kubera;
it was five yojanas in width, O Sage, and twice that in length.
It was surrounded on all sides by jewels shaped like crystal,
and it was provided with seven moats that were difficult to cross;
it was eternally adorned with millions of gems that resembled blazing fire.
It was provided with hundreds of streets lined with jeweled altars (6),
surrounded on all sides by throngs of merchants resplendent with various wares,
and adorned with variegated structures fashioned from gems shaped like vermilion (7).
Adorned with hundreds of millions of divine hermitages,
he went and beheld in their midst the excellent abode of Śaṅkhacūḍa,
which was exceedingly circular like the orb of the full moon.
With four moats filled with blazing crests of fire,
it was difficult for enemies to approach yet easy for others to traverse;
it was exceedingly high, touching the sky, and encircled by a rampart of jewels.
It was resplendent with twelve gates, each provided with gatekeepers;
it was enriched with artificial lotuses made of jewels and adorned with jeweled mirrors;
and it was beautified by a hundred thousand palaces inlaid with the finest of great gems.
It was adorned with jeweled staircases and graced by jeweled pillars;
[it was beautified] with jewel-encrusted painted doors and the like, provided with excellent jeweled finials, and resplendent with brilliantly shining rows of various jewels and gems. (12–13)
It was constantly guarded on all sides by hundreds of millions of dānavas—heroes possessing divine weapons, great strength, and prowess;
handsome, well-attired, and adorned with various ornaments. (14)
Having seen them, Puṣpadanta also beheld the gatekeeper;
at the gate stood a man with a spear in his hand, smiling, with tawny eyes, copper-colored, and terrifying. (15–16)
He related the account and departed with his permission;
having passed through the nine gates, he went into the inner city.
No one stopped the messenger, who was there in the form of a messenger.
Having gone to the inner gate, he spoke to the gatekeeper,
[requesting him] to inform the Lord of the entire account of the battle.
And having related that to him, the gatekeeper told the messenger that he might depart.
Having gone there, he beheld that most enchanting Śaṅkhacūḍa,
seated upon a wonderful golden lion-throne inlaid with the finest gems and provided with jeweled handles, situated in the midst of the circle of the Rāsa dance. (20)
It was always beautifully adorned with jewels and artificial flowers;
a captivating golden umbrella was held over it by an attendant, and it was served by hosts of attendants with fans and white chowries. (21–22)
O Sage, he was well-dressed, beautiful, and charming, adorned with jewel ornaments;
he wore garlands, unguents, and fine garments, and was surrounded by thirty million well-attired lords of the Dānavas. (23)
[He was surrounded] by another hundred crores of wandering [demons] bearing weapons.
Seeing him in such a state, Puṣpadanta, filled with wonder,
spoke of the events of the battle as they had been told by Śaṅkara.
Puṣpadanta said:
"O Indra among kings, O Lord, I am a messenger of Śiva named Puṣpadanta.
Listen as I speak that which has been spoken by Śaṅkara himself. (26)
"Bestow now the kingdom and the authority over the gods.
The gods have sought refuge in Śrī Hari, the supreme Lord of Gods.
Having given the trident to you, Hari has sent Śiva forth.
"Trilocana is at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river. [Tell him:
'Grant them a territory, or certainly engage them in battle.
Having gone there, what should I say to Śambhu? You ought to tell me that. (28–29)
Having heard the messenger's words, Śaṅkhacūḍa laughed and said, "I shall indeed come at dawn; you may go. Having departed, he quickly spoke to the Lord who was seated at the foot of the banyan tree.
[He took] that speech of Śaṅkhacūḍa and his retinue.
In the meantime, Skanda arrived in the presence of Śiva,
as did Vīrabhadra, Nandin, Mahākāla, and Subhadraka.
Viśālākṣa, Bāṇa, Piṅgalākṣa, Vikampana, Virūpa, Vikṛti, Maṇibhadra, and Bāṣkala; Kapilākṣa, Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, Vikaṭa, and Tāmralocana. (33)
Kālaṅkaṭa, Balībhadra, Kālajihva, Kuṭīcara, Balonmatta, Raṇaślāghin, Durjaya, and likewise Durgama—these are the eight Bhairavas. The eleven Rudras are remembered as being fierce (raudra). (34–39)
The Vasus, headed by Vāsava, and the twelve Ādityas are recorded;
as well as Hutāśana (Fire), Candra (Moon), Viśvakarman, and those two Aśvins;
Kubera, Yama, Jayanta, and Nalakūbara.
Vāyu and Varuṇa, as well as Budha and Maṅgala; Dharma, Śani, Īśāna, and the heroic Kāmadeva;
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugracaṇḍā, Koṭṭarī, and likewise Kaiṭabhī. || 37–38 ||
The goddess Bhadrakālī herself, possessing a hundred arms and terrifying in appearance,
is seated upon a celestial chariot inlaid with the finest of jewels;
she is clothed in red garments and adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Dancing, laughing, and singing with sweet voices in joy,
she grants fearlessness to her devotee while striking fear into the enemy.
She bears a formidable tongue that is exceedingly mobile and extends for a league.
A skull-bowl, circular in shape and deep, extending for a yojana;
a trident touching the sky, and a spear likewise extending for a yojana;
a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, arrows, and a terrifying bow.
A mallet, a pestle, a thunderbolt, a sword, and a radiant shield;
the Vaiṣṇava weapon, the Vāruṇa weapon, the Āgneya weapon, and the Nāgapāśa;
as well as the Nārāyaṇa weapon, the Brahmāstra, the Gāndharva, and the Gāruḍa.
The Pārjanya, the Pāśupata, the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon of Parvata,
the Māheśvara weapon, the Vāyavya, the Daṇḍa, and likewise the Sammohana—
these and various other weapons, including the supreme hundredfold divine missiles. (45)
Having arrived there, she stood together with thirty million yoginīs and thirty million formidable ḍākinīs;
as well as bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and brahmarākṣasas.
The Vetālas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras,
together with those [goddesses], Skanda bowed to the moon-crested Lord and,
by the command of Bhava, sat down in his father’s presence in the assembly hall.
Then, after the messenger had departed, the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa went inside and related the news to Tulasī.
Having heard the account of the battle, her throat, lips, and palate became parched.
The virtuous woman spoke sweetly with a grieving heart. Tulasī said:
"O lord of my life, O friend, stay for a moment upon my breast."
O God who presides over the vital breath, protect my life for even a moment!
(91) Enjoy that which is to be experienced throughout [my] births, whatever is truly desired by your mind.
Thirsting with my eyes, I behold you for a brief instant. (52)
My vital breaths tremble and my mind is constantly consumed by anguish.
Furthermore, I beheld a bad dream this very day at the final watch of the night.
Having heard Tulasī’s words, the lord of kings ate and drank.
The wise one spoke words that were beneficial, truthful, and appropriate.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said:
"Everything is joined by Time in the bondage of experience."

Auspiciousness, joy, happiness, suffering, fear, grief, and inauspiciousness—these come at the proper time; even trees with their branches appear according to the time, and in due course they become covered in flowers and fruits through the power of time. (55–56)
Their fruits indeed ripen in due time;
all of them, bearing fruit, pass away in their own time.
Beings come into existence in their time, and in their time they pass away.
O beautiful one, all things come into being in time and perish in time.
In time the Creator creates, and by time the Protector protects;
the Destroyer destroys in time, and they all proceed in due succession.
He is the Lord of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is always the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of all things in His entirety.
At the proper time, that very Lord, by His own will, having fashioned primordial nature, [acts].
Having created all things— both moving and non-moving—
that exist in the universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, they declare that everything is indeed artificial; for that which is perishable perishes in the course of time.
Worship the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Rādhā, who transcends the three qualities (guṇas);
the Lord of all, whose form is everything, the infinite Sovereign who is the Self of all—He who creates water with water, protects water with water, and [dissolves it] with water. 63.
One should take away water with water itself; therefore, worship that Kṛṣṇa constantly.
By his command the wind blows perpetually with great speed, and by his command the sun shines according to its season. (64–65)
Indra rains at every moment, and death moves among living beings at every moment;
fire burns at every moment, and the moon wanders like one terrified.
The root of death is Time, and the supreme Yama is the root of Yama.

Go for refuge to that Kṛṣṇa, the creator of even the Creator and the protector of even the Protector; the destroyer of even the Destroyer. Who is a kinsman, and to whom does he belong? O beloved, worship Him who is the kinsman of all. (67–68)
Who am I, or who are you? We were joined together in the past by destiny, and by that same karma we have been separated once again.
An ignorant person is timid in grief and calamity, but not so the wise man.
Happiness and suffering revolve indeed like the rim of a wheel;
you will certainly attain that beloved Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all,
for whose sake penance was performed by you formerly at Badarikāśrama.
"Indeed, you were obtained by me through austerity and by the boon of Brahmā.
O passionate woman, for the sake of Hari you performed penance; you shall attain Hari.
And in Vṛndāvana, you shall obtain Govinda in Goloka."
"I shall go to that world, having cast off this demoniac body.
There you shall see me, and I shall see you constantly.
[I have come] from Rādhikā’s curse to this Bhārata, which is very difficult to attain. (73–74)
"I shall go back to that very place once more; what cause for grief is there for me? Listen, my beloved!
For you, having cast off this body and assumed a divine form, will at that time attain Hari. Do not be despondent, O dear one!"
Having spoken thus at the end of the day,
he slept together with her on a beautiful bed anointed with flowers and sandalwood in that magnificent jewel-palace filled with various kinds of splendors. (76–77)
In a chamber illuminated by jewel-lamps, having obtained that beautiful woman, the jewel among women,
the king spent the night in play, curiosity, and auspicious delights;
he placed that beloved, who was weeping and deeply distressed, upon his chest.
To her, who was emaciated from fasting and submerged in an ocean of grief,
the Knower of Awakening again granted awakening through divine knowledge.
He [revealed] that supreme reality which had previously been bestowed by Kṛṣṇa at Bhāṇḍīra.

And he gave that to her; it was the supreme knowledge that removes all sorrow. Having obtained that knowledge, the goddess, with a serene face and eyes, played with joy, realizing that everything is utterly transitory.

O Sage, those two spouses, immersed in the ocean of bliss and overcome by the intensity of their play, were thrilled with horripilation over all their limbs; fainting in that secluded place, they were joined limb-to-limb, full of affection and eager for sexual union. (82–83)
And those two were likewise like two half-bodies of the Lord of the Universe, each being a half-woman and half-man;
Tulasī regarded the Lord of her life as supreme and dearer than her own life, and the King regarded her, the sovereign lady dearer than his life, as dearer than his own life. (84)
Those two beautiful and equal youths remained there, well-attired and comfortably asleep,
motionless from their pleasant enjoyment and exceedingly charming. For a moment, they became conscious and spoke of matters based on aesthetic sentiment (rasa).
They engaged for a moment in charming and divine conversation, and then, laughing,
they both chewed betel-leaf offered to one another;
with great affection, they also served each other with white fly-whisks.
For a moment they lay down in joy, and for a moment they remained seated;
for a moment they were engaged in play, filled with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva).
Being experts in that domain, there was no cessation from their amorous dalliance.

The two were constantly victorious; they were never defeated for even a single moment. (90) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Union of Tulasī and Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his mind, the king, who was solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa,
rose from his charming flower-bed during the Brāhma-muhūrta;
having discarded his night-garments, he bathed in auspicious water.
Having put on two washed garments and applied a radiant tilaka,
he performed his daily obligatory rites and paid homage to his beloved guru.
He beheld curd, clarified butter, honey, and parched grain— auspicious objects.
O Nārada, he devotedly gave to the Brāhmaṇas the finest jewels, the finest gems, the finest garments, and gold, as was his constant practice;
whatever priceless gems there were— pearls, rubies, and diamonds— he gave them all.
He gave to his brahmin preceptor an elephant-jewel,
a horse-jewel, and a charming cow-jewel for the sake of an auspicious journey.
For the sake of the brahmin’s welfare and for the sake of auspiciousness, he gave everything to that poor man.
With joy, he gave to the Brahmins a thousand treasuries, three hundred thousand cities, and a billion villages;
and having installed his son Sucandra as the king of the Dānavas, he made him the lord of kings.
Having entrusted his wife, the kingdom, all its prosperity, the multitude of subjects and followers, the mass of the treasury, and the vehicles and other assets to his son,
he himself donned his armor and stood with bow in hand.
Through his servants, he gradually assembled a collection of troops:
three hundred thousand horses, five hundred thousand elephants,
ten thousand chariots, and thirty million archers.
O Nārada, an immeasurable army was assembled by the lord of the Dānavas, consisting of three crores of shield-bearers and three crores of trident-wielders;
and within that army was a commander-in-chief who was highly proficient in the science of war.
He should be known as a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*), the foremost among car-warriors in battle.
Having appointed a commander over three hundred thousand *akṣauhiṇīs* of troops,
that lord of men also prepared a collection of musical instruments for thirty *akṣauhiṇīs*.
Remembering Śrī Hari in his mind, he emerged from the camp.
He ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna) inlaid with the finest of jewels and,
placing his elders at the forefront, proceeded to the presence of Śaṅkara.
On the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river is the auspicious Akṣayavaṭa;
there also is Siddhāśrama, known by name as the field of perfection for the Siddhas, and the place of Kapila’s asceticism, a sacred field in Bhārata. (16)
To the east of the western ocean and to the west of Malaya,
in the northern part of Śrīśaila and to the south of Gandhamādana,
it is five yojanas in width and a hundred times that in length.
The auspicious Puṣpabhadrā river is eternal and filled with water;
it is the beloved wife of the salt ocean, ever endowed with good fortune, resembling pure crystal, and bestowing great merit upon Bhārata. (18–19)
And having joined with the Śarāvatī, she emerged from the Himālayas;
keeping Mount Gomanta to her left, she entered the western ocean.
Having gone there, Śaṅkhacūḍa beheld the moon-crested Lord.
Seated at the foot of a banyan tree, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
established in the yogic posture, displaying a mudrā, and smiling;
resembling pure crystal and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Holding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, wearing a garment of tiger-skin, and excellent;
possessing the luster of molten gold, and bearing a mass of matted hair;
three-eyed, five-faced, and having a serpent as his sacred thread.
The conqueror of death, the one who brings about the death of Time and the death of the universe, the supreme;
the remover of death for his devotees, the peaceful, the beloved of Gaurī, the enchanting;
the bestower of the fruits of austerities, the giver of all prosperity. (24–25)
To the one who is easily pleased, whose face is serene, and who bestows grace upon his devotees;
to Viśvanātha, who has the form of the universe, who is the seed of the universe, and from whom the universe is born;
to the sustainer of the universe, the most excellent of all, and the cause of the dissolution of the universe.
The cause of all causes, the one who enables crossing the ocean of hell;
the bestower of knowledge, the seed of knowledge, the eternal bliss of knowledge.
Having descended from his celestial chariot, that lord of the Dānavas beheld him. (27–28)
Filled with devotion, he bowed his head in salutation along with everyone.
To his left was Bhadrakālī, and standing before her was Skanda.
Kālī, Skanda, and Śaṅkara then bestowed their blessings upon him.
Seeing the Dānava, all those led by Nandīśvara rose up.
They then engaged in conversation with one another there.
Having conversed, the king sat down in the presence of Śiva.
The blessed Lord Mahādeva, with a serene soul, spoke to him.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Brahmā is the creator of the worlds, the father of Dharma, and the knower of Dharma."
Marīci was his son, a righteous devotee of Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇava).
Kaśyapa was also his son, a most virtuous lord of progeny (prajāpati). Out of affection and devotion, Dakṣa gave thirteen daughters to him.
Among them, one was the virtuous Danu, who flourished through her good fortune.
Danu had forty sons, the Dānavas, blazing with splendor.
Among them was one named Vipracitti, possessed of great strength and prowess.

His son was the righteous Dambha, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses. Having taken Śukācārya as his guru for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, he chanted the supreme mantra at Puṣkara for a hundred thousand years.
Then you obtained him as a son, one who is supremely devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Formerly, you were a righteous cowherd among the eight Gopas, a personal attendant (Pārṣada). Now, due to the curse of Rādhikā, you are the lord of the Dānavas in Bhārata-varṣa.

The Vaiṣṇava indeed considers everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass to be illusory. Even the states of residing in the same world (sālokya), sharing the same power (sārṣṭi), having the same form (sārūpya), proximity (sāmīpya), and union (aikya) with Hari—
though these may be offered— they do not accept them without [the Lord's] service.

The devotee of Viṣṇu considered even the state of Brahmā or immortality to be trivial; he did not even reckon the status of Indra or Kubera among his concerns. What indeed could be the delusion regarding the domain of the gods for one such as you, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa?
"Give back the kingdom to the gods and show me your favor, O protector of the earth! Dwell happily in your own realm, and let the gods remain in their own places.
Enough with this enmity toward your brother; we are all born of the lineage of Kaśyapa."
Whatever sins there may be, even those such as the killing of a Brahmin,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sin of betraying one's kinsmen (44).
And if you consider, O King of kings, the loss of your own prosperity, [then you will understand].
In whom does equanimity prevail at all times and in all states?
(45) And when the dissolution of primordial nature occurs, there is the concealment of Brahman;
yet its manifestation comes forth again by the will of the Lord. (46)
Through austerity, knowledge, intellect, and memory are certainly established for the world.
That Creator also effects creation through knowledge in due order.
Dharma is most perfect in the Satya age, and it is always rooted in truth.
That [dharma] also remains as three parts in the Tretā age, as two parts in the Dvāpara age,
and as one part in the former part of the Kali age; its decline proceeds gradually until,
at the end of the Kali age, it is reduced to a mere fraction, like the digit of the moon on the new moon day.
The brilliance of the sun in summer is not such again in winter;
nor is that which it possesses at midday equal to what it has in the evening or the morning.
It rises in due time and gradually attains its state of childhood.
And after that, in due time, he again sets;
during the day he goes into concealment, and indeed during the time of a cloudy, rainy day;
when seized by Rāhu he trembles, and once more he returns to clarity.

Just as the moon is most perfectly full on the night of the full moon, it does not remain so forever; rather, it undergoes waning day by day. Then, with each successive new moon, it attains fullness once again.
In the bright fortnight, he is endowed with prosperity; in the dark fortnight, he is withered by consumption.
On a day eclipsed by Rāhu, he is withered; on a cloudy day, when thick clouds prevail, he is likewise withered.
At such times the moon becomes pure, yet its beauty is lost during the shifting of the seasons.

Bali shall now become Indra, his glory fallen into Sutala. In due time, the Earth—the supporter of all, the bearer of wealth—abounding in crops, will be submerged in water and, having met with calamity, will vanish from sight. (56)
All things perish in time and indeed arise from time alone.
Both the moving and the unmoving perish and come into being through time.
Such is the equanimity of the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
Since I am the conqueror of death, I behold the innumerable dissolution of primordial nature (prakṛti),
which is invisible, again and again, over and over. And that which is the form of primordial nature is remembered as the very Puruṣa.
That Self is the soul of all living beings, the supreme bearer of manifold forms.
Indeed, he who constantly performs the chanting of His names and qualities conquers time, death, birth, disease, old age, and fear. (60–61)
O King, he made Brahmā the creator and Viṣṇu the protector in this world;
and I was made the destroyer, because we are all subject to sense-objects.
Having appointed Kālāgnirudra to the task of destruction regarding these objects, O monarch...
I constantly perform the chanting of his name and qualities. By this knowledge, I am the conqueror of death and am free from fear;
out of fear of me, Death flees just as a serpent flees from Vainateya (Garuḍa).

Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Śarva— the Lord of all, the Omniscient, and the Creator of all— then ceased speaking in the midst of the assembly. Having heard those words, the king praised them again and again.
He spoke most beautifully to the god with supreme humility.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said:
"O Lord, everything that has been spoken by you is true and not false."
Nevertheless, listen to my report regarding a certain truth:
you have just now stated that there is great sin in harming one's kin;
yet, having seized Bali’s entire property, why was he sent away? (67–68)
I have extracted all his sovereignty by my prowess;
even that wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu) was not able to rescue him from Sutala.
How then could Hiraṇyākṣa, along with his brother, have been slain by the gods?

And how were the asuras, Śumbha and the others, struck down by the gods? Formerly, during the churning of the ocean, the nectar was consumed by the gods; we were the ones who bore the hardship there, while they were the recipients of all the rewards.
This universe is the plaything of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;
whenever He bestows it upon someone, that person then possesses sovereignty.
The perpetual conflict between the gods and the demons is always occasional.
Their defeat shall be your victory, and ours in due course of time. In this conflict between us, your journey would be fruitless;
for you are a relative of both parties, bound to the high-souled Lord. (73–74)
"Great shame arises now from competing with us,
and even greater would be the loss of fame in battle should we suffer defeat.
Having heard these words of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the Three-eyed One laughed and said:
To the lord of the Dānavas, who was both exceedingly sweet and extremely fierce as was fitting,
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"I shall have a battle with you all, who are born from the lineage of Brahmā."
O King, what great shame or infamy is there in defeat?
In the beginning, O monarch, Hari himself fought with Madhu and Kaiṭabha, as well as with Hiraṇyakaśipu and his own self. (77–78)
Furthermore, there was a battle with Hiraṇyākṣa by that wielder of the mace;
and in ancient times, a battle was also fought by me against the Tripuras and against Maya.
This indeed occurred concerning Prakṛti, the sovereign of all and mother of all.
Formerly, you engaged in a most wonderful battle with Śumbha and his followers.
You are a preeminent attendant of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
As for those Daityas who were slain, none of them were equal to you.

O King, what great shame is there for me in fighting with you—especially since I have been sent by Hari, the very refuge of the gods? Give back the kingdom of the gods; what is the purpose of this mere waste of words? (82)
"Do not wage war against me; this is my firm resolve," Śaṅkara said there and then fell silent, O Nārada. And Śaṅkhacūḍa rose up quickly along with his own followers.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and Śaṅkhacūḍa" within the "Episode of Tulasy," in the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having bowed his head to Śiva, the powerful lord of the Dānavas [spoke].
He quickly ascended the vehicle together with his ministers. At that time, they became agitated, afflicted by Skanda’s spear. Drums resounded in heaven, and a rain of flowers fell.
Right there in that terrifying battle, [he stood] upon Skanda.
Having seen the great, wondrous, and fierce battle of Skanda—
which brought about the destruction of the Dānavas like a natural dissolution— (3) [they were struck with awe].
The king, having ascended his celestial chariot, unleashed a rain of arrows.
The king’s shower of arrows was like a downpour from a cloud;
a great and terrible darkness arose, and a fire broke out.
All the other gods, including Nandīśvara and the rest, fled;
but Kārttikeya alone remained at the forefront of the battle.
[He stood] with mountains, serpents, rocks, and likewise trees.
He constantly rained down a shower of arrows that was difficult to withstand and terrifying.
Shiva’s son, covered by the king’s rain of shafts,
was like the sun shrouded by a dense cloud.
He cut asunder the formidable and terrifying bow-staff;
he shattered the divine chariot and sliced apart the chariot horses.
With a divine weapon, he rendered the peacock mangled and ruined.
He hurled a spear, radiant as the sun, which pierced his chest.
Having fallen into a swoon for a moment and then regaining consciousness,
he took up another divine bow that had been given to him by Viṣṇu in the past.
Having mounted a vehicle inlaid with the finest jewels, Agnibhū took up weapons and missiles and waged a fierce battle;
he [hurled] serpents, mountains, trees, and likewise boulders.
The son of Śiva, with divine weapons, angrily cut them all to pieces.
Guha indeed warded off the Āgneya weapon with the Vāruṇa weapon;
he effortlessly severed the chariot and the bow of Śaṅkhacūḍa.

I, together with my charioteer, hurled a spear as radiant as a meteor at the chest of the lord of the Dānavas, who was resplendent with his crown and diadem. Having fallen into a swoon, the king regained consciousness once more.
Having indeed mounted another vehicle, he quickly seized his bow;
that best of illusionists created a net of arrows through his power of illusion,
O Nārada, and shrouded Guha in the battle with that web of shafts.
He seized an unerring spear, radiant as a hundred suns,
possessing the form of the crest of the fire of universal dissolution, and enveloped by the splendor of Viṣṇu;
and with great force and in fury, Kārttikeya hurled it.
The spear, blazing like a mass of fire, fell upon his body.
Struck by that spear, the mighty Kārttikeya fell into a swoon;
Kālī took him in her arms and brought him into the presence of Śiva.
Śiva, by his mere glance, restored him to life through his divine play;
he granted him infinite strength, and the valiant one rose up.
Śiva then swiftly dispatched his own army and the gods.
A battle indeed commenced with the lords of the Dānavas and their armies.
Mahendra himself fought together with Vṛṣaparvan,
and Bhāskara quickly fought with Vipracitti.
Candra engaged in a great battle with Dambha;
Kāla with Kāleśvara; Hutāśana with Gokarṇa;
Kubera with Kālakeya; and Viśvakarman with Maya.
Mṛtyu was [conquered] by Bhayaṅkara, and likewise Yama by Saṃhāra;
Varuṇa by Kalaviṅka, and Samīraṇa by Cañcala; Budha by Dhṛtapuṣṭa, and Śanaiścara by Raktākṣa. (26–29)
Jayanta was born with Ratnasāra; the Vasus with hosts of splendors;
the two Aśvins with Dīptimant; Nalakūbara with Dhūmra;
Dharma with Dhanurdhara; and Maṅgala with Maṇḍūkākṣa. (27)
Īśāna was accompanied by Śobhākara and Piṭhara; Manmatha by Ulkāmukha, Dhūmra, Khaḍga, and Dhvaja;
and [Bhava] by Kāñcīmukha, Piṇḍa, Dhūmra, and Nandin. (28–29)
The Ādityas fought fiercely with Viśva and Palāśa;
the eleven great Rudras fought with the eleven terrifying ones;
and Mahāmārī fought with Ugradaṇḍa and the others.
Nandīśvara and all the others, together with the hosts of Dānavas,
fought in a great battle during that terrifying dissolution.
And Śambhu stood at the foot of the banyan tree along with Kālī and his son.
And all the hosts of soldiers fought continuously, O Sage. Adorned with jewel ornaments, Śaṅkhacūḍa dwelt upon a beautiful jeweled throne together with ten million Dānavas.
And all the warriors of Śaṅkara were defeated in battle;
all the gods fled, terrified and wounded. Skanda then displayed his wrath and granted fearlessness to the gods.
He indeed increased the strength of his own hosts through his splendor;
he himself alone fought against the multitudes of the Dānavas and slew a hundred akṣauhiṇīs in battle.
The lotus-eyed Kālī cast down the skull-bowl;
enraged, she drank the blood of the Dānavas— one hundred thousand skulls,
ten million lordly elephants, and one hundred million horses.
Taking [the head] with one hand, he playfully threw it into his mouth;
and a thousand headless trunks danced in the battle, O Sage.
The Dānavas were mangled and wounded by the net of arrows from Skanda.
Terrified, they all fled, despite their great strength and prowess.
Vṛṣaparvan, Vipracitti, Dambha, and Vikaṅkana—
all of them fought with Skanda in succession.
Kālī went to the battle, and Śiva protected Kārttikeya.
The heroes followed her, as did Nandīśvara and the others,
along with all the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras.
There were many royal treasures and hundreds of millions of clouds.
And she, having gone to the battlefield, let out a lion’s roar.
By that lion’s roar of the goddess, the Dānavas indeed fell into a swoon.
She let out a most inauspicious, loud, and piercing laugh again and again;
delighted, she drank the *mādhvīka* wine and danced upon the front lines of battle.
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugracaṇḍā, and Kauṭṭarī also drank the honey-wine.
The hosts of Yoginīs and Ḍākinīs, as well as the hosts of gods and others,
having seen Kālī, Śaṅkhacūḍa quickly arrived for battle. The Dānavas were seized with fear, but the King granted them freedom from fear.
Kālī hurled an *āgneya* weapon, resembling the crest of the fire of universal destruction;
the king effortlessly extinguished it with a *vāruṇa* weapon.
She then hurled a *vāruṇa* weapon that was fierce, great, and most wonderful.
And the lord of the Dānavas effortlessly cut it down with a Gāndharva weapon.
Kālī then hurled a Māheśvara weapon, resembling a crest of fire;
the king swiftly struck it down with a Vaiṣṇava weapon, as if in play. (49–50)
That goddess discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon with the accompaniment of mantras.
Seeing it, the king alighted from his chariot and prostrated himself; alas!
That weapon, resembling the crest of the fire of universal destruction, ascended upwards.
And Śaṅkhacūḍa fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff out of devotion.
She, for her part, discharged the Brahmāstra with effort, preceded by the proper mantras.
O great king, she brought that [opposing] Brahmāstra to extinction with her own Brahmāstra.
That goddess discharged a supreme divine weapon accompanied by mantras;
the king, however, brought it to extinction with a web of his own divine weapons.
The goddess then exerted great effort and hurled a spear a yojana in length.
The king indeed shattered it into a hundred pieces with a net of sharp weapons.
Then, in a rage, the queen seized the Pāśupata weapon with the accompaniment of mantras.
As she was about to hurl it, an incorporeal voice spoke to restrain her.

Death does not exist for this high-souled king in the Pāśupata [order], as long as this armor of Hari remains upon his neck; nor does it exist for the king’s wife Satī, as long as her virtue remains here in this world. (56–57)
"Until then, he shall have neither old age nor death"—this was the boon granted by Brahmā.
Having heard this, the virtuous Mahākālī did not cast that [weapon] away;
instead, in her wrath, she effortlessly seized a hundred million Dānavas.
The terrifying goddess rushed with speed toward Śaṅkhacūḍa;
the Dānava warded her off with an exceedingly sharp divine weapon.
She, the goddess, hurled a supreme sword that resembled the summer sun.
With divine weapons, that lord of the Dānavas shattered him into a hundred pieces;
yet the Great Goddess rushed toward him with speed to devour him again.
The illustrious lord of the Dānavas, the master of all supernatural powers, grew in stature once more.
And that supreme lord of all siddhas restrained her;
then the virtuous Kālī, filled with wrath and terrifying, struck him with a fist with great force,
shattering his chariot and killing his charioteer.
She hurled a trident resembling the flame of the fire of universal dissolution;
Śaṅkhacūḍa caught it effortlessly with his left hand.
Then the Goddess, with great fury and speed, struck him with her fist.
The Daitya wandered about in distress and for a moment fell into a swoon; regaining consciousness in an instant,
the powerful one rose up and did not engage in hand-to-hand combat with the Goddess, but bowed down before her.
He cut down the goddess’s weapon and seized him by his own splendor.
Being a devotee of Viṣṇu, he did not hurl a weapon at her out of devotion and because he regarded her as his mother.
Having seized the Dānava, the goddess whirled him around again and again.
And out of anger, he propelled him upward with great velocity.
The powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa fell from above with speed;
having fallen, he rose up again after bowing to Bhadrakālī.

Unwearied from the great battle, he joyfully ascended that most excellent chariot, which was enchanting and inlaid with the finest essence of jewels. And out of hunger, he [consumed] the blood and the abundant flesh of the Dānavas.
Having drunk and eaten, Bhadrakālī went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
She related the account of the battle in its entirety and in proper sequence.
Upon hearing it, Śambhu laughed at the destruction of the Dānavas.
O Lord, one hundred thousand of the lords of the Dānavas remain now in battle;
the rest, along with the arrogant kings, have been consumed by you.
Indeed, [you intend] to slay that lord of the Dānavas in combat with the Pāśupata weapon.
"Your king is not to be slain," such was the incorporeal voice that arose.
That Indra among kings, possessed of great wisdom and great strength and prowess,
did not hurl a weapon at me, but severed my arrow.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Battle between Kālī and Śaṅkhacūḍa," within the *Tulasī-upākhyāna* of the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, in the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard that truth, Śiva, who was an expert in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), [proceeded].
And Nārada, he himself went to the battlefield along with his own attendants.
Upon seeing Śiva, Śaṅkhacūḍa descended from his celestial chariot and,
prostrating like a staff upon the ground, bowed with supreme devotion.
Having prostrated before him, he swiftly ascended his celestial chariot;
he quickly donned his armor and seized his formidable bow.
The battle between Śiva and the Dānava lasted for a full year.
O Brahman, there was indeed neither victory nor defeat for those two.
The Blessed One had laid down his weapons, as had the Dānava;
Śaṅkhacūḍa stood upon his chariot, while the Bull-bannered Lord stood upon his bull.
And there arose a hundred of arrogant Dānavas.
The Lord restored to life those who had died in battle against Śambhu.
Then Viṣṇu, the master of great illusion, assumed the form of an old Brāhmaṇa.
Having arrived at the battlefield, he spoke to the lord of the Dānavas.
The old Brahmin said:
"O king of kings, give alms now to me, a Brahmin."
"You are the bestower of all prosperity, whatever is desired in my mind.
To me, who am aged, deprived of food, thirsty, and afflicted, you shall speak later; first, make your word true. (8–9)
"Om," said the king of kings, his face and eyes serene.
"I am a person seeking armor," he said through his illusory power.
Hearing that, the best of the Dānavas gave him the supreme armor.
Taking the divine armor, Hari himself departed;
assuming the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, he went toward Tulasī.
Having approached her through his illusory power, he indeed performed the act of impregnation.
Then Śambhu seized the trident of Hari for the sake of the Dānava—
a blazing weapon with the splendor of a hundred midday suns in the summer heat,
its tip presided over by Nārāyaṇa and its middle by Brahmā. (13)
Its root is presided over by Śiva, and its support is presided over by Kāla;
it is joined with a multitude of rays, resembling the crest of the fire of universal dissolution;
it is irresistible, invincible, never-failing, and the slayer of enemies. (14–15)
In its brilliance it was equal to a discus, capable of neutralizing all weapons;
distinct from those of Śiva and Keśava, it was difficult to wield and terrifying.
It measured one thousand *dhanus* in length and one hundred *hastas* in width.

O Nārada, once, as a divine sport, he whirled the entire cosmic egg— along with its living beings, its form of Brahman, its eternal nature, and its uncreated state— and cast it toward Śaṅkhacūḍa. (17–18)
The king, having abandoned his bow and assumed a yogic posture with his intellect, meditated with devotion upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Then,
whirling his trident, he hurled it down upon the demon.
And he reduced him, along with his chariot, to ashes with ease.
The king, assuming a divine form as a young boy dressed as a cowherd—two-armed, holding a flute in his hand, and adorned with jewel ornaments—[appeared]. (20–21)
Adorned with various excellent jewels and surrounded by millions of cowherds,
he ascended that vehicle which had come from Goloka and went to that city.
Having arrived, O Sage, he bowed his head before Rādhā and Mādhava.

O sage, having seen Sudāmā and those two [wives] with their faces and eyes radiant with joy, they embraced them with affection on their laps out of love for their lotus feet during the rāsa dance in Vṛndāvana.
Then the trident flew swiftly into the hand of the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin).
With that trident, Śaṅkara [struck] the mass of bones of the Dānava and,
out of affection, cast it into the salt-water ocean.
From the bones of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the genus of conch shells indeed arose.
Of various forms, excellent, pure, and fit for the worship of the gods;
the water from a conch shell is highly praised and supremely pleasing to the deities.
The nature of sacred waters is pure, yet it is not as purifying as that of Śaṅkara.
Wherever the sound of a conch resounds, there Lakṣmī remains firmly established.
He who has bathed with the water from a conch has effectively bathed in all sacred fords.
The conch is the abode of Hari; where there is a conch, there is Hari.
Right there is Lakṣmī ever present, and all inauspiciousness is driven far away—especially by the sound of conchs played by women and Śūdras.
Terrified and enraged, Lakṣmī departed from that place to another place.
And Śiva, having slain the Dānava, went to the world of Śiva,
joyful, mounted upon his bull and surrounded by his own attendants.
The gods attained their own realm, filled with supreme bliss. In heaven, the kettledrums resounded and the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang.
A continuous rain of flowers fell upon Śiva.
And the gods, as well as the foremost among the lords of sages, praised him.

(33) Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Introduction of Śaṅkha," within the "Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa" section of the *Tulasī-upākhyāna*, in the second book, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta-mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
The blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa indeed performed the act of impregnation.
In what form did he do so with Tulasī? You should explain that to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
And the Lord Nārāyaṇa, through his divine power,
assumed the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa and sported with that Rāmā;
having taken Śaṅkhacūḍa’s armor by means of his illusory power, Hari [did so].
Having assumed that form once again, he went to the house of Tulasī.
He sounded a drum in the vicinity of Tulasī’s door and awakened the beautiful lady by means of the sound of shouts of victory.
Having heard that, the virtuous woman, filled with supreme bliss,
gazed with great reverence through the window of the royal highway.
Having given wealth to the Brahmins, she caused auspicious rites to be performed.
He gave wealth to the bards, the mendicants, and the panegyrists.
Having descended from his chariot, the Lord went to the palace of the Queen—
a beautiful and most enchanting residence adorned with priceless jewels.
And seeing her beloved, who was so peaceful, standing before her, the lovely woman was filled with joy;
she washed his feet, bowed down, and wept.
Then, full of longing, she seated him upon a beautiful throne of jewels.
And she gave him betel-leaf, beautifully scented with camphor and other ingredients.
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my actions have become fruitful—for I behold the lord of my life, who had gone to the battlefield, returned once more to my home."
Smiling, casting side-long glances, filled with desire, and her hair standing on end with thrill, she asked her beloved about the events of the battle in a sweet voice. (11) Tulasī said:
"O Lord, how did your victory come about in battle against the destroyer of countless universes? Tell me that, O treasure-house of compassion.
Having heard Tulasī’s words, the Lord of Kamalā laughed and spoke.
In the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, he spoke these false words to her.
Śrī Hari said:
"O beloved, our battle lasted for a full year."
O passionate woman, the destruction of all the Dānavas occurred;
and Brahmā himself brought about our mutual affection.
Furthermore, the authority over the gods was granted by Brahmā in the past.
"I have returned to my own abode, and Śiva has gone to the world of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds lay down upon his bed.
O Nārada, the Lord of Ramā took his delight there together with Rāmā.

That virtuous woman, due to the intensity of her pleasure and the friction of their drawing together, reflected on everything and said, "Who are you? Tulasī said: 17. That virtuous woman, due to the intensity of her pleasure and the friction of their drawing together, reflected on everything and said, "Who are you? Tulasī said:
"Tell me, who are you? O Mistress of Māyā, I have been enjoyed by your Māyā.
Either my chastity has been destroyed by you, or else we shall curse you.
Having heard Tulasī’s words, Hari, out of fear of a curse, [remained silent]. (18–19)
O Brahmin, he effortlessly assumed his own most enchanting form.
Before him, the Goddess beheld the eternal God of gods, dark as a fresh rain-cloud and with eyes like autumn lotuses. (20)
Possessing the playful charm of ten million Cupids, adorned with jewel ornaments,
with a slight smile and a serene countenance, and graced by yellow garments—
seeing him, the passionate woman spontaneously fell into a swoon out of desire. (21)
And having regained consciousness once more, she spoke to him again:
"O Lord, you have no compassion; you are like a stone.
My husband, your master, was killed by you through deceit and the violation of dharma."
"O Lord, since you are devoid of compassion and resemble a stone, therefore, O God, become a stone-form upon this earth now.
Those who call you an ocean of mercy are deluded; of this there is no doubt. (24)
"How was this devotee, who committed no offense, killed for the sake of another?
You are wicked and claim to be all-knowing, yet you do not understand the suffering of others.
Therefore, in your very next birth, you shall forget even yourself. (25-26)
Having spoken thus, the great saintly woman fell at the feet of Hari;
afflicted with grief, she wept bitterly and lamented again and again.
And seeing her compassion, He who is an ocean of mercy [was moved].
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Kamalā, spoke to awaken her. The Blessed Lord said:
"O virtuous lady, you have performed penance for my sake in Bhārata for a long time."
For your sake, Śaṅkhacūḍa performed penance for a very long time;
having made you his beloved, that lustful man enjoyed [her] as the fruit thereof.
Now, it is fitting that the fruit of your own penance be given to you alone. (29–30)
"Having abandoned this body and assumed a divine form, you shall become equal to Ramā and sport with me in the Rāsa dance along with Ramā.
This body of yours shall take the form of a river, renowned as the Gaṇḍakī. || 31 ||
"May she be pure, a bestower of great merit upon men, and holy in Bhārata.
May the mass of your hair become sacred trees;
thus, born from the hair of Tulasī, she became renowned as Tulasī. (32–33)
O fair-faced one, among all flowers and leaves in the three worlds for the worship of the gods, Tulasī shall be the most preeminent form;
[so it shall be] in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in my presence.
O beautiful one, let the *tulasī* trees be the most excellent among flowers in Goloka,
on the banks of the Virajā, in the Rāsa dance, in Vṛndāvana on earth,
at the Bhāṇḍīra tree, in the lovely Campaka forest, and in the sandalwood grove. (35–36)
In groves of mādhavī, ketakī, kunda, mallikā, and mālatī,
let the trees there be givers of merit at those places where flowers are offered (37). And at the foot of a tulasī tree, in that most meritorious place which bestows great merit—

It shall become the presiding ground for all sacred fords (tīrthas), and therein indeed shall be the collective abode of all the gods. O fair-faced one, wherever the leaves of the *tulasī* fall in abundance, [there it shall be]. 38–39.

He who performs an ablution with the water from a *tulasī* leaf has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices; yet that satisfaction which Hari finds in such a rite would not be attained even by a thousand jars of nectar. (40)
Whatever satisfaction may arise for men from the gift of a *tulasī* leaf,
and whatever fruit a man obtains by the gift of ten thousand cows—
that same fruit he obtains, O virtuous lady, by the gift of a *tulasī* leaf. (41–42)
And whoever should obtain the water from a *tulasī* leaf at the time of death,
he is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. That man who daily drinks the water of *tulasī* with devotion—

He alone is liberated while living and shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. That man who, having offered tulasī daily, worships me, obtains the merit born of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
A person who, holding Tulasī in his hand and wearing it upon his body,
gives up his life at sacred pilgrimage sites, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
That man who wears a garland fashioned from Tulasī wood [attains the same].
At every step, he certainly obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
But he who holds a tulasī plant in his hand and does not accept it [as an offering] goes to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Indeed, that man who makes a false oath by Tulasī goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras. And he who obtains even a single drop of Tulasī water at the time of death—
Having ascended the jewel-vehicle, he proceeds to Vaikuṇṭha.
[This occurs] on the full moon day, the new moon day, the twelfth lunar day, or during the transit of the sun;
likewise when one has anointed oneself with oil, when one has not bathed, at midday, at night, or during the two twilights.

Those men who cut the *tulasī* during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) or at an inauspicious time, or when it is covered by night-dust, they cut off the head of Hari. A *tulasī* leaf remains pure for three nights even if it has been left overnight.

In a *śrāddha*, a vow, a gift, a consecration, or the worship of the gods—whatever is given to the true Viṣṇu, even if it has fallen upon the ground or into water, is pure; however, in other rites, even a pure *tulasī* leaf becomes impure through washing. (53–54)
The goddess who presides over the trees in the stainless Goloka will eternally engage in secret play with Kṛṣṇa. The goddess who presides over the rivers in Bhārata is the bestower of great merit.
And she shall become the wife of Lavaṇoda, who is a portion of myself.
And you yourself, O great virtuous lady, shall undoubtedly become equal to Ramā in my presence in Vaikuṇṭha and in the Rāsa dance.
"And I, assuming the form of a mountain, shall establish my presence upon the banks of the Gaṇḍakī in Bhārata due to your curse.
Indeed, there shall be diamond-worms and insects with adamantine fangs. (58)
They shall fashion my image within that stone cavity:
a four-wheeled form with a single door, adorned with a forest garland, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, known by the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (59–60)
One should know that the Lakṣmī-Janārdana [image] has four wheels, a single door, resembles a fresh rain-cloud, and is devoid of a forest garland (vanamālā).
That which has two doors, four wheels, and is provided with a "cow's footprint" (goṣpada) [is another type].
One should know that [the form] named Raghunātha is devoid of a forest garland (vanamālā).
One should know that the [form] named Dadhivāmana is extremely small, possesses two wheels, has the luster of a fresh rain cloud, and bestows happiness upon householders.
One should know that the deity Śrīdhara is very small, has two wheels, and is adorned with a forest garland; he always bestows prosperity upon householders.
[64] Furthermore, [the form of] Śrīnivāsa is large, circular in shape, and devoid of a forest garland.
The one named Dāmodara should be known as having two wheels, clearly and perfectly manifest.
The middle one, circular in shape with two wheels and pierced by arrows, should be known as named Raṇarāma, provided with an arrow and a quiver. (65–66)
The middle [type] has seven wheels and is equipped with an umbrella and quivers;
it should be known as the Rājarājeśvara, which bestows royal prosperity upon men.
The [third type] has fourteen wheels, is massive, and has the luster of a fresh rain cloud.
And that which is known as Ananta should be understood as bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga).
It is circular in shape, possesses two wheels, is endowed with beauty, and has the luster of a water-bearing cloud.
It should be understood as having a cow’s footprint and being central; this is the Madhusūdana [mudrā]. (68–69)
Sudarśana has a single wheel, while Guptacakra bears a mace. Hayagrīva is celebrated as having two wheels, resembling a horse's face.
O Sati, Vikaṭa has two wheels and an exceedingly wide mouth.
The one named Narasiṃha should be known as bestowing immediate detachment upon men.
(71) Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha, who has two discs, a wide-open mouth, and is adorned with a forest garland, should be known as always granting happiness to householders. (72)
At the doorway, one should recognize Vāsudeva, who possesses two wheels, is endowed with splendor, is symmetrical, and clearly manifest; he bestows the fruits of all desires.
Pradyumna has a subtle wheel and the luster of a fresh rain cloud.
If it has hollows and many perforations, it bestows happiness upon householders.
(74) Furthermore, when there are two wheels joined at a single point and the back is full, that should be known as the Saṃkarṣaṇa; it always grants happiness to householders. (75)
The wise declare that the *aniruddha* stone, which is yellowish in luster, circular, and exceedingly beautiful, bestows happiness upon householders.
Wherever there is a *śālagrāma* stone, there Hari is ever present.
In that very place dwells Lakṣmī, accompanied by all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Whatever sins there may be, including even the killing of a Brahmin, they all perish through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (77–78)
A kingdom shaped like an umbrella brings sovereignty; in a circular shape, there is great prosperity.
In the shape of a cart, there is suffering; on the point of a trident, death is certain.
In a distorted mouth, there is poverty; and in a tawny [shape], there is only loss.
If the ascendant wheel (lagnacakra) is split, there will be disease; if it is shattered, death is certain.
Vows, charity, consecrations, ancestral rites (śrāddha), and the worship of deities become highly meritorious through the presence of the Śālagrāma stone.

He who performs an ablution with the waters from the Śālagrāma stone has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices. Whatever merit is found in all acts of charity, as well as in circumambulating the earth, [is obtained by him]. (82)
In all sacrifices, at all sacred fords, and in all vows and fasts, all holy places desire his very touch.
He becomes liberated while living and supremely purified; of this there is no doubt.
By worshipping the Śālagrāma stone, a person certainly obtains that merit which results from the study of the four Vedas and the performance of austerities. Furthermore,
the man who constantly drinks the water from the Śālagrāma stone [obtains the same].

All sacred fords (tīrthas) desire its touch, which grants their heart's desire, bestows grace, and removes birth, death, and old age. One who is liberated while living and greatly purified goes to the abode of Hari at the end.
Right there, he indeed beholds the countless dissolution of material nature along with Hari; and being liberated from the duty of service, he remains in the state of servitude (dāsya).
Whatever sins there may be, including even the killing of a Brahmin, [are all destroyed].
And seeing him, they flee in fear like serpents at the sight of Vainateya.
By the dust of his lotus feet, the earth is instantly purified;
a hundred thousand ancestors of that man are delivered, and his own birth is rendered fruitful.
Whoever obtains the water from a Śālagrāma stone at the time of death,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
he attains the liberation of Nirvāṇa and is released from the experience of karma.
And he shall be dissolved into the foot of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
(92) He who, having held a Śālagrāma stone, speaks a falsehood, goes to Kūrmadaṃṣṭra for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā. (93)
He who touches a Śālagrāma stone and does not maintain his commitment goes to the Asipatra hell for more than a hundred thousand Manvantaras.
He who causes a separation between a Tulasī leaf and a Śālagrāma [suffers likewise].
In another birth, he shall suffer separation from his wife.
Indeed, whoever causes a breach in the *tulasī* leaves upon the conch shell shall likewise be deprived of his wife and afflicted by disease for seven births. (95–96)
The great wise one who keeps a Śālagrāma stone, Tulasī, and a conch together in one place shall become beloved by Śrī Hari. Indeed,
he who performs the act of depositing his seed even once in a woman [is likewise favored].
Upon their separation, mutual suffering will surely arise for them both.
You shall be the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa for the duration of one Manvantara;
your separation from Śaṅkha alone will be the source of your sorrow. (98–99)
Having spoken thus with reverence, Śrī Hari ceased;
and he, having cast off that body, assumed a divine form.
Just as Śrī, so too did she dwell upon the chest of Hari.
The Lord of Kamalā went with her to Vaikuṇṭha.
O Nārada, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā,
and Tulasī became the four beloved wives of the Lord Hari.
Immediately, the river Gaṇḍakī was born from that body;
and on its bank, by a portion of Hari, there arose a mountain that bestows merit upon men.
O Sage, even insects fashion various kinds of stone images there.
"Those that fall into the water and those that possess the luster of clouds are certainly known as *piṅgalās* situated on land due to the affliction of Hari.
Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Tulasī," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
Tulasī is worthy of worship by the entire world; she is pure and the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
Have I not heard of her ritual of worship and her hymn?
O Sage, by whom was she first worshipped and praised in ancient times?
Tell me, alas, by whom did she become your object of worship?
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the one whose banner is Garuḍa smiled and began to relate an ancient narrative of meritorious nature. (3)
Nārāyaṇa said: Having obtained Tulasī, Hari took his pleasure with Ramā; he treated her, who was equal to Ramā in fortune, with great honor. 4.
Lakṣmī and Gaṅgā could not endure her new union with him;
and Sarasvatī, out of jealousy, could not endure her good fortune and dignity.
In a quarrel, that proud woman struck her in the presence of Hari.
Out of shame and because of her humiliation,
that goddess— the sovereign of all siddhis, the wise and perfected yoginī—
vanished from sight out of anger; alas, she became invisible everywhere to Hari.
Not seeing Tulasī, Hari awakened Sarasvatī;
having obtained her permission, he went to the Tulasī grove.
Having gone there and bathed, he [offered] the virtuous Tulasī to Tulasī.
Having meditated upon her, he worshipped her and offered a hymn with devotion:

the ten-syllable mantra preceded by the seed-syllables of Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Kāma (Klīṃ), and Vāṇī (Aiṃ), followed by "Vṛndāvanī" ending in the feminine suffix ṅīp and concluding with the wife of Fire (Svāhā). 9–10.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ vṛndāvanyai svāhā.
O Nārada, by worshipping with this king of mantras, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree, according to the prescribed rite, a person shall obtain all perfections. 11.
O Nārada, she was gratified by ghee-lamps, incense, vermilion, sandalwood, food offerings, flowers,
and presents; and through the hymn of praise to Hari, she appeared from the tree.
Having sought refuge at his lotus feet, she went to him for auspicious protection.
Viṣṇu granted her a boon, saying, "Become one worthy of worship by the world;
I shall carry you upon my head and upon my chest."
"All the gods and others shall themselves bear you upon their heads.
Having spoken thus and taken her, the Lord departed for his own abode.
Nārada said:
"O highly fortunate one, what is the meditation, what is the hymn of praise, or what is the sequence of the ritual for worship of Tulasī? You should explain that to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
When she had vanished, Hari went to the Tulasī grove and, afflicted by the pain of separation, worshipped and praised Tulasī. (17) The Blessed Lord said:

Since trees and those who are like gods (vṛnda) exist together in one place, the wise know her as Vṛndā; I worship that beloved of mine. She was the goddess who existed in the beginning in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Therefore, she is known as Vṛndāvanī; I worship her, the auspicious one.
(19) Since she is worshipped continuously throughout the countless universes, I worship her who is named Viśvapūjitā, the one honored by the world. (20)
I remember with longing that Goddess who is the purifier of the universe, by whom all things are always rendered pure and beyond counting;
without her, even the gods are not satisfied by an abundance of flowers.
Out of grief, I wish to see that Puṣpasārā, who is pure;
for by the mere attainment of her through devotion, joy becomes certain for all.
Therefore, she shall be renowned as Nandinī, and she will indeed be pleased with me.
O beloved, I go for refuge to that Tulasī who is renowned because there is no goddess equal to her among all beings in the entire universe;
she whose form is the very life of Kṛṣṇa, who is eternally his most cherished and virtuous beloved. (24)
"By her, who is the life of Kṛṣṇa, may my life be protected.
(25) Having offered this praise, the Lord of Ramā stood there;
he beheld the virtuous Tulasī herself, bowing at his lotus feet. (26)

Seeing his beloved weeping out of pride— she who was honored by her own self-respect— the lover quickly took her onto his chest. Having received the command of Bhāratī, Hari then went to his own abode.
He quickly caused her to form a bond of affection with Bhāratī.
Viṣṇu granted her a boon, saying: "Be worshipped by the entire universe;
you shall be borne upon my head, and you shall be saluted and honored by me."
By the boon of Viṣṇu, that goddess became exceedingly pleased.
Sarasvatī embraced her and settled her in her own presence;
and Lakṣmī and Gaṅgā, O Nārada, likewise embraced her with smiles.
Then, with humility, he ushered into the house the virtuous Vṛndā,
the inhabitant of Vṛndāvana, the purifier of the universe, and the one honored by the world;
as well as Puṣpasārā, Nandinī, Tulasī, and Kṛṣṇajīvanī.

Whoever recites this eightfold name-stotra, which is endowed with the meaning of the names, after having worshipped her, shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). And on the full moon day of Kārttika, there is the auspicious birth of Tulasī.
There, worship of her was ordained by Hari in the past.
Whoever worships her with devotion there— she who purifies the universe—
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who offers a *tulasī* leaf to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārttika certainly obtains the fruit of giving ten thousand cows;
one without a son obtains a son, and one deprived of a beloved wife obtains a beloved wife.
One who is bereft of kinsmen shall obtain a kinsman merely by recollecting this hymn.
The sick man is released from disease, the bound man is freed from bondage;
the fearful one is liberated from fear, and the sinner is released from sin. (37–38)
Thus has this hymn been told; now hear the procedure for meditation and worship.
You alone know and understand that which is indeed declared in the Kāṇva recension.
As for what I shall say, one should worship her with devotion even without an invocation.
Through the sixteen modes of service, meditation destroys transgressions.
One should worship Tulasī—the essence of flowers, virtuous, beautiful, and like a blazing crest of fire for burning the fuel of all sins. (40–41)
O Sage, even among the goddesses there was no comparison for her among flowers;
she is celebrated as Tulasī, the most sacred form among all. She is to be worn upon the head by everyone, desired, and the purifier of the entire universe. (42)
"Worship her who grants liberation while living, who bestows final liberation, and who grants devotion to Hari.
Having thus meditated upon her, worshipped her, and praised her, the wise man should bow down.
The narrative of Tulasī has been told; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Tulasī," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
O Lord, I have heard this narrative of Tulasī, which is like nectar.
You ought to explain to me that narrative of Sāvitrī,
by which she was formerly manifested and heard as the mother of the Vedas;
by whom was the Goddess worshipped first, and by whom subsequently?
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, in the first [kalpa] the Mother of the Vedas was worshipped by Brahmā;
in the second, by the hosts of gods, and after that, by the assemblies of the learned.
And so, in ancient times in Bhārata, Aśvapati first worshipped him;
after that, the four social orders (varṇas) likewise worshipped him.
Nārada said:
"O Brahman, who was this Aśvapati, and by what means was Sāvitrī worshipped by him? Since she is worthy of worship by all, you ought to explain that to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, in the land of Madra there was a great king named Aśvapati;
he was the destroyer of the strength of his enemies and the dispeller of the suffering of his friends.
He had a great queen, his principal consort, who was a practitioner of dharma.

And she was known as Mālatī, just as Lakṣmī is to the wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu). O Nārada, that queen, a great virtuous woman, performed the worship of Sāvitrī with devotion according to the instruction of Vasiṣṭha.
The queen received no reply and did not see her;
she went home in sorrow, her heart burning with grief.
Seeing her thus distressed, the king indeed consoled her with prudent counsel.
Then, out of devotion to Sāvitrī, he went to Puṣkara for the sake of asceticism.
There, self-restrained, he performed penance for a hundred years.
Yet he did not see Sāvitrī; indeed, he received a rejection.
And the lord of men heard an incorporeal voice from the sky:
"O Nārada, perform ten lakhs of recitations of the Gāyatrī.
In the meantime, Parāśara arrived there.
The king bowed to him, and the sage spoke to the king.
Parāśara said:
"A single recitation of the Gāyatrī removes the sin committed during the day."
By reciting it ten times, one destroys the sins of men committed during the day and night;
by reciting it a hundred times, even the most severe sin accumulated over a month is destroyed; and by reciting it a thousand times, the defilement accumulated over a year is removed. (14–15)
A hundred thousand recitations destroy the sin committed in one lifetime; a million destroy the sins of three lifetimes;
and ten million destroy the sins committed throughout all lifetimes.
(15) Furthermore, such recitation brings liberation to the Brahmins, being ten times more effective than that.
Having formed the hand into the shape of a serpent’s hood and raised it upward,
the twice-born man, facing east, should recite the mantra with his head bowed and motionless.
Then, starting from the middle of the ring finger, he should proceed in a counter-clockwise direction around the left side.

This is the procedure for recitation on the hand, extending as far as the base of the index finger. O King, having fashioned a rosary from white lotus seeds or consecrated crystal beads, one should perform the recitation at a sacred ford or in a temple of the gods.
Having fixed the rosary upon seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree while remaining self-controlled, the wise one, having smeared it with *gorocanā*, should bathe it with the *gāyatrī*.
He should then recite the *gāyatrī* one hundred times over it according to the prescribed rule. (20–21)
Alternatively, having bathed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated the garland,
or else having bathed with the water of the Gaṅgā and being well-consecrated;
O royal sage, perform the recitation (japa) of one million [times] in this sequence.
You will behold Sāvitrī directly through the destruction of the sins of three births.
Day after day, you shall perform [this] constantly at the three junctions of the day—
at midday, in the evening, and always in the morning— remaining pure.

One who is devoid of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts. Whatever work he performs during the day, he shall not partake of its fruit. He who does not attend upon the morning twilight and does not worship the evening twilight [is likewise excluded].

He should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born like a Śūdra. But he who performs the three daily prayers (saṃdhyā) throughout his entire life is a Brāhmaṇa equal to the Sun in splendor and ascetic power at all times.
The earth was instantly purified by the dust of his lotus feet.
For that radiant twice-born man who is purified by the twilight prayers is liberated while living;
indeed, even sacred pilgrimage sites become pure merely by his touch.
Then, just as serpents flee from Vainateya (Garuḍa), sins surely depart.

Neither the gods accept worship nor do the ancestors accept the offering of rice-balls and libations from a twice-born man who acts according to his own will and neglects the three daily junctures (saṃdhyā).

A twice-born man who is devoid of Viṣṇu-mantras, who neglects the three daily junctions (sandhyā), and who omits the Ekādaśī fast, is like a serpent deprived of its venom. One who eats food not offered to Hari, a washerman, and a bullock-driver [are likewise excluded]. (31)
A Brahmin who eats the food of a Śūdra is like a snake devoid of poison;
so too is a Brahmin who burns the corpses of Śūdras, one who is the husband of a Śūdra woman, and one who serves as a cook for Śūdras—each is like a snake devoid of poison. (32–33)
The twice-born who accepts gifts from Śūdras, he who performs sacrifices for Śūdras, he who lives by the sword, he who lives by ink, and he who is like a serpent devoid of poison;
the Brahmin who eats the food of a woman without a husband, and he who eats the food of a woman who has just bathed after her menses. (34)
A Brahmin who lives off his wife,
a usurer, and one who sells the name of Hari—
O King, like a serpent devoid of venom, so is he who sells knowledge. (35–36)
"And that twice-born who eats twice a day at sunrise, who eats fish,
and who is devoid of stone-worship and other rites, is like a serpent without venom.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages [described] the entire sequence of the rules for worship.
And he spoke to him regarding Sāvitrī’s desired meditation and other practices (vv.
38–39). Having bestowed everything upon the lord of men, the sage departed for his own abode.
The king, having honored Sāvitrī, beheld her and obtained the boon.
Nārada said: What was the meditation of Sāvitrī, or what was the procedure for her worship?
Having given what hymn and what mantra did that Parāśara depart?
"By what ritual did King Aśvapati worship the Mother of the Vedas, and what boon did that king obtain? Tell me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, at an auspicious time, one who is self-restrained should,
as a practitioner of the vow, devoutly perform the rite on the fourteenth day as well.
This vow lasts for fourteen years and is endowed with the fruit of fourteen times seven.
Having offered fourteen oblations, as well as flowers, incense, and so forth,
along with clothing, a sacred thread, and food according to the prescribed rules,
he should then place an auspicious water-pot provided with fruits and branches.
O Sage, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā, one should worship the desired deity invoked within the water-pot (ghaṭa).
Now hear the meditation on Sāvitrī as it was described for the midday ritual.
The hymn of praise, the ritual procedure for worship, and the mantra that grants all desires;
[she who] has the luster of molten gold, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns at midday in the summer heat.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, adorned with jewel ornaments, wearing garments as pure as fire, she was intent on bestowing grace upon her devotees;
she is the giver of happiness and liberation, the peaceful and beloved consort of Brahmā, the Creator of the worlds. (48)

I worship you, the Mother of the Vedas, whose very nature is all prosperity and who bestows all riches; you are the presiding goddess of the Vedas, the embodiment of the Vedic scriptures, and the seed-form within the Veda itself. 49–50.
Having meditated with this meditation and placed a flower upon his own head,
the observer of the vow, having meditated again with devotion, should invoke the Goddess into the jar,
having offered the sixteen services preceded by mantras declared in the Vedas.
Having worshipped and praised her, one should thus prostrate before the Goddess according to the prescribed rite:
[offering] a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for bathing, unguents, incense, a lamp, food offerings, betel, and cool water. (52–53)
Garments, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, water for rinsing the mouth,
and a charming, excellent bed— these sixteen items should be given.
They may be fashioned from choice wood or made of gold and other precious materials.
The support of the gods and the bestower of merit has been constantly offered by me.
Holy water for the feet and the great, merit-bestowing, joy-inducing water—pure and forming an integral part of the worship—have been offered by me with devotion. (55–56)
This purifying arghya, accompanied by dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
bestowing merit and sprinkled with water from a conch shell, is offered by me to you.
Also, this fragrant āmalaka oil, which is the cause of bodily beauty.
"May you accept this bathing water offered by me with devotion.
(58) Produced on the Malaya mountain, increasing the beauty of the body, endowed with fragrance, and bestowing happiness—this has been offered by me to you. (59)

Produced from fragrant substances, meritorious, delightful, and bestowing divine scent—may this incense offered by me with devotion be accepted. It is beautiful to behold for all the worlds and the cause of radiant light. (60)
I have offered to you this seed for the destruction of darkness.
Please accept this food offering, which bestows contentment, nourishment, and joy; which destroys hunger, grants merit, and is sweet in form. (61–62)
