And this excellent, beautiful betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other fragrances, which bestows both contentment and nourishment, has been offered by me with devotion;
it is perfectly cool, perfumed, and the cause for the destruction of thirst. (63)
May the form of the life-force of the worlds and the very essence of vitality be accepted.
May the garment made of cotton and that produced by worms—both of which constitute the beauty of the body and enhance the splendor of the assembly—be accepted. (64–65)

"May this ornament, fashioned from gold and other precious materials, endowed with beauty and always bringing prosperity, bestowing happiness and merit—may it be accepted. It is strewn with various flowering creepers and possessed of manifold luster. (66)
"Please accept this garland, which bestows joy and merit;
and please accept this fragrance, rich with scent, which is the embodiment of all auspiciousness, the bestower of all auspiciousness, the most excellent, and the giver of merit. (67–68)
Pure, bestowing purity, and a great source of joy for the pure;
delightful and intended for sipping, this has been offered by me—please accept it.
It is fashioned from the essence of jewels and the like, and is joined with flowers and sandalwood.
Please accept this excellent bed, which bestows happiness and merit.
Please accept this fruit, produced from various trees, endowed with diverse forms,
consisting of fruit itself, and granting the fruit [of one's desires].

And accept this excellent, beautiful sindūra, which greatly enhances the splendor of the forehead; it is the ornament of ornaments—accept this sindūra, fashioned from a holy thread and joined with pure knots. (72)
Let the sacred thread be taken up with a Vedic mantra.
(73) Having offered these articles with the root mantra, the wise man should recite a hymn of praise.
Then, having bowed to the Brahmin, the observer of the vow should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (74)
They know the eight-syllable mantra to be preceded by Śrī, Hrīṃ, and Klīṃ, ending with the dative case of Sāvitrī and the wife of Vahni (svāhā). [79] Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sāvitryai Svāhā.

Learn from me as I describe to you the hymn recited at midday, which grants the fruit of all desires and serves as the very means of livelihood for Brahmins. In ancient times, Sāvitrī was bestowed by Kṛṣṇa upon Brahmā in Goloka.
But she did not go with him to the world of Brahmā, O Nārada.
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā praised the Mother of the Vedas with devotion;
thereupon, being highly pleased, that virtuous lady desired Brahmā.
Brahmā said: O Nārāyaṇī, whose very form is Nārāyaṇa, O eternal one, O you who have arisen from Nārāyaṇa, be gracious, O beautiful lady! (79)

O beautiful one, be gracious toward the twice-born, you who are the supreme essence of light, whose form is supreme bliss, and who are the very embodiment of the caste of the twice-born. O Goddess, eternal, eternally beloved, you whose nature is perpetual bliss.
O beautiful one, be gracious in the form of all auspiciousness!
O you who are the essence of all, the heart of the mantras of the Brahmins, higher than the highest;
O Goddess, bestower of happiness and liberation, O beautiful one, be gracious! 81–82.

O Goddess who bestows the splendor of Brahman, O beautiful one, be gracious for the sake of burning away the dense mass of the sins of the twice-born, which are like blazing flames of fire. Whatever sin a twice-born man commits through body, mind, or speech—[may it be destroyed]. (83)
"By the mere remembrance of that [mantra], it shall be reduced to ashes.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the worlds remained there in the assembly;
Sāvitrī, together with Brahmā, departed for the world of Brahmā.
Having praised King Aśvapati with this king of hymns,
he beheld Sāvitrī and obtained the boon desired in his heart.
Whoever recites this meritorious king of hymns at the three junctions of the day, [shall obtain the same].
One shall certainly obtain that fruit which is gained from the study of the four Vedas.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Sāvitrī Hymn" within the Sāvitrī Episode of the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, during the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having praised her and honored her according to the prescribed rites, King Aśvapati beheld there that goddess, whose splendor was equal to a thousand suns. She,
the virtuous one, being pleased, spoke to the king with a smile.
Just as a mother illuminates her own son with the radiance of her splendor pervading the quarters,
Sāvitrī said:
"O Great King, I know what is in your mind."
"I shall certainly grant everything desired by you and your wife.
Your beloved wife desires a virtuous daughter,
and since you pray for a son, both shall come to pass for you in due course."
Having spoken thus, that great goddess departed for the world of Brahmā.
The king went to his own home, and his daughter was born first.
From the wealth of the king, through Sāvitrī, Kamalā-kalā was born.
And King Aśvapati gave her the name Sāvitrī.
In the course of time, as she grew, she became more beautiful day by day; endowed with beauty and youth, she was like a digit of the moon in its bright fortnight.
Then Sāvitrī chose as her husband Satyavat, the son of Dyumatsena, who was endowed with manifold virtues.
And the king gave her to him, adorned with jewels and ornaments.
And he, out of curiosity, took her and went home.
(9) And when a year had passed, Satyavān, whose valor was truth, went for the sake of wood and fruit by his father’s command, filled with joy. (10)
Sāvitrī went there after him by the turn of fate.
Having fallen from the tree due to destiny, Satyavān gave up his life-breaths, O Sage. Yama then bound that personified soul, which was the size of a thumb.

Having taken her, he departed; thereafter, the virtuous woman followed after him. Then, seeing that beautiful lady, Yama, the lord of Saṃyaminī and the great preeminent among the righteous, spoke sweetly to the chaste woman.
Yama said:
"O Sāvitrī, oh, where are you going, having assumed a human body?
If you shall go together with your beloved, then cast off this body!"

A mortal cannot go to the world of Yama while still holding this perishable body composed of the five elements; for he is himself always subject to destruction. O Satī, when you were present in Bhārata, your husband’s time had indeed reached its full measure.
For the sake of experiencing the fruits of his actions, that truthful one comes to my house.
By action a living being is born; by action alone he perishes.
Through action alone one encounters pleasure, pain, fear, and sorrow. (16–17)
By one's own karma a living being becomes Indra; by one's own karma one becomes a son of Brahmā.
By one's own karma one becomes a servant of Hari, free from birth and other such conditions.
By one's own karma one certainly attains all perfections and immortality.

By his own action, O Viṣṇu, he may obtain the fourfold state of being in the same world as Viṣṇu (sālokya) and so forth; by his own action, a man may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa and liberation, as well as the status of a celestial being,
the status of a Manu, and the sovereignty of a king of kings.
And by action one attains the state of a lord of sages, and by action the state of an ascetic;
by one's own action one attains the status of a Kṣatriya, and by one's own action the status of a Vaiśya.
And by action alone one attains the status of a Śūdra, and by one's own action the status of an outcaste.
And by one's own karma one attains the state of a barbarian; there is no doubt in this.
By one's own karma one attains the state of a mobile being, and by one's own karma the state of an immobile being.
By one's own karma one attains the state of a mountain, and by one's own karma the state of a tree.
By one's own karma one attains the state of a beast, and by one's own karma the state of a bird;
by one's own karma one becomes a lowly creature, and by one's own karma a worm;
by one's own karma one becomes a serpent, and by one's own karma a gandharva. (24–25)
Through one's own karma one attains the state of a *rākṣasa*, through one's own karma the state of a *kinnara*;
through one's own karma the state of a *yakṣa*, and through one's own karma the state of a *kūṣmāṇḍa*.
Through one's own karma the state of a *preta*, and through one's own karma the state of a *vetāla*. (26)
And through one's own karma, one attains the state of a spirit (bhūta), a piśāca, or a ḍākinī;
through one's own karma, one attains the state of a daitya, a dānava, or even an asura.
By one's karma a living being becomes meritorious, and by its own karma it becomes a great sinner.
By action one becomes handsome or free from disease, and by action one becomes afflicted with a great malady.
By action one becomes blind, one-eyed, or deformed through one’s own deeds. (29) By action living beings go to hell, and by their own action they go to heaven.
By one's own action, one reaches the world of Śakra; by one's own action, the world of Sūrya. By one's action, the world of Candra; by one's own action, the world of Vahni.
By one's action, the world of Vāyu; and by one's action, the abode of Varuṇa. (30–31)
Likewise, by his own karma a man goes to the world of Kubera;
by his own karma he goes to the world of Dhruva and the world of Śiva;
and by his own karma he goes to the world of the stars and the world of Satya.
By one's own karma [one reaches] Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Maharloka;
by one's own karma, Pātāla; and by one's own karma, Brahmaloka.
By [this] merit, O Bhārata, one attains the holy land of Bhārata, which bestows all desired boons.
By one's own action one goes to Vaikuṇṭha and to the stainless Goloka;
by one's action one is long-lived, and by one's own action one has a lifespan of but a moment.
By one's action one lives for ten million kalpas, and by one's own action one's life is exhausted.
"O Sundarī, I have thus explained to you all this truth: that the lifespan in the womb lasts only as long as the movement of the *jīva*, and death occurs there through one's own karma.
Your husband has died by the power of his karma; go, my child, as you please. (36–37)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration that Karma is the Sole Cause of All," in the section on the ripening of karma within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second book, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Yama, the devoted wife Sāvitrī—
She praised him with supreme devotion, and that high-minded lady spoke to him.
Sāvitrī said:
"O Dharmarāja, what is the auspicious action of men, or what is the inauspicious?"
By what means do virtuous people utterly uproot karma?
What is the seed-form of karmas, and who is it that bestows the fruit of karma?
What is that karma, by what does it arise, and who indeed is its cause? (2–3)
Who experiences the fruit of action, and who remains entirely untainted?
Who is the embodied soul and what is the body? Who indeed is the agent of action?
What is consciousness, the mind, and the intellect? And what are the vital breaths of embodied beings?

Which are the senses, what is their defining characteristic, and who are their presiding deities? (5) Who is the enjoyer, or who is the one who causes enjoyment? What is enjoyment, and what is its cessation? Who is the individual soul (jīva), and who is the supreme self (paramātman)? You should explain these to me. (6)
Yama said:
"Action ordained by the Veda is the supreme auspiciousness within me;
however, that action which is non-Vedic is indeed inauspicious. (7)
The service of Viṣṇu by the virtuous is causeless and free from mental constructs;
it indeed consists in the uprooting of karma and bestows devotion to Hari.
It is heard in the Śruti that the man who is a devotee of Hari is liberated.
Free from birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and fear;
O virtuous lady, liberation is said in the Śrutis to be of two kinds, approved by all:
that which bestows the state of Nirvāṇa, and that which grants devotion to Hari for human beings. (9–10)
The Vaiṣṇavas indeed desire liberation in the form of devotion to Hari,
while other virtuous ones desire liberation in the form of *nirvāṇa*.
[He is] the seed-form of karma and the constant bestower of its fruit.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is of the nature of light and is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
He too possesses a form that is the cause of that [nature]; through Him, action comes into being.
The individual soul (jīva) experiences the fruit of its actions, while the Self (ātman) remains entirely untainted.
The embodied being, the individual soul (jīva), is indeed the reflection of the Self.
The body, composed of the five elements, is truly perishable.
Earth, air, space, water, and likewise fire—these are the elements.
These are the forms of the Sūtras regarding the creation of Hari in the process of creation:
"He is the agent, the enjoyer, the embodied one, the self, and the eternal provider of enjoyment; enjoyment, the various manifestations of power, expiation, and liberation itself. (15–16)
Knowledge, which is the seed of the distinction between the existent and the non-existent, becomes manifold;
it is proclaimed as the seed of the differentiation of objects.
In the Śruti, intellect (buddhi) is described as having the nature of discernment and as that which illuminates knowledge.
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed divisions of wind and constitute the form of strength for embodied beings.
They are the most excellent among the senses, a collective of lords, the impeller of actions, and truly difficult to restrain for those who possess a body. (16, 19)
The mind is known as that which is indiscernible and invisible, and which constitutes the differentiation of cognitions.
The eye, ear, nose, skin, tongue, and so forth are the sense organs.
They are the instruments of the embodied soul, their very form being the means for all actions and the impellers thereof. (20)
He is always in the form of an enemy and the form of a friend, bestowing both happiness and suffering.
The sun, the wind, the earth, speech, and other such deities are traditionally remembered as him.
Indeed, he who sustains the vital breath, the body, and so forth, is celebrated as the *jīva* (the individual soul).
The Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature,
the cause of all causes— Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is the Blessed Lord. Thus, everything that was asked has been told by me according to the scriptures.
"O child, go as you please to the wise ones who are the very embodiment of knowledge.
Sāvitrī said:
"Having abandoned my beloved husband, where shall I go—to you, the wise one who is an ocean of knowledge?"
Whatever question I ask you, you ought to answer it.
O Yama, by what action does the living soul go to which particular womb?
By what action, O Father, does one go to heaven, and by what to hell?
By what action does liberation come about, and by what does devotion to Hari arise?
By what action does one become diseased, and by what action does one become free from disease? By what action does one have a long life, and by what action does one have a short life? (27)
By what karma does one become miserable, and by what karma does one become happy?
(28) By what karma is one deprived of limbs, or one-eyed, or deaf?
Or by what karma is one blind, or wretched, or even heedless? (29)
By what means does one who is reviled, one who is excessively greedy, and even a slayer of men attain success?
By what means does one obtain the fourfold state of *sālokya* and the rest? And by what means does one attain the status of a Brahmin or the state of an ascetic?
O Brahman, by what karma is one attained to the enjoyments of heaven, and by what to Vaikuṇṭha? Or by what is Goloka reached—that which is the most excellent and free from all affliction?
Furthermore, how many kinds of hell are there, what is their number, and what are their names?
Who goes to which hell, and for how long does one remain there?
By what sinful deed is which specific disease produced?
You ought to explain all that I have asked you. (33–34)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Sāvitrī’s Question after Yama’s Speech," in the section on the ripening of karma within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second book, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Sāvitrī, Yama was struck with amazement.
Smiling, he began to speak of the ripening of the karma of living beings.
Yama said:
"O child, you are now a girl of twelve years in age."
Your knowledge is supreme among the ancient sages, yogins, and men of wisdom.
O virtuous lady, by virtue of the boon granted by Sāvitrī, you became a portion of Sāvitrī herself;
and in former times, O auspicious one, you were made equal to her by the king through his ascetic penance.
Just as Śrī is on the lap of the Lord of Śrī, and Bhavānī is on the chest of Bhava;
just as Rādhā is with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and Sāvitrī is on the breast of Brahmā;
and just as Mūrti is on the chest of Dharma, and Śatarūpā is with Manu. (4)
As Devahūti was to Kardama, as Arundhatī was to Vasiṣṭha;
as Aditi was to Kaśyapa, and as Ahalyā was to Gautama;
as Śacī was to Mahendra, and as Rohiṇī was to Candra. || 5–6 ||
As Rati is to Kāmadeva, as Svāhā is to the Consumer of Oblations (Agni), as Svadhā is to the ancestors, and as Saṃjñā is to the Maker of Day (the Sun);
as Varuṇānī is to Varuṇa, and as Dakṣiṇā is to the Sacrifice. (7)
"As Dharā [was born] from the Boar, and as Devasenā [was born] from Kārttikeya,
so may you be Saubhāgyā and Supriyā, O beloved Satyavatī;
thus a boon has been granted to you, as well as whatever else you desire."
"Choose, O illustrious goddess; I shall certainly grant you everything.
Sāvitrī said:
"I desire a hundred sons born of my own body from Satyavat."
"O highly fortunate one, this boon which I desire shall come to pass:
let there be a hundred sons for my father, and let sight be restored to my father-in-law;
let there be the recovery of the kingdom—thus is the boon I desire. (10–11)
"I shall go to the abode of Hari together with Satyavat before a hundred thousand years have passed. O Lord of the Universe, take back this body of mine;
I have a great curiosity to hear about the ripening of the karma of living beings."
"You should explain to me that seed of universal expansion.
Yama said:
"O great virtuous lady, everything you have conceived in your mind shall come to pass."
Listen as I describe the ripening of the karma of living beings:
the fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious actions is experienced throughout this sacred field of Bharata, and nowhere else. (14–15)
The Suras, Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and others, as well as men who perform actions—none of these have equal lives;
they experience the fruits of their actions according to their specific lifespans across all classes of birth. (16)
In particular, human beings wander through all the wombs;
they experience the supreme fruits of their previously acquired actions, both auspicious and inauspicious.
By means of auspicious action, they go to heaven and other such realms.
And by inauspicious karma alone, they wander in the hells.
Liberation consists in the uprooting of karma; that liberation is considered to be of two kinds:
the form of Nirvāṇa and service to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (19)

By evil action a living being becomes diseased, while by auspicious action he becomes long-lived; yet by certain [other] actions, one whose life was exhausted becomes long-lived, and one who was happy becomes miserable. Furthermore, by contemptible action, people become blind or otherwise deprived of their limbs. (20–21)
One attains success and other fruits through this most excellent rite.
O beautiful one, everything general has been told; now hear the specific details, which are very difficult to obtain even in the Purāṇas and the Vedas, yet provide sublime enjoyment. (22–23)
Among all castes in Bhārata, the human birth is difficult to obtain.
Among all [human beings], the Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent and praised in all rites.
(24) Furthermore, in Bhārata, the twice-born who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is even more venerable than that.
O virtuous lady, a Vaiṣṇava is of two kinds: one who has desires and one who is free from desires.
The one with desires is further divided into the primary (sakāma) and the devotee free from desire (niṣkāma).
The one with desires experiences the fruits of his actions, while the one free from desires is beyond all affliction.
Having abandoned the body, he goes to the stainless abode of Viṣṇu; for those free from desire, O Satī, there is no returning again. Those who serve the two-armed Kṛṣṇa, the Self, the Lord—
Those devotees who assume divine forms go to Goloka. And all those devotees of Nārāyaṇa who serve the four-armed Lord assume divine forms and go to Vaikuṇṭha. (28–29)
Having gone to Vaikuṇṭha, both those with desires and the Vaiṣṇavas return again to Bhārata; their birth occurs among the twice-born,
and in the course of time, they will gradually become free from desire.
He will certainly grant them pure devotion and a stainless intellect. (31) Others than the Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇas are possessed of desires throughout all their births;
they do not possess a stainless intellect, as they are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu. (32)

O virtuous lady, those twice-born who reside at sacred fords and are devoted to asceticism go to the world of Brahmā, yet they return again to Bhārata. The Brahmins in Bhārata who are devoted to their own duties and are devotees of the Sun [attain the same].
They go to the world of the Sun and return again to Bhārata.
(34) Those Brahmins devoted to their own duties—whether Śaivas, Śāktas, or Gāṇapas—they go to the world of Śiva and return again to Bhārata. (35)
Those Brahmins who worship other deities, yet remain devoted to their own duty while living in this world, go to the realm of Śakra and return again to Bhārata.
Those twice-born ones who are devotees of Hari, though free from desire, are devoid of their own specific duty.
Even they go to the world of Hari by the power of devotion in due course—oh!
But those Brahmins who are devoid of their own duty, who never serve the gods, who have fallen from right conduct, and who are childish, certainly go to hell. (37–38)
And likewise, the four castes who are devoted to their own specific duties certainly become partakers of the fruits of auspicious action alone;
but those who are devoid of their own duty surely go to hell.

In Bhārata, they indeed become partakers of the fruits of their actions. Brāhmaṇas devoted to their own duty give a daughter to a brāhmaṇa who is likewise devoted to his own duty; they go to the world of the Moon.
O virtuous lady, they dwell there as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
It is said that by the gift of a woman adorned with ornaments, the fruit is twofold.
Those who possess desire go to that world, but Vaiṣṇavas who are free from desire do not.
Those who are free from attachment to rewards go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Those who give products of the cow, silver, a wife, clothing, grain, fruit,
and water to Brahmins indeed go to that same world.
And they dwell in that world, O Satī, for as long as a manvantara; those people remain there for a very long time who give gold, cows, copper, and so forth, O Satī.
They go to the world of the Sun because of their purity and because they gave to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Sati, they dwell in that world for ten thousand years;
free from all ailment, they make a vast and long-lasting residence there.
He who gives land to Brahmins and abundant grains goes to the world of Viṣṇu, the enchanting Śvetadvīpa;
there he dwells indeed as long as the moon and sun endure.
The meritorious person who dwells in a vast residence finds a vast abode for himself.
Those people who give a house to a brāhmaṇa with devotion go to the world of the gods and remain there for a long time. (49–50)
If men give a gift on an auspicious day equal in size to the dust of their own home,
they shall dwell in a vast residence for as many years as there are grains of dust. To whichever deity a man gives a house, [he gains that same reward].
He goes to that world for as many years as there are grains of dust [in the water].
The merit in a mansion is fourfold; the fruit of a *pūrta* work is a hundredfold;
and in an excellent one, it is eightfold more than that—so said the Lotus-born One.
O virtuous lady, he who constructs a tank for all living beings in Bhārata goes to Janaloka for ten thousand years;
furthermore, a human being obtains a hundredfold greater merit from constructing a stepped well.

Likewise, by the providing of a causeway, one obtains the fruit of a tank (taḍāga). A reservoir (vāpī) is proclaimed as being four thousand bows in length, or even less than that, on level ground. || 55–56 ||

A maiden equal to ten ponds, if given to a worthy recipient, yields double the fruit if she is adorned with ornaments. The fruit of that [gift] is equal to the fruit obtained from a tank by clearing away its mud. (57)
By clearing away the mud from a pond, one obtains a fruit equal to that of constructing a pond oneself.
He who plants an Aśvattha tree and performs its consecration goes to the world of asceticism for ten thousand supreme years.
O Sāvitrī, he who gives a flower garden for the benefit of all beings shall certainly dwell in the world of Dhruva for ten thousand years.
And he who gives a celestial chariot to Viṣṇu in the land of Bhārata, O virtuous lady—
He too shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as a supreme Manvantara;
and when it is joined with a painting and is large, his fruit is fourfold.
By the gift of half a chariot or a palanquin, one certainly obtains the same fruit.
He who, endowed with devotion, gives a palanquin-temple to Hari,
shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as a supreme Manvantara.
O devoted wife, he who constructs a royal road provided with palatial mansions—
He too is honored in the world of Śakra for ten thousand years.
One obtains a fruit equal to that of giving to both Brahmins and gods.
For that which is given does not remain ungiven; it surely reaches the one who enjoys it.

Having enjoyed happiness such as that of heaven, they return again to Bhārata. They obtain birth in Brahmin families, progressively in those of superior and other ranks. 66. In Bhārata, the meritorious Brahmin, having enjoyed the supreme [bliss] of heaven and so forth, [returns].
Furthermore, he alone may become a Brahmin, and not those of the Kṣatriya or other castes;
even through hundreds of millions of kalpas of austerity, a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya does not attain the status of a Brahmin— this is heard in the Śruti.
Brahmins who have abandoned their own dharma go to various wombs;
and having experienced the portion of their karma, they may again obtain birth as Brahmins.
Karma does not perish even in hundreds of millions of kalpas until it has been experienced.
One must necessarily experience [the results of one's actions], even after hundreds of millions of eons.
One must necessarily experience the performed karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Through the company of deities at sacred fords and through the emanation of a multitude of bodies, one is purified.
"All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Departure to Places Corresponding to One's Karma," within the *Sāvitrī-upākhyāna* (The Narrative of Sāvitrī) concerning the ripening of karma, in the second book (*Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sāvitrī said:
"O virtuous one, you ought to explain to me by which specific actions meritorious men go to heaven or to other realms.
Yama said:
And he who bestows food upon a Brahmin in Bhārata is honored in the world of Śakra for a period equal to the quantity of that food.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
In this matter, there shall be no examination of the recipient, nor any restriction regarding time.
(3) If one gives a seat to the gods or to Brahmins, one will certainly be honored in the world of Agni for ten thousand years. (4)
He who gives a divine, milk-yielding cow to a brahmin is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for as many years as there are hairs on that cow;
on an auspicious day the merit is fourfold, and at a sacred pilgrimage site the fruit is a hundredfold.
A gift given in the field of Nārāyaṇa shall yield ten million times the fruit.
(6) He who gives a cow to a Brahmin in Bhārata with devotion is honored in the world of the Moon for ten thousand years. (7)
He who makes a gift of a cow with both faces to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for as many years as there are hairs on its body.
He who gives a Śāligrāma stone along with a cloth to a Brāhmaṇa—
He who gives a beautiful umbrella to a brāhmaṇa is honored in Vaikuṇṭha as long as the moon and sun endure;
he too rejoices in the abode of Varuṇa for ten thousand years.

O virtuous lady, he who gives a pair of sandals to a brahmin in Bhārata is honored in the world of Vāyu for ten thousand years. He who gives a divine and enchanting bed to a brahmin [attains great merit].

He who gives a lamp to a deity and to a Brahmin is honored in the world of the Moon for as long as the moon and the sun endure. He too is honored in the world of Brahmā for the duration of a Manvantara.
Having attained a human birth, he will certainly possess sight;
by that merit, O beautiful one, he does not go to the realm of Yama.
Indeed, he who bestows the gift of an elephant upon a brahmin in Bhārata [attains this].
He shall dwell upon the half-seat of Indra and the other gods in the celestial realm.
And he who gives a horse to a Brahmin in Bhārata rejoices in the world of Varuṇa for as long as fourteen Indras endure. (15–16)

O virtuous lady, he who indeed gives an excellent palanquin to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as a Manvantara. And he who gives a fan or a white chowrie to a Brāhmaṇa [attains the same merit].

He is certainly honored in the world of Vāyu for ten thousand years. And he who gives a mountain of grain to a Brāhmaṇa in Bhārata is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are grains of that mountain.
Then, having returned to his own birthplace, he shall live long and happily.
Both the giver and the receiver— these two— will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha,
that man who constantly chants the name of Śrī Hari in Bhārata.
He indeed becomes long-lived, and death flees from him.
That man who causes the swinging festival (dolana) of Hari to be performed on the final part of the night of the full moon in the land of Bhārata shall become a man liberated while living.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at the end to the abode of Viṣṇu;
he shall dwell there certainly for the duration of a hundred manvantaras.
The fruit [of a gift] under Uttaraphalgunī shall be twice as great as that.

"He shall live until the end of the kalpa," so said the Lotus-born One (Brahmā). Furthermore, he who makes an offering of sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa in Bhārata rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are sesame seeds.
Then, having returned to his own womb, he shall live long and be happy.
By the gift of [the cow] placed in a copper vessel, one obtains double the fruit.
[One should give] a beloved wife who is adorned, beautiful, provided with garments, and fit for enjoyment.
He who gives a devoted wife to a Brāhmaṇa in the land of Bhārata is honored in the world of the Moon for as long as fourteen Indras reign;
there he rejoices day and night together with a celestial nymph.
Then, for ten thousand years in the world of the Gandharvas,
he rejoices day and night with Urvaśī out of curiosity.
After that, he obtains a beautiful beloved wife for a thousand births.

That man who gives a fruit-bearing tree to a Brāhmaṇa— one that is beautiful, endowed with auspiciousness, tender, and sweet-sounding— is honored in the world of Śakra for as many years as there are fruits upon it. (30–31)

Furthermore, having returned to his own womb, he obtains an excellent son; and he who gives even a single gift of fruit to a Brāhmaṇa is praised as equal to one who has given a thousand fruitful trees. (32) He who gives the gift of fruit alone to a Brāhmaṇa [attains this merit].

Having dwelt in heaven for a very long time, he goes to Bhārata. He who gives a spacious house to a brāhmaṇa in Bhārata—one endowed with various articles and furnished with various crops—[attains this]. (33–34)
And he shall dwell in the world of Kubera for the duration of a manvantara. Thereafter, having returned to his own birthplace, he shall become great and wealthy.
O virtuous lady, this applies to whichever person [gives] beautiful land endowed with crops.
If one gives with devotion to a brahmin at a sacred place,
he will certainly be glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for a hundred manvantaras.
Having returned to his own birth, he shall become great and a possessor of land.
The earth does not abandon him for even a hundred future births.
He becomes illustrious, wealthy, possessed of sons, and a lord of subjects.
One should give a preeminent village, along with its inhabitants, to a twice-born man.
For a hundred thousand manvantaras, he is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha;
then, returning to his own birthplace, he will certainly obtain a hundred thousand villages.
Furthermore, the earth shall not abandon him for a hundred thousand births.

He who gives a city on the land of Bhārata to a Brahmin— a city that is well-populated, highly prosperous, endowed with the five kinds of crops, and provided with various lotus ponds, trees, and the enjoyment of fruits— [attains great merit]. (41)
He is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for a period equal to ten million reigns of Indra;
then, returning to his own birthplace, he becomes a lord of kings in Bhārata and obtains a hundred thousand cities—of this there is no doubt. (42–43)
The earth certainly does not abandon him for a million births;
he shall surely possess supreme sovereignty upon the surface of the earth. Indeed, he who [gives] a hundred cities and a region to a twice-born man... 44.
One who, endowed with supreme devotion, gives [land] joined with excellent progeny,
together with ponds and tanks and provided with various trees,
is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of ten million manvantaras. (45–46)
Having returned once more to his own birthplace, he shall become the lord of Jambūdvīpa,
endowed with supreme sovereignty on earth just like Śakra; indeed,
the earth shall never forsake him for ten million births.
He shall become a great lord of kings, living for the duration of an eon.
Furthermore, he who bestows his entire authority upon a twice-born man will,
without a doubt, obtain a fourfold reward from that act.

O devoted wife, for one who gives Jambūdvīpa to a Brāhmaṇa, the fruit shall be a hundredfold greater than that; of this there is no doubt. [This is superior even to] the merit of one who gives the earth with its seven islands and frequents all sacred bathing places.
For one who performs all austerities, observes all fasts,
bestows all gifts, and is a lord of all spiritual accomplishments— even for such a person,
there is indeed rebirth; but alas, for the devotee of Hari, there is none.
Indeed, the Vaiṣṇavas behold the protection of countless Brahmās;
they dwell in Goloka or Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Hari.
And the worshiper of the Viṣṇu-mantra, having cast off his human body, [attains that state].
He assumes a divine form that removes birth, death, and old age;
having attained the same form as Viṣṇu, he performs service to Viṣṇu.
And he beholds the countless dissolution of the material world in Goloka.
The gods and the perfected beings (siddhas), along with all things in their entirety, perish;
yet those devoted to Kṛṣṇa do not perish, for they remove birth, death, and old age.
He who offers tulasī to Hari during the month of Kārttika [attains this].
He rejoices in the abode of Hari for the duration of a yuga, equal to the measure of a leaf;
then, having returned to his own birth, he will certainly obtain devotion to Hari.
He shall become happy and long-lived upon the earth of Bhārata.

And he who offers a ghee lamp to Hari during the month of Kārttika rejoices in the abode of Hari for a year equal in measure to a *pala*. Having returned to his own birth, he will certainly attain devotion to Viṣṇu.
He shall become immensely wealthy, possessed of keen vision, and radiant.
He who bathes in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha at the time of dawn rejoices in the abode of Hari for sixty thousand yugas.
Having returned once more to his own birthplace, he will certainly attain devotion to Viṣṇu;
he shall become the foremost among those who have conquered their senses on the earth of Bhārata.
This applies to him who bathes in the Gaṅgā at Prayāga during the month of Māgha at the break of dawn.
He too rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a hundred thousand manvantaras.
Having returned to his own birthplace, he will certainly obtain the mantra of Viṣṇu;
and casting off the human body, he goes once more to the abode of Hari.

There is no returning from Vaikuṇṭha to the surface of the earth; having attained the very same form as Hari, he performs service to Hari. Constantly bathing in the Gaṅgā, he becomes purified on earth like the sun.
At every step, one certainly obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By the dust of his very feet, the earth is instantly purified;
and he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha as long as the moon and sun endure.
Having returned once more to his own womb, he shall become the most excellent among ascetics—
pure, learned, with senses well-conquered, and devoted to his own duty—
when the sun blazes intensely between the signs of Pisces and Cancer.
He who gives even water that is well-scented in Bhārata rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Having returned to his own birthplace, he shall become happy and free from deceit. (69–70)

He who offers sandalwood paste with devotion to Hari during the month of Vaiśākha rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for sixty thousand yugas. Upon returning to his own birth, he shall become handsome and happy. (71)

He who gives an offering of roasted barley flour (*saktu*) to a twice-born man in the month of Vaiśākha rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are particles of dust in that flour. Furthermore, he who performs the vow of Kṛṣṇa’s birthday (*kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī*) in Bhārata—
He is liberated from the sins committed throughout a hundred lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
He rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Then, having returned to his own birth, he will certainly attain devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Whoever observes Śivarātri right here in this land of Bhārata rejoices in the world of Śiva for the duration of seven manvantaras.
And whoever offers a bilva leaf to Śiva on the night of Śivarātri [attains the same]. (79)
For as many ages as there are leaves [in the manuscript], he rejoices in the abode of Śiva.
Having returned once more to his own birth, he will certainly attain devotion to Śiva;
he shall become possessed of learning, sons, prosperity, progeny, and land.
Or, in the month of Caitra or Māgha, the observer of the vow who worships Śaṅkara and dances with devotion day and night, holding a cane in his hand— for a month,
or half a month, or for ten, seven, or even five days. (78)

He too is honored in the world of Śiva for a period equal to a *yuga*. Indeed, that man who observes the Śrī Rāmanavamī festival in Bhārata rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for the duration of seven *manvantaras*.
Furthermore, having returned to his own birthplace, he will certainly attain devotion to Rāma;
he will become the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, great, and righteous.
Moreover, he who performs the great autumnal worship of Prakṛti—
With buffaloes, goats, rams, sugarcane, and likewise with cucumbers;
with food offerings and presents, as well as with incense, lamps, and the like;
and with dance, song, musical instruments, and various auspicious festivities. (82–83)

He shall dwell in the world of Śiva for the duration of seven manvantaras. Having returned to his own birth, he shall obtain pure intellect and attain unshakable prosperity that increases his sons, grandsons, and progeny. (84)

Endowed with great majesty and accompanied by elephants and horses, he shall indeed become a sovereign lord of kings; of this there is no doubt. Whoever worships Mahālakṣmī upon reaching the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, [shall attain these fruits].
Having constantly offered with devotion for one fortnight in the sacred field of Bhārata the sixteen excellent articles of worship to her,
he too rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha as long as the moon and sun endure.
Furthermore, having returned to his own birthplace, he shall become a sovereign lord of kings.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, having fashioned a Rāsa-maṇḍala and likewise created a hundred cowherds and a hundred cowherdesses... [88–89]
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā in an image made of stone or in a book of the Bhārata,
having offered the sixteen articles of service;
such a person shall dwell in Goloka for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Returning once more to Bhārata, he will certainly attain devotion to Hari (91).
Having gradually attained firm devotion as well as the mantra of Hari,
he casts off his body and returns once again to Goloka (92).
There, having attained a form similar to Kṛṣṇa, one becomes an attendant;
there is no falling back from that state, for he is great, removing both old age and death.
This applies to whoever observes either the Śukla (bright) or the Kṛṣṇa (dark) Ekādaśī.
He too rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Returning once more to Bhārata, he will certainly obtain devotion to Hari;
he goes again to Vaikuṇṭha, and there shall be no falling away for him.
The man who worships Śakra on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada is honored in the world of Śakra for sixty thousand years.
[This applies also] on a Sunday, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), or on the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
He who, having worshipped the Sun, partakes of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) in Bhārata,
is honored in the world of the Sun for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Returning again to Bhārata, he shall become free from disease and endowed with prosperity.

Whoever worships Sāvitrī on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is glorified in the world of Brahmā for the duration of seven manvantaras. Returning once more to the earth, he becomes illustrious and possessed of incomparable valor.

He too shall become long-lived, possessed of knowledge, and endowed with prosperity. (100) Whoever, being self-restrained and full of devotion, worships Sarasvatī on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having offered the sixteen types of ritual services; (101)
He is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the day and night of Brahmā endure.
Having attained rebirth once more, he shall become a wise and learned poet.
Furthermore, he who gives land, gold, and other such gifts to a Brāhmaṇa [attains these rewards].
In Bhārata, for as long as one lives, being endowed with devotion;
and for a number of years equal to the measure of hairs on a cow’s body, doubled, he rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu together with Hari amidst playful delights and auspiciousness. (103–104)
Then, returning here once more, he will certainly attain devotion to Viṣṇu.
Then, returning here again, he shall become a sovereign lord of kings, possessing cattle, sons, and wisdom; he shall be learned, possessed of knowledge, and happy in every respect. (105)

O Bhārata, whoever feeds sweet food to the Brāhmaṇas shall rejoice in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a goat. Then, returning once more to this world, he shall become happy and wealthy.

He who speaks or indeed gives the names of Hari in Bhārata becomes wise, long-lived, illustrious, and possessed of incomparable valor. And for as many ages as there are names [uttered], he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, having returned here once more, one will certainly attain devotion to Viṣṇu.
Indeed, if one should recite ten million names of Hari in the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa, one shall obtain a fruit ten million times greater than that.
(109) If one should recite ten million names of Hari in the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa...
Freed from all sins, he will certainly become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He does not undergo rebirth; he is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha. He attains the same form as Viṣṇu (sārūpya), and for him there shall be no falling back.
He who constantly worships Śiva by fashioning an earthen liṅga shall go to the abode of Śiva for as long as he lives;
for as many years as there are particles of dust in that clay, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Then, having returned here once more, he shall become a lord of kings in Bhārata. And whoever constantly worships the stone and drinks the water from the stone is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as a hundred Brahmās exist.

Then, having obtained a new birth and devotion to Hari which is very difficult to attain, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; for him there shall be no falling away. Indeed, all austerities and every single vow [are surpassed by this].
Having performed [this], he remains in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as fourteen Indras [reign].
Then, having obtained rebirth once more, he shall become a king of kings in Bhārata.
Thereafter, he shall be liberated, and no further birth exists.
He who bathes in all the sacred fords on earth after performing a circumambulation attains liberation; he shall not be born again on this earth.
Furthermore, he who performs the horse sacrifice in the meritorious field of Bhārata—
One shall dwell upon half of Śakra’s throne for as many years as there are hairs on a horse;
a human being obtains four times that fruit at the Rājasūya sacrifice. At the Naramedha, one obtains half the fruit of the Aśvamedha, and the same at the Gomedha. (119–120)
In the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice, one certainly obtains half of that [fruit] and a virtuous son;
in the *lāṅgaleṣṭi*, one obtains a fruit equal to that of the *gomedha*.
The same applies to the *vipreṣṭi*, and that same fruit is obtained in the *vṛddhiyāga*.
In the Padmayajña, a human obtains half of that fruit. In the Viśoka sacrifice, one attains freedom from sorrow and enjoys heaven for half the duration of a Padma.
In the Vijaya sacrifice, a victorious king becomes equal to a Padma in heaven.
In the *prājāpatya* [muhūrta], there is the attainment of progeny, and for kings, there shall be an increase of territory;
having obtained royal splendor in this world, one enjoys half of Padma’s [realm] in heaven.
In the *ṛddhiyāga*, there is great sovereignty, and heaven becomes equal to a lotus. (124)
O beautiful one, the Viṣṇuyajña is the foremost among all sacrifices;
it was performed by Brahmā in former times with great preparations,
during which, O virtuous lady, a quarrel arose between Dakṣa and Śaṅkara.
O Brahmins, Śeṣa cursed Nandin, and Nandin cursed the Brahmins out of anger.
For this reason, the moon-crested Lord destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Furthermore, in ancient times, Dakṣa Prajāpati performed a sacrifice for Viṣṇu. (126–127)
Dharma, Kaśyapa, Śeṣa, and Kardama; Svāyambhuva Manu and his son Priyavrata;
Śiva, Sanatkumāra, Kapila, and Dhruva. (128)
Through the abundance of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices, this ritual becomes equal;
one certainly obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūyas.
There is no sacrifice superior to the Viṣṇu-yajña that bestows such fruit as described in the Veda.
Living for many kalpas, he will certainly become liberated while alive;
through both knowledge and spiritual luster, he shall become equal to Viṣṇu in this world—just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, and Śiva is among the Vaiṣṇavas. (131)
Just as the Vedas are among all scriptures, and Brāhmaṇas among those in the stages of life (āśramas);
just as the Gaṅgā is among sacred fords (tīrthas), and Vaiṣṇavas among the pure;
just as Ekādaśī is among vows, and Tulasī is among flowers. (132–133)
As the moon is among the stars, as Garuḍa is among birds, as the primal nature (prakṛti) is among women, and as the earth is among supports;
as the mind is among the swift-moving and flickering sense faculties—so [is he]. 134.
Brahmā is the foremost among the Prajāpatis, and Prajāpati is the lord of the progenitors;
Vṛndāvana is the best among forests, just as Bhārata is among the lands; Śrī is the foremost among the glorious, and Sarasvatī is the chief among the learned. (139–136)
Durgā is the foremost among devoted wives, and Rādhikā is the foremost among those possessed of good fortune.
Likewise, O child, Viṣṇu’s sacrifice is the greatest among sacrifices.
By means of a hundred horse-sacrifices alone, one certainly attains the status of Śakra.
And Pṛthu himself attained the station of Viṣṇu by means of a thousand [merits].
This [attainment] is equal to bathing in all sacred fords, giving the sacrificial fee at all sacrifices,
and the very fruit of all vows and austerities.
The study of the four Vedas, as well as circumambulating the earth—all this is merely seed; service to Kṛṣṇa alone bestows liberation.
This is found everywhere in the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and the Itihāsas.
The worship of the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa has been described as the very essence.
Its description, its meditation, the chanting of His names and qualities, His hymn of praise, remembrance, salutation, and indeed the recitation of His mantra [are likewise essential]. (141–142)
The constant consumption of the water from His feet and the food offerings is indeed approved by all;
thus, O virtuous lady, this is desired by everyone.
Worship Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, who is beyond the material qualities and transcends primordial nature.
"Take your husband, my child; go happily to your own home.
All this has been told to you: the ripening of the actions of men, which is desired by all, approved by all, and which bestows the supreme reality upon men. (144–145)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ripening of Auspicious Karma," within the Sāvitrī-upākhyāna, in the dialogue between Sāvitrī and Yama, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the glorification of Hari from the mouth of Yama, Sāvitrī—
With tears in her eyes and her hair standing on end, she spoke again to Yama.
Sāvitrī said:
"The chanting of the names of Hari is the dharma that is the cause of uplifting one's own lineage."
For both listeners and speakers, it removes birth, death, and old age.
(2) Among gifts, vows, perfections, austerities, yogas, and Vedic studies, the service and glorification of Hari is supreme. (3)
Liberation, immortality, or even the attainment of all supernatural powers do not equal even a sixteenth part of the service rendered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
By what method shall I worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who transcends primordial nature?
O dear one, best among the knowers of the Vedas, speak to me, a foolish and helpless woman.
You have described to me the charming ripening of auspicious deeds for human beings;
you ought now to explain to me the ripening of inauspicious deeds as well. (5–6)
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, that virtuous woman, her neck bowed low with devotion,
praised Dharmarāja with a hymn declared in the Vedas.
Sāvitrī said:
I bow to that Dharmarāja, whom the Sun-god (Bhāskara) obtained as his son—a portion of Dharma—after propitiating Dharma through ascetic penance at Puṣkara in ancient times;
he who is the witness of all and possesses equanimity toward all beings. (8)
Therefore, I bow to him who is indeed called Śamana;
I bow to that Kṛtānta (the End-maker) by whom the ultimate end has been ordained for all living beings according to their karma and at the appointed time. 9–10.

I bow to that wielder of the staff who inflicts punishment upon those deserving of it for the sake of purifying sinners; he who is the instructor of all actions and who constantly ordains the entire lifespan of every being. (11)
I bow down to that Time, which is exceedingly difficult to ward off.
(12) I bow down to that Yama, who bestows the fruits of action upon living beings—he who is an ascetic, a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous, self-controlled, and a master of his senses. (13)
I bow to that all-knowing one who delights in his own self and is a friend to those who perform meritorious deeds;
who brings suffering to sinners, yet is a virtuous friend—I bow to him.
His birth was in the lineage of Brahmā, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
"I bow to that one who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman, the lineage of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, O Sage, Sāvitrī prostrated before Yama.
Yama then spoke to her, who was devoted to Viṣṇu, concerning the ripening of her karma.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this *Yamāṣṭaka* daily,
has no fear of Yama and is liberated from all sins.
O Nārada, even a great sinner who recites it daily with devotion [attains the same].
Yama makes him pure through a manifestation of his body; this is certain.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Yama Composed by Sāvitrī," in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having bestowed the Viṣṇu-mantra upon her according to the prescribed rites, Yama,
the son of the Sun, spoke to her concerning the ripening of her inauspicious karma.
Yama said:
Since you have heard of the various kinds of results from auspicious karma,
listen now as I describe the results of inauspicious karma.
Through virtuous action, the living being goes to various types of heavenly realms.
And by means of evil deeds, a man goes to various kinds of hells.
(3) There are various types of pits for the hells, and they have different names according to the various Purāṇas. (4)
O child, there are sixty-four pits in Saṃyamanī that are wide, deep, and bring suffering to living beings; they are terrifying, dreadful, and loathsome. (5)
Listen to their names as they are well-known in the sacred scriptures:
the Fire Pit, the Hot Pit, the Forgiving Pit, the Terrifying Pit, the Feces Pit, the Urine Pit, and the unbearable Phlegm Pit. (6–7)
The pit of feces, the pit of rheum, and likewise the pit of fat;
the pit of semen, the pit of blood, and the loathsome pit of tears;
the pit of bodily impurities, and indeed the pit of earwax. (8)
The pit of marrow, the pit of flesh, and the pit of nails are difficult to cross;
the pit of body hair, the pit of hair, and the pit of bones cause great suffering.
The heated pit of copper and the heated pit of iron grant immense torment. (9–10)
The pit of sharp thorns and the pit of poison, which bestows obstacles;
the pit of Dharma and the pit of heated liquor are also proclaimed.
There is the pit of boiling oil and the unbearable pit of teeth.
The Pit of Worms, the Pit of Pus, the Pit of Snakes which is difficult to endure;
the Pit of Mosquitoes, the Pit of Stinging Insects, the terrible Pit of Poison;
and the Pit of Vajra-fanged Scorpions, O lady of excellent vows. (12–13)
The Śara-pit, the Śūla-pit, and the terrifying Khaḍga-pit;
the Go-pit, the Nakra-pit, and the Kāka-pit, which is an abode of grief;
the Sañcāla-pit, the Vāja-pit, and the Bandha-pit, which is very difficult to cross. (14)
The pit of heated stones and the pit of sharp stones;
the pit of saliva, the sword-pit, and the most dreadful pit of powder;
the wheel-pit, the thunderbolt-pit, and the exceedingly fierce tortoise-pit. (15–16)
The Pit of Flames, the Pit of Ashes, and the Pit of Putridity, O beautiful one;
the Burning Sun, the Ink-Leaf, the Razor’s Edge, and the Needle-Mouth;
the Godhā-Mouth, the Crocodile-Mouth, the Elephant-Bite, and the Ox-Mouth. (17)
Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, Avaṭoda, Aruntuda,
Pāṃśubhoja, Pāśaveṣṭa, Śūlaprota, Prakampana,
Ulkāmukha, Andhakūpa, Vedhana, and Daṇḍatāḍana. (18–19)
The Net-Binding, the Body-Pulverizer, the Crusher, the Drier,
the Serpent-Flame-Mouthed, the Smoke-Blinded, and the Naga-Coil—
these, O Sāvitrī, are the pits that inflict suffering upon sinners.
And they were constantly guarded by appointed hosts of servants—terrible beings with staffs in hand, spears in hand, and nooses in hand;
with pikes in hand and maces in hand, intoxicated with pride, and fierce. (21–22)
[He was surrounded] by those possessed of darkness (tamas), devoid of compassion, and difficult to restrain from all sides;
by radiant ones who were fearless, with coppery-brown eyes;
and by excellent ones endowed with yoga, perfected in yoga, assuming various forms.
It was seen by those whose death was imminent, by sinners, and by all who subsist by living beings (butchers);
by Śaivas, Śāktas, Sauras, and Gāṇapatis devoted to their own duties;
and it was not seen by merit-makers, nor by perfected yogins.
Whether they are devoted to their own dharma or detached from it, independent,
powerful, or free from doubt— even by Vaiṣṇavas seen in dreams— [the goal is attained].
O virtuous lady, this description of the number of sacrificial pits has been told to you.
"Learn from me as I describe those in whose pond they dwell.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Hells," in the *Sāvitrī-upākhyāna* within the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Yama said:

O virtuous lady, a pure yogi devoted to the service of Hari, one who is perfected, observant of vows, an ascetic, a celibate student, and a renunciant—such a person does not go to hell. Furthermore, that man who [treats] his kinsmen with harsh speech and wickedness... [1]
The powerful one burns him and he enters a fire-pit.
Having remained there in that fire for as many years as there are hairs on his body, being burned in that fierce [fire], he attains the womb of a beast for three births. (2–3)
That fool who does not feed a Brahmin who has come to his house thirsty, agitated, and tormented, goes to the Taptakuṇḍa hell;
having remained there for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he suffers there in misery.
And for seven births, that bird shall dwell in a fire-pit on heated ground.
(5) That man who subjects his clothes to contact with alkaline substances on a Sunday, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on the new moon day, or on the day of a śrāddha ceremony— (6)
He goes to the Kṣārakuṇḍa hell for as many years as there are threads [in the land];
he shall enter the womb of a king in Bhārata for seven births.
He who seizes the property of a Brahmin, whether given by himself or by another—
For sixty thousand years he goes to Viṭkuṇḍa;
for sixty thousand years he remains there eating excrement;
and for sixty thousand years he becomes a worm in excrement on earth once again.
And he who constructs a tank upon another's tank shall,
by the fault of fate, become a reservoir of urine;
for as many years as there are particles of dust in that tank, he remains there, subsisting on its [filth].
In Bhārata, he shall indeed become a lizard for seven births.
(11) He eats sweets all alone, and he goes to a pit of phlegm;
eating that, he remains there for a full hundred years. (12)
For a full hundred years, he shall remain a *preta* in Bhārata;
thereafter, having become pure, he consumes phlegm, urine, poison, and pus.
[He who abandons] father, mother, teacher, wife, son, or daughter—
He who does not support the helpless goes to Garakuṇḍa;
he remains there for a full thousand years as one who eats that [filth].
Thence he goes to Bhūtayoni, and after a hundred years, he becomes pure.
Indeed, whatever man looks askance at a guest,
the ancestors and gods do not accept his water offering, for he is a sinner.
Whatever sins there may be, including even the killing of a Brahmin—
In this very world he suffers at the end, and he shall go to the pit of pus (dūṣikā-kuṇḍa).
Having eaten that for a full hundred years, he remains there;
thereafter, the man shall be poor on earth for seven births.
If, after giving wealth to a Brahmin, it is then given to another,
he remains in a pit of fat for a hundred years, eating that very substance.
Thereafter, he becomes a Caṇḍāla for three births, and only after that does he become pure.
He shall become a lizard for seven births in Bhārata;
thereafter he becomes a human being, yet poor and short-lived. Whether it be a man [who commits this] against a woman, or a woman against a man—then... [the same result follows].
He who causes semen to be drunk indeed goes to Śukrakuṇḍa;
having remained there for a full hundred years as one who consumes that [semen], he then becomes a worm in a womb on earth for a hundred years, after which he becomes pure. (21–22)
Having struck a Brahmin preceptor and caused him to bleed,
he shall remain for a hundred years in a pit of blood, subsisting upon that very blood.
Thereafter, he shall take birth as an outcaste for seven lifetimes in the land of Bhārata.
Then that person attains purification gradually.
Indeed, that man who laughs while seeing a devotee shedding tears, singing with a faltering voice, in the congregational chanting of the virtues of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [attains purification]. 24–25.
He shall dwell in a pit of tears, eating that [filth], for a hundred years.
Thereafter, he becomes a Caṇḍāla for three births, and only after that does he become pure.
A man whose heart is impure constantly practices wickedness.
He becomes a reservoir for the impurities of his body and remains so for ten years.
Thereafter, he enters the womb of a donkey for three births; for three births he enters the womb of a jackal, after which he certainly becomes pure. (27–28)

That man who laughs at a deaf person or indeed reviles him shall dwell for a hundred years in the cavity of that person's ear-wax, feeding upon it. Thereafter, he shall become deaf and impoverished for seven lifetimes.
For seven births he shall be deficient in limbs; thereafter, he will certainly attain purification.

(30) That man who, out of greed, kills a living being for the sake of his own protection, shall dwell in the Pit of Marrow for one hundred thousand years, as well as anyone who eats such a person's food. (31)
Then, for seven births, he shall become a hare and a fish;
thereafter, as a deer and other such creatures due to his karmas, he will certainly attain purification.
As for that man who, having raised his own daughter, sells her—
Out of greed for wealth, that great fool goes to the Pit of Flesh (māṃsakuṇḍa).
He remains there for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a maiden, eating that [flesh].
And the servant of Yama strikes him with blows within that pit.
Carrying a load of flesh upon his head, he shall lick streams of blood out of hunger.
Thereafter, that sinner in Bhārata shall become a worm among prostitutes and lechers for sixty thousand years,
and a hunter for seven lifetimes.
He becomes a boar for three births and a dog for seven births;
he becomes a frog for seven births and a leech for seven births;
he becomes a crow for seven births, and thereafter he shall certainly attain purification. (36–37)
O beautiful one, he who does not perform the act of shaving during vows, fasts, śrāddha ceremonies, and other such restraints is impure for all ritual acts;
and he remains in the pits of his nails and other [body hair].
He who eats on that very day [of the lunar month] shall be struck by a staff;
he who worships an earthen linga with its hair in Bhārata shall remain in Keśakuṇḍa for as many years as there are particles of dust on that hair.
At the end of that period, due to the wrath of Hara, he enters a Yavana womb;
after a hundred years, he attains purification and certainly regains his own family.
This applies to one who does not offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) for his ancestors at the station of Viṣṇu.
He remains for a year in a pit of bones amidst his own hair in a most terrible place.
Then, having returned to his own womb, he becomes lame for seven births and exceedingly poor; thereafter, indeed, he is purified through the staff (penance).
The great fool who has sexual intercourse with his own pregnant wife remains for a hundred years in a cauldron of molten copper.
He who eats the food of a woman without a husband, as well as the food of a woman who has just bathed after her menses, [suffers likewise].
And he remains for a hundred years in a red-hot iron cauldron;
then he enters the womb of a king’s servant for seven births.
Having become afflicted with great sores and impoverished, that man thereafter becomes purified.
For he who touches the property of the gods with hands smeared with hot ghee remains in the pit of that ghee for a duration of one hundred years.
And he who, permitted by a Śūdra, eats the food of a Śūdra [suffers the same].
And that twice-born man remains for a hundred years in a cauldron of boiling liquor.
Thereafter, he becomes a priest for Śūdras for seven births;
by eating the food at the funeral rites (śrāddha) of Śūdras, he then certainly becomes pure.
She who is corrupt in speech and harsh in her words, who constantly strikes her husband,
remains there in a pit of sharp thorns, eating that [thorn-fruit],
for the duration of four yugas, being beaten with a staff by the messengers of Yama.

Then Uccaiḥśravas remained pure for seven births thereafter. As for that cruel, base man who kills one who lives by poison, he remains in a pit of poison for a thousand years while consuming its food. (51–52)
Then he shall become a slayer of men and have a wound for seven births;
for seven births he shall be afflicted with leprosy, and thereafter he will certainly become pure.
Indeed, he who strikes a bull with a staff, or he who drives a bull [for a living], [shall suffer thus].
Whether acting independently or through the agency of a servant, he remains for four yugas in a pit of boiling oil at a sacred site (puṇyakṣetra) in Bhārata. Thereafter,
he becomes a bull for as many years as there are hairs on the bodies of cows.
O virtuous lady, he who kills a living being with his teeth, or with iron, or with a hook,
shall dwell in the Hell of Teeth for ten thousand years.
Thereafter, having returned to his own species, he shall be afflicted with diseases of the stomach.
Then, after one afflicted birth, that man becomes pure. But the Brāhmaṇa who eats meat in vain, who eats fish, or who eats food that has not been offered to Hari, goes to the Kṛmikuṇḍa hell. (57–58)
He remains there for a lifespan equal to the number of hairs on his own body, consuming that [food].
Thereafter, he becomes a member of a barbarian (*mleccha*) caste for three births, and then a twice-born (*dvija*).
As for the Brāhmaṇa who performs sacrifices for Śūdras and who eats the food at a Śūdra’s funeral feast (*śrāddha*), [he likewise undergoes this fate].

And one who burns the corpse of a Śūdra will certainly go to the Pit of Putridity (pūyakuṇḍa). O lady of virtuous vows, for as many years as there are hairs on the body of the sacrificer, he remains there, beaten by the messengers of Yama, subsisting upon that [putrid matter]. (60–61)
Then, having come to Bhārata, that Śūdra suffered for seven births as one afflicted by a great disease and poverty; thereafter, purified, he became a twice-born Brāhmaṇa once more.
And as for the man who kills a snake—whether small, fierce, or large— [he likewise suffers].
He goes to the Serpent-Pit for a number of years equal to the measure of hairs on his own body.
There, bitten by a serpent and struck by a messenger of Yama, he dwells as one who lives upon the excrement of serpents;
thereafter, he will certainly become a serpent. (63–64)
Then that person shall be short-lived and afflicted with leprosy;
his death will certainly come through great suffering by being devoured by a serpent.
This is the fate for one who, having devised a ritual, kills living beings and small creatures.
In a pit filled with gadflies and mosquitoes, he undergoes his birth, months, days, and years (66).
Day and night he is devoured by them while remaining without food and making cries;
his hands, feet, and other limbs bound, he is beaten by the messengers of Yama (67).
Then he shall become a small creature for as many births as are traditionally recorded;
thereafter he becomes a human being, but one who is physically deformed, and only after that does he become pure.
This applies to the fool who, having killed honey-bees, takes their honey.
In that very pit of poison, he is devoured by poisons for as many years as there are days he has lived;
he is burned and struck by the messengers of Yama.
Thereafter, he is born as a species of fly, and only then does the man become purified. (69–70)
He who inflicts punishment upon one who does not deserve it, and likewise inflicts punishment upon a Brahmin,
goes indeed to the *kuṇḍa* of insects with adamantine fangs;
he remains there day and night for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
And having been devoured by those [beings] who produce sound, the man then becomes pure.
(72) Furthermore, that king who, out of greed for wealth, inflicts punishment upon his subjects will certainly dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body within pits of scorpions. (73)
Thereafter, he is born as a species of scorpion for seven lifetimes.
Then, that man will certainly become deformed in his limbs and afflicted by disease. This applies to a Brahmin who bears weapons or who acts as a messenger for others.

The fool who neglects the twilight prayers and is devoid of devotion to Hari remains for as many years as he has hairs on his body within sacrificial pits and the like, or amidst arrows and the like. Constantly pierced by arrows and such, that man thereafter becomes purified.
He who, being negligent, imprisons his subjects in a dark prison for even a minor offense, goes to the Golakuṇḍa hell. That kuṇḍa is filled with boiling water, shrouded in darkness, and terrifying.
There is a pit for cattle filled with insects possessing sharp fangs;
pierced by those insects, one shall dwell there for a year, covered in hair.
Thereafter, he becomes a low-born servant, and after that, the man becomes pure on earth.
He who kills crocodiles and other creatures rising from a lake, even while it exists,
goes to Nakrakuṇḍa for as many years as there are teeth in the mouth of a crocodile.
Thereafter, he will certainly be born among the species of crocodiles and such in rivers and other waters.

Then, that man is indeed immediately purified by the staff alone. He who, out of lust, gazes upon the chest, hips, breasts, or face of another's wife—even if he is a lustful man in the merit-field of Bhārata—[is purified]. (81–82)
He shall dwell in Kākakuṇḍa, his eyes pecked out by crows;
thereafter, for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall be blind for three births;
and for seven births he shall be impoverished, extremely cruel, and a sinner.
In Bhārata, he becomes a goldsmith and then a gold merchant.
O beautiful one, he who steals copper or steals iron in Bhārata goes indeed to Vajrakuṇḍa for a number of years equal to the hairs on his own body.
In that very place, he who eats vajra-excrement and whose eyes are crushed by vajras,
being struck by the messenger of Yama, thereafter becomes a pure man.
In Bhārata, he who is a thief of the gods and a stealer of divine property [is likewise purified].
One must certainly dwell for a hundred years of one's own hair-counts in the extremely difficult Vajra-pit;
indeed, with one's body scorched by those vajras, without food, and making sounds while being struck by the messenger of Yama, the man thereafter becomes purified. (87–88)
The thief of silver, cows, parrots,
or the property of gods and Brahmins shall certainly dwell for a year in a pit of heated stones, his own body hair serving as the duration;
he remains a crane for three lifetimes and a white swan for three lifetimes.
For one birth he shall be a Śaṅkhacilla bird, and thereafter others as white-winged birds;
then he shall become a human being afflicted with blood disorders and colic.
Having lived a short life for seven births, the man shall thereafter become pure.
He who steals vessels made of tin, bronze,
or other metals belonging to a deity or a Brahmin shall certainly dwell in a pit of sharp stones for as many years as he has hairs on his body;
furthermore, he shall be born as a horse for seven lifetimes in the land of Bhārata.
Then he becomes possessed of extra limbs, and thereafter a sufferer of foot diseases; then he becomes pure [only after further penance].
He who eats the food of a prostitute, or lives by the livelihood of a prostitute, shall certainly dwell in the Pit of Saliva for as many years as there are hairs on his body. (93–94)
Beaten by the messenger of Yama, he who eats that [food] remains there;
thereafter he suffers from eye-pain, and then he is gradually purified.
That Brahmin on the land of Bhārata who serves Mlecchas or lives by selling ink— [he likewise undergoes this].
And he shall certainly dwell for a year equal to the number of his own hairs in a pit of boiling soot,
beaten by the messenger of Yama and eating that [soot] while remaining there.
Thereafter, O virtuous lady, he shall become a black-colored beast for three births.
In three births he shall become a goat, and in three births a black serpent;
thereafter he becomes a palmyra tree, and after that, the man becomes pure.
He who steals grain and other crops, or betel leaf, from gods or Brahmins [undergoes this].
He goes to a seat, a bed, or a powder-vessel;
there he shall dwell for a hundred years, struck by the messengers of Yama.
Thereafter, he shall become a ram and a cock for three births.

Then that man shall become on earth afflicted by coughing diseases, deprived of his lineage, poor, and short-lived; thereafter he becomes pure [only after atonement]. That man who, having stolen wealth from Brahmins, fashions a discus [from it], [suffers this fate].
He shall be beaten with a staff for a hundred years in the Vasvecakra hell;
thereafter, he shall become a human being as an oil-presser for three births.
Then he shall be afflicted by disease, a sick man, and deprived of his lineage, until finally he becomes pure.
O virtuous lady, if a man practices deceit toward his kinsmen and Brahmins,
he goes to Vajrakuṇḍa and shall dwell there for a yuga.
Thereafter, for seven births, he becomes crooked-limbed and deficient in his physical members.

He shall be poor, of low birth, and thereafter bereft of a wife, yet pure. Indeed, that Brāhmaṇa who eats tortoise meat on the day of Śayana shall dwell in Kūrmakuṇḍa for a hundred years, devoured by tortoises.
Then he would be born as a tortoise for three births, and as a boar for three births;
he would be a cat for three births and a peacock for three births—
[this is the fate] of one who steals ghee, oil, and so forth from gods or Brahmins.
That sinner indeed goes to the pit of flames and the pit of ashes;
having stayed there for a hundred years, he becomes a consumer of oil.
For seven births he shall be a fish, and thereafter a mouse, after which he becomes pure.
Whoever steals fragrant oil, the *dhātrī* fruit, or likewise aromatic substances from gods or Brahmins in the meritorious land of Bhārata,
shall dwell in the Durgandhakuṇḍa hell and always experience foul odors.
Then, for a period of a human year measured by his own body hair, he becomes foul-smelling. He remains foul-smelling for seven births, and for three births he is like musk.
Then, for seven births he is fragrant, and after that, he indeed becomes a human being. (111–112)
Indeed,
if one who is powerful should seize ancestral land in Bhārata through force, through wickedness,
or through violence, he shall dwell upon the Taptaśūla hell day and night. (113)

Just as a living being scorched in boiling oil wanders incessantly, so too the body that yields worldly experience does not perish; it is reduced to ashes, yet it is not destroyed. There, the sinner remains tormented for seven *manvantaras*.
Struck by a messenger of Yama, he makes no sound while remaining without food.
Then, for sixty thousand years, he becomes a dung-worm in Bhārata;
thereafter, he becomes landless and poor, and finally, he becomes pure.
Then, having returned to his own species, he becomes one of auspicious karma once again.
The most cruel man, devoid of compassion, cuts living beings with swords;
a slayer of men kills a man in the land of Bhārata out of greed for wealth. (117–118)
And he shall dwell in the Asipatra hell for as long as fourteen Indras [reign];
if he kills Brahmins therein,
then for a hundred manvantaras that sinner shall have his limbs perpetually severed by the edge of a sword.
Deprived of food and making sounds, he is struck by the messenger of Yama;
for a hundred births he becomes a Caṇḍāla in Bhārata, then a pig, then a dog for a hundred births, and a jackal for seven births. (120–121)
He becomes a tiger for seven births and a wolf for three births;
he will be a person with a birthmark on the cheek (*gaṇḍa*) for seven births and a buffalo for three births.
Furthermore, he who sets fire to a village or even a city [suffers this].
O virtuous lady, he might even dwell for three ages upon the edge of a razor with his limbs mangled;
thereafter, he would immediately become a *preta* with a mouth of fire and wander the earth.
For seven births he would feed on impurities, and for seven births he would be a firefly.
Then that man shall suffer from a great colic for seven lifetimes;
thereafter, having been afflicted with a wasting leprosy for seven lifetimes, the man becomes purified. (125) He who slanders others by whispering into their ears...

One who finds great delight in the faults of others and reviles gods and Brahmins shall dwell in the Sūcīmukha hell, pierced by needles, for three *yugas*. Thereafter, he shall become a scorpion and then a serpent for seven births.
For seven births he becomes a Vajrakīṭa worm; after that, a Bhasmakīṭa worm.
Thereafter he becomes a human being, but one afflicted by a great disease; only then does he become pure.
This is the fate for one who, as a householder, breaks through the wall of another's home and steals their property.
He goes to the mouth of a monitor lizard, and thereafter, for seven births, he becomes a member of the bovine species afflicted by disease;
for three births he is of the sheep species, and for three births he is of the goat species. (129–130)
Then he shall become a human being who is chronically ill and impoverished;
deprived of wife and kin, he shall suffer in torment until he becomes pure.
Furthermore, as a thief of common property, he goes to the Naramukha hell for the duration of a Yuga.
Thereafter he becomes a human being and suffers from a great disease; thereafter he becomes pure.
He kills cows, elephants, horses, and likewise men.
That great sinner goes to the state of being an elephant's bite for three *yugas*.
