Constantly struck with the tusk of Yama’s messenger, he shall become a member of the elephant species and a horse for three births; thereafter, he shall become a member of the bovine species and a mleccha, after which the man becomes pure. (134)
The man who prevents a thirsty cow from drinking water,
and who is devoid of service toward his parents,
goes to the hell called Gomukha, which is shaped like a cow's face and filled with boiling water and worms. (135)

There he remains tormented for the duration of a manvantara. Then that man, deprived of cattle, afflicted by great disease, and impoverished, becomes of the lowest caste for seven births; thereafter, the man becomes pure.

He who commits the transgressive killing of a cow or the killing of a Brahmin; he who approaches a woman with whom one should not have intercourse; he who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and is uninitiated;
he who accepts gifts at sacred fords (tīrtha); he who acts as a priest for a village; and he who serves as a temple-priest (devala). || 138 ||
The cook of Śūdras, one who is intoxicated, and the husband of a low-caste woman (139);
he who commits the slaughter of a cow, the slaughter of a Brahmin, the slaughter of a woman,
the slaughter of a friend, or the slaughter of an embryo— such a person is a great sinner in Bhārata (140).
He shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as fourteen Indras reign;
beaten by the messenger of Yama and being constantly pulverized,
he falls into fire for a moment and falls upon thorns for a moment.
For a moment in boiling oils and for a moment in boiling water;
for a moment on heated stones and then for a moment on heated iron.
Then, for hundreds of lifetimes as a pig, he becomes ten million times a thousand vultures. (142–143)
He shall be a crow for seven births, and a serpent for seven births;
thereafter, for sixty thousand years, he shall indeed become a worm in excrement.
After that, he shall become a eunuch, afflicted with oozing leprosy, and destitute.
"Afflicted by consumption, deprived of lineage, and then deprived of a wife—how may one become pure?
Sāvitrī said:
"What is the nature of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the sin of killing a cow, or what is the prescribed sin for those who act as their representatives?"
Who among men is forbidden as a consort, or who is one who has neglected the twilight prayers?
Who is an uninitiated man, or who accepts gifts at a sacred ford?
Who is a twice-born who officiates for a village, or what Brahmin is a temple-priest? (146–147)
Who is the cook for the Śūdras? Who is the intoxicated husband of a Vṛṣalī?
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me all the characteristics of these people.
Yama said:
O beautiful one, [one should worship] Śrī Kṛṣṇa and likewise in his earthen image, in Prakṛti;
or Śiva and in his Śivaliṅga, or Sūrya and in a sun-crystal;
or Gaṇeśa and in his very image—in this manner, everywhere.
He who conceives a sense of duality [between himself and others] incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who conceives a sense of duality toward his own guru, his chosen deity, his progenitor, or his mother, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. (150–151)

He who indeed treats with equality Vaiṣṇavas, other devotees, Brāhmaṇas, and others, shall incur the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. So too shall that fool who [treats with equality] the food offered to Viṣṇu and the food offered to others.

He who treats the water from the feet of Hari as equal to the water from the feet of another deity shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. [This applies] toward Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of all, the cause of all causes. (153)
To one who equates that which is the primordial source of all, the object of service for all gods, the inner self of all,
and though appearing in manifold forms through *māyā*, is in truth only one and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*),
with another, shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. (154–155)

He who prohibits the worship of the ancestors and the gods, as ordained by the Vedas in their proper sequence, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. Likewise, those who revile Hṛṣīkeśa as well as his devotees [incurs the same].
They incur the sin of killing a Brahmin, even though he is the purifier of purifiers,
auspicious, the very embodiment of Śiva, dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life,
the purifier of purifiers, and the eternal bliss of knowledge. (157–158)
Those who do not worship, and instead revile, the Lord Śiva—the preeminent deity of the Vaiṣṇavas and the gods—incure the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Those who revile the true Viṣṇu-māyā, which bestows devotion to Viṣṇu, [also incur that same sin]. 159.

They incur the sin of killing a Brahmin against her who is the embodiment of all powers, the mother of all, the essence of all goddesses, the primordial one worshipped by all, and the form of the cause of everything. (160–161)

Those men who do not observe these five meritorious festivals— the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, the supremely merit-bestowing Rāmanavamī, Śivarātri, Ekādaśī, and likewise the day of the Sun— [attain no spiritual fruit]. (162)
They incur the sin of killing a Brahmin and become more wicked than even Cāṇḍālas.
O child, those who perform purification and other rites in the water of the Ambuvīcī river in Bhārata incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. 163–164.

He who does not support his guru, mother, father, virtuous wife, son, or daughter, and who provides for no one who is destitute, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā). He whose marriage has not taken place, and he who does not see his own son—[these also incur such sin]. 165.
He who is devoid of devotion to Hari incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā).
He who eats what has not been offered to Hari and does not worship Viṣṇu daily—whether he be one who worships a meritorious earthen liṅga or otherwise—incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. (166–167)
Day after day he incurs the sin of killing cows; of this there is no doubt.
(169) He who gives the remnants of his food to cows, who employs a bull as a beast of burden, or who feeds food to those who drive bulls, will certainly incur the sin of cow-slaughter. (170)
The man who officiates at a sacrifice for the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), or who eats his food, incurs the sin of killing a hundred cows; of this there is no doubt.
He who offers a foot [as an oblation] into the fire and strikes cows with his foot [incurs the same].

One who enters his home without having washed his feet incurs the sin of killing a cow. He who eats with unwashed feet, sleeps with unwashed feet, or eats twice at sunrise, will certainly incur the sin of cow-slaughter. (172–173)
The twice-born who eats the food of one who has no heroic sons, he who lives by [prostituting] his own wife,
and he who neglects the three daily prayers (saṃdhyā), will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
Likewise, [he who fails to worship] the ancestors at the time of the lunar festivals (parvan) and the deities at the time of the lunar days (tithi).

He who does not honor a guest certainly incurs the sin of killing a cow. She who harbors a sense of duality between her own husband and Kṛṣṇa, and who strikes her beloved with harsh words, certainly incurs the sin of killing a cow. (175–176)
Having dug up a cow-path, he who sows grain there,
or does so in a pond or on its bank, shall certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
He who performs an act contrary to the prescribed expiation for the slaughter of a cow [incurs that same sin].

Out of greed for wealth or through ignorance, he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. In both royal and divine matters, the owner of the cow must not cause the cow to fall [into distress] with effort.
That fool who inflicts suffering [upon it] will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. (178–179)

He who steps over water, an offering of food, a flower, or grain belonging to one devoted to the worship of the deity, certainly incurs the sin of killing a cow. (180) He who constantly says "it does not exist," who is a speaker of falsehood and a deceiver—
One who hates the gods and one who hates the guru will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
(181) Furthermore, if upon seeing an image of a deity, a guru, or a brahmin, one does not bow out of negligence, he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. (182)

That twice-born man who, out of anger, does not grant a blessing to one who bows before him, nor imparts knowledge to a seeker of learning, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. The killing of a cow and the killing of a Brahmin are said to be extended [to these acts] by way of analogy. (183)
"What more do you wish to hear from the mouth of Sūrya as it was heard by me?
Sāvitrī said:
"Regarding the reality [of action], its extension, and the connection between sin and merit..."
"What is the difference between the deficient and the superior? You should explain that to me.
Yama said:
"In some cases, the actual [text] is superior, while the extended application is always inferior."
Wherein is the analogical [application] superior, and where is the literal [application] indeed inferior?
Or wherein is their equality, O virtuous one, according to the authority of the Vedas? He who shows no regard for that incurs the sin of murdering his preceptor. (186–187)
Because one projects the status of a father upon a teacher who was previously known as a learned brahmin and the bestower of knowledge and mantras, he is said to be superior in reality.
A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father, and likewise, [the teacher] is a hundred times more venerable than a mother. (188)
The teacher who imparts knowledge and mantra is to be honored, according to the Veda.
The wife of the teacher is even more worthy of reverence than the teacher himself.
Likewise, the wife of a deity and one's chosen deity are to be worshipped as desired. (189–190)

The Brahmin who is equal to Śiva and whose prowess is like that of Viṣṇu is superior to a king by virtue of his actual qualities, even if the king holds a delegated authority. All water is equal to the Gaṅgā, and all twice-born ones are equal to Vyāsa.
During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, their equality [in terms of impurity] occurs at that very time.
The Brahma-born (Brahmā) has declared that the sin resulting from the transfer of guilt is considered by all the Vedas to be fourfold when it is actual. 192–193.

The distinction regarding the extension of the rule for killing has been stated. Now listen as I tell you which women are forbidden to men; it is established in the Veda that one's own wife is permissible for all. (194)
The knowers of the Vedas declare that she who is other than these is also "unapproachable" (agamyā).
O beautiful one, I have described all that is common; now hear the particulars. Learn from me as I describe those women who are indeed "exceedingly unapproachable" (atyagamyā). 195–196.

The wife of a Brahmin among Śūdras, and a Śūdra woman who desires a Brahmin, are both extremely forbidden and highly censured in the world, the Veda, and for those devoted to their husbands (pativratā). If a Śūdra should approach a Brāhmaṇī, he incurs the sin of one hundred brahman-murders.
If a Brahmin woman also goes with him, she too will certainly go to Kumbhīpāka.
(198) If a Brahmin goes with a Śūdra woman, he becomes the husband of a Vṛṣalī; fallen from the caste of Brahmins, he is considered even lower than a Caṇḍāla. (199)
That funeral ball (piṇḍa) is equal to excrement, and that libation (tarpaṇa) is equal to urine;
likewise, when it comes to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, [the result] is the same.
Merit acquired over ten million lifetimes and merit earned through the practice of twilight prayers and austerity—[all are lost]. 200.

The enjoyment of a *vṛṣalī* by a twice-born man surely destroys [his merit], there is no doubt. A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, eats excrement, is the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, and eats on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) will certainly go to Kumbhīpāka hell. (201–202)
O virtuous lady, [one should not look at] the wife of a guru, the wife of a king, a co-wife, one's mother,
a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a mother-in-law, a pregnant woman, a sister,
the wife of a uterine brother, a maternal aunt, or one’s paternal grandmother. (203)
The Lotus-born One has declared that the mother’s mother, the essence of reality (tattvasāra), the sister, the brother’s daughter,
the female disciple, the disciple’s wife, the beloved of one’s nephew,
and even the wife of one’s brother’s son are women who must not be approached for sexual union.
Whosoever among the lowest of men should approach one or more of these women would, according to the Vedas, incur the guilt of a hundred Brahman-murders as if he were a violator of his own mother;
though unworthy of ritual acts, he is untouchable in the world and utterly censured in the Veda. (206)
That great sinner goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell, which is very difficult to cross.

He who performs the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) while impure, or he who does not perform the twilight prayers at all, or that twice-born man who neglects the three daily twilight prayers—he is devoid of the twilight rites. (207–208)
One who does not accept a mantra— whether Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, Saura, or Gāṇapa— due to egoism is considered uninitiated (adīkṣita).
Taking the current as the limit, for a distance of four cubits...
There, in that excellent place within the womb of the Gaṅgā, resides the Lord Nārāyaṇa. There, in the field of Nārāyaṇa at Kurukṣetra, the abode of Hari;
and at Vārāṇasī, at Badarī, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—210–211.
At Puṣkara, in the field of Bhāskara, at Prabhāsa and in the circle of Rāsa;
at Haridvāra, at Kedāra, at Someśvara, and at the purifying Badarī;
on the bank of the river Sarasvatī, and in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana. (212)
He who, out of desire, accepts gifts at the Godāvarī, the Kauśikī, the Triveṇī, the Himālaya, or elsewhere— such a recipient of gifts from sacred fords goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
One who performs sacrifices for anyone other than a Śūdra is proclaimed a village-priest (grāmayājī);
likewise, one who subsists on the worship of deities is proclaimed a temple-priest (devala).
One who subsists on the cooking for a Śūdra is remembered as a cook (sūpakāra). (215)
One who is devoid of the twilight worship (sandhyā-pūjā) and is heedless is considered fallen.
The characteristics of the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī-pati) were stated in the previous section.
These are the perpetrators of great sins (mahāpātakin); they go to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
"Listen, I shall describe to you those other pits into which they go; understand them.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hells for Sinners, the Praise of Śiva, and the Definition of Terms such as 'Brahmin-Slaughter' in the Retribution of Karma," within the Dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī in the Legend of Sāvitrī, in the Second Section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, during the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Yama said:
O virtuous lady, without service to Hari, one cannot obtain the destruction of karma.
Auspicious action is the seed of heaven, while hell results from evil action.
O devoted wife, he who eats the food of an unchaste woman or the food of a prostitute [falls].
Indeed, that twice-born man who approaches her goes to the Kālasūtra hell.
Having remained in Kālasūtra for a hundred years, he will certainly become a Śūdra.
In that birth he shall be diseased, and thereafter he may become a pure twice-born man again.
A woman who has only one husband is considered devoted to her husband (*pativratā*); in the second [period], she is remembered as unchaste (*kulaṭā*);
in the third, she should be known as wanton (*dharṣiṇī*); and in the fourth, she is remembered as a harlot (*puṃścalī*).
In the fifth, she is a courtesan (*veśyā*), and in the sixth, she is proclaimed to be a female twin (*yugmī*).

From this point forward, she is a great prostitute (mahāveśyā), untouchable among all castes. (5) That twice-born man who approaches an unchaste woman, a wanton woman, a harlot, a courtesan, or a great prostitute, goes to Avatoda. (6)
One who approaches an unchaste woman remains there for a hundred years; one who approaches a bold woman, four times that;
one who approaches a wanton woman, six times that; one who approaches a prostitute, eight times that;
and one who approaches a woman of the same caste, ten times that—of this there is no doubt. (7)
And one who lusts after a great courtesan shall dwell there for a hundredfold [duration];
for then he becomes "all-going," so said the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Right there, beaten by the messenger of Yama, he undergoes torment.
The partridge goes to unchaste women, and the crow goes to bold women;
the cuckoo goes to harlots, and likewise the wolf goes to prostitutes. The boar goes to female quadrupeds; for seven births in Bhārata, [these are their fates].
And the lover of a great courtesan becomes a silk-cotton tree in the cremation ground.
(11) He who, devoid of knowledge, eats during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, goes indeed to the Aruntuda hell for exactly one Candrāmnāya-year. (12)

Then he shall become a human being afflicted with diseases of the stomach, suffering from abdominal tumors, one-eyed, and toothless; thereafter he becomes pure. Furthermore, he who gives away a daughter already promised to one man to another [shall suffer likewise].
O virtuous lady, he who steals what has been given shall dwell for a hundred years upon a bed of dust, subsisting on that very dust. He who steals what has been given shall dwell for a hundred years,
bound by nooses and struck by the messengers of Yama, upon a bed of arrows.

Indeed, he who does not worship the earthen *śivaliṅga* with devotion goes, by the wrath of the Wielder of the Trident, to a most terrible state of being impaled upon a trident. Having remained right there for a hundred years, he becomes a beast of prey for seven births.
Thereafter, he shall become Devala and remain pure for seven births.
(17) He who inflicts punishment upon a Brahmin, causing that twice-born man to tremble with fear, shall dwell in Prakampana for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a Brahmin. (18)
She who looks upon her husband with a face full of wrath out of anger, speaks harsh words to him, and goes to the Ulkāmukha hell;
there the servant of Yama constantly places a flaming torch in her mouth. (19)
One should strike her on the head with a staff [the number of times] equal to the number of hairs on her body for as many years as there are hairs.
Thereafter, she shall become a human widow for seven births.
Having experienced the suffering of widowhood and having endured disease, she then becomes pure.
The Brāhmaṇī woman who was enjoyed by a Śūdra goes to the Andhakūpa hell;
there, she dwells day and night in darkness, subsisting on heated water and filth, extremely tormented and beaten by the messengers of Yama. (22)
And she remained submerged in the water for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
For a thousand births she was a crow, for a hundred births a sow, for a hundred births a hen, and for seven births a jackal. (23–24)
For seven births she shall be a female pigeon, and for seven births a female monkey;
thereafter, she shall become a Caṇḍālī woman, to be enjoyed by all in Bhārata.
Then she shall become a washerwoman, afflicted with consumption and a wanton woman.
Then the oil-maker shall be afflicted with leprosy, and thereafter she shall become pure.
The prostitute shall dwell in the piercing [of gems], while the couple indeed [reside] in the beating with a staff.
The great prostitute shall be in the binding with a net, and the unchaste woman in the powdering of the body.
O virtuous lady, a wanton woman who is indeed audacious in crushing [others] and likewise in withering them shall dwell there,
joined with torment and beaten by the messengers of Yama;
she must consume feces and urine there for the duration of a manvantara.
Then he becomes a worm in excrement for a hundred thousand years, and after that he becomes pure.
If a Brāhmaṇa should approach a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Kṣatriya a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya a Vaiśya woman, or even a Śūdra a Śūdra woman; || 30 ||
One who violates his own caste or another's wife goes to the Kaṣa hell together with her.
Having consumed the water of the Kaṣāya hell, which is heated by its own acidity, he shall dwell there for twelve years.
Thereafter, the Brāhmaṇa becomes purified; and in this same manner, so too do the Kṣatriyas and the others.
The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) has declared that women also become purified.
O devoted wife, if a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya should approach a Brāhmaṇa woman,
he becomes one who approaches his mother and shall go to the Śūrpakarṇa hell.
He was devoured along with his Brahmin wife by worms shaped like winnowing baskets;
he was beaten by a messenger of Yama and forced to consume boiling urine.
There, indeed, he undergoes torment for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.

For seven births he shall be a boar and then a goat; thereafter he becomes pure. He who, having taken Tulasī in his hand, does not fulfill his vow, or should utter a false oath, shall go to Jvālāmukha.
He who, having taken water from the Gaṅgā in his hand, does not fulfill his vow,
and he who, having extended his right hand, does not fulfill his vow— he shall go to Jvālāmukha, as if toward a stone image of a deity. (37)
Or if, having stayed even in a temple, he should go to Jvālāmukha;
or if, O virtuous lady, having touched a Brahmin, a cow, or fire—which is equal to Viṣṇu—he does not fulfill his vow, he shall go to Jvālāmukha. (38–39)
He who betrays a friend, he who is ungrateful, he who is a traitor to trust,
and he who gives false testimony— such a person shall go to Jvālāmukha.
These indeed dwell there for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Just as those scorched by glowing coals and beaten by the messengers of Yama [are purified], so too a Caṇḍāla who touches Tulasī becomes pure after seven births;
a Mleccha who touches the water of the Gaṅgā becomes pure after five births. (41–42)
O beautiful one, one who touches a stone becomes a worm in excrement for seven births;
one who touches an image becomes a worm in a wound for seven births thereafter,
and one who wipes with the right hand becomes a serpent for seven births.

Then that man shall become handless, and thereafter he shall be pure. One who speaks falsely in a temple shall become a *devala* for seven births. Furthermore, one who touches a Brahmin or others shall certainly become an *agrādānī*. 44–45.
Then, for three births, they become mute and deaf;
thereafter, O pure one, they are bereft of a wife, bereft of lineage, and bereft of intelligence.
Furthermore, they are betrayers of friends, ignoble, ungrateful, and afflicted with goiters.
A betrayer of trust becomes a tiger for seven births in Bhārata;
likewise, one who gives false testimony becomes a bear for seven births.
He destroys seven generations of ancestors, seven generations of descendants, and himself. (47–48)
A twice-born man who is devoid of daily rites and possessed of dullness,
who has no faith in the words of the Vedas and laughs mockingly at the virtuous;
one who is lacking in vows and fasts and is a reviler of the words of the righteous.
Even one who is crooked shall dwell for a hundred years as a crocodile in icy water;
he shall become an aquatic creature through a succession of a hundred births,
and thereafter, passing through various species of fish, he becomes pure.
Or whoever should commit the theft of wealth belonging to the gods or Brahmins,
having caused ten ancestors and ten descendants to fall,
goes himself to the realm of Dhūmāndha, which is filled with smoke and darkness.
Afflicted by smoke and subsisting on smoke, he shall dwell there for four yugas.
Thereafter, he shall be born as a mouse for a hundred births in Bhārata;
after that, he shall pass through various species of birds and species of insects.
Then he becomes various kinds of trees,
and then a man who is wifeless, lineage-less, a Śabara, and afflicted by disease;
thereafter he becomes a goldsmith and likewise a merchant of gold.
Then there is the Brāhmaṇa who serves Yavanas, and then the astrologer;
the Brāhmaṇa who subsists on astrology, the one who lives as a physician, the practitioner of medicine, the merchant, and he who sells iron, lac, mercury, and the like. (56–57)

He goes to Nāgaveṣṭa, surrounded indeed by serpents; bitten there by a serpent, he shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body. Thereafter, he shall become an astrologer and a physician for seven births.
The cowherd, the laborer, and then the conch-maker are pure (59).
O devoted wife, these well-known sacrificial pits have been described;
there are indeed other, lesser ones that are not so well known (60).
There are sinners among them who experience the fruits of their own actions;
they wander thus in *saṃsāra*. What more do you wish to hear?

(61) Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Pits for Sinners" within the "Fruition of Karma" section of the *Sāvitrī-upākhyāna*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second book, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*. (31)
Sāvitrī said:
"O Dharmarāja, highly fortunate one, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and who are the expounder of the various Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Pāñcarātras. (1)
That which is the essence of all, desired by all, and approved by all;
which, at the cessation of karma, exists as the seed-form, praiseworthy and bestowing happiness upon men;
which grants fame and dharma, and is the most auspicious of all auspicious things—(2).
Tell me, O observer of noble vows, that action by which people do not go to the Yāmya torments that grant the suffering of existence (3),
by which they neither see the pits there nor fall into them,
and by which birth and the rest may not occur (4).
What are the shapes of the pits, and what are their doctrines?
In what form do the sinners always remain right there?
When their own bodies have been reduced to ashes, men go to another world.
By what body do they experience enjoyment, whether auspicious or inauspicious?
(6) How is it that the body does not perish despite the long-term experience of afflictions?
O Brahmin, what is the nature of this body? You should explain this to me. (7)
Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard the words of Sāvitrī and remembering Hari, Dharmarāja bowed to his preceptor and began to tell the story, O Nārada.
Yama said:
O Vatsa, dharma indeed resides in the four Vedas and in the Saṃhitās;
in the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and the Pāñcarātra and other such texts;
and in all other scriptures and the Vedāṅgas, O lady of excellent vows.
Service to Kṛṣṇa is the most desired, the essential, and the auspicious;
it is the means of crossing over birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and suffering;
it is the embodiment of all auspiciousness and the cause of supreme bliss. (10–11)
It is the cause of all spiritual perfections, the means for crossing the ocean of hell, the sprout for the tree of devotion, and the cutter down of the tree of karma;
it is the staircase to the path of Goloka and the bestower of the imperishable state. 12.

O auspicious one, those who are servants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa do not see the sacrificial pits, the messengers of Yama, Yama himself, or the servants of Yama, even in their dreams— [for they bestow] the states of living in the same world (sālokya), sharing the same lordship (sārṣṭi), having the same form (sārūpya), and proximity (sāmīpya). || 13-14 ||
Those householders who enjoy the fruits of their actions but observe the vow of Hari,
who bathe in the sacred ford of Hari and do not eat on the day of Hari;
who constantly bow to Hari and worship the image of Hari— (15)
And they do not go to my terrible city of Saṃyamanī.
Nor do Brahmins who are purified by the three junctions of the day, endowed with pure conduct, devoted to their own duty, and tranquil, go to the abode of Yama. (16–17)

They, as well as others who enjoy the pleasures of heaven—pure gods and servants of the gods—go to and come from the mortal world and heaven; they are not truly liberated. Indeed, without service to Kṛṣṇa, men do not desire liberation. 18.
Even those devoted to their own duty, as well as those who have abandoned their own duty,
and the invincible servants of Yama traveling through the world of mortals,
become terrified of a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, just as serpents are of Vainateya.
I speak thus to that messenger who goes forth with noose in hand:
"You shall go everywhere—except to the hermitages of those devoted to Hari—to cut off the names of the worshippers of Kṛṣṇa's mantra. (20–21)
And Citragupta, like one terrified, joins his palms in reverence with his ten fingers;
furthermore, Brahmā performs the madhuparka offering and other rites for them.
Then, having transcended the realm of Brahmā, those virtuous ones proceed to Goloka.
And their misfortunes perish merely by their touch.
Just as wood and grass are consumed in a fiercely blazing fire,
so too does delusion encounter utter confusion upon seeing them, as if terrified.
Desire departs from the desirer, and greed and anger likewise cease when [the Self] is realized.
Death flees, as do disease, old age, sorrow, and fear;
so too do time, auspicious and inauspicious karma, joy, and enjoyment. (25)
O virtuous lady, I have told you which [beings] do not go to the realm of Yama.
Now listen; I shall describe the composition of the body according to the scriptures:
earth, air, ether, fire, and water—this is clear. (26–27)
And that which is the seed of the body for embodied beings, supreme in the Creator’s act of creation—
that body which is fashioned from the five elements beginning with earth—
is artificial, perishable, and here it shall be reduced to ashes. (28)
That living being, shaped like a person and the size of an old man’s thumb,
who bears a subtle body of that same form for the sake of experience—
that body shall not turn to ashes in the blazing fire within my abode. (29–30)
The body may perish by water, or after a long time of being struck by blows;
likewise, it is not destroyed by weapons or missiles, nor even by a very sharp thorn, nor by molten liquids, molten iron, or even heated stone. (31)

Even when embracing a heated image and even when standing extremely high, he is neither burned nor broken; yet he experiences intense suffering. O Goddess, I have related this account and its cause according to the sacred tradition.
"Learn all the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*); I shall describe them to you.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sāvitrī," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Yama said:
Every sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular, shaped like the orb of the full moon.
It is exceedingly deep and studded with various kinds of stones;
it is imperishable, enduring until the dissolution of the world, and fashioned by the will of the Lord.
That abode of the sinners, which bestows affliction, is of various forms;
it is described as a fire-pit consisting of blazing coals, endowed with flames a hundred cubits long, and extending for a *krośa* in every direction. (2–3)
It was filled with sinners making a great clamor,
and it was constantly guarded by my messengers who were striking them down.
It was full of boiling water and inhabited by predatory beasts.
It was a place of most terrible darkness, crowded with throngs of evildoers;
it was half a *krośa* in extent, guarded by my messengers who were struck by blows and made to utter cries of distress.
It was filled with water of caustic salt, surrounded by crocodiles, crowded with sinners, and terrifying as they cried out in lamentation;
it resounded with the cries of "Save me! from those being beaten by my messengers.
[The city] was filled with those moving about without food, their throats, lips, and palates parched;
it was full of excrement and urine, wailing and loathsome, permeated by an extreme stench, and inhabited solely by evildoers. (8–9)
And by my messengers who were beaten, by afflictions such as hunger,
and by those insects crying out "Save us!", it was devoured by those very insects.
It was filled with boiling liquid urine and swarming with urine-insects.

It is always infested by insects that bite those who have committed great sins; it measures one *gavyūti* in extent, is shrouded in darkness, and is constantly filled with the sounds of my terrible messengers,
whose throats, lips, and palates are parched as they strike [the sinners].
One *krośa* in extent, it is always filled with phlegm and constantly swarming with insects that feed upon it and are themselves devoured by sinful beings.
Another half-*krośa* is filled with poison and inhabited by those who consume that poison.
It is indeed filled with sinful beings devoured by insects and worms;
they are beaten by my messengers, who cause them to cry out and tremble—messengers who are like serpents with adamantine fangs, possessing parched throats and a most dreadful appearance. (14–15)
And for half a krośa, the eyes are filled with marrow and swarming with insects;
it is constantly crowded with sinners who are running about, being devoured by insects. And for a quarter of a krośa, it is filled with fat and is extremely difficult to endure.
It is filled with sinners who consume that [excrement], and with messengers who have been beaten;
it extends for four krośas and is full of filth, crowded with wailing sinners who are constantly tormented by fear and being devoured by white worms. (17–18)
It was a deep pool, filled with foul-smelling blood, measuring the size of a large pond;
it was crowded with sinful eaters and insects that had devoured them, and it was filled with the tears from the eyes of men, half of whom were joined by sinners. (19)
Filled with the bodily excretions of men, it was crowded with those sinners who were its food;
it was filled with my messengers, who were striking them, agitated, and devouring insects. (20–21)
It was filled with the earwax of men and joined by sinful beings who were its food;
it measured the size of a pond or a chariot, and was full of weeping creatures devoured by insects,
as well as the marrow of men and possessed of a most foul stench.

It was filled with great sinners and measured four times the size of a step-well (vāpī). It was completely packed with my messengers who had been struck down by those sinners, and it was crowded with wicked men; indeed, it was as terrifying as the dimensions of a step-well.
It was made terrifying by those who sold their daughters, by those who ate that [meat], by those eaten by insects, and by those crying out "Save us! while being struck with fear;
it was as vast as a pond or a chariot, and possessed the fourfold set of claws and so forth.
It is perpetually crowded with sinners struck by my messengers;
it contains a cauldron of molten copper filled with those turned face-upward toward the copper,
and it is always covered with hundreds of thousands of glowing copper images.
It was filled with each individual sinner embracing their own image and weeping, extending for the measure of two *gavyūtis*, crowded with my messengers who had been struck,
possessing streams of molten iron and joined with blazing embers. (28)
It is always covered by hundreds of thousands of glowing iron images, each one joined to all the others, constantly trembling out of fear, crying out "Save me!
Save me! as they are beaten by messengers. (29–30)
The Lohakuṇḍa is proclaimed to be two gavyūtis in extent, filled with great sinners, terrifying, and enveloped in darkness.
There is also the Dharmakuṇḍa, the Taptasurākuṇḍa, and likewise the Arddhakuṇḍa.
It is filled with sinners who eat that [fire] and are struck by my messengers.
Below the Śālmali tree is a pit of sharp thorns, measuring a hundred thousand *puruṣas* in extent and one *krośa* in depth, which causes great suffering. (32–33)
In the Dhanu measure, it is surrounded by extremely sharp thorns;
each one is pierced by thorns and inhabited by great sinners, who fall from the tops of the trees while being struck by my messengers. (34–35)
With parched palates, crying out "Give us water!", they were overcome by great terror; their heads were struck by sticks, and they moved about like living beings in boiling oil. (36)
It is one krośa in extent and filled with floods of poison from Takṣaka and other serpents;
it is crowded with sinners who are its food and with my messengers who strike them down. It is also filled with boiling oil and devoid of insects and the like.
It was filled with sinners who subsisted on that [meat], surrounded by those with glossy bodies;
it was joined by great evildoers who uttered plaintive cries, who were restless, and who were struck by messengers; it measured two gavyūtis in extent. (38–39)
The pit of weapons was enveloped in darkness, shrieking and terrifying;
it was surrounded by iron weapons with very sharp points shaped like spears. It had the nature of a bed of weapons and measured four *krośas* in extent. (40)
It was surrounded by outcasts and surrounded by those pierced by spears;
it was filled with my messengers whose throats, lips, and palates were parched,
and with those being tormented by insects and terrifying serpent-vehicles.
O virtuous one, it is filled with hideous beings with sharp teeth, shrouded in darkness,
and crowded with great sinners— some terrified, some devoured by insects,
some weeping and crying out, and others being beaten by my messengers. (43)
It is filled with an exceedingly foul stench, extending for half a *krośa* and saturated with pus;
it is crowded with sinners who consume that [pus] and with my messengers who strike them down.
It measures two *gavyūtis* in extent and is completely filled with cold water.
It was covered by tens of millions of serpents as large as palm trees;
it was crowded with sinners whose limbs were entwined by snakes and who were being devoured by them, as well as by my messengers who were striking them while they cried out in distress. (49–50)
There were three pits for mosquitoes and the like, filled with mosquitoes and such;
all were half the size of a treasury and occupied by great sinners,
bound by their hands, feet, and other limbs— kṣatriyas whose blood flowed from their wounds.
[The hell] is filled with those crying out "Hā! Hā! and moving about incessantly.
The pit of Vajra and Vṛścika is completely filled by those two;
half of the pond is occupied by sinners who have been stung by Vajras and scorpions.
There are three pits for those who discharge arrows and the like, filled with those very [weapons];
they are joined by those pierced sinners, half of whom are crimson with blood. There is also the Golakuṇḍa, filled with boiling mud and water, and enveloped in dense darkness.
It was filled with sinners being tormented and devoured by insects;
and half of it, as well as the whole, was filled with millions of aquatic crocodiles—terrible beings of deformed shapes—who were devouring the sinners. (51–52)
It was joined by hundreds of millions of those who feed on feces, urine, and phlegm,
as well as by sinners with deformed appearances and the size of a bow-length (*dhanurlakṣa*). There was also a pit for dogs and horses, which was completely filled with them.
It was constantly filled with devouring sinners who were incessantly making noise;
for a hundred bow-lengths it was joined with thunderbolts, always crowded with sinners,
and made of internal darkness, forever filled with the sound of those consumed by thunderbolts.
And there is the Vāpīdviguṇayāna, fashioned from heated stones,
resembling blazing coals, filled with moving sinners,
and further constructed of sharp rocks like the edge of a razor. (56)
It was crowded with those who have committed great sins, mangled by blood and water from their wounds;
filled with foul-smelling saliva, it was inhabited by sinful beings who serve as its food.
It resounded with deep cries from those being beaten by my messengers. (57–58)
[It is] a hundred bow-lengths full of boiling water resembling collyrium,
filled with moving sinners struck by my messenger;
it is a krośa long, full of liquid powders, and accompanied by sinners crying out.
By those who ate that [substance] and were consumed by fire, and by my messengers who struck them,
the pit— resembling a potter’s wheel and spinning incessantly—
was joined by sixteen very sharp spokes and filled with the whirling sinners. (60–61)
Exceedingly crooked and deep, measuring two *gavyūtis* in extent, it was fashioned in the shape of a cave and filled with boiling water;
it was crowded with great sinners who had devoured aquatic creatures. (62)
It was filled with moving creatures that made sounds, enveloped in darkness, and terrifying;
it was joined by tens of millions of hideous-shaped and most dreadful tortoises dwelling in the water,
and it was filled with those sinners who had been devoured by them.
It is always filled with masses of flames produced by radiant energy, accompanied by wailing sinners who are moving about and making sounds;
it is deep with their cries and covered with glowing ashes. (65)
It is joined with ever-moving sinners who have consumed ashes;
it is filled with heaps of heated stones and clods of earth;
and it is indeed filled with creatures whose limbs are scorched and who possess parched throats.

Resounding with cries, consisting of darkness, and deep, it is proclaimed as the Dagdhakuṇḍa (Boiling Cauldron) hell, filled with those struck by my messengers who are most cruel. It also contains water joined with waves and mixed with scalding lye.
It was filled with various kinds of deformed creatures of the water,
measuring two *gavyūtis* in extent, deep, and enveloped in darkness;
it was crowded with sinful beings who were its food, along with stinging aquatic monsters.
Moving about and crying out, yet unable to see one another,
they are cast into the terrifying *uttaptasūrmikuṇḍa* (the pit of the heated iron image),
and likewise beneath the tall palm tree of the *asipatravana* (the forest of sword-leaves).
And there is a pit measuring half a krośa, filled with falling leaves;
it is filled with the blood of sinners who fall from the tops of trees, even as those wicked ones cry out, "Save me! || 72-73 ||
Deep, shrouded in darkness, and infested with red insects—
that pit of sword-leaves is celebrated as terrifying;
it measures a hundred bows in extent and is crowded with razor-edged weapons.
Filled with the blood of sinners, razor-edged, and terrifying;
equipped with weapons such as needles and arrows, it is filled with a flood of the blood of the wicked.
Fifty bow-lengths in extent, it is needle-mouthed and a source of suffering. (75–76)
The mouth of a specific creature called a *godhā* is fearsome in shape;
it is deep, shaped like an elbow, and measures twenty *dhanus*.
It causes great suffering and is the ultimate mark of one who has committed a heinous sin.

And there is a pit, shaped like a human face, sixteen *dhanus* in measure, deep and resembling a well; it is constantly filled with those most wicked who were eaten by insects and whose faces were perpetually bowed down. (78–79)
The ground, shaped like a pool, was filled with a multitude of lordly elephants;
it was saturated with the blood of sinners struck down by elephant tusks, and was constantly filled with the cries of woe from those being devoured by insects. (80)
The elephant-bite [pit] is declared to be one hundred *dhanus* in measure.
The pit shaped like a cow’s mouth (*gomukha*) is indeed thirty *dhanus* in measure; it is proclaimed as the "cow-mouth," which inflicts suffering upon sinners. (81–82)

It was whirled around by Kālacakra, constantly terrifying, shaped like a jar, filled with darkness, and measuring two *gavyūtis* [in circumference]. It was a hundred thousand *manus* in measure, deep, and exceedingly vast. (83)
In some places, there is heated oil within the vicinity of the pits;
in some places, there are pits of heated iron and the like, as well as copper and so forth; and in some places, there are pits of heated stone within the vicinity. (84–85)
It was filled with the foremost of sinners and those who had committed great crimes (mahāpātakin), who could not see one another and were constantly making noise;
they were being beaten by my messengers with staffs and likewise with maces. (86–87)

O beautiful one, as many sinners as there are in all the pits— some reeling, some falling, some repeatedly fainting, and others struck down by my messengers who have fallen from great heights for a moment— [all these are being purified]. 88.
There are four qualities present there in the Kumbhīpāka hell, which is difficult to cross.
Having fallen into it for a very long time, they remain deprived of both enjoyment and a physical body.
And Kumbhīpāka is proclaimed to be the foremost of all the pits (kuṇḍas). 89–90.
There, the sinners are bound by the thread fashioned by Kāla;
they are raised up by my messengers and submerged again in an instant.
Likewise, they remain for a very long time within the pits, their breaths suppressed.
And their bodies and enjoyments, joined with excessive afflictions, are impermanent.
Struck by my messengers with staffs and even pestles, they are cast into that which is proclaimed as Kālasūtra, filled with boiling water. (92–93)
There is a pit and a fissure in the ground, shaped like a well and filled with scalding water, measuring twenty bow-lengths in extent;
it is constantly pervaded by great sinners whose limbs are being scorched. (94)
It is perpetually proclaimed as Avaṭoda because it was struck by my messengers;
there, within a distance of one hundred bows, is a pool where all the diseases of sinners suddenly manifest upon merely touching its water as they fall into it. (95–96)
Where all the obstructed and sinful ones suffer constantly, uttering cries of "Alas!
Alas!", that very place they know to be *Aruntuda*.
It is strewn with heated sands that are blazing and intensely burning.
Frequented by those sinful beings who consume that [flesh], it extends for a hundred bows' length and is filled with dust-eaters.
There, as the sinners fall, there is indeed a great trembling;
at the very moment of their descent, the sinner is indeed enveloped by the noose.
When the *kuṇḍa* indeed cries out, they know that to be its binding with nooses.
It is proclaimed to be twenty *dhanus* in measure and impaled upon a trident.
By the mere act of falling into it, the sinner becomes bound by the trident.
Where there is indeed trembling for the sinners as they fall, and where there is intense trembling for half a *krośa* in the freezing water;
indeed, my messengers cast flaming meteors into the mouths of the sinners there. (101–102)
It measured twenty *dhanus* and was filled with meteors;
it was one hundred thousand *manus* in extent, deep, and a hundred *dhanus* in depth;
and it was infested with various kinds of terrifying worms.
That which is known as Atyandhakāra (Extreme Darkness) is circular and shaped like a well;
it is filled with sinful beings who are devouring one another, unable to see each other, scorched by boiling water, writhing about, and devoured by insects. (104)
The Andhakūpa (Blind Well) is proclaimed as being filled with darkness and inhabited by those blind of sight;
there, sinners are pierced by multitudes of various kinds of weapons, and its depth is proclaimed to be twenty bow-lengths. 105–106.
Where sinners were struck with clubs by my messengers,
that pool, sixteen *dhanus* in measure, is known as Daṇḍatāḍana.
There, sinners are bound with great nets just like fish.

It is proclaimed to be thirty *dhanus* in measure and bound with a net (108). As the sinners fall into the pit, their bodies are pulverized; its interior is lined with iron plates and measures ten million *manavas* in depth (109).
Deep and filled with darkness, measuring twenty *dhanus* in extent—
that is proclaimed to be the powder of the bodies of those who have fainted and become inert.
Therein, the sinners are constantly crushed by my messengers with pestles.
That pit, measuring sixteen *dhanus*, is known as Dalana;
there, at the mere sight of it, the sinner’s throat, lips, and palate become parched.
And [the pit] measuring thirty *dhanus* consists of heated sands. (111–112)
That which measures one hundred mānas, is deep, filled with darkness,
and devoid of water-supplies, is proclaimed as *śoṣaṇa*.
It is completely filled for a distance of one hundred bows with various animal hides and decoctions.
Filled with foul odors and crowded with great sinners who eat those [filth],
there is a vast pit twelve *dhanus* in measure, shaped like a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*),
filled with heated iron sands, and inhabited by evildoers. (114–115)
O beautiful one, within that sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) which measures twenty bow-lengths, there are always flames of fire with mouths wide open;
it is entirely filled with sinners whose limbs have been consumed by those flames.
That great, perpetually distressing pit is known as Jvālāmukha;
by merely falling into it, the sinner becomes unconscious and tormented.
Furthermore, there is the Jihmakuṇḍa, half of which is lined with heated bricks. (117–118)
And it is filled with smoke and darkness, joined by sinners blinded by smoke;
that which is called "Blinded by Smoke" (Dhūmāndha) extends for a hundred bows' length and is bound by fetters of breath.
Upon merely falling there, the sinner becomes entwined by serpents.
A hundred bow-lengths filled with serpents is the *nāgaveṣṭana-kuṇḍaka*.
Listen as I have described these eighty-six types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), as well as their defining characteristics; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Hell-Pits in the World of Yama," within the Sāvitrī episode of the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Sāvitrī said:
"Grant me devotion to Hari, which is the very essence and exceedingly difficult to attain."
"O Lord, everything has been heard from you; nothing remains for me now.

Tell me something of the Dharma that consists of the glorification of the qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the seed for the upliftment of hundreds of thousands of men and the savior from the ocean of hell. (1–2)
It is the cause of the effects of liberation, the warding off of all that is inauspicious,
the shatterer of the trees of karma, and the remover of the flood of committed sins.
(3) How many kinds of liberations are there, and what is their defining characteristic?
The different forms of devotion to Hari, as well as the characteristics of the *niṣeka* rite;
and the fact that the female species was created by the Creator as devoid of knowledge of reality—O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me: what is that essential knowledge? (4–5)
Indeed, all forms of giving, fasting, bathing at sacred fords, religious observances,
and austerities do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of knowledge when ignorance prevails. (6) A mother exceeds a father a hundredfold in terms of venerability.
"O Lord, the teacher who bestows knowledge is a hundred times more worthy of worship than one's mother.
Yama said:
"Previously, every boon that was desired by you in your mind has been granted."
"Now, my child, by my boon, may you possess devotion to Hari.
O auspicious one, if you wish to hear the glorification of the virtues of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
which delivers the lineage of speakers, questioners, and listeners— [then listen]."
Even Śeṣa with his thousand mouths is not able to speak it, nor is the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya capable of speaking it even with his five mouths.
Even the Creator of the four Vedas and the Ordainer of the worlds [is unable]. 10.
Even Brahmā with his four faces, nor Viṣṇu who knows all,
nor Kārttikeya with his six faces, is certainly not able to describe it;
nor is Gaṇeśa capable, the teacher of the lords of yogins.
The four Vedas alone are the very essence of all scriptures;
even those who are wise do not know even a sixteenth part of his qualities,
and Sarasvatī herself is not capable of describing them, despite her utmost effort.

Sanatkumāra, Dharma, Sanaka, Sanātana, Sananda, Kapila, Sūryya, and those others who are the sons of Brahmā—even they, though wise, are unable to describe it; what then can be said of others whose intellects are dull? (14–19)
Neither the perfected ones (*siddhas*), nor the lords of sages (*munīndras*), nor likewise the yogis are able to describe [Him];
what then of others, or who are we ourselves in the matter of praising the qualities of the Blessed One?
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest meditate upon His lotus feet.
It is easily accomplished for those who are devoted to Him, but for others it is very difficult to attain.
Someone may know a little; the great proclamation of His qualities is known in its full extent by Brahmā, the sons of Brahmā, and others. (17–18)
Gaṇeśa, the teacher of the wise, knows that which transcends him;
and Śambhu alone, the omniscient one, knows that which transcends all.
To him [Gaṇeśa], this supreme knowledge was imparted in the past by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
In that very place, in the exceedingly secluded and beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala of Goloka,
a certain glorification of his qualities was recounted once more;
Śiva himself then related it for the sake of Dharma in the world of Śiva.
Dharma related that to Bhāskara at Puṣkara:
"O virtuous one, it was by propitiating Yama through austerity that my father obtained the earth.
Previously, I did not take possession of my own domain with such effort."
"O lady of excellent vows, endowed with dispassion, I desire to go for the sake of asceticism.
Then my father spoke to me concerning his virtues;
I shall relate that according to the tradition, though it is exceedingly difficult to comprehend—listen! (23–24).
He does not know His own qualities; what then can be said of another?
O fair-faced one, just as space does not know its own interior, so it is with Him.
The Blessed One is the inner self of all, the cause of all causes.
He is the Lord of all, the primordial source of all, the knower of all, and the bearer of all forms.
(26) He possesses eternal form, an eternal body, and eternal bliss;
he is formless, unrestrained, hornless, devoid of qualities, and without support. (27)
He is untainted, the witness of all, the support of all, and higher than the highest.
Nature (prakṛti) and its transformations, as well as the material beings born from those transformations, are He.
He Himself is the Person (puruṣa), He Himself is Nature, and He Himself is beyond Nature.
Though formless, he assumes a form for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees—extremely desirable, beautiful, and captivating;
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, a youth dressed as a cowherd. (29–30)
Charming, the abode of the playful beauty of ten million Cupids;
his eyes steal the splendor of autumn midday lotuses;
his face is resplendent with the beauty of ten million full moons of autumn. (31)
Adorned with jewel-ornaments inlaid with priceless gems,
(32) ever smiling and graced with a priceless yellow garment,
he is the supreme Brahman in form, blazing with the splendor of Brahman. (33)
He is pleasant to behold, peaceful, the beloved of Rādhā, and infinite;
he is being gazed upon from all sides by the smiling gopīs,
standing in the center of the rāsa circle upon a jeweled lion-throne.
Two-armed, sounding his flute, adorned with a forest garland;
(35) beautiful, with his chest radiant with the supreme gem, the Kaustubha; his body anointed with saffron, agallochum, musk, and sandalwood. (36)
Adorned with beautiful garlands of campaka flowers, lotuses, and mālatī blossoms,
and graced by a crest rich in the splendor of lovely campakas and shining with artificial jewels—
devotees, overflowing with devotion, meditate upon Him who is thus constituted. (37)
Out of fear of whom the Creator ordains the very creation of the worlds;
by whose command He records the deeds of all embodied beings according to their merit;
and by whose command He is the bestower of the fruits of austerities and actions. (38–39)
Viṣṇu is the protector of all, who constantly protects out of fear of Him;
Kālāgnirudra is the destroyer of all worlds, [acting] out of fear of Him;
and Śiva is the conqueror of death and the Guru of gurus for the wise. (40)
By the gift of that knowledge, he himself became the Lord of Siddhas, the Master of Yogins, and the All-Knowing One (41).
He was endowed with supreme bliss and possessed both devotion and detachment.
By his grace, the wind blows—the foremost of all swift-moving things (42).
O Sati, it is out of fear of her that the sun shines and blazes continuously;
by her command Indra sends rain, and Death moves among living beings.
By her command, fire burns even the most cooling water.
By his command, the guardians of the quarters protect the directions from great fear;
by his dread, the planetary wheels and the grahas indeed revolve;
out of fear they bear fruit, and out of fear of him even the trees blossom.
Out of fear, trees bear ripe fruits yet remain fruitless;
by his command, those dwelling on land do not live in the waters,
and likewise, by his command, those dwelling in the waters do not live on land.
I am the ordainer of rules, and it is out of fear of me that both dharma and adharma exist; time measures everything, and it is by my command that it revolves.
It is out of fear of me that Time and Death take away life at the improper hour.
Falling into a blazing fire or into a deep ocean, from the top of a tree onto a sharp sword, or into the mouths of serpents and other such creatures;
pierced by various weapons and missiles in treacherous battles—[in all these states, one remains mindful]. 49.
And while he lies upon a bed of flowers and sandalwood, protected by his circle of kinsmen, Death shall seize him at the appointed time through fear, employing rituals and mantras.
By whose command the wind supports the mass of waters, and the waters support the Tortoise; (50–51)
In the form of the tortoise, he supports Ananta, and he, in the form of the earth, bears the oceans, the seven mountains, and indeed everything; he assumes various forms,
since all beings dissolve within him at the end.
The lifespan of Indra is seventy-one divine yugas.
Twenty-eight such falls of Śakra constitute a day and night of Brahmā.
[This occurs] in twenty-five thousand five hundred and sixty [years]. 53–54.
Those who know the calculation of numbers understand that the lifespan of men in the *yuga* is equal to that of Śakra.
Thus, thirty such days constitute a month, and two such months are traditionally reckoned as a season (*ṛtu*).
Six such seasons make a year, and one hundred years is the span of Brahmā’s life.
Indeed, upon the falling away of Brahmā, there is the opening of Hari’s eyes;
they know that when his eyes are closed, there is the natural dissolution (prākṛta-laya).
At the time of dissolution, all beings—gods and others, moving and unmoving—are absorbed into nature.
The Creator (Brahmā) is dissolved in the Creator, and he [in turn] in Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s navel-lotus.
Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk and possesses four arms in Vaikuṇṭha,
is dissolved on the left side of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
All those beginning with Rudra and Bhairava, as many as there are followers of Śiva,
are dissolved into Śiva, the support of Śiva, within the eternal bliss of knowledge.
He is the presiding deity of knowledge for Kṛṣṇa, Mahādeva, and the Self.
Then, in an instant, he became dissolved in the knowledge of Hari.
All powers were dissolved in Durgā, who is the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu;
and she, in turn, was dissolved in the intellect of Kṛṣṇa as the presiding deity of the intellect.
And Skanda, who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, merged into his chest;
and the Lord of the Gaṇas, the sovereign of the gods, who is a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, merged into his arm.
O lady of virtuous vows, she [the goddess] who is a portion of Padmā merged into Padmā and into Rādhā. (62–63)
And all the Gopīs and indeed all the celestial women were there;
she is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breaths, and she resides within his very vital energies.
Sāvitrī is present in Sarasvatī, as are all the Vedas and Śāstras.
The speech of that very Supreme Self is established within his tongue;
the cowherds residing in Goloka are dissolved in his body hairs;
all the vital breaths of all beings are in his breaths, as are the winds and the fire.
The water dissolved in the fire of their stomachs at the tip of their tongues;
the Vaiṣṇavas, filled with supreme bliss, drank the nectar of the essence of the essence—the rasa of devotion—at the lotus feet [of the Lord]. (67)
The Virāṭ is subtle, yet merged within the Great One; in Kṛṣṇa, the Great One is the Virāṭ.
Within the pores of his very hair are all the worlds in their entirety.
By the mere closing of his eyes, the great dissolution occurs.
The opening of the eyes of that very Supreme Self is creation;
as much as there is creation in His closing of the eyes, so much is dissolution in their opening.
(70) And within a hundred years of Brahmā, there is creation therein, and then again, dissolution.
O lady of excellent vows, there is simply no number for the creations and dissolutions of Brahmā.
Listen now to the enumeration of the particles of dust on the earth:
for that Inner Self of all, a single blink of an eye constitutes a dissolution. (71–72)
Upon opening [the eyes], creation occurs again by the will of the Lord.
Who indeed is capable of proclaiming His qualities throughout all the cosmic eggs?
I have spoken exactly as it was heard from my father’s mouth and according to the scriptures.
And liberation has been described by those learned in the four Vedas as being of four kinds. Devotion to Hari, which is centered upon that [liberation], is even weightier than liberation itself.
One bestows the same world (*sālokya*) with Hari, while another, the supreme, bestows similarity of form (*sārūpya*). (74–75)
"Thus the tradition holds that [the Goddess] bestows proximity and indeed grants liberation;

devotees do not desire those [attainments], such as the state of a Siddha, immortality, or even the state of Brahmā, except through her service and the like. (73) They disregard even the status of a perfected being, godhood, and the nature of Brahman.
They know that the shattering of the fears of birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and so forth,
as well as the maintenance of the divine form, bestows the liberation of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, devotion devoid of service is liberation, while devotion accompanied by service increases that very service.

This is the distinction between devotion and liberation; now hear the definition regarding *niṣeka*. The wise know *niṣeka* to be the experience of the fruits of performed actions, as well as their destruction, which brings auspiciousness—the supreme service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (79)
"O virtuous lady, this knowledge of reality is indeed the essence of both the world and the Vedas;
it has been declared to be the destroyer of obstacles and the bestower of auspiciousness. Go, my child, as you please.
Having spoken thus, the son of the Sun (Yama) restored her husband to life.

Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon her, he prepared to depart. Seeing Yama departing, Sāvitrī bowed down to him and wept, grasping his feet; for separation from the virtuous causes extreme suffering. (82)
Seeing Sāvitrī weeping, Yama, that ocean of compassion, spoke to her with satisfaction; and he too wept, O Nārada. Yama said:
Having enjoyed happiness for a hundred thousand years in the meritorious land of Bhārata,
O auspicious one, you will finally go to Goloka, the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Having returned to your own home, O blessed lady, perform the vow of Sāvitrī.
For women, this is the cause of liberation for up to fourteen years. On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, there is the auspicious vow of Sāvitrī;
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, there is the auspicious vow of Mahālakṣmī. (86–87)
If she observes this vow for sixteen years, and for each year performs it for even a fortnight with supreme devotion, she goes to the abode of Hari.
And on every Tuesday, [she should worship] the goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.

Every month on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Ṣaṣṭhī, the bestower of auspiciousness; likewise, on the sun’s entry into Āṣāḍha, one should worship her in the mind as the giver of all perfections;
and on the full moon of Kārtika, one should worship Rādhā, the beloved who is dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life, during the Rāsa dance.
Having observed the fast on the eighth day of the bright fortnight every month,
one should worship the boon-bestowing Goddess Durgā— the illusory power of Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the distress of those in difficulty,
the primordial nature, the mother of the world, the virtuous Satī who possesses both husband and sons. (91)
A woman who, for the sake of wealth and progeny, worships with devotion chaste and pure wives, sacred yantras, and divine images—
having enjoyed happiness in this world, she goes at the end to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Having spoken thus, Dharmarāja departed for his own abode;
and Sāvitrī, taking her husband with her, went to her own home,
[relating] Satyavān and the events in their proper order.
And he spoke further of other kinsmen as well, O Nārada.
Sāvitrī’s father obtained his sons in due order;
her father-in-law regained his eyesight and his kingdom, and she herself obtained her sons through her boon.
Having enjoyed happiness for a hundred thousand years in the meritorious land of Bhārata,
that devoted wife went to Goloka together with her husband.
She was the presiding deity of the Sun and the presiding goddess of the mantra.
And because she is the *sāvitrī* of the Vedas, she is celebrated as Sāvitrī.
Thus, my child, this excellent narrative of Sāvitrī has been told, along with the ripening of the fruits of living beings' actions; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of Yama’s Instruction to Sāvitrī," within the *Sāvitrī-upākhyāna* of the second section (*Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus concludes the *Sāvitrī-upākhyāna*.
Nārada said:
In the dialogue between Sāvitrī and Yama, the most pure fame of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— of the Self, who is devoid of qualities and formless— was heard.
The truthful glorification of His qualities is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
Now, O Lord, I desire to hear the narrative of Lakṣmī.
By whom was she first worshipped, what is her nature, and by whom was she worshipped in ancient times?
O best among those who know the Vedas, tell me truly the glorification of her qualities.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahmā, in the beginning of creation, in the past, the Goddess was born from a portion of the left side of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, within the circle of the Rāsa dance. 4.
Exceedingly beautiful, dark-complexioned, and well-proportioned like a banyan tree;
she was like a lovely twelve-year-old girl, possessed of stable youth.
(5) She had the hue of a white campaka flower, was pleasant to behold, and captivating to the mind.
Her face was resplendent with the brilliance of ten million full moons of autumn;
her eyes were beautified by the splendor of autumn lotuses at midday.
And that goddess, by the will of the Lord, suddenly became twofold.
They were equal in form, complexion, splendor, age, brilliance, fame, dress, appearance, ornament, and virtue;
and likewise in their smiles, glances, speech, and gait. (8)
With a sweet voice, through proper conduct, and with conciliation, Mahālakṣmī was on his left side and Rādhikā on his right. First, Rādhā chose the Supreme Being who possesses two arms. (9–10)
And Mahālakṣmī, following after him, desired that charming one.
Out of respect for her, Kṛṣṇa indeed became twofold in form:
his right portion was two-armed, and his left portion was four-armed.
In ancient times, the two-armed one gave Mahālakṣmī to the four-armed one.
She by whom the universe is constantly perceived and beheld with a loving gaze,
and who is the greatest among goddesses— she is remembered as Mahālakṣmī.
The beloved of Rādhikā has two arms, while the beloved of Lakṣmī has four.
In Goloka, the two-armed Lord remained surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses;
the four-armed Lord went to Vaikuṇṭha together with Padmā.
In every respect, those two supreme ones, Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa, are equal;
and Mahālakṣmī, through her yoga, assumed various forms.
In Vaikuṇṭha, she is the supreme Mahālakṣmī, the most perfect.
She is the very embodiment of pure being, endowed with all auspiciousness;
she is indeed preeminent in her love among all beautiful women.
In heaven, she is the Fortune of Heaven itself, possessing the very form of Indra’s prosperity.
In the netherworlds and among mortals, she is the royal fortune (*rājalakṣmī*) in kings;
she is the household fortune (*gṛhalakṣmī*) in homes, and as a wife, she exists in every house by her fractional parts.
She is the very embodiment of prosperity for householders, the most auspicious of all auspicious things. (18–19)
She is the mother of cows, the fragrant Surabhi, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for those desiring the sacrifice;
she is the daughter of the ocean of milk, possessing the form of Śrī, and the lotus-like woman among lotuses.
She is the beauty and form in the moon, and she is adorned by the orb of the sun.
In ornaments, gems, and lotuses;
in kings, queens, and celestial women; in houses, all kinds of crops, and garments—likewise, she was present in that refined place. (21–22)
She was enchanting within the statues of the gods, in auspicious jars,
in rubies, in pearls, and in garlands;
she was indeed present in the finest gems, in necklaces, and in the sandalwood paste.
On beautiful tree branches, amidst new clouds, and among all things;
in Vaikuṇṭha, that Goddess was first worshipped by Nārāyaṇa,
in the second [kalpa] by Brahmā with devotion, and in the third by Śaṅkara.
And she was worshipped by Viṣṇu in the Ocean of Milk, O Sage,
as well as by Svāyambhuva Manu, by all the lords of men,
by the foremost of sages, by the best of ascetics, and by virtuous householders. (26)

She is worshipped by the Gandharvas and others, and by the Nāgas and others in the netherworlds (pātālas). O Nārada, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, a worship was performed with devotion by Brahmā throughout the entire fortnight within the three worlds.
In the months of Caitra, Pauṣa, and Bhādra, on an auspicious Tuesday,
this worship was created by Viṣṇu with devotion throughout the three worlds.
At the end of the year, during the transit of the sun into the month of Pauṣa, one should invoke the pure deity into the courtyard.
Manu worshipped her, and she became renowned throughout the three worlds.
Honored by the king with auspicious rites, Maṅgalā was indeed auspiciousness itself; she was likewise honored by Kedāra, Nīla, Nala, and Subala.
By Dhruva, son of Uttānapāda, by Śakra, and likewise by Bali;
by Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Manu, and Vivasvat;
by Priyavrata, Candra, Kubera, and Vāyu.
She is honored by Yama, Vahni, and Varuṇa;
thus she is always saluted and worshipped everywhere by all.
She is the presiding deity of all sovereignty and the very embodiment of all prosperity.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature and Worship of Lakṣmī," in the Lakṣmī-upākhyāna within the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
She is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, the most excellent one, and the resident of Vaikuṇṭha.
Mahālakṣmī is the eternal presiding goddess of Vaikuṇṭha.
(1) How did that goddess become the daughter of the ocean on earth?
What is her meditation (*dhyāna*), what is her armor (*kavaca*), and what is the entire sequence of the procedure for her worship (*pūjāvidhi*)? (2)
"By whom was she praised at the very beginning? You should explain that to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"In ancient times, Purandara had his fortune lost due to the curse of Durvāsas."
O Nārada, both the assembly of gods and the world of mortals became [distraught].
Lakṣmī, having abandoned heaven and the rest, being enraged and extremely miserable,
went and merged into Mahālakṣmī in Vaikuṇṭha, O Nārada.
Then the gods, overcome by grief and sorrow, went to the assembly hall of Brahmā.
Placing Brahmā at their head, they proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Having sought refuge in the supreme Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha, the gods [remained there].
They were exceedingly dejected, with their throats, lips, and palates parched.
At that time, by the command of Nārāyaṇa in the past,
Lakṣmī herself became the daughter of the ocean in a partial incarnation, appearing in the form of Śakra’s prosperity.
Then, having churned the Ocean of Milk together with the hosts of Daityas,
the gods obtained the boon of Lakṣmī and indeed beheld her there;
and after granting the boon to the gods and others, she gave a garland of forest flowers to Viṣṇu.
With a serene countenance, she, being pleased, granted [boons] to the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk (Viṣṇu).
And by virtue of that boon, the gods also regained their kingdom which had been seized by the asuras;
having worshipped and praised her, they became free from all calamities everywhere.
Nārada said:
O Brāhmaṇa, most excellent of sages, how did Durvāsas formerly curse Purandara? By what fault, O knower of Brahman, did he curse that most devoted practitioner of Brahman? 12.
In what form was the ocean churned by those gods and others?
By what hymn of praise did that Goddess appear directly before Śakra? And what was the conversation between the two? Tell me that, O Lord. (13–14)
Nārāyaṇa said: In ancient times, the lustful lord of the three worlds, intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine, engaged in dalliance in secret with Rambhā. (15)
Having sported with that lustful woman, his consciousness stolen away,
he remained there in the great forest, his mind agitated by passion.
[Meanwhile,] the bull among sages was departing from Vaikuṇṭha toward the peak of Kailāsa.
Indra beheld Durvāsas, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
the Lord who possessed the radiance of a thousand suns at midday in the summer heat,
shining like refined gold and intensely radiant with his mass of matted locks.
Wearing a white sacred thread, a bark garment, a staff, and a water-pot,
he bore a most brilliant forehead mark resembling the moon (19).
He was accompanied by a circle of disciples who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Seeing him, Purandara bowed his head in agitation;
filled with joy, he praised that group of disciples with devotion.
And by the sage, together with his disciples, auspicious blessings were bestowed upon him.
Viṣṇu gave him a most enchanting pārijāta flower,
which removes death, disease, old age, and sorrow, and bestows liberation.
Śakra, having taken the flower, became intoxicated by royal prosperity.
Out of delusion, he indeed placed it there upon the head of the elephant.
By the mere touch of that [liṅga], and by its form and qualities,
that elephant became equal to Viṣṇu in splendor, age, and radiance.
Having abandoned Śakra, the lordly elephant also went to the terrible forest;
O Sage, Mahendra was unable to protect him by means of his splendor.
And seeing Śakra having abandoned that flower, the lord of sages—
The one of great splendor, his eyes bloodshot with rage, cursed him.
Durvāsas said:
"O you who are intoxicated by prosperity, how can you treat me with such contempt?"
Out of pride, he cast away a flower given by me from the head of an elephant.
(27) A flower, an offering of food, a fruit, or water dedicated to Viṣṇu should be consumed merely upon receiving it; by rejecting it, a person becomes a slayer of a Brahmin. (28)
The man who would reject the auspicious offering to Viṣṇu that has come to him by fortune will have his prosperity lost, his intellect lost, and his knowledge lost.
But he who eats with devotion what has been offered to Viṣṇu, merely upon receiving it, [attains all blessings].
Having delivered a hundred men, he himself becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who eats the food offered to Viṣṇu and constantly bows to Hari,
or worships and praises Him with devotion, becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
By the wind touched by him, the multitude of sacred fords is instantly purified;

O fool, by the dust of his feet, the earth is instantly sanctified. [The food of] an unchaste woman, the food of a woman without a husband, and the food from a *śrāddha* performed by a *śūdra*—these too are likewise [purified]. (32)
That which is not offered to Hari, meat eaten in vain,
food given to a Śiva-liṅga, the food of those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras, the food of Brahmins who are physicians, and likewise the food of temple-priests (devala); || 33–34 ||
The food of those who sell their daughters, the food of those who live by [prostituting] their wives,

food that is not hot, stale food, the remnants of all kinds of eatables, the food of a twice-born man whose wife has a Śūdra husband, and the food of a twice-born man who drives an ox-cart— [these should be avoided]. 35.
The food of twice-born men who have not been initiated, the food of those who carry out corpses, and likewise the food of twice-born men who approach women who should not be approached;
the food of those who betray friends, the ungrateful, and those who violate trust. (36–37)
And likewise for those who give false witness, even if they be Brahmins—
all this is purified by eating the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu. A Śvapaca who serves Viṣṇu shall uplift ten million generations of his lineage.
A Brahmin who is not a devotee of Hari is incapable of protecting even himself.
(39) If, however, out of ignorance he accepts the *nirmālya* of Viṣṇu, he is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this. (40)
And having recognized this, one who accepts the food offering (*naivedya*) of Viṣṇu with devotion is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births; there is no doubt in this matter.
For [this was so] because a flower was indeed placed upon the head of the elephant out of pride.
Therefore, let Lakṣmī depart from you and go to the abode of Hari.
I am a devotee of Nārāyaṇa; I do not fear the Lord Brahmā, nor Time, nor Death, nor even Old Age—what others could I possibly count?

What can your father Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, or even my preceptor Bṛhaspati, do for me, who am free from fear of Hari? For he upon whose head this flower is placed is indeed the one to be honored first.
"Once the head of Śiva’s child has been severed, he will join this [head] back on.
Having heard this, Mahendra, seizing the child's two feet, wept aloud, afflicted by grief and overwhelmed with fear, and spoke to him: ||| 42–46 ||
Indra said:
"O Lord, a fitting curse has been bestowed upon me for my intoxication.
