Since my wealth has been taken away by you, grant me some measure of knowledge. (47)
Sovereignty is the seed of calamities and the cause for concealing true knowledge;
it is a bolt barring the path to liberation, and by its very firmness, it brings about the destruction of devotion to Hari.
It is the supreme sprout of birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and suffering. (48)
Blinded by the darkness of prosperity, one does not see the path to liberation.
O Sage, intoxicated by wealth and utterly deluded—even though he possesses consciousness—he is surrounded by kinsmen yet becomes a hater of his own kin, like one intoxicated by liquor. (49–50)
One who is intoxicated by success, heedless, blinded by sense objects, and overwhelmed;

one who possesses great lust and is reckless—such a person does not perceive the path of being (sattva). There are two kinds of those blinded by sense objects, known as the rajasic and the tamasic. (51)
One who does not know the scriptures is considered *tāmasa*, while one who knows the scriptures is said to be *rājasa*.
O bull among sages, two paths are indicated in the scripture:
one is the seed of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*), and the other is the cause of renunciation (*nivṛtti*).
Living beings move at the outset upon the path of activity, which is a road of suffering—
proceeding according to their own will, lacking clarity, and perpetually unrestrained;
through greed, they regard as happiness that which is afflicted and sweet only in its immediate impact.
In the seed of transformation and birth, which causes birth, death, and old age,
one wanders joyfully through the course of many births,
sequentially through various wombs ordained by one's own karma. (55–56)
Then, through the grace of Kṛṣṇa, a person attains the company of the virtuous;
among hundreds and thousands, only one becomes the means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Such a saintly person shall show the path to liberation by means of the lamp of pure being.
Then the living being exerts effort to break the bonds;
through the application of many births, through austerity, and through fasting, he then attains the path of liberation, which is free from obstacles and supremely blissful. (58–59)
This was heard from the mouth of the Guru on the occasion of a casual conversation;
nothing else was asked, for we were enveloped by a flood of worldly suffering.
Now, by destiny, this ocean of knowledge has been granted to me in my time of calamity.
This calamity has turned into prosperity for me, as it brings about my deliverance.
O Ocean of Knowledge, Friend of the Wretched,
O Treasure of Compassion, grant to me, who am now in distress, some essence of knowledge that leads to the further shore of existence.
Having heard Indra’s words, the eternal teacher of the wise laughed and, being exceedingly pleased, began to discourse upon knowledge. Durvāsas said:
"O Mahendra, oh, how auspicious! You desire to see yourself.
Though appearing at first glance to be a seed of suffering, it brings about happiness in the end;
it is the cause that shatters the pain and destruction of the torments within one's own womb. (64)
It is that which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to cross, turbulent, and hard to restrain;
it is the cause for cutting down the sprouts of the tree of karma, the savior of all; it brings about a continuous stream of contentment, and is the most excellent of all paths. (65–66)
Through charity, austerity, or vows such as fasting,
living beings obtain happiness such as the enjoyment of heaven by means of ritual action.
Having diligently severed the very root of all actions performed for the sake of desire— ||| 67 || |||

Now, this very absence of volitional intent is the seed of liberation. Whatever action one performs that is characterized by sattva, provided it is done without volitional intent and having offered everything to Kṛṣṇa, one merges into the Supreme Brahman.
The wise know this to be the liberation that delivers those caught in saṃsāra;
however, the Vaiṣṇavas, distressed by even a moment’s separation from service, do not desire it.
Having assumed an excellent body, they constantly perform service.
In Goloka or even in Vaikuṇṭha,
the Vaiṣṇavas desire liberation in the form of service to that very Supreme Soul, Hari. O Śakra, they are indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and are the uplifters of their own lineage.
Constant remembrance of Viṣṇu, chanting His names, worshiping Him, serving His feet, bowing down to Him, praising Him, and with devotion eating the food offerings (naivedya);
drinking the water from His feet, and the supreme repetition of His mantra. (73)
This shall be the seed of liberation for all and their desired goal. (74) This knowledge of the Conqueror of Death was given to me by the Conqueror of Death;
I am his disciple, and by his grace I am free from doubt in every respect. (75)
He who bestows devotion to Hari, which is very difficult to attain even in the three worlds, is the giver of birth, he is the guru, he is the kinsman, and he is the supreme among the virtuous;
whereas one who shows another path without the service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is not so. (76)
He surely destroys that [evil] and shall certainly partake in its destruction. (77) The name of Kṛṣṇa is the constant cause of auspiciousness for all worlds;
auspiciousness increases eternally, and there shall be no depletion of one's lifespan. (78)
Time, death, and indeed disease depart from them,
as do fever, distress, and grief— just as serpents flee from Vainateya.
Whether he be a Brahmin or even a dog-cooker (outcaste), one who is a worshiper of the Kṛṣṇamantra [is freed].
Having transcended the world of Brahmā, he goes to the supreme Goloka.
Honored by Brahmā with the madhuparka offering and other rites,
praised by the gods and the Siddhas, he becomes an embodiment of supreme bliss.
The essence of knowledge, the essence of austerity, the essence of Brahman, the supreme auspiciousness;
the essence of yoga as taught by Śiva is service at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, everything is purely and entirely illusory.
Worship the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Rādhā, who transcends primordial nature (prakṛti);
who is exceedingly blissful, the essential core, the supreme bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the giver of perfections (siddhis) and yoga, and the granter of all prosperity. (83–84)

Even for yogis who have attained perfection, for ascetics, and for those who practice austerities, all experience the fruits of their karma; however, this is not the case for those who serve Nārāyaṇa.
By the mere touch of whom even sin is reduced to ashes, [so is he].
Just as dry fuel cast into a blazing fire [is consumed],
so too do diseases, sins, and fears tremble;
and the messengers of Yama flee far away out of fear.
A person remains bound in the prison of *saṃsāra* by fate for as long as they do not receive the *mantra* of Kṛṣṇa from the mouth of a guru—
the cause for severing the shackles known as the experience of the multitude of performed actions. (88)
It cuts through the web of illusion and severs the noose of Māyā;
it is the staircase for the path to Goloka and the primary cause for crossing over [saṃsāra].
It is the very nature of the sprout of devotion, eternally increasing and imperishable. (89–90)
O Purandara, it is certain that this is the essence of all austerities, the means for attaining youth, and the core of all perfections, Vedic recitations, vows,
gifts, purifications at sacred sites, sacrifices, and so forth. (91)
"Of all acts of worship and fasts," so says the Lotus-born One, "a hundred thousand ancestors of men, a hundred for the paternal ancestors, and the same number for the maternal grandfather;
as well as one's father, mother, and teacher—[these are purified]. (92–93)
One should rescue one's uterine brother, wife, disciple, and servant; likewise, one's father-in-law, mother-in-law, daughter, and her son;
as well as oneself, one's fellow student, the teacher’s wife, and the teacher’s son. (94)
A powerful devotee shall be uplifted merely by receiving the mantra.
(95) Merely by receiving the mantra, a person becomes liberated while living;
the multitude of sacred fords is purified by contact with him, and the earth is instantly sanctified. (96)
Throughout the course of many births, a man remains devoid of initiation;
yet, by a mere fragment of merit, he may obtain the mantra of another deity.
Having performed service to the gods through his own actions for seven births, [he attains this].

And he obtains the mantra of Ravi, the witness of all rites. Having served the Sun-god for three lifetimes, the pure man shall obtain the supreme mantra of Gaṇeśa, which removes all obstacles. (98–99)
Having served him for three lifetimes, a person shall become free from obstacles;
by the grace of Vighneśa, that person shall obtain divine knowledge.
Then, having scrutinized with the lamp of knowledge, the one of great intelligence—
Having severed the blinding darkness of ignorance, a person should worship Mahāmāyā—
Prakṛti, Viṣṇu’s Māyā, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune,
the bestower of success, the embodiment of success, and the supreme Yoginī of perfection. (101–102)
Having served her— who is the embodiment of speech, who is Padmā, who is Bhadrā, whose very self is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa,
and who possesses manifold forms— for a hundred births, a man shall,
through her grace, become a possessor of knowledge and then enjoy the bliss of that knowledge.
Kṛṣṇa, the presiding deity of knowledge, the eternal Mahādeva;
Śiva, whose very nature is auspiciousness, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the cause of auspiciousness;
the embodiment of supreme bliss, and the giver of supreme bliss. (104–105)
It bestows happiness and liberation, and grants all forms of prosperity;
it confers immortality and supreme longevity, and is capable of granting the status of Indra or Manu with ease. (106)
It bestows the status of a lord of kings, grants knowledge, and bestows devotion to Hari.
By propitiating Him for three births through the grace of the quickly-pleased One,
and by the grace of the high-souled Śaṅkara, the Giver of All— 107–108.
By the very boon of the Giver of Boons, one shall certainly attain devotion to Hari.
Then, through association with His devotees, one shall certainly obtain the mantra of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, by means of the blazing lamp of stainless knowledge, one becomes a knower of reality.
One perceives everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass as nothing but false.
By the grace of the Treasure of Compassion, one may attain stainless knowledge;
by the boon of the Giver of Boons, one shall certainly obtain devotion to Hari.
Then one attains the peace that is the essence of essences, higher than the highest;
as long as one possesses the body in which the mantra was received within Bhārata-varṣa, so long does one remain.
Having cast off that body composed of the five elements, one shall bear a divine form.
He performs service in Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, or the abode of Hari;
endowed with supreme bliss and free from delusion and other such afflictions, there is no further birth nor return to this world, O Hari. (113–114)

Furthermore, having once held the mother’s breast, one should never drink milk again—except for those who worship the mantra of Viṣṇu, those who frequent holy sites such as the Gaṅgā, and those mendicants who abide by their own dharma; for them, rebirth does not exist. (115)

One should abandon sin at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and, having performed the ritual act, worship Hari. This is the natural duty (svadharma) for those who frequent sacred fords as ordained by the Creator.
Devoted to serving Him and other such acts, one should mutter His name-mantra.

He who is devoted to vows and fasts is indeed called a servant of Viṣṇu. He whose mind is always equal toward good food or bad food, or toward a clod of earth or gold, is celebrated as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī).
He should carry a staff, a water-pot, and only a red garment.
Always a traveler, he should not remain in one place; such a person is proclaimed a *saṃnyāsī*.
Free from greed and other vices, he eats the food of twice-born men of pure conduct.
But he who asks for nothing at all is celebrated as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī).

Neither engaged in worldly activity nor belonging to a [specific] stage of life (āśrama), having abandoned all ritual actions, he should constantly meditate upon Nārāyaṇa; he is celebrated as a renunciant.
Constantly observing silence, practicing celibacy, and avoiding all conversation, he should perceive everything as consisting of Brahman; such a person is celebrated as a *saṃnyāsī*.
Possessing an even mind toward all things, he is free from violence and deceit. (122–123)
Free from anger and egoism, he is celebrated as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī). Having eaten what has come to him unasked, whether sweet or savory,
and not begging for food out of desire to eat, he is celebrated as a renunciant.
He should not look upon the faces of women, nor should he stand near them;
he who does not touch even a wooden image of a woman is a true mendicant.
"This is the duty of renunciants," so said the Lotus-born One.
In the opposite case, there is destruction, and the fear of Yama’s realm arises.
For living beings, the suffering of birth and the suffering of Yama’s realm are exceedingly terrible.
O God, the suffering in the womb is equal in both the womb of a divine being and that of a pig.
Whether in the womb of small creatures or likewise of animals and so forth,
all those [beings] remember the karma arising from hundreds of previous births;
yet once the living soul has emerged from the womb, it surely forgets it through the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
Whether it be a god or even a worm, every living being protects its own body with effort.
When the semen of a man falls within the interior of the womb,
that semen, united with blood, instantly becomes [an embryo] at that very moment.
If the blood (ovum) is in excess, the child will resemble the mother; otherwise, it will have the form of the father.
On an even day a son is born, and on the opposite [an odd day] a daughter.
If the birth occurs on a Sunday, Tuesday, or Thursday, it will be a son.
A girl is born on the odd lunar days or on the other [even] days. He whose birth occurs in the first watch of the day has a short lifespan;
in the second, he is middling; and in the third, he becomes superior to that. (132–133)
In the fourth [period], one will be long-lived, corresponding to the nature of the *kṣaṇas*;
whether suffering or happy, it is according to the influence of past karma.
And in whatever kind of *kṣaṇa* birth occurs, such will be the nature of the delivery.
And thus do the wise discourse upon the moment of birth:
"The *kalala* increases day by day;
in the seventh [night] it takes the form of a jujube fruit, and in the [seventh] month it becomes like a mouthful. (135–136)
In three months, there is a mass of flesh devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs;
in the fifth month, the embodied being becomes complete with all its members;
and in the sixth month, O knower of all principles, the movement of the life-force (jīva) occurs.

Suffering like a bird confined in a cage, dwelling in a very small space, he consumes food and drink vomited by his mother while remaining in a place of impurity; uttering cries of "Alas! Alas! he should contemplate the Supreme Lord. (138–139)
Having thus experienced supreme torment for four months,
impelled by the vital wind at the proper time, he indeed emerges from the womb;
unacquainted with direction, place, or time, he is made forgetful by the illusory power of Viṣṇu.
Constantly joined with feces and urine, the infant remains in this state until childhood;
dependent on others and incapable of warding off even mosquitoes and the like, he is devoured by insects and other creatures, and being miserable, he cries out there again and again. (141–142)
Though blinded by the mother's breast-milk and unable to make his desired request,
no clear speech issued from him until the age of *paugaṇḍa*.
Having endured torment during that *paugaṇḍa* stage, he then attains youth once more.
The embodied soul, through [the power of] *māyā*, should no longer remember the agonies of the womb and so forth.
Afflicted by hunger and sexual desire, and entangled in various delusions and the like, one should diligently protect one's son, wife, and followers. 144–145.
Thus, he is indeed honored only so long as he remains capable;
but when they consider him incapable, his kinsmen treat him like an old bull.
When he is overcome by extreme old age and becomes dull-witted and utterly deaf, [he is abandoned].
Afflicted by cough, asthma, and other ailments, dependent on others, and like one utterly deluded, he repeatedly experiences constant remorse within that interval.
He did not visit the sacred fords of Hari, nor did he seek the company of the virtuous, all due to his lustful desires. (147–148)
"O God, if I should again obtain a human birth in Bhārata,
then I shall go to a sacred pilgrimage site and indeed worship Kṛṣṇa"— thinking such things as these in his mind, that dull-witted man, O God...
And when the time has arrived, the exceedingly terrible messenger of Yama seizes him.
He beholds the messenger of Yama, with noose in hand and staff in hand, his eyes extremely red with rage, his form distorted and formidable. (150–151)
Difficult to ward off by any means, most powerful and terrifying,
hard to behold, the knower of all accomplishments, unseen by all yet standing before one—
merely upon seeing him, one becomes greatly afraid and voids excrement and urine.

Then he would immediately abandon his life-breaths and indeed his body composed of the five elements. Taking the person, who is the size of a thumb, the servant of Yama places him within the body of experience and swiftly leads him to his own abode. (153–154)
The living soul, having gone there, beholds Yama, who knows all dharmas;
he is seated upon a lion-throne of jewels, smiling, perfectly steady, supreme, the knower of the deliberation between dharma and adharma, omniscient, and facing every direction. (155)
In ancient times, the Creator fashioned him as the sole sovereign over all;
he was clothed in garments pure as fire, adorned with jewel ornaments, and surrounded by throngs of attendants and thirty million messengers. (156–157)
Chanting the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with a rosary of pure crystal beads,
meditating upon His lotus feet, his body marked by horripilation,
speaking with a choked voice, his eyes filled with tears, and seeing with equanimity everywhere. (158)
Exceedingly beautiful and eternally possessed of stable youth, blazing with his own splendor, pleasant to behold and wise;
possessing the luster of the full moon in autumn, he stood before Citragupta. (159–160)
Seeing him, who is peaceful in form for those of meritorious soul and terrifying to sinners, an embodied being bows down and stands there filled with great fear.
According to the deliberation of Citragupta, whatever fruit is appropriate for each person [is bestowed].
And the son of the Sun performs both good and evil deeds;
thus, for living beings, there is no end to their coming and going.
The means for that cessation is the service of the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Thus everything has been told; ask for the boon you desire.
I shall grant you everything, my child, for there is nothing whatsoever that is unattainable for me.
Mahendra said:
"O auspicious one, you have attained the status of Indra; what is the use of such sovereignty?
O best of sages, O wish-fulfilling tree, grant me the supreme state.
Having heard Mahendra's words, the bull among sages laughed.
He spoke these true words, which were both Vedic and consistent with reason.
Durvāsas said:
"The supreme state is extremely difficult for those attached to sense-objects to attain, even from Mahendra."
And for those such as you, there is liberation neither in the cosmic dissolution nor in the dissolution of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Manifestation occurs during the process of creation, and concealment occurs during dissolution, just as waking and sleep occur in regular succession. (167–168)

Just as time revolves, so too do those possessed by sense-objects certainly revolve perpetually by the will of the Lord, following the sequence of the rim of a wheel. Just as one *pala* consists of sixty *vipalas*, so it is. (169)
Sixty *pala*s constitute a *daṇḍa*, and a *muhūrta* is twice that amount. Thirty *muhūrtas* make up a day and night.
The wise know that fifteen [such] days and nights constitute one *pakṣa*.
A month is defined by the two fortnights, the bright and the dark;
a season is proclaimed by those who know calculation to consist of two months;
three seasons constitute an *ayana*, and two of those [two *ayan*s] constitute a year.
And for forty-three hundred and thirty thousand years measured by human reckoning,
there is a cycle of four yugas;
[this occurs] within twenty-five thousand five hundred and sixty [years].
In each age (yuga), the lifespan of men is proclaimed to be equal to that of Indra and Manu.
When ten hundred thousand Indras have fallen, increased by eight thousand, the fall of Brahmā occurs; therein takes place the natural dissolution (prākṛtika-laya).

O child, the closing of the eyes of the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa is the dissolution, and likewise, their opening is the creation. It is heard in the Śruti that there is no end to the number of Brahmā’s creations and dissolutions.
"Just as there is no liberation for the particles of dust of the earth," so spoke Candraśekhara. "And regarding those [beings] that have been mentioned, there is no release for them.
O God, choose another boon, such as the nature of the Sṛṣṭisūtra."
Having heard the words of the Lord of Sages, O Sage, the Lord of the Devas was struck with wonder.
He chose as his boon the sovereignty he had formerly possessed;
having been told, "You shall obtain that very soon," he departed for his home. || 179–180 ||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of Durvāsas’s Curse upon Indra and Other Matters," in the dialogue between Durvāsas Muni and the Lord of the Suras, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārada said:
Having heard the qualities of Hari and having attained knowledge, Purandara [Indra]—
"What did he do upon returning home? You should explain that to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having heard the virtues of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he became free from passion."
Day by day, O Brahmin, he increased his dispassion.
Having gone from the sage’s hermitage to his home, he beheld Amarāvatī crowded with Daityas and hosts of Asuras, overwhelmed with fear. 2–3.
Seeing her despondent for her kinsmen, deprived of her relatives here and there,
utterly unstable as she was bereft of father, mother, wife, and others,
and seized by enemies, he went toward the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).
On the bank of the Mandākinī, Śakra beheld his preceptor, the Lord,
seated in the supreme waters of the Gaṅgā, meditating upon the Supreme Brahman;
facing the east and turned toward the sun, he was indeed possessed of faces in every direction.
With eyes full of tears, his hair standing on end, and filled with supreme bliss; most excellent and most venerable, most righteous and devoted to his duty;
the best among his circle of kinsmen and the most eminent among those who possess self-respect. (7)
He was the eldest among his circle of kinsmen and most beloved by the enemies of the gods.
Seeing his guru engaged in silent recitation (*japa*), the lord of the gods stood there;
at the end of the watch, seeing the guru rise, he prostrated before him.
Having prostrated at her lotus feet, he wept aloud again and again;
he then related the account of the Brahmin’s curse and so forth,
as well as how he had once more obtained a boon that is difficult even for the wise to attain.

Having heard the words of his disciple, Bṛhaspati—the lord of the gods and the best among the wise and virtuous—spoke this, his eyes reddened at the corners with anger: "By degrees alone shall the Lord of the Gods [recover] his own city, which has been seized by the enemy. (11–12)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O best of gods, you have heard everything; do not weep. Listen to these words:
one who knows policy should never be despondent in the face of calamity. (13)
Whether it be prosperity or adversity, it is perishable and dream-like;
it is dependent upon one's own prior karma, and one is oneself the agent of both. Furthermore, for all beings, this state indeed revolves constantly from birth to birth.
Following the very rotation of a wheel’s rim, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For everywhere in Bhārata, a person indeed experiences the fruit of his own actions—whatever good or evil he has done. (15–16)
"Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Whatever action has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced.
Thus it is stated in the Veda and by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
Having thus addressed one born of his own lineage within the Kauthuma branch of the Sāman Veda, [he spoke]:
"For all those who have performed their actions, birth occurs when a remainder of karma remains; and for them, it indeed happens in accordance with their merit, both in Bhārata and elsewhere. (18–19)
Through action one may incur the curse of a Brahmin, and through action one may receive auspicious blessings;
through action one may attain Mahālakṣmī, and through action one may meet with wretchedness. The karma accumulated over ten million births follows living beings.
For it does not abandon him without yielding its fruit, O Purandara, just like a shadow.
(21) Indeed, due to differences in time, place, and recipient, there may well be deficiency or excess in the results of actions. (22)
And in the gift of objects, O Bull, when the objects are equal and the day is the same, the merit is equal;
but when the days differ, it is ten million times greater, or even more than that, being incalculable.
And when objects are given in equal places, O Bull, the merit is equal.
In a different land, the merit is ten millionfold, or incalculable, or even greater than that.
(24) When the recipient is equal [to the donor], the merit for the objects and for the agent alone is equal.
When the recipient is of a different quality, it is a hundredfold, or incalculable, or even greater than that. (25)

Just as crops ripen in varying degrees— some meager and some abundant— depending on the differences in the fields of farmers, so too is the fruit [of giving] according to the difference in the recipient. On an ordinary day, a gift given to a Brahmin yields equal fruit.
On the new moon day coinciding with the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), the fruit shall be a hundredfold;
on the full moon day of the Cāturmāsya, the fruit is indeed infinite;
and during a lunar eclipse, the fruit is ten millionfold.
And during a solar eclipse, the fruit is ten times greater than that.
On the Akṣayā day, it is said to be inexhaustible and of incalculable fruit.
Likewise, on other auspicious days (puṇyāha), there shall be an increase in the fruit here.
Just as it is with giving, so it is with bathing, recitation, and indeed with meritorious deeds.
In this way, the fruit of men's actions should be understood to apply everywhere. Giving to a brahmin in an ordinary place yields a result equal [to that of a sacred site].
The fruit at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and in a temple of the gods is remembered as being a hundredfold;
indeed, at the Gaṅgā it is ten-millionfold, and at the immutable field of Nārāyaṇa,
as well as at Kurukṣetra, Badarī, and Kāśī, it is likewise ten-millionfold.
Just as it is indeed ten-million-fold [in merit], so too is it in the temple of Viṣṇu;
at Kedāra it is a hundred-thousand-fold, and likewise the fruit at Haridvāra.
At Puṣkara and in the field of Bhāskara, the fruit is ten-million-fold.
In this way, one should understand that the excellence of the fruit increases progressively in all cases.

(34) One obtains a fruit equal to that given to an ordinary Brāhmaṇa when giving to one who is pure, learned, and has conquered his senses at the three junctions of the day; [the fruit is] a hundred thousandfold. (35)
And for a wise person who worships the Viṣṇu-mantra, the fruit is ten millionfold.
In this way, it should be understood everywhere that the fruit is superior and the merit is superior.
Just as [one measures] with a staff, a thread, a bowl, or water.
Just as a potter fashions a jar from clay on the ground using a wheel,
so too does the Creator bestow the fruit [of actions] according to the thread of karma.
Worship that Nārāyaṇa by whose command the process of creation proceeds.
He is the ordainer of the ordainer and the protector of the protector in the three worlds;
he is the creator of the creator and the destroyer of the destroyer, the death of Death itself. He who remembers Madhusūdana during the great calamity of saṃsāra— ||| 39 ||
"Śaṅkara has said that for him, prosperity shall arise even from adversity.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Jīva embraced the Lord of the Gods, gave him auspicious blessings, and instructed him in his desired [wisdom].

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Karma," within the Narrative of Mahālakṣmī, in the Dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Mahendra, within the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahmin, having meditated upon Hari, Hari went to the assembly hall of Brahmā.
Placing Bṛhaspati at their head, together with all the hosts of gods,
they went quickly to the world of Brahmā; having seen the Lotus-born One,
O Nārada, all the deities, along with their preceptor, prostrated themselves.
The preceptor of the gods related the account to the all-pervading Brahmā.
Having heard that, the lotus-born one smiled and spoke to Mahendra.
Brahmā said:
"My child, you are born of my lineage, my wise great-grandson;
you are the disciple of Bṛhaspati and yourself the sovereign of the gods.
Your maternal grandfather is Dakṣa, a devotee of Viṣṇu and possessed of great prowess."

How could he who belongs to the three pure lineages be possessed of egoism? (5) How could he whose mother is devoted to her husband, whose father is pure and has conquered his senses, and whose maternal grandfather and maternal uncle are likewise, be possessed of egoism? (6)
Due to the faults of his father, the faults of his maternal grandfather,
the faults of his guru, and the faults of his conduct, a person will certainly become a hater of Hari.
The Blessed Lord, the inner self of all, dwells within all bodies.
From whose body he departs, that [body] becomes a corpse at that very moment.
Śaṅkara is indeed the mind, the lord of the senses, and the form of knowledge;
Viṣṇu is the stainless primordial nature (prakṛti), and the blessed Satī is the intellect (buddhi).
Sleep and the other powers are all these manifestations (*kalā*) of *prakṛti*.
And the reflection of the Self is the individual soul (*jīva*), the experiencer who bears the body.
When the Lord of the Self departs from the body, they all depart in a state of agitation.
Just as attendants follow a king of men traveling on the road—
Śiva, Śeṣa, Viṣṇu, Dharma, and the great Virāṭ—
we are his portions, as are his devotees; yet you have trampled upon that flower of his.

O God, that lotus foot which was worshipped by Śiva with a flower was given by Durvāsas; it was ordained by fate and not made by anyone else. That flower, fallen from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, rested upon his head.
Indeed, the worship of that [deity] should take precedence over all other gods.
You have been deceived by fate, and fate is most powerful;
who indeed is able to protect a foolish person devoid of fortune? (14–15)

Indeed, Mahālakṣmī, the servant of that Lord, becomes enraged and abandons him who does not regard Kṛṣṇa—the Lord of Śrī, worshipped by all—as such. She, who was obtained in the past by you through a hundred sacrifices while you were initiated as a priest. (16)
That fortune has now departed in anger because of your rejection of Kṛṣṇa’s floral remains (nirmālya).
Now go to Vaikuṇṭha along with me and my preceptor;
having served Śrīnātha there, you will obtain prosperity by his grace.
Having spoken thus, that Brahmā, together with all the hosts of gods,
quickly went to Vaikuṇṭha, where the Lord of Śrī was with her.
Having gone there, [he beheld] the Supreme Brahman, the eternal Blessed One.
Having seen him whose nature is splendor, blazing with his own radiance,
possessing a brilliance equal to hundreds of millions of suns at the midday of summer—
peaceful, without beginning, middle, or end, the beloved of Lakṣmī, and infinite.
He was praised and bowed to by the four-armed attendants and by Sarasvatī;
he was served with devotion by the four Vedas and by Gaṅgā.
All the gods, led by Brahmā, prostrated before him with their heads.
Bowed down with devotion and with eyes full of tears, they praised Puruṣottama.
Brahmā himself, with palms joined in reverence, related the account;
and all the deities wept, having been deprived of their respective offices.
And he saw the host of gods seized by calamity, overwhelmed with fear,
stripped of garments and ornaments, deprived of their mounts and the like,
devoid of splendor, robbed of their fortune, and uncircled by their attendants. (25)
Seeing them terrified, Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of fear for those in distress, spoke.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Do not fear, O Brahmā, nor you gods; what cause for fear is there while I am present?"
I shall grant you imperishable prosperity that increases supreme sovereignty.
Furthermore, let my words be heard, which are appropriate for the occasion, beneficial, true, essential, and bringing happiness in the end. (27–28)
The countless people dwelling in the universe are perpetually under my control;
yet, just as I am independent, so too am I subject to the will of my devotees.
Indeed, whoever is angry with my devotee—who is devoted to me alone—is unrestrainedly offending me.
I certainly do not stay in that house along with Padmā.
Durvāsas is a portion of Śaṅkara, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and one who is devoted to me;
it was because of his curse that I, together with Śrī, departed even from your home.
Where there is no sound of the conch, no *tulasī*, and no worship of the stone [Śāligrāma], where there is no feeding of Brahmins, Lakṣmī does not dwell there.
O gods, wherever there is censure of my devotees and of me, [Lakṣmī does not dwell there].
Then Mahālakṣmī, becoming greatly enraged, departs due to that humiliation.
Even from the house of that fool who, devoid of devotion to me, eats on the day of Hari or on my own birth-day, Śrī likewise departs. (33–34)
He who sells human beings, he who sells his own daughter,
from whose house a guest does not eat, and from whose house my beloved departs;
he who goes to the houses of sinners and those who eat the food of a Śūdra’s funeral feast (śrāddha).
Then, greatly enraged, Kamalālayā departs from the temple.
And when a Śūdra burns a corpse or a Brāhmaṇa is devoid of fortune,
the Goddess who dwells in the lotus departs from that house in anger.
The lotus goddess Kamalā flees from the house of that Brāhmaṇa who is a cook for Śūdras or a driver of bulls, fearing the drinking of his water (38).
A Brāhmaṇa who serves Yavanas, a Devala, or one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras [is likewise abandoned].
And Vaiṣṇavī departs from that house, fearing the drinking of its water.

From the house of one who betrays trust, a slayer of friends, a slayer of men, an ungrateful person, or a Brahmin who approaches a woman who should not be approached—that is, my wife—she likewise departs. (39–40)
A twice-born man who is impure of heart, cruel, violent, and a reviler;

one born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇa mother; and the goddess [who dwells] in his house—[all these] go [to that state]. So too does the Brahmin who is the son of an unchaste woman, and her husband, who is a great sinner.
If she eats the food of one who has no heroic sons, from that man the mother of the world departs;
likewise, if he cuts grass with his fingernails or scratches the earth with them, or if he is crooked or wears dirty clothes, she departs from his house. (42–43)
The Brahmin who eats twice a day, sleeps during the day,
and engages in sexual intercourse by day departs from the beloved of Hari.
That Brahmin who is devoid of proper conduct and who accepts gifts from a Śūdra [likewise departs].
For from that foolish man who is uninitiated, she departs in restlessness.

Moreover, from him who sleeps with greasy feet or naked, being weak in wisdom, and who is constantly talkative about matters contrary to dharma, the virtuous woman indeed departs from his house. (49–50)
If one who has bathed his head with oil should touch another limb,
or play a musical instrument against his own body, Lakṣmī departs from that house.
Likewise, a twice-born man who is devoid of vows and fasts, who neglects the twilight prayers, or who is impure— [Lakṣmī likewise leaves him].
He who is devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu goes from there to Haripriyā.
He who indeed reviles a Brāhmaṇa and constantly hates them,
being a perpetrator of violence and devoid of compassion, goes from there to Sarvaprasū.
Wherever there is worship of Hari and the auspicious glorification of Hari,
there dwells that Goddess Kamalā, the source of all auspiciousness.
Wherever, O Grandfather, there is praise of Kṛṣṇa and his devotee, [there she dwells].
And that goddess, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, dwells there eternally.
Wherever there is the sound of a conch, a conch-shell, a sacred stone, or a tulasī leaf—
there she herself resides, through service, worship, and meditation.
Where there is worship of the Śiva-liṅga and the auspicious glorification of it, where there is worship of Durgā and the recounting of her qualities, and where Padmanivāsinī resides;
where there is service to the Brahmins and the auspicious feeding of them—[there one should dwell]. (93)
"The worship of all the gods shall take place there; O virtuous one, you shall have a lotus-like face.
Having spoken thus to all the gods, the Lord of Ramā said to Ramā:
"O Ramā, take birth in the Ocean of Milk by means of a portion of yourself."
Having spoken thus to her, the Lord of the World spoke again to Brahmā:
"O Lotus-born One, churn the ocean and give Lakṣmī to the gods.
Having said this, O Sage, the God who is the beloved of Kamalā vanished from sight.
After a long time, the gods went to the Ocean of Milk.
Having made Mount Mandara their churning-stick and the tortoise their base,
and having made Vāsuki their rope, they churned the ocean.
They obtained Dhanvantari, the desired nectar, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, various jewels, the jewel among elephants, and a vision of Lakṣmī;
and she, O sage, gave a forest garland to the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
To Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the Delightful One, the virtuous Vaiṣṇavī—
praised and worshipped by the gods, by Brahmā, and by Śaṅkara—
bestowed upon the abode of the gods a vision that releases one from the curse of Brahmā.
O Nārada, by the grace of Mahālakṣmī and her granting of boons, the gods regained their own realm which had been seized by the terrifying Daityas.
Thus has this entire, excellent narrative of Lakṣmī been told.
"What more do you wish to hear that is both conducive to happiness and essential?

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Churning of the Ocean," in the Lakṣmī-narrative within the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said:
The chanting of Hari’s names is auspicious; that which has been heard is the supreme knowledge.
Please speak of the desired narrative of Lakṣmī, as well as her meditation, hymns of praise, and so forth—she who was formerly worshipped by Hari, and thereafter by Brahmā and the other gods. (1)

By what method or by what rite was she worshipped through meditation in the past? Or by what hymn was she praised by Śakra when he had fallen from his kingdom, along with the hosts of gods? You ought to explain that to me. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having previously bathed in the sacred ford and put on two clean garments,
Śakra placed the pitcher in the Ocean of Milk and worshipped the six deities.
Having worshipped with devotion Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā, as well as with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings;
and having invoked there Mahālakṣmī, whose form is supreme sovereignty.
The Lord of Gods performed the worship with Brahmā as his domestic priest (purohita). O Sage, while the sages, the Brāhmaṇas, the Guru, and the gods and others stood before him,
Śiva— the Lord of Gods, whose nature is knowledge and bliss— [was worshipped].
O Nārada, having taken a flower from the pārijāta tree and anointed it with sandalwood paste, he meditated upon the goddess Mahālakṣmī and worshipped her;
the meditation was that which had been previously declared by Brahmā and is taught in the Sāmaveda.
Through that meditation on Hari, understand this which I shall tell you:
[meditate on] the Supreme Goddess dwelling in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus,
her excellent hands graced by the luster of ten million full moons of autumn.
Blazing with her own splendor, beautiful to behold and captivating,
resembling molten gold, she was Satī herself in embodied form;
richly adorned with ornaments of jewels and graced by yellow garments.
I worship the auspicious Mahālakṣmī, who has a face brightened by a gentle smile, who is beautiful, possesses stable youth, and bestows all prosperity;
having meditated upon her with this visualization, one should be well-provided with offerings. (12–13)
Having worshipped according to the words of Brahmā, he offered sixteen types of oblations with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, each preceded by its respective mantra—
praiseworthy, delightful, and excellent offerings that are difficult to obtain. (14)
"O Mahālakṣmī, please accept this wonderful seat, inlaid with priceless jewels and fashioned by Viśvakarman;
and here is pure water from the Gaṅgā, honored by all and desired. (19)
O Abode of Kamala,
let the water of the Ganges— pure, joined with flowers, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and other offerings,
and held within the interior of a conch— be accepted as the form of the fire that consumes the smoke of sin, O Dweller in the Lotus. (16–17)
O beloved of Śrī Hari, please accept this fragrant oil and scented water from the *āmalaka* fruit— the very seed of bodily beauty—
as well as this resinous substance combined with various aromatic ingredients. (18)
O Beloved of Kṛṣṇa, please accept this pure incense.
O Goddess, please accept this sandalwood, produced on the Malaya mountain, the essence of trees, enchanting, fragrant, and bestowing happiness. (19–20)
O Supreme Goddess, let this lamp, which is the very nature of the eye of the world, the cause of the total destruction of darkness, and pure in form, be accepted;
it is presented as various offerings and endowed with various flavors. (21)
May you accept this food offering, which provides manifold flavors.
(22) Food is the very nature of Brahman and the cause of the preservation of life;
may you accept this sweet food, which bestows contentment and nourishment. (23)
"May this well-cooked rice, unbroken and perfectly prepared, combined with sugar and cow's products—
sweet, delightful, and exquisite *paramānna*— be accepted upon the lotus.
And may this [offering], cooked with sugar and cow's products, sweet and most captivating, [be accepted]."
"O Lakṣmī, please accept this svastika offered by me.
O Kamalā, please accept these various kinds of delightful, ripe fruits—sweet-tasting and fruit-bearing. (25–26)
"O beloved of Acyuta, please accept this cow's milk, which is produced from the land of Surabhi, most delicious and very enchanting; it is indeed the nectar of mortals.
It is endowed with a most sweet flavor, arising from the essence of the sugarcane plant. (27)
"O Goddess, please accept this jaggery, whether cooked by fire or uncooked.
O Goddess, please accept this sweet dish produced from the flour and dust of barley and wheat grains, anointed with well-cooked jaggery and cow's products."
"O Goddess, please accept this flour-cake (piṣṭaka) offered by me, which is prepared from grain flour, cooked, and adorned with svastikas and other designs;
it is made from various ingredients and resembles a tree or a mountain. (30)
"Please accept this sugarcane juice, sweet and full of flavor;
it provides cool air and is supremely refreshing during the heat.
And please accept this lotus, this white chowrie-fan. || 31-32 ||
And take this excellent, beautiful betel, well-scented with camphor and other spices.
O Goddess, please accept this betel, which removes numbness of the tongue.
It is well-perfumed, cooling, and a cause for the destruction of thirst.
O Goddess, please accept this life-sustaining water that is the very essence of the world’s vitality.
O Goddess, please accept these garments made of cotton and silk, which are the seeds of bodily beauty and the constant increasers of splendor.
Please accept this ornament, fashioned from jewels and gold, which increases physical comfort, bestows beauty, brings prosperity,
and is supremely endowed with manifold splendor through its arrangement of various flowers. (36)
"O Goddess, please accept this pure garland, beloved in the celestial realm;
it is the purifier, the very embodiment of purity, and the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
O Goddess, please accept this delightful fragrance produced from fragrant substances."
"O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, accept this beautiful water for sipping (ācamanīya), which is the water of sacred bathing-places (tīrtha)— pure and always bestowing purity—
woven with the essence of jewels and joined with flowers and sandalwood. (39)
"Accept this excellent couch, richly adorned with jewel ornaments.
Whatever rare substance exists on earth that is difficult to obtain,
O Goddess— whatever is fit for enjoyment and enriched with divine ornaments— let that substance be accepted."
O bull among gods, having offered these substances with the root mantra,
he recited the root mantra with devotion ten lakhs of times according to the prescribed rite.
By that recitation of ten lakhs, the perfection of the mantra was indeed attained.
The mantra was given by Brahmā, and the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) is always present.
Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kāmavāṇī, and then Kamalavāsinī;
ending with Svāhā, this twelve-syllabled Vedic king of mantras is thus formed. (43–44)
Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ kamalavāsinyai svāhā.
By this mantra, Kubera attained all sovereignty;
likewise did Dakṣa, the Lord of the Kings of Kings, and Manu Sāvarṇi. (49)
By means of this mantra, Maṅgala became the lord of the seven continents;
likewise Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, Kedāra, and King Nṛpa—
these lords of kings attained perfection through this mantra, O Nārada.
When the mantra was perfected, Mahālakṣmī granted her vision to Śakra.
Seated upon a celestial chariot inlaid with a multitude of supreme jewels, bestowing boons, she covered the earth consisting of seven continents with her radiance. (47–48)
Having the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, adorned with jewel ornaments,
her face bright with a slight smile, she bestows grace upon her devotees;
wearing a garland of jewels, she possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Having beheld that peaceful mother of the world, Purandara,
his entire body marked with horripilation, his eyes filled with tears, and his hands joined in reverence,
offered praise with self-restraint using the "King of Hymns" bestowed by Brahmā.
And there, with that very Vedic mantra which bestows all desired objects, Indra said:
"Om, salutations to the one who dwells in the lotus; salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī."
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇapriyā, Sārā, and Padmā. Salutations again and again to the lotus-petal-eyed one and the lotus-faced one.
Salutations again and again to Padmāsanā, Padminī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Salutations again and again to her whose very nature is all prosperity, who bestows everything;

salutations again and again to the giver of happiness, the giver of liberation, and the giver of spiritual perfections (siddhis). Salutations again and again to the bestower of devotion to Hari and the giver of joy.
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇeśā, who resides upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa. Salutations again and again to her whose very form is the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, to her who is enriched with jewels.
Salutations again and again to Mahādevī, the presiding deity of prosperity.
Salutations again and again to the presiding deity of crops, to Sasyalakṣmī;
salutations again and again to her whose nature is intellect, to the giver of intellect.
In Vaikuṇṭha she is Mahālakṣmī, and in the ocean of milk she is Lakṣmī.
She is the glory of heaven in the abode of Indra, the royal fortune in the palace of kings,
the household prosperity in the home of housewives, and the tutelary deity of the house.
She is Surabhi, the mother of cows, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and she who desires the sacrifice.
You are Aditi, the mother of the gods; you are Kamalā, O dweller in the lotus.
You are Svāhā in the offering of oblations, and you are remembered as Svadhā in the offering to the ancestors.
For you are indeed the very form of Viṣṇu, the support of all, the Earth.
You are the very embodiment of pure being, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
you are free from anger and violence, the bestower of boons, and possessed of a beautiful countenance.
You are the supreme giver of the ultimate truth and the highest bestower of service to Hari.

Without you, the entire world is reduced to ashes and rendered worthless; without you, the universe is like one dead while living, resembling a corpse. Indeed, you are the supreme being for all, appearing in the form of every kinsman.
Without you, a kinsman can never be spoken to by his relatives;
deprived of you, one is bereft of kin, but united with you, one possesses all kinsmen.
You are the very embodiment of the causes for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Just as you are the mother of suckling infants during their infancy,
so too are you always the mother of all beings in every respect throughout the entire universe.
Even if a child has been weaned from the breast and deprived of its mother, yet lives by the power of fate—
Deprived of you, no person whatsoever can certainly live.
O Mother, you whose very nature is most gracious, be gracious to me;
O Eternal One, grant me possession of that enemy as my object of focus.
O beloved of Hari, O Sovereign of the Gods, as long as we are deprived of you, deprived of our kin, and deprived of all prosperity like mendicants, so long [grant us favor].
Grant us the kingdom, grant us fortune, and grant us strength.
Grant me fame, grant me wealth, and indeed grant me sons;
O beloved of Hari, grant me desire, grant me intellect, and grant me enjoyments.
Grant me knowledge, grant me dharma, and grant all desired good fortune. (70–71)
"Indeed, [grant him] full authority, as well as power,
majesty, victory, prowess in battle, and supreme sovereignty.
Having spoken thus, Mahendra, together with all the hosts of gods, [bestowed these upon him].
With eyes full of tears, he bowed his head again and again.
Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Śeṣa, Dharma,
and Keśava all repeatedly offered exemptions for the sake of the gods.

Having granted a boon to the gods, Lakṣmī, being well-pleased in the assembly of the deities, gave a beautiful flower garland to Keśava. And the gods, being satisfied, departed each to their own abode, O Nārada.
The Goddess went joyfully to the lap of Hari, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
And Brahmā and Īśāna both departed for their respective abodes, O Nārada,
after they had affectionately bestowed auspicious blessings upon the gods.
The man who recites this hymn of great merit at the three junctions of the day shall become a great sovereign of kings, equal to Kubera;
and if he should recite the Siddha-stotra, that man becomes like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru).
By reciting [this] five hundred thousand times, men shall achieve perfection in the hymn.
(79) If one who is self-restrained should recite this perfected hymn for one month, he will undoubtedly become a great king, endowed with supreme happiness. (80)
Nārada said: "O Lord, you previously stated that for whomsoever the flower given by Durvāsas rests upon his head, all worship is performed before him. (81)
That very flower was placed upon the head of the lordly elephant;
for it was from that [elephant] that Gaṇeśa was born, and he had gone to the forest while intoxicated.
O Sage, formerly, when the head of Gaṇapati was severed by the gaze of Śani, [that flower was used].
Hari himself placed the elephant’s head upon its shoulder.
(83) Having worshipped the six deities just mentioned, Purandara, together with the gods, then worshipped Lakṣmī in the Ocean of Milk. (84)
"Aha! The speech of the ancient narrators is difficult for men to understand.
O best among those who know the Vedas, explain its clearly manifest conclusion.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

When Durvāsas, the bull among sages, cursed Śakra, at that time his birth did not even exist; yet he appeared at the moment of worship. For a very long time, the gods wandered about in misery due to the curse of Brahmā.
Thereafter, O Sage, they attained that fortune through the boon of Hari.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Lakṣmī," in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
The narrative of Śrī Lakṣmī is complete.
Nārada said: O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, O Lord, you are indeed equal to me in form, in qualities, in fame, in splendor, and in radiance. (1)
You alone are the foremost among the wise, as well as among the perfected ones and the yogis; you are the supreme among ascetics, sages, and knowers of the Vedas.
You have understood this great and most wonderful narrative concerning Mahālakṣmī. 2.
Now tell me some other secret narrative,
one that is extremely well-guarded, useful in every respect,
not revealed in the Purāṇas, declared in the Vedas, and endowed with dharma. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Brāhmaṇa, how many kinds of narratives, difficult to obtain and hidden within the Vedas, remain undisclosed from the Purāṇas? 4.
"Among those, tell me, O illustrious one, which is the essence that you wish to hear; I shall explain that to you again later.
Nārada said:
*svāhā* is praised for the offering of oblations to the gods in all rites;
*svadhā* is commended for offerings to the ancestors; and *dakṣiṇā* is the best of all.
[6] Such is their conduct, birth, fruit, and preeminence.
"I wish to hear from your mouth; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas!
Sauti said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the bull among sages smiled and spoke.
He began to relate an ancient tale as told in the Purāṇas.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the beginning of creation, the gods formerly went out for the sake of food.
Having gone to the most enchanting assembly hall of Brahmā in the world of Brahmā, which is difficult to reach,
O Sage, they made a request concerning food.
Having heard this and having given his promise, Brahmā resorted to the feet of Śrī Hari.
For the Blessed One, in a portion of his being, became the very form of sacrifice.
Whatever oblation was given to those [gods] by the Creator during the sacrifice,
the Brahmins and the Kṣatriyas and others offered that oblation with devotion.
O bull among sages, the gods did not receive that gift at all.
All those deities, being despondent, returned once more to their assembly hall.
Having gone there, they reported the cause of their lack of food. (12–13)
Having heard this in his mind, Brahmā went for refuge to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
by His command, he worshipped Prakṛti while meditating upon her. Prakṛti, who is the embodiment of all powers, did so through her own portion. (14)
There appeared the burning power of Agni in the form of Svāhā (15),
which eclipsed the splendor of the midday sun in the summer heat.
She was an exceedingly beautiful woman, delightful and captivating to the mind (16).
With a face brightened by a slight smile, she who bestows grace upon her devotees spoke thus before the Creator: "O Lotus-born One, choose a boon.
Having heard those words, Brahmā addressed her with agitation. (17–18)
Brahmā said:
"Become the burning power of Agni and his beautiful wife;
for without you, the consumer of oblations is unable to burn even what is offered to him. (19)
Whatever oblation a person offers to the gods at the end of a mantra while uttering your name,
the gods receive it with great joy.
O Gṛheśvarī, you are the very embodiment of Agni’s prosperity and the personification of Śrī.
"O Mother, you are eternally worshipped by the gods, humans, and others.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, she became despondent;
then the Goddess herself spoke her own intention to the Self-born One.
Svāhā said:
"O Brahman, I shall worship Kṛṣṇa through austerity for a very long time;
everything else besides Him is merely an illusion, like a dream. (23)
You are the ordainer of the worlds, and Śambhu, the Lord who has conquered death;
Śeṣa sustains the universe, and Dharma is the witness of embodied beings.
You are the one to be worshipped by all at the beginning, the Lord of the hosts among the gods.
Nature (Prakṛti), the mother of all, is honored by everyone through her grace;
likewise, the seers and sages are honored by serving him.
I meditate upon his lotus feet with a state of being one with Brahman. || 25-26 ||
Having said, "The lotus-faced one is the lotus-born," and in accordance with her attainment of the lotus,
the lotus-born goddess went to the lotus-like abode of the Lord for asceticism. There, the lotus-born goddess performed penance on one foot for a hundred thousand years.
Then she beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond the material qualities and transcendent of nature. Seeing His exceedingly beautiful form, the lovely woman,
longing for the Lord of Desire, fell into a swoon out of passion.
Having understood her intention, the Omniscient One spoke to her; and lifting her, whose limbs were worn thin by long asceticism, onto his lap, Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"And in the Vārāha [incarnation], you shall become my wife through a portion of yourself,
O lovely one, as the maiden named Nāgnajitī, the daughter of Nagnajit.
Now, O beautiful lady, become the burning power of Agni and his wife."
"Purified by my grace, you shall become the very form of the limbs of the mantra.
And Vahni, having worshipped you as the mistress of his home with a spirit of devotion,
will take delight together with you, who are as delightful as Rāmā."
Having spoken thus and consoled the Goddess, O Nārada, the Lord vanished.
Then, at the command of Brahmā, Agni arrived there in great trepidation,
having meditated upon that Mother of the Universe with the meditations prescribed in the Sāmaveda.
Having worshipped him, he praised him and took her hand according to the sacred mantras.
Then, for a hundred divine years, he took delight with Rāmā in that exceedingly secluded and beautiful place which always provides the pleasure of union.
And by the power of the Fire-god himself, she became pregnant;
and that goddess bore him for twelve divine years.
Then she gave birth to sons who were beautiful and captivating.
The Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya fires, in their proper order;
and the sages, the ascetics, the Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, and others—
having uttered the mantra ending with "svāhā," they constantly offer the oblation.
O Brahmin, for one who receives a praiseworthy mantra joined with *svāhā*, all success shall come from the mere act of receiving it;
he is like a snake devoid of venom or a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas.

A woman devoid of service to her husband is like a man devoid of knowledge, or like a tree devoid of fruit and branches; indeed, such a tree is censured. Likewise, a mantra devoid of the *svāhā* exclamation does not swiftly bestow its fruit. (41–42)
All the twice-born were fully satisfied, and the gods received their oblations;
indeed, every ritual act became fruitful through the mantra ending with "svāhā. Thus has this entire, excellent narrative of Svāhā been described.
"It bestows happiness, it bestows liberation, and it is the essence; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
"O Lord of Sages, [tell me] the procedure for the worship of Svāhā, as well as her meditation and hymn of praise."
"O Lord, tell me that by which Vahni, having performed worship, offered praise to her.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"The meditation, the hymn as declared in the Sāmaveda, and the procedure for worship—"

I speak; listen, O Brahmin, and hear with careful attention. At the commencement of all sacrifices, whether at a Śālagrāma stone or in a ritual jar, one should worship Svāhā with diligence and perform the sacrifice for the attainment of its fruit.
"I worship Svāhā, who is a constituent part of the mantra, whose very nature is the perfection of the mantra,
who is perfected, who bestows success upon men, and who grants the fruits of ritual actions.
Having meditated thus and having offered the water for the feet and other honors with the root mantra, the person—
O Sage, listen to the root hymn; by praising it, one obtains all accomplishments (siddhis).
With the mantra "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ svāhā to the Goddess who is the consort of Fire," he who worships that Goddess certainly attains all desired objects. (49–50)
Vahni said:
Svāhā is the primordial portion of Prakṛti, whose form consists of the limbs of mantra and tantra;
she is the bestower of the fruits of mantras, the sustainer of the worlds, and the virtuous Satī. (51)
She is the very nature of accomplishment, the perfected one, and the bestower of success to men at all times.
She is the power of fire that burns, whose form is superior even to the vital breath. She is the essence of worldly existence and the deliverer from the terrible cycle of transmigration.
She is the life-force of the gods and the nourisher of the gods.
(53) Whoever recites these sixteen names endowed with devotion shall attain all perfections both in this world and in the next. (54)
He shall not be deficient in any limb; for him, all undertakings are auspicious.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one without a wife obtains a beloved.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Narration of Svāhā’s Birth and Other Matters," in the Svāhā-episode within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Thus ends the narrative of Svāhā.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate the excellent narrative of Svadhā.
It indeed brings satisfaction to the ancestors and increases the fruit of the śrāddha rites.
At the beginning of creation, the Creator fashioned the hosts of ancestors:
four embodied ones and three whose nature is pure radiance. (1–2)
Having beheld the seven groups of ancestors, who were beautiful and embodied in the form of spiritual perfection,
he prepared for them food preceded by the ancestral *śrāddha* and water libations (*tarpaṇa*).
[3] From the ritual bathing up to the water libations, and from the conclusion of the *śrāddha* up to the worship of the deities.

The daily rites (āhnika) for Brahmins, including the three daily junctures (trisandhyā), are heard of in the Śruti. That Brahmin who does not constantly perform the daily ancestral offerings (śrāddha), libations (tarpaṇa), the bali offering, and the chanting of the Vedas at the three junctures is like a serpent deprived of its venom.

O Nārada, he who is devoid of service to Hari and eats what has not been offered to Śrī Hari has his impurity (sūtaka) ending only with his ashes; he is unfit for ritual action. Brahmā, having created the śrāddha and other rites, departed for the sake of the ancestors.
The ancestors do not receive [the offerings] when Brāhmaṇas and others give them.
All of them, hungry and dejected, went to the assembly hall of Brahmā;
they all made their report to that very Ordainer of the worlds.
And Brahmā created a mind-born daughter who was captivating;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, possessed a radiance equal to the autumnal moon,
and was learned, virtuous, beautiful, and chaste.
Having the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, adorned with jewel ornaments,
pure, a portion of Prakṛti, smiling, bestowing boons, auspicious,
named Svadhā, possessing beautiful teeth, Lakṣmī endowed with all auspicious marks. (10–11)
She bore upon her lotus-feet the imprints of a hundred lotuses;
she was the wife of the Pitṛs, lotus-faced, born of the lotus, and lotus-eyed. To the Pitṛs, who were gratified, he gave that daughter, the very embodiment of contentment.
He indeed gave this secret instruction to the brahmins:
"Having uttered the mantra ending with *svadhā*, say, 'Give to the ancestors.
In that manner, the brahmins formerly gave the gift to the father. (13–14)
*svāhā* is prescribed for the offering to the gods, and *svadhā* is the best for the offering to the ancestors.
In all cases, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is praised; a sacrifice without a fee is ruined.
The ancestors, the deities, the Brahmins, the sages, and likewise human beings [are the recipients].
They performed worship and praised Svadhā with supreme reverence; she was peaceful and gratified.
The gods and others were satisfied, their desires fulfilled, as were the brahmins and the ancestors by the boon of the goddess Svadhā. (16–17)
Thus has this entire, supreme narrative of Svadhā been told, which brings satisfaction to all. What more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
O great sage, best among the knowers of the Vedas, I desire to hear with diligence the rules for the *svadhā* offering, the ritual worship, the meditation, and the hymn of praise; please speak.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahman, that meditation and praise are declared in the Vedas and are approved by all.
You know everything; I shall indeed speak for your knowledge and for your spiritual advancement.
[This should be done] on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Śarad, under the Maghā asterism, on the day of the Śrāddha ceremony.

Having worshipped Svadhā with diligence, one should then perform the śrāddha. That brahmin who, possessing a sense of ego, performs the śrāddha without worshipping Svadhā will not partake of the fruit; this is likewise true for the libations of the śrāddha.
I worship the mind-born daughter of Brahmā, who is eternally possessed of stable youth,
who is worthy of worship by the ancestors and the gods, and who bestows the fruit of śrāddha rites.
(23) Having thus meditated, [one should worship her] in a beautiful vessel or, alternatively, in an auspicious śālagrāma stone.
One should offer her water for the feet and other honors with the root mantra; so it is heard in the Śruti.
Having uttered the great mantra—“Oṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Svadhādevyai Svāhā”—and having worshipped and praised her, the twice-born should prostrate before her. (24–25)
"Listen, O best of sages, son of Brahmā, you who are learned, to this hymn which was composed by Brahmā in the past; it grants all desires to human beings. Brahmā said:
By the mere utterance of "svadhā," a person becomes one who has bathed in a sacred ford (tīrtha);
he is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
If one should remember "svadhā, svadhā, svadhā" in this way three times, [the same result follows].

One obtains the fruit of a *śrāddha* as well as that of the two timely libations (*kālatarpaṇa*). He who, with a concentrated mind, hears the *svadhā* hymn at the time of a *śrāddha*, shall obtain the merit of hundreds of *śrāddhas*; of this there is no doubt. (28–29)
The man who recites "Svadhā, Svadhā, Svadhā" thus at the three junctions of the day shall obtain a beloved, modest, and virtuous wife, as well as a son endowed with excellent qualities.
You are like the very life-breath of the ancestors and the embodiment of the livelihood of the twice-born.
And you are the presiding goddess of the *śrāddha*, the bestower of the fruits of the *śrāddha* and other rites.
Go outside my mind for the sake of pleasing the ancestors, for the satisfaction of the twice-born, and for the prosperity of householders. (31–32)
O lady of noble vows, you are eternal, your very nature is eternal, and you are the embodiment of the qualities (guṇas).
Your manifestation and disappearance occur during creation and dissolution.
Oṃ, svasti, namaḥ, svāhā, svadhā, and likewise dakṣiṇā—you are all these.
These six have been described in the four Vedas as the most excellent for those engaged in ritual action.
In ancient times, you were the cowherd girl Svadhā, a companion of Rādhikā in Goloka;
because Kṛṣṇa held you upon his own chest, you are remembered as Svadhā.
Destroyed by the curse of Rādhikā, you came from Goloka to this world;
formerly, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, you were seen by her while embraced by Kṛṣṇa.
By the merit of that embrace with Kṛṣṇa, you have become my mind-born daughter.

Unsatisfied in amorous play with her four husbands, that beautiful gopī Svāhā was formerly a friend of Rādhikā. Because she herself spoke to Kṛṣṇa during their union, she is celebrated as Svāhā. || 37-38 ||
In the past, she was seen by Rādhā embracing Kṛṣṇa for a very long time in the circle of the rāsa dance, intent on amorous play;
by her curse, she was cast down from Goloka and came to this world.
By the merit of embracing Kṛṣṇa, she became the beloved of Agni. She is of pure form, supreme, and worshipped by gods and men;
by the mere utterance of her name, a person is liberated from sin. (40–41)
The cowherd woman named Suśīlā, who was formerly a friend of Rādhikā,
dwelt upon the right lap of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
She, however, having been cast down from Goloka by his curse, came to this world.
By the merit of embracing Kṛṣṇa, she became Dakṣiṇā.
She was beloved by her husband, skilled in lovemaking, and praised in all activities.
Because she resided on the right side of her husband, she was celebrated as Dakṣiṇā. (43–44)
"By the will of the Lord, in ancient times, three daughters— Svadhā, Svāhā, and Dakṣiṇā— were born for the sake of fulfilling the ritual acts of those engaged in karma.
Having spoken thus in the assembly within the world of Brahmā, that Brahmā [departed].
And she stood there suddenly; immediately, Svadhā herself became manifest.
Then he gave that very lotus-faced one to the ancestors.
Having received her, those ancestors departed, filled with great joy.
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this meritorious hymn of Svadhā,
he becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and shall obtain the fruit of reciting the Vedas.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of Svadhā and Her Worship," within the Svadhā Episode of the second section, the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, in the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the narrative of Svadhā. Nārāyaṇa said: The highly praised, sweet, and supreme narrative of Svāhā and Svadhā has been told.
I shall relate the narrative of Dakṣiṇā; listen with careful attention.
Long ago, in Goloka, there was a cowherd girl named Suśīlā, the beloved consort of Hari—excellent, foremost among the companions of Rādhā, blessed, venerable, and enchanting.
She was exceedingly beautiful, a fortunate woman, virtuous, and possessed of fine teeth;
she was likewise learned, endowed with good qualities, chaste, and beautiful in form.
She was skilled in the arts, soft-limbed, lovely, and lotus-eyed. (2–3)
She possessed beautiful hips and lovely breasts; she was youthful and had the well-proportioned build of a banyan tree.
With a face brightened by a slight smile, she was adorned with jewel ornaments.
She had the luster of a white campaka flower, lips red like the bimba fruit, and eyes like those of a deer.
She was highly proficient in the treatises on love, a passionate woman with the gait of a swan; (5) she was enamored by his inner disposition, knew his heart, and was the beloved wife of Kṛṣṇa;
she understood aesthetic flavor, was a connoisseur of rasa, and yearned for the rasa of the Lord of Rāsa during the Rāsa dance. (6)

In former times, Madhusūdana sat upon the right lap in front of Rādhā; with his face bowed down in fear, he remained there. And seeing Rādhā, the most excellent and best among the gopīs, standing before him...
Proud, with a flushed face and eyes like red lotuses;
her limbs trembling with anger, she was wrathful and displayed her indignation.
With quivering lips, she was intent on speaking harshly out of rage.
Perceiving that she was approaching with great speed,
the Blessed One, fearing conflict, immediately vanished from sight.
As he was fleeing— calm, the support of all beings, and possessed of a beautiful form—
Seeing him, the cowherd girl Suśīlā trembled and hid herself out of fear.
Seeing that peril there, hundreds of thousands and millions of cowherd girls stood with palms joined in reverence, terrified, their necks bowed low in devotion.
Crying out "Protect us! Protect us! again and again, O Goddess, they went for refuge at her lotus feet out of fear.
There were three hundred million cowherds, including Sudāmā and the others.
O Nārada, they went for refuge to his lotus feet out of fear.
And the Supreme Goddess, perceiving that her beloved was indeed fleeing, cursed her virtuous companion who was also fleeing with him. (14–15)

"From this day forward, if that Gopikā comes to Goloka, she shall be reduced to ashes by the mere act of her arrival. Having spoken thus, the Goddess of gods and goddesses remained right there in her wrath.
In the midst of the *rāsa*, Rāseśvarī called out to the Lord of the *rāsa*.
Not seeing Kṛṣṇa before her, Rādhā, distressed by separation,
O observer of noble vows, perceived even a single moment as equal to ten million ages.
"O Kṛṣṇa! O Lord of my life! Come, O you who are dearer than my very life!
O God presiding over my vital breaths, my life-breaths depart without you.
The pride of a woman increases day by day through the good fortune of her husband. (19)
If she is a virtuous wife, then because of her, one’s wealth shall always increase through righteousness.
For noble women, the husband is their kinsman, their presiding deity, and their constant refuge;
he is the supreme embodiment of prosperity and the personification of happiness. (20–21)
He is the giver of Dharma, the constant giver of happiness, the giver of joy, and the giver of peace;
he is the bestower of honor, the giver of respect, the one worthy of honor, and indeed the crusher of pride.
He is the essence of essences, the Lord, and the increaser of his kinsmen.
And among all kinsmen, no relative is seen to be equal to a husband.
He is called "bhartṛ" (supporter) because of his supporting [her], and "pati" (lord) because of his protecting her.
Furthermore, he is the "svāmī" (master) because he is the lord of her body, and the "kānta" (beloved) because he fulfills her desires. (23–24)
He is a kinsman because he binds one with happiness; he is most dear because he gives affection;
he is a lord because he bestows sovereignty; he is the leader of life because he is the master of one's vital breaths;
and he is the lover because he grants delight—there is no one dearer than the beloved. (25)
A son is born from the seed of the master; therefore, he is dear to him.
To those of noble birth, a master is always dearer than even a hundred sons.
A woman born of an ignoble family is incapable of discerning her beloved.
It is equivalent to bathing in all sacred fords, initiation into all sacrifices,
circumambulating the entire earth, and indeed all forms of austerity;
it is equal to all vows and the like, as well as all the great gifts.
Whatever meritorious fasts there are, and whatever other [virtues] exist everywhere—
such as service to one's guru, service to Brahmins, service to the gods, and so forth—
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to the feet of the Lord. (29–30)
Among gurus, Brahmins, and beloved deities, the husband is the most venerable for all;
just as the giver of knowledge is dear to men of noble birth,
so too is he to the three hundred million gopīs and the cowherds.
By His grace, I am the sovereign mistress of the countless cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) situated therein,
as well as of Lakṣmī and the other cowherd women;
yet, because the nature of womanhood is difficult to overcome, I do not know that Beloved.
Having spoken thus to Kṛṣṇa, Rādhikā meditated upon him there with great devotion.
She soon attained him and indeed sported with him there.
O Sage, then that Goddess Dakṣiṇā was cast down from Goloka.
Having performed austerities for a very long time, he entered the body of Kamalā.
Then all the gods and others, having performed a most difficult sacrifice, did not obtain its fruit; dejected, they went to Brahmā.
Having heard the petition of the gods and others, the Lord of the World,
being well-considered through their devotion, meditated and received their response. And the Blessed Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakṣmī [emerged] from his body.
Having extracted the mortal fortune, he gave it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmā.
Brahmā gave her to the Sacrifice for the sake of completing the rites of the virtuous.
Having worshipped her according to the rules, the Sacrifice joyfully praised Ramā.
She possessed the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to ten million moons;
she was exceedingly lovely, beautiful, and most enchanting.
Her face was like a lotus, her limbs were tender, and her eyes were as long as lotuses.
He whose body is like a lotus beheld Kamalā, who is worthy of worship by the one seated upon a lotus;
she was clad in garments pure as fire, possessed of lips like the *bimba* fruit and beautiful teeth,
and was a virtuous woman bearing a mass of braided hair adorned with garlands of jasmine.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, adorned with jewel ornaments,
richly dressed, well-bathed, and enchanting the minds of sages;
[she was anointed] with drops of musk along with fragrant sandalwood pastes.
Extremely radiant in the area below her head with a dot of vermilion (sindūra),
endowed with most excellent hips, possessing large buttocks and breasts,
she was the very embodiment of the support for the god of love, yet tormented by his arrows. 44–45.
Upon seeing her, who was so exceedingly beautiful, Yajña fell into a swoon;
he then took her as his wife according to the path prescribed by the sacred ordinances.
Having taken her to a secluded place, he remained there for a hundred divine years.
Yajña, filled with joy, sported together with Rāmā, who delights him.
That goddess bore the divine embryo for twelve years;
thereafter she gave birth to a son, the very fruit of all ritual actions.
The giver of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the bestower of the fruits of virtuous deeds;
when the rite is complete, his son is the one who yields the fruit.
Sacrifice, together with the sacrificial fee, the son, and the fruit [is perfected].
