"Thus those learned in the Vedas know him to be the bestower of the fruits of actions.
And when, O Sage, the sacrifice, having obtained the sacrificial fee and the son as the giver of fruit,
bestowed the fruit upon all those performers of ritual acts," ||| 50-51 ||
Then the gods and others, satisfied and with their desires fulfilled,
all departed for their own abodes after hearing this from the mouth of the Speaker of Dharma (Dharmavaktra).
And having performed the ritual act, the performer should quickly bestow the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

O Sage, it is stated in the Vedas that one obtains the fruit at that very moment. Even when the ritual action is complete, if the performer does not give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins at that time—whether due to fate or through ignorance—[the result is lost]. (53–54)
When a muhūrta has passed, it will certainly become twofold;
when one night has passed, it becomes sixfold;
indeed, after three nights it is tenfold, and after seven days it is then doubled.
In one month, it is said that [the merit] of Brahmins increases a hundred-thousandfold;
when a year has passed, it becomes three-crore-fold.
All the ritual actions of the patrons would indeed become fruitless.
That man who steals the property of a Brahmin is impure and unfit for ritual acts;
by that sin he becomes a sinner, impoverished, and afflicted with disease. Lakṣmī departs from his house after having uttered a most dreadful curse. (58–59)
The ancestors do not accept that śrāddha offering or libation given by him;
likewise, the gods do not accept his worship or the oblation into the fire offered by him.
The giver does not give the gift, and the receiver does not ask for it.

Both of them go to hell, like a jar with its rope severed. (61) If the sacrificer does not bestow the sacrificial fee upon the petitioner, he becomes a thief of the Brahmin’s property and will certainly go to the Kumbhīpāka hell. (62)
He shall dwell there for a hundred thousand years, beaten by the messengers of Yama.
Thereafter, he becomes a Caṇḍāla, afflicted by disease and impoverished. He shall indeed cause seven generations of his ancestors from previous births to fall [into hell].
"Thus it has been told, O brahmin; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
"O sage, who enjoys the fruit of that ritual action which is devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)?"
"Tell me the ritual for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as performed by the sacrificers of old.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Sage, how indeed can there be a fruit for a rite that is devoid of a sacrificial fee?"
In a ritual accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), the fruit alone comes forth.
O Sage, whatever collection of materials was used in the rite, Bali consumed it all.
O Sage, that had been given to Bali by Vāmana in the past.

Food for a *śrāddha* offered by one who is not learned in the Vedas, as well as any gift that does not constitute a *śrāddha*; whatever items for worship belong to Brahmins whose wives are *vṛṣalīs*; a sacrifice not performed by an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); and the worship of an impure person. (68)
The ritual action of one who lacks devotion toward the guru is consumed by Bali; of this there is no doubt.

(69) Now, listen as I shall proclaim all that pertains to the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—the meditation, the hymn of praise, and the sequence of the worship rite—as it is declared in the Kāṇva recension. (70)

In ancient times, having obtained her as his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), Yajña—who was himself skilled in ritual action—was infatuated by her beauty; overcome by desire, he offered praise to her. Yajña said: 71. Yajña said:
"O beloved, formerly you were a gopī of Goloka, the supreme and most excellent among the gopīs; you were Rādhā’s equal, her companion, and the darling of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, during the great festival of Rādhā at the rāsa dance—"
Therefore, she is indeed Dakṣiṇā, for she manifested from the right side of Kṛṣṇa.
Formerly, you were known as Suśīlā because of your most auspicious character;
however, due to residing in a portion of Kṛṣṇa’s right side and because of Rādhā’s curse, you have become Dakṣiṇā.
"O beloved, you have descended from Goloka and appeared before me through my good fortune.
Show mercy this very day and make me your husband.
O Goddess, you alone are always the bestower of the fruits of the actions performed by all beings."
And without you, all the actions of everyone are fruitless.
Just as a tree on the surface of the earth is deprived of its fruits and branches, so too,
without you, the action of those who perform it does not shine.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and even the guardians of the quarters and others are not capable of bestowing the fruit of action without you.
Brahmā himself is the form of action, and Maheśvara is the form of the fruit.
I am Viṣṇu, the embodiment of sacrifice; you are the essence of these [elements].
(79) The giver of the fruit is the Supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature;
even the Lord Kṛṣṇa himself is not capable without you. (80)
"O beloved, you alone are my power in birth after birth;
O fair-faced one, I am capable in every action only when together with you.
Having spoken thus, the deity presiding over the sacrifice stood before him.

That goddess became pleased; Kamalākalā attended upon him. And whoever recites this hymn of praise to Dakṣiṇā at the time of a sacrifice shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter.
In the Rājasūya, Vājapeya, Gomedha, and Naramedha sacrifices;
in the Aśvamedha, the Lāṅgala, and the glorious Viṣṇuyajña;
in the Dhanada, Bhūmida, Phalgu, Putreṣṭi, and Gajamedha sacrifices. (84)
In the iron sacrifice, the gold sacrifice, the removal of eye diseases, the Śiva-sacrifice, the Rudra-sacrifice, the Indra-sacrifice, and in bondage;
in the Varuṇa-rite, the ball-game, and the crushing of enemies. (85–86)
In the Śuci-sacrifice, the Dharma-sacrifice, the Recana, the Pāpamocana,
the Bandhana, the Karma-yāga, and the auspicious Maṇi-yāga—
whosoever recites this hymn at the commencement of these [rites], [attains success]. 87.
And it is certain that such an action will be completed without obstacles and with all its constituent parts.
This hymn has been declared, as well as the method of meditation and worship;
the wise person should perform the worship and offer the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) either at a Śālagrāma stone or in a water-pot.
I worship Dakṣiṇā, born from a portion of Lakṣmī and Dakṣa, a part of Kamalā,
who is skillful in all rites, the bestower of the fruits of all actions,
whose very nature is the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu, who possesses excellent character, and who grants auspiciousness.
Having meditated thus, the wise one should worship the Giver of Boons with this very root mantra.

O Nārada, having offered water for the feet and other articles to the Goddess according to the Vedic injunctions, the discerning practitioner should recite: "Oṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Hrīṃ Dakṣiṇāyai Svāhā. (91–92)
One should worship with devotion according to the prescribed rite, offering the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which is honored by all.
Thus has been told this entire, supreme narrative concerning the *dakṣiṇā*,
which bestows happiness, grants delight, and yields the fruit of all ritual actions.
And whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this narrative of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā),
no action shall result in physical deformity upon the land of Bhārata.
A sonless man shall certainly obtain a son endowed with virtuous qualities.
One devoid of a wife shall obtain a most excellent wife— one of virtuous character, beautiful, of noble form, possessed of sons, humble, sweet-spoken,
devoted to her husband, firm in her vows, pure, of noble birth, and most distinguished. (96)
One devoid of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one devoid of wealth shall obtain wealth.
One devoid of land shall obtain land; one devoid of progeny shall obtain progeny.
Likewise, in times of distress, separation from kinsmen, calamity, or imprisonment— (97–98)
Having heard this for one month, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.

(99) Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Origin of Dakṣiṇā and the Ritual for Her Worship," in the Dakṣiṇopākhyāna of the second section, the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, within the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
And many goddesses have heard this supreme narrative.
O Brahmin, best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the life-story of the others as well.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Brahmin, the conduct of all these goddesses exists separately within the Vedas.
Among the goddesses previously mentioned, which ones do you wish to hear about?
Nārada said:
The sixth is Maṅgalacaṇḍī, who is a portion of Prakṛti manifested through the mind.
I wish to hear the account of their origins and deeds according to the truth.
Nārāyaṇa said:
She who is the sixth part of Prakṛti is proclaimed as the sixth [digit];
she is the presiding deity of the child, the Māyā of Viṣṇu, and the bestower of children. Among the Mothers, she is renowned by the name Devasenā.
She is more dear than life, virtuous, the wife of Skanda, and firm in her vows;
she bestows long life upon children, is a worthy recipient, and provides protection.
Always remaining by the side of the infant, she is indeed a Yoginī who has attained perfection through yoga.
O Brahmin, hear the procedure for the history [of this] within the ritual for her worship—
[a procedure] heard from the mouth of Dharma, which is supremely bestowing happiness and sons.
King Priyavrata was the son of Svāyambhuva Manu.
The lord of yogis, always devoted to ascetic practices, would not have taken a wife;
yet, by the command of Brahmā, he diligently took a wife.
O sage, although he had been married for a very long time, he did not obtain a son.
Kaśyapa also caused that Putreṣṭi sacrifice to be performed; the sage gave the sacrificial oblation (caru) to his beloved wife Mālinī. Having consumed the oblation, she immediately became pregnant.
And that goddess bore him for twelve years by divine power. Then, O Brahmin, she gave birth to a boy with the luster of gold,
endowed with all limbs, dead, yet with wide-open eyes.
Seeing him, all the women—the wives of his kinsmen—indeed wept.
His mother, firm in her vows, fell into a swoon out of grief for her son.
O Sage, the king took the boy and went to the cremation ground.
There in the forest, placing his son upon his chest, he wept.
Not abandoning the infant, the king prepared to give up his life;
through this most agonizing grief for his son, he forgot the yoga of knowledge.
In that interval, he beheld there a celestial chariot,
resembling pure crystal, resplendent with the finest jewels,
eternally blazing with brilliance, and adorned with silken garments.
It was resplendent with flower garlands, richly adorned with various wonderful colors;
there he beheld the goddess, lovely and heart-stealing, possessing the hue of a white campaka flower and endowed with beautiful, firm youth. (17–18)
Seeing her before him— her face bright with a gentle smile, adorned with jewel ornaments,
full of compassion, perfected in yoga, and bestowing grace upon her devotees—
the king praised her with the utmost reverence. (19)
Having left the boy on the ground, he performed her worship.
O Nārada, seeing her—who possessed a radiance like the summer sun, blazing with splendor, yet peaceful and beautiful as the consort of Skanda—the king questioned her. (20–21)

Priyavrata said: "Who are you, O most beautiful one? O lovely lady, whose beloved wife are you, O woman of excellent vows? Whose daughter are you, O lady of noble hips—you who are blessed and honored among women? (22)
Having heard the words of the lord of men, that Devasenā, who bestows auspiciousness upon the world and provides protection for the gods, spoke:
"In former times, she was the army of the gods when they were terrified by the Daityas. (23)
And he granted victory to them, and because of that, she became known as Devasenā.
Devasenā said: "I am the mind-born daughter of Brahmā, the sovereign Devasenā."

Having created me from his mind, O protector of the earth, the Creator gave me to Skanda. Among the Mātṛkās, I am renowned as Skandasenā and Suvratā; I am celebrated as Viśva-Ṣaṣṭhī because I am the sixth part of Prakṛti.
I am the giver of sons to the sonless, and the giver of what is dear to those who love; I am the giver of wealth to the poor, and to those who act, I am the bestower of auspicious deeds.
I am happiness, suffering, fear, grief, joy, and indeed, auspiciousness itself.
Prosperity and adversity—all comes about through karma.
Through karma one has many sons, and through karma one's lineage is destroyed.
Through karma one is handsome, and by one’s own karma one is constantly afflicted by disease. (28–29)
By action one has a dead son, and by action one is long-lived;
by action one possesses virtues, and by action one is deficient in limbs.
Therefore, O King, action is supreme above all things, as is heard in the Śruti.
"Lord Hari, who is the very form of karma, bestows the fruit through that [karma].
Having spoken thus, O Sage, that goddess took the child and suddenly restored him to life by means of her great knowledge, as if in play. (31–32)
The king beheld that boy, smiling and radiant as gold;
and Devasenā saw him looking at the king and at the sky itself. Taking the child, the queen prepared to ascend into the heavens.
Then the king, with his throat, lips, and palate parched, praised her once more. (34) By that hymn of praise from the king, the goddess became truly satisfied.
O Brahmin, she spoke to the king regarding the action ordained by the Vedas. (35)
Devasenā said:
"You are the king in the three worlds, the son of Svāyambhuva Manu;
having caused my worship to be performed everywhere, perform it yourself. (36)
Then I shall give you a son, a charming lotus of the family, renowned by the name Suvrata, virtuous and highly learned;
one who remembers his past births, a lord among yogis, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa. (37)
He who performed a hundred sacrifices, the most excellent, and honored by the Kṣatriyas;
he who possessed the auspicious strength of a hundred thousand rutting elephants;
the archer, the virtuous, the pure, and truly beloved by the wise. (38–39)
"A yogin, a man of knowledge, one perfected in form, an ascetic,
renowned throughout the worlds, and a giver of all prosperity"—
having spoken thus, that goddess gave the child to him.
And King Suvrata accepted him for the sake of his worship;
the Goddess, having granted him an auspicious boon, went to heaven.
The great king, with a joyful heart, returned to his own home.
Having arrived, he related the news concerning his son.
O Nārada, the men and women became joyful and well-pleased;
they performed auspicious rites everywhere for the sake of the son.

He worshipped the Goddess and gave wealth to the Brahmins. And every month, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, the king diligently caused a great festival for the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī to be celebrated everywhere.
On the sixth day after birth,
she performed the worship of children with great care; likewise, on the twenty-first day, she performed the auspicious rites for children and the ceremony of first feeding them solid food.
He himself increased [the practice] everywhere and performed it;
O observer of noble vows, hear from me the meditation, the ritual of worship, and the hymn of praise,
which was heard from the mouth of Dharma and spoken by Kauthuma.
O Sage, a wise person may fashion an image on a *śālagrāma* stone, in a water-pot, at the root of a banyan tree, or even upon a wall, and worship it—
an image that is a pure sixth part of *Prakṛti*, well-established, and firm in its vows. (48)

I worship Devasenā, the supreme goddess, who bestows noble sons, grants auspiciousness, is the very embodiment of compassion, and is the mother of the world; she possesses the hue of a white campaka flower, is adorned with jewel ornaments, and is of most sacred form. (49–50)
Having meditated thus and placed a flower upon his own head, the wise one,
firm in his vows, should again meditate and worship the virtuous goddess with the root mantra,
using water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for rinsing the mouth, as well as perfumes, incense, and lamps.

With various kinds of food offerings and auspicious fruits, a person should recite the eight-syllable great mantra according to their capacity, preceded by the ritual procedure: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, Svāhā. (92–93)
Having praised Him there, one who is endowed with devotion and composed in mind should bow down.
O Sage, he who recites eight hundred thousand times the eight-syllabled great mantra—the hymn declared in the Sāmaveda which bestows the fruits of wealth and sons—[attains his desires]. 54.
"The Lotus-born One has indeed said that he shall obtain a son.
Listen, O best of sages, to this hymn which brings auspiciousness to all, which grants the desires of all, and which is hidden even in the Vedas, O Nārada. (56–59)
Priyavrata said:
Salutations to the Goddess, the Great Goddess; salutations again and again to Siddhi and Śānti.
Salutations again and again to the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the giver of happiness and the giver of liberation. 57.
Salutations again and again to the giver of boons, the giver of sons, and the giver of wealth;

salutations again and again to the giver of happiness, the giver of liberation, and to Goddess Shashthi. (58) Salutations again and again to her who is the form of the sixth part of Shakti, and to the Perfected One.

Salutations again and again to Māyā, Siddhayoginī, and the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. Salutations again and again to Pārā and Pāradā, and to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī; salutations to Sārā and Sāradā, the Pārā of all actions.
Salutations again and again to the goddess who presides over children, to Goddess Shashthi;
to the auspicious one who bestows well-being, and to the giver of the fruits of actions.
Salutations again and again to Goddess Shashthi, who is manifest before her devotees.
Salutations again and again to Goddess Shashthi, who is worthy of worship by all in all their undertakings, the beloved of Skanda, and the protector of the gods;
salutations to her whose nature is pure being and who is ever worshipped by men.
Salutations again and again to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, who is free from violence and anger.
O Sovereign of the Gods, grant me wealth, grant me a beloved wife, and grant me a son.
Grant me righteousness, grant me fame; salutations again and again to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
"Grant me land, grant me progeny, grant me knowledge, O highly honored one!
Grant me auspiciousness and victory; salutations again and again to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī!
Having thus praised the goddess, Priyavrata obtained a son.
And by the grace of Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, O Indra among kings, he shall become illustrious.
O Brahmin, whoever hears this hymn to Ṣaṣṭhī for a year, even if childless, obtains a son who is excellent and long-lived. (67)
And she who listens to this with devotion for one year,
being liberated from all sins, even if she has long been barren,
shall give birth to a son who is heroic, virtuous, learned, and illustrious.
By the grace of Ṣaṣṭhī Mātṛ, she shall indeed become long-lived. And that woman who is barren like a crow or whose children have died,
having heard [this] for a year, shall obtain a son by the grace of Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
When a child is afflicted by disease, if the father or mother hears [this prayer],
the child is liberated from that month-long affliction through the grace of Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, Her Worship, Hymns, and so forth," in the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa within the Second Part of the First Section of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O son of Brahmā, the narrative of the sixth [chapter] has been told according to the scriptures;
now listen to that account of the goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍī. 1.
All her worship and so forth, as heard from the mouth of Dharma,
is indeed desired by all the learned as being in accordance with the Vedas.
Caṇḍī dwells within Caṇḍā, remaining awake amidst the circle of enemies.
She who is skilled in auspicious rites is Maṅgalā, and she is indeed Caṇḍikā.
(3) The word *caṇḍī* is found in the name Durgā, while *maṅgala* refers to the daughter of Mahī.
She who is the beloved goddess Maṅgalā shall be known as Maṅgalacaṇḍikā. (4)
Maṅgala was of the lineage of Manu and the lord of the earth with its seven continents.
His worshipful and beloved goddess was Maṅgalacaṇḍikā;
she is Durgā, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti, appearing through a different form.

The supreme Goddess, whose form is compassion and who is directly perceptible, was worshipped in the past by Śaṅkara as his chosen deity; she was also worshipped by Viṣṇu, who was impelled by him, during the terrible slaughter of Tripura. (6–7)
On a difficult mountain plateau and in a state of distress,
when the vehicle had fallen from the sky, having been cast down by the Daitya in his rage,
Śaṅkara, instructed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, praised Durgā.
And she became this Maṅgalacaṇḍī through a transformation of form.
She spoke before Śambhu, saying, "O Lord, there is no fear for you.
And the Blessed One, the Lord of All, assumed the form of a bull.

"By his command, O Bull-bannered One, I shall become the very embodiment of the power of war; with myself as the soul and Hari as my helper, O Lord of Gods, slay the Daitya who strikes down the feet of the deities. (11)
Having spoken thus, that goddess, the power (*śakti*) of Śambhu, vanished.
With the weapon given by Viṣṇu, the Lord of Umā struck him down.
O chief of sages, when the Daitya had fallen, all the gods and great seers [rejoiced]. (12–13)
The gods, their necks bowed in devotion, praised Śaṅkara;
immediately, a rain of flowers fell upon the head of Śambhu.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, being well-pleased, bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
Instructed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, having bathed well and being pure,
worshipped that Goddess, the auspicious Maṅgalacaṇḍikā,
with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and various kinds of oblations.
O Sage, with flowers, sandalwood, and various kinds of food offerings made with devotion,
as well as with goats, rams, buffaloes, and excellent, illusory *gaṇḍa* animals,
along with garments, ornaments, garlands, milk-rice, and flour-cakes. (17)
With honey and nectars, with various kinds of ripe fruits,
with songs, dances, instrumental music, festivals, and hymns of praise to Kṛṣṇa—
having meditated according to the prescribed rule by means of the meditation described for midday. (18–19)
O Nārada, he gave the ritual substances with the root mantra alone:
*oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sarvapūjye devi maṅgalacaṇḍike aiṃ krūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the twenty-one-syllable mantra. (20)

He is worthy of worship, even as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), granting all desires to his devotees. By ten hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) of the mantra alone, men shall attain mastery over the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*). He who attains mastery over the mantra becomes Viṣṇu himself, the granter of all desires.
O Brahman, listen now to the meditation (dhyāna) as declared in the Vedas and approved by all:
[one should meditate upon] the Goddess, sixteen years of age, beautiful, in the full bloom of youth, enriched with every form and quality, with delicate limbs, and captivating to the mind. (22–23)
Having the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, with a radiance equal to ten million moons;
wearing garments of fire-purified silk, adorned with jewel ornaments;
bearing a mass of braided hair decorated with garlands of jasmine flowers.
She has full lips, beautiful teeth, and is pure, with a face resembling an autumn lotus;
her countenance is brightened by a gentle smile, and her eyes are like lovely blue lotuses.
She is the sustainer of the world and the bestower of all prosperity upon all beings.
I worship her, the excellent one who is like a boat in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
(27) O Sage, listen now to this meditation on the Goddess and to this hymn of praise with which Śaṅkara, seized by distress, offered worship while remaining self-restrained. (28)
Śaṅkara said:
Protect, protect, O Mother of the World, O Goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā!
O Destroyer of the multitude of calamities, O Bestower of joy and auspiciousness! 29.
O Caṇḍikā, skilled in joy and auspiciousness; O Śubhā, skilled in auspiciousness and O Maṅgalacaṇḍikā!
O Maṅgalā, worthy of auspiciousness and O Maṅgala of all auspicious things! 30.
O Goddess who bestows auspiciousness upon the virtuous, O abode of auspiciousness for all!
You are to be worshipped on Tuesday, as the deity who grants the desired blessings of auspiciousness;
you are eternally to be worshipped by King Maṅgala, the descendant of the lineage of Manu. (31–32)
O Goddess presiding over auspiciousness, the most auspicious among all auspicious things;
O support of auspiciousness in saṃsāra, O bestower of the auspiciousness of liberation;
O essence and support of auspiciousness, you are at the further shore of all karmas.
"O bestower of auspiciousness, you are to be worshipped every Tuesday.
Having praised Maṅgalacaṇḍikā with this hymn and having performed worship every Tuesday, Śambhu, the auspicious Śiva, departed.

Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this auspicious hymn of the Goddess, for him there shall be eternal auspiciousness; may no inauspiciousness ever befall him. In the beginning, the Goddess Sarvamaṅgalā was worshipped by Śambhu.
On the second [day], the Goddess was worshipped by Maṅgala and by the planet [Mars].
On the third, Bhadrā was worshipped by Maṅgala and by the king.
On the fourth, on a Tuesday, she was worshipped by beautiful women.
In the fifth [kalpa], Maṅgalacaṇḍikā was worshipped by men desiring auspiciousness;
she was always worshipped by the lords of the universe in every world. Thereafter, having been fully honored everywhere, she became the Sovereign of the Gods (Sureśvarī). (38–39)
O Sage, whoever with a concentrated mind listens to this auspicious hymn of the Goddess, recited by the gods and others, by sages, by Manus, and by human beings—
for him there shall be eternal auspiciousness; may there never be anything inauspicious for him.
Their sons and grandsons flourish, and auspiciousness increases day by day.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn and Other Matters in the Legend of Maṅgala," within the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O son of Brahmā, the narrative of these two has been told according to tradition.
Now hear the account of Manasā, as it was heard from the mouth of Dharma;
she is the divine daughter of Kaśyapa, born of his mind.
Therefore, she is Manasādevī because she sports with the mind;
or because she meditates with the mind upon the Supreme Self, the Lord, she is Manasādevī, for she sports by means of this yoga. (2–3)
That goddess, a Vaiṣṇavī and a perfected yoginī, delights in the Self;
having performed penance for three ages for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, the Lord beheld her for a moment upon seeing the body of Jaratkāru. (4)
The Lord named him Jaratkāru, the "Protector of the Gopīs.
Out of compassion, that ocean of mercy granted her her desire and caused worship to be performed for him, and furthermore, he performed it himself.
In heaven, in the world of the Nagas, on earth, and up to the world of Brahma,
while many were chanting, that Gauri was beautiful and captivating;
therefore, that virtuous lady became renowned as Jagadgauri and was worshipped.
That goddess is a disciple of Śiva; therefore she is celebrated as Śaivī.
O Nārada, she is exceedingly beautiful and a devotee of Viṣṇu; therefore she is Vaiṣṇavī.
She was the protector of the lives of the serpents during Janamejaya’s sacrifice. (8–9)
She is renowned as Nāgeśvarī and likewise as the sister of the Nāgas. Because she is capable of neutralizing poison, she is Viṣahāriṇī.
She obtained the perfected Yoga from Hara; therefore, she is Siddhayoginī.
It is the great secret knowledge, the supreme *mṛtasañjīvinī* (the reviver of the dead);
the wise declare it to be endowed with that great wisdom.
She was indeed the mother of the ascetic Āstīka, the lord of sages.
She was the renowned mother of Āstīka, known by the name Jaratkāru.
She was the beloved wife of the great-souled sage Jaratkāru, that lord of sages;
she was thus the beloved of the yogi Jaratkāru, who is honored by the entire world. (13–14)
Oṃ, salutations to Manasā.
Jaratkāru’s daughter, the world’s Gaurī, Manasā, the perfected Yoginī;
she is Vaiṣṇavī, the sister of the Nāgas, Śaivī, and likewise the sovereign of the Nāgas. 15.
Jaratkārupriyā, Āstīkamātā, Viṣaharī,
and Mahājñānayutā— this goddess is worshipped by the entire universe.
Whoever recites these twelve names at the time of worship [shall obtain great merit].
There is no fear of nāgas for him, nor for those born of his lineage.
[This applies] when there is a bed threatened by nāgas, or a dwelling seized by nāgas;
when one is wounded by nāgas, in a fortress of nāgas, or when one's body is encircled by nāgas. (17–18)
By reciting this hymn, one is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
Upon seeing one who recites it daily, the host of nāgas flees.
By reciting the mantra ten hundred thousand times, the perfection of the hymn is attained by men.
He for whom this hymn is perfected becomes capable of consuming poison;
having made a multitude of serpents his ornament, he shall have the serpent as his vehicle.
That man becomes a great adept, with serpents as his seat and serpents as his bed. (20–21)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn of Mānasā and Other Matters," in the *Mānasopākhyāna* within the second section (*Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O best of sages, hear now the procedure for worship and the hymn of praise.
And the meditation, as prescribed in the Sāmaveda for the ritual of worshiping the Goddess, is as follows:
[She is] possessing the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, adorned with jewel ornaments, wearing garments pure as fire, and having a serpent as her sacred thread. 1–2.

I worship her who is endowed with great wisdom, the most excellent among the wise and the virtuous, the presiding goddess of the Siddhas, herself perfected and the bestower of perfection. (3) Having thus meditated upon that goddess, one should worship her with the root mantra alone.
With various food offerings, lamps, flowers, incense, and ointments;
(4) the root mantra declared in the Vedas bestows the desires of devotees.
The twelve-syllabled mantra, known as the Root Wish-Fulfilling Tree (*mūlakalpataru*), is perfectly accomplished. (5)
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ aiṃ manasādevyai svāhā"—thus it is proclaimed.
By reciting this mantra five hundred thousand times, men shall attain mastery over the mantra.
He who attains mastery over the mantra becomes a perfected one (siddha) upon the surface of the earth.
Poison is like nectar for him, and he becomes equal to Dhanvantari.
O Brahmin, he who diligently invokes the Goddess at the Āṣāḍha saṃkrānti under the *guḍāśākhā* trees and worships her with devotion until the end of the month— [attains these results]. (7–8)
He who offers a bali-oblation to the goddess named Mānasī on the fifth lunar day will certainly become wealthy, possessed of sons, and renowned for his fame.
The procedure for worship has been declared; now listen to her narrative.
I shall relate, O illustrious one, that which was heard from the mouth of Dharma:
"In ancient times, the human beings on earth were overcome by fear of the *nāgas*.
Whomever the *nāgas* devour, O Nārada, they do not survive. (10–11)
Terrified and requested by Brahmā, Kaśyapa then created the mantras according to the seeds of the Vedas and the instruction of the Creator; thereafter,
he created that mental goddess who presides over the mantras.
Through that mental austerity, she indeed became Mānasā.
Having been born as a maiden, she went to the abode of Śaṅkara;
having worshipped him with devotion on Kailāsa, she praised the Moon-crested Lord.

And for a thousand divine years, the daughter of the sage attended upon him; and Maheśa, who is easily pleased, became truly gratified with her. He bestowed great knowledge upon her and taught her the Sāman.
O Sage, he gave the eight-syllabled mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree:
the seed-syllables of Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Kāma, followed by the vocative ending in -ṅe, and then the word "Kṛṣṇa.
Thus: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya*.
The armor named *Trailokyamaṅgala*, the sequence of worship,
the hymn of praise which is worthy of all adoration, the meditation that purifies the worlds,
and also the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) as declared in the Vedas and approved by all. (17–18)
Having obtained from Mṛtyuñjaya the supreme knowledge that conquers death,
the virtuous Satī went to Puṣkara for ascetic penance at the command of Śaṅkara.
Having performed penance for three yugas for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul—
That goddess became perfected; she beheld the Lord before her.
Seeing her, who was young and emaciated, the ocean of compassion, Hari, out of pity, caused worship to be performed and performed it himself.
And the Lord granted her a boon: "May you be worshipped in every birth.
Having bestowed the boon upon the auspicious lady, the All-pervading One immediately vanished;
she was thus worshipped for the first time by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.

In the second [kalpa], she was worshipped by Śaṅkara himself, by Kaśyapa, by the god [Sureśvara], by Manu, by the sage [Muni], and by Ahi, the son of Manu; thus she became renowned throughout the three worlds. (23–24)
In ancient times, Kaśyapa gave her to Jaratkāru, the lord of sages.
Without being asked, that best of sages accepted her by the command of Brahmā.
Having performed the marriage, the great yogi rested for a long time through his ascetic power.
He slept at the foot of a banyan tree on Puṣkara, upon the lap of the Goddess.
That sage fell asleep, remembering the Lord, the Master of Sleep. The sun set, and evening arrived. (26–27)
Having reflected there with her mind, that virtuous woman,
out of fear of violating dharma, performed a mental recitation;
she did not perform the evening twilight rite, which is a constant duty for the twice-born.
"My husband will incur sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—[he] who does not attend to the morning [prayer] and does not worship at the evening [prayer];
he shall always be impure and constantly incur sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. (29–30)
Thinking, "This was spoken by the Vedas," he attempted to awaken that sage.
But having understood her intent, that best of sages became exceedingly enraged.
Jaratkāru said:
"O virtuous woman of excellent vows, how have you caused my sleep to be interrupted?
For her who harms her husband, vows and the like are in vain;
likewise, whatever penance, fasting, religious observances, or charity she may perform [is fruitless]. (32)

For a woman who does what is displeasing to her husband, everything becomes fruitless. (33) By her through whom the husband is honored, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is honored; for Hari himself, in the form of the husband, is the very essence of the vow of devotion to one's husband. (34)
All forms of giving, all sacrifices, the visiting of all sacred fords,
all austerity, every vow, and whatever fasting and so forth there may be;
all dharma, truth, and the worship of all the gods.
All of those do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to one's husband.
(36) She who performs service to her husband in the most meritorious land of Bhārata-varṣa goes to Vaikuṇṭha along with her lord, to the abode of Brahman. (37)
She who does what is disagreeable to her husband and speaks unpleasantly even when it is pleasant—O virtuous lady, hear now the fruit of that woman born of an ignoble family:
she shall go to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (38)
"Then she will become a Cāṇḍālī woman, deprived of husband and sons.
(39) Having spoken thus, the best of sages' lips began to quiver.
The virtuous woman trembled in her mind with fear and spoke to her husband: (40)
Manasovāca said:
"O illustrious one, O observer of noble vows, you have broken your sleep only out of fear of violating the twilight rites. Grant peace to me, who am wicked. (41)
"And he who causes the interruption of passion, food, or sleep—
especially for one's master— he shall go to the Kālasūtra hell.
Having spoken thus in her mind, the goddess [placed herself] at the lotus-feet of her master.
Overcome with devotion and fear, she fell down and wept again and again.
Seeing the sage enraged and prepared to curse Śrīsūrya,
O Nārada, the Blessed One arrived there together with Sandhyā.
Having arrived there, Bhāskara himself, humble and disciplined, spoke appropriately to the best of sages along with her. Śrī Sūrya said:

"O Brahmin, seeing that it was the time of sunset and fearing a lapse in my religious duty, I awakened you; at that time, the sun had not yet set. O venerable Brahmin, O sage, forgive me; it is not fitting for you to curse me."
The hearts of Brahmins are always like fresh butter;
their anger lasts for only half a moment, after which the world becomes ashes.
Furthermore, the twice-born are capable of creating [the world] again; there is no one more powerful than a Brahmin.
Born of the lineage of Brahmā and blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
he should constantly meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the eternal light of Brahman.
(49) Having heard the words of the Sun, the twice-born one indeed became satisfied.
Having received the blessings of the Brahmins, Sūrya returned to his own abode.
And the Brahmin, for the sake of fulfilling his vow, mentally abandoned her as she wept,
filled with grief, and tormented by a burning heart.
Emaciated by fear in her calamity, she remembered her gurus— Śambhu, Hari, and Vidhi— as well as Kaśyapa, her progenitor.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the Gopīs, and Śambhu himself arrived there.
And Vidhi and Kaśyapa, reflecting within their minds,
beheld the beloved deity who is beyond the qualities (guṇas) of primordial nature (prakṛti);
they praised him with supreme devotion and bowed down again and again.
He paid homage to Śambhu, as well as to Brahmā and Kaśyapa.
He then asked this question: "How have you come here?
Having heard those words, Brahmā immediately spoke what was appropriate for the occasion.
Having offered salutations to the lotus feet of Hṛṣīkeśa, he said to him:
"If your virtuous and righteous lawful wife has been abandoned even in thought, then indeed bring about the birth of a son through her for the sake of establishing dharma. (56–57)
Whether he be an ascetic, a student of sacred knowledge, a mendicant, or even a forest-dweller,
one should become a sage only after producing offspring through his wife.
However, he who is devoid of passion and abandons his beloved wife without having produced offspring [is at fault].
That austerity and its merit would leak away, just as water does from a winnowing basket.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Jaratkāru, the lord of sages,
brought about that contact with her navel through yoga, preceded by mantras.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon her, the gods departed filled with joy;
and Jaratkaru, likewise filled with joy in his mind, was also filled with joy.
By the mere touch of the sage’s hand, a fetus was immediately conceived.
The best of sages spoke thus to her who had conceived by his mind alone:
Jaratkāru said,
"By this embryo, O lady, a son shall be born to you through my mind."
The most eminent among those who have conquered their senses, the most righteous, and the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas;
radiant, ascetic, illustrious, and endowed with all virtues;
he was the best among the knowers of the Vedas, as well as among yogis and men of wisdom.
And that son, devoted to Viṣṇu and righteous, shall uplift his lineage;
indeed, all the ancestors dance with joy at the mere birth [of such a son].
She who is devoted to her husband, virtuous, beloved by her husband, and sweet-spoken—[she too brings this same merit]. 65.
A mother who is most righteous, of noble birth, and a guardian of the family;
a kinsman who bestows devotion to Hari, and whatever is desired that grants happiness;
and one who severs bondage and shows the path of Hari—he is a father. (66–67)
She who bears the embryo and she who releases one from dwelling in the womb;
he who imparts the mantra of Viṣṇu is the Guru who bestows devotion to Viṣṇu.
The Guru is the giver of knowledge, and that knowledge is the contemplation of Kṛṣṇa.
Since the entire universe, moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has appeared and disappeared [from Him], what other knowledge could there be?
Whatever knowledge is born of the Vedas or born of yoga, its essence is the service of Hari. (69–70)
And that which is the essence of all principles, yet other than Hari, is a mere mockery.
Knowledge has been imparted by me to you; for he who bestows knowledge is indeed one's master.
Through knowledge one is liberated from bondage; therefore, he who inflicts bondage is truly an enemy.
He who bestows knowledge conjoined with devotion to Viṣṇu is indeed a guru.
He is an enemy and a slayer of disciples, for he does not liberate them from bondage—from the suffering born of a mother’s womb as well as from the beating by Yama. (72–73)

How can he who does not liberate one be a guru? For he is indeed a father and a kinsman. How can he who does not show the path of Kṛṣṇa—which is of the nature of supreme bliss and imperishable—be such a kinsman to men? 74.
"O virtuous lady, worship the Supreme Brahman, Acyuta Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa).
By service to Him, your past karma will certainly be eradicated from its very root.
O beloved, you were abandoned by me through a ruse; please forgive this fault of mine."
In those virtuous women endowed with forbearance, anger does not exist due to their inner strength.
(76) O Goddess, I am going to Puṣkara to perform austerities; go as you please.
I am fearful of any interruption to my meditation upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (77)
For those who tread the path of worldly activity, their affection for women, wealth, and the like is directed toward these things;
whereas the desires of those who are free from longing rest upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
(78) Having heard the words of Jaratkāru, she became distressed with grief in her mind.
With tearful eyes, she spoke with humility to her beloved,
as Manasovāca said:
"O Lord, I have been abandoned by you because of my fault in disturbing your sleep."
"O kinsman, wherever I remember you, there you shall come to me.

The separation from a kinsman is the greatest affliction; the separation from a son is even greater than that. But the separation from one's lord of life is the most supreme of all, surpassing even the severance of one's own vital breaths. (80–81)
He is the husband of those devoted to their husbands, dearer than a hundred sons;
he is dearer than everything else to women, and for that reason he is called "the Beloved" (Priya) by the wise.
He is as dear to those with only one son as he is to Vaiṣṇavas in Hari.

As eyes are to the one-eyed, as water is to the thirsty, as food is to the hungry, and as a woman is to the lustful; as another’s property is to thieves, and as a paramour is to unchaste women. (83–84)
"O Lord, just as the minds of the learned are ever fixed on the scriptures, and as those of merchants are on trade,
so too are the minds of virtuous women ever fixed on their beloved.
Having spoken thus, the goddess fell at her husband's feet with her mind.
The sage, a treasure-house of compassion, took her onto his lap for a moment out of pity;
with tears from his eyes and his mind, he bathed her.
Fearing separation, she in turn served the sage’s lap with her own tears.
Then, by means of that knowledge, both of them became free from sorrow.
Constantly remembering the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
the brāhmaṇa departed for ascetic practice after having properly awakened his beloved.
In his mind, he went to Kailāsa, the abode of his guru Śambhu.
Pārvatī mentally consoled Manasā, who was emaciated by grief,
with extremely auspicious and comforting words in the temple of Śiva.
On an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, the virtuous woman gave birth to a son who was a portion of Nārāyaṇa and a teacher of the wise and the yogis;
while still in the womb, he had heard great knowledge from the mouth of Śaṅkara.
He became a great yogi, the teacher of yogis and the wise. Śiva caused the birth ceremony to be performed for the child and recited auspicious blessings; he also taught the Vedas to Śiva.
Śiva gave three hundred thousand jewels to the Brahmins;
Pārvatī gave a hundred thousand cows and various kinds of gems;
and Śambhu [bestowed] the four Vedas as well as the other Vedāṅgas.
She taught her son the supreme knowledge that conquers death (Mṛtyuñjaya).
She possessed devotion toward her own husband, as well as toward her chosen deity Hari and her guru; because of this, her son became Astīka indeed.

By the command of Śaṅkara, he went to Puṣkara to perform penance for Viṣṇu. Having obtained the great mantra of the Supreme Soul and having performed penance for three hundred thousand divine years, that one whose wealth is austerity completed his ascetic practice.
The great yogi arrived to pay homage to the Lord Śiva.
Having bowed to Śaṅkara and placed the boy before him,
she then went in her mind to the hermitage of her father, Kaśyapa.
Seeing his daughter together with her son, the Lord of Creatures attained great joy.
O Sage, he gave a hundred lakhs of jewels to the brahmins and fed countless brahmins for the welfare of the child. (100)
Aditi, Diti, and the others likewise attained supreme joy.
Accompanied by her sons, she then remained for a very long time in her father’s abode.
I shall now relate her story further; listen to it.
Then, O Brahmā, due to the fault of fate and his own past actions, the curse of a Brahmin suddenly fell upon Parīkṣit, the son of Abhimanyu. "When seven days have passed, Takṣaka shall bite you."
Having touched the water of the Kauśikī, Śṛṅgin uttered this curse.
Upon hearing news of that, the king went to Gaṅgādvāra;
he stayed there for seven days and listened to the compendium of Dharma.

When a week had passed, Dhanvantari saw Takṣaka on the road as he was traveling to see the king; he perceived that he could save him. A conversation took place between the two, and there was great mutual affection.
Takṣaka gave the excellent jewel of Dhanvantari of his own accord.
Taking it, he departed with a mind full of contentment and joy. Takṣaka soon beheld the king seated upon his couch.

The king went to Vaikuṇṭha, remembering Hari, his guru, again and again. O sage Janamejaya, he caused the funeral rites for his father to be performed and conducted a sacrifice known as the Sarpasatra.
The multitude of serpents gave up their lives through the power of Brahmanic luster.
Takṣaka, terrified, sought refuge with Mahendra.
Then the assembly of Brahmins prepared to slay both Indra and Takṣaka.
Then the gods and the sages approached Manu in their minds.
And Mahendra, trembling with fear, praised her in his presence.
Then Āstīka arrived there at his mother's command and [proceeded to] the sacrifice.
He requested from the king the boon that the lives of Mahendra and Takṣaka be spared. Out of compassion and at the command of the Brāhmaṇas, the best of kings granted the boon;
having completed the sacrifice, he joyfully gave sacrificial fees to the Brāhmaṇas.
The Brahmins, sages, and gods, having approached Manasā in their minds,
worshipped her mentally and praised her individually.
Śakra, having prepared the necessary offerings, was ever devoted and pure.
He worshipped Manasā and praised her with supreme devotion.
Then, having offered the oblation with the sixteen types of service,
he, being thoroughly satisfied, gave what was pleasing at the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the king of the gods.
Having mentally worshipped the Goddess, they departed for their own abode.
Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
With what hymn did Mahendra praise the virtuous Manasā?
I wish to hear, in accordance with reality, the sequence of the ritual for her worship.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having bathed well, purified himself, sipped water for ritual purification (ācamana), and put on two clean garments,
he devoutly seated the Goddess upon a jeweled lion-throne with water from the celestial Gaṅgā held in a precious pitcher.
Mahendra bathed Manasā with Vedic mantras;
he clothed her in two beautiful garments purified by fire;
and, filled with devotion, he anointed all her limbs with sandalwood paste and offered water for her feet and the arghya offering.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā—that is, the group of six deities—he then worshipped that Satī with the mantra:
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Manasādevī. || 123 ||

With the ten-syllable mantra, Hari joyfully offered all sixteen types of services as was appropriate; impelled by Brahmā, he worshipped with devotion those offerings that are otherwise difficult to obtain. (124–125)
There, indeed, he played various kinds of musical instruments.
A rain of flowers fell from the sky upon Manasa.
By the command of the Brahmins, and by the command of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, the god [appeared] there.
With eyes filled with tears and his body covered in horripilation, he offered praise.
Mahendra said:
"O Goddess, I desire to praise you, the most excellent and supreme among virtuous women."
I am not now able to praise you, who are higher than the highest and supreme.
In the Veda, the definition of hymns is that which goes beyond the description of inherent nature;
O lady of virtuous vows, I am not capable of describing the qualities of your own nature.
You are of the nature of pure being, free from anger and violence;
for that reason, the sage was not cursed by me when you abandoned him.
O virtuous lady, you have been honored by me like Aditi, my own mother. (130)
O Goddess of the gods, you are like a sister in the form of compassion and like a mother in the form of forgiveness. My life and my wife and children have been protected by you;
I shall honor you as worthy of worship, and my affection for you shall increase.
O Mother of the World, although you are eternally worthy of worship here in this world,
nevertheless I shall increase your worship again and again.
Those who shall worship you with devotion on the day of the Āṣāḍha-saṃkrānti— ||| 132-133 ||
On the fifth lunar day known as Manasī, or at the end of the month, or on a daily basis, their sons, grandsons, and others, as well as their wealth, increase;
they become illustrious, famous, learned, and endowed with virtues. (134)
Those people who, out of ignorance, do not worship you but instead revile you,
shall be deprived of fortune (lakṣmī) and will always face fear from serpents.
You are the Fortune of heaven in Svarga, and a portion of Kamalā in Vaikuṇṭha.
The lordly Jaratkāru, the sovereign of sages, was a portion of Nārāyaṇa;
your father created you through his ascetic power, his splendor, and his mind.
For the sake of our protection alone, you were thus conceived by him in his thought.
Capable of worshipping with the mind, you are a perfected yoginī by your very nature.
Therefore, O Manasādevī, may you be worshipped and saluted.
You whom the gods constantly and fervently worship with devotion through the mind. (138–139)
Therefore, those who know the ancient lore call you Manasādevī. You are the Goddess whose nature is *sattva*, because of your constant devotion to *sattva*.
For whatever one constantly contemplates, one attains a hundred times that very thing.
Having praised Indra with his mind and taken that sister,
who was adorned with ornaments, garments, and finery, he departed for his own abode.
That goddess remained for a long time in her father’s house together with her son.
Constantly honored by her brothers, she was respected and saluted by all.
O Brahman, Surabhi came there from Goloka and, having been well-honored,
she bathed her with milk and worshipped her with great reverence.
She then described the nature of knowledge, which is difficult for all to attain.
Honored by the gods at that time, she returned once more to the heavenly realm.
Whoever, having worshipped her, recites this hymn—the seed of merit—[shall obtain great rewards].
For him, and for anyone who shall be born in his lineage, there is no fear of serpents.
When one recites this perfected hymn, poison becomes equal to nectar.
By merely performing five hundred thousand recitations, a person becomes a master of the hymn.
"He shall also certainly become one who sleeps upon a serpent and has a serpent as his vehicle.

(147) Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin, Worship, Hymn, and Other Matters Concerning the Legend of Manasā," in the *Manasopākhyāna* within the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
"Or who is that goddess Surabhī, who has come from Goloka?
O Brahman, I desire to hear her life story in its true essence.
Nārāyaṇa said:
The presiding goddess of cows, the primordial source of cows, the progenitor of cows,
the preeminent Surabhi, born in Goloka—
listen as I relate the account of the creation of all things from the beginning. (2)
By him, that birth took place long ago in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
(3) Once, the Lord of Rādhikā, accompanied by Rādhā and surrounded by cowherd women, went out of curiosity to the holy Vṛndāvana. (4)
Out of curiosity, he sported there in secret; then, though he was one who acts according to his own will, a desire to drink milk arose within him.
He then effortlessly created the goddess Surabhi from his left side.
Seeing the cow Surabhi together with her calf— yielding milk,
beautiful to the calves, and adorned with jewels— he milked her into a jeweled vessel;
she yielded a supreme milk that surpassed nectar and removes both birth and death.
The Lord of the Gopīs himself drank that warm and sweet milk. Through the milk and by the spilling from the vessel, a lake was formed, long and wide, extending for a hundred yojanas all around. (8)

That beautiful Kṣīrasarovara is famous throughout Goloka. By the will of the Lord of the Lake, that pond quickly became fashioned with jewels and served as a pleasure-pool for the gopīs and for Rādhā. (9–10)

Suddenly, there appeared hundreds of thousands of millions of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus). Indeed, as many Surabhis with their calves emerged from the pores of her skin. Their sons and grandsons were born in numbers beyond counting.
The creation of cows was described by her, and by them the world was filled.
O Sage, in ancient times the Blessed One performed worship of Surabhi;
thereafter, that worship became difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
On the following day, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the worship of Surabhi took place accompanied by lamps; this was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
[The details of] the meditation, the hymn, the root mantra, and whatever sequence of ritual procedures for the worship [were revealed]. 14.
O highly fortunate one, listen to what is declared in the Vedas; I shall tell it to you.
(15) "Om, salutation to Surabhi"—this six-syllable mantra is perfected by a hundred thousand recitations alone, serving as a wish-fulfilling tree for devotees. (16)
The meditation established in the Yajurveda is worshiped by all;
it bestows prosperity, growth, liberation, and the fulfillment of all desires.
It is the supreme embodiment of Lakṣmī, the highest companion of Rādhā. (17)

I worship that goddess Surabhi, the presiding deity of cows, the primordial source of cows, the progenitor of cows; she who is of pure form, worthy of worship, the granter of all desires to her devotees, and by whom the entire universe is purified. (18–19)

A twice-born man should worship Surabhi in a water-pot, on the head of a cow, upon a tethering post for cattle, or among cows; or in a *śālagrāma* stone, in water, or in fire. On the following day, endowed with devotion, he should perform the worship in the forenoon accompanied by lamps.
And he who worships Surabhi shall himself become worthy of worship on earth.
(21) Once, in the three worlds, during the Vārāha-kalpa, by the illusory power of Viṣṇu, milk was suddenly carried away; then the gods and others were filled with anxiety. (22)
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, they then praised Brahmā.
And by his command, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, praised Surabhi.
Mahendra said:
Salutations to the Goddess, to Mahādevī, and salutations again and again to Surabhī.
Salutations to you, O Mother of the World, whose very nature is the seed of cows.
Salutations to the beloved of Rādhā, and salutations again and again to her who is a portion of Padmā.

Salutations to the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, and repeated salutations to the mother of cows; salutations to her who is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree and the bestower of all prosperity. Salutations again and again to the giver of fortune, the giver of wealth, and the giver of intelligence.
Salutations again and again to the giver of auspiciousness, to the gracious one, to the giver of cows;
salutations again and again to Yaśodā, the giver of happiness, the knower of dharma.
Merely by hearing this hymn, the Mother of the World became pleased and joyful.
She appeared right there in the eternal world of Brahmā;
having granted Mahendra his desired boon, which is difficult for all to obtain,
she departed for Goloka, and the gods and others returned to their own abodes.
O Nārada, the entire universe suddenly became filled with milk;
from that milk came clarified butter, from that the sacrifice, and from that the satisfaction of the gods.
Whoever recites this highly meritorious hymn endowed with devotion, [attains the same fruit]. (29–30)
He shall possess cattle and wealth, and become renowned and meritorious;
he is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at the end to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
He shall dwell there for a very long time and perform service to Kṛṣṇa;
O son of Brahmā, he shall never again be born in this world of saṃsāra.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin, Worship, and Other Matters Concerning Surabhi," in the *Surabhyupākhyāna* (The Episode of Surabhi) within the *Nāradanārāyaṇasaṃvāda* (The Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa), in the second section (*Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrībrahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārada said: O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, O you who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa, O Blessed One who are a portion of Nārāyaṇa, tell me the story of Nārāyaṇa. 1.
I have heard the account of Surabhī, which is exceedingly captivating;
it is a secret among all the Purāṇas, praised by those who know the ancient lore.
Now I desire to hear the supreme narrative of Rādhikā.
Its origin, that meditation, the hymn of praise, and the supreme armor—3.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, [he spoke] to the eternal Blessed One.
The Lord of Siddhas, the bestower of perfection, whose nature is all things, the supreme Śaṅkara;
with a blossoming face, joyful and smiling, praised by the sages;
delighting Kumāra in the [narrative] of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
The narration of the Rāsa festival and the description of the Rāsa circle;
and at the conclusion of that narration, when the opportunity arose, the radiant Pārvatī, smiling, questioned her beloved of her life. (6)
While offering praise, she was terrified; then, consoled by the Lord of her life, the Great Goddess, the sovereign of the gods, spoke to that Mahādeva:
"The unprecedented account of Rādhikā is very difficult to find even within the Purāṇas. || 7–8 ||
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Lord, I have heard the entirety of the Āgamas, all of which are unsurpassed, as well as the Pāñcarātra and other scriptures, the treatises on ethics, and the yoga of the yogis. (9)
The scriptures of accomplishment (*siddhi-śāstra*) of the Siddhas, the various and captivating Tantras,
the scripture of devotion (*bhakti-śāstra*) for the devotees of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
and the life-stories of all the Goddesses [shall emerge] from your lotus-like mouth. (10)
Now I desire to hear the supreme narrative of Rādhikā.
(1.1) That which was heard in the Śruti and is highly praised regarding Rādhā has been told by Vyāsa in brief within the Kāṇva recension; tell it now from your own mouth. (1.2)
And at the time of narrating the scripture, you previously accepted that the utterance of the Lord cannot possibly be false. Therefore,
[you must accept] its origin, its meditation, and the supreme majesty of its name.

O Lord, who are compassionate toward your devotees, please now tell me—the devoted one—the procedure for worship, the life-story, the hymn of praise, and the supreme armor; as well as the method of propitiation and the desired manual of worship. (14–15)
"Why was this not told before, at the time of the narration of the Āgamas?
Having heard these words of Pārvatī, the Blessed Lord, whose face is fivefold, became downcast of countenance, his throat, lips, and palate parched. (16)
Fearing the violation of his own truth, he remained silent and reflected;
through meditation, he remembered Kṛṣṇa, his chosen deity and ocean of compassion.
Having obtained his permission, he spoke to her, who was half of his own body. (17–18)
"I was forbidden by the Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, at the time of beginning the scripture during the course of narrating the story of Rādhā:
'You are half of my own body; you are not different from me in essence. (19)
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, Kṛṣṇa granted me permission to speak,
O Satī, of the life-story of Rādhā, the beloved of my chosen deity— a narrative that must be kept strictly secret, yet which bestows happiness and devotion to Kṛṣṇa. (20–21)
"O Durgā, I know all that is excellent regarding the past and the future;
yet neither Brahmā nor the Lord of Serpents knows that secret which I know, nor does Sanatkumāra, nor the eternal Dharma. (22)
Neither the lords of the gods, nor the lords of sages, nor the lords of the perfected ones, nor the foremost of the siddhas are more powerful than I;
yet you, who are stronger than I, are prepared to give up your life.
Therefore, O Queen of the Gods, I shall tell you that which must be kept secret.
Listen, O Durgā, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret:
the life-story of Rādhikā, which is difficult to attain and bestows great merit.
Long ago, in the beautiful Vṛndāvana, in Goloka, within the circle of the rāsa dance—

And in a portion of Śataśṛṅga, within a grove of *mālatī* and *mallikā* jasmine, the Lord of the World sat there upon a beautiful jeweled throne. The Blessed One, who is composed of his own will, became eager for dalliance. (26–27)

In that *mallikā* grove, everything came to pass by the mere will of that Lord of the worlds who desired to sport, for he consists of his own free will. In that very moment, O Durgā, he became twofold in form.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa became her right side and Rādhikā her left half;
she was a beautiful woman, the queen of the rāsa dance, eager for dalliance.
Adorned with ornaments of priceless jewels, she sat upon a jeweled throne.
Clad in garments as pure as fire, possessing the luster of ten million full moons,
with a radiance like the color of molten gold, she shone with her own splendor.
Smiling, with beautiful teeth and a pure face resembling an autumn lotus, she was perfectly stainless.
Wearing a beautiful braid adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers,
and bearing a jeweled necklace with a radiance like the summer sun,
she was further graced by a brilliant pearl necklace that resembled a stream of the Ganges.
She bore a pair of breasts that were joined, rounded, and lofty like Mount Sumeru;
they were firm, beautiful, visible, marked with patterns of musk,
auspicious, and worthy of blessings.

Afflicted by the weight of her hips and loins, that beautiful woman in the bloom of youth was seen by the Lord of Rasikas, who was himself overcome with desire. Having gazed upon his beloved, he, the beloved of the world, became eager for dalliance. (35–36)
Having seen him, who was most beautiful, she held [him] before Hari.
For that reason, O Great Goddess, he is called Rādhā by those who know the ancient lore.
Rādhā worships that Kṛṣṇa, and he worships her; they are mutually devoted to one another.
The virtuous always declare that there is complete equality between the two.
While chanting the name of the embrace during the *rāsa*, he remembers the dwelling and the running;
therefore, that Lord speaks of a secret rendezvous with Rādhā there.
By the utterance of the syllable *rā*, the devotee attains liberation, which is very difficult to obtain.
By the utterance of the syllable *dhā*, O Durgā, one indeed hastens to the feet of Hari. In ancient times, Rādhā, the mistress of the rāsa dance, was born from the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa.
And from a minute fraction of a portion of her, the divine women came into being.
The syllable *rā* signifies "to take" (or "giver"), and *dhā* is expressive of "nirvāṇa.
Because she thereby attains liberation (*mukti*), she is celebrated as Rādhā.
The multitude of gopīs arose from the pores of Rādhā’s skin;
all the cowherds arose from the pores of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s skin.
From the left portion of Rādhā’s body, she became Mahālakṣmī.
She became the presiding goddess of that house, Gṛhalakṣmī;
she is the four-armed goddess who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha as the consort of Viṣṇu.
And Rājalakṣmī, the bestower of royal prosperity, is a portion of her.
Her partial manifestations are the mortal fortune in every house of householders;
she is the presiding deity of the lamp and the very goddess of the home.
She herself is Rādhā, the wife of Kṛṣṇa, who dwells upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa.
And the goddess who presides over the vital breath (prāṇa) is that very same Supreme Self.
O Pārvatī, everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is entirely false.
Worship the true, supreme Brahman, the Lord of Rādhā, who transcends the three guṇas.
The supreme Pradhāna, the highest, the Supreme Self, the Lord;
the first of all, the one to be worshipped by all, free from desire, beyond Prakṛti;
consisting of His own will, eternal in form, whose body is for the grace of His devotees. 49.
And the form of the gods distinct from him is indeed material (prākṛta).
His life-force is Rādhā, endowed with manifold good fortune;
she is the mother of Mahāviṣṇu, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti.
The virtuous always and eternally serve the proud Rādhikā,
whose lotus feet are easily attained by them yet extremely difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain.
Even in their dreams, the cowherds do not behold the lotus feet of Rādhā.
The Goddess herself, the beloved, exists in the form of a shadow upon the lap of Hari.
And he, O dear one, is the foremost of the twelve Gopas, known as Rāyaṇa;
he is an incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a lord whose prowess is equal to that of Viṣṇu.
Due to the curse of Sudāmā, that goddess came from Goloka to the earth;
she was born in the house of Vṛṣabhānu, and her mother was Kalāvatī.

(55) Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of Rādhā’s Birth, Her Worship, and Other Matters," within the Legend of Rādhā, in the Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, which is part of the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*. (48)
Pārvatī said:
How did that goddess receive the curse from Sudāmā? And how indeed could a servant curse his own master’s beloved, the consort of the God? 1.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret, which is hidden in all the Purāṇas, bestowing auspiciousness, devotion, and liberation. (2)
Once, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, on a portion of the mountain named Śataśṛṅga within the Rāsa-maṇḍala of Goloka,
the Lord of Rādhikā took the fortunate gopī Virajā, who was equal to Rādhikā.

Adorned with jewel ornaments, the Blessed One engaged in play upon a couch inlaid with priceless gems, set upon a bed of flowers, within a pavilion fashioned of jewels and provided with jeweled lamps. (4–5)
Reddened with musk and saffron, well-perfumed with excellent sandalwood,
and adorned with clusters of fragrant jasmine garlands—
there was no cessation from lovemaking for the couple, who were experts in the art of passion. (6)

Those two, mutually impassioned and governed by the enjoyment of pleasure, passed through a measured time of a hundred thousand *manvantaras*. Yet, for Goloka—which is devoid of birth and other such conditions—this was but a very short period of time. (7–8)
Having learned of the four messengers, they then spoke to Rādhikā;
hearing this, the sovereign lady became exceedingly enraged and abandoned Hari.
Though exhorted by her friends, her face and eyes remained flushed with anger.
Having cast off her jeweled ornaments and put on two pure,
bright garments of fire-refined silk, the virtuous lady wiped away her play-lotus, her priceless jewel-adorned mirror, her radiant vermilion, and her decorative leaf-patterns.
Having washed the red lac from her face with handfuls of water,
her heavy braid hanging loose, her hair disheveled, trembling,
clad in white garments, emaciated, and divested of all ornaments— (12)— she stood there.
Though restrained by her dear friends, she went quickly to the side of the vehicle; with her lower lip quivering in anger, she called out to the group of her companions,
while her limbs trembled incessantly as she was surrounded by the gopīs.
Praised by them, who were filled with devotion yet also trembling with fear, he ascended a divine chariot made of priceless jewels;
it was ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas in length. (15)
It was equipped with a thousand wheels and adorned with various wonders; it shone with fine, variegated silken garments and was graced by mirrors fashioned from priceless jewels.
[He was adorned] with thousands of flower garlands possessing the splendor of strings of great jewels and Indra-jāla gems;
endowed with beautiful palaces containing jars of excellent gems;
and together with three hundred thousand crores of gopīs, his dear companions. (17–18)
O beloved,
having heard the clamor, the cowherd Sudāmā, a personal attendant of Kṛṣṇa,
made Kṛṣṇa alert and fled together with the other cowherds on that very chariot adorned with flower garlands. (19)
Terrified by fear, Kṛṣṇa abandoned the virtuous Virajā;
though Kṛṣṇa himself was immersed in his own love, he vanished from sight. Knowing the time had come, that virtuous woman reflected within her heart with indignation.
Terrified by the wrath of Rādhā, she abandoned her life-breaths at that very moment.
There, the hosts of Virajā’s attendants, overwhelmed and trembling with fear,
immediately sought refuge with the virtuous Virajā out of dread.
O daughter of the mountain, in Goloka she indeed became that river;
extending for ten million yojanas and a hundred times as long, she encircled Goloka like a beautiful moat. (23–24)
Then there were other small rivers and even gopīs;
O beautiful one, all the rivers and their parts exist in every universe.
These seven oceans on earth are the Virajā and Ānandā.
Then the highly fortunate Rādhā, the supreme mistress of the rāsa dance,
having returned and not seeing Virajā or Kṛṣṇa, went back to her own home.
Kṛṣṇa then went to that Rādhā together with eight cowherds.
Although he was repeatedly turned away at the door by the vigilant gopīs,
the queen beheld Kṛṣṇa and rebuked him then;
Sudāmā likewise rebuked her in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Enraged, that goddess, the sovereign of the gods, cursed Sudāmā:
"Go! Enter an asura womb; go far from here quickly!
And Sudāmā cursed her in turn: "Go from here to Bhārata! (29–30)
O Bhava, there you shall dwell with the principal Gopīs and your own [consorts],
and there your separation from Kṛṣṇa shall last for a hundred years.
There, the Blessed Lord will also effect the removal of the earth's burden.
Having thus cursed him, Sudāmā bowed to his mother and Hari;
with eyes full of tears and overcome by delusion, he then prepared to depart.
Rādhā followed after him, her eyes filled with tears and she was deeply distressed.
"O child, where are you going?"—having uttered these words, she was distressed by the separation from her son.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, enlightened her with his divine knowledge:
"O lady of beautiful countenance, do not weep; you shall soon regain your son."
And that asura Śaṅkhacūḍa became the husband of Tulasī.
With his body pierced by my trident, he indeed went to Goloka.
The virtuous Rādhā, in the Vārāha-kalpa, went to Gokula in Bhārata.
And that maiden indeed became the daughter of the Vaiśya Vṛṣabhānu. The goddess Kalāvatī, born not from a womb and conceived by Vāyu,
gave birth to Vāyu through her illusory power (māyā) and manifested herself there.
Twelve years later, having seen her in the bloom of fresh youth,
he entered into a relationship with her while she was with a Vaiśya named Rāyāṇa.
Having established a shadow-form in that house, she vanished from sight.
The marriage of that Vaiśya with Chāyā took place.
When fourteen years had passed, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, out of fear of Kaṃsa and by means of a stratagem, went to Gokula in the form of an infant. (39–40)
Yaśodā was the mother of Kṛṣṇa; Rāyaṇa was his uterine brother.
In Goloka, being a portion of Gopa-Kṛṣṇa, he became Kṛṣṇa’s maternal uncle through that relationship.
[In the holy forest of Vṛndāvana, he was with Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā.]
The Ordainer of the worlds caused the marriage to be performed according to the sacred rites.
(42) The cowherds did not see the lotus feet of Rādhā even in their dreams;
Rādhā herself rested on the lap of Hari, while her shadow remained in the palace of Nanda. (43)
In ancient times, Brahmā performed austerities for sixty thousand years at Puṣkara,
desiring a vision of the lotus feet of Rādhikā;
and [he did so] in Nanda’s cowherd settlement in Bhārata, for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden.
And by the fruit of his austerity, he beheld those lotus feet. For some time, that Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, indeed took delight with Rādhā in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana in Bhārata-varṣa.
Then, indeed, a separation occurred due to the curse of Sudāmā.
There, Kṛṣṇa brought about the removal of the earth’s burden.
When a hundred years had passed, however, on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), [he departed].
Rādhā beheld Kṛṣṇa, and he beheld her; thus they gazed upon one another.
Then the knower of reality departed for Goloka together with Rādhā.
Kalāvatī and Yaśodā also traveled together with Rādhā.

Vṛṣabhānu and Nanda went to the supreme Goloka; all the cowherds and the cowherd women who had gathered there also departed. And the shadow-forms of the cowherds and cowherd women attained liberation in his presence.
O Pārvatī, they beheld them right there together with Kṛṣṇa;
thirty-six million crores of gopīs and an equal number of gopas,
being liberated, went to Goloka along with Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā.
Droṇa was Prajāpati, Nanda was Yaśodā, and Dharā was his beloved wife;
through their former austerities, they attained the Supreme Self, the Lord.
Vasudeva was Kaśyapa, and the virtuous Devakī was Aditi.
In every kalpa, by their very nature, there is a mother of the gods and a father of the gods.
Rādhā’s mother is Kalāvatī, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs;
Vasudāmā also came from Goloka, as did Vṛṣabhānu. (54–55)
Thus, O Durgā, has this supreme narrative of Rādhikā been told;
it bestows prosperity, removes sin, and increases one’s sons and grandsons.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is of two forms: the two-armed and the four-armed.
In Vaikuṇṭha he is four-armed, and in Goloka he himself is two-armed.
The wives of the four-armed one are Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī,
Gaṅgā, and Tulasī— these goddesses are the beloveds of Nārāyaṇa.

That Rādhā is the wife of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, born from half of his own body; she is a virtuous woman equal to him in splendor, age, beauty, and virtue. (59) A wise person should first utter the name of Rādhā and afterwards say the name of Kṛṣṇa.
In case of transgression, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
And on the full moon day of Kārttika, in Goloka within the Rāsa-maṇḍala, he performed the worship of Rādhā and the great festival associated with her.
Having fashioned that armor from a pill of the seven precious gems,
Hari wore it upon his neck and on his right arm along with the cowherds.
Then, having performed meditation with devotion, he recited this hymn of praise.
Madhusūdana chewed the betel nut that Rādhā had already tasted.
Rādhā is worthy of worship by Kṛṣṇa, and the Lord, the Master, is worthy of worship by her.
One who creates division between these two, who are each other’s chosen deity, shall go to hell. (63–64)
In the second [kalpa], she was worshipped by me, Brahmā, according to the Dharma,
as well as by Ananta and Vāsuki, by Ravi and Śaśin in the past,
and by Mahendra, the Rudras, and Manu, the son of Manu.
She was worshipped by the lords of the gods, the lords of the sages, and by all the worlds.
In the third [kalpa], she was worshipped by the lord of the seven continents,
and in Bhārata by Suyajña, together with his sons and friends, filled with joy.
Cursed by a brahmin, afflicted by a divine calamity,
seized by disease in his hand, and tormented by suffering,
that king, his royal fortune fallen away, regained his kingdom through the grace of Rādhāvara.
Having praised the Supreme Goddess with the hymn composed by Brahmadatta,
he placed her impenetrable armor upon his neck and arms;
then, meditating, he performed worship at Puṣkara for a hundred years.
The lord of the earth departed for Goloka by means of a jeweled vehicle.
Thus, everything has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of Rādhā’s Curse from Sudāmā and Other Events," within the Legend of Rādhā, in the Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, which is part of the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Pārvatī said:
Who was that king Suyajña, and in which lineage did he arise?
How was he cursed by the brāhmaṇas, and how did he obtain Rādhikā? (1)

How could he have served the supreme goddess, the wife of Kṛṣṇa who is the soul of all and who is worshipped by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, while bearing excrement and urine? In former times, Brahmā performed penance for sixty thousand years.

How did the Lord, the All-pervading One, formerly behold that virtuous Mahālakṣmī at Puṣkara for the sake of obtaining the dust of her lotus feet? Though she was difficult even for you to behold, how did she become visible to human beings? (3–4)
How did the Creator of the three worlds give that armor to him?
