You ought to explain her meditation, the ritual of worship, and her hymn of praise.
(5) Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, Svāyambhuva Manu was indeed the first of the Manus;
he was the son of Brahmā, an ascetic, the lord, and the husband of Śatarūpā.
His son was Uttānapāda, and his son was Dhruva.
O Daughter of the Mountain, Dhruva’s fame is renowned throughout the three worlds.
His son was Utkala, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
he performed a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices at Puṣkara.

With joy, he gave all the jewel-encrusted vessels to the Brahmins; at the conclusion of the sacrifice, during that great festival, the king gave to the Brahmins a thousand heaps of priceless gems, radiant with splendor.
O beloved of the worlds, having witnessed that splendid sacrifice,
the Creator appointed King Suyajña as its presiding priest in the assembly of the gods.
And that King Suyajña was born of the lineage of Manu.
A giver of food, a giver of jewels, indeed a giver of all prosperity— he,
filled with joy, constantly gave ten lakhs of cows adorned with jeweled horns to the Brahmins, along with ritual fees.
Filled with joy, he constantly gave away twelve lakhs of cows; and,
O Pārvatī, he daily fed six crores of Brahmins with well-cooked meats.

Day after day, he fed a hundred thousand cooks until they were completely satiated with foods to be sucked, chewed, licked, and drunk; thereafter, he provided them with a full measure of food seasoned with soup,
containing cow products but devoid of meat.

And at the time of the meal, the brahmins did not praise Suyajña, who was born of Manu’s lineage; rather, they praised his ancestors. On that day, at the conclusion of Suyajña’s sacrifice, thirty-six hundred thousand crores [of ancestors] were honored.
O beautiful one, the brahmins partook of excellent food until they were fully satiated;
yet, being unable to carry all the jewels they had received to their own homes, they gave some to the cart-drivers and dropped some along the way. (18)
And at the conclusion of the feeding of the Brahmins, the king gave [gifts] to other Brahmins.
Nevertheless, a thousand heaps of food remained there.
Having performed the sacrifice, the mighty-armed one dwelt in his own assembly hall.
On a beautiful jeweled lion-throne, adorned with ten million parasols fashioned from the finest essence of the best gems, well-prepared with silk cloths,
and beautifully anointed with sandalwood and other substances, as well as lovely sandalwood sprouts.
Adorned with full water-pots joined with branches and with *rambhā* trees, it was refined by sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and forest vermilion;
it was attended by the Vasus, Vāsava, Candra, Indra, Rudra, and the Ādityas. (22–23)
In this very place, which was graced by sages such as Nārada and Manu, as well as by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
a certain brahmin arrived in the meantime.
He was coarse, dressed in soiled garments, and his throat, lips, and palate were parched.

Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, anointed with garlands and sandalwood paste, he—smiling and with palms joined in reverence—blessed the king. The king bowed to him, yet did not rise up even slightly. (25–26)
The members of the assembly did not rise, and they laughed only slightly.
Having paid homage even to the sages and the gods, that best of the twice-born,
standing there unrestrained, cursed the king out of anger.
"Go far away from this kingdom; be deprived of royal fortune and become a commoner!
May you soon become afflicted with leprosy that oozes, devoid of intellect, and tormented by calamities!
Having spoken thus, trembling with rage, he prepared to curse those present in the assembly. (28–29)
Wherever they laughed, all the members of the assembly rose;
they all offered their salutations, and the submarine fire (Vāḍava) abandoned its wrath.
Having bowed down and approached him, the king wept, overwhelmed by fear.
With a heart burning with grief, he departed from the midst of the assembly.
A Brahmin of hidden form, blazing with the splendor of *brahman*, followed behind him;
and after him, all the sages set out, overcome with fear.
"O Brahmin, stop! Stop! they cried out again and again.
Pulaha, Pulastya, Pracetas, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Kratu likewise [spoke].
Śukra and Bṛhaspati, as well as Durvāsas and Lomaśa;
Gautama, Kaṇāda, Kaṇva, Kātyāyana, and Kaṭha; Pāṇini, Jājali, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Vibhāṇḍaka.
Taittiri, Āpiśali, and Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism; Sanaka, Sananda, Voḍhu, Paila, and Sanātana;
the venerable Sanatkumāra, and the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (36)
Parāśara, Jaratkāru, Saṃvarta, and Karabha;
Bharadvāja, Vālmīki, Aurva, and Cyavana; Agastya, Atri, Utathya, Saṅkarta, Āstīka, and Āsuri. (37–38)
Śilāli, Lāṅgali, Śākalya, Śākaṭāyana, Garga, Vatsa, Pañcaśikha, Jamadagni, Devala,
Jaigīṣavya, Vāmadeva, the Vālakhilyas, and others.
Śakti, Dakṣa, Kardama, Praskanna, and Kapila;
Viśvāmitra, Kautsa, Ṛcīka, and Aghamarṣaṇa—these and other sages, the ancestors, Agni, and the beloved of Hari. (40–41)
All the world-protecting deities followed behind the brahmin;
O Goddess, they enlightened the brahmin and established him in his dwelling.
Those experts in ethics spoke to him in due order regarding the principles of conduct.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Episode of Suyajña," within the "Episode of Rādhā" from the "Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī," occurring in the "Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa" in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Brahman, what did the brāhmaṇas—the sons of Brahmā—say to that brāhmaṇa?
"You are a knower of ethics; you ought to explain those words of ethics to me.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Having gratified that brahmin with praise and humility..."
O lady of beautiful countenance, the assembly of sages began to speak in due order.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Sattva, and likewise Yaśas followed after you."
The ancestors, Agni, and likewise the gods, possessing excellent character and great sovereignty, arrived from the houses of kings after having caused the king’s fortune to fall away.
O best of the twice-born, may you be pleased; for the Vāḍava fire is easily satisfied.
The hearts of Brahmins are as tender as fresh butter;
they are pure, utterly stainless, and polished by asceticism, O Sage.
Forgive me, come, O Lord of Brahmins, and purify the king’s palace.
Bestow upon him your blessing with the dust from your holy feet.
Bhṛgu said:
"If a guest returns from one's house with his hopes frustrated..."

The ancestors, the gods, and likewise the sacred fire—these all depart disappointed because of the refusal of hospitality from the guest. "Forgive us; come, O best of Brahmins, and purify the king's palace. (7–8)

"He who does not honor a guest incurs a fault equal to that of those who kill women, those who kill cows, the ungrateful, those who slay Brahmins, and those who violate the teacher’s bed. Pulastya said:
Those who look upon a guest who has arrived at their home with a crooked glance transfer their own sin to him and depart taking his merit away.
"Forgive the fault of the king, and go, my child, as you please."
The king did not rise due to the fault of his own past actions; therefore, please forgive him.
Pulaha said:
"O King, he who disregards a brāhmaṇa because of royal splendor or learning..."

"The Brahmin who is devoid of the three daily prayers, the Kṣatriya who is bereft of prosperity, he who neglects the Ekādaśī fast, and he who has been deprived of the food offerings to Viṣṇu—forgive them! Come, O best of Brahmins, and purify the king's palace. (12–13)
Kratu said:
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, he who shows contempt for a Brāhmaṇa becomes devoid of consecration (dīkṣā). 14.
"He will certainly become destitute of wealth, destitute of sons, and destitute of a wife.
Forgive me, O Blessed One; come and purify the king's palace.
Aṅgiras said:
"He who, having become a wise Brahmin, treats another Brahmin with contempt,
shall become a bullock-carrier for seven births in Bhārata.
Marīci said:
"He who, being devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, shows contempt for the Lord, for a Brāhmaṇa, or for a guru in the merit-field of Bhārata— [he becomes such].
Kaśyapa said:
He who, upon seeing a Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa, treats him with false contempt;
he who is devoid of Viṣṇu-mantras and remains averse to His worship.
Pracetās said:
He who, upon seeing a guest who is a Brāhmaṇa, does not rise to greet him,
shall be devoid of devotion to the ancestors on this earth in Bhārata;
that fool shall attain the womb of a crane for seven births.
"Go quickly, O best of the twice-born, and grant auspicious blessings to the king.
Durvāsas said:
"Whether it be a preceptor, a brahmin, or even an image of a deity—"
Having seen [you], if one does not quickly bow down, he shall become a pig on this earth.
He becomes a false witness and likewise a betrayer of trust.
Forgive us everything; please accept our hospitality. (21–22)
The king said:
"Dharma has been explained by you, the best of sages, through parables.
Having made everything perfectly clear, please enlighten me, for I am indeed deluded. (23)

"O best of yogis, tell me: what fault is there for those who kill women, those who kill cows, those who are ungrateful, those who violate the wives of their gurus, and likewise those who kill Brahmins? Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, for killing a cow out of desire, a man should wander to sacred pilgrimage sites for one year,
subsisting on barley and barley-gruel and drinking water from his hand;
then he should bestow a hundred divine cows along with ritual fees upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Having given [gifts], one is released from sin; having fed a hundred twice-born brahmins, one is likewise freed.
But even when a penance has been performed, one is not released from all sins;
due to the residue of sin, one becomes miserable and indeed becomes a *caṇḍāla*.
In the case of a killing by extension (*ātideśika*), one experiences half that fruit.
One is not released from all sins merely by a secondary form of expiation (*prāyaścittānukalpa*).
Śukra said: [28]

The sin incurred by killing a woman is certainly twice that of killing a cow; one will surely dwell in the Kālasūtra hell for sixty thousand years. Thereafter, that great sinner shall become a pig for seven births.
Then he becomes a serpent for seven births; after that, he is purified.
Bṛhaspati said:
"The sin incurred by one who commits the murder of a Brahmin is double that of the murder of a woman."
He will certainly dwell for a hundred thousand years in the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell.
Thereafter, that great sinner becomes a worm in excrement for a hundred years.
Then he becomes a serpent for seven births; after that, he becomes pure.
Gautama said:
O Indra among kings, the fault of an ungrateful person is four times that of killing a Brahmin.
It is certain that no atonement for the ungrateful is declared in the Vedas. 33.
The king said:
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the characteristics of the ungrateful.
How many kinds of ungrateful people are said to exist, and what is the fault in each case? (34)
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Sixteen types of ungrateful persons are described in the Sāmaveda;
each one experiences the respective fruit according to their individual fault. (35)
When the Kṛta age, truth, merit, one's own duty, austerity, and steadfastness prevail;
when promises, generosity, and the protection of one’s own community are maintained;
and when duties toward gurus, duties toward the gods, rites for desired ends, and the worship of the twice-born are observed. (36)
One who destroys these— daily duties, trust, and the imparting of another's dharma—
is considered the most sinful and is known as ungrateful (kṛtaghna).
For such people, there are worlds [of suffering], and their birth occurs among different species.
O Indra among kings, those sinners go to whichever hells there may be;
and those various hells certainly exist in the world of Yama.
Suyajña said:
"Who, having done what, do these ungrateful ones go to the Raurava hells?
O Lord, I wish to hear this for each case; you ought to tell it to me.
Kātyāyana said:

Having made a vow in the form of an oath, he who kills the truth and does not protect it is ungrateful; he shall dwell indeed in the Kālasūtra hell for the duration of four yugas. For seven births he shall be a crow, and for seven births a bat.
Then that Śūdra, having suffered from a great disease for seven lifetimes, became pure thereafter.
Śrī Sanandana said:
"Having performed a meritorious deed, he speaks [thus] solely for the sake of increasing his fame."
That ungrateful person dwells upon a glowing iron pillar for three yugas;
for five births he is a frog, for three births a crab;
then he becomes mute, afflicted by a great disease, and impoverished, after which he becomes pure.

Sanātana said: That brahmin who abandons his own duty, who neglects the three daily junctions (saṃdhyā), who bathes without offering libations, and who bathes while omitting the food offerings (naivedya) to Viṣṇu—[is fallen]. 45.
He who is devoid of the worship of Viṣṇu, devoid of the mantras of Viṣṇu,
and devoid of the Ekādaśī fast on the day of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s birth,
as well as he who eats on Śivarātri and on the day of Rāmanavamī— 46.
He who neglects the rites for his ancestors and other such duties is known as ungrateful (*kṛtaghna*).
He dwells in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as fourteen Indras reign;
thereafter, he certainly becomes a *caṇḍāla* for seven births. (47–48)
For a hundred births he becomes a vulture, and for a hundred births a pig;
thereafter he becomes a Brāhmaṇa who serves as a cook for Śūdras.
After that, he is born seven times as a Brāhmaṇa who drives oxen.
And for seven births he shall be the cremator of the dead for Śūdras. Having been born as a twice-born man in Bhārata for seven births as the husband of a Vṛṣalī,
and having experienced a mere fraction of his own enjoyments, he wanders about and goes to the Raurava hell.
Again and again he enters a sinful womb and hell; thereafter, he becomes a donkey for five births and a cat for five births.
Then, after five births, he becomes a frog, and from that point on, he gradually attains purification.
Suyajña said: [It is forbidden] for Śūdras in the preparation of food, in the cremation of the dead for Śūdras, in eating the food of Śūdras, or even in sexual union with a Śūdra woman. 54.
"What fault is there in Brahmins, or likewise in the driving of bulls?
Having considered all of this, O Sage, tell me your certain conclusion.
Parāśara said:
A Brahmin who is weak in knowledge and serves as a cook for Śūdras dwells indeed in the Asipatra hell for seventy-one yugas. Thereafter, he becomes a donkey and then a mouse for seven births.
After seven births as an oil-pressing insect, that man becomes pure.
Jaratkāru said:
"Whether by means of a servant or by himself, that brahmin who acts as a bullock-driver..."
O King, he became famous and renowned throughout the land of Bhārata as a person ungrateful for favors.
The sin incurred by constantly beating a bull is equal to the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by placing a burden upon the back of a bull, that sin becomes twofold. (58–59)

He who drives a bull that is hungry or thirsty in the heat of the sun incurs the sin of one hundred killings of Brahmins; of this there is no doubt. For those who drive bulls, the food of Brahmins becomes excrement and their water becomes urine.
O King, they shall have no right to perform worship of the ancestors or the gods.
They shall dwell in the Pit of Saliva for as long as the moon and sun endure;
there, their food shall certainly be excrement and their drink urine.
At the three junctions of the day, the servant of Yama shall strike him with a trident;
he places a flaming torch in his mouth and constantly cuts him with a needle.
For sixty thousand years, he shall become a worm in excrement.
Then the crow [remained] as such for five births, and likewise the crane for five births;
the vulture for five births and the jackal for seven births.
Thereafter he was a poor Śūdra, then one afflicted with a great disease, and finally he became pure.
Bhāradvāja said:
O Indra among kings, he who burns the corpse of Śūdras is remembered as ungrateful; by that act, he certainly incurs the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa according to their age. 66.

One becomes pure from wandering through hells equal to those [of the person one has cremated] by cremating the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa; whatever fault there is in cremating the corpse of Śūdras, that same fault shall exist in eating the food at a Śrāddha ceremony for Śūdras. (67–68)
Vibhāṇḍaka said: That base Brāhmaṇa who eats at a Śrāddha for Śūdras is a drinker of spirituous liquor and a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; he is excluded from the worship of the ancestors and the gods. (69)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, I shall declare the fault regarding Brāhmaṇas who have sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman; listen attentively to what is declared in the Vedas. (70)
That Brahmin who is the foremost among the ungrateful and who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* shall dwell in Kṛmidaṃṣṭra for as long as fourteen Indras endure; there,
the Brahmin shall become a consumer of worms, overwhelmed by the servants of Yama.
He constantly embraces that image made of heated iron;
thereafter, he certainly becomes a worm in the womb of a prostitute for a thousand years, and after that, he is purified as a Śūdra. (72–73)
Suyajña said:
O sage, tell me of the fruit of the actions of others who are ungrateful.
Even a Brahmin’s curse is praiseworthy for me; for whom is there prosperity without adversity? (74)
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose; my life is fruitful, since these liberated sages and gods have come to my home.

(75) Thus ends the section on Rādhā within the dialogue between the King and the Sages, which is part of the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, contained in the second book of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the conversation between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
The fifty-first chapter, titled "The Ripening of Karma.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Lord, tell me what the fruit of the actions of other ungrateful people is.
What did those sages, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, say to them?
Śrī Maheśvara said:
O beloved, while all the sages were present, the lord of kings posed this question.
Thereupon, the great seer Nārāyaṇa began to speak.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Whoever should seize the property of a Brahmin, whether given by himself or given by another,"
He should be known as ungrateful; hear now the fruit [of his action], O lord of the earth:
for as many particles of dust as are moistened by the teardrops of the brahmins, for that many thousands of years he remains impaled upon a stake.
He must consume glowing coals as food and drink only heated urine;
he lies upon burning coals and is beaten by the servants of Yama.
At the end of that, the great sinner is born as a worm in excrement.
For sixty thousand years, according to the measurement of the gods, [this shall last] in Bhārata.
Then the human being will become deprived of land and deprived of progeny;
he will be poor, wretched, diseased, a Śūdra, and thereafter, though censured, pure.
Nārada said:
That lowest of men who destroys the fame of others or his own fame is known as ungrateful; hear now the fruit of that action. (8)
O King, that sinner shall dwell even in a blind well for as long as fourteen Indras reign,
constantly being devoured by insects, mongooses, and vultures;
thereafter, he indeed drinks the water of boiling lye forever.
"From this point on, he shall be a serpent for seven births, and thereafter a crow for five; after that, he becomes pure.
Devala said:
"He who should seize the property of a Brahmin, the property of a guru, or even the property of a deity..."
He should be known as ungrateful and a great sinner in this world of Bhārata.
He shall dwell in a pit for as long as the fourteen Indras endure;
thereafter he becomes a drinker of spirits, then a Śūdra, and finally pure.
Jaigīṣavya said: One who,
devoid of devotion, fails to protect his father, mother, and teacher—
even if he strikes them with mere words— is remembered as a traitor (kṛtaghna).
And that unchaste woman who constantly strikes her husband with words is renowned in Bhārata as an ungrateful sinner;
those two will certainly go to the most terrible fire-pit.
In that fire he shall dwell indeed as long as the moon and sun exist;
thereafter he shall become leeches for seven births, and after that he becomes pure.
Vālmīki said:
Just as the nature of being a tree does not abandon its presence in all trees,
so too, O King, does ingratitude persist among all sins.
He who gives false testimony out of desire, anger, or fear—
He who speaks with partiality in an assembly is remembered as ungrateful (kṛtaghna).
Furthermore, O King, he who destroys even a mere fraction of merit is an ungrateful person;
indeed, ungratefulness consists in the destruction of the merit of all people in every respect.
O King, whoever gives false testimony or partial testimony in the land of Bhārata shall certainly dwell in the Serpent-Pit for as long as a thousand Indras;
there he will be constantly surrounded by serpents, terrified, and indeed devoured.
And beaten by the messenger of Yama, he eats all excrement and urine.
There, in Bhārata, he becomes a lizard for seven births;
for seven births he becomes a frog together with his seven ancestors. (20–21)
Then he would indeed become a *śālmali* tree in a great forest;
then he would become a mute man, then a *śūdra*, and thereafter pure.
Āstīka said:
By approaching the wives of one's guru, a man becomes one who has approached his mother;
for men who approach their own mothers, no atonement exists.
O best of kings, such is the fault regarding those who approach their mothers, as stated in the *Bhārata*.
And likewise for Śūdras who have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman;
indeed, the same fault shall apply to a Brāhmaṇī woman for having sexual intercourse with a Śūdra.
The same applies to those who have intercourse with virgins, daughters-in-law, wives of sons, or mothers-in-law. (24–25)
O King of kings, I shall describe the fault regarding sisters-in-law and sisters, as spoken by the Lotus-born [Brahmā]:
"That great sinner who engages in sexual intercourse with these women [commits a grave offense]. (26)
Even while living, he would be as good as dead; he is a Caṇḍāla and indeed untouchable.
He has no right to behold the solar disc, nor to the Śālagrāma stone, its water, or the leaves and water of the Tulasī plant.
A sinful man who is equal to a dog cannot even touch the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha) nor the water from the feet of a brahmin;
he does not deserve to offer salutations to the gods, his guru, or a brahmin.
That food contains more excrement than nourishment, and likewise the water contains more urine;
neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor the Brahmins accept it in Bhārata.
By the wind from their bodies, even a sacred bathing place becomes a "charcoal-bearer" (a place of impurity).
For seven nights a twice-born man must indeed fast due to such contact with a deity;
moreover, the earth is burdened and unable to bear that weight.
Because of that sin, the region falls, just like the land of one who sells his own daughter.

From touching him, from conversing with him, and from sharing his bed, seat, or food, men incur an equal sin; of this there is no doubt. He too shall dwell in Kumbhīpāka for as long as a hundred Brahmās.
Day and night he wanders there incessantly in a whirlpool of fire;
scorched by flames and beaten by the messengers of Yama,
thus the great sinner constantly experiences the torments of hell.
And subsisting on excrement everywhere, he is then cast into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
When the great and terrible dissolution of nature has passed, and at the commencement of a new creation, he may become such a being once again. (36–37)
For sixty thousand years he shall become a worm in excrement;
thereafter he becomes a Caṇḍāla, deprived of a wife and impotent. For seven births he remains pure, yet remains a galat-kuṣṭhī (one with trickling leprosy) and impotent.
Then he may become a Brahmin who is blind, afflicted with leprosy, or a eunuch;
having passed through seven such births, the great sinner becomes pure.
The sages said:
Thus everything has been told by us to you according to the scriptures.
A fault equal to these would arise from the neglect of guests.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, certainly offer your salutations and lead him to his home.
Having honored the Brahmin with effort and received his blessing, [he was told:
"Go to the forest, O Great King, and perform austerities immediately;
once liberated from the Brahmin's curse, you shall return once more."
Having spoken thus, all the sages departed quickly for their own abodes,
as did the gods, the kings, and their circles of kinsmen, O Pārvatī.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Ripening of Karma," within the Narrative of Rādhā, in the Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, which is part of the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
When the hosts of sages had departed after hearing about the fruits of human actions, what did that best of kings do, overwhelmed as he was by the curse of a Brahmin? (1)
O Lord, what did the guest or the Brāhmaṇa do then? Did he go to the king’s palace or not? You ought to tell me that.
Maheśvara said:
When the assembly of sages had departed, the king,
seized by reproach and urged on by his most virtuous domestic priest Vasiṣṭha,
fell prostrate like a staff upon the ground at the feet of the brāhmaṇa.
Having abandoned his anger, the best of the twice-born gave him auspicious blessings.
Seeing the Brahmin smiling, free from anger, and full of compassion, the best of kings, with tearful eyes and palms joined in reverence, spoke: (4–5)
The king said: "In what lineage were you born, O Lord, and what is your name? What is your name as well—tell me that—and where is your residence, and how did you come here? (6)
Viṣṇu himself, disguised as a Brahmin and concealed in human form,
was manifestly Agni incarnate, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
"O Blessed One, who was your guru and your chosen deity in Bhārata?"
"How is this appearance of yours now possible for one so full of knowledge?
(8) Accept the entire kingdom, sovereignty, and the treasury;
O Sage, make my son your own servant, and me, a woman, your slave. (9)
"Rule over the earth consisting of seven seas and seven continents,
enriched by the eighteen sub-continents and adorned with mountains and forests;
being my servant, become an emperor in Bhārata."
"Sit upon this excellent lion-throne inlaid with the finest essence of jewels.
(11) Having heard the king's words, the bull among sages laughed and spoke the supreme reality, unknown and difficult for all to attain. (12)
The guest said:
Marīci was the son of Brahmā, and Kaśyapa himself was his son.
All the sons of Kaśyapa attained the desired status of divinity. (13)
Among them, Tvaṣṭṛ, possessed of great wisdom, performed supreme austerity;
for a thousand divine years at Puṣkara, he practiced difficult penance and worshipped Hari, the supreme God of gods, for the sake of the Brahmins. (14)
From Nārāyaṇa he obtained a boon: a son who was a radiant brahmin.
Thereupon, the radiant Viśvarūpa, whose wealth was asceticism, became the domestic priest when Vācaspati had departed in anger. (15–16)

O King, my father Virūpa, the son of Viśvarūpa, cut off that Brāhmaṇa—who was offering oblations of clarified butter to the Daityas, his maternal grandfathers—at the command of his mother. Śunāsīra then severed him. (17)
And I am a twice-born named Sutapa, a Kaśyapa free from passion.
Mahādeva is my guru, the bestower of learning and wisdom.
My chosen deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the soul of all, beyond primordial nature.

I meditate upon that lotus-foot; I have no desire for worldly prosperity. Even the states of *sālokya*, *sārṣṭi*, *sārūpya*, and *sāmīpya* belonging to the Lord of Rādhikā—these, if granted by Him, I do not accept without the auspicious service of His feet.
O Lord of Men, I consider the state of Brahmā or immortality to be like a reflection in water—transient, false, and merely a delusion obscured by devotion;
so too the status of Indra, Manu, or Soma. (21–22)
"I do not consider it a mere line of water; by whom is kingship reckoned as such?
O King, having heard of the arrival of the sages at the sacrifice of Suyajña, I have come to inspire in you a longing for devotion to Viṣṇu.
"You have been solely favored by me; you have not been cursed by me now.
You have been lifted up from having fallen into the terrible, deep ocean of worldly existence.
For holy places do not consist of water alone, nor are the gods made of clay or stone. (24-29)
Furthermore, those devotees of Kṛṣṇa purify others merely by their sight, even over a long period of time.
O King, depart from this house and bestow the kingdom upon your son.
Having entrusted your beloved, virtuous wife to your son, go quickly to the forest, my child.
O protector of the earth, everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is entirely illusory.
Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhā, the Supreme Soul, the Sovereign who is attainable through meditation but difficult to propitiate even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other gods. (27–28)
Through manifestations and disappearances of the material elements, which are beyond primordial nature,
Brahmā is the creator, Hari is the protector, and Hara is the agent of destruction;
even the guardians of the quarters and the lords of the directions wander about by his illusory power.
By whose command the wind blows, the sun always becomes the lord of the day, and the moon, the lord of the night, eternally brings about the lushness of crops;
by whom, in due time, death occurs for all beings throughout the entire universe. (30–31)
Śakra pours rain at the proper time, and Agni burns according to the proper time;
likewise, Yama, the ruler of the universe and restrainer of creatures, acts like one who is afraid [of transgressing his own laws].
Time destroys at the proper time, and at the proper time it creates and protects.
In one's own country indeed is the ocean, and in one's own country is the earth;
in one's own country are the mountains, and from one's own country are the netherworlds (pātālas).
O King of kings, there are the seven heavenly worlds, and the earth with its seven continents exists within one's own country.
Indeed, there are seven netherworlds (pātāla) joined with mountains and oceans;
and by these worlds, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), submerged in water, takes the form of a bubble.
Within each individual egg, there truly exist Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
O King, the gods, humans, nāgas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others—
from the netherworld (pātāla) up to the world of Brahmā— this entire mass of beings is indeed this very supreme, artificial cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 36–37 ||
In the navel-lotus of the Virāṭ Viṣṇu, who is the minute one reclining upon the waters,
he remains just as a lotus seed resides within the pericarp of a lotus flower;
even so, he lies upon a bed of water that is completely submerged.
The great yogi meditates indeed upon the ordinary self as being beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
he is one who fears time and [meditates upon] Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Time, the Self, and the Sovereign.
He exists within the vast expanse of Mahāviṣṇu, sharing the space of a single pore of his skin.

In the pores of the hairs on his body, O protector of the earth, there exist all the universes, each one individually. Even Kṛṣṇa is unable to calculate the number of the cosmic eggs within the hairs of Mahāviṣṇu's body; what then can be said of anyone else? (40–41)
Mahāviṣṇu is primordial, yet he too is always born from the cosmic egg (ḍimba).
By the will of Kṛṣṇa, that egg arises from the womb of Prakṛti.
Mahāviṣṇu, the support of all, is afraid of Time and remains apprehensive.
He meditates at will upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Time, as his own self and the Supreme Sovereign.
And thus, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all others who abide in the entire universe—
the Great Virāṭ, the Minor Virāṭ, and everyone else— are eternally composed of primordial nature (prākṛtika).
She is the sovereign primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), consisting of all seeds;
dissolved in time within the Lord of Time, the Dark One, she meditated upon him.
Thus, all beings—both those of the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and those derived from it—are afraid of time.
Manifested and withdrawn by time within the Supreme Self—thus has all this great knowledge, so difficult to obtain, been told.
It was granted by Śiva as my Guru; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Instruction on Hospitality to Suyajña," within the Legend of Rādhā, in the Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, which is part of the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
The King said:
"What is the support of the Great Viṣṇu, who is himself the support of all?"
O Lord of Sages, how long is the lifespan of one who fears death?
(1) And for how long is the lifespan of a base person, of Brahmā, and likewise of Prakṛti;
as well as the lifespan of Manu, Indra, Candra, and Sūrya? (2)
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, having carefully considered what is declared in the Vedas regarding the maximum lifespan of other ordinary people, please tell me:
what world could that possibly be, situated above all the worlds? (3)
"Speak, O illustrious one; cut away my doubt.
The sage said:
"O King, Goloka is more vast than all worlds, equal to the sky."
Thus, he is eternally in the form of a cosmic egg (ḍimba), produced by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
it was filled with water by a drop from Kṛṣṇa’s mouth as He played,
weary from His sport at the beginning of creation, intent upon the first act of emanation.
O King, for him who is joined with his own *prakṛti* by means of a *kalā*,
there exists therein the vast support of Mahāviṣṇu, the support of the universe.
O protector of the earth, *prakṛti* belongs to that which has arisen from the child conceived within the womb.
And the Great Virāṭ lies reclining upon a vast reservoir of water.
He is proclaimed to be a sixteenth part of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhā;
his form is dark like a blade of dūrvā grass, he is smiling, and he has four arms. (8–9)
Wearing a forest garland, glorious, and adorned with yellow garments;
above in the sky is that very Vaikuṇṭha of Viṣṇu, which is eternal.
It is the Self, equal to space, eternal, and as expansive as the orb of the moon.
Arisen from the will of the Lord, unperceivable and without support, it is as vast as space and fashioned from heaps of jewels.
Therein dwells the glorious Nārāyaṇa, wearing a garland of forest flowers and possessing four arms. (11–12)
The Lord is the master of Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī;
He is surrounded by His attendants, beginning with Sunanda, Nanda, and Kumuda.
He is the Lord of all, the Master of all perfections, whose very form exists for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees.
And Śrī Kṛṣṇa became twofold: two-armed and four-armed.
The four-armed one is in Vaikuṇṭha, while He Himself as the two-armed one is in Goloka.
Fifty crores of yojanas above the world of Vaikuṇṭha [lies Goloka].
Goloka is circular in shape and superior to all worlds;
it is adorned with palaces inlaid with priceless jewels, featuring pillars and staircases fashioned from the finest essence of gems. (16)
It was resplendent with gates adorned with the reflections of the finest jewels and shining with golden pitchers,
and with pavilions variegated by various wonderful paintings;
it extended for ten million *yojanas* in width and was a hundred times that length.
It is beautifully encircled by hundreds of peaks strewn with the Virajā river;
it is equal in length and breadth to half the river, and it is endowed with Vṛndāvana, which measures half the size of the mountain. (18–19)
Adorned with a dancing circle (rāsa-maṇḍala) whose inhabitants are half that size,
Goloka itself is situated in the midst of rivers, mountains, forests, and so forth,
just as the beautiful pericarp is in the center of a lotus. 20.
There, O King, the Lord of the Gopīs was constantly joined by Rādhikā, the Queen of the Rāsa, within the circle of the Rāsa dance, together with the cows, cowherds, and gopīs;
He was two-armed, holding a flute in His hand, appearing as a child in the form of a cowherd boy. || 21–22 ||
Wearing garments purified by fire, adorned with jewel ornaments,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, resplendent with a necklace of jewels,
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, and graced by a jeweled parasol. (23)
Thus he was served by his beloved cowherds with white chowries;
he was adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste, and gazed upon with smiles and sidelong glances by the well-attired gopīs.
The extent of the world has been described according to my ability and according to the scriptures.
Now listen to the measurement of time as it was heard from the mouth of Śambhu.
A vessel made of six palas, deep and four finger-breadths wide [is required].
A vessel made from a gold māṣaka, with holes [drilled] at intervals of four finger-breadths, is submerged in water;
the time it takes for the water to fill that vessel, as well as the time for one daṇḍa, constitutes one muhūrta, and four of those [muhūrtas] constitute one yāma. (28)
A day consists of eight watches (yāmas), and fifteen of those constitute a fortnight (pakṣa).
A month consists of two fortnights, and twelve months make a year.
Indeed, one month for humans is a single day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs).
The dark fortnight is declared to be the day, and the bright fortnight is proclaimed to be the night.
For humans, a year constitutes a day and a night for the gods;
indeed, the northern course (of the sun) is the day, and the southern course is the night.
And the lifespan of humans and others, O King, corresponds to the respective age (yuga).
Now hear concerning the primary nature and its derivatives, beginning with Brahmā.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga). (32–33)
Listen attentively to these twelve thousand divine verses:
four, three, two, and one thousand [years] constitute the Kṛta and the other ages respectively;
for each of these, the dawn (saṃdhyā) and the twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) are proclaimed to be two thousand years.
The four yugas are measured by thirty-four lakhs and twenty thousand [years] according to the human reckoning;
and by seventeen lakhs and twenty-eight thousand [years]. (35–36)
The Kṛta Yuga is proclaimed by those skilled in calculation to consist of one hundred twenty-six thousand human years.
The Tretā Yuga is proclaimed by those who know time to be measured [in the same manner]. (37)
The duration of the Dvāpara age is stated by those who know the numbers to be four hundred and thirty-two thousand years, measured at eight lakhs and sixty-four thousand. (38)
Those wise ones who know time understand that the Kali Yuga arises indeed from pride in manhood (nṛmāna).
In that age, seven days of the week and sixteen lunar days (tithis) are recorded;
day and night, the two fortnights, the month, and the year are likewise established.
In that same manner, O king of kings, that wheel revolves; even so do the four ages, as well as the yugas and the manvantaras.
Indeed, a manvantara consists of seventy-one divine yugas.
In this manner, fourteen Manus indeed revolve in succession.
Twenty-five thousand, five hundred and sixty years,
along with a Nara-Mānava Yuga, is recorded as one supreme Manvantara.
O lord of men, listen from me to the account of the most righteous Manus,
which was heard from the mouth of Śiva—
the truth concerning the first Manu, the son of Brahmā, and his devoted wife Śatarūpā.
The most excellent among the righteous, the most venerable lord among men,
the son of Svayambhū, a disciple of Śambhu, devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu,
liberated while living, and possessed of great wisdom— such was your great-grandfather. (45–46)
He indeed performed a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices on the banks of the Narmadā;
three hundred thousand Aśvamedhas and three hundred thousand Naramedhas,
as well as four hundred thousand Gomedhas— great and wonderful rites performed according to the prescribed rules.
He fed three million Brahmins daily with well-cooked meat from five hundred thousand cows seasoned with ghee,
along with hard foods, soft foods, lickables, drinkables, and very rare sweet delicacies.
And a hundred thousand priceless jewels, ten crores of gold pieces,
a hundred thousand divine cows endowed with golden horns and well-worshipped,
and a hundred thousand garments for the lords of sages, purified by fire.
He gave land abundant with all kinds of crops, a hundred thousand lordly elephants,
three hundred thousand excellent horses adorned with gold,
a thousand precious chariots, and a hundred thousand palanquins.
Three crores of golden vessels filled with desired food and water;
three crores of golden ornaments; betel-leaf highly scented with camphor and other fragrances;
and a bed of gold worth three crores.
Adorned with platforms inlaid with the finest gems fashioned by Viśvakarman,
and resplendent with variegated cloths purified by fire and clusters of garlands,
he constantly gave these to the Brāhmaṇas out of devotion to Viṣṇu and by the command of Śiva.
Having received from Śaṅkara the knowledge of the Kṛṣṇamantra, which is very difficult to obtain,
and having attained the state of service to Kṛṣṇa, he indeed went to Goloka.
Seeing his own son liberated, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) became exceedingly joyful.
Being satisfied, the Creator praised Śaṅkara and created another Manu.
Since he was the son of Svayambhū, he is known as Svāyambhuva Manu.
And the second Manu was Svārociṣa, the son of Vahni.
The king was generous, most righteous, great, and equal to Svāyambhuva.
The other two sons of Priyavrata were two Manus, the best among the virtuous.
They, the third and the fourth, were devotees of Viṣṇu and the foremost of ascetics.
And those two were disciples of Śaṅkara, devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Raivata was the fifth Manu, the most excellent among the righteous;
and the sixth is to be known as Cākṣuṣa, who was devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Śrāddhadeva, the son of Sūrya, is the seventh Manu, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Sāvarṇi, the son of Sūrya, is the eighth Manu, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
The ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi, who is wholly devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
The tenth is Brahmasāvarṇi, who is proficient in the knowledge of Brahman. After him, the eleventh Manu is remembered as Dharmasāvarṇi;
he is most righteous, most excellent, and devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
And the wise Rudrasāvarṇi is recorded as the twelfth Manu;
likewise, the righteous Devasāvarṇi is the thirteenth Manu;
and the greatly wise Candrasāvarṇi is the fourteenth.
Indeed, for as long as the lifespan of the Manus lasts, so long does that of the Indras last.
A day of Brahmā is said to be delimited by fourteen Indras;
his night is of equal duration, O King, and that is the nocturnal period of Brahmā.
She is to be known as Kālarātri, as proclaimed in the Vedas. O King, within a day of Brahmā, a minor kalpa is proclaimed. Mārkaṇḍeya, of great asceticism, lived for seven kalpas.
Indeed, all the worlds below the realm of Brahmā were consumed there by the fire from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa, which suddenly arose;
the Moon, the Sun, and the sons of Brahmā certainly fled to the realm of Brahmā. (68–69)
When the night of Brahmā has passed, the Creator brings about creation once again.
That period of Brahmā’s night is called the minor dissolution (kṣudrapralaya).
During that night, the gods, the Manus, and likewise humans and other beings are consumed by fire.
Thus, thirty days and nights constitute a month of Brahmā,
and twelve such months indeed form a year belonging to Brahmā.
O King, when fifteen such years of Brahmā have thus passed—
The daily dissolution (*dainaṃdina-pralaya*) is proclaimed in the Vedas;

it is described by the ancient knowers of the Vedas as the "Night of Delusion" (*moharātri*). During that time, all things—including the moon, the sun, and the lords of the directions—are utterly destroyed.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the Manus, and the Mānavas;
the Ṛṣis, Munis, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and others; as well as Mārkaṇḍeya, Lomaśa, Pecaka, and other long-lived ones. (74)

King Indradyumna, the tortoise Cākūpāra, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Baka—all of them indeed perished there. All the worlds below the realm of Brahmā, as well as the abodes of the nāgas, were likewise destroyed. (76–79)
All of them, including the sons of Brahmā and others, went to the world of Brahmā.
When the daily dissolution had passed, Brahmā created the worlds once again.
Thus, the supreme lifespan of the Prajāpati lasts for a hundred years.
O King, upon the dissolution of Brahmā, there shall be a Mahākalpa;
that very period is proclaimed by the ancients here as the "Great Night" (Mahārātri).
And at the dissolution of Brahmā, the multitude of cosmic eggs is submerged in water.
The mother of the gods, Sāvitrī, the Vedas, Dharma, and the rest—
all have perished, as has Death and Prakṛti, without Śiva. Likewise, Nārāyaṇa and the Vaiṣṇavas residing in the universe have dissolved away.

Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer, together with all the hosts of Rudras, is dissolved into Mahādeva Mṛtyuñjaya; that quality of darkness (tamas) [is thus absorbed]. And by the falling away of Brahmā, a nimeṣa of Prakṛti occurs.
O King, at the end of a single blink of an eye, the creation of Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, and Mahāviṣṇu occurs again by the will of Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa is devoid of blinking, beyond the qualities (guṇas), and transcendent to primordial nature (prakṛti).
The duration of a moment (*nimeṣa*) for those possessing qualities is measured by the divisions of time.
For the qualityless, eternal, and beginningless-and-endless [Brahman],
a *daṇḍa* is said to consist of a thousand moments of *prakṛti*.
A day for her is proclaimed to consist of sixty *daṇḍas*.
Thirty nights and days make a month, and twelve months make a year.
When one hundred such years have passed, there is the dissolution of Prakṛti into Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

And when Prakṛti has dissolved into Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that is the dissolution of the material world (prākṛta-laya). Having withdrawn all things, she alone—who is the mother of Mahāviṣṇu—Mūlaprakṛti, the Sovereign Goddess, dissolves into the chest of Kṛṣṇa. (87–88)
The wise call her Durgā, the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu;
she is the supreme, virtuous Nārāyaṇī, whose very nature is all-powerful energy, and who is the attributeless Goddess presiding over the intellect of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself. 89.
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others are deluded by her māyā;
those Vaiṣṇavas call that supreme Mahālakṣmī Rādhā.
And Mahālakṣmī is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, forming half of his body.
And [he praised] the Goddess who presides over the vital breaths, who is dearer than life itself and most excellent;
the power consisting of steadfast love, who is beyond attributes (nirguṇā) and belongs to the Attributeless One (nirguṇasya).
Nārāyaṇa and Śambhu, having withdrawn their many attendants... [92]
The Lord, whose nature is pure being, merged into Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond all qualities.
O King, the cowherds, the cowherd women, and the cows along with their calves—
all merged into Prakṛti, and Prakṛti itself merged into the Supreme Lord.
All those minor Viṣṇus are dissolved into Mahāviṣṇu;
Mahāviṣṇu is dissolved into Prakṛti, and she likewise into the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Prakṛti and Yoganidrā are both within the two eyes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, by means of his illusory power (māyā) and by the will of the Lord,
he established a state of sleep for the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana for as long a period of time as is proclaimed to constitute one day of Prakṛti.
And upon a priceless bed of jewels, honored with garments purified by fire,
and made fragrant by the scent of perfumes, sandalwood, heaps of garlands, breezes, and other such things—
during his subsequent wakefulness, the entire creation comes into being once again.
Thus, all ordinary beings, with the exception of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa), [attain liberation].
Saluting Him, remembering Him, meditating upon Him, worshipping Him,
and chanting His qualities destroys even the greatest of sins.
"All this has been told to you, O Great King, exactly as it was heard from Mṛtyuñjaya and according to the scriptures. What more do you wish to hear?
Suyajña said:
Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer of all universes and characterized by the quality of *tamas*,
is dissolved at the end of Brahmā’s life into Śiva, the conqueror of death, who is the essence of *sattva*.
Śiva, in turn, is absorbed into the attributeless Śrī Kṛṣṇa during the dissolution of material nature (*prākṛta-laya*).
How was it heard that your guru’s name is Mṛtyuñjaya?
How is it that your mother is the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti of Mahāviṣṇu, upon whose body hairs innumerable universes indeed exist? (103–104)
Sūtapā said:
At the end of Brahmā, the daughter of Death, the destroyer of all worlds beginning with Brahmā, vanished like a reflection in water, O lord of men. (105)

In the dissolution of millions of Brahmās, how many times has Śambhu been absorbed by Time into the qualityless essence of pure being? My Guru, Śiva, has eternally conquered the daughters of Death. (106)
"Śambhu has never been conquered by death; this is heard in the Śruti at every Kalpa.
O King, Śambhu is indeed [the manifestation] of Nārāyaṇa and of Prakṛti. The dissolution of eternal beings occurs within the Eternal One, yet that Māyā is not real. (107–108)
He is himself the Person, devoid of qualities, yet by time he becomes possessed of qualities himself;
he is himself Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, and by his māyā he is himself Prakṛti. His portion is eternally equal to him, just like a spark from a fire.

Whosoever were created by Brahmā, such as the Rudras, Ādityas, and others, they all, being subject to destruction, were conquered by the maiden Death in every kalpa. But Śiva was not created by Brahmā; he is the Truth, eternal, and primeval.
O King, how many Brahmās arise from His single blink?
Then, at the beginning of creation, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Teacher of the Universe,
performed the infusion of His potency within Prakṛti in the sacred forest of Vṛndāvana.
Born from her left shoulder in the Rāsa dance, she is the supreme Mistress of the Rāsa (Rāseśvarī).
That Rādhā bore the embryo for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā;
thereafter, she gave birth to the infant in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance.

Seeing the child, her heart was tormented with grief; she became enraged and cast that child down into the cosmic egg (Viśvagolaka). Having abandoned her offspring, the Great Goddess wept again and again.
Kṛṣṇa, the knower of yoga, awakened her by means of great yoga.
From that embryo was born the Mahāvirāṭ, the support of all.
Suyajña said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; my life has attained its purpose.
Even this curse has taken the form of a boon, serving as the cause for my devotion.
Devotion to Hari, the most auspicious among all auspicious things, is exceedingly difficult to attain.

O Brahmin, even the fivefold devotion prescribed in the Vedas is not equal to that by which my devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, may arise—a devotion that is very difficult for all to attain; therefore, perform it, O great sage. (119–120)
For holy fords are not merely made of water, nor are gods made of clay or stone;
they purify only after a long time, whereas those devoted to Kṛṣṇa purify by their mere sight.
And among all stages of life, the birth of the twice-born is the most excellent.
Among them, those who are devoted to their own duties are excellent in Bhārata;
among them, the worshiper of Kṛṣṇa’s mantra and one intent on devotion to Kṛṣṇa is superior;
and the great, pure one who constantly eats the *naivedya* is even more excellent than that. (122–123)
"O Sage, having obtained you— the supreme ocean of great knowledge, a disciple of Śiva, and the best among the twice-born, Vaiṣṇavas— to whom else shall I go for refuge?
O Great Sage, I am now suffering from leprosy due to your curse."
"How can I, being impure, perform penance for which I am not qualified?
Suta-pa said:
"She is the eternal Viṣṇu-māyā, the bestower of devotion to Hari."
She bestows favor upon those whom she favors and grants them devotion;
yet she does not grant it to those whom Māyā deludes, and she deceives them with transient wealth. (126–127)
Worship that Rādhā, who consists of love for Kṛṣṇa, who is the presiding deity of the vital breaths,
who is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇā), and who bestows all perfections. Through service to her grace, you will quickly go to Goloka.
She was served by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is worshiped by all; she was honored [by him].
(129) Having served that Nirguṇa, who is difficult to propitiate and attainable only through meditation, devotees go to Goloka after many births and after a very long time. (130)
By serving her, who is composed of compassion, devotees indeed attain [their goal] without delay.
She is the mother of Mahāviṣṇu and the embodiment of all prosperity.
Drink the water from the feet of the Brahmins for a period of one thousand years.

And you shall be free from disease, possessing a form like that of Kāmadeva. (132) As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of a Brahmin, for that long the ancestors drink water from lotus leaves. (133)
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, they are all present in the ocean;
and whatever sacred fords exist in the ocean, they are likewise present at the feet of the Brahmins.
Indeed, the water from the feet of the Brahmins is the destroyer of sins and diseases.
It is equal to the waters of all sacred fords, auspicious, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Janārdana, the God of gods, is the Brāhmaṇa in human form;
indeed, all the deities partake of whatever substance is offered by a Brāhmaṇa. (135–136)
Having spoken thus, the brahmin took his offerings and departed for his home, saying, "I shall return at the end of a year.
O Śivā, with devotion, the king then drank the water from the brahmin's feet.
He honored the brahmins and fed them for a year.
When the year had passed, the king was freed from his disease.
Then the best of sages, Sutapas, the leader of the Kaśyapa lineage, arrived.
He gave that king the ritual procedure for the worship of Rādhā, as well as the hymn, the armor, the mantra, and the meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda.
Then, saying, "O King, depart quickly for the sake of penance," the sage [dismissed him].
The king departed from his own residence and hurriedly went to the fortress.
All his kinsmen, fainting with grief, wept for three nights;
his wives also gave up their lives, and his son indeed became king. (141–142)
Having gone to Puṣkara, Suyajña performed a most difficult penance;
for a hundred divine years, the king recited the supreme mantra.
Then he beheld the Supreme Goddess stationed upon her chariot in the sky.
By the mere sight of him, he became free from sin;
he abandoned his human body and assumed a divine form.
That goddess, by means of that vehicle fashioned from the finest jewels, [departed].
Having led the king to Goloka, she then departed;
there the king beheld Goloka,
surrounded by the Virajā river and encircled by the beautiful mountain Śataśṛṅga.
It is endowed with Śrī Vṛndāvana and adorned with the Rāsa-maṇḍala;
it is beautified by multitudes of cows, cowherds, and gopīs who serve [there], and by most enchanting palaces inlaid with the finest of gems. (147–148)
It was resplendent and beautifully adorned with various wonderful and diverse [features],
graced by thirty-seven pleasure-groves provided with wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa),
strewn with pārijāta trees, and surrounded by the cows of plenty (kāmadhenu).
Extremely vast like space and circular like the orb of the moon, it is situated fifty crore yojanas even above Vaikuṇṭha;
remaining in the void without support, it is eternally fixed by the will of the Lord. (150–151)
The Self is eternal and equal to space, and it is extremely difficult for us to attain.
I am Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the great Virāṭ.
[I am] the assembly of Dharma, Kṣudra-virāṭ, Gaṅgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī. (152)

You are Viṣṇu’s Māyā, Sāvitrī, and Tulasī; you are Gaṇeśvara, Sanatkumāra, and Skanda; you are the Ṛṣis Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Kapila, Dakṣiṇā, and Sacrifice; and you are the sons of Brahmā and the Yogins. (153–154)
Pavana, Varuṇa, Candra, Sūryya, Rudra, Hutāśana,
the worshiper of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, and the Vaiṣṇavas residing in Bhārata—
Goloka has been seen by these, but never by others. (155)
And there, upon that very same stainless lion-throne made of jewels, he is seated—
adorned with jeweled garlands and crowns, decorated with jewel ornaments, and resplendent in perfectly pure yellow garments as bright as fire. (156–157)
His entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste; he appeared as a youth in the form of a cowherd.
Dark as a fresh rain cloud, his eyes were like white lotuses, and his face was like the full moon of autumn—charming and adorned with a gentle smile. (158)
Two-armed, with a flute in hand, His form is for the grace of His devotees;

He is the Supreme Brahman consisting of His own will, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), attainable through meditation, difficult to propitiate, and exceedingly rare for us to encounter. (159–160)
He was served by his beloved twelve cowherd boys with white chowries,
and gazed upon by throngs of most enchanting cowherd girls who were smiling and perpetually struck by the arrows of love, yet possessed of eternal youth. (161)
Clad in garments as pure as fire and adorned with jewel ornaments,
the king then beheld right there Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme, standing in the center of the *rāsa* circle as shown by Rādhā. (162–163)
It was praised by the four Vedas, which had assumed beautiful and enchanting embodied forms;
it was exceedingly captivating to the Rāgiṇīs and the Rāgas;
and, O Śivā, the music emerging from the mouths of the mechanical instruments was heard.
Together with you, who are eternal and primordial by nature,
[he whose] lotus feet are perpetually worshipped with unbroken *tulasī* leaves,
anointed with musk and saffron, and smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste. (165–166)
It was exceedingly beautiful, graced by offerings of *durvā* grass, unbroken rice grains, and *pārijāta* blossoms, as well as by pure, stainless waters used for the *arghya* offering;
it was most serene, independent, and the cause of all causes.
The inner self of all, the Lord of all, the life of all;
the supreme support of all, the most worshipful, the eternal light of Brahman;
the embodiment of all prosperity and the bestower of all riches. (159–168)
He is the embodiment of all auspiciousness and the cause of all auspiciousness;
he bestows all auspiciousness and is the auspiciousness of all auspicious things.
Seeing him, the king was terrified and quickly descended from his chariot.
With eyes full of tears and his body bristling with joy, he bowed his head in prostration.
The Supreme Self granted him His own service, auspicious blessings,
steadfast and true devotion to Himself, and that which is very difficult for us to attain.
Descending from her own chariot, Rādhā sat upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest;
served by her very dear gopīs with white chowries,
she was addressed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa with a smile and honored.
"Arising suddenly with devotion and indeed with great excitement, one should first utter the name of Rādhā and afterwards that of Kṛṣṇa Mādhava;
so it is proclaimed in the Vedas by the ancient knowers of the Vedas. (174–175)
Those who speak of perversion and those who revile Rādhikā— the power consisting of pure love who is dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life and the progenitress of the universe—
they are cooked in the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (176)
For a hundred lifetimes they remain deprived of wives and sons and are afflicted by disease.
Thus, O Durgā, has this supreme narrative of Rādhikā been told.
You are that very Satī, the Goddess, the Vaiṣṇavī, and the eternal one.
Nārāyaṇī, Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the sovereign Goddess—
by means of that Māyā you question me, you who are all-knowing and possess every form.
(179) You are the supreme presiding deity among the womankind, the highest, remembering your former births, and most excellent.
The narrative of Rādhikā has been told; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Goloka by Suyajña," within the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, which is part of the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section, the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Here concludes the legend of Suyajña.
Śrī Pārvatī said: While the mantras of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and those of you other lords remain [in use], how did that Vaiṣṇava king indeed receive the mantra of Rādhā? 1.
What is the ritual procedure, what is the meditation, what is the hymn of praise, and what is the armor?
What mantra did he give to the king? Tell me that method of worship.
Śrī Maheśvara said:
When the king asked the question, "O Brahmin, whom should I worship?
and "O sage, by worshipping whom do I quickly attain Goloka?",
the best of Brahmins spoke to that lord of kings.
And by serving Him, you shall attain His world after many births.
(4) Worship Rādhā, the supreme goddess who presides over His very life-breath;
through the grace of her compassionate nature, one quickly attains that state. (5)

Having spoken thus, he gave him the six-syllabled mantra of Rādhikā: "Oṃ Rādhe," ending in the dative case and concluding with the wife of fire (svāhā). He likewise taught him breath control (prāṇāyāma), the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa).
He taught him the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), as well as the meditation (*dhyāna*) which is very difficult to attain,
the hymn (*stotra*), and that armor (*kavaca*), out of devotion.
The king, in that very sequence, recited the supreme mantra.
And that meditation, declared in the Sāmaveda and the most auspicious of all auspicious things—
by means of which meditation Kṛṣṇa formerly worshipped her—
she who has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower and a radiance equal to ten million moons. (9)
Her face was like the full moon of autumn, her eyes like autumn lotuses;
she possessed beautiful hips and lovely buttocks, with excellent, ripe bimba-fruit lips. She was enchanting, with a row of teeth that were the very image of strings of pearls.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, she bestows grace upon her devotees;
she wears garments as pure as fire and is adorned with necklaces of jewels.
She is graced with jeweled armlets and bracelets, and resplendent with jeweled anklets.
She was resplendent with a pair of variegated jeweled earrings,
her cheeks shining like the radiance of the sun;
she was adorned with a neck-ornament inlaid with priceless gems.
She is radiant with a crown and diadem inlaid with the essence of the seven precious gems;
she is adorned with jeweled rings and beautified by jeweled loops;
she bears a mass of braided hair graced with garlands of jasmine flowers.
And [he saw] the goddess presiding over form, who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut,
served by beloved cowherd girls with white chowries;
and [he saw her] with drops of musk together with drops of sandalwood paste below.

She was radiant beneath her beautiful parting, marked with a dot of vermilion, and was constantly worshipped with devotion by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. Endowed with the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa, she was the most excellent woman, dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life. (16)
She is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath, beyond the qualities (nirguṇā), and higher than the highest;
she is the creator of Mahāviṣṇu and the bestower of all prosperity;
she grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa, is peaceful, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), and the sovereign Goddess. (17–18)

I worship Rādhā, the auspicious Mistress of the Rāsa, who is the power of Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇavī), the illusory energy of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā), and composed of love for Kṛṣṇa; she stands in the center of the Rāsa-maṇḍala, seated upon a jeweled throne, united with the Lord of the Rāsa in every Rāsa. 19.
Having meditated and placed a flower upon [the deity's] head, one should again meditate upon the Lord of the World.
Having meditated once more, one should offer a flower and the sixteen services:
a seat, clothing, water for the feet, the arghya offering, and fragrant unguents.
Incense, a lamp, beautiful flowers, bathing water, and jewel ornaments;
various kinds of food offerings, betel leaf, scented water, honey-mixture (madhuparka), and a jeweled couch—these are the sixteen modes of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra). (21–22)
Each was offered with devotion by the king along with Vedic mantras.
O Durgā, hear now the mantras spoken in the Vedas and approved by all:
[these were used for] the object fashioned from the essence of jewels by Viśvakarman.
"O Rādhā, please accept this beautiful and excellent lion-throne for the worship services.
O Goddess, please accept this garment, which is inlaid with priceless jewels, invaluable, exceedingly fine, purified by fire, and stainless. (24–25)
"O Rādhā, please accept this auspicious water from all sacred fords, contained within a vessel made of the essence of the seven precious gems, for the purpose of washing Your feet;
and [this water] held in a right-spiraling conch shell, together with dūrvā grass, flowers, and sandalwood. (26)
O Rādhā, please accept this *arghya*, purified and prepared with the waters of sacred fords.
(27) O Rādhā, accept from me this fragrance, produced from earthly substances, made exceedingly fragrant, auspicious, and pure. (28)
O Goddess of gods, please accept this unguent, which is smooth sandalwood powder mixed with musk and saffron, endowed with fragrance,
combined with tree resin and earthly substances. (29)

O Goddess, accept from me this incense produced from the crest-flames of a mass of fire. O Supreme Sovereign, accept this jewel-lamp, rich in splendor, which dispels fear in the darkness and is adorned with priceless gems.
O Supreme Goddess, please accept this exceedingly beautiful and charming *pārijāta* flower, anointed with fragrant sandalwood;
and this fragrant, very smooth, and most enchanting powder of *āmalakī*.
"O Goddess, please accept this bath-powder mixed with Viṣṇu-oil.
O Rādhā, please accept these ornaments of mine—armlets, bracelets, and so forth—set with priceless jewels and eternally beautiful. (33-34)
O Goddess, please accept this seasonal fruit grown in the proper time and place, such as sweetmeats like *laḍḍukas*, as well as *paramānna* and other delicacies for the ritual offering (*naivedya*).
Also, accept this excellent and beautiful betel leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other ingredients.
"O Goddess, please accept this betel leaf, sweeter than all enjoyments.
O Supreme Sovereign, please accept with devotion this food, most delicious and enchanting, served by me in a vessel of jewels. (36-37)
"O Goddess, please accept this couch, inlaid with the finest essence of jewels, draped with fire-purified silk, and richly adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste.
(38) Having thus worshipped the Goddess, one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
The observer of the vow should diligently worship the Goddess and the female leaders during the rite, O Dear One,
proceeding from the east in clockwise order with devotion and the fivefold offerings, as well as the beloved attendants. (39–40)
Mālāvatī in the eastern corner, Mādhavī in the southeast;
Ratnamālā in the south, and the virtuous Suśīlā in the southwest;
Śaśikalā in the west, and Pārijātā in the northwest. (41)

Furthermore, the practitioner of the vow should offer Padmāvatī in the north and Sundarī in the northeast; he should also present garlands of jasmine, mālatī, and lotus. He likewise performs the ritual dismissal as prescribed in the Sāmaveda.

O Goddess, you are the mother of the worlds, the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu; you are the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath, the auspicious one who is dearer to him than his own life. You are the power consisting of love for Kṛṣṇa, and you are the very embodiment of good fortune within Kṛṣṇa. 44.
O Rādhā, bestower of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, salutations to you, the giver of auspiciousness!
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life has attained its purpose;
for I have worshipped her who is herself worshipped by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
She who is Rādhā on the chest of Kṛṣṇa, endowed with all auspicious fortune; she who is the form of the Queen of the Rāsa dance in the Rāsa circle; she who is Vṛndā in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
and she who is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa in Goloka and in the grove of Tulasī trees.
Campāvatī sports in the company of Kṛṣṇa in the Campaka grove;
Candrāvalī in the Moon-grove; and Satī on Mount Śataśṛṅga.
Virajā and Darpahantrī sport in the forest on the banks of the Virajā.
Padmāvatī is in the lotus forest, Kṛṣṇā is in the Black Lake,
Bhadrā is in the bower-cottage, and Kāmyā is indeed in the Kāmyaka forest.
Mahālakṣmī is in Vaikuṇṭha, and Vāṇī is upon the chest of Nārāyaṇa.
In the Ocean of Milk she is Sindhu-kanyā; in the mortal world she is Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari.
In all of heaven she is Svarga-lakṣmī, the destroyer of the suffering of the gods.
She is the eternal Viṣṇu-māyā, Durgā upon the chest of Śaṅkara.
By a portion [of yourself], you are Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, upon the chest of Brahmā;
by a portion, you are the lawful wife of the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
and by a portion, you are Tulasī and Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world. (53)
The cowherd women (gopīs) arose from the pores of [Her] body; they are portions of Her digits (kalāṃśas). Rohiṇī is Rati.
Kalā is the form of a digit, as are Śatarūpā, Śacī, Diti, Aditi—the mother of the gods and beloved of Hari—who are all portions of Your digits.
"O auspicious one, worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, through the acquisition of a portion of Your power, may the goddesses and the wives of the sages [grant] devotion to Kṛṣṇa and service to Kṛṣṇa for me.
Having thus performed the ritual circumambulation and offered praise, one should recite the armor-verse (*kavaca*).
This auspicious hymn, composed in the past, bestows devotion and servitude.
He who worships thus daily becomes equal to Viṣṇu in the land of Bhārata;
liberated while living and purified, he certainly goes to Goloka. (57–58)
O Śivā, he who worships Rādhā on the full moon day of Kārttika,
following this sequence every year, shall obtain the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice.
That meritorious person shall be endowed with supreme sovereignty in this world.
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes at last to the abode of Viṣṇu.
In this manner, at the very beginning and in due order, in the forest of Vṛndāvana during the rāsa dance, that virtuous Rādhā was formerly praised and worshipped by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (60–61)
And on the second day, she was likewise worshipped by the Creator (Dhātṛ) in due order.
Having obtained the Mother of the Vedas through your boon, the Creator [worshipped her];
and Nārāyaṇa, having worshipped Bhāratī, attained Mahālakṣmī.

Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, likewise obtained Gaṅgā, Tulasī, and the supreme purifier of the worlds, as well as Sindhusutā; for previously, at my command and by the order of Kṛṣṇa, when the daughter of Dakṣa had died, [he brought them forth].
You alone have become Durgā, and she was worshipped at Puṣkara.
Kaśyapa obtained Aditi, and Candra obtained Rohiṇī;
Kāma obtained Rati, and Dharma obtained his wife Mūrti, who was devoted to her husband.

Having worshipped that devoted wife, both the gods and the sages obtained through her very boon dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. Thus has the procedure for worship been told; now hear the hymn of praise.
Śrī Maheśvara said:
Once, while the Lord was deeply attached to Tulasī and to a gopī in the Tulasī grove, the proud Rādhā became invisible to him. 68.
Having playfully withdrawn all her own forms and all her constituent powers (kalās),
all the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others—
became deprived of their sovereignty, stripped of their splendor, separated from their wives, and indeed afflicted.
Having deliberated together, they all went to Śrī Kṛṣṇa for refuge.
(70) Satisfied by their hymn of praise, having bathed and performed worship, that pure Supreme Soul praised the virtuous Rādhikā before them all. (71)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "It is exactly so; I am dear to you, and your delight is indeed in me.
It is very clear today that your words were deceitful, O fair-faced one. (72)

"O Kṛṣṇa, you are my life-breath and my very soul"—this is what you have constantly said out of love; that which you spoke eternally has now swiftly come to pass. Therefore, O Mother of the World, all your words have proven false.
The hearts of women are like the edge of a razor in every respect.
Listen to these true words that I speak:
"O Rādhā, you are the presiding deity of my five vital breaths; you are dearer to me than life itself. (74–75)
I am not able to protect you, for my life-breaths depart without you;
indeed, who can live anywhere without their presiding goddess?
You are the Mother of Mahāviṣṇu, the Sovereign Primordial Nature (Mūlaprakṛti).
You are with attributes by your portion, yet you are yourself indeed without attributes.
You are the form of light, formless, yet possessing a physical form for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees;
assuming various forms according to the diverse inclinations of your devotees.

In Vaikuṇṭha you are Mahālakṣmī, and in Bhārata, the field of merit, you are Bhāratī, the mother of the virtuous; likewise, you are Satī and Pārvatī. You are Tulasī, whose form is merit, and Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world. (79)
In the world of Brahmā you are Sāvitrī, and by a portion of yourself you are Vasundharā;
in Goloka you are Rādhikā, the sovereign mistress of all the cowherds.
Without you, I am indeed lifeless and incapable of all actions.
Śiva is powerful through you, his Śakti; without you, he is but a corpse.
Brahmā himself is the creator of the Vedas only in conjunction with you, the Veda itself.
Nārāyaṇa, the protector and lord of the world, is so only through you, Lakṣmī.
The sacrifice yields its fruit only when accompanied by you as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Śeṣa sustains the creation, having placed the earth upon his head;
likewise, Śiva, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, bears you in the form of the Gaṅgā upon his crest.
Without you, the entire world is powerless and like a corpse;
with your speech, everyone becomes a speaker, but without you, even a charioteer is mute.
Just as a potter is always capable of making a jar from clay, [so are all beings through you]. (89)
In order to bring forth creation, I am likewise [united] with Prakṛti and with you;
without you, I am inert and lack power everywhere.
You are the embodiment of all powers; come into my presence.
In fire you are the power of burning; fire is not capable without you.
You are the very nature of beauty in the moon; without you, it is not beautiful.
Indeed, you are the form of radiance in the sun; without you, it is not luminous.
"O beloved, without you and Rati, Kāma has no friend among women.
Having offered this praise, the Lord of the World attained her;
the gods became endowed with splendor, accompanied by their wives, and united with their powers.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the entire world became possessed of women;
and by her grace, Goloka became filled with cowherdesses.
Having thus praised the beloved of Hari, the king departed for Goloka.

The man who recites this hymn to Rādhā composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa attains devotion to Kṛṣṇa and His service; of this there is no doubt. He who, being pure, listens to this for one month during a separation from his wife [attains the same]. (92–93)
He who, being devoid of a wife and devoid of fortune, listens for one year [to this], will before long obtain a wife who is virtuous, beautiful, and faithful.
(94) He who, being devoid of a wife and devoid of fortune, listens for one year [to this], will before long obtain a wife who is virtuous, beautiful, and faithful. (95)
O Pārvatī, in former times you were obtained by me through this hymn of praise;
and when the daughter of Dakṣa had died,
Sāvitrī was formerly obtained by Brahmā through this same hymn, by the command of the Supreme Self.
Formerly, when the hosts of deities were bereft of fortune due to the curse of Durvāsas,
that most difficult-to-attain Śrī was regained by those gods through this hymn.
Furthermore, one who desires a son obtains a son by listening to it for one year.
By the grace of this hymn, one who suffers from a great disease shall be freed from illness.
(98) Furthermore, he who worships it on the full moon day of Kārttika and recites it shall attain unshakable prosperity and obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (99)
If a woman hears this hymn, she shall be endowed with the good fortune of her husband.
Whoever hears this hymn with devotion will certainly be liberated from bondage.
(100) He who daily recites it with devotion, having worshipped Rādhā with devotion—
He departs for Goloka, liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.

(101) Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Worship and Hymn of Śrī Rādhā," within the Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, which is part of the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
I have heard the ritual for worship and the hymn of praise, which are most wonderful;
now, by your grace, tell me the armor-verse (*kavaca*), which I shall hear.
(1) Śrī Maheśvara said:
Listen, O Durgā, I shall declare this most wonderful armor (kavaca), which was formerly recited to me by the Supreme Self in Goloka;
it is the supreme secret reality, the embodiment of the entire multitude of mantras. (2)
By retaining and reciting which, Brahmā attained the Mother of the Vedas;
by retaining which, I became your lord, the Mother of All, the Sovereign of the Gods;
and by retaining which, Nārāyaṇa obtained Mahālakṣmī. (3–4)
Having held that which is beyond the qualities (*nirguṇa*) and transcendent of *prakṛti*,
the all-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa became endowed with power in order to perform creation in the past;
and having held that same [power], Viṣṇu, the protector, attained the Daughter of the Ocean.
For this reason, Śeṣa bears the cosmic egg upon his head like a mustard seed;
and the great Virāṭ bears cosmic eggs within each and every pore of his skin.
Because he supports them through meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), he has become the support of all.
By its retention and recitation, Dharma becomes a witness everywhere;
by its retention, Kubera became the lord of wealth in Bhārata;
and by its recitation and retention, Indra became the all-pervading lord of the gods.
