Through recitation and retention, Manu became the lord of kings and the sovereign;
through holding it, the illustrious Candra performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Through recitation and retention, Hari himself became the Sun, the lord of the three worlds. (9–10)
By wearing and reciting which, the fire purifies the world;
by wearing which, this wind blows and purifies the three worlds;
and by wearing which, Death indeed moves with autonomy among living beings. (11)
And twenty-one times the son of Jamadagni, Rāma, made the earth devoid of kṣatriyas by virtue of his study and mastery [of this science].
And it was through holding it and reciting it that the pot-born Agastya drank the ocean. (12–13)
The Lord Sanatkumāra, the teacher of the wise, [attained perfection] by wearing it;
as did the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who were liberated while living and perfected.
By wearing and reciting it, Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, became a perfected one.
From whom Kapila is the Lord of Siddhas, and from whom Dakṣa is the Prajāpati;
from whom Bhṛgu hates me, and Kūrma bears Śeṣa;
from whom Vāyu is the support of all, and Varuṇa is the wind. (15–16)
Because Śiva is Īśāna, the lord of the quarters, and Yama, the punisher;
because he is Kāla and Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer of the worlds;
and because by holding him within himself, Gautama became a perfected one (siddha) as did Kaśyapa, the lord of progeny. (17)
And he obtained the daughter of Vasudeva as a single portion of that [divine] part.
Formerly, upon the separation from his own wife, Rāma— the foremost of sages—
obtained Sītā, who had been carried away by Rāvaṇa in the past.
In ancient times, Nala obtained the virtuous Damayantī;
Śaṅkhacūḍa, the great hero and lord of the Daityas, [obtained her] from him;
and since Vṛṣa carries me across difficult terrain, just as Garuḍa carries Hari.
Thus did those perfected ones and the sages of old attain complete success;
for by wearing this, Mahālakṣmī becomes the bestower of all prosperity,
Sarasvatī becomes the most excellent among the virtuous, and Rati becomes full of playful delight.
Since Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, attained perfection [thereby];
since Sindhu-kanyā, the mortal Lakṣmī, obtained Viṣṇu [through it];
and since Tulasī, by wearing which, became purified as Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world. (23)
By wearing which the Earth became rich in all crops and the support of all;
by wearing which Manasādevī indeed attained perfection and was worshipped by the universe;
and by wearing which Devamātā obtained Viṣṇu as her son. (24–25)
And because of her devotion to her husband, Lopāmudrā attained Arundhatī;
and since the virtuous Devahūtī obtained the son Kapila, his mother likewise obtained two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda. (26)

And your mother also attained you, because she is the goddess Girijā. In this way, all the hosts of Siddhas shall obtain all sovereign powers through this armor (kavaca) of the auspiciousness of the world, whose [author] is Prajāpati.
The seer of this [mantra] is Gāyatrī, and the goddess herself is Rāseśvarī.
Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One should reveal it to a disciple who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and a Brāhmaṇa. (29)
By giving it to a deceitful disciple of another, one shall meet death.
O beloved, the kingdom may be given, the head may be given, but the armor must not be given;
this was worn around the neck with devotion by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
And it was seen by me in Goloka, as it was seen by Brahmā and Viṣṇu in the past: "Oṃ Rādhe," ending in the dative case and concluding with the word for the wife of fire (Svāhā).
May this mantra, worshipped by Kṛṣṇa and like a wish-fulfilling tree, protect my head. (32)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rādhikāṃ [ending with the dative case] and likewise ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā);
may this always protect the skull, the pair of eyes, and the pair of ears.
Oṃ eṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rādhikāyai [ending with the dative case] and likewise ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā).

May the King of Mantras always protect the head and the mass of hair. Oṃ rāṃ—ending with the dative case of Rādhā and followed by the wife of Fire (svāhā)—may this bestower of all accomplishments protect the cheeks, the nose, and the mouth. (35)
Klīṃ Śrīkṛṣṇapriyā [ending in] ṅe, followed by namaḥ, may protect the throat. (36) Oṃ Rāṃ Rāseśvarī [ending in] ṅe, followed by namaḥ, may protect the shoulders.
Oṃ Rāṃ Rāsavilāsinyai Svāhā, may this always protect the back. (37)
"Obeisance to the one who sports in Vṛndāvana—svāhā! May she always protect my chest.
Obeisance to the one who dwells in the forest of Tulasī—svāhā! May she protect my hips.
[The mantra] beginning with the Praṇava (Om), ending with 'svāhā', and ending with the feminine suffix '-ī', [should be recited as] 'Kṛṣṇaprāṇādhikāyai svāhā'. || 38 ||
May she protect my pair of feet and all my limbs continuously from every side.
May that Rādhā protect me in the east; may Kṛṣṇa’s beloved protect me in the southeast.
May the Queen of the Rāsa dance protect me in the south; may the Mistress of the Gopīs protect me in the southwest. (39–40)
May she who is devoid of qualities protect me in the west; may she who is worshipped by Kṛṣṇa protect me in the northwest.
May the Sovereign Lady, the Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), protect me constantly in the north.
May the Sovereign of All, worshipped by all, protect me always in the northeast.
In water, on land, and in the sky, in dream as well as in waking—
may she, the mother of Mahāviṣṇu, protect me constantly everywhere.
O Durgā, this supreme armor, which is the auspiciousness of the entire world, has been told to you.
This supreme secret, more secret than the secret, must not be given to anyone whatsoever.
Out of affection for you, I have declared it; it must not be spoken to anyone.
[Only after] having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
By wearing it on the neck or the right arm, one becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, the armor-mantra (kavaca) becomes perfected.
If the armor-mantra is perfected, one cannot be consumed by fire.

O Durgā, in former times, from this armor, King Duryodhana was certainly skilled in the solidification of water and the solidification of fire. And formerly, at Puṣkara, it was given by me to Sanatkumāra.
On the occasion of the solar eclipse at Mount Meru, he gave it to Sāndīpani;
and what was given by him to Balla, he in turn gave to Duryodhana.
By the grace of this armor, a man shall become liberated while still alive.

Whoever constantly recites this with devotion and is a worshiper of its mantra shall always become equal to Viṣṇu and obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing in all the holy fords and by giving all possible gifts—
By all vows and fasts, by circumambulating the earth, by initiation into all sacrifices, and by the constant protection of truth;
by the constant service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and by the eating of the food offered to Kṛṣṇa (naivedya). || 51-52 ||
Whatever fruit a person may obtain from the study of the four Vedas,
that same fruit one certainly obtains from the recitation of this armor (*kavaca*).
[This holds true] at the royal gate, in the cremation ground, and in a forest infested with lions and tigers.
In a forest fire, in a crisis, in fear accompanied by robbers and thieves,
in a prison, when overwhelmed by calamity, or in a terrible and firm bondage—
one who is afflicted by disease shall be liberated through the recitation of this armor-mantra (kavaca).
Thus has this been told, O Durgā; this is yours alone, O Maheśvarī.
You yourself, who possess all forms, being Māyā, ask me through Māyā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus, repeatedly remembering the narrative of Rādhikā and Mādhava,
his entire body became marked with horripilation and his eyes filled with tears.
There is no god equal to Kṛṣṇa, and no river equal to the Gaṅgā.

There is no sacred ford superior to Puṣkara, and no caste higher than the Brāhmaṇa. Just as there is nothing subtler than an atom, nothing greater than Mahāviṣṇu, and nothing more vast than the sky, O Nārada, so it is indeed.
O Nārada, just as a knower is not superior to a Vaiṣṇava, nor a lord of yogis superior to a Śaṅkara, so too by him alone were lust, anger, greed, and delusion conquered;
Śiva was perpetually devoted to meditation on Kṛṣṇa, both in dream and in waking.
As is Kṛṣṇa, so is Śambhu; there is no difference between Mādhava and Īśa.
As Śambhu is among the Vaiṣṇavas and as Mādhava is among the gods, so too, my child, is this armor the most excellent among all armors.
The word "śi" signifies auspiciousness, and the letter "va" denotes a giver.
He who is the bestower of all auspicious things is proclaimed as Śiva. He who constantly bestows welfare and prosperity upon all people in the universe [is Śiva]. (63)
The auspicious is said to be liberation; he is thus remembered as Śaṅkara.
To Brahmā and the other gods, and to the sages who proclaim the Vedas—to those great ones, he is celebrated as the god Mahādeva. (64–65)
She is the Great One, worshipped by all, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), and the Sovereign Lady.
And her husband, the God who is worshipped, is remembered as Mahādeva;
he himself is the Lord of all the great beings situated within the universe.
And for that reason, the wise call him Maheśvara.
O son of Brahmā, you are blessed that your guru is Maheśvara;
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you who bestow devotion, what is it that you ask me?

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of Her Mantras and Other Matters," within the Legend of Rādhikā, in the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Here concludes the Legend of Rādhā.
Nārada said:
O Brahman, I have heard the entire narrative, which is exceedingly and most wonderful. Now I desire to hear the supreme account of Durgā.
Durgā is Nārāyaṇī, Īśānā, Viṣṇumāyā, Śivā, and Satī.
The Blessed Lady Śarvāṇī is eternal and true; she is Sarvamaṅgalā, Ambikā, Vaiṣṇavī, Gaurī, Pārvatī, and the Sanātanī. These names, as declared by Kauthuma, bestow auspiciousness upon all. (2–3)
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the meaning of all sixteen names and the desired boon [they grant], as declared in the Vedas and approved by all.
By whom was she worshipped first, and by whom in the second instance in ancient times?
"In the third or the fourth [manvantara], by whom has she been worshipped everywhere?
Nārāyaṇa said:
"In the Viṣṇu-Veda, he established the meaning of the sixteen names."
Having understood this, you ask again; I shall explain it according to the tradition.
(6) The word *durga* refers to the Daityas, great obstacles, the bondage of worldly existence, and karma;
as well as to grief, suffering, hell, the rod of Yama, and birth. (7)
In great fear and in extreme disease, the word *āśa* denotes a destroyer.
That Goddess who indeed destroys these [afflictions] is celebrated as Durgā.
She is equal to Nārāyaṇa in fame, splendor, forms, and qualities.
This is the power (*śakti*) of Nārāyaṇa; therefore, she is remembered as Nārāyaṇī.
(9) The word *īśāna* signifies "for the sake of all accomplishments," and the syllable *ā* denotes a giver. She who bestows all accomplishments is likewise proclaimed as Īśānā. (10)
In the beginning, at the time of creation, Māyā was created by Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
The entire universe is deluded by this Māyā; thus she is celebrated as Viṣṇumāyā.
O Śivā, you are of auspicious form, the bestower of welfare, and the beloved of Śiva.
Because she is a beloved and a giver, she is proclaimed by Śiva as "Śivā.
Presiding over right intellect and existing in age after age, she who is devoted to her husband and of virtuous character is celebrated as "Satī. (12–13)
Just as the Blessed Lord is eternal, so too is the Blessed Goddess;
yet she has become concealed by her own *māyā* within that Lord during the dissolution of the material world.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, everything is entirely false and artificial.
Durgā is the very nature of truth, just as the Blessed One (Bhagavān) is Prakṛti.
All perfections, sovereign powers, and so forth exist within her in every age.
Since "bhaga" is understood to mean perfection and the rest, she is remembered as Bhagavatī.

She brings about liberation for all from birth, death, old age, and so forth, as well as for all things moving and unmoving situated within the universe; therefore, she is celebrated as Śarvāṇī. Furthermore, the word *maṅgala* signifies liberation, and the syllable *ā* denotes a giver.
She alone bestows all liberations; she herself is Sarvamaṅgalā (the Auspicious One of All).
Joy, prosperity, and well-being are proclaimed as "maṅgala";
because she grants all of these to everyone, she is therefore Sarvamaṅgalā.

The word *ambā* is a term for mother, always used in the sense of salutation and worship. Because she is worshipped and honored by the worlds as their mother, she is *Ambikā*. She is a devotee of Viṣṇu, has the form of Viṣṇu, and is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu’s power (*śakti*).
Because she was created by Viṣṇu during the act of creation, she is celebrated as Vaiṣṇavī.
(21) She is fair-complexioned, yellow, stainless, and resides within the supreme, pure Brahman;
this power of that Self is therefore proclaimed as Gaurī. (22)
Śambhu is the Guru of all, and his Śakti is Satī;

Kṛṣṇa is the Guru, and his Māyā is Gaurī—thus she is proclaimed. [23] This applies across the divisions of lunar days (tithis), the divisions of festival days (parvas), the divisions of Kalpas, and other such distinctions.

Because she is renowned among those [mountains], she is celebrated as Pārvatī; and because she is well-proclaimed as "parvan" during a special great festival, she is likewise known as such. Furthermore, she who is the presiding deity (adhidevī) of that [festival] is proclaimed as Pārvatī.
The goddess who is the daughter of Parvata manifested upon the mountain;
because she is the presiding deity of the mountain (parvata), she is celebrated as Pārvatī. She is called "sanā" because she exists at all times, and "tanī" because she is pervasive.
O great sage, the meaning of these sixteen names has been proclaimed as eternal, existing everywhere and at all times. Now,
listen to the narrative from the Vedas according to the traditional scriptures.
She was worshipped first by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
in Vṛndāvana at the beginning of creation, and in the Rāsa-maṇḍala in Goloka;
and secondly, she was worshipped by Brahmā, who was terrified by Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
In the third [instance], she was worshipped with devotion by Mahendra, who had been deprived of his glory due to a curse from Durvāsas in the past, as he was incited by Tripura against Tripurāri.
In the fourth [instance], the blessed Satī, the Goddess, was worshipped with devotion.
Then, O Sage, she was always worshipped everywhere throughout all the worlds by the lords of sages, the lords of perfected beings (siddhas), the gods,
and the foremost of munis; she had manifested long ago within the splendors of all the deities.
All the gods gave her weapons and ornaments.
By that Durgā, the Daityas beginning with Durga were slain;
she restored their own kingdom to the gods and granted them whatever boon they desired.
In another kalpa, she was worshipped by the high-souled King Suratha,
a disciple of Medha, with earthen images on the riverbank,
along with rams, buffaloes, black antelopes, and mandakas.
O Sage, having offered goats, sugarcane, cucumbers, birds,
and sacrificial oblations, as well as the sixteen services prescribed in the Vedas;
and having meditated, donned the armor (kavaca), and worshipped according to the rules.
Having offered this exemption, the king obtained the boon as he desired;
and the merchant attained liberation after performing worship on the riverbank.
Both the king and the merchant praised [the deity] with tears in their eyes and palms joined in reverence.
He cast that earthen image indeed into deep, clear water.
Not seeing that earthen image washed away by the water, O lord of men,
the Vaiśya then wept and went to another place.
Having performed difficult penance at Puṣkara,
that Vaiśya abandoned his body and went to Goloka by the grace of Goddess Durgā.
And the powerful king, being honored, returned to his own kingdom, which was now free of all thorns.
The king enjoyed his pleasures for sixty thousand years; then,
having entrusted his wife and his kingdom to his son,
he became Manu Sāvarṇi through the power of time after performing austerities at Puṣkara.
"Thus, O child, O best of sages, has the narrative of Durgā been told to you in brief according to the scriptures. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Derivation of the Names of Durgā and Others," in the *Durgopākhyāna* (Narrative of Durgā) within the second book (*Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
From whose lineage was born King Suratha, the best among the righteous? And how did he indeed attain knowledge from Medhas, the foremost of the wise? 1.
O Brahmin, from which lineage was Medhas born, O best of sages? Where did that conversation between the king and the sage take place?
And where, O Lord, did the friendship between this king and the Vaiśya originate?
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, I wish to hear this from Vyāsa; please speak.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Atri was the son of Brahmā, and his son was Niśākara."
Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, he indeed became the king of the twice-born (the Moon).
And from his wife Tārā, the wife of his guru, there was born a son, Budha.
Budha’s son was Caitra, and his son is remembered as Suratha.
Nārada said:
O great sage, how was his son born from Tārā, the wife of his guru? Alas, tell me of this transgression of the Veda! 6.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Intoxicated by prosperity and possessed of great lust, he roamed along the banks of the Ganges;
[he approached] Tārā, the wife of the preceptor of the gods, who was most virtuous and devoted to her husband.
She was well-bathed, beautiful, and lovely, with full and elevated breasts;
she possessed shapely hips and a sumptuous waist, and was slender at the middle and captivating.
She had beautiful teeth and tender limbs, and was endowed with fresh youth.

Clad in fine garments and adorned with jewel ornaments, she was radiant in the middle of her beautiful forehead with a spot of musk, a spot of sandalwood paste below it, and a spot of vermilion. 9–10.

By the wind, her lower garment was displaced; she was full of desire, with blood-red eyes, a face like the autumnal full moon, and excellent lips like the ripe bimba fruit. She was smiling yet had her face bowed in shame at the sight of the moon.
O Sage, seeing her walking toward her own home with the gait of an elephant in rut, the moon, overcome by the god of love, cast aside his shame;
with his entire body covered in horripilation and filled with desire, he spoke to her. (12–13)
Candra said: O best among women, most excellent among those who possess aesthetic sensitivity, you who are highly clever and constantly captivate the minds of the wise—wait but a moment! (14)
Having served Prakṛti for thousands of births in the ocean of desire,
Bṛhaspati attained you, O lady of broad hips, through the fruit of his asceticism.
Oh, what a pity that the Creator has joined you with such an unrefined ascetic!
You, O excellent woman, are ever devoted to the savory [pleasures] and afflicted by desire.
What happiness indeed is known in the union of the ignorant?
The union of the clever with the clever is an ocean of bliss. (16–17)
O Goddess, you too have been burnt by desire in vain;
who knows the mind of a woman—whether it be due to her actions or her own faults?
Day after day, this rare and fresh youth passes away in vain. (18)
Your husband, though advanced in age, remains in the prime of youth;
and Bṛhaspati, ever engaged in ascetic practice, dwells in meditation upon his desired self, Kṛṣṇa, both in sleep and in waking.

You, who know the essence of all desires, are free from desire yet seek the desired object; constantly meditating upon the erotic passion of youths within yourself as a passionate woman, your mind’s desire is for another, distinct from what your husband seeks. (21)
And what joy can there be in the union of two whose objects of desire are different?
Rejoice, taking me with you, in the springtime forest of Mādhavī during the season of Vasanta, upon a couch of Vāsantī flowers anointed with fragrant sandalwood.
In a secluded sandalwood forest, fragrant with blossoming flowers, may you,
a fortunate young woman, rejoice right there.
In the sandalwood grove of campaka trees, amidst the cool campaka breeze...
"Play with me upon this delightful bed of *campaka* flowers!
Having spoken thus, the intoxicated Madana, more beautiful than the God of Love himself, fell at the feet of the Goddess on the bank of the Mandākinī. (25)
With her path blocked by Candra, her throat, lips, and palate parched,
Abhītā, her eyes like red lotuses, spoke with anger.
Tārā said:
"Shame on you, O Moon! I consider you a mere blade of grass—a rogue obsessed with the wives of others.
Due to the misfortune of Atri, you are his son; your birth and life are in vain.
O wretch, having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, you consider yourself powerful! (28)
Your merit has become fruitless, since your mind is set upon the wives of Brahmins.
He whose heart is fixed on the wives of others is impure in all ritual acts;
being a sinner, he does not partake in the fruits of his deeds and is to be censured by everyone everywhere.
"You are destroying my chastity; you shall be seized by consumption (yakṣman).
It is heard in the Vedas that one who is excessively exalted meets with a fall.
Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of the pride of the wicked, will crush your arrogance."
"O child, abandon me, your mother; truth will bring you well-being.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Tārakā wept again and again, and she made Dharma, Sūrya, Vāyu, and Hutāśana her witnesses.
O sage, having heard the words of the stars regarding Brahmā, the Supreme Self, ether, wind, earth,
day, night, twilight, and the entire host of gods,
he was not afraid, but rather grew enraged.
Taking the beautiful woman by the hand, he quickly placed her upon the chariot;
and that traveler who moves as fast as thought drove the enchanting vehicle.
Having taken Manoharā, he sported with her in a most delightful manner.
In Vispandaka, Suravana, Candana, and Puṣpabhadraka; at Puṣkara on the riverbank, in the flowering forest of Puṣpaka;
and upon a bed of fragrant flowers, with the breeze of flower-scented sandalwood. (37)
In a secluded valley of the Malaya mountains, anointed with smooth sandalwood paste—
on every mountain and by every river— as the two of them indulged in amorous dalliance,
a hundred years passed in joy like a single moment, O Nārada. (38–39)
The moon became terrified and sought refuge among the Daityas, while Śukra remained resplendent as their powerful preceptor. Out of compassion, the descendant of Bhṛgu granted him freedom from fear.
They laughed at Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods and their great adversary;
the powerful sons of Diti, rejoicing in the assembly, laughed aloud.
And they granted freedom from fear to him who was terrified and stained with disgrace.
Through the destruction of Sati’s very existence within the most sinful lunar orb, the hare-form became a stain—a defilement upon the spotless [moon].
Śukra, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, spoke to him who was greatly terrified: ||| 43 ||
"It is beneficial, truthful, consistent with the Vedas, and brings about happiness in the end.
Śukra said:
"O, you are the grandson of Brahmā and the son of the venerable Atri!"
"O son, this ill-conducted deed of yours is ignoble and brings no glory.
It is like a drop of wine cast upon a mass of nectar— a stain upon the stainless circle of fame that was the excellent fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice."
Abandon the wife of Bṛhaspati—the teacher of the gods, most eminent among the virtuous Brāhmaṇas—who is as noble as one’s own mother;
she is the wife of Śambhu, the lord of the deities, the son of the preceptor, and the progenitor of the Vedas. (47)
Of his grandson, who was constantly blazing with the spiritual luster of Brahman in the lineage of Aṅgiras;
and that "the virtues of even an enemy should be spoken of, and the faults of even a teacher should be spoken of"—this is the innate nature of the virtuous born of noble lineages. (48–49)
"He is my enemy, the preceptor of the gods, and the supreme lord of the universe, the maker of the night;
nevertheless, he has been described as my 'natural brother' in the assembly of dharma.
For where there are people who are most righteous, there the eternal dharma resides. (50)
Where there is Dharma, there is Kṛṣṇa; where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory.
A cow gives birth to one calf, a tigress to five, and a lioness to seven.
Those who commit violence go to their destruction; Dharma protects the righteous.
Although the gods, the preceptors, and the brahmins are capable of protecting [one],
they nevertheless do not protect a sinful person who destroys dharma.
[This applies] regarding the approach of unchaste women, the wives of brahmins, or toward the gods and brahmins.

The sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa is certainly incurred; and by approaching those women when they have arrived [for intercourse], that sin becomes one-fourth. And if one approaches the virtuous wives of Brāhmaṇas by force, [the sin is likewise incurred]. 54.
"The sin of a hundred Brahman-murders would indeed be incurred; this is heard in the Śruti.
Practice dharma, O illustrious one, and abandon the Brāhmaṇī now. Having felt remorse for the sin, desisting from it yields great fruit. (55–56)
Indeed, by this means, your sin shall surely be removed.
For it is the law of righteousness that [one must protect] a god who has come for refuge in fear;
one who is unarmed, terrified, wretched, and seeking shelter. (57)
The most unrighteous person who does not protect [his subjects] will certainly dwell in Kumbhīpāka.
On the other hand, the protector [of his subjects] obtains the fruit of hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices;
endowed with supreme sovereignty, he shall abide here in accordance with Dharma.
Having spoken thus, the preceptor of the Daityas bathed on the banks of the Mandākinī in heaven;
he bathed him [the image] and performed the worship of Viṣṇu.
That auspicious food offering (naivedya) was produced from the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu.
He fed Candraka with the meritorious water of the Gaṅgā.
O Sage, having placed that terrified man—who was equipped for evil deeds—upon his lap, he spoke thus to him while repeatedly remembering Lord Hari, holding *kuśa* grass in his hand. (61–62)
Śukra said: "O Hari, if my austerity is true, if the fruit of worship is true, if the fruit of vows is indeed true, and if the fruit of truthful speech is true— " (63)
If the fruit of bathing at sacred fords is true, if the fruit of giving is truly true,
and if the fruit of fasting is true, then you shall be liberated from sin.
[This applies even to] a Brahmin who is devoid of the three daily prayers and bereft of the worship of Viṣṇu.
May he not incur that most terrible and exceedingly dreadful sin of the moon;
may that sinner who, having deceived his own wife, goes to another's wife,
go to a horrific hell through the sin of Rudra.
That immoral and foul-mouthed woman who strikes her beloved with words shall surely go for a Yuga to the Lālāmukha hell, cursed by the sin of the moon.
And that twice-born man who eats food offered to Hari without first offering it as *naivedya* eats in vain.
May he who digs the earth, a base man, go for four yugas to Kālasūtra as a result of his lunar sin;
may he go to Kālasūtra for a hundred yugas as a result of his lunar sin. (68–69)
And she who, having deceived her own husband, goes to another man—
let her enter the fire-pit for four *yugas* as atonement for the sin against the Moon.
She who destroys the fame of others with her own dust brings only infamy upon herself.
May that sinner who does not support his father, mother, or wife go for a yuga to the Candrapāpa and Kumbhīpāka hells;
and may he certainly become a Caṇḍāla by the sin of [neglecting] his own guru through the Candrapāpa rite. (71–72)

May that sinner who eats the food of an unchaste woman, the food of a woman whose husband is absent, the food of a woman who has just bathed after her menses, or the food of a woman during her period, certainly go to the Candrapāpa hell; may he,
by that sin, go to Kumbhīpāka for the duration of four yugas.
Therefore, having emerged from that [state], the sinner enters the womb of a Cāṇḍāla woman.
Furthermore, he who is a great sinner commits the act of village-dharma (sexual intercourse) during the day;
or he who, driven by lust, approaches a pregnant woman or one who is menstruating out of desire.
Let that sinful Candrapāpa go to the most terrible hell;
let him, by virtue of that sin, go to Kālasūtra for the duration of four yugas—
[he] who gazes upon the face, the hips, or even the breast of another's wife.

May he who is consumed by lust go to that Moon which is stained by sin; may he, due to the Moon's transgression, become a consumer of saliva for the duration of four yugas. Having emerged from that state, may he become a Cāṇḍāla, blind, and a eunuch.
On the new moon, the full moon, the solstices, the fourteenth, and the eighth days,
as well as on Sundays, he who eats meat, lentils, or breadfruit,
and practices vulgar sexual conduct— let that man go to the sin of Candra.
By that sin, may he go to the Kālasūtra hell for four yugas.
Having emerged from there, the sinner enters the womb of a Caṇḍāla;
for seven births he shall be diseased, impoverished, and indeed hunchbacked.
May that great sinner who eats on the eleventh day, on the day of Kṛṣṇa’s birth (the eighth day), or on Śivarātri, go to the Candrapātaka hell;
may he go to Kumbhīpāka for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
By that sin, may he attain the womb of a *cāṇḍāla* woman.
[Likewise for consuming] milk placed in copper, honey-wine (*madhvīka*), or even ghee when one is impure;
as well as coconut water in a bronze vessel, or milk mixed with salt. (83–84)
The twice-born who repeatedly drinks the water remaining from his bath and likewise eats the rice remaining from his meal while the sun has not yet set—
may that terrible and unavoidable sin of the moon fall upon him. (85)
May he go, by that sin, to the blind well for four yugas.
May the Brahmin Devala, who sold his own daughter, who drove oxen, who burned the corpses of Śūdras, and who served as their cook, [go there]. (86–87)
May that sinner who destroys the *aśvattha* tree and reviles Viṣṇu and his devotees go to the terrible *candrapāpa* hell;
and from that sin, may the transgressor go to the *taptasūrmī* hell.
May he be burned perpetually for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Having emerged from that, the sinner enters the womb of a Caṇḍāla;
for seven births he is a Caṇḍāla, and for five births he is a bull.

The one who defiles a sacred ford becomes a donkey for a hundred births, a pig for seven births, a crow for seven births, and indeed a dung-worm for five births; he becomes a leech for a hundred births, and thereafter may he become pure. 91.

He who eats meat in vain, as well as food cooked for his own sake alone— that great sinner, having consumed what was not given, shall incur the sin of the moon (Candrapātaka). By that lunar sin, let him go to the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) for four Yugas.
Then, for seven births, let him be a serpent and an animal;
for he who is a Brahmin usurer, one who lives off his own wife, a physician, a seller of the names of Hari, or one who sells his own limbs. (93–94)
One who speaks only of his own dharma, one who praises himself,
a seller of ink, a washerman, and one who supports a wanton woman—
let that man incur the sin of the moon, and let the moon itself be free from its fever.
May he go by that evil to a most dreadful impalement upon a stake;
may he remain pierced there as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Then, may that man become poor, diseased, devoid of initiation, and a mere beast.
One who sells lac, meat broth, sesame seeds, salt, horses, and iron is a slayer of men; let him,
along with a Brahmin who is a potter or a thief, go to the Candrayāna penance.
May he go by that evil deed onto a razor-sharp path, most difficult to endure;
may he be cut there for as long as a thousand Indras.
Having emerged from that, may he become a jackal for seven births.
For seven births he was a cat, for five births a buffalo;
for seven births a bear, and for seven births a dog.
(101) He was born as a fish for a hundred births, and as a female crab for five births.

He was a lizard for a hundred births, an ass for seven births, and for seven births a frog; thereafter he became a base human being—a leather-worker, a washerman, an oil-presser, and a carpenter. (102–103)
"A boatman, a seller of human flesh, a hunter, a goldsmith,
a potter, and an ironworker— after these come a Kṣatriya, and after that a twice-born.
Having thus made the moon pure, he spoke to Tārakā.
"O great virtuous lady, abandon the moon and go to your husband," said the twice-born man.
"Even without a formal penance, you are purified because your mind is thus cleansed.
A woman who is not of her own will, when overcome by a powerful paramour, is not defiled. (106)

Having spoken thus, Śukra likewise addressed the moon and the virtuous Tārā; with a smile, he bestowed auspicious blessings upon them both. Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Removal of the Faults of Tārā and Candra," in the Durgopākhyāna of the second section on Prakṛti within the great and holy [Brahmavaivarta] Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
What did Bṛhaspati do during the abduction of Tārakā? How did he win back that virtuous woman? You should explain this to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing that Tārā was delayed even as she was bathing,
the Guru himself dispatched a disciple to the Ganges to search for her.
The disciple went and learned the facts of the matter from the mouths of the people.
Weeping, he spoke to his own guru regarding the abduction of Tārā, O Sage.
Having heard the news that his beloved had been carried off by the Moon, the preceptor of the gods fell into a swoon for a moment; then, having regained consciousness, [he spoke].
He wept aloud with his disciples, his heart burning with anguish;
overcome by grief and shame, he lamented again and again.
(5) Addressing his disciples, he spoke words of wisdom in accordance with the Vedas.
With tearful eyes, [Bṛhaspati spoke] to those with tearful eyes, who were afflicted by grief and emaciated by sorrow.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O children, I do not know by whom I have been cursed; I am unaware of the ultimate cause."
He who acts in opposition to the Dharma undoubtedly encounters suffering.
(7) He whose virtuous wife, who speaks kindly, is not present in his home, should go to the forest; for him, the home is like the forest. (6)
He whose wife, devoted to him, has been carried off by an enemy must go to the forest; for him, the forest is like home. Alas, he from whose house a virtuous and beautiful wife has departed!
He by whom a devoted wife, whose duty is to serve her husband, has been carried away by fate—by him the forest should be entered;
for him, as the forest is, so is his home. (10–11)

He who has no mother in his house, or whose wife is not well-disciplined, should go to the forest; for him, the home is just like the forest. Even if a home is full of wealth and kinsmen, it is empty if it is bereft of a beloved wife.
He should go to the forest; as is the forest, so is the home.
Homes devoid of a wife are equal to forests, while homes with a wife are true homes.
It is said that the housewife is the home; a mere building is not called a home.
One who is impure and devoid of a wife, when performing rites for the gods or the ancestors,
shall not partake in the fruit of whatever action he performs during that day;
he is like a dull fire lacking the power of combustion.
Like the sun bereft of its radiance, like the moon devoid of its splendor;
like a living being deprived of power, or like the self (ātman) without a body;
like that which is supported without its support, or like the Lord (Īśa) without primordial nature (prakṛti). || 16–17 ||

Just as a sacrifice is not capable of yielding fruit without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), so too the totality of ritual materials is the very root for bestowing the fruit of actions. Just as a goldsmith is not capable of his craft without gold, [so it is with the performance of rites]. (18)
Just as, O twice-born ones, a potter is not capable [of his work] without clay,
so too a householder is never capable of performing any ritual action without the presiding deity of the home, who is his own wife endowed with her own power. (19–20)
All rites have their root in the wife; likewise, houses have their root in the wife.
All happiness for householders in the home always has its root in the wife.
Joy always has its root in the wife, and auspiciousness has its root in the wife.
The world of transmigration has its root in the wife; the fragrance of life has its root in the wife. (22) As a chariot is to those who ride in chariots, so is a home to householders;
and as a charioteer is to them, so is the beloved wife to householders. (23)

And the jewel among women, the foremost of all jewels, even if taken from a lowly family, is like one accepted by a householder; so said the Lotus-born One (Brahmā). Just as a lotus is without water, or as a lotus is without beauty—
"In the same way, for men who are householders, their own home is [empty] without their wife.
Having spoken thus, that guru repeatedly entered his house and repeatedly emerged from the house,
overcome with grief.
Again and again he fell into a swoon and regained consciousness;
repeatedly he wept aloud, remembering over and over the virtues of his beloved.
Then, in the meantime, he was enlightened by the great sage and by the wise ones.
Accompanied by his true disciples and other sages, he went to the abode of Purandara.
That preceptor was honored by the Lord of the Maruts with hospitality;
he then related his own story to him, which was as unpleasant as a thorn in the heart. (28–29)
Having heard the words of Bṛhaspati, Mahendra, whose eyes were like red lotuses and whose lips quivered with anger, spoke to him. Mahendra said:
"Let a thousand messengers go out on a mission of espionage—
extremely skillful, capable, and for the purpose of ascertaining the truth—
as to where the sinner Candra is, along with my mother Tārā. (31)
"I shall go there, fully prepared, together with all the hosts of gods. Cast away your anxiety, O illustrious one; everything will turn out well.
This fortress, though difficult to penetrate, contains the seeds of prosperity; for whom, indeed, is there fortune without adversity?"
Having spoken thus, O Sage, Śunāsīra dispatched a thousand messengers skilled in that task;
those messengers indeed traveled for a hundred years through a desolate wilderness.
Having wandered through all the worlds, they reached Śakra, who was extremely difficult to overcome.
Seeing the Moon in the abode of Śukra, having approached him and been freed from his fever, yet still accompanied by Tāraka and filled with fear, they reported this to the Lord.
Having heard this, Śunāsīra, his face bowed down, spoke to Bṛhaspati, tormented by grief and with a heart burning with anguish. Mahendra said:
Listen, O Lord, I shall speak that which brings about happiness in the end.
Abandon your fear, O illustrious one; all will turn out well.
Śukra was not conquered by you, nor was the son of Diti by me.
Having reflected on this, Candra went for refuge to the Poet (Kavi).
"Go quickly to the world of Brahmā along with us;
we shall go together with Brahmā to Kailāsa to see Śaṅkara. (39–40)
Having spoken thus, Mahendra, distressed along with his preceptor,
went to the world of Brahmā, which is pleasant to behold and free from affliction.
Having seen Brahmā there, he bowed down together with his preceptor.
He related the entire account to the supreme Lord of the gods.
Having heard the words of Mahendra, the lotus-born one laughed and, filled with humility,
spoke what was beneficial, true, and the essence of political wisdom.
Brahmā said:
To him who inflicts suffering upon another in every way, the eternal Teacher Kṛṣṇa gives suffering in return. 44.
I am the creator and the protector of creation, the eternal Viṣṇu;
and as Rudra is the destroyer, Śiva bestows auspiciousness.
Dharma is indeed the witness of all and the cause of everything, existing without interruption.
All the gods are possessors of sense-objects and followers of Kṛṣṇa’s command.
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, and Saṃvarta—who had conquered his senses—were the three sons of Aṅgiras, masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (46–47)
The preceptor gave nothing at all to the youngest, Saṃvarta;
he became an ascetic and meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord.
To the middle son, Utathya, he gave his virtuous wife who was pregnant.

He carried off that brother’s wife against her will out of lust. Whoever, driven by desire, should carry off his brother’s wife when she is unwilling, incurs the sin of a thousand Brahman-murders; of this there is no doubt. (49–50)

He goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. A man who abducts his brother’s wife or one who violates his mother, having emerged from that [hell] as a sinner, is born as a worm in excrement. (51)
Having remained there for thousands of millions of years, that sinner,
O Purandara, shall then become a great evildoer for another thousand million years,
existing as a worm within the pit of a prostitute’s womb.

For stealing a brother’s wife, one becomes a vulture for ten million births and a dog for a hundred births; likewise, he who, though being powerful, does not give his inheritance to one who is weak, [suffers the same]. (54)
He goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (95) Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons if it has not been experienced;
one must inevitably experience the fruit of whatever action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—one has performed. (56)

"Let Bṛhaspati, the son of the preceptor of even Śiva, the teacher of the world, ascertain the situation regarding the Lord, the foremost among the powerful. Let all the hosts of gods, equipped for battle and with their mounts, assemble. (57)
"Let the sages who dwell on the banks of the Narmadā indeed remain neutral. Afterward, I too shall go to that holy bank of the Narmadā.
Let the preceptor and his son also go quickly to the abode of Śiva. (58–59)

Mahendra said: How is it that Bṛhaspati, the son of the preceptor, became the teacher of the creator of the Vedas, of the perfected ones (siddhas), of the yogins, and of Śambhu, the conqueror of death? 60.
"Aṅgiras was your son, and Bṛhaspati was his son.
O Mahādeva, how can you, who are more knowledgeable than him, be the disciple of your father, the Guru?
Brahmā said:
O Purandara, this story is very well-guarded in the Purāṇas.
Listen as I relate this ancient account:
in former times, the wife of Aṅgiras had children who died due to the fault of her past actions.
And she performed a vow for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. She observed for one year the vow known as Puṃsavana;
the blessed Sanatkumāra caused her to perform that vow.
Then the Supreme Soul, full of compassion, the Supreme Brahman consisting of His own will, whose form is for the sake of showing grace to His devotees, arrived from Goloka.
That ocean of mercy spoke to Suvratā, who was accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Praised by her as she stood bowed down, with tearful eyes and full of humility,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Accept this fruit of your vow, endowed with my own splendor."
"Eat, O daughter, by my boon; he shall be born from a portion of myself.
By my boon, O virtuous lady, Bṛhaspati shall become your husband and son—he who is the teacher of the gods and the foremost among the great sages. (67–68)
"By my boon, he who shall be born [of you] will indeed be my son through my boon.
This son of mine shall dwell long in your womb.
He shall be the one born of the boon, the one born of valor, the one born of the field, and likewise the protector. (69)
"Vidyā, Mantra, and Suta—thus the seventh son was taken.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Rādhikā departed for his own realm.
This Śrī Kṛṣṇa-vara-putra is himself the Guru of the Lords of Knowledge.
In ancient times, he bestowed upon Śiva the great knowledge of Mṛtyuñjaya;
then, for three hundred thousand divine years, he performed penance on the Himalayas,
[bestowing] his entire yoga-knowledge, his own peerless and supreme splendor.
[He gave him] his own power, Viṣṇu’s Māyā, and his own portion, the bull as a vehicle;
[he gave him] his own trident, his own armor, and his own twelve-syllable mantra.
Thus praised by him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is full of compassion and higher than the highest, [bestowed these upon him].
In the world of Śiva, she is Śivā, the illusion (māyā) of Viṣṇu, the beloved of Śiva.
This eternal power (śakti) of Nārāyaṇa has manifested;
she is the eternal manifestation of the splendor of all the gods. (73–74)
She slew the multitude of Daityas and bestowed the realm upon the gods.
At the end of the kalpa, that Satī, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti),
who was a perfected yoginī through yoga, cast off her body at the sacrifice of her father.
That virtuous daughter of the mountain became distressed by her husband’s reproach;
in time, through her dark austerities, the beautiful woman attained Śaṅkara.
Indeed, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the preceptor of Śambhu, the Supreme Soul, higher than the highest.
This excellent son of Kṛṣṇa is Bṛhaspati himself; for this reason, he is the preceptor of the gods and the son of Śiva’s own guru. Thus has been told everything, which is most secret and ancient.
Thus, the primary connection has been described by me as it was heard;
now listen as I relate another, traditional account.
Durvāsas and Garuḍa were indeed the powerful partial incarnations (aṃśa) of Śaṅkara. 79–80.
Then those two disciples of Aṅgiras, or rather the sons of their preceptor,
when Satī had died due to the curse of Dakṣa,
forgot their own knowledge and themselves because of their delusion. (81)
Prompted by Kṛṣṇa, Aṅgiras caused him to remember [his former state]. For this reason, let that Bṛhaspati, my son and the preceptor of Śiva, go quickly to Kailāsa himself.
"Go there to the banks of the Narmadā, fully armored along with the gods.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the Creator of the worlds fell silent;
the Preceptor went to Kailāsa, and Mahendra went to the banks of the Narmadā. (84–85)

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Bṛhaspati’s Journey to Kailāsa," within the Legend of Durgā, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said:
O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences!
I have thoroughly drunk in the great narrative issuing from the moon of your mouth.
Now I wish to hear what Bṛhaspati said after going to Śiva on Kailāsa, the giver of all prosperity. (1–2)
"Was he the creator and ordainer of the world, or what did he say in reply?
Having considered all this, speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas.
(3) Nārāyaṇa said:

Having gone quickly to Kailāsa, the preceptor, his glory diminished, bowed before Śaṅkara and stood before him with his neck bent low in shame. Seeing the son of the preceptor, Śambhu rose from his seat of kuśa grass.
He quickly gave him an embrace and auspicious blessings.
Having seated him on his own throne, Śiva indeed asked after his welfare with these words.
To him, who was frightened and ashamed, Śiva spoke these sweet words.
Śrī Śaṅkara said: "O brother, why are you in such a state—miserable, with a soiled body, eyes full of tears, and ashamed? Tell me the cause of this."
O sage, was your austerity deficient, or were you deficient in the twilight prayers?
Or was that service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa lacking due to some misfortune of fate?
Or were you devoid of devotion toward your guru, or perhaps toward your chosen deity?
Or what [being] who has sought refuge and come for protection is there that you are unable to guard?
(9) Or is your guest turned away? Or are your dependents hungry?
Or is your wife independent of you? Or is your son a transgressor? (10)

Is your disciple ill-disciplined, or do your servants give you contrary answers? Is your fortune turned away from you, or is your guru angry with you? [For you are] most venerable, most excellent, and one whose mind is eternally contented.
O Guru, Vasiṣṭha is indeed your most beloved, the best among the virtuous!
(12) Is it that your chosen deity is angry, or are the Brāhmaṇas angry?
Or are the Vaiṣṇavas angry, or is your enemy powerful? (13)
Or was it the separation from your kin, or a conflict with a powerful foe? Was your position seized by an enemy, or were your kinsmen and wealth taken away?
Or by whom, O Sage, was this reproach directed at you—by wicked men or by sinners?
By which kinsman or beloved one have you been abandoned?
Or has a kinsman been abandoned by you out of world-weariness or perhaps anger?
Have you failed to bathe at a sacred ford, or have you failed to give gifts on auspicious days? (15–16)
Whether heard from the mouth of a wicked person or otherwise, reviling one's guru or reviling one's kin—indeed, for the virtuous, reviling one's guru exceeds death;
likewise is the reviling of the wicked born of an ignoble lineage. (17)
Thus, among the wicked here, immorality is constant for those destined for hell;
but in Bhārata, the virtuous, who praise others, are indeed meritorious, ever endowed with auspiciousness, and always shine with a pure mind. (18–19)
In his son, in fame, in water, in abundant prowess,
in sovereignty, in majesty, and in subjects, lands, and wealth;
in his speech, in his intellect, in his nature, and in his conduct— (20)—
The hearts of men arise according to their conduct and their dealings. Whatever is in their hearts, such is their auspiciousness;
whatever was their prior merit, such is their disposition of mind.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva ceased speaking in his own assembly.
Then Bṛhaspati himself, the great orator, spoke to him.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Lord, why do I relate this account which is truly beyond words?
Beings, under the power of karma, perform various deeds throughout many births;
in birth after birth, a living being experiences the fruit of its own actions.
For that karma is not destroyed in the land of Bhārata without its being experienced;
O Lord, pleasure, pain, fear, and sorrow for men in Bhārata—some indeed say these arise from one's own performed karma. (25)
Some say it is by fate, while others say it is by nature;
for its courses are threefold, O you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
And one is the generator of action oneself, while action indeed has fate as its cause.
The nature of human beings arises from their own previous karma.
And for all living creatures, in every birth, pleasure, pain, fear, and sorrow arise from their own selves through their own actions. (28–29)
For the individual soul (jīva) is always endowed with qualities and is the experiencer of the fruits of its own actions;
whereas the Self (ātman) is the nourisher, the witness, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
That very Self is to be served by all, and it is the bestower of the fruits for everyone. (30)
He indeed creates destiny, as well as inherent nature and action itself.
(33) Through action, men experience shame, praise, and joy;
yet I shall tell you the story of the seed of shame as well. (32)
Having spoken thus, Bṛhaspati related the entire account to him.
Upon hearing it, the Lord of Gaurī then became downcast with shame;
the rosary slipped from the hand of the Trident-bearer, who was overcome with anger.
And there was an immediate trembling in his eyes, which were like red lotuses.
Śiva is the friend of Rudra, the Lord who destroys, and of Viṣṇu, the Protector;
he is to be praised by the Creator and honored as the Supreme Self of one's own self. (34–35)
And to Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond all qualities and the Lord of Nature, O Nārada,
Śiva began to speak out of anger, his throat, lips, and palate parched. (36) Śiva said:
May there be auspiciousness here for the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas who are true beings;
may there be misfortune at every step for those who are non-Vaiṣṇavas and are wicked.
And as for that person who, though well-established, inflicts suffering upon the Vaiṣṇavas— (37) — [he shall suffer likewise].
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is his destroyer, and there shall be obstacles at every step for him.
The hearts of those who are not Vaiṣṇavas are never pure or stainless;
the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s mantra is the cause of the mind’s purity.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and the karma of those people is destroyed through the worship of the Viṣṇu-mantra.
Oh, what a most pure nature belongs to the servants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa!
Though his wife had been abducted and he was in a state of swoon, the Guru did not curse his enemy;
for the Guru was most excellent, free from anger, and righteous.
Even though this enemy had slain a hundred of his sons, the sage did not curse him.
Indeed, by the mere breath of my brother Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods,
Śatacandra would certainly have been reduced to ashes in an instant;
nevertheless, out of fear of violating dharma, he did not curse him.
The ascetic power of one who is cursed and perpetually overcome by anger surely diminishes.
Alas! This son of Atri is wicked, a lecher after another's wife, and deceitful—toward a wise Vaiṣṇava ascetic and a son of Brahmā.
The sons of Brahmā are most righteous, as are the Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas;
some are gods, some are twice-born (dvijas), and some are Daityas—thus they are considered to be of three kinds.
Those brāhmaṇas who are characterized by sattva are gods, and likewise those characterized by rajas are [Daityas].
The Daityas were characterized by darkness (tamas), fierce, exceedingly powerful, and ever-arrogant.
The Brahmins were devoted to their own duties and dedicated to Nārāyaṇa;
those gods who were Śaivas and Śāktas were honored with worship, whereas the Daityas were devoid of such honor.
Those desiring liberation are devotees of Viṣṇu; the Brāhmaṇas desire service [to him];
the gods and asuras likewise desire sovereignty, as do those characterized by tamas.
For the Brāhmaṇas, their own duty is the worship of Kṛṣṇa, which they desire.

Those Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who are free from desire and independent attain the supreme state of the Supreme Being, who is beyond qualities and even beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). Other worshippers, however, along with others, undergo dissolution into primordial nature at the time of its reabsorption.
Among the social classes, Brāhmaṇas are the best if they are virtuous Vaiṣṇavas.
A dog-eater is better than twice-born men who are devoid of Viṣṇu-mantras.
Whether they are fully matured or not yet matured, those who are Vaiṣṇavas are indeed virtuous.
The Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu constantly protects them;
just as dry grass is always reduced to ashes in a fire,
so too is sin among the devotees of Viṣṇu, like wood in a consuming flame.
The wise declare that he into whose ear the Viṣṇu-mantra enters from the mouth of the Guru is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, supremely purified;
[he purifies] a hundred generations of paternal ancestors and a hundred generations of maternal ancestors.
The Vaiṣṇavas indeed uplift their own sisters and their mother;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā, those who offer the cakes uplift the consumer of the cakes,
as do the Vaiṣṇavas for hundreds upon hundreds of men.
By the mere reception of this mantra, a person becomes liberated while living;
Yama, therefore, is greatly terrified of him, as a serpent is of Vainateya.
Indeed, even the sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā and others purify in the land of Bhārata.
O Lord of Speech, by the mere touch of those who worship the mantra of Kṛṣṇa,
all the sins that sinners have committed, however many they may be at a sacred ford,
are destroyed by the mere touch of a Vaiṣṇava. (59–60)
By the dust from the lotus feet of those who worship the mantra of Kṛṣṇa,
people are instantly liberated from their sins, and the entire earth becomes purified;
indeed, the wind, the purifying breeze, fire, and the sun all purify everything.
These [deities] are indeed purified by the mere touch of the Vaiṣṇavas through his divine play.
I, Brahmā, Śeṣa, Dharma, and the witness of all actions—these, being delighted, long for the company of the Vaiṣṇavas. (62–63)
In Bhārata, the fruit for all beings occurs in accordance with their karma;
however, it does not exist in Vaiṣṇava, just as there is no sprout in a perfected grain.
The Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, destroys the prior karma of those devotees.
The ocean of mercy indeed grants his own state to them out of compassion.
To the son of Bhṛgu, the foremost among the radiant Vaiṣṇavas, that weak and frightened Candra went for refuge. (65–66)
Sudarśana was not capable of conquering the powerful Śukra;
nevertheless, I shall rescue Tārā by means of the mantra of my guru.
Worship the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa, the Self, the Lord.
"When the Blessed One is well-pleased, you shall obtain a wife effortlessly.
O brother, I shall grant you his supreme mantra, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree,
which destroys the sins of ten million births, and which is the cause of all auspiciousness."
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, everything is perishable like a reflection in water.
Take refuge in Govinda, the Supreme Self, the Lord.
As long as there remains in men here the desire for worldly existence, the desire for enjoyment, and the desire for the pleasure of women— (70)
Until one receives the mantra of Hari from the lotus-like mouth of the Guru;
having obtained that mantra which is so difficult to attain, a person indeed becomes free from craving. Vaiṣṇavas do not desire even the status of Indra or immortality.
Indeed, they do not desire liberation without service and devotion to Hari.
A devotee does not desire the Lord’s liberation, which is the churning of devotion;
rather, knowledge, victory over death, and all perfections are what he desires.

Even the perfection of speech and the status of a creator are not desired by devotees. For he who, abandoning devotion to Kṛṣṇa, desires worldly objects, is deceived by the māyā of Viṣṇu; he has cast aside nectar and swallowed poison.
I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Ananta, Kaśyapa,
Kapila, Kumāra, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
Svāyambhuva Manu, Prahlāda, and Parāśara. (75–76)
Bhṛgu, Śukra, Durvāsas, Vasiṣṭha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Bali, the Vālakhilyas, Varuṇa, and Hutāśana;
Vāyu, Sūrya, Garuḍa, Dakṣa, and Gaṇapati himself. (77)
"These are the supreme, most excellent devotees of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
and those who are His eminent portions are likewise devoted solely to Him.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara gave him the Kalpataru mantra.
O Sage, [the mantra consists of] the seed-syllables of Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Kāma, followed by the word "Kṛṣṇa" ending in the vocative case.
O Sage, [I shall now describe] the supreme procedure for worship, the hymn, and the armor-mantra (kavaca),
as well as its preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) and meditation on the pure bank of the Mandākinī.
Having received that mantra from Śaṅkara, the teacher of the world,
the Guru became despondent within the ocean of existence and spoke to him.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Give your command, O Lord of the World; I am going to perform penance for Hari.
Let Tārā remain right there, for I have no need for her.
O Lord, I perceive everything as equal to poison and subject to decay. (83)
"I take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is truth, eternal, and beyond the material qualities.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O sage, having abandoned a woman who has been seized by another, penance is not praiseworthy."
For one who has been highly esteemed, a malicious reputation is worse than death.
(85) Go forward, O illustrious one, to this bank of the Narmadā;
where Brahmā and the other gods reside, there I shall go with haste. (86)
Having heard the words of Śiva, the preceptor of the gods himself departed;
and the illustrious Śaṅkara arrived at the bank of the Narmadā.
Seeing Śaṅkara together with his attendants, his face and eyes were serene.
All the deities, as well as the Manus and the sages, prostrated themselves.
Śambhu bowed his head to Viṣṇu and the lotus-born Brahmā.
Viṣṇu affectionately offered a seat and an embrace to Maheśa.
In the meantime, Bṛhaspati arrived there;
he prostrated before Mahādeva, Viṣṇu, and the lotus-born Brahmā,
as well as Sūrya, Dharma, Ananta, Nara, me, and the lords of the sages.
He dwelt there in that assembly with devotion toward his own guru and father;
and having reflected in his mind upon the proper course of action, he spoke there in that assembly:
"The Lord Viṣṇu himself [is present], as well as Brahmā and the moon-crested Śiva. (91–92)
Viṣṇu said:
"Both you and the sages should quickly go to the seashore and dispatch some neutral person to Śukra."
There will undoubtedly be great hardship through conflict alone;
yet, by my blessing, the Preceptor of the Gods shall certainly regain Tārā.
And being praised by the gods, Śukrācārya shall become truly satisfied.
Indeed, Śukra was not conquered by the gods because he was protected by the discus of Kṛṣṇa.
Being entreated by you both and by your hymn of praise, I have come from Śvetadvīpa, well-pleased by that hymn. (95–96)
"O Śukra, let all the deities enter into this seat made of *asī* leaves!
By means of this hymn, even the most powerful enemy shall be brought under control"—so says the Śruti.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds vanished on the spot.
He was praised by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, who bowed down and worshipped him.
O Nārada, when the Lord of the worlds had departed for Śvetadvīpa, all the gods were likewise filled with anxiety and dejected in mind. (98–99)
Having addressed the sages and the gods in that assembly, Brahmā spoke this essence of ethics,
which was approved by Śaṅkara.
Brahmā said:
"O sons, our affection is equal toward Daityas and Devas alike—toward me, Śambhu, Dharma, and Viṣṇu, the witness of all;
and the Moon has sought refuge with Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas. (101)
Śukra has not been conquered by the gods, yet he is honored by the sons of Diti.
O gods, for the sake of Tārā, I shall go to the abode of Śukra;
let all of you go to the shore of the ocean at the command of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the worlds went into the presence of Śukra.
O Sage, the gods and the brāhmaṇas then proceeded to the sandy shore of the ocean.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of the Means for Delivering the Saved Souls as Taught by Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Second Part of the First Section of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
Thereafter, what further secret transpired between the Asura and the Deva?
O Blessed One, I wish to hear it; my curiosity is great. (1)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Brahmā went to the abode of the high-souled Śukra,
which was crowded with various hosts of Daityas and adorned with pavilions of jewels.
It was surrounded by fifty crores of disciples who were exponents of the Veda,
and it was a fortress encircled by seven moats.
It was protected by hosts of guards and by hundreds of crores of Daityas.
The Creator of the worlds beheld the son of Bhṛgu in the assembly hall,
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with cloaks fashioned from rubies, and praised by hosts of sages and Daityas. (4–5)

Seeing his grandson reciting the supreme Brahman— Kṛṣṇa, the Self, the Lord— who possesses the splendor of ten million suns and is eternally blazing with the luster of Brahman, the Creator (Brahmā) was delighted in his heart.
O Nārada, Śukra considered himself successful, as did his son and grandson,
upon seeing the Grandfather, the creator and lord of the worlds.
Terrified, he rose up suddenly and prostrated with palms joined in reverence.
Having taken them, he worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings;
he praised him with supreme devotion and fervor according to the scriptures—
him who was the bestower of knowledge and mantras, and the giver of all prosperity.
The Lord of the worlds, being satisfied by Śukra’s hymn of praise alone— the giver of the fruits of all one's own actions and the most excellent in every respect—
quickly descended from his chariot and sat there in that assembly.
On an excellent jeweled throne offered by Śukra with his own head,
which was fashioned by Viśvakarman, beautiful and blazing with splendor,
Śukra bowed down to Brahmā, Kumāra, Śakuna, and Kratu.
O sage, with palms joined in reverence, she bowed with devotion to Vasiṣṭha, Marīci, Sananda, Sanātana, Kapila, Pañcaśikha, Voḍhu, Aṅgiras, Dharma, and me, Nara. (13–14)
The righteous king honored each one individually with due respect as was fitting; he had them seated upon thrones set with jewels.
All of them, their faces beaming with joy and their hearts filled with delight, bowed down in salutation.
And the hosts of sages praised the Sustainer according to the sacred tradition.
Having offered praise to them all, that poet, with palms joined in reverence, his eyes filled with tears, his hair standing on end, bowed down and spoke with humility. (16–17)
Śukra said:
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived;
for I have seen the Lord Vidhātṛ himself in his own abode. 18.
And his sons, the eternal Blessed Ones, were seen by me in person.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest, being pleased, spoke thus to me:
"O child, welcome to you; may I make you successful in your purpose. (19)
To inquire after the welfare of those who delight in their own Self is merely a mockery.
[O sages,] you are capable of making me pure; tell me the purpose for your arrival here.
Speak further, or else command me: what may I do for you?
Brahmā said:
"Distressed by our long separation, I have come to see you, my grandson.
Separation from sons and grandsons is more painful than death. (22)
"Is it well with you, O best of sages, and with your two sons and your wife?
Is it well with your own duties, with your desired rites, and even with your austerities?
Day by day, your cherished worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa remains uninterrupted. (23)
Your service to your own guru must be constant and uninterrupted. (24) The worship of the guru and his wife is the cause of all auspiciousness;
it destroys sin, mental anguish, disease, and grief, bestows merit and joy, and is auspicious. (29)
When the Guru is pleased, the beloved deity of men here is satisfied;
and when the beloved deity is satisfied, all the gods are satisfied.
For those sinners here whose Guru, the Brahmin, and the God are enraged— (26)
And for them there is no merit, and obstacles arise at every step.
But, O child, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond material nature, the Lord who is the inner self of all and devoid of the modes of nature, is eternally pleased with you because of your devotion. (27–28)
I, your preceptor, am pleased with you, as am the Creator of the worlds.
When I am pleased, Hari is pleased; when Hari is pleased, all the deities are pleased.
Now listen to me, O wise one, regarding the reason for my arrival here.
Having abducted Tārā, the virtuous wife of Bṛhaspati— the son of the Guru and Śiva himself, who was sent by the gods and is indeed the destroyer of the universe—
the Lord of the Night has come for refuge to you alone. (30–31)
O dear son, Śambhu, Dharma, Sūrya, Śakra, and Ananta,
as well as the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the guardians of the quarters, and the lords of the directions—
three crores of deities, fully equipped for battle, are advancing.
Now, upon the shore of the ocean, there are nāgas, kimpuruṣas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and guhyakas;
bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and brahmarākṣasas;
as well as kirātas and gandharvas. (33–34)
"In the battle for Tārā, I stand as a mediator along with my sons.
Give up Tārā, or else give up the war and the amorous Candra.
Śukra said:
"Let all the gods come, armored and fierce in battle!
I shall fight them all, excluding Maheśa, the supreme teacher of us all.
The Daityas said: "Śambhu is the teacher of both sides; he is to be honored and worshipped at all times."
Dharma is the witness of all, and you alone are the Grandsire.
We do not consider others to be even equal to blades of grass.
Let them come and we shall fight; go and tell [them so], O Teacher of the World. (37–38)
"O Lord, if Maheśvara comes out of compassion for the preceptor’s son,
we shall employ the Āgneya weapon and afterwards we will fight.
Brahmā said:
Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer of the universe and the best among the powerful—
O children, who indeed will engage in battle with him?
Bhadrakālī, the mother of the world, who bears a sword and a skull-bowl.
Who indeed will engage in battle with that invincible one?
That goddess has a thousand arms, is adorned with garlands of severed heads,
possesses a face a yojana in length, and is ten yojanas in width.

Her fearsome teeth were seven *tāla* trees in height, and her tongue was a *krośa* in length, exceedingly flickering and terrifying. These servants of Śaṅkara were extremely fierce, armored, and formidable. (43)
Atibhīma, Bhairava, and Nandi, who is fierce in battle—all these attendants of Śiva possess great strength and prowess. Vīrabhadra and the other heroes are as radiant as ten million suns. (44–45)
To Śeṣa, who possesses a thousand heads, the entire universe is but an ornament upon the circle of his hoods, appearing as small as a mustard seed; who indeed could be a warrior equal to him?
Even Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer, is but a servant of that Lord Śambhu.
Of the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Tripura, who blazes with the splendor of Brahman—
by whose irresistible Pāśupata weapon the entire universe would be reduced to ashes, what need is there to mention the Daityas? || 47-48 ||
By whose trident the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa was pierced—[he who is] Sudāmā, the foremost attendant of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
radiant like thirty million suns, most wonderful. (49)
He who has the *rādhākavaca* around his neck, the lord of all the hosts of Daityas,
the slayer of Madhu, Kaiṭabha, and Hiraṇyakaśipu—
that Lord Viṣṇu himself comes from Śvetadvīpa.
Having spoken thus in the assembly, the Creator of the worlds fell silent.
Then the son of Diti, the sovereign of the Dānavas, laughed and said:
Prahlāda said:
Salutations to you, O Sustainer of the World, the primordial Lord of all!
You are the one worthy of worship by all and the protector of all; what more shall I say before you?
You are the slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu, as well as of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
That discus named Sudarśana belongs to that Kṛṣṇa, who is the most perfect being and the inner self of all;
it will instantly consume our world and us as well, being unbearable to behold.
Therefore, neither Śambhu is powerful, nor is the Pāśupata weapon, O Creator;
neither Kālī, nor Śeṣa, nor the gods headed by Rudra [are powerful] compared to Him, in whose body-hairs all the worlds reside, O Lord of the Universe. (56)

Of the all-supporting, all-pervading Lord, who is even vaster than the vast, that great Virāṭ is indeed but a sixteenth part. He is infinite; he is not merely gross, nor is Kālī greater than him. (58)
"Let all the gods come and engage in battle now!
I have no fear of arrows, nor do I fear the Pāśupata weapon from Hara.
Homage to that Blessed One, Śiva, whose form is auspicious! (59)
Salutations to Ananta and to the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, O Lord of Creatures!
By the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I am fearless and free from affliction.
O Brahman, I possess no strength of my own; that which is the strength of the Lord is my strength.
In the past, our father died due to his own sin, namely the reviling of Viṣṇu;
likewise, Śaṅkhacūḍa was killed through persistence, and Madhu and Kaiṭabha through pride.
Tripura, though he was our servant, is not even counted among the ranks of heroes.
Nevertheless, urged by him, that Maheśvara, seated upon his chariot,
having spoken thus in the assembly, the best of the Dānavas fell silent;
and then, O Nārada, the Creator of the worlds spoke once again.
Brahmā said:
"O child, perform with great devotion the service of both the Daityas and the gods, for their mutual conflict is the cause of destruction, while serving them is the cause of all auspiciousness. (65)
"O Tārā, give alms to me, a mendicant and a seeker of knowledge.
O King, when a mendicant turns away from a householder, that householder incurs all the sins.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Indra among kings, protect your own fame; you are a lion to both gods and demons!
What need is there to speak of the fame of him whose mendicant is the Creator of the World?
Sanātana said:
"You have not been conquered even by the lords of the gods, led by Brahmā and Īśāna.
Protected by the discus of Kṛṣṇa, you are a Vaiṣṇava, meritorious and pure.
Sanandana said:
He whose chosen deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the Soul of all, beyond material nature—and whose spiritual master is the Vaiṣṇava Śukra; by whom could that great soul be defeated?
(69) Sanaka said:
The meritorious man is not conquered by anyone; the sinner is conquered by his own sins. The lamp of merit does not go out even by the wind of heresy.
The sages said:
"O illustrious Candra, give back Tārā, who is dearer to your preceptor than life itself!
Protect your own reputation for a very long time; we entreat you again and again.
(71) Prahlāda said:
While my Lord is present in person, a servant does not shine.
Speak of my master as the creator, the Guru Śukra, the best among the virtuous;
he is the sovereign lord over disciples and the master of the holy ones. (72)
All sovereignty was previously offered to the Lord of Sages by the Guru;
we are his servants, those to be nourished, and attendants of our own Guru.
And those disciples who carry out the Guru’s command are truly well-faring.
Having heard the words of Prahlāda, Śukra made a request to the sage;
O Sage, he gave back Tārā and the moon, which had been soiled.
Having returned Tārā and the moon, Śukra bowed at the feet of Brahmā.

Having paid homage to the sages, he departed for his own city with a bowed head. Prahlāda, together with his followers, having bowed with devotion at the feet of Brahmā and having saluted each of the hosts of sages, went to his own home.

O sage, Brahmā beheld Tārā, who was devoted to her own station and bowed before him; she had a downcast face out of shame, was weeping, and was pregnant. And the Creator, having placed the bowing Moon upon his lap by means of his illusory power, [spoke].
Filled with compassion, he spoke to the dejected and terrified Tārā:
"O Tārā, abandon fear of me; for while I am present, what cause for fear can you have?
By my boon, you shall be endowed with great fortune through your husband."

A weak woman who is seized by a powerful man shall not fall from her state if she is devoid of desire; purified by penance, she is not defiled by the paramour. But a woman with desire who, out of passion, consorts with a paramour for her own pleasure [is indeed defiled]. 81.
She is not purified by penance if she has been abandoned by her husband;
she is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Her food is excrement, her water is urine, and even her touch bestows all manner of sin.
"O auspicious one, tell me whose womb it is—whether that of a sinner or that of someone abandoned by the virtuous. Go, my child, to the house of your preceptor;
cast aside your shame, O noble lady, for everything is the result of past deeds."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Satī then said to him:
"O Father, I am currently carrying the embryo of Candra by my own karma. O Prajāpati, all [the gods] are witnesses for me, though I am weak. (85–86)
"When the merciless and evil-minded Candra seized me," having said this, the goddess Tārakā gave birth there to a beautiful boy of golden luster,
blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Taking his son and bowing to Brahmā and Īśvara, Candra went to his own abode; Brahmā went to the shore of the ocean,
and he granted fearlessness to the virtuous Tārā from her teacher and even from the gods.
Having bestowed his blessing upon Śambhu and Dharma, Brahmā departed for his own world;
the gods went to their respective abodes, and Bṛhaspati returned to his own home.
Having obtained a woman devoted to him in heart, he was delighted in mind.
Born from the womb of Tārakā, he himself was Budha;
he was radiant, a virtuous planet, a Brahmin, and the great son of Candra.
It was he who, having reached the Citrā star in the secluded Nandana grove, [attained his goal].
Having seen that beautiful, lotus-eyed girl in a secluded place— born from the womb of Ghṛtācī by the seed of Kubera,
a young maiden of sixteen years standing in the full bloom of youth. (93)
The son of the Moon took her as his wife by the Gāndharva rite; then, in secret, he begot an offspring upon her. Upon Citrā, he became King Caitra, the sovereign of the realm.
The righteous and powerful king indeed rules over the earth consisting of seven islands.
There are a hundred rivers of clarified butter, hundreds of rivers of curds,
hundreds of rivers of milk, and sixteen rivers of honey.
There were ten rivers of oils, heaps of a hundred thousand measures of sugar,
and a constant heap of a hundred thousand sweetmeats and *svastika* cakes; as well as the meat of fifty million cows, along with cakes and excellent cooked rice.
O Sage, the Brahmins enjoy the abundance of these rivers:
a hundred thousand cows, a hundred thousand gems, a hundred thousand jewels, ten million pieces of gold, and a hundred thousand fine garments. (99)
The king gave to a twice-born man an exceedingly beautiful vessel adorned with jewels, which he offered constantly until the end of his life.
And his son was Caitra, and [his other son] was King Adhiratha.
His son was Suratha, a universal monarch of great renown;
having attained supreme knowledge from Medhas, the best of sages,
he formerly resorted to the illusory power of Viṣṇu in the sacred land of Bhārata.
In the autumn season,

O best of sages, that great king Virādha, the ruler of the Kalinga country and the foremost among the Vaiśyas, performed a grand worship on the bank of the river together with that wise man. (103–104)
His son was the great yogi Drumina, the best among the wise.
Drumina, a learned Vaiṣṇava, performed difficult austerities at Puṣkara;
having attained meditative absorption, he became the foremost of the wise Vaiṣṇavas.
Cast out by his wicked sons and wife out of greed for wealth,
he nevertheless constantly gave away ten million gold pieces and drank water;
having served the eternal Viṣṇu-māyā, he attained liberation.
O Sage, the king attained the status of Manu and a kingdom free from all thorns.
The Creator, the Lord of the three worlds, spoke these sweet words.
