(108) Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Guru’s Attainment of Tārā and the Birth of Budha," within the Durgopākhyāna of the second section, the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (61)
Nārada said: How did the king obtain great knowledge from that best of sages? And how did the Vaiśya attain liberation from Medhas? You should explain this to me. (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The grandson of Dhruva was the powerful Nandin, the son of Utkala;
he belonged to the lineage of Svāyambhuva Manu, was truthful in speech, and had conquered his senses. 2.
Taking a hundred *akṣauhiṇīs* of troops,
he besieged the city of Kolā belonging to the high-minded Suratha.
O Nārada, a continuous battle took place for a full year.
The long-lived Vaiṣṇava King Suratha conquered [his enemies].
(4) Alone and terrified, having been cast out by Nandin, he mounted his horse at night and went into the dense forest. (5)
There, on the bank of the river Puṣpabhadrā, he saw a Vaiśya.
O Sage, a great affection arose between those two who had become like kinsmen.
Together with that Vaiśya Medhas, the king went to the hermitage.

Puṣkara is indeed a field of merit difficult to attain for the virtuous in Bhārata. (7) There the king beheld that sage of intense splendor, who was proclaiming to his disciples the reality of Brahman, which is very difficult to obtain. (8)
The king and the merchant bowed their heads to the eminent sage.
The sage honored them both and bestowed auspicious blessings upon them.
He then inquired after their welfare and asked each of them their caste and name separately.
The king gave his reply in due order to the bull among sages.
Suratha said:
"O Brahmana, I am King Suratha, born of the lineage of Caitra."
"Expelled from my own kingdom by the powerful Nandin, what means shall I employ now? How may the kingdom become mine again?
O illustrious one, tell me that, for I have come to you for refuge."
This Vaiśya, though virtuous, was cast out from his own home by his sons, his wife, and fate, all through greed for wealth;
yet he constantly gave ten million jewels to a Brāhmaṇa day after day. (13)
Though forbidden by his sons, wives, and kinsmen, and though rejected by them in anger, he sought them out again with grief;
yet, detached, wise, and pure, he did not return to his home. (14–15)
And the sons, out of grief for their father, abandoned their home and went to the forest;
having given gifts to the brahmins, they became detached from all ritual actions.
Service to Hari, which is very difficult to attain, was desired by this Vaiśya as well.
"How does one who is free from desire attain it? You should explain that to me.
Śrī Medhā said:
"The illusory power of Viṣṇu, which is difficult to overcome, veils him with its māyā."
And by the command of the attributeless Kṛṣṇa, the universe consisting of the three qualities exists.
She, who is composed of compassion, bestows her grace upon those righteous ones; out of that grace, she grants them devotion to Kṛṣṇa, which is very difficult to attain. (18–19)
O King, those deceivers for whom Māyā does not show compassion—she binds them with her illusion, like a net born of delusion, leading them to miserable states;
she constantly causes them to wander in this perishable and impermanent cycle of existence. || 20 ||
Abandoning the Supreme Lord, they perform acts while maintaining the notion that He is eternal;
they serve another deity and mutter its mantra, having falsely conceived some pretext in their minds out of greed. (21–22)

Having served the deities, who are portions of Hari, throughout seven births, they then serve Prakṛti through her very nature and grace. Having served the compassionate Viṣṇu-māyā throughout seven births, [they then attain liberation].
They obtain devotion to Śiva, who is eternal bliss consisting of knowledge.
And by serving Śaṅkara, the Lord who presides over knowledge, they quickly attain devotion to Viṣṇu from Maheśvara. (24–25)
Then those attached to sense objects worship Viṣṇu as possessing qualities (saguṇa).
Through the knowledge of that pure being, men indeed perceive stainless knowledge. Having served Viṣṇu who possesses qualities, those men are virtuous (sāttvika) Vaiṣṇavas.
They obtain devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is devoid of material qualities and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
His saintly devotees receive his flawless mantra;
by serving the God who is beyond the modes, they themselves become free from the modes.

Those Vaiṣṇavas indeed witness the dissolution of innumerable Brahmās; they constantly perform service in the stainless Goloka. That best of men who receives the Kṛṣṇa-mantra from a devotee of Kṛṣṇa [attains this].
He shall uplift a thousand of his male ancestors,
and likewise uplift a thousand maternal grandfathers as well as his mother.
Having uplifted his servants and others, he goes to Goloka.
In this most terrible ocean of worldly existence, she who is the very embodiment of a helmsman constantly ferries the wretched across by means of the boat of devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
and as Vaiṣṇavī, she cuts through the bonds of their own karma for the devotees of Viṣṇu.
O King, that power of the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is like a sharp weapon, is twofold:
the power of discernment (*vivecikā*) and the power of concealment (*āvaraṇī*).
The former grants [liberation] to the devotee, while the latter [grants it] to others who are beyond the Supreme.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the very nature of truth; therefore, everything else is perishable.
"Discriminative intellect" is the eternal wisdom of the Vaiṣṇavas. This intellect is my eternal form, Śrī, and it is the covering [of the self]. (35)
"O King, alas for those non-Vaiṣṇavas, the wicked who merely enjoy the fruits of their actions! I am the son of Pracetas and the grandson of Brahmā;
having attained knowledge from Śaṅkara, I worship Kṛṣṇa as my own Self. (36–37)
"Go, O King, to the riverbank and worship the eternal Durgā.
The God will grant you the obscuring intellect, for you are a seeker;
but to the Vaiṣṇava Vaiśya who is free from desire, it is the Vaiṣṇavī [intellect] that He grants. (38)
"The compassionate one will surely grant you pure, discerning intellect.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages, that ocean of mercy,
bestowed upon them the ritual for the worship of Durgā, as well as her hymn, armor, and mantra.
The Vaiśya attained liberation by serving her who is full of compassion;
the king obtained his kingdom, the status of a minister, and his desired supreme sovereignty.
Thus has this entire excellent narrative of Durgā been told.
"It bestows happiness, it bestows liberation, and it is the essence; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Fulfillment of the Desires of Suratha and the Vaiśya," within the narrative of Durgā, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (Prakṛti-khaṇḍa) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārada said:
O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me by what means did the king serve the Supreme Nature? 1.

By what means did the Vaiśya named Samādhi worship the Lord—who is free from desire, devoid of qualities, and all-pervading—through the instruction of Prakṛti? Or what was the ritual of worship, the meditation, and the mantra itself? (2)
What hymn or what armor did the great sage give to the king?
What supreme knowledge did he give to that Vaiśya, Prakṛti?
And by what means did Prakṛti suddenly manifest herself directly before them both?
Having attained that knowledge, what rare state did the Vaiśya reach?
And what became the destiny of the king? I wish to hear about that as well.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having received from the sage Medhas the mantra,
the hymn of praise, the armor of the Goddess, the meditation, and the preliminary rites,
both the king and the Vaiśya recited the supreme mantra at Puṣkara. (6)

Having bathed there for a year at the three times of day, he then became purified. There, the Sovereign Mūlaprakṛti appeared in person and granted the king the boon of sovereignty, the status of a Manu, and his desired happiness.
She bestowed upon the Vaiśya that most difficult-to-attain knowledge which is kept secret—
that very same [knowledge] which was previously given by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, to the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
Seeing the Vaiśya fasting and exceedingly distressed, she, who is composed of compassion, [bestowed it upon him].
She wept, taking him— who was motionless and breathless— into her lap;
and repeatedly crying out, "O child, regain your consciousness!",
she, who is the very embodiment of consciousness, bestowed consciousness upon him once more.
Having regained consciousness, the Vaiśya wept before Prakṛti.
She, who is exceedingly full of compassion, spoke to him with grace.
Śrī Prakṛti said:
"Choose a boon, my child, whatever dwells in your mind—
whether the state of Brahmā, immortality, or something even more difficult to attain than that;
or the status of Indra, or the status of Manu, or indeed the attainment of all supernatural powers."
"I will not give you something empty, perishable, and a deception for children.
The Vaiśya said:
"O Mother, neither the state of a Brahmin nor immortality is desired by me."
Therefore, I do not know what it is that you desire, for it must be exceedingly difficult to obtain. Having sought refuge in you alone, grant me whatever you wish;
you ought to bestow upon me a boon that is imperishable and the essence of all things.
Prakṛti said:
"There is nothing that cannot be given by me to you; I shall grant whatever you desire, for you shall go to Goloka, a station indeed very difficult to attain. (17)
O highly fortunate one, accept that knowledge which is the essence of all things and is very difficult even for the divine sages to obtain; go, my child, to the abode of Hari.
[Remember Him,] offer salutations, meditate upon Him, worship Him, and chant His virtues.

Hearing, meditating, serving, and offering everything to Kṛṣṇa—this indeed is the ninefold characteristic of devotion for Vaiṣṇavas. [It results in] the shattering of birth, death, old age, disease, and the blows of Yama. 19–20.
For the sun alone constantly takes away the lifespan of people—
especially of the wicked, the sinful, and those devoid of the ninefold devotion (navadhā-bhakti).
But the devotees of Viṣṇu, whose minds are fixed upon Him, are long-lived.
They are liberated while living, free from sin, and exempt from birth and other such conditions.
[These are] Śiva, Śeṣa, Dharma, Brahmā, Viṣṇu the Great Virāṭ,
Sanatkumāra, Kapila, Sanaka, and Sanandana.
Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Dakṣa, and the eternal Nārada; Bhṛgu, Marīci, Durvāsas, Kaśyapa, Pulaha, Aṅgiras, Medhāvī, Lomaśa, Śukra, Vasiṣṭha, and Kratu. (24)
Bṛhaspati, Kardama, Śakti, Atri, Parāśara;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Bali, Prahlāda, and Gaṇeśvara; Yama, Sūrya, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Candra, and Hutāśana. (25–26)
Akūpāra, Ulūka, and Nāḍījaṅgha, born of the Wind;
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Kūrma, Indradyumna, and Vibhīṣaṇa—these nine were endowed with devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (27)
These are great, most righteous, and likewise the foremost among devotees.
O Lord of the People, those who are devoted to Him are His very portions, eternally liberated while living,
and they remove the sins of sacred fords and the entire earth.
Above are the seven heavens and the earth with its seven continents;
below are the seven netherworlds, and this indeed is the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
O son, there is no end to the number of such universes.
And thus, in every universe, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and other gods,
as well as divine sages, Manus, and human beings;
all stages of life exist everywhere, yet they are all bound by Māyā.
Within a single pore of Mahāviṣṇu reside all the universes;
he is the Great Virāṭ, who is a sixteenth part of Kṛṣṇa and of the Self.
Worship the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, who is eternal, devoid of qualities, and infallible.
The Lord who is beyond primordial nature, Kṛṣṇa, the desired Self—He who is effortless, formless, changeless, and stainless;
free from desire, free from opposition, eternal bliss, and everlasting. (34, 39)

He whose form consists of all things and is composed of His own will, whose body is the embodiment of grace toward His devotees; He who is the supreme essence of light, the bestower of all prosperity;
He who is unattainable through meditation and difficult even for Śiva and other yogis to propitiate. (36)
The Lord of all, worthy of worship by all, the bestower of all desires to all;
the support of all, the omniscient, the supreme source of all bliss;
the giver of all dharma, the All, the omniscient, whose form is the vital breath.
The true nature of all phenomena, the cause of all causes,
the giver of happiness, the giver of liberation, the essence, the supreme form, the bestower of devotion,
the giver of service, the giver of righteousness, and the granter of all perfections to the virtuous. (39)
Everything else besides that is perishable, artificial, and ever-changing.
[It is] the Supreme beyond the supreme, pure, most perfect, and auspicious.
Go as you please, my child, to the Blessed Lord Adhokṣaja.
Having taken up this two-syllable mantra "Kṛṣṇa," which bestows the state of being Kṛṣṇa’s servant,
go to Puṣkara, that difficult-to-reach place, and recite it one million times.
By reciting it exactly one million times, the perfection of the mantra shall be yours.
Having spoken thus, that Blessed Lady vanished right there.
O Sage, the Vaiśya bowed to her with devotion and went to Puṣkara;
having performed difficult austerities at Puṣkara, he attained the Lord Kṛṣṇa.
By the grace of the Blessed Lady, he became a servant of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Dialogue between Prakṛti and the Vaiśya," within the "Account of Durgā" in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O highly fortunate one, hear now that very sequence as declared in the Vedas, by which the king attained that supreme state:
having bathed and sipped water, the great king then performed the three-fold assignment (nyāsa).
He performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) for his own limbs and the mantras of those limbs;
then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the purification of the conch,
and having meditated upon the Goddess within the earthen image, he then performed the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Having meditated again, he worshipped with devotion;
and having established Kamalālayā on the right side of the Goddess,
that most righteous one worshipped her with a spirit of devotion and with great reverence.
O Nārada, having invoked the six deities into the pitcher before the Goddess, he worshipped them with devotion according to the prescribed rites:
Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā.
Having worshipped and paid homage to the group of six deities,
the wise man should then meditate upon the Great Goddess with devotion through this meditation,
O Sage; and this meditation, as declared in the Sāmaveda, is the supreme wish-fulfilling tree.
One should constantly meditate upon the Great Goddess, the Sovereign Primordial Nature (Mūlaprakṛti);
she who is eternal, worthy of worship and salutation by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
Nārāyaṇī, the Illusion of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā), the Power of Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇavī), and the bestower of devotion to Viṣṇu.
She who is the essential nature of all, the support of all, and higher than the highest;

she whose nature consists of all knowledge, all mantras, and all powers; she who possesses attributes and is yet devoid of attributes, the existent one, the supreme, composed of her own will, and the eternal truth. (10)
The mother of Mahāviṣṇu, born from half the body of Kṛṣṇa;
the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the power (śakti) of Kṛṣṇa, the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s intellect;
she who is praised by Kṛṣṇa, worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, and saluted by Kṛṣṇa—she who is composed of compassion.
She possesses the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to ten million suns;
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and she bestows grace upon her devotees.
She is the goddess Durgā, possessing a hundred arms, the destroyer of great misfortune. (13)
The virtuous one, beloved of Trilocana, who possesses the three qualities and has three eyes;
she whose form is the very life-breath of Trilocana, who bears a pure crescent moon upon her crest, and who wears a mass of braided hair adorned with garlands of jasmine. (14–15)
She has a circular left face that enchants the mind of Śambhu;
she is radiant with a pair of jeweled earrings upon her cheeks,
and she wears an elephant-tusk earring on the right side of her nose.

She bore upon her ears many priceless jewels; she was exquisitely adorned with a row of teeth that put even strings of pearls to shame; her lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit; she was most gracious and supremely auspicious. (17–18)
Resplendent with a pair of cheeks made beautiful by rows of variegated leaf-patterns;
adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets;
enriched with ornaments of jeweled bangles and graced by a jeweled waist-belt. 19.
Her mass of fingers was radiant with clusters of jeweled rings;
she was exquisitely beautiful with lines of red lac clinging to the nails of her toes;
she wore garments as pure as fire and was anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste.

Bearing a pair of breasts adorned with a spot of musk, she possessed every beauty and virtue; she moved with the slow gait of a lordly elephant, was exceedingly lovely, tranquil, and perfectly accomplished in the yogic perfections. (22)
She is the ordainer of the Ordainer, the sustainer of all, and the bringer of auspiciousness;
her face is like the full moon of autumn, exceedingly beautiful,
with a spot of musk and a drop of sandalwood paste below it.
Her forehead is eternally radiant with a dot of vermilion;
her eyes possess the luster of lotuses at midday in autumn;
and she is resplendent on all sides with two beautiful lines of collyrium.
Her form was irreproachable in its playful grace, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids;
she sat upon a jeweled lion-throne, radiant with a crown of excellent gems—the very embodiment of the Creator’s artistry in creation and the Protector’s compassion in preservation. (26–27)
At the time of dissolution, she is the supreme destroyer of the Destroyer, possessing the form of destruction;
she is the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
In ancient times, during the battle with Tripura, she was praised by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
In the battle between Madhu and Kaiṭabha, she was the embodiment of Viṣṇu’s power;
she was the slayer of all Daityas and the destroyer of Raktabīja.
And during the slaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, she took the form of the power of Nṛsiṃha.
"I always worship the power of Varāha in the Vārāha incarnation during the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa— that which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman and the embodiment of all powers.
Having meditated thus, the wise one should place a flower upon his own head.
Having meditated again with devotion, one should then perform the invocation (āvāhana).
Then, having taken up the image of Prakṛti, a person should recite this mantra: "Then, one should diligently perform the ritual placement of the life-force (jīvanyāsa) with this mantra. (32–33)
Come, come, O Blessed Mother, eternal one from the world of Śiva!
Accept my autumnal worship, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Come here, O you who are worshipped by the world; stay, stay, O Great Goddess!
O Mother, O Ambikā, be firmly established within this image;
O Acyutā, let your vital breaths come here along with those of the presiding deities.
Let all your powers also come here swiftly.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, and likewise ending with the wife of fire (svāhā) for Durgā; having recited this, [one should say]: "May the vital breaths always abide here in Sadāśiva.
O Caṇḍikā, may the presiding deities of all the senses come here.
"May those powers come here; may the lords come here!
(38) Having thus invoked with "May he come here," he performs the ritual dismissal (*parihāra*).
O best of Brahmins, listen with a concentrated mind to this mantra: (39)
Welcome, O Blessed Mother, beloved of Śiva, from the world of Śiva!
Grant me your grace, O Auspicious One; O Bhadrakālī, salutations be unto you!
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose; my life has become fruitful.
"O Durgā, O Consort of Maheśvara, since you have come to my abode from such a difficult place,
today my birth has become fruitful and my life meaningful,
because I am worshipping Durgā in the holy land of Bhārata. (41–42)
The wise man who worships you, the worshipful Durgā, in Bhārata,
attains supreme sovereignty here and goes to Goloka at the end.
Furthermore, having performed the worship of Vaiṣṇavī, the intelligent one shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
And having fully worshipped Māheśvarī, one goes to the world of Śiva.
Worship is threefold—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa;
that of the Blessed Goddess, as declared in the Vedas, is likewise classified as superior, middling, and inferior.
The worship of the Vaiṣṇavas is indeed *sāttvika*, while that of the Śāktas and others is *rājasa*. That of the uninitiated, the wicked, and others is recorded as *tāmasa*.
However, the supreme Vaiṣṇava worship is free from the taking of life.
The Vaiṣṇavas go to Goloka by virtue of offering oblations to the Vaiṣṇavīs.
Those who follow Māheśvarī and those who are Rājasic, when accompanied by the offering of oblations, as well as the Śāktas and others who are Rājasic, likewise go to Kailāsa. (47–48)
By that worship of yours, even Kirātas go to the third heaven.
O Mother of the worlds, you alone bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life;
you are the very embodiment of all powers of the Supreme Soul, Kṛṣṇa.
You are the remover of birth, death, old age, and disease, and you are higher than the highest.
You are the giver of happiness and liberation, auspicious, and the eternal bestower of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
O Nārāyaṇī, O Mahāmāyā, O Durgā, O destroyer of misfortune!
"By the mere remembrance of Durga, one crosses over difficult passages here for men.
Having thus performed the rite of avoidance on the left side of the Goddess,
the practitioner should place a conch shell upon the Tripadī.
There, having offered full water along with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and sandalwood,
and holding [the conch] with his right hand, a person should recite this mantra:
"O conch, you are the merit of merits and the most auspicious of auspicious things."
"In a former kalpa, you were the pure Pavitraka born from Śaṅkhacūḍa.
(54) Then, having placed the vessel for the *arghya* offering according to this rite, the wise man should worship the Goddess with the sixteen services (*upacāras*) after making the offering. (55)
Having fashioned a triangular mandala with water and *kuśa* grass,
the righteous practitioner should there worship Kūrma, Śeṣa, and the Earth.
He should place a tripod there, and upon that tripod, a conch shell.
Then, having added water to the extent of three parts in the conch, one should worship it [with these words]:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, and Kauśikī! 57–58.
Svarṇarekhā, Kanakhala, Pāribhadra, and Gaṇḍakī; Śvetagaṅgā, Rudrarekhā, Pampā, Campā, and Gomati;
Padmāvatī, Triparṇāśā, Vipāśā, Virajā, and Prabha.
"O Śatahradā and O Gaṅgā of the Celas, take up your residence in these waters!
One should worship there in the water Agni, Sūrya, Candra, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Śiva with Tulasī and sandalwood."
One should sprinkle all the food offerings with that water.
Then, one should indeed present each of the sixteen services (upacāras) individually:
the seat, clothing, water for the feet, water for bathing, and unguent.
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), fragrance, the water of honor (arghya), flowers, desired food offerings (naivedya), again the water for sipping (ācamanīya), betel leaf, jewel ornaments,
incense, a lamp, and a bed— these are the sixteen services (upacāras). (63–64)
"O beloved of Śaṅkara, please accept this excellent and supreme lion-throne, fashioned from priceless jewels and resplendent with various colorful designs;
it originates from the thread of Ananta and was created by the will of the Lord. (65)
O Auspicious One, please accept this garment purified by a blazing fire.
O Goddess Durgā, please accept this pure water of the Ganges contained in a vessel of priceless jewels for the purpose of washing your feet.
O Supreme Goddess, please accept this fragrant, unctuous liquid of *āmalakī* which is very difficult to obtain, as well as this well-ripened *viṣṇutaila*,
along with fragrant melted sandalwood smeared with musk and saffron. (68)

O Mother of the World, please accept this fragrant unguent. O Great Goddess, please graciously accept this honey-mixture (madhuparka), which is contained in a vessel of jewels, most pure, and highly auspicious. (69–70)
O Goddess, accept from me this fragrant powder of roots, blended with aromatic substances— most pure and worthy of auspicious rites—
as well as this sacred offering placed in a conch vessel, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). (71)
"O Caṇḍī, accept from me this arghya, the water of the Mandākinī from heaven;
and accept this most fragrant, excellent flower born of the Pārijāta tree.
O Mother of the World, let these various garlands of flowers and other offerings be accepted. (72–73)
"O Śivā, please accept this divine offering of prepared food, uncooked rice, flour-cakes, milk-rice and the like, sweetmeats, and fruit-laddus.
[Please accept] this well-scented, cool water, thoroughly refined with camphor and other ingredients. (74)
"O Daughter of the Mountain, please accept this which has been offered by me with devotion.
O Goddess, please accept this beautiful betel-roll, scented with camphor and other fragrances and made from the powder of betel leaves, which provides all enjoyments."
"O Goddess, please accept this ornament, which by the will of the Lord is inlaid with the essence of priceless jewels and brings beauty to every limb;
it is also powdered resin of young trees combined with fragrant substances. (77)
O Goddess, please accept this incense, purified by the flames of the sacrificial fire. O Supreme Sovereign, please accept this most holy lamp, a special divine jewel that dispels dense darkness.
"O Goddess, please accept this divine and supreme couch, strewn with heaps of the finest jewels and woven with fine fabrics.
O Sage, having thus worshipped Durgā, one should offer a handful of flowers.
Then, one should diligently worship the eight goddesses who are the leaders:
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Aticaṇḍā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍā, and likewise Caṇḍavatī. (81–82)
Likewise, upon an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship these [deities] starting from the east in sequence;
having worshipped them with the five offerings, one should worship the Bhairavas starting from the center—
first Mahābhairava and likewise Saṃhārabhairava.
Asitāṅgabhairava and Rurubhairava, Kālabhairava and likewise Krodhabhairava; Tāmracūḍa and Candracūḍa—these are indeed the final pair of Bhairavas. (84–85)
Having worshipped these, one should indeed worship the nine Śaktis in the center;
there, in the eight-petaled lotus, one should worship with devotion in the center Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, and likewise Māheśvarī. (86)
Having worshipped the nine Śaktis— Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Kārttikī,
as well as Sarvaśaktisvarūpā, Pradhānā, and Sarvamaṅgalā—
one should worship the deities within the water-pot (ghaṭa).
Having worshipped Śaṅkara, Kārttikeya, Sūrya, Soma, Hutāśana,
Vāyu, Varuṇa, as well as the Goddess’s handmaidens and the young brahmin student (baṭu),
and having duly honored the sixty-four Yoginīs according to the prescribed rites.
Having offered the *bali* offering according to his capacity, the wise man performs a hymn of praise (90).
Having tied the armor (*kavaca*) around his neck and recited it with devotion,
the discerning one should then perform a circumambulation and offer salutations (91).
And listen, O best of sages, to the procedure for the offering of the sacrifice:
one should offer a goat, a ram, or other auspicious animals such as a buffalo that represents Māyā.
Through the gift of Māyā’s enemy, Durgā remains well-pleased for a thousand years.
From a buffalo one obtains [the fruit] for a hundred years, and from a goat for ten years;
from a ram for one year, and likewise from pumpkin gourds, birds, and deer; from black antelopes for ten years, and from gaṇḍaka deer for a thousand years. (93–94)
O Nārada, [one may offer] animals made of flour for six months,
and for one month, well-ripened fruits and unbroken grains (akṣata). [The animal should be] young, free from disease, possessing horns, and endowed with auspicious marks.
If the gold is pure, of unaltered quality, well-refined, and substantial, Caṇḍikā destroys the son of the donor by means of a young and strong child;
by means of an old one, she destroys the elders; and even by means of a thin one, she destroys beloved kinsmen. (96–97)
Wealth [is indicated] by an extra limb, and likewise offspring by a missing limb;
a beloved woman by a broken horn, and a brother by being one-eyed. Death occurs through a club-like [mark], while obstacles arise from various head-marks.
One who has fallen from prosperity destroys his friend by means of copper-backed [arrows], and due to the loss of his tail [he is ruined].
O best of sages, hear now the true nature of those who have transcended illusion;
I shall describe that which is declared in the Atharvaveda, for there is a loss of fruit in its transgression.
A youth who is bereft of father and mother, free from disease, married, initiated, and devoid of another's wife;
one born of a goat, pure, and nurtured by a virtuous Śūdra. (101)
Having given wealth to its owners exceeding the price paid for it,
the performer, after bathing the image, should worship it with garments, sandalwood paste,
garlands, incense, vermilion, curd, gorocanā, and other offerings. (102–103)
Having rotated that wheel with effort by means of a servant,
and having released it at the end of the year, one should offer it to Durgā.
Furthermore, at the junction of the eighth and ninth lunar days, one should present the Māyātīrtha itself.

Thus has everything regarding the offering of the *bali* been explained in its proper context. Having praised the *bali*, offered it, and donned the armor (*kavaca*), the wise man should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Specific Details Regarding the Ritual of Worship, the Sacrificial Offering, and the Characteristics of the Animal Victim," in the *Durgopākhyāna* (The Legend of Durgā) within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the second section (*Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārada said:
"O highly fortunate one, I have heard everything; it is the supreme excellence, like the essence of nectar."
"O Lord, tell me the hymn, the armor, the fruit of the worship, and the proper time.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"One should awaken the Goddess under the asterism Ārdrā, and cause her entry under Mūla alone."
Having worshipped her with the Uttarā [Phalgunī] constellation, one should dismiss her on the day of Śravaṇā.
But by performing the awakening of the Goddess on the ninth lunar day conjoined with Ārdrā,
a human being obtains the fruit of a hundred years of worship.
By entering at Mūla, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice (naramedha).
Having performed the ritual dismissal of the Goddess on Śravaṇā, a person obtains fortune, sons, and grandsons; of this there is no doubt.
O Nārada, even in the absence of an auspicious conjunction of the stars, a man obtains the merit of circumambulating the earth by performing worship on the ninth day;
having performed the awakening rite, he should worship throughout the fortnight.
On the tenth day, one should perform the dismissal for the sake of obtaining the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Having performed worship on the seventh day, the wise man should offer an oblation (bali).
On the eighth day, worship is recommended, but it should be devoid of the offering of an oblation.
On the eighth day, by the offering of a bali sacrifice, misfortune arises for men.
On the ninth day, a wise person should devoutly offer a bali according to the prescribed rite.
O best of Brahmins, through the offering of the bali, Durgā becomes pleased with men.
One incurs no sin arising from violence in the performance of a sacrificial rite.
The one who releases [the animal], the giver, the one who cuts it, the one who nourishes it, the protector,
the one who binds it in front, and the one who binds it behind— these seven are not perpetrators of slaughter.
"He who kills him, he does not kill him"—this is indeed what is declared in the Vedas.
For that reason, the Vaiṣṇavas perform the worship of Viṣṇu.
Having thus worshipped with devotion for a full year, Suratha—
Having bound the armor around his neck, he praised the Supreme Goddess.
Pleased by his hymn of praise, she appeared before him in person.
He beheld the Goddess before him, radiant with a splendor like that of the summer sun.
Having seen her—the supreme, excellent one whose nature is splendor, both with attributes and without attributes—desirable and situated in the midst of a circle of light;
she who consists of her own will, whose form is compassion, and who bestows grace upon her devotees. (15)

Then the lord of kings, his neck bowed low with devotion, praised her once more. (16) Pleased by that hymn of praise, the Mother of the World, smiling with compassion, spoke these truthful words to the lord of kings out of her devotion. (17)
Prakṛti said:
"O King, having approached me in person, you choose wealth as your boon.
I shall now grant you the wealth that you desire. (18)
"O Great King, having conquered all enemies and obtained a kingdom free from thorns, you shall become the eighth Manu, Sāvarṇi. And in the end, O lord of men, I shall bestow knowledge upon you. (19)
That dull-witted person who, having directly attained Me, the Supreme Soul Śrī Kṛṣṇa, chooses worldly opulence instead of devotion and service to Him,
is indeed deceived by Māyā; he is like one who would reject nectar and consume poison.
Everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is indeed perishable;
the eternal, true, supreme Brahman is Kṛṣṇa alone, who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
I am the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest, being higher than the highest.
She is both with attributes and without attributes, always supreme and consisting of her own will;
she is eternal and non-eternal, possessing all forms, and the cause of all causes.
She is the seed-form of all things, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), and the Sovereign Goddess.
In the auspicious and delightful Vṛndāvana, in Goloka within the circle of the Rāsa dance, I am Rādhā, dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
I am Durgā, the illusory power of Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the intellect. (25)
I am Lakṣmī, and in Vaikuṇṭha I am the goddess Sarasvatī herself.
From the world of Brahmā, I am Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, and Brahmāṇī.
I am Gaṅgā, Tulasī, and the Earth, the support of all.

"O King, through my various powers of *māyā*, I am all women. I, who was created by Kṛṣṇa with the mere play of a frown—the very same frown by which the Great Virāṭ was created—[am now united with him]. (28)
Indeed, within the pores of his body, there are always all things;
they are both innumerable and created by his illusory power (māyā). And everyone constantly perceives permanence in that which is impermanent. (29–30)
The earth, endowed with the seven oceans and consisting of seven continents, lies there;
beneath it are the seven netherworlds (pātālas) and likewise the seven celestial realms (svarlokas).
Thus, this manifold universe, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), was created by Brahmā.
In every cosmic egg, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
yet the knowledge that Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of them all is the highest of the high.
So too is it the supreme goal of the Vedas, of vows, of sacred fords, and of austerities.
It is remembered that Kṛṣṇa is the very essence of all the gods.
That fool who is devoid of devotion to Him is certainly dead while still alive.
And even the sacred pilgrimage sites are purified by the wind from the touch of His devotee.

And one who worships that mantra is known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Merely by receiving the mantra, a person becomes Nārāyaṇa, even without recitation, without austerity, without pilgrimage, and without ritual worship. (36–39)
Having thus delivered one hundred of his maternal grandfathers and a thousand of his paternal ancestors, he goes to Goloka.
O lord of men, this essential knowledge has been told to you.
"At the end of the Manvantara, when my enjoyments have ceased, I shall bestow devotion upon you toward Hari.
(38) Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of Kalpas if it has not been experienced;
whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced. (39)
To whomsoever I grant favor, I shall bestow upon them stainless,
unwavering, and very firm devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
To whomever I apply deception, I shall bestow wealth upon them.
"In the morning, [it is seen] as having the nature of a dream, false, and consisting of delusion.
(41) "Thus has this knowledge been told to you; go, my child, as you please.
Having spoken thus, the Great Goddess vanished right there. (42)
Having obtained the kingdom and having bowed to her, the king departed for his home.
Thus, O child, has this excellent narrative of Durgā been told to you.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Knowledge," within the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa in the *Durgopākhyāna*, in the Dialogue between Prakṛti and Suratha, in the second section (*Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārada said:
"Everything has been heard; indeed, nothing remains uncertain.
O best of sages, tell me the armor and the hymn of Prakṛti. (1)
Nārāyaṇa said:
In ancient times, she was praised by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
in Goloka during the month of Madhu, after he had worshipped her in the joyful circle of the Rāsa dance.
In the past, during the second battle between Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
at that very time when her life was in peril, Durgā was praised there by Brahmā;
and in the fourth [instance], the Goddess was praised with devotion by the enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
O Sage, in the past, during the most terrible battle of Tripura,
the Goddess was praised by Śakra and all the gods in the fifth [chapter], as well as during the slaying of the demon Vṛtra in that horrific crisis of life.

Then she, who is higher than the highest, was praised and worshipped in every kalpa by the lords of sages, by Manu, and by humans such as Suratha and others. O Brahmin, listen now to this hymn which destroys all obstacles.
It bestows happiness, grants liberation, is the essence, and is the cause for crossing over worldly existence.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
You alone are the mother of all beings, the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti), and the Sovereign Goddess.
You alone, consisting of the three *guṇas*, by your own will, are the primordial one in the process of creation.
For the sake of the task to be accomplished, you appear endowed with qualities (*saguṇā*), yet in reality you are yourself devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā*).
You are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman—truthful, eternal, and everlasting.
She whose essential nature is light, the supreme one whose form is the grace bestowed upon devotees;
she who is the nature of all, the sovereign of all, the support of all, higher than the highest.
She is the nature of the seed of all, worthy of worship by all, and without any external support.
She is omniscient, auspicious in every way, and the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
She is the very nature of all intellect and the embodiment of all powers.
The Goddess bestows all knowledge; she is all-knowing and the source of all that exists.

You are *svāhā* in the offering to the gods, and you yourself are *svadhā* in the offering to the ancestors; you are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in every gift, the embodiment of all power. You are sleep, you are compassion, you are thirst, and you are the beloved of the Self.

She is the forbearance of hunger, the sovereign peace, the eternal creation, faith, nourishment, lassitude, modesty, splendor, and compassion. She is Śrī, the embodiment of prosperity for the virtuous and misfortune for the wicked in this world. (13–14)
She is the form of joy for the meritorious and the sprout of strife for the sinful;
she is the power consisting of eternal karma for all living beings at all times. She bestows her own state upon the gods and is the compassionate nurse of the Creator. (15)
For the welfare of all the gods, she is the destroyer of all asuras.
She is the yogic sleep (yoginidrā), the embodiment of yoga, and the bestower of yoga upon yogins.
She is the very nature of perfection for the perfected ones (siddhas), the giver of perfection, and the Siddhayoginī.
Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Viṣṇumāyā, and Vaiṣṇavī; Bhadradā, Bhadrakālī, and she who strikes fear into all the worlds (18);
the village goddess in every village, and the household goddess in every house.
You are always the fame and the standing of the virtuous, while you are the censure of the wicked.
In great battles, you are the great pestilence in the form of the destruction of the evil;
yet for the disciplined, you are the very embodiment of protection, acting for their benefit like a mother.
You are always to be saluted, worshipped, and praised by Brahmā and the other gods;
you are the Brahman-nature of the Brāhmaṇas, the asceticism of ascetics, the knowledge of the learned, and the intellect of the wise and virtuous. (21)
You are the nature of intelligence and memory, and the creative intuition of those possessed of genius.
You are the majesty of kings and the form of commerce for the merchant class.
In the act of creation you are the very essence of creation, and in the act of preservation you are the form of protection.
Likewise, at the end, you are Mahāmārī, worshipped by all throughout the universe;
you are Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Moharātri, and the Enchantress (Mohinī).
You are my Māyā, difficult to overcome, by which the entire world is deluded.
"By which even a learned man, being deluded, does not perceive the path to liberation.
(25) Thus, this hymn to Durgā, which destroys all difficulties, was composed by Ātman.
Whoever recites it at the time of worship shall attain their desired success. (26)
A barren woman, one who gives birth only to daughters, one whose children die, or one who is unfortunate—
by hearing this hymn for one year, she will certainly obtain a virtuous son.
Even one who is bound with firm fetters in a most terrible prison, [is liberated].
Having heard this hymn for one month, one is certainly released from bondage.
(28) One afflicted by consumption, suffering from trickling leprosy, great colic, or high fever—having heard this hymn for one year, is immediately freed from disease. (29)

One who is distressed due to separation from a son, separation from subjects, or separation from a wife, shall obtain [their reunion] by reciting this hymn for one month; there is no doubt about this. Whether at the royal gate, in a cremation ground, in a great forest, or on a battlefield—
Upon hearing this hymn in the presence of violent creatures, one is liberated.
Even in the event of a house fire, a forest conflagration, or being surrounded by an army of bandits, one attains safety merely by hearing this hymn; of this there is no doubt. (31–32)

"Even one who is extremely poor and foolish, if he recites this hymn for a year, shall become possessed of knowledge and wealth; of this there is no doubt. (33) Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Durgā," within the Legend of Durgā, in the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (66)
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, proficient in all branches of knowledge, please tell me the armor of Prakṛti known as the "Deluder of the Cosmic Egg. (1)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, my child, I shall speak of the armor (kavaca) which is very difficult to obtain;
it was formerly told out of compassion by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself to Brahmā. 2.

Everything was told by Brahmā for the sake of dharma on the bank of the Jāhnavī; and out of compassion at Puṣkara, the Lord graciously gave it to me. Having taken that [weapon], the enemy of Tripura formerly destroyed Tripura.
That which Dhātṛ wore and thereby dispelled the fear of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
that which Bhadrakālī wore and slew Raktabīja;
and that which Mahendra wore and thereby attained the abode of Kamalā—[that is this]. (4)
By wearing which Mahākāla became long-lived and righteous;
by wearing which the great wise Nandin was filled with joy;
and by wearing which the great warrior Rāma became a terror to his enemies.
By wearing which Durvāsas, the best among the wise, became equal to Śiva.
Oṃ Durgāyai Svāhā—may this mantra ending in the dative case and concluding with "Svāhā" protect my head.
This six-syllabled mantra is a wish-fulfilling tree for devotees.
O Sage, there is no deliberation (*vicāra*) regarding the reception of the *manas* in the Vedas.
(8) Merely by receiving the mantra, a person becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
May my mouth always protect [me] with "Oṃ Durgāyai namaḥ" at the end. (9)
Oṃ Durgā protects the throat; may she always protect mine.
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—may this mantra protect my shoulders continuously.
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ—may it always protect my back from all sides.
May *hrīṃ* protect my chest, and may *śrīṃ* constantly protect my hand.
(11) May *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ* protect all my limbs, both in sleep and likewise in waking.
May Prakṛti protect me in the east, and may Caṇḍikā protect me in the southeast. (12)
May Bhadrakālī protect [him] in the south, and Maheśvarī in the southwest; may Vārāhī protect in the west, and Sarvamaṅgalā in the northwest;
may Vaiṣṇavī protect in the north, and likewise Śivapriyā in the northeast.
"May the Mother of the World protect me in water, on land, and in the atmosphere.
(14) Thus, O child, this armor (*kavaca*) which is very difficult to obtain has been told to you.
It must not be given to just anyone, nor should it be spoken of to anyone at all. (15)
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste, he who wears this armor is indeed Viṣṇu himself; of this there is no doubt.
[This is equal to] wandering through all the holy fords and performing circumambulations of the entire earth.
O Sage, whatever fruit the world obtains, that is gained through this wearing [of the armor].
By merely reciting it five hundred thousand times, this becomes certainly perfected.
And in the world, a weapon whose armor has been perfected does not pierce one in times of distress. (17–18)
Death does not come to him; he may certainly enter water or fire [and remain unharmed]. He becomes liberated while living and himself becomes a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
If he possesses the armor of perfection (siddhakavaca), he will certainly become equal to Viṣṇu.
O Sage, this section concerning Prakṛti has been told, which is superior even to the fragments of nectar.
That very one who is Mūlaprakṛti, whose son is Gaṇeśvara,
performed the Kṛṣṇa-vow and thereby obtained Gaṇapati as her son.
And by his own portion, the Lord Kṛṣṇa became the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Having heard this section of the Prakṛti, which is most pleasant to hear and like unto nectar,
one should feed him with curd-rice and give him gold.
One should indeed give a beautiful, auspicious cow along with her calf out of devotion (O Sage).
One should satisfy the reciter with garments, ornaments, and jewels,
as well as with flowers, decorations, clothing, and various offerings.
One should worship the book in this manner, endowed with devotion and faith.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him who listens after having performed [the worship] in this way.
By his grace, one’s sons, grandsons, and others increase, and one becomes illustrious.
Lakṣmī dwells in that person's home, and at the end [of their life], they shall attain Goloka.
They shall obtain the service of Kṛṣṇa and unwavering devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

(26) Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Brahmāṇḍa-mohana-kavaca," in the Durgopākhyāna of the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa within the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (67)
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Here ends the second section, the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to the illustrious Veṅkaṭeśa.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
Now begins the third section, the Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa, in the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (1).
Nārada said:
I have heard the *Prakṛti-khaṇḍa*, that supreme ocean of nectar,
which is most excellent, desirable, and increases the knowledge of the ignorant.
Now, I have come here to hear the section concerning the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
That birth and life-story of the man is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
(3) O best of gods, how was he born from the auspicious womb of Pārvatī?
And by what means did the Goddess obtain such a son? (4)
Of which deity was that portion [an emanation], and how did he take birth?
Was he born without a womb, or was he born from a womb?
What was that Brahmanic splendor, and what was his prowess?

What is penance, what is knowledge, or what is that stainless fame? How can there be worship of him before all others, while Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, and the Creator—the Lord of the universe—remain [as supreme]? (6–7)
In the Purāṇas, his birth is proclaimed as being hidden;
how is it that he has the face of an elephant, a single tusk, and a large belly?
Tell me all of this, for I have a great curiosity to hear it.
It is very extensive, O fortunate one, and exceedingly captivating.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall tell you a most wonderful secret.
It removes the torment of sin and destroys all obstacles;
it bestows all auspiciousness, is the essence of all, and is enchanting to all who hear it.
It grants happiness, is the seed of liberation, and cuts away the very root of evil. (10–11)
Born from a mass of splendor for the sake of the gods who were oppressed by the Daityas,
the Goddess, having destroyed the hosts of Daityas, became the daughter of Dakṣa;
and that Goddess was named Satī because of her censure of her husband in the past.
Having cast off her body through yoga, she was born from the womb of Śailapriyā.
With joy, Parvata gave that Pārvatī to Śaṅkara.
Having taken her, Mahādeva went to a secluded forest.
Having prepared a bed made delightful for pleasure and adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste,
O Nārada, he took his delight with her on the bank of the Narmadā in a flower garden for a period of one thousand divine years.
Between the two of them, there arose a great passion, beginning with the "reverse" acts.
By the mere touch of Durgā’s limbs, Śiva was rendered unconscious by love;
she too, unconscious from the touch of Śiva, did not wake day or night.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, filled with the songs of male cuckoos, enriched by the blossoming of various flowers, and resounded with the humming of bees;
it was made fragrant by a breeze embracing sweet-smelling blossoms. (18)

Seeing their amorous dalliance there in that place which was exceedingly pleasant and devoid of all other living beings, the gods fell into deep anxiety. Placing Brahmā at their head, they went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa. (19–20)
Having bowed to him, Brahmā related the desired account.
All the deities remained motionless like painted dolls.
Brahmā said:

For a period of a thousand years according to the measurement of the gods, Śaṅkara, intent on sexual union, remained motionless; yet that yogi did not cease. And upon the conclusion of their sexual union, O Lord of the World, the couple—
"What kind of offspring will be born? You should tell me the truth. The Blessed One said:
"O Sustainer of the World, there is no cause for anxiety; everything will be auspicious."
How could there be suffering for those who have taken refuge in me?
Therefore, together with the host of gods, exert yourselves with effort to employ whatever means will certainly cause that [enemy’s] prowess to fall to the earth. (24–25)
And when that semen of Śambhu falls into the womb of Pārvatī,
then an offspring shall be born who will crush both gods and demons.
Thereupon, all the gods, headed by Śakra, [shall act] at the command of Nārāyaṇa.
They proceeded to the banks of the Narmadā, while Brahmā went to his own abode.
Right there, on the outer region of the mountain valley, all the supreme gods became dejected of face and overwhelmed with fear.
Śakra [sent] Kubera; Kubera likewise [sent] Varuṇa;
Samīraṇa [sent] Varuṇa, and Samīraṇa [sent] Yama;
Yama [sent] Hutāśana, and Hutāśana [sent] Bhāskara.
"Candra, as well as Bhāskara, and Īśāna and Candra himself—
thus the gods incite the gods to the interruption of his pleasure,
saying to one another, 'Bring about the destruction of Hara’s amorous delight. (30–31)
Standing at the gate, the crooked-headed Śakra spoke to Maheśvara.
Indra said: "What are you doing, O Mahādeva? O Lord of Yogins, salutations be unto you!"
"O Lord of the World, O Seed of the World, O Destroyer of the fear of devotees!
(33) Having said, "Hari has gone," the Sun-god approached him;
standing at the gate, terrified and afflicted by fear, he spoke with his squinting eyes. (34)
The illustrious Sūrya said:
What are you doing, O Mahādeva, protector of the worlds?
O best of gods, O highly fortunate one, O Lord of Pārvatī, salutations be unto you! 35.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Sūrya departed from there out of fear. Then Candra arrived and spoke with his neck bent.
Candra said:
"What are you doing, O Lord of the three worlds? O Three-eyed One, salutations be unto you!
You who delight in the Self, who are self-sufficient, and whose hearing and chanting are meritorious.
(37) Having spoken thus, the Lord of Night, filled with fear, fell silent.
Even the Wind-god, standing at the door, beheld him and spoke respectfully:
The Wind-god said:
"What are you doing, O Lord of the World? O Kinsman of the World, salutations be unto you!"
"O eternal one, you who exist in the form of the seeds of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa!
(39) Having heard this praise, he who is expert in yoga and knowledge did not abandon his amorous passion, though he desired to leave it out of fear of Pārvatī. (40)
Seeing the gods, who were afflicted by fear yet intent on offering praise once more,
Maheśa abandoned his pleasurable enjoyment and Pārvatī, who was clinging to his neck;
as he rose up, filled with both terror and shame.
That seed fell upon the earth, and from it Skanda was born.
Later, I shall relate that most enchanting story;
for now, listen to what you desire regarding the account of Skanda’s birth.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having abandoned his passion, Mahādeva beheld the gods before him.
"Run away! she said out of compassion, fearing Pārvatī.
|| 1 || The gods, terrified by the cause of Pārvatī’s curse, fled;
even the Destroyer of the entire universe trembled from fear of Pārvatī. || 2 ||
Rising from her bed, Durgā did not see the gods before her;
she then suppressed within her own body the fire of wrath that had arisen.
"From this day forward, let those gods be rendered powerless," she declared.
The goddess, becoming exceedingly enraged, indeed cursed those gods.
Then Śiva beheld Śivā, her eyes bloodshot with anger,
weeping with a downcast face as she scratched the surface of the earth.
Seeing her distressed and with eyes bloodshot with anger, Śiva,
the Lord of Gods, took her by the hand and placed her upon his chest.
Trembling with extreme fear, he spoke these sweet words.
Śaṅkara said: O daughter of the best of mountains, O blessed and enchanting one, O you who are the very embodiment of my good fortune and the presiding deity of my life-breaths, why are you angry?
"O Mother of the World, tell me what you desire that I shall do for you.
Within this entire multitude of cosmic eggs, what is impossible for us two?
O beautiful one, be gracious toward me who am innocent."
"By destiny, my fault remains unknown; you ought to perform a rite of pacification for me.
United with you, I am Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness upon all.
Without you, O Lord, I am like a corpse, eternally inauspicious."
You are primordial nature (*prakṛti*), you are intellect (*buddhi*), and you are power, forgiveness, and compassion (11).
You are contentment as well as nourishment; you are peace and indeed forbearance.
You are hunger, shadow, sleep, lassitude, and faith, O Goddess of the gods (12).
You are the nature of all supports and the embodiment of all seeds.
O Śivā, speak now words full of flavor, preceded by a smile.
Quickly revive me, who am dead, having been scorched by the poison of your anger. 13–14.
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, endowed with forgiveness, spoke sweetly with a grieving heart. (15) Pārvatī said:
What shall I say to you, who are omniscient, possessing all forms, delighting in the self, whose desires are fulfilled, and who dwells within all bodies?
A lustful woman might speak of her husband as one possessed by desire for his mind, lacking wisdom. (16)

I shall tell you that which is known in the hearts of all and desired within their hearts. O Maheśa, though it is a secret most carefully guarded by all women and a cause for shame, I shall tell it to you even though it is not to be spoken of before anyone.
O Lord of the Gods, among all pleasures and amidst the riches of women, the enjoyment of a virtuous man in secluded places is the supreme happiness;
and there is no sorrow for a woman equal to that which arises from its loss. (19)
For beloved women, the grief caused by separation from their lovers is most cruel.
Just as the moon wanes day by day during the dark fortnight,
so too does a beloved woman waste away moment by moment without her lover.
For all [living beings], it is the fever of anxiety; for garments, it is the distress of storage;

for virtuous women, it is separation from their beloved; and for horses, it is mating. For those who have enjoyed pleasure, the first [misfortune] is the loss of delight, and the second is the discharge of virility. (22)
And the third sorrow, exceeding all others, is childlessness.
(23) Though I have obtained you, my beloved, who are the delight of the three worlds, I have no son.
For the life of a woman who is bereft of a son is useless. (24)
Merit arising from austerity and charity brings happiness in future lives;
and a son born of a noble lineage bestows happiness both in this world and the next.
A virtuous son is a portion of his master and bestows happiness equal to that of his master.
And a bad son is a firebrand to his family, causing nothing but mental anguish.
(26) A husband shall certainly take birth from a portion of himself within the womb of virtuous wives.
A chaste wife is equal to a mother and is always a source of benefit. (27)
An unchaste woman is like an enemy and is a constant source of suffering;
she is traditionally remembered as being of three kinds: corrupt in speech, corrupt in her origins, and simply unchaste.
O Lord of the Lords of Yogins, tell me: what remedy shall I employ?
"O ocean of means, bestower of the fruits of all ascetic penances!"—
having spoken thus, the goddess Pārvatī stood with her face bowed.
Laughing, the god Śaṅkara enlightened Pārvatī.
He began to speak words that were measured, affectionate, and very beautiful— words which are the seed of virtuous sons, bestowing happiness and serving as the cause for the destruction of suffering.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Listen, Pārvatī; I shall speak, and it will be well for you.
In the three worlds, the accomplishment of one’s purpose occurs indeed through the proper means. 1.
I shall tell you of a most auspicious means that generates joy in the mind, which is the seed-form for the accomplishment of all desires.
O lady of beautiful countenance, perform the vow after having worshipped Hari.
And you shall observe for one year the vow known as Puṇyaka—supreme, like a wish-fulfilling tree for desires, yielding great and firm fruit;
it is bliss-giving, merit-bestowing, essential, bestowing sons, and granting all happiness. (3–4)
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and Hari is among the gods;
just as I am among Vaiṣṇavas, O beloved, so are you among goddesses.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes, and Puṣkara is among sacred fords.
O Śivā, just as the Pārijāta is among flowers and Tulasī is among leaves,
just as the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is remembered as the most meritorious among auspicious dates, and just as Sunday is the most merit-bestowing among days of the week; || 6 ||
As Mārgaśīrṣa among months, and as Mādhava among seasons;
as the year among years, and as the Kṛta age among the ages (yugas);
and as the mother among venerable gurus who bestow knowledge.
A virtuous wife is like the mind of those who are trustworthy;
she is like a jewel among riches and a husband among beloved things;
she is like a son among kinsmen and the wish-fulfilling tree among all trees. (8–9)
Among fruits, the mango is supreme; likewise, among years, Bhārata;
among forests, Vṛndāvana; and among women, Śatarūpā.
As Kāśī is among cities, and as the Sun is among luminous bodies.
Just as the moon is among those that grant happiness, and Kāmadeva is among the beautiful;
as the Vedas are among the scriptures, and Kapila is among the perfected ones (siddhas); as Hanumān is among the monkeys, and the face of a Brāhmaṇa is among sacred fields (kṣetras). (11–12)
Just as knowledge and captivating poetry are to the Yaśodās, as the sky is to all-pervading things, and as the eye is to the limbs;
so too are the stories of Hari among all riches, and meditation upon Hari among all joys. (13)

Among all touches, the touch of one's son is supreme; among the cruel, the rogue is foremost; among evils, falsehood is the worst; and among sinners, the unchaste woman is the most wretched. Among merits, truth is supreme; and among austerities, service to Hari is the highest. (14–15)
Just as clarified butter is among products of the cow, as Brahmā is among ascetics;
as nectar is among edible things, and as rice is among grains;
as water is among meritorious gifts, and as fire is among pure things. (16)
Gold is the foremost among luminous things, and sweet speech among pleasant things.
(17) Garuḍa is the foremost among birds, and Indra’s mount among elephants.
Kumāra is the foremost among yogins, and Nārada among divine sages. (18)
Citraratha is among the Gandharvas as Jīva is among the intelligent; Śukra is among the great poets as Purāṇaka is among poetic compositions;
the ocean is among flowing waters as the earth is among those possessing forbearance. (19)
Just as liberation is the foremost among gains, and devotion to Hari among all riches;
just as the Vaiṣṇavas are the purest among castes, and the *praṇava* among syllables;
just as the Viṣṇu-mantra is the chief among mantras, and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the source among seeds. (20–21)
Just as speech is among the learned, and as the Gāyatrī is among meters;
as Kubera is among the Yakṣas, and as Vāsuki is among the serpents;
as you are among the mountains, and as Surabhi is among cows. (22)
As the Sāmaveda is among the Vedas, as Kuśa grass is among blades of grass;
as Lakṣmī is among givers of happiness, and the mind is indeed among those things that move swiftly;
as the syllable *a* is among letters, so is my father among those who wish me well. (23–24)
Among all forms, the Śālagrāma is like Viṣṇupañjara among weapons;
as the five-faced lion is among quadrupeds, so is the human being among living creatures.
As the mind is among the senses, so is the weak digestive fire among diseases. (25)
Just as I am among the strong according to their power, so too am I among those who possess power. I am the Great Virāṭ among gross things and the atom among subtle things;
just as Indra is among the sons of Aditi and Bali is among the Daityas.
Just as Dadhīci is among givers and Prahlāda among the virtuous,
as the Brahmāstra is among weapons and the Sudarśana among discuses;
as Rāmacandra is among men and Lakṣmaṇa among archers.
The support of all, the one to be served by all, the seed of all, and the giver of all; as Kṛṣṇa is the essence of all and as the merit of all vows, so it is.
O highly fortunate lady, perform this vow which is difficult to attain in the three worlds.
"And by the power of this very vow, your son shall become the most excellent of all.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa is to be propitiated through vows; he is the granter of the desires of all.
By serving him, a person is liberated along with ten million ancestors."
He who, having received the mantra of Hari, performs service to Hari,
makes his birth in Bhārata fruitful for himself;
he certainly goes to Vaikuṇṭha, having delivered ten million ancestors.
Having become an attendant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he rejoices happily in that very place.
(33) Having uplifted his uterine brothers, his own servants, his kinsmen, his companions, and his wives, the devotee goes to the abode of Hari. (34)
Therefore, O Girijā, accept the mantra of Hari, which is very difficult to obtain.
Recite that mantra during this vow; it is the cause of liberation for the ancestors.
Having spoken thus, the god Śaṅkara departed together with Girijā.
And quickly [he brought her] to the bank of the Jāhnavī; O Sage, with great affection he gave her the enchanting mantra of Hari, along with its armor (kavaca) and hymn (stotra),
and he explained to her the rules for the ritual of worship.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the rules for the vow, Durgā was delighted in her mind.
She began to inquire about the entire procedure for the vows.
Pārvatī said:
"O best among those who know the Vedas, tell me the entire procedure for the vows."
O Lord, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, supreme beyond the supreme!
(2) What are the substances and fruits appropriate for the vows?
O Master, what is the procedure along with its restrictions and permitted foods, and what is the fruit thereof? (3)
"Give me a virtuous priest appointed for my service,
as well as Brahmins for the offering of flowers, servants for the procurement of materials,
and whatever other things are required that I have not yet considered. (4)
He is the master of women and the giver of all; employ all of this [upon him].
(5) In childhood, the father is always the protector;
in middle age, the husband; and in the remainder [of life], the son—such are the three stages for virtuous women. (6)
Then King Aśoka, having given his daughter— who was as dear to him as his own life— to that lord of beings,
attained peace by entrusting his beloved to his son.
And that woman, accompanied by her three kinsmen, became supremely fortunate.
That which is slightly deficient is middling, and that which is entirely deficient is the lowest on earth.
She who stands near these [three] is praiseworthy throughout the three worlds; she is censured when associated with others. All this has been heard in the Śruti regarding renunciation (saṃnyāsa). 9.
"You, the Blessed One, are the self of all, the witness of all, and the knower of all.
Grant me a boon of a son who shall be the cause of my own spiritual fulfillment.
Thus was it offered to the Great-Souled One by means of the inference derived from the realization of one's own self.
"I am one who knows all inner intentions and knows awakening; what more can I teach you?
Having said this, Pārvatī affectionately fell at her husband's feet.
And the Blessed One, an ocean of compassion, began to speak.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the procedure, the observances, and the fruit;
as well as the fruits and the materials that are suitable for the vow. 13.
A hundred pure Brahmins were appointed to offer fruits and flowers;
a hundred servants were assigned to fetch wealth;
a hundred thousand female slaves were stationed there, along with a family priest.
Accept Sanatkumāra for the sake of the vow— he who knows the ordinances of all vows, who has mastered the Vedas and Vedāntas,
the most eminent among the devotees of Hari, the omniscient one, the best among the wise,
and my equal. (15–16)

O Goddess, O Beloved, at a pure and auspicious time, preceded by supreme observance, the commencement of the vow on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is auspicious. Having made the body perfectly clean, one should first perform the consecration of the head.
Having fasted on the preceding day and carefully purified his clothing,
the observer of the vow should rise from his bed at the time of dawn,
wash his face, and bathe in pure water.
Having sipped water and purified himself with effort while recollecting Hari,
and having offered the *arghya* to Hari with devotion, he should quickly return home;
then, having put on two washed garments and seated himself upon a pure seat.
Having sipped water, applied the *tilaka*, and completed his daily rites (*svāhnika*),
he should again set up the water-pot according to the rules, preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*).
Then, having carefully performed the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the family priest (*purohita*).

One should perform this vow, which is a resolve ordained by the Vedas. O Goddess of Devas, the materials for the vow and the sixteen regular ritual offerings must always be given to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (23)
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya),
bathing water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), garments, ornaments,
fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood paste. (24–25)
The sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) and betel leaf well-scented with camphor and other ingredients—
O beautiful one, these substances constitute the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of worship.
O Goddess, if even a small portion is lacking, a deficiency in the ritual limbs arises.
Just as a man who is deficient in a limb performs a rite that is likewise deficient in a limb,
so too when the ritual action is defective, a loss of the fruit arises.
One hundred and eight flowers of the *pārijāta* tree [should be offered] to Viṣṇu.
O Durgā,
one hundred thousand white campaka flowers, unblemished and desired,
should be offered daily with devotion to Hari for the sake of one's own beauty of form. (28–29)
One hundred thousand unblemished lotuses with a thousand petals should be offered with devotion to Hari for the sake of the beauty of one's face;
likewise, a thousand mirrors set with priceless jewels [should be offered].
One hundred thousand blue lotuses should be offered with devotion to Kṛṣṇa for Nārāyaṇa alone,
O Goddess of Gods, as an integral part of the vow, for the sake of the radiance of his eyes and for the sake of [attaining] beauty of the eyes. (31–32)

A hundred thousand beautiful white chowries originating from the Himalayas should be offered to Keśava alone for the sake of the beauty of his hair. A thousand caskets fashioned with priceless jewels [should likewise be given].
A hundred thousand Bandhūka flowers should be offered to the Lord of Rādhā for the sake of the beauty of the hair of the cowherd girl and for the sake of the beauty of the nose.
Furthermore, they should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the color of His gentle lips and lower lip. (34–35)
O Daughter of the Mountain, one hundred thousand pearls should be offered with devotion to the Lord of Goloka for the sake of the beauty of His teeth,
and one hundred thousand mouthfuls of gems for the sake of the beauty of His cheeks. (35)
O Daughter of the Mountain King, during this vow, an offering must be given to Maheśvara.
And a hundred thousand jeweled nooses must be given to Brahmeśvara.
O Mistress of Life, the observer of the vow should, with devotion, offer [an oblation] to the one whose form is the region below the lip.
And one hundred thousand ear-ornaments fashioned from the finest gems should be given to the Lord of All for the sake of the beauty of his ears;
and likewise, one hundred thousand jars of honey-wine fashioned from jewels.
A thousand jars made of jewels and filled with nectar should be given to Viśveśvara for the sake of the beauty of one's own voice;
and they should be given to Kṛṣṇa, O Goddess of Gods, for the sake of the beauty of one’s speech. (40–41)
And one hundred thousand jewel-lamps should be given to the one who assumes the guise of a cowherd,
to the one in the form of a youth, for the sake of the beauty of his vision.
A thousand vessels of jewels, shaped like dhattūra flowers, [should be offered].

A thousand lotus stalks fashioned from the essence of excellent jewels should be given to Gorakṣaka for the sake of strength and beauty. And they should be given to Caṇḍakapāla for the sake of the beauty of his arms. (43–44)
O Nārāyaṇī, O you who observe the vow of Hari, one hundred thousand red lotuses should be offered to the Lord of the cowherd women for the sake of the beauty of His hands;
and one hundred thousand rings fashioned from the finest gems should be given. (45)
And for the sake of the beauty of the fingers, one should give [gems] to Deveśvara;
and a hundred thousand excellent, white, and captivating sapphire gems should be given to Munīndranātha for the sake of the beauty of the nails. (46–47)
One hundred thousand most enchanting necklaces made of the essence of the seven precious gems should be given to Madanamoha for the sake of the beauty of his chest;
and one hundred thousand very beautiful, well-ripened bilva fruits [should also be given]. 48.
It should be given to Siddhendranātha for the sake of the beauty of the breasts;
it should be beautiful, with leaves in the shape of round, excellent jewels.
It should be given to Padmālayeśa for the sake of the beauty of the body.

A thousand navels fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems should be offered to Padmanābha for the sake of attaining the beauty of his navel. A thousand chariot wheels fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems [should likewise be offered].
And for the sake of the beauty of the hips,
a hundred thousand most enchanting golden plantain pillars should indeed be offered to the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi) for the purpose of the loveliness of the buttocks of Śrīnivāsa. (52–53)
One hundred thousand unfading and unblemished lotuses from the beds of the *śatapatra* lily should be offered to the Lotus-eyed One for the sake of the beauty of his feet;
and likewise, one thousand *khañjana* birds fashioned of gold.
And for the sake of attaining beauty of gait,
a thousand royal swans and a thousand lordly elephants fashioned with gold should be given to Lakṣmīśvara for the purpose of securing a [divine] state of existence. (55–56)
And one hundred thousand golden umbrellas should be given to Nārāyaṇa,
variegated with the finest jewels for the sake of the beauty of his head;
and, O Sovereign Lady, one hundred thousand unbroken *mālatī* flowers [should be offered].
One should give [this] to the Lord of Vṛndāvana for the sake of laughter and beauty.
Indeed, one hundred thousand priceless jewels should be given to Nārāyaṇa, O lady of virtuous vows, for the fulfillment of the vow and for the sake of character and beauty. (98–59)
Resembling clear crystal and possessing the excellence of a thousand of the finest jewels,
this should be given to the Lord of the Sages for the sake of the beauty of the mind.
Resembling the essence of coral and possessing a thousand of the finest gems—
One should devotedly give to Kṛṣṇa [gems] for the sake of increasing the passion of his beloved;
and one should diligently offer a hundred thousand *māṇikya* jewels of the finest quality to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of securing the good fortune of one's master for ten million births.
The kūṣmāṇḍa, the coconut, the jambīra, and likewise the śrīphala—
these fruits should be offered to Hari for the sake of obtaining a son.
Furthermore, one hundred thousand gems of the finest quality should be diligently offered to Kṛṣṇa.
For the increase of the master’s wealth throughout countless lifetimes,

the observer of the vow should cause Śrī Hari to hear various kinds of musical instruments, such as the excellent bronze cymbals and others, for the sake of increasing prosperity during the vow. (64–65)
Milk-rice, flour-cakes, and ghee mixed with sugar—delightful offerings should be given with devotion to Hari for the increase of the Master’s enjoyment.
A hundred thousand fragrant flower garlands and unbroken grains of rice are desired. (66)
One should offer [these] with devotion to Hari for the sake of increasing devotion to Hari.
(67) And various kinds of food offerings—delicious and sweet—should be presented, O Durgā, for the purpose of attaining the pleasure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (68)

O lady of virtuous vows, various kinds of flowers, along with *tulasī*, should be offered with devotion for the pleasure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa during the vow. Furthermore, the observer of the vow should feed a thousand Brahmins every day.

O Goddess, for the sake of the growth of one's own spiritual harvest, in vow after vow and birth after birth, one hundred handfuls of flowers should be offered daily and completely during worship; and a hundred prostrations should be performed for the increase of devotion. (70–71)

O lady of excellent vows, during this rite you should eat sacrificial food for six months, fruits and the like for five months, clarified butter for a fortnight, and water for a fortnight. You should offer a hundred jewel-lamps and maintain a fire day and night.
Having prepared a seat of *kuśa* grass at night, one should constantly observe the vigil during the vow.
[The stages of desire are: recollection, praise, play, gazing, secret conversation, resolve, determination, and the completion of the act. (73–74)
Sexual intercourse in dreams must be abandoned by one observing the vow for the sake of the purity of that vow.
O Goddess, when the vow is fully completed, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) follows immediately thereafter.
[One should offer] three hundred and sixty-six locks of hair together with garments.
May he give this, together with food, the sacred thread, and an offering.
