(76) There shall indeed be one thousand three hundred and sixty feedings of Brahmins;
there shall indeed be one thousand three hundred and sixty oblations of sesame seeds. (77)
Indeed, one thousand three hundred and sixty pieces of gold are to be given as the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the completion of the vow.
On the day of completion, I shall describe another sacrificial fee.
O Goddess, the fruit of this vow is that firm devotion to Hari shall arise;
one’s son shall become equal to Hari, renowned throughout the three worlds;
and there shall be beauty, the good fortune of a husband, sovereignty, and abundant wealth. (79–80)
"The seed of all desired accomplishments in birth after birth—thus has it been told, O Goddess; perform this vow, O Maheśvarī.
Having said, "A virtuous son shall be yours," he indeed ceased speaking. 81–82.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Puṇyaka Vrata," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the ritual procedure for the vow, Durgā was delighted in her mind.
Again she asked her beloved about a divine and auspicious account of a vow:
Śrī Pārvatī said: "O Lord, what is this wonderful vow, and what is its ritual procedure and fruit?"
Speak further on that discourse: by whom was this vow revealed?
(2) Now begins the narrative of the meritorious vow.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Śatarūpā, the wife of Manu, distressed by grief for her son,
went to the abode of Brahmā and spoke to him.
(3) Śatarūpā said:
O Brahman, by what means can a son be born even to a barren woman?
Tell me that, O Sustainer of the World, O Cause of the cause of creation!
O Brahman, her birth, as well as her sovereignty and wealth, would otherwise be fruitless.
Nothing at all shines in the home of those who have sons without a son.
(5) The merit arising from austerity and charity brings happiness in future births;
liberation bestows happiness, but for those with sons, it is the son who bestows joy. (6)

Upon seeing the face of her son, a daughter will certainly obtain the fruit arising from a hundred horse-sacrifices— the very cause of protection from the hell named Put. O ascetic, tell me, who am filled with distress, the means for the birth of a son.
In that case, it would be well; otherwise, I shall go to the forest with my husband.
Take the kingdom, sovereignty, wealth, and the earth filled with subjects.
Father, what is the use of these to us two who are childless and have no sons? (8–9)
A wise man does not venture to look upon the inauspicious face of one who has no son;
a sonless man feels shame even at the thought of showing his own face.
Or else, having consumed poison, I shall enter the fire.
"A home devoid of sons and grandsons, and bereft of women, would be inauspicious.
Having spoken thus, she wept before Brahmā himself.
And the Treasure of Compassion, seeing her, began to speak.
Brahmā said: Listen, my child, I shall explain the means for obtaining a son, which brings happiness, is the seed of all sovereignty and other blessings, bestows all desires, and is auspicious.
This most meritorious vow is to be observed on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
And during the bright fortnight, one should perform [the rite] after propitiating Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of all;
this should be done for a year, destroying all obstacles.
O lady of virtuous vows, the materials to be offered in the vow have been declared by the Vedas.

"O auspicious lady, having performed the vow prescribed in the Kāṇva recension, which grants the fulfillment of all desires, you shall obtain a son whose prowess is equal to Viṣṇu. Having heard the words of Brahmā, she performed that supreme vow.
She obtained two charming sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda (17).
Having performed her vow, Devahūti obtained as a son Siddheśvara—
Kapila, who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, meritorious, the bestower of merit, and auspicious (18).
Having performed this rite, the auspicious Arundhatī obtained a son, Śakti;
and having performed the vow, Śakti’s beloved wife obtained a son, Parāśara.
And Aditi, having performed the vow, obtained a son, Vāmana.
Having performed this, the sovereign Śacī obtained her son Jayanta;
having performed this, the wife of Uttānapāda obtained her son Dhruva;
and having performed this, the wife of Kubera obtained Nalakūbara.
Sūryaputrī obtained Manu by performing this supreme vow; Atripatnī obtained her son Candra by performing this supreme vow;
and the wife of Aṅgiras obtained [her son] by performing this supreme vow. (22)
By the power of this [Bhṛgu], Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, was born as his son.
Having observed a vow, Bhṛgu’s wife obtained as a son Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas,
who was a portion of Nārāyaṇa and the foremost among all those endowed with splendor.
Thus has been told, O Goddess, the most excellent of all vows.
Perform this, O auspicious one, O daughter of Himālaya, O blessed lady;
it brings happiness to the wives of great kings and to goddesses alike. 29.
"O great virtuous lady, this vow is dearer than life itself to virtuous women.
By the power of this vow, the Lord of the cowherd maidens, the Sovereign of all beings, shall himself become your son. (26–27)
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Śaṅkara ceased there;
and that goddess, being delighted, undertook the vow at the command of Śaṅkara.
Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
It bestows happiness, it bestows liberation, it is the essence, and it is the cause of the birth of Gaṇeśa.

(29) Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Meritorious Vow," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Śaunaka said:
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, Nārada was delighted in his heart.
O virtuous one, rich in asceticism, tell me what he asked again.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, Nārada, with a joyful mind,
began to inquire about the procedure for commencing the vow.
(2) Nārada said:
O best of sages, tell me in what manner this auspicious vow was performed by Pārvatī at the command of her husband,
by virtue of which the Lord of Beings obtained birth through that excellent vow.
"O Brahmin, you ought to explain to us in what manner that [is accomplished].
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having related the divine narrative as well as the procedure for the vow..."
Śiva himself, the ordainer of austerities, went forth to perform penance;
Hari, intent on the worship of Hari, assumed a distinct form;
he was habituated to contemplating Hari and devoted to meditation upon Hari. (5–6)
Filled with supreme bliss and possessing eternal joy of knowledge,
he did not perceive day or night while remembering the mantra of Hari externally.
With a delighted mind, the goddess Pārvatī, by her husband’s command, [acted].
She dispatched her servants and brahmins for the sake of the vow.
Having brought all the materials suitable for the rite,
that auspicious lady began the vow at a favorable moment.

The blessed Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, arrived; he was a personified mass of splendor, blazing with the luster of Brahman. And Brahmā himself came from the world of Brahmā, joyful and accompanied by his wife.
For Maheśvara, the Blessed One, arrived in great haste;
as did Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, four-armed and accompanied by Lakṣmī—
the Blessed One, the protector, teacher, and sustainer of the worlds, together with his attendants.
Wearing a forest garland, dark-complexioned, and adorned with jewel ornaments,
and likewise having gathered all necessary provisions, O Nārada, he departed by means of a jeweled vehicle,
accompanied by Sanaka, Sananda, Kapila, and Sanātana. (13)
Āsuri, Kratu, Haṃsa, Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Aruṇi, Yati, Sumati, Vasiṣṭha with his followers,
Pulaha, Pulastya, Atri, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras. (14–15)
Agastya, Pracetas, Durvāsas, and Cyavana; Marīci, Kaśyapa, Kaṇva, Jaratkāru, and Gautama;
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, Saṃvarta, and Saubhari.
Jābāli, Jamadagni, Jaigīṣavya, and Devala;
Gokāmukha, Vakraratha, Pāribhadra, and Parāśara;
Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Vibhāṇḍaka. (17–18)
Mārkaṇḍeya and Mṛkaṇḍu, Puṣkara and Lomaśa; Kautsa, Vatsa, Dakṣa, Bālāgni, and Aghamarṣaṇa;
Kātyāyana, Kaṇāda, Pāṇini, and Śākaṭāyana.
Śaṅkara, Apiśali, Śākalya, and Śaṅkha—
these and many other sages with their disciples, O Sage,
as well as we two sons of Dharma, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, are equal [in this]. (20–21)
The guardians of the quarters, as well as the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
and all the mountains with their retinues, came for the vow of Pārvatī;
so too did Himālaya, the king of mountains, together with his children and his wife.
Accompanied by his retinue and followers, adorned with jewel ornaments,
and having likewise gathered the necessary provisions along with various materials— whatever gems, rubies, and jewels were suitable for the vow— [he set out]. (23–24)
Various kinds of objects are difficult to find in the world:
a hundred thousand gems of elephants, three hundred thousand gems of horses, ten hundred thousand gems of cattle, and one hundred million pieces of gold. (25)
Likewise, there were four hundred thousand pearls, a thousand *kaustubha* gems, and [an equal number] of *rucaka* diamonds and *sparśa* gems;
and the curious king [received] a hundred thousand *bhāras* of various delicious substances.
Anantaratnaprabhava arrived at the vow for a son;
likewise, Brāhmaṇas, Manavas, Siddhas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas, as well as renunciants, mendicants, and bards, came for the vow of Pārvatī. (27–28)
Vidyādharīs, dancers, and throngs of celestial nymphs (apsarases),
along with various kinds of musical instruments, arrived at the temple of Śiva.
And the royal road of Kailāsa was beautifully prepared with sandalwood paste.
Richly adorned with threads of mango sprouts and beautified by plantain trunks,
decorated with *dūrvā* grass, grains, fruits, leaves, parched rice, and flowers,
the hosts joyfully beheld that [palace] fashioned from rubies. (30–31)
These inhabitants of Kailāsa, all endowed with supreme bliss, were honored by Śaṅkara upon lofty lion-thrones. Śunāsīra was the superintendent of gifts, and Kubera was the guardian of the treasury.
The Sun himself was the director, and the Lord of Waters was the attendant.
There were thousands of rivers of curds and likewise of milk;
there were thousands of clarified butters and hundreds of molasses.
Thousands of *mādhvīka* liquors, hundreds of oils,
and even millions of buttermilk preparations were prepared for Pārvatī’s vow,
O Nārada; and there were hundreds of millions of jars of nectar.
O Nārada, there were heaps of sweetmeats and sugar, as well as heaps of flour made from barley and wheat mixed with ghee;
and there were heaps of full svastika-shaped cakes, each numbering one hundred thousand.
There were heaps by the ten million of parched grains prepared with molasses;
there were ten crores of heaps of flattened rice and śāli rice; O Sage, as for the heaps of excellent rice, no number can be found.
O great sage, during Pārvatī’s vow on Mount Kailāsa, there were mountains of gold, silver, coral, and precious gems;
as well as milk-rice, flour cakes, and most enchanting śāli rice.
Lakṣmī prepared the cooked rice and side dishes seasoned with ghee.
Śiva, together with Nārāyaṻṇa and the hosts of celestial sages, partook of the meal.
A hundred thousand brahmins served as the distributors of food.
And he gave them betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other ingredients,
to those hundreds of thousands of highly skillful Brahmins seated upon jeweled thrones.
And [he gave it] to Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, as he sat upon his jeweled throne.
He was being served by his attendants with smiling faces and white whisks;
he was being praised by sages, Siddhas, and hosts of gods;
and he was joyfully watching the dances of the Vidyādharīs with a smile.
O Brahmin, having heard the enchanting music of the Gandharvas,
Śaṅkara affectionately questioned Brahmā, the Lord of Brahmā:
"Impelled by Brahmā, you ought to perform the desired vow that is appropriate."
In that assembly hall filled with hosts of celestial sages, with his hands joined in reverent salutation (saṃpuṭāñjali),
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O Lord, O Śrīnivāsa, O Master, listen to my words."
O Hari, you are the bestower of the fruits of austerities, of penances, and of ritual actions;
you are the one worshipped by all, the object of vows, silent recitations, sacrifices, and rites of worship.
O Hari, you are the wish-fulfilling tree for all desires, existing as the seed-form of everything.
O Brahman, Pārvatī desires to perform a most meritorious vow;
she is seeking a son, afflicted by grief and tormented in her heart. She is distressed by the futility of her seed due to the interruption of her pleasure caused by the gods. (49)

That virtuous woman, having been awakened by me with various nectars of speech, now performs her vow while praying for a worthy son and the good fortune of her husband. Without those two, she finds no contentment and desires to give up her own life. (50–51)

Formerly, having abandoned her own body at a sacrifice for the ancestors, that proud woman obtained rebirth on the Himalayas due to my censure. You know the entire account; why do I speak to you, the omniscient one?
O knower of reality, speak to her who is distressed, for she brings about auspicious results in the end.
O Lord of All, the fickle nature of women is difficult to restrain; it is hard to abandon even for us—yogis, perfected ones, and ascetics alike. (53–54)

By those who have conquered their senses and subdued their anger, the form of a woman—which is a cause of delusion, a casket of all illusions, and a means for increasing desire—is perceived as the Brahmā-missile of the god of love: difficult to pierce and the cause of victory. (55)
And it was fashioned by the Creator according to rule, as the foremost of all things, preceded by ritual ordinance;
it is the bolt upon the door of liberation, the obstructer of devotion to Hari, and the cutter of the rope that serves as the tethering-stake for the bonds of saṃsāra. (56–57)
It is the seed for the destruction of dispassion and the constant increaser of passion; it is a city of reckless acts and the eternal abode of faults;
it is a field for mistrusts and is itself deceit personified.
It is the constant locus of egoism, a jar of poison with the face of nectar;
it is unattainable by all and always difficult to propitiate;
it is rich in conduct aimed at achieving its own ends and is the cause of the sprout of strife. (59–60)
"O Brahman, you have related everything; you ought to tell me what must be done.
Every action, when deliberated upon, brings about happiness in the end.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus and gazed upon the face of Brahmā, the Blessed One ceased speaking in the midst of the assembly after praising the Lord of Kamalā.
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Universe smiled.
He began to speak words of policy that were beneficial.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"This is a most meritorious vow, the very essence, for the sake of producing a lineage of virtuous women."
O Lord of Pārvatī, your wife wishes to perform that which is the seed of your lordly fortune—
[a rite] impossible for all others to accomplish, difficult to propitiate, the bestower of the fruits of all desires,
the giver of happiness, the essence of bliss, and the bestower of liberation. (64–69)
The Self is the nature of the witness, eternal, and of the nature of light;
it is without support, untainted, free from limiting adjuncts, and free from disease.
It is the life-breath of the devotees, the Lord of devotees, and the one who bestows grace upon devotees.
For he who is difficult for others to propitiate is the supreme accomplisher of his devotees.

Indeed, the Blessed Lord is subject to devotion; though he has attained all perfections, he remains free from worldly fruit. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are but partial manifestations (kalās) of that Supreme Person.
The Great Virāj, whose portion is this world, yet remains untainted and beyond primordial nature;
the imperishable, the restrainer, the fierce one, whose form manifests for the grace of his devotees;
the fierce seizer among all seizers, and the one who effects the restraint of the planets.
And within three crores of births, nothing can be accomplished without you.
For a man who has obtained birth in Bhārata may indeed attain devotion to Hari;
yet, having served minor deities for seven births [he remains bound]. (70–71)
By that blessing alone, he obtains the Sūrya-mantra;
having fully propitiated the Sūrya-mantra during three births in Bhārata, the human being joyfully attains the Śaiva-mantra, which bestows all things. (72)
Having thus served you alone with supreme devotion for seven lifetimes,
he attains the *māyā-mantra* through the grace of your lotus feet.
And having propitiated the supreme *Māyā-Nārāyaṇī* for a hundred births, [he attains the same].
A human being attains the state of Nārāyaṇa, which is worthy of service,
by serving that portion [of the Lord] here in this most rare field of merit for a year.
Having served that portion, one attains devotion to Kṛṣṇa, which is caused by association with devotees.
Having attained mature devotion after wandering repeatedly throughout Bhārata,
one attains fully ripened devotion through service to devotees;
then, O Śiva, by the grace of the devotee and the blessing of the gods—
One obtains the supreme mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which bestows the fruit of liberation (nirvāṇa).
The vow of Kṛṣṇa and the mantra of Kṛṣṇa grant the fruits of all desires.
Through long-term service to Kṛṣṇa, the devotee becomes equal to Kṛṣṇa himself.
At the time of the great dissolution, the fall of all beings is indeed certain;
however, there is no fall for the devotees of Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable saints.
The servants of Kṛṣṇa rejoice in the indestructible Goloka.
O Śiva, those free from anxiety laugh at the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
You are the destroyer of all, O Maheśvara, yet you do not [destroy] your devotees; Māyā deludes everyone except for my devotees, by virtue of my grace.
Māyā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, is the mother who bestows devotion to Kṛṣṇa upon all.
Without the service of Māyā, one does not attain devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
And that Māyā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, is the sovereign primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti).
She is dear to Kṛṣṇa, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, equal to Kṛṣṇa, and imperishable. She is of the nature of light and assumes forms by her own will;
she manifested through her splendor for the sake of subduing the asuras among the gods.

Having slain the hosts of Daityas, Dakṣa obtained through his ascetic penance a birth from the wife of Dakṣa in the land of Bhārata, after many lifetimes. Having abandoned her body at her father’s sacrifice due to your censure, she became Satī.

The eternal Goddess, the power of Kṛṣṇa, went to Goloka. Having assumed her form, which is the supreme refuge of qualities and beauty, you wandered repeatedly throughout Bhārata and became despondent in the past, O Hara. (86–87)
Awakened by me on the banks of a river at Śrīśaila,
she soon obtained birth from Śailakāntā;
may that virtuous, auspicious woman of excellent vows perform meritorious deeds.

O Śaṅkara, the merit of this meritorious vow is equal to that of thousands of Rājasūya sacrifices. O Three-eyed One, this vow—which involves the expenditure of wealth—is not achievable even by all the most virtuous women. (89–90)
"By the power of Puṇyaka, you yourself shall become the Lord of the Lords of Beings (Bhūteśanātha). Born from the womb of Pārvatī, you will be an excellent son;
for he is himself the Lord of the hosts of gods and a treasure-house of compassion. (91)
He shall become renowned as Gaṇeśa throughout the three worlds;
by the mere remembrance of him, the destruction of obstacles will certainly occur.
For this reason, on account of the worlds, the omnipresent Lord shall be named Vighnanighna (the Destroyer of Obstacles). || 92-93 ||
Because various kinds of substances are to be given during the merit-bestowing rite (*puṇyaka*),
and because he became pot-bellied after eating them, he is remembered as Lambodara.
Due to the gaze of Śani, his head was severed and joined back on by the elephant-faced one.
Because he is an elephant-faced infant, he bestows all perfections upon all.
Since the axe of Paraśurāma indeed broke his tusk, for that reason the infant is renowned by the name Ekadanta (the Single-Tusked). //96-99//
"He is worthy of worship by all the gods and is the sovereign of our worlds. By my boon, his worship shall indeed take place at the very beginning of all [other] worship.
Having first fully worshipped him among all the gods during their rites, people [shall then worship the others]."
One obtains the fruit of worship without obstacles; otherwise, it is in vain. Having propitiated Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, Agni, and Durgā, one may then worship another deity. (98–99)
Through the worship of Gaṇeśa, obstacles shall be eradicated for all the worlds;
through the worship of the Sun, one becomes free from disease; through the worship of the pure Śrī Viṣṇu, one attains purity;
and there is liberation, the destruction of sin, fame, and supreme sovereignty. (100)
The knowledge of reality is the seed of perfect contentment for those who worship Śaṅkara.
The worship of the Fire-god is proclaimed to produce the purification of one's own intellect;
through the knowledge derived from worshipping the fire consecrated by ritual, death [occurs] with wisdom.
By serving Śaṅkara and Agni, one becomes both a donor and an enjoyer.
The supreme worship of Durgā bestows devotion to Hari and is auspicious;
without the worship of these three, the three worlds are the opposite [of their true nature]. (103)
Thus, O Mahādeva, this sequence is certain to exist in every kalpa.
These [principles] are eternally present, constant, and devoted to creation;
their manifestation and disappearance occur by the will of the Lord.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari ceased speaking there on the floor of the assembly.
The gods, the brahmins, and Śaṅkara along with Pārvatī were greatly delighted.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Acceptance of the Vow and the Command," in the Gaṇeśa-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (Chapter 6)
Nārāyaṇa said: Having received the command of Hari, Hara, with a joyful mind, spoke with affection to Pārvatī auspicious words concerning his conversation with Hari. (1)
Having received the command of Śiva, Śivā, her mind filled with joy,
played auspicious musical instruments during the auspicious vow.
Having bathed well, the fair-toothed and pure woman wore two washed garments.
Having firmly established a jeweled pitcher upon white grain,
adorned with mango sprouts and beautifully decorated with fruits and unbroken rice,
and made radiant with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron; (3–4)
Seated upon a jeweled throne, rich in jewels, that virtuous daughter born from a jewel honored the preeminent sages who were seated upon jeweled lion-thrones;
she also honored the excellent family priest who was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.

Having placed before him, with devotion, the guardians of the quarters adorned with jewels, sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and ornaments, and having worshipped according to the prescribed rites the gods, humans, and serpents; (6–7)
Having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara with supreme devotion—
[the deities] resplendent with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron—
and likewise with pure garments cleansed by fire, as well as with excellent jewels and ornaments; || 8 ||
O sage, having worshipped them with various ritual offerings during the auspicious occasion,
the Goddess commenced her vow, preceded by the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana).
She invoked her chosen deity, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, into an auspicious water-pot.
With devotion, he offered the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāras) in their proper sequence.
Whatever various items are to be performed or given during the vow,
he presented them all, each yielding its respective fruit.
And she, the virtuous Suvratā, with devotion gave all that offering prescribed for the vow— which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds—
and having given all the materials, that Satī [offered them] with Vedic mantras.
She caused a *homa* sacrifice to be performed three hundred thousand times with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Having honored the guests, she likewise fed the Brahmins;
that virtuous goddess, herself firm in her vows, fed them, O you of excellent vows. (13)
She performed this ritual with its full procedure every day for an entire year.
On the day of completion, the brahmin family priest said to her:
"O lady of excellent vows, O lady of excellent vows, give me my fee as a husband. (14–15)
Having heard those words and lamented in the assembly of the gods,
Mahāmāyā fell into a swoon, her mind deluded by Māyā.
And seeing her thus unconscious, those bulls among sages laughed.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu sent Nārada [to Śaṅkara].
Then, requested by the members of the assembly to awaken Śivā, Śiva—the best among speakers—made an effort to speak. (17–18)
Śrī Mahādeva said: "Arise, O blessed lady; welfare shall be yours, there is no doubt. Now, regaining your senses, listen to my words. (19)
Having said this to Śivā, whose throat, lips, and palate were parched,
Śiva placed her upon his chest and restored her consciousness—
[speech that was] beneficial, truthful, measured, and entirely conducive to future happiness. (20)
He began to speak of that which brings glory and yields fruit:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which has been established by the Veda; it is approved by all, desired, and for the sake of dharma, as declared in the assembly of dharma. (21-22)
O Goddess, among all ritual acts, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the very essence; it is eternally the bestower of glory and fruit, O virtuous one, in every righteous deed.
Whether it be for the gods or the ancestors, O beloved, whether performed regularly or on specific occasions—23.
Whatever rite is devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), all of that becomes fruitless;
and by such an act, the donor will certainly go to the Kālasūtra hell.
Then, at the end, he meets with wretchedness, tormented by his enemies.
If the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) intended for a Brahmin is not given at that very moment, then once that hour has passed, the fee shall become double;
once a day has passed, it becomes fourfold; and after a fortnight, it becomes a hundredfold. (29–30)
In one month, it becomes five hundredfold; in six months, four times that;
but when a year has passed, the ritual becomes fruitless.
And the giver goes to hell for as long as a thousand years.
Through sin, one suffers the loss of sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty;
his dharma is destroyed, and when his actions are devoid of dharma, [he falls].
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O most virtuous one, knower of dharma, engaged in righteous deeds, protect your own dharma!
For there shall be protection for all when one's own dharma is preserved.
Brahmā said:
And whoever, for some reason, does not protect the Dharma—
when the Dharma is destroyed and the knower of Dharma has perished, the perpetrator of that act is himself destroyed. (30) Dharma said:
"O virtuous lady, protect me with effort by bestowing the gift of a husband.
O great saintly woman, while I remain [with you], everything will be auspicious.
The gods said:

"O great virtuous lady, protect the Dharma; O chaste one, fulfill your vow! When your vow is complete, we shall make you one whose heart's desire is fulfilled. The sages said: [The sages said: "O great virtuous lady, protect the Dharma; O chaste one, fulfill your vow! When your vow is complete, we shall make you one whose heart's desire is fulfilled. "O virtuous lady, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* sacrifice, give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmin.
O knower of dharma, while we are standing here, what ill fortune could possibly happen?
Sanatkumāra said:

"O Śivā, grant me auspiciousness; otherwise, let the fruit of my vow perish—the fruit of the long-accumulated austerity of my own self. O virtuous lady, I am indeed the fruit of that sacrifice which was performed without the sacrificial fee. (34)
"I shall obtain the full fruit of the sacrificer's ritual.
Pārvatī said:
"O lords of gods, what is the use of my ritual? O sage, what is the use of my sacrificial fee?"
What is the use of a son or of dharma where the husband is the sacrificial fee?
What indeed is the fruit of worshipping trees if the earth itself is not worshipped? When the cause has departed, how can there be an effect; whence the grain, whence the fruit? (36–37)
If the life-breaths have been abandoned by one's own will, what purpose would there be for the bodies?
What purpose is there for an eye deprived of the power of sight?
O lords of the gods, a husband is equal to a hundred sons for virtuous women.
If the husband must be given away as part of a vow, what is the use of that vow or even of a son?
For the lineage and the offspring depend solely upon the husband;
where the root is destroyed, that enterprise is fruitless.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"A master is even more important than a son, and righteousness is more important than a master.
When righteousness has perished, what is the use of a son or a master to one who is most virtuous? (41)
Brahmā said:
O lady of virtuous vows, the highest duty is toward one's master; from duty comes truth.
Truth is action performed according to one's resolve; do not let your vow fall away. 42.
Pārvatī said:
"O knower of the Vedas, listen to my words: the word 'sva' is defined in the Vedas as signifying wealth; he who possesses that [wealth] is the owner."
"His giver is always his master, yet he does not attain the status of being his own master.
Oh, what a lack of order this is, resulting from the ignorance of you who claim to know the Vedas! Dharma said: [44] Dharma said:
"O virtuous lady, no one other than his wife is capable of giving another husband.
A husband and wife are certainly inseparable; in the act of giving, two equals become two.
Pārvatī said: 45. [Note: The verse number provided in the source is 45. Pārvatī said:
"The father gives [his daughter] to the son-in-law, and he takes his daughter;
this has never been heard otherwise by those devoted to the Vedas, for so it is stated in the Śruti.
The gods said:
O Durgā, you are the very nature of intelligence, and we are intelligent through you.
O knower of the Vedas, who among those who discourse on the Vedas is capable of defeating you?
In the meritorious vow, you have been designated as both the presiding deity and the sacrificial fee.
"That which is heard in the Śruti is Dharma; that which is contrary to it is indeed Adharma.
Pārvatī said:
"Who can reach a definitive conclusion by relying solely upon the Veda?"

Who would abandon the worldly Veda, which is powerful, and the conduct of the world? O wise gods, understand that in the Veda, the Puruṣa is certainly more venerable than Prakṛti; why do I speak like a child?
Bṛhaspati said:
"O virtuous lady, there is no creation without the male, nor is there [creation] without Prakṛti.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the creator of both; Prakṛti and Puruṣa are equal. (51)
Pārvatī said:
Kṛṣṇa, the creator of all, is that Person who, by means of a portion, possesses qualities;
the Person is indeed greater than Prakṛti, and she is not greater than him. (52)
In the meantime, in that assembly, the gods and sages beheld in the sky a chariot fashioned from the essence of the finest gems,
surrounded by attendants and accompanied by dark-complexioned, four-armed beings.
Surrounded by forest garlands and adorned with jewel ornaments,
he joyfully descended from his vehicle and approached the floor of the assembly hall.
The lords of the gods praised that deity who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
The Lord, possessing four arms, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
the beloved of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī; peaceful and most enchanting;
visible with ease to devotees, yet invisible to non-devotees even through ten million births. (95–96)
Possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids and a radiance equal to ten million moons,
adorned with beautiful ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels,
he is to be served by Brahmā and the other gods, and is constantly praised by his attendants. (57)
Enveloped and surrounded by the celestial sages who were completely shrouded in its radiance,
he caused him to sit upon an excellent jewel-throne;
and Brahmā, Śakti, Śiva, and the others bowed their heads to him in salutation.
With their hands joined in the *sampuṭa* gesture, all of them had their limbs covered in horripilation and their eyes filled with tears.
He, who was smiling and well-versed in awakening others, questioned them all with a sweet voice;
thus enlightened, he began to speak.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O wise ones, it is not proper for you to speak with such pride;
for all beings in the universe are endowed with power, and it is by that very power that they live. (62)
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the entire material world is real, truly real—except for me; yet by me, Śakti has been manifested.
And she, the Goddess, has appeared from me through my will for the sake of creation.
And she remains withdrawn within me during the dissolution of creation;
she is Prakṛti, the creator of creation, the supreme mother of all.
My Māyā is equal to me, and for that reason she is remembered as Nārāyaṇī.
For a very long time, Śambhu performed austerities while meditating upon me;
therefore, I bestowed upon him this [power] which is the very embodiment of the fruit of his penances. And I prescribed this vow for the sake of instructing the world, and not for my own sake alone.
She herself is the bestower of the fruits of vows and austerities throughout the three worlds.
(67) All beings are deluded by her *māyā*; what, then, could be her own true vow?
Her vow and its fruit are to be accomplished again and again in kalpa after kalpa. (68)
The lords of the gods, who are portions of My own self, as well as Brahmā, Śakti, and Maheśvara;

the Kalās and those whose forms are portions of Kalās, along with the individual souls, the gods, and others—just as a potter is unable to fashion a jar without clay, [so too am I unable to create without these]. (69)
Just as a goldsmith is unable to fashion an earring without gold,
so too am I unable to create my own manifestation without Śakti.
Furthermore, it is the consensus of all philosophical systems that creation is primarily dependent upon Śakti.
For I am the Self, untainted, invisible, and the witness of embodied beings;
all bodies are material, perishable, and composed of the five elements.
I am eternal, the indweller of the body, whose form is the very embodiment of the sun.
That Prakṛti is the support of all; I am the Self of all within the worlds.
(73) I am the Self, the mind, Brahmā, the embodiment of knowledge, and Maheśvara.
I am the five vital breaths, Viṣṇu himself, the intellect, and the sovereign Prakṛti. (74)
Intelligence, sleep, and all these others are the modalities (kalās) of Prakṛti;
and she is this very daughter of the Mountain King—thus it is described in the Veda.
I am the eternal Lord of Goloka and the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.

There itself, the Lord of Devas, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is four-armed and surrounded by his attendants, exists with two arms, himself surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses. He is situated fifty crores of yojanas above Vaikuṇṭha.
And my abode is Goloka, where I am the Lord of the Gopīs.
He who is to be worshipped through vows is the two-armed form, and he is the bestower of its fruit;
for whatever form one contemplates, that very form is the bestower of its fruit.
O Śivā, complete your vow by giving an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having given the appropriate price once more, you shall take the Lord.
Just as cows are the body of Viṣṇu, so too is Śiva the body of Viṣṇu.

"O auspicious lady, having given the price for the cow to the twice-born, take back your husband. For it is the opinion of the Śruti that just as the husband is always capable of giving away his wife as part of a sacrifice, so too is she empowered to give away her husband. (80–81)
Having spoken thus in the midst of the assembly, he vanished right there.
They were delighted and she, being greatly rejoiced, prepared to give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* for Śiva, she gave that auspicious fee to Śiva.
Having said "Svasti," the prince took [the hand] in the assembly of the gods.
Durgā, terrified, her throat, lips, and palate parched, spoke to the Brahmin with palms joined in reverence and a heart burning with anguish. (83–84)
Pārvatī said:
"In the Veda it is established that the value of a cow is equal to my husband.
I shall give you a hundred thousand cows; O twice-born one, give me back my lord. (85)
"Then I shall give various gifts to the Brahmins;
for this body, being devoid of a self, is unable to perform any action.
Sanatkumāra said:

"O Goddess, what need have I for a hundred thousand beautiful cows? By returning the cows in exchange for a priceless jewel that has been given, every person in the three worlds becomes their own giver. (87)
Is the object of action that which is desired by the agent alone, or rather by the desire of another?
(88) Placing a naked mendicant before me, I shall wander through the three worlds, becoming the cause of smiles for the crowds of boys and girls. (89)
Having spoken thus, O Sage, the radiant son of Brahmā took Śaṅkara and established him in the presence [of the gods] within the assembly of the deities.
And Pārvatī, seeing Śiva being taken away by Kumāra, [was filled with grief].
With her throat, lips, and palate parched, she prepared to give up her body.
Reflecting in her mind that this was indeed difficult to overcome, the virtuous woman thought:
"The beloved deity has not been seen, nor has the fruit of my vow been attained."
In the meantime, the gods, together with Pārvatī,
suddenly beheld in the sky a supreme mass of splendors,
blazing in the ten directions and surpassing the brilliance of ten million suns. (93)
In front of Mount Kailāsa, accompanied by all the gods and others,
[he saw] that vast, mandala-shaped abode of all, covered with hosts of attendants.
Having seen that, they praised the Blessed One in succession.
Viṣṇu said: "All the cosmic eggs reside within the pores of his hair; he is this very one who is the Great Virāṭ, yet you are but a sixteenth part of him. Who are we? (96)
Brahmā said:
O Lord, I am capable of seeing that which is visible and employed by the Vedas, and I am able to praise and describe it; yet, being devoted to that Supreme, what more can I praise? ||| 97 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said:
I, the deity presiding over knowledge, praise that which is supreme knowledge—You, the all-pervading Lord who is beyond all description and composed of Your own will. 98.
Dharma said:
What shall I praise—that form of splendor which is invisible during [His] incarnations yet visible to all living beings, and which is a physical manifestation for the grace of His devotees? (99)
The gods said:
"Who are we, mere fragments of Your portions, that we should be capable of praising You?
Even the Vedas are not able to praise Him, nor is Sarasvatī capable. (100)
The sages said:
"Though we are learned, having studied the Vedas, we are unable to praise the cause of the Vedas—you who are beyond both speech and mind. (101)
Sarasvatī said:
Those who discourse on the Vedas declare me to be the goddess presiding over speech;
yet they are unable to praise you even slightly, for you are beyond both speech and mind. 102.
Sāvitrī said: "O Lord, I am the mother of the Vedas, created by you in the past through a portion of yourself; how can I, with the nature of a woman, praise the cause of all causes? (103)
Lakṣmī said:
I am the beloved of Viṣṇu, who is a portion of you, and I am the nourisher of the world.
Why should I praise one created from a fraction of you, the causal seed of the worlds? (104)
Himālaya said: "O Lord, the virtuous laugh at me, the lowly one, who am attempting to praise you, the supreme immobile being; for what can I praise you, being incapable of such praise? (105)
O Sage, after all the gods had praised him in succession, they ceased;
and all the goddesses and sages prepared to praise Pārvatī, who, wearing matted locks and clad in washed garments, was steadfast in her vow during her religious observance. (106)
Impelled by Śiva, she worshipped the Supreme Soul who is to be propitiated through vows;
she was Satī, whose form was composed of splendor, appearing like a blazing flame of fire, the mother of all worlds and the bestower of the fruits of all ascetic practices. (107–108)
Pārvatī said:
O auspicious Kṛṣṇa, you know me; I am not able to know you.
Who indeed knows you—the knowers of the Vedas, the Vedas themselves, or even the authors of the Vedas? (109)
Your own parts do not know You; how then shall Your fractions know You? Do You Yourself know the Reality, or are others capable of knowing it?
You are subtler than the subtle, unmanifest, yet greater than the great and more gross than the gross.
You are the All-pervading, the Universal Form, the Eternal Seed of the Universe.
You are the effect and you are the cause, even the cause of causes.
You are the Lord whose nature is splendor, formless and without support. (111–112)
Untainted, devoid of qualities, the witness, delighting in your own self, you are higher than the highest.
You alone are the Lord of Prakṛti, the seed of the Virāṭ, and the Virāṭ form itself.
For the sake of creation, by means of a portion [of yourself], you possess qualities and consist of Prakṛti. (113)
You are primordial nature (prakṛti) and you are the person (puruṣa); there can be no other Veda anywhere.
You are the individual soul (jīva), the witness, and the enjoyer, being the reflection of your own Self.
You are action (karman), you are the seed of action, and you are the bestower of the fruits of actions.
Yogis meditate upon your bodiless splendor;
some [meditate] upon the four-armed, peaceful, charming beloved of Lakṣmī;
and the Vaiṣṇavas [meditate] upon the embodied, lovely, and captivating form. (115)
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, wearing yellow garments, supreme, two-armed, lovely, youthful, and darkly beautiful;
peaceful, the beloved of the cowherd girls, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (116–117)
Thus, devotees constantly serve that Radiant One with joy;
how could yogis meditate upon that which is apart from the Radiant One?
O God, it was by the splendor of the gods who formerly bore that radiance [that they were empowered]. 118.
Manifested for the sake of slaying the demons and praised by Brahmā,
I am eternal, consisting of the nature of light; O Lord, having assumed a physical form and fashioned a lovely female body, I have presented myself.
"By means of your illusory power, I previously deluded the Asuras with my own māyā;
having slain them all, I went to that Himālaya, the king of mountains. Thereafter, O Lord, I was praised by the gods who were oppressed by Tārakākṣa."
In my birth as Bhava, I was born from the wife of Dakṣa as Śivā;
having abandoned my body at Dakṣa’s sacrifice due to the censure of Śiva, I became the daughter of the Mountain King through his own ritual action. (122–123)
Through manifold austerities, Śiva was attained even in this birth;
the omnipresent Yogi, entreated by Brahmā, took my hand.
Yet, through the divine illusion (māyā), I did not perceive that splendor born of passion.
"I praise you alone for that reason, O Lord, for I am distressed by the suffering caused by my son.
Now, through this vow, I desire to obtain a son such as yourself.
For the Veda, along with its auxiliary branches, has ordained that one's own master is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 125–126 ||
"O ocean of compassion, having heard all this, you ought to show mercy to me.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Pārvatī ceased speaking there.
Whoever, being well-restrained, hears this hymn of praise to Pārvatī in Bhārata—

One surely obtains a virtuous son whose prowess is equal to that of Viṣṇu. By eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) for a year and worshipping Hari with devotion, one obtains the fruit of a most meritorious vow; of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmā, this hymn of praise to Viṣṇu increases all prosperity;
it bestows happiness and liberation, it is the essence, and it augments the good fortune of one's master.
It is the seed of all beauty and the increaser of a mass of glory. (130)
It bestows devotion to Hari and grants the knowledge of reality, intelligence, and happiness.

(131) Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of Pārvatī’s Hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa," within the section on the "Vow of the Auspicious Gift" in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the third Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the hymn of praise by Pārvatī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion,
revealed his own form, which is invisible to all and exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Having offered praise, the Goddess, devoted to her vow, fixed her mind entirely upon Kṛṣṇa.

In the midst of splendors, he beheld His own form, which deludes all; [a form] fashioned from the essence of excellent gems, adorned with diamonds, endowed with garlands of rubies, filled with jewels, and enchanting. (2–3)
Wearing yellow garments as pure as fire, the supreme bestower of lineage,
dark-complexioned with a garland of forest flowers around his neck, adorned with jewel ornaments,
youthful in age, dressed in variegated attire, and marked with sandalwood paste.
His face was graced with a beautiful smile, worthy of praise, and it put to shame the autumnal moon.
He was adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers and wore a crest of peacock feathers.
Surrounded by cowherd women, he shone upon the breast of Rādhā.
Seeing her son, who was as beautiful as ten million gods of love, a charming abode of playful grace,
exceedingly joyful, beloved by all, and the bestower of grace upon his devotees—
the beautiful Rūpavatī beheld him who was worthy of her.
Having obtained that [boon] at that very moment, he chose a boon with his mind.
Having granted whatever was desired in his mind, the Lord of Boons,
after bestowing the wished-for gift upon the gods, vanished along with that splendor.
Having awakened the prince, those filled with compassion gave that incomparable naked child there to the joyful queen of the gods. Durgā, moreover, bestowed various jewels upon the Brahmins.
And Viśvananditā gave gold to the monks and the bards;
she fed the Brāhmaṇas, the gods, and the mountain-dwellers as well,
and she worshipped Śaṅkara with unsurpassed offerings.
She caused the drum to be sounded and had auspicious rites performed;
she had beautiful music related to Hari sung.
Having completed the vow and given gifts, that Durgā, smiling, [departed].
Having fed everyone, he then ate together with his master.
Having offered excellent and beautiful betel, exquisitely scented with camphor and other ingredients,
to all of them in due order, he ate it with him out of curiosity.
Upon a beautiful bed resembling the foam of milk, furnished with a couch of excellent gems and scented with flowers, sandalwood, musk, and saffron,
the Supreme Goddess lay down in secret with her Lord. (16)
And in a certain delightful portion of Kailāsa,
in a sandalwood forest made fragrant by a breeze rich with scented flowers,
resounding with the humming of bees and filled with the songs of male cuckoos. (17)
There Ambikā, that goddess fond of pleasure, conversed with him.
And at the moment of the emission of the seed, Viṣṇu, by means of his illusory power (māyā),
assumed the form of a brahmin and arrived at the house of Rati.
O Sage, [he saw] a mendicant with matted hair, without oil, wearing tattered rags, possessing exceedingly white teeth, yet tormented by thirst;
his body was exceedingly emaciated, and he bore a brilliant tilaka. (20)
With many modulations of voice, piteous, and with a form made wretched by misery,
the very old man, a beggar for food, leaning upon his staff at the door of Rati, being exceedingly frail, called out to Mahādeva. (21–22)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "What are you doing, Mahādeva? Protect me, who have come to you for refuge; seven nights of my vow have passed, and I am hungry, longing for the breaking of the fast. (23)
"What are you doing, O Mahādeva? O dear father, O ocean of compassion!
Look at this old man, seized by old age and tormented by thirst.
Mother, arise and give me food today, and auspicious water!"
O you who are born from the emergence of infinite jewels, protect me who has come to you for refuge! (25) O Mother, O Mother, O Mother of the World, come! I am not standing outside;
I am perishing with thirst while my own Mother stands here. (26)
O Sage, hearing this intonation of voice as Śiva was rising,
his seed fell upon the bed and not into the womb of Prakṛti at that time.
Terrified, Pārvatī stood up, covering herself with a fine garment.
Śaṅkara arrived at the outer gate together with Pārvatī.
There he beheld a wretched brahmin, afflicted by old age,
aged, with trembling limbs, leaning upon a staff.
Seeing that ascetic, who was unpeaceful and whose throat, lips, and palate were parched,
making obeisance and offering praise to the two with supreme devotion,
Nīlakaṇṭha heard his words there, which were like nectar.
Being pleased, he spoke with supreme affection and laughed at him.
Śaṅkara said:
"O brahmin-sage, best among those who know the Vedas, tell me, where is your home?"
"What indeed is your name? I wish to know it immediately.
Pārvatī said:
"O Brahmin, from where have you come? You have arrived here by my good fortune."
Today my birth has become fruitful, for a Brāhmaṇa is a guest in my home.
(33) By him who honors a guest, the three worlds are honored.
O twice-born one, the gods, the Brāhmaṇas, and the gurus are established right there [in the guest]. (34)

The sacred fords (tīrthas) certainly reside perpetually at the feet of guests; by using water mixed with that which has washed their feet, a householder obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords and being initiated into all sacrifices.
(35) He has bathed in all sacred fords and is consecrated in all sacrifices.

By him who has honored a guest according to his own capacity and as is appropriate, all great gifts have been bestowed upon this earth. By him who has honored a guest in Bhārata with devotion, [all great gifts have been bestowed]. (36–37)
Whatever various kinds of merits are indeed declared in the Vedas, others do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of serving a guest. From whose house a guest departs unhonored...
The ancestors, the gods, the sacred fires, and the gurus follow behind when they are not honored.
Whatever sins there may be, including the killing of a Brahmin and others, one incurs them all by failing to honor a desired guest. (39–40)
The Brahmin said:
"O knower of the Vedas, you know the Vedas; perform the worship prescribed in the Vedas.
O mother, I am afflicted by hunger and thirst, and I have heard your words. (41)
When a man afflicted by disease, fasting, or observing a vow of starvation, desires to partake of an offering through the power of his mind, Pārvatī said: 42. Pārvatī said:

"O Brahmin, what do you desire to eat that is so difficult to obtain even in the three worlds? I shall give it to you to eat today; make my birth fruitful. The Brahmin said: 43. O Brahmin, what do you wish to eat that is very difficult to find in the three worlds? I will give it to you to eat today; make my birth fruitful. The Brahmin said:
O Suvratā, you have gathered every kind of offering for your vow—various kinds of sweet and desirable foods. Hearing this, he arrived, saying:
"O Suvratā, I am your son; you shall worship me first."
Having given sweet things that are difficult to find even in the three worlds—(45)—the fathers are said to be of five kinds, and the mothers are remembered as being of various kinds;
O virtuous lady, the sons are declared by the exponents of the Vedas to be of five kinds. (46)

The giver of knowledge, the giver of food, the protector from fear, the progenitor, and the giver of a daughter in marriage—these are remembered in the Vedas as the fathers of men. The wife of one's guru, the nurse who suckled one at the breast, and the father’s sister [are likewise to be honored]. 47.
One's mother’s sister, her co-wife, the wife of one’s son, and she who provides food;
the servant, the pupil, the dependent, the son born of virility, and the refugee;
and the four sons of dharma—the son born of virility is the sharer of the wealth. (48–49)
"O Mother, afflicted by hunger and thirst, I am old and have come to you for refuge. Now, to you who are barren, I am both a son and one without a protector.
[Please give me] flour-cakes, milk-rice, and well-cooked fruits. (50)
Various kinds of flour products originating from different times and places;
cooked food, *svastika* cakes, milk, sugarcane, and products derived from sugarcane;
ghee, curd, *śāli* rice, and side dishes prepared with ghee. (51–52)
Laddukas made of sesame seeds, sweet foods with jaggery,
and other things unknown to me that were equal to nectar;
and excellent, beautiful betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other fragrances— 53.
"Bring these substances—mobile, perfectly pure, and sweet—and scented.
Whatever substances I have eaten that caused my belly to become beautiful and large, you shall give those to me, produced from an inexhaustible mine of jewels. (54–55)
Your Lord is the creator of the three worlds and the bestower of all prosperity.
You are the very embodiment of Mahālakṣmī, the granter of all sovereignty.
[There is] a delightful jeweled throne, priceless and adorned with gems.
You shall grant me beautiful, fire-purified garments that are very difficult to obtain;
likewise, O virtuous one, you shall grant the mantra of Hari, which is very difficult to obtain, and firm devotion to Hari.
You alone are always present as the beloved of Hari and the power of Hari.
O Mother, what is there that cannot be given to one's own son— the knowledge named Mṛtyuñjaya, which bestows the power of giving and happiness, as well as all spiritual accomplishments—
once the mind has been made perfectly pure through constant devotion to dharma and austerity? (59)
I shall perform the sacrifice for the sake of the Supreme, not for the sake of desire which is the cause of rebirth.
(60) From one's own desire one performs action, and from action comes experience alone.
Experience should be known as twofold—auspicious and inauspicious—and these two are the causes of pleasure and pain. (61)
O Mother of the World, why does suffering or happiness not arise [at will]?
Everything is the experience of one’s own karma; therefore, the wise person abstains from it.
Indeed, the virtuous constantly and joyfully uproot karma itself.
Through the cultivation of the thought of Hari, by that very austerity, and through association with devotees, the pleasure arising from the contact of the senses with their objects is destroyed;
meanwhile, the pleasure consisting of conversation about Hari is eternal. (63–64)
For the virtuous who are habituated to the remembrance of Hari, their true life does not pass away.
For them, neither Time nor even the Lord of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya) is certain [to prevail].
Those devotees live for a long time; they are long-lived in Bhārata.
Having realized all perfections, they move everywhere at will.
These devotees of Hari remember their births; they know ten million lifetimes, relate stories of them, and take birth joyfully according to their own desire. (66–67)
Furthermore, those who are themselves purified purify sacred fords by their own divine play.
They wander here in this field of merit for the sake of service and for the benefit of others;
by the touch of the feet of Vaiṣṇavas, the earth becomes instantly sanctified.
For as long as it takes to milk a cow, they dwell at that sacred ford (tīrtha).
Those who know the ancient lore declare that he into whose ears the Viṣṇu-mantra enters from the mouth of the Guru is a Vaiṣṇava purified by the sacred ford.
In Bhārata, through devotion, they effortlessly deliver a hundred ancestors and a hundred descendants of men, as well as their brothers and mothers;
and ten ancestors and ten descendants of their maternal grandfathers.
They rescue their mother from the terrible beating by Yama.
Those men who obtain the sight and embrace of a devotee have visited all sacred fords and are consecrated in all sacrifices.

Devotees whose minds are constantly fixed on Hari are not smeared by sins, just as fires are not satiated by any kind of fuel or as winds are not obstructed by any substances. At the end of thirty million births, one attains birth as a human being.
Through ten million births as a human, he attains association with devotees.
From association with devotees, the sprout of devotion arises and becomes truly alive;
yet from the mere sight of one who is not a devotee, it withers away.
It blossoms again merely through conversation with a Vaiṣṇava;
its sprout is indestructible and grows in every birth.
O virtuous lady, for that tree as it flourishes, the fruit is service to Hari.
Upon the ripening of his devotion, he shall become an attendant of Hari.
It is certain that at the time of the great dissolution, his destruction shall not occur;
even during the withdrawal of the entire creation, including the world of Brahmā and its creator.
Therefore, O Mother, grant me always devotion to Nārāyaṇa;
for without you, O Viṣṇu-māyā, devotion to Viṣṇu would not exist.
For the sake of instructing the world, perform your own penance and worship of yourself toward one who possesses that [devotion].
"You are the bestower of fruits upon all, eternal in form and everlasting.
In kalpa after kalpa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the form of Gaṇeśa, shall be your son;
he will quickly come into your lap. Having said this, he vanished.
Having made himself invisible and assuming the form of a child,
the Lord went to Pārvatī’s bedchamber situated within the palace.
And when Śiva’s seed was deposited upon the bed, he became mixed with it.
He beheld the pinnacle of the house as if a child had been born;
possessing the luster of the color of pure campaka flowers and a radiance equal to ten million moons, he was pleasant for all people to behold and increased the brilliance of their eyes. (84–85)
His body was exceedingly beautiful, capable of enchanting even the god of love;
he bore a peerless happiness that put the autumnal moon to shame, and he possessed lovely eyes that mocked the beauty of charming lotuses. (86)
Bearing a pair of lips that put the ripe bimba fruit to shame,
his forehead and cheeks were supremely captivating; and possessing a beautiful tip of the nose that mocked the beak of Indra’s bird.

Bearing a most excellent form, peerless in all its limbs throughout the three worlds, he lay upon a beautiful couch, moving his hands and feet. (89) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Gaṇeśa," in the *Gaṇeśakhaṇḍa*, the third part of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (8)
Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, when Hari had vanished, Śarvāṇī Durgā and Śaṅkara then searched for the brāhmaṇas and wandered about on all sides. 1.
Pārvatī said:
"O best of Brahmins, O very aged one, where have you gone, afflicted by hunger?
O father, grant me your sight; O Lord, protect my life! || 2 ||
"O Śiva, arise quickly and seek out the brahmin!
For a moment he has become invisible to us both.
O Lord, a guest who departs from the house of a householder without having received worship—" || 3 ||
If he departs afflicted by hunger, what is the use of his life in vain?
(4) His ancestors do not accept his offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) or the water libation (*tarpaṇa*);
the Fire-god does not accept his oblation, nor do the gods accept his flowers or water. (5)
The sacrificial offering, the flower, the water, and the ritual substance [of one who is] impure are equal to liquor;
the funeral cake is like excrement, and its touch destroys merit.
(6) In that interval, an incorporeal voice arose there.
Afflicted with grief, she heard that Durgā was united with Kaivalya (liberation).
"Be at peace, O Mother of the World! Behold your own son in the palace—Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, the Supreme and Most Perfect One. (7–8)
That eternal splendor, which is the fruit of the tree of most meritorious vows,
which yogis constantly meditate upon with perpetual joy,
and which the Vaiṣṇava deities— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others— indeed meditate upon.
To that worshipful one, whose worship is performed at the very beginning of every eon after eon;
by the mere remembrance of whom all obstacles are destroyed;
and who is the very embodiment of a mass of merit—behold your own son in the palace. (10–11)
Behold, O son, that eternal form of light which you have meditated upon age after age— the bestower of liberation, the embodiment of grace toward devotees,
the seed that fulfills your desires, and the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of your asceticism. (12)
"Behold your own handsome son, who puts even ten million Cupids to shame!
This is no Brahmin afflicted by hunger; he is Janārdana in the form of a Brahmin.
Why do you lament? Where is the old man, and where is the guest?"
O Nārada, having spoken thus, Sarasvatī fell silent;
and the virtuous lady, terrified upon hearing the voice from the sky, went to her own abode.
There she beheld the child lying on his couch, smiling with joy. (14–15)
Beholding the roof-peak of his house, which possessed a splendor equal to a hundred moons,
illuminating the surface of the earth by the very mass of his own radiance,
he was seen joyfully moving about upon his couch according to his own will. (16)
Seeing him crying out "Umā!

and weeping while desiring her breast, she was terrified by that wondrous sight; having gone into the presence of Śaṅkara, she, who is the auspiciousness of all auspicious things, spoke to Giriśa. (17–18)
Pārvatī said:
O Lord of All, come to my home, which bestows the fruit of austerities;
having come to this residence, behold him whom you meditate upon in kalpa after kalpa. 19.
Quickly behold the face of your son, the great festival of meritorious seed,
the cause of protection from the hell named Put, and the means of your own deliverance.
It is equivalent to bathing in all sacred fords and the sacrificial fee of all sacrifices.
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of this sight of one's son.
Whatever merit is gained from all forms of giving and whatever from circumambulating the earth,
it does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of seeing one's son.

Whatever merit is gained through all forms of austerity, by fasting, and by religious observances, does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit arising from a virtuous son. Whatever merit is gained by feeding Brahmins and whatever by serving the gods—
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit gained from obtaining a virtuous son.
Having heard Pārvatī’s words, Śiva, his mind filled with joy,
quickly returned to his own abode together with his beloved.
He beheld his son upon the couch, resembling molten gold;
he was that very same exceedingly enchanting form which resided within his heart.
Taking that son from Durgā’s couch and placing him upon his breast—
She said to him: "I am submerged in an ocean of bliss born from tasting you, having obtained you—the eternal and perfect one—who are like a priceless jewel;
just as the mind of a pauper is upon suddenly acquiring great wealth. (26–27)

Just as the minds of women become completely fulfilled when their beloved returns after a long absence abroad, so too did my mind become fulfilled. To me, who had only one son, the news that he had gone away for a very long time and had now returned was like a story [of a long-lost child].
"O child, just as she was delighted upon seeing you, so am I now.
Just as a person is thrilled to recover a fine jewel that had been lost for a very long time, so am I, having obtained my son after a drought-like period. (29–30)
Just as the mind of one who has been blind for a very long time, remaining without support, becomes completely full upon obtaining a perfectly clear eye, so too is it with me;
even though I have fallen into a terrible and difficult-to-cross ocean of distress. (31)
Just as one who is without a boat finds a boat, so too is my mind fulfilled;
and just as those whose throats are parched with thirst find very cool and well-scented water after a long time, so too is my mind fulfilled. (32–33)

And for those fallen into a forest fire who stand without refuge, my mind is likewise full once it has found a refuge free from fire; so too for those long famished who perform vows and fasts. (34–35)
"Seeing excellent food before me, my mind is likewise filled.
Having said this, Pārvatī placed her young son upon her lap there and,
with a heart full of supreme bliss, affectionately gave him her breast.
With a joyful heart, the Blessed One took the boy onto his lap;
he kissed him on the cheek as prescribed by the Vedas and joyfully bestowed his blessings upon him.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Child Gaṇeśa," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having gone outside for the sake of their son’s auspiciousness,
that couple joyfully gave various kinds of jewels to the twice-born.
Śaṅkara caused various gifts to be given to bards and mendicants, and he had diverse musical instruments played. And Himālaya gave a hundred thousand jewels to the twice-born.
A thousand lordly elephants and three hundred thousand horses;
ten lakhs of cows and five lakhs of gold pieces;
pearls, rubies, gems, and whatever other excellent jewels there may be. (3–4)
Viṣṇu, filled with joy, gave to the Brāhmaṇas various other gifts— clothes and ornaments, as well as all manner of priceless jewels produced from the Ocean of Milk— and the Kaustubha gem.
Brahmā joyfully bestowed upon the Brahmins, for their desire, excellent gifts that are exceedingly difficult to obtain within this creation.
Likewise, Dharma, Sūrya, Śakra, the gods, and the sages [did so].
The Gandharvas, the mountains, and the goddesses gave gifts in succession:
thousands of rubies, hundreds of gems, hundreds of *kaustubha* stones, and hundreds of diamonds. (7–8)
Filled with joy, they [offered] thousands of the finest emeralds,
hundreds of thousands of cows as jewels, a thousand jewel-like elephants,
and other priceless white-colored gems out of curiosity. 10.
There, Brahmā joyfully gave to the Brāhmaṇas a hundred lakhs of gold pieces and garments purified by fire;
and the Ocean of Milk gave a necklace of priceless gems, difficult to find in the three worlds.
The goddess Sarasvatī gave him a most pure and essential gem that outshone the rays of the sun; it was adorned with rubies and diamonds, radiant, and set within a beautiful kaustubha stone. (12–13)
That Sāvitrī joyfully gave him a necklace— the essence of the three worlds— crafted from a multitude of excellent gems, as well as all her ornaments,
a hundred thousand gold coins, and various kinds of wealth. (14)

And Kubera joyfully gave hundreds of priceless jewels. Having bestowed gifts upon the brahmins, O Sage, they all, filled with supreme bliss, beheld the infant during the festival for the son of Śiva. || 15–16 ||
Incapable of bearing their burdens, the Brahmins and the bards moved along the road, stopping again and again; being timid regarding their wealth,
they all, once rested, recounted stories of those who had given in the past.
The Buddhas listen with joy, O Sage, as do the youthful monks.
There, Viṣṇu, being greatly delighted, caused the drum to be sounded;
he provided the music and had them perform a dance.
O Nārada, he caused him to recite the Vedas and the Purāṇas;
he brought the lords of sages and joyfully honored them;
he caused blessings to be bestowed and had auspicious rites performed.
Together with the goddesses, the god bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
Viṣṇu said:
"O child, may you possess knowledge equal to Śiva and a supreme lifespan."
"In prowess you shall be equal to me; become the lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Brahmā said:
The world shall be filled with your fame, and you shall be worshipped by all for a long time."
"May worship before all beings be exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Dharma said:
"May you be as truly righteous as I; such a person is rare to find."
He is omniscient, endowed with compassion, a devotee of Hari, and equal to Hari himself.
Mahādeva said:
"Become a giver equal to me, a wise devotee of Hari."
"O beloved of my life, may you be learned, meritorious, peaceful, and self-controlled.
Lakṣmī said:
"May my presence abide eternally in your home and in your body."
"A devoted wife equal to me—tranquil, beloved, and enchanting.
Sarasvatī said:
"Equal to me is excellent poetry and the power of retention."
"O son, may your memory and power of discernment become exceedingly great.
Sāvitrī said:
"O child, may I, the mother of the Vedas and the knower of the Vedas, become so before long."
And he was devoted to the recitation of my mantra, the most eminent among the exponents of the Vedas.
(27) Himālaya said:
May there be constant and eternal devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by supreme wisdom.
"Be virtuous like Śrī Kṛṣṇa and devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Menakā said:
"Be as profound as the ocean and as handsome as the god of love."
"Endowed with glory, be equal to the Lord of Glory; in dharma, be equal to Dharma.
Vasundharā said:
"In character, be like me—forgiving, a refuge for all, and possessed of every jewel."
"O child, may you be free from obstacles, a subduer of obstacles, and a refuge of auspiciousness.
Pārvatī said:
"He is a great yogi equal to my father, a perfected one, the bestower of perfection, and auspicious."
"May the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya be exceedingly proficient.
Thus did the ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas all offer their blessings;
and the brahmins and bards likewise offered every auspicious benediction.
Everything has been told to you, my child— this narration of the birth of Gaṇeśa, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, which destroys all obstacles.
Whoever hears this supreme lord of auspiciousness shall find happiness thereby.
Endowed with all auspiciousness, he shall become an abode of auspiciousness.
The childless obtains a son; the poor obtains wealth;
the wretched obtains courage; and it is the eternal bestower of prosperity.
One seeking a wife obtains a wife; one seeking offspring obtains offspring.
The sick obtain health, and the unfortunate obtain good fortune.
One who has lost a son, lost wealth, or whose beloved is away shall regain them. (36)

One who is overcome by grief always attains bliss; there is no doubt about this. O Sage, whatever merit a mortal gains from hearing the narrative of Gaṇeśa, that very fruit one certainly obtains from hearing this chapter.

And whoever has this Chapter on Auspiciousness (Maṅgalādhyāya) in their home shall always be endowed with auspiciousness; of this there is no doubt. And he who, with a concentrated mind, listens to it at the time of a journey or on a holy day—
He obtains every desired object through the grace of Śrī Gaṇeśa.

(40) Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Auspicious Origin of Gaṇeśa," in the Gaṇeśa-khaṇḍa of the third book of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having offered his most excellent blessing upon the preeminent jeweled lion-throne,
Hari sat there in that assembly together with the gods and the sages.
To his right was Śaṅkara, and to his left was Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures.
In front [of him] was Dharma, the witness of the worlds and the best among the righteous.
Likewise, O Brahmin, near Dharma sat Sūrya, Śakra, the Moon (the storehouse of digits), the gods, the sages, and the mountains upon comfortable seats. (2–3)
The ranks of dancers danced, the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang,
and the Vedas praised Hari— the essence of the scriptures and the delight of the ears—
in this interval, having come there to behold the son of Śaṅkara.
The great yogi Śanaiścara, the son of the Sun, arrived.
With his face deeply bowed and his eyes slightly closed,
he remembered Kṛṣṇa both internally and externally, his mind fixed solely on Kṛṣṇa.
Feeding on the fruits of austerity, radiant and resembling a blazing flame of fire,
he was exceedingly handsome, dark-complexioned, and clad in yellow garments— an excellent being.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, Dharma, Ravi, and the gods, [he departed].
With their permission, he went to see Bālaka, the Lord of Sages.
Having reached the main gate, he spoke to the gatekeeper Viśālākṣa, who possessed prowess equal to Śiva and held a trident in his hand. || 8-9 ||
Śanaiścara said:
"O servant of Śaṅkara, by the command of Śiva, I am going to see the Child, at the request of the gods headed by Viṣṇu and of the sages. (10)
"O wise one, give me permission to go into the presence of Pārvatī.
Once I have seen the child again, my mind will become attached to worldly objects.
Viśālākṣa said: "I am not a bearer of commands for the gods, nor am I a servant of Śaṅkara."
"I am not able to grant passage without the permission of my mother," he said;
having spoken thus, he went inside and, impelled by the command of Śiva,
the large-eyed one then joyfully granted passage to the Lord of Planets.
Śani, having gone inside, bowed with his neck bent low;
he joyfully beheld Pārvatī seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, smiling, and constantly served by five female companions with white fly-whisks. (14)
Having enjoyed the fragrant betel-leaf offered by her friend, she was dressed in garments purified by fire and adorned with jeweled ornaments;
holding her son to her breast, she watched the dance of the female performers. (15–16)
Seeing the son of the Sun prostrate, Durgā quickly addressed him;
having inquired after his auspicious welfare, she bestowed upon him her auspicious blessings.
(37) Pārvatī said:
"Why is your face so dejected? I wish to hear this now.
Do you not see me, O virtuous one, as a mere child, O Lord of Planets?
Śani replied:
O virtuous lady, all enjoy the fruit of their own austerity;
and whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is performed, it is not destroyed even in ten million kalpas.
By that very action, a living being is born in the abodes of Brahmā, Indra, Aryaman, or Yama.
By action one is born in human homes, and by action among animals and the like;
by action one goes to hell, and by action one goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
By one’s own action one becomes a lord of kings, O Indra of kings, and by one’s own action one becomes a servant.
By his own karma one is eternally handsome; by one's own karma one is afflicted with disease.
By one's own karma, O Mother, one becomes a master of sense-objects; yet by one's own karma one remains untainted.
By one's own karma a person in this world becomes wealthy; by one's own karma one is beset by wretchedness.
By one's own action one becomes a good householder, and by one's own action a thorn to one's kinsmen;
by one's own action one has a good wife and good sons, and is perpetually happy.
By one's own action one is childless, has a bad wife, or is without a wife at all. (23–24)
O beloved of Śaṅkara, hear this most secret history,
which is unfit to be told in the presence of one’s mother and is a cause for shame.
From my very childhood, I have been a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, with my mind solely intent on meditating upon Kṛṣṇa.
Constantly devoted to ascetic practices, yet always also attached to sensual objects,
her father gave that exceedingly radiant maiden, who was ever intent on penance, in marriage to Citraratha. (26–27)
Once, having bathed after her menses and having dressed herself in beautiful attire, she—
adorned with jewel ornaments and enchanting the mind of the sage—
beheld him meditating on the foot of Hari, herself deluded by passion. (28)
Approaching me with a smile and tremulous eyes,
she cursed me— who was devoid of external perception and whose mind was absorbed in meditation— for not seeing her due to the loss of my season, out of anger. (29–30)
"Because you did not guard your season, I was not seen by you;
and whatever object you have seen, O fool, all of it is destroyed.
And I, having desisted from meditation, was then pleasing that virtuous woman."
She was unable to release the curse and fell into deep remorse.
"Therefore, O Mother, I do not see any object with my own eyes.
Consequently, with my face naturally bowed down out of fear of harming living beings," [I remain thus].
O Sage, having heard the words of Śanaiścara, Pārvatī laughed;
all the hosts of dancers and Kinnarīs laughed loudly.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Cause of Śani’s Downcast Gaze," within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard those words, Durgā remembered Hari, the Lord;
she spoke thus: "The world indeed is subject to the will of the Lord. (1)
And that goddess, by the power of fate, spoke out of curiosity to Śani:
"Look at me and my child; who can ward off the flow of destiny?
Having heard Pārvatī's words, Śani reflected within his own heart.
"I see him; do I not see the son of Pārvatī? Alas!
If this child were seen by me, his obstacle would surely be brought about.
Otherwise, it is most auspicious to protect oneself beforehand. (3)
Having spoken thus, the righteous Śani, having made Dharma his witness,
set his mind on seeing the boy, but not his mother.
Previously dejected in spirit, his throat, lips, and palate were parched.
And with the corner of his left eye, he beheld the face of the child.
By the mere glance of Śani, O Sage, the head was severed.
Śani closed his eyes and stood with his face bowed down.
And he remained in the lap of Pārvatī; his entire body was blood-red. Having gone to the desired Goloka, he entered the head of Kṛṣṇa.
That goddess fell into a swoon, lamenting intensely again and again.

And all those gods, the goddesses, the mountains, and all the Gandharvas dwelling on Kailāsa stood motionless upon the earth, holding the child to their chests, like figures in a painting, filled with wonder. (8–9)

Seeing them all unconscious, Hari mounted Garuḍa and went to the Puṣpabhadrā river situated in the northern direction. On the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river, he indeed beheld him standing in the forest.
There he saw the lordly elephant sleeping with his mate, his head turned toward the north;
beautiful and overcome by the exhaustion of sexual union, his mind filled with supreme bliss as he surrounded his young ones. (11–12)
With great joy, he swiftly severed that head with the Sudarśana discus alone;
he placed it, dripping with blood and captivating to behold, upon Garuḍa.
