Through the tossing of the elephant’s severed limbs, the female elephant regained consciousness.
Then, speaking of the impurity [of her state], she awakened her young ones;
afflicted by grief, she wept and lamented together with her young ones.
She praised the Lord who is the beloved of Kamalā, the peaceful one who smiles.
The Supreme One, wearing yellow garments, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
seated upon Garuḍa, the beloved of the world, who whirls the Sudarśana [discus],
the all-pervading Lord capable of destroying the *niṣeka* and the progenitor of the *niṣeka*.
To the one who bestows the enjoyment of conception and is the cause of liberation from worldly enjoyment,
the Lord, pleased by her praise, granted a boon to that brahmin.
Having severed the head and trunk of one elephant, he joined them to another elephant.
The omniscient one restored him there through the knowledge of Brahman;
he joined the elephant’s lotus-foot to every limb.
"O elephant, you shall live together with your followers until the end of the kalpa."
Having spoken thus, he, who travels at the speed of thought, went indeed to Kailāsa.
Having taken [the head] from the hand of Pārvatī and placed the child upon his own chest,
he properly joined that beautiful head to the boy.
The Lord, whose nature is Brahman, through his divine play and by means of the knowledge of Brahman,
quickly restored him to life with the utterance of the syllable "Huṃ.
Having awakened Pārvatī and placed that infant upon his lap...
Kṛṣṇa awakened her with spiritual instructions.
Viṣṇu said:
"From Brahmā down to a mere insect, every being experiences the fruit of its own karma."
O Śiva, do you not know that you are the very nature of the consciousness of the world?

(23) For living beings, the experience of hundreds of millions of kalpas arises constantly through their own karma; it manifests perpetually in every womb according to their auspicious and inauspicious deeds. (24)
Indra may obtain birth in the womb of an insect through his own karma;
and an insect, indeed, may become Indra through the fruit of past karma.
Even a lion is unable to kill a fly without [the influence of] the past.
A mosquito is capable of killing an elephant by means of its own prior [karma].
(26) Happiness, suffering, fear, sorrow, and joy are the fruits of action.
From good action comes happiness and joy; from other [actions], namely evil action, come the others. (27)
In this very world, as well as in the next, there is the experience of the fruits of action through both auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
And Bhārata is a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) fit for the accumulation of karma;
it is the bestower of the fruits of action and the ordainer even of destiny itself.
The death of death, the time of time, the one who performs the consecration of even the consecration;
the destroyer of even the destroyer, the protector of even the protector, higher than the highest—Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, is himself the most perfect Supreme Being. (29–30)
We are but portions of that Supreme Person from whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara arise;
the Mahāvirāṭ is a mere fraction of Him, and within the pores of His hair lies the entire universe.
Some are portions of His attributes, and some are even portions of those portions.
There Vināyaka remained, [guarding] the entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having heard the words of Śrī Viṣṇu, Pārvatī was thoroughly delighted;
having bowed to that wielder of the mace (Gadādhara), she gave her breast to the infant.
Pleased and urged by Śaṅkara, Pārvatī,
with palms joined in devotion, offered praise to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Kamalā.
Viṣṇu, in turn, bestowed his blessing upon the child and the mother of the child.
He placed the Kaustubha gem, his own ornament, around the neck of the boy.
Brahmā gave him his own crown, and Dharma indeed gave him a jewel-ornament.
In due order, all the goddesses gave jewels as was appropriate.
Mahādeva, his mind exceedingly joyful, praised him;
and the gods, sages, mountains, Gandharvas, and all the women likewise [praised him],
having seen Śiva and Śivā, along with the child restored to life from death.
O Nārada, he gave ten million jewels there to the Brahmins;
and he bestowed hundreds and thousands of horses and elephants upon the bards there for the sake of reviving the dead child.
The Himalaya was satisfied, and the gods there were indeed delighted. They gave gifts to the Brahmins and to the bards, as did all the women.
He fed the Brahmins and caused auspicious rites to be performed.
The Lord of Ramā taught him the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
Seeing Śani filled with shame, Pārvatī, manifesting her anger,
cursed him in the midst of the assembly, saying, "May you become devoid of limbs."
Seeing Śani cursed, Sūrya, Kaśyapa, and Yama likewise arose in great rage, intent on departing from the abode of Śaṅkara. With blood-red eyes and red faces, their lips quivered with anger.
Having made Dharma their witness, they prepared to swear an oath against Viṣṇu.
Brahmā, urged by the gods and impelled by Viṣṇu, enlightened them [regarding] Pārvatī, whose face was flushed with red and whose lower lip quivered with anger. 44–45.
There, all the deities, the timid sages, and likewise the mountains, spoke in due order to Brahmā according to the occasion. Kaśyapa said:
This was ill-fated due to a previous curse from his wife;
he beheld the child with great effort at the command of the mother.
Śrīsūrya said:
Making that Dharma his witness, by the command of her son’s mother,
she beheld the Son of Pārvatī with great effort;
for she saw how she had cursed my innocent son.
"And there will be the breaking of his limbs; of this there is no doubt.
Yama said:
"Having personally given the command, how could she herself have cursed him?"
"We shall curse him; what unrighteousness is there in harming one who seeks to kill?
Brahmā said:
"Pārvatī, enraged and out of feminine fickleness, uttered a curse."
"May all the virtuous ones forgive me by their very word.
Having granted you entry into this fortress and permission to see your son,
how can you curse an innocent guest who has come to your house?"
Having spoken thus, and having taken Śani and informed Pārvatī,
he offered him to her for the sake of releasing the curse.
O Sage, Pārvatī became pleased by the word of Brahmā.
On that day, the Sun, Yama, and Kaśyapa became pacified.
There, Pārvatī— propitiated by Śiva and served by Brahmā— being well-pleased, spoke to Śanaiścara.
Pārvatī said:
"O Śani, by my boon, may you become the king of the planets and a beloved of Hari;
may you be long-lived and a lord of yogins—for what calamity can there be for one who is devoted to Hari? (56)
"From this day forward, may your devotion to Hari be firm and free from obstacles.
Since my curse is unfailing, you shall now become somewhat lame.
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī, being pleased, took the boy to her breast.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, she dwelt in the midst of women; then,
O Brahmin, Śani, with a joyful mind, departed for the presence of the gods after bowing with devotion to that Ambikā, the Mother of the World.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of Śani’s Vision of Gaṇeśa, the Falling of Gaṇeśa’s Head, Viṣṇu’s Reattachment of Gaṇeśa’s Head, and the Curse of Śani," in the Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, at an auspicious time, Viṣṇu, together with the gods and sages, [proceeded].

He worshipped that child with unsurpassed offerings. "O best of gods, worship has been offered by me to you first of all; therefore, O child, become a lord of yogis who is worthy of worship by all," he said to him.

Hari gave him a forest garland and the knowledge of Brahman which bestows liberation; having granted all perfections, he made him equal to himself. He also gave him beautiful articles and the sixteen modes of worship.
Together with the sages and the gods, he performed a hymn of praise using these names:
Vighneśa, Gaṇeśa, Heramba, Gajānana, Lambodara, Ekadanta, Śūrpakarṇa, and Vināyaka. (4–5)
These eight names bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
He caused them to grant his blessing and brought those sages there;
Dharma gave him the Siddhāsana, and Brahmā gave him a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
Śaṅkara gave the yogic belt and the very rare knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
Śakra gave a jeweled lion-throne, and Sūrya gave two jeweled earrings.
Candra gave a necklace of rubies, and Kubera gave a crown.
The Fire-god gave him a garment purified by fire;
Varuṇa gave a jeweled parasol; Vāyu gave a jeweled ring;
and [the Ocean] gave an excellent bracelet fashioned from choice gems produced in the Milk Ocean.
O Sage, Padmālayā gave him anklets and armlets;
Sāvitrī gave a neck-ornament, and Bhāratī a radiant necklace.
In due order, all the gods and goddesses gave him wedding gifts.
The Earth gave him sages, mountains, various jewels,
and a mouse as a vehicle.
In due order, the gods, goddesses, sages, mountains, and others [bestowed their gifts].
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Manus, and Mānavas likewise [offered] various kinds of substances, both savory and sweet; and they all performed worship in due order with devotion. (13–14)
O Nārada, Pārvatī, the mother of the worlds, her lotus-face smiling, seated her son upon a jeweled throne,
having honored him with water from all sacred fords collected in jeweled pitchers. (19)
Then Satī joyfully bathed him with mantras declared in the Vedas, assisted by the sages; she gave him two garments purified by fire,
and offered water for his feet and the respectful arghya-offering with the waters of the Godāvarī and the Gaṅgā.
Having brought water from the Puṣkara lake together with dūrvā grass, unbroken grains, flowers, and sandalwood,
[he offered] the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) again;
then the honey-mixture (madhuparka) in jeweled vessels, and the spirituous liquor (āsava) mixed with sugar.
There was bathing water and Viṣṇu-oil prepared by the two celestial physicians,
a multitude of beautiful ornaments set with priceless gems,
and hundreds of other flowers from the Pārijāta tree.
Various flowers such as *mālatī* and *campaka*,
leaves worthy of worship along with *tulasī*,
and sandalwood, *aguru*, musk, and saffron should be offered with reverence. (20)
He offered a multitude of jewel-lamps and incense on all sides;
he presented food offerings dear to Him, including mountains of sesame laddus,
and mountains of laddus made from the flour of barley and wheat.
There were mountains of cooked foods, delicious and enchanting;
mountains of *svastika* cakes mixed with delicious sugar;
and mountains of parched grain (*lāja*) and flattened rice (*pṛthuka*) smeared with molasses.
With joy, he gave away hundreds of thousands of mountains of rice, flour-based foods, and various side dishes, along with hundreds of thousands of jars filled with milk;
and for the sake of worship, he also gave hundreds of thousands of jars filled with curd.
And Sundarī [offered] three hundred thousand jars of honey;
respectfully, five hundred thousand jars of ghee and gold;
and countless fruits of pomegranates and bilvas. (25–26)
O Nārada, with great joy he gave him countless fruits of dates, wood-apples, rose-apples, and various others; as well as mangoes, jackfruits, plantains, and coconuts. (27)
O illustrious one, he gave those other fruits which were ripe, produced in the proper season and place, delicious, and sweet;
as well as water that was clear, perfectly pure, and exquisitely scented with camphor and other perfumes.
Ganges water for drinking, and again water for sipping; O Nārada, excellent and beautiful betel-leaf scented with camphor and other fragrances, and a hundred golden vessels filled with edible foods.
The ministers, beloved of the king of mountains, worshipped the son of the mountain-born goddess.
Om Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ! Salutations again and again to Gaṇeśvara, who is the embodiment of Brahman, who is beautiful, and who bestows all supernatural powers; salutations to the Lord of the Universe.
Having offered these substances with devotion by means of this very mantra,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all the others there became exceedingly joyful.
This thirty-two-syllable garland-mantra grants all desires.
It bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and grants all perfections.
(34) By merely reciting it five hundred thousand times, the practitioner attains mantra-siddhi.
He who achieves mantra-siddhi is indeed Viṣṇu himself in this world of Bhārata. (35)
And obstacles flee by the mere recollection of its name.
He becomes a great orator, attains great accomplishment, and is endowed with all perfections. It is certain that he directly becomes a master of speech and attains the status of a guru. (36)
The great lord of poets, possessed of virtue, and the teacher of teachers to the learned—
having worshipped him with this mantra, the gods, overflowing with bliss,
played various kinds of musical instruments during the festival. (37–38)
They fed the Brahmins and caused a festival to be celebrated; they gave gifts to them and especially to the bards.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Viṣṇu, having honored that Lord of the Gaṇas in the midst of the assembly, praised with supreme devotion the destroyer of all obstacles:
"O Lord, I desire to praise you, the eternal light of Brahman. (40)
One is not at all able to describe him appropriately, for he is effortless,
the most excellent of all gods, the teacher of the Siddhas and Yogins,
the embodiment of all forms, the Lord of all, whose very nature is a mass of knowledge. 41–42.
Unmanifest, imperishable, eternal, and the true nature of the Self;
like the wind, untainted, unimpaired, and the witness of all;
situated on the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, where the boat of *māyā* is exceedingly difficult to find. (43)
He is the embodiment of the helmsman and the bestower of grace upon his devotees.
He is the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the giver of boons, and even the Lord of those who grant boons.
He is the perfected one, the very nature of perfection, the bestower of success, and the means for attaining success.
It is beyond meditation, yet the object of meditation; it is not accomplished by meditation, yet it is righteous.
It is the very nature of Dharma, the knower of Dharma, and the bestower of the fruits of both merit and demerit.
It is the seed of the trees of worldly existence and the sprout that rests upon it. (46)
This form of women, men, and neuter beings is beyond the reach of the senses.
It is the primordial source of all, the foremost object of worship, worthy of universal adoration, and an ocean of virtues.
By its own will, Brahman is with attributes (saguṇa), and again by its own will, it is without attributes (nirguṇa).
You are yourself the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), yet you are the natural state beyond primordial nature.
Even Ananta, with his thousand mouths, is unable to praise you;
neither is Pañcavaktra capable, nor is Caturānana.
"Sarasvatī is not capable, nor am I capable of praising you;
even the four Vedas are not capable—what then of those who merely recite the Vedas?
Having thus offered this praise in the assembly of the lords of sages and the gods, [he remained silent].
And Sureśa, the Lord of Ramā, together with the gods, ceased [speaking].
Whoever should recite this hymn to Gaṇeśa composed by Viṣṇu—endowed with devotion and with a concentrated mind—at evening, at dawn, and at midday; || 51-52 ||
O Sage, Vighneśa constantly destroys those obstacles;
he, the progenitor of all auspiciousness, always increases every form of well-being.
Whoever goes forth at the time of a journey after reciting this with devotion to him, [attains success].
For him, the accomplishment of all desired aims occurs indeed; of this there is no doubt.
Even a bad dream seen by him turns into a good dream.
Never shall he suffer from the terrible affliction of the planets.
There shall be the destruction of enemies and the increase of kinsmen;
the perpetual destruction of obstacles and the perpetual, perfect prosperity.
Fortune shall be stable in the home, with the increase of sons and grandsons.
Having attained all sovereignty in this world, one shall indeed obtain the station of Viṣṇu at the end;
and by the grace of Gaṇeśa, one shall also certainly obtain the fruit that belongs to all holy places, sacrifices, and all great gifts. || 57-58 ||
Nārada said:
"I have heard the hymn of praise to Gaṇeśa and his enchanting ritual worship;
now I wish to hear the armor-verse (kavaca), which provides protection in this present time. (59)
Nārāyaṇa said: When the worship had been properly concluded, Śanaiścara spoke to Viṣṇu— the savior of all and the teacher of the worlds— amidst the assembly.
Śanaiścara said:
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the armor (kavaca) of the Destroyer of Obstacles, for the destruction of all suffering and the pacification of sin. (61)
A dispute arose between us regarding power and illusion.
And for the sake of pacifying that obstacle, I wear this armor.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:

The armor of Vināyaka is difficult to obtain in the three worlds; it is well-guarded in the Purāṇas and rare even in the Āgamas. It was spoken in the Kauthuma branch of the Sāmaveda, enchanting to the mind.
This supreme armor of Vighnanātha removes all obstacles.
O son of the Sun, one may give away a kingdom, one may give away one's head, and one may even give up one's life;
yet such an armor as this must never be given, even in a crisis involving one's life.
He who, by his own will and through his *māyā*, manifests and withdraws [the world], is eternal and has a single tusk; O Vatsaka, this is his armor.
His worship and hymn of praise exist continuously in every *kalpa*.
Indeed, before this birth, sages served him;
just as in my own incarnations there is the assumption of a physical body,
so too was there the birth of the Lord of the Gaṇas from the womb of the Mountain’s Daughter.
Wearing which all the sages in Bhārata became liberated while living,
and all the gods became free from fear and crushers of the enemy host;
death does not even approach those who wear this armor out of fear.
There is no loss of life, no evil, and no defeat within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
By reciting [this] one million times, the armor (kavaca) becomes perfected.
He who has perfected the armor is capable of conquering death.
By the mere recitation [of this], one becomes one whose armor is well-perfected, eloquent, long-lived on the surface of the earth,
victorious everywhere, and worthy of worship.
This meritorious garland-mantra is a protective armor, auspicious and beautiful.
For those who bear [this], all sins are certainly destroyed.
(73) Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, brahmarākṣasas,
ḍākinīs, yoginīs, yakṣas, vetālas, bhairavas, and so forth— (74)
Child-seizing spirits, malevolent planets, and likewise field-protectors and others—
those who are fearful flee at the mere sound of the *varman*.
Mental afflictions, physical diseases, and fearsome sorrows likewise [depart].
They do not come into the possession of those [who are unworthy], just as serpents do not come into the possession of Garuḍa.
One should reveal [this teaching] to a straightforward disciple who is devoted to the guru;
by giving it to a wicked person or to the disciple of another, one shall meet with death.
Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor that deludes the cycle of existence;
the meter is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Lambodara himself.
Its application is proclaimed to be for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (78)
O Sage, this is the essence of all armor-mantras:
*oṃ gaṃ huṃ śrīgaṇeśāya svāhā*. May it protect my head;
may this thirty-two-syllable mantra always protect my forehead. (79)
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ gam—may this indeed constantly protect the eye.
May Vighneśa constantly protect [me] at the palate on the surface of the earth.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīm—may this supreme [mantra] constantly protect the nose.
Oṃ gauṃ gaṃ, svāhā to Śūrpakarṇa; may this protect my lower lip. May the sixteen-syllable mantra protect my teeth, palate, and tongue.
Oṃ laṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Lambodara; may it always protect my cheek. (81)

Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ vighnanāśāya svāhā—may this always protect the ear. (82) Oṃ śrīṃ gaṃ gajānanāya svāhā—may this always protect the shoulder. Oṃ hrīṃ vināyakāya svāhā—may this always protect the back. (83)
Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ—may this Kaṅkāla protect the supreme chest;
may he who destroys obstacles always protect the hands, the feet, and all the limbs.
May Lambodara protect in the east, and Vighnanāyaka in the southeast.
May Viśveśa protect [him] in the south, and Gajānana in the southwest (nairṛtyā).
May Pārvatī’s son protect [him] in the west, and Śaṅkara’s son in the northwest (vāyavyā). And may the portion of Kṛṣṇa, who is the most perfect being, protect [him] in the north.
May the single-tusked Heramba protect me in the northeast, and may he protect me from above.
May the Lord of Ganas, who is worshiped by all, protect me from below and on all sides.
And may the Guru of yogis protect me both in sleep and in wakefulness. (87)
Thus, my child, I have told you this most wonderful armor named Saṃsāramohana, which embodies the entire multitude of mantras.
It was given long ago by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance.

O son of the Sun, I have granted this supreme boon—which is worthy of worship by all, a deliverer from all distress—to me, who am humble in Vṛndāvana; and you shall not give it to anyone else. (89–90)

He who, having worshipped the Guru according to the rules, wears this armor (kavaca) either on his neck or on his right arm, is indeed Viṣṇu himself; of this there is no doubt. [This is equal to] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
Other lords of mantras do not equal even a sixteenth part of this armor (*kavaca*).
(92) He who worships the son of Śaṅkara without knowing this armor—though he may recite the mantra a hundred lakhs of times—the mantra will not grant success. (93)
Thus ends the armor known as the "Delusion of Saṃsāra.
Having bestowed this upon the son of the Sun, the Lord of the Gods ceased speaking.
Filled with supreme bliss, the gods stood nearby. (94)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Worship, Hymn, and Armor of Gaṇeśa," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
And all the gods in that assembly were delighted in their minds.
The Gandharvas, sages, and mountains beheld that most magnificent festival. In the meantime, Durgā, her lotus-like face beaming with a smile,
bowed down and spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, there in the assembly.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, you are the protector of all the worlds; I am not outside the world.
O Master, how was the infallible potency of my lord preserved, O Prabhū?"
"When the interruption of your pleasure was brought about by the gods incited by Brahmā,
by which god indeed was the semen that fell upon the earth taken up?
Let all the gods search for it respectfully before you."
"How can this world remain without a king while you are its sovereign?
Having heard Pārvatī’s words, the Lord of the World laughed and spoke,
even as the hosts of gods and the hosts of sages stood by.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, listen to my words; you have heard the speech of Pārvatī. By whom was that infallible seed of Śiva, which was formerly [emitted], taken away? (7)
"Bring him quickly to the assembly; otherwise, you shall deserve punishment here.
What king is he who does not rule, yet who oppresses his subjects and is partial?
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, they deliberated among themselves.
Terrified by the words of Śiva, they all spoke before Hari.
Brahmā said:
"By him, that seed was discharged upon the holy land of Bhārata."
"May he be deceived here on this auspicious day during this meritorious rite.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"By whom my seed was cast away upon the holy land of Bhārata..."
"Let him be deceived in this service and worship of you.
Yama said:
"Let him be deceived in this protection of one who has come for refuge."
And by that very power, his seed was cast out during the vow of Ekādaśī.
Indra said:
"By that power, [he was freed] from the sin of those who are sinful, for it effects liberation from sin."
"Let my fame be lost in this matter, but let that meritorious deed endure.
Varuṇa said:
"O Hari, let there be a birth for me here in the Kali age in the land of Bhārata."
And let him be one who has caused the fetus of the wife of a Śūdra-priest to be miscarried by that means.
Kubera said:
Let him be a stealer of deposits, a betrayer of trust, and a destroyer of friends.
May he be a destroyer of truth and ungrateful, by whom that power was taken away.
Īśāna said:
"And may he be a thief of others' property here in this Bhārata."
"May those by whom his vital energy was extracted be killers of men, traitors to their gurus, liars, and adulterers in the land of Bhārata.
The Rudras said:
"May they be speakers of falsehood and adulterers in Bhārata."
Those who are constantly devoted to reviling their guru, and by whom his virility was taken away;
Kāmadeva said:
"That fool who, having made a vow, does not fulfill it due to delusion."
He who took it would become a vessel for that sin.
The two celestial physicians said:
"In the nourishment of one's mother, father, teacher, and likewise of one's wife and sons..."
"May those two by whom that prowess was seized be deceived.
All the gods said:
"And may they become givers of false witness here in this Bhārata."
"Childless and impoverished are those by whom that seed was indeed taken.
The celestial wives said:
"Let them be censured by their own husbands; let them go to another man."
"May they be deprived of their intellect, by whom that valor was indeed withheld.
Having heard the words of the gods and the goddesses, Hari himself [summoned] Dharma,
the witness of actions, as well as the Sun, the Moon, and the Fire-god.
The Creator, Protector, and Ruler of the three worlds spoke to the Wind, the Earth, the Water, the Twilight, and Night and Day, O Sage. Śrī Viṣṇu said: 23. Śrī Viṣṇu said:
That prowess which was not taken away by the gods—who has now taken it away?
That [prowess] of the Blessed Maheśa, the teacher of the world, is unfailing.
And you all are witnesses to every action at all times.
"What has been brought forth by you? Or what kind of thing should you say?
(25) Having heard the words of the Lord, they trembled in the assembly;
consulting with one another, they spoke in turn before Hari: (26)
Śrīdhara said:
As Rati was rising up, her seed fell upon the surface of the earth.
I realized that it was infallible due to the intense wrath of Śaṅkara. 27.
The Earth said:
"O Brahman, being unable to bear that seed, I cast it into the fire long ago; since it was exceedingly difficult to carry, you ought to forgive me, for I am weak. (28)
Agni said:
"I was unable to bear your seed, so I cast it into the forest of reeds.
O Lord of the World, what fame or what manliness is there for one who is weak? (29)
Vāyu said: His seed fell upon the arrows, and immediately a boy was born, O Viṣṇu, exceedingly handsome on the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā. (30) Śrīsūrya said:

Seeing the infant crying, I, unable to remain during the night, set out toward the Astachala mountain, impelled by the wheel of time. (31) The Moon said: Having encountered the crying infant, the group of Kṛttikās took him up.
O Viṣṇu, having departed from Badarikāśrama, he went to his own abode.
Then the Water spoke:
"Having brought this weeping child here, give your breast to him who seeks it."
They caused that son of the Lord, whose radiance surpassed even the sun, to grow.
At twilight, they spoke; now he was the foster-son of the six Kṛttikās. Out of love, they themselves gave him the name Kārttikeya.
Rātri said:
They did not allow the boy to pass beyond the range of their vision—he who was the object of their love even more than their own lives, and whose son was his very nourisher. (35)
Day spoke:
"Whatever objects there are in the three worlds that are difficult to obtain, praised, and delicious, they indeed fed him with those. (36)
Having heard those words of theirs, Madhusūdana was satisfied.
With delighted minds, they all addressed Hari in the assembly hall.
Upon receiving news of her son, Pārvatī was also joyful at heart.
He gave ten million jewels and vast wealth to the Brahmins;
he gave all kinds of garments to the Brahmins.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Menā, Sāvitrī, and all the women [were there].
Viṣṇu and all the gods gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas.

(39) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Birth of Kārttikeya," in the Gaṇeśa-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, having received news of his son, Śaṅkara,
urged by Viṣṇu, the gods, the sages, and the mountains,
dispatched messengers of great strength and prowess along with Pārvatī. (1)
Vīrabhadra, Viśālākṣa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kabandhaka;
Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Vajradanta, Bhagandara;
Godhāmukha, Dadhimukha, and one resembling a blazing crest of fire. (2–3)
One hundred thousand for the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) and three hundred thousand for the spirits (bhūtas);
four hundred thousand for the vetālas and five hundred thousand for the yakṣas;
four hundred thousand for the kūṣmāṇḍas and three hundred thousand for the brahmarākṣasas.
Four hundred thousand *ḍākinīs* and three hundred thousand *yoginīs*,
as well as Rudras and Bhairavas whose prowess is equal to Śiva’s,
and others of deformed appearance beyond counting, O Nārada. (5–6)
All those messengers of Śiva, with various weapons and missiles in their hands,
surrounded the radiant abode of the Kṛttikās.
Seeing them, all the Kṛttikās became overwhelmed with fear in their minds.
And they took up Kārttikeya, who was blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
The Kṛttikās said:
"O child, countless armies have completely surrounded us."
"We do not know whose these terrifying [forms] are, O child.
Kārttikeya said:
"Cast away your fear, O auspicious ladies; why should you have fear while I am present?"
"The ripening of karma is difficult to ward off; by whom, O mothers, can it be prevented?
(10) In the meantime, the commander Nandikeśvara, standing before Kārttikeya, spoke to them. (11)
Nandikeśvara said:
"O brother, hear from me the auspicious news concerning my mother,
regarding the Lord of the Gods who was sent forth, and regarding Śaṅkara, the Destroyer."
On Mount Kailāsa, all the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others,
dwell in assembly, celebrating the auspicious festival of Gaṇeśa.
Then the Daughter of the Mountain King [Pārvatī] addressed that Viṣṇu, the protector of the worlds.
Having awakened him, he spoke of the reason for his search.
Viṣṇu questioned those gods in turn for the sake of obtaining [the means],
and they each gave a reply as was appropriate.
There, in the abode of the Kṛttikās,
all the gods, beginning with Dharma— the witnesses of both dharma and adharma—
spoke to the Lord concerning the secret dalliance that had formerly taken place between Pārvatī and Śiva. (16)
And as Śambhu was being gazed upon by the gods, his semen fell to the earth.
The earth cast it into the fire, and the fire [cast it] into the forest of reeds (śaraka).
Then it was received by these Kṛttikās; "Go now," they said. (17)
Viṣṇu, together with the gods, will perform your consecration;
O Lord, having obtained all weapons, he will slay Tāraka.
You are the son of the Destroyer of the Universe; these [goddesses] are not capable of protecting you. 18.

Just as a dry tree in its own hollow is unable to protect the fire, so too you, though radiant among all people, do not shine in their homes; like the king of birds falling into a great well, he does not appear resplendent. 19.

You provide light to the world; you are not obscured by the brilliance of these [senses], just as the sun is never obscured by the rays of a person. O Śambhu, you are Viṣṇu, pervading the universe; you are not an object to be pervaded by them.
Just as space is not pervaded by anything, yet it pervades all;

so you, the Lord of Yogins, are not smeared by worldly enjoyment, even while sustaining it. Just as the Self is never tainted by the actions and enjoyments of living beings, so too are you unstained. (21–22)
You are the support of all and the Lord; without the Immortal (Amṛta), stability could not exist, just as there can be no abode for the ocean—the refuge of rivers—within a small stream.
Indeed, the dwelling place of the Lord of All cannot possibly be found in the home of the Kṛttikās.
Just as the dwelling of a garuḍa is within the belly of a lowly sparrow,
so too the gods do not know you, whose form is the grace bestowed upon devotees—
a mass of virtues and splendors, just as those devoid of yoga do not know the nature of knowledge.
And how can the Kṛttikās know you, who are ineffable—
just as those of deluded mind, being devoid of devotion, cannot know the supreme devotion for Hari? O brother, those who do not know him treat him with disrespect.
Just as frogs do not respect a single lotus that serves as their common dwelling.
Kārttikeya said:
"O brother, I know everything, including all knowledge pertaining to the three periods of time."
O wise one, what praise can there be for you, since you have taken refuge in the Conqueror of Death?
O brother, those whose births are determined by their past actions do not find lasting peace within whichever wombs they may inhabit. (28–29)
Whoever exists there— whether virtuous or deluded, whether experiencing the fruits of their karma—
they too hold him in high esteem, being deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
At present, the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu is the mother of the worlds.
The primordial Viṣṇu-māyā, who is eternally auspicious to Viṣṇu,
became the wife of the Lord of Mountains; she took birth in the womb in Bhārata,
and having performed severe penance, she obtained Śaṅkara as her husband.
Everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is entirely false and artificial.
All things arise from Kṛṣṇa and at the proper time dissolve back into Him alone.
In every kalpa, she is the mother of the world; in every birth, she is my mother.
Bound by the illusion of birth, I am eternally engaged in the process of creation.
Truly, all women in this world arise from Prakṛti;
some are portions [of her], some are fractions, and some are even parts of a fraction.
The Kṛttikās, who possess knowledge, are Yoginīs who are portions of Prakṛti. I was constantly nourished by their breasts with offerings;
I am the foster-son of them, my mothers, because of their nursing and other acts of care. (36)
And her son was born from the power of your master;
O Nandikeśvara, I am not born of the womb of the daughter of the Mountain King.
She is my mother according to dharma, as are all these women who are universally esteemed.
The wet-nurse, the one who bore the child, the giver of food, and the wife of one's preceptor;
the wife of one's chosen deity, the wife of one's father, and daughters;
a pregnant woman, a daughter, a sister, the wife of one's son, and the mother of one's beloved—[these must not be looked upon with lust]. 39.
The mother’s mother, the father’s mother, and likewise the beloved sister of one’s uterine brother;
the sister of one’s mother and father, and similarly the maternal aunt—these sixteen are recorded in the Vedas as the mothers of all people. (40–41)

And these daughters of Brahmā, who possess the knowledge of all accomplishments and are endowed with supreme sovereignty, are not insignificant; they are honored throughout the three worlds. And you, impelled by Viṣṇu, are great, equal to the son of Śambhu.
"Go; I shall go with you, for I will behold the assembly of the gods.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nandin and Kārttikeya," in the *Gaṇeśa-khaṇḍa*, the third part of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus and quickly awakened him, the son of Śaṅkara addressed the Kṛttikās with these appropriate words. Kārttikeya said:

"I shall go to the abode of Śaṅkara and behold the assembly of gods; I shall also see my mother and my circle of kinsmen. Grant me your permission, O mothers! For the entire world is subject to destiny, as are birth and auspicious deeds."
Union and separation do not depend on anything other than destiny;
yet that destiny itself is dependent upon Kṛṣṇa, for he is superior to destiny.
The virtuous constantly worship the Supreme Self, the Lord.
He is able to increase destiny by his own sport or bring it to destruction;
yet his devotee is not bound by destiny and is imperishable—this is the certain conclusion.
Therefore, worship Govinda and abandon delusion, which brings only sorrow.
It bestows happiness, grants liberation, is the essence that removes the fear of birth and death;
it generates supreme bliss and cuts through the snare of delusion—that which all, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, eternally worship. (6–7)

Who am I in this ocean of worldly existence, and who are you, who are of my own nature? All of this, gathered together like foam by the currents of karma, is subject to either union or separation through the contemplation of the Lord. (8)
The wise know that the cosmic egg is dependent on the Lord and not independent.
(9) All three worlds are as impermanent as bubbles in water;
those of deluded mind, through their own illusion, treat what is impermanent as if it were real. (10)
"Those who dwell there, even if their minds are dark, are not defiled, just like the wind.
Therefore, O Mothers, abandon delusion and grant your command.
Having spoken thus and bowed to them, he [departed] together with the attendants of Śaṅkara.
The Blessed One set out on his journey, remembering Śrī Hari in his mind.
In the meantime, he saw there an excellent chariot,
fashioned by Viśvakarman, beautiful and resplendent with diamonds.
It was fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems and adorned with rubies;
it was beautified by clusters of garlands of *pārijāta* flowers,
and it was brilliantly illuminated by mirrors of the finest jewels and white yak-tail whisks.
It was a magnificent vehicle, adorned with beautiful and variegated palaces fit for play;
it possessed a hundred wheels, was exceedingly vast, moved at the speed of thought, and was enchanting to the mind.
It was dispatched by Pārvatī and surrounded by her excellent attendants. (15–16)

As the vehicle was ascending, they suddenly regained consciousness with hearts burning in grief; with their hair disheveled and tormented by sorrow, they saw Skanda before them and were utterly paralyzed by extreme anguish. (17)
As if driven mad by fear, they began to speak right there.
The Kṛttikās said:
"O child, what shall we do? Where shall we go? We have you as our sole refuge."
"Leaving us behind, where are you going? This is not your duty now. Our son was raised by us with affection according to our own dharma;
it is not the dharma for a son to abandon his mother and her kin when they are devoted to him. (19–20)
Having spoken thus, all the Kṛttikās placed that son upon their breasts;
they again fell into a swoon, agonizing from the separation from their child.
Then Kumāra indeed awakened them with words concerning the supreme self (adhyātma).
O sage, he ascended the chariot together with those women and his attendants.
[He saw] a brāhmaṇa with a full water-pot, a courtesan, white grains, a mirror,
curd, clarified butter, honey, parched rice, flowers, dūrvā grass, and white unbroken grains.
A bull, a lordly elephant, a horse, a blazing fire, gold,
full vessels, various kinds of ripe fruits,
a woman accompanied by her husband and sons, a lamp, and an excellent jewel. (24)
O Sage, he saw before him these auspicious objects: a pearl necklace, a garland of flowers, fresh meat, and sandalwood;
and on his left side, a jackal, a mongoose, a jar, and a corpse, which brought him good fortune. (25–26)
The royal swan, the peacock, the wagtail, the parrot, and the cuckoo; the pigeon, the śaṅkhacilla bird, the ruddy goose, and the auspicious [animals];
the black antelope, the cow, the yak, and the white chowrie.
He saw a cow accompanied by its calf and an auspicious banner to the right;
he also heard various kinds of musical instruments and the sound of auspicious proclamations,
as well as enchanting songs and the resonance of bells and conchs.
Having seen and heard the auspicious news, he indeed went to his father’s palace in an instant,
filled with joy, by means of a chariot that travels at the speed of thought.
Having reached Kailāsa, the prince [sat] at the root of the imperishable banyan tree.
She stood for a moment with the Kṛttikās and her foremost attendants.
Pārvatī, having performed auspicious rites, proceeded along the enchanting royal road;
the city was adorned on all sides with rubies and sapphires.
It was adorned with clusters of plantain trunks and fine silken cloths,
joined with sprouts of sandalwood and beautifully graced by full water-jars;
it was pervaded by the waters of those full jars and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
It was resplendent with countless jewel-lamps and the finest of gems;
it was always filled with the festivities of actors, dancers, and courtesans; and it was attended by bards and groups of brahmins holding *dūrvā* grass and flowers in their hands. (34–35)
It was filled with virtuous women who possessed sons,
as well as Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Tulasī, and Rati; Arundhatī, Ahalyā, Diti, Tārā, and Manoramā.
Aditi, Śatarūpā, Śacī, Sandhyā, Rohiṇī,
Anasūyā, Svāhā, Saṃjñā— the beloved of Varuṇa— Ākūti, Prasūti, Devahūtī, and Menakā. (37–38)
Placing before him Ekapāṭalā, Ekaparṇā, Mainākakāminī, Vasundharā, Manasā,
Rambhā, Tilottamā, Menā, Ghṛtācī, Mohinī, and Śubhā, he arrived. (39)
Urvaśī, Ratnamālā, Suśīlā, Lalitā, Kalā,
Kadambamālā, Surasā, Vanamālā, and Sundarī—
these and many other hosts of Apsarases, O best of Brahmins, [attended him]. (40–41)
Devoted to singing and dancing, smiling and elegantly attired,
they all went forth with joy, their hands clapping in rhythm.
The gods, sages, mountains, gandharvas, and likewise the kinnaras [did the same].
All went forth, greatly rejoicing, to follow the youth’s immersion.
Accompanied by various kinds of musical instruments, and together with the Rudras, the Pārṣadas,
the Bhairavas, and the Kṣetrapālas, Maheśvara went along with them.
Then Śaktidhara, seeing Pārvatī from afar, was filled with joy;
quickly descending from his chariot, he prostrated himself with his head at her feet.
He likewise saluted the host of goddesses headed by Padmā and the wives of the sages.

Having diligently addressed everyone with supreme devotion, Śivā looked upon Kārttikeya, took him onto her lap, and kissed him. Śaṅkara, the gods, the mountains, and the goddesses—the wives of the mountains—all did likewise. (46–47)
The goddesses headed by Pārvatī, as well as Lord Śaṅkara,
all the mountains, and the sages bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
Then Kumāra, together with his attendants, arrived at the abode of Śiva.
He beheld Viṣṇu in the midst of the assembly, reclining upon the Ocean of Milk (Kṣīroda),
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with ornaments of precious gems,
and accompanied by Dharma, Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Ārka, Vahni, Vāyu, and others. (49–50)
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, he bestows grace upon his devotees;
he is praised by the lords of sages and the lords of gods, and served with white chowries.
Beholding that Lord of the worlds, [the devotee] bows his neck in devotion.
With all his limbs covered in horripilation, he prostrated with his head;
he bowed with joy to Brahmā, Dharma, the gods, and the lords of sages,
greeting each of them individually there and receiving auspicious blessings from them.
Having addressed them all individually, Śaṅkara sat upon a golden throne together with Pārvatī and bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Kārttikeya," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Viṣṇu, the beloved of the world, being delighted and having determined an auspicious moment, seated the six-faced one upon a beautiful throne of jewels. 1.

Out of curiosity, he played various kinds of musical instruments, such as cymbals made of bell-metal, and various types of mechanical devices. [2] And with waters filled from all sacred fords, consecrated by Vedic mantras, [he performed the ritual].
With joy, he bathed him with hundreds of jars filled with excellent gems.
[He offered] a crown inlaid with the essence of fine jewels, auspicious armlets,
and many ornaments studded with priceless gems.
He joyfully gave him divine garments purified by fire, the Kaustubha gem born from the Ocean of Milk, a forest garland, and a discus;
Brahmā gave him a sacrificial thread, and the Vedas gave him the Mother of the Vedas.
Dharma gave him the twilight mantra, the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, the hymn of praise, and the armor of Hari;
(6) as well as a water-pot, the Brahmā-weapon, and the lore that crushes enemies.
He bestowed upon him divine righteousness, a righteous mind, and compassion toward all living beings. (7)
It is the supreme knowledge that conquers death, which brings understanding of all scriptures;
it is the most enchanting knowledge of reality that bestows eternal happiness.
It is the essence of yoga, the essence of spiritual attainment, and the very difficult-to-attain knowledge of Brahman.
Śiva gave him the trident, the Pināka bow, the axe, the Śakti spear, and the Pāśupata bow,
along with the discharge and withdrawal of the weapons of destruction.
The Lord of the Waters (Varuṇa) gave him a white parasol and a garland of jewels.
The Lord of Nectar gave a lordly elephant and a lordly horse, along with a jar of nectar and a treasury of nectar;
Sūrya gave a chariot that travels at the speed of thought and a beautiful armor;
Yama gave the staff of Yama, and Hutāśana (the Fire-god) gave a great spear.
All the gods joyfully gave him various weapons and means;
Kāmadeva, filled with delight, gave him the science of love (kāmaśāstra);
and the Ocean of Milk gave him priceless jewels, specifically a pair of exquisite jeweled anklets.
Pārvatī, smiling, joyful, and with a mind full of supreme bliss, [honored] Mahāvidyā, Suśīlā, Vidyā, Medhā, Dayā, Smṛti,
the most pure Buddhi, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Kṣamā, and Dhṛti. (13)
And with joy, he granted her firm devotion to Hari and the state of being a servant of Hari.
Prajāpati gave Devasenā—adorned with jewel ornaments, well-disciplined, virtuous, beautiful, and most enchanting. (14–15)
He himself bestowed her upon him according to the marriage rite with Vedic mantras—
her whom the learned call Mahāṣaṣṭhī, the nurse of Śiśu. And having consecrated the prince, all the gods returned to their own abodes.
The sages and the Gandharvas, having bowed down to the lords of the world, [departed].
O dear one, Śaṅkara praised Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, and Dharma;
he prostrated before Hari and embraced Dharma, O Nārada.
And the lord of mountains, honored by Śaṅkara, departed with joy along with his retinue;
all those who had gathered there likewise went forth filled with bliss.
Maheśvara, joined with supreme delight, remained together with the Goddess.
After some time, Śaṅkara brought all of them back and bestowed prosperity upon the high-souled Gaṇeśa through marriage;
Pārvatī, her mind filled with joy, [did likewise] together with her two sons and their attendants.
She served the lotus feet of her lord, which grant all desires.
Thus has everything been told: the consecration of Kumāra, his marriage, and the worship of Gaṇeśa at that wedding.
"The attainment of a son for Pārvatī and the assembly of the gods—what desire is in your mind? What more do you wish to hear? (23).

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Marriage of Kumāra and Gaṇeśa and the Coronation of Kumāra," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (17)
Nārada said:
O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, I ask you something, for I am beset by a great doubt. (1)
O Lord, how could there be any obstacle for the Great-Souled Śaṅkara, the Lord of the thirty gods, the master who destroys all obstacles?
He is the most perfect, the glorious one, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest.
Golokanātha himself, as the son of Pārvatī through his own partial incarnation—
oh, O All-pervading Lord, how can you explain to me the severing of that Blessed One’s head by the gaze of the Lord of Planets? (3–4)
Nārāyaṇa said: Listen attentively, O Brahmā, to this ancient history, by which this obstacle befell Vighneśa, O Nārada. (5)
Once, Śaṅkara, who is exceedingly compassionate, struck the Sun with his trident, dividing him into eight supreme parts— [the Sun] who was the slayer of Sumālī and Mālī.
The illustrious Sun, by means of his unerring trident and his splendor equal to a thunderbolt, [was thus struck].
He immediately lost consciousness and fell down from the chariot.
Kaśyapa beheld his son dead with eyes wide open;
placing him upon his chest, he lamented intensely and repeatedly out of grief.
The gods raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! and were overwhelmed with fear;
the entire world became blinded, enveloped in darkness.
Seeing his son rendered lusterless, Kaśyapa cursed Śiva.
The ascetic Prajvana, the grandson of Brahmā, possessed of Brahmanic splendor, said:
"Just as the chest of my son was pierced by you today with a spear, so too shall the head of your son be severed; of this there is no doubt. (10–11)
And Śiva, his anger having dissolved, being quick to grant satisfaction,
instantly restored it to life with the fullness of the knowledge of Brahman.
He is the portion of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, and consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
And Sūrya, having regained consciousness, rose up before his father. Devoted to Śaṅkara, who is kind to his devotees, he bowed with devotion to his father.
Having learned of Śambhu’s curse, he became enraged at Kaśyapa. (13–14)
He did not accept the objects of the senses at all, but spoke thus in anger:
"I shall abandon the objects of the senses and worship Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
everything else is trivial, impermanent, and perishable without the Lord. (15)
Having abandoned auspiciousness for the sake of truth, the wise man should not desire inauspiciousness.
(16) Then Brahmā, impelled by the gods, arrived there in great haste;
having awakened the Sun, the Unborn One established him in his respective domains. (17)
Having bestowed blessings upon him, Śambhu and Brahmā joyfully departed for their own abodes;
Kaśyapa likewise returned to his own domain, as did the Sun.
Then Mālī and Sumālī became afflicted by disease.
"Leper-like, with all their limbs fallen away, powerless and robbed of their luster—Brahmā himself said to them both: 'Worship the Sun;
you two have been thus rendered lusterless and defiled by the wrath of Sūrya. (19–20)

Having related the armor of the Sun, the hymn of praise, and the entire procedure for worship according to the rules, the eternal Brahmā departed for the world of Brahmā. Then, O Sage, those two went to Puṣkara and worshipped Ravi.

Having bathed at the three periods of the day and reciting the supreme mantra with devotion, they then obtained a boon from the Sun and returned to their own original forms. Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Obstacles by Vighneśa," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
O Lord, what is the hymn and what is the armor (kavaca) that was [revealed] by Brahmā, the witness of the world?
Formerly, this was bestowed upon the Sun, the Supreme Self, by two Dānavas.
O highly fortunate one, you ought to tell me everything regarding his method of worship, or what mantra destroys disease.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the Blessed One, the ocean of compassion, spoke the hymn, the armor-armor (kavaca), the mantra, and the procedure for his worship. 3.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the sequence for the ritual of worshipping the Sun, including the hymn and the armor-mantra (kavaca), which liberate one from all sins and diseases. 4.
The two Daityas, Sumāli and Māli, became afflicted by disease.
They remembered Brahmā, the bestower of the Śiva-mantra, in order to offer him praise. Brahmā went to Vaikuṇṭha and questioned the Lord of Kamalā.
Beholding Śiva dwelling right there in the presence of Hari,
Brahmā said:
"The two Daityas, Sumālin and Mālin, became afflicted by disease."
"O Hari, tell me, what is the means for the destruction of their affliction?
Viṣṇu said:
"Having performed service to the Sun at Puṣkara for a full year,"
"By the grace of the Destroyer of Disease (Śiva), those two shall be liberated.
Śaṅkara said:
"The hymn to the Sun, the armor, the mantra, and the supreme Kalpataru [mantra]."
O beloved of the world, grant these two to that Great-Souled One who is the destroyer of disease.
Hari himself is the bestower of prosperity from afar and the giver of all;
the Sun is the healer of disease, and he [the Great-Souled One] is the object of his [Hari’s] grace, O Creator.
Having obtained the mantra from those two, Brahmā went to the abode of the Daityas.
Then, seeing him and bowing down, they offered him a seat.
To them, who were afflicted by disease, Brahmā himself, a treasury of compassion, spoke.
Stiff, devoid of food, and filled with the foul stench of pus.
Brahmā said:
Having taken the armor, the hymn, the mantra, and the sequence of the ritual of worship.
"O dear ones, having gone to Puṣkara, worship the Sun with prostrations.
They both said:
"By what rite or by what mantra shall we worship him, O Creator?"
"What is the hymn of praise, or what is the armor? Tell that to us both now.
Brahmā said:
"Having performed the bath at the three periods of the day with this mantra, [one should worship] Bhāskara."
By serving the Sun with devotion, you two shall become free from disease.
With this mantra— *Oṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavate sūryāya paramātmane svāhā*— you should worship the Maker of Day with full concentration.
Having worshipped with devotion and indeed offered the sixteen types of oblations,
you two shall certainly attain liberation for as long as a year.
I now bestow upon you both this unprecedented armor.
That which was previously given by the Guru to Indra with affection (17),
[was bestowed] upon him who possessed a thousand female organs due to the curse of Gautama,
and who had been liberated from sin through the abduction of Ahalyā during a time of distress (18).
Bṛhaspati said:
O Indra, listen; I shall proclaim this most wonderful armor (kavaca), wearing which the sages in Bhārata became purified and liberated while living. 19.
Disease does not approach one who wears this armor out of fear,
just as serpents flee upon seeing the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa).
One should reveal it to a pure disciple who is devoted to the guru.
By giving this to a wicked person or to another's disciple, one shall meet with death.
Prajāpati is the seer of this armor, which is unique in the world;
its meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Sun himself.
Its application is proclaimed for the destruction of disease and the attainment of beauty.
(22) It is the essence that instantly removes illness and destroys all sins.
Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, may the mantra "Svāhā to the illustrious Sūrya" protect my head. (23)
May the eighteen-syllable mantra protect my skull at all times.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ sūryāya svāhā—may this protect my nose.
May Sūrya protect my eyes, and may Vikartana protect my pupils. (24)
May Bhāskara protect my lower lip; may Dinakara always protect my teeth.
May Pracaṇḍa protect my cheek, and Mārtaṇḍa likewise my ear.
May Mihira always protect my shoulder, and Pūṣan always protect my shanks.
May Ravi protect my chest forever; may Sūrya himself always protect my navel.
May he who is saluted by all the gods always protect my skeleton.
May Bradhna always protect my hands, and may Prabhākara protect my feet.
"May the Lord Vibhākara protect all my limbs constantly.
Thus, O child, this most enchanting armor has been told to you;
it is named Jagadvilakṣaṇa, and it is very difficult to obtain within the three worlds.
In ancient times, it was given to Manu by Pulastya at Puṣkara;
and it has been given by me to you. O sir, do not give this to anyone whatsoever! By the grace of this armor, you shall be freed from your illness.

You shall become free from disease and endowed with prosperity; of this there is no doubt. Whatever fruit a man obtains by offering oblations for a hundred thousand years, that fruit he surely attains by wearing this armor (kavaca).
If a fool worships the Sun without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca),
then even if he recites the mantra ten lakhs of times, the accomplishment of the mantra (mantrasiddhi) will not arise.
Brahmā said:

"O children, by wearing this armor and performing the hymn of praise to the Sun, you two shall certainly be freed from disease. This hymn of praise to Sūrya, as declared in the Sāmaveda, grants liberation from illness. (34)
It is the essence that removes all sins, the supreme bestower of wealth and health.
Brahmā said:
That is the supreme Brahman, the eternal abode whose nature is light.
I desire to praise you, who bestow grace upon your devotees;
the eye of the three worlds, the lord of the world, and the liberator from sin; the giver of the fruits of ascetic penances, and the eternal inflictor of suffering upon the wicked. (36–37)
He is the bestower of fruits according to one's karma, the seed of karma, and the ocean of compassion.
He is the form of karma, the form of action, yet formless—the seed of all karma. He is a portion of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, and his nature consists of the three *guṇas*.
The giver of freedom from disease and the destroyer of disease, the remover of sorrow, delusion, and fear;
the bestower of happiness, the giver of liberation, the essence, the granter of devotion, and the fulfiller of all desires;
the Lord of all, the embodiment of all forms, and the witness of all actions. (39)
Manifest to all the worlds yet invisible, he is captivating to the mind;
ever bestowing delight and subsequently granting aesthetic bliss, he is the giver of all perfections.
He is the very embodiment of accomplishment, the Lord of Siddhas, and the supreme teacher of the perfected ones.
This king of hymns has been proclaimed as the supreme secret among secrets.
He who recites it constantly at the three junctions of the day is liberated from diseases.
Blindness, leprosy, poverty, illness, grief, fear, and strife [are likewise dispelled].
O Lord of the Universe, by the grace of the Sun-god, his [suffering] will certainly perish:
whether he is afflicted with leprosy, emaciated, blind, or suffering from great ulcers; or seized by consumption, plagued by severe pain, or beset by various other diseases. (43–44)
Having observed this for a month and partaken of sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*), one is certainly liberated from [sin] upon hearing [this];
one obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), of this there is no doubt.
Go quickly to Puṣkara and worship the Sun, O sons!
Having spoken thus, that Creator went joyfully to his own abode.
By serving that Sun-god, those two became free from disease.
Thus it has been told, my child; what more do you wish to hear?

Having praised Vighneśa—the remover of all obstacles, the essence, and the destroyer of impediments—with this hymn, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (48) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Causes of Obstacles," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (19)
Nārada said: Born from a portion of Hari and equal to Hari in intellect, you ought to hear my question, [endowed as you are] with splendor and prowess. (1)
That which was heard regarding the obstacle of him who is the destroyer of obstacles is most wonderful.
And that very cause of the obstacle [was told] from the mouth of the Cause of the Universe.
Now I desire to hear that supreme [teaching] which shatters all doubt.

While many other beings were present— both those with excellent vital breaths and those possessing various beautiful forms— the son of the Lord of the Three Worlds stood there for the purpose of approaching the elephant-faced one, O Lord of the Lotus-born. (3–4)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Nārada, listen to the reason for the elephant-faced form, which is secret among all the Purāṇas and very difficult to find even in the Vedas. (5)
It is the deliverance from all sufferings, the cause of all prosperity,
the remover of calamities, the secret for liberation from sin,
and the life-story of Mahālakṣmī, which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things. (6)
It bestows happiness, grants liberation, and yields the fruits of the four aims of life.
Listen, my dear, for I shall relate this ancient history—a secret of the Pādma-kalpa that I formerly heard from the mouth of my father. (7–8)
Once, Mahendra went to the river Puṣpabhadrā;
he was intoxicated by the pride of great prosperity, full of desire, and endowed with royal splendor.
On its bank, in a beautiful flower garden that was a place of extreme seclusion—
In an exceedingly inaccessible forest, devoid of all living beings,
filled with the humming of bees and the sounds of male cuckoos,
and rendered fragrant by winds laden with scented flowers. (10–11)
There he beheld Rambhā, who had arrived from the world of the Moon;
she was a seeker of love, desiring rest from the fatigue of amorous play,
and was proceeding to the hermitage of Madana, longing for the sport she desired.
She was alone, free from worldly thought, yet her mind was stirred by the god of love;
she possessed beautiful hips and fine teeth, was youthful, with lips like the bimba fruit and eyes like lotuses;
she was burdened by the weight of her large hips and moved with the gait of an elephant in rut.
With a smiling face like the autumn moon, she bears beautiful side-long glances;
she wears a lovely braid adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers,
clad in garments pure as fire, and decorated with jeweled ornaments.
Joyfully wearing vermilion together with a drop of musk,
her eyes shining with collyrium dark as the petal of a blue lotus,
and her cheeks resplendent, adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings; || 16–17 ||
She bore a pair of breasts that were exceedingly high, very firm, adorned with rows of fine lines, and a source of pleasure for connoisseurs;
she was endowed with all beauty, richly dressed, fortunate, and eager for amorous dalliance. (18)
He chose the most excellent Apsaras, who was dearer to the gods than their own life-breath, pure, moving at her own will, delightful, possessing exceedingly stable youth,
endowed with virtues and beauty, tranquil, and capable of enchanting the minds of sages. (19–20)
Having seen her, who was exceedingly rich in beauty, Indra was tormented by her sidelong glances;
due to his super-sensory restlessness, he began to speak.
Indra said:
"Where are you going, O lady of beautiful hips? Where have you gone, O enchanting one?
For I have seen you at last, O auspicious and fortunate one!
Having heard your message before me, I have been searching for you."
My mind is attached to you, and I truly do not take account of any other woman.
(23) One who desires well-scented water would never seek muddy water; one who desires sandalwood would not seek mud, nor would one who desires a lotus seek a water-lily. (24)
One seeking nectar would not desire liquor; one seeking milk would not seek turbid water.
Indeed, he who sleeps upon fragrant flowers would not desire a bed of weapons;
one destined for heaven would not desire hell; and one accustomed to fine enjoyments would not desire foul food. (25)
A man living with the wise should not desire the company of women;
who would wish for an ornament of iron after casting away a jewel-encrusted one?
What deluded person would wish to go elsewhere without embracing you, O woman of great wisdom?

Having abandoned the Gaṅgā, what wise person would desire any other river? (27) Even those who seek boons and living beings who desire happiness increase their attachment to the objects of the senses at every step. (28)

Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the Blessed One descended from the lordly elephant and stood before her, filled with desire. Hearing those words, Rambhā became intensely eager for great amorous dalliance.
With her face bowed like a lotus, her body covered in horripilation,
her countenance smiling, she restored his consciousness with a sidelong glance, the display of her breasts and hips, and words imbued with playful jests. (30–31)
Measured, substantial, very sweet, smooth, tender, and pleasing,
and with its seed dependent upon man, she began to speak.
Rambhā said:

I shall go wherever I desire; what fruit is there for you in questioning me? Friendship with the wicked is not a source of contentment for rogues, just as a bee may obtain the nectar of all flowers out of greed. (33)
Wherever there is a superior sweetness, there he remains constantly;
likewise, a woman full of desire wanders perpetually in this world like a bee.
For, due to her fickleness, she shall extract pleasure from various men, just as the wind [draws scents] from everywhere.
Just as a creeper depends on trees for its branches, so does a woman depend on a man who possesses limbs.
A lustful woman, fickle like a crow, departs after having enjoyed the fruit;
she pursues her own purpose only so long as it serves her interest. (36)
Their persistence is in accordance with their function, just as fire persists within wood.
(37) As long as there is water in a pond, aquatic creatures remain therein;
but when the drying up of the waters begins, they move once more to another place. (38)

"You are the lord of the gods and the desired one of amorous women. Those who possess aesthetic sensitivity always desire from happiness a man who is a connoisseur of rasa—one who is youthful, sensitive, tranquil, well-attired, handsome, and beloved. (39)
A passionate woman desires one who is virtuous, wealthy, pure, and handsome.
(40) But women do not at all desire one who is ill-behaved, sickly, old, deprived of sexual vigor, stingy, or ignorant. (41)
"What fools do not desire you, such an ocean of virtues?
Accept here, as you please, this maidservant who shall carry out your commands.
Having spoken thus, she looked at him with a smile and drank him in with her sidelong glance.

Burning with the fire of desire and her modesty melting away, she stood near him. (43) Perceiving the state of mind of her who was afflicted by love, he, who was an expert in the science of love, took her onto a bed of flowers and dallied with her. (44)
In secret, he kissed the mature, beautiful, and excellent woman who was naked;
she, with lips like a ripe bimba fruit and beautiful teeth, kissed him in return.
O Sage, through various kinds of amorous play, such as the inverted posture and others, [they enjoyed themselves].
In her he truly became happy, like the god of love incarnate.
With their minds possessed by passion, the two of them were unaware of day or night;
their hearts were fixed on one another, afflicted by desire, and devoid of discernment.
And having played upon the dry land with her, that Lord of the Gods went to the waters of the Puṣpabhadrā river for the purpose of sporting in the water.
He joyfully engaged in water-sports with her for a moment.
He sported again and again, moving from water to land and from land to water.
In the meantime, the eminent sage Durvāsas, accompanied by his disciples, was traveling along that same path from Vaikuṇṭha to the abode of Śaṅkara.
And seeing that lord of sages, the lord of gods, his mind paralyzed with pride, suddenly approached and bowed; he, in turn, bestowed blessings upon him.
[He offered] that *pārijāta* flower which had indeed been given by Nārāyaṇa.
And that [flower] was given to Mahendra by the high-souled lord of sages.
Having given the flower, the illustrious one, a treasure-house of compassion, spoke to him;
the best of sages recounted whatever little of its unprecedented majesty there was.
Durvāsas said:
O Lord of the Gods, victory comes from every quarter for that person upon whose head rests this flower, offered to Nārāyaṇa, which removes all obstacles. (94)
He shall become the foremost leader of all the gods, honored at their head;
Mahālakṣmī, like his very shadow, shall never forsake him,
[endowed] with knowledge, splendor, intellect, valor, and strength.

The illustrious one, superior to all gods and equal to Hari in prowess, does not accept [an offering] upon his head out of devotion if it is offered by a base person through egoism; such a person, having lost his fortune, is shunned by those of his own caste. Even the *naivedya* of Hari itself [is rejected].
Having spoken thus, he who is a portion of Śaṅkara went indeed to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Standing near Rambhā, he cast [the curse] upon the head of the elephant;
seeing her fortune fallen because of that, she departed for the abode of the gods.

An unchaste woman, fickle and base, desires a suitable man and no other. Having abandoned the King of the Gods (Indra), the mighty Gajarāja entered the great forest, leaving him behind by his own splendor.
Right there, having encountered a female elephant in rut, he enjoyed her by force.
Consequently, that woman, seeking pleasure, became subject to his will.
There in that forest, a multitude of offspring was born to the two of them.
Having cut off the head of Hariścandra, he joined it to the boy.
Thus has it been told, O child; what more do you wish to hear?
Also, the cause for the joining of the elephant's face, which destroys all sins. 62.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Cause for Bestowing the Elephant Face upon Gaṇapati," in the third section, the Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
O Lord, by what means were those gods deprived of their splendor through the curse of Brahmā?
And that secret of theirs was to be concealed and was very difficult to obtain.
How did these [gods] attain that Kamalā, the mother of the worlds?
And what did Mahendra do? You ought to tell us that. (1–2)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having been defeated by Gajendra and by Rambhā, that one of very dull intellect, fallen from his glory and filled with wretchedness, went to Amarāvatī. (3)
O Sage, he beheld that city devoid of joy— joyless itself,
seized by wretchedness, bereft of kinsmen, and overwhelmed by hosts of enemies.
Having heard this from the mouth of the messenger, he went to the preceptor’s abode.
He went to the assembly of Brahmā together with the hosts of gods.
Having arrived, Śakra, along with the deities, as well as Bṛhaspati, bowed down to him;
and, self-restrained, he praised him with Vedic verses and with hymns.
Vākpati related the matter of creation to that Prajāpati.
Having heard it, Brahmā, with a downcast face, began to speak.
Brahmā said: "O Indra of the gods, you are my great-grandson; O King, you are ever ablaze with splendor."
The husband of Lakṣmī, who is equal to Śacī, was always lustful for the wives of others.
By the curse of Gautama, you became marked with the sign of the female organ in the assembly of the gods;
furthermore, you were devoid of shame and remained lustful for the wives of others. (8–9)
For one who is devoted to the wives of others, from where could there be fortune or fame?
He is censurable and filled with sin in all assemblies forever.
This very *naivedya* of Śrī Hari was given to you by Durvāsas.
"O elephant, Rambhā, whose heart was captivated by you, placed [her hand] upon your head. Where is that Rambhā, who is to be enjoyed by all? And where are you now, struck down by misfortune?
She, the bestower of all happiness, has abandoned you and departed in an instant. (11–12)
A fickle courtesan desires one who possesses wealth and not one who is destitute;
seeking ever the new, she reviles the former.
O child, that which has passed away is gone; what is accomplished does not return.
"Worship Nārāyaṇa with devotion for the sake of attaining Padmā. Having said this, he who was solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa gave him the hymn and the armor (kavaca) of the Creator of the World,
as well as the mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
Together with them and his preceptor, he indeed recited the desired mantra;
having received the *kavaca* from him, he praised Hari at Puṣkara for one year,
remaining without food in the auspicious and merit-bestowing land of Bhārata.
He served the Beloved of Kamalā for the sake of attaining Kamalā. Having approached him, Hari granted him his desired boon:
the Lakṣmī-stotra, the kavaca, and the mantra that increases sovereignty.
Having given it, Indra went to Vaikuṇṭha and to the Ocean of Milk;
O Sage, having taken the armor and offered praise, he reached the abode of Padmā.
Having conquered his enemy, the Lord of the Gods indeed regained Amarāvatī.
And every one of the gods reached their own desired abodes.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Attainment of Śakra and Lakṣmī," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
"O ascetic, tell me what hymn and what armor Lord Hari bestowed upon him after manifesting himself; and likewise, what did the Lord of Lakṣmī give to Mahālakṣmī? Nārāyaṇa said:
Having performed austerities at Puṣkara, the Lord of the Gods desisted.
Seeing him distressed, Hari himself appeared right there.
Hṛṣīkeśa said to him, "Choose a boon as you desire."
And he chose Lakṣmī as his boon; the Lord joyfully granted it to him.
Having bestowed the boon, Hṛṣīkeśa began to speak words that were beneficial, true, essential, and bringing happiness in the end.
Śrī Madhusūdana said: "O Śakra, take this armor which destroys all suffering, generates supreme sovereignty, and crushes all enemies. (5)
And in the past, when the world was submerged in water, it was given to Brahmā;
by holding it, Vidhi—the best of the worlds—became endowed with all sovereignty, and from that [source] all the Manus became endowed with all sovereignty. (6)
The seer (ṛṣi) of this armor (kavaca), which bestows all sovereignty, is Brahmā;
the meter (chandas) is Paṅkti; and the deity is that supreme Goddess herself whose abode is the lotus.
Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed to be for the sake of spiritual perfection, sovereignty, and happiness.
Wearing which armor, a person shall be victorious everywhere.
(8) May Padmā protect my head; may the beloved of Hari protect my throat.
May Lakṣmī protect my nose; may Kamalā protect my eyes. (9)
May Keśavakāntā protect the hair; Kamalālayā, the mother of the world, may she always protect the pair of cheeks; and Sampatpradā, the bestower of prosperity, may she always protect the shoulder.
Oṃ Śrīṃ, Svāhā to Kamalavāsinī; may she always protect the back.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Padmālayā; may she always protect my chest.
May Śrī protect my skeleton; salutations to you for the pair of my arms.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, namaḥ to Lakṣmī; may she protect my feet perpetually for a long time.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ padmāyai svāhā—may this protect the hips.
(12) Oṃ śrīṃ mahālakṣmyai svāhā—may this always protect all my limbs.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mahālakṣmyai svāhā—may this protect me from every side. (13)

Thus, O child, I have told you this supreme armor (*kavaca*), which brings about all prosperity, bestows all sovereignty, and is most wonderful. He who, having duly worshipped his guru, wears this armor, [attains success]. (14)
Whether worn on the neck or on the right arm, he shall be victorious over all;
Mahālakṣmī never abandons his home,
and she remains with him constantly, like a shadow, in birth after birth.
That dull-witted person who worships Lakṣmī without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) will find that even after a hundred lakhs of recitations, the mantra does not grant success. Nārāyaṇa said:
And having given him the armor and the sixteen-syllable mantra,
the Lord of the World, who acts for the welfare of the worlds, was well-pleased. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ namo mahālakṣmyai svāhā.
And out of compassion, O great sage, he gave that meditation—
declared in the Sāmaveda, to be kept secret, very difficult to attain,
hard for even the perfected lords of sages to obtain, certain, bestowing success, and auspicious— to him and to Indra. (19–20)
Having the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, with a radiance equal to a hundred moons,
wearing garments as pure as fire, adorned with jewel ornaments,
her face bright with a slight smile, she bestows grace upon her devotees.
Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, self-abiding and most enchanting,
peaceful and the beloved of Śrī Hari— he should worship her, the mother of the worlds.
Having meditated thus upon the captivating Lakṣmī, the lord of the gods [attained his goal].
O Vāsava, having worshipped her with devotion and the sixteen types of offerings,
and having praised her with this hymn which is about to be spoken,
you shall bow down, receive a boon, and attain peace.
O Lord of the Gods, listen to this hymn of praise to Mahālakṣmī which bestows happiness;
I shall recount it, for it is a profound secret difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Nārāyaṇa said:

O Goddess, I desire to praise you, yet even the lords are not capable of praising you. Who indeed is able to describe her who is beyond the reach of the intellect, subtle, whose form is splendor, eternal, and enriched with irresistible qualities? (27)

O Mother of the Universe, what can I possibly praise You? You are composed of Your own will, formless, yet possessing a form for the sake of bestowing grace upon Your devotees; You are beyond the reach of speech and mind.
You are the Supreme, the primordial seed within the ocean of worldly existence, and the further shore of the four Vedas. (28)

And what more need I describe? I shall describe her who is the presiding deity of all crops and of all forms of prosperity; the mother of yogins and their yogas, of knowledges and the wise, and of the Vedas and those who know the Vedas. (29–30)
Without whom the entire world would certainly be seedless and fruitless;
and without whom there could be no happiness for suckling infants—
be gracious, O Mother of the worlds, and protect us who are exceedingly distressed.
We have taken refuge in the lotus feet of you; we have come for protection.
Salutations again and again to the Mother of the World, whose very nature is Power!
Salutations again and again to the giver of knowledge, the giver of intellect, and the giver of everything! 32–33.
Salutations again and again to the bestower of devotion to Hari, the giver of liberation;
