salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī, the all-knowing, the giver of everything.
(34) Bad sons may exist somewhere, but bad mothers exist nowhere at all.
Where does a mother go, leaving behind that fault of her son?
O Mother, grant me a vision, as if to those who suckle at your breast!
Have mercy, O ocean of compassion, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!

Thus, O child, has this auspicious hymn of Padmā been told—bestowing happiness, granting liberation, essential, conferring welfare, and bestowing prosperity. Whoever recites this highly meritorious hymn at the time of worship, [attains these fruits]. (37)
"Mahālakṣmī shall never forsake his home.
Having spoken thus to him, Śrī Hari vanished right there.
By his command, the Lord went to the Ocean of Milk together with the gods.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn, Armor, and Worship of Lakṣmī," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
And Indra, his mind filled with joy, together with his preceptor and the gods, [proceeded].
He went quickly to the shore of the Ocean of Milk for Padmā;
having tied the armor, adorned with excellent jewel-beads, around his neck,
he repeatedly remembered and recited the divine hymn in his mind again and again.
Filled with devotion, they all praised the one whose abode is the lotus;
with tearful eyes, distressed, and their necks bowed in devotion, they offered their hymns.
Having heard their praise, she immediately appeared before them in person.

Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, possessing a splendor equal to a hundred moons, O Sage, she by whom the entire world is pervaded and who is the very essence of the universe—she, the Mother of the World, spoke these beneficial and essential words to them as was appropriate: 3–4. "O Sage, she by whom the entire world is pervaded and who is the very essence of the universe—she, the Mother of the World, spoke these beneficial and essential words to them as was appropriate."
Śrī Mahālakṣmī said:
"O children, I do not wish to go to your homes; I am not able to do so now.
Having seen you fallen due to the curse of a Brahmin, I am afraid of that Brahmin's curse. (5)
All Brahmins are my very life-breaths, and they are eternally dearer to me than a son. Whatever means of subsistence is given by the Brahmins, that I shall always rely upon.
Let the Brahmins, being satisfied, command me; I shall go according to your instruction.
Those ascetics are certainly not capable of performing worship for me.
(7) If, by some ill fortune of fate, they were cursed by gurus, brahmins, gods, mendicants, or Vaiṣṇavas, they would always remain so. (8)
And the Lord Nārāyaṇa fears the curse of a Brahmin;
for the Lord is the seed of all, the eternal Lord of all.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, the Brāhmaṇas were delighted in their minds.
They all arrived with smiles, blazing with the splendor of Brahmanic power:
Aṅgiras, Pracetas, Kratu, and Bhṛgu;
Pulaha, Pulastya, Marīci, and Atri. (10–11)
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
the venerable Sanatkumāra, who is Nārāyaṇa himself in essence;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha. (12)
Durvāsas, Kaśyapa, Agastya, Gautama, and Kaṇva;
Aurva, Kātyāyana, Kaṇāda, and likewise Pāṇini;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Lomaśa, and the venerable Vasiṣṭha himself.
The Brahmins worshipped the Goddess with various offerings;
and the gods, with devotion, offered forest-grown oblations as gifts.
Having praised her with devotion, the lords of sages joyfully performed her propitiation.
"Come to the abode of the gods and to the world of mortals, O Mother of the Universe!
(16) Having heard those words of theirs, the Mother of the World, being well-pleased and desirous of departing, spoke to them fearlessly by the command of Brahmā: (17)
Śrī Mahālakṣmī said:
"O twice-born ones, by your command I shall go to the homes of the gods;
listen now to those among the inhabitants of Bhārata whose house I do not enter. (18)

I dwell permanently in the homes of those who are meritorious, who know the path of sound policy, and who are householders or kings; I protect them like my own children. Whomever my guru, the gods, mother, father, and kinsmen may be angry with—
I do not go to the house of one who neglects guests and the ancestral world;
nor do I go to the home of one who is a habitual liar, who never studies the Vedas, who is devoid of goodness, and who is ill-behaved. (20–21)
I do not go to the house of one who is devoid of truth, one who misappropriates what has been deposited, one who gives false testimony,
one who betrays trust, or one who is ungrateful. (22) Nor do I go to the home of one who is overwhelmed by anxiety, overwhelmed by fear, overwhelmed by enemies, or a perpetrator of great sins.
"Overwhelmed by debt and extremely wretched, I do not go to the houses of sinners.
Deprived of initiation, afflicted by grief, dull-witted, and always conquered by women, I never go even to the home of an unchaste woman who has neither husband nor son. (23-24)

I do not go to the house of one who is constantly possessed by strife and harsh speech, nor to the home where women hold the dominant position. I do not go where there is no worship of Hari nor any chanting of His virtues. (25)
I have no desire for his praise; I do not go to his house.
(26) Indeed, [the house] of one who sells girls or the Vedas, a slayer of men, and a perpetrator of violence—I do not go to that man's house, which resembles the abode of hell. (27)
He who, out of miserliness, does not support his mother, father, wife, the wife of his teacher, his teacher, his son,
his helpless sister, his daughter, or those kinsmen who have no other refuge,
but always accumulates wealth for himself— (28) — [he is a sinner].
O Lords of Munis, I do not go to those houses which are like the abodes of hell— those whose teeth, clothing, and heads are filthy and coarse, and whose eating and laughing are distorted. (29–30)
I do not go to the house of that dull-witted man who, having voided urine or excrement, looks upon it;
nor to the house of him who sleeps with unclean feet, or who sleeps naked and excessively drowsy. (31)
I do not go to the house of one who sleeps at twilight or who sleeps during the day.
I do not go to the house of one who, having first applied oil to the head, touches another part of the body, or who applies it later to the limbs. (32–33)
I shall not go to the home of one who, having applied oil to his head and body, voids excrement or urine; who bows down or picks up flowers;
or who cuts grass with his fingernails or scratches the earth with his nails. (34)
I do not go to the house of one who has filth on his limbs or feet.
(35) I do not go to the house of one who, though possessed of knowledge and virtuous conduct, seizes the property of a Brahmin—whether given by himself or by another—or the property of a deity. (36)
That karma which a foolish and deceitful person performs devoid of sacrificial fees—
that sinner, bereft of merit, I do not go to his abode.
(37) Furthermore, one who lives off the knowledge of mantras, a village priest, and a physician—
I do not go to the house of one who is a cook for a king, nor of Devala;
(48) nor of one who, out of anger, obstructs a marriage or a religious rite; nor of one who engages in sexual intercourse during the day. (39)
Having spoken thus, Mahālakṣmī vanished;
she bestowed her gaze upon the abode of the gods and upon the mortal world, O Nārada.
All the deities and sages, filled with joy, bowed down to her.
They quickly returned to their own abode, which was now abandoned by enemies and joined by friends. (41) In heaven, kettledrums resounded and showers of flowers fell;
O Sage, the gods regained their own kingdom and the stable Goddess Kamalā. (42)

Thus, O child, has this supreme life-story of Lakṣmī been told—bestowing happiness, bestowing liberation, and full of essence. What more do you wish to hear? Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Life of Lakṣmī, Including the Cause of Gaṇapati’s Elephantine Face and His Conflict with the Brāhmaṇa," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third book of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. Chapter 23.
Nārada said:
O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, born from a portion of Hari,
by your grace I have heard the entire auspicious account of Gaṇeśa.
"O Brahmin, how is it that this infant has only one tusk, when the face of the king of elephants was endowed with two tusks by Viṣṇu? You ought to explain where his other tusk has gone."
"You are the Lord of all, omniscient, compassionate, and affectionate toward your devotees.
(3) Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, his lotus-like face blossomed with a smile.
He began to recount the life-story of Ekadanta.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate this ancient history."
The life-story of Ekadanta is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
(5) Once, O Sage, Kārtavīrya went out on a hunt;
having slain many deer, he became exhausted. (6)

When the day had passed and night had fallen, the king remained there in the forest near the hermitage of Jamadagnya, fasting along with his army. In the morning, the king bathed in the lake, purified himself, and adorned himself.
Then, having devoutly recited the mantra given by Ātreya,
the sage beheld the king, whose throat, lips, and palate were parched;
with affection and respect, the sage gently inquired after his welfare.
The king bowed with agitation to the sage, who was as radiant as the sun;
and he, out of affection, bestowed auspicious blessings upon him as he prostrated.
The king then related the account of his fasting and other observances.
In his agitation, the sage invited the terrified king.
Having informed him [of the matter], that best of sages departed for his own abode with joy. He related this event to Kāmadhenu as if he were afraid.
She said to the frightened sage: "What fear do you have while I am present?
O Sage, what king is there who is capable of feeding the world with me?
Whatever substance you request that is worthy of being fit for a king's meal," [I shall provide it].
I shall give you everything that is difficult to obtain in the three worlds:
(14) various vessels made of gold and silver, and countless eating bowls as well as cooking pots suitable for food. (15)
She presented the sage with bowls filled with sweet foods,
as well as various kinds of delicious, ripe fruits,
such as jackfruit, mangoes, wood-apples, coconuts, and others. (16)
There were countless heaps of sweet *laḍḍuka* cakes piled high,
as well as various foods made from barley and wheat flour;
there were mountains of cooked rice and mountain caves of *paramānna*.

With joy he gave rivers of milk and ghee, as well as rivers of curd; likewise, he gave heaps of sugar and mountains of sweetmeats (modaka). With delight, he presented mountains of flattened rice and excellent śāli rice.
And he gave him a full betel-roll, exquisitely scented with camphor and other ingredients;
and out of affection, he also gave beautiful garments and ornaments worthy of a king. Having prepared these offerings, the sage gave the charming articles. (20–21)
He fed the king along with his army as if in sport.
O lord of men, whatever object was difficult to obtain was provided in abundance.
Seeing this, the king was filled with wonder and spoke to the attendants: 22.
The king said:
"O minister, these objects are rare and unheard of;
behold, they have suddenly appeared before me, though they were unattainable for me. (23)
And by the king’s command, the minister, having seen everything in the sage’s house,
related the great and wonderful account to the king. (24) The minister said:
"O Great King, behold all this; understand the hermitage of the sage.
It contains a fire-pit provided with sacrificial wood, *kuśa* grass, flowers, and fruits;
it is crowded with black antelope skins, sacrificial ladles (*sruva* and *sruc*), and throngs of disciples. (25)

Devoid of all prosperity such as houses, seats, and so forth, they were seen wearing tree-bark garments and bearing matted hair. Only that single, enchanting Kapilā was seen in one part of the house. (26–27)
With beautiful limbs, possessing the luster of Rudra’s complexion, and with eyes like red lotuses, she blazed there with splendor, radiant as the full moon;
she was the repository of all prosperity and virtues, appearing like the beloved of Hari himself. (28)
Thus enlightened, the king of evil intellect, bound by the noose of Time at the command of his minister, begged the sage for that cow.
What indeed is merit, what is intelligence, and what is Time? Time is the strongest of all.
By fortune, the meritorious and wise lord of kings requested [a boon] from the twice-born.
In the land of Bhārata, meritorious action arises from merit and takes a meritorious form;
from sin, sinful action arises, which is terrifying in its nature. (31)
Through merit, men experience heavenly enjoyment and are born in a holy place;
through sin, living beings experience hell and undergo a contemptible birth.
O Nārada, as long as karma remains, there is no escape for living beings.
By that means, the virtuous constantly bring about the exhaustion of karma.
That is true learning, that is true austerity, that is true knowledge, he is the true teacher, and he is the true kinsman—
indeed, he is the mother, he is the father, and he is the son— who brings about the exhaustion of that [karma].
For living beings, the experience of auspicious and inauspicious karma is a terrible disease;
the physician of devotion cures it through the elixir of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Māyā grants that devotion when she herself has been served throughout successive births. (36–39)
The Mother of the World, who bestows wisdom upon her devotees, is supremely satisfied;
yet she never grants Māyā to that supreme devotee for whom she has bestowed [wisdom], so as to delude him with Māyā, nor does she ever grant him discernment [for such a purpose]. (37)
The king, deluded by illusion, having diligently brought the sage [to him],
spoke with joy, humility, and devotion, his palms joined in reverence.
The king said:
"O Kalpataru, grant me alms—grant me the wish-fulfilling cow, the bestower of desires!
O Lord of devotees, O you who bestow grace upon your devotees, for me, your devotee, there is nothing that cannot be given by givers such as yourselves in this land of Bhārata. (40)
It is heard that in ancient times Dadhīci gave his own bones to the deities.
O ascetic rich in penance, you are capable of creating a multitude of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) in Bhārata by the mere play of a frown, O mass of austerity! 41–42.
The sage said:
"O King, you speak of a transgression, O rogue and deceiver!
How, O monarch, shall I, a brahmin, give a gift to a kṣatriya? (43)

O King, this Kāmadhenu was given by the Supreme Soul, Kṛṣṇa, to Brahmā in Goloka; she is dearer to him than his own life and must not be given away at a sacrifice. O protector of the earth, she was then given by Brahmā to Bhṛgu, who was as dear to him as a son.
And Kapilā, my paternal cow, was given to me by Bhṛgu.
Born in Goloka, she is a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
How could I, by mere play, be capable of creating another Kapilā? || 45–46 ||
"O fool! I am no plowman to be roused by such praise; I am a wise man.
Without this guest, I am capable of reducing everything to ashes in an instant.
Go home, go home; do not increase my anger! (47)
"Behold your sons, wives, and others, O base man afflicted by fate!
(48) Having heard those words of the sage, that lord of men became enraged;
bowing to the sage, he, constrained by destiny, departed toward the midst of his army. (49)
Having gone into the presence of his army with his lips quivering in anger,
he dispatched his servants to bring the cow by force.
Then that bull among sages went into the vicinity of Kapilā and wept.
With his mind overwhelmed by grief, he related the account.
Seeing the Brahmin weeping, Surabhi spoke to him—
she who is the very embodiment of Lakṣmī and who bestows grace upon her devotees.
Surabhi said:
Whether he be Indra or even a plowman, one is the master to give away one's own property;
as the ruler, the protector, and the giver, one has perpetual authority over one's own possessions. (53)
"O ascetic, if you give me to the king of men of your own free will, I shall go with him by my own desire and at your command.
Or, if you do not give me, I shall not leave your house. (94)
"O King, drive away the enemy with the army given by me.
Why do you weep, O omniscient one, with a mind deluded by illusion?
Union and separation are brought about by time, not by the self. (55–56)
Who are you to me? Who am I to you? Our connection is merely joined by time.
For as long as there is a connection, so long does the sense of "mine" exist;
the mind knows only that a certain object belongs to itself. (57)
"And there shall be suffering for him upon its destruction, as long as his ownership over it remains.
Having said this, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) brought forth various weapons,
missiles, and armies possessing a radiance equal to the sun.
Three crores of sword-bearers emerged from the mouth of Kapila;
five crores of trident-bearers issued forth from his nose;
and a hundred crores of bow-wielders streamed out from his two eyes.
Three crores of heroes bearing staffs issued from his skull;
three crores bearing spears issued from his chest;
and ten billion with maces in hand emerged from the region of his back.
Thousands of musical instruments issued from the soles of his feet; three crores of princes emerged from the region of his calves;
and three crores of Mleccha tribes issued forth from his private parts.
Having given his armies to Kapila and granted him safety, he said, "Let the armies fight; you must not go. The sage, filled with joy by the abundance of provisions gathered, became truly exultant.
Urged by the king, the servant told the king everything:
the account of the Kapilā army and the defeat of his own forces.
Having heard that, the tiger among kings became terrified, his mind filled with fear.
Having dispatched messengers, he brought forth his armies from his own country.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Commencement of the Battle between Jaḍa, Agni, and Kārtavīrya," occurring in the context of the inquiry regarding the state of having a single tusk, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Remembering Hari with a grieving heart, the enraged Kārtavīrya dispatched a messenger to the presence of the sage,
saying: "O best of sages, grant me either battle or the desired cow."
Having carefully considered what was appropriate for my servant and guest,
the bull among sages, upon hearing the words of the messenger,
laughed and spoke everything that was beneficial, true, and the essence of political ethics to the messenger.
The sage said: "I saw the king who had been fasting; he was brought to my home by me. He was fed various kinds of food according to his capacity and as was appropriate.
Then the king asked for a tawny cow (kapilā), who is dearer to him than life itself."
"O messenger, unable to give her away, I shall certainly give battle.
Having heard those words of the sage, the messenger related everything to the king of men in the midst of the assembly; he was clad in armor and filled with fear.
And the sage said to Kapilā, "What shall I do now?
Without a helmsman, a boat is lost; likewise, without me, the army is lost.
And Kapilā gave him various weapons.
And [I shall give you] instruction in the science of war and useful counsel on making peace.
(8) O Brahmin, may victory be yours; you will certainly triumph in battle.
Your death shall not come, O Sage, unless by means of a divine weapon—this is the truth. (9)

"O Brahmin, it is improper for you, a disciple of Dattātreya and a wielder of power, to engage in battle with the king; indeed, such an act would be in vain. Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, the high-minded Kapilā ceased speaking. (10)
O Sage, having prepared his army and taken all his forces with him, that wise king then went to the field of battle;
the king set out for war and bowed down before the bull among sages.
A battle occurred between the two armies that was exceedingly difficult [to withstand].
(12) The entire royal army was forcibly defeated by Kapila’s army;
and in the fray, he effortlessly shattered the king’s variegated chariot. (13)
That army of Kapila’s sons joyfully cut that strung bow;
the king of men was unable to conquer the armies of the sons of Kapila.
He [the king] then rendered those armies weaponless with a rain of weapons.
By the rain of arrows and the rain of weapons, the king indeed fell into a swoon.
Only a small remnant of the king's army remained, and a few fled.
O Sage, seeing that the lord of men, his royal guest, had fainted, the lord of sages [acted].
And the treasure-house of compassion, out of mercy, withdrew that army. Having gone there, he saw that the artificial army had dissolved into the Kapilā river.
The sage quickly gave the dust from his feet to the king.
The compassionate one bestowed a blessing, saying, "May there be victory!
Having sprinkled him with water from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), he restored that king to life.
Regaining consciousness, the king rose up from the field of battle.
With palms joined in reverence, he bowed his head with devotion to the best of sages.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon the king, the sage embraced him;
then, having bathed him once more, he fed him with great care.
"The hearts of Brahmins are always like fresh butter;
those of others are always like the edge of a razor—difficult to manage and harsh.
The best of sages said to him, "Go home, O lord of the earth. (21)
The King said:
"O mighty-armed one, give me either the field or the cow desired by me.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Jamadagni and Kārtavīryārjuna," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third book of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of the king—which were beneficial, truthful, and the essence of political ethics—the best of sages began to speak. (1)
The sage said:
"Go home, O illustrious one, and protect the eternal dharma.
It is certain that all prosperity remains stable as long as dharma endures forever."
O King, seeing you fasting, I brought you home and performed your worship according to the prescribed rites and to the best of my ability. Now,
seeing you unconscious, [I offer] the dust of your feet as an auspicious blessing.
"I gave [it], yet I hesitated; it was not even proper to speak.
Having heard those words, the king bowed to the bull among sages, mounted another chariot, and said, "Give me battle! || 4-5 ||
The sage, having donned his armor, proceeded to fight him;
the king, his mind struck by anger, fought him there.
With a weapon given by Kapila, he caused that [sage] who had laid down his weapons to take them up again.
And by the power bestowed by Kapila, he fell into a swoon once more.
Having regained consciousness again, the lotus-eyed king fought with the sage there once more, filled with wrath. (7–8)
The bull among kings discharged the Āgneya weapon in battle;
the sage effortlessly extinguished it with the Vāruṇa weapon.
Then the lord of men hurled the Vāruṇa weapon at the sage in the conflict.
With the Vāyavya weapon, that sage effortlessly quelled it.
Then, O best of kings, the king hurled the Vāyavya weapon in battle;
the best of sages instantly neutralized it with the Gāndharva weapon. (10–11)
And the best of kings hurled the Nāga weapon at the forefront of the battle;
the best of sages joyfully destroyed it in an instant with the Gāruḍa weapon.
Then he [hurled] the great Māheśvara weapon, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns.
The best of kings hurled [it], illuminating the ten directions;
with the divine Vaiṣṇava weapon, which pervades the three worlds, the sage Nārada extinguished it with great effort. (13–14)
The sage then discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon with the accompaniment of mantras.
Upon seeing that weapon, the great king bowed down and sought refuge;
having whirled upward and blazed for a moment, it illuminated the ten directions. (15)
There, like the fire of universal dissolution, he himself vanished.
And that sage hurled the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon at the front of the battle;
by it the king fell into sleep and slept as if dead.
Seeing the king asleep,
the sage then instantly severed his charioteer, the vehicle, the bow, and the arrow with a crescent-headed shaft;
he also cut off the crown, the parasol, and the armor with a razor-edged arrow.

With his various weapons, he rendered the king's grass-like army and multitude of horses powerless; then, laughing, the sage effortlessly bound all the king’s ministers with the Nāga-weapon itself and stationed them upon the field of battle. (19–20)
The sage awakened him with ease by means of a mantra alone;
he then showed the king to all the bound ministers.
Having shown the king to them, he released them at that very moment.
Having offered a blessing to the king of men, he said, "Go home.
Then the king, rising up in anger, strenuously raised his trident and hurled it at that best of sages; the sage struck him with a *śakti* weapon.
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived at the battlefield;
through his excellent counsel, he generated mutual affection between them.
Satisfied on the field of battle, the sage bowed down to Brahmā.
Then the king, having bowed to the sage and performed the prescribed rites, departed for his own city;
the sage went to his own hermitage, and the lotus-born Brahmā returned to his own world.
Thus has this been briefly told; I shall relate something else to you.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cessation of the Battle between Jamadagni and Kārtavīrya," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having remembered Hari and returned home, the king’s mind was filled with wonder.
He returned once more to the great forest to the hermitage of Jamadagni’s son. There were four hundred thousand chariots and ten million chariot-warriors;
the number of lordly horses, lordly elephants, and foot-soldiers was beyond counting.
Accompanied by a thousand lords of kings of great strength and prowess,
and endowed with immense prosperity, he was capable of conquering the three worlds;
with joy, he surrounded the hermitage of Jamadagni on all sides.
O Sage, Kārtavīryārjuna himself, standing in his chariot and clad in armor,
caused those staying at the hermitage of Jamadagni to fall into a swoon through fear by means of the clamor of his army, the sounds of musical instruments, and great tumults. (4–5)
Entering the hut, the powerful one seized the auspicious Kapilā;
that evil-minded man, who took refuge in what is untrue, set his mind on going to the city.
The best of sages stood up, taking up his bow along with its arrow.
Alone, with his body released [from armor], having bowed to the cow and remembering Hari,
and having diligently comforted all the people staying in the hermitage,
he came fearlessly to the battlefield before the king. (7–8)
That sage fashioned a net of arrows preceded by mantras,
covering his hermitage with them as if with human armor;
then that bull among sages fashioned another net of arrows.
With those very [arrows], he warded off the entire army in due order.
The whole host was completely enveloped by the sage with a net of shafts;
they were all hidden away like leaves within a cage.

Having seen the best of sages, the king descended from his chariot and, together with the lords of men, bowed before him with devotion and palms joined in reverence. Having offered salutations and received the sage’s auspicious blessings, he ascended the vehicle.
And having ascended his own vehicle with a joyful mind, that best of kings,
together with other monarchs,
hurled missiles, weapons, clubs, and spears at the preeminent sage; yet the sage struck them down as if in play.
The sage discharged a divine weapon, which the king effortlessly cut down.
The king then hurled a spear, which the sage struck down at that moment.
Furthermore, the bull among sages created another net of arrows.
And with floods of weapons that were difficult to ward off, he cut them into pieces;
bound by a net of arrows, they were unable to flee.
Then, by means of the *jṛmbhaṇa* (yawning) weapon, the sage caused them all to yawn.
Seeing the king asleep along with his entire army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, the Lord of Sages did not strike him. Instead,
he joyfully seized the weeping Kapilā, who was overwhelmed by grief.
Having awakened him and placed him at the front, he prepared to go to his own hermitage.
In the meantime, O Nārada, the king regained consciousness and,
seizing his bow with an arrow, restrained the sage.
Terrified, Kapilā fled from the battlefield to her own abode;
and the sage, taking up his bow with an arrow, stood there without fear.
Then that best of kings discharged the Brahmā weapon at the sage.
By means of the Brahmāstra, the weapon of the lord of sages was instantly extinguished.
With his own divine weapon, the best of sages cut apart the king’s bow along with its arrow,
as well as his chariot, his charioteer, and his formidable armor.

Then the king, greatly enraged, saw that spear, which could slay a single man, being offered by Datta right before him. Having bowed to Datta, he took that formidable spear; and having bowed to it, he [took] that fierce spear.
Right there, he pulverized that splendor which was equal in radiance to a hundred suns—
the splendor of all the gods, of Nārāyaṇa,
of Śambhu, of Brahmā, and of Māyā as well, O Nārada. (24–25)
There, that yogi invoked [the goddess] with mantras;
he illuminated the sky and the ten directions with his splendor.
Seeing her hurling [the weapon], the gods cried out with cries of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
Standing in the sky and watching the battle with hearts full of sorrow,
Kārtavīryārjuna himself hurled that spear and crushed it;
yet that blazing spear immediately fell upon the chest of the sage.
Having split open the chest of the sage, the spear went to the presence of Hari;
it was then returned by Hari to Datta, who was the treasury of all weapons and missiles.
Having fallen into a swoon, that sage gave up his life at that very moment.
Having wandered through the sky, she went to the world of Brahmā.
Seeing the sage dead in battle, Kapilā wept repeatedly;
crying out "O father! O father! she departed for Goloka.
She related everything concerning the Lord Kṛṣṇa in Goloka,
who was seated upon a jeweled throne and surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses;
how he had formerly been given to Brahmā by Kṛṣṇa, and by Brahmā to Bhṛgu.
O Brahmin, out of affection, she went to Puṣkara and, having bowed down before Bhṛgu for the sake of Jamadagni,
she departed toward the multitude of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus).
By a single drop of her tears, a heap of jewels appeared in the mortal world.
Then the king, having slain him and restored his own army to consciousness,
performed the rites of atonement and returned to his own city with joy.
Hearing that her lord was dead, the virtuous Reṇukā departed.
Placing the sage upon her breast, she fell into a swoon for a moment.
Then, having regained consciousness, that devoted wife did not weep;
instead, she cried out, "Come, dear child Bhṛgu! Rāma! Rāma! Rāma!"
Bhrigu arrived swiftly from Puṣkara in an instant;
moving as fast as thought and skilled in yoga, he bowed with devotion to his mother.
Seeing his father dead and his virtuous mother afflicted by grief, Rāma [was moved].
Having heard the news of the battle, as Kapilā was departing in grief, he lamented there intensely, crying, "O father! O mother!
Then the lord of yogis prepared a funeral pyre with sandalwood and clarified butter.
Taking Rāma upon her breast, Reṇukā quickly kissed him on the cheeks and head; she wept loudly and profusely again and again, crying:
"O Rāma, O Rāma, O mighty-armed one, where shall I go, forsaken by you? (41)
Calling out "O child, O child," he lamented thus repeatedly and intensely:
"O child, you who are dearer to me than my own life, listen to my words!
O son, after performing the remaining funeral rites for your parents, do not go to war."
"Stay at home in happiness, my son, and perform eternal asceticism;
battle with fierce kṣatriyas is by no means pleasant.
Disregarding his mother's words, he indeed made that vow.
"Twenty-one times I shall surely make the earth devoid of kings.
I will slay Kārtavīrya, that lowest of Kṣatriyas, with ease,
and likewise satisfy my ancestors with the blood of the Kṣatriyas."
Having spoken thus before his mother, he lamented again and again;
he then instructed his mother with words that were beneficial, true, and the essence of political wisdom.
Rāma said:

The great fool who does not kill one who violates his father’s command or one who intends to slay his father will certainly go to the Raurava hell. So too shall he who sets fire to dwellings, who administers poison, who holds a weapon in hand, or who steals wealth.
One who seizes land or a wife, one who harms his father or kinsmen,
one who is constantly lazy, one who is a reviler, and one who speaks harshly—
these eleven are the most sinful, deserving of death according to the Veda. (49–50)
"Taking the wealth of the twice-born, banishing them from their place,
shaving their heads, and beating them— the wise declare these to be equivalent to killing.
In the meantime, Bhṛgu himself arrived there.
Exceedingly terrified and high-minded, with a heart burning with anguish,
Reṇuka and Rāma stood bowed upon seeing him.
He spoke to them that which is declared in the Vedas and is for the benefit of the world beyond.
Bhṛgu said:
"O son, you are a wise man born of my lineage; why do you lament?
Everything in this world of transmigration, both moving and unmoving, is like a bubble upon the water. (54)
"O son, contemplate Kṛṣṇa, whose essence is truth and whose seed is truth.
That which has passed away, my child, has passed away; what has gone will never return.
Whatever is to be, that indeed shall be; whatever is destined to happen, that shall come to pass. (55)
By whom can the fruit of one's own previously acquired karma be warded off?
(56) Whatever has been, is, and will be has been determined by Kṛṣṇa;
O child, by whom can that determined karma be warded off? (57)
The seed of illusion belongs to the deceivers, and their body is composed of the five elements.
O son, their name is preceded by convention and is like a dream at dawn.
Likewise, hunger, sleep, compassion, peace, forgiveness, beauty, and so forth [are likewise illusory].
When the Supreme Self departs, the vital breaths, the mind, and the intellect depart as well;
all the powers follow Him, just as servants follow a great king. Therefore, worship that Kṛṣṇa with diligent effort.
Who are the fathers of whom, and who are the sons of whom, O son?
Driven by their own actions, all are cast into this most difficult-to-cross ocean of existence.
The wise do not weep at all; therefore, do not weep now, my son.
From the falling of weeping tears for the deceased, hell is certain.
And when kinsmen weep by uttering the name of the deceased as a conventional designation,
they will certainly not reach him even after weeping for a hundred years.
The earth takes up its own earthly portion, consisting of bone, skin, and so forth;
likewise, water takes up its own watery portion, and the sky its own ethereal portion.
Similarly, air takes up its own airy portion, and fire its own fiery portion. (63–64)
All have dissolved into all; who indeed will come from weeping?
Reduced to nothing but the hearing of their names, their fame, their deeds, and mere stories, perform that action for the sake of the next world which is prescribed by the Vedas.
He alone is a kinsman and he alone is a son who acts for the benefit of the next world.
Having heard those words of Bhṛgu, [the king] abandoned his grief at that very moment;
and the great virtuous Reṇukā began to attend upon him.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Jamadagni and Paraśurāma’s Vow," in the Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa of the third book of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Reṇukā said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, I shall now follow my lord of life."
"This man, the bestower of honor, died on the fourth day of his fertile period, yet he has died today.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me: what arrangement should be made here?
You have come to me suddenly due to the merit of many lifetimes."
Bhṛgu said: "O great chaste lady, follow your meritorious husband;
the fourth day is pure for all the rites of a master.
On the fourth day she is pure for her husband, but not yet pure for rites concerning the gods or the ancestors. (3)

In rites for the gods and for the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day. (4) Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, even so does a virtuous wife, taking her husband with her, proceed to heaven. (5)
There he rejoices with his master for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Beyond that, O virtuous woman, enjoy the fruits of your karma, both auspicious and inauspicious.
He is a true son who offers devotion, and she is a true wife who follows him.
He is a kinsman who bestows gifts; he is a disciple who honors the guru.
He is the chosen deity who protects; he is the king who guards the subjects.
And he is the master who is capable of directing one’s mind toward what is dear to the Dharma in this world.
That guru is a bestower of dharma who grants devotion to Hari.
These [qualities] are certainly praised in the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
(9) Reṇukā said:
"O Sage, O ascetic, tell me among women in Bhārata: who is capable of going along with her own husband, and who is incapable?
Bhṛgu said:

Women with young children, those who are pregnant, those who have not yet reached puberty, as well as menstruating women, unchaste women, those afflicted by wasting diseases, those who neglect service to their husbands, those who are faithless, and those who speak harshly— [these should not be seen]. 11.
If, by fate, these women do not obtain their beloved,
then— having placed the consecrated fire before them— they follow their husband as he lies upon the funeral pyres, provided that they are beloved wives and thus attain him. (12–13)
Those women who follow their beloved attain him alone,
sharing with him the enjoyment of merit in heaven, birth after birth.
O virtuous lady, this definitive rule for householders has been declared to you.
Listen now to the destination of those Vaiṣṇavas who have died at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Wherever a virtuous wife follows her Vaiṣṇava husband,
she goes together with her lord to Vaikuṇṭha, into the presence of Hari.
O Nārada, there is no difference for devotees whether they die at a sacred ford or elsewhere;
the fruit of death is equal for those liberated ones who have realized Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, there is no falling back for those two, even when the great dissolution occurs.
A man should worship that Nārāyaṇa, and a woman [should worship] Kamalālayā.
Having died at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with knowledge, he certainly goes to Vaikuṇṭha;
there, together with his wife, he rejoices for as long as a hundred Brahmās exist.
Having spoken thus to Reṇukā there, that Bhṛgu addressed the son of Jamadagni with all the words prescribed by the Vedas, which were appropriate for the occasion:
"Come, O blessed child; abandon this inauspicious grief."
"O Bhṛgu, lay your father on his back with his head toward the south.
Clothe him in fresh garments and a new sacred thread.
With tears no longer in your eyes, stand facing the south. (21–22)
And receive with affection the fire produced from the *araṇi* wood;
perform the remembrance of all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) upon the earth.
[23] And [remember] the sacred fords such as Gayā and those meritorious mountain peaks.
Kurukṣetra, the Gaṅgā, and the Yamunā, the best of rivers;
the Kauśikī and the Candrabhāgā, which destroy all sins;
as well as the Gaṇḍakī, Kāśī, the Panasā, and likewise the Sarayū.
The Puṣpabhadrā, the Bhadrā, the Narmadā, and the Sarasvatī;
the Godāvarī, the Kāverī, the Svarṇarekhā, and Puṣkara;
as well as Raivata, Varāha, Śrīśaila, and Gandhamādana.
Again and again, he repeatedly recalled the Himalayas, Kailāsa, Sumeru, and the mountain of jewels; Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, the holy forest of Vṛndāvana, Haridvāra, and Badarī. (27–28)
Having offered sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and fragrant flowers,
and having covered him with a cloth, place him upon the funeral pyre.
You, moreover, [should apply] a golden probe to his ears, eyes, nose, and mouth.
Having performed the churning, O dear one, give it respectfully to the Brahmins.
Having given a copper vessel with sesame seeds, a cow, silver,
and gold along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), bestow the fire upon them without any hesitation.
Oṃ! Having committed an evil deed, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
when a man has come under the power of the time of death and reached the state of the five elements—
endowed with both merit and demerit, and enveloped by greed and delusion— 32.
"May he go to all the limbs [of his body] and to the divine worlds.
(33) Having recited this mantra and circumambulated his father, give the fire to Janaka while remembering Hari with this mantra. (34)
"Oṃ! You were born in our family; may another [son] be born from you.
Now say, 'To this one, for the heavenly world, svāhā!
O Bhṛgu, together with your brothers, place the fire upon the head."
Bhṛgu performed all of that together with his kinsmen at the command of Bhṛgu.
Then Reṇukā, having placed her son upon her breast,
spoke these few words which bring happiness in the end.
Non-opposition in the ocean of existence is the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
opposition is the seed of destruction and the cause of all calamities.
Indeed, one must not engage in hostility with fierce Kṣatriyas.
And a formal pledge must be made once my words have been heard.
Having deliberated with Brahmā and Bhṛgu, his divine counselor, the virtuous should perform the auspicious consultation as is appropriate. (39–40)
Having spoken thus, she abandoned her beloved, placed him upon her breast,
and fell asleep upon the funeral pyre while remembering Hari;
then Rāma, together with his brothers, set fire to the pyre.
Together with his brothers and the disciples of his father, he lamented.
Having uttered the words "Rāma, Rāma,
Rāma," that virtuous woman was reduced to ashes before the son of Jamadagni.
Upon hearing the name of their master, the messengers of Hari arrived there;
they were all mounted on chariots, dark-complexioned, and possessed of beautiful four arms. They bore conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses, and wore garlands of forest flowers.
Wearing crowns and earrings, and clad in yellow silk garments,
they placed that Reṇukā upon their chariot and went to the abode of Brahmā;
taking Jamadagni with them, they proceeded to the presence of Hari.
And that couple remained in Vaikuṇṭha in the presence of Hari,
constantly performing service to Hari, who is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
Then, O Nārada, Rāma, together with the Brahmins and Bhṛgu—
Having performed the remaining funeral rites for his parents, he gave wealth to the Brahmins:
cows, land, gold, garments, a beautiful celestial bed provided with a golden vessel,
water, food, and sandalwood.
A jewel-lamp, a silver mountain, and an excellent golden throne;
betel-leaf with a fragrant scent together with a golden base;
an umbrella, sandals, and a charming garland of flowers. (50)
Having given fruits, roots and the like, as well as delicious and enchanting food and wealth to the Brahmins, he went to the world of Brahmā.
He beheld that world of Brahmā, fashioned from gold.
There he beheld Brahmā, encircled by a golden rampart and adorned with golden pillars; blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, and decorated with ornaments of precious gems.
He was surrounded by lords of sages who had perfected themselves through austerities and the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
he was looking on with a smile and joy at the dance of the Vidyādharīs, while listening to the music being performed by singers. (54)
Adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
the bestower of the fruits of austerities, the giver of all prosperity, the sustainer of the entire universe, and the supreme Lord who is its creator. (55–56)
Seeing the imperishable Lord Kṛṣṇa, who was reciting the most perfect Brahman,
teaching the secret yoga, and questioning the circle of disciples,
Bhṛgu bowed before him with devotion.
Having wept loudly, he spoke of his own circumstances.
Bhṛgu said: "O Brahmā, O Creator, I am born of your lineage, the son of Jamadagni. You are our grandfather; what can I say to you who know all things?"
When my father, who was observing a fast, encountered the king who had come out hunting,
he caused him to break his fast with the goods given by Kapilā.
Out of greed for that Kapilā cow, King Kārtavīryārjuna himself [acted].
"Having said, 'He caused my mother to be slain,' he wept aloud.
Checking his tears, that ocean of compassion spoke again:
'O Teacher of the World, my virtuous mother followed me, leaving me behind. (61–62)
Now I am without a protector; you are my mother, father, and guru.
You are my creator, sustainer, and giver; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
I have come to your assembly by the command of my maternal grandfather and mother.
O Lord of the World, by means of skillful stratagem, bring about the destruction of my enemies.
He who protects the distressed is a king, he is most righteous, he is compassionate, and he is illustrious; he is worthy of worship and possesses enduring prosperity. (64–65)
"He who looks upon the wealthy and the wretched as equals, yet does not protect his subjects—
from his body the Goddess of Fortune departs in anger, and he shall be deprived of his kingdom.
Having heard the words of the young brahmin, Brahmā, the ocean of compassion, [acted].
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, he held him to his chest.
And having heard Bhṛgu’s vow— which was exceedingly difficult to perform, terrible, and destructive of many living beings— the four-faced Brahmā was struck with wonder.
Thinking that all this must come about through action,
he spoke in his mind to that son of Jamadagni regarding that which brings happiness in its ultimate fruition.
Brahmā said:
"O child, this vow is difficult to fulfill, for it involves the destruction of many living beings.
This creation must have come into being through the will of the Blessed Lord;
O son, this creation was brought forth by me with great effort, indeed by the command of the Lord."
Your vow regarding the destruction of creation is supreme, cruel, and merciless.
(71) You desire to make the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times;
because of the fault of a single Kṣatriya, you wish to destroy that entire caste. (72)
The perpetual creation by the fourfold classes— Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—
is manifested and withdrawn again and again by Hari alone;
otherwise, your previous vow would have been contradicted.
The accomplishment of your purpose shall come to pass with great effort.
Go to the world of Śiva, my child; seek refuge in Śaṅkara.
There are many kings upon the earth who are servants of Śaṅkara.
"Without the command of Maheśa, who indeed is capable of slaying them?
For they bear the divine armor of Śakti and of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, strive diligently to devise a means that is auspicious and the seed of victory."
All undertakings initiated with skillful means succeed.
Receive from Śaṅkara the armor-mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
it will surely overcome the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Śākta splendors that are otherwise difficult to conquer. (77–78)

Your guru is Śiva, the Lord of the worlds, in birth after birth. A mantra obtained from anyone other than me is not fit for you; that which is obtained from me shall be the proper rite. Through action a mantra is obtained, and through action a guru is obtained.
Those for whom these [weapons] present themselves of their own accord will certainly possess them.
O Bhṛgu, having taken up this excellent armor named Trailokyavijaya,
you shall render the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
"Śaṅkara will give you the divine Pāśupata [weapon].
By means of that mantra given by him, you shall conquer the host of Kṣatriyas.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means Spoken by Brahmā," in the section concerning Bhṛgu’s journey to the world of Brahmā, within the *Nārada-Nārāyaṇa Saṃvāda* of the third *Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Brahmā and having bowed to the Teacher of the World, he departed for Śiva’s realm, prosperous and having obtained a boon from him. 1.
One hundred thousand *yojanas* above the world of Brahmā lies Vaikuṇṭha, which is distinct from it;
it is indescribable, rich in exquisite beauty, supported by the wind, and enchanting.
To its south is Gaurīloka, and to its north is [Vaikuṇṭha] itself.
That which is below is the eternal world (dhruvaloka), remembered as being beyond all worlds.
Above them is Goloka, fifty crores of yojanas in extent.
Beyond that there is no world; it is remembered as being at the very summit of all.
That lord of yogis, traveling by means of his mind alone, beheld the world of Śiva—
a place of great wonder, devoid of any comparison or object of comparison—
and filled with the most excellent of lordly yogis, who were masters of perfected sciences and vidyās. (5)
It was frequented by meritorious beings purified by ascetic penances lasting for millions of kalpas;
it was surrounded by groves of wish-fulfilling trees that grant all desires,
and it shone with countless herds of wish-granting cows (kāmadhenus).
It was adorned with rows of groves of *pārijāta* trees,
endowed with tens of thousands of flower gardens, and always exceedingly beautiful;
it was graced by splendid jeweled altars fashioned from the essence of the finest gems.
It was adorned on all sides by hundreds of divine royal highways,
joined by hundreds of millions of mansions constructed from streams of the finest jewels,
enriched with various wonderful paintings and radiant with jars made of the most excellent gems.
In the delightful center of that place, he beheld the abode of Śaṅkara,
most enchanting, with walls constructed from the essence of the finest jewels;
it was exceedingly high, touching the sky, and as white as the waters of the milk-ocean.
It was provided with sixteen gates and adorned with a hundred palaces (12).
These were constructed of priceless jewels, decorated with jeweled staircases,
and featured jeweled pillars and doors embellished with diamonds (13).

There, in front of the temple, he beheld the lion-gate, adorned with networks of rubies, radiant with jars of excellent gems, and made exceedingly beautiful by various diverse and variegated paintings. (14)
The house was resplendent with door-panels inlaid with the finest essence of jewels,
and it was always adorned with altars both inside and out,
fashioned from rubies and great emeralds. (15–16)
He beheld two terrifying gatekeepers of fearsome form, painted with various beautiful and variegated colors;
they had mouths with large, formidable fangs, were devoid of passion, and possessed blood-red eyes. (17)
Resembling two scorched mountains, they possessed great strength and prowess;
their limbs were adorned with ashes, and those two excellent ones wore tiger-skin garments.
They had tawny eyes and wide eyes, wore matted locks, and each had three eyes.
Bearing tridents and sharp-edged spears, they blazed with the splendor of Brahman.
Seeing them, he was terrified and agitated in his mind, and being humble and disciplined, he spoke somewhat to those two mighty ones who were ill-behaved. (20)
He related his entire history before him.
Having heard the words of the brahmin, they became filled with compassion;
having received the command of the high-souled Śaṅkara through his messenger, they departed.
The two excellent attendants of the Lord gave him permission to enter.
Having received that command, Bhṛgu entered while remembering Hari.
He beheld sixteen exceedingly beautiful gates, one after another.
Having seen those [gates] appointed by doorkeepers and adorned with various wonderful paintings,
he beheld with great wonder the assembly hall of the Trident-bearer (Śiva),
crowded with hosts of various Siddhas and frequented by throngs of great sages.

There he beheld Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest; he was made fragrant by a breeze rich with the scent of the Pārijāta tree, the supreme deity holding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, and clad in a tiger skin. 26.26–27ab.
His limbs were adorned with supernatural powers, and he wore a serpent as a sacred thread;
he sat upon a jeweled lion-throne, decorated with ornaments of gems.
He is the Great Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness, the seed of Śiva, and the refuge of Śiva.
Delighting in the Self, with all desires fulfilled, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
with a slight smile and a serene countenance, intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees;
whose very nature is eternal light, and whose form exists for the welfare of the worlds.
Wearing a mass of matted locks and accompanied by the daughters of Dakṣa;
the bestower of the fruits of austerities and the giver of all prosperity;
resembling pure crystal, with five faces and three eyes. (30)
He was proclaiming the secret Brahman to his disciples by means of the *tattva-mudrā*;
he was being praised by the lords of yogins and served by the lords of *siddhas*,
and was constantly attended by the foremost attendants with white chowries.
He meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, the most perfect and supreme,
consisting of His own will, transcending the qualities (guṇas), the remover of old age and death, the ultimate,
the form of light, the primordial source of all, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond material nature (prakṛti). 33.
Meditating upon supreme bliss, his body covered in horripilation,
he was singing aloud with a melodious voice and tearful eyes— him, an ocean of virtues,
surrounded by the lords of beings, the hosts of Rudras, and the guardians of the sacred fields. (34)
Upon seeing him with reverence, Paraśurāma bowed his head;
he saw Kārttikeya to his left and Gaṇeśvara to his right,
as well as Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, and Vīrabhadra before him.
In his lap, he beheld that beloved Gaurī, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
With supreme devotion and great joy, he bowed his head before them all.
Seeing Hara, he began to offer praise out of intense delight.
With faltering words, dejected, with tearful eyes and deeply distressed, he joined his palms in reverence; peaceful yet afflicted by grief, he [addressed] the destroyer of sorrow.
(38) Paraśurāma said:
O Lord, I desire to praise you, yet I am entirely unable to praise you.
How can I praise that which is the imperishable and undecaying seed, the effortless one?
O Lord of Gods, being of deluded intellect, I am not capable of making a proper connection [of words]; nevertheless, I praise you. (39)
The Vedas are not able to praise You; who here is capable of praising You? (40) You are beyond speech, intellect, and mind; the essence of essences, higher than the highest;
attainable through knowledge alone, perfected, and served by the Siddhas. (41)
That which is like space, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and likewise immutable;
the foundation of the universe and yet not a system, independent and the seed of all systems;
unattainable through meditation, difficult to propitiate, yet easily mastered by the compassionate treasury of mercy.
Save me, O ocean of compassion, O friend of the distressed, for I am most wretched!
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived;
for what was never seen even in a dream by devotees, I now behold with my own eyes.
I bow to that Maheśvara, from whose single part (kalā) the hosts of gods beginning with Śakra arise, and from a fraction of a part (kalāṃśa) the moving and unmoving world;
he who assumes the form of a woman, the form of a eunuch, and the form of a man.
I bow to that Maheśvara, the support of all and the form of all.
(46) I bow to that Maheśvara, who is the nature of the sun, the nature of the moon, and the sacrificial fire; who is the nature of water and the nature of wind. (47)
I bow to that Maheśvara, the terrifying destroyer of infinite worlds of creation, who in a mere moment, as if in play, [devours all].
He is Time, the Death of Death, the Kali age, the seed, and that which is born of Time.
"I bow to that Maheśvara who is both unborn and the source of all beings.
Having spoken thus, Bhṛgu fell at the lotus-feet [of the Lord],
and He, being well-pleased, bestowed a blessing upon him.

Whoever recites this hymn composed by the son of Jamadagni with devotion, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Śiva. (51) Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of Paraśurāma to Kailāsa," in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa within the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa. (29)
Śaṅkara said:
Who are you, O boy? Whose son are you? Where is your dwelling? How is this hymn [composed]?
Or what desired thing shall I do for you? Speak now. (1)
Pārvatī said: I see you overwhelmed by grief, dejected, and greatly astonished—though you are extremely young in age, peaceful, and the best among the virtuous in your qualities. 2.
Bhṛgu said:
"I am the son of Jamadagni, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu;
Reṇukā is my mother, and I am Paraśurāma by name, O Lord. (3)
"O ocean of compassion, purchase me, your servant, with the commodity of knowledge.
O Lord, you who are kind to the distressed, protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (4) My father [said], "The king has come out hunting while I am fasting."
Having brought him in, he offered hospitality with the items given by Kapilā.
Out of greed for Kapilā, the dull-witted king had him executed.
Seeing him dead, Kapilā departed for Goloka.
My mother has followed [Yama], and I am now truly without a protector.
You are my father and Śivā is my mother; O Lord, protect me like a son.
A vow was made by me out of grief, which is indeed exceedingly difficult to fulfill.
"I shall render the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times;
I shall slay Kārtavīrya, the murderer of my father, in battle.
O Blessed One, you ought to fulfill this for me. (8–9)
Having heard the words of the brahmin and having seen the mouth of the Durgā, Hara’s face became downcast, and she [Pārvatī] had her lips and palate parched. Pārvatī said: 10. Pārvatī said:

"O ascetic, you are the son of a brahmin, yet out of anger you desire to make the earth kingless; O young student, this is a great act of rashness. Being unarmed, you wish to slay the lord Saṃsārarjuna, who possesses a thousand arms."
O boy, the armor of Śrī Hari was bestowed by Datta upon that Rāvaṇa, whose defeat was achieved merely by the playful knitting of his eyebrows; and he also gave you an infallible spear,
by which indeed your father was slain.
Whoever recites the mantra of Hari and His hymns of praise day and night—who on this earth could possibly slay him? I see no such person here on the surface of the earth.
O Brahmin, go home; what can Śaṅkara do?
"And other kings are my servants; what fear can you have of them while I am present?
Kālī said:
"O brahmin boy, you rogue! You wish to leave the world without kings."
Just as Vāmana desires to seize the moon with his hand,
so do you, with the aid of Digambara, wish to slay my servants— who have performed sacrifices, possess great merit, and are endowed with great strength and prowess. (16–17)
Having heard their words, he wept aloud out of grief;
suddenly, in their presence, he prepared to give up his life.
Hearing the Brahmin’s weeping, Śaṅkara, the ocean of compassion, [appeared].
Beholding Durgā and Kālī, and having understood their intention, the All-pervading Lord,
the Master of all who is affectionate toward his devotees, obtained their consent and immediately began to speak to the son of Jamadagni.
Śaṅkara said:
"From this day forward, my child, you are as great to me as a son.
I shall grant you a secret mantra, difficult to obtain in the three worlds. (21)
And I shall give you such a most wonderful armor;
by my grace, you will slay Kārtavīrya with ease.
O twice-born one, you will render the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
"The world shall become filled with glory; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara gave him a most difficult-to-obtain mantra, the supreme and most wonderful armor named Trailokyavijaya.
O Nārada, he explained the hymn of praise and the ritual procedure for worship preceded by the *puraścaraṇa*,
the practice for the attainment of mantra-siddhi according to the proper sequence of observances,
the place of accomplishment, and the number of days required.
At that very moment, he taught him the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and so forth;
as well as the Nāgapāśa, the Pāśupata, and the extremely rare Brahmāstra;
and likewise the Nārāyaṇāstra, Āgneya, Vāyavya, and Vāruṇa [astras].
The Gāndharva and Gāruḍa [sciences], as well as the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon;
the mace, the spear, the axe, and the supreme, unfailing trident;
and the mantras for various kinds of weapons and missiles, according to the prescribed rites. (28)
The withdrawal of weapons and missiles, the two quivers with inexhaustible arrows,
the protection of oneself and the fixing of arrows, the sequence for victory in battle,
various forms of illusory warfare, and the *huṃkāra* preceded by mantras.
Hara bestowed upon him the protection of his own army, the crushing of enemy forces,
various kinds of incomparable stratagems for the perils of battle,
and the deluding lore (*mohinī-vidyā*) that removes death at the time of destruction. (31)
Having stayed for a long time on the shoulder of his guru and mastered all branches of knowledge,
he achieved perfection in the mantra at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and after bowing to them, he departed.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Paraśurāma’s Acquisition of Weapons and Missiles Granted by Śiva," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said: O Blessed One, I wish to hear which mantra, hymn, and armor the Blessed Lord Hara compassionately bestowed upon Paraśurāma. (1)
Who is the one to be propitiated by this mantra? What is the fruit of the armor (kavaca), and what is the fruit of the hymn of praise? You ought to tell me that. (2) Nārāyaṇa said:
For the Blessed One himself, the most perfect, is indeed to be propitiated through mantra;
he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, the Master and Sovereign of the cowherds and cowherdesses.
(3) [This is] the most wonderful armor named Trailokyavijaya.

He gave to Paraśurāma, in the presence of the Jewel Mountain, this king of hymns of great merit, which arises from the yoga of prosperity— a mantra named the Wish-Fulfilling Tree that bestows the fruit of all desires. (4–5)
On the bank of the Svayaṃprabhā river, within a grove of pārijāta trees,
in the hermitage of the world-deity and in the presence of Mādhava,
Mahādeva said: "Come, O blessed one, you who have arisen from the lineage of Bhṛgu."
"You are dearer to me in affection than a son; therefore, take up this armor.
Listen, O Rāma, I shall proclaim that which is most wonderful in the universe, known as the *Trailokyavijaya*, which brings victory to Śrī Kṛṣṇa."

Formerly, in Goloka, within Rādhikā’s hermitage in the midst of the Rāsa-maṇḍala in the forest of Vṛndāvana, Śrī Kṛṣṇa bestowed upon me this most secret reality, which embodies the totality of all mantras. (9)
I shall tell you that which is more meritorious than merit itself, out of supreme affection:
by holding and reciting it, the Goddess, the Sovereign of Mūlaprakṛti, slew Śumbha, Niśumbha, Mahiṣa, and Raktabīja. (10–11)
Having held this, I— the destroyer of the worlds and knower of all principles—
easily destroyed Tripura, though it was previously invincible and difficult to endure.
Having held this, Brahmā created the supreme creation through its recitation.
That which the Lord Śeṣa holds, supporting the entire universe;
that which the king of tortoises holds, supporting Śeṣa with ease;
and that which the Lord Vāyu himself, the all-pervading support of the universe, holds—[that is this earth]. (13–14)
By holding which Varuṇa became perfected, and Kubera the lord of wealth;
by holding and reciting which Indra himself became the sovereign of the gods;
and by holding which the sun himself shines in the world as a mass of splendor.
By holding and reciting this, the Moon attained great strength and prowess.
By holding and reciting it, Agastya drank up the seven oceans;
and by its splendor, he rendered the Daitya named Vātāpi as if consumed by fire. (16–17)
By bearing and reciting which, the Goddess Vasundharā became the support of all;
by bearing and reciting which, Gaṅgā, the purifier of the worlds, became sanctified;
and by bearing which, Dharma, the witness of the worlds and the best among the upholders of dharma, [attained his status]. 18.
She is the presiding goddess of all vidyās; it is she whom Sarasvatī assumes, by wearing whom Lakṣmī becomes the giver of food to the worlds, higher than the highest;
and it is she whom Sāvitrī bears and from whom she gives birth to the Vedas through recitation.
The Vedas, which proclaim the Dharma, became pure through holding and reciting this; the Fire-god, the bearer of oblations, became radiant through holding and reciting it;
and the blessed Sanatkumāra, the best among the wise, attained his preeminence by holding it. (21)
It should be given to a devotee of Kṛṣṇa who is virtuous and high-souled.
By giving it to a rogue or to the disciple of another, one shall meet with death.
Prajāpati [is the seer] of this armor (kavaca) that conquers the three worlds.
The seer is Gāyatrī and the meter is also Gāyatrī; the deity is Rāseśvara himself.
His application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of victory over the three worlds.
This armor (kavaca), which is higher than the highest, is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
May the Praṇava protect my head; "Obeisance always to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
May the five-syllable mantra remembered as "Kṛṣṇāya Svāhā" protect the skull.
And may "Kṛṣṇa" protect the eyes, while "Kṛṣṇa Svāhā" protects the pupils.
May the mantra "Oṃ *haraye* namaḥ" always protect my creeper-like eyebrows.
May "Oṃ *goviṃdāya* svāhā" constantly protect my nose. May "Oṃ *gopālāya* namaḥ" always protect my two cheeks from all sides. (26–27)
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the cowherd women; may he always protect my ears.
Oṃ, salutations to Kṛṣṇa; may he eternally protect the pair of my lips. Oṃ, svāhā to Govinda; may he always protect the rows of my teeth. (28)
May *pātu* protect the area below the teeth of Kṛṣṇa; may *klīṃ* always protect the area above the teeth. (29) May *oṃ śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā* always protect my tongue;
may *rāseśvarāya svāhā* always protect my palate. (30)
"Oṃ Rādhikeśāya svāhā"—may this protect my throat forever.
"Namo gopāṅganeśāya"—may this protect my chest forever.
"Oṃ Gopeśāya svāhā"—may this protect my shoulders forever. (31)

Salutation to Him in the form of a youth, Svāhā; may He always protect my back. (32) May Mukunda protect my belly eternally; salutation always to Him. Oṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Svāhā—may this protect my hands always. (33)
Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu; may he always protect my pair of arms.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Blessed One; may he always protect my fingernails.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa; may he always protect the hollows between my fingernails.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, may the one with the lotus-navel (Padmanābha) always protect my navel.
(35) Oṃ sarveśāya svāhā, may he always protect my skeleton.
Oṃ gopīramaṇāya svāhā, may he always protect my hips. (36)
Oṃ, may the feet of the Lord, the Beloved of the Gopīs, always protect me.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Rasikeśa; may He always protect everything.
Oṃ keśavāya svāhā; may this protect my hair forever.
"Oṃ namaḥ kṛṣṇāya svāhā"—may this always protect my *brahmarandhra*.
"Oṃ mādhavāya svāhā"—may this always protect my body hairs.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rasikeśāya svāhā"—may this always protect everything. (38–39)
May Kṛṣṇa, the most perfectly complete, always protect me in the eastern direction;
may he himself, the Lord of Goloka, protect me in the south-eastern direction;
and may he, whose nature is the perfect Brahman, always protect me in the southern direction.
May Kṛṣṇa protect me in the southwest; may Hari protect me in the west.
May Govinda protect me eternally and constantly in the northwest.
May the crest-jewel of the connoisseurs of rasa always protect me in the north.
May He who sports in Vṛndāvana always protect me in the northeast;
may the Lord of the life-breath of Vṛndāvana protect me from above.
May Mādhava, the recipient of offerings and possessor of great strength, always protect me.
May Nṛsiṃha protect me always in water, on land, and in the atmosphere. (44) May Mādhava protect me constantly in sleep and in waking;
may the all-pervading Lord, the untainted inner self of all, protect me from every side. (45)
Thus, O child, I have related to you that which embodies the entire multitude of mantras.
This most wonderful armor named Trailokyavijaya was heard by me from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa; it must not be spoken of to anyone.
Having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rules, he who should wear the armor (kavaca) [attains success]. || 47 ||
Whether on the neck or on the right arm, he too is Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
And wherever that devotee dwells, there Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall dwell.
If one's armor were perfected, he would become liberated while living.
One shall certainly obtain the fruit of worship for ten million years. || 49 ||
Thousands of Rājasūya sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
Indeed, ten thousand horse-sacrifices and ten thousand human-sacrifices [are equal to it]. ||50||
These very same great gifts, as well as circumambulating the earth, [yield the same merit].
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of this Trailokyavijaya.
The observance of vows and fasts, the study of one's own sacred texts, and austerity.
And all bathing at sacred fords do not equal even a fraction of this. || 52 ||
There is the state of being a perfected one, immortality, and even servitude to Śrī Hari.
If one’s armor is perfected, one certainly attains everything. He whose armor is perfected is one who has recited it ten lakhs of times;
he whose armor is perfected will certainly become omniscient. 54.
If one of very dull intellect should worship Kṛṣṇa without knowing this armor (*kavaca*),
the mantra will not grant success even if recited for ten million kalpas.
Having taken this armor, O child, rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas.
Indeed, for twenty-one times, he was always fearless and joyful, acting with ease.
O son, a kingdom may be given, a head may be given, and even life itself may be given;
but such armor as this must never be given, even in a life-threatening crisis.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Kavaca upon Paraśurāma," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Bhṛgu said:
O sage, you have now obtained this armor which provides eternal protection for all limbs.
It bestows happiness, it bestows liberation, it is the essence, and it is the cause for the destruction of enemies. 1.
Now, O Lord, [tell me] the mantra of the Blessed One, the hymn of praise, and the ritual procedure for worship.
Give [protection] to me, who am without a protector, O guardian of those who have sought refuge! ||2||
Mahādeva said:
Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect one; svāhā!
Among mantras, this great king of mantras consists of seventeen syllables. (3)
This bull among sages has attained perfection through five hundred thousand recitations.
The fire sacrifice (havana) should be one-tenth of that, and the consecration (abhiṣecana) one-tenth of that.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is one-tenth of that, and the sprinkling (mārjana) is one-tenth of that.
And one hundred gold pieces is the sacrificial fee for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). || 4 ||
O Sage, for a man who has attained mastery over mantras, the entire universe is as if in the palm of his hand.
He is capable of drinking the oceans and is the Lord who can destroy the entire universe.
One who possesses a body composed of the five elements is capable of going to Vaikuṇṭha.
By the mere touch of the dust of his lotus feet, |||
All sacred fords are purified, and the earth is instantly sanctified.
O Sage, listen from my mouth to the meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda, which bestows both devotion and liberation upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All. (6–7)
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like blue lotuses, his face like the full autumn moon, he was enchanting with a gentle smile;
he was the captivating abode of the playful beauty of ten million Cupids. (8)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with ornaments of precious gems,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, wearing excellent yellow garments,
and being constantly gazed upon by the smiling gopīs. (9–10)
Adorned with a garland of full-blown *mālatī* flowers and a forest garland (*vanamālā*),
he bears a crest rich with *kunda* blossoms and graced by the moon.
He eclipses the splendor of the sky filled with the moon and stars.
I worship Him whose every limb is adorned with jewels, who rests upon the breast of Rādhā,
who is served by the lords of the Siddhas, the lords of the Munis, and the lords of the gods,
and who is praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the Vedas.
Having meditated upon Him with this meditation and having offered the sixteen types of ritual services,
a person who worships with devotion shall attain omniscience.
[14] These include the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the seat (āsana), as well as clothing and ornaments.
A cow, water for honoring, honey-mixture (madhuparka), and an unsurpassed sacrificial thread;
incense and lamps, food offerings, and again water for sipping;
various kinds of flowers and well-scented betel leaf. (15–16)
A captivating divine bed adorned with musk, agallochum, and sandalwood,
as well as garlands and three handfuls of flowers, should be offered with devotion to the Blessed One.
Then, having performed worship of the six limbs, one should subsequently worship Gaṇeśa.
One should worship with a spirit of devotion these seven foremost attendants: Śrīdāmā, Sudāmā, Vasudāmā, Haribhānu, Candrabhānu, Sūryabhānu, and Subhānu. (18–19)
One should worship with devotion Gopīśvarī, Rādhikā, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti, the power of Kṛṣṇa who is worthy of Kṛṣṇa’s worship;
as well as the peaceful hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, myself, Brahmā, and Pārvatī. (20)
Having worshipped Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Pṛthvī, and all the gods along with their attendants—
the group of six deities— again with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra),
the wise one should thereafter worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the proper sequence.
Having worshipped the six deities— Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Vahni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā— one should also worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva).
One should worship Gaṇeśa for the destruction of obstacles and Bhāskara for the destruction of disease.

One should worship Vahni for the purification of the self, Śrī Viṣṇu for the sake of liberation, Śaṅkara for the sake of knowledge, and Durgā for the sake of supreme sovereignty. This is the fruit of worship; the opposite occurs when there is no worship.
Then, having performed the circumambulation and having worshipped the chosen deity with devotion, one should recite with devotion the hymn proclaimed in the Sāmaveda; listen to that.
Mahādeva said:
I bow to the Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the eternal supreme light,
the untainted Supreme Self, the cause of all;
the God who is greater than the gross, more subtle than the subtle, and the Transcendent.
I bow to Him who makes all that is visible invisible, who acts according to His own will;
I bow to the Lord who has form and is formless, who possesses attributes and is without attributes, who is the support of all, who is everything, and whose form is His own will. (28–29)

I bow down to the All-pervading Lord, who possesses an exceedingly beautiful and incomparable form, yet who also bears an extremely formidable appearance. He is the very essence of action and the witness of all actions.
I bow to the fruit and the giver of the fruit, who possesses every form.
(31) The creator, the protector, and the destroyer through his portions and distinct manifestations—I bow to that Puruṣa who assumes various forms by means of his partial energies. (32)

I bow to that which is higher than the highest, which is itself the eternal form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and, through its own *māyā*, is itself the Person (*puruṣa*); it is beyond both of these and is eternally itself. It assumes the forms of female, male, and neuter by means of its own *māyā*.

I bow to that God who is himself Māyā and himself the wielder of Māyā. I bow to him who is the deliverer from all sufferings, the cause of all causes, the sustainer of all universes, and the seed of all.
I bow to that Lord of the World, who is the sun among all luminous bodies, the submarine fire among all castes, and the moon among the stars;
who is indeed Śaṅkara among the Rudras, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the wise. (36)
I bow to that Lord of the World who is Śeṣa among the Nāgas;
I bow to that Teacher of the World who is Brahmā among the Prajāpatis, Kapila himself among the Siddhas, and Sanatkumāra among the sages. (37–38)

I bow to Him who is Viṣṇu among the gods, who is Prakṛti herself among the goddesses, who is Svāyambhuva Manu among the Manus, and who is the Vaiṣṇava among human beings; I bow to him who is Śatarūpā among women, and who possesses manifold forms. (39)
I bow to Him who is the embodiment of all things: the spring among the seasons, Mārgaśīrṣa among the months, and the eleventh lunar day among the dates;
He who is the ocean among rivers and the Himalaya among mountains.
I bow down to him who is the earth among the patient;
among leaves, the *tulasī* leaf;
and among trees in the form of wood, the *kalpa* tree—I bow to that Lord of the World. (41–42)
Among flowers I am the Pārijāta, and among crops I am rice;
among foods I am the nectar of immortality—these various forms I revere.
Among lordly elephants I am Airāvata, and among birds I am Vainateya.
I bow to Kāmadhenu, the best among cows, who possesses every form;
I bow to that which is gold among radiant things and barley among grains;
