and I bow to the lion, the most excellent form among beasts. (44, 49)
I bow to that supreme boon-granter who is Kubera among the Yakṣas, Bṛhaspati among the planets, and Mahendra among the guardians of the quarters;
who is the collection of the Vedas among the scriptures, and Sarasvatī among the learned. 46.
I bow to that which is the letter *a* among letters, the foremost;
(47) among mantras, the Viṣṇu-mantra; among sacred fords, the Gaṅgā herself;
and indeed, among the senses, the mind—I bow to that which is the most excellent of all. (48)
I bow to him who is the Sudarśana among weapons, the Vaiṣṇava fever among diseases, and the Brahman-splendor among splendors—the most excellent one.
He is indeed the strength of the strong and the mind of those who move with speed. (49)
I bow to that Time which is distinct from all things subject to time.
I prostrate before that Essence who is the giver of knowledge among gurus, the mother among kinsmen, and the one who grants birth among friends. (50–51)
I bow to him who is Viśvakarman among artisans, Kāmadeva among those endowed with beauty, and the devoted wife among wives;
he who is the son among beloved ones and the king among men. (52)
I bow to that Śālagrāma, which is the most distinguished among all yantras. (53) I bow to that which is Dharma, the seed of all auspicious things; the Sāmaveda among the Vedas;
and the embodiment of truth among all dharmas—the most distinguished one, I bow to him. (54)

I bow to Him who is the very nature of coolness in water, the form of fragrance in the earth, and the form of sound in the sky; I prostrate before Him who is the Rājasūya among sacrifices and the Gāyatrī among meters. 55.
I bow to Citraratha, the most venerable among the Gandharvas.
(56) He who is the essence of milk, the purifier of all things that purify, and the hymn of merit-bestowing gifts—to Him, the bestower of auspiciousness, I bow. (57)
I bow to him who is the form of grass among blades of *kuśa*, the form of disease among enemies, and the form of tranquility among virtues;
to the Great One who is the form of splendor, the form of knowledge, and the form of all things. 58.
I bow to that self-existent Lord who is entirely beyond definition;
to Him who, like the wind among all supports, is the soul of those whose form is eternal, and who, like space among all pervasive things, is the most pervasive—I bow to Him. (59–60)
That which is indefinable, even a wise man is not able to praise it;
and who indeed is capable of praising that which is beyond definition?
Even the Vedas are unable to praise Him, and Sarasvatī herself has become rendered mute.
And who, even if wise, is capable of praising Him whose limits of speech and mind are beyond reach?
(62) I bow to Him whose nature is pure radiance, whose form is the embodiment of grace toward devotees, who is exceedingly beautiful, and whose appearance is dark-hued. (63)
I bow to the two-armed youth with a flute at his mouth, who is smiling with joy and is constantly gazed upon by the cowherd girls;
I bow to the enchanting one who has consumed the betel nut offered by Rādhā.
I bow down to that Lord seated upon a jeweled lion-throne;
adorned with an abundance of jewel ornaments and served by white chowries,
I bow to him who is attended by the foremost of his attendants, the cowherd youths.

I bow to the Lord of Rasikas, who is situated in the midst of the circle of the rāsa dance within the beautiful interior of Vṛndāvana, and who is eager for the joy of the rāsa. [67] On the great mountain Śataśṛṅga, in Goloka, upon the jewel-mountain;
I bow to the one who sports upon the delightful, dustless sands;
to the most perfect, peaceful, and enchanting beloved of Rādhā.
I perpetually prostrate before Kṛṣṇa, who is Truth and the very nature of Brahman. (68–69)

The person who recites this hymn of Śrī Kṛṣṇa at the three junctions of the day shall become a bestower of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation in this world of Bhārata. By the grace of this hymn, one shall obtain service to Hari and devotion toward Him.

In this world, he will certainly become equal to Viṣṇu and worthy of worship by the entire universe. As the lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis), though peaceful, he goes at the end to the abode of Hari.
He shines with splendor and fame upon the earth like the sun.
He shall be liberated while living and a devotee of Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
He will always be free from disease, virtuous, learned, possessed of sons, and wealthy.
He will certainly become one who possesses the six superknowledges, the ten powers, and the ability to travel by mind alone.
"By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he shall forever become omniscient, all-seeing, a bestower of all perfections, and equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Thus has this hymn been told; my child, you must go to Puṣkara."

Having accomplished the mantra-siddhi there, you shall afterwards obtain your desire. O best of sages, by my blessing and through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, make the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times at your pleasure.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Hymn," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third book of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having bowed to Śiva, that Bhṛgu, filled with joy, [bowed] to Durgā and Kālī.
Having gone to the Puṣkara-tīrtha, he indeed accomplished the perfection of mantra. Filled with devotion, he remained without food for a month;
meditating on the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, he performed the restraint of breath (vāyurodha).
Opening his eyes, he beheld the sky filled with light;
illuminating the ten directions and eclipsing the sun,
he saw a jeweled chariot situated in the midst of a circle of radiance.
There he beheld a most beautiful and excellent man,
whose face was bright with a gentle smile, who bestows grace upon his devotees.
Prostrating himself like a staff with his head, he chose that Lord as his boon.
"I shall make the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
Grant me that firm and unfailing devotion to Your lotus feet,
and grant me forever the service to Your lotus feet, which is so very difficult to attain.
Having granted him a boon, Kṛṣṇa vanished right there.
Bhrigu, having bowed down, went to that supreme and transcendent abode;
and his right limb throbbed, indicating the highest auspiciousness.

He beheld the fulfillment of his desires, the arising of conviction, and auspicious dreams; day and night, his mind became serene and expansive. Having spoken to all his kinsmen, he remained at home filled with joy. (9)
Having repeatedly summoned his own disciples, the disciples of his father, groups of brothers, and kinsmen,
he performed various mantras;
and at an auspicious moment, he recounted to them his own history from beginning to end.
Together with them, the powerful Rāma became intent on departure. He beheld auspicious omens and heard sounds indicative of victory;
he understood in his mind all that his own triumph and the destruction of his enemies would be.
And at the time of his departure, the sage suddenly heard before him the sound of "Hari," the roar of lions, and the sounding of bells and drums;
he also heard the music of a celestial voice saying, "Victory shall be yours."
Having heard such various auspicious signs— the auspicious gestures of the ship, the sound of the clouds bringing victory— the Blessed One set out on his journey.
He saw before him Brahmins, bards, astrologers, and mendicants.
He saw before him a virtuous woman accompanied by her husband and son, wearing various ornaments, with a smiling face, and holding a burning lamp.
He likewise saw Śiva and Śivā, a full water-pot, a blue jay, and a mongoose.
As he went along, Rāma saw signs indicative of a successful journey:
a black antelope, an elephant, a lion, a horse, a rhinoceros, a hippopotamus, a yak, a royal swan, a ruddy goose, a parrot, and a cuckoo. (17–18)
The peacock, the wagtail, the śaṅkhacilla, the cakoraka, the pigeon, the crane, the kāraṇḍava, the cātaka,
and the sparrow; the lightning, the bow of Indra, the sun, and the auspicious radiance of the sun.
Fresh meat, a live fish, a conch shell, gold,
ruby, silver, pearl, the lord of gems (sapphire), coral,
curd, parched grain, white grain, white flowers, and saffron. (20–21)
A leaf, a banner, an umbrella, a mirror, and a white chowrie;
a cow accompanied by its calf, as well as a king seated upon a chariot;
milk, clarified butter, betel nut, nectar, and likewise milk-rice (pāyasa).
A Śālagrāma stone, a ripe fruit, a svastika, sugar,
honey, a cat, a bull, a ram, a mountain mouse,
the rising of the sun when covered by clouds, and the lunar disc. (23–24)
Musk, a fan, water, turmeric, clay from a sacred ford,
white mustard seeds, black mustard, dūrvā grass, a young brāhmaṇa, a young girl,
a deer, a courtesan, a bee, camphor, one dressed in yellow garments, and a cow.
Urine, cow dung, the dust raised by cows, and the marks of cow hooves;
(26) a cow-pen, the path of cows, a delightful cow-shed, and the auspicious movement of cows;
an ornament, a divine image, a blazing fire, and a great festival; (27)

He beheld auspicious copper, crystal, venerable vermilion, garlands, sandalwood, fragrance, diamonds, and gems on his right side. He received the scent of fragrant breezes and the auspicious blessings of the Brahmins. (28–29)
Having thus understood this auspiciousness, he departed filled with joy.
When the sun had set, he reached the vicinity of the banks of the Narmadā.
There he beheld the divine and most enchanting Akṣayavaṭa tree.
Extremely high and vast was that supreme hermitage of great merit;
it was the site of the asceticism of Paulastya, filled with fragrant breezes.
There, near Kārtavīryārjuna, he remained together with his attendants.
Attended by servants, he slept upon a bed of flowers;
exhausted and filled with supreme bliss, he fell into slumber.
When the night had passed, that Bhṛgu beheld a beautiful dream.
That which was not conceived by the mind, nor produced by wind, bile, or phlegm;
[dreaming] of mounting elephants, horses, mountains, palaces, cows, or trees, or of bearing fruit; and of oneself weeping or being devoured by worms. (34–35)
He saw himself being made to board a boat, anointed with sandalwood paste, wearing a garland of flowers, and adorned with yellow garments;
yet his entire body was smeared with feces and urine, and covered with fat and pus. (36)
He saw himself playing a most excellent lute (vīṇā).
On the bank of a river, he saw himself with broad lotus petals,
having consumed milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with curd, clarified butter, and honey.
He saw himself having eaten betel-leaf and receiving the blessings of the Brahmins;
he saw himself beholding fruits, flowers, and lamps;
and [he saw] ripe fruit, milk, and hot food mixed with sugar.
And he saw himself again and again having eaten the svastika;
he saw his own self terrified and fleeing, being devoured by a leech, a scorpion, a fish, and a serpent.
Then the twice-born one beheld himself as a mandala of the moon and the sun,
looking with a smile upon a woman accompanied by her husband and son,
together with a well-attired maiden and the smiling brahmin.
He saw himself embraced by one who was pleased and thoroughly delighted;
he saw himself as a tree laden with flowers and fruit, as a divine image,
and as a king mounted upon an elephant or seated in a chariot— indeed, he beheld himself in all these forms.
The Brahmin saw himself entering the house, dressed in yellow garments, adorned with jewel ornaments,
and carrying a conch shell, crystal, a white garland, pearls, and sandalwood. (45)
Bhārgava indeed beheld himself seeing gold, silver, and jewels;
he saw an elephant, a bull, a serpent, a white [horse], and a white chowrie; and he saw a blue lotus and a mirror. (46–47)
In a dream, Bhṛgu beheld his own self seated upon a chariot rich with the nine gems and adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers; he was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
and [beheld] rows of lotuses, a full water-pot, curd, parched grain, clarified butter, and honey.
Bhṛgu indeed saw in his dream a leafy parasol and one who held it;
he saw a row of cranes, a row of swans, and a row of maidens observing vows; and Bhṛgu indeed saw in his dream them worshipping a bright water-pot.
In a dream, Bhṛgu beheld Hara and Hari worshipping a multitude of twice-born brahmins seated within a pavilion; they had said to him, "May there be victory!
and there was a perpetual rain of nectar, leaves, and fruits.
Bhṛgu indeed saw a rain of flowers and sandalwood in his dream;
he saw fresh meat, a live fish, a peacock, and a white wagtail;
and Bhṛgu indeed saw a lake and sacred fords in his dream.
Bhṛgu beheld in his dream a pigeon, a parrot, a blue jay, a conch, a hawk, and a cātaka bird; he saw a tiger, a lion, a cow, yellow pigment, turmeric, and an excellent mountain of white grain. (54)
Bhṛgu indeed saw a blazing fire and dūrvā grass in his dream;
he also saw a multitude of temples and a worshipped Śiva-liṅga;
and Bhṛgu indeed saw an honored earthen image of Śiva in his dream.
Bhṛgu saw in his dream various foods made from the flour of barley and wheat, and he ate them again and again; likewise,
he saw women dressed in divine garments and adorned with jeweled ornaments.
The descendant of Bhṛgu committed an act of incest in a dream;
he beheld a dancing courtesan and drank blood and wine. In that dream, the descendant of Bhṛgu had all his limbs smeared with blood. (58–59)
O Nārada, at dawn during his dream, Rāma joyfully ate the flesh of yellow-colored birds and of humans; furthermore,
he saw himself suddenly bound with fetters and wounded by a weapon.
Having seen [the dream], he awoke at dawn and rose while remembering Hari.
Exceedingly delighted by the dream, he performed his morning rites. In his mind, he realized with certainty: "I shall surely conquer the enemy."
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having performed his morning rites and deliberated with them, he...
Bhṛgu dispatched a messenger to the hermitage of Kārtavīrya. That messenger, arriving swiftly while the king was seated in the royal assembly surrounded by his ministers, spoke to the lord of kings.
The messenger of Rāma said:
"In the vicinity of the Narmadā riverbank, at the root of the imperishable banyan tree, that Bhṛgu is together with his brothers; you ought to go there. (3)
"O Great King, wage war against your kinsmen and relatives!
He will make the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
Having spoken thus, the messenger of Rāma returned to the presence of Rāma.
The king, having donned his armor, was prepared to go to battle.
Seeing her lord departing for the conflict,
Manoramā restrained him and caused him to remain in her presence.
O Sage, having seen Manoramā with a serene face and eyes, King Kārtavīryārjuna spoke these heartfelt words to her in the midst of the assembly. (7) Kārtavīryārjuna said:
"O beloved, the great son of Jamadagni is challenging me alone;
he stands on the bank of the Narmadā with his brothers, having obtained from Śaṅkara weapons and mantras, and from Hari armor. (8)
He desires to make the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
My vital breaths tremble and my mind is repeatedly agitated;
my left limb throbs constantly. Listen, my beloved, to the dream I have seen. (9–10)
I saw myself mounted upon a donkey, anointed with oil,
wearing a garland of *auḍha* flowers and red sandalwood paste (11),
dressed in red garments, and adorned with ornaments of iron.
O virtuous lady, you saw him playing and laughing with a heap of extinguished charcoal;
the earth covered in ashes yet adorned with *japā* flowers;
and the sky devoid of the sun and moon, yet filled with the twilight.

I saw a widow with disheveled hair dancing, her nose severed, wearing garments of red cloth, and laughing with a loud, boisterous laugh; she was holding an arrow and standing upon a funeral pyre devoid of fire, covered in ashes. (14)
O Goddess, I beheld a rain of ashes, a rain of blood, and even a rain of fire;
I saw the earth strewn with ripe palm fruits and covered with bones, along with a multitude of skull-bowls accompanied by severed hair and nails. (19–20)
He saw a mountain of salt and heaps of cowrie shells,
as well as caves of powders and oils that were invisible at night;
he also saw invisible flowering trees of Aśoka and Karavīra.
I saw a palm tree laden with fruit, and right there a falling fruit; a full water-jar fell from my own hand and shattered. Thus I beheld the lunar orb as it was descending from the sky.
I saw the solar disc falling from the sky onto the earth;
I saw the fall of meteors, comets, and the eclipses of the moon and sun;
and I saw a man of deformed appearance with a hideous face, naked as the directions themselves.
And as he approached before me, I beheld him, terrifying to behold.
At night, I saw a twelve-year-old girl, adorned with garments and ornaments, departing from my house in a state of great wrath, saying, "I am leaving his home. (21–22)
"O Indra among kings, give me your command; I am going from your house to the forest.
When you spoke thus to me, I saw you at night in my grief.
The brahmin was angry and cursed me, as did my preceptor, the renunciant.
On the wall, he indeed saw painted figures dancing;
and at night, I saw myself constantly tormented by flocks of restless vultures, crows, and buffaloes.
O Īśvarī, I saw those who were being crushed by oil-presses and whirled about by oil-makers; they were naked, with nooses in their hands. All the singers danced and sang songs in my house.
At night, I perceived marriage as the supreme bliss;
[I saw] people making love and even pulling each other's hair.
At night, I witnessed a battle between crows and even dogs.
O beloved, at night I saw large lumps of flesh and a cremation ground filled with corpses; I saw red garments and white garments.
There was a woman dressed in black, black-complexioned, naked, and with her hair disheveled.
And a widow embraced me at night, O beautiful one, though I did not see her.
A barber shaved my head and the rows of my beard, O beloved;
and I saw my chest marked with nail-scratches at night.
O beautiful one, I saw a vast heap of leather thongs for sandals,
and a potter’s wheel spinning on the ground;
and I saw that withered tree rising up, whirling in a whirlwind.
O lady of excellent vows, O noble one, I beheld a headless trunk full of pride during the night; I also saw a garland of skulls being ground to powder by a whirlwind,
and I beheld one with exceedingly terrible teeth.
"During the night, I saw spirits and ghosts with disheveled hair, vomiting fire, who constantly terrified me;
as well as another man who was like one whose life was burnt away, like a scorched tree, and utterly seized by disease. (35)
And at night, I saw even a low-born man who was maimed;
I also saw the sudden collapse of houses, mountains, and trees,
and repeatedly, at night, I saw the falling of thunderbolts.
And at night, everywhere in every house, I constantly beheld the howling of dogs and jackals, repeatedly;
[I saw beings] with their heads downward and feet upward, with disheveled hair and naked as the sky. (38)

I saw a man wandering and moving about upon the ground. O Lord, having heard at dawn the sound of a distorted cry and weeping in the village and other places, I have awakened; tell me now what remedy there is.
Having heard the words of the king, with a heart burning with grief,
she spoke to that lord of kings in a faltering voice while weeping.
Manoramā said:
O Lord, O most excellent lover, O best among all mountains!
O Master of my life, who is dearer to me than life itself, listen to these auspicious words.
The illustrious son of Jamadagni, a portion of Nārāyaṇa, is possessed of great strength.
He is the disciple of the Lord who is the creator and destroyer of the world;
abandon battle with that Rāma, whose vow it is to rid the earth of kings twenty-one times. (43–44)
"Having conquered the wicked Rāvaṇa, you too consider yourself a hero.
But he was not conquered by you, O Lord; he was defeated by his own sin.
For one who does not protect righteousness—who on earth can protect him? (45)
That fool perishes by himself; though living, he is indeed dead.
You, who are a constant witness to the auspicious and inauspicious, the dharma of action, who delight in the self and abide within your own heart—you, a fool, do not perceive this.
O King, whatever sons, wives, and other forms of sovereignty belong to those of virtuous dharma—
all that is impermanent and perishable like bubbles on the water.
Realizing that this worldly existence is like a dream, the wise remain here in Bhārata.
They constantly meditate upon the Dharma and perform austerities with devotion. (49) That knowledge which was given by Datta has all been forgotten by you.
O evil-minded one, if it were so, how could your mind be set upon the injury of a Brahmin? (50)
Having gone hunting for the sake of pleasure, he fasted there in a brahmin’s hermitage;
yet, after eating delicious and unprecedented delicacies, he pointlessly killed a brahmin.
He who brings about the humiliation of his guru, a brahmin, or the gods— (51) —[suffers this fate].
His beloved deity is angry, and calamity is near him.
O Indra among kings, remember the lotus feet of Dattātreya;
devotion to the guru destroys all obstacles for everyone.
Having duly honored the Guru-deva, seek refuge in that Bhṛgu.
When the Brahmin and the God are pleased, there is no harm for Kṣatriyas.
O King, the king is indeed the servant of the Brahmin, and the Vaiśya is the servant of the king.
Śūdras are the servants of all, especially those of the Brāhmaṇa.
For a Kṣatriya, seeking refuge with another Kṣatriya brings constant infamy;
however, seeking refuge with teachers, gods, and the twice-born brings great renown. (59, 96)
"O Indra among kings, honor the Brahmin, who is greater even than the gods.
When the Brahmin is fully satisfied, all the deities are satisfied.
Having spoken thus to the king, the great chaste lady took him upon her lap.
Looking at his face again and again, she lamented and wept.
"Stay for a moment, O Great King," she said once more; "O Great King, take your bath, and I shall feed you what you desire. (58–59)
"O handsome one, I shall apply an unguent mixed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron upon all your limbs.
O Lord, remain for a moment on the lion-throne, and for a moment upon my breast."
In the assembly hall, upon a couch strewn with flowers, I beheld that beautiful one. O King, the husband of virtuous women is indeed superior to a hundred sons in his love;
this has been declared by Lord Hari himself in the Vedas. (61–62)
Having heard the words of Manoratha, the king, who was supremely wise,
enlightened that queen and gave her a reply once more.
Kārttavīryārjuna said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall speak; everything you have said has been heard by me.
Furthermore, the words of those afflicted by grief are not to be praised in assemblies.
Happiness, sorrow, fear, grief, quarrel, and even joy—[all these arise from the mind].
O beautiful one, all karma becomes fit for experience in its own time.
Time bestows kingship; time brings death and rebirth.
Time creates the cycle of existence, and time again withdraws it.
Janārdana, in the form of Time, performs the act of preservation;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Time of time and the Ordainer of the Ordainer.
He is the destroyer of even the Destroyer, the protector of the Protector, and the performer of all actions. (67)
He, who is the very form of action, bestows the fruit of actions through austerity.
When he exists, what living being could be slain by whom, indeed, without [his] action?
As the creator, he creates the creation, and as the destroyer, he destroys it again.
He who protects all beings and whose command they must obey;
by whose command the wind blows constantly, agitated by fear; by whose command death perpetually moves about, and the sun shines incessantly. (69–70)
Indra rains, Agni burns, and Time wanders about like one afraid.
All immobile things stand still, and all mobile things constantly move.
At the proper time, trees become covered in flowers, laden with fruit, and endowed with new shoots.
By His command, things wither away in due time and grow again in due time;
by His command, creation itself appears and disappears. By His command everything comes to be; nothing occurs according to the will of men. (72–73)
"The Lord Jamadagnya, a portion of Nārāyaṇa and possessed of great strength, will rid the earth of kings twenty-one times;
his vow shall never be in vain. (74)
"O lady of virtuous vows, I know for certain that I am to be slain by him.
Having realized all this future, why do I seek refuge?
For those who are established in honor, ill-repute is worse than death. (75–76)
Having spoken thus, the king of kings prepared to go to battle;
he caused musical instruments to be played and had auspicious rites performed.
There were a hundred crores of kings and three lakhs of lordly elephants.
Having taken with him a hundred *akṣauhiṇīs* of great strength and prowess—
consisting of horses, elephants, and likewise foot soldiers,
as well as innumerable chariots— he prepared to depart. (78–79)
Seeing him intent on departure, having donned his armor and holding his inexhaustible bow with an arrow, that virtuous woman became motionless;
she stood for a moment in the pleasure-chamber, placing her beloved against her breast.
Beholding his lotus-like face, she kissed it again and again.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Armoring of Kārtavīryārjuna," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third book of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Manoramā, having placed her lord for a moment upon her breast,
mentally reflected upon everything she had heard from the mouth of her master regarding the future;
she then brought her sons before her, as well as her kinsmen and her own attendants.
She remembered the feet of Hari and thought, "O Sage, may this truly come to pass.
Having pierced the six chakras through yoga and established the vital breath (vāyu) at the crown of her head,
she [focused] upon the thousand-petaled lotus situated in the Brahma-aperture (brahmarandhra).
Having drawn the mind away from sense objects— which are like bubbles on water—
and having established and bound that restless mind through knowledge within the partless Brahman,
one should renounce the two kinds of action, uprooting them so as never to arise again.
In that situation, he gave up his life-breaths, yet nothing was dearer to him than his life-breaths.
Seeing her dead, the king lamented and wept;
casting off his armor and placing her upon his chest, he spoke to her.
The king said:
"O beautiful one, arise! I will not go to the field of battle.
Look at me, you who possess consciousness! Thus he lamented again and again. (7)
"O Manoramā, arise! Go home with me.
O beautiful lady, I shall not engage in battle with Bhṛgu.
"O Manoramā, arise! O lovely one, go to Śrīśaila."
"There, I shall play with you just as before.
Arise, O beloved, let us go to the delightful Godāvarī;
I shall perform water-sports with you just as before."
"O beautiful one, arise in my mind; go to Nandana, O lovely one!
I shall sport in the solitude on the banks of the Puṣpabhadrā river.
O beautiful one, arise in my mind; go to Malaya, O lovely one!"
I shall sport with you there in that sandalwood grove,
which is made fragrant by a cool, scented breeze,
filled with the humming of bees and resounding with the songs of male cuckoos. (12–13)
Apply anointment of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
O smiling one, look upon me with all my limbs smeared with sandalwood paste.
O beloved, compose words that are exceedingly sweet and like nectar.
"And why do you not now put an end to this distortion of your curved eyebrows?
(15) Having heard the king's weeping, an incorporeal voice arose:
"Be steadfast, O Great King; why do you weep? (16)
You are the best among those of great wisdom by the grace of Dattātreya.
Behold this entire world as beautiful as a water bubble.
That virtuous woman, a portion of Kamalā, went to the abode of Kamalā.
"Go yourself to Vaikuṇṭha after fighting on the field of battle.
Having heard these words, the lord of men abandoned his grief;
he then prepared a divine funeral pyre with sandalwood logs.
Having caused the funeral pyre to be prepared, he had her cremated through his son;
with joy, he gave various kinds of jewels to the Brahmins,
as well as various kinds of gifts and diverse garments.
Out of joy, he gave [the wealth] to the brahmins through the merit of Manoramā.
O Sage, the sound "Eat! Eat! Give constantly! Give!
resounded everywhere throughout Kārtavīrya’s hermitage.
Then, whatever wealth was situated in the treasuries and under his own authority,
the king joyfully gave it to the Brahmins through the merit of Manoramā.
The king went to battle with a grieving heart.
Accompanied by hosts of troops and innumerable musical instruments,
the king beheld auspicious sights on every path before him;
nevertheless, he proceeded toward the battle and did not return home again.

One with disheveled hair, one whose nose has been cut off, one weeping and naked, another dressed in black garments, or even a widow; one who is corrupt in speech, corrupt in her womb, afflicted by disease, or a procuress—(these are not to be accepted). 26.
And likewise one who has lost her husband or sons, a *ḍākinī*, or a harlot;
a potter, an oil-presser, a hunter, or one who lives by catching snakes;
one with tattered clothes, one with extremely coarse limbs, one who is naked, or one wearing saffron robes. (27–28)
One who sells fat, as well as one who sells a maiden;
a corpse burnt on a funeral pyre, ashes, and extinguished embers;
a man bitten by a snake, a snake, a monitor lizard, a hare, and poison.
The food prepared for a *śrāddha*, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the ritual grass (*moṭaka*), and likewise sesame seeds;

one who serves as a priest for the gods (*devala*), one whose vehicle is a bull, one who eats the food of a *śūdra*’s *śrāddha*, one who cooks for a *śūdra*, one who performs sacrifices for a *śūdra*, and one who performs sacrifices for an entire village. (30–31)
A doll made of *kuśa* grass, one who performs the cremation of a corpse, an empty jar, a broken jar, oil, salt, and a bone;
cotton, a tortoise, powder, a barking dog—[these are inauspicious omens]. (32)
And on the right, he sees a jackal making a terrifying sound;
[he sees] cowries, a barber’s razor, shorn hair, nails, and filth;
as well as quarreling, lamentation, and people engaged in such acts. (33–34)
One who is inauspicious, one who weeps, one who causes grief;
one who gives false testimony, a thief, and a murderer of men; the husband of an unchaste woman, the son of an unchaste woman, and one who eats the food of an unchaste woman. (35–36)
One who seizes the property or wealth of deities, gurus, or brahmins;
a thief who misappropriates what has been given; a violent person, a slanderer, or a wicked man;
one who is disaffected toward his father and mother; and one who destroys twice-born men or the holy fig tree (aśvattha). || 37 ||
One who destroys the truth, one who is ungrateful, one who seizes what has been deposited, one who betrays a Brahmin friend, one who is thus wounded by treachery, one who violates trust,
one who reviles gurus, gods, and the twice-born, and one who harms his own body— [these are excluded]. (38–39)
One who kills living beings, one who is deficient in limbs, and one who is merciless; one devoid of vows and fasts, one devoid of initiation, and a eunuch;
one with a body afflicted by disease, one who is one-eyed, and one who is deaf. (40)
A Pulkasa, one whose linga has been severed, one intoxicated by liquor, and likewise liquor itself;
one who is reviled, one vomiting blood, a buffalo, and likewise a donkey;
urine, feces, phlegm, a withered person, and a human skull. (41–42)
A fierce wind, a rain of blood, the falling of trees, a wolf, a boar, a vulture, a hawk, a heron, and a bear;
a noose, dry wood, a crow, and likewise sulphur—these are the omens. (43–44)
A Brahmin who accepts gifts, one who subsists on Tantras and mantras,
a physician, red flowers, medicinal herbs, and even chaff;
bad news, news of death, and the terrible curse of a Brahmin.
On the road, the king encountered foul-smelling winds and harsh sounds;
his mind became dejected and his vital breaths were incessantly agitated.
A throbbing in his left limbs and a numbness of the body came upon the king. (46–47)
Nevertheless, the king, free from hesitation, beheld the field of battle;
accompanied by his entire army, he entered the arena of war.
Having quickly descended from his chariot and seeing Bhṛgu before him, [he approached].
Together with the lords of kings, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff out of devotion.
Rāma bestowed upon them the desired blessing, "Go to heaven";
for the blessings of Brahmins are inviolable and must be endured.

Having prostrated before Bhṛgu, the lord of kings, together with other lords of kings, immediately ascended at once his chariot, which was equipped with various weapons. There were also various kinds of musical instruments, such as kettledrums and drums.

He suddenly caused [the music] to be played and gave wealth to the Brahmins. Then Rāma, the best among those who know the Vedas, spoke words that were beneficial, truthful, and the essence of political ethics to the king of kings in the assembly of the lords of kings.
Paraśurāma said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, most righteous one born of the lunar dynasty;
you are the disciple of the wise Dattātreya, who is a portion of Viṣṇu. 54.
Having been learned yourself and having heard the Vedas from the mouths of those who know the Vedas,
how can you, being of evil intellect, now commit violence against the virtuous?
How could you, out of greed, previously strike down a Brahmin who was free from worldly desire?
The Brahmin woman, tormented by grief, went along with her husband.
"O King, what will become of you in the next world from the killing of these two?
This entire cycle of existence is utterly false, like water on a lotus leaf. (56–57)
Now, both good reputation and ill repute remain as nothing more than mere stories.
Alas, for the virtuous, what is more than a mockery than this ill repute?
Where has Kapila gone? Where are you? Where is the dispute? And where is the sage? (58)
That which was performed by the wise king was not performed by a plowman.
Indeed, seeing you, the Lord, observing a fast, his virtuous father caused him to break the fast;
the fruit of that act has been bestowed upon him by you.
The Veda was studied according to rule and given day after day to the Brahmins;
the world is filled with fame—how then could there be infamy in old age?
He was a supreme giver, most righteous, illustrious, meritorious, and wise.
"Equal to Kārtavīryārjuna has never existed, nor will there ever be," so say the bards upon the surface of the earth. Such is the ill-fame of him who was celebrated in the Purāṇas. (62–63)
O King, harsh speech is more unbearable to living beings than even a sharp weapon;
yet, even in the midst of crisis, no double-tongued speech has ever issued from the mouths of the virtuous.
I shall not grant you this duplicity; I shall speak only what is relevant.
"Give me an answer, O Indra among kings, in this assembly of the lords of men.
There are those born of the lineages of the Sun, the Moon, and Manu present in this hall.
Speak the truth in the assembly, and let the ancestors and the gods listen. (65–66)
"Let all the lords of kings, who are capable of speaking both truth and falsehood, listen!
For the virtuous, seeing with impartiality, do not speak with partiality.
Having said this, the son of Renuka ceased speaking on the field of battle.
The king, equal to Bṛhaspati, began to speak.
Kārtavīryārjuna said:
"Listen, O Rāma, you who are a portion of Hari, a devotee of Hari, and one who has conquered his senses."
From whose mouths you have heard the Dharma, you are the teacher of even those teachers.
Or, one who performs the contemplation of Brahman through action—even with an impure intellect—but remains devoted to his own duty and is pure, is therefore called a Brāhmaṇa. (69–70)
Perform your actions constantly through mental reflection both internally and externally.
He who always speaks at the proper time while remaining silent [otherwise] is indeed called a sage (muni).
Whether toward gold or a clod of earth, in a house or a forest, or toward very fragrant sandalwood or mud—[remain the same].
He who practices the meditation on equality is proclaimed a yogin.
He who contemplates Viṣṇu in all living beings with a mind of equanimity,
and who offers devotion to Hari— he is remembered as a true devotee of Hari.

For Brahmins, asceticism is their wealth; asceticism is like a wish-fulfilling tree, ascetic practice is like a cow of plenty, and there is a constant longing for asceticism. Likewise, sovereignty is for Kshatriyas, and trade for Vaishyas.
A Kṣatriya’s excessive desire for asceticism is highly censured;
a Brāhmaṇa’s excessive desire for debate is likewise severely condemned. One who is passionate performs actions characteristic of the *rājasa* nature out of passion.
One who is blinded by passion and characterized by the quality of *rajas* is proclaimed a "king" (*rājan*).
O Sage, it was out of passion that I indeed requested the wish-fulfilling cow;
what fault has arisen for me, a passionate Kṣatriya? (77–78)
Whence, and for which sage, could there be a wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) without you?
There is no longing for battle or for enjoyment, yet there is transgression against you all—
[namely] this army of thirty akṣauhiṇīs belonging to the lords of kings, numbering three crores.
"O Sage, it was not right for you to kill me as I approached alone.
Even when one who has mastered the Vedāṅgas comes to kill you, there is no fault in killing him; I did not become a slayer of a Brahmin by that act. (80–81)
"Indeed, no expiation has been prescribed in the Vedas for those who commit violence;
their execution is the appropriate penalty," so said the Lotus-born One.
By your father, those kings of great strength and prowess were slain.
Now these princes and children have gathered here.
Fulfill that vow which was made by you: "I shall make the entire earth devoid of kings twenty-one times. (83–84)
War is the duty of Kṣatriyas; death in battle is not censured.
For Brāhmaṇas, "svāhā" [is the call] in battle—this is a mockery in the world and in the Veda.
In every age, the strength of Brāhmaṇas whose wealth is austerity lies in their speech.
Peace and rites for prosperity are the duty of Brahmins, not the practice of war;
battle is the strength of Kṣatriyas, while trade is the strength of Vaiśyas; begging is the strength of mendicants, and service to Brahmins is the strength of Śūdras. (86–87)
Devotion is the strength of Hari; service to Hari is the strength of Vaiṣṇavas; and Hari himself is their strength.
Violence is the strength of the wicked, while austerity is the strength of ascetics.
Dress is the strength of courtesans, and youth is the strength of women. (88)
For kings, strength is majesty; for children, weeping is strength.

For the virtuous, truth is strength; for the wicked, falsehood is always their strength. For followers, following [their leader] is strength; and for those with little, accumulation is strength. (89–90)
Knowledge is the strength of the learned; fortitude is the strength of the bold.
Wealth is the strength of the wealthy, and especially so for those who are pure.
Discernment is the strength of the tranquil; unity is the strength of the virtuous. (91–92)

Virtue is the strength of the virtuous, and theft is the strength of thieves; sweet speech is the strength of the deceitful, and unrighteousness is the strength of harlots. Violence is the strength of predatory beasts, and service to her husband is the strength of chaste women. (93)
For the gods, [the power is] granting boons and curses; for disciples, service to the teacher;
for householders, dharma; for servants, service to the king;
for those who offer praise, hymns of praise; and for celibate students, the Veda. (94–95)
Good conduct is the strength of ascetics, and renunciation is the strength of those who have taken up the life of a *saṃnyāsin*.
Sin is the strength of evildoers, and Hari is the strength of the weak.
Merit is the strength of the virtuous, and the king is the strength of his subjects. (96)
The fruit is the strength of trees, and water is the strength of aquatic creatures;
water is the strength of crops, and water is the strength of fish.
Peace is the strength of kings, and especially the strength of Brahmins.
"A peaceful Brahmin engaged in the exertion of battle has never been seen nor heard of.
While the divine Nārāyaṇa stands present, how could there be any other reversal?
Having spoken thus, the lord of kings ceased speaking on the field of battle.
Having heard those words of his, he immediately became silent.
Then all of Rāma’s brothers, those great heroes with sharp weapons and swords in hand, began to engage in battle at his command.
Seeing them intent on battle, the mighty King of Matsya,
Maṅgala— the abode of auspiciousness— began to engage in the fight.
That lord of kings warded them off as well with a net of arrows.
Then the sons of Jamadagni cut through the net of arrows.
O Sage, the king discharged a divine weapon possessing the brilliance of a hundred suns; but the sages effortlessly severed it as well with the Māheśvara weapon.
With a divine weapon, the sages severed the bow along with the arrow,
as well as the king’s chariot, his charioteer, and even his armor.
Seeing the king with his weapons laid down, the sages were overwhelmed with joy.
He took up the trident of the wielder of the trident with the intent to slay the king of the fish.
At the moment the trident was being hurled, an incorporeal voice arose:
"O best of Brahmins, cast aside the trident; for the trident of Śiva is indeed never in vain."
In former times, the divine armor of Śiva was given by Durvāsas;
it resides upon the neck of Matsyarāja and protects all his limbs. [108] O King, request this armor, which bestows life itself.
Then the king struck at the discarded spear for a long time;
O Sage, having reached the king, that spear shattered into a hundred pieces.
Upon hearing a voice from the sky, Śṛṅgin assumed the garb of a renunciant.
The great son of Jamadagni requested armor from the king;
and the king gave him the supreme armor that grants victory over the entire universe.
Having taken that armor, he struck [his enemy] with a trident alone.
And the king of the Matsyas fell, he whose face was like a hundred moons,
who was exceedingly powerful, virtuous, and born of the Lunar dynasty.
Nārada said:
"Tell me the armor of Śiva which was worn by Matsyarāja.
O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O best of Brahmins, hear the armor of the high-souled Śaṅkara,
named Brahmāṇḍavijaya, which protects all limbs.
In ancient times, it was bestowed by Durvāsas upon the wise King Matsya.

Having bestowed the six-syllable mantra which destroys all sins, (115) and while the armor-mantra remains upon the body, there is no death for living beings. Whether against missiles, weapons, water, or fire, success is certain; of this there is no doubt. (116)
By wearing and reciting which Bāṇa effortlessly attained the state of Śiva;
by wearing which Nandikeśvara became equal to Śiva;
and from the retention of which Vīrabhadra, the best of heroes, and Sāmba became [so]. (117)
King Hiraṇyakaśipu himself was a conqueror of the three worlds;
and Hiraṇyākṣa became victorious because he indeed held [this mantra].
For by holding and reciting it, Durvāsas attained perfection and was honored by the entire universe.

The great yogi Jaigīṣavya [attained his state] through the recitation and the practice of dhāraṇā; and by retaining this [knowledge], Vāmadeva, Devala, Pavana himself, Agastya, and Pulastya likewise became honored by the entire world. (120)
"Oṃ namaḥ śivāya"—may this always protect my head.
"Oṃ namaḥ śivāya svāhā"—may this always protect my forehead.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ śivāya svāhā"—may this always protect my eyes.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ, salutation to Śiva; may he protect my nose.
(122) Oṃ namaḥ śivāya śāntāya svāhā; may he always protect the throat. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ, salutation to the performer of dissolution, svāhā; may he always protect the ears. (123)

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ pañcavaktrāya svāhā—may this always protect my teeth. Oṃ hrīṃ maheśāya svāhā—may this always protect my lower lip. (124) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ trinetrāya svāhā—may this always protect my hair.
Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ, svāhā to Mahādeva; may this always protect the chest.
(125) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ, svāhā to Rudra; may this always protect the navel.
Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Īśvara; may this always protect the back. (126)
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ mṛtyuñjayāya svāhā—may this always protect the eyebrows and the arms. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīm īśānāya svāhā—may this always protect the sides.
Oṃ hrīm īśvarāya svāhā—may this always protect my belly.

Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Mṛtyuñjaya; may this protect my arms forever. (128) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīm, svāhā to Īśvara; may this protect my hands. Oṃ, svāhā to Maheśvara Rudra; may this always protect my hips. (129)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Bhūtanātha; may he always protect my feet. Oṃ, svāhā to Sarveśvara, the All-pervading; may he always protect my feet.
(130) May Bhūteśa protect me in the east, and may Śaṅkara protect me in the southeast.
May Rudra protect me in the south, and Sthāṇu in the southwest;
may Khaṇḍaparaśu protect me in the west, and Candraśekhara in the northwest;
may Giriśa protect me in the north, and Īśvara himself in the northeast. (131–132)
May Mṛḍa always protect me from above, and may Mṛtyuñjaya himself protect me from below;
in water, on land, and in the atmosphere, in sleep and in waking, may he ever protect me.
May Pinākin, who is affectionate toward all and kind to his devotees, protect me, his devotee, with love. (133)
Thus, O child, this most wonderful armor has been told to you.
By reciting it one million times, success will certainly be attained.
If one becomes a master of this armor, one will surely become equal to Rudra.
Out of affection for you, I have disclosed this which must not be told to anyone.
This armor, declared in the Kaṇva recension, is highly secret and very difficult to obtain.
It is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices.
All [other means] are not worth even a sixteenth part of this armor.
By the grace of this armor, a person shall become liberated while living;
he will certainly become omniscient, a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis), and one who travels at the speed of thought.
He who worships the Lord Śaṅkara without knowing this armor (kavaca),
even if he recites the mantra a hundred lakhs of times, it will not grant success.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Armor of Śaṅkara," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third book of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
When the king of the fish had fallen, the king, skilled in warfare, dispatched lords of kings who were experts in weaponry to the battle. 1.
Bṛhadbala, Somadatta, Vidarbha, the lord of Mithilā,
the sovereign of Niṣadha, and likewise the sovereign of Magadha—
these great car-warriors arrived at the battle to fight against the son of Jamadagni.
O Nārada, together with armies consisting of three akṣauhiṇīs,
all the heroic brothers of Rāma, with sharp weapons in their hands,
warded them off with their own missiles at the forefront of the battle.
Those heroes, with great effort, warded off each of the groups of Bhṛgu’s sons individually with a web of arrows and divine weapons. Seeing them defeated, he quickly advanced in the battle.
With the Pināka bow in hand, that Bhṛgu-like Jamadagnya of great strength, resembling a blazing crest of fire, hurled a serpent-noose. The mighty Somadatta cut it asunder with a Gāruḍa weapon.
Bhṛgu struck Somadatta with the trident of Śaṅkara;
he struck Bṛhadbala with a mace, Vidarbha likewise with his fists,
Maithila with a mallet, and the king of Niṣadha with a spear.
Having struck down all the Māgadha kings with his foot-strikes and slain the soldiers with a web of missiles in battle— like the fire of universal destruction—
the mighty son of Jamadagni pursued Kārtavīrya.
Seeing him approaching to fight, the kings and great chariot-warriors came forward to engage in battle, having warded off Kārtavīrya;
likewise, there were hundreds from Kānyakubja and hundreds from Saurāṣṭra.

There were hundreds of royal leaders and likewise hundreds of lords of heroes; hundreds of gentle men from Vanga, ten from Maharashtra, as well as those of the Gurjara race and hundreds of Kalingas. (12–13)
Having created a web of arrows, Bhṛgu cut it down at that very moment.
Having severed it, Rāma rose up like the sun emerging from the mist.
For three nights, Rāma fought with them upon the field of battle.
In that manner, he cut through an army of twelve akṣauhiṇīs with his axe,
as easily as one might sever a cluster of plantain trunks with a sword.
Having thus destroyed the army, he slaughtered the host of kings with the trident of Śiva.
Seeing all of them slain, Sucandra, born of the Solar dynasty,
arrived accompanied by a hundred thousand lords of kings and with twelve akṣauhiṇīs of troops for the battle. (17)

In the battle, he fought Rāma with fury, like one lion against another. Having slain a hundred thousand kings with the trident of Śaṅkara, the powerful Bhṛgu then destroyed twelve akṣauhiṇīs of troops with his battle-axe.
Having destroyed all the armies, the powerful one fought with Sucandra.
Bhṛgu himself discharged the serpent-missile (*nāgāstra*) at him,
but the lord of men cut that serpent-noose (*nāgapāśa*) apart with the *gāruḍa* weapon.
The king laughed at Bhṛgu again and again in the battle;
and Bhṛgu, at the forefront of the fray, hurled the Nārāyaṇa weapon,
which possessed a radiance equal to a hundred suns, in order to slay him.

Seeing that weapon, O tiger among kings, he immediately descended from his chariot; having laid down his arms, he prostrated himself and praised Nārāyaṇa Śiva. Abandoning him as he lay thus bowed, [the weapon] went to the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord Rāma, the king of archers, was struck with amazement.
Then Bhr̥gu, desiring to slay him, furiously hurled a spear, a mace, a lance, a sharp-edged spear, as well as a club and an axe. (24–25)
Seated upon the chariot of Sucandra, Kālī seized them all;
he hurled the trident of Śiva, and it became a garland for the king.
Rāma beheld Bhadrakālī, the mother of the world, before him.
Carrying a garland of severed heads, with a hideous and terrifying face,
Bhṛgu then cast aside his weapons, missiles, and the Pināka bow, and,
with his neck bowed low in devotion, offered praise to that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā).
Paraśurāma said:
Salutations to the beloved of Śaṅkara; salutations again and again to you, the essence. Salutations to the destroyer of misfortune; salutations again and again to you, Māyā. (29)
Salutations, salutations to the Mother of the World, the Creator of the World; salutations, salutations.
Salutations be to You, the Mother of the World, the Cause; salutations, salutations.
Be gracious, O Mother of the worlds, O You who perform the creation and destruction [of the universe].
I go for refuge to your two feet; make my vow fruitful.
And when I am turned away from you, who is capable of protecting me?
Be gracious, O auspicious one, toward me, your devotee, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees.
"O fair-faced one, you ought to make fruitful that boon which was granted to me by you all in the world of Śiva in the past. Having heard this praise of Reṇukā, Ambikā became pleased.
Having said, "Do not fear," he vanished right there. Whoever recites this hymn composed by Bhṛgu with devotion shall indeed be delivered from great danger as if by sport.
He shall be honored throughout the three worlds and victorious right there;
he shall become the foremost among the wise and a crusher of the ranks of his enemies. In the meantime, Brahmā [addressed] Bhṛgu, the best among the upholders of dharma.
Having arrived, he spoke the secret to Rāma alone.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, O highly fortunate Rāma, to this secret which has existed from the very beginning."
The cause of Sucandra’s victory and the very fruit of his vow—
the great ten-syllable vidyā— was formerly bestowed upon Sucandra by Durvāsas, as well as the armor of Bhadrakālī, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (38–39)
The armor of Bhadrakālī is extremely difficult even for the gods to obtain.
He upon whose neck this armor rests is the crusher of all enemies;
it is highly venerable, auspicious, and the cause of victory over the three worlds.
While that armor remains, who on earth is capable of conquering you?
Let Bhṛgu go for the sake of alms and make a request to the king;
he is a king born of the Solar dynasty, a donor, and supremely righteous. (41–42)
"He will certainly bestow his life-breaths, his armor, and all his mantras.
O Sage, Bhṛgu, having gone into the presence of the king in the guise of a renunciant,
requested alms and [bestowed] the mantra and the most wonderful armor.
And the king gave him that mantra and armor with the utmost reverence.
Then Bhṛgu struck the king with the trident of Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Bhṛgu and Kārtavīrya," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. (36)
Nārada said:
O Lord, O omniscient one, I now desire to hear from you the armor-mantra (kavaca) and that ten-syllabled vidyā of Bhadrakālī. (1)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare the ten-syllabled Great Vidyā (Mahāvidyā), as well as the armor (kavaca) which must be kept secret and is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. 2.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ kālikāyai svāhā"—this is the ten-syllable mantra.
Indeed, Durvāsas gave it to the king at Puṣkara during a solar eclipse.
In ancient times, the perfection of this mantra was achieved through ten lakh recitations alone.

By reciting this supreme armor (*kavaca*) five hundred thousand times, he became one whose armor was perfected; he returned to Ayodhyā and, through the power of that armor, conquered the entire earth. (4–5)
Nārada said:
I have heard the ten-syllable lore (vidyā), which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. Now I wish to hear the armor (kavaca); O Lord, tell it to me. (6)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O best of brahmins, I shall declare the most wonderful armor (kavaca), which was formerly given out of compassion by Nārāyaṇa to the wielder of the trident (Śiva). (7)
O Sage, in the past, during the terrible slaughter of Tripura and for the sake of Śiva’s victory,
that very [weapon] was given by the wielder of the trident to Durvāsas;
and it was given by Durvāsas to the high-souled Sucandra.
The most secret reality, the embodiment of the entire multitude of mantras:
OṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ KLĪṂ KĀLIKĀYAI SVĀHĀ—may this protect my head.
KLĪṂ—may it always protect the skull; HRĪṂ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ—may these protect the eyes. (10)
Oṃ hrīṃ trilocane svāhā! May she always protect my nose. Klīṃ kālike rakṣa rakṣa svāhā! May she always protect my teeth.
Klīṃ bhadrakālike svāhā! May she protect the pair of my lips.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Kālikā; may this always protect my throat. (12) Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Kālikā; may this always protect the pair of ears.
Oṃ krīṃ krīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Kālī; may this always protect my shoulders. (13)
Oṃ krīṃ, svāhā to Bhadrakālī; may she always protect my chest.
Oṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Kālikā; may she always protect my navel. (14) Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Kālikā; may she always protect my back.
*Oṃ raktabījavināśinyai svāhā!* May [this mantra] always protect my hands. (15) *Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ muṇḍamālinyai svāhā!* May it always protect my feet.
*Oṃ hrīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai svāhā!* May it always protect all my limbs. (16)
May Mahākālī protect me in the east, and Raktadantikā in the southeast;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect me in the south, and Kālikā in the southwest;
may Śyāmā protect me in the west, and Caṇḍikā in the northwest. (17)
May Vikaṭāsyā protect [me] in the north, and Sāṭṭahāsinī in the northeast.
May Lolajihvā protect me above, and may she who is primordial Māyā always protect me below.
May Viśvaprasū always protect me in water, on land, and in the atmosphere.
Thus, O child, I have told you this which embodies the entire multitude of mantras;
it is the essence of all armor-mantras (kavacas), higher than the highest.
By its power, King Sucandra became the lord of the seven continents.

By the power of this armor, Māndhātṛ became the lord of the earth; likewise Pracetas and Lomaśa attained perfection. For it was by its power that Saubhari and Pippalāyana became the foremost among yogins.
If one should possess this perfected armor, he would become the lord of all accomplishments.
All great gifts, ascetic penances, and likewise vows—certainly, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of this armor. (23)

If one worships Kālī, the mother of the universe, without knowing this armor (kavaca), the mantra will not grant success even if recited a hundred lakhs of times. (24) Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Armor of Bhadrakālī," in the Dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa within the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa. (37)
Nārāyaṇa said: O Brahmin, when Sucandra— the crest-jewel of the lords of kings— had fallen,
Puṣkarākṣa set forth accompanied by an army of three akṣauhiṇīs.
The great King born of the Solar dynasty, the son of Sucandra, was a servant of Mahālakṣmī; he was prosperous and resplendent like the sun. The enchanting armor of Mahālakṣmī hung around his neck.
Then, endowed with supreme sovereignty and victorious over the three worlds,
all the brothers of the wise son of Reṇuka,
holding various weapons and missiles in their hands, saw him and came forward to engage in battle.
The king of kings likewise cut them down with a net of arrows; and those heroes effortlessly cut through that net of arrows as well. Those heroes then shattered the king's chariot with five arrows.

They struck the charioteer with five arrows and the horses of the chariot with ten. O brahmins, they swiftly cut that bow with seven arrows and [the remaining] five arrows, while the host of his brothers [were struck] by Śaṅkara’s trident.
And those heroes effortlessly destroyed an army of three akṣauhiṇīs;
then, in order to slay the king of men, they hurled Śiva’s trident.
That trident became like a garland of lotuses around the neck of the king. (8)
The brahmins, their fires blazing with rage, hurled spears, iron clubs, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, mallets, and maces;
yet those weapons were reduced to powder upon contact with the body of the mountain.
All the brothers were struck with wonder at the great sage Bhṛgu. Then Kārtavīryārjuna himself dispatched his chariot, bow, weapons, various missiles, and his entire army.
O Sage, the mighty lotus-eyed king, having mounted his chariot, unleashed a most terrible net of arrows. Those heroes, with weapons and missiles in their hands, cut through that net of arrows.

The king indeed put them all to sleep with a soporific spell. Seeing his brothers asleep with their entire bodies mangled by wounds, the mighty son of Jamadagni awakened them in accordance with reality.
Having awakened them and turned them back, he went to the front of the battle.
In his anger, desiring to slay the king, he swiftly hurled a battle-axe.
Having severed the king's crown, the axe indeed fell to the ground.
Then the mighty son of Jamadagni quickly seized his axe;
at that moment, he hurled Śaṅkara’s trident with the accompaniment of mantras.
Having severed the king’s earring, it returned to the presence of Śiva.
The king indeed discharged a web of arrows to slay that Rāma;
and the son of Reṇukā effortlessly cut through that web of arrows.
In due order, the king hurled various weapons accompanied by mantras.

Bhṛgu, the best among wielders of weapons, cut that [missile] down in due order. Bhṛgu discharged various missiles after performing great aimings; the great king, however, cut them down with ease, by means of his own aimings alone. (19–20)

Rāma aimed and discharged the Brahmāstra with its accompanying mantra; the King, however, extinguished it effortlessly by means of his own aim alone. Rāma [discharged] all missiles and weapons, with the exception of the Pāśupata.
Agitated by anger, the king hurled [the weapons], and Rāma cut them down;
O Sage, Rāma then praised Śiva, bowed to him, and took up the Pāśupata weapon.
And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a brahmin, spoke: (22–23).
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O child Bhṛgu, what are you doing? You are the best among the wise;
why do you cast the Pāśupata weapon out of anger and delusion to kill a human being? (24)
By the Pāśupata [weapon] alone, the entire universe would quickly be reduced to ashes.
This weapon is the destroyer of all, save for the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Alas, even the Sudarśana is not at all capable of conquering the Pāśupata!
And Hari’s Sudarśana, which crushes all other weapons;
the Pāśupata of Khaṭvāṅgin, and the Sudarśana of Hari himself—these are the foremost of all weapons in the three worlds. (26–27)
"O Brahmin, abandon the Pāśupata [vow]; listen to my words so that you may conquer the mighty King Puṣkarākṣa, and so that you may now defeat Kārtavīrya, who is otherwise invincible. (28)
Listen attentively; I shall tell you all of that.
This armor (*kavaca*) of Mahālakṣmī is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
It was worn around the neck with devotion by Puṣkarākṣa according to the prescribed ritual.
Furthermore, the most wonderful armor of Durgatināśinī was worn upon the right arm by the son of Puṣkarākṣa;
by the power of that armor, those two were capable of conquering the entire universe.
"O Sage, while those two—the Conqueror of the three worlds and the armor—are present within my body, I shall go for alms;
I will perform that begging so that your vow may bear fruit. (32–33)
Having heard the words of the brahmin, Paraśurāma, his mind filled with trepidation and his heart tormented, spoke to the aged brahmin. (34) Paraśurāma said:
"I do not know, O one of great wisdom, who you are wearing the form of a brahmin. Speak quickly to me, for I am ignorant; then go to the presence of the king.
Having heard these words of the son of Jamadagni, the brahmin himself laughed.
Having said, "I am Viṣṇu," the Lord departed to beg for alms.
Having approached them, he requested the two armor-plates from them;
and by means of Viṣṇu’s illusory power (māyā), they both gave the armor-plates to Viṣṇu.
Having taken the armor, Viṣṇu departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Nārada said:
O great sage, by whom was the armor of Mahālakṣmī given?
I have a great curiosity to hear about the armor of Durgā belonging to King Puṣkarākṣa and his son;
you should tell me by whom that which is so difficult to obtain was given. (38–39)
And what is the nature of their armor, or what is its fruit?
What are the two mantras like? Tell me that, O Teacher of the World.
(40) Nārāyaṇa said:
Sanatkumāra bestowed upon the wise Puṣkarākṣa the armor (kavaca) of Mahālakṣmī, as well as her ten-syllable mantra (daśākṣara-mantra),
her secret hymn of praise, and her life-story. 41.
The meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda and the captivating worship were also given;
furthermore, the armor (kavaca) of Durgā was bestowed by Durvāsas in the past,
as well as the secret hymn of praise and the ten-syllable mantra.
Later you shall hear all that most wonderful account of the Goddess, and how [the mantra] was granted at her request during the commencement of the great battle.
Listen also to the mantra of Mahālakṣmī; I shall tell it to you.
"Oṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in the lotus"—this is most wonderful.
O Sage, hear now the meditation as declared in the Sāmaveda and the procedure for worship, which was imparted by Kumāra to the wise Puṣkarākṣa. (45–46)
Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, the virtuous beloved of Padmanābha,
whose abode is the lotus, whose face is like a lotus, whose eyes resemble lotus petals,
who is fond of lotus flowers, and who reclines upon a bed of lotus blossoms.
I joyfully worship her who smiles, who holds a lotus in her hand like a lotus-pond, who is adorned with a garland of lotuses,
who is richly decorated with lotus ornaments, who increases the splendor of the lotus,
and who gazes upon a forest of lotuses. (48–49)
One should worship with a lotus flower upon an eight-petaled lotus made of sandalwood.
Having fully worshipped Gaṇa and offered the sixteen types of service (upacāra),
the practitioner should then offer praise and bow down with devotion.

"O Brahmin, listen to the armor; I shall tell you the essence of all things. Listen, O chief of sages, to the supreme and auspicious armor of Padmā, which was given by Padmanābha to Brahmā within the lotus of his navel."
Having obtained the armor, Brahmā created the universe within that lotus;
by the grace of Padmālayā, he became endowed with Lakṣmī. Having received the boon from Padmālayā, Pādma became the lord of the worlds.
O Nārada, on the Padmakalpa, the most wonderful armor was given by Pādyaka to the wise Sanatkumāra, his beloved son;
and that which had been given by Kumāra to Puṣkara [was likewise bestowed]. || 54–55 ||
By retaining and reciting which, the great Brahmā became the lord of all siddhis,
endowed with supreme sovereignty and possessed of all prosperity;
and by giving which, Kubera became the lord of wealth and the master of riches.
O Sage, because of its recitation and retention, the glorious Svāyambhuva Manu [attained his state]; because of it, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda became possessed of fortune;
and because of its retention, Pṛthu immediately became the lord of the earth.
By the grace of this armor, Dakṣa himself became the lord of progeny;
and by its grace, Dharma became the witness of actions and their protector.
Wearing it upon his right arm, Viṣṇu reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
And Śeṣa, who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, wears it around his neck out of devotion.
By wearing it, Kaśyapa, the lord of progeny, obtained Vāmana;
and from its wearing, the glorious Mahendra became the sovereign of all the gods. (60–61)

King Marutta became blessed because of his practice of *dhāraṇā*; the illustrious Nahuṣa, the sovereign of the three worlds, [attained that state] through the practice of *dhāraṇā* upon which he meditated.
Khaṭvāṅga conquered the entire universe by reciting and practicing *dhāraṇā*.
Since the illustrious Mucukunda, the great son of Māndhātṛ,
was the progenitor of this armor which is the seat of all prosperity;
and since the seer is Bṛhatī and the meter is the goddess Padmālayā herself.
The application [of this mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
it is the great seed of merit and the most wonderful armor of the great ones.
Oṃ hrīṃ, may [the mantra] "svāhā to her who dwells in the lotus" protect my head.
Śrīṃ may protect my skull, and Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī, [protect] my two eyes.
(66) Oṃ Śrīṃ, svāhā to Śrī—may this always protect my pair of ears.
Oṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ, svāhā to Mahālakṣmī—may this protect my nose. (67)
Oṃ śrīṃ, may Padmālayā always protect my teeth; svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ, may Kṛṣṇapriyā always protect the cavities of my teeth. Oṃ śrīṃ, may Nārāyaṇeśā always protect my throat.
Oṃ śrīṃ! May she who is beloved by Keśava always protect my shoulders. Oṃ śrīṃ! Svāhā! May she who dwells in the lotus always protect my navel.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! May the Mother of the World always protect my chest. 69–70.
Oṃ śrīṃ moṃ, svāhā to Kṛṣṇakāntā; may she always protect my back.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Śrī; may she always protect my hands.
Oṃ, svāhā to Śrīnivāsakāntā; may she always protect my feet. (71)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Śrī; may she always protect all my limbs.
(72) May Mahālakṣmī protect me in the east, and Kamalālayā in the southeast.
May Padmā protect me in the south, and Śrī, the beloved of Hari, in the southwest. (73)
May Padmālayā protect me in the west; may she herself protect me in the northwest. May Kamalā protect me in the north, and Sindhukanyakā in the northeast.
May Nārāyaṇī protect me above, and may Viṣṇupriyā protect me below. (74)
May she, who is dearer to Viṣṇu than his own life-breath, protect me constantly and from all sides.
(79) Thus, O child, I have narrated to you this most wonderful armor (*kavaca*), which embodies the multitude of all mantras and bestows all sovereign powers. (76)

The righteous person who, having duly honored his guru, wears this armor obtains a fruit even greater than that which one gains by giving a golden mountain equal to Mount Meru to a twice-born brahmin. (77)
Whether on his neck or on his right arm, that illustrious one shall possess fortune in every birth;
Lakṣmī shall abide unshakably in his house for a hundred generations. He shall certainly become invulnerable to the lords of the gods and the lords of the asuras. (78–79)

He who wears this armor around his neck is possessed of all merit, is wise, and is as if initiated into all sacrifices; he has bathed in all sacred fords. This must not be given to anyone whatsoever, even out of greed, delusion, or fear.
One should reveal this to a disciple who is devoted to the guru and seeks refuge.
Without knowing this armor (*kavaca*), if one recites [the mantra] for Lakṣmī or the Lord of the World—even if recited ten million times—the mantra will not grant success. (81–82)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrī Lakṣmī Kavaca," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārada said:
O Brāhmaṇa, you have narrated the enchanting armor (kavaca) of Padmā.
O Lord, please tell me the supreme armor of Durgatināśinī—
[that armor] which is equal to the life-force of a lotus-seed, which is the cause of vitality and strength,
which is the essence of all armors, and which is the means for serving Durgā. (1–2)
Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall recite the auspicious hymn of Durgā, which was formerly bestowed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself upon Brahmā in Goloka. 3.
In ancient times, Brahmā gave [this mantra] to Śaṅkara during the battle with Tripura;
Rudra, having received it with devotion, destroyed Tripura.
Hara gave it to Gautama, and Gautama gave it to Padmākṣa.
From which Padmākṣa arose, the victorious lord of the seven continents;
by holding and reciting which Brahmā became possessed of knowledge and power on earth,
and Śiva became omniscient and the teacher of yogins.
And Gautama, the best of sages, became equal to Śiva.
For this armor (*kavaca*) of the conquest of the universe, Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*),
and the goddess Durgatināśinī is the *gāyatrī* meter.
Its application is proclaimed for victory over the universe.
It is a sacred pilgrimage site for the great ones, a most wonderful armor.
Om Hrīṃ, may [the mantra] "Svāhā to the destroyer of misfortune" protect my head.
Oṃ Hrīṃ! May [the goddess] protect my skull; and Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! May she protect my two eyes.
(9) May she protect the pair of my ears; and always, Oṃ Durgāyai Namaḥ!
And may Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ protect my nose from all sides at all times. (10)
May *hrīṃ śrīṃ krūṃ* protect the teeth, and may *klīṃ* protect the pair of lips.
May *klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ* protect the throat, and may *durge* protect the two cheeks.
O Mahākālī, may *durge svāhā* protect the shoulders continuously.

May the breast [of the goddess] protect me on all sides—svāhā! To her who destroys calamities, svāhā! O Durgā, O Durgā, protect my two flanks; svāhā! May she always protect my navel. O Durgā, O Durgā, grant me protection; may she protect my back on all sides—svāhā! (12–13)
Oṃ hrīṃ durgāyai svāhā—may she always protect my hands and feet.
Oṃ hrīṃ durgāyai svāhā—may she always protect all my limbs.
(14) May Mahāmāyā protect me in the east, and may Kālikā protect me in the southeast.
May Dakṣakanyā protect [me] in the south, and Śivasundarī in the southwest (nairṛtya).
May Pārvatī protect [me] in the west, and Vārāhī always in the northwest (vāruṇa). May Kuberamātā protect [me] in the north (kauberya), and Īśvarī always in the northeast (aiśānya). (15–16)
May Nārāyaṇī protect [me] above, and may Ambikā always protect me below;
may Jñānapradā protect my knowledge, and may Nidrā always protect me in sleep. (17) Thus, O child, has been told to you that which embodies the entire multitude of mantras.
This most wonderful armor named Brahmāṇḍavijaya—
by it, a man obtains that fruit which is gained by bathing in all sacred fords, performing all sacrifices, and observing all vows and fasts. (18–19)
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste,
whoever wears this armor upon his neck or right arm shall be a conqueror of the three worlds and a crusher of all enemies. (20)
Without knowing this armor (*kavaca*), one might worship the Goddess who destroys misfortune;
yet even if the mantra is recited a hundred lakhs of times, it will not bestow success.
O Nārada, the armor as declared in the Kāṇva Śākhā has been described as the giver of success.
It must not be given to anyone whatsoever; it is to be guarded as something very difficult to obtain.

(23) Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Armor of Durgatināśinī," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having seized him and Viṣṇu having then departed for Vaikuṇṭha,
the descendant of Bhṛgu struck the thousand-eyed Indra along with his son,
after having fought diligently for seven days with the Brahmāstra.
Even though he was deprived of his armor, the king fell down along with his son.
When the Thousand-Eyed One had fallen, the great hero Kārtavīryārjuna himself arrived, accompanied by two hundred thousand akṣauhiṇīs. 3.
Having mounted a golden chariot adorned with the finest jewels and surrounded by various weapons, he stood at the forefront of the battle.
In that conflict, Paraśurāma beheld that lord of kings.
[He was] accompanied by tens of millions of lords of kings, enriched with ornaments of precious gems;
[he himself was] adorned with a jeweled parasol and decorated with precious ornaments, his entire body anointed with sandalwood, smiling and most enchanting. (5–6)
Having seen that lord of sages, the king descended from his chariot;
having bowed down, he ascended the chariot again and stood there together with the hosts of kings.
Then Rāma bestowed upon him auspicious blessings appropriate for the occasion.
And he said to him, whose purpose was already accomplished, "Go to heaven with your followers.
O Nārada, a battle then took place there between the two armies;
the disciples of Rāma and his exceedingly powerful brothers fled.
With all their limbs mangled and wounded,
having been tormented by Kārtavīrya with the king’s net of arrows, Rāma— the best among wielders of weapons—
could see neither his own army nor the royal army. (9–10)
Rāma discharged the Āgneya weapon, and the battlefield became filled with fire;
the king effortlessly extinguished it with the Vāruṇa weapon alone.
Rāma then discharged the Gāndharva weapon, accompanied by mountains and serpents.
The great king effortlessly discharged the Vāyavya weapon;
Rāma then hurled the Nāga weapon, which was difficult to ward off and terrifying.
The great king effortlessly discharged the Gāruḍa weapon. (12–13)
The Lord, the descendant of Bhṛgu, hurled the Māheśvara weapon;
the King, however, effortlessly extinguished it with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
O Nārada, Rāma then hurled the Brahmāstra for the destruction of the king.
That life-extinguishing weapon was neutralized in battle by the Brahmāstra.
Then the king, for the sake of destroying Paraśurāma in the conflict, seized the spear given by Dattātreya, which is infallible when preceded by the appropriate mantra. (15–16)
And Rāma beheld a trident, possessing a brilliance equal to a hundred suns,
intensified like the cresting flame of the fire of universal dissolution, and irresistible even by the gods.
O Nārada, that trident fell upon Rāma in the battle.
That Bhṛgu fell into a swoon and collapsed while remembering Hari.
When Rāma had fallen, all the gods were overwhelmed with fear;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara arrived there at that battle.
And Śaṅkara, the possessor of great knowledge, by means of his great knowledge and through divine play,
quickly restored the Brahmin to life at the command of Nārāyaṇa.
And Bhṛgu, having regained consciousness, beheld the gods standing before him.
He bowed down with supreme devotion, his neck bent low with shame.
(21) Seeing the lords of the gods, the king, his neck bent low with devotion, prostrated himself with his head and forehead and praised the lords of the gods. (22)

Thereupon the blessed Dattātreya, compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees, arrived at the battlefield for the sake of protecting his disciple. Filled with wrath, Bhṛgu seized the Pāśupata weapon.
Upon seeing Dattadatta, Bhṛgu became paralyzed with astonishment.
Paralyzed, Rāma beheld the king at the forefront of the battle,
protected in the fray by Kṛṣṇa, who was accompanied by various attendants.
He was always performing circumambulations with his Sudarśana discus blazing,
smiling, and praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
he was accompanied by hundreds of cowherds and wore the attire of a cowherd.
Singing with a flute in his hand, which bore the likeness of a fresh rain-cloud, [he appeared].
In that interval, an incorporeal voice arose there:
"The armor has been bestowed by Datta upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (27–28)
O Nārada, on the king’s right arm there was a jewel-studded ring;
and when Śambhu, the preceptor of the yogis, had accepted the armor as alms,
Bhṛgu then became capable of slaying the king.
Having heard the incorporeal voice, Śaṅkara assumed the form of a brahmin;
having begged for alms, he brought the armor belonging to the king—
the armor of Kṛṣṇa which had been given by Śambhu to Bhṛgu.
In the meantime, the gods went to their own supreme abode.
And Paraśurāma replied to the king in the midst of the battle.
Paraśurāma said:
"O King of Kings, arise and engage in battle with boldness!
For men, victory comes at the right time, and defeat comes at the wrong time.
[By you] the Veda has been studied according to rule, gifts have been bestowed, and the entire earth has been well-governed."
The battle was fought by you with perfect skill, yet I have now been rendered unconscious.
All the lords of kings were conquered, and Rāvaṇa was defeated as if in play.
I myself was conquered, but having been granted a trident by Śambhu, I have been restored to life once more.
Having heard Rāma’s words, the supremely righteous king bowed his head in devotion to him and spoke these truthful words. The king said:
