What has been studied, what has been given in charity, or what land has been well-governed?
How many kinds of kings like me have passed away upon the surface of the earth?
[Your] intellect, splendor, valor, and various military strategies— 37.
O Lord, my prosperity, sovereignty, knowledge, and worldly power of giving;
my conduct, humility, learning, status, and supreme austerity—all these have indeed vanished upon union with Manoramā. (38–39)
And that virtuous woman, born from a portion of Padmā, is as dear to me as my own life;
she is my partner in sacrifices like a mother, and she sports with me in affection as my companion.
From childhood, she has always been my companion by my side on the bed, at the meal, and in battle.
Without her, I am like a snake deprived of its life-force, devoid of poison.
You have not seen my battle with her before; this is the first cause for my grief.
O Brahmin, there is a second cause for my grief: that I have been struck down by a brahmin. (41–42)

In due time, a lion kills a jackal, and a jackal likewise kills a lion; in due time, a deer kills a tiger, and a gazelle kills a lordly elephant. In due time, a fly kills a buffalo, and likewise a serpent kills Garuḍa.
The servant praises the king of kings at the proper time, and the king [praises] the servant;
and at the proper time, a human praises Indra, while Brahmā shall perish.
Having become latent within the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa at the proper time, that primordial nature (prakṛti) [remains there].
All the gods, and all things moving and unmoving situated within the three worlds, shall die;
all go to dissolution in time, for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the time of time, the creator of the creator, according to His will.
He is the destroyer of even the destroyer, the protector of the protector, and higher than the highest.
He is more massive than the most massive, subtler than the subtlest, and yet more attenuated than the thin.
He is beyond the atom, he is time, and he is the one who divides time.
He whose every hair is a universe is that Puruṣa, the Mahāvirāṭ;
he is a sixteenth part of the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
From him was born the Kṣudravirāṭ, the ultimate cause of all.
He who is the creator Brahmā himself, born from whose navel-lotus [the world arose],
did not reach the end of the lotus-stalk of his own navel despite his efforts;
after wandering for a hundred thousand years, he finally came to rest in his own place.
Then he performed penance there for a hundred thousand years, subsisting only on air.
Thereafter, he beheld Goloka and Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with His attendants—
surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses, two-armed, and holding a flute.
Having seen him seated upon a jeweled lion-throne with Rādhā resting upon his chest,
and having received his permission and prostrated again and again,
he understood the will of the Lord and set his mind upon creating the world.

That Śiva, who is the creator and destroyer, was born from the forehead of the Creator (Brahmā). Viṣṇu is the protector, the Kṣudravirāṭ, and the dweller in Śvetadvīpa. Furthermore, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the causes of creation.
In all beings, everywhere, there exist those born from a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
they too are deities of the material nature, and the Great Virāṭ is likewise of the material nature.
Prakṛti is the source of everything, yet Śrī Kṛṣṇa is beyond Prakṛti.
Even the Supreme Lord is not able to effect creation without that power, Prakṛti;
the Lord of Māyā cannot bring about creation without Māyā.
And she [Māyā] remains concealed within Kṛṣṇa, the agent of both creation and dissolution.
She is manifested at the time of creation, and that Great Goddess is eternal.
Just as a potter is unable to make a mat without clay,
so too a goldsmith is incapable of making an earring without gold.
And that power, at the time of creation, by the will of the Lord, becomes fivefold:
Rādhā, Padmā, Sāvitrī, Durgā, and the goddess Sarasvatī—she who is the presiding deity of the vital breath of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (61)
That Rādhā is proclaimed to be more beloved than life itself;
she is the presiding goddess of sovereignty and the bringer of all auspiciousness.
And she is proclaimed as Lakṣmī, whose very form is supreme bliss.
She who is the presiding goddess of knowledge, difficult even for the Supreme Lord to attain;
she who is the mother of the Vedas and the Shastras, is celebrated as Savitri.
She who is the presiding goddess of the intellect, whose nature is that of all powers— 64.
She who is the essence of all knowledge, she who is Durgā, the destroyer of difficulties;
she who is the presiding goddess of speech, who always bestows the knowledge of the scriptures;
she who is born from the throat of Kṛṣṇa—she is the goddess Sarasvatī. (65–66)

In the beginning, the Goddess herself, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti, divided herself fivefold. Thereafter, through the very process of emanation, she manifested in many ways by means of her creative power (kalā). Women are portions of Prakṛti, and men are portions of Puruṣa.
And at the time of creation through Māyā, existence would not occur without Him.
O Brahmā, in every universe, creation always originates from Brahman;
Viṣṇu is the protector, and Śiva is the destroyer who eternally bestows auspiciousness.

"O Rāma, this knowledge was given to me by Dattātreya at Puṣkara during the time of my initiation on the full moon day of Māgha, in the presence of the most excellent of sages. Having spoken thus, Kārtavīrya bowed to Rāma with a smile.
Taking up his bow along with arrows, he quickly mounted the chariot.
Then Rāma struck the royal army with the Brahmāstra;
remembering Śrī Hari, he effortlessly slew the king with the Pāśupata weapon. (71–72)
Thus,
remembering Śiva, Rāma effortlessly rendered the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times in succession—
whether they were in the womb, on their mother’s lap, as infants, as youths, or as adults. (73)
Rāma indeed slew the Kṣatriya in order to fulfill his vow. And Kārtavīrya went to Goloka, into the presence of Kṛṣṇa; and Paraśurāma, remembering Śrī Hari, departed out of satisfaction.
Having seen the earth rendered kingless twenty-one times, Maheśvara,
along with the gods, sages, goddesses, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, beheld Paraśurāma and became filled with awe. (76)
And all of them, O Nārada, showered flowers upon the head of Rāma.
In heaven the kettledrums resounded and a cry of joy arose;
indeed, the entire world was filled with the glory of Paraśurāma.
Brahmā, Bhṛgu, Śukra, Vālmīki, Cyavana,
and Jamadagni came from the world of Brahmā, filled with great joy;
their entire bodies were covered with horripilation, and they arrived full of bliss and devotion.
All of them, holding *dūrvā* grass and flowers in their hands, offered auspicious blessings.
Rāma prostrated before them, falling upon the ground like a staff;
first Brahmā took him onto his lap, and [the others] did so in succession, addressing him as "Father."
Then Brahmā, the preceptor of the world, spoke to Paraśurāma regarding that which is the essence of the Vedas, endowed with ethics, and bringing happiness in its ultimate result. Brahmā said:

Listen, Rāma, I shall proclaim the supreme words spoken in the Kāṇva Śākhā, which bestow all prosperity, are indeed true, and are universally esteemed. Among all those worthy of worship, he alone is the most beloved, the most worshipful, and the highest. (83)
Janaka is remembered as the father because of giving birth and because of protecting;
O Sage, the giver of food is a father even more venerable than the one who gives birth.
Without food, the body perishes, whereas the origin from a father is eternal.
The mother is a hundred times more worthy of worship, honor, and salutation than those two;
indeed, she is declared to be weightier because of her bearing and nourishing the child in the womb.
The beloved deity, as heard in the sacred scriptures, is a hundred times more worthy of worship than those [three].
The Guru who bestows knowledge, wisdom, and mantras is superior even to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva). The son of the Guru is like the Guru, and the wife of the Guru is even more so.
When the deity is angry, the Guru protects; but when the Guru is angry, no one can protect.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, dearer than the most beloved Brāhmaṇas.
The Guru indeed bestows knowledge, and that knowledge grants devotion to Hari.
Who else is a kinsman beyond him who bestows devotion to Hari?
From whom one, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, may obtain the lamp of knowledge;
and having obtained it, may see clearly—who else is a kinsman beyond him? (90–91)
By reciting the *sumantra* bestowed by the guru, one then obtains knowledge;
through omniscience and spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*), what friend could be greater than that? Everywhere, one triumphs with ease through the lore (*vidyā*) bestowed by the guru.
Who in this world is a kinsman greater than she by whom even the Worshipful One is honored?
That fool, whether blinded by ignorance or blinded by wealth, who does not worship the Guru, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such crimes; of this there is no doubt. (93–94)
One should serve the Guru with the understanding that he is a human being, even if he is poor, fallen, or lowly.
Even one who has bathed at sacred pilgrimage sites is not pure and lacks qualification for spiritual rites.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is your chosen deity, and your Guru is Śaṅkara himself.

"Go for refuge, O son, to the Guru who is most worthy of worship by the gods. Since you have rendered the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times, and since you have attained devotion to Hari—that auspicious one—go to him for refuge. (96–97)

Take refuge in the Guru, who is auspicious, whose form is auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, the cause of auspiciousness, the one to be worshipped by Śiva, auspicious himself, and peaceful. (98) The Lord of Goloka, the Blessed One, has assumed the form of Śiva through his partial incarnation.
Whoever is one's chosen deity is the guru; go to that very one for refuge.
(99) In all living beings, Kṛṣṇa is the Self, Śiva is knowledge, and I am the mind.
O son, Viṣṇu’s vital breaths are that Prakṛti, endowed with all powers. (100)
Take refuge in that Guru, the giver of knowledge, whose nature is knowledge, the eternal seed of knowledge, the conqueror of death, the death of time,
whose form is the light of Brahman, and whose body is the grace bestowed upon devotees. 101.
Go for refuge to the omniscient, eternal Lord.
Having performed austerities for a hundred thousand years, Prakṛti obtained Him as her Lord—her beloved, her dear husband; go for refuge to that Guru. (102–103)
Having spoken thus, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) departed together with the sages.
And Rāma, O Nārada, set his mind upon going to Kailāsa.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Bhṛgu’s Journey to Kailāsa," in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa within the third section, the Gaṇeśa-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having donned the armor of Hari and having rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas,
Rāma went to Kailāsa to pay homage to his guru, Śiva.
To see the preceptor’s wife, Śivāmbā, and those two sons of the preceptor—
Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśvara— who were equal to Nārāyaṇa in their virtues,
that high-souled Bhṛgu, traveling as fast as thought, arrived there at that very moment.
He beheld a delightful mountain, exceedingly captivating to the mind. (3) It was resplendent with royal roads that resembled pure gold, adorned with enchanting jewels as bright as clear crystal. (4)
It was encircled by jeweled altars the color of vermilion-red,
joined with clusters of pearls, and filled with pavilions of gems.
It was further endowed with hundreds of millions of divine abodes belonging to the Yakṣas.
Adorned with doors, pillars, and stairs fashioned from jewels,
[the city was graced] with divine golden jars, silver ones, and white chowries;
it was filled with gems and gold and surrounded by hosts of Yakṣa lords.
It was resplendent with throngs of beautiful women, richly adorned with jewel ornaments and radiant;
and with girls and boys playing,
smiling constantly, and shining as they moved about freely like painted dolls.

It was strewn with clusters of *pārijāta* trees and with fragrant, blossoming lotuses from the banks of the celestial river; it was filled with hosts of *siddhas* resting under the *kalpa* trees and preceded by the wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadhenu*).
It was frequented by meritorious persons skilled in the perfected sciences (siddhavidyā).
There were imperishable banyan trees with a shadow extending for three hundred thousand yojanas,
each measuring a hundred yojanas in width and possessed of a hundred trunks.
Adorned with countless branches bearing innumerable fruits in their hands,
crowded with flocks of various birds making most enchanting sounds,
and shaken by a fragrant, cool breeze, [the forest] was thus embellished. (12–13)
With a thousand flower gardens, a hundred lakes,
and hundreds of thousands of abodes for the lords of the Siddhas fashioned from jewels and gems—
Rāma, seeing the city, was exceedingly joyful in heart.

He beheld before him the beautiful and glorious abode of Śaṅkara (15). It was inlaid with hundreds of gems worth gold, with golden-colored jewels, and adorned with the finest of precious stones; it had been fashioned by Viśvakarman (16).
The wall was fifteen yojanas in height and four yojanas in width;
it was square, with four corners, and exceedingly beautiful.
Its gate was provided with jeweled doors adorned with various colorful designs.
It was joined with altars of supreme jewels and adorned with pillars of precious gems.
To its right, O Nārada, was the lordly bull, and to its left was the lion;
[there were also] Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Piṅgalākṣa, and Bhayaṃkara.
Viśālākṣa, Bāṇa, the mighty Virūpākṣa,
Vikaṭākṣa, Bhāskarākṣa, Raktākṣa, Vikaṭodara,
Saṃhārabhairava, Kālabhairava, and Bhayaṅkara.
Rurubhairava, who resembles Īśāna, and Mahābhairava;
Kṛṣṇāṅgabhairava, and the fierce Krodhabhairava;
Kapālabhairava, and Rudrabhairava as well. (21–22)
The lords of the Siddhas and other hosts of Rudras, the Vidyādharas and the Guhyakas;
the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Brahmarākṣasas;
the Vetālas and Dānavas, as well as the lords of Yogins wearing matted hair. (23)
He beheld yakṣas, kimpuruṣas, and kinnaras.
Having seen them and received the command from Nandikeśa, the descendant of Bhṛgu addressed them and,
overflowing with joy, entered within.
He beheld a hundred palaces inlaid with the finest essence of jewels,
resplendent with blazing jars made of priceless gems,
and adorned with spotless mirrors fashioned from priceless jewels and pearls. (26)
It was resplendent with door-panels fashioned from the essence of diamonds (hīrasāra),
endowed with thousands of pillars set with gems and yellow orpiment (gorocanā),
and beautifully adorned with stairways wrought from the finest jewels.
He beheld the inner door, adorned with various paintings and resplendent with networks of garlands strung with rubies and pearls. He also saw Kārttikeya on his left and Gaṇeśvara on his right.
O Nārada, [he saw] Vīrabhadra of massive body and prowess equal to Śiva,
along with the principal hosts of attendants and the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas),
all seated upon jeweled lion-thrones and adorned with jewel ornaments. (30–31)
Having addressed them, Bhṛgu— possessed of great strength and prowess,
with an axe in hand— that Paraśurāma prepared to depart.
As he was going, Gaṇeśa said to him, "Wait a moment!"
"Mahādeva is now asleep, possessed by slumber.
(33) "Having received the Lord's command, I shall come here in a moment and go with you; brother, stay here for now. (34)
Having heard the words of Gaṇeśa, the exceedingly powerful Paraśurāma,
a speaker equal to Bṛhaspati, began to speak.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Kailāsa," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Paraśurāma said:
"O brother, I shall go to the inner apartments to pay my respects to the Lord;
having bowed with devotion to my mother, I will go home in haste."
Having effortlessly deprived the earth of its kings twenty-one times,
it was by his grace that Kārtavīrya and Sucandra were slain;
from him various sciences and diverse weapons, so difficult to obtain, were acquired.
I now desire to behold that Guru, the Lord of the worlds,
who possesses both form and formlessness, whose very body is the grace bestowed upon devotees,
who is Truth itself, whose nature is truth, and who is the eternal Brahman-light. (3–4)

The Lord of Sages, who consists of his own will, an ocean of compassion, a friend to the distressed, delighting in the Self, whose desires are fulfilled, both manifest and unmanifest, higher than the highest;
the creator of all things high and low, invoked by many, and held in supreme honor. (5)
The ancient Supreme Self, the Lord, without beginning or end, imperishable;
the most auspicious among all auspicious things, the cause of all auspiciousness;
the bestower of all auspiciousness, peaceful, the giver of all sovereignty, the excellent one. (6–7)
"Quickly propitious, with a gracious countenance, affectionate toward those who have come for refuge,
bestowing fearlessness upon devotees, loving toward his devotees, and impartial in vision"—
having spoken thus, Paraśurāma stood before Gaṇapati.
There, the Lord of the Gaṇas spoke with sweet words:
"Wait a moment, wait a moment; listen to these words, O brother!
A man accompanied by a woman must never be seen while standing in a secluded place."
That lowest of men who sees a man united with a woman,
or who causes a disruption of their pleasure, shall certainly go to the Kālasūtra hell.
There that wicked one remains as long as the moon and the sun exist.

O twice-born one, a wise man should especially not look upon his father, his teacher, or the Lord of Beings while they are engaged in secret sexual union. Should anyone, whether out of lust or anger, look upon them when intent on sexual intercourse, [he incurs great sin]. (12–13)
For him, separation from his wife will certainly occur for seven lifetimes.
That deluded man who, out of lust, gazes upon the hips, the chest, or the face of another's wife, will surely become blind. (14)
Having heard the words of Gaṇeśa, the descendant of Bhṛgu laughed and,
O Sage, spoke these harsh words to him with great anger.
Paraśurāma said:
"Aha! What unprecedented speech, endowed with political wisdom, have I heard!
Aha! This is exactly so; it has never been heard thus from the mouth of a lord.
This statement was heard by those who are lustful and subject to transformation."
Indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in a child who is free from change.
"O brother, I shall go to the inner apartments; why do you remain here, O boy?
I will act according to what I see, performing my duty as the occasion requires. (17)
It has not been established at all that "your father and mother are [the same as mine]";
rather, Pārvatī and Parameśvara are the parents of the worlds.
By whom has it not been established that Pārvatī is the woman and Śambhu is the man? (18–19)
Śaṅkara is all forms, and Pārvatī is all forms. What play can there be for one who has transcended the qualities (guṇas), or whence could there be its cessation, O All-pervading Lord?
Play, shame, fear, and cessation belong only to the vulgar, not to the Sovereign.
And seeing me standing there, how could my parents feel shame?
How can there be shame for shame itself, and from where would that shame come for the Lord of Shame (Śiva)?
Does shame incur shame, or does fire incur heat? || 21–22 ||
O brother, cold encounters coldness, and the summer heat encounters only burning;
fear encounters fear, so what can death itself fear?
(23) Whence does fever come to destroy fever, and how is it that one disease consumes another disease?
Is there no destroyer for the destroyer? Does Time itself fear Time? (24) In your view, does the Creator create the Creator, or does the Protector protect the Protector?
Does hunger ever consume hunger, or does thirst ever reach thirst? (25)
Sleep regards sleep as its own, and Śrī regards Śrī as her own; Śānti regards Śānti as her own, and Puṣṭi regards Puṣṭi as her own.
Does Tuṣṭi regard Tuṣṭi as her own, and Kṣamā regard Kṣamā as her own?
The Supreme Self is the self of the individual soul; does Power ever fear another power? (26)
O Lord, desire and anger, greed and delusion—these do not afflict Your own self. Compassion is not bound by compassion, nor is will bound by will.
What transformation can there be in knowledge and intellect? Old age does not afflict You, O Old Age.
Thought is not seized by thought; the eye does not see the eye. (28) Does joy attain delight? Does sorrow afflict sorrow?
What is calamity for calamity? And whence comes prosperity for prosperity? (29)
From where would the power of retention come from *medhā*, or the act of remembering from *smṛti*?
It is universally accepted that the Sun is not consumed by his own radiance;
therefore, O brother, you have now acted quite the opposite.
"He has not been heard from the mouth of my guru, nor seen, nor has he been heard of even in the Vedas.
Having said this, Paraśurāma, laughing incessantly,
joyfully set his mind upon entering that cave quickly.
Having heard those words of Rāma, the Lord of the Gaṇas, who had conquered his anger and whose nature is pure sattva, laughed and spoke to him. The Lord of the Gaṇas said:
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, one attains knowledge from those who know it.
Knowledge obtained from the mouth of a father or a brother is difficult to find; only the fortunate may obtain it.
Such learned and distinguished knowledge is rare even among the wise.
O brother of dull intellect, listen to this report of mine:

he who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) is untainted and is indeed not joined with powers (śakti). Desiring to create, when that which is devoid of qualities resorts to power, it becomes possessed of qualities (saguṇa).
O Great Sage, all bodies whatsoever that are fit for enjoyment— whether they be material or otherwise— with the sole exception of the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
yogis meditate upon Him as being of the nature of pure light. (37)
Devoid of hands, feet, and the like, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—
the Vaiṣṇavas, those devotees who bestow grace upon their followers, bow down to Him.
From where did that light arise, O wonder, without [any other] luminous being?
Within the light is the eternal body, dark and beautiful, with two arms, holding a flute in His hand, smiling, and clad in yellow garments;
He is adorned with ornaments of exceedingly priceless and excellent jewels. (40)
By the grace of the All-pervading Lord, they behold His form within the light;
then, by the will of the Lord, they indeed become appointed to service.
Neither yoga nor austerity is worth even a sixteenth part of this service.
When Kṛṣṇa, intent on creation, joyfully brought forth Prakṛti,
His seed was cast into her womb, and from that seed a cosmic egg (ḍimbha) came into being.
After a hundred thousand divine years, the embryo emerged from the egg.
Then there arose a breath, and from that, wind indeed came into being.
Along with the breath, O brother, a drop emerged from the mouth;
from that, a mass of water suddenly appeared before Hari.
And the child remained in that water for a hundred thousand divine years;
then he suddenly became the Great Virāṭ, the support of the universe.
As many as are the hairs on the body of that Great Soul, [so many worlds exist].
There are certainly as many existing cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) as there are;
and within each of those very eggs, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara exist, as do the gods, the sages, and all things moving and unmoving. 47–48.
O sage, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari became the breath of life for the Great Virāṭ and for all people;
and then Mahāviṣṇu, by means of a portion [of Himself], became the Lesser Virāṭ.
In the lotus of its navel is Brahmā; from its forehead is born Śaṅkara;
and Viṣṇu, who dwells in Śvetadvīpa, is his portion and the protector.
Thus, in every individual egg (universe), there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
And Hari himself, assuming various forms through his own partial manifestations (*svāṃśakalā*),
then became endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*) and possessed of all powers.
How could he— the great one, consisting of pure consciousness— be devoid of shame and other such qualities?
At all times worthy of every enjoyment and endowed with all powers, he is considered by all to be beyond shame;
for how could shame have departed from that Goddess who is the very embodiment of modesty? (53–54)
Durgā is all-powerful by nature, and she is the daughter of the mountain.
She possesses modesty and other virtues that are always esteemed by all.
Furthermore, there is the fivefold *prakṛti* who belonged to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Rādhā, Padmā, Sāvitrī, Durgā, and the goddess Sarasvatī—
she who is the presiding deity of the vital breaths of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
that beloved Rādhā, who is dearer to him than his own life, dwells upon his chest. (56–57)
She who is the presiding goddess of knowledge, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā;
Lakṣmī herself, the embodiment of all prosperity, belonging to Nārāyaṇa;
and Sarasvatī, having become twofold, emerged from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa. 58.
Sāvitrī is the beloved of Brahmā and herself of Nārāyaṇa;
she is the goddess presiding over the intellect, the mother of knowledge, endowed with power.
She is Durgā, the beloved of the Trident-bearer (Śiva). How could shame have departed from her? (59–60)

O brother, Prakṛti indeed became fivefold in Goloka, because these primary energies manifested in many ways through her portions (kalā). O best of Brahmins, Vaikuṇṭha is eternally said to be beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
There is an imperishable and eternal place, which remains constant even during the dissolution of nature;
there dwells the Lord Nārāyaṇa, possessing four arms and a portion of Kṛṣṇa’s essence,
wearing a forest garland and yellow robes, together with his Śakti, Padmā.
Kṛṣṇa himself, in Goloka, is two-armed and darkly beautiful;
smiling, with a flute in his hand, he stands upon the breast of Rādhā. Always accompanied by cows, cowherds, and cowherd girls, he assumes the form of a cowherd.
He is most perfectly complete, glorious, devoid of [material] qualities, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
He consists of His own will, is independent, and bears the form of supreme bliss. The gods are born from His creative power (kalā), and the Great Virāṭ is His sixteenth part.
From which all things, both gross and subtle, come into being; and there they dissolve again in this very same way, over and over again.
Goloka is fifty crore yojanas above Vaikuṇṭha.
"There is no world beyond that, nor is there any Lord superior to Kṛṣṇa.
This I have heard from the mouth of Śambhu and have told it to you, O twice-born one.
Wait a moment now, brother, for the Lord is intent upon sexual union."

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Gaṇeśa and Paraśurāma," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Gaṇeśa, that wise one then [acted] out of affection.
With an axe in hand, Rāma was indeed prepared to go forth fearlessly.
Then the Lord of the Gaṇas, seeing this, rose up quickly with effort;
out of affection, he restrained him and again offered humble salutations.
Rāma urged him on, uttering "Hum" again and again.
Then, amidst the dragging of hands, a battle of words ensued.
At that time, Bhṛgu set his mind upon hurling his axe.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", Kārttikeya addressed him in the assembly:
"O brother, how can you discharge this unfailing weapon against the son of your preceptor?
You ought not to strike the son of your guru as if he were the guru himself. (4–9)
As he was angrily brandishing his axe, his eyes like the petals of a red lotus,
Gaṇeśa restrained him and said to him, "Desist!
Rāma then urged Gaṇeśa forward again out of anger.
Deprived of his pride, Gajānana fell down before him with force.
Then Gajānana, the son of Śiva, having risen and made Dharma his witness,
enlightened him once more, having conquered his anger.
"Turn back, turn back!"—thus he cried out again and again.
"O Lord, what power do you have for entry without the command of the Supreme Lord?
You are surely my brother and my guest by virtue of our connection through sacred knowledge."
"And because he was a disciple dear to the Lord, it was indeed endured by him for that reason.
For neither I nor Kārtavīrya are kings; you are but insignificant creatures.
Therefore, O Brahmin, you do not know me, the son of Viśveśvara."
"Stay for a moment, turn back from the battle, O guest of the Brahmins!
In another moment, I shall go into the presence of the Lord together with you.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Heramba, he laughed again and again;
bowing to Hari and Śaṅkara, he set his mind upon hurling the axe. As Rāma was angrily casting the axe, Gajānana [beheld him].
Seeing him on the verge of death, the Lord of Gods, having made Dharma his witness,
increased that trunk to ten million yojanas by means of yoga.
Standing there, the Lord of Yogis whirled it around again and again.
Having coiled him around a hundred times and whirled him about there,
he lifted him up with great force, just as Garuḍa seizes a small snake;
[he then traversed] the seven continents, the mountains, Mount Meru, and all the oceans.
In an instant, he showed Rāma, who had been struck down by yoga—
devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs, inert, and with all his limbs trembling.
Then the destroyer of pride made that arrogant one whirl around once more.
The Lord of the Gods showed Nārada the world of Bhūḥ, the world of Bhuvaḥ, and the world of Svaḥ;
then Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Dhruvaloka beyond that;
and finally Gaurīloka and Śambhuloka.
Having displayed the cosmic egg, he drank up the seven oceans;
then he vomited them out again as water containing Sanaka, crocodiles,
and sea-monsters, and cast it there into the deep waters of the ocean.
As he was about to die while crossing over, [the Lord] playfully seized him again;
having whirled him there once more even above the cosmic egg,
He showed him Vaikuṇṭha, where the four-armed Lord dwells with Lakṣmī.
Having whirled him there for a moment by means of his yogic power, the Lord of Yogis then,
through his yoga, playfully enlarged his hand and showed him Goloka and the sovereign river Virajā.
Vṛndāvana, the lordly mountain Śṛṅgavān with its hundred peaks, and the circle of the rāsa dance;
together with the gopīs, gopas, and others, [he beholds] Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beautiful Śyāmasundara—two-armed, holding a flute in his hand, smiling, and most enchanting. (25)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and adorned with jewel ornaments,
possessing a splendor like ten million suns, and resting upon the breast of Rādhā—
having thus shown Kṛṣṇa and bowing down again and again. (26–27)
In an instant, having whirled him around again and again as he hung suspended,
and beholding Kṛṣṇa— the beloved deity who destroys all sins—
he cast far away Bhṛgu’s sin, including the murder of an embryo. (28)
The torment born of sin would not be destroyed without its being experienced;
yet Rāma experienced only a small portion of it, and the remainder vanished upon seeing Kṛṣṇa. Regaining consciousness in an instant, he fell violently to the ground.
The immobilization of Gaṇeśa by Bhṛgu came to an end;
he then remembered the armor and the hymn bestowed by his guru, which are very difficult to obtain,
as well as his chosen deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa and his guru Śambhu, the teacher of the world.
O Sage, he hurled an axe that was as effective as Śiva and possessed a splendor a hundred times greater than the sun at midday in summer;
and seeing his father’s weapon to be so unfailing, Gaṇapati himself [acted].
He seized it with his left tusk, but the weapon became useless;
for, having struck it down with force and severed the tusk along with its root,
the axe returned to Rāma’s hand by the power of Mahādeva.
With great alarm, the gods raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! in the sky.
Vīrabhadra, Kārttikeya, the Kṣetrapālas, and the attendants [watched].
Then the tusk fell to the ground, dripping with blood and making a sound.
He fell like a mountain of crystal smeared with red chalk.
O Brahmin, by that great sound the earth trembled with fear;
all the people dwelling on Kailāsa fell into a swoon for a moment out of terror.
At that moment, sleep was shattered for Śambhu, the Lord of the World and Master of Sleep. He emerged in haste with Pārvatī and saw Heramba before him, his red face wounded by the blow. 38.
O Sage, Pārvatī quickly questioned Skanda, who had broken teeth, whose anger was conquered, and who was smiling yet ashamed: "Why is this, my son?
And he, out of fear, related to her the entire account from beginning to end. (39–40)
Durgā became enraged and wept again and again out of compassion;
placing her son upon her breast, she spoke before Śambhu, addressing him with grief, fear, and humility. (41)
The virtuous lady, having bowed down, spoke to her husband, the remover of the distress of those who prostrate before him.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause of Gaṇeśa’s Broken Tusk," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Pārvatī said:

Everyone in the world knows Durgā, the servant of Śaṅkara. Her maidservants are free from all expectations; indeed, their life is in vain [if they are not so]. To the Lord, all things—from blades of grass to mountains—are equal.
"O Lord, it is fitting for you to investigate whose fault it is—that of the disciple who is the son of a slave-girl. For you are the foremost among those who know the Dharma;
Vīrabhadra, Kārttikeya, and the attendants are present as witnesses. (2–3)

Who would speak falsely as a witness? Or rather, these two brothers are equal [in that regard]. When enemies and friends are equal in testimony, this is the determination of dharma for the virtuous. (4) A witness who, though knowing the facts, should state the testimony in court otherwise—
Whether out of desire, anger, greed, or fear,
he who [commits such an act] is cast into the Kumbhīpāka hell along with a hundred men;
there he shall dwell together with them as long as the moon and the sun endure.
I am capable of awakening you, for I am the judge of both;
nevertheless, my command has been openly defied by you in the hearing of the assembly where the king’s servants reside. (7)
O Lord, just as a firefly is like nothing on the earth once the sun has risen, so too is my own merit;
for though I attained Your lotus feet through long austerity, I have constantly been afraid out of fear of being abandoned. (8–9)
Whatever was uttered out of anger and grief, that supreme [speech] was spoken through delusion;
forgive that, O Lord of the World, because of your intense affection for your son.
If you have abandoned me, then what is the use of that son?

For a virtuous woman born of a noble lineage, her husband is worth more than a hundred sons. But she who is born of an ignoble lineage, being ill-behaved and devoid of knowledge, does not respect her husband; she is contemptible due to the fault of her parents. (11-12)
A woman of noble birth always regards her beloved—whether he be despised, fallen, foolish, poor, diseased, or dull-witted—as equal to Viṣṇu;
he is like fire or the sun, the foremost among all who possess splendor. (13)
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of the splendor of a devoted wife.
Great gifts, meritorious deeds, vows, fasts,
and ascetic penances do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to her husband.
"Whether it be a son, a father, a kinsman, or even a brother—
for women born of noble families, no one is equal to their husband.
Having said this, Durgā beheld Bhṛgu standing before her husband.
She spoke to that fearless one who was serving the lotus feet of Śambhu.
Pārvatī said:
"O Rāma, O highly fortunate one, you are a scholar born of the lineage of Brahmā."
You are the son of Jamadagni and indeed a disciple of the Guru of yogis.
Your mother is the virtuous Reṇukā, a portion of Padmā born of a noble lineage;
her father is a Vaiṣṇava, and her maternal uncle is even more so. (18–19)

And you, O virtuous one, are the grandson and maternal uncle of King Reṇuka, who was born of the lineage of Manu; you are a hero who has taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu. I do not understand by whose fault you, who are otherwise invincible, have become so impure-minded.
Without him, people were corrupted by their own vices; [he alone] possessed a pure mind.
Having obtained an unfailing axe and having approached his Guru, that ocean of compassion, he performed a test upon a Kṣatriya and subsequently became a father of a son.
"The giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor is both appropriate and prescribed in the Vedas.
[If you fail,] alas, I shall sever even the head of your son whose tooth was broken!
If you stand before us after defeating Gaṇeśvara in battle..."
Having obtained these boons, you have become honored in the world and throughout the three realms.
By means of the axe of unerring power and through the grace of Śaṅkara,
even a jackal is capable of killing a lion, and a mouse-eater [a cat] is capable of killing a tiger.
The Lord of the Gaṇas is capable of slaying even hundreds of millions of those like you;
yet, as the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, he does not kill even a fly.
This Lord of the Gaṇas is equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor and is a portion (aṃśa) of Kṛṣṇa himself.
Other regions are but portions of darkness; therefore, worship is performed before him.
By the power of his vow and by the boon of Śaṅkara, he attained [this state];
for through most bitter grief, there is no prosperity without adversity.
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī, out of anger, prepared to kill that Rāma.
Rāma, having mentally bowed to his guru Kṛṣṇa, remembered him.
In the meantime, Durgā saw a twice-born man before her.
He was exceedingly dwarfish and youthful, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
he had white teeth, wore white garments, and had a white sacred thread;
he carried a staff and held a parasol, was most radiant, and was brilliant with a sectarian mark (tilaka).
Wearing a garland of *tulasī*, smiling and most enchanting;
adorned with jeweled armlets and bracelets, and decorated with a necklace of gems;
his feet graced by jeweled anklets, and radiant with a crown of excellent jewels. (32)
Adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings that grace his cheeks,
he displays the *sthiramudrā* with his left hand toward his devotees,
while showing the *abhayamudrā* with his right; he is the Lord of Devotees, affectionate toward those who take refuge in him.
Accompanied by groups of girls and boys, and by the citizens with smiles upon their faces,
he was joyfully gazed upon by all the inhabitants of Kailāsa, including the elderly.
Seeing him, Śambhu, along with his attendants and his son, was filled with agitation.
With devotion, he prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before Durgā with his head bowed.
The boy bestowed a blessing that grants all desires upon them all.
Seeing him, all the boys were filled with great wonder and fear.
Having offered those sixteen services with devotion to him, Śiva performed the worship of the Most Perfect One as prescribed in the Vedas; then,
with his neck bowed, he praised Him with a hymn recited in the Kāṇva recension.
With all his limbs marked by horripilation, Śaṅkara himself spoke to the eternal Blessed One,
who was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and whose form was completely concealed by an exceeding brilliance. (39–40)
Śaṅkara said:
Among those who delight in the Self, an inquiry after their welfare is a profound mockery;
for they are the eternal foundation of well-being, being themselves well-disposed and bestowers of well-being. 41.
In this [auspicious] transit, my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived.
O Brahmin, you have arrived as a guest due to the arising of the fruit of service to Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect one, exists for the sake of delivering the world.
For in a mere fraction of the sacred field of Bhārata, the ocean of mercy [resides].
(43) By whomsoever a guest is honored, all the deities are honored.
When a guest is satisfied, Hari himself is satisfied with that person. (44)
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing in all sacred fords, by every kind of gift,
by all vows and fasts, by initiation into all sacrifices,
and by all various types of ascetic penances— both regular and occasional— [is attained here].
These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of serving a guest.
(46) If a guest departs from one's house disappointed and angry, the merit accumulated over ten million lifetimes is certainly destroyed for that person. (47)
The killer of a woman, the killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the guru’s bed, the reviler of one's father, mother, or teacher, the murderer of a human,
(48) the one who neglects the twilight prayers, the self-destructive, the destroyer of truth, and the reviler of Hari.
One who steals the property of a Brahmin or a sanctuary, one who gives false testimony,
a betrayer of friends, an ungrateful person, a driver of bulls, a cook for others,
one who burns corpses, a priest for a village, and a Brahmin who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* (a woman of low caste). (49–50)
One who eats food at a *śrāddha* ceremony for a Śūdra, one who officiates as a priest at *śrāddhas* for Śūdras, one who sells a daughter in marriage, and one who sells the name of Śrī Hari;
[and those who sell] lac, meat, sesame seeds, salt, and [other] sesame products. (51)
A seller of horses and likewise of cows, a Brāhmaṇa in Bhārata who neglects the observance of Ekādaśī, and a Brāhmaṇa who serves Kṛṣṇa [only for gain]—
these are great sinners, censured throughout the three worlds. (52–53)
And they fall into the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred lifetimes as Brahmās.
Even greater than these is he who turns his back on a guest.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, Śrī Hari himself was satisfied;
the Lord of the World spoke to him in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
(95) Viṣṇu said: "I have come from Śvetadvīpa, having learned of your tumultuous outcry."
For the protection of this Rāma, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, at this time—
O Śiva, with the discus in hand, I protect these devotees of Kṛṣṇa from any inauspiciousness anywhere, except for my guru and others. (56–57)

"I am not one who falls [into sin] when the Guru is angry, for there is no sinner greater than one who treats the Guru with contempt; nor is there anyone more sinful than he who neglects service to the Guru.
He is to be honored and worshipped above all, for he is the progenitor of all. (58)
"Aha! By whose grace a human being perceives all things.
He is Janaka because he gives birth, and he is the father of men because he protects them;
furthermore, by expanding [the creation] through his portion, he is Prajāpati."
A mother is a hundred times more worthy than a father because of her nourishing and her bearing the child in her womb;
indeed, the progenitor is to be saluted, worshipped, and honored like the Earth herself.
One who provides food is a hundred times more worthy of salutation, worship, and honor than a mother.
Without which the perishable body and Viṣṇu, who bestows food through his partial incarnation (kalā), would not exist.
It is traditionally taught that the supreme desired deity is a hundred times more venerable than the giver of food;
the teacher who imparts knowledge and mantras is a hundred times more venerable than that.

He who, with the eye of the lamp of knowledge, reveals all objects of purpose that are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance—he alone is a true kinsman; no other is so. Through the mantra bestowed by the Guru, one may obtain the desired happiness through austerity.
One who is devoted to that [knowledge] attains omniscience and all accomplishments; no other kinsman is truly such a relative.
Through the lore bestowed by the guru, one conquers everything everywhere.
Therefore, who indeed in this world is more worthy of worship than a kinsman superior to that? (65–66)

Whether blinded by ignorance or blinded by wealth, the fool who does not serve the Guru is tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. (67) One should behave toward the Guru with the same attitude one would toward a human being, even if he is poor, fallen, or lowly.

Even one who has bathed at sacred fords is neither pure nor qualified for ritual acts. O Śiva, he who out of deceit fails to support his father, mother, wife, the wife of his teacher, or his preceptor, is a perpetrator of a great sin.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, and the Guru is the embodiment of the Sun.
The Guru is likewise the Moon, Indra, Vāyu, Varuṇa, and Agni.
For the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, is himself the Guru, possessing all forms.
(71) There is no scripture superior to the Veda, nor any deity higher than Kṛṣṇa;
there is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, and no flower superior to the Tulasī leaf. (72)
There is no one more patient than the son of the Earth; there is no other who is more dear.
There is no power greater than destiny, and no vow superior to Ekādaśī.
There is no yantra superior to the Śālagrāma, and no sacred field greater than Bhārata.
Just as Vṛndāvana is the most meritorious among all sacred places;
as Kāśī is among those that grant liberation; as Śiva is among the Vaiṣṇavas;
there is no woman more virtuous than Pārvatī, nor any self-controlled one greater than Gaṇeśa. (74–75)
There is no kinsman equal to knowledge, nor is there anyone higher than the guru.
There is no doubt that the wife and son of the one who bestows knowledge are equal to him.
And [thus] there occurred an insult to Rāma regarding the guru’s wife and his son.
"I have come to your abode for the purpose of performing the supreme act of sweeping.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Nārada, having spoken thus to Śambhu and addressed Durgā,"
There the Blessed One spoke these supreme words, the essence of truth.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim my auspicious speech."
It is endowed with ethics, the essence of the Vedas, and brings about happiness in the end.
O Pārvatī, just as Gajavaktra (Gaṇeśa) and Kārttikeya are [to you], so too is Paraśurāma Bhārgava; there is no doubt in this matter.
There is no difference in affection toward these [sons] between you and Śaṅkara;
having considered everything, O omniscient Mother, do what is appropriate.
This dispute between a son and his father has arisen due to the fault of destiny.
For who indeed is able to overcome destiny? Destiny is most powerful.
O child of lovely countenance, look at what is called "son" in the Vedas:
he is renowned as Ekadanta, saluted by all the gods. (82–83)
O Goddess, O Mother, listen attentively to this supreme hymn of eight names of the Son (*putranāmāṣṭaka*), as declared in the Sāmaveda, which removes all obstacles. (84) Viṣṇu said:
O Mother, beloved of Hara, hear from me the eight names of your son: Gaṇeśa, Ekadanta, Heramba, Vighnanāyaka, Lambodara, Śūrpakarṇa, Gajavaktra, and Guhāgraja. (85)
The essence of all hymns, the supreme remover of all obstacles—
Ga signifies knowledge, and Ṇa signifies liberation;
I bow down to Gaṇeśa, the Supreme Brahman who is the Lord of those two.
The word *eka* signifies "principal," and *danta* denotes "strength.
Strength is the principal [quality] of all; therefore, I bow to the One-Tusked One (*Ekadanta*).
The syllable *he* expresses the meaning of "the wretched," and *ramba* signifies a "protector. (88)
I bow down to Heramba, the protector of the distressed.
(89) *Vighna* signifies calamity, and *nāyaka* has the sense of one who shatters;
I prostrate before that Vighnanāyaka, the destroyer of adversity. (90)
I bow to that Lambodara, whose large belly hangs down due to the food offerings presented by Viṣṇu and the various gifts bestowed by his father;
and whose ears, shaped like winnowing baskets, act as warders-off of obstacles.
I bow to Śūrpakarṇa, who possesses prosperity and the form of knowledge;
I bow to that lovely Gajavaktra, whose face is like that of a lordly elephant, upon whose head the flower-garland granted by Viṣṇu was placed by the sage. 92–93.
Born before Guha, he manifested in the abode of Hara.
I bow to the God who is born before Guha, worshipped foremost by all the gods.
O Durgā, this supreme octet of names is endowed with manifold powers.
This auspicious hymn of eight names, endowed with manifold meanings—
whosoever recites it daily at the three junctions of the day shall be happy and victorious in all things;
from him, obstacles flee away just as serpents flee before Vainateya.
By the grace of Gaṇeśvara, one will certainly become a possessor of great knowledge.
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring a wife obtains a virtuous woman.
Even one who is extremely dull-witted will certainly become a lord among poets and possessed of learning.
"You are our son; look at the Veda and likewise do not harbor anger toward us.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn to Gaṇeśa," in the third section, the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having enlightened Pārvatī, Viṣṇu spoke to Rāma:
"That which is beneficial, essential, the essence of ethics, and brings about happiness in the end.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Rāma, you are now truly at fault in the view of the Śruti,
for out of anger you stood in an inauspicious state after breaking the tusk of Gaṇeśa.
[Now] having praised the supreme Gaṇapati with this very hymn spoken by me..."
Praise Durgā, the mother of the universe, according to the ritual prescribed in the Kāṇva recension.
(3) She is the supreme power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the world, and is of the nature of intellect.
If she is enraged with you, your intellect will be destroyed. (4)
This [Śakti] is the very nature of all powers; by her, the world possesses power.
By her, Kṛṣṇa—though devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—is possessed of power.
Without this Śakti, Brahmā is unable to effect creation.
O twice-born one, in this most terrible age when the host of gods was seized by the asuras, we— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— were born from her;
for Satī had previously manifested as the splendor of all the gods.
Having slain the asuras by the command of Kṛṣṇa and having granted them their station,
he then took birth from the wife of Dakṣa due to the former penance of Dakṣa.
Having become the wife of Śaṅkara, [he was again born] through the censure of his husband.
In former times, Satī, having cast off her body, took birth from the wife of the Mountain King (Himavat).
Through penance, she obtained Śaṅkara, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis;
and through service to Kṛṣṇa, she obtained as a son Gaṇapati, who is a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
"O child, do you not know that very one whom you meditate upon constantly?
He is indeed the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the son of Girijā [Pārvatī] in a partial incarnation.
Bowing with palms joined in reverence, praise Durgā, the beloved of Śiva."
She is auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, devoted to Śiva, the seed of Śiva, and the sovereign of Śiva.
[She was praised] in the past by the King of Hymns to Śivā, composed by Śūla, when Brahmā was impelled during the terrible slaughter of Tripura. (12–13)

Having spoken thus, he quickly went to the abode of Śrī, the dwelling place of Fortune. After Hari had departed, Rāma, remembering Hari, prepared to offer praise with the hymn bestowed by Viṣṇu, which removes all obstacles. (14)
And for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, O Nārada,
having bathed in the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā with palms joined in reverence,
and having prostrated before his guru, the Lord of Devotees, he put on two clean garments. (15–16)
Having sipped water for purification and bowed his head to her with his neck bent low in devotion, his entire body bristling with horripilation and filled with tears of joy, Paraśurāma said:
17. Paraśurāma said:

She appeared in embodied form from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect being, in Goloka, in the past when he was intent upon creation. She possessed the splendor of ten million suns and was adorned with garments and ornaments.
Wearing garments as pure as fire, smiling and most enchanting;
endowed with fresh youth, adorned with the reddish glow of vermilion;
bearing a gracefully flowing mass of hair decorated with garlands of jasmine flowers. (19–20)
Oh, how indescribable you are, bearing such a beautiful form!
You are the bestower of liberation to those seeking release, the very ordinance of Mahāviṣṇu himself.
Upon seeing you, the enchantress of all, he was deluded for a mere moment. (21)
Having suddenly become bashful, she ran away in haste with a smile;
for that reason, Rādhā is celebrated by the virtuous as the Sovereign Mūlaprakṛti.
Frightened, Kṛṣṇa then quickly performed the act of impregnation upon her.
From that, a great embryo was produced, and from that, the Great Virāṭ was born;
within whose pores all the cosmic eggs reside.
Indeed, by the power of Rādhā’s delight, He became her very breath.
That breath became a great wind; he is Virāṭ, the sustainer of the universe.
By the very water of the sweat of fear, the cosmic egg overflowed.
That Virāṭ, the abode of the universe, indeed became a mass of water. (25–26)

Then, dividing yourself fivefold and assuming five forms, you become the form that presides over the life-breath (prāṇa) of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul; those who know the ancient lore call that Rādhā, who is superior even to Kṛṣṇa’s own life-breath. (27)
The wise proclaim that Sāvitrī, who is the embodiment presiding over the Vedas and the mother of the Vedic scriptures, is of pure form.
You are Śānti, the embodiment presiding over sovereignty, and you are of peaceful nature.
The wise call that Lakṣmī, who is pure and whose nature is goodness (sattva).
She is the goddess presiding over passion (rāga), white in form, and the mother of the virtuous.
O, those who know the scriptures proclaim her to be Sarasvatī, the knower of the scriptures. (29–30)
She is the intellect, the knowledge, and the embodiment of all power as its presiding deity;
she is the most auspicious among all that is auspicious, the very form of all auspiciousness, now residing in the abode of Śiva, the seed of all auspiciousness. (31–32)
O Śivā, you are of the very nature of Śivā; you are Lakṣmī in the presence of Nārāyaṇa;
you are Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, and the beloved of Brahmā;
and you are Rādhā of the Lord of the Rāsa, the most perfect Supreme Being.
You are of the nature of supreme bliss, belonging to Him whose nature is supreme bliss.
By a mere fraction of a fraction of a portion of Your power, even the wives of the gods [exist].
You are knowledge; you are all women, the seed-form of all beings.
Chāyā is the wife of the Sun; Rohiṇī, who deludes all, is the wife of the Moon. Śacī is the wife of Śakra; Rati, the sovereign mistress, is the wife of Kāma.
Varuṇānī is the wife of the Lord of Waters; the woman beloved as dear as life is the wife of Vāyu.
For Svāhā is the beloved of Agni, and Sundarī is the beloved of Kubera;
Suśīlā is the beloved of Yama, and Kaiṭabhī is the beloved of Nairṛta.
Aiśānī shall be the beloved of Īśāna, and Śatarūpā is the beloved of Manu.
Devahūti was the wife of Kardama, and Arundhatī was the wife of Vasiṣṭha.
Lopāmudrā was the wife of Agastya, as was Aditi, the mother of the gods. Ahalyā was the wife of Gautama, and Vasundharā, the support of all, was the wife of Viśvāmitra.

The Gaṅgā and Tulasī, as well as whatever other excellent rivers exist upon the earth— all these others, O Ambikā, are [manifestations] of Your own portions. You are the household fortune (gṛhalakṣmī) in the homes of men, and the royal fortune (rājalakṣmī) among kings.

You are the ascetic practice of the ascetics, and you are the Gāyatrī of the Brāhmaṇa. You are the embodiment of the quality of goodness (sattva) for the virtuous, and the sprout of strife for the wicked.
You are the form of light for the attribute-less (nirguṇa), and the power (śakti) for the one with attributes (saguṇa).
In the sun you are of the nature of light, and in fire you are the burner;
in water you are of the nature of coolness, and in the moon you are of the nature of splendor.
On earth you are of the nature of fragrance, and in the ether you are of the nature of sound.
Hunger, thirst, and so forth, as well as you yourself, are all the powers of living beings.
You are the nature of all seeds and the essential form within saṃsāra.
You are the memory, intelligence, and intellect, as well as the power of knowledge of the wise.
You are that auspicious knowledge, the progenitor of all wisdom, which was given out of compassion by Kṛṣṇa to the wielder of the trident (Śiva), by means of which Śiva became the conqueror of death;
you are also those threefold powers of creation, preservation, and destruction.
You alone are that [power] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; salutations be to you!
I bow my head to that Goddess whom the Creator, terrified and trembling with fear of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, praised and was thereby liberated. 48–49.

In the battle with Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Viṣṇu became possessed of power by praising you, O Sovereign Goddess Durgā; I bow down to you. When the charioteer had fallen in the great battle with Tripura, O Śivā—
I bow down to that Durgā whom all the gods praised.
(51) Śambhu himself arose in the form of a bull along with Viṣṇu;
having praised her, he destroyed Tripura—I bow down to that Durgā. (52)
I bow down to that Durgā by whose command the wind blows, the sun shines incessantly, Indra sends rain, and Agni burns;
indeed, by whose command Time itself revolves perpetually with great speed. (53)

Death stalks all living beings; I bow down to that Durgā. (54) By whose command the Creator creates the creation and the Protector protects it, and the Destroyer destroys it at the proper time—I bow down to that Durgā. (55)
I bow to her, without whom the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself—though of the nature of light and devoid of qualities—is unable to perform creation.
(56) Protect, protect me, O Mother of the World; forgive my transgression.
"For how could a mother be angry at the fault of her children?
Having spoken thus, Paraśurāma bowed to her and wept.
Durgā was pleased by his agitation and granted him the boon of fearlessness.
"Be immortal, O son; my child, attain steadfastness.
By the grace of all, may victory be yours forever.
May the Lord Hari, the inner self of all, be perpetually pleased. (59)
May you have devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, toward Śiva who bestows auspiciousness, and toward your guru.
(60) If one possesses eternal devotion toward their chosen deity and their guru, then all the gods, whether pleased or enraged, are not able to harm them. (61)
"You are a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and indeed a disciple of Śaṅkara;
since you praise the wife of your guru, who here would be able to kill you?
Oh, no misfortune ever befalls the devotees of Kṛṣṇa anywhere!"
O Bhṛgu, for those fortunate ones who are devoted to the Moon, even if they are not devoted to other gods, the Moon is powerful and well-pleased;
what can the weak hosts of stars do to them, even if they are angry? (63–64)
"But for whom the great king, being pleased, provides protection,
what can even angry and weak servants do to him?
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī, being satisfied, gave her blessing to Rāma.
He went quickly to the inner apartments, and a cry of joy arose.
Indeed, whoever recites this hymn declared in the Kāṇva Śākhā at the time of worship,
or likewise in the morning at the time of departure, shall certainly obtain his desired object.
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter.
One desiring knowledge obtains knowledge, and one desiring progeny shall obtain progeny.
One who has lost his kingdom shall regain his kingdom, and one whose wealth is lost shall obtain wealth. (68)
Whether it be a teacher, a deity, a king, or a kinsman who is angry with someone,
by the grace of this King of Hymns, that person shall be satisfied and granted boons.
Even one seized by bandits, one seized by serpents, or one seized by enemies, even in the midst of terrifying danger—
One seized by disease shall be liberated merely by recollecting this hymn.
Whether at the king’s gate, in a cremation ground, in a prison, or in bondage, or even submerged in a mass of water, one is released merely by remembering it. (70–71)
In cases of severe discord with one's master, discord among sons, or discord among friends,
one will certainly obtain one's desired object merely by recollecting this hymn. She who, having prepared sacrificial food (haviṣya), listens to this King of Hymns for a year, [attains her goal].
Having worshipped Durgā with devotion, even a woman who has long been barren gives birth;
she obtains a divine son who is wise and long-lived. And one who is unfortunate shall obtain good fortune by listening [to this] for six months. (73–74)

A woman who has given birth only once before (a *kākavandhyā*) or whose children have died will certainly obtain a son if she listens to this King of Hymns with devotion for nine months. A mother of daughters who is childless will [obtain a son] if she listens for five months.
Having worshipped Durgā in a water-pot, she certainly obtains a son.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Durgā Composed by Paraśurāma," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having praised her with the hymn spoken by Hari, that Paraśurāma, his mind blossoming with joy,
extolled the Lord of the Gaṇas;
he also performed worship with devotion and various kinds of food offerings.

Having worshipped his brother with devotion using incense, lamps, perfumes, and flowers— with the exception of *tulasī*— and having bowed to his preceptor and his preceptor’s wife at the command of Śaṅkara, that Rāma prepared to depart. (2–3)
Nārada said: When Rāma performed the worship of the Lord Gaṇapati with various kinds of food offerings and flowers, how was it done without tulasī? 4.
Tulasī is the most venerable, auspicious, and captivating of all flowers;
why does Gaṇeśvara not accept her worship, which is the very essence?
Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Nārada, I shall relate an ancient history,
the hidden and captivating account of the Brahmakalpa.
Once, the goddess Tulasī had reached the bloom of fresh youth.
Wandering to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) through asceticism, she who was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa beheld on the bank of the Gaṅgā the Lord of the Gaṇas (*Gaṇeśa*), endowed with youth,
exceedingly handsome, pure, smiling, and clad in yellow garments. (7–8)
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments,
he was meditating upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, which destroy birth, death, and old age—
the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, the teacher of the lords of yogins. (9)
To him, who was handsome, free from desire, and captivating, she, though full of desire, spoke.
(10) Tulasī said:
"O God, O elephant-faced one of peaceful form, what are you meditating upon?"
"How is it that your body is pot-bellied and how is it that you have the face of an elephant?
How is it that there is a single tusk in your mouth? Tell us the reason for this, both here and in the hereafter.
Abandon your meditation, O illustrious one; evening has arrived. (11–12)
Having spoken thus, the goddess Tulasī laughed again and again;
yet she was deeply tormented in her heart by the most cruel arrows of Kāma.
O Sage, having sprinkled a little water upon the principal limb of Gaṇeśa...
With the tip of his forefinger, he struck Kṛṣṇa’s mind, which had become motionless. O Nārada, his consciousness was shattered by that meditation;
for the breaking of meditation brings sorrow, as it causes the cessation of that [state] and yields grief. (14–15)
Abandoning his meditation and remembering Hari, he beheld before him a woman endowed with fresh youth, smiling, and tormented by desire.
And Lambodara, seeing her, [greeted her] with the utmost humility.
The self-controlled Gaṇeśvara, peaceful and smiling, spoke to the peaceful woman who was afflicted by desire:
"Who are you, my child? Whose daughter are you? O auspicious mother, tell me."
It constantly causes evil and brings inauspiciousness, for it is the destroyer of the meditations of ascetics. May Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, grant you well-being and destroy all obstacles;
through his grace, O auspicious lady, no misfortune shall arise from the fault caused by the interruption of that meditation.
Having heard the words of Gaṇeśa, she, afflicted by love, spoke to the god with a smile and a sidelong glance in a sweet voice. Tulasī said: 20. Tulasī said:
"I am the daughter of the son of Dharma (Yama), a young and ascetic maiden.
My penance is for the sake of a husband; O Lord, please become my husband.
Having heard these words of Tulasī, Gaṇeśa remembered Śrī Hari.
The highly wise Gaṇeśa spoke to that intelligent woman with sweet words:
"O Mother, I have no desire for the terrible taking of a wife."

For the taking of a wife leads only to suffering and never to happiness. Sexual union is destructive to devotion to Hari, it causes the failure of ascetic penance, it acts as a bolt on the door to liberation, and it is a noose for the bondage of worldly existence. (23–24)
That which causes perpetual dwelling in the womb, that which cuts away the knowledge of reality,
and that which is the undertaking of doubts— even by the lowliest of men— should be abandoned.
This house is the source of all causes and a casket for every illusion.
"A multitude of rash acts and, in particular, a host of faults [will result].
Turn back, O illustrious lady; look for another lover as your husband.
For the union of a lustful woman with a lustful man alone would be virtuous. (26–27)
Having heard these words, she cursed him out of anger:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, your wife shall become unchaste; of this there is no doubt.
(28) Having heard this, the best of gods, the son of Śiva, cursed her in return.
"O Goddess, you will undoubtedly be seized by an asura.
Thereafter, due to the curse of the great ones, you shall become a tree.
Having said this to her, "You shall be a woman of great asceticism," Nārada fell silent. (29–30)
Upon hearing the curse, Tulasī wept again and again.
She praised the best of gods, and he, being pleased, spoke to her.
Gaṇeśvara said:
O charming one, you shall become the very essence of all flowers;
O highly fortunate one, by a portion of yourself, you shall be the beloved of Nārāyaṇa himself.
You shall be dear to all the gods, and especially to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Devotion grants liberation to men; I am not to be enjoyed by you eternally.
Having spoken thus, that best of gods departed once more for asceticism.
Absorbed in the worship of Hari, he went to the vicinity of Badarī.
The goddess Tulasī departed with a grieving heart.
Without food, she performed penance at Puṣkara for a hundred thousand years,
O Nārada, following the curse of the lord of sages and Gaṇeśa.
O Sage, she became the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa for a very long time.
Then that lord of the asuras was slain by the trident of Śaṅkara.
That beloved of Nārāyaṇa attained the state of a tree through a portion of her essence.
This history has been told to you; it was heard long ago from the mouth of Dharma.
It bestows liberation, is essential, and has been proclaimed through the Purāṇa.
Thereafter, that Paraśurāma went to the forest for ascetic penance.
Having prostrated before Śaṅkara and having fully worshipped Durgā and Gaṇeśvara, the Lord of Gaṇas—
honored and saluted by all the foremost of the lords of gods and sages—
remained happily in the presence of Pārvatī and Śiva. (39–40)
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this section on Gaṇapati certainly obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
One who is childless obtains a son through the grace of Śrī Gaṇeśa.
He was steadfast, heroic, wealthy, virtuous, and long-lived;
he was illustrious, possessed of sons, learned, and a sovereign among great poets;
he was the foremost of those who have conquered their senses and a giver of all prosperity. (42–43)
One shall obtain a Vaiṣṇava who is virtuous, of good conduct, praiseworthy, non-violent, compassionate, and proficient in the knowledge of reality;
having worshipped Gaṇeśa with devotion using garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste. (44)
Having heard this section on Gaṇapati, even a woman who has never borne a child will give birth;

one whose children have died, or one who bears only daughters like a crow, shall certainly obtain a son, O Brahmin. Even a woman who is pure yet intent upon defiling the blameless shall likewise obtain a son.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by hearing the entire Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa,
that same fruit he obtains by hearing this excellent section (khaṇḍa),
provided he listens with supreme devotion, having formed a longing for it in his mind.
To him, Gaṇeśvara, the best of the gods, grants everything desired.
Having diligently heard this section on Gaṇapati for the destruction of obstacles,
[one should offer] a golden sacred thread, a white umbrella, and a garland.
A svastika, sesame sweets (tilalaḍḍukas),
and indeed ripe fruits produced according to the season and region are given to the reciter.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Arrival of Paraśurāma and the Fruits of Hearing this Section," in the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the third section, the Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa, in the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Om. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to Śrī Sarasvatī.
Om. Salutations to the beloved of the gopīs.
Now begins the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa from the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
Then one should utter the victory-hymn to the Goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa.
Nārada said:
"O Brahman, I have first heard the enchanting Brahmakhaṇḍa."
From the lotus-like mouth of Brahmā, [I heard] that which is most wonderful.
Then, having quickly come into your presence at his word,
I have heard the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa, which is more excellent than a fragment of nectar.
Therefore, my restless mind, though not yet satiated, desires to hear further the distinguished *Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa*, which destroys the cycle of birth for both the whole and the part,
as well as the *Śrīkṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa*, which destroys the cycle of birth and so forth for human beings. (3)
It is the lamp of all principles, the destroyer of karma, and the bestower of devotion to Hari;
it instantly generates dispassion and cuts away the disease of worldly existence;
it is the cause of the seeds of liberation and the supreme means of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. (4–5)
It is an elixir for shattering the diseases of karma and its enjoyments,
the cause of the staircase for attaining the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
the very life of the Vaiṣṇavas, and the supreme purifier of the worlds. (6)
Speak at length to me, your devotee, disciple, and one who has come for refuge.
By what request was Kṛṣṇa impelled to descend to the earth?
For he alone is the Lord, the most perfect in every respect. (7–8)
In which age, for what reason, and where did he indeed manifest?
Who was his father Vasudeva, and who was Devakī?
Tell me, in whose lineage did this birth occur—this excellent mockery performed through Māyā?
What did Hari do upon arriving, and in what form? (10) Why did He depart from the maternity chamber for Gokula out of fear of Kaṃsa?
O Sage, how could the Lord, who is the master of fear itself, have fear of Kaṃsa, who is like a mere insect? (11)
What indeed did Hari do in Gokula while disguised as a cowherd? Why did the Lord of the Universe sport with the cowherd women?
Who were the cowherd women, and who were the cowherds appearing in the form of children?
Who was Yaśodā, and who was Nanda? What merit did he indeed perform?
How was the meritorious goddess Rādhā, a resident of Gokula, born as a cowherd girl in Vraja, becoming the beloved of Hari? (13–14)
How did the cowherd women attain the Supreme Lord, who is so difficult to propitiate?
And why did He depart for Mathurā again, abandoning them?
Having accomplished the removal of the earth's burden, what did He do before He departed?
O illustrious one, whose name is meritorious to hear and glorify, please tell us the story of Hari, which is very difficult to obtain— a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence,
and a shears that cut through the shackles of attachment to the pleasures of rebirth. (16–17)
Like a blazing crest of fire for the burning of the fuel of sins, it destroys the transgressions of millions of births for those who have heard it;
it is liberation itself, as delightful as nectar to the ear and the destroyer of the ocean of sorrow. (18)
O Treasure of Compassion, grant knowledge to me, your devoted disciple.
[This is superior] to asceticism, recitation, great charity, visiting sacred fords on earth, the study of the Vedas, fasting, religious vows, or even the worship of the gods. (19–20)
Whatever fruit a man obtains from initiation in all sacrifices,
that fruit does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving knowledge.
I have been sent by my father into your presence to bestow knowledge.
"Having reached the ocean of nectar, who else would wish to drink anything else?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"I have recognized you; you are blessed, a mass of merit embodied in a beautiful form."
O purifier of your lineage, you wander through the worlds to sanctify them.
Indeed, the hearts of people are immediately and clearly revealed by your speech, whether toward a disciple, a wife, a daughter, a grandson, or even a kinsman. (23–24)
In one's son, grandson, speech, valor, misfortune, woman,
old age, enemy, and learning, the hearts of men are known.
You are liberated while living, you are pure, and you are a devoted worshiper of the Wielder of the Mace (Viṣṇu).
You purify the entire earth, the support of all, with the dust of Your feet;
You purify all the worlds by the sight of Your own form.
Therefore, You desire to hear the most auspicious narrative of Hari.
Wherever there are stories of Kṛṣṇa, right there are all the deities,
as well as the sages, the seers, and all the sacred fords.
Having heard the stories, at the conclusion of the narration, those virtuous ones go to a state free from calamity.
Those places where the auspicious narrations of Kṛṣṇa occur become true holy pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
One who immediately speaks the narrations of Kṛṣṇa, having uplifted hundreds upon hundreds of his own people,
purifies his entire lineage of those possessed of scriptural learning.
The questioner purifies his own lineage merely by asking the question;
the listener purifies his own family and his kinsmen merely by hearing it.
One who has performed austerities for a hundred lifetimes obtains this birth in the land of Bhārata.
Having heard the nectar of Hari’s stories, one makes one's birth fruitful:
worship, salutation, the chanting of mantras, service, constant remembrance, glorification, and the desired hearing of his qualities. (32–33)
O Nārada, by performing these nine characteristics of devotion— offering oneself and serving Him— one makes one's birth fruitful;
no obstacle shall arise for such a person, and their supreme lifespan shall not perish.
Time does not pass him by, just as a serpent cannot overtake Garuḍa;
nor does Hari himself leave his side for even a moment.
The supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, quickly attend upon him.

The Sudarśana discus indeed revolves day and night by his side for his protection at the command of Kṛṣṇa; who indeed is capable of doing him harm? Even the servants of Yama do not approach his presence, even in a dream. (37)

Just as moths do not approach a blazing fire once they have seen it, so too diseases, calamities, sorrows, and even the Brahmins do not approach him. O Sage, Death itself does not go near him out of fear of death. (36–39)
The ṛṣis, munis, siddhas, and all the gods are satisfied;
and he, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, is everywhere free from fear and happy.
And may you always have ultimate delight in the stories of Kṛṣṇa.
For the inherent nature of Janaka certainly resides in his offspring.
O best of Brahmins, what praise could there be for your birth from the mind of Brahmā?
In whatever family one is born, such will be one's disposition. (41–42)
The father is the creator of the worlds, who by means of service to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa constantly and eternally manifests the characteristic of ever-new devotion;
he for whom there is delight in the stories of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the breaking forth of tears and horripilation. (43)
With his mind immersed in that very [Lord], he is called a devotee by the wise.
(44) He who knows everything—sons, wife, and so forth—as belonging to Śrī Hari, and who [serves] with his body, mind, and speech, is called a devotee by the wise. (45)
Those who, free from attachment and filled with joy, meditate upon the lotus feet of Śrī Hari in solitary places or at sacred fords— they are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
They possess compassion for all living beings and perceive this entire world as Kṛṣṇa.
He who knows [this] is a possessor of great wisdom; he is indeed considered a Vaiṣṇava devotee.
Those who constantly sing His names, chant His qualities and mantras, perform the act of hearing, and recite His stories—they are the supreme Vaiṣṇavas.
He whose mind is quickly gladdened to joyfully offer whatever desirable objects he has obtained to Hari— that devotee is the best among the wise.
His mind [is fixed] upon the lotus feet of Hari day and night, both in dreams and in waking consciousness.
That Vaiṣṇava indeed experiences the fruits of his past karma externally.
The wise declare that person to be a most purified Vaiṣṇava into whose ear the Viṣṇu-mantra has fully entered from the mouth of the guru. (50–51)
A devoted person shall rescue seven ancestors from the past, seven descendants from the future, seven maternal grandfathers and their kin, his uterine brothers, his own mother, his mother’s mother,
his wife, his daughter, his kinsmen, his disciple, and his own grandson. (52)
A Vaiṣṇava should always rescue both male and female servants in this manner.
A Vaiṣṇava always desires the touch and sight of holy places;
by association with them, the sins committed by those sinners are destroyed.
For as long as Vaiṣṇavas remain in a place— even for the duration of a single milking—
