all holy pilgrimage sites on the surface of the earth are present there.
Certainly, a sinner who dies there is liberated and goes to the abode of Hari.
In the same way, [the merit] is as great at the confluence of the Gaṅgā of Knowledge, when there is remembrance of Kṛṣṇa,
as it is in a grove of Tulasī, in a cow-pen, in the supreme temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
in Vṛndāvana, at Haridvāra, or in other sacred fords (tīrthas).
The sins of sinners depart through immersion and bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha).
Their sins are destroyed by the breeze from the touch of a Vaiṣṇava;
indeed, the very sins they have committed are unable to remain. 58.
Just as dry grass is quickly consumed in a blazing fire, so too,
whatever men behold a devotee traveling on the path, the sins accumulated by them over seven lifetimes will certainly perish. (59–60)
Those who revile Hṛṣīkeśa, his devotee, or one whose nature is merit—
surely the merit they have earned over a hundred lifetimes perishes.
They are cooked in the most terrible and fearsome Kumbhīpāka hell.
Even if they have been devoured by swarms of insects as long as the moon and sun endure,
merit is certainly destroyed by the mere sight of him.
Only after bathing in the Gaṅgā and bowing to the Sun does the wise man then become purified.
Merely by the touch of a Vaiṣṇava, the sinner becomes liberated;
Madhusūdana, dwelling within his heart, surely destroys his sins.
Thus, O Brahmin, have the qualities of Viṣṇu and the Vaiṣṇava been described.
"Now, listen as I relate to you the birth of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Introduction to the Praise of the Qualities of Viṣṇu and His Devotees," in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Or rather, O Kṛṣṇa, by whom was He entreated that the All-pervading Lord came to the surface of the earth? Having performed this or that on the earth, He returned to His own abode.
[He came] for the means to remove the burden and for the endeavor to slay the wicked.

I shall tell you everything, having reflected well according to the prescribed method. Now, listen as I relate to you how Hari assumed the guise of a cowherd and came to Gokula, and by what means Rādhā became a cowherd girl.
The slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa was previously heard by you in brief; now listen as I relate it to you again in great detail. (4) Furthermore, a quarrel arose between Śrīdāmā and Rādhā.
Śrīdāmā and Śaṅkhacūḍa indeed became [his sons] due to her curse.
Śrīdāmā cursed Rādhā: "Go to a human womb;
having become a cowherd woman in Vraja, wander upon the surface of the earth."
Terrified by the curse of Śrīdāman, she spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"I shall become a gopī, for Śrīdāman has cursed me.
O destroyer of fear, tell me what means I shall employ."
Without you, O Lord of Time, how shall I sustain my own life? Without you, even a single moment would become a hundred yugas;
through the mere absence of the blink of an eye, my mind would become blind.
O Lord, day and night I drink with my two eyes, which are like *cakra* birds, your face that resembles the full autumn moon and is filled with hunger;
you are my self, my mind, and my life-breaths, while I carry only this body. 10.
You are the power of vision and the eye; you are life and supreme wealth.
(11) In dream and in waking knowledge, I remember your lotus feet within my mind.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, I cannot live for even a moment without your service. (12)
Having heard those words, Kṛṣṇa consoled Sundarī;
placing his beloved upon his chest, he made her fearless.
"O fair-faced one, I shall go to the surface of the earth during the Vārāha Kalpa."
I have also determined for you a descent to earth and a birth together with me.
O Goddess, having gone to Vraja, I shall sport with you in the forest of Vraja;
you are dearer to me than my own life—why, then, do you fear while I am present?
Having spoken thus to her, Hari, the Lord of the universe, ceased speaking there.
For this reason, the Lord of the world went to Nanda’s cowherd settlement. What fear could he have of Kaṃsa, he who brings an end to all fears?
Under the very pretext of fear, Māyā went into the presence of Rādhikā.
Having assumed the dress of a cowherd, he sported with her;
and for the sake of fulfilling his vow, he also sported with the cowherd women. (17–18)
Requested by Brahmā, the omnipresent Kṛṣṇa descended to the earth;
having relieved the burden of the world, the Lord returned to his own abode.
(19) Nārada said:
And how did the quarrel between Śrīdāman and Rādhā come about?
Having previously related it in brief, now tell it again in full detail.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, Śrī Hari himself sported with Rādhā in the great forest, in a secluded rāsa-maṇḍala in Goloka. Due to the enjoyment of bliss with Rādhikā, he was not aware of his own self or anything else.
Having built a monastery and departed without asking her, Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to another beautiful gopī named Virajā for the sake of amorous pastimes.
And in the forest of Vṛndāvana, there was a fortunate Virajā who was equal to Rādhikā.
Her companions were hundreds of millions of beautiful gopīs;
that gopī was dearer to Kṛṇa than his own life, blessed among women, and worthy of honor.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, she beheld Hari nearby.
Śrī Hari beheld her, whose face resembled the autumnal moon;
she was enchanting, smiling, and gazing with sidelong glances.
She was eternally sixteen years of age, possessing the blossoming bloom of fresh youth. (25–26)
Seeing her— richly adorned with the splendor of jewel ornaments, decorated with white garments,
her entire body covered in horripilation, and tormented by the arrows of Kāma—
Śrī Hari quickly sported with her.
In a solitary, great forest, within a pavilion of jewels upon a bed of flowers, Virajā fell into a swoon out of curiosity for Kṛṣṇa’s amorous charms;
she placed her Lord of Life, who resembled ten million gods of love, against her breast. (28–29)
Seeing Śrī Hari, who was seated in the jeweled pavilion and embraced by her,
Rādhikā’s friends made their report to her.
Having heard their words, she fell asleep and became angry.
That goddess, whose eyes were like red lotuses, wept bitterly.
She said to them: "O great goddesses, you are capable of showing that [man] to me.
If you speak the truth, come along with me."
"I shall bestow upon Gopī and Kṛṣṇa their due reward.
Who will protect her now while I am inflicting punishment?
Bring Ailā quickly along with her beloved Hari."

With an inner face smiling and a face of nectar upon a vessel of poison, you will not grant me, your servant, permission to come into your presence. Go instead to that very same beautiful pavilion; the Lord protects it. (34–35)
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, some gopīs were filled with fear;
standing before her with their palms joined in reverence, all of them, their necks bowed in devotion, spoke to that beloved and virtuous lady. (36)
The friends said:
"We shall show you that all-pervading Lord together with Virajā.
Having heard their words, the beautiful woman mounted the chariot.
He went together with three hundred and sixty million gopīs.
[The chariot] was fashioned from the essence of the finest jewels, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
and was adorned with thirty million pitchers made of the essence of the finest gems.
It was resplendent with variegated rows [of jewels] and adorned with victory banners;
it was equipped with a hundred thousand wheels, moved at the speed of thought, and was enchanting to the mind.
It was beautifully decorated with ten million pillars fashioned from the finest gems.
Adorned with various wonderful and diverse, most enchanting [ornaments],
they were embellished in their centers with gems having the appearance of vermilion;
and there were artificial lions made of jewels, positioned above the wheels of the chariot.
It was resplendent with four hundred thousand [temples] adorned with variegated bells and enriched by the beauty of diverse,
painted figurines; and it shone with a million pleasure-palaces constructed from the finest gems.
It was adorned with door-panels made of the finest gems and decorated with variegated horses;
it was provided with water-jars made of the essence of the best jewels, radiant with crests,
and furnished with articles for enjoyment as well as materials for attire.
It was adorned with jeweled couches and provided with vessels and jars made of gems;
it was endowed with a multitude of altars made of emeralds,
and possessed tens of millions of staircases made of saffron-colored jewels.
It was beautifully adorned with syamantaka, kaustubha, and excellent rucaka gems,
as well as hundreds of millions of artificial lotuses; it shone,
moreover, with wonderful groves and exquisite ponds.
Its summit was radiant with a pinnacle fashioned from the essence of the finest jewels;
it rose a hundred yojanas high and extended ten yojanas in width,
resplendent with tens of millions of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers.
With the captivating blossoms of *kunda*, *karavīra*, and likewise *yūthikā*;
of the most beautiful *campaka* and *nāgeśa*;
and of the fragrant *mallikā*, *mālatī*, and *mādhavī* flowers. (50–51)
It was resplendent with clusters of kadamba trees and garlands,
and it shone with wreaths of thousand-petaled lotuses;
it was further adorned with gardens of variegated flowers, lakes, and forests.
And among all chariots, it was the supreme Vāyuvaha, the most excellent;
it was covered with the finest of subtle and exquisite cloths,
and was provided with hundreds of thousands of jeweled mirrors.
It was endowed with ten million white yak-tail whisks and ten million vajras;
it was anointed with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
and it shone with ten million couches made of *pārijāta* flowers.
Equipped with millions of bells and joined by millions of banners;
with millions of jeweled couches and variegated vajra-canopies; anointed with sandalwood and decorated with saffron from campaka flowers. (56–57)
Adorned with flower-filled cushions and accompanied by those fit for amorous dalliance,
and embellished with beautiful objects that were both invisible and unheard of—
having swiftly descended from such a chariot, the beloved of Hari [alighted].
O sage, the goddess went suddenly to that jeweled pavilion.
At the entrance, she beheld a charming gatekeeper, surrounded by a hundred thousand cowherds, his lotus-like face smiling. (59–60)
To the cowherd named Śrīdāma, the beloved servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Goddess, her eyes like red lotuses, spoke with anger: "Go far away! Go far away, you servant so greedy for sexual pleasure! (61)

"What kind of beloved woman, devoted to me, shall I see belonging to your master? Having heard these words of Rādhikā, the mighty one, staff in hand, stood fearlessly before her; he did not allow her to depart.
With their lips quivering in anger, Rādhikā and her companions quickly dispatched Śrīdāmā along with his servants by force.
Hearing the tumultuous clamor of the gopīs, Hari himself—
And having realized that Rādhā was enraged, he vanished; indeed,
Viraja vanished at the mere mention of the name "Rādhikā," and seeing Rādhā afflicted by fear, he too gave up his life through yoga.
Instantly, that body there took on the form of a river;
it became a circular expanse pervading Goloka itself,
extending for ten million yojanas across an exceedingly low plateau.
It was ten times as long [as its width], beautiful, and a supreme mine of various jewels.

(68) Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Introduction to the Virajā River," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, having gone to the chamber of love, Rādhā did not see Hari;
seeing Virajā in the form of a river, she went home. Śrī Kṛṣṇa, seeing his virtuous beloved Virajā in the form of a river—
She wept aloud on the banks of the Virajā, which were enchanting with their waters.
"Come near me, O most excellent of beloveds!
O fortunate one, O beautiful lady, how shall I live without you? (2-3)
O Goddess who presides over the river, become manifest in embodied form!
By my blessing, be a beautiful woman, endowed with form, lovely, and the most excellent among women.
From your former appearance, become now even more fortunate through the granting of auspiciousness and other blessings.
"O virtuous one, your former body has become like a river.
Arise from the water and come forth, having assumed an excellent form.
O beautiful goddess, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) have been swiftly granted by me."
And by the command of Kṛṣṇa, Virajā, having assumed an excellent body,
appeared before Hari like the beautiful Rādhā herself—
clad in yellow garments, with a smiling lotus-face. (7)
Beholding her lord of life with sidelong glances,
she— oppressed by the weight of her hips and buttocks, possessing full and elevated breasts,
proud among the proud women, and walking as slowly as a lordly elephant— [beheld him]. (8–9)
She was beautiful among the beautiful, blessed and honored among women;
she possessed the luster of the color of a lovely *campaka* flower, with excellent lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit, and her row of teeth was as enchanting as the seeds of a ripe pomegranate. (10)
Her face is like the full moon of autumn, her eyes are like blossoming blue lotuses;
she is adorned with a dot of musk along with a dot of vermilion, enriched by the beauty of lovely leaf-designs, and endowed with a most beautiful braid of hair. (11–12)
Her cheeks were adorned with jeweled earrings, and she was decorated with a garland of gems;
the tip of her nose was set with elephant-pearls, and she shone with pearl necklaces.
She was radiant, her hands graced by beautiful jeweled bracelets, armlets, and conch-shell ornaments.
Rich with the sound of networks of small bells and adorned with jeweled anklets,
the Lord of the World, upon seeing that beautiful woman, quickly embraced her out of an overflow of love and kissed her again and again. (14–15)
The omnipresent Lord, having obtained his beloved in private, repeatedly engaged in various kinds of amorous play, including inverted positions and the like. She,
though free from passion (*virajā*), became filled with passion (*rajoyuktā*) as she held his infallible seed.
Immediately, right there, that virtuous woman became blessed and pregnant;
she bore the Lord’s child for a hundred divine years,
and then, in that very place, she gave birth to seven beautiful sons.
That mother, the beloved wife of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
remained there seated comfortably together with her seven sons.
Once, in a secluded part of the Vṛndāvana forest, she was with Hari.
The virtuous woman continued to dwell there, her mind intent upon the adornment of her beauty. In the meantime,
her youngest son, tormented by fear of his brothers, went to his mother’s lap.
Seeing her son terrified, that ocean of compassion abandoned her;
she took the child onto her lap, while Kṛṣṇa went to Rādhā’s house.
Having awakened the child, that virtuous woman did not see her beloved by her side.
There, her mind unsatiated with passion, she lamented intensely.
Out of anger, she cursed her own son: "You shall become the salt-water ocean;
never shall any living beings drink your water."
He cursed all the children: "O fools, go to the surface of the earth!
O fools, depart for the enchanting Jambudvīpa on the earth;
you shall have no single place of residence, but shall dwell separately."
May they remain forever happy, establishing their dwellings on every island;
may they sport in solitude with the rivers situated upon those islands.
And due to his mother’s curse, the youngest indeed became the salt-water ocean.
The youngest spoke of the mother’s curse to the boys;
all the boys, filled with sorrow, went to their mother’s place.
Having heard the account, they all descended to the surface of the earth.
Having bowed at their mother’s feet, with bodies humbled by devotion,
the seven oceans and seven continents stood in their respective divisions, O Sage, each doubling in size from the youngest to the eldest. (29–30)
The oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water—
[from these] their waters shall become available upon the earth for the sake of crops.
Thus the seven oceans pervade the earth consisting of seven continents.
All the children wept, overcome with grief for their mother and brothers;
and the virtuous woman wept bitterly, distressed by the separation from her sons,
fainting from sorrow for her sons and for her husband.
Perceiving her submerged in an ocean of grief, the Lord of Rādhikā returned with his lotus-like face beaming with smiles.
Upon seeing Hari, she abandoned both her sorrow and her weeping.
Seeing her beloved, she became immersed in an ocean of bliss. Afflicted by love, she placed Śrī Hari on her lap and sported with him.
And Hari became truly pleased with her, who had been abandoned by her son.
With a gracious countenance and eyes full of affection, He granted her a boon:
"O beloved, I shall certainly come to your abode forever;
you shall become as dear to me as Rādhā herself. (37)
"By the grace of my boon, you shall behold your sons constantly.
Having spoken thus to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was dwelling near Virajā,
Rādhā’s companions saw him and reported this to the Goddess.
Hearing this, the goddess became enraged and went to sleep in her chamber of wrath.
In the meantime, O Nārada, Kṛṣṇa went to the presence of Rādhikā;
he stood at the door of Rādhikā's quarters together with Śrīdāmā.
Seeing Hari at the Rāsa dance, Rāseśvarī became angry and spoke to her beloved before him:
"O Hari, there are many more beautiful women than me in Goloka;
go to their presence—what need have you for me? (41-42)
The beloved Virajā became a river;
even so, having abandoned her body out of fear of me, go toward her.
Having built a temple on her bank, stay, stay, and go toward her!
She became a river, and you ought to become a river as well.
The union of a river with a river is virtuous;
there is supreme affection between those of the same kind, finding pleasure together in resting and in eating.
Oh, alas! Upon hearing that the play of the crest-jewel of the gods with the river has occurred, the great multitude will immediately have smiling faces.
But those who call you the Lord of All—what do they truly know in reality?
"The Blessed One, the soul of all beings, desires to enjoy the river.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Rādhikā, filled with wrath, ceased speaking;
accompanied by hundreds of thousands of gopīs, she did not rise from her bed upon the ground.
Some held chowries in their hands, some wore fine silken garments;
some carried betel-leaves in their hands, and some excellent women held garlands. Some carried scented water, and some excellent women held lotuses in their hands.
Some held vermilion in their hands, and some held wine;
some held jeweled ornaments, and some carried collyrium. Some had flutes and lutes in their hands, and some held combs.
Some had fans in their hands, and some had mechanical instruments in their hands;
some of those most excellent women had fragrant oils in their hands;
some had cymbals in their hands, and some had mirrors in their hands.
Some played the mṛdaṅga, muraja, muralī, and tānaka drums;
some were skilled in vocal music, some were intent on dancing, some held playthings in their hands, and some held honey in their hands. (53–54)
Some held vessels of nectar in their hands, while others held footstools;
some held garments and articles of attire, and some were attendants at her feet.
Some had their hands joined in the *añjali* gesture, and other excellent ones were intent on offering hymns of praise.
O Sage, how many kinds of women are there before Rādhikā?
Some always reside outside in their millions upon millions;
some are appointed at the door as companions and cane-bearers. (56–57)
Standing at the door, they did not allow Kṛṣṇa to enter the interior.
To that Lord of her life standing before her, Rādhā spoke again:
"This is unbecoming, improper to say, unsuitable, and exceedingly harsh. (58)
Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, O beloved of Virajā, O Hari, go before me!
Why do you distress me, O restless one, O most greedy thief of my pleasure? (59)
"Go quickly to Padmāvatī, or to the delightful Ratnamālā;
or else go to Vanamālā, who is peerless in beauty.
O Lord of Rivers, O Lord of Gods, O Teacher of the teachers of the gods! (60)
I have recognized you; may it be well with you. Go, go away from my hermitage!
O you who are ever addicted to the worldly dealings of humans, depart for Bhārata from Goloka and take birth in a human womb.
"O Suśīlā, O Śaśikalā, O Padmāvatī, O Mādhavī!
Let this rogue be turned away; what purpose does he have here?
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, the gopīs spoke to Hari.

Some spoke thus: "O Hari, go to another place for a moment; we shall indeed return once Rādhā’s anger has been dispelled—[that which is] beneficial, true, disciplined, essential, and appropriate for the occasion. (64, 69)
Some spoke thus with affection: "Go for a moment inside the house;
by you alone was Rādhā raised, so whom else will she speak to when you are not here?
O Sage, some spoke thus out of love for Hari regarding Rādhikā.
"Go to Vṛndāvana for a moment, until her pride has been removed," some said to the Lord with joking words; "O lover, remove the pride of this proud woman through devotion. (67–68)
The Kāścanas said: "O Lord, go to that other wife of yours who is so lustful. O Master, how shall we do what is appropriate for one such as you?
Thus spoke the Kāścanas to Hari, who stood before them with a smile.
"Go near and, rising up, perform the removal of my pride.
Thus the gopīs spoke these harsh words to their lord of life:
"Who is now capable of beholding the lotus-face of Rādhikā? (70–71)
Some spoke thus to the Lord: "O Hari, go to another place;
at the time when your anger has subsided, there shall be your return.
Thus did those bold and excellent women speak to him.
"We shall tear you apart if you do not go into another house.
Some of the most excellent women restrained Mādhava—the Lord of All, whose face was smiling, who was composed, free from anger, and the Supreme Master. (73–74)
While the Gopīs were warding off the cause of the cause of the universe,
Śrīdāmā suddenly became enraged once Hari had gone inside the house.
Out of anger, Śrīdāmā spoke to the supreme sovereign Rādhikā.
[She was] angry, with eyes like red lotuses and red lotus-like eyes.
Śrī Dāma said:
"O Mother, why do you speak such harsh words to my lord?"
O Goddess, without due reflection, you utter rebukes in vain.
[He is] Brahmā, Ananteśa, the Lord of Gods, the cause of the causes of the universe; the Lord of Vāṇī, Padmālayā, Māyā, and Prakṛti, and the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). || 77–78 ||

You are performing a mockery against one who delights in his own self and whose desires are fulfilled. Understand that you are the foremost of goddesses, and by whose service you have become the supreme sovereign of all through the mere worship of his feet. (79)
O auspicious lady, do you not know that I am capable of saying this?
By the mere play of a frown, Kṛṣṇa is able to create millions upon millions of goddesses like yourself; yet you do not know Him who is beyond all attributes.
In Vaikuṇṭha, Śrī eternally performs the service of washing the lotus feet of this Śrī Hari with her hair, out of devotion;
and Sarasvatī does so by means of hymns as beautiful as nectar to the ears. (82)
You do not know that Lord whom Prakṛti, who is Māyā and the seed-form of all, constantly praises with devotion;
you do not know him, O proud woman, whom she constantly praises with devotion. (83–84)
The Vedas constantly praise but a sixteenth part of His majesty;
they never know Him, nor do you know Him, O beautiful lady—He whom the all-pervading Brahmā, the progenitor of the Vedas, [praises] with his four mouths. (85)
O Goddess, Śaṅkara, the teacher of yogis, praises and serves his lotus feet with his five faces;
filled with tears and with hair standing on end from joy, he worships his lotus feet. (86–87)

Śeṣa, with his thousand mouths, constantly praises the Supreme Self, the Lord, who serves His lotus feet with devotion. Dharma is the protector of all and the witness of the worlds; he is the Lord of the universe. (88)
And with devotion, he constantly serves his lotus feet with joy—
[he who is] Viṣṇu himself, the all-pervading Lord residing in Śvetadvīpa,
as well as his partial incarnation (aṃśa), and likewise that which is upheld as the supreme Imperishable (akṣara). || 89-90 ||
Even the lords of the gods, asuras, and sages, the Manus, humans, and the wise, do not serve His lotus feet; indeed, they do not behold them even in a dream.
Therefore, quickly casting aside your anger, take refuge in the lotus feet of Hari.
By the mere play of a frown of Him who is the creator and destroyer [of the universe],
the fall of this very Brahmā occurs in the space of a single blink.
Even in a single day of His, twenty-eight Indras fall.
"Thus, for that Creator of the world whose lifespan is one hundred and eight years, who are you, or who else, O Rādhā? Everything is under the control of my Lord.
Having heard these words of Śrīdāman, which were exclusively harsh and brilliant—
O Brahmin, she, the mistress of Hari’s life, immediately became enraged;
the mistress of the *rāsa* dance went outside and spoke harshly to him, her lips quivering, her hair disheveled, and her eyes like red lotuses. (95–96)
Rādhikā said:
"O you wretch, O great fool, listen, you vile servant!
You know every matter, yet you do not know your own master. (97)
"O lowest of the Vraja people, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is your lord, not ours!
You know your own father, yet you constantly praise him and revile your mother, just as the demons and the gods have always and continuously reviled one another. (98)
"Since you revile me thus, O fool, therefore become an asura!
O cowherd, depart from Goloka and enter an asura womb.
You have been cursed by me today, O fool; who is capable of protecting you? (99-100)
Having spoken thus to him, Rāseśvarī fell asleep and ceased her speech.
Her companions served her with chowries and handfuls of jewels.
And having heard her words, his lip quivered with anger.
And Śrīdāmā cursed her, saying, "Go to a human womb.
Śrīdāmā said: "Since you possess anger like that of a human woman, therefore you shall become a human woman on earth. (102)
"You shall become so, of this there is no doubt; you have been cursed by me, O Ambikā.
By means of a shadow, a portion, or even through the influence of another power, a deluded woman named Rāvaṇa’s wife shall speak of you upon the surface of the earth. (103)

Rāpāṇa, a Vaiśya who is a portion of Śrī Hari, will become a great yogi born from a womb in the forest of Vṛndāvana due to Rādhā’s curse. Having reached Kṛṣṇa in Gokula, you shall sport with Him in the woods. (104–105)
"Your separation from Hari shall last for a hundred years;
then, having regained that Lord, you will return to Goloka.
Having spoken thus to her and bowed down, he departed before Hari.
Having gone there and bowed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she related the account of the curse. She told him everything in its proper sequence and wept bitterly once more.
To him who was weeping, he said: "Go to the surface of the earth."

"Indeed, there shall be no conqueror of yours in the three worlds; you shall become the lord of the Asuras. In due time, having cast off this body by the trident of Śaṅkara, you will come into my presence at the end of fifty yugas through my blessing."
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he, overcome with grief, said to him:
"You shall never again make me devoid of devotion to you.
Having spoken thus and bowed to Śrī Hari, he departed from his own hermitage.
Afterwards, that goddess departed and wept again and again;
crying out, "Where are you going, my child? the virtuous lady lamented intensely.
Śrīdāmā also, having bowed to her, wept, overwhelmed with love.
He himself became Śaṅkhacūḍa, the husband of Tulasī.
When Śrīdāman had departed, that goddess went into the presence of the Lord.
She reported everything, and Hari gave her a reply.
And Kṛṣṇa consoled his beloved, who was afflicted with grief.
In due time, Śaṅkhacūḍa met his end,
and Rādhā went to the earth along with Hari during the Vārāha incarnation.
O Sage, he obtained birth in Gokula in the house of Vṛṣabhānu.
Thus, everything has been told—the auspicious narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the essence of all that is desired. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Birth of the Seven Oceans and the Origin of Rādhā’s Curse upon Śrīdāmā," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
By whom was Kṛṣṇa requested, and for what reason did he come to the earth?
The Lord of the World arrived; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas!
Nārāyaṇa said:
Formerly, in the Vārāha-kalpa, that Earth was oppressed by a heavy burden.

She became deeply afflicted with grief and went to Brahmā for refuge. Together with the gods, whose minds were greatly distressed by the oppression of the Asuras, she went to that inaccessible assembly hall of the Creator.
In her, he beheld the Lord of Gods, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
joyfully attended by the lords of sages, the lords of seers, and the lords of perfected beings;
smiling with delight, he was gazing upon the dance of the throngs of Apsarases.
He had heard the enchanting music of the Gandharvas;
he was chanting the two syllables "Kṛṣṇa," the supreme Brahman;
his body was marked with horripilation, and his eyes were filled with tears of blissful devotion. (5–6)

O Sage, having bowed with devotion to the Four-faced One along with the gods, she reported everything—the burden of the Daityas and so forth. With eyes full of tears, her hair standing on end, she praised him and wept. (7)
The Sustainer of the World said to her: "Why do you praise and why do you weep?
O blessed lady, tell me how you have come; it shall turn out well for you.
Be firm, O auspicious one; what fear can there be for you while I am present?"
Having comforted the earth, Brahmā respectfully questioned the gods:
"O gods, how have you come into my presence?
Hearing these words of Brahmā, the gods spoke to the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati): [9–10]
O Lord, the earth is oppressed by burdens and we are seized by bandits;
you alone are the creator of the worlds, so quickly provide us with relief.
O Brahman, you are our refuge; it behoves you to grant us peace.

"O Grandfather, we are afflicted with suffering by that very burden by which this earth is oppressed; therefore, remove that burden. Having heard the words of the gods, the Ordainer of the World questioned her.
"Cast away your fear, my child; stay happily near me.
O lotus-eyed one, whom are you unable to bear as a burden?
O blessed lady, I shall remove it; prosperity will surely be yours. (14)
Having heard his words, she whose face and eyes were serene spoke to him regarding her own suffering— she who was thus afflicted by this or that. (15) The Earth said:
Listen, my dear, I shall speak of my own mental anguish.
One ought not to speak to anyone other than a trusted kinsman. (16) The female species is eternally weak and must be protected by her own kin.
O father of the world, I have been censured by Janaka, Svāmiputra, and others who are well-acquainted with me; yet, when questioned by you, I feel no shame in speaking.
Listen as I tell you of those whose burdens have oppressed me. (17–18)
Those who are devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and those who revile His devotees—
these great sinners are incapable of bearing even my weight.
(19) Those who are devoid of the practice of their own dharma and who have abandoned their daily obligatory duties;

Those who lack faith in the Vedas are oppressed by their burden. Those who do not provide sustenance for their father, mother, teacher, wife, sons, or dependents are likewise incapable of bearing a burden. (20–21)
O dear one, I am oppressed by the burden of those who speak falsely, who are devoid of compassion and truth, and who revile their gurus and gods;
as well as by the burden of the betrayer of friends, the ungrateful, and the giver of false testimony. (22)
I am oppressed by the burden of those who betray trust and those who misappropriate deposits;
[I am oppressed] by the burden of those who indeed sell auspicious hymns, Sāman chants, and the singularly auspicious name of Hari. (23–24)
The killer of living beings, the traitor to his guru, the village priest, the hunter, the cremator of corpses, and the eater of food from a Śūdra—by the weight of these, she was oppressed.
Her various vows, such as worship, sacrifice, fasting, and other observances [were likewise burdened]. (25)
Oppressed by the burden of those fools who cause destruction;
oppressed by the burden of those wicked ones who always hate cows, brāhmaṇas, gods, and Vaiṣṇavas, as well as Hari, the stories of Hari, and devotion. (26–27)
"O Creator, I am oppressed by the weight of Śaṅkha and the others;
I am even more thoroughly oppressed by the weight of the Daityas who are superior to them.
Thus was the entire report of my suffering related.
"If I am to be well protected by you, O Lord, then provide a remedy.
Having spoken thus, the Earth wept again and again.
Seeing her weeping, Brahmā, the ocean of compassion, spoke to her.
"I shall remove your burden even by means of the Dasyus;
for even through strategic means, O Earth, all tasks are indeed accomplished.
In due time, my Lord will effect the removal of the burden."
The mantra, the auspicious jar, the Śiva-liṅga, saffron,
madhuka wood, sandalwood, musk, clay from a sacred ford (tīrtha),
a fragment of a sword-blade, crystal, and ruby. 32–33.
Sapphire, sun-crystal, rudrākṣa, the root of kuśa grass,
the śālagrāma stone, the conch, tulasī, an image, water,
the conch, a row of lamps, a sacred stone fit for worship, and a bell. (34)
One should likewise offer flower remains (*nirmālya*), food offerings (*naivedya*), an emerald,
a consecrated sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) with knots, a mirror, a white chowrie,
yellow orpiment, a pearl, a mother-of-pearl shell, and a ruby.
The Purāṇa-saṃhitā, fire, camphor, and likewise an axe;
silver, gold, coral, and indeed gems; Kuśa seeds, water from sacred fords, and products of the cow—cow's urine and cow dung. (36–37)
O beautiful one, those fools who shall place these [images] upon you will certainly be cooked in the Kālasūtra hell for ten thousand years.
Brahmā, having consoled the Earth together with the deities, [departed].

The Creator of the worlds went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara. Having reached that delightful hermitage, Vidhi beheld Śaṅkara dwelling at the foot of the imperishable banyan tree on the bank of the celestial river.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with the bones of Dakṣa’s daughters, he held a trident and a battle-axe;
he was five-faced and three-eyed, surrounded by various siddhas and served by hosts of lords of yogins. (41)
He was looking all around with a smile and joy at the dance of the Apsarases, and out of curiosity he was listening to the music of the Gandharvas;
he was gazing with affection at Pārvatī with his sidelong glance. (42–43)
He was chanting the single auspicious name of Hari with his five mouths,
his body marked by horripilation as he held a rosary made of lotus seeds from the Mandākinī;
in that interval, Brahmā stood before that Dhūrjaṭi.
Together with the earth and the hosts of gods, their necks bowed low,
Śaṅkara rose quickly upon seeing the Teacher of the World with devotion;
he prostrated with his head out of great affection and then received blessings from him.
All the deities bowed down to Śaṅkara, who bears the moon upon his crest.
The Earth prostrated herself with devotion, and Hara bestowed his blessing upon her.
Then Prajāpati related the entire account to the Lord of Pārvatī.
Upon hearing this, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, quickly lowered his face.
Having heard of the distress of their devotee, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord became afflicted with grief; then Brahmā enlightened them both.
Then Brahmā and Maheśa, having diligently consoled the hosts of gods and the Earth, sent them back to their home.
Thereupon, the lords of the gods quickly arrived at the abode of Dharma.
Having deliberated with him, they went to the abode of Hari—
the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha, the highest station that removes old age and death,
sustained by Vāyu, and most excellent, situated above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Extending ten million yojanas upward from the world of Brahmā is that eternal realm,
wondrously fashioned of jewels, which cannot be described by poets;
it is adorned with royal highways made of rubies and sapphires.
All those gods, traveling by mind, reached that enchanting inner apartment of Hari; having entered it, they beheld Śrī Hari seated upon a jeweled throne and adorned with ornaments of gems. (54)
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets;
shining upon the regions of his cheeks with a pair of jeweled earrings;
clothed in yellow garments and embellished with a forest garland. 95–96.
Peaceful, beloved of Sarasvatī, with his lotus feet held by Lakṣmī; possessing the grace of ten million Cupids, with a smiling face and four arms;
served by his attendants Sunanda, Nanda, and Kumuda. (57)

O Sage, the lords of the gods, including Brahmā and others, bowed with devotion before Him, whose every limb was anointed with sandalwood paste, who shone with a crown of supreme jewels, who is the embodiment of supreme bliss, and who bestows grace upon His devotees. (58)
With their necks bowed in devotion, they praised him with supreme faith;
overwhelmed by the weight of supreme bliss, their bodies were covered in horripilation.
(99) Brahmā said: I bow to the beloved of Kamalā, the peaceful, the infallible one who grants all desires.
We gods,
the Manus, the lords of sages, and human beings, as well as all moving and unmoving entities,
are but fragments of Your portions— born from You, O stainless one, by means of a minute fraction of a fraction of a portion. (60–61)

Śaṅkara said: [I bow to] you—the imperishable and the unchanging, the manifest and the unmanifest, the Lord, who is without beginning yet possesses a beginning, whose form is bliss, and who embodies all forms. (62)

Who is capable of praising Him, the cause of the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, the cause of all causes, the knower of success, the bestower of success, and whose very form is success? (63) Dharma said:
The wise should describe that reality which is established in the Veda;
for who is capable of explaining that which is ineffable in the Veda? That stainless one whose qualities and form are beyond conception—[who can describe Him]? (64)
Apart from that, what praise can I offer to the one who is devoid of attributes?
O great sage, by reciting this hymn of six verses addressed to Brahmā and the other gods, a person is liberated from distress and obtains their desires. (69)
Having heard the praise of the gods, Hari himself said to them:
"Go you to Goloka; I shall go afterwards with Śrī.
As for those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, they are residents of Śvetadvīpa."
These shall go to Goloka, as will the goddess Sarasvatī, my infinite Māyā, Kārttikeya, the lord of the Gaṇas, and Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas; they will certainly follow after him. (68)
There, I am the two-armed Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā and the gopīs;
here, I am joined with Kamalā and surrounded by Sunanda and others. And as Nārāyaṇa, I am Kṛṣṇa who dwells in Śvetadvīpa.
"All these gods, beginning with Brahmā, are known as my very own portions (kalās).
By a minute fraction of a portion of a portion (kalā-kalāṃśa-kalayā), the gods, demons, humans, and others [are formed].
Go now to Goloka, and your purpose shall be accomplished."
"We shall follow behind for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal of everyone.
Having spoken thus in the midst of the assembly, Hari himself became silent.
Having bowed to all the deities, they departed for the wondrous Goloka.
It is a wondrous, supreme abode, the highest remover of old age and death.
Extending fifty crore yojanas above Vaikuṇṭha,
it is supported by the wind and fashioned by the will of the All-pervading Lord.
And that garden was indescribable; eager to depart, those gods, all traveling as fast as thought, reached the bank of the Virajā river. Seeing the riverbank, the gods were filled with supreme wonder.
Resembling pure crystal, it was very extensive and captivating;
it was endowed with mines of pearls, rubies, and supreme jewels, and it shone with rows of black, white, yellow, and red gems. (76–77)
In some places, beautiful coral sprouts had emerged;
it was adorned with rows of mines of the finest, priceless gems, and endowed with the most wonderful sources of the Creator’s invisible treasures. (78)
O Sage, in some places it was a source of rubies and sapphires;
in other places it was endowed with rows of emerald mines;
in some places there were mines of syamantaka gems, and in others mines of rucaka gems.
In some places it possessed the luster of priceless yellow gold and was endowed with mines of excellent gemstones; in some places it was a mine of jewels, and in others a mine of the Kaustubha gem;
in other places it was a supreme mine of jewels that are beyond description.

Having seen here and there various excellent and delightful places of residence— truly a supreme wonder— the lords went to its further shore. There they beheld the most beautiful Śataśṛṅga, the best of mountains.
It was resplendent with rows of groves of *pārijāta* trees,
surrounded and encircled by *kalpa* trees and *kāmadhenu* cows;
it extended ten times further in length than its height of ten million *yojanas*.
Measuring fifty billion yojanas, it is the size of a mountain plateau.
Upon its very summit is the Rāsa-maṇḍala, shaped like a rampart, ten yojanas in extent, circular in form, and most excellent. (85–86)
It was filled with thousands of flowering and fragrant flower gardens,
crowded with swarms of bees;
it shone with pleasure-palaces furnished with all the requisites for amorous delight.
It was endowed with thousands of millions of jeweled pavilions (88),
furnished with jeweled staircases and excellent jeweled pitchers,
and adorned by pillars made of emeralds (89).
It was encrusted all around with rubies the color of vermilion,
adorned with captivating sapphires set in the center,
and it shone with various kinds of gems forming a jeweled rampart.
It was adorned with four doors fitted with panels,
provided with cords and knots and hung with mango sprouts,
and surrounded on all sides by clusters of plantain trunks.
O Sage, it was endowed with white grains, leafy clusters, fruits, and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass;
it was anointed with the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
and it was surrounded by millions of groups of cowherd girls.
Adorned with jewel ornaments, resplendent with garlands of gems;
decorated with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and jeweled anklets;
and graced on the cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings. (94–95)
Their hands were resplendent with fingers graced by beautiful jeweled rings,
and their toes shone with clusters of jeweled anklets;
they were adorned with precious ornaments and radiant with crowns of excellent gems.
Adorned with ornaments of pearls from the lord of elephants shining upon his trunk,
together with a dot of vermilion, radiant at the base of his forehead;
possessing the beautiful hue of campaka flowers and anointed with liquid sandalwood paste.
Clad in yellow garments, with lips as enchanting as the bimba fruit, their radiant faces eclipsed the splendor of the full autumn moons;
with eyes that robbed the beauty of autumn-blooming lotuses. (99)
Adorned with musk-encrusted vessels, radiant with lines of applied kajjala,
graced by clusters of full-blown mālatī garlands, and beautified by their braided locks (kabara),
they were further crowded by swarms of bees greedy for honey and intent on its scent.
By her very graceful gait, which eclipsed the movement of elephants and *khañjana* birds; by her arched eyebrows joined with smooth smiles;
and by her row of teeth shining like the seeds of a ripe pomegranate. (101–102)
Adorned with prominent noses as beautiful as the beaks of the king of birds, they were bent by the weight of their breasts which resembled the pair of temples of a lordly elephant;
they were bowed down by the heavy burden of their firm hips and full buttocks. (103)
Their minds were shattered by the amorous gestures of the god of love;
they were eager to behold the beauty of the Full Moon’s face reflected in mirrors, and their hearts were devoted to the service of Rādhikā’s lotus feet. (104–105)
It was protected by throngs of beautiful women at the command of Rādhikā,
and it was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of pleasure-lakes encircled by white, red, crimson, and ruby-hued lotuses. (106)
It was always filled with swarms of honey-bees humming sweetly,
endowed with thousands of flowering flower-gardens, and possessed of ten million bower-cottages furnished with beds of flowers. (106–107)
O Sage, it was adorned with enjoyments, wealth, camphor, betel, and garments;
surrounded on all sides by jewel-lamps, white chowries, and mirrors;
and beautified by various garlands of flowers. (109)
Having seen that circle of cowherds, they went out from the mountain.
Then they beheld a wise, delightful, and beautiful forest—the forest named Vṛndāvana, dear to Rādhā and Mādhava. (110–111)
Their very playground was filled with groves of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa),
stirred by gentle breezes moistened by the waters of the Virajā river,
and made fragrant by heaps of flowers and lotus leaves smeared with musk.
Where is there a place as lovely as this, filled with the warbling of cuckoos perched upon fresh sprouts (113), and adorned with clusters of *helika* and *kadaṃba* trees,
as well as *mandāra*, *campaka*, and *candana* trees? (114)
The forest was made fragrant by the scent of sweet-smelling flowers; it was a grove of gods, filled with clusters of mangoes, oranges, jackfruit trees,
as well as palmyra palms and coconut trees.
O Nārada, [there were trees] of rose-apples, jujubes, and especially dates; of wood-apples, hog-plums, and citrons;
and of plantains, bilva-fruits, and pomegranates—[all] most beautiful. (116–117)
It was resplendent with clusters of trees laden with well-ripened fruit—
of *pippalī*, *śāla*, and likewise *aśvattha* trees;
and it was beautified by lovely *nimba*, *śālmali*, and *tittiḍī* trees.
It was always crowded with clusters of various other trees;
it shone on all sides with multitude upon multitude of *kalpa* trees;
and there were *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *kunda*, *ketakī*, and *mādhavī* creepers. (119–120)
O Sage, it was filled with clusters of these [flowers] along with *yūthikā* blossoms, and with those fifty crores of charming bower-cottages,
illuminated by jewel-lamps and made fragrant with incense.
It was perfumed by scented breezes carrying the fragrance of erotic unguents;
it was furnished with couches of flowers anointed with sandalwood and adorned with networks of garlands;
and it resounded with the sweet warbling of bees greedy for honey as they smelled the nectar.
He was surrounded by throngs of gopīs resplendent with the beauty of jewel ornaments, and protected by fifty million gopīs under the command of Rādhikā. (124)
There, the grove of thirty-two [trees] is delightful, most beautiful, and captivating to the mind.
An excellent, secluded place situated within Vṛndāvana.
O Sage, [he was] like a celestial being with fruits that were perfectly ripe, sweet, and delicious.
And it was filled with assemblies of cow-pens and herds of cattle.
With a thousand flowering and fragrant flower gardens.
It was filled with swarms of bees greedy for honey and intent on its scent.
And it was resplendent with the amorous sports of fifty crores of gopīs.
Of those whose forms were equal to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the chariots were] with excellent [parts] encrusted with fine jewels. 128.
Having beheld the beautiful Vṛndāvana, the lords went to Goloka.
It is circular in shape all around and extends for ten million yojanas. || 129 ||
O Sage, it was encircled by a wall of jewels, endowed with four gates, and provided with hosts of cowherds and gatekeepers. (130)
With hermitages inlaid with jewels and endowed with various enjoyments.
Accompanied by fifty crores of gopīs who were servants of Kṛṣṇa. ||131||
With hundreds of millions of hermitages belonging to the hosts of cowherd devotees.
It was further endowed with exceedingly vast [ornaments] strung with excellent jewels. ||132||
And by means of the hermitages of the attendants, which were even more distinguished and extraordinary than those.
It was joined by ten crores of the foremost attendants, who bore the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and were adorned with priceless jewels. || 133 ||
It was endowed with ten million hermitages constructed from excellent jewels.
By means of the excellent hermitages of the gopīs, who are the pure devotees of Rādhikā.
It was endowed with thirty-two crores of materials fashioned from the seven precious gems (sadratna),
and adorned by ten crores of most enchanting palaces for those female attendants, constructed from jewels, gems, and other precious substances. (135–136)
Those devotees on the land of Bhārata who have been purified by austerities performed over a hundred lifetimes.
And those who are devoted to the worship of Hari and who bring about liberation through their actions. || 137 ||
O sage, their minds were intensely absorbed in dreams, in knowledge, and in meditation upon Hari.
Chanting "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa" and "Kṛṣṇa" day and night. || 138 ||
By the most enchanting dwellings of those devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Constructed from excellent gems and jewels, and endowed with various articles of enjoyment. || 139 ||
Adorned with flower-beds, flower-garlands, and white chowries; enriched by the splendor of jeweled mirrors and set with emeralds (marakata);
possessing crests joined with clusters of priceless jewel-pitchers; and covered within with fine fabrics—[the city was] endowed with hundreds of millions [of such palaces]. (140–141)
Having seen that wonder, the gods went a certain distance away with joy.
There, the lords of the world beheld the beautiful Akṣayavaṭa tree. || 142 ||
O Sage, it is five yojanas wide at its base and twice that height.
Endowed with a thousand trunks and possessed of the arrangement of branches.
It was strewn with ripe red fruits and adorned with jeweled pedestals.
At the foot of that tree, they beheld their beloved children, who were of the very form of Kṛṣṇa.
Clad in yellow garments, they were enchanting and intent on play.
There they saw the foremost attendants of Hari, their entire bodies anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments. Then,
not far from there, they beheld a charming royal highway.
O Sage, it was surrounded by a jeweled pavilion fashioned from gems the color of vermilion,
as well as sapphire, ruby, diamond,
and emerald, and it was provided with altars constructed all around.
Smeared with the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
provided with curd, parched grain, fruits, flowers, and sprouts of dūrvā grass;
and adorned with the tender leaves of śrīkhaṇḍa tied with knots of fine thread. (148–149)
It was resplendent with clusters of plantain pillars smeared with saffron,
and with jars adorned with excellent gems and provided with branches bearing fruit;
these were likewise anointed with vermilion and saffron, and smeared with fragrant sandalwood.
It was adorned with trees decorated with flower garlands,
surrounded by throngs of cowherd girls intent on their play, and featured jeweled staircases fashioned from precious gems. 151–152.
They were resplendent with garments as pure as fire, beautiful white chowries and mirrors, and various flower garlands upon wonderful jeweled couches;
they were provided with sixteen gates and guarded by gatekeepers. (153)

Seeing those delightful mansions on all sides surrounded by moats and encircled by walls of jewels, and anointed with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron, those gods became eager to depart. (154–155)
They traveled quickly for some distance and then beheld a beautiful hermitage, O Nārada, belonging to Rādhikā, the Queen of the Rāsa dance,
the Goddess of gods, and the most excellent of gopīs— a place wonderfully constructed.
Belonging to Kṛṣṇa, who is dearer than life itself, it is enchanting with its beautiful objects;
it is entirely indescribable and has not been fully defined even by the learned.
It is of a very lovely circular shape and measures six gavyūtis in extent. (157–158)
It was endowed with a hundred palaces, blazing with the luster of jewels;
it was a magnificent structure fashioned from heaps of priceless, exquisite gems, and it was beautifully adorned with deep moats that were impossible to cross. (159)
It was surrounded by wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and interspersed with hundreds of flower gardens;
it was encircled by walls inlaid with highly precious gems, provided with pedestals of fine jewels, and equipped with seven gates. (160–161)
O Sage, it is circular and adorned with various joined jewels;
O Sage, from the seven principal gates, it is arranged step by step;
and thus, on all sides, it is provided there with sixteen doors.
And having seen the wall, a thousand bows in height,
adorned with clusters of beautiful small jars made of excellent jewels,
blazing with splendor and most delightful, the gods were filled with supreme wonder. (163–164)
Then, having circumambulated [it], they went some distance with joy;
as they proceeded forward, that hermitage remained behind them,
and they beheld other hermitages belonging to cowherds and cowherdesses.
O Sage, repeatedly beholding all around the entire hermitage— both that of the cowherds and that of the cowherd-maidens— which was fashioned from priceless jewels numbering a hundred crores,
and which was ever more delightful and ever newer; (166–167)
Having beheld the entirety of Goloka, the gods went forth with their limbs bristling with joy;
they saw that very same delightful forest of Vṛndāvana in its circular form, as well as Mount Śataśṛṅga and the Virajā river outside of it. (368)
The gods went to that stainless realm and saw it as entirely empty;
they beheld Goloka, which is supported by the wind, composed of excellent jewels, and wonderful, fashioned by the will of the Lord through the influence of Rādhikā’s command. (169–170)
Joined by thousands of lakes, that place was exclusively an abode of auspiciousness.
There the gods beheld a most enchanting dance, as well as the beautiful singing of the daughters [of the sages], which was imbued with the virtues of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. (171)
O Sage, upon merely hearing the nectar of that song, the gods fell into a swoon;
then, regaining consciousness in an instant, those gods, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, beheld a supreme wonder, enchanting in every place. (172–173)
All the gopīs, assuming various costumes, were seen;
some held mṛdaṅga drums in their hands, while others, excellent women, held vīṇās;
some held chowries in their hands, and others had their palms joined in rhythmic clapping.
Some had hands playing musical instruments and were adorned with jeweled anklets;
those excellent women resounded with the sound of a network of fine jewel-bells. Others had jar-like breasts and were intent on various types of dance. (175–176)
Some were heroines dressed as men, and some of them were heroes dressed as heroines;
some wore the attire of Kṛṣṇa, while others wore the attire of Rādhā;
some were weary of union, and others delighted in embracing.
Seeing them absorbed in play, the Lords of the Universe smiled;
O Nārada, as they proceeded for some distance, they beheld many hermitages and the residences of Rādhā’s principal companions.
There, indeed, were thirty-three gopī companions of Rādhikā who were her equals in form, in virtues, in dress, in youth, in loveliness, and in age. (180)
Their attire was indescribable; now hear their names:
Suśīlā, Śaśikalā, Yamunā, Mādhavī, Ratī, Kadaṃbamālā, Kuntī, Jāhnavī, and Svayaṃprabhā. (181–182)
Candramukhī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Sumukhī, Sukhā; Padmālayā, Pārijātā, Gaurī, and Sarvamaṅgalā;
Kālikā, Kamalā, Durgā, Bhāratī, and Sarasvatī. (183)
Gaṅgā, Ambikā, Madhumatī, Campā, Aparṇā, Sundarī,
Kṛṣṇapriyā, Satī, Nandinī, and Nandanā—
these are her equals, fashioned from excellent jewels, and beloved by Rādhikā. (184–185)
These [palaces], uniform in form, variegated with precious gems and elements,
adorned with various kinds of wonderful patterns, and exceedingly beautiful,
shone with peaks crowned by clusters of priceless jewel-vases. (185)
They likewise beheld white hermitages constructed of the seven precious gems.
(187) Furthermore, there is no world above the Egg of Brahmā;
everything above it is composed of emptiness, and creation itself ends there. (188)

There is no creation whatsoever below the seven netherworlds (rasātala). Beneath those is water, darkness, the unattainable, and the invisible. Listen to me regarding everything from the end of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and beyond. 189.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Goloka," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having beheld the entirety of Goloka, those gods were delighted in their hearts.
They returned once more to the very main gate of Rādhā’s palace,
which was constructed of excellent gems and jewels and featured a pair of altars made of turmeric-colored gemstones interspersed with diamonds.
They beheld the unsurpassed Vīrabhānu stationed at the gate, adorned with a door-panel fashioned from priceless jewels;
he was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and embellished with ornaments of gems.
Clad in yellow garments and radiant with a crown of excellent jewels,
they joyfully presented everything to the gatekeeper at the most wonderful and marvelous door, which was variegated with diverse and brilliant colors. (4–5)
The gatekeeper spoke fearlessly to those lords of the gods:
"I am not currently authorized to let anyone enter or grant passage without a command.
He then dispatched his servants to the very abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O Sage, having obtained the permission of Hari, he allowed the gods to depart.
After conversing with him, the gods went toward the second, most excellent gate—which was even more wonderful, beautiful, and captivating. (Verses 5–7)
And they saw Candrabhānu, who was stationed at the gate, O Nārada—
a beautiful youth, dark-complexioned, holding an excellent golden cane,
seated upon a jeweled throne, and adorned with ornaments of gems. (9)
Adorned by a multitude of cowherds numbering five hundred thousand,
the gods addressed him and proceeded to the third, most excellent gate;
which was exceedingly beautiful, variegated, and blazing with the luster of jewels.
And at the gate, O Nārada, they beheld Sūryabhānu,
a two-armed youth, darkly beautiful, with a flute in his hand,
and his cheeks radiant with a pair of jeweled earrings. (12)
They sent that most excellent messenger, who held a jewel-studded staff and was the supreme servant of the Lord of Rādhā;
surrounded by nine hundred thousand cowherds like a sovereign of kings,
the gods addressed him and proceeded to the fourth gate.

They beheld Vasubhānu, the lord of Vraja, stationed at the gate— he who was distinct from them, delightful, brilliantly radiant with the luster of jewels, adorned with most wonderful and diverse ornaments, and exceedingly captivating. (15)
A youthful and most beautiful youth, with hands holding jeweled staffs, supreme;
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and adorned with jewel ornaments;
with lips like the ripe bimba fruit, smiling, and exceedingly charming. (16–17)
Having addressed him, the gods proceeded to the fifth gate,
which was brilliantly illuminated by various wonderful paintings situated upon diamond walls.
There, they indeed beheld the gatekeeper Devabhānu.
Seated upon a beautiful throne, adorned with ornaments of jewels;
with a crest of peacock feathers and decorated with a necklace of gems;
radiant with excellent jeweled earrings set with kadamba flowers. (19–20)
Anointed with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
and equal in splendor to the best of great kings, he was surrounded by ten million subjects.
Having conversed with that staff-bearer, the gods departed filled with joy.

They beheld the Lord of Vraja, Śukrabhānu, stationed at a gate that was unique, adorned with sixfold rows of variegated patterns, flanked by a pair of diamond walls, and decorated with garlands of flowers. (22–23)
Richly adorned with the splendor of various ornaments and accompanied by ten million subjects,
his cheeks touched by the sprouts of sandalwood and radiant with earrings—
the gods, having addressed him, quickly went to the seventh gate.
They beheld the beloved of Hari stationed at the gate— a being of manifold and variegated forms, utterly distinct from the six [elements], radiant with the luster of jewels,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands of flowers. (25)
Adorned with beautiful ornaments and captivating jewels of precious gems,
he shone like a lord of kings accompanied by twelve hundred thousand cowherds;
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, his lotus-like face was smiling.
Having addressed him who held a staff in his hand, the lords of the gods departed with joy.
They beheld the eighth gate, which was wondrous and distinct even from the seven;
they saw its gatekeeper, Supārśva, who was exceedingly beautiful.
Smiling, the most excellent of the beautiful, radiant with a sandalwood tilaka,
his lower lip like the bandhujīva flower, adorned with jeweled earrings,
enriched by the splendor of all ornaments, and holding a staff of jewels— [he is] the Supreme Lord. (29–30)
Accompanied by twelve hundred thousand cowherds and young calves,
the gods then quickly went to the desired ninth gate,
which was constructed of excellent diamonds and gems and provided with four altars.
They beheld [the palace] resplendent with networks of garlands fashioned in unprecedented and variegated designs;
and they saw the gatekeeper Subala, of graceful form, enriched by the beauty of various ornaments, worthy of adornment, and captivating. (32–33)
Adorned with twelve hundred thousand vajras and exceedingly beautiful,
they addressed him who held a staff in his hand and proceeded toward the gate.
Seeing that distinguished tenth gate, they were filled with wonder.
O Sage, they beheld one who was entirely indescribable, unseen and unheard before;
they saw the gatekeeper Sudāmā,
beautiful and charming, whose form was indescribable, like that of Kṛṣṇa himself.
Surrounded by hosts of twenty-one million cowherds,
the gods, upon merely seeing him with staff in hand, went to another gate—
the eleventh gate, which was most variegated, great, and wonderful. (37)
And there he saw Śrīdāmā, the lord of Vraja, standing as the gatekeeper;
he was equal to the son of Rādhikā, adorned with yellow garments, and seated upon a jeweled throne fashioned from priceless gems. (38–39)
Adorned with ornaments of priceless jewels, it was exceedingly beautiful;
it shone with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron;
and it was radiant with excellent jeweled earrings that graced its cheeks and temples.
Resplendent with a variegated crown fashioned from the finest of the seven jewels;
adorned on all his limbs with clusters of garlands of full-blown mālatī flowers; surrounded by ten million cowherds; and more brilliant than the king of kings. (41–42)
Having conversed with him, the gods joyfully went to the gate known as the twelfth,
which was provided with altars fashioned from priceless jewels;
it was a wondrous sight, O Sage, difficult for all to attain, unseen and unheard of before.

The gods beheld a beautiful and most enchanting painting situated upon a diamond wall at the gate; it was watched over by excellent cowherd women, endowed with fresh youth and adorned with jewel ornaments. (44–45)
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with heavy braided hair,
they were decorated on all their limbs with networks of fragrant mālatī garlands;
they were further embellished with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and jeweled anklets.
Adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings that illuminated their cheeks,
they were anointed with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
they were bent low by the weight of their full hips and oppressed by the burden of their buttocks.
The most excellent and beloved of even Hari among the hundreds of millions of gopīs—
seeing those gopīs by the tens of millions, the gods were filled with wonder.
O Sage, having conversed with them joyfully, they departed through the gateway.

And then, O Brahmin, they gradually beheld at those three gates the most excellent women among the cowherds— extremely captivating, the best of the best, beautiful, blessed, venerable, and splendid. (50–51)
They were all endowed with good fortune and were dear to Rādhikā;
they were adorned with beautiful ornaments and possessed the fresh bloom of youth.
Having thus seen the three gateways, he heard of this wonderful dream through his knowledge.
Invisible, exceedingly beautiful, and indescribable even by the wise—
having conversed with those various goddesses, the astonished lords departed for the sixteen-gated, enchanting entrance within the interior of Rādhikā.
O Sage, he was the foremost of them all, protected by throngs of cowherd women and surrounded by a multitude of thirty-three companions,
endowed with their various and inexpressible qualities. (55)
Endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with jewel ornaments,
decorated with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and jeweled anklets,
and graced upon their hips with networks of excellent jeweled bells. (56–57)
Adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings that illuminated their cheeks,
and with clusters of blossoming mālatī garlands shining upon their chests;
with moon-like faces that eclipsed the splendor of the full-moon autumn lotuses.
Enveloped by a multitude of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers,
with lower lips like ripe *bimba* fruits and lotus-faces smiling,
they were adorned with rows of teeth resembling the seeds of ripe pomegranates. (59–60)
O Sage, they shone with trunks having the hue of beautiful campaka flowers, slender at the waist,
adorned with elephant-pearls,
and possessing the warm luster of the lovely beaks of the king of birds.
Bowed down by the weight of their breasts, which were as firm as the temples of lordly elephants,
and oppressed by the burden of their full hips, those goddesses— whose minds were fixed on the feet of Mukunda and who were devoid of blinking— beheld the door. (62–63)
It was beautified by a pair of altars made of *lasadramaṇi* jewels,
and it was always joined by clusters of pillars made of emeralds.
Its central area shone with gems having the appearance of vermilion.
Adorned with networks of garlands made of *pārijāta* blossoms,
and rendered fragrant everywhere by the breezes carrying their touch—
the gods beheld that supreme wonder within the inner chamber of Rādhikā. (65–66)

With their bodies covered in horripilation, their necks slightly bowed, and their eyes filled with tears from the overflow of devotion, they departed quickly after speaking with him, their sole desire being the sight of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (67)
From afar, the gods beheld the excellent inner chamber of Rādhikā (68),
situated in the midst of the mansions, a charming four-winged hall (catuḥśāla),
most exquisite, constructed from the essence of priceless jewels. (69)

It was adorned with pillars made of various gems and jewels set in vajra-frames, and it shone with networks of garlands of *pārijāta* flowers; it was further graced by clusters of pearls, rubies, white yak-tail whisks, and mirrors. (70)
O Sage, it was adorned with jars filled with the essence of priceless jewels;
its beautiful courtyard was embellished by clusters of jeweled pillars, each tied with knots of fine silk thread and provided with sprouts of sandalwood. (71–72)
Combined with the liquids of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
together with white grains, white flowers, coral, fruits, and rice;
with leaves, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, parched grain, and decorated with nirmocana—(73).
It was resplendent with jeweled jars filled with fruit and adorned with vermilion and saffron, and graced by garlands of *pārijāta* flowers;
it was made fragrant everywhere by scented breezes laden with blossoms. (74–75)

It was adorned with all manner of substances that are indescribable and undefined, and it shone with whatever rare objects exist within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); it was beautifully embellished with clusters of garlands made from the blossoms of the Pārijāta tree.
O Nārada, they were elegantly reclining on beds of jewels, covered with garments of fine cloth; there were millions of jeweled jars and precious vessels, as well as beautiful, priceless ornaments,
all of which adorned them.
Resounding with the sounds produced by various kinds of musical instruments,
and beautifully heard through the lutes and stringed instruments of the gopīs’ music,
it was enchanted, O Nārada, by the sounds of the drums and cymbals.
Surrounded by throngs of cowherds who were equal to Kṛṣṇa himself, and resplendent with numerous groups of gopīs who were the companions of Rādhā;
it was beautifully filled with the sound of songs concerning the abundance of the virtues of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. (80–81)
Having thus beheld the interior, the gods were filled with wonder.
They heard sweet singing and witnessed an exquisite dance.
There, all the gods stood with their minds absorbed in one-pointed meditation.
The lords of the thirty gods beheld a beautiful jeweled lion-throne,
measuring a hundred bows in circumference and circular in shape,
and provided with clusters of small jars made of excellent gems. (83–84)

O Brahman, it was adorned with variegated puppets and flowering groves; there was a mass of splendor there, equal in radiance to ten million suns, blazing with light—a great and wonderful marvel. (85)
It extended upwards and all around to the height of seven palm trees;
it eclipsed the splendor of all others and was free from the exhaustion of great effort.
It was all-pervading, the seed of all things, and the supreme producer of vision and light. (66–87)
Having beheld that form of radiant splendor, those gods, intent on meditation, bowed down with supreme devotion, their necks bent low in piety;
their eyes were filled with tears due to the union with supreme bliss. (88)
With all their limbs covered in horripilation and their desires fulfilled,
those lords of the gods bowed down to that Lord, whose nature is radiant splendor.
Rising there, absorbed in meditation, they set out before that light.
Having meditated thus, O Nārada, the Creator of the worlds placed Śaṅkara on his right and Dharma on his left, and with palms joined in reverence,
he praised them with a mind one-pointedly absorbed in meditation through the intensity of his devotion.
The Supreme Lord, the Self beyond the highest, transcending all qualities.
Brahmā said:
[I bow to] the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the giver of boons, and the cause of all givers of boons.
I bow to the one who is the cause of all beings, whose form is splendor.
(93) I bow to the splendorous form, the auspiciousness of the auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the support of all auspiciousness. (94)

I bow to that which is established everywhere, untainted, the very form of the Self, higher than the highest; which is effortless and inconceivable, whose nature is radiant light, the eternal Brahman, both with and without qualities. 95.
I bow to the form of light, which is both with form and without form;
I bow to that form of light, which is ineffable, manifest and unmanifest, one, consisting of its own will, and possessing all forms. (96–97)
The Supreme One, who assumes three forms for the sake of the differentiation of the three qualities (guṇas)—by a mere fraction of You all have been created; what do they know beyond the Veda?
[98] He is the support of all, the form of all, the seed of all, yet himself without seed.
I bow to the one who is the end of all, the infinite, whose form is splendor. (99) The object of perception has the nature of the six qualities and is to be described by the wise.
What more can I describe? I bow to that which is the object of perception, whose form is splendor. (100)
I bow to that which is bodiless yet possesses a form, which is a sense-organ yet transcends the senses; which, though not a witness, is the witness of all, whose nature is radiant light;
which, though footless, is worthy of movement, and which, though eyeless, is the seer of all. (101)
I bow to that form of splendor which is the enjoyer, yet devoid of hands and mouth.

(102) I bow to that form of splendor which is described in the Veda as an entity that the virtuous are capable of describing; and I bow to that form of splendor which is not described in the Veda. (103)

I bow to that whose nature is light, which is the lord of all yet is itself without a lord, which is the beginning of all yet is itself without a beginning, which is the self of all yet is itself without a self. I am the creator of the world and myself the progenitor of the Vedas.

Dharma is the protector, Hara is the destroyer; yet no one at all is capable of praising You. Through Your service, this Dharma has been ordained for protection, and by Your command, he is the destroyer when the time appointed by You arrives. (105–106)
"By serving your lotus feet, I am the creator of all things without exception;
and you, O Lord, are the bestower of fruits upon those who perform rituals and the master of us, your devotees.
Having become worldly enjoyers within this cosmic egg which resembles a reflection," [107]
Thus, how many kinds of servants are there among those infinite beings? Just as there is no counting the grains of sand, so too there is no counting those most minute ones.
Who is capable of praising the Lord who is the progenitor of them all? (108–109)
In every single pore of his hair is one entire Brahmāṇḍa;
that very [universe] is but a sixteenth part of that great Viṣṇu, who is you yourself.
All yogis meditate upon this desired form of yours.
Devoted to the service of Your devotees, they worship Your lotus feet.
O Lord, reveal to us the youthful, most beautiful, charming, and desirable Yakṣa, who is in accordance with our mantra and meditation. 111–112.
The supreme Lord, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, wearing yellow garments, two-armed, with a flute in His hand, smiling and most enchanting;
His crest adorned with peacock feathers and His form graced by clusters of jasmine flowers. (113)
Anointed with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
adorned with the finest ornaments made of priceless jewels;
and radiant with a crown and diadem fashioned from priceless gems. (114–115)
His moon-like face eclipses the luster of autumn blossoms;
it shines with a lower lip resembling a ripe *bimba* fruit, and is enchanting with a row of teeth like the seeds of a ripe pomegranate. (116)

And who would not be eager to behold Your desired form— standing at the root of the *kelīkadaṃba* tree, intent on the rasa of the *rāsa*, with a body [adorned] by the smiles from the faces of the gopīs, and seated upon the breast of Rādhā? (117–118)
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the Universe bowed down again and again;
and Dharma himself, Śaṅkara, being gratified by this hymn of praise,
likewise bowed repeatedly with eyes filled with tears.
Even as he remained there, the lords of the gods again performed a hymn of praise.
O Sage, that entire hermitage was pervaded by the splendor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This king of hymns was composed eternally by Brahmā, Īśa, and Dharma.
Whoever recites this at the time of Hari’s worship, being endowed with devotion,
shall obtain firm and unwavering devotion to Hari, which is very difficult to attain,
as well as the state of servitude that is hard even for the gods, demons, and the lords of sages to reach. (122)
He shall certainly attain the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as the fourfold [liberations] such as *sālokya*;
even in this very life, he will be renowned and honored like Viṣṇu himself.
It is most certain that he will achieve perfection of speech and perfection of mantra.
Endowed with all beauty, he filled the world with his fame. His son possessed learning and poetic skill, and Fortune (Kamalā) was ever-steadfast.
His wife was devoted to her husband, virtuous, well-behaved, and the subjects were stable and loyal. (125)
And there shall be eternal fame, and at the end, one’s destination will be in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Recitation of the King of Hymns to Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Description of Goloka within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having meditated and offered praise, those gods remained before that splendor;
they beheld within the midst of the radiance a most lovely body, possessing the hue of a water-laden cloud, smiling, and exceedingly beautiful. (1)
Her form is supremely gladdening and deludes the minds of the three worlds.
(2) With her cheeks and temples, she is adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings;
and with her two lotus-feet, she is resplendent with excellent jeweled anklets. (3)
Resplendent with garments the color of fire-purified turmeric and gems,
adorned with beautiful ornaments fashioned at will from the finest of precious jewels, yet appearing as if they were naturally inherent to his very form.
Charming with a bimba-fruit-like lower lip joined by a playful flute, (5) gazing with gracious eyes, and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees;
radiant with a chest and armor adorned with excellent jewel-beads. (6)
There they beheld a woman named Rādhikā, radiant with the brilliant luster of the excellent jewels set in the Kaustubha gem;
she was gazing at her smiling beloved with sidelong glances, while he gazed back at her.
She was resplendent with a row of teeth that surpassed a string of pearls;
her face was brightened by a gentle smile, and her eyes were like autumn lotuses.
Her enchanting face put to shame the luster of the full autumn moon.
Her face was radiant with lips that eclipsed the luster of the bandhūjīva flower;
she was graced by two lotus-like feet adorned with a pair of tinkling anklets.
Her rows of toenails shone, surpassing the brilliance of the finest jewels.
Having covered her [the image], which shone like saffron and was adorned with red lac upon its feet,
she [the goddess] was further graced by a girdle of priceless, exquisite jewels around her hips;
she wore garments purified by fire and was resplendent with the brilliance of priceless gems.
Adorned with the finest essence of great jewels, set with tinkling bells in the middle;
