decorated with necklaces of excellent gems, armlets, and bracelets;
and possessing radiant earrings fashioned from the essence of the best of jewels upon her cheeks.
Adorned with the finest jewels upon her ears as ear-ornaments,
with the tip of her nose graced by the beak of the king of birds and the pearls of the lord of elephants,
she shone with the weight of her curly tresses adorned by a garland of *mālatī* flowers. (14–15)
She was beautifully adorned on her chest with a garland of Kaustubha gems;
her garments were radiant with clusters of Pārijāta flower garlands;
and her fingers were embellished by a multitude of jeweled rings.
Adorned with divine conch ornaments decorated with various colors,
beautified by charming shell-ornaments fashioned from fine threads,
and exquisitely graced by strings of beads made from the essence of excellent gems. (17–18)
Clad in a garment the color of molten gold, her beautiful form was concealed;
she was graceful with her hips and loins, her chest was heavy with full breasts, and she was adorned with every ornament graced by exquisite beauty. (19)
Seeing that excellent sovereign lady, all the thirty gods were struck with wonder;
their every desire fulfilled, all those deities offered praise.
Brahmā said:

O Lord, let the bee of my mind wander constantly upon the lotus of Your feet with love and devotion; grant me that service which consists of the most firm and mature devotion toward embodied beings, serving as the medicine for the pacification of the heat arising from the enjoyment of worldly power. Śaṅkara said: My mind-fish, submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, wanders perpetually in this pit of terrible saṃsāra.
Remove this most censurable sense-object which takes the form of creation and destruction, and grant me devotion at Your lotus feet.
Dharma said:
O My Lord, may I have union with Your own people; may it be a sharp sword for cutting the bonds of sense-objects.
"Grant me devotion to Your lotus feet in birth after birth, for Your lotus feet are the sole cause for granting me a place [in Your heart].
Having offered this praise, they stood before the Lord of Rādhikā, the fulfiller of desires, who sat alone in complete absorption.
Having heard the praise of the gods, the Ocean of Compassion,
his lotus-like face smiling, spoke these words— beneficial and true—
to them. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

"Stay or go, O gods; there is no doubt in this. It is not appropriate at this time to inquire after the welfare of those who have taken refuge in Śiva. Be free from anxiety right here; what cause for concern is there for you while I am present? (26)
I abide within all living beings; indeed, I am directly manifest through this hymn of praise.
Whatever intention you hold, I know it all with certainty. Furthermore, whatever action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—will truly come to pass in its time, I know it.
O gods, whatever action there is, whether great or small, all is produced by Time.
At their respective times, trees always bear fruit and flowers;
at the proper time, they possess ripe fruits, and at the proper time, they are endowed with ripened fruit.
Happiness and suffering, misfortune and prosperity, grief, anxiety, the auspicious and the inauspicious— these,
which arise at all times, are rooted solely in the fruits of one's own karma.
Indeed, in the three worlds, there is no one who is beloved to another, nor anyone who is disliked.
At the proper time, due to the force of circumstances, all indeed become both unpleasant and pleasant.
O kings, you have surely seen here on earth how even Manus,
having fallen under the power of time through the ripening of the fruits of their own actions, have all passed away.
And now, for you in Goloka, whatever moment has passed,
on earth that same moment has already become seven Manvantaras.
Seven Indras have passed away there, and the eighth, the Lord of Gods (Indra), is now present.
The wheel of time indeed revolves day and night for me;
even Indras, humans, and kings have all fallen under the power of time.
My fame on earth and my merit now remain as nothing more than a mere story.
Even now, there have been many wicked kings on earth who reviled Hari and possessed great strength and prowess;
yet all these kings will certainly fall under the sway of the power of time.
Even though this time has arrived, the wind blows incessantly;
by my command, fire burns and the sun indeed scorches.
Diseases exist within bodies, and death moves among living beings.
"All these clouds are raining by my command.
The Brahmins are devoted to the status of a Brahmin, and those whose wealth is austerity are devoted to penance.
The celestial rishis are devoted to the Brahman, and the yogins are devoted to yoga. (39–40)
All of them, terrified by fear of me, are devoted to their own duties and dharma;
yet my devotees alone are free from doubt and are the ones who uproot karma.
I am the God of time, the Time of time, the Ordainer, and even the Creator himself.

He who destroys the destroyer, who protects the protector, and who is higher than the highest—by my command, he shall be the destroyer; for that reason, he is known by the name Hara. You are the creator of the universe for the sake of creation, and the protector through the preservation of dharma.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, I am the Lord of all.
I am the giver of the fruits of one's own actions and the one who eradicates karma. As for those whom I shall withdraw, who indeed could be their protector?
"No one shall be the slayer of those whom I protect;
indeed, I alone am the destroyer, the creator, and the protector of all.
Yet, I am not capable of destroying my devotees, who possess eternal bodies. (45–46)
My devotees are my constant followers, ever intent on worshipping my feet.
I am eternally present near those devotees for the sake of their protection.
All things in the universe perish and arise again and again; [but my devotees do not]. 47.
"My devotees do not perish; they are free from doubt and free from calamity.
Therefore, all the wise desire service [to Me] rather than any other boon.
Those who entreat Me for service are blessed; all others are cheated. (48-49)

The fear of birth, death, old age, and disease, as well as the torments of Yama, exist for other performers of ritual actions, but never for devotees. Devotees are not smeared by sins; they perform all actions while remaining untouched by merit.
I certainly shake off their karmic enjoyments.
I am the life-breath of my devotees, and they are the life-breath of me as well.
They meditate upon me constantly, and I remember them day and night. (51–52)
The discus named Sudarśana has sixteen spokes and is exceedingly sharp.
Not even a sixteenth part of its splendor exists among all living beings.
Having bestowed that discus upon his devotee for the sake of their desired protection, [he departed].
I have neither peace nor joy when I am in their presence.
I have no peace even in Vaikuṇṭha or in Goloka by the side of Rādhikā;
wherever those devotees reside, there I remain day and night.
Rādhā, dearer to me than my own life-breaths, remains upon my chest day and night;
you, O lords of the gods, are Lakṣmī, more precious to me than life itself, yet no one is dearer to me than my devotee.
And whatever substance is given by a devotee, I eat with devotion, O lords of the gods.
I do not eat what is given by one who is not my devotee; indeed, Bali himself eats his own offering. (57) Having abandoned their wives, sons, and kinsmen, they meditate upon me day and night;
leaving you aside, I constantly remember them day and night. (58)
When wicked people certainly commit violence against my devotees, against brahmins, against cows, against sacrifices, or against deities,
they perish before long, just as blades of grass are consumed by fire. (59)
When I have arrived as their slayer, there shall be no protector for them.
O gods, I shall go to the earth; you all go to your own abodes.
And you too, in the form of partial incarnations (aṃśa), go quickly to the surface of the earth.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds summoned the cowherds and cowherdesses and spoke these sweet words, which were true and appropriate for the occasion:
"O cowherds and cowherdesses, listen! Go to the supreme Nanda’s settlement."
"O Rādhikā, you too go quickly to the house of Vṛṣabhānu.
She is the virtuous beloved of Vṛṣabhānu, the daughter of Nanda the cowherd, and the daughter of Subala; she is born from a portion of Kamalā. (63–64)
The mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, auspicious and honored among women—her birth formerly took place in the home of a cowherd in Vraja due to the curse of Durvāsas.
Go quickly to Nanda’s Vraja; take birth in her house.
O lotus-faced one, I take you as my own in the form of a child.
O Rādhā, you are dearer to me than my own life, and I am likewise dearer to you than your own life;
for there is never any difference between us, we are truly one body.
Upon hearing this, O Sage, Rādhikā there wept, overwhelmed with love;
she drank in the moon-like face of Hari with her eyes, which were like those of a cakora bird.
And the cowherds and cowherd girls obtained birth upon the surface of the earth.
In every auspicious mansion of the most excellent cowherds,
in the meantime, they all beheld a supreme chariot adorned with diamonds and the finest essence of precious gems. (69–70)
Adorned with a hundred thousand white chowries and ten thousand mirrors,
it was embellished with fine saffron-colored cloth purified by fire;
and it was made exceedingly beautiful by a thousand jars of excellent jewels.
It was resplendent with networks of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers;
it was joined by the foremost of his attendants, auspicious, and composed of gold.
It was of incomparable nature as pure light, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns. (72–73)
There he saw a person, dark-complexioned, beautiful, and lovely;
holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus; wearing yellow garments, most excellent, adorned with a crown, earrings, and a forest garland. (74)
Smeared with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
four-armed, with a smiling face, and eager to bestow grace upon devotees;
adorned with ornaments made of the most excellent essence of precious gems and jewels. (75–76)
To her left is the beautiful goddess, white in color and captivating;
she is richly adorned with the splendor of jewel ornaments and graced with yellow garments. Her face is like the full autumn moon, and her eyes are like autumn lotuses.
She has lips like a ripe bimba fruit, is smiling, and is captivating;
she holds a flute and a vīṇā in her hands, is intent on bestowing grace upon her devotees, is the presiding goddess of knowledge, and is Sarasvatī, whose form is wisdom. (78–79)
To her right was another beautiful [form], possessing a luster equal to a hundred moons;
she had the hue of molten gold, was smiling, and was exceedingly charming.
Her beautiful cheeks were illuminated by two earrings made of excellent jewels.
Adorned with priceless garments inlaid with jewels of inestimable value;
beautified by armlets and bracelets made of priceless gems;
accompanied by the sweet sound of anklets composed of the finest essence of excellent jewels.
Her waist was adorned with a girdle of excellent jewels and tiny bells;
her chest shone with a garland of *pārijāta* flowers;
and her braided hair was entwined with a wreath of full-blown *mālatī* blossoms. (83)
Her face was beautifully adorned, eclipsing the splendor of the autumn moon;
she bore a tilaka-mark of vermilion joined with a spot of musk, and her eyes were like autumn lotuses anointed with exquisite kohl. (84–85)
Beholding Nārāyaṇa, who was joined with a playful lotus attached to his thousand-petaled [crown], and who gazed back at her with his side-long glance,
she quickly descended from the chariot together with her wife and his attendants. (86)
And he went to the beautiful assembly hall, which was filled with cowherds and cowherdesses.
The gods, the cowherdesses, and the cowherds stood there with joy and palms joined in reverence,
[listening] to the hymn composed by the celestial rishis according to the Sāmaveda.
Having gone there, the god Nārāyaṇa dissolved into the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing that supreme marvel, they all were filled with astonishment.
In the meantime, from a chariot made of gold...
Having descended himself, Viṣṇu, the protector and lord of the worlds,
arrived— four-armed, adorned with a forest garland,
wearing yellow garments, glorious, smiling, and most enchanting. (90–91)
Richly adorned with the splendor of all ornaments and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
they rose up upon seeing him and, bowing down, offered praises, O Sage;
and he too remained absorbed right there within the form of the Lord of Rādhikā.
Seeing that great marvel, they were filled with supreme wonder.
While the body of Hari, the dweller of Śvetadvīpa, was thus dissolved,
in that very interval, someone arrived swiftly and with great haste.
Resembling pure crystal, he is known by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns, arrived;
and seeing him, all praised Viṣṇu, the Lord.
Having arrived with his shoulders bowed, he praised the Lord of Rādhikā;
and with devotion, O Nārada, he prostrated himself before the Thousand-headed One.
We two, the sons of Dharma known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, [were also there].
I became absorbed in the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, and Phālguna became inferior.
Brahmā, Īśa, Śeṣa, and Dharma indeed stood together in that one place.
In the meantime, the gods beheld an excellent chariot.
It was fashioned from the finest essence of gold, furnished with various types of seats and accessories;
it was joined with the most excellent of gems, provided with garments purified by fire, accompanied by white chowries, and adorned with mirrors. (99–100)
It was resplendent with a multitude of jars made of the essence of the seven precious gems;
it was beautifully adorned with networks of garlands of *pārijāta* flowers; it was equipped with a thousand wheels, capable of traveling at the speed of thought, and enchanting to the mind. (101)
It was as excellent as the heat of the midday sun in summer that scorches all things;
it was brilliantly illuminated by a multitude of pearls, rubies, and diamonds; and it was adorned with variegated mechanical puppets, flower-lakes, and groves. (102–103)
O Sage, this preeminent chariot of the gods and the Dānavas was constructed with great effort by Viśvakarman out of devotion to Śaṅkara;
it is fifty yojanas in height and four yojanas in width.
It was adorned with pleasure-pavilions joined by women equal to Rati herself.
There they beheld the Goddess, adorned with ornaments of jewels,
whose radiance eclipsed the luster of refined gold.
She is the sovereign primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), whose form is splendor,
incomparable, and endowed with a thousand arms equipped with various weapons;
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and she is intent upon bestowing grace upon her devotees.
Resplendent with excellent jeweled earrings resting upon her cheeks and temples;
beautified by tinkling anklets fashioned from the essence of the finest gems;
and graced in her midsection by a girdle of supreme jewels. (108–109)
Adorned with armlets and bracelets made of the finest jewels,
her chest was radiant with garlands of mandāra flowers;
she possessed firm hips and a broad pelvis, and was bent slightly by her full, elevated breasts.
Her face was captivating, surpassing the luster of the autumnal full moon;
her eyes were like autumn lotuses marked by a brilliant line of kohl;
and she was adorned with variegated patterns made of sandalwood, agallochum, and musk. (111–112)
Adorned with rows of teeth that eclipse the luster of strings of pearls,
her excellent braided hair was entwined with garlands of full-blown *mālatī* flowers;
the tip of her nose, like the beak of the king of birds, was adorned with a pearl from the lord of elephants.
Resplendent with a garment as pure as fire and blazing intensely, she joyfully ascended the back of a lion together with her two sons;
then, quickly descending from the chariot, she prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (114–115)
Accompanied by her two sons, the fair-faced goddess spoke.
Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, having bowed to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme,
prostrated before Śaṅkara, Dharma, and the lotus-born Brahmā.
Seeing those two lords of the thirty gods from afar, the deities rose up.
The gods offered their blessings and settled them nearby;
filled with joy, the gods engaged in constant conversation with the two of them. (117–118)
The gods stood in the midst of the assembly before the Lord Hari;
the cowherds and cowherdesses were for the most part filled with wonder.
Kṛṣṇa, his lotus-face smiling, spoke to Kamalā.
"Go, O virtuous lady, to the house of Bhīṣmaka, which is filled with various jewels. O Goddess, take birth in the womb of the princess of Vidarbha.
Having gone to Kuṇḍina, O Satī, I shall take your hand in marriage."
Seeing Pārvatī, those goddesses rose up with haste and seated the Goddess upon a beautiful throne of jewels,
O best of Brahmins; for Pārvatī is the presiding deity of Lakṣmī, Vāc, and Aditi.
Having conversed there as was appropriate, they sat upon a single seat;
and those cowherd girls conversed with them with great affection. In their presence, some of the cowherd women spoke joyfully. (123–124)
There, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe, spoke to Pārvatī:
"O auspicious Goddess, you shall take birth in the beautiful cowherd settlement of Nanda in the form of a partial incarnation,
within the womb of Yaśodā by means of Nanda's seed."
O Mahāmāyā, you who perform creation and destruction, may my birth be fruitful!
I shall cause your worship to be performed with devotion in every village and throughout the entire surface of the earth, in cities and in forests alike. (126–127)
There, O Śivā, filled with joy, human beings will worship you, the presiding goddess,
with various divine substances and offerings in the maternity chamber at the mere touch of your ground. (128)
My father, having established me there, will take you and depart.
Merely by seeing Kaṃsa, you shall go to the presence of Śiva.
Having accomplished the removal of the burden, I too shall go to my own hermitage.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari quickly said to the six-faced one:
"O child, O Lord of the Gods, you shall go to the surface of the earth in the form of a partial incarnation; take birth from the womb of Jāmbavatī."
"Let all the deities go to the surface of the earth with a portion [of themselves];
I shall certainly bear the burden of the earth.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Rādhikā remained upon his excellent throne.

The gods and goddesses, as well as the cowherds and cowherd girls, stood there, O Nārada. In the meantime, Brahmā arose before Hari and, with palms joined in reverence and full of humility, spoke to the Beloved of the World. (134)
Brahmā said:
"O Lord, pay heed to the petition of your servant.
O illustrious one, give your command: whose [is it], and at what place on earth?"
The master is the lord of his servants, always providing for their protection and upliftment. (136) That servant is ever-devoted who carries out the command of the Lord.
Which deities [reside] in what form, and which goddesses in which aspect? (137)
"Where on this earth is there space for whom, and what shall be their subject matter?
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the Lord of the World replied:
"I shall tell you, according to the rules, where there is room for each."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Kāmadeva is the son of Rukmiṇī; Rati is the virtuous Māyāvatī, who remained in the house of Śambara in the form of a shadow. (139)
"You shall become his son, indeed by the name Aniruddha.
Bhāratī shall become the daughter of Bāṇa in Śoṇitapura.
The infinite Lord of the World, the son of Rohiṇī, shall emerge from the womb of Devakī. (140–141)
Because he drew forth the embryo through his illusory power (*māyā*), the Lord is named Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Kālindī, the daughter of the Sun, appeared on the surface of the earth as a portion of the Gaṅgā;
and by half a portion, Tulasī became Lakṣmaṇā, the princess.
She shall be Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas, and by name Satī Nāgnajitī;
she shall become Vasuṃdharā, Satyabhāmā, the queen Śaibyā, Sarasvatī, Rohiṇī, and Mitravindā—these shall be the names of the princesses. (143–144)
Ratnamālā was born from a portion of Sūrya’s wife, and Suśīlā from a portion of the Lord of the Universe (Viṣṇu). Svāhā’s portion became Rukmiṇī; these and others are the nine wives.
Jāmbavatī arose from half a portion of Durgā; thus, ten queens are recorded.
"Let Śailaputrī go to the home of Jāmbavān with half a portion.
Long ago, by the command of Śaṅkara on Kailāsa, Pārvatī [spoke thus] regarding Viṣṇu,
who was residing in Śvetadvīpa and was traveling toward Kailāsa.
"O beloved, grant me an embrace; there is no fault in my knowing this.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Rādhikā, how did Śiva’s command come to that goddess?"
Formerly, during a conversation with Viṣṇu, the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa [spoke]. (148) The Blessed Lord said:
"In ancient times, all the deities went forth to see Gaṇeśa."
Viṣṇu himself went from Śvetadvīpa to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Having seen Gaṇeśa, he was delighted and sat upon a comfortable seat.
Everyone beheld with ease that body which enchants the three worlds.
Wearing a crown and earrings, clad in excellent yellow garments,
beautiful, with a dark complexion, endowed with fresh youth,
and anointed with the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. (151)
Abounding in the splendor of jewel ornaments, with a lotus-face smiling, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, and surrounded by his attendants;
saluted by all the gods, worshipped and praised by Śiva. (152–153)
Seeing Viṣṇu, Pārvatī, whose face and eyes were gracious, covered her face with her garment out of modesty;
for she was beholding again and again his exceedingly beautiful form. (154)

Covering her face, she gazed without blinking; with a smile and sidelong glances, she beheld him of most wonderful appearance. Immersed in an ocean of bliss, she became covered in horripilation. (159–160)

For a moment he beheld him with five faces, white in color, and three eyes; bearing a trident and a club, he was as beautiful as ten million gods of love. For a moment he beheld him as dark-complexioned, with one face and two eyes.
Having seen him with four arms, clad in yellow garments, adorned with a forest garland—
one who is described as either a single Brahman manifested in different forms or as non-dual—
that Māyā became filled with desire through the power of Viṣṇu’s Māyā. (158–159)
And the three gods who are my portions— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
are surpassed by him because he consists of the quality of *sattva* and possesses excellence over them.
Seeing him with devotion, Pārvatī’s body was covered with horripilation.
He worshipped the Supreme Self, the Lord, with his mind.
And Śaṅkara himself understood Durgā’s inner intention;
for the Blessed One is the inner self of all, the inner controller, and the Lord of the universe.
Hara himself summoned Durgā to a secluded place and spoke to her;
he enlightened her with various beneficial, truthful, and unerring words.
(163) Śrī Śaṅkara said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, understand my petition:
bestow upon Hari, the Supreme Self, the auspicious sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra); may it be well with you.
I, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are but the one eternal Brahman.
You are the singular Veda, devoid of [dualistic] Vedas, the one who distinguishes the forms of sense objects.
You are the single primordial nature (prakṛti), the mother of all, possessing every form.
You are the self-existent Speech (Vāṇī) and Lakṣmī upon the breast of Nārāyaṇa.
"O virtuous lady, know that you, Durgā, are within my breast; this is the spiritual truth.
Having heard these words of Śiva, the Sovereign of the Gods spoke to him.
(167) Pārvatī said:
O friend of the distressed, O ocean of mercy, how could you show me such lack of compassion?
Having obtained you as the Lord of the worlds through long and arduous penance, O Master,
it does not behove you to abandon a servant like me.
"O Maheśvara, do not, do not speak such unworthy words!
O Mahādeva, I shall certainly carry out the fulfillment of your word.
Having obtained birth in another body, O Hara, I shall worship Hari."
Having heard these words, Maheśvara ceased speaking;
the bestower of fearlessness laughed aloud and granted Pārvatī freedom from fear.
To fulfill that vow, Pārvatī [resided] in the house of Jāmbavat.
"O Creator, she who is truly named Jāmbavatī will obtain birth.
Brahmā said:
"When how many kinds of kings are established on earth, how [will] Pārvatī [be born]?"
I obtained birth in the despised house of Bhālluka in Bhārata.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the Tretā age, during the incarnation of Rāma, the portions of the gods descended to the earth.
A portion of the Himalaya, there was a servant named Jāmbavān, a bear.
By the boon of Rāma, he became long-lived and endowed with splendor;
possessed of great strength, he maintains the power of ten million lions. (174–175)
Durgā went to the earth by means of a portion [of herself] into the house that was her father’s share.
First, listen from my mouth as the account of the former [birth] is told.
Indeed, let the lineages of all the gods go to the earth.
O Creator, let the princes become my allies in battle;
let all the princesses be graced by a portion of Kamalā,
and let them become my sixteen thousand queens.
This Dharma, in the form of a partial incarnation, is Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu;
Bhīmasena arises from a portion of Vāyu; Arjuna is indeed the wielder of the thunderbolt himself;
and Nakula and Sahadeva are born from portions of the celestial physicians.
Sūryāṃśa and Karṇavīra were Vidura, who was Yama himself;
Duryodhana was a portion of Kali, and Śaṃtanu was a portion of the Ocean.
Aśvatthāman was a portion of Śaṅkara, and Droṇa was born from a portion of Agni.
The illustrious and mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna was a portion of Agni;
Abhimanyu was a portion of the Moon; Bhīṣma was born from the Vasus;
Vasudeva was a portion of Kaśyapa; and Devakī was a portion of Aditi.
Nanda the cowherd was a portion of Vasu, and Yaśodā was a portion of Vasukāminī.
Draupadī was a portion of Kamalā, born from the sacrificial fire-pit.
Subhadrā was a portion of Śatarūpā, born from the womb of Devakī. (183–184)
"Let the gods go to the earth with a portion as bearers of the burden;
let the wives of the gods also go to the surface of the earth with a fraction [of themselves].
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the Blessed One became silent.
Having heard the entire exposition, Prajāpati dwelt there;
O Nārada, Vāgdevī was on Kṛṣṇa’s left, Kamalālayā on his right,
and all the deities as well as Pārvatī were in front.
The gopīs and gopas were all around, situated upon the chest of Rādhā.
In the meantime, that Queen of Vraja spoke to Him. (188) Rādhikā said:
Listen, O Lord, Master; I shall speak the words of your servant.
My life-breaths burn constantly, and my mind wavers.
I am unable to close my eyes from beholding you. (189)
"O Lord, how shall I traverse the surface of the earth without you?
After only a short time, there will surely be a reunion with you;
O Lord of my life, tell me the truth—it shall indeed happen in Gokula. (190–191)
To me, a single moment in your absence will become like a hundred ages.
Whom shall I look upon? Where shall I go? Or who will protect me?
[I shall have no mother, father, kinsman, brother, sister, or son. 192.

"O Lord of my life, without you I think of nothing else. O Master of Māyā, if you conceal me from the world by means of your power, then truly swear an oath that you will restore my former glory. (193–194)

O Madhusūdana, may my mind-bee wander perpetually from moment to moment within the honeyed lotus-feet of Your Samādhi. And wherever, or in whatever womb, this birth of mine may occur— (195) — [may it be so].
"You shall grant me the remembrance of yourself and my desired service.
You are Kṛṣṇa and I am Rādhikā; our fortune of love is such that I do not forget it on this earth. Grant me this supreme boon. (196–197)
"Just as the vital breaths depart with the body and the shadow with the form, so too may our birth come to an end; O Lord, grant me this boon.
Let there be no interruption of our eyes' blinking while we are on earth. (198)
Even having come there, O Lord, grant me a boon somewhere.
O Hari, by what means could Your body be made dearer than my own life?
Is it by the self, or by the flute, or by the feet, or even by the mind? (199–200)
"How many kinds of women or men are there, O Puruṣṭuta?
Nowhere is there a beloved equal to me in beauty and power.
By what portion of your body was I fashioned?"

This alone is the difference between us two: there is no [other] reason why my mind is fixed upon you. Just as my self, my mind, and my vital breaths are established in you, so too are your self, your mind, and your vital breaths established in me.
"Therefore, due to this separation lasting even for a moment, my distressed mind is consumed;
when the news of our separation is heard, my very life-breaths burn incessantly.
Having spoken thus, that goddess remained right there in the assembly of the gods.
Holding her lotus-like feet, she wept aloud again and again.
Then Kṛṣṇa, taking her onto his lap and wiping her face with his garment, enlightened her with various words that were true, factual, and beneficial. (205–206)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Goddess, listen; I shall declare the supreme spiritual yoga which effects the cutting away of sorrow, and which is difficult even for the lords of yogis to attain. (207)
O beautiful one, behold the entire universe as the relationship between the container and the contained.
There is no possibility of the contained existing apart from its container. (208) The flower is the support of the fruit, and the sprout is the support of the flower.
The trunk is the support for the shoots, and the tree itself is the support for the trunk.
The sprout, endowed with the power of the life-force (jīva-śakti), is also supported by the tree.
The root is the support for the single sprout, and the earth is the support for the root.
Śeṣa is the support of the earth, and the tortoise is indeed the support of Śeṣa;
Vāyu is the support of the tortoise, and I alone am the support of Vāyu.
You are my very nature as a support, and I abide within you at this moment.
You are the aggregate of powers and the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the Sovereign;
you are the very form of the body, possessing the nature of the substratum of the three qualities (guṇas).
I am your self, devoid of desire yet active in conjunction with you.
From the Puruṣa, virility is produced, and from virility, the lineage itself;
and the woman, who is the substratum for both, is a portion (kalā) of Prakṛti.
Where is the self without a body, and where is the body without the self?
O Goddess, and where is the preeminence of those two today without you?
O Rādhā, there is no difference anywhere between us two, the seed and the sprout of worldly existence.
Where there is the Self, there is the body; why this modesty regarding their lack of distinction? (215–216)
Just as whiteness resides in milk and burning power in fire,
as fragrance in the earth and coolness in water, so do [these qualities] abide in you and me. Just as there is a unity between whiteness and milk, and between burning power and fire...
There is no difference between us, just as there is none between the scent of the earth, water, and coolness.
Without me you are lifeless, and I am invisible without you;
O beautiful one, it is certain that I am not able to exist without you. (218–219)
Just as a potter is not able to make a jar without clay,
and a goldsmith is incapable of making an ornament without gold;
so too, just as the Self is eternal by its very nature, you yourself are Prakṛti.
Endowed with all powers, the support of all, and eternal;
equal to my own life-breath, Lakṣmī, Vāṇī, and Sarvamaṅgalā;
and Brahmā, Īśa, Ananta, and Dharma—you are my beloved, dearer to me than my very life. (221–222)
O Rādhikā, all these gods and goddesses are standing nearby;
if she were not superior even to them, how could she be situated upon your chest?
O virtuous Rādhā, abandon the shedding of tears and this fruitless delusion.
"Abandoning all doubt, go fearlessly to the house of Vṛṣabhānu.
O beautiful one, having filled Kalāvatī’s womb with wind for nine months, secure the fetus by means of your illusory power (māyā)."
When the tenth month has arrived, manifest yourself upon the earth;
having set aside your own true form and assumed the form of an infant,
appear in the presence of Kalāvatī at the time of the expulsion of the wind.
"Surely you will fall to the ground, stripped of your garments, and weep. And you shall be born from a non-womb in Gokula;
I too shall be born from a non-womb, for there is no conception of us within a womb. (227–228)
"Merely by touching the ground, he will cause me to reach Gokula.
For your sake, I shall go, having employed a ruse out of fear of Kaṃsa.
And I shall be joyfully received in Yaśodā’s house as the delight of Nanda."

"O auspicious Rādhikā, by my boon, you shall always have the memory [of me] at the proper time; preceded by my embrace, you shall see me constantly. I shall sport freely and eternally in the forest of Vṛndāvana. (230–231)
Enter Gokula, the cowherd settlement, with three hundred and twenty-one million gopīs,
as well as with thirty-three companions such as Suśīlā and others;
and having established countless gopīs within Gokula itself.
Having comforted them with words of awakening and with measured, nectar-like speech, O Rādhikā, I shall establish my friend Gopāla right here;
afterwards, I will go to Vasudeva’s hermitage and then to the city of Mathurā. (233–234)
"Let those who are dearer than the dearest go to Vraja for the sake of sport in my company;
let ten million cowherds obtain birth in the houses of the cowherds.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Śrī Kṛṣṇa became silent.
The gods and goddesses, the cowherds and cowherd-maidens, indeed dwelt there.
Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, and Dharma, as well as Śivā, Padmā, and Sarasvatī, praised that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme, with supreme joy.
Out of devotion, the cowherds and cowherd girls, distressed by the fever of separation,
praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa there and prostrated themselves, overwhelmed with love—
for their beloved who is dearer than life, the husband who has fulfilled Rādhā’s every desire.

Seeing Rādhā overwhelmed by fear, filled with tears, extremely distressed, and trembling with the fever of separation, Hari himself became deeply moved by her devotion; and having heard her words of awakening, he spoke to her personally. (239–240)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Great Goddess, who are dearer to me than my own life, be steadfast and abandon fear.
As you are, so am I; what cause for anxiety is there while I remain present? 241.

However, I shall tell you something: there is indeed one inauspicious thing. O beautiful one, due to the ripening of karma born from Śrīdāman’s curse, my separation from you will last for a full hundred years.
My arrival in Mathurā shall indeed take place thereafter;
there, I shall effect the removal of the burden [of the earth], the liberation of my parents from bondage, and the deliverance of the florist, the weaver, and Kubjikā. (243–244)
Having caused the Yavana to be slain, the liberation of Mucukunda,
the construction of Dvārakā, the witnessing of the Rājasūya sacrifice,
and the marriage of sixteen thousand royal maidens. (245)
Likewise, the subduing of even one hundred and ten enemies, the assistance rendered to a friend, and the burning of Vārāṇasī;
there, the causing of Hara to yawn and the cutting off of Bāṇa’s arms. (246–247)
The abduction of the Pārijāta tree and whatever other deeds [he performed];
his journey on a pilgrimage to sacred fords and the meeting with the assembly of sages;
his conversation with his kinsmen and the completion of his father’s sacrifice.
Furthermore, at an auspicious moment, I shall manifest myself there together with you; and right there, I shall grant a vision of the Gopīs to you.
Having bestowed upon you the spiritual [teachings], I shall again speak the truth with you.
"From this point forward, there shall be no separation from me day or night.
O beloved, when a period of a hundred years has passed during our time apart, you shall return again to Vraja. (250–251)
There will be a constant union with you in my dreams;
and as for him who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, his journey to Dvārakā within a hundred years is certain— this alone is well-ascertained.
Furthermore, there will be a *rāsa* dance with you in that forest (253).
Having again performed the supreme cleansing of the grief of my parents and the cowherd girls,
and having relieved the burden [of the earth], I shall return once more (254).
O Rādhā, even with you, along with the cowherds and the cowherd-maidens,
and together with my own voice, Padmā, I— who am a portion of Nārāyaṇa and the eternal Supreme Soul—
shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.

Śvetadvīpa shall become the abode of Dharma and the residence for my portions; the portions of the gods and goddesses likewise shall go to their own abodes. Then, once again, my establishment here in Goloka with you shall take place.
"Thus everything regarding the future, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been told;
O beloved, who can ward off that which has been ordained by me?
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa placed Rādhā upon his chest.
He stood still, and all the gods and the wives of the gods stood still, filled with wonder.
Śrī Hari spoke to the gods and the goddess in a manner appropriate for the occasion:
"O gods, go to your own abodes, which are suitable for your respective domains, for the sake of your duties."
"Go, Pārvatī, to Kailāsa with your husband and two sons.
All the tasks assigned by me shall come to pass in due time.
O Queen of Vraja, there shall be the birth of all [of us] through a portion [of our being]. (261)

Having prostrated before the god Lambodara— the lord of both the small and the great— and having bowed with devotion to Śrī Hari, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, the gods joyfully departed for their own abodes,
[having paid homage] to Puruṣottama.
Eager to perform the task assigned by Hari, they went to the earth;
a place appointed by their Lord that is difficult even for the gods to attain. Kṛṣṇa said to Rādhikā, "Go to the house of Vṛṣabhānu."

"O beloved, accompanied by the previously designated hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, I shall go to Mathurā, to the abode of Vasudeva; afterwards, under the pretext of fear of Kaṃsa, I will come to Gokula, to your presence. (265–266)

Rādhā, whose eyes were like red lotuses, bowed down before Śrī Kṛṣṇa and wept profusely in his presence, distressed by the prospect of being separated from her love. Stopping again and again as she went along, she would walk forward and then return repeatedly. (267)
Returning again and again, she gazed repeatedly at the face of Hari;
remaining without blinking, she drank in the Lord’s countenance with her eyes like *cakora* birds, a face filled with nectar and resembling the full moon of autumn. (268–269)
Then, having circumambulated the Supreme Goddess seven times and bowed down to her seven times, she stood once more before Hari. And three hundred and twenty-one million gopīs arrived as well.
And a multitude of cowherds, numbering ten million, arrived.
Together with the multitudes of cowherds and cowherd girls, O Nārada, Rādhikā bowed to him once more and remained there. (271–272)
Accompanied by thirty-three companions among the cowherd girls, the beautiful woman,
having bowed down along with the multitudes of cowherds, departed for the earth;
they went to Nanda’s Gokula, the place ordained by Hari.
Rādhā went to the house of Vṛṣabhānu and to the houses of the cowherd women and cowherds.
When Rādhā had gone to the earth along with the cowherd women and cowherds, Śrī Hari immediately became eager to go to the earth as well. (274–275)
Having conversed with the cowherds and cowherd-maids and having enjoined them to their respective duties,
Hari, the Lord of the Universe, who travels by the power of his mind, departed for Mathurā.
[276] As for whatever offspring Devakī and Vasudeva had previously—
Immediately after that, Kaṃsa killed six sons;
however, by the command of Hari, he drew out the seventh embryo—the remaining portion—by means of his illusory power (māyā), placed it in the womb of Rohiṇī, and departed. (277–278)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
[Tell me] of that supreme excellence of Kṛṣṇa, which produces great merit.
Speak, O fortunate one, of that birth which removes birth, death, and old age.
Whose son was Vasudeva, and whose daughter was Devakī? Which Vasu was Devakī, or what was the nature of the marriage between the two? Tell me this. (1–2)
How did the cruel Kaṃsa kill his six sons?
On which day was the birth of Hari? I wish to hear this according to the truth.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Kaśyapa and Vasudeva, as well as Devakī, the mother of the gods,
obtained Śrī Hari as their son solely through the fruit of their past merits.
From Devamīḍha and Māriṣā, the great Vasudeva was born.
Upon his birth, the host of gods sounded the dundubhi drum and the great ānaka drum with immense joy; because he was the progenitor of Śrī Hari,
the ancient sages call him Ānakadundubhi.
The illustrious Devaka, born of the Yadu lineage, was the son of Āhuka;
he was an ocean of knowledge, and his daughter was Devakī.
Garga, the preceptor of the Yadu clan, established a matrimonial alliance with Vasu.

Devaka caused [the ceremony] for Devakī to be performed according to the rules and as prescribed. With great preparations made, at an auspicious moment, Devaka indeed gave Devakī to him (Vasudeva) in marriage.
Thousands of horses and hundreds of elephants,
hundreds of beautiful female slaves adorned with ornaments,
and various kinds of goods and diverse jewels.
O Nārada, [he gave] the finest jewels, diamonds, and golden vessels;
a maiden adorned with excellent gems, possessing a radiance like a hundred moons, enchanting the three worlds, blessed, venerable, and the most excellent of women. (11–12)
Taking her— who was the support of beauty, the support of virtue, possessed of a lovely smile and arched eyes,
fit for a new union, and whose fresh youth had just blossomed—
he placed her upon his chariot at the time of departure. (13)

Kaṃsa was delighted, acting as an attendant at his sister’s wedding ceremony. At that very moment, as Kaṃsa was walking near her chariot, an incorporeal voice arose in the sky, addressing Kaṃsa: [14–15]
"Why are you joyful, O Indra among kings? Listen to these true and beneficial words:
indeed, the eighth pregnancy of Devakī shall be the cause of your own death.
Upon hearing this, the mighty Kaṃsa, sword in hand, [rushed toward] Devakī.
Driven by the words of the gods, out of fear and anger, that most wicked man prepared to kill her.
Seeing him intent on killing her, the highly wise Vasudeva—
learned in policy and expert in the treatises of statecraft— instructed him.

Vasudeva said: "O King, you do not understand the science of politics; listen to my beneficial words, which bring fame, destroy faults, are prescribed by the scriptures, and are appropriate for the occasion. (19)
O King, if this is indeed your eighth conception, which is Death itself,
how can you, a man, bring ill repute upon yourself by killing her?
For even in the slaying of small creatures or of those who are harmful, a wise man [refrains].
By renouncing even a single kārṣāpaṇa coin at the time of death, one is liberated. The killing of small, harmless creatures results certainly in a hundredfold [retribution];
therefore, the lotus-born Brahmā has declared this as the expiation for the time of death.
For the intentional killing of distinguished beings and animals such as cattle,
Manu has declared that the sin is certainly a hundredfold greater than that;
for the killing of men of Mleccha tribes, it is a hundredfold greater still.

Whatever sin one incurs by killing hundreds of Mlecchas, a man incurs that same sin by killing a single virtuous Śūdra. And whatever sin one incurs by killing hundreds of virtuous Śūdras, [one incurs that same sin by killing a single virtuous Vaiśya]. (24–25)
One certainly incurs that very sin by the single act of killing a cow;
the sin incurred by killing a Brāhmaṇa is ten times that of killing a cow. A man incurs a sin equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa by killing a woman.

For a sister is especially worthy of support, and she has come for refuge. O King, by killing her, the sin of killing a hundred women would be incurred. [Yet] austerity, recitation, charity, worship, and visiting sacred fords— 27–28. For a sister is especially worthy of support, and she has come for refuge. O King, by killing her, the sin of killing a hundred women would be incurred. [Yet] austerity, recitation, charity, worship, and visiting sacred fords—
The wise man performs the feeding of Brahmins and fire-offerings for the sake of attaining heaven;
yet the virtuous constantly perceive that all existence is like a bubble in water and equal to a dream, and thus they practice dharma with diligence. (29)
"O most righteous one, O sun to your own lineage, abandon your sister!
O King, how many kinds of wise men are there in this assembly? Ask them: what will be the offspring of her eighth pregnancy? (30–31)
"I shall grant you a boon; what need have I for it?
Or rather, O best of the wise, I shall give you all those children whom you may have; who is dearer to me than you?"

"O Indra among kings, abandon your sister, who is as dear to you as a daughter and has always been raised by humans with the gift of sweet food and drink. Having heard Vasudeva's words, the king abandoned his sister.

Vasudeva, having taken his beloved, went to his own palace. O Nārada, he gradually begot six children, whatever was born; Vasu gave them to him [Kamsa], and Satyaka killed them one by one in succession.
Out of fear, Kaṃsa provided protection for Devakī’s seventh pregnancy;
however, Māyā drew him out into Rohiṇī’s womb and protected him. The guards reported that a miscarriage had indeed occurred.
From that [Māyā], the Lord, the master Saṃkarṣaṇa, came into being.
Indeed, she conceived an eighth embryo which was filled with wind (Vāyu).
When the ninth month had passed and the tenth was at hand, [he was born].
And the Blessed One, the all-seeing, cast his gaze upon the womb.
By that very glance, the goddess Rūpavatī herself— already the most excellent among all women—
immediately became four times more beautiful.
Kaṃsa beheld Devakī, her face and eyes blossoming with joy;
blazing with splendor like an illusion pervading the ten directions, she was as if the very collection of celestial lights embodied in form. (41)
Upon seeing her, the lord of the asuras was filled with the utmost wonder.
Thinking, "From this womb shall come offspring that is the very seed of my own death," Kaṃsa spoke thus and took great care to provide for her protection.
She protected Devakī and Vasudeva at the seven gates.
And when the tenth month was complete, the fetus became fully developed;
O Nārada, she became one whose movements were laborious and who appeared as if insentient.
And when the womb was filled with wind, the Lord Ajita remained untainted;
he indeed took up his abode within the lotus-bud of Devakī’s heart.
And she, bearing the universe as her embryo, remained within the interior of the temple.
She remained there in a state of mental dullness and became overwhelmed by affliction.
The goddess stayed for a moment, stood up for a moment;
she would walk a single step for a moment and then indeed sleep there for a moment. (46–47)
And seeing Devakī, the high-minded Vasudeva, quickly perceiving that the time of delivery had arrived, remembered Hari, the Lord,
in that most beautiful palace illuminated by jeweled lamps. 48.
Agitated by fear, he placed his sword, iron, water, and fire; a man skilled in mantras and his wife’s kinsmen;
and, trembling, a learned Brahmin and his relatives with respect. (49–50)
In the meantime, two watches of that night had passed.
The sky was overspread with clouds accompanied by momentary flashes of lightning;
winds blew, and the guards fell asleep.
Motionless upon their beds, they were unconscious as if dead.
In the meantime, the lords of the thirty gods arrived there;
Dharma, Brahmā, and Īśa praised the Supreme Lord dwelling within the womb.
The gods said:
"You are the source of the universe, yet you are without origin; you are infinite and indeed immutable.
You are the very nature of light, O sinless one, possessing attributes and yet devoid of attributes—the Great One. (54)
Out of regard for his devotees, he possesses form, yet is formless, unrestrained,
without parts, the support of all, fearless, free from affliction,
devoid of limiting adjuncts, untainted, effortless, and the ender of death.
He rejoices in his own self, his desires are fulfilled, he is unblinking and eternal.
He consists of his own will, he is the cause of all, he is everything, and the substratum of all qualities.
He is the giver of happiness and the giver of suffering; he is the fortress and the end-maker of the wicked.
He is fortunate and unfortunate, eloquent, difficult to propitiate, and insurmountable;
he is the cause of the Vedas, the Vedas themselves, the limbs of the Vedas, the knower of the Vedas, and the all-pervading Lord.
Having spoken thus, the gods bowed down again and again.
With eyes brimming with tears of joy, they all rained down flowers.
(59) Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites these forty-two names, attains firm devotion, service to Hari, and their desired fruit. (60)
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa composed by Brahmā and the others in the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having thus offered this praise, those gods returned to their own abodes. (61)
O Sage, a rain of water fell and the city of Mathurā became motionless; the night became thick with terrible darkness. When seven muhūrtas had passed and the eighth had arrived, [the Lord appeared].
In an auspicious moment superior to all, which is difficult to perceive even beyond the Vedas;
when the planets are auspiciously aligned, whether visible or invisible;
at midnight, on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī), under the Rohiṇī asterism. (63–64)
O Sage, when the moment of the *jayantī* conjunction coincided with the rising of the half-moon,
the Sun and the other planets became terrified; having repeatedly observed that moment,
they then departed for the auspicious sign of Pisces, leaping across the sky in succession.
All the planets situated there became perfectly propitious.
By the command of the Creator, those eleven [deities] remained there with affection for a moment. The clouds rained down, and very cool breezes blew. (66–67)
The earth was exceedingly serene, and the ten directions were tranquil.
The sages, the Manus, as well as the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras—
along with the gods and goddesses— rejoiced, and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
The lords of the Gandharvas and the Vidyādharīs sang, O Nārada;
the rivers flowed joyfully and the fires blazed with delight.
In the heavens, kettledrums resounded and enchanting flutes played. (69–70)
A great rain of *pārijāta* flowers fell;
the Earth, assuming a female form, went to the maternity chamber.
There was a sound of "Victory!", a sound of conch shells, and the cry of "Hari! indeed arose.
In that interval, the virtuous Devakī fell there;
then a wind issued forth from Devakī’s womb.
Right there, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, having assumed a divine form, appeared.
From the lotus-bud of Devakī’s heart, Hari indeed manifested;
his body was exceedingly lovely and most enchanting, with two arms, a flute in hand, and shimmering crown and earrings. (74)
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, He is intent on bestowing grace upon His devotees.
Adorned with ornaments made of the finest jewels and gems,
He is dark as a fresh rain cloud and resplendent in yellow garments.
Anointed with the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
with a face like the full autumn moon and lips as enchanting as the *bimba* fruit;
wearing a crest of peacock feathers and radiant with a crown of fine gold. (77)
With three folds in the middle of his abdomen and adorned with a forest garland (vanamālā), his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa and resplendent with the Kaustubha gem;
youthful in age, peaceful, beautiful, and the supreme object of Brahmā and Īśvara. (78–79)
O Sage, Vasudeva beheld [the child] before Devakī;
with supreme devotion he offered praise and was filled with great wonder.
With palms joined in reverence, his neck bowed low in devotion, he stood there.
Tears filled his eyes and his hair stood on end as he stood with Devakī and the other women.
Vasudeva said:
"You, who are beyond the senses, unmanifest, imperishable, devoid of qualities, and all-pervading—"
And for all [beings], the Supreme Lord, the Self, who cannot be attained through meditative absorption (dhyāna)—
who consists of His own will, who possesses all forms, who assumes forms by His own will,
the supreme, untainted Brahman, the eternal seed-form— [is the goal]. (82–83)
Greater in magnitude than the gross, all-pervading, exceedingly subtle, and invisible;
abiding within all bodies as the witness-form, itself unseen;
possessing a body yet devoid of qualities, it is the supreme collection of all attributes. (84)
I praise the Lord, who is both nature and the lord of nature, who is the product of nature and yet beyond nature;

who is the lord of all, whose form is everything, who brings an end to all, and who is imperishable; who is the support of all yet has no support, who is without expansion—how can I fully praise that all-pervading Lord? (85–86)
Ananta is incapable of praising him, as is the goddess Sarasvatī;
likewise, the five-faced Śiva and the six-faced Kārttikeya are unable to praise him.
Even the four-faced Brahmā, the author of the Vedas, is forever unable to praise him.
Even Gaṇeśa is not capable of praising you, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis.
(88) Why do the sages, the deities, the lords of munis, and the sons of Manu praise only you, who are invisible even in their dreams? (89)
The Vedas are incapable of praising Him; what then can the learned praise?
You ought to become a child once again, casting off this very body.
That man who recites this hymn composed by Vasudeva at the three junctions of the day [attains his goal].
One attains devotion and servitude at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
one obtains an excellent son who is a servant of Hari endowed with virtues;
one swiftly overcomes distress and is liberated from the fear of enemies. (91–92)
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa composed by Vasudeva in the glorious Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Vasudeva, Hari himself spoke to him.
With a serene countenance, glorious, and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"By the very fruit of your austerities, I am now your son."
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you—and it shall come to pass without a doubt.
Long ago, O best of ascetics, you were the Prajāpati Sutapas;
your wife was named Pṛśni, and she was propitiated by you through your ascetic penance."
"Seeing me there, the wise one chose a son like myself;
I granted you this boon: 'Your son shall be equal to me.
O dear one, having reflected in my mind after granting you this boon, [I thought as follows]."
"Therefore, there is no one equal to me in this world; for that reason, I am your son.
By the power of your asceticism, you yourself are Kaśyapa.
You are Sutapā, O Mother of the Gods, and this Aditi is devoted to her husband."
Now you, Kaśyapa, are my father Vasudeva;
Devakī, the mother of the gods, is born from a portion of Aditi.
From you, through a portion of yourself, I was born as your son Vāmana in the womb of Aditi.
"Now I am fulfilled by the fruit of your austerities, my son.
Whether you regard me as your son or rather as Brahman—
having attained me, O man of great wisdom, you shall become liberated while living."
"Taking me quickly, go to Vraja and to Yaśodā’s house.
O dear one, having placed me there, depart while assuming your illusory form.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari became a child right there.
He saw his dark-complexioned son lying naked upon the ground.
Having seen the boy there, he was deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu; what indeed was this deceptive state of exhaustion, and why was the maternity chamber so unprecedented?
Having spoken thus and consulted with his wife, Vasudeva took the child upon his breast and went to Nanda’s cowherd settlement. Reaching Nanda’s station quickly, he entered the maternity chamber.

He beheld Yaśodā lying upon her bed, overcome by sleep; he saw Nanda also steeped in slumber, as well as everyone else staying there in the house. He beheld the naked infant girl, who resembled molten gold.
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, she was looking toward the pinnacle of the house.
Upon seeing her, Vasudeva was filled with the utmost wonder.
Having placed his son there, he quickly took the girl and departed.
He went joyfully to Mathurā, to the maternity chamber of his beloved wife.
He placed the great illusory power (Mahāmāyā) and the infant girl right there;
seeing her wailing, Devakī was delighted.
By her very weeping, that young girl awakened the guards.
Rising quickly, the guards then seized the girl;
having taken the girl, they went into the presence of Kaṃsa.
Devakī and Vasudeva then departed in grief.
And having seen the auspicious young girl wailing piteously, O great sage, Kaṃsa was not at all joyful; indeed, no compassion arose within him.
As that most cruel man was going to strike her with a stone after seizing her,
Vasudeva and Devakī spoke to him with the utmost respect:
"O Kaṃsa, best of kings, you who are learned in the treatises on ethics!"
Listen to these words, which are true, endowed with wisdom, and pleasing:
O kinsman, you have shown no mercy by slaying our six sons;
now, in my eighth pregnancy, there is a weak girl. (115–116)
"O weakling, what sovereignty will you have on the surface of the earth after killing a woman? Are you capable of slaying a mere woman at the forefront of battle?
Having spoken thus to him in the assembly hall, Vasu and Devakī—
She wept there in front of the evil-minded Kaṃsa.
Having heard their words, the evil-minded Kaṃsa spoke to her.
(118) Kaṃsa said:

Listen to my words and understand them; I shall enlighten you. Even the Creator, by means of destiny, is capable of striking down a mountain with a blade of grass, or likewise a lion or a tiger with an insect, or an elephant with a mosquito.
A young one [overcomes] a great hero, and small creatures [overcome] a large one;
a mouse [overcomes] a cat, and a frog a serpent.
In this way, the offspring overcomes the progenitor, and even the food overcomes the eater. (121)
Water is destroyed by fire, and fire by dry grass;
even the seven oceans were swallowed by a single creature, a bird.
Indeed, the course of destiny is wondrous and difficult to comprehend within the three worlds.
"By fate, this girl will be capable of destroying me;
I shall kill the girl, there is no need for deliberation here.
Having spoken thus, Kaṃsa then seized the girl.
Kaṃsa began to strike him, but then Vasu said to him:
"O King, you have struck in vain; O treasure-house of compassion, give me back my child.
Having heard this, O great sage, Kaṃsa, who knew how to deliberate, was pleased.
As he was thus reflecting, an incorporeal voice arose right there:
"O fool Kaṃsa, whom do you kill without understanding the course of Hari?
At some time or other, your slayer will manifest himself. (127)
Upon hearing the voice of the gods, the king abandoned the girl.
Vasudeva and Devakī, filled with joy,
took her and went to their own home, placing the daughter upon their chests.
Having recovered her as if she were dead, he gave wealth to the Brahmins. O Brahmin, that supreme sister of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, was renowned as Ekānaṃśā, born from a portion of Pārvatī. (130)

Vasu, however, gave her with devotion at the time of Rukmiṇī’s wedding in Dvārakā to Durvāsas, who was a portion of Śaṅkara. Thus has been narrated everything concerning the glorification of Kṛṣṇa’s birth.
O Sage, it destroys birth, death, and old age, and bestows happiness and merit.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada," in the Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said:

"Tell me of the Janmāṣṭamī vow, the most excellent of all vows. Now, please explain generally the fruit of the Jayantī conjunction. O Great Sage, what is the fault in its non-performance, or what is the rule regarding eating?"
O Lord, please speak now after due reflection upon the fruit of fasting as it is well-regarded on Jayantī,
as well as the rules for the vow, the procedure for worship, self-restraint,
and the breaking of the fast.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having prepared the sacrificial oblation on the seventh day and likewise remaining self-restrained during the breaking of the fast,
one should rise at the time of dawn on the following day.

Having performed his morning duties and bathed, O Brahmin, he should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding a vow or a fast. Whatever fruit is obtained through bathing and worship when the day of Manu and other such festivals arrives—

O twice-born one, on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, the fruit becomes ten-millionfold. On that lunar day, whoever offers even a mere measure of water to the ancestors has performed a Śrāddha at Gayā for a hundred years; of this there is no doubt. (6–7)
Having bathed and performed his daily rites, he constructed a lying-in chamber equipped with clusters of fire fueled by iron fragments and guarded by groups of protectors;
therein were various kinds of materials and the instruments for cutting the umbilical cord.
A wise man should diligently station a woman in the form of a nurse (dhātrī).
O Nārada, there should be beautiful articles for worship consisting of the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra),
as well as eight sweet fruits and indeed various substances.
Jatiphala, kamkola, pomegranate, and bilva fruit;
likewise coconut, citron, pumpkin, and fragrant cloth;
as well as a seat, clothing, water for the feet, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka). (11)
The water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), water for bathing (snānīya), as well as a bed;
perfume, flowers, food offerings (naivedya), betel leaf, ointment;
incense, lamps, and ornaments—these indeed are the sixteen modes of service (upacāra). || 12–13 ||
Having washed his feet and put on two clean garments,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and taken his seat, he should first recite the benediction (svastivācana).
Then, having placed the water-pot (ghaṭa) and worshipped the five deities, he should proceed.
Having performed the invocation into the jar for the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
[one should invoke] Vasudeva and Devakī, Yaśodā and Nanda,
Rohiṇī and Baladeva, as well as the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī and Vasundharā. (15–16)
To Rohiṇī and Brāhmaṇī, and to the eighth, the deity of the site;
to Hanumān and Vibhīṣaṇa along with Aśvatthāman;
and to Kṛpa, Paraśurāma, Vedavyāsa, and Mṛkaṇḍaka. (17)
Having performed the invocation of all [the deities], one should then perform meditation upon Hari.
Placing the flower upon His head, the wise man should meditate again.
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the meditation as declared in the Sāmaveda.
Formerly, Brahmā spoke thus to the high-souled Kumāra:

"That supreme one, who is praised for a few days by Brahmā, Īśāna, and Ananta with their respective attributes— he is a child, possessing the luster of a blue lotus, exceedingly beautiful, with a smiling lotus-face."

I worship that which cannot be accomplished through meditation even by the lords of sages, the hosts of munis, or the assemblies of Siddhas; that which is unattainable for the masters of yoga, inconceivable, incomparable, and the very form of the Witness.
(21) Having meditated upon it and offered a flower, one should offer all of that as an oblation.
Thus the observer of the vow should perform the rite; O Sage, listen to the sequence of mantras:
"O Hari, let this beautiful seat, rich in all splendor, fashioned from excellent gems and jewels, and variegated with its diversity, be accepted. (22–23)
"O Hari, please accept this garment, purified by fire and fashioned by Viśvakarman, inlaid with molten gold and adorned with paintings (24).
And for the purpose of washing your feet, here is water contained in a golden vessel."
"O Hari, please accept this pure, stainless, and beautiful water for washing the feet (pādya).
O Hari, please accept this supreme substance for bathing— honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sugar combined, placed within a golden vessel."
"O Hari, please accept this *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, white flowers, and pure water, combined with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk.
This delicious, clear water has been perfumed with fragrant substances. (27)
"O Supreme Lord, please accept this pure water for sipping.
O Viṣṇu, please accept this well-perfumed oil blended with fragrant substances.
O Hari, please accept this bathing water consisting of the juice of *āmalaka*."
"O Hari, please accept this most enchanting bed, fashioned from the essence of excellent gems and jewels, covered with a fine cloth;
as well as the powder of various trees mixed with their roots and liquids. (30)
O Hari, please accept this fragrance blended with liquid musk. O Hari, please now accept these fragrant flowers, infused with saffron and most beloved by all the gods.
"O Hari, please accept this food offering (naivedya) as prescribed for the Svastika rite, provided with sweet substances, joined with well-cooked fruits; [accept] the laḍḍukas,
modakas, clarified butter, milk, jaggery, and honey."
O Hari, please accept this freshly churned curd and buttermilk as an offering.
[Please accept] the cool, well-cooked milk pudding mixed with sugar,
and betel leaf— the essence of enjoyment— blended with camphor and other ingredients.

O Supreme Lord, please accept this which has been offered with devotion. O Supreme Lord, please accept this beautiful *abīra* powder, blended with the liquid extracts of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
"O Hari, let this incense be accepted—it is the excellence of the essence of various trees, endowed with fragrance, and accompanied by fire;
it is most dear to all the gods, the sole cause for destroying terrible darkness, and the bringer of auspiciousness. (37–38)
"O Hari, let this lamp, well-kindled and light-giving, be taken.
O Hari, let this pure, stainless water, mixed with camphor and other fragrances—the life-sustainer of all seeds—be taken for drinking. (39)
"May this excellent garland, composed of various flowers and strung with fine thread,
which is the finest ornament for the body, be accepted.
Having offered these materials and other substances required for worship," (40–41)
Furthermore, wealth situated in the place of the vow must indeed be offered to Hari.
Fruits, seeds of trees that are sweet and beautiful, which truly cause the increase of the lineage—O Supreme Lord, please accept them. 42.
The observer of the vow should worship each of the invited deities individually.
Having worshipped them with a spirit of devotion, he should offer three handfuls of flowers to Sunandana,
Nandaka, Kumuda, the cowherds, the cowherd women, and Rādhikā.
Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, Brahmā and Śiva and Śivā; Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, as well as the guardians of the quarters and the planets;
Śeṣa and Sudarśana, and likewise the foremost attendants.
Having worshipped all the gods and prostrated on the ground like a staff,
and having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya) to the Brahmins, one should give them a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, with a spirit of devotion, one should listen to the narrative as told in the chapter on the birth [of the Lord].
Then, seated upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, the observer of the vow should keep a vigil.
At dawn, having performed his daily rites and joyfully worshipped Śrī Hari,
he should feed the Brahmins and cause the glorification of Hari to be recited.
Nārada said: Having thoroughly examined the meaning of the Vedas and the ancient Saṃhitās, [I shall explain] the regulation of the times for vows as declared in the Vedas and accepted by all. 49.
"O Sage, best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me: what is the fruit of fasting, keeping vigil, and observing vows? And what is the sin incurred by eating there?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

If the eighth lunar day, conjoined with the asterism [Śravaṇā], is seen during the latter half of the night, that alone is the primary time; Hari himself was born therein. Because it brings victory and merit, it is remembered as Jayantī.
Having fasted there and performed the vow, the wise man should keep a vigil.
"This time is the foremost occasion for all expiations and is approved by all"—such is the word of those who know the Vedas, as spoken by Brahmā in the past. (52–53)
Having kept a vigil there and observed the fast while performing the vow, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births; of this there is no doubt.
One should take great care to avoid the eighth lunar day when it coincides with the seventh.

Even that [Aṣṭamī] should not be observed when it is joined with the seventh lunar day (Saptamī). For it was on an unblemished Aṣṭamī under the asterism of Rohiṇī that the son of Devakī was born, endowed with the distinguished auspicious marks of one who is protected by the Vedas and Vedāṅgas. 55.
When the Rohiṇī asterism has passed, the observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
At the end of the lunar day, the observer of the vow, having remembered Hari and performed the worship of the deity,
should take the purifying fast-breaking meal, which destroys all sins for men.
It is a constituent part of the fast, yielding fruit and being the cause of spiritual success.
In all fasts, breaking the fast during the day is prescribed;
otherwise, if the breaking of the fast is performed at night, there will be a loss of the fruit.
One should not perform the breaking of the fast at night, except during the Rohiṇī vow.
One may break the fast at night, avoiding the "great midnight" (mahāniśā).
Breaking the fast in the forenoon is recommended after having performed worship of the Brahmins and the gods.
One should perform [the vow] with the consent of all, except for the Rohiṇī-vrata.
If Jayantī, conjoined with Wednesday and Monday, is obtained,
the observer of the vow, having performed it then, shall not undergo residence in a womb again.
If at sunrise there is even a small portion of the eighth lunar day and the ninth is complete,
and it is conjoined with Mercury and the Moon and associated with the Rohiṇī asterism,
such an occasion may not be found even in a hundred years, or it may indeed be found.

There, the observer of the vow should perform the rite; he shall deliver ten million men. Even for devotees of meager fortune who lack the capacity for such vows, Mādhava becomes pleased simply by their performing a single fast. (64)
Through devotion, various offerings, and keeping a vigil at night,
the enemy of the Daityas bestows the fruit arising from the Jayantī vow.
One who does not practice stinginess regarding wealth shall obtain the full fruit.
One who practices stinginess regarding wealth obtains a corresponding fruit.
Furthermore, a wise person should not break the fast on the eighth lunar day or under the asterism Rohiṇī;
for such an act would destroy previously accumulated merit as well as the fruit earned through the fast.
It destroys the merit of the lunar day eightfold and that of the asterism fourfold.
Therefore, one should diligently perform the breaking of the fast at the end of the lunar day.
When the end of the lunar day occurs while the "great night" (mahāniśā) has arrived— || 68–69 ||

On the third day, O best of sages, the wise man performs the breaking of his fast (*pāraṇa*). But when six *muhūrtas* have passed, it is indeed the middle of the night; O Nārada, by eating there, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Betel leaf, fruit, and water are equal to beef, excrement, and urine;
for pure men, they are unfit to be consumed—what then need be said of cooked rice?
They say the night consists of three watches, excluding the first and the last [four-hour periods]. (71–72)

At both twilights, which are designated as the beginning and end of the day, and on the pure eighth day of the birth [of the Lord], having performed the vow of keeping a vigil, one is liberated from the sins committed in a hundred births; there is no doubt in this matter. (75)
If a man fasts on the pure Janmāṣṭamī day alone,
even without keeping a vigil, he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Whatever [sin] was committed in childhood, in youth, in middle age, or in old age— [all that is purified].

One is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this. But that lowest of men who eats on the birthday of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shall become a violator of his mother's bed and incur the sin of a hundred murders of Brahmins.
The merit accumulated over ten million births is certainly destroyed for him.
He is unworthy and perpetually impure in rites for the gods and the ancestors;
in the end, he shall dwell in the Kālasūtra hell as long as the moon and sun endure.
Devoured by worms with sharp fangs that are like spears, the sinner then rises up; if he should obtain a birth in Bhārata, he shall become a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years. (79)
For a hundred births he was a vulture, for a hundred births a boar;
for a hundred births a beast of prey, and for seven births a jackal;
for seven births a serpent, and for seven births a crow. (80–81)
Thereafter, that man shall become mute, afflicted with oozing leprosy, and perpetually diseased;
thereafter he shall become a killer of animals, and thereafter a snake-catcher;
at the end of that, he shall become a robber, devoid of dharma, and a vulture.
Then he may become a washerman, then an oil-presser;
then he may become a temple-priest (devalaka), a Brāhmaṇa who is perpetually impure. If one is unable to observe the fast, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa.
He should give away wealth until what has been consumed becomes doubled;

or he should recite the mantra of the Goddess a thousand times, or perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). Thus, a man should perform these twelve [observances] according to his purpose during that vow.
Thus, O child, has been related that which was heard from the mouth of Dharma:
the procedure for vows, fasts, and worship, as well as what occurs when they are not performed.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow, Worship, and Fasting of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
Having established Kṛṣṇa in Gokula at the home of Yaśodā, Vasu Nanda went to his own house; what did that great lord do? (1)

O Sage, describe in sequence what Hari did there, for how many years the Lord remained, and what his childhood playthings were. Also relate the vow that was previously made by Rādhā together with Him in Goloka.
By what method was Hari’s vow fulfilled?
Tell me, what is the region named Vṛndāvana like, and of what nature is it?
O Lord, having set aside the Rāsa dance and the water-sports, please describe it.
What penance did Nanda perform, and what did Yaśodā and Rohiṇī do?
Furthermore, where did the birth of Hari and the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) previously take place?
This is the unprecedented narrative of the Moon-portion (Pīyūṣakhaṇḍa), remembered as belonging to Śrī Hari.
Especially from the mouths of poets, something new surely emerges at every step.
(6) Furthermore, describe yourself the very sport of the circle of musical notes.
Poetry is praised for its description of what is absent; the description of the new is most excellent. (7)
"You are the direct portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis.
Whosoever is a portion of another, that person is happy only through the happiness of that [source].
You two have described the feet of Hari, and you both are dissolved within them."
"You alone are a direct portion of the Lord of Goloka, great and equal to Him.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, Vighneśa, Kūrma, Dharma, and I myself—"
Nara, Kārttikeya, and we nine are portions of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Oh, by whom can the majesty of the Lord of Goloka be described?
We ourselves do not know Him, nor do the Vedas; how then could the learned scholars?
The Boar, the Dwarf, Kalki, the Buddha, Kapila, and Mīnaka—
O Sage, these and many other portions (aṃśas) and digits (kalās) truly exist in manifold ways.
[12] The Tortoise, Nṛsiṃha, Rāma, and the all-pervading Virāṭ of Śvetadvīpa.

Kṛṣṇa, the most perfectly complete, is himself present both in Vaikuṇṭha and in Gokula. In Vaikuṇṭha, the beloved of Kamalā possesses four arms due to a difference in form; in Goloka and Gokula, he himself is the beloved of Rādhā and possesses two arms.
Yogis constantly place His splendor within their hearts;
devotees [place] His lotus feet [therein]. Without a radiant one, how could there be radiance?
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe the penance of Yaśodā and Nanda.
And because they beheld the face of Hari during Rohiṇī;
Nanda, the foremost of the Vasus, was by name Droṇa, rich in asceticism.
His wife was the virtuous Dharā, who as an ascetic woman became Yaśodā. (16–17)
Rohiṇī, the mother of the serpents, and Kadrū, the progenitor of snakes—
learn of their birth and life story as I relate it to you.
Once, upon Mount Gandhamādana, Dharā and Droṇa [dwelt]...
O sage, in the meritorious land of Bhārata-varṣa, in the vicinity of Gautama’s hermitage,
they performed austerities there for ten thousand years on the secluded bank of the Suprabhā river for the sake of beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (19–20)
Droṇa did not see Hari, nor did the ascetic Earth;
out of world-weariness, they prepared a fire-pit and stood ready to enter it.
Seeing them desirous of death, an incorporeal voice arose:
O best of the Vasus, you two shall behold the glorious Lord Hari on earth in Gokula in the form of a son—
He who is difficult to perceive even for yogis in other births, who is unattainable through meditation even by the wise, and who is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods. (22–23)
Having heard this from the Earth, Droṇa and Aṅgiras went happily to their own abode.
Having obtained birth in Bhārata-varṣa, they beheld the face of Hari.
Thus has the life-story of Yaśodā and Nanda been narrated to you.
Listen to the conduct of Rohiṇī, which is most secret even to the thirty gods.
Once, O sage, on the day of the Flower Festival, the mother of the gods made a request to Kaśyapa through a female messenger.
