The beautiful goddess, having bathed well and adorned with jewel ornaments,
assumed various garments and beheld her face in a mirror;
it was marked with a spot of musk together with a dot of vermilion.

Richly adorned with the splendor of jeweled earrings and decorated with leaf-shaped ornaments, his nose-tip was joined with elephant-pearls and was exceedingly beautiful; his face was like the full autumn moon and his eyes were like autumn lotuses. (28–29)

Endowed with arched eyebrows that playfully curve, resplendent with variegated kohl, and graced by a row of teeth resembling the seeds of a ripe pomegranate; possessing lips like a ripe bimba fruit, he is always beautiful and smiling. (30)
Extremely lovely and enchanting even to the minds of the lords of sages—
seeing her face thus transformed, Sundarī, remaining in her own home,
watched the path of her husband while being tormented by the arrows of Kama. (31–32)
Aditi heard news that Kaśyapa was united with Kadrū,
staying upon her breast at the commencement of the gathering of the essence of jewels.
Upon hearing this, that virtuous woman became enraged— her hopes shattered and distressed by the loss of her pleasure.
Out of love, she did not curse her husband; rather, she cursed the mother of the serpent:
"May she, though righteous, be unworthy of a temple; may that destroyer of dharma go far away from the heavenly world and back to her human birth. (34–35)
Having heard this, Caradvārā cursed the mother of the gods:
"May she enter a human womb and be born from a placenta among mortals.
Kaśyapa then enlightened Kadru, the mother of the serpents.
"O lady of pure smiles, you shall go to the mortal realm with me at the proper time.
Cast off your fear, obtain happiness, and you shall behold the face of Śrī Hari.
Having spoken thus, Kaśyapa departed from Aditi’s house. (37–38)
The omnipresent Lord fulfilled her desire;
and during that season, Mahendra became the bull among the gods.
Aditi became Devakī, and Rohiṇī became the mother of serpents.
Kaśyapa and Vasudeva, the great father of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
O sage, everything that was to be kept secret has now been told.
Now, O sage, hear the account of the birth of Baladeva.
O sage, by the command of Vasudeva, the virtuous Rohiṇī— the jewel among wives and the beloved consort of the infinite, immeasurable Lord who possesses a thousand heads—
went to Gokula.
Fleeing out of fear of Kaṃsa for the sake of Saṃkarṣaṇa’s protection,
Māyā then, by Kṛṣṇa’s command, placed Devakī’s seventh embryo into the womb of Rohiṇī there in Gokula. (43–44)

Having then established the embryo [within herself], she went to Kailāsa. After a few days had passed, Rohiṇī gave birth in the house of Nanda to a son who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, a lord with the luster of refined silver.
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, he blazed with the splendor of Brahman.
At his very birth, the gods rejoiced;
then, in heaven, the kettledrums, tabors, drums, and other instruments resounded.
Filled with joy, the gods raised shouts of victory and blew their conchs.
Nanda, delighted, bestowed various kinds of wealth upon the brahmins.
The nurse cut the umbilical cord and bathed the infant.
Adorned with all their ornaments, the gopīs sang the word "Victory!
(jaya). Nanda, with the utmost devotion, celebrated the festival for his son as if he were another's.
Then, Yaśodā joyfully gave gifts to the gopīs and the brāhmaṇas.
Wealth, various articles, oil, and vermilion— thus,
O child, has been described the penance of Yaśodā and Nanda,
as well as the account of the birth of the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) and the life of Rohiṇī.
Now listen to that desirable festival of Nanda’s son,
which bestows happiness, grants liberation, is the essence, removes birth, death, and old age,
is auspicious, is the life-story of Kṛṣṇa, and is the very life of the Vaiṣṇavas. (52–53)
Destroying all inauspiciousness and bestowing devotion and service to Hari,
Vasudeva established Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the house of Nanda;
then, taking the girl [Yaśodā], he joyfully went to his own home.
O Sage, her life story has been told and heard from you in person.
Now hear the auspicious deeds of Kṛṣṇa in Gokula.
When Vasudeva had gone home, Yaśodā and Nanda likewise [remained]. (55–56)
In the auspicious lying-in chamber, a hall of victory filled with joy,
she beheld her son upon the ground, possessing the luster of a fresh rain-cloud—
exceedingly beautiful, naked, and gazing toward the pinnacle of the house. (57)
With a face like the full moon of autumn, eyes like blue lotuses, weeping and laughing, his body entwined with a flute;
his two hands well-positioned, full of love for his lotus feet. (58–59)
Seeing Hari together with his mother, Nanda became overjoyed.
A nurse bathed the infant with cool water;
the cowherd women, out of delight, cut the umbilical cord and cried "Victory! for him.

All the cowherd women arrived, with their broad hips and swaying breasts; the young girls, the companions, and the wives of the brahmins also came. They all offered their blessings to the woman who had given birth and joyfully gazed upon the infant.
Some, praising him, took him onto their laps and stayed there;
Nanda, having bathed with his clothes on and put on two clean garments,
performed the traditional rites there with a joyful heart.
He fed the Brahmins and had auspicious rites performed;
he caused musical instruments to be played and gave wealth to the bards.
Then Nanda, filled with joy, bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins.

O Sage, [he offered] with reverence seven mountains of sesame seeds, along with six kinds of gems, corals, and diamonds; a hundred measures of gold, silver, a mountain of grain, clothing, and a thousand beautiful cows. (66)
Curd, milk, sugar, fresh butter, clarified butter, honey;
(67) sweet foods, a multitude of excellent *laḍḍuka* sweets, and delicious *modaka* cakes;
land abundant with all kinds of crops, and horses with the speed of the wind; (68)
Having offered betel leaves and oils, he became joyful;
indeed, he appointed Brāhmaṇas, as well as groups of elderly cowherd women who were knowers of mantras, to guard the lying-in chamber. (69)
He caused the Vedas to be recited, which contain the singular auspiciousness of Hari’s name;
and with devotion, through the agency of Brahmins, he worshipped the deities.
He also honored the elderly cowherd women, who were adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Smiling and moving swiftly, they arrived at Nanda’s palace;
and various classes of astrologers, experts in the science of astronomy,
arrived at Nanda’s palace, their speech perfected and holding books in their hands.
Smiling, the wives of the brahmins, their female companions, elderly ladies,
and young girls accompanied by their children came to Nanda’s house;
to them also he gave jewels and various kinds of wealth.
Having respectfully offered excellent garments, silver, and thousands of cows to them,
Nanda joyfully paid his respects with humility.
They all bestowed their blessings upon him and beheld the supreme child.
Thus the bull among the Vrajas had accumulated the necessary provisions.
He had the astrologers calculate his future, both auspicious and inauspicious.
In this manner, the boy grew like the moon in the bright fortnight.
At Nandālaya, Halī indeed drank from his mother’s breast.
Then Rohiṇī, delighted by that festival for her son, joyfully gave them oil, vermilion, betel, and wealth, O Sage. (78)
Having bestowed blessings upon their heads, they returned to their own abodes.
Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, and Nandā remained in the house, filled with joy.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Festival for Nanda’s Son," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Kaṃsa, seated upon a golden throne in the midst of the assembly, heard a truthful, incorporeal voice in the sky. 1.
"What are you doing, O great fool? Perform that which is for your own welfare!
The time has come for you upon this earth; remain, O lord of men, in the means [of salvation].
Having given his son to Nanda, Vasudeva [departed]—he who was your end."
Having taken the girl and given her to you, he remains there employing his illusory power (māyā). This girl is a portion of Māyā, and Vāsudeva himself is Hari;
he is growing up in Nanda’s house in Gokula as your slayer.
The seventh embryo of Devakī was growing in the house of Nanda.
The seventh embryo of Devakī did not bring forth a son of nectar;
indeed, Māyā placed him within the womb of Rohiṇī.
And there, the remaining portion was born as the exceedingly powerful Baladeva. Both of them grew up in Gokula in the house of Nanda during that time.
Having heard these words, the king became one whose neck was bowed low.
Suddenly overcome with anxiety, the king, distracted in mind, abandoned his food.

Having summoned Pūtanā, who was dearer to him than life itself, the king, skilled in statecraft, spoke to his sister in the midst of the assembly: 8–9. [He spoke] to his sister, the virtuous woman, in the middle of the hall.
Kaṃsa said:
"O Pūtanā, go to Gokula for the sake of my purpose, to the house of Nanda.
Having smeared your breast with poison, give it to the infant immediately."
"O child, you who travel by mind and are skilled in the science of illusion (māyā-śāstra),
O yoginī, having assumed an illusory human form and having obtained the great mantra of Durvāsas, go forth, you who can travel everywhere. (10–11)
"O well-established one, you are capable of assuming every form.
Having spoken thus to her, O Nārada, the great king remained in the assembly;
Pūtanā, moving at will, departed after bowing to Kaṃsa.
Having the luster of molten gold, adorned with various ornaments, she bore a mass of braided hair entwined with garlands of jasmine;
joyfully, she wore vermilion marked with a spot of musk. (13–14)
Making a sweet sound with her anklets and girdle,
she reached the cow-pen, which was difficult to behold and as enchanting as Nanda’s own abode;
it was surrounded by deep moats that were impossible to cross.
It was fashioned from divine stones and constructed by Viśvakarman;
it was adorned with sapphires, emeralds, and rubies,
and made radiant by its crests of divine golden pitchers, variegated and brilliant.
It was surrounded by walls that touched the sky, provided with four gates,
fitted with iron doors, and attended by gatekeepers;
it was beautiful, delightful, and encircled by throngs of beautiful women.
It was filled with pearls, rubies, emeralds, and wealth consisting of full precious gems;
it was strewn with golden vessels and surrounded by ten million cows, as well as by servants to be maintained and hundreds of thousands of cowherds. (19–20)
Accompanied by thousands of maidservants busy with their tasks,
the virtuous and most enchanting woman entered the hermitage with a smile.
Seeing her entering, the cowherd women looked on and gave their approval.
Or has Lakṣmī, the dweller in the lotus, or Durgā come here to see Kṛṣṇa?
(22) The cowherd women and cowherds bowed down to her and inquired after her welfare;
they offered her a throne, water for her feet, and indeed provided her with a place to stay there. (23)
She inquired after the welfare of the cowherds and the child;
that virtuous woman sat there with a smile and respectfully accepted the water for her feet.
All the cowherd women said to her, "O Goddess, who are you here now?"
"Where is your dwelling? What is your name? Or what is your business here? Tell us.
Having heard their words, she too spoke charmingly:
"I am a cowherd girl residing in Mathurā; at present, I am seeking a Brahmin. (25–26)
"I have heard from the mouth of the oral teacher that truth which indicates auspiciousness:
'In this advanced age, there is a great son of Nanda.
Having heard this, I have come to see him and to bestow my desired blessing."
"Bring my son; having seen him and offered him my blessing, I shall depart.
Hearing these words of the brahmin woman, Yaśodā, her heart filled with joy, bowed her son and placed him in the lap of the brahmin lady. (28–29)
Placing him upon her lap, that virtuous woman kissed him again and again;
seated comfortably, the meritorious and faithful lady gave Hari her breast to drink.
"O beautiful cowherd girl, what a wonderful child this is! she exclaimed.
"This boy is equal to Nārāyaṇa in his virtues," he said.
Having drunk the poisoned breast-milk while staying upon her chest, Kṛṣṇa laughed;
he drank that poisonous milk along with her life-breaths as if it were nectar.

The virtuous woman abandoned the child; having given up her life-breaths, she fell down, O Sage, with her face turned upward and her features distorted. Casting off her gross body, she entered into her subtle body.
He quickly ascended the chariot fashioned from the essence of jewels (34),
surrounded by the most excellent and divine attendants who were exceedingly beautiful,
adorned with a hundred thousand white chowries and a hundred thousand mirrors (35).
The bridegroom was adorned with a fine cloth purified by fire,
accompanied by various wonderful and variegated jars made of excellent gems;
he was seated upon a beautiful chariot with a hundred wheels, which was encircled by the brilliance of jewels.
Placing those attendants upon their chariot, they departed for the supreme Goloka.
Seeing that wonder, the people and the cowherd women were utterly amazed;
and Kaṃsa, having heard all of it, was likewise filled with astonishment.
O sage, Yaśodā took the child, placed him on her lap, and gave him her breast;
she then had auspicious rites performed for the infant through the mediation of brāhmaṇas.
And Nanda joyfully burned [the sacrificial] body of hers.
Having obtained a fragrance equal to sandalwood, agallochum, and musk...
(40) Nārada said:
Who was that virtuous woman in the form of a Rākṣasī, and how did she become so meritorious?
By what merit did he go to the temple of Kṛṣṇa upon seeing him?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having seen the charming form of Vāmana at the sacrifice of Bali...
Balakanyā Ratnamālā felt maternal affection for him.
In her mind she thought, "He is like my own son;
if Kṛṣṇa would drink from my breast, I shall place him upon it."
Knowing her mind to be full of longing for a grove,
the ocean of mercy, who fulfills all desires, gave her a breast in another birth.
O sage, the demoness Pūtanā gave Kṛṣṇa a breast containing poison.
"Through devotion he attained the state of his mother; whom can we worship but Hari?
(45) Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you this most excellent and exceedingly sweet glorification of the virtues of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, step by step. (46)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Pūtanā," in the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, in the section concerning the childhood of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once upon a time, the virtuous Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda, was in Gokula.
While she was absorbed in her household chores, having placed the child upon her breast,
Śrī Hari perceived with his mind that Tṛṇāvarta, in the form of a whirlwind, was approaching Gokula; he then became weighed down by a great burden.
O sage, Yaśodā, overcome by the weight [of the child], then laid the boy to rest and went to the Yamunā.
In that interval, an asura assumed the form of a whirlwind.
Having seized him and whirled him around, the master of illusions went a hundred yojanas away;
he shattered the branches of the trees and rendered the cowherd settlement blind,
and then he suddenly fell back down upon that spot.
The Asura also, through the touch of Hari,
went to the abode of Hari after ascending a beautiful chariot and bringing about the exhaustion of his own karma.
He was the king born in the Pāṇḍya country who had become an Asura due to the curse of Durvāsas.
By the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, he went to Goloka. O Sage, when he had departed in the form of a whirlwind, the cowherds and cowherd girls were overwhelmed with fear;
they did not see the boy there, lying upon his bed.
Overwhelmed by grief and fear, they all struck their own chests;
some fell into a swoon, while others wept.
Searching about, they saw the boy in Vraja.
With all his limbs grey with dust, standing within a flower garden,
on a certain outer part of the shore of a lake devoid of water,
he was constantly gazing at the sky and speaking in a state of terrified distress. (10–11)
Taking the child and quickly placing him against his chest,
Nanda gazed repeatedly at his face and wept, overcome with grief.
Seeing the child so swiftly, Yaśodā and Rohiṇī also wept.
Placing his face upon her breast, she kissed it again and again.
Yaśodā, her face and eyes radiant with joy, caused the boy to be blessed with auspicious rites, bathed him, and gave him her breast to suck.
Nārada said:
O Brahmin, having reflected well, please relate this ancient history: how did Durvāsas curse the king born in the Pāṇḍya country? 15.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The powerful King Sahasrākṣa, the sovereign of the Pāṇḍya country, took a thousand women with him, being tormented by the arrows of desire. 16.
On the enchanting and solitary Gandhamādana mountain,
the king sported on the delightful banks of rivers and in beautiful flower gardens, performing various kinds of amorous gestures, including the inverted and other such acts.
(17) O King, [he performed] various types of erotic charms, such as the *viparīta* and others.
He left his body marked by the nail-scratches and tooth-bites of amorous women.
Having assumed a thousand forms, that lord of kings, a master of yoga,
performed sports on dry land and engaged in aquatic play.
All the women were without garments, and the king’s wives were naked;
they sported on the charming bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river.
In the meantime, a great sage arrived there.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of disciples, he was traveling toward Śaṅkara.
Upon seeing the sage, the intoxicated king neither rose nor bowed;
neither with speech nor with his hand did he offer a greeting.
Seeing this, he became enraged and, with his lips quivering, cursed the king:
"O most sinful one, become an asura! Fallen from yoga, go to the earth!
O lowest of men, you must remain there in Bhārata for a hundred thousand years. (23)
Then, by the touch of Hari’s feet, you will certainly go to Goloka.
O queens, in various places you shall take birth in Bhārata;
in the houses of great kings, you will become beautiful consorts to great kings.
Having spoken thus, the lord of sages departed for the abode of Śaṅkara;
the compassionate hosts of disciples raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
When the lord of sages had gone, the king wept upon the bank of the river.
The beautiful women, distressed by separation, wept piteously.
(27) Repeating again and again, "O Lord, O best of lovers!
Where shall we go without you, or where will you go? (28)
"We shall not dwell with you in this most secluded place.
You will not rule the kingdom, nor shall we go home.
We shall not behold your face, which eclipses the radiance of the autumn moon. (29)
"We will not bring him back with our outstretched arms"—
having said this, they all wept, placing the lord of men at their head;
and grasping the feet of the king on the riverbank, they fell into a swoon.

O Nārada, having prepared a sacrificial fire-pit together with the women, the king, recollecting the lotus feet of Hari, entered the blazing fire. All the gods, stationed in the sky, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (Hāhākāra).
Thus spoke the sages, for destiny is indeed most powerful.
And that king Tṛṇāvarta went to the abode of Hari.
The queens obtained their desired births in the land of Bhārata.
Thus has been related everything concerning the supreme majesty of Hari, as well as the liberation of the king from the cause of the sage’s curse.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Tṛṇāvarta," in the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. 11.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, in the palace, that wife of Nanda, having placed Govinda upon her breast with great joy, gave him her breast as he was hungry. 1.
In the meantime, the cowherd women arrived at Nanda’s house—
the elderly, the companions, and the young girls accompanied by their children.
Having quickly laid the insatiable child upon his bed, the virtuous women [entered].
Rising up with joy, she performed the auspicious rites of hospitality;
filled with delight, the cowherd woman gave them oil, vermilion, and betel-leaf, as well as sweet foods, garments, and ornaments. (3–4)
In the meantime, O sage, the all-pervading Lord of Māyā, the almighty Kṛṣṇa, being hungry,
moved His foot through His power of illusion;
that foot fell upon the skillfully crafted cart.
From the blow of Viśvaṃbhara’s foot, that [cart] was indeed reduced to powder.
The cart was shattered; its broken wooden parts fell there, and curds, milk, butter, ghee, and honey spilled out.
Seeing this wonder, the cowherd women fled from fear of the boy;
they saw the broken cart with the infant inside the firewood, as well as a heap of shattered vessels and much spilled cow's milk. (8)
Having pushed aside the wooden beams, she seized the child out of fear.
Yaśodā gave her breast to him, whose every limb was protected by Māyā; though he cried from hunger, she wept bitterly with grief.
The cowherd boys asked, "How did he break the cart?
We see no cause whatsoever; how wonderful that it happened so suddenly!
All the boys spoke thus, and the cowherds said, "Listen to my words."
"By a kick from Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s foot, the cart was surely shattered.
Upon hearing those words, the cowherds and cowherd-maidens laughed with joy; however, the people in Vraja did not believe it and said, "This is false. (12–13)
The eminent brāhmaṇas performed a rite for the child’s well-being;
placing his hand upon the child’s body, the twice-born one recited the armor (kavaca).
"O best of brāhmaṇas, I shall tell you that armor which provides protection from all [dangers]."
That which was previously given by Māyā to Brahmā at his navel-lotus,
while the Lord of the World was asleep upon the waters as the Water-Sleeper—
to him who was afraid and offering praise out of fear of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Yoganidrā said:
"Cast away your fear; what cause for fear is there while Hari stands by?
And while I am present, O Brahman, remain at ease, O Lord of the Universe. (17)
May Śrī Hari protect your face; may Madhusūdana protect your head.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect your eyes; may the Lord of Rādhikā protect your nose.
May Mādhava protect the pair of your ears, your throat, and your skull. (18)
May Govinda protect my cheek, and may Keśava himself protect my hair.
May Hṛṣīkeśa protect my lower lip, and Gadāgraja my row of teeth.
May Rāseśvara protect my tongue, and the all-pervading Vāmana my palate. (19–20)
May Mukunda protect the chest, and may the slayer of Daityas protect the belly.
May Janārdana protect the navel, and may Viṣṇu protect my genitals.
May Puruṣottama protect the pair of hips and the private parts.
May the all-pervading Lord of Jānakī protect your pair of knees at all times;
may Nṛsiṃha protect your pair of hands in every crisis;
and may Varāha, who was born from the lotus, protect your pair of feet.
May Nārāyaṇa protect from above, and may the Lord of Kamalā protect from below.
May Gopāla protect in the east, and may the slayer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa protect in the southeast (Agni).
May Vanamālī protect in the south, and may Vaikuṇṭha protect in the southwest (Nairṛti).
And Vāsudeva himself, the protector of the virtuous, [resides] in the western quarter; may he, the unborn Viṣṭaraśravas, protect you constantly in the northwestern quarter;
and may the one whose seat is the lotus always protect you in the northern quarter with his splendor.
May Īśvara protect [me] in the northeast; may the Conqueror of Enemies protect me everywhere.
May Rāghava protect me in water, on land, in the atmosphere, and during sleep.
Thus, O Brahman, has this most wonderful armor been described.

Formerly, when I was remembered by Kṛṣṇa out of compassion, I was granted [this weapon] by him. In the battle with Śumbha, which was aimless and most terrible, he was instantly defeated by me as soon as I reached it while stationed in the sky. (28–29)
By the power of his armor, he fell upon the earth and died.
Having previously waged a terrifying battle in the sky for a hundred years,
when Śumbha was dead, the compassionate Govinda remained stationed in the heavens.
Having bestowed the garland and the armor, he departed for Goloka.
O Sage, out of compassion, this account of another kalpa has been told;
by the power of the armor, there is no internal fear.
"Millions upon millions of creators have been seen by me as they perished;
yet I, together with Hari, am always constant through every kalpa.
Having spoken thus and bestowed the armor, she vanished from sight.
The lotus-born Brahmā remained free from fear within the lotus of his navel.
And having placed this supreme armor upon a golden pill, the wise man who always binds it around his neck or his right arm [is protected]. (34–35)
No fear arises for him from poison, fire, water, or enemies.
Whether in water, on land, or in the sky, while awake or asleep, the Lord protects him—
in battle, during the fall of a thunderbolt, in calamity, or in life-threatening danger.
Merely by recollecting this armor, one immediately attains fearlessness.
Having bound this armor around his neck in ancient times, Śaṅkara slew the lord of the Asuras, who was difficult to overcome, against Tripura with effortless ease. (37–38)
Having donned this armor, Kālī devoured the Raktabīja;
having worn this [armor], the Thousand-Headed One sustains the universe like a single sesame seed.
We two, as well as Sanatkumāra, are witnesses to the deeds of all beings.
"By the power of this armor, we shall be victorious everywhere.
(40) The twice-born one placed the armor around the neck of that infant Nanda;
and Hari himself wore his own armor around his neck. (41)

Thus, O sage, the entire power of the armor of Hari, as well as the incomparable power of the infinite Acyuta, has been told. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Armor-Recitation and the Description of Yoga-Nidrā for the Breaking of the Cart," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O great sage, listen to another account of the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, which destroys obstacles, removes sins, and bestows supreme merit. 1.
Once, the wife of Nanda, having placed Kṛṣṇa upon her breast while seated on a golden throne, gave her breast to him as he was hungry. In the meantime, a certain eminent brāhmaṇa arrived there.
Surrounded by a multitude of disciples and blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
he was reciting the Supreme Brahman with a rosary of pure crystal;
carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in white garments, his teeth shone brilliantly.
He was the personified Jyotirgrantha, a master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas;
he wore a mass of matted hair resembling molten gold,
possessed a face like the full autumn moon, fair limbs, and lotus-like eyes.
The lord of yogis, a disciple of Dhūrjaṭi and a pure devotee of the Wielder of the Mace (Viṣṇu),
his glorious hand formed the gesture of exposition as he joyfully taught his disciples,
as if effortlessly performing various kinds of commentaries on the Vedas. (6–7)
The four Vedas, as if having become one and embodied through their splendor, were present there;
he was like the very throat of Sarasvatī herself, uniquely proficient in the established doctrines, and solely devoted to meditation upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa day and night. (8)
For that lord of perfected beings was liberated while living, omniscient, and all-seeing.
Upon seeing him, Yaśodā rose up and prostrated;
she offered him water for his feet, a cow, the honey-mixture, and a golden throne.
The child joyfully and with a smile paid homage to the lord of sages;
and the sage mentally offered hundreds of prostrations to Hari.
With affection, he bestowed a blessing consisting of Vedic mantras.
She bowed down to her disciples, and they bestowed blessings upon her.
With devotion, she offered water for the feet and other honors to each of the disciples individually. Having washed the feet of her disciples, she sat down upon a comfortable seat.

With palms joined in *añjali*, she prepared herself to ask, holding the boy upon her lap with her neck bowed in devotion; yet, though she desired to inquire about the one who delights in his own self and is the source of all auspiciousness, she was not yet able to do so. (14)
Nevertheless, I now inquire after your welfare.
You ought always to forgive the fault of this weak and witless woman;
for the virtuous always exercise forbearance toward the faults of a fool.
Are you Aṅgiras, or perhaps Atri, Marīci, or Gautama? Or are you Kratu, or Pracetas, Pulastya, or Pulaha (17)? Or are you Durvāsas, Kardama, Vasiṣṭha, or even Garga?
Are you Jaigīṣavya, Devala, or the all-pervading Kapila himself? (18) Or are you Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, or Sanātana?
Are you Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Āsuri, or perhaps Saubhari? (19)
Was it Viśvāmitra, or Vālmīki, or Vāmadeva, or Kaśyapa; was it Saṃvarta, or Utathya, or Kaca, or Bṛhaspati;
or Bhṛgu, Śukra, Cyavana, or even Nara and Nārāyaṇa?
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śukadeva, and Jaimini;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Lomaśa, Kaṇva, and likewise Kātyāyana; Āstīka, or Jaratkāru, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Vibhāṇḍaka. (21–22)
Are you Paulastya, or Agastya, or Śaradvān, or Aṅgiras?
Or are you Śamīka, Ariṣṭanemi, Māṇḍavya, or Paila?
Or perhaps Pāṇini, Kaṇāda, Śākalya, or Śākaṭāyana? (23)
Aṣṭāvakra, Bhāguri, or Sumantu, or indeed Vatsa;
Jābāla, Yājñavalkya, and Vaiśampāyana; as well as Yati, Haṃsa, Pippalāda, Maitreya, and Karuṣa. (24–25)
Upamanyu, Gauramukha, Aruṇi, Aurva, Kakṣīvān,
Bharadvāja, Vedaśiras, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Śaunaka—
among these men of virtuous fame, who are you? Tell me, O Lord.
"If I am not worthy of an answer, nevertheless you ought to speak.
Whether a male servant or a female servant, who is capable [of serving] a master or lord?
He who is constantly engaged in the service of another—whom would he question, other than that person?"
I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my life is fruitful.
By the touch of the dust of your lotus feet, the sins of ten million births are destroyed.
By the contact with the water from your feet, the earth is instantly purified.
By your mere arrival, my hermitage has become a sacred ford (tīrtha).
O Brahmin, those great souls who have been heard of in the Vedas as the essence of revelation—
I have seen one such person through the arising of the fruits of my former merit.
The Vedas, personified like midday suns in the summer heat, are his disciples;
they instantly purify my lineage, Gokula, with the dust of their feet.
They ought to bestow a blessing upon this child with a gracious mind.

"A complete blessing is immediately and certainly granted by the words of a Brahmin's benediction. Having spoken thus, the virtuous wife of Nanda stood before the sage with devotion and dispatched a man to bring Nanda.

Having heard Yaśodā’s words, the bull among sages laughed, and the hosts of disciples laughed as well, illuminating the ten directions. [Her speech was] beneficial, truthful, endowed with wisdom, and supremely conducive to great merit. (35)
Filled with joy, the great sage Śuddhabuddhi spoke to her.
Śrī Garga said:
"Your words are like nectar, worldly yet appropriate for your family."
In whichever family one is born, one becomes exactly like that [family].
(37) Among all the cowherds and lotuses, Giribhānu was the sun.
His virtuous wife, equal to Padmā, was named Padmāvatī. (38)
Her daughter is Yaśodā, you who increase glory;
and the preeminent among cowherds, the beloved Nanda, has been obtained. O auspicious lady, you are that Nanda, and he is the child by whom [you] have been reached.
"I know everything; I shall speak it all in the presence of Nanda.
I am Garga, the family priest of the Yadu lineage for a long time. I have been dispatched by Vasudeva for this task, which cannot be accomplished by anyone else. (40–41)
In the meantime, Nanda arrived as soon as he heard [the news];
he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, bowing his head to that bull among sages.
He also bowed with his head to the disciples, and they bestowed their blessings upon him.
Rising quickly from their seats, Yaśodā and Nanda took him by the hand,
and that best of the learned, Garga, went into a beautiful inner chamber;
Nanda and Yaśodā, along with their son, were filled with joy.
Then, O sage, Garga spoke these hidden words to him in a secluded place.
Śrī Garga said:
"O Nanda, I shall speak words that will bring you happiness."
"Listen to that by which I was sent forth by Vasudeva.
The infant was entrusted to me by Vasudeva in the lying-in chamber:
'This is the son of Vasudeva, and he is certainly his eldest. (45–46)

"The maiden who was carried away by him to Mathurā out of fear of Kaṃsa—for her first-feeding ceremony and for the naming ritual, I have been sent by him in secret; O twice-born one, exert yourself in that undertaking. (47)

This child, whose nature is the fullness of Brahman, has come to the earth through his *māyā* to remove its burden; he is served by the Creator himself. He is the Lord of Goloka, the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhikā. (48)
He who is Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha and the beloved of Kamalā, he who dwells in Śvetadvīpa and is the father Viṣṇu—he too is the Unborn (Aja).
Kapila and others are portions of him, as are the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (49)
"Has a mass of all splendors indeed arrived in embodied form?
Having revealed that Vasu, he has become a child;
now he has come from the maternity chamber to your abode."
And this one, born of an improper source, has appeared upon the surface of the earth;
having filled his mother’s womb with air through his illusory power (*māyā*), Hari manifested and,
showing his true form to Vasu, departed.
In age after age, O cowherd, there is a difference in his color and a difference in his name:
he was white, yellow, and likewise red, and now he has attained blackness.
In the Satya Yuga, he was white in color, endowed with exceedingly intense splendor.
In the Tretā age he was red in color, and in the Dvāpara age this all-pervading Lord was yellow.
In the Kali age, the glorious one is black in color, a veritable mass of splendors.
Because he is the most perfect Brahman, he is remembered as Kṛṣṇa.
What is this syllable *ṛ*, which expresses Brahmā and signifies the infinite?
The syllable *ṣa* expresses Śiva, and the syllable *na* expresses Dharma.
The syllable *a* is a designation for Viṣṇu, the dweller on the White Island (*Śvetadvīpa*). (56–57)
The syllable *visarga* is traditionally held to express the meaning of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
He is a mass of all splendors, whose very nature consists of all forms;
he is the support of all and the seed of all, and for that reason he is known as Kṛṣṇa. (58)
The syllable *kṛ* signifies the uprooting of karma; *ṣi* does not denote servitude. (59) The syllable *a* denotes the giver; therefore, he is remembered as *Kṛṣṇa*.
*Kṛ* signifies the absence of activity, while *ṇa* denotes devotion. (60)
The letter *a* signifies attainment; therefore, he is remembered as *Kṛṣṇa*.
The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies nirvāṇa, and the syllable *na* denotes liberation.
The letter *a* signifies the giver; therefore, he is remembered as *Kṛṣṇa*. (61)
By the mere recollection of ten million names of the Blessed One, a person surely obtains that same fruit which is obtained by recollecting "Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever merit arises from such recollection, the same likewise arises from speaking or hearing [those names]. (62–63)
From the mere remembrance of it, the sins of ten million lifetimes are destroyed.
Among all the names of Viṣṇu, this is the essence of essences, higher than the highest— (64)—
the beautiful and auspicious name "Kṛṣṇa," which bestows devotion.
By the utterance of the syllable *ka*, the devotee attains liberation from birth and death;
by the syllable *ṛ*, incomparable servitude; by the syllable *ṣa*, the desired devotion;
and by the syllable *na*, co-residence with Him as well as equality with Him in time.
One attains similarity with Him through the emission [of breath]; of this there is no doubt.
Merely by the utterance of the letter *ka*, the servants of Yama tremble;
by the utterance of the letter *ṛ*, they do not remain; and by the letter *ṣa*, all sins are destroyed.

From the utterance of the syllable *na*, diseases flee; from the syllable *a*, death itself surely flees. O Lord of Vraja, all these things, being terrified by the utterance of Kṛṣṇa’s name, certainly run away at the mere effort of remembering, speaking, or hearing it.
The servants of Kṛṣṇa run, carrying the chariot from Goloka.
Even the most learned scholars are able to calculate the number of particles of dust on the earth,
but the virtuous are not capable of describing the extent of the power of His name.
Formerly, the greatness of this name was heard from the mouth of Śaṅkara;
my guru knows something of its qualities and the power of its names.
So too do Brahmā, Ananta, Dharma, the celestial sages, Manu, and the Manusyas. (71–72)
Even the Vedas do not know even a sixteenth part of his greatness.
Thus, O Nanda, has the greatness of your son been described,
according to my intellect and knowledge, as heard from the mouth of my guru.
Kṛṣṇa, the one clad in yellow garments, the destroyer of Kaṃsa, and Viṣṭaraśravas;
the son of Devakī, the Lord of Śrī, the son of Yaśodā, Hari;
the eternal, the infallible, the infinite, the Lord of all, who assumes all forms.
The support of all, the goal of all, the cause of all causes;
the kinsman of Rādhā, the very self of Rādhikā, the life itself of Rādhikā;
the breath of Rādhā, the lord of Rādhikā, and the lover of Rādhikā himself. (76)
The companion of Rādhikā, the fulfiller of Rādhā’s heart’s desire;
the one for whom Rādhā is his wealth, whose body is Rādhikā, whose mind is attached to Rādhikā;
the thief of Rādhikā’s heart, the Lord who is dearer to him than her own life-breaths. (77–78)

The most perfect Brahman is Govinda, whose banner bears Garuḍa. These names of Kṛṣṇa, which remove birth and death, have been heard by you from my mouth; keep them in your heart, O Nanda of auspicious gaze, and protect yourself.
The definition of the names of the youngest [brother] has been completed as it was heard.
Now hear from my mouth the conventional meaning of the name of the eldest, Halin.
Because he drew [the embryo] out of the womb (*garbhasaṃkarṣaṇāt*), he is remembered by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Because there is no end to him even within the Vedas, he is remembered as Ananta (the Infinite).
Baladeva is so called because of his abundance of strength, and Halin because he wields a plow.
Śitivāsas is named from his blue garments, and Musalin from his weapon, the mace.
Because he enjoyed himself with Revatī, he is himself Revatīramaṇa;
and because he dwelt in the womb of Rohiṇī, the high-minded one is Rauhiṇeya.
Thus has the name of the eldest son been declared as it was heard.
"I shall go home; O Nanda, remain happily in your own abode.
Upon hearing the words of the brāhmaṇa, Nanda became stunned;
Nanda’s wife was motionless, and the boy laughed of his own accord.
Having prostrated before him, Nanda spoke these words with humility. With his hands joined in *añjali* and his neck bowed low in devotion, Nanda said:
Nanda said:
If you have departed, then who else is great enough to perform the rite?
O auspicious-eyed one, having performed the ceremony yourself, perform the *annaprāśana* (first feeding) under [the child's] name.
Furthermore, the multitude of names beginning with "Rādhāprāṇa" and so forth has been declared as ten. || 87-88 ||
"Who indeed is her Rādha, and whose daughter is she for certain?
Hearing Nanda's words, the bull among sages laughed and said:
"I shall tell you the supreme truth, a secret that is hidden. (89)
Śrī Garga said:
Listen, O Nanda, I shall relate an ancient history (itihāsa),
the account of Goloka from former times, which was heard from the mouth of Śaṅkara.
A great quarrel arose between Śrīdāman and Rādhā.
Due to Śrīdāman’s curse and by divine destiny, the gopī Rādhā was born in Gokula as the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, and her mother was Kalāvatī. (91–92)
Born from half the body of the Lord Kṛṣṇa, this virtuous lady is his equal;
she who dwells in Goloka has now come here by the command of Kṛṣṇa.
This goddess, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti, was not born from a womb.
Having filled her mother’s womb with wind through her illusory power (māyā),
Satī assumed the form of an infant at the moment the wind was about to exit;
by the instruction of Kṛṣṇa, this illusion manifested upon the earth.

That Rādhā flourished in Vraja like a digit of the moon in the bright fortnight; she was the personified form of half of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s splendor. Though she is one form, she has become twofold; this distinction is described in the Veda.

"Is this a woman, or is that a man? Or is that a beloved woman, and this a man? (97) "The two forms are equal in brilliance, and equal in appearance, in quality, in prowess, in intellect, in knowledge, and even in prosperity. (98)
Yet, by going before him, she has become his superior in age;
he constantly meditates upon her, and she remembers this beloved one.
She has been fashioned from his life-breaths, and he is her life-breaths incarnate.
His supreme coming to Gokula was in accordance with Rādhā’s desire.
That which was previously performed in Gokula was done to make his acceptance meaningful;
indeed, Hari’s coming to Gokula was under the pretext of fear of Kaṃsa. 100–101.
For the sake of fulfilling his vow, how could there be fear for the Lord of Fear?
The etymology of the word "Rādhā" is described in the Sāmaveda;
Nārāyaṇa spoke it to Brahmā within the lotus of his navel. (102)
Brahmā related that to Śaṅkara in the world of Brahmā:
"In former times, on the peak of Kailāsa, Maheśvara said to me: 'O Nanda, listen; I shall tell you of that which is difficult for even the gods to attain. (103–104)

The syllable *ra* indeed casts off the sins of ten million births and the experience of the fruits of karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious; the syllable *ā* shall cast off dwelling in the womb, death, and disease—[the supreme liberation desired by the lords of gods, asuras, and sages]. (105)
The letter *dhakāra* causes the loss of longevity, and the letter *ākāra* constitutes the bondage of worldly existence.
Through hearing, remembering, and speaking [of this mantra], these perish without a doubt.
Indeed, the letter *repha* bestows unwavering devotion and service (*dāsya*) at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. (106–107)
The syllable *Dha* bestows everything desired, eternal bliss, and mastery over the entire multitude of perfected beings (*siddhas*). It grants co-residence with [the deity] at that very same time,
as well as the power of equal status (*sārṣṭi*) and the form of equality (*sārūpya*), and the knowledge of reality identical to that of Hari.
He perceived his form as a mass of splendor, like the power of generosity in Hari;
he possessed the power of yoga and a mind fixed on yoga, remembering Hari at all times.
Through the practice of recollecting the teachings of the Vedas, he destroyed the web of delusion and all sin. (109–110)
Disease, grief, death, and Yama tremble before this; of this there is no doubt.
For from it has been heard even a slight exposition of Rādhā and Mādhava.
And as it was spoken according to my knowledge, I am unable to describe it in its entirety.
O Nanda, the marriage of these two shall take place at Vṛndāvana in the distant future.
The Creator of the World, acting as the priest with joy and making the sacred fire his witness, shall perform the liberation of Kubera’s son and the eating of cow-products. (112–113)
The slaying of Dhenuka alone in the forest and the eating of palm-fruits;
then the effortless slaying of Baka, Keśin, and Pralamba;
the liberation of the wives of the twice-born, and the enjoyment of sweet food and drink. (114)
The breaking of Śakra’s sacrifice; the protection of the cowherds from Indra;
the stealing of the gopīs’ garments; likewise, the fulfillment of their vow; the returning of the garments to them; and the granting of boons according to their desires. (115–116)
He will captivate their hearts and bring them under his control.
This most delightful Rāsa festival, which increases the joy of all, takes place at night during the spring full moon within the circle of the Rāsa dance. (117)
Having fulfilled the desires of the gopīs through their fresh amorous union,
he will, out of curiosity, engage in water-sports with them.
His separation from them, caused by the curse of Śrīdāmā, shall last for a hundred years.
Together with Rādhā, he will be accompanied by the cowherds and the cowherd girls.
Therein will be his arrival at Mathurā, which increases the grief of the gopīs,
as well as their subsequent awakening and the bestowal of spiritual knowledge.
He will immediately provide protection for Sridaman and Akrura;
then, having mounted the chariot, he will proceed again toward Mathura, crossing the Yamuna with his father, brothers, and the Vraja people in Vraja. (121–122)
Having shown the gift of knowledge to Akrūra, he manifested his own self within the water;
and out of curiosity, in the evening, he showed himself from the city to all,
performing the liberation from bondage for the garland-maker, the weaver, and the hunchbacked woman.
The breaking of Śaṅkara’s bow, the showing of the sacrificial site,
the slaying of the elephant-heroes, the appearance before the king,
the immediate slaying of Kaṃsa, and the liberation of his parents from their fetters. (124–125)
And there was your awakening and the consecration of Ugrasena;
the removal of grief for his wives through knowledge;
and the initiation of your brother, performed by your preceptor from his own mouth. (126)
The giving away of the preceptor’s son, the return home,
the deception of the wicked Yavana and his royal armies,
the construction of Dvārakā, and the liberation of Mucukunda. (127–128)
The journey to Dvārakā with the Yādavas out of curiosity,
the wandering about with groups of women, and sporting together with them—
[all this] increases their good fortune as well as that of their sons, grandsons, and descendants. (129)
The liberation of the gem from its false stain,
assistance rendered to the Pāṇḍavas, the removal of the earth's burden, and so forth— all these were accomplished effortlessly by Dharmaputra during the Rājasūya sacrifice. (130–131)
The abduction of the *pārijāta* tree, the crushing of Śakra’s pride,
the fulfillment of Satyā’s vow, the severing of Bāṇa’s arms,
the trampling of Śiva’s armies, and the supreme yawning of Hara. (132)
The abduction of Bāṇa’s daughter and the liberation of Aniruddha;
the burning of Vārāṇasī and the destruction of the poverty of the brahmins; the granting of a son to a brahmin and the subduing of the wicked. (133–134)
In the course of a pilgrimage to sacred sites, she met with you all;
and having stayed together with Rādhā, she returned again to Vraja.
Then, having dispatched Dvārakā, she sent forth the supreme portion of Nārāyaṇa.
Having accomplished everything,
this Lord, the protector of the worlds, will indeed go to Goloka together with Rādhā;
and Nārāyaṇa, along with you, shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.
The abode of Dharma, the two sages, Viṣṇu, and the Ocean of Milk—
thus, O Nanda, has the future as determined by the Vedas been told.
Now hear the purpose for which I am traveling.
Perform the rite on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha at an auspicious moment;
specifically on a Thursday under the Revatī nakṣatra when the moon and stars are pure, with the moon situated in Pisces as the ascendant and the lord of the ascendant in full aspect. (139–140)
On that most rare day, which is highly auspicious for merchants, excellent in its astrological configuration, delightful, and supremely beneficial for all purposes—
having deliberated with the learned scholars, perform your work filled with joy. (141)
Having spoken thus, that lord of sages came outside and said:
"Nanda and Yaśodā were delighted and indeed undertook the preparations for the ritual.
In the meantime, the cowherds and cowherd-women went to see Garga.
Boys and girls alike came to the house of Nanda;
they beheld that best of sages, who was like the midday sun in summer,
surrounded by throngs of disciples and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
He joyfully spoke of the hidden yoga to the perfected one who questioned him;
he was looking with a smile at the attendants of Nanda’s palace—
the excellent one, seated upon a golden lion-throne and bearing the *yogamudrā*.
Beholding with the eye of knowledge the past, the present, and the future;
beholding the Lord within the heart as a perfected being through the power of mantra;
[he saw] such a child, smiling, lying on the lap of Yaśodā outside.
Having seen that form which was manifested through the meditation bestowed by Maheśa, his heart’s desire fulfilled, he was filled with supreme joy;
with eyes brimming with tears and his body covered in horripilation, he was immersed in an ocean of devotion. (148–149)

To him who was performing worship and prostration in his heart through the practice of yoga, they bowed their heads; he, in turn, bestowed blessings upon them. The sage remained seated on his seat, while they departed for their own abodes with joy.

Nanda, filled with joy for himself and his kinsmen, joyfully dispatched auspicious letters to those relatives staying at a distance. He also sent a stream of curd, a stream of milk, and a stream of clarified butter, all overflowing. || 151-152 ||
He saw, by chance, extensive channels of molasses, oil, and honey;
channels full of fresh butter and curd;
and channels of sugarcane water, all overflowing with ease. (153)
He offered high mountains of Śāli rice, a hundred mountains of flattened rice (pṛthuka),
seven mountains of salt,
seven mountains of sugar, and seven mountains of sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka). || 194–195 ||
And there, from ripe fruits, sixteen mountains [were made],
as well as mountains of barley and wheat flour, of cooked *laḍḍuka* balls,
of sweetmeats (*modaka*), and mountains of *svastika* figures. (156)
O Nārada, there were seven exceedingly high mountains of cowrie shells (197),
and a temple of betel leaves prepared with camphor and other ingredients— extensive, devoid of doors, and filled with scented water (158).
Endowed with joy, he offered sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
along with various kinds of gems, diverse types of gold, beautiful pearls, and corals. (159)
Out of affection, Nanda had various kinds of beautiful garments and ornaments prepared for his son’s first feeding ceremony;
[the child] was adorned with these refined decorations and anointed with lovely liquid sandalwood paste.
Out of curiosity, he had the courtyard draped with plantain pillars and fresh mango sprouts tied together with fine cloth;
it was further adorned with auspicious jars filled with fruits and sprouts. (162)
It was adorned with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and flower garlands;
it shone with heaps of wreaths and excellent garments, as well as with offerings of cows, honey-mixtures (madhuparka), and seats, O Nārada. (163–164)
It was provided with heaps of fruits and water-jars,
as well as various kinds of musical instruments that were rare and exceedingly charming—
namely, ḍhakkās, dundubhis, and likewise paṭahas.
It resounded with the sounds of ensembles of mṛdaṅga and muraja drums and other instruments, as well as flutes, cymbals, bronze gongs, and mechanical bows;
it was filled with the dancing of the Vidyādharīs and the whirling of Bhṛṅgin. (166–167)
Accompanied by the musical performances of the Gandharva leaders, filled with thousands of melodic modulations,
and resounding with the sounds of golden lion-thrones and chariots—
at this juncture, the bard spoke joyfully to Nanda.
The lords of the cowherds and their kinsmen, the cowherds, arrived;
likewise, the princes—mounted on horses, mounted on elephants, and seated in chariots, adorned with jewel-encrusted ornaments—arrived in haste. (169–170)
Giribhānu arrived accompanied by his wife and his servants,
along with four hundred thousand chariots, an equal number of elephants,
ten million horses, and likewise palanquins.
Who is capable of counting the throngs of lords of sages, lords of ascetics, wise brahmins,
bards, and mendicants gathered nearby,
as well as the cowherds and cowherd girls? (172–173)
"Look! Having come and gone outside," he said, standing in the courtyard.
Upon hearing this, the Lord of Vraja approached them, brought them back, settled them in the courtyard, and quickly honored them.
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground before the assembly of sages and others, he, being well-composed, offered them water for their feet and other honors;
thus Nanda’s Gokula became filled with wealth and kinsmen.
Indeed, no one there was able to hear anyone else's voice.
For three muhūrtas, Kubera, out of joy and for the pleasure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
filled all of Gokula with a rain of gold.
And all the groups of kinsmen, having seen Nanda’s prosperity, bowed their necks and playfully feigned ignorance out of curiosity.
Nanda, having performed his daily rites, purified, and wearing two washed garments, [proceeded].

Adorned with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron, he washed the feet of Garga and the lords of sages and sat upon a beautiful golden throne. Then, having received the permission of Garga and the great sages, the Lord of Vraja departed. (179–180)
Having remembered Viṣṇu and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) preceded by the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana),
and having performed the rites prescribed in the Vedas,
he joyfully fed the boy in accordance with the words of Garga. (161)
And at an auspicious moment, he bestowed the auspicious name "Kṛṣṇa" upon the Lord of the World;
having fed him with ghee and performed the naming ceremony, he caused musical instruments to be played and had auspicious rites performed. (182–183)
With joy, he gave various kinds of gold and diverse riches, as well as foodstuffs and garments, to the Brāhmaṇas;
and he bestowed abundant gold upon the bards and beggars. (184)
And they were all overcome by the weight [of the food] and unable even to move.
He fed sweet, perfectly delicious, and enchanting food to the Brahmins, his kinsmen, and especially to the mendicants. (185–186)
"Let it be given! Let it be given! Eat!
Eat!"—such was the exceedingly loud sound that arose constantly in Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
Jewels were bestowed in abundance, as were garments and ornaments.
There were coral ornaments, golden ones, and those made of the finest gems;
and there were beautiful golden vessels fashioned by Viśvakarman. Having gone to Garga, the bull among the inhabitants of Vraja offered them with humility. (188–189)
Filled with humility, he bestowed loads of gold upon his disciples,
and even gave complete amounts to the remaining brahmins, O Nārada.
(190) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having taken Śrī Hari with him, Garga departed in secret with joy;
bowing down to that Lord, he praised Him with supreme devotion, his eyes filled with tears, his hair standing on end, and his neck bowed low in devotion. (191)
Joining his palms in reverence, he spoke to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Garga said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the worlds, destroyer of the fear of Your devotees!"
Be gracious toward me, O Lord; grant me service at Your lotus feet.
My father gave me wealth, but what need have I for it?
Grant me unwavering devotion, O bestower of fearlessness upon Your devotees. (193–194)

O Lord, I have no desire whatsoever for the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, nor for yogic attainments or liberations; nor do I long for the essence of knowledge or immortality, nor even for the status of Indra or Manu, nor for the fruits of the heavenly realms for a long time. (195)
I have no desire in my mind for anything other than serving your feet.
O Brahman, I do not accept sālokya, sārṣṭi, sārūpya, sāmīpya, or aikya—these five forms of liberation—if they are desired without the service of your feet. (196–197)
I have no desire to dwell even in Goloka or Pātāla;
rather, may there be constant remembrance of Your lotus feet for me.
Having obtained Your mantra from Śaṅkara through the ripening of the fruits of several births—
I am omniscient and all-seeing; may I have access everywhere.
O Ocean of Compassion, Friend of the Wretched, show mercy at Your lotus feet!
Protect me by granting fearlessness; what can death do to me? (199–200)

Through service to your lotus feet, he became the lord of all, the conqueror of death, and the end-maker; he became the teacher of yogis. Through service to your lotus feet, Brahmā became the creator of the worlds.
O Brahmin, he upon whom fourteen Indras fall in a single day—
through service to your feet, Dharma has become the witness of all his actions,
as well as their protector and bestower of fruits, having conquered Time, which is so difficult to overcome. (202–203)
By serving whose lotus feet the thousand-headed Śeṣa bears the entire universe like a mustard seed, and as Śiva bears poison upon his neck;
she who bestows all prosperity and is higher than the highest among goddesses.

Lakṣmī constantly performs the cleansing of Your feet with her hair. She, who is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) in the form of the seed and the power (*śakti*) of all things, became devoted solely to that [cleansing] by remembering again and again Your lotus feet. (205–206)
Pārvatī is the embodiment of all forms; she is the intellect in the form of all beings.
Through service to your feet, O Beloved, she obtained Śiva, the Lord.
She who is the Goddess presiding over knowledge, the Mother of Wisdom, Sarasvatī—[is she not you?].
Having worshipped your lotus feet, she became worthy of worship by all.
Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, purifies the three worlds;
through service to your feet, she is the refuge of Brahmā and of the Brahmins. (208–209)

The earth, whose womb contains jewels, sustains the world through her patience; and all crops are produced by the service of your lotus feet. Rādhā, born from a portion of myself, is equal to you in splendor.
Having placed its foot upon your chest, it serves you; what need is there to mention others?
Just as the gods such as Śarva and the goddesses such as Padmā [are your attendants], O Lord, grant me a protector; for the grace of the Sovereign is impartial. (211–212)
"O Lord, I shall not go home, nor shall I accept your wealth;
having made me yours, protect me as a servant devoted to the service of your lotus feet.
Having thus offered praise, with eyes full of tears, he fell at the feet of Hari.
And he wept profusely with devotion, his body covered in horripilation.
(214) Having heard Garga’s words, Kṛṣṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, laughed and said to him himself: "May you have devotion unto me. (215)
The person who recites this hymn composed by Garga at the three junctions of the day will certainly attain firm devotion, service to Hari, and the power of remembrance.
[216] From the perils of birth, death, old age, disease, grief, delusion, and the like—
One who is intent on serving the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s devotee becomes one who has crossed over [the ocean of worldly existence].
(217) Such a person rejoices together with Kṛṣṇa at the same time as Kṛṣṇa; never shall there be any separation for him from Hari. (218)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having composed a hymn of praise to Hari, the sage joyfully gave it to Nanda and said to him, "O cowherd, I am going home; give me leave. (219)
"Aha! How wondrous is this saṃsāra, enveloped by the net of delusion!
The meeting and separation of men are like the foam upon the ocean.
Having heard these words of Garga, Nanda wept.
For the separation from the virtuous exceeds death itself.
(221) Then all the cowherds, headed by Nanda, and the cowherd women, weeping, [beheld] the Lord of Sages surrounded by all his disciples as he prepared to depart. (222)
They bowed with supreme affection and showed him due respect, O Sage.
Having bestowed his blessings, the best of sages joyfully departed for Mathurā.
The ṛṣis, the munis, the kinsmen, and the cowherds likewise followed.
All departed for their own homes with full treasuries and joyful hearts;
all the bards went forth with their desires completely fulfilled,
[honored] with sweet substances, excellent garments, superior horses, and golden ornaments.
The mendicants, having eaten until their bellies were full to the throat, were unable to move;
exhausted by the excessive weight of the gold and garments, yet filled with joy, some walked very slowly while others lay down upon the ground. (226)
Some stood on the path, and some rose up;
some spoke there with great joy, and some laughed.
[They gathered] many remaining items of cowrie shells that had been left behind. (227–228)
Some took them up, while others stood there displaying them;
some performed dances, and some sang there.
Some recounted various ancient verses.
The stories of the kings Marutta, Śveta, Sagara, and Māndhātṛ;
of Uttānapāda, Nahuṣa, Nala, and others; and the accounts of the deeds of Śrī Rāma, Aśvamedha, and Rantideva.
From the mouths of the elders, these stories were heard by various kings;
some recounted them, while others had already heard them.
Some paused at every station, and others fell asleep at every stop.

Thus, everyone, being greatly delighted, went joyfully to their own abodes. Nanda and Yaśodā, thrilled with joy, placed the child upon their chests and remained in their beautiful residence, which resembled the palace of Kubera.
Thus the two boys grew, resembling the crescent of the white moon;
joyfully grasping the tail of a cow and a wall, they stood up.
Day by day, they were capable of speaking half a word, or even a quarter of a word.
O Sage, increasing the joy of their parents as they walked about the courtyard,
the boy Hari became capable of walking two steps or even one step;
indeed, he was able to move about the courtyard or the house on his knees.
For Saṃkarṣaṇa himself was indeed older than Kṛṣṇa by one year; thus,
increasing each other's joy and growing day by day,
the two boys moved about in Gokula, capable of walking with joyful strides.
Having clearly spoken these words, O Sage, those two who were Māyā in the form of children departed. Garga went to Mathurā to the hermitage of Vasudeva;
he bowed to him and inquired after the welfare of his two sons.
The sage related to him that auspicious and most great festival;
and upon merely hearing it, he became immersed in tears of joy.
Devakī, with supreme affection, questioned him again and again.
Bathed in tears of joy, she wept again and again.
Having bestowed his blessings upon them, Garga departed for his own home with delight;
they both remained in their own residence, which was like the palace of Kubera.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In that kalpa in which this story takes place, you were Upabarhaṇa, the preeminent Gandharva and the husband of fifty beautiful women. (244)
And you were their beloved, more dear than life itself, a youth skilled in the arts of love.
Then, due to the curse of Brahmā, you became the son of a Brāhmaṇa’s slave-girl.
Now, however, through eating the remnants of Viṣṇu's food, you have become the son of Brahmā.
The All-Seeing and All-Knowing One, through his service to Hari, became the reminder [of these deeds].
The life-story of Kṛṣṇa, beginning with the ceremony of first feeding solid food (annaprāśana), has been told;
now I shall relate to you another that destroys birth, death, and old age.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Naming Ceremony and the Description of Kṛṣṇa’s First Feeding of Solid Food," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, the wife of Nanda went to the Yamunā for the purpose of bathing.
Seeing the house filled with cow products, Madhusūdana laughed.
He ate the curd, milk, clarified butter, buttermilk, and the delightful fresh butter, as well as whatever else was situated within the house. (1–2)

Having bathed and returned to her own home, the cowherd woman saw the boy, who was about to perform the purification of his face with cloths after eating and drinking honey, fresh butter (*hyaṅgavīna*), *svastika*-butter, and that which remained in the cart. (3)

Seeing the cow-pen empty, the vessels broken, and the jars of honey and other contents overturned, he questioned the boys: "Aha! What is this marvelous deed? Tell me the truth; by whom has this most dreadful act been committed? (4–5)
Having heard Yaśodā’s words, all the boys said,
"The boy truly ate [the curd], and he did not give any to us at all.
Hearing the words of the children, Nanda’s wife became enraged.
Taking up a cane, she with eyes like red lotuses ran after him;
yet she was unable to seize Govinda as he fled.
He was unattainable even by Śiva and others through meditation, and difficult to reach even for yogins.
Having wandered about, Yaśodā, overcome by the heat, stood there exhausted,
her soul possessed by anger, with her throat, lips, and palate parched.
Seeing his mother thus resting, the compassionate Puruṣottama [acted].
The Lord of the Universe stood before his mother with a smile. Taking him by the hand, the goddess brought him to her own abode;
having tied Madhusūdana to a tree with a cloth, she beat him.
Having bound Kṛṣṇa, Yaśodā went toward her own home;
Hari, the Lord and Master of the worlds, remained at the foot of a tree.
O Nārada, by the mere touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the tree] suddenly [became golden] there.
A tree resembling a mountain fell down, making a terrifying sound.
Then a divine man, beautifully attired, appeared from the tree;
mounting a celestial chariot, he departed for his own abode ahead of them.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, who was adorned with golden ornaments—
a youth, smiling, fair-complexioned, and decorated with jewel-encrusted jewelry—
the Queen of Vraja, seeing the falling tree, became terrified with fear. (15)
She took that crying, dark-complexioned beauty onto her lap.
Then the cowherds and cowherd women from Gokula arrived at her house;
they rebuked Yaśodā and joyfully performed the propitiatory rites for the infant. (16–17)
In this extremely advanced age, this son was born;
all that wealth, grain, and jewels were for the sake of his son.
O Queen of Nanda’s cowherd settlement, it is known as a truth that you possess no wisdom.
Whatever has not been eaten by one's son is entirely fruitless on this earth.
Having tied her son to the foot of a tree for the sake of cow-dung while she was preoccupied with household chores, the tree fell down by chance. (19–20)
By the falling of the tree, the cowherd girl was saved, while the boy, by good fortune, survived.
When the foolish boy had perished, what use were material objects?
The Brahmins and the bards then offered auspicious blessings.
The twice-born performed the chanting of Hari’s names for them.
Having done this, all the people departed for their own homes.
Then Nanda, whose eyes were like red lotuses, spoke to his wife.
Nanda said:
"I shall go to the sacred ford this very day, taking the child upon my neck;
or else, you may go from the house—what need have I for you? (24)
A large pond is superior to a hundred wells; a lake is equal to a hundred ponds;
a sacrifice is superior to a hundred lakes; and a son is superior to a hundred sacrifices.
The merit arising from austerity and charity bestows happiness in future births.
A virtuous son bestows happiness both in this world and in the next.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a kinsman greater than a son.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Nanda remained in his own palace.
Yaśodā and Rohiṇī were indeed occupied with household chores.
Nārada said:
"Who was that well-attired man in Gokula who had taken the form of a tree?"
"O Blessed One, by what cause did he indeed attain the state of being a tree?
Nārāyaṇa said:
"He was the illustrious son of Kubera, known by the name Nalakūbara."
He went to the Nandana grove for the sake of sport together with Rambhā,
to a secluded and charming flower garden on the shore of a lake near a banyan tree,
where the air was fragrant with the scent of blossoms.
Having prepared a bed of flowers illuminated by jewel-lamps,
infused with the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
and surrounded on all sides by flower garlands and silken cloths. || 31 ||
There, having brought Rambhā, he sported with her according to his desire.

[He enjoyed] the eightfold erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and the pleasures such as the inverted positions, as well as the sixfold kissing (*cumbana*), each as it has been described in its proper place. ||32–33||

The Lord of Rasikas, an expert in the science of love, joyfully engaged in the threefold embrace through the union of his limbs and members, and performed the dalliance of scratching with nails, biting with teeth, and using his hands,
moving from water to land and from land to water. (34)
The sage Devala beheld Rambhā engaged in amorous enjoyment—
naked, with disheveled hair, her hips and breasts full,
her limbs marked by nail and tooth wounds, and her body covered in horripilation.
He beheld that amorous woman looking at her lord of life with joy and a smile, her eyebrows knit in a playful curve;
she was radiant with a pair of jeweled earrings upon her cheeks. (37)
Adorned with various garlands of jewels and flower garlands,
joined with a network of tinkling bells, and marked with dots of vermilion— [he saw] him,
thrilled with horripilation and filled with love, unable to rise because of her.
"O most wicked one, become a tree!"— thus spoke the bull among sages.
He cursed Rambhā, who was afflicted by desire, saying, "Become a human woman," and further,
"You shall be a beautiful beloved to Janamejaya."
"Go to Gokula yourself and become a tree," [he said].
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by the mere touch of you, you shall return home again.
O Rambhā, through union with Indra, you too will certainly return. 41–42.
Having spoken thus, that sage departed for his own abode;
the illustrious son of Kubera likewise went to his own home.
Thus has it been told, O Brahmin; now I shall relate to you the narrative of Rambhā.
In the house of Sucandra, Rambhā obtained birth in Bhārata.
She became a beautiful and excellent maiden, the very embodiment of Lakṣmī.
King Sucandra, the lord of monarchs, adorned her with ornaments. (44–45)
He gave her, who was endowed with various charms, to Janamejaya;
she became the fortunate and excellent queen of Janamejaya.
In various places and in secluded spots, the king took his pleasure with her.
Once, when the best of kings had been initiated for the horse sacrifice,
Śakra remained in his palace after having hidden the horse.
Thinking the sacrificial horse was beautiful, the lovely woman approached it out of curiosity.
That virtuous woman went joyfully to see the horse alone;
Śakra, having assumed the form of a groom, violated that chaste lady.
Though she tried to ward him off, he took his pleasure there with her.
Śakra fell into a swoon and was unconscious day and night.
Through mere sexual union, she abandoned her body by means of yoga.
Out of shame and fear for the king, Śakra departed for heaven.
Having heard this and seeing her dead, the king lamented repeatedly and bitterly.
Having completed the sacrifice, he gave full sacrificial fees to the brahmins.
Rambhā, having cast off her human body, went indeed to heaven.
Thus has been told everything concerning the shattering of the Arjuna tree,
O great sage, as well as the liberation of Nalakūbara and Rambhā;
this sacred account of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds removes birth, death, and old age.
Thus everything has been told; I shall tell you more besides.

(94) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Breaking of the Arjuna Tree," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, Nanda went to Vṛndāvana; there,
at the Bhāṇḍīra tree in the grove,
he tended the cattle and made them drink from a lake of delicious water, and he drank from it himself.
And he dwelt at the foot of a tree, placing the child upon his own chest. In the meantime, O Sage, Kṛṣṇa, whose form is a human manifestation of Māyā,
suddenly caused the sky to be covered with clouds by means of his power of illusion.
Seeing the sky covered with clouds and the interior of the forest turned dark,
[he heard] the great roar of a tempestuous wind and the terrible sound of thunderbolts,
as well as extremely thick torrents of rain and the trembling trees.
Seeing the calves fallen thus, Nanda was indeed seized by fear:
"Alas, how shall I go to my own hermitage leaving the cow-calf behind?
If I do not go home, what will become of the child? (5-6)
While Nanda was speaking thus, Śrī Hari then wept;
and out of fear of milk, he held his father’s neck.
In the meantime, Rādhā arrived in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Moving with a gait that puts to shame the royal swans and the khañjana birds;
(8) her face, beautiful as it is, possesses the luster of the full moon in autumn;
her eyes steal the splendor of lotuses at midday in the autumn season; (9) she is radiant with the brilliant kajjala of various stars, which serve as the lashes around her eyes.
Her nose was capable of destroying the praise of the beautiful beauty of the beak of the king of birds;
it was radiant with large pearls worthy of adorning the expanse of her middle; she was adorned with the style of a braided hair-tuft and encircled by a garland of *mālatī* flowers. (10–11)

Her earrings were like the rays of the midday sun in summer, and the splendor of her pair of lower lips surpassed that of ripe bimba fruits. She was radiant with a row of teeth that shone like a string of pearls, and her smile possessed the brilliant luster of slightly blossomed kunda flowers. (12–13)
Adorned with a drop of musk and a dot of vermilion, holding a skull-cup joined with a jasmine flower, she is endowed with beauty and is virtuous;
her cheeks are of very lovely circular shape and are covered with horripilation. 14.
Adorned upon her chest with necklaces made of the finest essence of precious gems;
joined by a pair of firm breasts possessing the beautiful form of *śrīphala* fruits; endowed with the splendor of decorative leaf-patterns; and radiant with the luster of excellent jewels. (15–16)
She possessed a most charming and beautiful belly of perfectly rounded shape,
adorned with three diverse folds and a deep-set navel (17). Adorned with a network of girdles fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems, she—
by means of the knitting of her eyebrows, which were the very essence of the weapons of Love— enchanted the minds of the lords of yogis (18).
Joyfully bearing a pair of firm hips that put the mountains to shame, and feet that eclipsed the luster of land-lotuses,
she was adorned with jeweled ornaments and anointed with the liquid of lac-dye. (19)
The red lac of her feet was eclipsed by the splendor of the finest jewels;
she was made radiant by tinkling anklets fashioned from the essence of excellent gems.
Adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and beautiful conch shells, [she shone]. (20–21)
Resplendent with garments as pure as fire, shimmering with a multitude of jewel rings, she was like the radiance of beautiful campaka flowers gathered into a single body;
she was a brilliant play-lotus endowed with a thousand petals. (22)
Holding a jeweled mirror in order to behold the beauty of Śrīmukha’s face,
Nanda saw her in that secluded place and was filled with the utmost wonder—
she who eclipsed the splendor of ten million moons and illuminated the ten directions. (23–24)
With eyes full of tears and his neck bowed low in devotion, he prostrated before her:
"I know you from the mouth of Garga as one dearer to Hari than even Lakṣmī;
I know this [Lord] to be the supreme, attribute-less, and infallible Mahāviṣṇu."
Nevertheless, I, a human being, have been deluded by the Māyā of Viṣṇu.
O auspicious lady, take my lord of life and go as you please;
later, you shall give me back my son once his desires have been fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, she gave her the crying boy out of fear;
Rādhā took the boy and laughed sweetly with joy.
She said to Nanda with effort, "This secret must not be revealed."
"O Nanda, I have been seen by you as the fruit of the results of many lifetimes has arisen.
You are wise; from the words of Garga, you know the entire cause.
Go back to Gokula; our conduct there is not to be told and must be kept secret. (29–30)
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Vraja, whatever is desired in your heart;
I shall grant it to you effortlessly, even if it be difficult for the gods to attain.
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, the Lord of Vraja spoke to her:
Grant devotion to your feet; I have no desire for anything else.
You shall grant us residence in your presence, which is very difficult to attain.
O Mother of the worlds, O Supreme Goddess, grant this to both of us.
Having heard the words of Nanda, the Supreme Goddess said:
"I shall now grant you incomparable service; let there be devotion for me.
Let [your devotion] be toward the lotus feet of us two and of you both, day and night."
In your ever-blossoming hearts, let there be a remembrance that is exceedingly difficult to attain.
By my boon, neither Māyā nor you two shall remain concealed;
at the end, having cast off your human bodies, you shall go to Goloka. (36–39)
Having spoken thus with joy, she pressed Śrī Kṛṣṇa to her own chest; then,
lifting him up with her arms as far as she desired,
she embraced him against her breast out of passion and kissed him again and again.
With every limb marked by horripilation, he remembered the circle of the *rāsa* dance.
(38) In the meantime, Rādhā beheld a pavilion made of excellent illusory jewels, provided with a hundred jeweled pitchers. (39)

Richly adorned with various and manifold paintings, it was beautified by wonderful groves; it shone with clusters of pillars made of gems shaped like vermilion (40). It was provided with a flower-bed consisting of a multitude of jasmine garlands, combined with the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, kasteria, and saffron (41).
It was endowed with various luxuries and equipped with a divine mirror;
it was adorned with networks of garlands made of the finest gems, pearls, and rubies, and provided with door-panels fashioned from the essence of the most excellent jewels. 42.
It was adorned with exquisite garments and excellent clusters of banners;
it possessed seven staircases made of saffron-colored jewels;
and it was joined by flowering flower gardens frequented by bees.
Having seen the pavilion, that goddess joyfully entered within.
There she beheld betel-leaf prepared with camphor and other ingredients,
as well as water— clear, cool, and enchanting— contained in a gem-studded jar.
O Nārada, there were jeweled jars filled with nectar and honey;
and a lovely youth, dark and beautiful, possessing the grace of ten million Cupids and adorned with sandalwood paste. (46)
He was reclining upon a bed of flowers, smiling and most enchanting;
