(47) clothed in yellow garments, with a serene face and eyes;
adorned with ornaments fashioned from the finest of precious gems, and beautified by tinkling anklets; (48) and endowed with armlets and bracelets crafted from the essence of excellent jewels.
His cheeks were resplendent with two earrings made of the finest jewels;
his chest was brilliantly illuminated by the Kaustubha, the sovereign gem; the radiance of his face eclipsed the light of the full autumn moon;
and his eyes released the splendor of a blossoming autumn lotus.
Beholding him, who was adorned with peacock feathers entwined with jasmine garlands,
wearing a triple-crested crown, gazing at the jeweled palace,
and seeing his lap empty of children— he being in the bloom of youth— [he was struck with wonder]. (51–52)
Although she is the very embodiment of all memory, she was nevertheless filled with wonder;
beholding the most enchanting form of the Queen of the Rāsa dance, she became infatuated.
Out of desire, she joyfully drank in the moon of her face with the cakora-birds of her eyes.
Rādhā, free from blinking and longing for their first union,
her entire body marked with horripilation, smiling and overcome by love—
there Hari spoke to her, whose lotus-face was radiant with a smile.
And seeing her with sidelong glances, fit for a new union,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhā, do you remember the events of Goloka in the assembly of the gods?"
"Today, O beloved Rādhā, I shall fulfill that which was previously promised by me;
for you, O fair-faced one, are dearer to me than life itself.
Just as you are, so am I; there is certainly no difference between us."

Just as whiteness exists in milk, as burning power exists in fire, and as fragrance exists in the earth, so do I exist perpetually within you. Just as one cannot make a pot without clay, nor a earring without gold, [so it is with me and you]. (58–59)
Just as a potter and a goldsmith are never capable [of creating their respective objects] without [their tools],
so too am I unable to perform creation without you.
You are the substratum of creation, while I, O Acyuta, am the form of the seed.
"Come, O virtuous one, and place me upon your breast as you lie on the bed.
You are my very splendor and the true form of my body, just as an ornament is to the physical frame.
For people will say of me that I am Kṛṣṇa only when I am separated from you."
And then they too beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with you alone as the Supreme.
You are Śrī, you are prosperity, and you are the very embodiment of the substratum.
You are the embodiment of all powers, while I am the imperishable one who possesses all forms.
When I am of the nature of fire, you are likewise of the nature of fire;
when I am bodiless, you are likewise bodiless.
O beautiful one, through yoga I am always the nature of all seeds.
And you are the very nature of Śakti, assuming the forms of all women;
you are the nature of a portion of my own body, the primordial Prakṛti, the Sovereign Goddess.
O fair-faced one, in power, intellect, and knowledge, you are equal to me.
And that lowest of men who creates a sense of difference between us two—
his dwelling shall be in Kālasūtra for as long as the moon and sun endure;
he casts down seven generations of ancestors and seven generations of descendants into the depths.
The merit accumulated over ten million births is certainly destroyed for those lowest of men who,
out of ignorance, revile us two;
they shall be cooked in a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
To those who utter the sound "rā," I, being moved by fear, grant supreme devotion.
To those who utter the sound "dhā" from behind, I go out of a longing to hear them.
And those who serve me by offering the sixteen types of ritual honors—

Whatever joy arises within me throughout the span of my life, may that joy be even greater than that which arises from the word "Rādhā. O Rādhā, you are not as dear to me as the one who speaks the name of Rādhā. (71–72)
Brahmā, Ananta, Śiva, Dharma, and the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa; Kapila, Gaṇeśa, and Kārttikeya, who is dear to me;
as well as Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, and Prakṛti. (73)
My beloveds and the gods are likewise dear to me, yet they are not equal to you. They are all as dear to me as my own life, but you, being virtuous, are dearer to me than my very life.
They reside in various places, whereas you reside upon my chest.
"I, who am Kṛṣṇa in essence, he whose four-armed form always bears his beloved upon his chest— myself, I shall marry you. Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa remained upon the delightful couch.
With her neck bowed low in devotion, Rādhikā spoke to her Lord.
Rādhikā said:
"O All-pervading One, I remember everything and I know everything; how then could I forget?"

As for what you say: "By the grace of your lotus feet, I am everything"—where are there any who are not dear to the Lord, and where are there any who are dear? Just as those who do not remember me [do not receive my grace], so too is there no lack of compassion from you toward them.
He is capable of turning grass into a mountain and a mountain into grass;
yet his compassion remains equal toward the worthy and the unworthy, and toward both prosperity and adversity.
While I stand and you lie down, that moment passes away in conversation.
At that moment, I am unable to endure even what feels like an eon;
place your lotus-feet upon my chest and my head.
My mind is immediately tormented by the fire of separation from you.
My gaze fell first upon your lotus-feet;
indeed, I was not able to behold any other body without great hardship.
Only after seeing each individual limb did my sight finally rest upon your peaceful, lotus-like face.
Having seen her lotus-like face, she was not able to go elsewhere.
Upon hearing Rādhikā’s words, Puruṣottama laughed and spoke to her what was beneficial and true, as established by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"That matter has already been settled by me there; it is not to be contested.
Stay for a moment, O blessed one; I shall do what is beneficial for you, my beloved. (86)

The time has itself arrived to fulfill your heart's desire. O Rādhā, neither I nor anyone else is able to thwart that which was previously inscribed for someone and ordained for a specific time; such is the power of destiny.
"I am the ordainer even of the Ordainer; whatever has been written for whomsoever—be they Brahmā and the others or even the lowly—that can never be annulled.
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived before Hari. (88–89)
Holding a garland and a water-pot, with four faces slightly smiling,
he went and bowed to that Kṛṣṇa and praised him according to the scriptures (90).
With eyes full of tears, his hair standing on end, and his neck bowed low in devotion, he offered praise.
Having praised and bowed down, the Sustainer of the World went into the presence of Hari;
having again bowed with devotion to the Lord, he went into the presence of Rādhikā.
With devotion, he bowed his head at the lotus-feet of his mother.
In great agitation, he joyfully and quickly washed [the Lord] with the water from his water-pot, which was encircled by a mass of matted locks; then,
with palms joined in reverence, he praised Him again according to the sacred scriptures.
Brahmā said:
O Mother, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, your lotus feet have been seen by me—
feet which are very difficult for all to attain, and especially so in Bhārata-varṣa.
In the past, I performed austerities for sixty thousand years at the Puṣkara tīrtha dedicated to Bhāskara, the Supreme Self Kṛṣṇa. Hari himself, the bestower of boons, came there to grant me a boon.
When it was said, "Choose a boon," she joyfully chose her own desired wish:
"O You who transcend all qualities, show me right now, this very moment, the lotus feet of Rādhikā, which are difficult for even all [the gods] to attain. (97)
Having been addressed with "So be it," this Hari spoke to me, the ascetic:
"I shall show myself at the proper time; my child, for now, you must be patient.
For the command of the Lord is never fruitless; by him, the lotus-feet were beheld.
O Mother, this is now the desire of everyone in Goloka and Bhārata:
all goddesses are certainly portions of Prakṛti, born of her nature;
you, however, were produced from half the body of Kṛṣṇa and are equal to Kṛṣṇa in every respect. (100)
"You are Śrī Kṛṣṇa and this Rādhā; you are Rādhā or Hari himself.
"By whom has it been established that I have not seen this in the Vedas?
O Mother, just as Goloka exists above and outside the cosmic egg," || 101-102 ||
O Ambikā, you are Vaikuṇṭha and the Unborn, and likewise you are the Unborn.
Just as in the entire universe there are those who live by the portions of a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
so too do you, whose nature is Śakti, abide within all of them.
Men are portions of Hari, while all women are portions of you.
You are the self in the form of this body, for you alone are its support.
O Mother, you exist with his vital breaths, and he, the Lord, exists with yours.
"Alas, by what artisan and for what reason was this created?
For Kṛṣṇa is eternal, and you likewise, O Mother, are eternal.
By whom was it determined that you are a portion of him, or he a portion of you?"
"I am the creator of the worlds and the progenitor of the gods myself.
Having heard this from the mouth of their guru, people indeed become wise;
yet they are unable to speak even a hundredth part of his actual virtues. (107–108)
Whether it be the Veda, a scholar, or anyone else, who is capable of praising you?
O Mother, knowledge is always the progenitor of hymns, and intellect is the mother of knowledge;
you, O Mother, are the mother of intellect—who indeed is capable of praising you?
Indeed, a wise person is capable of speaking of that object which has been seen by all;
but who is capable of describing an object that has neither been seen nor heard?
Neither I, nor Maheśa, nor Ananta—no one at all—is capable of praising you. (110–111)
Sarasvatī and the Vedas—what capable person is able to praise [the Lord]?
You should not reproach me for what has been stated here according to the scriptures and as it was taught.
The compassion of the Lord of lords is equal toward both the worthy and the unworthy.
"In the case of people who must be protected, there is fault at one moment and virtue at another;
even a mother or a father forgives everything out of affection.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the worlds stood before the two of them.
Having bowed at the lotus feet of all that is venerable and desired,
the man who recites this hymn composed by Brahmā during the three junctions of the day will certainly attain devotion and the state of a servant at the feet of Rādhā and Mādhava. (115)
Having eradicated karma and conquered death, which is so difficult to overcome,
and having transcended all worlds, he goes to the supreme Goloka.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the praise of Brahmā, Rādhikā said to him:
"O Creator, choose a boon that resides in your heart.
Hearing Rādhikā's words, the Ordainer of the World spoke to her.
"And grant me devotion to the lotus feet of you two.
When Brahmā had spoken thus, Rādhā quickly replied, "So be it.
Then the Creator, the Lord of the worlds, bowed again to her with devotion.

Then Brahmā, having kindled the sacrificial fire between the two of them and having meditated upon Hari, performed the oblation according to the prescribed rite. Rising from his bed, Kṛṣṇa sat down in the presence of the fire.

Following the ritual procedure prescribed by Brahmā, the father himself performed the oblation. Having again caused Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā to bow down, he himself had the marriage-thread ceremony performed and conducted seven circumambulations.
Then, having caused Rādhā to circumambulate the fire clockwise once more,
the officiant (vidhi) led Kṛṣṇa forward and settled him there;
he then caused Śrī Kṛṣṇa to take her hand.
The knower of the Vedas placed Rādhikā’s hand upon the chest of Hari and taught Mādhava the seven mantras declared in the Vedas. Then the Prajāpati placed Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s hand upon the back of Rādhā.
He established three mantras and caused Rādhikā to recite them.
Through Rādhā, Brahmā joyfully placed a garland of pārijāta flowers, hanging down to her knees, upon the neck of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (126–127)

Having again caused Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā to bow down, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] placed a beautiful garland upon Rādhā’s neck with his own hands; then the Lotus-born once more had Śrī Kṛṣṇa take His seat. 128.
On His left side was Rādhā, smiling and with her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa;
having caused them both to join their palms in *puṭāñjali*,
O Nārada, Brahmā taught Mādhava and Rādhikā the five mantras declared in the Vedas.
Having bowed down and having offered Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā back [to Him],
Brahmā stood before Hari with devotion, just as a father does for his daughter.
In the meantime, the gods were filled with joy and their hair stood on end.
They sounded kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and other instruments;
indeed, a rain of flowers from the pārijāta trees fell.
The foremost of the gandharvas sang, and the hosts of apsarases danced.
Brahmā praised Śrī Hari, and He, smiling, said to him:
"Grant me the southern gift of devotion to the lotus feet of you two.
Having heard Brahmā's words, Hari himself spoke to him: [133–134]
"May you possess firm devotion to my lotus-feet.
Go to your own abode; may it be well with you, there is no doubt in this.
O child, perform the task assigned by me at my command."
O Sage, having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
the Creator of the worlds bowed to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and departed for his own abode with joy.
When Brahmā had gone, that goddess, smiling, [looked at them] with a sidelong glance.

She beheld the face of Hari and, her entire body marked with horripilation and tormented by the arrows of love, she covered her face out of modesty. Having bowed to Śrī Hari with devotion, she went to the bed of Hari.
Having fashioned a tilaka on her forehead with a paste of sandalwood and aguru, mixed with musk and saffron, she placed it upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa;
she also offered a beautiful jewel-vessel filled with nectar and another filled with honey. (139–140)

The lord of the earth gave [it] with devotion to Hari and partook [of it]. And Rādhā respectfully gave Kṛṣṇa excellent and beautiful betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other spices; Hari partook of it.
Smiling, Rādhā consumed the nectar-like juice given by Hari;
she then ate the betel nut offered by him in the presence of Hari.
Kṛṣṇa joyfully gave the chewed betel nut to Rādhikā. (142–143)
He ate with supreme devotion and drank from her lotus-like face.
Madhusūdana requested the betel-chewed by Rādhā;
Rādhā laughed and did not give it, but said joyfully, "It is enough. (144)
Mādhava himself applied the finest liquid paste of sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron upon every limb of Rādhikā—
she whose single lotus-foot he, as Kāma, meditates upon eternally. (145)
O Sage, that Madana was brought under his control for the sake of pleasing Rādhā;
indeed, the Lord—who consists of his own will—was conquered by him at every moment through his servants' servants, out of mere curiosity. 146–147.
Taking her by the hand, Kṛṣṇa placed her upon his chest;
he loosened her garment and performed the four kinds of kissing.
Through their amorous combat, the tiny bells were shattered.
O Sage, through kissing the redness of her lips was lost; through embracing, her leaf-patterned tilaka; through passion itself, her braided hair and the vermilion forehead-mark;
and through the reverse-intercourse and other acts, the mark of red lac vanished. (149–150)
With every limb marked by horripilation from their first union, Rādhā fell into a swoon and was conscious neither by day nor by night;
she embraced him limb for limb, body for body. 151.
Kṛṣṇa, who was learned in the science of love, displayed the eightfold erotic sentiment;
then, embracing her again as she smiled with sidelong glances,
he indeed caused all her limbs to be wounded by his nails and teeth.
Right there, the heart-stealing sound of bracelets, tinkling bells, and anklets arose, born from the battle of love. Then, having drawn her back again and settled her upon the bed—
In a secluded place, Kṛṣṇa, who was an expert in the science of love, out of curiosity stripped Rādhā of her hair-braid, her garments, and her ornaments;
and Rādhikā likewise stripped him of his topknot, his attire, and his finery. (155–156)
Neither of those two, who were experts in their respective duties, suffered any loss whatsoever.
Mādhava took the jeweled mirror from Rādhā’s hand,
while Rādhikā forcibly took the flute from Mādhava’s hand.
Mādhava forcibly carried away the heart of Rādhā;
Rādhikā, in turn, stole the mind of Mādhava from the *rāsa* dance.
When the battle of passion had ended, she with her curved eyes smiled.
Out of affection, she gave the flute to the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa, for his part, gave her a mirror and a radiant toy-lotus. He fashioned a beautiful braid of hair and applied a tilaka of vermilion.
Hari thus assumed a costume of such variegated leaves;
even Viśvakarmā did not know how to fashion such a dress for Kṛṣṇa, so what need is there to mention his companions? This was when Rādhā set about preparing the attire.
Having abandoned both the form of an infant and that of childhood,
he saw Acyuta in the form of a child, weeping and afflicted by hunger,
just as Nanda had given him when he was frightened. 163.
Sighing deeply with a heart tormented by grief, Rādhā—
afflicted by sorrow and distressed by separation— looked here and there for him and, overcome with despair, addressed Kṛṣṇa with these plaintive words: (164–165).
"O Lord of Māyā, how can you perform such a trickery against me, your own servant?
Having spoken thus, Rādhā fell down and wept. Kṛṣṇa wept right there, and an incorporeal voice arose.
"Why do you weep, O Rādhā? Remember the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa!
Until the circle of stars appears and night arrives here, you shall eternally enjoy your desired dalliance with Hari. (167-168)
"Having created a shadow [of him] in your own home, come here yourself and do not weep.
Placing the Lord of my life, the Lord of Maya in the form of a child, upon your lap, abandon your grief and go home. Thus was Sundarī consoled.
Having heard these words, Rādhā took the boy onto her lap;
she beheld a flower garden, a forest, and a pavilion made of precious gems.
Then Rādhā quickly departed from Vṛndāvana for the home of Nanda.
O Nārada, that goddess, who travels by mind alone, in half a moment—
her tongue moist with well-anointed sweet nectar and her eyes red—
prepared to give the infant to Yaśodā and spoke thus: (172)
Having thus taken this child— stout, weeping, and afflicted by hunger—
I shall undergo torment on the road, for he was given to me by your master in the cow-pen.
O child, my garment has been soaked during this most foul day, overcast with clouds.
"O blessed lady, take the child and, giving him your breast, comfort him;
O virtuous one, stay at ease, for I am going home which has been abandoned for a long time. (175)
Having spoken thus and handed over the boy, she departed toward her own home.
Yaśodā, taking the boy, kissed him and gave him her breast. Meanwhile, Rādhā remained outside her house engaged in household chores.
There he constantly took delight with Hari night and day.
Thus, O child, has the auspicious life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa been told; it bestows happiness, grants liberation, and is meritorious. Now I shall relate another to you. (178)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Marriage and Union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, Mādhava, together with the boys and accompanied by Balarāma (Halin),...
O Sage, having eaten and drunk, Madhusūdana went to the auspicious forest for the sake of sport.
There, Madhusūdana engaged in various kinds of play with the boys, and having finished that, he drove the cattle.
From there, Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to Madhuvana together with the herds of cattle.
Having drunk the sweet water there in the forest, that one of great strength [proceeded].
There, a certain powerful Daitya appeared, white in color and terrifying.
With a face of distorted form and the appearance of a crane, he was like a mountain.
And having seen Gokula with the children in the cow-pen, Balarāma and Keśava [acted] just as Agastya effortlessly swallowed Vātāpi and everything else.
Seeing Hari seized by the serpent, all the gods were overcome with fear;
terrified, they ran about with weapons in hand, crying out "Alas! Alas!
Indra hurled his thunderbolt, which was fashioned from the bones of the sage.
The crane did not die from that; rather, he burned one of his wings.
The Moon, afflicted by cold, discharged the *nīhāra* (fog) weapon, by which the Dānava was pained.
The Son of the Sun (Yama) hurled the *yamadaṇḍa* (staff of Yama), but it became blunted against him.
By means of the Vāyavya weapon, Vāyu went to another place;
and Varuṇa, being afflicted by that, rained down a shower of stones.
And Hutāśana burnt his wings with fire.
By Kubera’s crescent moon [weapon], his foot was indeed severed;
and by Īśāna’s trident, the asura became unconscious.
Then the ṛṣis and munis, out of fear, offered blessings to Kṛṣṇa.
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
burned all the limbs of the Daitya, both inside and out.
Having vomited all that up, the Dānava gave up his life-breaths.
Having slain Baka, the powerful one went with the children and the cattle to a most enchanting grove of *kadamba* trees for play.
In the meantime, an asura there assumed the form of a bull. (13–14)
By name he was Pralamba, powerful and a great rogue, as firm as a mountain.
Seizing Hari with his two horns, he indeed whirled him about there.
All the boys fled, weeping and overcome by fear.
The powerful one laughed upon realizing his brother was the Lord.
He spoke to the boys, asking, "What is this fear?
Then Śrī Madhusūdana himself took hold of that horn.
Having whirled him about in the sky, he cast him down upon the earth.
Striking the ground, the lord of the Daityas gave up his life-breaths. All the boys laughed, danced, and sang with joy.
Having swiftly slain Pralamba along with Balarāma, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa tended the cattle and went to the Bhāṇḍīra forest.
Seeing Mādhava approaching, the powerful Keśin, lord of the Daityas, [advanced]. (19–20)
Scratching the earth with his hoof, he swiftly encircled him;
then, placing Hari upon his head, the bull, being pleased, leaped ninety yojanas into the sky,
whirled him around, and landed back upon the surface of the earth.
That wicked one seized Hari and chewed him out of anger.
Alas, with his teeth shattered from chewing the one whose body was like a thunderbolt, the Daitya,
consumed by the splendor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, gave up his life upon the earth.
In heaven, kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell. In the meantime, the attendants of divine form arrived there, mounted upon chariots, possessing two arms and clad in yellow garments.
Wearing crowns and earrings, adorned with forest garlands, holding playful flutes in their hands, and delighting with the tinkling of their jingling anklets;
with all their limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, these excellent ones wear the attire of cowherds. (25–26)
With faces brightened by gentle smiles and hearts eager to bestow grace upon their devotees,
they mounted a blazing chariot constructed of the finest jewels and arrived at the Bhāṇḍīra forest, where Hari was present.
Clad in divine garments and adorned with jewel ornaments,
having bowed to Hari and offered praise,
the three Vaiṣṇava men cast off their bodies and departed for the supreme Goloka.
Having attained birth in the womb of a demoness, they became the attendants (pārṣadas) of Kṛṣṇa.
Nārada said:
Who were those divine persons, the Vaiṣṇavas who took the form of Daityas?
"O illustrious one, tell me what most wonderful deed was performed.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, I shall relate an ancient history."

I heard from the mouth of Maheśa at Puṣkara during the solar festival that Śaṅkara, when questioned by the assembly of sages, by me, by Dharmarāja, and by Brahmā, spoke while engaged in a discourse on the qualities of Hari. 32.
O illustrious son of Brahmā, listen attentively as I relate in detail this story that purifies the world. On Mount Gandhamādana, the lord of the Gandharvas, the Wind-god, [spoke]. (33–34)
O sage, that great and most excellent ascetic was devoted to the service of Hari;
he had four sons who were the foremost among the Gandharvas,
and they remembered the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa in their dreams, in their waking knowledge, and day and night.
And those disciples of Durvāsas, devoted to the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
daily offered a lotus, performed his worship, and drank water.
Vasudeva, Suhotra, Sudarśana, and Supārśvaka— (36–37).
Four of the best of Vaiṣṇavas performed penance at Puṣkara.
Having practiced penance for a long time, they became masters of perfected mantras.
The eldest, Durvāsas, having attained yoga, became the foremost among yogis.
Having attained perfection and remaining celibate, he blazed with the splendor of Brahman;
instantly casting off his body, he became an attendant of Kṛṣṇa.
Once, those brothers of his went to the Citrasaras lake.
O Sage, at sunrise, seeing Vaiṣṇavas going out to gather lotuses for the worship of Kṛṣṇa after having collected them,
all the servants of Śaṅkara bound them and departed.
The strong ones, having seized the weak, went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Having seen Śaṅkara, they all prostrated themselves on the ground with their heads.
Bestowing a supreme blessing upon them quickly, Śiva spoke to them.
With a face brightened by a slight smile and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees, Śiva said:
"Who are you who have stolen the lotuses from Pārvatī’s lake? (43–44)
For the sake of fulfilling her vow to Pārvatī, Satī constantly offers a thousand lotuses daily to Hari, who must be guarded by a hundred thousand yakṣas;
she does so with devotion during this three-month vow that increases the fortune of her husband.
Having heard the words of Śiva, all the Vaiṣṇavas, with palms joined in reverence and their necks bowed in devotion, spoke to him out of fear. The Gandharvas said: 46. The Gandharvas said:
"O Lord, we are the foremost of the Gandharvas, the sons of Gandhavāha.
O Master, having offered a lotus to Hari, we drink the water.
O Protector, we do not know of this lake guarded by Pārvatī. (47–48)
"Take all these lotuses and make them bear fruit for you!
We will not give you the lotuses today; O Hara, we shall drink the water today!
Or rather, how could we not drink it, since they have been given to you?"
Having constantly meditated upon whose lotus feet we worship with a lotus, O Lord, we have become purified by offering that very lotus directly to him.
For Brahman is indeed one and without a second; where is the body, and where is the embodied form? (50–51)
The body and the diversity of forms are due to Māyā, arising from the grace bestowed upon devotees.
Nevertheless, O Lord, you alone are my master; therefore, please accept these lotuses.
Since our hearts are not yet fully satisfied, O Acyuta, reveal that [divine] form to us.
Two-armed, lovely, youthful, and darkly beautiful;
holding a flute for diversion in His hand, wearing yellow garments, supreme;
with one face and two eyes, anointed with sandalwood and aguru paste. 53–54.
With a face brightened by a slight smile, adorned with jewel ornaments,
his chest made radiant by the supreme gem Kaustubha;
with a crest of peacock feathers and decorated with garlands of jasmine.
Adorned with rows of garlands of *pārijāta* blossoms, enchanting as the abode of the playful beauty of ten million Cupids,
he was beheld by throngs of gopīs with smiling, sidelong glances;
endowed with fresh youth, he rested upon the breast of Rādhā.
"Praised by Brahmā and the other gods, worthy of worship, the object of meditation, and the desired goal;
delighting in his own self, with all desires fulfilled, and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees"—
having spoken thus, the preeminent Gandharvas stood before Śambhu, their bodies marked with horripilation from hearing of the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard the words of the Gandharvas, Śiva, his eyes filled with tears from hearing the description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form, spoke to them: "I myself have recognized you as the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas;
wander over the earth to purify it with the dust of your lotus feet."
I indeed cherish the desire for the sight of the devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For the company of the virtuous is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
O Pārvatī and you gods, you are always dear to me.

I am dear to myself and to my devotees, and the Vaiṣṇavas are dear to us as well. However, O highly fortunate ones, listen to that which was previously accepted by me so that it does not become fruitless regarding the performance of Pārvatī’s vow.
Those who, during the interval between their vows, have plucked the lotuses from the fragrant lake,
will without doubt quickly go to an asuric womb;
for indeed, no inauspiciousness exists anywhere for the devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having attained a human birth, you will certainly go to Goloka.
You are eager to see the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa directly;
O dear ones, you will surely behold Him in the Vṛndāvana forest in Bhārata-varṣa.
Then, having seen Kṛṣṇa and attained death, you, the best of Vaiṣṇavas,
shall mount a divine chariot and go to the abode of Hari.
Now, you are eager here to behold His desirable form.
Having said, "Behold all that," Śiva revealed it to them.
Having seen that form, those lords of the Dānavas, with tearful eyes, bowed down to the one who possesses all forms and returned to their birth as Dānavas. (70)
In former times, Vasudeva, Suhotra, and the demon Baka were liberated;
so too were Sudarśana, this Pralamba, Keśin himself, and Supārśvaka—
having seen his unsurpassed form through the granting of a boon by Hara.
Having met their death at the hands of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they went to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this wonderful deed of Hari been told—the liberation of Baka, Keśin, and Pralamba, which brings about liberation. (73)
Nārada said:
"O highly fortunate one, by your grace I have heard all that was wonderful.
Now I wish to hear what vow Pārvatī performed."
Who is to be propitiated in this vow? What is its fruit, and what is the rule of restraint?
O Blessed One, what are the materials required for the vow? For how long is the vow, and what is the description regarding its consecration? (72–76)
"O Lord, speak after due reflection; I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "There is a vow lasting three months called the 'Increaser of a Husband’s Good Fortune' (Patisaubhāgyavardhana). 77.
O sage, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, together with Rādhikā, is to be propitiated.
The commencement [of the vow] takes place at the equinox (viṣuva), and its conclusion occurs during the southern transit of the sun (dakṣiṇāyana).
On the preceding day, one must restrain oneself and certainly consume only sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Having bathed on the day of the sun's entry into Aries (vaiśākhasaṃkrānti) and made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
the observer of the vow should worship [the deity] in a water-pot, a gem, a śālagrāma stone, or in water.
Having worshipped the five deities, he should meditate with devotion upon Rādheśa.
Now learn of the meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda, which I shall describe to you:
[He is] dark as a fresh rain-cloud, clothed in yellow silk garments, with a face like the full moon of autumn, endowed with a gentle smile. (81)
With eyes like lotuses blooming in autumn, adorned with charming marks,
repeatedly enchanting the minds of the gopīs,
beheld by Rādhā, and resting upon the breast of Rādhā. (82–83)
I worship Him who is being praised by Brahmā, Ananteśa, Dharma, and others.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa with concentration and having joyfully invoked Him through that meditation, the observer of the vow should then meditate upon Rādhikā;
this is the meditation prescribed for midday.
To Rādhā, the mistress of the rāsa, the beautiful one, eager for the delight of the rāsa-dance;
to her who stands in the center of the rāsa-maṇḍala, the presiding deity of the rāsa;
to her who dwells upon the chest of the Lord of the rāsa, the connoisseur of rasa, beloved by the connoisseurs of rasa. 85–86.
She was the most excellent of connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, beautiful, and eager for dalliance;
her eyes shed the luster of rows of autumn lotuses;
she was endowed with the knitting of curved eyebrows and delighted by the sound of her anklets.
Her face was like the full moon of autumn, enchanting with a slight smile;
she possessed the beautiful hue of a campaka flower and was adorned with sandalwood paste. She was joined by a drop of musk together with a dot of vermilion. (88–89)
Adorned with rows of beautiful leaves, radiant in garments as pure as fire,
her lovely cheeks were made brilliant by two earrings of excellent gems;
her chest was resplendent with a necklace of the finest essence of jewels.
I worship her who is adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and tinkling bells, and graced by the resonant sound of anklets fashioned from the essence of excellent gems;
she who is served by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, who is served even by Brahmā and the other gods;
she who is praised by the Lord of All, and who is the seed of all.
Having meditated thus, one should worship her together with Kṛṣṇa.
Having offered the sixteen services daily with devotion, the observer of the vow should joyfully present everything individually and separately. (93–94)

O Sage, the observer of the vow should daily perform a divine oblation of one thousand and eight offerings; he should diligently offer one hundred and eight oblations while uttering with devotion, "Svāhā to Kṛṣṇa."
One should daily offer with devotion one hundred and eight fruits of the *rasāla* and the plantain—whether raw or ripe—along with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
And, O Sage, one should daily feed a hundred Brahmins with devotion. (96–97)
The observer of the vow should perform the fire sacrifice daily with one hundred and eight oblations.
He should offer these with devotion to Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhikā.
O Nārada, he should perform the oblation with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
One should constantly play musical instruments and cause the glorification of Hari to be performed.
Having done this for three months, one should thereafter perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Listen, O Nārada, to the procedure for that day of consecration. (99–100)
And ninety thousand lotuses, as well as unbroken grains of rice; O best of Brahmins, one should diligently feed nine thousand Brahmins with excellent, savory, and sweet foods.

One should offer nine thousand seven hundred and twenty fruits, as well as various kinds of most enchanting substances as an oblation (naivedya). Having established the consecrated fire, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa). 102–103.

Having offered ninety thousand oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds, one should devotedly present ninety sesame-laddukas, accompanied by garments, food, and sacrificial threads with their fruits,
all honored with perfumes and flowers.
One should give ninety jars filled with cold water.
Having performed such a vow, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, according to the measure prescribed for a dakṣiṇā in the Vedas. 106–109.
And a thousand bulls, each endowed with golden horns— thus,
O Brahmin, has been described the three-month vow that produces an excellent lineage and increases a husband’s good fortune.
By the power of this vow, she shall possess good fortune for a hundred births;
indeed, she will certainly become the mother of virtuous sons for a hundred lifetimes.
Furthermore, there shall never be any separation between her husband and her sons. (108–109)
The son shall become like a servant, and the husband shall act according to her word.
At every moment, she, being virtuous, shall be endowed with devotion to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
By the power of her vow, she shall attain knowledge and the constant remembrance of Hari.
Furthermore, a vow prescribed in the Sāmaveda was previously performed by us both.
Listen as I tell you that which is the most excellent of all vows:
the virtuous Śatarūpā, belonging to Svāyambhuva Manu, [performed it]. (111–112)
Having first appointed Agastya as their domestic priest,
that was performed by Devahūti; and then,
O Sage, according to the injunctions of the Śrutis, Ākūti likewise appointed Pulastya as her domestic priest.
Rohiṇī performed that ritual, having appointed Rati as her domestic priest;
Gautama served as her priest out of devotion to him. Tārā, the beloved wife of her guru, also performed that vow with devotion.
Vasiṣṭha was his priest, having gathered a great store of provisions;
and having seen that vow performed by Śakra and Śacī, as well as by the wife of his guru,
Bṛhaspati, his priest, likewise gathered a great store of provisions.
And Svāhā performed a vow that was entirely extraordinary.
Marīci, his family priest, had gathered all the necessary materials in great abundance.
O Brahmin, seeing this, Pārvatī joyfully spoke to Śaṅkara.
With her hands joined in the *puṭāñjali* gesture, the goddess, her neck bowed low with devotion, spoke:
Pārvatī said:
"Give me your command, O Lord of the World; I shall perform this supreme vow. (118–119)
O Lord, the worship of Hari is the supreme vow among all our vows and the cause of all auspiciousness;
it surpasses what is sacrificed, what is given, the recitation of the Vedas, visiting holy fords, and circumambulating the earth. (120)
It does not merit even a sixteenth part of the worship of Hari.
For one who has external and internal remembrance of Hari at every moment—that very person is liberated while living; liberation occurs simply by the sight of him.
By the dust of his lotus feet, the earth is instantly purified;
by the mere sight of him, he purifies the three worlds.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Śeṣa, and you, O Lord of Gaṇas, [are all purified]. 123.
By meditating again and again upon whose lotus feet one becomes great and equal to him in splendor;
whoever constantly meditates upon whom, he certainly attains that very person.
Through virtue, splendor, intellect, and knowledge, he becomes equal to that being.
Through the remembrance, meditation, austerity, and service to Kṛṣṇa, I have indeed obtained the Blessed Lord as my master and even as my son;
everything was effortlessly attained by me, and at that time my heart was completely fulfilled. (126)
"My lord is one such as you; my sons are Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśvara;
my father is Himādri, and I am a portion of Kṛṣṇa—O Lord, what is difficult for me to attain?
Having heard these words of Pārvatī, Śaṅkara himself was well-pleased.
With his body covered in horripilation, he laughed and spoke sweetly.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O Īśvarī, you are the very embodiment of Mahālakṣmī; what is impossible for you?"
You are the embodiment of all prosperity and the form of infinite power.
O Goddess, he in whose house you reside is a vessel of sovereignty;
for one in whose house Lakṣmī does not dwell, death is better than life.

O bestower of auspiciousness, through devotion to you, I, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are capable during the time of dissolution and at the time of creation by your grace. Who indeed is Himālaya, who am I, and who are Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśvara? (131–132)

"Deprived of you we are powerless, yet with you we are masters. You are endowed with the qualities of a devoted wife, as were those women of old heard of in the Vedas. Having received the command of the Lord, O devoted wife, perform your vow."
"Perform this vow in a manner distinct from those by whom it has already been performed.
Let the venerable Sanatkumāra be the presiding priest (purohita) for your vow;
I too shall be the donor of lotuses, Brahmins, and ritual materials. (134–135)
O beautiful one, appoint Kubera as the guardian of the treasury of wealth;
I myself shall be the superintendent of charity during the vow, and Śrī herself shall be the giver of riches.
Vahni-deva shall be the reciter, and Varuṇa the provider of water. (136)
The Yakṣas are the carriers of the ritual objects, and their supervisor is the six-faced Kārttikeya.
Pavana himself is the performer of the consecration of the site in this vow;
Śakra himself is the attendant, and Candra is the presiding authority over the vow. (137–138)

O beloved, Sūrya is the expounder of the nature of giving; having given the substance prescribed for a vow according to what is appropriate and inappropriate and as is fitting, O beautiful one, give flowers to Hari with even greater fruit than that, as it has been ordained. (139)
O Goddess, after feeding the Brahmins who have been restrained by their vows,
extend an invitation with devotion to an even greater number of Brahmins, beyond counting.
On the day of completion, [offer] gold, gems, pearls, and coral.
"Having given the sacrificial fee prescribed for the vow, give everything to the twice-born.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara caused her to perform that vow;
Durgā performed the vow, which was distinct from all others.

"O Brahmin, thus has been told what vow was performed by Pārvatī. The Brahmins were unable to carry the jewels [required] for Pārvatī’s vow. The entire history has been heard; now hear the matter at hand, O Nārada. (143–144)
Having slain those lords of the Dānavas along with the children in Gokula, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose childhood deeds are ever new at every step,
went to his own home, which resembled the palace of Kubera.
And the news of the forest was joyfully told to everyone by the children.
Upon hearing this, they were all struck with wonder, while Nanda fell into a state of fear.
He then summoned the elder cowherds, as well as the elder cowherd women.

Having deliberated with them, the Lord of the Gopas employed a stratagem appropriate for the occasion. O Sage, having devised that plan, he prepared to leave that place and immediately spoke to them all regarding his departure for Vṛndāvana.
Having heard Nanda’s command, they all prepared to depart—the cowherds and cowherdesses, as well as the boys and girls. Together with Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the boys set out with joy. (149–150)
Singing songs together and arrayed in various costumes, some were players of the flute, some were players of the horn,
some had their hands clapping rhythm, and others held lutes in their hands. (151)
Some had arrows and mechanical devices in their hands, and some had horns in their hands;
some cowherd boys had fresh sprouts as earrings, some had flower buds as earrings, and some had full-blown flowers as earrings. (152–153)
Some had wreaths of fresh flowers, and some had garlands reaching down to their knees;
some had crests of sprouts, and some had crests of blossoms.
O best of Brahmins, all these cowherd boys numbered nine crores.
O sage, millions upon millions of cowherd girls and their companions went there with joy;
likewise, millions of elderly women with broad hips and swaying breasts,
as well as young cowherd girls who were the companions of Rādhikā.
Those fortunate women, Suśīlā and the others, adorned with various ornaments and dressed in divine garments, went forth joyfully with smiles upon their faces;
some having mounted palanquins, and some having mounted chariots. (157)

Mounting a chariot adorned with gold, the goddess Rādhā, accompanied by them and decorated with jeweled ornaments, departed; likewise Yaśodā and Rohiṇī, also adorned with jeweled ornaments, went forth. (158–159)
Mounting a chariot adorned with gold, Nanda went forth;
Sunanda, Śrīdāmā, Giribhānu, Vibhākara,
Vīrabhānu, and Candrabhānu joyfully set out, mounted upon elephants.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva, adorned with jewel-encrusted ornaments, mounted a golden chariot and departed with supreme joy. Accompanied by crores upon crores of cowherds—both elders and those in the prime of youth—they went forth. (161–162)
Some mounted on horses, some on elephants, and others on chariots—
the cowherds, the attendants of Nanda, filled with joy and exultant— proceeded,
while others were mounted on bulls or donkeys, intent upon the performance of music.
There were another three hundred and seventy million maidservants of Rādhikā, filled with joy and smiling, adorned with golden ornaments;
some held vermilion in their hands, and others carried collyrium. (164–165)
Some held balls in their hands, and some held dolls;
some excellent women held objects of enjoyment, and others held articles for play.
Some held garments and ornaments, while other excellent women held garlands.
Some gopīs joyfully set forth with musical instruments in their hands;
some carried garments purified by fire, and others bore liquids of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. (167–168)
Some were devoted to music, and some were delighted by wonderful tales;
millions upon millions of beautiful women set forth, accompanied by palanquins.
Millions upon millions of horses and millions upon millions of chariots followed.
By the tens of millions and indeed by the tens of millions were the carts filled with goods;
by the tens of millions and indeed by the tens of millions were the lordly bulls that drew the goods;
and by the tens of millions and indeed by the tens of millions were ten lakhs of elephants.
Equipped with elephant goads, they went to the forest of Vṛndāvana.
O Sage, having all arrived at Vṛndāvana and seeing the houses empty,
they all stood at the foot of the trees in their respective places as was appropriate.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to the cowherds, "O Vrajas, stay in your most beloved homes today. Having heard these words spoken by Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
the cowherds asked, "Where are those homes, O Kṛṣṇa?"
Having heard these words of theirs, Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In this place there are houses, gracious and fashioned by the gods. (175)
Without the favor of the gods, no one at all is able to see [it].
O cowherds, stay today after having fully worshipped the forest deities;
tomorrow morning you will surely behold the beautiful homes with joy.
"Perform worship of the goddess Caṇḍikā, who dwells at the foot of the banyan tree, with incense, lamps, food offerings, oblations, flowers,
and sandalwood. Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, the cowherds fully worshipped the deity.
Having enjoyed their pleasures during the day, they slept there joyfully at night.

(178) Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Departure for Vṛndāvana Following the Slaying of Baka, Pralamba, and Keśin," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
While the inhabitants of Vraja were asleep in the forest of Vṛndāvana at night,
and while the Lord of Sleep lay fast asleep upon the breast of his mother,
and while the gopīs were also sleeping upon their beautiful couches.
And among some whose minds were attached to the union with the pleasure of youths; among some accompanied by children; among some accompanied by female friends;
among some seated in carts; and among some seated in chariots. (2–3)

In that place, more enchanting than even heaven, which was filled with the moonlight of the full moon and made fragrant by the breeze carrying the scent of various kinds of flowers; when all living beings had become motionless and the fifth muhūrta had passed— (4)
There arrived the Blessed One, the teacher of teachers to artisans, wearing fine, divine garments and a captivating garland of jewels;
he was adorned with incomparable jeweled ornaments and glorious crocodile-shaped earrings. (5–6)
Advanced in both knowledge and age, he was as handsome as a youth;
exceedingly beautiful and glorious, his splendor was equal to that of Kāmadeva.
Together with thirty million artisans who were experts in specialized crafts... [7]

Multitudes of yakṣas, the servants of Kubera’s forest, arrived with their hands bearing jewels, gold, gems, and iron weapons. Some were dressed in crystal and precious stones, while others had long shoulders. (8–9)
Some have hands of ruby, while others, the most excellent, have hands of sapphire;
some have hands of syamantaka gem, and likewise those of moonstone;
others have hands of sunstone, and other excellent ones have hands that radiate light.
Some had axes in their hands, while others were excellent carriers of refined iron;
some carried fragrant woods and the finest jewels;
some held chowries in their hands, and others carried mirrors. (11–12)
Some were carriers of golden vessels, jars, and other items;
and Viśvakarmā, having seen the most enchanting collection of materials,
began to construct the city after meditating upon Kṛṣṇa of auspicious gaze.
Five yojanas in extent, it is the most excellent and supreme region in Bhārata;
a field of merit, the essence of all holy fords, and most dear to Hari.
For those dwelling there who seek liberation, it is the cause of the highest nirvāṇa. (14–15)
It is a staircase to Goloka, granting the desires of all;
there itself is an exceedingly beautiful four-winged mansion with four halls, provided with excellent stone door-panels, pillars, staircases, and steps. (16)

Then, with ease, he fashioned [the city] with a crest radiant with variegated puppets and flower-pots (17), joined by courtyards and altars constructed from the stone of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) (18),
and enclosed by stone walls (18). Delighted, he joyfully constructed it with gems having the appearance of crystal, provided with two gates— one large and one small— as was appropriate (19).
It was adorned with staircases made of sandalwood, pillars fashioned from *śaṅku* wood,
doors of excellent iron, and radiant silver pitchers;
it was further beautified by ramparts constructed from the essence of diamond.
Having established the settlement for the cowherds in their respective places as was appropriate,
he then began once more to construct a beautiful residence for Vṛṣabhānu,
which was provided with walls and moats and possessed four excellent gates.
It was a beautiful four-winged palace (catuḥśāla) constructed of great jewels,
adorned with excellent mattresses made of the finest essence of gems,
and featuring most lovely staircases fashioned from gold-colored jewels.
It was adorned with door-panels made of the finest iron and decorated with artificial paintings;
every beautiful mansion shone with golden domes.
And in a certain secluded, most enchanting part of that hermitage—
O Sage, within the garden of beautiful campaka trees,
he constructed a palatial dwelling for Kalāvatī to enjoy with her husband out of curiosity, using a preeminent and magnificent jewel. (29–30)
It was fitted with nine ascending stairs fashioned from sapphire;
it possessed a multitude of pillars and door-panels made of sandalwood;
it was exceedingly lofty, delightful, and distinct in every respect. (27)
Nārada said: "O Blessed One, who was Kalāvatī, and whose wife was that captivating woman, for whose sake the celestial architect built such a delightful house with great effort? (28)
Nārāyaṇa said: Kamalāṃśā Kalāvatī, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs,
became the beautiful Sundarī, devoted to her husband, the wife of Vṛṣabhānu.
She whose daughter Rādhā is dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa,
born from half a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and equal to Him in splendor;
and by the dust of whose lotus feet the earth was purified.
And in whom the virtuous constantly desire firm devotion.
Nārada said:
O sage, while staying in Vraja, how [did you see] the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs?
By what merit did that man obtain her who is so very difficult to attain? (31) Who indeed was Vṛṣabhānu, the lord of Vraja, in a former life—what a great soul he was!
And by whose austerity did Rādhā become his daughter? (32)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the great sage, the best among the wise,
smiled and spoke with affection to him regarding this ancient history.
Nārāyaṇa said:
In ancient times, three daughters were born from the mind of the Pitṛs—Kalāvatī, Ratnamālā, and Menakā, all exceedingly rare. And Ratnamālā, filled with desire, chose Janaka as her husband.
Menakā [gave birth] to Himālaya, the lord of mountains and a portion of Hari;
and Sītā, the wife of Śrī Rāma, who was the goddess Śrī herself and devoted to truth, was born not from a womb as the daughter of Ratnamālā. (36)
She was formerly Satī, the daughter of Menakā, who became Pārvatī. She was not born from a womb; she is the eternal Māyā of Hari.
Through her ascetic penance, she obtained as her husband the god Hara, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa. (37–38)
Kalāvatī [married] Sucandra, who was born of the lineage of Manu.
And that king, an expansion (aṃśa) of Hari, having obtained Kalāvatī,
considered himself the most excellent among the virtuous and exceedingly handsome.
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what attire! Oh, her fresh youth!
(40) Her limbs are most tender and graceful, and her face surpasses the autumn moon.
Oh, her gait is rare indeed, putting to shame both the elephant and the wagtail! (41)
Her pair of hips, exquisitely graceful and fashioned like plantain trunks, was capable of deluding even the minds of the lords of sages with her sidelong glances.
O Sage, her two breasts were exceedingly firm, plump, and elevated.
Her pair of lovely hips was fashioned like the wheels of a chariot;
her hands and feet were red, and her lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit. Her row of teeth was enchanting, resembling the seeds of a ripe pomegranate. (43–44)
His eyes were like the radiance released from lotuses at midday in the autumn;
his form was adorned with ornaments made of excellent jewels.
Thinking thus and seeing him, he was tormented by the arrows of Kāma.
Mounting a divine chariot together with his beloved,
the lover sported in secret in various enchanting places,
in the delightful valley of the Malaya mountains, where the breeze was scented with sandalwood and aloe.
Upon a bed of beautiful campaka flowers that brings the pleasure of delight,
in a flower garden of mālatī and mallikā in full bloom,
and in a secluded grove of ketakī trees on the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river.
In a forest on the shore of the western ocean, devoid of living beings;
in the Nandana grove, in the valley of Mount Mandara, or in the forest on the banks of the Kāverī;
on every mountain, in every delightful place, by every river, and at every stream—49–50.
In every island, he enjoyed himself in secret with Vāmā;
due to the intensity of their new union, he was unaware of day or night.
Thus, those thousand years passed for him as if they were but a single moment.
Having established a monastery for a very long time, he became detached from worldly life.
He went with her to the Vindhya mountain for asceticism,
to that most excellent and highly praised Pulaha-hermitage, a sacred site in Bhārata.
There the king performed austerities for a thousand divine years;
desiring liberation, free from longing, abstaining from food, and with a lean belly,
O best of sages, he fell into a swoon while meditating on the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.

Seeing her husband motionless, abandoned by his five vital breaths, his body smeared with flesh and blood and his frame clinging to the bones, that virtuous woman moved far away from the anthill that had enveloped his limbs. (55–56)
Afflicted by grief, Kalāvatī wept aloud in that solitary place;
crying out "O Lord, O Lord! and placing him who had fainted upon her breast, she, devoted to her husband, lamented in great distress. (57)
Seeing the king fasting, emaciated, and covered with veins,
and hearing her weeping, the creator of the worlds, the lotus-born one, a treasure-house of compassion, appeared out of pity. (58-59)
Placing him quickly upon his lap, the all-pervading Lord wept.
Brahmā, the knower of Brahman, sprinkled the king’s body with water from his water-pot and,
through the knowledge of Brahman, restored life to it.
The lord of men, having regained consciousness and seeing Prajāpati before him—who was as radiant as Kāma—bowed down to him. Satisfied, he said to him: "Choose a boon according to your desire."
Having heard the words of Vidhi, he chose the desired Nirvana.
"O Ocean of Compassion, you have prepared to grant a boon out of mercy.
[Thus spoke] the glorious one, whose face was serene and whose lotus-like countenance was smiling.
Having made this inference in her mind, with her throat, lips, and palate parched,
the virtuous Kalāvatī, trembling with fear, spoke to him as he stood prepared to grant a boon.
Kalāvatī said:

"O Lotus-born One, if you grant liberation to the king of men, then tell me, O Brahmā, what will be the fate of this woman? And without her husband, O Four-faced One, what beauty can there be for women? (65–66)
In the Śruti it is heard that for a woman devoted to her husband, the husband alone is her vow.
The husband is her guru, her chosen deity, and his very essence is austerity and dharma.
To all women, there is no kinsman dearer than the husband; there is no one higher than the master.
O Brahmin, service to the husband is superior to all dharmas and is very difficult to attain.
For one who is devoid of service to her lord, everything—whatever vows, gifts, austerities, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth—becomes fruitless. (68–69)
Bathing in all sacred fords, circumambulating the earth,
initiation into all sacrifices, whatever great gifts there may be,
the recitation of all the Vedas, and all forms of austerity— [all these are equaled by this]. (70)

Feeding Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and the service of the gods—these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the service of one's master. Those women who are devoid of service to their master speak harshly to their master. (71–72)
They fall into the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure;
there, worms the size of mustard seeds bite them day and night, and they incessantly utter a harsh, distorted sound. (73)
They joyfully consume urine, phlegm, and excrement;
and the servants of Yama place a flaming torch into their mouths.
Having experienced such suffering in hell, they enter the womb of worms.
"They consume blood, flesh, and excrement for a hundred births.
Having heard this from the mouths of the learned, as determined in the Vedic statements, I know somewhat; you are a woman, while the All-pervading Lord is the progenitor of the Vedas.
O Acyuta, you are the teacher of teachers, as well as of the learned, the yogis, and the wise;
since you are thus omniscient, why do you not enlighten me?
If this beloved one, who was dearer to him than life itself, has indeed been liberated, [then tell me]. (77–78)
"O Brahmin, who is the protector of my virtue and my youth?
In childhood, my father was the protector; having honored him, he gave me to a worthy recipient.
Always, the husband is the protector, and in his absence, his son. (79)
It is traditionally taught that women have three protectors during the three stages of life.
Those who are independent are ruined; they are excluded from all dharma.
Born of an ignoble family, they are unchaste women with depraved minds.
O Lotus-born One, the merit accumulated by them over a hundred lifetimes perishes.
Just as the affection for a son is equal in childhood, youth, and old age, so too is the longing of devoted wives for their beloved constant at all times. (82)

The affection of mothers for their own infant sons, even when those children are exceedingly beautiful, does not equal even a sixteenth part of the love that virtuous wives have for their husbands. [This love lasts] until the infant’s weaning from the breast, and until the husband’s consumption of his desired food. (83–84)
The hearts of virtuous women are constantly fixed upon their beloveds, whether in sleep or in waking consciousness.
The end of suffering for them is the separation from kinsmen, and even greater than that is the grief for their sons;
there is no suffering for a woman more terrible than that of her husband.

Just as an unskilled woman is consumed by grief when her food is scorched on a blazing fire, so too is a skilled woman consumed by the fire of separation from a clever lover. For virtuous women, there is no thirst for food or water when they are without their husband. (86–87)
In the fire of separation, the mind is consumed like dry grass in a blaze.
Indeed, there is no kinsman greater than the beloved; indeed, there is no one dearer than the beloved.
Indeed, there is no deity greater than the beloved; indeed, there is no teacher greater than the beloved.
Indeed, there is no duty higher than the beloved; indeed, there is no wealth higher than the beloved.
Indeed, there is no life-breath higher than the beloved; indeed, for a woman, there is nothing higher than the beloved—just as the minds of Vaiṣṇavas are submerged in the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. (89–90)
As [the love] of a mother for her only son, as that of lustful men for women,
as that of misers for their wealth acquired over a long time,
as that of the fearful for their fears, and as that of the learned for the scriptures— 91.
Just as infants [long] for the taking of the breast, as artisans for their crafts,
and as unchaste women for a lover, so too do virtuous women for their beloved;
O Brahmin, it is not possible to live even for a single moment without him.

For those women whose minds are destroyed by grief at being deprived of a virtuous husband and who are submerged in the sorrow of another, death is life and life is worse than death; for them, food and drink [serve only] as a matter of time. (94)
Alas, the grief for a beloved increases through the consumption of [forbidden things] in a contrary manner.
For virtuous women who associate with the righteous, there is the excellent shadow of their own karma;
whereas others, at the end of their bodies of enjoyment, become virtuous woman after woman in birth after birth.
"O Sustainer of the World, if you do not release this [man] without me,
then, O Lord, having cursed you, behold, I shall commit the slaughter of a woman.
Having heard Kalāvatī’s words, the Creator, filled with wonder, spoke.
With a mind agitated by fear, he spoke words that were beneficial and like nectar.
Brahmā said:
"O child, I will not grant you liberation, nor will I [grant it] to my lord without you."

"O Mother, I am not currently able to grant liberation along with you; for it is universally agreed that liberation is difficult to attain without [experiencing] worldly enjoyment. One who enjoys sense-objects attains the state of Nirvana upon the cessation of those enjoyments. (99)
"O Satī, enjoy the pleasures of heaven with your husband for a thousand years of the gods.
Thereafter, your birth shall take place in Bhārata;
when Rādhikā herself becomes your daughter, Satī. (100–101)
Upon liberation while living, you two shall go together to Goloka.
O best of kings, enjoy pleasures with this woman for some time;
she is indeed virtuous and endowed with goodness, so you ought not to curse me.
"Being liberated while living, equanimous, and with their minds fixed on the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, they desire service to Hari—which is difficult to attain—and not mere liberation.
Having spoken thus and granted those two boons, He stood before them. (103–104)
Having bowed to him, those two were delighted, and Brahmā departed for his own abode.
In due time, having enjoyed the pleasures of Bhārata—which is supremely merit-bestowing, divine, and desired even by Brahmā and the other gods—they both returned. (105)
Sucandra and Vṛṣabhānu obtained birth in Gokula within the womb of Padmāvatī by means of Surabhānu’s seed;
he was a portion of Hari who remembered his former births, like the moon in its bright fortnight.
There, in the house of Vraja, the lord of Vraja grew day by day—
he who was all-knowing, a great yogi, whose mind was fixed on the lotus feet of Hari,
a kinsman of Nanda, generous, handsome, virtuous, and wise. (108)
In Kānyakubja there was a woman named Kalāvatī, born not from a womb;
she was a great saint, beautiful, and possessed of a portion of Kamalā, and she remembered her former births.
In Kānyakubja there was a most excellent king, Bhaṇḍana, who was of wide stride. (109–110)

Having reached her at the conclusion of the sacrifice—she who had arisen from the sacrificial pit, naked, laughing, and endowed with beauty like a young girl whose breasts have not yet been nourished;
blazing with splendor and possessing the luster of molten gold—he beheld her. (111)
Placing it upon his chest, the king of kings joyfully gave it to his beloved wife.
Mālavatī, filled with great delight, gave her breast and nourished the child.
On the day of the first feeding of solid food, at an auspicious moment in the midst of virtuous people, [she performed the ceremony].
And at the time of protecting the maiden's name, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O King, protect the maiden named Kalāvatī.
Having heard these words, the lord of the earth did accordingly.
He gave wealth to the Brahmins, the mendicants, and the bards;
he fed everyone and celebrated a magnificent festival.
In the course of time, that Rūpavatī reached the bloom of youth. (115–116)
Exceedingly beautiful and youthful, she captivates the minds of sages;
her complexion has the luster of a lovely campaka flower, and her face resembles the autumnal moon.
With a countenance brightened by a gentle smile, her eyes are like full-blown lotuses. (117)
Afflicted by the weight of her hips and loins, and bent low by the burden of her breasts, she walked along the royal road with the slow, majestic gait of a lordly elephant.
And Nanda, filled with joy, beheld her as she proceeded upon the path. (118–119)
Although he was self-controlled and wise, he nevertheless fell into a swoon;
yet, being alarmed, he quickly and respectfully questioned the people passing on the road:
"Whose daughter is this who is going along? To him, the people replied.

King Bhanandana had a daughter named Kalāvatī, who was blessed by the grace of Kamalā and born in the royal palace. Out of curiosity, she was going to her friend’s house for the sake of play. (121–122)
"Go, go, O best of the Vrajas!"—having spoken thus, the people departed.
With a joyful heart, Nanda went to the royal palace;
quickly alighting from his chariot, he entered the king's assembly hall.
Rising up, the king greeted him and offered him a golden throne.
They engaged in extensive and pleasant conversation with one another. Then Nanda, bowing low with humility, spoke words regarding their kinship.
Nanda said:
"Listen, O Indra among kings, I shall speak auspicious and specific words. Now, form an alliance with a distinguished man through your daughter. (126)
The illustrious Vṛṣabhānu, the son of Surabhānu and lord of Vraja, was an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, virtuous, handsome, and highly learned;
he was endowed with perpetual youth, a yogi, and a youth who remembered his past lives. (127)
Your daughter was born not from a womb, but emerged from the sacrificial fire-pit;
she is enchanting to the three worlds, peaceful, a portion of Kamalā, and possessed of every art. He is worthy of your daughter, and your daughter is worthy of him.
"O King, the union of a wise woman with a wise man is full of merit.
Having spoken thus in the assembly, Nanda fell silent.
Then, O Sage, that best of kings, bowing low with humility, spoke to him.
Bhānandana said:
O Lord of Vraja, this relationship is indeed subject to destiny; it is not something to be achieved by me.
Prajāpati is the ordainer of yoga, and I am merely the giver of birth.
Who is whose wife or daughter, and who is the groom along with his retinue?
Destiny is the cause for all, bestowing fruits in accordance with one's past actions.
That which is destined to be and the deeds performed are unfailing; so it is heard in the Vedas.

Otherwise, every effort of one who lacks mastery is as fruitless as [the labor of] the Creator; for if the beloved of Vṛṣabhānu has been written by the Creator to be my daughter, she was already so in the past—who am I, or who else, that could prevent it? (134)
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the lord of kings, his neck bowed in humility, respectfully fed him with sweet foods. Then,
having received the king's permission, Vrajarāja returned to Vraja.
Having gone there, he spoke in the assembly of Surabhāna;
and Surabhāna, with effort and through Nandana,
respectfully and swiftly established the alliance by means of Garga.
At the time of the wedding, the lord of kings gave a vast dowry:
a jewel among elephants, a jewel among horses, gems, and jeweled ornaments.
Having obtained Kalāvatī, Vṛṣabhānu was filled with joy. (138–139)
She played in that secluded and beautiful place, unaware of day or night;
she was distraught at the absence of her Lord due to the lack of even a blink of an eye. And Vṛṣabhānu was likewise distressed in an instant without her.
And that girl, possessing the form of a magical human, was a rememberer of her past births;
Vṛṣabhānu, an expansion of Hari who likewise remembered his past births, was filled with joy.
And their love grew, ever-new day by day. (141–142)
She was always full of desire and mature, and he was a youth equal to the god of love.
In time, a daughter was born to them, who became that very Rādhikā;
she had previously been [Śatadhanu] by the curse of Sudāmā and the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (143)

And she, though born of an improper source and possessing a dark life-force, became such that by the mere sight of her, those two were liberated. (144) This history has been told; now hear the subject at hand.
Resembling a blazing crest of fire in consuming the fuel of sins,
Viśvakarman, the foremost of artisans, went joyfully to the hermitage of Vṛṣabha and then departed for another place together with his own attendants.

Having mentally envisioned a beautiful stretch of land measuring one *krośa*, the knower of reality began to construct a hermitage for the high-souled Nanda; and having used his intellect to discern a site that was distinct from all others in every respect, he proceeded with the work.
It was an excellent city, provided with four deep moats that were difficult for enemies to cross,
dug out and lined with stone;
these moats were filled with flowering groves, blooming on both their banks.
O Sage, it was surrounded on all sides by beautiful, blossoming *campaka* trees that were most enchanting, and by the fragrance of scented winds;
as well as by mangoes, *guḍālī* trees, jackfruit, dates, and coconuts.
With pomegranates, bilva fruits, bhṛṅgas, jambīras, and nāgaraṅgas;
with tall āmrātakas and clusters of jambu trees laden with fruit; and with groves of plantains, ketakīs, and kadambas. (151–152)
Adorned on all sides with those blossoming fruits— oh, how wonderful!—
which were always desirable, secluded, and fit for play,
he constructed an excellent path at the secret location of the moats. (153)
It was always difficult for those on the opposing side to traverse, yet easy for its own people;
by means of a signal, it was marked by jeweled pillars covered with very little water—a boundary established by pillars that was neither crowded nor expansive. (154, 159)
And upon the upper part of the moat, he constructed an exceedingly beautiful wall,
measuring one hundred bow-lengths and rising to a great height;
the measurement of its stone foundation was twenty-five cubits.
It was constructed from rubies shaped like vermilion and was exceedingly beautiful.
It was joined with two gates on the exterior and likewise with seven within, secured by door-leaves made of the finest jewels. 157–158.

It was resplendent with pitchers made of emeralds set with various jewels, and it was beautifully adorned with door-panels fashioned from the finest gems. Having constructed Nandālaya, which was crowned by a pinnacle shining with pitchers crafted from the essence of gold, he then wandered through the city once more. (159–160)
And he constructed various beautiful royal highways,
with platforms fashioned from the transformations of Raktabhānu and well-built towns;
and on both banks, all around, he established enchanting embankments.
It was resplendent on all sides with jewel-pavilions suitable for trade belonging to merchants,
blazing on both the right and the left;
then, having gone to Vṛndāvana, he constructed the Rāsa-maṇḍala.
Beautiful, circular in shape, and encircled by a wall of jewels; extending for a yojana on all sides and provided with jeweled altars,
it was adorned with nine crores of pavilions fashioned from the finest essence of gems.
Adorned with various paintings suitable for amorous enjoyment and provided with beds for pleasure;
made fragrant by the wind carrying the scent of diverse kinds of flowers;
furnished with jeweled lamps and radiant with golden pitchers. (165–166)
Having fashioned the site for the *rāsa* dance, which was beautifully adorned with flowering gardens and blossoming lakes, he proceeded to another place before him.
Upon seeing the lovely Vṛndāvana, he became truly delighted.
Within Vṛndāvana, in various secluded spots,
having carefully determined them with his intellect and reflected upon them in his mind,
he established thirty distinct and beautiful forests there. (168–169)
And he fashioned [a place] specifically for the sport of Rādhā and Mādhava;
then, in a secluded and exceedingly beautiful spot near Madhuvana,
at the foot of a banyan tree on the western bank of the lake.
To the east of the Campaka grove, in the midst of a Ketakī forest,
he further constructed for the two of them a jeweled pavilion, exceedingly beautiful and surrounded by four altars. (171–172)
It was resplendent with hundreds of cotton mattresses fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems;
it was adorned with nine beautiful doors featuring various paintings made of priceless jewels. (173)
It was adorned all around on the walls, both at ground level and above, with thirty million artificial jewel-encrusted and variegated pitchers;
it was surrounded by nine turrets fashioned from great, supreme gems. (174–175)
Its summit was radiant with a pinnacle fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems;
it was adorned with banners and arches, beautified by white chowries, and illuminated on all sides and in front by mirrors made of priceless jewels. (176)

A hundred bow-lengths high, resembling a crest of fire, and a hundred cubits in circumference, it is circular in shape. Its interior is most excellent, adorned with things like jewels, and decorated with nets of garlands made of cloths as pure as fire. (177–178)
It was perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron, combined with garlands and cushions made of *pārijāta* flowers;
it was fit for fresh amorous dalliance and served to increase desire. (179–180)
It was adorned with rows of *mālatī* and campaka flowers,
and provided with betel leaves mixed with camphor, served in vessels set with precious gems;
[the pavilions] were inlaid with diamond-hard materials and hung with lattices of pearls.
It was strewn with jars of the essence of jewels, well-provided with jeweled pedestals,
and furnished with jeweled lion-thrones variegated with jewel-inlay;
it was beautifully sprinkled with droplets of water from oozing moonstones.
Having created a delightful pleasure-house provided with cool, scented water and articles of enjoyment, he returned once more to the city; there,
he inscribed the names of those whose palaces they were.
Filled with joy, Viśvakarman, together with his disciples and hosts of yakṣas,
bowed to the Lord of Sleep who was fast asleep and departed for his own abode, O Sage.
Thus, in every way, everything belongs to the virtuous through the grace of the Blessed One.
By the will of the Lord, this wondrous city came into existence upon the earth.
Thus has been told the entire auspicious life-story of Hari; it bestows happiness and removes sins. What more do you wish to hear? (187)
Nārada said:
O knower of the true reality, tell me the etymology or the derivation of the name "Vṛndāvana" for this forest in Bhārata, and its essential truth. (188)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the sage Nārāyaṇa, with joy, laughed and spoke the entire ancient truth. (189)
Nārāyaṇa said: O Brahmin, in ancient times, during the Satya Yuga, there was a king named Kedāra who was himself the lord of the seven continents; he was always devoted to truth and righteousness.
He took delight together with women and with his hosts of sons and grandsons.
The righteous king protected all his subjects like his own sons;
yet, despite performing a hundred sacrifices, he did not obtain the desired status of Indra.

Having performed various kinds of merit himself without desiring its fruit—performing all obligatory and occasional rites with the sole aim of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa—King Kedāra was unequaled; such a king has never existed before, nor will there ever be another again. (193)

Having entrusted the kingdom to his sons, he—being an exclusive devotee of Hari—went to the forest for asceticism at the instruction of Jaigīṣavya, taking with him his beloved wife who enchants the three worlds; there he meditated constantly upon Hari. (194–195)
O Sage, there exists the eternal Sudarśana discus;
having performed austerities for a long time in its presence, that best of sages departed for Goloka.
And the sacred ford named Kedāra came to be known by his name.
Even now, any living being who dies there shall certainly be liberated immediately.
His daughter was the ascetic Vṛndā, a portion of Kamalā;
she, being an expert in the Yoga scriptures, did not choose any suitor as her husband.
Durvāsas gave her that mantra of Hari which is very difficult to obtain.
Detached from the world, she abandoned her home and went to the forest for asceticism.
For sixty thousand years, she performed penance in a most secluded place.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared before her.
With a gracious countenance and full of splendor, he said, "Choose a boon.
Seeing her beloved, whose beautiful form was peaceful, Rādhikā [beheld him]. (200–201)
Afflicted by the arrows of love, she immediately fell into a swoon;
and quickly she chose him as her boon, saying, "Be my husband. Having said "So be it," he enjoyed himself with her in secret for a long time.
And she went to Goloka with Kṛṣṇa out of curiosity. Rādhā became equal to him in good fortune and became the most excellent of the gopīs.
Where Vṛndā performed her penance, that place is known as Vṛndāvana.
O best of sages, was the sport performed here by Vṛndā?
Or rather, O child, listen now to another history that bestows merit;
understand it as "Vṛndāvana," for I shall tell it to you. (205)

Kuśadhvaja had two daughters, Tulasī and Vedavatī, both of whom were experts in the Dharmaśāstras and were detached from worldly existence and its activities. Having performed austerities, Vedavatī attained the supreme Nārāyaṇa. (206–207)

She is celebrated everywhere as Sītā, the daughter of Janaka. And Tulasī, having performed austerities and formed a longing for Hari, by chance, due to the curse of Durvāsas, came into the presence of the demon Śaṅkha. (206)
Afterwards, having obtained her beloved and charming husband, the Lord of Kamalā,
that queen of the gods, by Hari’s curse, took the form of a tree;
