and by her curse, Hari likewise became the Śālagrāma stone.
And thus Sundarī remained constantly upon the breast of the stone.
You have been told the entire extensive account of Tulasī’s life;
nevertheless, O Sage, I have spoken a little more here by way of digression. (211)
O ascetic, this very place is the site of that penance;
therefore, the wise call it by the name Vṛndāvana.
Or rather, I shall tell you another supreme reason—listen.
In the land of Bhārata, there is a sacred field named Vṛndāvana.
Because the name "Vṛndā" was heard in the Vedas as one of the sixteen names of Rādhā, that beautiful forest where she sports is therefore remembered as Vṛndāvana. (213–214)
In ancient times, for her pleasure in Goloka, Kṛṣṇa created that forest on earth for the sake of sport; it is known by her name as Vṛndāvana.
Nārada said:
O Teacher of the World, what are the sixteen names of Rādhikā? Tell them to me, your disciple; I have a great curiosity to hear them.
I have already heard the thousand names as they are set forth in the Sāmaveda.
Nevertheless, O Lord, I desire to hear from you their sixteen names—
whether they are the inner ones or others besides them—
for they are of a meritorious nature and desired by devotees. (217–218)

The names of the Mother of the World, which are difficult for all to obtain, purifying, and the cause even of the worlds—Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: [219] [He spoke] their names, their etymologies, and how they are difficult for all to attain; [names that are] purifying and the very cause of the worlds.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Rādhā is the mistress of the rāsa dance, the dweller of the rāsa, and the queen of connoisseurs.
She is dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, and identical in nature to Kṛṣṇa.
Born from the left side of Kṛṣṇa, she is the embodiment of supreme bliss. (220)
Kṛṣṇā, Vṛndāvanī, Vṛndā, and Vṛndāvanavinodinī;
Candrāvatī, Candrakāntā, and she whose face resembles a hundred moons—these are the essential names, as well as those internal to them. (221–222)
She who is thus perfected as "Rādhā"— wherein the syllable *rā* signifies the granting [of gifts] and she herself bestows liberation— is celebrated as Rādhā.
Because she is the wife of the Lord of the Rāsa dance (*rāseśvara*), she is remembered as Rāseśvarī.
Because she dwells in the *rāsa*, she is called Rāsavāsinī.
Furthermore, because she is the supreme sovereign (*īśvarī*) of all the goddesses who are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*), the wise of old proclaim her to be Rasikeśvarī. (224–225)
She is dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
and she has been proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa herself to be dearer than his own life. She is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, exceedingly dear to him, or rather, Kṛṣṇa is always dear to her.

Because she was spoken of by all the hosts of gods as such, she is remembered as the beloved of Kṛṣṇa (Kṛṣṇapriyā). Since she is capable of manifesting the form of Kṛṣṇa effortlessly through her mere glance, she is similar to Kṛṣṇa in all her aspects; therefore, she is the very embodiment of Kṛṣṇa (Kṛṣṇasvarūpiṇī).
She who was born from the left half of Kṛṣṇa as the supreme Satī was proclaimed by that Kṛṣṇa as "Kṛṣṇavāmāṅgasaṃbhūtā" (Born from the Left Half of Kṛṣṇa).
She is the mass of supreme bliss herself, existing as the personified Satī.
Therefore, she is celebrated by the Vedas as being of the nature of supreme bliss.
The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies liberation (*mokṣa*) and also denotes excellence; the syllable *ā* signifies the giver (*dātṛ*). Thus, she is proclaimed as Kṛṣṇā.
There exists Vṛndāvana; because she belongs to it, she is remembered as Vṛndāvanī. Or else, she is celebrated as the presiding deity (adhidevī) of Vṛndāvana.
The word *vṛnda* signifies a group of female companions (*sakhīnām saṅghaḥ*), and the letter *a* is also expressive of existence (*asti-vācaka*). 232.
She who possesses a multitude of friends is celebrated as Vṛndā;
for she indeed possesses delight in Vṛndāvana. Therefore, the Vedas call her Vṛndāvanavinodinī (the one who delights in Vṛndāvana). ||233-234||
Because the curved moon of her fingernails is ever-present there, she is celebrated by Kṛṣṇa as Candrāvalī;
for her radiance is always equal to the moon, both day and night. (235)
She was proclaimed by Hari with joy as Candrakāntā;
since the radiance of the autumn moon exists upon her face day and night,
she was therefore proclaimed by the Sage as Śaraccandraprabhānanā.
This [work], consisting of sixteen names and accompanied by an explanation of their meaning, was given by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā in the lotus of his navel;
and in ancient times, it was given by Brahmā to Dharma, my father. (238)
It was given to me with righteousness and compassion during the solar festival (Ādityaparvan),
at the great sacred site of Puṣkara, on an auspicious day in the assembly of the gods, while the majesty of Rādhā was being extolled, with a most gracious mind. (239–240)
O Sage, this hymn of great merit has been given by me to you.
O Great Sage, it must not be given to a reviler or to one who is not a Vaiṣṇava.
That man who recites this hymn three times a day for as long as he lives—
May there be devotion here to the lotus feet of Rādhā and Mādhava.
In the end, one shall obtain their service and become their eternal companion.
Having attained the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the like, as well as an eternal form— (242–243)
By means of all vows, gifts, and fasts accompanied by every form of restraint;
by the recitations of all four Vedas together with their entire contents;
and by the performance of all sacrifices and pilgrimages as prescribed by the rules.

By circumambulating the entire earth seven times, by protecting those who have come for refuge, and by bestowing knowledge upon the ignorant; and whatever fruit is obtained even from the sight of the gods and the Vaiṣṇavas—[all that is attained through this]. (245–246)
That [other merit] does not equal even a sixteenth part of the recitation of this hymn.
By the power of this hymn, a person shall become liberated while living.
Nārada said:
O Lord, this most wonderful hymn, which is extremely difficult to obtain, has been attained;
likewise, the armor (*kavaca*) of the Goddess, which brings victory over *saṃsāra*, has also been obtained.
This hymn was composed with great effort, and it too is difficult to find.

Having heard the wonderful stories of Kṛṣṇa through the grace of your lotus feet, I now desire to hear what secret there is; please tell me that. And O Sage, having seen the city in the morning, what did the cowherds say?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
When the night had passed and Viśvakarman had departed, at the time of dawn all the people remained awake. (251)
Having risen and beheld the city, which was unlike anything they had ever seen, the inhabitants of Vraja exclaimed, "What a marvel! What a marvel!
Some spoke to the cowherds, asking, "From where has this come about? (252)
"I do not know in what form whom shall he manifest upon the earth," Nanda thought in his mind, recollecting the words of Garga;
for by the will of Śrī Hari, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, [is subject to His power]. (253–254)

For Him, by the mere play of whose knitting of the eyebrows all things from Brahmā down to a blade of grass have appeared and disappeared— what is there that is impossible for Him, and why? Indeed, within the pores of His very hair lie all the cosmic eggs.
O, what indeed is impossible for that Great Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari?
(256) Brahmā, Ananta, Īśa, and Dharma meditate upon whose lotus feet;
what is impossible for that Lord who has assumed the form of a human through his Māyā? (257)
Wandering through that city again and again, looking at every house,
and reciting the names [of the Lord] to everyone, Nanda and the eager Vṛṣabhāna chose an auspicious moment and bestowed a residence upon them all. (258)
Together with his attendants, he joyfully established his residence in the hermitage (259).
And all those dwelling in Vṛndāvana, their faces and eyes radiant with joy,
entered their own excellent hermitages with delight (260).
All the cowherds rejoiced in their respective charming abodes;
the boys and girls, filled with great joy, played together,
while Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva also joined the children out of curiosity.

He played in that very place, in various charming spots. (262) Thus, O Nārada, everything regarding the construction of the city, as well as the Rāsa-maṇḍala of the women in the forest, has been told. (263)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the City of Śrī Vṛndāvana," in the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, oh, what a wonderful secret and most enchanting mystery!
The life-story of Kṛṣṇa has been heard; it is supremely bestowing happiness and liberation.
Sūta said:
Having heard about the construction of the city, Nārada, the best of sages—
He asked about another most enchanting account of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds.
Nārada said:
O best of sages, the narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s life is like nectar.
"O Ocean of Knowledge, speak to me, your disciple who has come for refuge.
(3) Having heard the words of Nārada, Nārāyaṇa himself, with joy, spoke of the supremely wonderful life-story of the Supreme Lord. (4)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, Mādhava went to the glorious Madhuvana forest on the banks of the Yamunā, which was filled with lotuses, accompanied by Balarāma and the boys. 5.
Then the boys played with thousands of cows;
they were exhausted, overcome by thirst, and tormented by hunger.
With supreme joy, the cowherd children spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"O Kṛṣṇa, hunger afflicts us; tell us, what shall we do, O servants?
(7) Having heard the words of the children, the ocean of mercy, with a serene face and eyes, spoke these beneficial and truthful words to them. (8)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O children, go to the pleasant sacrificial ground of the brahmins;
quickly beg food from those brāhmaṇas who are intent upon the sacrifice. (9)
All the Brahmins of the lineage of Aṅgiras were performing a sacrifice in their own hermitage near the Śrīvana forest— Brahmins who were experts in the Śruti and Smṛti.
All those Vaiṣṇavas, free from desire and seeking liberation, were worshipping me.

They do not recognize me through my illusory power, for I am in the form of an illusory human. (11) If these brahmins, intent on their sacrifices, do not give food to you, then quickly ask their wives, who are compassionate toward their children. (12)
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the best of boys went before the brāhmaṇas and stood with their necks bowed. Then the boys quickly said, "O best of the twice-born, give us food! (13)
Some twice-born men did not hear [the news], while others, having heard it, remained where they were.
They went to the kitchen where the brahmin women were cooking. Having arrived, the young wives of the brahmins bowed with their necks bent low.
Having bowed down, all the children said: "O mothers, wives of the brahmins who are devoted to their husbands, give food to us children who are afflicted by hunger.
Having heard the words of the children and having seen those charming ones, [the women spoke].
The virtuous wives, their lotus-like faces smiling, inquired with great respect.
The wives of the brahmins said:
"Who are you? By whom have you been sent? What are your names, O wise ones?"
"We shall give you excellent food of many kinds, accompanied by various side dishes.
Having heard the words of the Brahmin women, all those cowherd boys—affectionate, laughing, and robust—spoke to them with great joy. (18–19)
The boys said:
"Sent by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, we are greatly oppressed by hunger.
O mothers, give us food; we shall go quickly to their presence. (20)
Not far from here, within the Bhāṇḍīra forest at the foot of a banyan tree in Madhuvana, Rāma and Keśava are dwelling. Having rested and being hungry, they both beg for food, O mothers.
"What should be given, or what should not be given? Tell us quickly now!
(22) Having heard the words of the cowherds, their eyes filled with tears of joyful bliss;
their entire bodies were covered in horripilation, as their minds longed for His lotus feet. (23)
Filled with joy, they placed in vessels of silver, bronze, and silver— most enchanting rice mixed with various condiments, as well as milk-rice, flour cakes, savory curd, milk, ghee, and honey. (24)
All those wives of the brahmins departed into the presence of Kṛṣṇa (25).
Having conceived various desires in their minds, they were eager to go;
those chaste and blessed women were longing for the sight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa (26).
Having gone there, they beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma together with the boys,
dwelling at the foot of a banyan tree like the moon amidst the stars—
dark-complexioned, in the bloom of youth, and clad in yellow silk garments.
Beautiful, smiling, peaceful, the beloved of Rādhā, and captivating;
with a face like the full moon of autumn, adorned with jewel ornaments, and graced by a pair of jeweled earrings upon his cheeks. (28–29)
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets, he wears a radiant jeweled garland that reaches down to his knees;
his neck and chest are resplendent with a wreath of *mālatī* flowers. (30)
His body was adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
he possessed excellent nails and beautiful cheeks, and his noble lips were like the ripe bimba fruit.
He bore exquisite teeth that shone like the seeds of a ripe pomegranate. (31–32)
Adorned with peacock feathers and with his topknot bound, he is higher than the highest;
he shines at the roots of his ears with a pair of *kadamba* flowers, and though unattainable through meditation even for yogins, he is eager to bestow grace upon his devotees. (33)
Having thus beheld the Lord being praised by Brahmā, Īśa, Dharma, Śeṣa, Indra, and the lords of sages,
the wives of the twice-born bowed with devotion and offered hymns of praise to Madhusūdana, according to their own respective levels of knowledge.
The wives of the Brahmins said:
"You are the Supreme Brahman, the Abode; you are free from desire and devoid of egoism. You are without qualities and formless, yet you yourself manifest with form and qualities. (36)
The Supreme Self is the witness-form, untainted, and formless.
You are both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and the cause beyond those two.
Furthermore, you are the three deities remembered as presiding over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

They— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— are all your portions and the seeds of all things. O Lord, you are the progenitor of that Great Virāṭ, the Great Viṣṇu, within whose every pore the entire universe resides, O All-pervading One.
You are radiance and yet the radiant one; you are knowledge and the knower, devoted to that [knowledge].
You are inexpressible in the Veda; who here is capable of praising you, O Lord?
You are the thread of creation beginning with Mahat, as well as the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
You are the seed of all powers, whose very nature consists of all powers.
You are the Lord of all powers, the All, the eternal refuge of all power.
You are effortless, self-luminous, the bliss of all, and the Primeval One.
Oh! Though you are devoid of form, you possess all forms;
though you are not a possessor of senses, you know the objects of all the senses.
Sarasvatī herself becomes stupefied in your praise and in your description.
Maheśa, Śeṣa, Dharma, and Brahmā himself became inert;
so too did Pārvatī, Kamalā, Rādhā, Sāvitrī, and even the progenitor of the Vedas.
Even the Veda itself falls into a state of insentience; who then among the learned is capable [of fathoming this]? 44–49.
"O Lord of the lords of the life-breaths of women, what praise can we offer?
Be gracious to us, O God, friend of the distressed; have mercy!
Thus spoke those wives of the brahmins at his lotus feet.

With a gracious face and eyes, he granted them fearlessness. Whoever recites this hymn composed by the wives of the brahmins at the time of worship shall attain the same state as the wives of the brahmins; of this there is no doubt. (47–48)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing them fallen at his lotus feet, the glorious Madhusūdana spoke, saying, "Choose an auspicious boon; it shall be granted. 49.
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the wives of the brāhmaṇas were filled with joy.
With their necks bowed in devotion, they spoke these words to him with piety.
(50) The wives of the twice-born said:
O Kṛṣṇa, we do not accept any other boon; our longing is for Your lotus feet.
Grant us Your own servitude and that firm devotion which is so difficult to attain.
O Keśava, may we behold Your lotus-face at every moment.
"O Lord, show us favor; we shall not go home again.
Having heard the words of the brahmin’s wife, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion and lord of the three worlds, said "Om" and remained in the assembly of the boys.
Sweet food, resembling nectar, was served by the wives of the brahmins;
having fed the children, the Lord himself then ate.
In the meantime, a supreme chariot made of gold [appeared] there.
And the wives of the brahmins beheld it falling from the sky—
adorned with jeweled mirrors, furnished with ornaments of precious gems,
bound with pillars of jewels, and radiant with excellent jeweled pitchers. ||55-56||
Adorned with white chowries, draped in garments as pure as fire, and resplendent with networks of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers;
it was equipped with a hundred wheels, traveled at the speed of thought, and was utterly enchanting. (57)
He was surrounded by divine attendants adorned with forest garlands,
wearing yellow garments and decorated with jewel ornaments;
they were endowed with fresh youth, dark-complexioned, and exceedingly charming.
With two arms holding flutes, wearing the excellent attire of cowherds,
and with their curly topknots bound with peacock feathers and guñjā garlands,
they quickly descended from the chariot and bowed at the feet of Hari.
The wives of the brāhmaṇas spoke so as to ascend the chariot. Having bowed to Hari, the wives of the brāhmaṇas went to their desired destination, Goloka;
they immediately became gopīs, having cast off their human bodies.
Having created the shadow of Hari by means of his Viṣṇu-māyā,
the omnipresent Lord himself sent those brahmins back to their homes;
and the brahmins, with minds extremely distressed, [departed] for the sake of their wives.
While searching, they saw beautiful women on the road.
Upon seeing them, all those brāhmaṇas, filled with humility, spoke to them; their entire bodies were marked with horripilation, and their faces and eyes were radiant with joy. (64–65)
The Brahmins said:
"Oh, you are most blessed, for the Lord has been seen by you!
Our lives are in vain, and even our recitation of the Vedas is useless. (66)

In the Vedas and Purāṇas, they are proclaimed everywhere by the learned as all the manifestations of Hari; Hari is the progenitor of all. Austerity, recitation, vows, knowledge, the Vedas, study, and worship—
Hari bestows the fruit of all holy baths at sacred fords and of fasting.
(68) For one by whom Śrī Kṛṣṇa has been served, what is the use of the fruits of austerities?
For one by whom the wish-fulfilling tree has been obtained, what is the use of any other tree? (69)
"For one in whose heart Śrī Kṛṣṇa resides, what is the use of performed rituals?
Or rather, what manliness is there in crossing a well compared to the ocean?
Having spoken thus, the brahmins took the excellent women.
They returned to their own homes delighted and took pleasure together with them.
Then, their love for him increased even more in all activities and pastimes;
through his power of *māyā*, he showed such courtesy toward the brāhmaṇas that it was beyond their comprehension.

Then that very Nārāyaṇa, the eternal and perfect Brahman, went quickly to his own abode along with the children by means of his power. Thus has been told everything regarding the supreme majesty of Hari.
"Previously, this was heard from the mouth of Dharma; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
"O Indra among sages, by what merit did [he become] the husband of brahmin women?"
The sovereign state of those perfected in the yoga of the Lord of Sages is difficult to attain.
Who were these meritorious women who formerly dwelt upon the surface of the earth?
By what fault did they come [to this state]? Speak, O Destroyer of Doubt! (75–76)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The wives of the seven sages were supreme, peerless in beauty, virtuous, well-behaved, most righteous, and devoted to their husbands. (77)
All were in the bloom of youth, with full hips and breasts;
they wore divine garments and were adorned with jeweled ornaments.
They possessed the luster of molten gold, and their lotus-like faces were smiling.
Capable of deluding even sages with their sidelong glances,
Anala, tormented by the fire of passion, beheld their beautiful breasts, hips, and faces and desired them. (79–80)
Standing at the place of the fire, with his mind intent on sexual union,
he touched their limbs with his crest-lock and became captivated by their hearts. Those devoted wives, whose minds were fixed solely upon the lotus-feet of their husbands, did not perceive this.
Seeing them again and again, Agni was infatuated with their limbs.
Knowing the mind of the Fire-god, the venerable sage Aṅgiras cursed him, saying: "Become a devourer of all things."
The fire-god, having become conscious, praised the bull among sages;
with his face bowed in shame, he trembled at the ascetic power of Brahman.
The excellent sage, enraged that the amorous women had been touched, uttered a curse.
"Go, you who are joined with sin, to a human womb indeed!
You shall obtain birth in the land of Bhārata in the house of Brāhmaṇas. And twice-born men born of your own lineage shall perform your marriage. (85–86)
Having heard the words of the sage, they wept, overwhelmed with love.
With their hands joined in *añjali*, they all spoke to that best of the wise.
The wives of the sages said:
"O best of sages, do not abandon us; we are sinless and devoted to our husbands.
We were unaware [of your presence] and were touched by another; you ought not to forsake us.
You should not inflict punishment upon us, who are your devotees and servants. (88)

"When shall we behold your lotus feet? O Sage, for virtuous women, the cruel separation from their beloved is always more unbearable than being cut by a sword, struck by a thunderbolt, or hit by any other weapon. [This applies even] toward great sages who are most excellent in Brahman and endowed with virtues, yet are other than their beloveds."

"O Lord of Brahmins, having abandoned those who have become such as these, how shall we go to the surface of the earth? If we must go, O best of brahmins, tell us when our return here will take place;
and may the fault of contact with ignorance not befall us, as ordained by the sacred rules."
Ahalyā, however, regained her husband after the assault by Indra;
she was purified through sexual union, whereas we were deprived of even his touch.
O most virtuous one, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, reflect upon this.
"You are the son of the Creator of the Universe and the best among all knowers of the Vedas.
(94) When women flee to their husband for refuge out of fear of others, to whom do they go for refuge when they are themselves agitated by fear of their own husband? (95)
"O most righteous one, grant fearlessness even to those who are full of fear!
Who is unable to inflict punishment upon a son, a pupil, or a wife? Whether weak or strong, one is indeed the master of one's own possessions. (96)
"No one else is capable of protecting [them] from selling their own substance.
Having heard these words of the women, the compassionate bull among sages wept out of love upon beholding their lotus-like faces. (97–98)
Though he was a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, the best among the wise and the yogis,
even he fell into a swoon regarding the separation from his wife;
all became afflicted with grief, their minds distressed by the loss.
Beholding their faces, they stood like wooden puppets.
(100) Having lamented for a very long time, that best among those who know all the Vedas, having consulted with his brothers, spoke to them while afflicted by grief. (101)
Aṅgiras said:
"Listen, for I shall speak words that are indeed true.
It is heard in the Vedas that those who experience the fruits of their own actions must undergo that experience until the karma is exhausted. (102)
The enjoyment of you all has certainly gone along with us.
Once enjoyment has passed away, it is not described in the Veda that enjoyment can ever return.
And whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, was performed by the doers in Bhārata—
Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of births without being experienced.
(104) He who enjoys a beloved woman enjoyed by another is the lowest of men;
he is cooked in the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (109)
She is unfit for offerings to the gods or the ancestors; being joined with evil, she is unworthy of ritual cooking.
By embracing her, a husband loses his prosperity and is destroyed by his own vital energy.
For him, the deities and the ancestors [are likewise lost] regarding the offering of oblations and the libations.
"Those who act thus do not become happy," so said the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Therefore, the wise man protects his wife with great effort;
otherwise, the husband becomes a partaker of sin and will certainly go to hell. (107–108)
At every step, a wise man guards his beloved with vigilance;
for a woman is neither a sacred vow nor a holy ground, but a casket of faults.
One ought always to protect both one's wife and one's cooking vessel.
She who is impure due to contact with another, yet always pure when touched by her own husband;
and she who, having abandoned her own lover, goes to another—such a low woman goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (110–111)
And the messengers of Yama, having stationed her within the midst of hell,
strike her with blows from their staffs if she rises even from afar;
[they also employ] insects the size of mustard seeds, possessing sharp fangs and being most terrible.
There they constantly bite the unchaste woman day and night;
she, assuming a distorted form and voice, cries out perpetually out of fear.
Sustaining a subtle body, she did not die from the blows.
Having enjoyed pleasure for but half a moment, she is destroyed by infamy in this world;
fallen in the next world, she shall obtain such a fate as this—namely, that a woman who has been touched by another should still harbor desire for yet another. (115)
The Lotus-born One further stated that such a wicked woman must also be abandoned. Therefore, women who have been carefully concealed from others by skillful [husbands],
who do not look upon the sun, and who are pure, are called devoted wives (*pativratā*).

She who acts according to her own will, independent, and like a sow—she is certainly always internally corrupt and destined for another. And she who is to be won over by her husband, remaining steadfast out of fear of the family dharma. (118)
That beloved woman will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha together with her beloved.
Go now to the earth, to the human womb you desire;
by the mere sight of Kṛṣṇa, you shall surely go to Goloka. (119–120)
Shadows of you have been created by Hari through his yogic power (yogamāyā).
Having stayed in the house of the brāhmaṇa, they will certainly come back to us;
there is no doubt that you will again become our wives through a portion [of yourselves].
"And your curse upon me has become a source of great blessing.
Having spoken thus, the sage ceased, overcome with grief.
They, having come to the earth due to that curse, became the wives of Brahmins.
Having offered food to Hari with devotion, they departed for the abode of Hari.
It became certain that for them, even a curse was superior to wealth;
for contemptible and base wealth is worse than calamity, while calamity is better than great fortune.
Ah! The anger of the virtuous immediately conduces to their own benefit.
(125) Without adversity, whose greatness could there be on this earth?
Brahmin women were liberated from their husbands by being abandoned by them. (126)
Thus has been narrated in its entirety the supreme life-story of Hari.
Oh, how enchanting is this account of liberation for the meritorious!
O best of Brahmins, the narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is ever-new at every step.

For there is no satiety for those who possess learning; by what means is one satisfied in regard to the highest good? (128) Whatever is delightful has been told, and whatever was heard from the mouth of the Guru.
Tell me what you desire; what more do you wish to hear? (129)
Nārada said:
O ocean of mercy, O teacher of the world, please tell me that auspicious account of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds which you previously heard from the mouth of your guru. (130)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of the celestial sage, the Ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa himself began to proclaim another account of the greatness of Kṛṣṇa. 131.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Episode of the Liberation of the Brahmin’s Wife," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, Hari, together with the boys but without Baladeva, [went forth].
He went to the bank of the Yamunā where the abode of Kāliya was located.
Having eaten ripe fruit in the forest growing on the banks of the Yamunā, he—
being composed of his own will and overcome by thirst— drank the pure water.
He tended the cattle in the forest together with the boys;
he played with them and established his herd there.
His mind was immersed in play, and the children were filled with joy.
O Sage, having grazed upon fresh grass, the cows drank poisoned water;
and having drunk that water laced with poison through the cruel machinations of Death, they instantly abandoned their lives by the flames of *kālakūṭa* poisons. (4–5)

Seeing the herd of cows dead, all the cowherds, overwhelmed with anxiety and fear, their faces dejected, spoke to the slayer of Mura. Having understood everything, the Lord of the World restored the cattle-pen to life.
At that very moment, the cows rose up and beheld the face of Śrī Hari.
Kṛṣṇa, having climbed a kadamba tree growing on the bank of the Yamunā’s waters,
fell in human form into the abode of the serpent, amidst the serpents.
And the rising of the water reached a measure of one hundred cubits;
O Nārada, there the young girls experienced both joy and despair.
Seeing the serpent Kāliya in human form, he was overwhelmed with rage.
The serpent quickly seized Śrī Hari, like a man grasping heated iron;
his throat and belly scorched by the Brahmanical luster, he became agitated,
and saying, "My life-breaths are departing," he then began to vomit.
With his teeth shattered and his face smeared with blood from chewing upon the black vajra-limbs,
the serpent— crushed by the Earth-bearer and intent on giving up his life— stood before the Lord, who rose above his head. (12)
He vomited blood and fell down unconscious, O Sage.
Seeing him unconscious, the serpents wept, overwhelmed with affection;
some fled in fear, while others entered their holes.
Seeing her beloved facing death,
the virtuous Surasā wept out of affection before Hari along with the other nāginīs;
she quickly bowed to Śrī Hari with palms joined in reverence and in fear.
Holding His lotus feet, she spoke to Him, agitated by fear.
Surasā said:
"O Beloved of the world, O Giver of honor, grant me my husband and my honor."
To women, the husband is dearer than life, and there is no other kinsman as devoted as he.

O Lord of the entire world, O Lord of my life, O infinite ocean of love, O true friend, do not bring about the slaughter of my husband! O Friend of the whole universe, O ocean of Rādhikā’s love, O Dispeller of the Creator, grant me this boon: let him remain my husband here! Even the Three-eyed Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Kārttikeya, along with their hosts of mouths, are unable to praise You, for their speech is rendered dull by the very act of attempting to hymn Your glory.

Indeed, all the Vedas and even the other gods are capable of making you the object of their praise; yet, O virtuous one, they belong to You alone. (19) How can I, a person of poor intellect, compare with women who are lowly, or with the Lord who is the refuge of the world and beyond the range of the eyes?
Yet, O Lord, I desire to praise You—that very Lord who is praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śeṣa, and who, though bodiless, is the Master of men. (20)

Whom else but You could Pārvatī praise, she who is afraid of becoming the object of Your hymns; whom else but You could Padmā praise, the mother of the multitude of Vedas? Immersed in the impurities of the Kali age and bewildered regarding the scope of hearing the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and Śāstras, how can I possibly desire to praise You?
Lying upon a jeweled couch, adorned with jewel ornaments, Your limbs graced by the beauty of gemstone decorations, You remain seated upon the breast of Rādhā.
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, his lotus-like face smiling,
he is constantly immersed in the bliss of the surging ocean of the essence of love;
his crest is adorned with clusters of garlands of jasmine and *mālatī* flowers.
His mind was delighted by the fragrant scent of *pārijāta* blossoms;
his body was marked with horripilation due to the agitation caused by the flowers, accompanied by the sweet warbling of male cuckoos and the humming of bees. (24–25)

I praise that Nāgavallabhā, who always joyfully partook of the betel-roll offered by her beloved; whom even the Vedas, though wise, are rendered speechless and unable to extol—how then can I describe her, she who is beyond all definition? (26)
I bow to your lotus feet, served by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa;
served always by Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, and Jāhnavī—the mothers of the Vedas—as well as by hosts of Siddhas, lords of sages, and Manus. (27–28)

Salutations to You, who are without cause yet the cause of all, the Lord of all, and higher than the highest; to the self-luminous one, the supreme and the inferior, and the sovereign of both the high and the low. O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of gods and asuras, Lord of Brahmā, Lord of Śeṣa, Lord of the Prajāpatis!
O Lord of Sages, Lord of Manus, Lord of the moving and the unmoving, Lord of Siddhis, Lord of the Siddhas, Lord of the Gaṇas, protect me!
(30) O Lord of Dharma, Lord of the righteous, Lord of the auspicious and inauspicious, Lord of the Vedas, and You who are not fully defined even within the Vedas;
O Lord of all, whose self is all, friend of all, Lord of living beings, Sovereign of souls, protect my Master! (31)

Having thus offered praise, the beloved of Nāgeśa stood with her neck bowed in devotion, holding his lotus feet. The man who recites this hymn composed by the wives of the Nāgas at the three junctions of the day [attains the fruit].
Freed from all sins, he goes at the end to the abode of Śrī Hari.
In this world he attains devotion to Hari, and at the end he certainly obtains the status of a servant.
Having become an attendant (pārṣada), he attains the fourfold [liberations] beginning with sālokya.
Nārada said:
Having heard the words of the serpent’s wife, what did the Lord Hari himself—the delighter of all—say, his eyes wide with joy? (39)
"O illustrious one, tell us this most wonderful secret.
Sūta said:
"Having heard the words of Nārada, the Blessed One, the seer of all, [replied]. (36)
At every step, Madhuvṛnda spoke to the Supreme Soul.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of the serpent’s wife, Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke to him. (37)
With her hands joined in *añjali* at her feet, she fell down, overwhelmed by fear.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Arise, arise, O Queen of Serpents! Choose a boon; cast away your fear. (38)
"O Mother, by my boon, take your beloved who is free from old age and death.
Leaving the pool of the Yamunā, go to your own home;
O child, go together with your husband and the cowherd community, and be happy. (39)
From this day forward, O Mistress of Nagas, you have become my daughter;
and this son-in-law is dearer to me than my own life, of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious one, by the mark of my lotus feet, Garuḍa shall [protect] your husband.
Having offered praise with devotion, she will bow down at my feet.
"Abandon your fear of Garuḍa; go quickly to Ramaṇaka.
O child, emerge from the lake and choose a boon as you desire."

Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she, with a serene face and eyes, spoke with tearful eyes, her neck bowed in devotion. Surasā said: "O Lord of Givers of Boons, if you will grant me a boon now as well," (43–44)
You ought to grant me firm and unwavering devotion to your lotus feet.
May my mind wander within your lotus feet like a bee;
may there never be any forgetting of your remembrance.
"May my good fortune rest with my own beloved; may this husband of mine be the best among the wise. "O Lord, fulfill this very prayer," having spoken thus, the female serpent set out before Hari.
The virtuous woman beheld the face of Śrī Hari, whose countenance was like the full moon of autumn;
with eyes that did not blink, she drank in his face, her entire body bristling with horripilation and overflowing with tears of joy. 48.
Beholding the beautiful boy and feeling maternal affection for him, she, overflowing with an excess of devotion, spoke once more:
"I will not go to Ramaṇaka; there is no purpose in going there. (49-50)

Let the serpent create the cycle of worldly existence; make me your own servant! O Kṛṣṇa, I have no desire for the fourfold states beginning with *sālokya* (residing in the same world as you), for they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the service of your lotus feet. (51)
But he who desires any other boon besides service at your feet,
having obtained a birth difficult to find in Bhārata, is himself deceived.
Having heard the words of the serpent’s wife, his lotus-like face blossomed with a smile.
With a serene mind, the illustrious one spoke thus: "Om.
In that interval, O Sage, a divine chariot constructed from the finest essence of precious gems arrived swiftly, blazing with splendor.
Accompanied by the foremost of his attendants, and adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments;
possessing a hundred wheels, the speed of the wind, moving as fast as thought, and captivating the mind—
[the chariot] descended swiftly from the chariot, along with the dark-complexioned Śyāma and his dark servants.
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa and led her away, they went to the supreme Goloka.
Hari, having fashioned an illusory form by his own splendor, gave it to the serpent;
and he, deluded by Viṣṇu’s māyā, perceived nothing at all.
Descending from the head of the serpent, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion,
out of mercy quickly placed his hand upon Kāliya’s head.
Regaining consciousness immediately, he beheld Hari standing before him.
With palms joined in *añjali* and eyes filled with tears, the virtuous Surasā immediately bowed to Hari; overwhelmed by love, she wept.
With eyes brimming with tears and her body marked by horripilation due to the intensity of her devotion, she [remained] thus.
Seeing her become silent, the ocean of compassion spoke:
"If the Lord’s mercy is always equal toward the worthy and the unworthy," Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: [61]
"Choose a boon, Kālīya, whatever dwells in your mind.
O child, you are dearer to me than my own life; remain in happiness and cast away your fear.
I bestow grace upon him who is exceedingly devoted to me, for he is born from a portion of myself. (62–63)
Having subdued him somewhat, I shall grant you my favor.
That lowest of men who kills serpents born of your lineage will certainly incur a sin equal to that of killing a Brahmin. (64)
Whoever strikes with a staff upon the marks of my lotus feet,
his sin shall be double that of killing a Brahmin;
having uttered a most terrible curse, Lakṣmī shall depart from his house.
The decline of his lineage, lifespan, and fame will be certain;
by my word, he will surely go to the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred years.
Furthermore, swarms of insects the size of you will bite him incessantly.
At the end of his enjoyments, having obtained birth [again], his death shall come from being bitten by him.
And for those born in his lineage, there shall be fear of your lineage. And those who, upon seeing my footprint marked with a beautiful lotus, [behold yours]... 69.
They shall bow down with devotion and be liberated from all sins.
Go quickly to Ramaṇaka; abandon your fear of the Lord of Birds.
Seeing the mark of my foot upon your head, he will bow down to you with devotion.
"You and those born of your lineage shall have no fear of Garuḍa anywhere.
By my boon, may you today become the chief of all your kinsmen, the serpents.
O child, what supreme boon do you desire? Choose it now."
"Abandoning fear, tell me how I may destroy your suffering.
Hearing these words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kāliya trembled with dread;
joining his palms in reverence, the serpent spoke to Him. (73)
Kāliya said:
"O All-pervading Lord, O Giver of Boons, I have no desire for any other boon.
Grant me devotion and remembrance of Your lotus feet in birth after birth."

Whether one’s birth be in the family of Brahmā or even among the animal wombs, it is equal [in value]; that birth alone is fruitful wherein there is mindfulness of your lotus-feet. Residence in heaven is fruitless if there is no mindfulness of your feet. (75–76)
For one intent on meditation upon your feet, whatever that state may be—
whether for a moment or ten million kalpas, or even until the end of a human life—
if it proceeds through service to you, it is fruitful, whether it be with parts or without parts.
There is no exhaustion of life for those who serve the lotus-feet of Your Honor;
nor do they experience birth, death, disease, grief, affliction, or fear.
Whether in the state of Indra, or immortality, or even the exceedingly rare state of Brahmā— [these are not their goals]. (78–79)

Devotees have no desire whatsoever other than service at your feet; they regard even the fourfold attainment of *sālokya* and the rest as equal to a tattered old rag or even to something brand new. O Brahmin, this mantra of yours has been obtained by me from Ananta and others. (80–81)
By the very power of meditating upon you, through your grace, I have become your own color.
And having recognized me as a devotee— whether yet unripe or otherwise— the Garuda himself,
possessed of firm devotion, carried me far from that place and humbled [my enemies].
And you, O Lord of Boons, having bestowed firm devotion upon me—[I said:
"He was told: 'I am your devotee; you are not able to abandon me now, having seen my head marked with the signs of your lotus feet. (83–84)
"He is now unable to abandon me, who am both flawed and endowed with virtues.
Furthermore, O Lord, the lords of the Nāgas are my worshippers; therefore, I am not to be slain by him.
Except for that infinite Guru, I have no fear from anyone anywhere. (85)

That which the lords of gods, the gods, sages, Manus, and men perceive in dreams or through meditation—that has come within the range of my vision. By favor toward your devotees, you have appeared with form; O All-pervading Lord, how could there otherwise be a physical body for you?
He possesses qualities and is with form, yet he is without form and devoid of qualities.
He consists of his own will, the abode of all, the seed of all, and the eternal.
He is the Lord of all, the witness, the self of all, and the bearer of all forms.

Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, and Dharmeṃdra—those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—are dull-witted in attempting to praise that Lord; yet even a serpent shall praise that all-pervading One.
O Lord, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, forgive this most wretched man! (89–90)
O Kṛṣṇa, because of your wicked nature and ignorance, you have been chewed by me.
Just as the sky cannot be struck by weapons, nor seen, nor leaped over;
nor can it be touched, nor covered—so too are you pure radiance.
Having spoken thus, the lord of serpents fell at his lotus-feet.
Saying "Om," the gratified Hari granted him every boon.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this hymn composed by the king of serpents— || 92-93 ||
For those belonging to his lineage, there shall be no fear of that very serpent.
He will always be able to sleep on the earth, having made a bed of serpents.
For him, there is truly no difference between poison and nectar when it comes to consuming them.

When seized by a *nāga*, when struck by a *nāga*, or when facing the end of life from consuming poison, a human being becomes healthy through the mere recollection of this hymn. Having written this hymn on birch bark, one should wear it around the neck or on the right arm. (vv. 96, 99)
He who maintains this with devotion does not face fear even from serpents.
In that house where this hymn resides, no serpent stays;
there, certainly, there shall be no fear of poison, fire, or thunderbolts.
In this world, one shall constantly obtain devotion and remembrance of Hari;
and at the end, having purified one's own lineage, one certainly attains the state of service [to Him].
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having granted a boon to the lord of the Nāgas, the Lord of the World again spoke these sweet words, which bring about happiness in the end. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Go,
O lord of serpents, together with your own assembly, by way of the waters of the Yamunā to the supreme Ramaṇaka, which is like the city of Indra.
Having heard Hari’s command, the serpent wept, overwhelmed with love.
"O Lord, when shall I behold your lotus feet?
she asked, having prostrated herself a hundred times before the Lord together with her female companions.
Then the lord of the *nāgas*, distressed by separation, departed by way of the waters. (102)
And the water of the Yamunā lake became like nectar;
O Nārada, all living beings became serene because of that.
Having gone there, he beheld the palace, which was supreme and like the city of Indra.
And by the command of the ocean of compassion, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman.
There the lord of the nāgas dwelt together with his wife and his sons—
free from fear, filled with joy, and entirely devoted to the meditation upon Hari.
Thus has been related everything concerning the wonderful deeds of Hari; they are bliss-giving, liberating, essential, and supreme. What more do you wish to hear? Sūta said:
Having heard the words of the great seer, Nārada, overwhelmed with joy,
questioned the seer— who is the destroyer of all doubts— regarding his own doubt.
(107) Nārada said:
"O Teacher of the World, tell me how Kālīya, having abandoned his former abode, went to the other bank of the Yamunā. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Nārada, I shall relate an ancient history (itihāsa) which I heard from the mouth of Dharma on Mount Malaya during a solar eclipse,
in the context of the narrative of Kṛṣṇa, on the western shore at Suprabhā. (109–110)
Pulaha asked about dharma as it was being recounted in the assembly of sages.
To him, that treasure-house of compassion spoke this wonderful narrative.
"O Brahmin, listen; what I heard there, I shall relate to you."
By the command of Śeṣa, the hosts of Nāgas, out of fear,
perform the worship of Garuḍa every year on the full moon day of Kārtika with joy,
using flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sacrificial oblations.
Having bathed well at the great holy site of Puṣkara, they were filled with devotion;
yet Kālīya, being exceedingly arrogant, did not perform their worship.
He prepared himself to forcibly devour the offerings intended for the serpent-worship.
The serpents made their defense and spoke words arrogant with pride;
yet they were not capable of stopping him, and so the Lord of Birds appeared.
Seeing the Lord of Birds, the serpents [submitted] for the sake of protecting Kālīya’s life.
O Sage, they fought with their vital power (prāṇa-śakti) until sunrise; then,
all of them, terrified by the splendor of the Lord of Birds,
fled and sought refuge in Ananta, the bestower of fearlessness upon all.
Seeing the serpents intent on flight, that ocean of compassion remained there without fear; Kālīya beheld him and,
O Sage, remembering the lotus feet of Hari, he fought.
For a moment, their battle was exceedingly fierce;
then the lord of serpents, defeated by the splendor of Garuḍa,
fled in fear and went to the pool of the Yamunā.
Due to the curse of Saubhari, the king of birds was not able to go there;
out of fear, the serpent remained there, and his attendants departed afterwards.
Nārada said:
But how did the curse of Saubhari come to be upon Garuḍa?
And why was he, the vehicle of the Lord, unable to go to that lake?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Having performed austerities there for a thousand divine years, the great perfected one Saubhari meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa; and while he was thus meditating on the bank near the waters of the Yamunā, [the Lord appeared]. (123–124)
Together with his herd, he wanders about joyfully and without fear;
repeatedly tossing his tail high in every direction out of great delight, he circumambulates the sage and goes back and forth filled with joy. (125)

Seeing the noble-souled Sakula again and again, the lord of birds seized him with his beak near the great sage. As he was departing with the fish in his mouth, the king beheld him with eyes full of wrath.
Provoked by the sage’s gaze, the fish fell into the water;
and the lord of sages spoke to it as it prepared to take him up again.
Out of fear of Garuḍa, the fish remained near the sage. (128)
Saubhari said:
"Go far away, go far away from my presence, O king of birds!
What fitness do you have to seize my fierce life-breath right before me?"
"Knowing that you are the vehicle of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you hold yourself in high esteem.
Yet Kṛṣṇa is capable of creating millions of vehicles such as yourself;
with the mere play of a frown, I shall quickly reduce you to ashes. (130–131)
"You are the vehicle of the Lord; we are not your servants.
O King of Birds, from this day forward, if you come to my lake, you will certainly be reduced to ashes instantly by my curse. (132)
Having heard the words of the Lord of Sages, the Lord of Birds set forth.
Remembering again and again the feet of Kṛṣṇa, he bowed to him and departed.
O best of Brahmins, from this day forward, the king of birds shall constantly [serve]. (133–134)
Merely by hearing of the lake, a trembling certainly occurs.
And the history that was told, which was heard from the mouth of Dharma—listen now to this auspicious account, which is fundamental, delightful to hear, and accompanied by its secret teachings. (135)
Having realized this after a long time, Hari did not emerge from that water.
Out of delusion, the boys fell into despair and wept on the bank of the Yamunā; some, overwhelmed by grief, beat their own chests. (136–137)
Some fell to the ground and lost consciousness without Hari;
others, overcome by the pain of separation, sought to enter the lake. Some of the cowherd boys cried out to prevent them from doing so.
Having lamented, some were even prepared to give up their lives.
Among them, some who possessed knowledge protected [the others] with great effort;
some cried out "Alas! Alas!", while others cried "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! || 139-140 ||
Some set out for Nanda’s presence to deliver the news;
others remained gathered there, afflicted by grief, delusion, and fear, saying:
"What shall we do? Where has Hari gone from us?"
"O son of Nanda! O Kṛṣṇa, you who are dearer than life itself!
O kinsman, grant us your sight!"—thus indeed did their departing vital breaths speak.
In that interval, certain boys [arrived] in the presence of Nanda. (142–143)

Extremely agitated, weeping and overwhelmed by grief, they quickly reached Yaśodā and Balarāma at their very source. With eyes like red lotuses, the cowherds and cowherd girls reported the news to them. (144)

Having heard the news, they all went quickly, overcome with grief; [145] they reached the bank of the Kalindanandinī (the Yamunā) and wept together with the boys. Having arrived, they all gathered together and wept, fainting from sorrow. [146]
Some offered resistance as Ambā was entering the lake;
the cowherds and cowherd girls, out of grief, beat her limbs.
Some lamented there, while others fell into a swoon.
A certain woman restrained Rādhā as she was entering the lake;
and out of grief, she fell into a swoon on the riverbank as if dead.
Having lamented most bitterly, Nanda fell into a faint again and again. (148–149)
Weeping yet again, he fell once more into a swoon.
While Nanda lamented intensely and Yaśodā was emaciated by grief,
the cowherds and cowherd-maidens likewise saw Rādhikā in a state of extreme unconsciousness.
To all the weeping boys and girls who were overcome with grief,
Balarāma— the best among the wise— awakened them all.
Śrī Baladeva said:
"O cowherds, cowherd girls, and boys, all of you listen to my words!
O Nanda, best among the wise, remember the words of Garga:
[He is] Śeṣa, who sustains the world, and Śaṅkara, who destroys it. (152–153)
Why is there defeat on earth for both the Ordainer and the Disposer?
The atom is the supreme arrangement; it is grosser than the gross and higher than the high.
Though it exists, it is invisible even to yogis, for its conjunction [is beyond reach]. (154)
There is no collection of directions, nor is space itself tangible;
even the Lord of All is subject to sublation—thus the Śrutis have clearly declared.
The Self is not visible, not the mark of arrows, not to be slain, and indeed not an object of sight.
Those who know the inner self understand that he is neither consumed by fire nor subject to injury;
for this very body of Kṛṣṇa exists solely for the purpose of being meditated upon by his devotees.
He is the pervasive Lord whose nature is light, the Self without beginning, middle, or end.
When the cosmic egg was submerged in water, Janārdana lay upon the waters. Brahmā, born from the lotus at his navel, met with calamity in the lake of that Lord.
O father, if even a mosquito were capable of swallowing the entire cosmic egg, [then what need is there to speak of others]? (158–159)
"Even so, the serpent would not be able to devour that Lord.
Thus has been told everything concerning the unsurpassed spiritual [teaching], the hidden essence of yogis, which serves as the cause for cutting through doubt. (160)
Having heard the words of Baladeva and recollecting the speech of Garga,
Nanda, the people of Vraja, and the women of Vraja abandoned their grief.
Everyone considered it to be awakening, except for Yaśodā and Rādhikā.

In this matter of being separated from their kinsmen, their minds were not established in awakening. In the meantime, O Sage, the men of Vraja and the women of Vraja, being very joyful, beheld Kṛṣṇa as he was rising up from the water. (163)
With a face like the full moon of autumn, smiling and most enchanting; wearing ungreased garments yet appearing lustrous, with sandalwood paste and collyrium unfaded;
adorned with all ornaments and blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
with a crest of peacock feathers and the flute held to his mouth—[I behold] Acyuta.

Upon seeing the boy, Yaśodā placed him upon her breast and, with a smile, her face and eyes radiant with joy, she kissed his lotus-like mouth. Nanda and Rohiṇī likewise joyfully took him onto their laps. (166–167)
All, their eyes unblinking, gazed upon the glorious face of Hari.
Blinded by love, all the boys embraced Hari. And the gopīs drank in his moon-like face with the *cakra* birds of their eyes. (168)

In the meantime, a forest fire suddenly surrounded the cowherd settlement along with all of them within the depths of the woods. Seeing the fire, as vast as a mountain, enveloping the interior of the forest on all sides— || 159–170 ||
Everyone considered it their own destruction and fell into fear amidst the crisis.
All the inhabitants of Vraja, with palms joined in reverence, praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
even the children and the gopīs were terrified, their necks bowed low in devotion. (171)
The children said:
"O Brahmin, just as our family has been protected by you in all times of distress,
so again, O Madhusūdana, provide protection from this forest fire."
You are our chosen deity; you alone are our family deity.
O Lord of the World, you are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the worlds.
You are Agni, or Varuṇa, or even Candra, or indeed Sūrya.
Yama, Kubera, Pavana, Īśāna, and the other deities;
Brahmā, Īśa, Śeṣa, Dharma, Indra, the lords of sages, and the Manus are remembered [as such].
Likewise, humans, Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kiṃnaras [are also included]. 175.
Whatever beings there are, both moving and unmoving, they are all your manifestations. The appearance and disappearance of all things likewise occurs by your will.
Grant us fearlessness, O Govinda; extinguish this fire.
"We take refuge in you; protect us who have come for shelter.
Having spoken thus, they all stood meditating upon his lotus feet.
The forest fire, however, receded due to the nectar-like glance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
And when the forest fire had moved far away, they danced, filled with joy.
(179) All calamities perish merely by the remembrance of Hari. Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this highly meritorious hymn, (180) [attains all auspiciousness].

He shall have no fear of fire throughout birth after birth. Whether seized by enemies, in a forest fire, in calamity, or in a life-threatening crisis, by reciting this hymn one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (181)
The enemy army shall go to destruction, and one shall be victorious everywhere.
In this world, one attains devotion to Hari, and at the end, one will certainly obtain the state of servitude [to Him].
(182) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, listen: after extinguishing the forest fire, Śrī Hari went together with them to his home, which resembled the palace of Kubera. Nanda joyfully gave abundant wealth to the brāhmaṇas. (183)
He caused his circle of kinsmen and relatives to take their meal;
he performed various auspicious rites and the chanting of Hari’s names;
and filled with joy, he had the Vedas recited through the agency of Brahmins.
Thus everyone rejoiced in every house within the Vṛndāvana forest,
their minds solely absorbed in meditation upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In this manner, the entire auspicious narrative of Hari has been told.
[He was] like a fire for burning the logs of the sins of the Kali age.

(187) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Subduing of Kālīya and the Liberation from the Forest Fire," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, after eating, drinking, and being anointed with unguents along with the boys and Balarāma, Mādhava went to the forest of Vṛndāvana;
there the Blessed Lord played with them out of a sense of playful curiosity.
While their minds were absorbed in play, that Gokula went far away.
To test his power, the Creator, the Lord of the worlds,
concealed the cows, the calves, and even the boys.
Having understood his intention, the omniscient one, the doer of all,
that lord of yogis, again performed all of that through his yogic power (*yogamāyā*).
Śrī Hari, having caused Gokula to be driven away, went to his own home.
With his mind intent on the joy of play,
the Blessed One spent one year in this manner every day,
going with Balarāma and the boys to the Yamunā along with the cattle. (5–6)
Having recognized his power, Brahmā, his neck bowed with shame,
came to the abode of Hari at the foot of the Bhaṇḍīra banyan tree.
There he beheld Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by a multitude of cowherds.
Just as the full moon shines together with its host of stars,
[he was] seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, laughing with joyful smiles,
clothed in yellow garments, and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets that radiate splendor;
made radiant upon the surface of his own cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings;
possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids; the abode of grace, and enchanting. (10)
His body was honored with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
he was adorned with clusters of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers; he was dark as a fresh rain-cloud and possessed the bloom of newly emerged youth. (11–12)
Adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers and a crest of peacock feathers, he was further embellished by the natural splendor of his own limbs as if by ornaments;
his beautiful face eclipsed the radiance of the full autumn moon. (13)
With lower lips like ripe bimba fruits and a nose like the beak of the king of birds;
with eyes that shed the splendor of autumnal midday lotuses; enchanting with a row of teeth that puts to shame a string of pearls;
and with his chest made radiant by the Kaustubha, the sovereign of gems.
The peaceful, beloved of Rādhikā, the most perfect Supreme Being—
seeing the Lord in such a state, he bowed down, utterly amazed;
beholding that Īśvara again and again, he prostrated himself repeatedly.
Whatever was seen within the lotus of the heart, that very form appeared externally as well.
That form which was first seen in front was later seen all around;
O sage, having seen everything there in Vṛndāvana as equal to Kṛṣṇa.
Meditating again and again upon that form, the Teacher of the World remained there.
Brahmā beheld the cows, the calves, the children, the creepers, the shrubs, and the climbing plants—indeed, the entirety of Vṛndāvana—in a dark blue form. (19–20)
Having seen this supreme marvel, Brahmā again entered into meditation;
O Sage, he beheld the three worlds as nothing other than Kṛṣṇa.
Where was the tree, where the mountain, where the earth, and where the oceans?
Where are the gods, where the Gandharvas, where the lords of sages, and where are human beings?
Where is the self, where the seed of the universe, where heaven, and where this very world?
By his own vision, Brahmā beheld all of this through the illusory power (māyā) of Hari.
Where is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the worlds, and where are these illusory manifestations?
Seeing everything as permeated by Kṛṣṇa, he was unable to say anything at all.
Holding back his mind with the thought, "What shall I praise? What shall I do? (24).
Remaining there, the Sustainer of the World prepared to perform his recitation (japa).
Having assumed a comfortable yogic posture, he joined his palms in reverence;
with all his limbs covered in horripilation and eyes filled with tears, he appeared exceedingly humble. (25–26)
Having diligently bound together through yoga the six channels— iḍā, suṣumnā, the middle one, piṅgalā, nalinī, and dhurā—
as well as the mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, and the beautiful maṇipūra, [one should proceed]. (27)
Having bound the six chakras, which are pure and known as the supreme command, and having caused them to leap, he performed the ritual procedure for those six chakras in sequence;
bringing them to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), he effected the binding of the vital air (vāyubandha). || 28–29 ||
Having bound that central breath and drawn it into the heart-lotus,
he caused that breath to circulate and joined it with the central channel.
Having done this, he became motionless, just as he had been rendered so by Hari in the past.
He recited the supreme mantra, the ten-syllabled mantra of Him alone.
Having performed the recitation for a moment while repeatedly meditating upon His lotus feet,
O Sage, he beheld [the Lord] consisting of all splendor within the lotus of his heart.
Within that splendor was a form exceedingly beautiful to behold:
two-armed, with a flute in hand, adorned with yellow garments; with flaming crocodile-shaped earrings placed at the base of his ears;
with a face bright with a gentle smile, and intent upon bestowing grace upon his devotees. (33–34)
Having seen that which was perceived in the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), in the heart, and even outside,
and having beheld this supreme wonder, he praised the Supreme Lord.
O Sage, he offered that hymn of praise which had previously been given by Hari in the single ocean.
With his neck bowed in devotion, he [approached] that Lord according to that ritual.
Brahmā said:
"O you who are the form of all, the Lord of all, the cause of all causes."
I bow to Him who is inexpressible in every way, whose form is Śiva;
(37) whose body is dark and beautiful like a fresh rain-cloud, who dwells within all living beings, yet remains untainted as their witness. (38)
Delighting in its own self, with all desires fulfilled, pervading the world yet transcending the world;
the essence of all things, the seed-form of all, eternal;
the support of all, the bestower of all, endowed with all powers. (39)

I praise the All-pervading Lord, who is to be propitiated by all, the teacher of all, and the cause of all auspiciousness; who is the very essence of all mantras, the bestower of all prosperity, and the most excellent; who is endowed with power and yet free from it, and whose nature is his own will.
I bow to Śaktīśa, the seed of power, the supreme one who assumes the form of power;
who, in this terrible ocean of worldly existence, is equipped with the boat of power;
the compassionate helmsman, who is affectionate toward his devotees.

I praise Brahman, whose nature is the Self, who is both exclusively one and yet manifold, both stained and indeed stainless; who possesses attributes and is also devoid of attributes, whose form is his own will;
who is the god presiding over all the senses and the like, and who is the very abode of the senses. 43–44.

I bow to the Supreme Lord, who is the essential nature of all the senses, who is the Virāṭ form, who is the Veda itself, the progenitor of the Vedas, who embodies all the limbs of the Vedas, and whose essential nature is within all. 45.

I worship the son of Yaśodā, the substance more essential than the most essential, unprecedented and indefinable; independent yet dependent, present in all bodies, invisible and beyond inference. (46–47)

I worship the Lord of Yogīs, who exists as that which cannot be accomplished even by meditation; I bow to that Sovereign of the Earth, who stands in the midst of the Rāsa circle, who is eager for the joy of the Rāsa dance, and who is served by the Gopīs. 48.
I bow to that Lord of Yoga, who is eternally existent for the virtuous and non-existent even for the wicked; who is to be attained through yoga and is served by Śiva.
I bow to the seed of mantras, the king of mantras, the giver of mantras, the bestower of fruits, and the fruit itself.
I bow to that supreme among the supreme, whose very nature is the perfection of mantras.
I bow to him who is happiness and suffering, the giver of happiness and the giver of suffering, merit itself,
the bestower of merit, the granter of auspiciousness, and the seed of all that is auspicious.
Having thus offered praise and given the cows and the boys, O Sage,
he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, wept, and bowed down;
then, opening his eyes, the Creator of the worlds looked upon him.

Whoever constantly recites this hymn composed by Brahmā with devotion shall enjoy happiness in this world and, at the end, go to the abode of Śrī Hari. He attains incomparable service and a station in the presence of the Lord.
And having obtained the proximity of Kṛṣṇa, he shall become a foremost attendant (pārṣada).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When the cause of the universe has departed to the world of Brahmā within Brahman...
The all-pervading Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to His own abode along with the boys.
The cows, calves, and children returned home at the end of the rainy season;
through the illusory power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they all believed it had been another day.
At that time, the cowherd girl Gopālikā was not at all able to do that.
Is everything created by a yogi something new, or is it ancient?
Thus has the entire auspicious life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa been told.
It bestows happiness, grants liberation, is meritorious, and brings about well-being at all times.

(59) Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Episode of the Abduction of the Cow-Calf," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, on one occasion, Nanda, filled with joy in the cowherd settlement and intent on performing a sacrifice for Indra, had drums beaten;
he prepared curds, milk, ghee, buttermilk, fresh butter, jaggery, and honey.

"Taking these, let them perform worship for Śakra," he said. "Whosoever are here in this city—cowherds and cowherd-women, boys and girls, as well as brahmins, vaiśyas, and śūdras—let them do so with devotion. (2–3)
Thus, filled with joy, he himself caused [the proclamation] to be heard;
he erected a sacrificial post in a beautiful and spacious place,
and there he offered silken garments and a charming array of garlands.

Having bathed and performed his daily rites, he donned two clean garments with devotion; having washed his lotus-feet, he sat upon a golden throne, anointed with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. || 5-6 ||
With various types of vessels, with Brahmins and priests,
with cowherds and cowherdesses, and together with boys and girls;
in the meantime, the city-dwellers arrived there.
Having gathered great provisions and equipped with various means,
all the sages— tranquil, masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and accompanied by their hosts of disciples— approached him who was blazing with the splendor of Brahman. (8–9)
Garga, Gālava, Śākalya, Śākaṭāyana,
Gautama, Karuṣa, Kaṇva, Vātsya, Kātyāyana,
Saubhari, Vāmadeva, Yājñavalkya, and Pāṇini.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Gauramukha, Bharadvāja, and Vāmana;
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Śṛṅgin, Sumantu, Jaimini, and Kaca;
Parāśara, Maitreya, and Vaiśampāyana as well. (11–12)
How many kinds of brahmins, mendicants, and bards were there?
Kings, vaiśyas, and śūdras also gathered for the great festival.
Having seen the lords of sages, as well as the brahmins and the rulers of the earth, Nanda [was filled with joy].
He rose from his golden throne, and the Vrajas likewise arose.
Having bowed down, he caused the lords of sages, the brahmins, and the kings to be seated;
and having obtained their permission, he dwelt there again with joy.
And he gave the command to prepare the cooking near the sacrificial post. Having respectfully summoned a hundred Brahmins skilled in culinary arts, gems and lamps blazed all around that place. (16)
The place was made fragrant by incense that rendered it as if blind to the senses;
there were various kinds of flowers and diverse garlands, along with many varieties of unprecedented and most enchanting food offerings. (17–18)
O Nārada, the place of the sacrificial posts was filled with sesame-sweets (tilalaḍḍuka), a thousand maṇḍakas, and completely covered with svastikas;
and there were a thousand jars full of sugar, O Sage.
There were jars filled with excellent, sweet *laḍḍuka* sweets made from the flour of barley and wheat,
cooked in ghee and specially prepared;
as well as delightful fruits ripened on trees and beautiful plantains.
There were fruits that were fully ripe and produced in their proper season and place;
O Nārada, there were hundreds of thousands of jars of milk and as many jars of curd;
there was a hundred jars of honey and a thousand jars of clarified butter.
Three hundred thousand jars were certainly filled with buttermilk;
five hundred thousand jars were certainly filled with molasses;
and one thousand jars were filled with sesame oil. (23–24)
O Brahmin, various excellent bulls capable of carrying goods fit for enjoyment,
as well as diverse vessels made of gold and silver and golden seats,
arrived in the presence of the sacrificial pole.
Garments worthy of choice and beautiful ornaments,
as well as various kinds of musical instruments— charming and sweet— the musicians played their resonant instruments during the festival. (25–27)
He brought thousands of goats, hundreds of buffaloes,
and indeed hundreds of thousands of rams there;
even hundreds of rhinoceroses came into the presence of the staff-bearer.
All the glances were guarded by guards;
who is capable of counting the boys and girls, the trees and tree-women, as well as the youths and young women? (29–30)
Having heard the music of the singers and seen the dancing of the dancers during that great festival, all the people were enchanted.
Rambhā, Urvaśī, Menakā, Ghṛtācī, Mohinī, and Rati [were there].
Prabhāvatī, Bhānumatī, Vipracitti, Tilottamā,
Candraprabhā, Suprabhā, Ratnamālā, Madālasā,
Reṇukā, and Ramaṇī, O Brahmin— these women came to the festival. (32–33)
By their dancing, singing, and the sight of their breasts, faces, and hips; by their beauty and their sidelong glances, the men fell into a swoon.
In the meantime, Hari himself arrived swiftly.
Together with the cowherd boys and the powerful Balarāma,
all the people, seeing him, were bewildered and overwhelmed with joy;
they rose up from nearby, struck with fear, their bodies covered in horripilation.
He was returning from his place of play, peaceful and of beautiful form, accompanied by the sounds of his flute, pipe, and horn;
he was adorned with ornaments made of the finest jewels and with the Kaustubha gem. (37)
Beholding his dark-complexioned form anointed with a paste of sandalwood and agallochum,
his face like an autumn lotus at midday, reflected in a jeweled mirror together with a beautiful sandalwood crescent and a drop of musk. (38–39)
His forehead shone like the sky graced by the moon,
and his dark throat and chest were made radiant by a garland of *mālatī* flowers,
like the spotlessly clear autumnal sky adorned with a flight of cranes.
His dark-complexioned body was adorned with beautiful yellow garments, shining constantly like a rain cloud illuminating the earth with lightning;
his coiled topknot was fashioned from jasmine flowers and guñjā berries. (41–42)
Just as the sky shines when illuminated by a rainbow and the constellations,
and just as [the face] is beautifully adorned with the luster of jeweled earrings and a smiling countenance,
so too does the autumn lotus in full bloom shine with the rays of the sun.
O sage, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, sages, and cowherds,
having prostrated themselves, seated him upon an auspicious jeweled throne.
That Lord of the World sat in their midst upon a gem-studded seat.
Just as the autumnal moon shines in the sky amidst the stars, so did he appear.
Having heard of him, they all spoke to the Supreme Lord of the worlds—he who is composed of his own will, beyond the qualities (guṇas), the embodiment of light, and eternal. (46)

Having seen the great festival, Hari, who was an expert in the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*), quickly spoke to his father regarding that policy which is difficult for all to attain. (47) Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Oho! O King of Ministers, O observer of noble vows, what are you doing here?
Who is to be propitiated, and what is the worship? What would be the fruit of that worship? Or what is the means for attaining that fruit, and who is the friend through that means? (48–49)
When the deity is angry, what can there be [to prevent it], or what obstacle could there be to worship?
When the deity is pleased, what fruit does he bestow here or in the hereafter? Some [deities] bestow fruit in this world, while none whatsoever do so in the next.
Some worship is prescribed neither here nor there; some is prescribed in both places.
Worship not ordained by the Vedas is a vessel for total ruin.
Is this worship of yours now [ordained], or is it merely according to human custom?
"Have you seen the god? Where is he, for whom this worship is intended? Does your god eat visibly, or does he not eat visibly?
That worship is most excellent which is offered to the god who eats visibly. (53)
Janārdana, in the form of a brahmin, personally eats the sacrificial offering (naivedya).
When the brahmin is fully satisfied, all the deities are satisfied.
What need has he for the worship of the gods who is engaged in the honoring of the twice-born?
By him who has honored the brāhmaṇas, all the deities have been honored. (56) If one offers the food-oblation to the deity but does not give it to the twice-born,
that food-oblation becomes as ashes and the worship becomes fruitless.

By giving the offering to the deity to a Brahmin, the gratified Lord grants an eternal and infinite boon and returns to his own abode. But if a fool, having offered the food to the deity, eats it himself, [he incurs sin]. (57–58)
One who steals what has been given, having consumed the property of the gods, shall go to hell.
One must not consume what is offered by a deity, nor the *naivedya* (food offering) except that of Hari.
Among all deities, the consumption of *naivedya* from Viṣṇu is most highly praised.

Food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu is excrement, and water is urine. This rule applies to all, but especially to Brāhmaṇas: if a wise person gives an object to a Brāhmaṇa without first having given it to the God, [it is as if he were eating filth]. (60–61)
Having eaten from the mouth of a Brahmin, the gods are satisfied and proceed to heaven.
Therefore, with every effort, perform the worship of Brahmins,
who bestow excellent fruits in this world and in the next.
Recitation, austerity, worship, sacrifice, charity, and great festivals—of all these rites, the satisfaction of the Brahmins is the essence; it is their sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Within the bodies of those who give the sacrificial fee, all the deities reside. (63–64)

All sacred fords reside in their feet, and all holy waters are contained within the dust of their feet and the water used for washing the feet of Brahmins. By touching them, one obtains the fruit arising from bathing in all sacred fords.
O Ballava, diseases perish through eating [this] with a spirit of devotion;
one is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes—of this there is no doubt.
Even one who has committed the five kinds of sin, O Vraja, is purified if he bows down before a brāhmaṇa.
Having bathed in all sacred fords, he is liberated from all sin;
by the mere touch of a Brāhmaṇa, the sinner becomes purified.
It is declared in the Veda that one is released from evil through the sight [of such a person].
Whether ignorant or wise, a brāhmaṇa is the very form of Viṣṇu.
Those brāhmaṇas who serve Hari are dear to Viṣṇu, even more so than his own life.
The power of twice-born ones who are devotees of Hari is difficult to find even in the Vedas.
By the dust of whose lotus-feet the earth is instantly purified, their footprints are proclaimed to be sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
By the mere touch of them, the sin of [neglecting] sacred fords is destroyed; likewise by embracing them, by constant conversation with them, and by eating the remnants of their food. (71–72)

By both seeing and touching [him], one is liberated from all sins. Whatever merit arises from bathing at all sacred fords during a pilgrimage, that same merit one obtains simply by seeing this brahmin, the servant of Hari. (73)
