Those brahmins who, having given food to Hari, always eat [what remains]—by eating their leftovers, a man attains service to Hari. But if one eats even out of delusion, without having first given with devotion to Hari, [he does not attain this]. (74–75)

A substance resembling feces may become like water, and that which is like urine may become pure. If a Śūdra is a devotee of Hari and is eager to eat the *naivedya*, he gives raw rice to Hari, cooks it himself, and eats it. (76)
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas have the right to worship the Śālagrāma stone;
likewise, Śūdras do not have the right even to worship Hari.
O Lord of the Cowherds, if you do not give these articles to the Brāhmaṇas, [the world will perish]. (77–78)
All [these] will undoubtedly be reduced to ashes.
One ought to give food for the sake of merit to all living beings;
by giving it to distinguished living beings, one obtains a distinguished fruit.
Therefore, by giving to human beings, one obtains an eightfold reward.
By giving food to Vaiśyas, the merit for Śūdras is twofold;
and by giving food even to Kṣatriyas, it becomes twice that of the Vaiśyas.
By giving food to Brahmins, one obtains a hundredfold [merit] compared to Kṣatriyas;
the fruit for a Brāhmaṇa who knows the scriptures is a hundredfold more than that for ordinary Brahmins;
and one certainly obtains a hundredfold more than that for those who know the scriptures by giving to a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted [to the Lord]. (81–82)
Having given food to Hari, he eats with devotion and respect.
Whatever fruit is obtained by one who gives to Viṣṇu and to a devotee of the Brahmins, that same fruit is surely attained by feeding a devoted Brahmin. (83)
When the devotee is satisfied, Hari is satisfied; and when Hari is satisfied, the deities are satisfied.
They become perfected just as the branches [thrive] from the watering of the root.
If one offers these substances to a single deity, [all are pleased]. (84–85)
If all the gods are enraged, what can the gods do?
Or else, give half of the objects to Govardhana.
He is known as Govardhana because he constantly nourishes the cows.

O dear one, he who constantly gives fresh grass to cows possesses on this earth as much merit as Govardhana itself. Whatever merit is found at sacred pilgrimage sites and whatever merit is gained from feeding Brahmins, [he attains all that]. (87–88)
Whatever merit lies in all vows and fasts, and in all forms of austerity;

whatever merit lies in great gifts, and whatever merit lies in the service of Hari; whatever merit lies in wandering the earth, and whatever may lie in all sacred utterances— [all that is attained by him]. (89)

Whatever merit a man may obtain from all sacrifices and from the initiation ceremony, that same merit the wise man obtains by giving grass to cows. And he who, out of desire, restrains a cow after it has eaten its fill of grass, [incurs sin]. (90–91)
The killing of a Brahmin shall befall him, yet he is purified through expiation.
All the gods reside in the limbs of the cow, and all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) reside in her hooves.
O Father, Lakṣmī herself always dwells in her private parts.

Indeed, the man who makes a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with earth smeared from a cow’s footprint becomes instantly purified by bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); for him, there is victory at every step.
That very place where cows stand is proclaimed to be a sacred ford.

A man who gives up his life there will certainly be liberated immediately. That lowest of men who destroys the body of a Brāhmaṇa or a cow incurs a sin equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt. (95)
"Those men who kill Brahmins who are portions of Nārāyaṇa, as well as cows,
go to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Śrī Kṛṣṇa became silent.
Filled with joy, Nanda, his face beaming with a smile, spoke to him.
Nanda said:
"This is the traditional worship of the high-souled Mahendra. (98)
It brings about good rain and accomplishes the delightful growth of all crops.
Crops are the life-breath of living beings; from crops, the living sustain their lives.
And those dwelling in Vraja worship Mahendra through human effort.
"For a great festival at the end of the year, for the sake of prosperity and the removal of obstacles.
(100) Having heard these words, Mādhava laughed loudly along with Bala and spoke again to his father with joy. (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Oh, I have heard your most wonderful and extraordinary speech!
This world and its scriptures are objects of ridicule and are even censured within the Vedas. (2)
There is no discernible cause anywhere from which rain is produced by Śakra.
Today, an unprecedented statement on policy has been heard from your mouth.
Listen to the wisdom of those who possess sacred learning, O father; do not speak what is improper.
The virtuous know everywhere the words spoken in the Sāmaveda.
Put forth your questions and various mantras in this assembly;
let them speak the ultimate truth regarding whether rain indeed comes from Indra.
For from the sun water is born; from water come the plants and trees.
From them come grains and fruits; from them all living beings subsist.
And when the water is drawn up by the sun, it arises again from that [sun] in due time.

The sun, the clouds, and all other such things were ordained by the Creator. In whichever year a particular cloud, elephant, and ocean are considered to preside, the lord of the crops, the king, and the minister—these too were ordained by the Creator. (7–8)
It has been determined that all those things— water and the like, as well as crops and grasses—
exist indeed year after year, kalpa after kalpa, and age after age.
An elephant, taking the desired water from the ocean with its trunk...
One should give that to the cloud; impelled by the wind, the cloud should give it at various places on the earth and at appropriate times as is fitting.
Manifested by the will of the Lord, it shall not be subject to obstruction. (110–111)
Past, present, and future; great, small, and middling—by whom, O dear one, can that karma ordained by the Creator be averted?
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, was created by his, the Lord’s, command.
In the beginning, food was created, and afterwards it is known as the "living being" (jīva).
Through practice, that indeed becomes one's nature; from nature, action arises.
From actions, living beings experience the enjoyment of pleasure and pain. (13–14)
Torture, birth, death, disease, grief, and fear;
the arising of prosperity or calamity, learning or poetry, fame or infamy;
merit and residence in heaven, and sin and dwelling in hell. (15)
For human beings, enjoyment, liberation, and service to Hari are accomplished through action.
Indeed, the Lord is the progenitor of all, as well as the source of the practice of virtuous deeds;
He is both the sustainer and the giver of the fruit, and everything occurs by His will. (16–17)
By whom Virāṭ was fashioned, by whom the principles (tattvas), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the world [were fashioned]—
[by whom] the Tortoise, Śeṣa, the Earth, and everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass [were fashioned].
By whose command the Wind supports the Tortoise, and he [the Tortoise] supports Śeṣa.
The serpent Śeṣa supports the earth with his head, and she, in turn, supports all that is moving and unmoving.

By whose command the life-breath of the world always blows through the three worlds, and by whose command the maker of beautiful light (the sun) heats the terrestrial globe after completing its revolution. (19–20)
Fire burns and death moves among all living beings;
at the appointed time, trees produce flowers and fruits;
and now, the oceans swiftly sink down into their respective places.
Worship that Lord with devotion; for what power does Śakra possess?
(22) Of how many kinds are the cosmic eggs that have appeared and vanished?
And of how many kinds are the ordinances [of fate] brought about by the mere play of his brow’s knitting? (23)
He is the death of death, the time of time, and the very law of the Ordainer.
O dear one, take refuge in Him; He will provide protection for you.
Alas! A single day and night passes for Him as the twenty-eight Indras fall.
The falling of even a single blink of the eye of that Lord, the attributeless Self and creator of the worlds, exceeds one hundred and eight [blinks].
While the Lord remains in such a state, the worship of Śakra is a mere mockery. (25–26)
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Śrī Kṛṣṇa became silent;
and the sages present in the assembly praised the Blessed Lord.
Nanda, thrilled with horripilation and joyful, stood in the assembly with eyes full of tears.
If men endowed with joy are surpassed by their sons, [then what need is there for others?
(28). Having received the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he performed the recitation of auspicious blessings; in due order, he then conducted the formal selection of all [the participants] there. (29)
Then Parvata performed the worship of the lords of sages,
as well as of the wise brahmins, the cows, and the sacred fire with great reverence.
There, when the worship was completed during that sacrifice and the grand festival, [he offered oblations].
The tumultuous sound of various kinds of musical instruments arose;
there was the sound of "Victory!", the blare of conchs, and the cry of "Hari! And the bull among sages recited the auspicious Vedic hymns.
Ḍiṇḍi, the foremost of bards and the beloved minister of Kaṃsa,
recited loudly before him the auspicious Maṅgalāṣṭaka.
Kṛṣṇa, having gone to the edge of the mountain, manifested his divided form.
"I am a mountain; I eat solid things. Choose a boon," he said.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to Nanda, "Father, look at this mountain before you.
Ask for a boon; may it be well with you," he said.
That cowherd chose as his boon service to Hari and devotion to Hari.
Having enjoyed the offering and granted the boon, He vanished from sight.
Then the protector of the cowherds fed the lords of sages and the brāhmaṇas.
He gave wealth to the bards, the Brahmins, and the sages.
Having given gifts to the sages and the Brahmins as well, Nanda, filled with joy,
went to his own abode accompanied by his followers, placing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at the head.
He gave silver, cloth, gold, an excellent horse, and likewise a jewel,
as well as various kinds of food and wealth, to the bard Ḍiṇḍi.
Having praised and bowed to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the sages and brahmins departed.
All the Apsarases, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras departed; likewise,
all the kings and cowherds who had been invited to the great festival,
having bowed down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, went forth with respectful devotion.
In the meantime, Śakra,
the lord of the gods, his lips quivering with rage upon hearing the various censures regarding the destruction of the sacrifice,
quickly ascended his chariot along with the Maruts and the clouds.

He went to the enchanting Vṛndāvana forest, the city of Nanda. O Nārada, all the gods, experts in the science of warfare, followed behind with weapons and missiles in their hands, having mounted their chariots in anger.
By the sounds of the wind, the sounds of clouds, and the terrifying sounds of armies,
the entire city trembled and Nanda was seized with fear.
Distraught with grief, he addressed his wife and spoke to his own retinue.
Having brought her to a secluded place, Nanda, who was an expert in the treatises on statecraft, said:
"O Yaśodā, come here; O Rohiṇī, listen to my words."
"O beloved, take Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and go far away from Vraja.
Let the boys, girls, and women depart to a distance, overwhelmed by fear.
And let the strong cowherds remain here by my side. (47)
"And afterwards we shall emerge from this peril to our lives.
Having spoken thus, the best of cowherds, out of fear, called to mind Śrī Hari with his hands joined in *añjali* and his neck bowed low in devotion.
He praised the Lord of Śacī with a hymn recited from the Kāṇva branch.
Nanda said:
"Indra is the lord of the gods, Śakra, the son of Diti, and the elder brother of Pavana."
He is the thousand-eyed one, the lord of the female organ (Bhaga), and the son of Kaśyapa;
he is Biḍaujas, Sunāsīra, Marutvān, and Pākaśāsana;
he is the glorious father of Jayanta, the lord of Śacī, and the slayer of the Daityas.
Vajrahasta, Kāmasakha, Gautamīvratanāśana;
Vṛtrahā, Vāsava, and Dadhīcidehabhikṣuka; Viṣṇu, Vāmanabhrātṛ, Puruhūta, and Purandara. (52–53)

Lord of the day, performer of a hundred sacrifices, Sutrāman, breaker of mountains, the all-pervading one; bull among the gods, enemy of Bala, crusher of Jambha, refuge of the deities; Śakra, Duścyavana, Turāṣāṭ, and he whose vehicle is the clouds. (54)
Ākhaṇḍala, Hari-haya, Namuci-prāṇanāśana,
Vṛddhaśravas, Vṛṣa, and Daityadarpaniṣūdana—
these forty-six names are certainly destroyers of sin. (55–56)
If a person recites this hymn spoken by Kauthuma daily,
even in the midst of great calamity, Śakra, with thunderbolt in hand,
protects him from severe excessive rain, showers of stones, and the falling of lightning bolts. (57)

Never shall there be fear for him; Vāsava himself shall be his protector. O Nārada, in whichever house this hymn exists and the meritorious one who knows it, there shall be no falling of thunderbolts nor any shower of stones.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the hymn from the mouth of Nanda, Madhusūdana became enraged.
Blazing with the splendor of Brahman, he spoke words of counsel to his father.
Whom do you praise, O coward? Who is this Indra? Abandon your fear in my presence!
(61) I am capable of reducing [the enemy] to ashes in half a moment with effortless ease.
Indeed, I shall protect the cows, the calves, the children, and the women who are overcome by fear. (62)
"Stay fearlessly, having placed [the mountain] within the hollow of Govardhana.
Hearing the boy's words, he (Vṛndāvana) did so with great joy.
Hari held that mountain like a staff with his left hand.
In that interval, O Sage, although it was illuminated there by the luster of jewels,
it suddenly became blinded, shrouded by dust;
and a mass of clouds accompanied by wind covered the sky.
In Vṛndāvana, there was incessant and excessive rain;
there were showers of stones, showers of thunderbolts, and most terrible falls of meteors.
Consequently, everything fell far away from the touch of the mountain.
O Sage, that undertaking was as fruitless as an effort made by one who lacks power.
Seeing all of that rendered futile, Śakra immediately became enraged;
he seized his unfailing thunderbolt, which had been fashioned from the bones of Dadhīci.
Seeing him with the thunderbolt in hand, Madhusūdana laughed;
he paralyzed both his hand and that exceedingly terrible thunderbolt.
The Lord rendered that paralysis, along with the host of gods, futile.
They all stood motionless, like statues against a wall.
Śakra, yawned by Hari, immediately fell into a state of drowsiness;
in that drowsiness, he beheld the entire world there as being composed entirely of Kṛṣṇa.
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, adorned with jewel ornaments,
clothed in yellow garments, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
with a face bright with a gentle smile, and intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees. (72)
Seeing all this world of moving and non-moving beings with every limb anointed with sandalwood paste—
a sight most wonderful— he immediately fell into a swoon;
yet, right there, he recited the mantra previously bestowed upon him by his guru.
He beheld an intense light situated upon a thousand-petaled lotus;
within that [light], he saw a divine form, exceedingly beautiful,
a dark and handsome body with the splendor of a fresh rain-cloud.
Blazing with makara-shaped earrings fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems;
his crest radiant with a crown of shimmering, supreme jewels;
his throat and chest made resplendent by the blazing Kaustubha, the lord of gems; and adorned with jewels in his armlets, bracelets, and anklets.
Having perceived the inner and the outer as equal, he praised the Supreme Lord.
Indra said:
"The imperishable, supreme Brahman, the eternal form of light."
He who transcends the qualities (*guṇātīta*), is formless (*nirākāra*), consists of His own will (*svecchāmaya*), and is infinite (*anantaka*).
To those who meditate upon Him with devotion and for the sake of service, He is the supreme one who assumes various forms—
white, red, yellow, and dark— in accordance with the succession of the ages (*yuga*).
In the Kṛta age, he is white in luster and form, and in the Satya age, he has the nature of truth;
in the Tretā age, he is the color of saffron, blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
and in the Dvāpara age, he is yellow in color, adorned with yellow garments.

I bow to the Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is dark-complexioned in the Kali age, the most perfect Supreme Lord, whose form is as beautiful and deep blue as the finest rain-cloud, the sole delight of Nanda, the joy of Yaśodā,
the supreme one who steals the consciousness of the cowherd girls and is dearer than life to Rādhā.

He was joyfully playing the sound of his flute for amusement, possessed of incomparable beauty and adorned with jewel ornaments; he was the Lord, bearing a tranquility that surpassed the loveliness of ten million Cupids. (84, 89)
In some places in the Vṛndāvana forest, he was playing together with Rādhā;
in another secluded forest, he was seated upon the breast of Rādhā;
and in yet another place, he was engaged in water-sports with Rādhā.
In one forest he was arranging the mass of Rādhikā’s hair;
in another, he was applying red lac to Rādhikā’s feet; and in yet another, he was joyfully taking back her betel that she had been chewing. (87–88)
Seeing Rādhā somewhere, and being seen by her with a sidelong glance; having fashioned a garland somewhere and given it to Rādhā;
and going somewhere with Rādhā to the circle of the Rāsa dance.
In one place, he was wearing a garland placed around his neck by Rādhā;
in another, he was sporting together with the cowherd girls;
and in yet another, he was walking away after taking Rādhā, leaving her behind.
In one place, he was eating food given by the wives of Brahmins;
in another, he was eating palm fruits together with the children;
and in yet another, he was joyfully stealing the clothes of the cowherd women.
In one place, he was calling out to a herd of cows along with some children;
in another, he had placed his lotus-feet upon the head of Kāliya;
and in yet another, he was joyfully producing the playful sound of his flute.
Somewhere, while he was singing beautiful music together with children,
Śakra praised Hari with the *Stavendra* hymn and bowed down in fear.
[This occurred] because of what had been granted previously by his preceptor and by the demon Vṛtra in battle.
Out of compassion, Kṛṣṇa gave to Brahmā, who was performing austerities,
the eleven-syllable mantra and the armor (kavaca) possessing all characteristics.
Formerly, at Puṣkara, this was given by Brahmā to Kumāra.

O Sage, this hymn composed by Indra was given to the preceptor Aṅgiras by Kumāra; and whoever recites it daily with devotion shall certainly attain firm devotion and, at the end, obtain the state of servitude [to the Divine]. (98)
A person is liberated from birth, death, old age, disease, and sorrow;
indeed, he does not see the messenger of Yama or the abode of Yama even in a dream.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard Indra’s words, the Abode of Śrī was pleased;
out of affection, he granted him a boon and established the mountain.
Then, having bowed to Hari, Śakra departed together with his attendants.
All the people dwelling in the caves departed from the cave to their homes;
they all regarded Kṛṣṇa as the most perfect, all-pervading Lord. Placing those residing in Vraja at the forefront, Hari proceeded to his own abode.
With his entire body covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears of devotion, Nanda praised that son, the eternal, perfect Brahman. (3) Nanda said:
Salutation to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to Him who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins.
Salutation again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the benefactor of the world, Govinda.
Salutation to the God who is the friend of Brahman, to Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Salutations be to You, the abode of the light of infinite millions of cosmic eggs.
Salutations to the witness of the forms of the Fish and others, who exists in the form of the individual soul.
Salutations to You, the untainted, devoid of qualities, and formless.
Salutations to You, whose essential nature is exceedingly subtle, yet who are more gross than the grossest;
to the Lord of all, to the All, whose form is light—salutations be to You!
To You whose form is most directly perceptible, yet who are unattainable through meditation even for yogins.
To the one worthy of worship by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, who possesses an eternal form;
to the Abode of the four castes throughout the four ages,
endowed with the qualities designated as white, red, yellow, and dark.
Salutation to the Guru who is the embodiment of yoga for the yogi, and also the Guru of yogis;
salutation to the Lord of Siddhas, the perfected one, the Guru of the Siddhas.
To him whom Brahmā is unable to praise, and whom Viṣṇu is unable to praise.
He whom Rudra is unable to praise, whom Śeṣa is unable to praise;
whom Dharma is unable to praise, whom Ravi is unable to praise;
and whom even Lambodara and Ṣaḍānana are unable to praise— (12)
All the sages, beginning with Sanaka, are unable to praise Him;
Kapila, the teacher of the lords of the Siddhas, is not capable of praising Him;
nor are the two ṛṣis, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, able to perform His praise. (13–14)
Who else of dull intellect could be capable of praising the Supreme beyond the supreme?
Neither the Vedas, nor speech, nor Lakṣmī, nor Sarasvatī are capable;
even Rādhā is not capable of praising Him—so what can the learned ones praise? 15.
O Brahman, forgive every offense at every moment.
O ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, protect me in this ocean of worldly existence!
Long ago, by performing penance at a sacred ford, the eternal son was obtained.
Grant me devotion and service at Your own lotus feet.

Whether it be the state of Brahmā, immortality, or even residence in the same realm as You (sālokya) and so forth—these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the service rendered at Your lotus feet. (18)
O Lord, what do the wise count as the attainment of Indrahood or the status of a god, or the achievement of perfection and heaven;
or kingship and long life? Indeed, all this that has been mentioned, beginning with the state of Brahmā, [is of no account]. (19–220)
What comparison can possibly befit even half a moment of association with Your devotee?
For who is capable of fathoming You, O Lord, when that devotee is Your equal?
Yet, by means of a mere conversation lasting half a moment, he is able to reach the further shore [of understanding]. //21//
Through association with devotees, one indeed becomes capable of practicing devotion in many ways.
It flourishes through the watering of the conversation of your devotees, who are like clouds;
however, from the heat of conversation with non-devotees, it withers away instantly.
And through the sprinkling of the remembrance of your qualities, that supreme sprout of devotion born of the mind—which has already arisen—clearly flourishes at that very moment;
it must not perish but must be constantly and perpetually nurtured, moment by moment. (24)
Then, having attained the state of Brahman for the sake of the devotee's livelihood,
He surely grants him that unsurpassed fruit which is service to Hari.
If, having attained that rare servitude, he indeed becomes a servant, || 25-26 ||
"By that very certainty, all fear and the like have been conquered.
Having spoken thus, Nanda stood before Hari with devotion;
Kṛṣṇa, with a gracious countenance, granted him his desired wish. (27)

Whoever constantly recites this hymn composed by Nanda with devotion shall attain firm devotion and immediately obtain the state of servitude to Hari. After performing austerities at the sacred ford (tīrtha) together with the Earth, Droṇa— || 28–29 ||
In former times, Brahmā gave him that hymn which is very difficult to obtain;
[he also gave] the six-syllable mantra of Hari and the armor that provides all protection.
At Puṣkara, Saubhari, being pleased, gave these to him here.
That very armor, that hymn, and that mantra are exceedingly difficult to obtain.
By the sage who is a portion of Brahmā, this mantra, hymn, and armor were given to Nanda as he was performing austerities; likewise, the chosen deity and the guru [were bestowed]. 31–32.
Whatever knowledge one has acquired in the past, one certainly does not abandon it.
Thus has been told this wonderful hymn, the narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which bestows happiness, grants liberation, is the very essence, and releases one from the bonds of worldly existence. (233)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Destruction of Indra’s Sacrifice," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, the Lord of Rādhikā, together with Balarāma and the boys, [went forth].
He went to that palm grove filled with ripe fruits.
There dwelt a Daitya named Dhenuka, who was the guardian of the trees, possessed the form of a donkey, had strength equal to ten million lions, and was the destroyer of the pride of the gods. (1–2)
The body is like a mountain, and the eyes are like wells;
the rows of teeth are like a line of plow-poles, and the snout is a mountain cave.
The tongue, measuring a hundred cubits, is flickering and terrifying.
His navel was like a whirlpool, and his voice was terrifying.
Seeing the grove of palm trees, the blameless young women were filled with joy;
with the lotuses of their faces smiling, they spoke to Kṛṣṇa out of curiosity. (4–5)
The children said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, Lord of the universe!
O you of great strength, brother of Balarāma, best among all the powerful! (6)
O Lord, bestower of grace upon devotees, grant us your attention for even half a moment to our petition;
we are hungry children and your devotees.
Behold these sweet and beautiful palm fruits.
"To break, to shake, to fell the trees, and [to gather] the fruits;
the various colored flowers and ripe ones that are difficult to obtain—if you give us the command, O Kṛṣṇa, we are capable of performing these deeds. (8–9)

But here is the Daitya Dhenuka, who has the form of a donkey; he is powerful, possesses great strength and prowess, and has not been conquered by all the gods. He is the great minister of Kaṃsa and is difficult for anyone to restrain.
He is a destroyer of all living beings, yet he is the protector of the forests.
O beloved of the world, best among speakers, having reflected well upon this, tell us:
is it proper or improper, and should this deed be done or not? (11–12)
Having heard the words of the children, the Blessed One Madhusūdana spoke these sweet and comforting words to the boys.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O children, what fear do you have of the Daitya? You are my companions;
break down the trees, shake them, and eat the fruits without fear!
Having received the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the powerful boys [did so].
And hungry ones, desiring fruit, flew up to the tops of the trees.
O Nārada, they caused various kinds of ripe fruits—sweet and beautiful—to fall. (15–16)
Some broke the trees and even shook them;
some raised a clamor, while others danced there.
And the powerful boys descended from the trees.
While returning after gathering fruits, they beheld a preeminent Daitya—
of great strength, massive body, and terrible appearance, in the form of a donkey—
approaching with great speed and making a fierce noise. (18–19)
Seeing him, they all wept and, out of fear, cast away their fruits;
they cried out repeatedly and intensely, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!
and said, "Come, O Kṛṣṇa, O ocean of compassion, protect us! (20)
O Saṅkarṣaṇa, protect us; let not our vital breaths depart to the Dānava.

O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, Hare, Murāri, Govinda, Dāmodara, Friend of the Distressed, Lord of the Gopīs, Lord of the Cowherds, O Infinite Nārāyaṇa, protect us, protect us from this ocean of worldly existence! 22.

O Lord of the helpless, whether in fear or safety, in good fortune or misfortune, and amidst joys or sorrows, we have no other refuge in this ocean of worldly existence than You; O Mādhava, protect us, protect us!
Victorious, victorious, O Ocean of Virtues, O Kṛṣṇa, sole kinsman of Your devotees, protect, protect these children who are beset by manifold fears!

"Kill this lord of the Danuja clans, who increases the pride of the strength of our divine race; having slain him, let us increase our own. (24) Seeing the distress of the children, Mādhava, the destroyer of fear and lover of his devotees, arrived at the place where the children were with Balarāma.
(25) Saying, "There is no fear, there is no fear," he ran forward with great haste. (26)
With a face brightened by a slight smile, he granted fearlessness to the children.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, and the boys, they danced and abandoned their fear.
Remembrance of Hari bestows fearlessness and is the giver of all auspiciousness.
Seeing the demon devouring the children before him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Madhu, addressed the powerful Balarāma and said: Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
This son of Bali, a Dānava named Sāhasika, was once a donkey cursed by Durvāsas in the past. This most sinful one, possessed of great strength and prowess, is to be slain by me. (29)
"I shall kill him; you, Bala, protect the children!
he said. "Taking all the children, go far away.
Having seized them, Bala quickly departed in haste at his command.

Seeing Kṛṣṇa, who resembled a blazing crest of fire, the lord of the Dānavas, possessed of great strength and prowess, swallowed him playfully out of anger. [32] He became intensely scorched by that extreme splendor and desired to die.
Out of fear, the Daitya swallowed the radiant Lord again;
but seeing that the Lord had been released—exceedingly beautiful, peaceful, and blazing with the splendor of Brahman—the Daitya let him go. (33–34)
Merely by the sight of Kṛṣṇa, his former memory returned;
he recognized himself as Kṛṣṇa, the supreme cause of the worlds.
Having beheld that Lord whose nature is splendor, the Dānava offered praise.
According to the scriptures, according to his birth, he transcends all qualities and is beyond the reach of the Vedas.
The Dānava said:
"You are Vāmana, a partial incarnation (aṃśa) who came as a beggar for the sacrifice of my father."
The usurper of the kingdom and the stealer of prosperity, who gave me my son, wife, and land—O hero Bali, lord of all, compassionate toward devotees, who have fallen under the power of devotion!
Quickly destroy me, a sinner, who by your curse have taken the form of a donkey. (37–38)
"O Lord of the World, due to the curse of the sage Durvāsas, I have had such a contemptible birth;
and my death has been declared by that sage to come from you, by means of a sixteen-spoked wheel, exceedingly sharp and of great brilliance. (39)

O Lord of the worlds, grant me true devotion; O Giver of Liberation, show me favor. You, the protector of the Vedas and the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, became the Boar through a portion of yourself in order to uplift the Earth. 40–41.
You are Nṛsiṃha yourself, the perfect one, for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu,
for the purpose of bestowing grace upon Prahlāda, and for the protection of the gods.
O ocean of compassion, you are the restorer of the Vedas through your Fish incarnation.
For the sake of bestowing knowledge upon the king and for the protection of the gods and brahmins, you are Śeṣa;

and as the Tortoise, you are the support [of the earth] through a portion of yourself for the purpose of creation. You are the universe itself, the support of the world, and through yet another portion, you are the Thousand-headed One who upholds the world.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, you, and Jānakī for the sake of deliverance;
the slayer of the ten-necked one and the builder of the bridge across the ocean;
and in a partial incarnation, the great Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni.
O Lord of the Earth, you shall be the destroyer of kings twenty-one times.
You are Kapila by partial incarnation, the teacher of the Siddhas and the preceptor of preceptors;
you are the bestower of knowledge upon your mother and the author of the Yoga Śāstra.
By a portion [of his being], the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa were the best among the wise;
and you, having become the son of Dharma, are the one who expands the world.
Now, in the form of Kṛṣṇa, you are yourself the most perfect Supreme Being.
The eternal one who is the seed-form of all incarnations;
the life of Yaśodā, the perpetual one who increases the singular bliss of Nanda;
the presiding deity of the life-breaths of the gopīs, and the one dearer than life to Rādhā. (49–50)
The son of Vasudeva, the peaceful one, the destroyer of Devakī’s sorrow; born not from a womb, the glorious one, the remover of the earth’s burden;
the storehouse of compassion who granted the state of motherhood even to Pūtanā. (51)
He who brings liberation even to Bakas, Keśin, and Pralamba;
O Lord who consists of Your own will, who transcend the material qualities, and who shatter the fear of Your devotees—be gracious, O Lord of Rādhikā! Be gracious and grant me liberation! 52–53.
O Lord, deliver me, the son of Gārdabhīya, from the ocean of worldly existence!
I am a fool, yet I am your devotee’s son; you ought to rescue me.
Even the Vedas, Brahmā and the other gods, and the lords of sages are unable to praise you.
How can I praise him who transcends all qualities—he who was formerly a Daitya and is now Khara?
O Ocean of Mercy, act in such a way that I may have no further birth;
for having beheld your lotus feet, who would ever return to the cycle of worldly existence?
"Brahmā is your praiser, and Khara is your praiser; you ought not to mock them.
For one who is a lord and wise, compassion is equal toward both the worthy and the unworthy.
Having spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas stood before Hari.

With a serene countenance, the glorious one became exceedingly pleased. Whoever recites this hymn composed by the Daitya daily with devotion shall effortlessly attain the states of *sālokya*, *sārṣṭi*, and *sāmīpya* with Hari. (58–59)
In this world, devotion to Hari is difficult to attain; at the end [of one's life], servitude to Him is very rare to obtain.
One may acquire knowledge, prosperity, skill in poetry, sons, grandsons, and fame.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the hymn of praise, the Lord of the Daityas, that ocean of compassion, consented, thinking,
"Alas, how can I bring about the destruction of such a devotee?
Having granted him his remembrance, Hari himself withdrew [the power of] that memory.
For the killing of a praiser, even if he speaks ill, is not ordained by the Lord.
The Dānava, through his illusory power, forgot his own [true nature] regarding Viṣṇu;
indeed, that evil speech took its seat upon his throat.
With his lower lip quivering in anger, the Daitya spoke to Śrī Hari:
"O sage, seized by fate and deprived of my senses, I am desirous of death this very moment.
The Daitya said: "O evil-minded child of man, you certainly desire to die!"
"Today I shall dispatch you to the abode of Yama.
O child, if you come to my palm grove seeking life, you shall not go home again, nor indeed shall you see your kinsmen. (65-66)
Neither Kaṃsa, nor Jarāsandha, nor Naraka is equal to me.
Even the gods tremble before me constantly; who else on earth could be my equal? Indeed, even Śiva, the agent of universal destruction, is not capable of destroying me.
Neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Mṛtyu, nor even Kāla himself [can do this].
Having broken my palm trees and felled their fruits, why indeed do you act with such sudden arrogance? Ah, by whose power is this? (68–69)
"Tell me truly, O boy, who are you? You are so desirable and exceedingly handsome.
Why have you come here to grant me life, which is so difficult to obtain?
Having spoken thus, the powerful one placed him upon his head and set him in motion.
Desperate for death, he hurled Śrī Kṛṣṇa from afar.
Having brought him down to the ground, he struck him with his two tusks;
yet by the mere touch of Kṛṣṇa’s body, those two tusks were shattered.
O Sage, the Daitya, his tusks shattered, provoked that Lord to anger;
he seized Him in order to chew Him, but his own teeth were broken.
With his mouth scorched by the Lord's splendor, he released Him at that very moment.
Burning with agitation and rage, he tore at the earth with his claws.
Having crushed his tail and let out a terrifying sound, he went to the place where the children were; the boys fled in fear.
The exceedingly powerful Balarāma struck him on the head with his fist;
the Asura then fell into a swoon.
Regaining consciousness in a moment, he went into the presence of Hari.
Pained by that fist-blow, he fell into a swoon once more;
then, regaining consciousness, he rose up overwhelmed with agony.
He discharged a large quantity of semen and urine, and was seized by fear.
In an instant, having reached the juncture of moments, that Dānava of great strength and prowess placed Govinda upon his head and crushed him;
having pulverized him, he threw him to the ground again and again. (79)
Mādhava uprooted that palm tree and struck [the demon] with it.
(80) Just as pain would arise for the Dānava from a blow of a sword, so too did it come to the Daitya from the striking of the palm tree. (81)
Having uprooted Govardhana, the Lord struck him down.
O great sage, that king of mountains fell upon him with great force.
From the blow of the mountain, the mighty one fell into a swoon.
His limbs became mangled and he vomited blood;
yet in an instant, regaining consciousness, the asura rose up in rage, seized a preeminent mountain, and hurled it at Mādhava. (83–84)
Seeing the mountain leaping up with speed, the Lord Madhusūdana seized it with his right hand as if it were a stalk of sugarcane;
out of curiosity, he set that mountain back in its original place.
Seizing the tip of the Daitya’s ear, he cast it far away.
Then, leaping up with great speed,
he coiled around Hari and scraped the earth with his sharp-pointed hoof.
Seizing Śrī Hari with speed and placing him upon his head, the great asura,
who could travel as fast as thought, leaped playfully a hundred thousand yojanas.
And for a moment, the battle between the two became invisible.
Then, seizing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Again, for a muhūrta, a battle took place between the two on the ground.
With joy, Hari laughed and praised the lord of the Dānavas.
The life of Bali, my devotee, is blessed and supreme. May it be well with you, O lord of the Dānavas; my child, attain final liberation.
My vision is the seed of well-being and the ultimate cause of nirvāṇa.
"Obtain a most excellent, supreme, and heart-stealing abode!
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa remembered his supreme discus;
he seized that Sudarśana, which was equal to ten million suns in brilliance.
Having whirled it around, he effortlessly cast that unsurpassed, sixteen-spoked [discus], which was incapable of being slain even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
the head of the great-souled Dānava fell to the ground. (94)
A mass of splendor arose, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns.
Beholding the realm of Hari merged within the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, oh, that preeminent among Dānavas attained supreme liberation. (95–96)
All the gods and sages stationed in the sky, filled with great joy,
rained down flowers of the *pārijāta* tree there.
In heaven, the kettledrums resounded and throngs of *apsarases* danced.
The hosts of Gandharvas sang and the sages praised him with joy.
(98) Having offered their hymns of praise, all the gods and the sages, overwhelmed with delight, departed.
And the boys came there, having witnessed the slaughter of Dhenuka. (99)
Bala, the best among the strong, praised Puruṣottama;
all the boys offered praise and danced, filled with joy. Having given ripe fruits to Kṛṣṇa and Bala, they continued their celebration.
The boys, their minds filled with great joy, devoured everything.
Having eaten and drunk, O Brahmin, Hari quickly went to his own abode along with the boys and the child, after having slain the lord of the Dānavas by his power.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Dhenuka," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
By what sin did Bali attain the state of a donkey?

By what fault did Durvāsas curse the lord of the Dānavas? Or by what merit, O Lord, did that sovereign of the Dānavas suddenly attain oneness with and liberation into the state of the mighty Śrī Hari? (1–2)
O Sage, O destroyer of doubts, speak, having explained everything in great detail!
Oh, how wonderful—the poetry in the mouth of the poet is ever-new at every step! (3) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, my child, I shall relate an ancient history heard of old from the mouth of Dharma on Mount Gandhamādana;
it is an account from the Pādma Kalpa, wonderful and most enchanting.
It is endowed with the narrative of Nārāyaṇa, the supreme nectar for the ears.
In whichever Kalpa this story exists, there you shall be Upabarhaṇa,
living until the end of the Kalpa, possessed of splendor, beautiful, and endowed with perpetual youth.
And you were the husband of fifty amorous women, devoted to the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra).
By the boon of Brahmā, you became Su-kaṇṭha, the lord of song.
Moment after moment, they drank in your beautiful lotus-face.
All of them were without blinking, tormented by the arrows of desire.
It has been heard that they were fashioned by the Creator from their very life-breaths, like you;
as companions, they do not live by day or night without you.
And in flower gardens, in secluded and delightful places here and there;
in the deep recesses of mountains, in caves, and by rivers;
and in lovely forests, and in cremation grounds devoid of living beings. || 9–10 ||
And they sported with you according to their desires.
Then, by the power of fate and due to a curse from Brahmā, you became the son of a maidservant;
now, however, through eating the remnants of Viṣṇu's food, you have become the son of Brahmā.
A great and eminent Vaiṣṇava, living for incalculable eons,
he perceives all through the vision of knowledge and is the beloved disciple of Dhūrjaṭi.
O Sage, hear from me the account of that eon.
Having expanded upon the account of the Daityas, I shall relate this story which is like nectar.
Once, the powerful son of Bali, named Sāhasika,
having conquered the gods by his own splendor, set out for Mount Gandhamādana.
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with jewel ornaments,
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, and accompanied by a vast army— just at that moment, Tilottamā came along that path.
She was the most excellent among the Apsarases in beauty, assuming various guises;
she possessed the lovely hue of the campaka flower, was adorned with jeweled ornaments, was endowed with fresh youth, and was tormented by the arrows of Kama. (17–18)

With a slight smile and a serene countenance, wearing divine garments, her eyebrows slightly arched, she moved with the slow gait of a lordly elephant. Beholding her breasts, her thighs, and her moon-like face, the impetuous youth—
When her garment was blown away by the wind, she fell into a swoon.
She beheld the son of Bali, exceedingly handsome,
wearing a garland of full-blown mālatī flowers and in the bloom of youth.
Seeing him, whose face was like the full moon of autumn, smiling and most enchanting,
she was struck with wonder and, out of desire, cast a sidelong glance at him. Desiring the moon, she went to the world of the moon for the sake of sport.
Under what pretext did she, intoxicated and longing for love, remain there?
Repeatedly looking at his face with her sidelong glance and smiling, she again and again covered his face with her garment. (23–24)
With every limb covered in horripilation and endowed with righteous action,
there arose a moist itching sensation in the womb of her who was intoxicated by desire;
she forgot the moon-crested Lord and the aspirations of Bali’s son.
Oh, who in this world knows the mind of a harlot? It is truly difficult to understand.
For he who places his trust in a harlot is mocked by fate;
he is cast out from his reputation, his dharma, and his own family.
Upon obtaining a desired new [husband], the former one perishes.
Then, since she is governed by her own karma, who indeed could be dear or undear to her?
[This applies] toward a deity, a rite for the ancestors, a son, a kinsman, or even a husband.
The mind of a wanton woman is always cruel in matters of amorous dalliance.
(29) That wanton woman looks with an eye of nectar upon one who knows the art of love and values him more than her own life;
yet she looks with a poisonous eye upon one who bestows jewels and is a connoisseur of gems. (30)
There is no place at all for unchaste women anywhere.
The species of unchaste women is even more cruel than that of human killers.
It is certain that for everyone, there is an expiation at the end of all enjoyments.

O best of Brahmins, as long as the moon and sun endure, such compassion as other women have for even killing an insect is not found in unchaste women; indeed, they destroy their own ancient beloved. (32–33)
Upon seeing a beloved man, she destroys him with ease through some stratagem.
Having obtained a new lover who knows the art of love, she regards the former as equal to poison.
Whatever sins exist on earth in the land of Bhārata, they reside solely in unchaste women.

There are none more wicked than these; they remain [in that state]. (39) The food of a woman who has been defiled by a paramour is certain to be a source of all sins. It must not be offered in rites for the gods or the ancestors, nor should water be given to them in such rites. (36)
Food is certainly excrement and water is urine when given by unchaste women to the ancestors and the gods; having offered it and eaten it,
one goes to hell for a hundred years, being cooked in the most dreadful Kālasūtra.
In that terrible darkness, worms bite him day and night.
(38) Furthermore, if that lowest of men should by chance eat the food of an unchaste woman, his merit accumulated over seven lifetimes is certainly destroyed. (39)
There is a loss of life, fortune, and fame both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, one's wife—the vessel of ripening [merit]—must be protected with effort.
By beholding an unchaste woman, merit is gained and the success of one’s journey is certain.
Touching her is a great sin, which is purified by bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Bathing, giving gifts, vows, recitation, and the worship of deities—all these are fruitless for unchaste women; their life in Bhārata is in vain. (41–42)
The story of the unchaste woman has been told according to the scriptures, as well as that which is difficult to understand;
now hear, O Nārada, their conversation as it occurred there.
Then, having regained consciousness and seeing her, the son of Bali—
Afflicted by desire and intoxicated, he went to the presence of the unchaste woman.
She, whose side-glances were crooked and whose hips and breasts were full, spoke with joy while bashfully covering her face with her garment. (44, 49)
The impetuous one said:
"Who are you? Whose daughter are you? Whose beloved are you, O lovely woman?
Where are you going yourself, O fair-browed one, and to which meritorious and charming man? (46)
O beautiful one, you who go to him whom you seek— go indeed— but you ought to make me your servant, I who have been purified by asceticism at the end of an eon and now desire only to enjoy you.
Buy me, a servant eager for pleasure, with the merit of your love-making.
You are greedy for love, O wanton woman; grant me love!
(48) An embrace with you was ordained by Fate itself.
Once it has been determined by Him, O beloved, who can prevent it? (49)
"Speak words like nectar with a smile, O beautiful one!
Quickly bind me in the noose of your creeper-like arms in this secluded place.
O auspicious lady, give me a seat upon your own thigh, which resembles gold."
Display your pitcher-like breasts, which are worthy of being a vessel;
O beautiful woman, rend them with the sharp weapon of your sidelong glance.
Wounded by the serpent of desire, make them free from pain by the touch of your feet.
Give me, who am hungry, the sweet nectar of your lower lip;
show me your beautiful teeth, which resemble the seeds of a ripe pomegranate. O beautiful one, I wish to behold your deep navel and the three folds of your waist.
I always have the desire to loosen the knot of my lower garment;
I gaze upon my lovely hips, which enchant the minds of sages and cause the eyes to lose their luster like autumnal lotuses at midday. (54–55)
"Show me your serene face, which resembles the full autumn moon.
Having heard those words, she, afflicted by love and desiring the destruction of his pride, spoke to him, her mind tormented by the arrows of Kāma. (56)
Tilottamā said:
"O Lord, a husband such as you is the heart's desire of all women.
You are the son of Bali, most righteous, handsome, virtuous, and young."
You are skilled in the arts of love, beloved, and proficient in the treatises on desire;
you are always pleasing to women and naturally well-attired.
[One should seek] one who is well-dressed, handsome, peaceful, beloved, self-controlled, and free from disease.

A passionate woman desires you—you who are skilled in the arts of love, a connoisseur of virtues, youthful, aesthetic, and pure; charming to women, compassionate, powerful, virtuous, a lord, a donor, devoted, and beloved. (60)
"O beloved, all these virtues certainly reside in you, my love.
Those women who do not desire you are ignorant and deceived.
Having come from the house of the Creator, I shall bring you satisfaction. (61)

"Having assumed this disguise for the sake of Candra, his beloved wife will today commit a transgression of dharma by merely embracing another man. And the lives of those who do not protect their dharma are in vain. (62)
Those who do not know the embrace of the Moon are proclaimed to be fools;
they alone, while still within their mother’s womb, are not wise regarding the heroic sentiments.
[Their] own physician is Madana, the Moon is Marutvān, and [their] Nalakūbara is...
Those women who have not been embraced by these [men] are deprived of the acts of love.
Day and night, my mind shall contemplate their play, especially that of Kāmadeva, who is skilled in the arts of love. (64–65)
"Today is his day of delight, with embraces as beautiful as the moon's crest and conversation sweeter than nectar; therefore, let his mind dwell upon that.
Having heard Tilottamā’s words, the son of Bali laughed.
And with desire and his hair standing on end, he spoke to her in that secluded place.
Sāhasika said:
"O Tilottamā, you were created by Brahmā out of curiosity."

Therefore, she is the most excellent among the Apsarases, the sovereign mistress of those who relish the refined aesthetic sentiment. By means of the destruction of Sunda and Upasunda, she was created with great effort by Brahmā in ancient times as the repository of all beauty and virtue. (68–69)
O Omniscient One, you know everything; you are an expert in the art of sexual union.
Out of joy, I wish to hear the words from your heart;
tell me, O fair-faced one, who is most dear to you and what is your true nature? (70)
"I wish to hear, O beautiful one, who it is that must necessarily be protected;
for among the Gandharvas, the gods, and even the meritorious kings—among all these, you are as dear as their own life-breath—who else is more beloved to them? (71–72)
Having heard the words of the Asura, Tilottamā laughed and, looking at him with a sidelong glance, covered her face.
That which is the essence, situated within, unmanifest, and most secret—[is truth]. (73)
He spoke these words from his mind, which remained unknown even to the wise.
Tilottamā said:
"O reckless man, the thoughts and words of unchaste women must be told."
It is the supreme cause of derision for all women;
the conduct of women is difficult to understand for everyone, and the mind and speech of unchaste women are especially difficult to fathom. (75–76)
The learned man knows everything up to the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Śāstras;
he knows the end of the quarters, of the directions, and of the celestial women. To women, an old man is more unpleasant than poison and even more so than a jewel. (77)
If a youth who steals all one's possessions is dearer than even one's own life, then upon seeing a handsome young man, an unchaste woman becomes distressed;
she loses her very senses, especially when she beholds him well-attired. (78–79)
Without blinking, she would drink in his face with both eyes.
Water would flow from her vulva, and immediately there would be itching;
her mind became exceedingly restless and unsteady, and all her limbs trembled.
Her body has become numb and scorched by the fire of passion.
If, having approached him in secret, she engages in clear conversation with him, repeatedly showing him her smiling face and casting side-long glances; (81–82)
Likewise, if she is unable to bring him under her control because he has conquered his senses, she should show him her own body and speak these words clearly within:
"If the hero is difficult to win over, there will be suffering for me birth after birth until the end of time. (83)
Having obtained one equal to him, that unchaste woman forgets him.
Who on this earth is disliked by unchaste women, or who is beloved?
He who is highly skilled in the arts of love is dearer to them than their own life.
Having obtained a superior new husband, son, brother, father, or mother,
she abandons everything effortlessly, as if in play—
neither by gifts, nor by honor, nor by truth, nor by praise. (86)
She cannot be won over by favors or by affection without exquisite pleasure.
Whether on the bed or at the meal, in sleep or in waking, day or night, unchaste women constantly long for the embrace of a virtuous man. (87–88)

For those skilled in the arts of love, the nature of the harlot—difficult to master through meditation even over a long period—is exceedingly cruel; she desires ever-new [lovers]. Thus, the conduct of all unchaste women has been described by me. (89)
Listen to the words from my heart, which are not to be spoken and must be kept secret:
I have lovers dearer to me than the Gandharvas and the gods—youthful, heroic in love, and experts in the science of erotics. (90–91)
In particular, I possess a supreme affection for the moon;
indeed, Kāma is dearer to me than everything else.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, anyone as dear to me as Kāma.
"By the mere remembrance of Smara, my mind has quickly become very affectionate.
Thus I have related everything concerning myself and women as well.
O Great King, give me your command; I shall go into the presence of Candra. || 93-94 ||
"Having come from the place of the Moon to your own station with perfect certainty, O Lord of Daityas, I shall bring you satisfaction; of this there is no doubt.
Upon hearing this, the son of Bali laughed aloud again and again.
Looking at him with a sidelong glance, she laughed, afflicted by love;
under a pretext, she revealed her pair of firm breasts,
which had the luster of a beautiful campaka flower, being round, plump, and prominent.
Her hips were very firm and beautiful, putting to shame the trunk of a plantain tree;
her face was smiling with side-long glances, and her cheeks were covered in horripilation.
Having reached a secluded place, her consciousness was overcome by passion. (98)
With all her limbs bristling with thrills, she drank in his face with her eyes (99).
Again and again, beholding his form and his attire,
she covered his face out of emotion with her fine garment (100).
Seeing her exceedingly enamored, the wise Balinanda, himself a lover eager to understand the state of mind of those filled with passion, questioned her.
Sāhasika said: 101. Seeing her so intensely impassioned, the very wise son of Bali, a lover himself, questioned her, being eager to discern the disposition of those possessed by desire.
Sāhasika said:
"What will you do with me? Tell me the truth, O lotus-eyed one.
I shall attend to other duties; I am unable to remain for very long.
My dear, the use of force toward women is not the dharma of those who follow dharma."
Especially for those who are highly learned, this is not appropriate for our own family. (103) Either provide us with love-making, or go to the presence of the gods to engage in pleasure.
Or else, who is capable of subduing an unchaste woman who wanders after many men? (104)
Having heard the words of the Dānava, her throat, lips, and palate parched, considering herself most wretched and pierced by the weapon of Love, Tilottamā said:
105. Tilottamā said:
"Tell me how it is that you, my beloved, dearer to me than life itself, have become thus;
or how is it that you are filled with anger? Accomplish what you desire.
If I go to the presence of the moon while leaving you thus turned away from me..."
"By your curse, an obstacle shall arise for him right there immediately.
Build a monastery—may prosperity be yours—for Hari himself will carry it out. For him who guards his pride as a woman at every step, there shall be auspiciousness at every step. (107–108)
"The fool who, disregarding a woman, proceeds as the lowest of men— Pārvatī, the virtuous one, will bring him misfortune at every step.
Having heard the words of Tilottamā, the son of Bali laughed.
The wise man, who was proficient in the treatises on love, understood her state of mind.
Having discerned her feelings, he, who was skilled in the science of love and knew the heart's inclinations,
took her by the hand, embraced her, and kissed her lotus-like face.
And he went with her to the cave of Gandhamādana.
Having gone there, he beheld a place devoid of living beings. He established jewel-lamps and most enchanting incense.
Having prepared a bed that provided great pleasure, he slept with her;
deluded by passion, he engaged in various forms of amorous dalliance.
Tilottamā perceived him to be more discerning than even a god. (113–114)
The Queen of Rasikas became delighted by their inverted dalliance;
intoxicated by their new union, she did not perceive day or night.
Then Tilottamā, out of amorous desire, spoke to the son of Bali.
Having joyfully placed the Lord of her life upon her chest between her breasts,
Tilottamā said:
"O beloved, when shall I behold your enchanting moon-like face?"
"When will such an auspicious day come for me again?
[117] "O Dānava, what is this marvelous form or quality of yours?
Surely there is no one else more skilled in the erotic sentiment than you. [118]
In time, you will forget me, just as a six-legged insect forgets its former state;
yet for women, the embrace of a virtuous man remains in the heart for as long as life lasts.
The company of the righteous occurs on auspicious days through the merit of those who possess merit. (119)
The severance of contact with the virtuous is a cause of suffering that exceeds even death;
it is more difficult to obtain than a meal of nectar or residence in heaven.
Association with the virtuous is full of happiness, whereas association with the wicked is worse than poison. (120–121)
"Stay a moment, O Great King; grant me another embrace. My life-breaths shall depart along with my heart only when they leave with you.
Having spoken thus, the unchaste woman affectionately placed him against her breast.
With her body covered in horripilation from the touch of his entire form, she fell into a swoon out of joy;
and through the embrace and conversation of that unchaste woman, he became exceedingly lustful,
just as a blazing fire increases all the more when fed with clarified butter.
O Sage, the asura again performed the eightfold amorous decoration (śṛṅgāra) and the ninefold kissing (cumbana), each in its proper place and as was fitting;
he further engaged in various sports with his nails, teeth, and hands. (125)
The jingling of small bells and bracelets produced a loud sound;
by that, the meditation of the sage Durvāsas was indeed interrupted,
even though he remained unseen there, concealed within the anthill.
As they performed yogic postures in the cave of Mount Gandhamādana and meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
their gaze did not fall upon the great sage standing nearby.
"For those whose souls are possessed by desire and whose minds are destroyed by desire, there is no knowledge.
(128) Suddenly regaining consciousness and blazing with the splendor of Brahman, the sage opened his eyes and beheld the two of them before him. (129)
Not knowing day from night, joined together and infatuated by desire,
the radiant, all-pervading Lord, an emanation of Rudra, became enraged upon seeing them.
With eyes like red lotuses, he spoke to them at the conclusion of his diversion.
His mind distressed by the interruption of the lotus-feet of him who had attained the states of meditative absorption, Durvāsas said:
"Arise, you donkey-shaped one, shameless, lowest of men! (131)
The son of Bali, who was preeminent in devotion, possessed a splendor equal to that of a beast.
Even gods, humans, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas—save for beasts—constantly feel shame before their own kind. (132–133)
"Moreover, you are devoid of wisdom and shame, especially as one of the ass species.
Therefore, O best of Dānavas, enter the womb of an ass now!
And you, Tilottamā, arise—you are shameless and a wanton woman!"
"O Daitya, such is your longing for the womb of a cow and the state of a Dānava.
Having spoken thus, the sage stood there blazing with wrath. And those two, rising up terrified and ashamed, praised the sage.
The impetuous one said:
"You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Maheśvara himself;
you are the sacrificial fire and the sun, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. (137)
"O Blessed One, O treasure-house of compassion, forgive this offense; grant us your grace!
He who constantly forgives the offenses of the deluded is a true Lord.
Having spoken thus, O Sage, the lord of the Daityas wept loudly before the ascetic.
Having placed blades of grass between his teeth, he fell at her lotus feet.
Tilottamā said:
"O Lord, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, have mercy!"
And in the creation of Brahmā, the entire female species is indeed deluded.
Therefore, O Lord, she is excessively intoxicated, unchaste, and perpetually afflicted by lust; in such a woman, shame, fear, and consciousness do not exist.
Having spoken thus and wept, he went for refuge to the sage.
On this earth, knowledge arises for some only through adversity.
Seeing the distress of those two, compassion arose within the sage. (142)

Durvāsas said: O Dānava, whether it be a curse or a favor, it must come by the power of destiny; likewise, whether it be great fame or ill-repute, it is certainly produced by one's previous actions. (143)
A person born of a noble lineage is the son of Bali, a devotee of Viṣṇu. From Janaka you have become a devotee of Viṣṇu; I know this of you with absolute certainty.
For the very nature of the father surely resides in the offspring. (144)
Just as the hoof-mark of Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon the head of the Kālīya serpent, O child, attain liberation even after reaching the womb of a donkey;
for the fruit of former worship of Kṛṣṇa is never lost for the virtuous, however long it may take. (145–146)
Go quickly to Vṛndāvana, to the Tālavana forest, and to the vicinity of Vraja.
Having cast off your life-breaths by the discus of Hari, you will certainly attain liberation.
O Tilottamā, you shall become the daughter of Bāṇa in Bhārata.
"By means of a wordplay on the grandson of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you shall become purified once again.
Having spoken thus, O great sage, that muni ceased speaking.
They both bowed to the bull among sages and departed for their respective places.
Thus was related the entire account of the Daitya born as Khara.
Tilottamā was indeed the daughter of Bāṇa, while Uṣā was the beloved of Aniruddha.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Episode of the Curse of Brahmā upon Tilottamā and the Son of Bali," in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, listen to the hidden account of the sage Durvāsas.
Aho! How could there have been a union with a wife for him who was one whose vital seed is drawn up? 1.
Seeing their amorous display, the sage indeed became filled with desire.
Even for one who has conquered his senses, the fault of association arises from contact with the wicked. Suddenly, a longing for sexual union arose within his heart.
Having performed austerities there, he, afflicted by passion, meditated upon a desirable woman. In the meantime, the lord of sages,
Aurva, was traveling along that path together with his daughter, who was seeking a virtuous husband.
In a former kalpa, while Brahmā was performing austerities, a son was born from his thighs;
he was a lord of yogis who remained celibate (ūrdhvaretas), and thus he is remembered as Urva.
His daughter, born from his knees, was the renowned Kandalī by name.
Praying to Durvāsas, no one else was pleasing to her mind.
(6) Indeed, that best of sages stood before the sage Durvāsas together with his son, exceedingly gracious and resembling a blazing flame of fire. (7)
The Lord of Sages, seeing that Lord of Sages before him, rose up with haste and bowed down filled with joy. There, Aurva, filled with joy, embraced Durvāsas.
He told the sage everything regarding the maiden’s desire.
Aurva said:
“My daughter, named Kandalī, is renowned and captivating.”
But a mature maiden, meditating on you alone and having heard [of you] from the mouth of a messenger,
is a daughter born without a womb (ayoni-saṃbhavā), capable of enchanting the three worlds,
the repository of all beauty and virtues, yet joined with a single defect. (10–11)
"Exceedingly overcome by quarrelsomeness and speaking harshly out of anger,
one should not abandon a substance endowed with manifold virtues because of a single defect.
Having heard the words of Aurva, the sage was filled with both joy and sorrow.
He saw before him a maiden endowed with virtue and beauty;
her face was like the full moon of autumn, her eyes were like autumn lotuses, her countenance was bright with a gentle smile, and she possessed full hips and breasts. (13–14)
Seeing her endowed with fresh youth, gazing with sidelong glances,
richly adorned with jewel ornaments, and clad in garments as pure as fire,
the sage, afflicted by the arrows of desire, was infatuated upon beholding her. (15)
With a grieving heart, he spoke to that best of sages.
Durvāsas said:
"The form of a woman is an obstruction to the path of liberation in the three worlds."
Constant distraction from ascetic practice is the perpetual cause of delusion;
it is a supreme fetter, difficult to bear within the prison of saṃsāra, and unbreakable even by the great swords of knowledge wielded by Śaṅkara and others. (17–18)
And that which is beyond the clinging shadow and beyond the experience of karma;
beyond the senses and the support of the senses, and beyond both knowledge and the intellect (19).
As long as the body exists, there is the clinging shadow; and until the end of experience, there is experience itself.
The body, the senses, the individual soul, and knowledge belong to one who lacks self-control; likewise, the intellect belongs to one who lacks self-control until the end of life.
One who possesses a virtuous wife remains happy birth after birth;
as long as one has a living wife, there is no breaking of the continuity of births.
As long as one lives, so long does enjoyment bring happiness;
yet, O Lord of Sages, the service of Hari’s lotus feet is supreme above all else.
While I was meditating upon Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, an obstacle indeed arose for me.

I do not know by what fault of karma from a previous birth my mind became filled with desire upon seeing the amorous dalliance of the Daitya with a harlot; that fruit was surely bestowed by the Creator. (23–24)

"However, O Sage, I shall certainly forgive your hundred bitter words toward my daughter, and I shall grant you the fruit thereof. For the endurance of a woman's bitter speech is the highest form of censure in every respect. (25)
One who is conquered by women is exceedingly censured among the virtuous in the three worlds.
Having placed your command upon my head, I shall take your daughter.
A man who abandons a loving wife who has come to him would go to the Kālasūtra hell.

"If a man of controlled senses should abandon a wanton woman who has approached him in secret out of desire, he does so out of fear of violating dharma; yet through such unrighteousness, he would go to hell.
Having spoken thus before the sage, Durvāsas fell silent.
O sage, the silent sage (Muni) gave his daughter to him according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas.
Durvāsas said, "May there be well-being," and the sage gave him a dowry.
Having performed the formal offering of the maiden, he wept out of sheer emotion.

Afflicted by the separation from his own daughter, that sage fell into a swoon; for the flood of grief caused by the loss of one's offspring does not spare even one who delights in the self. Regaining consciousness in an instant, he awakened his daughter.
Fainted from the separation from her father, weeping and filled with grief—
Aurva said:
"Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the essence of political ethics, which is very difficult to attain."
That which is beneficial, truthful, declared in the Vedas, and brings about happiness in the end;
one's own husband is the supreme kinsman both in this world and in the next.
For there is no one dearer than a husband to women of noble family, nor is there any teacher greater than he. (33–34)
Worship of the gods, religious observances, charity, austerity, fasting, and recitation;
bathing in all sacred fords, initiation into all sacrifices, circumambulation of the earth, and service to Brahmins and guests. (35)
All these do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to one's husband.
What is the use of these things for one devoted to her husband or for one who is not, O Bhārata?
For when the husband is first distressed, he becomes desirous of the commencement of happiness.
In all the scriptures, it is taught that service to the husband is the supreme duty.
Constantly perceiving her beloved through her own wisdom as superior even to Nārāyaṇa, she will perpetually perform service at his lotus-feet. (37–38)
O Sage, out of jest, anger, delusion, or contempt,
she will never utter harsh words to her husband, whether in his presence or in his absence. Nor shall there be on the earth of Bhārata any woman whose speech is corrupted by passion.
There is no atonement prescribed in the Vedas for one who utters harsh words to her husband; such a woman faces a hundred births in hell.
For her who, though surrounded by every virtue, speaks cruelly to her husband, the merit accumulated over a hundred lifetimes is certainly destroyed. (40–41)
Having given away his daughter and having instructed her, the bull among sages departed;
he, who delights in his own self, remained joyfully in his own hermitage together with his wife. When his mind was enveloped by the desire for union, that lover attained his beloved.
"Aha! For those of meritorious deeds, every desire is fulfilled by mere wish.
O great sage, having prepared a bed conducive to pleasure, that best of sages took his beloved by the hand at an auspicious moment and slept with her in a secluded place.
Although that bull among sages had been ignorant of the essence of women since birth,
he was nevertheless an expert in sexual union and proficient in the science of love;
he performed various kinds of amorous dalliance according to the prescribed rules.
Merely by their first union, Kandali fell into a swoon;
the best of sages likewise fell into a swoon and was not conscious day or night.
Thus, O Sage, he engaged in amorous dalliance there every single day.
The union of the clever woman with the clever man was perfectly matched.
The lord of sages, having abandoned his asceticism, became attached to domestic life.
Kandalī constantly engages in quarrels with her husband.
The Lord of Sages sought to awaken the passionate woman with words of counsel;
yet she understood nothing of it, for she took delight in quarreling.
She did not become peaceful even by means of the knowledge bestowed by her father.
For one's own nature, which is difficult to transcend, does not diminish through awakening.
She constantly utters harsh words toward her beloved without cause. By her, the world was made to tremble; by her, he was made to tremble with anger. 50–51.
The ocean of mercy forgave the harsh words she spoke and remained established in patience;
he constantly awakened her from her delusion immediately.
In that time, the hundred verses of harsh speech were completed.
Out of compassion, he forgave more than a hundred harsh words.
(53) The mind of the sage was surely consumed by his wife’s bitter speech; thus, the karma of that woman who had uttered such harsh words was brought to completion. (54)
Delighting in his own self and compassionate, he was unable to restrain his anger;
out of delusion, he cursed the woman, saying, "Become a heap of ashes!
At the mere gesture of the sage, she was indeed reduced to ashes.

Thus, for those who are excessively haughty, there is no welfare in the three worlds. When the body had been reduced to ashes, that reflection of the Self—the living soul (jīva) situated in the intermediate space—humbly spoke to the Lord: (56–57).
Jīva said:
O Lord, you are all-seeing; with the eye of eternal knowledge, you know everything, O Omniscient One. What can I possibly teach you? (58)
Whether it be pleasant speech or harsh speech, anger and even distress;
greed, delusion, and desire, as well as hunger, thirst, and the like;
obesity and emaciation, destruction, the visible and the invisible, and all that arises—[all these belong to the body]. (59)
All the attributes of the body belong neither to the *jīva* nor to the *ātman*.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—such is the body, composed of the three *guṇas*. Understand that it is of various kinds; I shall describe them to you. (60–61)
O Sage, some [beings] have a predominance of *sattva*, some a predominance of *rajas*, and some a predominance of *tamas*;
nowhere is there equality.
From the arising of *sattva* comes the desire for liberation, and from the quality of *rajas* comes the desire for action.
From the quality of darkness (tamas) arise violence toward living beings, anger, and indeed egoism.
From anger, harsh speech inevitably follows; through harsh speech, enmity comes to be.
Through that enmity, one immediately becomes disliked; for who on this earth is not someone's enemy? (63–64)
Who is dear and who is undear? Who is a friend and who is an enemy?
The senses are the seeds of both enmity and friendship everywhere.
To women, their husband is dearer than life; to a husband, his wife is dearer than life.
Hostility arose instantly between the two due to that harsh speech;
in a mere moment, O Lord, everything that had transpired was indeed caused by the fault of passion.
Forgive all this offense; tell me now what ought to be done.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where will my birth be?
"In the three worlds, I shall become your wife and no other's.
Having spoken thus, Jīva became silent.
With his mind stolen away by grief, that sage fell into a swoon;
alas, even one who delights in his own self and possesses great wisdom loses consciousness!
For the separation from a wife is, for the wise, a sorrow greater than all others. (69–70)
Regaining consciousness in an instant, he prepared to cast off his life-breaths;
having assumed a yogic posture there, he performed breath-retention (*vāyudhāraṇa*). In the meantime, a young Brahmin arrived at that place.
Carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in red garments, and bearing the supreme *lakṣmī*;
smiling, dark-complexioned, and blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
very young in age, peaceful, wise, and the best among those who know the Vedas. (72–73)
Upon seeing him, Durvāsas bowed down with great agitation;
he caused him to stay right there and honored him with devotion.
Then the young Brahmin, having offered him a blessing, spoke.
Upon seeing him and through his blessing, all suffering vanished from the sage.
Remaining for a moment in the form of a child, the wise one, who was proficient in the science of ethics, spoke to him a flood of policy that was like nectar. (75–76)
The child said:
"O omniscient preceptor, by the grace of your mantra you know everything.
O Brahmin, what reality am I, who am distressed by grief, asking you? (77)
Austerity is the duty of Brahmins; the three worlds are to be accomplished through austerity. Having abandoned your own dharma, what are you doing now, O sir?
In the three worlds, who is whose wife, who is whose husband, or to whom does anyone belong?
Hari employs illusion (māyā) to deceive fools:
"This wife of yours is false, and by him she has now vanished in an instant.
For that which is real is not invisible, and that which is false does not endure for long.
And Ekānaṃśā, the sister born of Vasudeva and daughter of Hari,
who arose from a portion of Pārvatī, being virtuous and long-lived—
she, ever beautiful in every kalpa, shall become your wife.
"Give your mind joyfully to ascetic practice for a few days;
[then] the *kandalī*, a species of banana tree, will appear upon the earth—auspicious, fruit-bearing, lovely, born but once, and exceedingly rare. (82–83)
"In another kalpa, she shall become your wife in a peaceful form.
It has been heard in the Vedas that the subduing of one who is excessively haughty is appropriate.
Having spoken thus, Janārdana quickly assumed the form of a brahmin.
Having bestowed knowledge upon the Brahmin, he vanished;
the sage, having abandoned all delusion, set his mind upon ascetic practice.
Kandalī became a species of banana tree upon the surface of the earth.
O Sage, the Daitya went to the palm grove and assumed the form of a donkey; Tilottamā, the daughter of Bāṇa, likewise became so at that time.
The lord of the Daityas, having abandoned his life through Viṣṇu’s discus, attained his heart’s desire.
Having attained the lotus-feet of the Sage, which are exceedingly difficult to obtain,
Tilottamā returned to her own abode at the proper time;
her heart's desire was completely fulfilled by the embrace of Kṛṣṇa’s grandson.
Having thus heard this supreme and beautiful narration of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
word by word, what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Bali’s Son," occurring in the context of the eating of palm fruits, within the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
O Brahmin, I have heard the wonderful and auspicious deeds of Hari;
indeed, they are exceedingly captivating when coming from your own lips. (1)
