When the hermit’s daughter had died due to the curse of the sage Durvāsas, what did he do upon returning? Tell me that, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
As the sage was performing austerities on the bank of the river Sarasvatī,
his washed garment, which was being held up by the wind, fell from above.
When the cloth had fallen upon the earth, the lord of sages abandoned his ascetic practice.
Through meditation, he perceived the entire crisis concerning his daughter.
Though overwhelmed with grief, he went quickly to his son-in-law’s hermitage;
he drenched the dust of the earth continuously with drops from his eyes.
Having approached the vicinity of his home with a distressed mind,
the Brahmin called out again and again, "O child Kandalī!
Recognizing the voice of his father-in-law, Durvāsas was overwhelmed with fear.
She quickly emerged and fell at his lotus-like feet. Having bowed to her father-in-law, she lamented intensely out of grief and related the news from the very beginning to that best of sages.
Upon hearing the news, the great sage was overcome with grief and fell to the ground;
he lost consciousness, motionless like one who is dead.
O Sage, seeing him as if dead, Durvāsas felt distress in his mind.
With great effort, he restored consciousness to the great sage.
Having quickly regained his senses, the sage spoke to him who stood before him—the son-in-law, who was filled with grief, terrified, and with his neck bowed in prostration. || 10-11 ||
His eyes were filled with tears from great sorrow, and his red lotus-like eyes were bloodshot;
trembling constantly from anger, he was terrified, his lower lip quivering.
Aurva said:
"O Brahmin, you are the grandson of Atri, the lord of the world.
Why have you inflicted such a severe punishment for a very minor offense?
Your birth is from a portion of Śaṅkara, and you are the disciple of that Teacher of the World."
He is a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, omniscient, and himself endowed with all virtues.
Your mother is Anasūyā, a great saintly woman who is a portion of Kamalā.
I do not know by what fault such a thought has arisen in you.
He whose father is virtuous and whose mother is a virtuous woman—yet their son is devoid of compassion! Oh, how subtle is the path of the Veda!
My daughter, who is dearer to me than my own life, has been joyfully entrusted to you.

Endowed with great virtues and mixed with only slight faults, the punishment for one whose speech is corrupt is indeed abandonment; so it is heard in the Śruti. If you have abandoned her out of anger, though she was protected with effort by your father. (17–18)
"Since my offspring was reduced to ashes by you for such a minor offense, there will undoubtedly be a great defeat for you;
this applies always to all living beings, whether they be great or small creatures. (19)
"The Blessed One, the storehouse of compassion, is the creator, the protector, and the teacher.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages lamented again and again; crying out, "O Mother! O Child! Alas! he went to his own abode in anger.
When the Lord of Sages had departed, Durvāsas lamented intensely once more;
for the sorrow that had been forgotten through knowledge became doubled again.
Indeed, the fire of grief, which had been extinguished by the ashes of knowledge over time, flared up anew.
By providing fuel for the fire of his longing through the sight of his kinsmen, he grew strong once again.
(23) Repeatedly remembering his beloved and lamenting there over and over, he awakened himself and set his mind upon ascetic practice. (24)
Thus has the entire cause of the sage’s curse been told;
in the course of time, his unbearable humiliation came to pass.
Nārada said:
Durvāsas was a portion of Śaṅkara and equal to Śiva in splendor. Who, being so powerful and great, could have brought about his humiliation? Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, King Ambarīṣa, a great lord of kings born of the solar dynasty, had his mind constantly fixed upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
he found no delight in his kingdom, nor in his wives, nor in his sons, nor in his subjects. (27)
Even amidst prosperity acquired through meritorious deeds, his mind does not dwell for even a moment upon it.
Day and night, that righteous one meditates with joy upon Hari within the knowledge at the end of his life.
Having great mastery over his senses, peaceful, and devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu— (28–29).

He is devoted to the vow of Ekādaśī and intent upon the worship of Kṛṣṇa; he is unattached to all worldly actions and performs them only when dedicated to Kṛṣṇa. He possesses the extremely sharp Sudarśana discus of Hari, which has sixteen spokes.
Equal in splendor to Indra and possessing a radiance like ten million suns (31),
it was being praised by Brahmā and others, and worshipped by gods and asuras;
it was constantly protected by the Lord for its preservation in the presence of the king (32).
Having observed the Ekādaśī vow, when the day of Dvādaśī arrives,
one should bathe and perform worship at the proper time according to the prescribed rites; then,
having given gifts of gold, silver, and other valuables to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having fed the Brahmins, he remained there for the sake of a meal. In the meantime, O Sage, a certain ascetic Brahmin arrived— he was hungry,
carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in white garments, and wearing an excellent tilaka.
With matted hair, extremely emaciated, terrified, and with his throat, lips, and palate parched,
the venerable Durvāsas arrived there before the king.
And seeing that lord of sages, he rose and prostrated himself before him.
Having affectionately offered water for his feet, he gave him a golden throne.
(37) Having bestowed blessings upon him, the brahmin sat upon a comfortable seat.
The king, filled with joy, asked him: "What is your command? Tell me what you desire. (38)
Having heard the words of the king of men, the great sage said to him:
"O King, give food to me who am hungry according to the prescribed rites.
However, having first chanted the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra, I shall indeed arrive before long."
"O King, wait for a moment," having said this, the sage departed.
When the brahmin had gone, the royal seer fell into an insurmountable anxiety;
seeing that the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) was almost at its end, he was overcome with fear.
In the meantime, having joyfully bowed to the Guru as he arrived there and reported everything, the king spoke:
"O tiger among sages, the sage does not come; the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is passing away."
"In this crisis, having deliberated upon what ought to be done according to the prescribed rules,
speak quickly, O best of sages, regarding my welfare or misfortune.
Having heard the king's words, the bull among sages spoke with haste.
[It is] beneficial, truthful, declared in the Vedas, and bringing about happiness in the end.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the twelfth day has passed, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should indeed be performed on the thirteenth day.
Having destroyed the fruit of the fast, he certainly kills the one observing the vow.
It is heard in the Śruti that his sin shall be equal to the murder of a Brahmin;
the Lotus-born One has declared that his food is equivalent to liquor.
If a fool does not feed a guest who has arrived, that guest,
terrified and hungry, eats [his merit] and will certainly go to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Staying there for a hundred years, the man shall attain the state of a caṇḍāla.
He shall be afflicted by disease and impoverished in birth after birth.
Therefore, what more subtle point can we say now in this supreme crisis?
Having considered the dharma of both [parties], I tell you: provide protection. 48–49.
"Protect the fruit of your fast, O King, by drinking the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet. Having quickly drunk that water, even eating [forbidden food] becomes as if not eaten.
Having spoken thus, O great sage, the son of Brahmā ceased speaking.
Remembering the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, he drank a little of that water.
In the meantime, O Brahman, the lord of sages arrived;
the omniscient one, out of anger, tore out his own matted hair before the king.
Then, O Indra among kings, a man resembling a flame of fire rose up swiftly;
with sword in hand and most terrifying, he was intent on slaying the king.
And Hari beheld that [demon], who possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns, as he held his discus.
He cut down the Kṛtyā-puruṣa who was intent on slaying the Brāhmaṇa.
Seeing Sudarśana, the Brāhmaṇa fled, overwhelmed by fear;
subsequently, the twice-born one beheld him resembling a blazing crest of fire.
Having traversed the entire cosmic egg, he became despondent and overwhelmed with great fear;
considering him to be the Lord of the World, he went to Brahmā for refuge.
Crying out, "Save me! Save me! he entered the assembly hall of Brahmā. (56)

Having risen, Brahmā asked the lord of sages, "O Muni, is all well? He related the entire account from its very beginning to Brahmā. Having heard it, Brahmā sighed and, overwhelmed with fear, spoke to him.
Brahmā said:
O child, by whose power have you gone to curse a servant of Hari?
He who is protected by the Blessed Lord—who in the three worlds could slay him? (59)

Śrī Hari, who is affectionate toward his devotees, constantly protects the discus for the sake of guarding both small and great devotees. O twice-born one, he who is a fool and hates a Vaiṣṇava— who is as dear to Viṣṇu as his own life— [is destroyed].
Hari, the Lord, is capable of destroying even the one who brings about his own destruction.
"O child, go quickly to another place; there is no protection for you now.
Otherwise, the Sudarśana discus will slay you along with me. (61-62)
"What is this that is capable of burning the world of Brahmā and the cosmic egg in an instant?
Since its splendor is equal to that of Viṣṇu, by whom else can it be warded off?
Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Brāhmaṇa then fled.
Terrified, he went to Kailāsa and sought refuge with Śaṅkara out of fear.
Out of fear, he said to Śaṅkara, "O treasure-house of compassion, protect me!
The omniscient Śiva did not inquire after the welfare of the brahmin.
The destroyer of the worlds in an instant, the Lord of the most wretched among the wretched, said:
"Be firm, O best of the twice-born; listen to my words.
Śaṅkara said:
"O sage, you are the grandson of the Creator of the worlds and the son of Atri;
you are a knower of the Vedas and omniscient, yet your action is like that of a fool.
For nowhere—in the Vedas, in the Purāṇas, nor in the Itihāsas—is such a deed found anywhere. (67)
Though he has been described as the Lord of all, you do not know him like a fool.
I, Brahmā, Indra, the Ādityas, and likewise the Vasus; Dharma and Indra, all the gods, the lords of sages, and likewise the Manus—[all these are subordinate to him]. (68–69)
By whose mere playful knitting of the eyebrows [the worlds] appear and disappear—
by whose power do you slay that devotee who is dearer to him than life?
I, Brahmā, Kamalā, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Rādhikā [are all subject to his will].
For there are no devotees superior to those who love with pure affection, and such devotees are dear to Him in every way.
(71) The Lord, the inner self of all, constantly protects both small and great devotees with diligent effort, by means of His unbearable discus. (72)
Having yoked his irresistible wheel, which was equal to himself in splendor, he nevertheless did not perceive [the danger] and went forth to protect [them] himself;
yet, upon hearing the names of his own virtues, he was overcome with great agitation. (73)

Hari is always present in the company of His devotees, like a shadow; indeed, there is no one dearer to Him than His beloved devotee, who is more precious to Him than His own life. Yet, if she herself hates His devotees, the Lord quickly abandons her.
O twice-born one, Brahmins are dear to all, even more so than their own bodies.
Devotees are dearer to Hari than the Brahmins and even dearer than his own life-breaths.
Who, indeed, in the three worlds, is dear or who is not dear to the Lord? (76)
One should constantly and perpetually worship and meditate upon Him who remains.
O Brahmā, during the great dissolution when the multitude of cosmic eggs is submerged in water, there shall be no destruction for any of His devotees. (77–78)
Worship Govinda, O Brāhmaṇa; remember his lotus feet.
All calamities perish even from the remembrance of Śrī Hari.
Go quickly to Vaikuṇṭha; Vaikuṇṭha is your refuge.
"The Lord, an ocean of compassion, will surely grant you fearlessness.
In the meantime, Kailāsa was pervaded by the splendor of the discus,
just as the surface of the earth is brilliantly illuminated by the rays of the sun.
All the inhabitants of Kailāsa were scorched by the terrifying flames;
crying out, "Save us! Save us! they sought refuge in Śaṅkara.
Seeing that unbearable discus, Śaṅkara, the ocean of compassion, [acted].
With great affection, he bestowed a blessing upon the Brahmin along with Pārvatī:
"If splendor, truth, and austerity have been long accumulated, then let this twice-born man, though he has committed an offense and is afraid, be free from his distress. (83–84)
Pārvatī said:
Since my Lord, a Brāhmaṇa who has sought refuge, has come to my meritorious lands, may he quickly be freed from his fever by my blessing and great fear [of him]. 85.
Having spoken thus, Śivā ceased out of compassion;
Śiva, the lord of gods, bowed and went for refuge to Vaikuṇṭha.
Having reached the abode of Vaikuṇṭha by means of his mind, the lord of sages departed.
Having beheld Sudarśana, he subsequently entered the inner apartments of Hari.
There the brahmin saw the supreme Śrī Hari seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and clad in yellow garments.
Dark-complexioned, four-armed, peaceful, the beloved of Lakṣmī, and captivating;
richly adorned with the splendor of jewel-ornaments and decorated with a garland of gems;
his face bright with a gentle smile, he is intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees. (89)
His crown was radiant with its crest fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems;
he was served by the foremost among the great attendants with white yak-tail whisks;
his lotus-feet were worshipped by Lakṣmī, and he was praised before him by Sarasvatī; he was surrounded by Sunanda, Nanda, Kumuda, Pracaṇḍa, and others.

Seeing the Lord in such a state— singing praises of His qualities through musical instruments and beholding his desired object— he prostrated himself like a staff and offered hymns of praise to the Supreme Lord with a chant from the Sāmaveda.
Durvāsas said:
"Save me, O Beloved of Kamalā! Save me, O Treasure of Compassion!
O Friend of the Wretched, O Lord of the Most Forlorn, O Ocean of Mercy, O Master! (94)
O creator of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, O ordainer who art yourself the Ordainer;
O death of death, O death of time, save me from this ocean of distress!
You are the dissolution of the Dissolver, the Lord of all, and the Cause of all.
O seed of the great Viṣṇu-tree, protect me in the ocean of worldly existence!
O you who are solely devoted to rescuing those who have come for refuge from grief, affliction, and fear;
O Blessed One, save me, who am terrified; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you!

That primordial reality which exists within the Vedas, even the Vedas themselves are not capable of praising; Sarasvatī herself has become speechless—how then can the learned praise it? Śeṣa, with his thousand mouths, would fall into a state of stupor in attempting to praise it. (97)
The five-faced one has become stunned, and the four-faced one has become stunned.
(99) If the Vedas, the authors of the Smṛtis, and even Speech itself are unable to praise You, who am I—a Brahmin learned in the Vedas and Your disciple—to offer praise, O Giver of Honor? (100)
When twenty-eight cycles of Manus and Mahendras have passed,
for that Creator whose lifespan is one hundred and eight days and nights,
his fall occurs at the mere opening of his eyes.
"What am I to praise, O Lord, who am inexpressible? Protect me!
Having offered this hymn of praise, he fell at the lotus-feet [of the Lord], overwhelmed by fear, and drenched them with the water from his lotus-eyes.
This hymn to Hari, the Supreme Soul, composed by Durvāsas,
bestows merit, is proclaimed in the Sāmaveda, and is named "The Auspiciousness of the World.
Whoever, though beset by distress, recites it with devotion and self-restraint—
Nārāyaṇa, having arrived swiftly out of compassion, protects him [in these places]:
at the king’s gate, in the cremation ground, in a prison filled with fear, when overwhelmed by enemies, in terror of bandits, and in the presence of violent beasts. (105–106)

When surrounded by the king’s army and when the ship has sunk in the great ocean, one is liberated merely by the recollection of this hymn; there is no doubt in this matter. (107) Thus ends the Śrīkṛṣṇastotra composed by Durvāsas in the Śrībrahmavaivarta [Purāṇa].
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the sage’s hymn of praise, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, smiled and spoke sweetly with joy, like a shower of nectar. 108.
The Blessed One said:
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you through my boon.
However, always listen to my words, which are true and bring happiness. (109)
And others may gain knowledge by hearing the scriptures from the mouths of the virtuous;
for the virtuous indeed move about as the scriptures incarnate.
Furthermore, any action contrary to the Vedas is utterly despised by all.
If a wise person acts after having known this, he is superior even to one who is dead while living.
O Brāhmaṇa, the greatness of the Vaiṣṇavas has been heard by everyone everywhere in the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and the Itihāsas. (111–112)
I am indeed the life-breath of the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Vaiṣṇavas are my life-breaths. That fool who hates them is indeed a destroyer of my own life-breaths.
Having abandoned sons, grandsons, wife, kingdom, and prosperity— ||| 113 || |||

To those who constantly meditate upon me, who is dearer to me than they? My life-breaths, nor Lakṣmī, nor Śaṅkara, nor Bhāratī, nor Brahmā, nor Durgā, nor Gaṇeśvara are more beloved to me than my devotees. (114–115)
There are no Brahmins, nor Vedas, nor the Supreme Mother of the Vedas;
there are no cowherd girls, nor cowherds, nor Rādhā, who is dear to the one who bows down.
Thus has everything been told—truthful, essential, and real.

They do not seek praise for these [virtues], and they hold them dearer than their own lives. Those fools who hate me—deprived of knowledge, deceived, and ignorant of the Self—they go to hell for a long time. (117–118)
Those who hate my devotees, who are dearer to me than life itself—
for them I am the swift punisher in the hereafter, consigning them to hell for a long time.
I am the sovereign power of all, the Lord, and the protector.
I am neither all-pervading nor independent; day and night, I am subservient to my devotees.
Whether in Goloka or Vaikuṇṭha, this form—be it two-armed or four-armed—is merely my outward appearance; in the presence of my devotee, my very life-breath resides.
As it has been said: "Whatever is given by a devotee is to be consumed by me;
even food unfit for consumption, if given by another, is like nectar.
[To him spoke] Ambarīṣa, the best of kings, who was free from desire and non-violent.
"How can you kill one who is compassionate by nature and devoted to the welfare of all living beings?
Those virtuous ones who constantly show compassion toward all creatures—those fools who hate them, I myself shall be their slayer. (123–124)
"I am unable to protect you from this enemy who harms my devotees.
Go to the abode of Ambarīṣa; he is capable of protecting you.
Nārāyaṇa said: [125]

Having heard these words, the Brāhmaṇa, overwhelmed by fear and dejected in mind, stood there remembering the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. In the meantime, Brahmā and Śaṅkara, together with Bhavānī, [arrived].
O best of sages, Dharma, Indra, and the other gods arrived;
having prostrated before the Supreme Soul, the Lord, they all offered praise with their entire bodies covered in horripilation and their necks bowed in devotion. (127–128)
Brahmā said: O You whose own nature is untainted, O You who are eager to bestow grace upon Your devotees, protect this preeminent Brāhmaṇa who has committed an offense against Your devotee. 129.
Mahādeva said:
O Friend of the Wretched, Lord of the World, this brahmin is not outside the universe.
Protect him, who has committed an offense, who is miserable, and who has come to you for refuge. 130.
Pārvatī said:
"Ambārīṣa is indeed your devotee; neither the twice-born, nor we gods, are so.
You are the lord of all; therefore, protect this brahmin who has committed an offense. (131)
Dharma said:
"O Lord, you are the progenitor of all, their protector, and the sovereign who wields the rod of punishment.
How can it be that a father kills his own child for the sake of a child? (132)
Indra said:
O Lord, you who possess constant compassion and equanimity toward all living beings, it behoves you now to drink this which has become the fruit of my transgression. (133)
Rudra said:
It is now appropriate for you to perform what is fitting to bring about peace;
you ought to protect the root that has been firmly established. (134)
The Guardian of the Quarter said:
"It is not heard in the Śruti that you ought to punish a Brahmin who has committed an offense;
rather, the True Lord always protects him after having pacified the offense. (135)
The planets said:
"O fool, all the gods are enraged with him who hates a Vaiṣṇava.
We shall constantly inflict suffering upon him; you ought to protect him afterwards. (136)
The sages said:
"O Lord, when a brahmin has been defeated, we are all as good as dead.
To inflict punishment upon a single individual would bring shame among our own kind. (137)
Atri said:
"By you alone was this son given to me—one who is wrathful yet always devoted to your service.
Possessed of your own splendor, he does not fear anyone in the three worlds. (138)
Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, forgive the offense; the Brahmin has come to you for refuge.
O God, the twice-born praise the Brahmins; you ought not to kill a Brahmin. (139)
Sarasvatī said:
"I shall inform the Lord of the gods, the progenitor who grants desires according to the Vedas.
O Blessed One, you are the master of all; it behooves you to protect us all. (140)
The attendants said:
"By the mere remembrance of you, there shall be all auspiciousness for everyone; all calamities depart. Protect this one who has come to you for refuge. (141)
The dancers said:
"O destroyer of poverty, we are your perpetual beggars;
now grant us alms and provide protection for this twice-born man. (142)
Having heard their hymn of praise, the Lord, who is compassionate toward those seeking refuge,
smiled and spoke these words that cause the satisfaction of all. The Blessed One said:
"Listen all to my words, which are endowed with wisdom and bring about happiness:
by your command, I shall certainly provide protection for the Brahmins.
However, let this man go from Vaikuṇṭha back to the abode of Ambarīṣa."

"Let the sage perform his meal-breakfast there for the great pleasure of the king. (145) A certain Brahmin, having become his guest, was intent on pronouncing a curse upon him. But Sudarśana, protecting that Brahmin who was intent on killing him— (146)
Frightened, he wandered the earth joyfully for a full year.
That king of kings, along with his wife, was filled with grief while observing the fast.
Then I too observed the fast, for the sake of my devotee’s fasting.
Just as a mother does not eat upon seeing her infant son who is still nursing at her breast, so too,
by my blessing, O best of sages, may he be instantly freed from his fever; moreover,
my discus shall not inflict any injury upon him on that path.
"Today, I am surely free from anxiety and shall enjoy happiness;
for whatever substance is given by a devotee out of affection, having made it like nectar, that I may enjoy.
But as for the wealth given by Lakṣmī, I am not the master to enjoy it. (150)
"Without the offering of food, the Lord is not able to grant satisfaction.
(151) "O Lord of Sages, O one of great wisdom, go, my child, to the king's palace.
Let all the gods and goddesses, as well as the sages, go to the house. (152)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari quickly went joyfully to his inner apartments.
All, filled with joy, bowed to the Lord of the Universe and departed.
And the Brahmin, traveling as fast as thought, went to the king’s palace.
And that Sudarśana discus possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Having fasted for a year until his throat, lips, and palate were parched, the king,
seated upon his throne, beheld the preeminent sage before him.
Rising immediately in great haste, he bowed with reverence and joy;
having fed the Brahmin with sweet food, he himself ate.
Having eaten, the best of the twice-born was satisfied and bestowed a supreme blessing.
He went quickly to his own abode and praised [it] again and again.
On the way, the best of brahmins, his mind overwhelmed with wonder, spoke:
"Oh, how difficult it is to attain the majesty of the Vaiṣṇavas! thus said the twice-born one.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Liberation of the Sages," in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
O Sage, the fault incurred by the transgression of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) has been heard from your mouth.
"The defeat of the sage, as well as the protection of the king by Hari—oh!
Now I desire to hear that which is wished for by all;
tell me with certainty the procedure for this Ekādaśī vow. (1–2)
"Aha! Something has been heard by me in the Vedas, yet it remains uncertain due to differences of opinion.
I have a great curiosity to hear the cause of the Vedas from your own mouth.
Nārāyaṇa said:
This Ekādaśī vow is difficult even for the gods to attain;
it is the most excellent austerity among ascetics, generating supreme delight for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Just as Kṛṣṇa is to the gods, and just as Prakṛti is to the goddesses.
As the Brahmin is among the stages of life, as Śiva is among the Vaiṣṇavas;
as Gaṇeśa is among those worthy of worship, as Vāṇī is among the learned;
as the Vedas are among the scriptures, and as the Jāhnavī is among the sacred fords. (5–6)
Just as gold is among luminous things, as a Vaiṣṇava is among living beings,
as knowledge is among riches, and as a beloved wife is among those who possess attachments;
just as Rudra is among the Pramathas, and as the intellect is among all that is auspicious.
As the self is to the senses, as the mind is to the flickering faculties;
as a mother is to the wives of one's elders, as a husband is to his kinsmen;
as destiny is to the powerful, and as time is to those who measure all things—so [is he]. (8–9)
O Sage, just as good character is to friends, and disease is to enemies;
just as fame is to those who possess it, and a home is to householders;
and just as a rogue is to the violent, and a harlot is to the wicked. (10)
He is the lord of luminaries among the radiant, and the earth among those who endure;
he is nectar among things to be consumed, and fire among those that burn;
he is Śrī among the givers of wealth, and Satī among virtuous women. (11–12)
Just as Brahmā is among the lords of creatures, as the ocean is among rivers, as the Sāman is among the Vedas, and as Gāyatrī is among meters;
as the Aśvattha is among trees, and as Tulasī is among flowers. (13)
Just as the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is among months, and as Madhu is among the seasons;
as Sūrya is among the Ādityas, and as Śaṅkara is among the Rudras;
as Bhīṣma is among the Vasus, and as the Bhārata is among the [epic] ages, O Bhārata. (14–15)
Just as you are among the celestial seers, and as Bhṛgu is among the Brahman-seers;
as Rāma is among kings, and as Kapila is among the Siddhas;
and as Sanatkumāra is the foremost among yogis and the wise. (16)

As Airāvata is among the lordly elephants, as the Śarabha is among beasts, as the Himālaya is among mountains, as the Kaustubha is among gems, and as the Sarasvatī is among rivers by virtue of her meritorious nature; (so is she). 17–18.
Just as Citraratha is the foremost among the Gandharvas and Nārada is the best,
just as Kubera is among the Yakṣas and Sumālī among the Rākṣasas,
so too is Śatarūpā the most excellent and supreme among women.
Just as Svāyambhuva Manu himself is the foremost among Manus,
just as Rambhā is the foremost among beautiful women, and just as Māyā is the foremost among those possessed of power,
so too is this Ekādaśī vow the best among all vows.
And this must always be performed by the four castes,
especially by ascetics, Vaiṣṇavas, and Brāhmaṇas;
for truth [destroys] all sins, including even the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.

Indeed, there are [these sins] depending upon boiled rice on the day of the vow of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. That dull-witted person who, having eaten these sinful things, eats [rice] on that day, becomes a great sinner even here and certainly goes to hell in the end. (23–24)
Those who disregard the authoritative rules for Ekādaśī established according to the number of Yugas shall dwell in the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell and then fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla;
thereafter, for seven births, they shall be afflicted with wasting diseases.
"Afterwards, one shall be liberated from sin," so said the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Thus has been told, O Brahmin, whatever fault there is in that eating;
and the fault in transgressing the Dvādaśī has also been heard as previously declared by me.
Listen as I tell you the fault in transgressing the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*);
it was heard by me in the past from the mouth of Dharma, and is the very essence extracted from the Vedas.
That fool who, out of ignorance, should transgress even a single sixteenth part (*kalā*) of the tenth day— [incurs great sin].
Fortune departs swiftly from that house after pronouncing a terrible curse.
In this world, there will certainly be the destruction of his lineage and the loss of his fame.
At the end, O twice-born one, he shall dwell in a blind well for a hundred manvantaras.
On whichever day the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth lunar day occurs,
one should eat on that day, fast on the following day, and perform the vow;
having performed the vow on the twelfth day, one should break the fast on the thirteenth day.

For those observing the vow, there is no fault in transgressing the twelfth day [of the lunar fortnight]. Where the eleventh day is complete and at dawn it is only slightly [longer], one should fast on that [eleventh] day; and the second [day] is also [to be observed] if the following [eleventh] increases in length. || 32-33 ||
Where, at dawn, three lunar days (tithis) exist for sixty *daṇḍas*,
householders perform the fast first, as do ascetics (*yati*) and others;
having observed the fast on the following day, one should perform the daily obligatory rites (*nityakṛtya*).
The wise person should perform the entire vigil for the vow on the preceding day itself.

Having performed the daily rites on that previous day for the vow, one should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the following day, once the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) has passed. (35–36)
For Vaiṣṇavas, ascetics, widows,
mendicants, and likewise for celibate students, all [of these days] are to be observed as fasts. However, householders who are not Vaiṣṇavas observe only the bright fortnight (śukla).

O Nārada, there is no fault for them in transgressing the dark fortnight (the *kṛṣṇa* Ekādaśī) according to the Vedas. That Ekādaśī which falls in the interval between the *Śayanī* and *Bodhinī* [Ekādaśīs] and is of the dark fortnight— only that one should be observed as a fast by a householder, never any other dark Ekādaśī.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this decision been declared as heard in the Śruti.
Now listen to the procedure for this vow; I shall describe it to you.
Having prepared the sacrificial food (haviṣya) in the forenoon, one does not eat again, nor does one drink water.
Alone, one should sleep at night upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
(41) Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed the morning duties, and having then completed the daily obligatory rites, one should thereafter perform the ritual bath. (42)
Having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the vow and fast with the intent of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and having performed the twilight prayers (sandhyā) and libations (tarpaṇa), one should carry out the daily rites (āhnika).
Having performed the regular worship (nityapūjā) during the day, one should gather the materials required for the vow.
Having performed the sixteen-fold service as prescribed by the revealed injunctions:
(44) a seat, clothing, water for the feet, the arghya offering, flowers, unguents, incense, a lamp, food offerings, a sacrificial thread, and ornaments; (45)
Having brought together perfume, bath-powder, betel, honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water again,
one should perform the vow at night during the day;
having purified oneself by sitting upon a seat and wearing two washed garments.
Having sipped water for purification and bowed to Śrī Hari, one should perform the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana).

At an auspicious moment, having placed the auspicious jar— smeared with fruits, twigs, and sandalwood paste— upon a beautiful base of grain, [one should act] according to the Vedic injunctions and with joy as prescribed by the sages.
Having invoked the group of six deities, the wise practitioner should perform the worship with separate grains and with the five excellent offerings:
Gaṇeśvara, Dinakara, Vahni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā.
Having worshipped and bowed down to these, one should then perform the vow while remembering Hari.
(50) If one performs any rite—whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—without having first propitiated the group of six deities, all of it shall be fruitless. (51)
Thus everything has been told, including that which constitutes the constituent parts of the vow as declared in the Kaṇva recension. O great sage, hear now the desired vow;
having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme, according to the meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda.
Having placed a flower upon his head, he should again practice meditation.
Listen to this secret meditation, which is desired by all;
it must not be revealed to one who is not a devotee, for it is supreme and dearer than life to a devotee. 93–94.
His body was as dark and beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud; his unsurpassed face possessed the splendor of the full autumnal moon;
and his eyes released the radiance of the lotuses that bloom at sunrise in autumn. (55)
Adorned with jewel ornaments that surpassed the splendor of his own limbs' beauty,
he was constantly beheld by the corners of the cowherd girls' eyes— eyes that were both gracious and highly suggestive— as if he were fashioned from their very life-breaths. (56–57)
Standing in the center of the *rāsa*-circle, eager for the joy of the *rāsa* dance; like a *cakora* bird drinking the nectar of the autumn moon that is Rādhā’s face;
His chest made radiant by the Kaustubha, the king of jewels;
and resplendent with clusters of garlands of *pārijāta* flowers. (58–59)
Adorned with a crown of blazing crest-jewels fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems,
his hand rests upon a flute held for his own delight; he is worshiped by gods and asuras alike,
unattainable through meditation, difficult to propitiate, and saluted even by Brahmā and the other deities.

I worship that Lord who is the cause of all causes. O Nārada, having meditated upon Him with this [mantra] and having invoked Him, one should offer the sixteen types of oblations and worship Him with devotion using these mantras.
"O Supreme Lord, please accept this seat made of gold, adorned with the finest jewels, and enriched with various wonderful patterns;
as well as this garment, purified by fire and fashioned by Viśvakarman. (63)
O Lord of Rādhikā, please accept this which is beyond all price.
O ocean of compassion, please accept this fragrant, cool water, fit for washing the feet, contained in a golden vessel. 64–65.
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, please accept this pure arghya, accompanied by water from a conch shell, anointed with flowers, dūrvā grass, and sandalwood.
It is beautifully scented, consisting of white flowers, sandalwood, and aguru."
"O cause of all things, accept this which immediately produces joy! O Kṛṣṇa, accept this excellent sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, and uśīra—this unguent desired by everyone.
It is the essence of a particular tree, blended with various substances."
"May this incense, endowed with fragrance and bestowing happiness, be accepted.
May this lamp, brilliantly shining day and night, fashioned from the essence of jewels, and the seed for the destruction of darkness, be accepted once again. (69-70)
"O one who delights in your own self, please accept these various kinds of pure substances— sweet and fragrant, such as things to be sucked and so forth—
and this [thread] made of golden fibers, joined with the *sāvitrī* knot. (71)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, please accept this beautiful necklace fashioned by my hand;
O delighter of Nanda, please accept these ornaments for all the limbs, set with priceless jewels and blazing with luster. (72-73)
The foremost and most worthy of description in all auspicious rites—
O Friend of the Wretched, please accept this fragrance that bestows blessings.
[74] This captivating Viṣṇu-oil, produced from the leaves of the *dhātrī* and *śrīphala* trees, is here.

O Blessed One, please accept that which is desired by all the worlds. O Lord, please accept this betel-leaf offered by me, which is desirable to all and beautifully scented with camphor and other fragrances.
O Beloved of the Gopīs, please accept this most delicious, sweet honey that brings joy to all, contained within a vessel made of the finest jewels;
as well as the pure, most sacred, and fragrant water of the Jāhnavī. (77)
"O Madhusūdana, please accept this water for sipping once more.
Having thus offered the sixteen services with joyful devotion,
the devotee should diligently offer flowers and garlands while reciting this mantra.
"O Lord, please accept this garland, the most excellent of ornaments, strung with white thread and composed of various kinds of flowers.
Thus the practitioner, observing the vow, should offer a handful of flowers while reciting the root mantra.
The wise devotee, with palms joined in *añjali*, should offer that praise with devotion:
The devotee said:
O Kṛṣṇa! O Lord of Rādhikā! O Master, ocean of compassion!
Rescue me from the terrible and fearsome ocean of saṃsāra!
O Lord, grant liberation to me, who am distressed by the exhaustion of hundreds of births and bound by the shackles of the noose of my own karma.
Behold me, who have come to you for refuge, prostrate at your lotus feet.
Protect me, who have come to you for refuge, terrified by the fear of the bonds of worldly existence.
[I am] devoid of devotion, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of the Vedic injunctions.
O Lord, make that which is devoid of the *vastu-mantra* complete;
O Hari, even when a rite is deficient in its constituent parts due to ignorance regarding the injunctions prescribed in the Vedas,
everything shall become complete merely by the utterance of Your name.
Having thus praised and bowed to him, and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇa,
the observer of the vow should then hold a great festival and perform a vigil.
If, after performing the vow and fasting, one indulges in sleep, [the merit is lost].

Furthermore, he should consume water and shall obtain half the fruit of the vow. O best of Brahmins, with effort he should partake of *haviṣya* food only once, while reciting this mantra and remembering the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (88–89)
"Indeed, food is the life-force of living beings, created by Brahmā in ancient times.
O you who possess the form of Viṣṇu, grant me the fruit of my vows and fasts.
He who thus performs this supreme vow with devotion in Bhārata—

One will certainly uplift seven ancestors and seven descendants, as well as oneself. A man will surely uplift his mother, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, daughter, son-in-law, and servant. (91–92)

Thus has been told, O Brahmin, the vow concerning the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. It bestows happiness and liberation; it is the essence. Now I shall tell you something else. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ekādaśī Vow," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate once more the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the stealing of the gopīs' garments and the granting of their desired boons. 1.
In the first month of the winter season, the cowherd women, deluded by desire,
prepared sacrificial food with devotion for the entire month;
having bathed on the bank of the Yamunā, they fashioned an image of Pārvatī made of sand.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and invoked [the deity] with the mantra, they perform worship constantly (3).
With charming sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
and with various kinds of flowers as well as many sorts of garlands (4).
With incenses, lamps, food offerings, garments, and various fruits, O Sage;
with gems, pearls, corals, and also with various kinds of musical instruments— [I worship you],
O Goddess, Mother of the worlds, who brings about the creation, preservation, and end [of the universe].
"O lady of virtuous vows, grant us the beloved son of Nandagopa.
Having performed the ritual dismissal with this mantra, O Goddess of the Gods,
and having then made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should worship her with the root mantra.
The mantra, as declared in the Sāmaveda, is fresh and accompanied by its seed-syllable:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the illustrious Durgā, the destroyer of all obstacles.
(8) [One should offer] flowers, garlands, food offerings, incense, and likewise auspicious lamps.

With this mantra and with devotion, they all, filled with joy, gave [the gift]. (9) Having performed the recitation of this mantra a thousand times with devotion using a garland of coral, and having offered praise, they prostrated themselves on the ground with their heads. (10)
"O auspicious one, most auspicious among all that is auspicious, O Śivā, bestower of all desires!
Grant me my wish, O Goddess; salutations to you, the beloved of Śaṃkara.
Having spoken thus, he performed prostration and gave the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
And all the food offerings went to the houses of the Brāhmaṇas.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, listen to the King of Hymns (Stavarāja) with which they praised Pārvatī.
Out of devotion, all the cowherd women [worshipped her], who bestows the fruit of all desires.
(13) When the world was a single, terrible ocean, devoid of Rudra and the Sun,
and when all moving and non-moving beings were submerged in water as dark as collyrium, (14)
In ancient times, this was given to Brahmā by Hari while reclining upon the waters.
Having bestowed all this upon him, the Lord of the Universe entered into sleep.
Within the lotus of his navel, the Creator of the World [was born], along with Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Afflicted, he offered praise to the Sovereign Primordial Nature (Mūlaprakṛti).
Brahmā said:
"O Durgā! O Śivā! O Abhayā! O Māyā! O Nārāyaṇī! O Sanātanī!"
"O Victorious One, grant me auspiciousness; salutations to you, O Sarvamaṅgalā!
The syllable *da* is proclaimed to signify the destruction of the Daityas;
the syllable *u* is the signifier for the destruction of obstacles, as sanctioned by the Vedas. (17–18)

The letter *ra* signifies the destruction of disease, and *ga* signifies the destruction of sin; the letter *a* is proclaimed to signify the destruction of fear and enemies. By the mere recollection of her name, these [afflictions] are certainly destroyed. (19)
Therefore, Durgā is proclaimed by Hari as the power (śakti) of Hari.
The word *durga* signifies adversity, and the letter *a* signifies destruction;
she who eternally destroys adversity (*durga*) is proclaimed as Durgā. (20–21)
The syllable *duḥ* signifies the lord of the Daityas, while the syllable *gā* denotes destruction.
Because she destroyed him in ancient times, she is proclaimed as Durgā by the wise.
Furthermore, the syllable *śa* signifies auspiciousness, and the syllable *ī* denotes excellence.
The syllable *va* denotes a collection, and the syllable *ka* denotes a giver.
Therefore, Śivā is proclaimed as the bestower of the most excellent assembly [of auspicious qualities].
Because she is the personified mass of auspiciousness, she is therefore proclaimed as Śivā. (23–24)
For the syllable *śi* signifies liberation (*mokṣa*), and the syllable *va* signifies the giver;
she who herself bestows nirvāṇa is celebrated as Śivā.
The syllable *a* signifies fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the destruction of fear, and it signifies the giver. 25.
She who immediately bestows fearlessness is celebrated as Abhayā (Fearlessness).
The word *mā* denotes sovereignty (*rājyaśrī*), and *yā* signifies leading (*prāpaṇa*).
She who immediately leads one to that [sovereignty] is celebrated as Māyā.
The word *mā* signifies liberation (*mokṣa*), and the word *yā* denotes leading (*prāpaṇa*).
That which constantly leads one [to that liberation] is proclaimed as *māyā*.
She is the half-body of Nārāyaṇa and is equal to him in splendor.
Because she always resides within his body, she is remembered as Nārāyaṇī;
she is the eternal designator of the one who is beyond qualities (nirguṇa) and eternal.
She who is proclaimed to be eternally constant, beyond qualities, and ancient is the Sanātanī.

The word *jaya* signifies auspiciousness, and the syllable *yā* denotes a giver. She who constantly bestows victory (*jaya*) is celebrated as *Jayā*. Furthermore, the word *sarva* is auspicious and denotes complete sovereignty. (31)
The letter *Ā* is the word for "giver," and she who gives that is Sarvamaṅgalā.
This eightfold name is the essence, endowed with a thousand meanings of the names;
it was given by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā within the lotus of his navel. (32–33)
Having given that to him, the Lord of the worlds fell asleep.
Then Madhu and Kaiṭabha, intent on killing Brahmā and Durgā, approached;
and Brahmā, having bowed down, offered this hymn of praise.
Then Durgā, being directly praised, gave the armor to Brahmā—(35)—the divine armor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, named "The Protector of All. Having given it to him, that Mahāmāyā indeed vanished from sight. (36)
They performed a hymn of praise while guarding their sleep with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
By the grace of that sleep and by the power of the hymn itself,
the Blessed Lord Janārdana arrived there in the form of a bull.
Together with Śakti and Durgā, for the sake of Śaṅkara’s victory,
Jayā placed Śaṅkara along with his chariot upon her head and granted him fearlessness;
she raised him very high and bestowed victory upon him.
By the power of this hymn alone, Brahmā obtained the armor;
and having obtained the excellent armor, he certainly attained fearlessness.
Brahmā gave this supreme hymn and the armor to Maheśa.
And in the battle with Tripura, when Hara’s charioteer had fallen and Hari [Viṣṇu] was unconscious, Hara took up the Brahmā-weapon while remembering Śrī Hari;
and having obtained the hymn and the armor, he destroyed Tripura. (41–42)
By means of this hymn of praise, having offered worship to Durgā,
the cowherd girls obtained Śrī Hari as their beloved through the power of this stotra.
This hymn composed by the cowherd girls is named *Sarvamaṅgala*.
It immediately bestows desired objects and destroys all obstacles.
(44) That person—whether a devotee of Śiva, Viṣṇu, or Śakti—who daily recites this at the three junctions of the day with devotion, is liberated from distress. (45)
At the king's gate, in a cremation ground, in a forest fire, or in a life-threatening crisis;
when seized by the fear of predatory beasts, or sinking in a great ocean with one's boat;
when overwhelmed by enemies in battle, or fallen into the misfortune of prison. (46)
In the event of a curse from a guru, a curse from a Brahmin, or an insurmountable rift among kinsmen;
when one has fallen from their station, fallen from wealth, or fallen from their caste, and is overwhelmed by grief;
when there is a separation from a husband, a separation from a son, or when one is afflicted by the poison of a wicked man or a serpent—(in these circumstances, one should seek refuge). 47–48.
Merely by remembering this hymn of praise, one is immediately liberated and becomes fearless;
one instantly obtains whatever is desired, as well as unsurpassed sovereignty over all things, and firm devotion to Hari in this world along with constant mindfulness of Him. (49)
"And by the grace of Pārvatī, he obtains service [at her feet] at the end.
(50) Thus ends the *Sarvamaṅgalā-stotra* composed by the cowherd girls in the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
By means of this king of hymns, they constantly praised the Goddess.

For as long as a month, the women of Vraja prostrated themselves with supreme devotion. (51) When the month was thus complete, on the day of its conclusion, the gopīs went to bathe, having placed their garments upon that bank. (52)
O Nārada, there were various kinds of substances of jewel-like value— yellow, red, white, beautiful, and variegated—
which covered the banks in countless numbers, making the shore exceedingly splendid.
Fragranced by the wind with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk;
adorned with various kinds of food offerings, fruits produced in specific seasons and regions, incense, lamps, vermilion, and saffron. (54–55)
Out of curiosity, the gopīs became intent on playing in the water;
naked and absorbed in their sports, their minds were entirely fixed upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
And Kṛṣṇa, seeing their garments and various belongings, [took them].
Taking the garments and other articles, he ate them together with the children.
Having gone a great distance, all the cowherds stood there filled with joy.
First, having gathered the clothes into a heap, they placed it upon their shoulders, being exceedingly greedy for them.
Śrīdāmā, Sudāmā, and likewise Vasudāmā; Subala, Supārśva, Śubhāṅga, and Sundara;
Candrabhānu, Vīrabhānu, and likewise Sūryabhānu.
Vasubhānu, Ratnabhānu, and Gopāla are remembered as the twelve;
Śrīkṛṣṇa and Baladeva are the fourteen principal ones.
O Sage, the cowherds who were the companions of Hari numbered in the tens of millions.
Taking up their garments, they all stood together at a distance;
there, by the hundreds, they formed heaps with their faces turned upward.
Having joyfully gathered some cloth and made a heap, they remained there.
Having ascended to the top of a Kadamba tree, Hari spoke to the Gopikās.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O all you cowherd girls, you have failed in the performance of your vow."

"Having heard my words, perform the ritual and sport according to the dictates of love. When the month suitable for the vow has arrived and the auspicious rite is prepared, how can you remain naked in the water, thereby causing the failure of the vow's essential components? (64–65)
"By whom have your wrap-around garments, the flower garlands, and all those articles required for the vow been taken away just now?
(66) As for her who bathes naked during the vow, Varuṇa himself became enraged; his attendants then carried off her clothes and belongings. (67)
"How will you go about naked, and how will your vow not be violated? How can she, who is to be propitiated by your vow, fail to protect these objects?
Thinking thus, Bali praised that venerable Goddess.
Such a goddess as yours is not capable of protecting you;
how could that Queen of the Gods be capable of granting the fruit of your vow?
She who is capable of bestowing the fruit is capable of every action. (69–70)
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the women of Vraja fell into deep anxiety.
They saw the bank of the Yamunā stripped of its clothes and belongings;
they were filled with despair at the sight of the water and, being naked, they wept bitterly.
"Where have our clothes and belongings gone? they asked us there.
Feeling dejected, all those cowherd girls, with palms joined in *añjali* and full of devotion and humility, spoke to him right then and there. (72–73)
The cowherd girls said: "O Lord, these garments are for your maidservants; please know this yourself, for you ought to touch them. (74)
O knower of the Vedas, it is now appropriate for us to take those articles fit for the vow which belong to the gods, even if they have not been given and were previously taken back;
having worn these washed garments, we shall perform the vow. (75)
"O Govinda, consume other objects with [this] object!
In the meantime, Śrīdāmā showed them a bundle of clothes and ran far ahead of them.
Seeing the cowherd boy clothed, the supreme sovereign of them all, Śrī Rādhikā—
drenched in water and filled with anger— spoke to all her companions.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Suśīlā, O Śaśikalā, O Candramukhī, O Mādhavī;
O Kadambamālā, O Kuntī, O Yamunā, O Sarvamaṅgalā;
O Padmamukhī, O Sāvitrī, O Pārijātā, and O Jāhnavī! 79.
O Sudhāmukhi, O auspicious Padmā, O Gaurī, O Svayaṃprabhā;
O Kālikā, Kamalā, Durgā, O Sarasvatī, O Bhāratī;
O Apūrṇā, Rati, Gaṅgā, Ambikā, Satī, Sundarī! (80–81)
"O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, Madhumatī, Campā, Candananandinī!
All of you, rise up together and, having bound him, bring the cowherd here!
At Rādhā’s command, they all rose quickly from the water in anger.
The cowherd women went forth naked, covering their private parts with their hands.
Thousands of other cowherd women who accompanied them followed quickly in that same manner,
their eyes bloodshot with anger.
All the young girls ran with speed after Śrīdāmā;
and as he ran with haste, carrying his bundle of clothes,
Śrīdāmā went quickly to where the cowherds were with their garments.
The cowherd women, accompanied by Balarāma, ran swiftly after them;
they quickly surrounded the cowherds who had stolen the garments. Out of fear, the boys fled to where Kṛṣṇa was with the clothes.
They quickly chose the boys together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Out of fear of the gopīs, the cowherds gave their garments to Mādhava.
Mādhava then placed them, one by one, upon the branches of a tree.
The Kadamba tree shone with various kinds of garments. Having placed all the bundles of clothes upon its branches, Kṛṣṇa spoke these joking words to the gopīs: (89–90)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O cowherd girls, you who are now naked, what will you do now? Quickly join your palms in supplication and make a request for clothes! (91)
"Go and speak to Rādhikā, your own Goddess;
having joined your palms in supplication, ask her quickly for garments.
Otherwise, I shall not give you clothes. (92)
"What will Rādhā, the mistress of you all, do for me now?
Or what will that goddess who is to be worshipped through vows do for me? Tell Rādhikā everything that has been said in this manner. (93–94)

Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, all those cowherd girls glanced at him with the corners of their eyes and went into the presence of Rādhikā. Having gone there, they reported everything that Hari himself had said.
Upon hearing this, Rādhā laughed and became afflicted with desire.
Hearing their words, her body bristling with horripilation, the virtuous lady, smiling with bashfulness, did not go to Hari’s abode. (96–97)
Having performed a yogic posture in the water, she meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa—
the supreme, desired-granting object of worship for Brahmā, Śiva, Ananta, and Dharma.
Repeatedly remembering those lotus feet, her eyes became filled with tears.
Out of overflowing love, she praised the Supreme Lord, who is beyond all qualities.
Rādhikā said:
"O Lord of Goloka, O Lord of the gopīs, O my Master, O Beloved of my life!"
O friend of the distressed, O Lord of the distressed, O Sovereign of all, salutations be unto You!
(100) O Lord of the cowherds, O Lord of the multitude of cows, O increaser of Yaśodā’s joy, O son of Nanda, O eternal bliss, O perpetual joy, salutations be unto You! (101)
O You whose wrath shattered Śatamanyu, O destroyer of the pride of Brahmā, O subduer of Kālīya, O Lord of my life, O Kṛṣṇa, salutations be unto You!
O Śiva, O Infinite Lord, O Lord of Brahmā, O Lord of Brāhmaṇas, O Supreme beyond the supreme! 102.

O you whose nature is Brahman, O knower of Brahman, O seed of Brahman, salutations be unto you! (103) O seed of the tree of the moving and the unmoving, O one who transcends the qualities, O essence of the qualities, O seed of the qualities, O support of the qualities, O Lord of the qualities, salutations be unto you! (104)
O Lord of the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, O you whose very nature is perfection;
O ascetic, through your austerity, O you who are the seed-form of austerity, salutations be to you!
You who make that which is inexpressible into something expressible.
O you whose nature is that [of all things], the seed of those two, the seed of all—homage be to You!
(106) I am Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Durgā, Gaṅgā, and the mother of the Vedas;
homage again and again to Him by the worship of whose feet I am eternally honored. (107)
"Salutation to that Blessed One, by whose touch and by whose meditation day and night even the sacred pilgrimage sites are purified.
Having spoken thus, that goddess cast her body into the water.
With her mind and vital breaths fixed upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that virtuous woman remained as motionless as a pillar.
(109) The man who recites this hymn to Hari composed by Rādhā at the three junctions of the day will certainly attain devotion to Hari, the state of servitude, and the supreme goal of Rādhā. (110)
He who recites this with devotion during times of misfortune shall immediately attain prosperity.
Property that has been long gone, stolen, or lost shall be recovered.
There shall be an increase of wealth for him, and his mind shall become supremely serene.
One seized by anxiety who recites this with devotion shall attain supreme bliss.

(112) In times of crisis involving a rift with one's husband, a rift with one's son, or a rift with a friend, if one should recite it with devotion for a month, one will immediately obtain a vision [of the deity]. (113)
If a young maiden listens to this hymn with devotion for one year,
she will certainly obtain a virtuous husband who is equal to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa composed by Rādhā in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
O sage, having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet while standing in the water and having offered this praise, Rādhikā opened her eyes and, seeing the entire world as consisting of Kṛṣṇa,
beheld the bank of the Yamunā filled with garments and riches.
Upon seeing this, Rādhikā thought it was either a state of lethargy or a dream.
In whatever place, upon whatever support, and with whatever materials it had previously been situated—even including the garments—the Gopa maidens found all of that exactly as it was. (116–117)
Having emerged from the water and performed their desired vow,
all those goddesses, having obtained the boon, returned to their own abodes.
Nārada said:
O Lord, what is the procedure for this vow, what is its name, and what is its fruit?
What substances are to be given, and what sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is to be offered there?
And at the conclusion of the vow, what was the most enchanting secret that occurred?
"O highly fortunate one, having made this division, tell the story of Nārāyaṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the bull among sages laughed.
The teacher of the teachers of the lords of poets began to tell a story.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O child, listen to me regarding the entire procedure for the observance of vows."
The vow known as Gaurīvrata, when performed by a woman in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
bestows upon men virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation, and grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
This vow is celebrated in various regions and is recorded as having both prior and subsequent rites.
It grants desires to those who long for them, and its fruit is characterized by beauty.
Having fasted on the preceding day and washed her garments, being self-restrained,
she should go with devotion to the riverbank at dawn during the transit of the sun into the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having put on clean garments and bathed with various substances, the maiden, having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) into the water-pot, should worship the six deities:
Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Nārāyaṇa, and Śiva. (125–126)
Having worshipped Durgā with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should commence the vow.
Having fashioned a square and very extensive pedestal beneath the water-jar, it should be well-prepared with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. (127)
Having fashioned an excellent ten-armed goddess out of sand,
and having placed vermilion in a skull-cup with sandalwood paste and camphor beneath it,
one should meditate upon her and then, with palms joined in reverence, invoke the Goddess.
Having first recited this mantra, one should then commence the worship:
"O Gaurī, O you who occupy half the body of Śaṅkara, just as you are the beloved of Śaṅkara, so too, O auspicious one, make me a most rare and beloved wife to my husband. (129–130)
Having recited this mantra, one should meditate upon the Goddess, the Mother of the World.
Listen, O Nārada, as I shall declare that secret meditation, proclaimed in the Sāmaveda, which grants all desires and is difficult even for the lords of sages to attain. (131)
By means of this, the perfected ones (siddhas) meditate upon Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune—she who is auspicious, beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, and seated upon the chest of Śiva;
she whose face is bright with a gentle smile, who is firmly established, and possessed of beautiful eyes. (132–133)
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with jeweled ornaments,
decorated with jeweled bracelets, armlets,
and jeweled anklets, and graced by a pair of jeweled earrings upon her cheeks.
Mālatī, her tresses entwined with bees clinging to her garlands,
bearing a beautiful musk dot along with a vermilion tilaka;
wearing fire-purified raiment and a jeweled crown, she was most enchanting, radiant with a necklace of gems set with the finest of precious stones.
Adorned with hanging clusters of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers, she possessed full and firm hips and was bent by the weight of her breasts;
slightly stooped from the burden of fresh youth, she was captivating to the mind. (137–138)
She was being praised by Brahmā and the other gods, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
her lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit, and she resembled the beautiful campaka flower;
she shone with a single row of teeth that put to shame even a string of pearls.
I worship the Goddess who bestows the fruit of liberation, whose face is like the autumnal moon.
(140) Having meditated thus and joyfully placed a flower upon [her] head, the observer of the vow, taking up a flower with devotion and meditating once more, should perform the worship. (141)
Having constantly offered the sixteen services there with great joy,
the practitioner of the vow, with gladness and devotion, should then praise [the deity] with the previously mentioned mantra and likewise offer salutations with the previously mentioned hymn. (142)
Having offered salutations with devotion and being self-restrained, one should listen to the narrative.
Nārada said:
[I shall describe] the vow, the procedure for the vow, the fruit, and the wonderful hymn of praise.
Now I wish to hear the auspicious narrative of Gaurī’s vow (gaurīvrata).
By whom was this vow performed previously, and by whom was it revealed on earth?
O destroyer of doubts, explain all of this in great detail. (144–145)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The virtuous daughter of Kuśadhvaja was named Vedavatī;
she performed this vow at the great holy site of Puṣkara.
On the day of completion, the Mother of the World appeared in person, accompanied by a hundred thousand yoginīs and possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
the Supreme Goddess was seated upon a chariot fashioned from gold. (147)
With a face brightened by a slight smile, Pārvatī spoke to that well-composed woman:
"O Vedavatī, may it be well with you; choose a boon according to your desire."
"By your vow I am pleased; I shall grant you your desire.
Having heard Pārvatī’s words and seeing her with a joyful mind, O Nārada, that virtuous woman, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down and spoke. (149–150)
Vedavatī said: "O Goddess, grant me my desired boon: Nārāyaṇa as my husband;
I have no longing for any other boon than firm devotion at His feet. (151)
Having heard the words of Vedavatī, the Mother of the World laughed and,
quickly descending from her chariot, spoke to that beloved of Hari.
Pārvatī said:
O Mother of the World, it is known that you are Lakṣmī herself, the virtuous Satī;
you have come here to purify Bhārata with the dust of your feet.
O chaste lady, by the dust of your feet, the earth is instantly purified. (153)
O Supreme Goddess, all sacred fords are purified by you.
O ascetic woman, perform penance for the sake of instructing the world;
you are the beloved consort of Nārāyaṇa, dear to him in birth after birth.
Viṣṇu will descend to the earth to remove its burden;
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, being complete, will come to subdue the wicked and to grant liberation to his two devotees who have fallen due to a Brahmin’s curse.
And in Ayodhyā during the Tretā age, there shall also be the manifestation of Hari.
You yourself, assuming the form of a child, go to Mithilā;
having obtained you as his daughter born not from a womb, Janaka too—
She will protect Sītā with diligence, and you shall become [her husband].
Having gone to Mithilā, Rāma too will perform your marriage.
You shall be the beloved of Nārāyaṇa in kalpa after kalpa.
Having spoken thus and embraced her, Pārvatī went to her own abode.
Having gone to Mithilā, that virtuous woman assumed the form of a child and,
by means of her illusory power, stayed happily within the furrow of a plow.
O Nārada, Janaka beheld her naked with her eyes closed,
possessing the hue of molten gold, weeping, and endowed with splendor;
having seen her, he took her and placed her upon his chest.
As he was departing, an incorporeal voice arose right there:
"Accept the maiden Kamalā, who is born not from a womb;
Nārāyaṇa shall be your son-in-law—this is my word. (163)
Having heard that divine voice, the sage then took the girl and,
filled with joy, went and gave her to his own wife for her protection.
When she had attained youth, that virtuous woman obtained Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.

By the power of this vow, Vasiṣṭha, out of a spirit of devotion, revealed on earth his beloved husband, the Lord of the three worlds. Rādhā, having performed this vow, obtained Śrī Kṛṣṇa as her life’s dearest love.
And by the power of this vow, the cowherd women also reached him.
Thus, O Brahmin, has the story of the Gaurī-vow been told.
And whatever young girl performs this vow in Bhārata, [she attains her desire].
She attains a husband equal to Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus those gopīs performed the vow for the duration of one month.
Day after day, they praised that Goddess with the previous hymn.
On the day of completion, the gopīs, filled with joy, performed their vow and praised the Supreme Goddess with the hymn declared in the Kaṇva recension.
By means of that hymn, having praised her, Sītā, who was devoted to truth,
immediately regained her beloved, lotus-eyed Rāma.
Jānakī said:
O you whose nature is power, the support of all, the substratum of the qualities, ever united with Śaṅkara—grant me a husband; salutations be to you!
O you who, through the forms of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, possess the forms of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Salutations to You, who exist in the form of the seed of the seeds of creation, preservation, and destruction.
O Gaurī, knower of Your husband’s innermost secrets, devoted to Your husband’s vow; O faithful wife, grant me a husband whose devotion is fixed on his wife—salutations to You! 174.
O you who are the most auspicious of all that is auspicious, O you who are endowed with all auspiciousness,
O seed of all auspiciousness, salutations to you, O all-auspicious one!
O beloved of all, O seed of all, O destroyer of all that is inauspicious!
O Sovereign of all, O Mother of all, salutations to you, beloved of Śaṅkara!
O Eternal One, whose nature is the Supreme Self, who are of perpetual form;
O You who possess form and are formless, who are the form of all—homage be to you! 176–177.
Hunger, thirst, desire, compassion, faith, sleep, lassitude, memory, and forgiveness—all these are your powers, O Nārāyaṇī; salutations be to you.
Shame, intelligence, contentment, nourishment, peace, prosperity, and growth—[all these are yours]. 178.
All these are your powers; O you who possess every form, salutations be to you!
O you whose nature consists of both the seen and the unseen, and who bestow the seed and the fruit of those two;
O Great Illusion, who are entirely beyond definition, salutations be to you!
O Śivā, endowed with the auspiciousness of Śaṅkara, O bestower of good fortune! O Goddess, grant me my beloved husband Hari and prosperity; salutations be unto you.
Having praised Śivā with this hymn on the day of completion—
Those who bow with supreme devotion obtain Hari as their husband.
Having enjoyed the happiness of a lover in this world and obtained a husband who is higher than the highest, they ascend a divine chariot and go at last into the presence of Kṛṣṇa. (182–183)

Thus ends the hymn to Pārvatī composed by Sītā in the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa. On the day of completion, Rādhā, joined by the gopīs, bowed to the Goddess, offered praise, and fulfilled the vow. (184)
Having joyfully given a thousand cows and a hundred pieces of gold to the brahmins, and having bestowed a sacrificial fee upon a learned brahmin, she prepared to go to her own home;
meanwhile, she respectfully fed a thousand brahmins. (189)
He played musical instruments and gave wealth to the mendicant.
In that interval, Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress,
appeared from the sky, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
With a face brightened by a slight smile, accompanied by hundreds of Yoginīs,

seated upon a lion, possessing ten arms, and adorned with ornaments of precious gems— having swiftly descended from her divine chariot made of gold and furnished with trappings of the finest jewels, she embraced Rādhikā to her chest. (188–189)
Seeing the goddess, the cowherd women bowed down, filled with joy.
Durgā bestowed her blessing upon them, saying, "Your desires shall be fulfilled.
Having granted a boon to the cowherd women and addressed them with respect, she departed. (190)
Durgā, her lotus-like face smiling, spoke to Rādhikā.
Pārvatī said:
"O Rādhā, O Mother of the Universe, you who are dearer than the very life-breath of the Lord of All."
O you who possess a form that is both illusory and human, this vow of yours is for the sake of instructing the world.
[You have visited] Goloka’s Lord, Goloka itself, Śrīśaila, the banks of the Girijā, the divine and glorious Rāsamaṇḍala, and the enchanting Vṛndāvana. (192–193)

O beautiful one, do you perhaps remember the conduct of the thief of delight, which steals away the minds of women— the conduct of those learned in the treatises on love? You are born from half the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and are equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor.
O Goddess, how is it that you, being a human, are a portion of a fraction of yourself? You are the very life-breath of Hari, and Hari himself is yours;
according to the Veda there is no difference between the two, so how is it that you are a human? (195–196)

In the past, even though Brahmā performed austerities for sixty thousand years, he did not behold Your lotus feet; how then can You, being a human woman, [be seen by me]? And by the command of Kṛṣṇa, O Goddess, You assumed the form of a cowherd girl.
How have you come to this earth while Śānta is still alive?
Suyajña, the best of kings born in the lineage of Manu, has indeed departed for Goloka from your presence; how is it that you, being a human woman, remain here? (198–199)
Bhṛgu rendered the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times by means of your mantra. How is it that you, though being human, [were able to do so] from his armor?
Having obtained your mantra from Śaṅkara and having perfected it at Puṣkara—

How did you, being a mere mortal woman, slay Kārtavīrya? (201) And how did you, being a mere mortal woman, break the tusk of the high-souled Gaṇeśa out of pride? How was it that he felt fear of you? (202)
When I was uplifted by anger, you were capable of reducing me to ashes;
yet, having arrived, how is it that you, though being a human woman, protected me out of love for me?
In kalpa after kalpa, and in birth after birth, Kṛṣṇa shall be your husband.

O Mother of the World, this vow was undertaken by you for the sake of the welfare of the world. Oh, how is it that through the curse of Śrīdāman and for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, you have established yourself upon the earth; how is it that you, being divine, have become human? (204–205)
Born from no womb, you are the remover of birth, death, and old age.
Being a virtuous human, how can you be the daughter of Kalāvatī?
When three months had passed, in the enchanting month of Madhu...
O virtuous lady, in the secluded and pure Rāsa-maṇḍala at night, which is most suitable for yoga,
you shall sport with joy together with Hari and all the gopīs in the forest of Vṛndāvana. (207–208)
O Rādhā, who can prevent this play written by the Creator for you upon the surface of the earth in kalpa after kalpa, together with Śrī Hari?
Just as I am endowed with good fortune through Śrī Hari, the beloved of Hara. || 209 ||
O beautiful one, may you likewise be endowed with good fortune by Kṛṣṇa;
just as whiteness resides in milk, as burning power in fire,
as fragrance in the earth, and as coolness in water, so shall your abiding presence be in Kṛṣṇa.
Whether she be a goddess, a human, a Gandharva woman, or likewise a Rākṣasa woman—
none has been more fortunate than you, nor will there ever be.
You are higher than the highest, beyond all qualities (guṇātīta), and are saluted by Brahmā and the other gods.
"By my boon, Kṛṣṇa himself shall become subject to you.
O virtuous lady, he who is worshipped by Brahmā, Ananta, and Śiva shall come under your control.
Though difficult for all yogins to propitiate and unattainable through meditation, he shall be yours."
"And you, O Rādhā, are most fortunate; among all womankind, none is your superior.
Together with Kṛṣṇa, you shall later go to Goloka.
Having spoken thus, O sage, Pārvatī immediately vanished on the spot.
Rādhikā prepared to go along with the cowherd girls.
In that interval, Kṛṣṇa went before Rādhikā.
Rādhā beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the youthful and beautiful dark one.
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with various ornaments,
he is decorated with a garland of jasmine reaching down to his knees and a forest-garland (vanamālā);
his face is bright with a slight smile, and he is intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees.
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, his eyes like autumn lotuses,
his face like the full moon of autumn, radiant with a crown of excellent jewels,
and possessing teeth resembling the seeds of a ripe pomegranate— he was most enchanting. (219–220)
Holding a flute for diversion in one hand and a playful lotus in the other,
possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, enchanting as the abode of grace,
transcending all attributes, and being praised by Brahmā, Ananta, Śiva, and others. (221)
He is the very nature of Brahman, devoted to Brahman, and cannot be fully defined even by the Vedas.
He is unmanifest, the unmanifest Imperishable, the eternal form of light.
He is auspiciousness itself, the support of all auspiciousness, the auspicious one who bestows auspiciousness.
Seeing that wondrous form, she bowed to him in agitation.
Seeing him, Rādhā, tormented by the arrows of love, fainted;
yet, with her eyes cast askance, she gazed again and again at his lotus-face with a smile.
Out of shame, she repeatedly covered her face. Seeing her, Hari, with a serene countenance and eyes, spoke while standing before the entire assembly of cowherd girls.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā, who are dearer to me than my own life, choose a boon that you desire.
O all you cowherd girls, choose each a boon according to your wish. (227)
Having heard the words of Kṛṣṇa, Rādhikā chose a boon from that wish-fulfilling tree of all intentions, and the cowherd girls were greatly delighted. Rādhikā said:
O Lord, may my mind’s bee wander constantly upon the lotus of Your feet,
just as a honeybee hovers over a lotus to drink its nectar and taste the essence of devotion.
May You be the lord of my life in birth after birth.
Grant me that most rare devotion to Your lotus feet.
May my mind be constantly immersed in the remembrance of You, in Your qualities, in dreams, in waking consciousness, and day and night;
this is my constant aspiration.
The cowherd girls said: "O Lord of our lives, just as you are with Rādhā, so shall you be our bond of life day and night; O Master of our breaths, you shall protect us in every birth. (232)
Having heard their words, the glorious one, whose face was serene and who increases the joy of Yaśodā, replied, "So be it.
He then gave to Rādhikā a play-lotus endowed with a thousand petals. (233)
The Lord of the World affectionately gave a beautiful garland of *mālatī* flowers;
the Lord of the Gopīs, laughing with supreme delight, gave a multitude of garlands and flowers to the Gopīs and spoke thus: (234–239).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "When three months have passed, you shall perform pastimes with me in the delightful Vṛndāvana forest, within the beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala. (236)
"As I am, so are you; no difference between us is heard in the Śruti.
I am indeed your life-breath (*prāṇa*), and you are my life-breath, O Lord.
Your vow is for the sake of protecting the world, and not for your own sake, my dear ones. (237)
Having come from Goloka, you shall also depart with me.
Go quickly to your own abode; in birth after birth, you are dearer to me than even my own life—of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari remained there on the bank of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā).
All the cowherd girls stood gazing at Kṛṣṇa again and again,
their faces beaming with joy, smiling, and their eyes cast askance.
With eyes like those of the *cakora* bird, they drank in the moon-like face of Hari with joy.
Having repeatedly granted him victory, they quickly departed for their homes.
And Hari, being well-pleased, went to his own abode together with the children.

Thus has been narrated in its entirety the auspicious life-story of Hari, including the stealing of the gopīs’ garments, which brings happiness to all the worlds. (243) Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Episode of Stealing the Gopīs’ Garments," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. (27)
