Nārada said: When three months had passed, tell me in what manner their physical union with Hari took place. (1)
What is the nature of Vṛndāvana? What is the character of the Rāsa-maṇḍala? How did Hari, who is one, come to have so many consorts, and by what means did their play come to be?
This ever-new subject is a source of great curiosity for me to hear.
Tell me, O highly fortunate one, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious! (3) Tell me of the narrations that are the essence of the Purāṇas, and of the wonderful Rāsa-yātrā of Hari.
Indeed, all the pastimes of Hari upon this earth are most enchanting. (4)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the sage Nārāyaṇa himself, smiling with a very serene face, began to speak. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Once, O sage, on the auspicious thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, when the moon was full at its rising, Śrī Hari went to the forest of Vṛndāvana at night.
Scented by the breeze carrying the fragrance of *yūthikā*, *mālatī*, *kunda*, and *mādhavī* flowers; enchanting with the sweet humming of bees;
filled with fresh sprouts and resounded by the cries of male cuckoos.
It was joined with nine hundred thousand perfumes and was exceedingly beautiful;
it was well-scented with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
and provided with betel leaves mixed with camphor and other articles for enjoyment.
It was beautifully adorned with various couches prepared for dalliance, featuring campaka flowers combined with musk and sandalwood;
it was illuminated by radiant jewel-lamps and made fragrant with incense.
Adorned with various flowers and resplendent with networks of garlands,
the circular Rāsa-maṇḍala was situated right there,
beautifully prepared with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron. (11–12)
It was adorned with flowering flower gardens and well-maintained pleasure lakes filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, resounding with the cries of water-fowls;
these beautiful play-grounds were capable of removing the fatigue of amorous dalliance.
It was cleansed by extremely pure water filled with substances resembling clear crystal, and by white grains mixed with curd;
it was beautifully adorned with a lovely cluster of plantain trunks. (14–15)
Adorned with beautiful thread-bindings joined with mango sprouts,
and decorated with auspicious jars filled with vermilion and sandalwood paste (16), as well as with jasmine garlands and coconut fruits,
Madhusūdana beheld that circle of the *rāsa* dance and laughed. (17)
There, out of curiosity, he produced the sound of his flute as a diversion,
which served to increase the passion of the lustful gopīs.
Upon hearing that, Rādhikā immediately fainted, overcome by love.
Her body became like a pillar, her mind one-pointedly absorbed in meditation.
(19) Regaining consciousness in an instant, she again heard that sound;
she sat, stood up, and rose up again and again in great agitation. (20)
Having abandoned her necessary duties, she quickly departed from the house;
looking around in the four directions,
she followed after him while meditating upon the lotus feet of the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Illuminating [the place] with their splendor and adorned with ornaments made of the essence of excellent jewels, they emerged outside, terrified, their minds captivated by the bridegroom;
abandoning family custom, they were fearless and deluded by passion. (22–23)

Those thirty-three companions, known as Suśīlā and the others, who were the most beloved of Rādhikā and the foremost among the gopīs, departed. After them followed other gopīs; learn from me their number.
Sixteen thousand women, equal in dress, age, beauty, and virtue, followed due to their attachment to Suśīla; sixteen thousand others followed behind Candramukhī. (25–26)
Eleven thousand women of the Mādhavī clan set forth;
thirteen thousand women of the Kadamba-mālā clan departed;
and ten thousand friends of Kuntī are recorded to have gone as well.
Fourteen thousand went following the Yamunā;
nine thousand went as companions of the Jāhnavī;
and nine thousand went with Padmā as their leader.
Fifteen thousand companions of Sāvitrī departed from Vraja; ten thousand companions of Pārijātā also departed;
and seven thousand followers of Svayaṃprabhā left Vraja.
Fourteen thousand gopīs with faces like nectar departed;
fourteen thousand auspicious gopīs departed;
fourteen thousand lotus-like gopīs departed. (31–32)
Fourteen thousand Gopīs who were Gaurīs and Padmās went forth;
sixteen thousand Gopīs known as Sarvamaṅgalās went forth; and sixteen thousand Gopīs known as Kālikās went forth. (33)
Thirteen thousand women from the lotus-dwellings departed;
sixteen thousand cowherd women followed Durgā;
and thirteen thousand followed behind Sarasvatī. (34–35)
Ten thousand followed behind Bhāratī from the cow-pen;
fourteen thousand accompanied Aparṇā;
and ten thousand companions followed behind Rati.
Fourteen thousand companions of Gaṅgā set forth;
sixteen thousand followed behind Ambikā; and thirteen thousand gopīs followed behind Satī. (37–38)
Ten thousand accompanied Nandinī;
thirteen thousand followed behind Sundarī;
and sixteen thousand followed behind Kṛṣṇapriyā. (39)
Sixteen thousand [cowherds] followed behind Madhumatī;
thirteen thousand cowherd women followed behind Campā;
and sixteen thousand [women] followed behind Candanālī.
They all gathered together there and stood joyfully for a moment.
Then some gopīs arrived there with garlands in their hands,
and others came from Vraja with beautiful sandalwood paste in their hands.
Some arrived there joyfully with white chowries in their hands;
some cowherd girls arrived there with musk in their hands; and some cowherd girls arrived there carrying saffron.
Some among them arrived there carrying betel-leaf boxes, while others, cowherd girls, arrived swiftly carrying golden garments to where Candrāvalī was with joy. 49.
All of them, having gathered together in one place, smiling and filled with joy,
assumed the dress of Rādhikā and departed from that spot with delight.
On the way, they repeatedly chanted the name of Hari.
They reached the beautiful Vṛndāvana and beheld the circle of the Rāsa dance (47)—
a sight more lovely than the heavens, graced by the rays of the full moon,
utterly secluded, in full bloom, and perfumed by the breeze carrying the scent of flowers (48).
There, they all heard the sweet sound of the male cuckoo, which arouses desire in women and causes even sages to be infatuated;
it was exceedingly subtle, melodious, and more enchanting than the humming of bees.

At an auspicious moment, Rādhikā entered the circle of the rāsa dance together with all her companions, her mind absorbed in meditation upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa— [the circle] where female bees were clinging to their union with the honey of blooming flowers. (50–51)
Beholding Rādhā there from afar, Kṛṣṇa was filled with joy;
overcome by love and smiling, he followed her with affection as she stood amidst the throngs of her friends, adorned with ornaments of precious gems. (52)
Clad in divine garments, smiling, with arched eyes, walking with the gait of a lordly elephant, beautiful, and enchanting the minds of sages;
she was exceedingly captivating in her youthful appearance, dress, and form. (53–54)
She possessed a supreme beauty characterized by the weight of her hips and buttocks;
she had the lovely hue of a campaka flower and a face resembling the autumnal moon,
and she bore a mass of braided hair adorned with garlands of jasmine.
Rādhā beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the youthful and beautiful dark one,
endowed with fresh youthfulness and adorned with jewel ornaments—
charming, the abode of the playful beauty of ten million Cupids. (56)
Beholding her, who was dearer than life itself, looking back at him with sidelong glances;
[beholding] that most wonderful form, supreme and incomparable in every respect;
wearing various garments and a crest-lock, smiling with joy. (97–58)
Gazing again and again with the corners of her slanted eyes,
the virtuous woman, smiling, covered her face out of modesty;
then, tormented by the arrows of Love, she immediately fell into a swoon.

Her entire body was covered in horripilation, and she became senseless. (60) Pierced by the love-arrows of her sidelong glances, Hari—intent on the pleasure of play—fell into a swoon; yet he did not fall down, but remained like a pillar. (61)
His flute fell away, as did his radiant toy-lotus,
his second yellow garment, and a peacock feather from his body.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, he went joyfully into the presence of Rādhā.
Placing her upon his chest, he embraced her with affection and kissed her.
(63) Merely by the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the virtuous woman regained consciousness;
embracing her lord of her life, who was dearer to her than her own breath, she kissed him. (64)
O sage, Kṛṣṇa captivated the heart of Rādhā, and she his;
that connoisseur of aesthetic delight went with Rādhā to the pleasure-chamber, which was furnished with jeweled lamps and adorned with jeweled mirrors. (65)

It was adorned with beautiful beds of campaka flowers smeared with sandalwood paste, and provided with betel leaves mixed with camphor and various articles of enjoyment. There, Kṛṣṇa, filled with joy, spoke together with Rādhā. (66–67)
Madhusūdana chewed the betel nut offered by Rādhā;
the Queen of the Rāsa dance joyfully consumed the betel nut given by Kṛṣṇa;
and the Lord joyfully gave her the chewed betel nut that had been offered to Rādhā. (68)
Afflicted by passion, she laughed and quickly devoured it after breaking it apart.
Mādhava joyfully begged for the betel-chewed by Rādhā;
Rādhikā, being afraid, did not give it and fell at his lotus-feet.
In the meantime, there, full of desire and intent upon amorous play, the Lord slept together with Rādhā upon a charming bed of pleasure;
he performed the eight varieties of erotic sentiment, including the inverted positions and the rest.
And he, the Lord of Connoisseurs, performed the appropriate striking with nails, teeth, and hands,
as well as the eight supreme types of kisses that are kept secret in the treatises on love,
which captivate the hearts of passionate women. (72–73)
Afflicted by love, he pressed his limbs against their limbs and his minor members against their minor members,
providing pleasure to the amorous women there.
Those two were skilled in the erotic arts and highly learned in the treatises on love.
And there was no cessation of the battle of passion for either of the two.
(75) Thus, having assumed various forms in every beautiful house, he took delight with the cowherd women in the most enchanting circle of the *rāsa* dance. (76)
O Sage, nine hundred thousand gopīs and likewise eighteen hundred thousand gopas were present in the circle of the rāsa dance;
they had their hair disheveled, were naked, and their ornaments were scattered.
Their garments were disarrayed, and they were intoxicated and swooning from passion;
O Nārada, they were constantly accompanied by the sounds of bracelets, tinkling bells, armlets, and anklets set with fine jewels. (78–79)
Having thus played on the dry land, they joyfully went into the water.
Having played there in the water until they were now thoroughly exhausted,
they quickly emerged from the water and put on their garments.
They beheld their lotus-like faces in mirrors made of fine jewels;
they joyfully donned sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and flower garlands,
and regained their senses.
Having eaten betel-leaf with camphor out of curiosity,
they all beheld their lotus-faces in a stainless mirror set with fine jewels.
One woman, afflicted by love, drew Kṛṣṇa toward her by force out of curiosity.
One seized the flute from his hand and pulled at his garment;
another, intoxicated by passion, stripped Mādhava naked, but after mocking him, she gave back his yellow cloth. (84–85)
Having said, "Listen to the reasoning," one woman took hold of her husband;
she kissed him on the cheek and, embracing him again and again,
she pressed her bimba-red lips against his moon-like face, which was marked by a smile and sidelong glances, while her breasts rose high.
One woman, out of desire, displayed her very graceful hips;
another, holding her beloved by the hand and resting him against her waist,
fashioned a crest-ornament adorned with garlands of jasmine.
One woman, having pulled out her topknot, gave him a peacock feather;
another wound a garland of *guñjā* seeds around his topknot;
and [another] gave it to her husband out of desire, for the sake of increasing their love. (89)
One woman, having pulled another by force and stripped her naked out of desire,
sent her onto the lap of Kṛṣṇa, which was smeared with sandalwood paste.
Others, having embraced their beloveds out of desire, danced and sang.
And a certain woman made him dance by force;
out of curiosity, Kṛṣṇa pulled away the garment of another,
leaving her naked, and gave her garment to someone else.
Kṛṣṇa drew Rādhā toward him and settled her upon his chest;
he then fashioned her beautiful braid with exquisite artistry. He applied vermilion to her forehead along with spots of musk.
Out of curiosity, she placed a very fine sandal-paste mark of the moon beneath it;
she drew a most graceful leaf-design upon her beautiful cheek.
Having carefully donned a lovely garment of fire-purified cloth, she stood there.

Taking the beautiful jeweled anklets from her feet, he cleaned her lotus-like feet and applied lovely lac-dye. Having adorned her with ornaments and anointed her with unguents, he decorated her completely. (96–97)
Having given her a garland of *mālatī* flowers, he kissed her again and again;
he applied collyrium to her two lotus-like beautiful eyes,
and placed upon the bridge of her nose a rare elephant-pearl.
And she made nail-marks upon the region of her hips and on her breasts;
she bit her excellent, ripe bimba-fruit-like lower lip with her teeth.
This she did on a lovely, secluded bank by a lake in a flower garden.
Outside, at the lovely rising of the moon, the ground was anointed with flowers and sandalwood;
it was made fragrant by a breeze scented with aloe and sandalwood;
it resounded with the humming of bees and the songs of male cuckoos. (101)
Having assumed many forms, the supreme teacher of yogis once again manifested amorous passion, captivating the hearts of the gopīs,
O Nārada, with the tinkling of small bells, bracelets, and anklets.
There, due to the intensity of their passion, a beautiful sound arose;
all of them reached a state of swoon from the mere act of their first union.
They became motionless as mountains, their bodies covered in horripilation.
When the passion had subsided, they regained consciousness once more;
they struck one another with their nails and teeth.
Kṛṣṇa dealt blows with his fingernails upon the breasts of those women. (105–106)
He indeed made nail-marks upon their very firm hips.
Their waist-knots, their braided hair, and their small bells became loosened;
their fine garments, elegant attire, and beautiful ornaments fell far away. (107)
The Lord of Connoisseurs, out of joy, performed sixteen kinds of amorous union (*śṛṅgāra*): nine types of embracing and eight types of kissing.
He joined his limbs with the limbs of the women, and his minor members with their minor members. (108–109)
The lover, full of desire, embraced the longing women with affection. The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*), and its measure is defined by those parts.
Those learned in the science of love (*kāmaśāstra*) know its various divisions according to these distinct parts.

The Lord of Rasikas composed twelve types of Prakṛta; thereafter, the Lord composed even more than that as described in the Kāmaśāstra, concerning the actions of women at the beginning, middle, and end of amorous play. (111–112)
Then the Lord performed even more than that for the sake of her pleasure.
Marked by the lines of the gopīs’ bracelets and the red lac from their feet, Kṛṣṇa’s body shone like a mountain with red chalk. (113)

When the *rāsa*-maṇḍala had thus come into being, filled with the full assembly, all the gods arrived there along with their wives and followers; mounted upon golden chariots and surrounded by their own retinues, they came out of curiosity. (114)
With all their limbs bristling with horripilation and tormented by the arrows of love—
ṛṣis, munis, siddhas, and likewise pitṛs;
vidyādharas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras.
Accompanied by their wives, they arrived and beheld him with great joy.
He had mounted a divine chariot fashioned from gold, beautifully adorned with jewels and equipped with ornaments of the finest gems. (116–117)
It was most enchanting, draped in fire-purified cloth;
it was accompanied by white chowries and possessed a mirror of fine gems and a lotus;
it had a hundred wheels, was adorned with variegated patterns, moved at the speed of thought, and was captivating to the mind. (118)
The Blessed Lord Śaṅkara arrived together with Pārvatī, his crest resplendent with a water-pot fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems.
On his left side was Mahākāla, and on his right was Nandikeśvara. (119–120)
In front was Kārttikeya, and the Lord himself, Gaṇeśvara;
all the attendants, such as Piṅgalākṣa and others, were around the two of them.
Likewise, there were all the Kṣetrapālas and the eight Bhairaveśvaras. (121)
Durgā, with a smiling face and arched eyes, stands upon his chest;
and Brahmā, together with Bhāratī, is seated upon a chariot made of gold.
To his left are the Seven Sages, and to his right are Sanaka and the others.

Dharma was seated upon a golden chariot and served as the witness of all actions; his consort Satī stood upon his chest with a smiling face, her curved eyes gazing longingly at the perfect rāsa dance. (124)
All the attendants were on every side, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Mahendra was there with Śacī, and the Moon, the storehouse of digits, with Rohiṇī;
Vahni himself was present along with Svāhā, and Sūrya together with Saṃjñā. (125–126)
And Kāma arrived, placing Rati upon his chest. All the planets and the guardians of the quarters came as well, accompanied by their wives.
Remaining in the sky, they beheld the lake and the circle of the rāsa dance.
Some there were bewildered, and some fell into a swoon;
for a moment, all the gods, smiling and filled with joy,
showered a rain of sandalwood paste and a rain of flowers.
The lords of sages showered rains of garlands mixed with musk.
Having witnessed the *rāsa*, the wives of the gods, tormented by the arrows of Kāma,
experienced the essence of passion on the dry land and then went to the waters of the Yamunā.
And Kṛṣṇa, the eternal, perfect Brahman, together with Rādhā,
and the illusory forms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa accompanied by the gopīs,
being tormented by the arrows of love, joyfully engaged in play in the water. (131–132)
Mādhava himself, filled with desire, gave water to Rādhikā; and she, afflicted by passion, offered three handfuls of water to Mādhava. He took her garment, and she indeed became naked.
Hari broke her garland and loosened her braid;
the application of vermilion was wiped away, as was her attire, by the dashing of water.
The variegated coloring of her eyebrows and the tint of her lips were lost, and the collyrium from her eyes was washed off. (134–135)
Having embraced her while she was naked, Hari submerged into the water;
by nature, he remained sporting with her within the interior.
And having shown that naked Gopikā, who was bent over in play, [he departed]. (136)
Smiling, she sent him far away into the waters of the Yamunā.
Rising up with speed, she seized Mādhava by force;
having taken his flute, she angrily cast it far away.
Having seized that yellow garment, he made him naked;
he cut off his forest garland and gave him water again and again. Having pulled Hari back once more, he cast him into the water.
The Lord of the World plunged into the deep current of the sage’s stream.
Rising quickly, Mādhava seized her, laughed, and,
having drawn her naked against his chest, kissed her again and again.
Thus all those forms, together with the gopīs, sported out of curiosity in the enchanting waters on the banks of the Yamunā. Having gone to the shore with her, Hari, naked, was submerged by her.
She requested that garment from him, and he, smiling at the virtuous woman, gave the cloth to Rādhikā; Mādhava likewise gave her a beautiful garland.
He gave the garment to Hari, and the Queen of the Rāsa dance gave him the flute.

With supreme devotion, she applied sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron to all the limbs of Kṛṣṇa as he sat upon her lap. Having fashioned a charming crest that captivated the hearts of amorous women, [she adorned him]. 145.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa again adorned Rādhikā’s most enchanting braid with beautiful garlands of jasmine flowers;
having performed the refinement of her earrings, he fashioned a row of leaf-shaped ornaments.
She joyfully applied vermilion upon her forehead along with drops of musk; beneath that, she placed a very fine and beautiful mark of sandalwood paste resembling the moon.
She also joyfully made nail-marks—dense upon her breasts, thighs, and chest.
Having given her that [garment], he indeed had her clothe herself in a cloth purified by fire.
Having applied the liquid essence of sandalwood, agallochum, musk,
and saffron to his chest and having smeared it there, he kissed her again and again.
Having embraced her again, she placed a garland around her neck;
having adorned her with ornaments, she placed anklets on her feet.
She then applied red lac-dye to her feet and to the nails of her toes once more.
In this manner, he assigned the cowherds and the cowherd-maidens to their respective groups.
Then, intoxicated, they proceeded once more to the beautiful circle of the rāsa dance—
a place suited for amorous play, filled with the moonlight of the full moon, and utterly secluded.

Having seen the blossomed flower, the mistress was able to gather it, which was made fragrant by the enchanting flowers of the mādhavī, ketakī, kunda, and mālatī, as well as by those of the campaka, yūthī, and mallikā. (154)
And out of curiosity, Rādhikā assigned the gopīs their tasks:
she appointed some to the work of weaving garlands, some to the preparation of betel-leaf, and others to the grinding of sandalwood paste. (155–156)

Smiling, with eyes cast askance, the beautiful Sundarī affectionately gave Kṛṣṇa a garland, sandalwood paste, and betel nut offered by the gopīs. Some others engaged him in the activity of singing his praises. (157)
And some played upon mṛdaṅgas, murajas, and other instruments (158).
Thus, having found delight in the rāsa dance with Hari through his playful grace,
she wandered everywhere in charming, secluded places (159).
In delightful flower gardens and on the banks of lakes;
in every lovely cave and by rivers and streams;
in extremely secluded places, in cremation grounds, and in mountain ravines.
And among the desires of women, [he dwells] in the thirty-three forests:
in Bhāṇḍīra, in the beautiful Śrīvana, likewise in the Kadamba forest, in the Tulasī forest, in the Kunda forest, and in the Campaka forest. (161–162)
In the Nimbā forest, in Madhuvana, and likewise in the Jambīraka grove; in the coconut grove, in the betel-nut grove, and in the plantain grove (163);
in the Badarī grove, in the Bilva grove, and in the orange grove.
In a grove of *aśvattha* trees, in a bamboo grove, in a grove of pomegranates;
(164) likewise in a grove of *mandāra* flowers, in a palm grove, in a mango grove;
in a grove of *ketakī*, in a grove of *aśoka*, and in a grove of date palms. (165)
O Sage, [he dwelt] in groves of *āmrātaka*, in thickets of *jambū* trees, in forests of *śāla* trees; on mountain ridges, in woodlands, in lotus ponds, and in groves of *jāti* jasmine;
in formidable thickets of banyan trees, as well as in forests of sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*).

In that forest of blossoming *kesara* trees, which was extraordinary in every respect, he thus dallied out of curiosity and passion for thirty days and nights. Nevertheless, his mind remained unfulfilled, and nothing at all came of it. (167–168)
The desire of passionate women is not quenched by erotic indulgence;
rather, it increases ever further, like a fire fed by a stream of clarified butter.
Then the gods, the goddesses, and likewise the sages departed for their own abodes.
They all praised him and were filled with wonder and joy. In every house of the lords of men, they took birth in Bhārata;
for those goddesses, who were intensely devoted to the sentiment of love, had been partially consumed by the fire of desire. (170–171)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Rāsa-dance," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, then all the cowherd girls, intoxicated by desire, [proceeded].
And the exceedingly haughty women of pride did not regard the Lord as their husband.
Some, with smiles and sidelong glances, spoke thus: "O Kṛṣṇa, lift up this mālatī flower and give it to me as a garland."
Some said, "O Kṛṣṇa, take us upon your lap!
And one woman, having taken hold of Śrī Hari’s shoulder, climbed up onto it.
Another, intoxicated with pride, spoke to her beloved of her life.
"Put on your own yellow garment for me," said one woman to that Lord. "Give me vermilion," said another. One woman said to her lord of life, "Come quickly now! (4–5)
"Having finished grooming the curls, fashion my braid," some urged;
others sent sandalwood paste to the cowherd for his own body and dress,
and for the purpose of ornaments on the ears of the two [wives].
One woman, gazing at his lotus-face with a smile, spoke with supreme desire according to a prior secret agreement for sexual union. Another,
forcibly drawing Kṛṣṇa toward her, seized his flute.
Having stripped off his yellow garment and left him naked, the passionate women carried him away. Some proud women spoke thus to Madhusūdana:
"Give us the liquid lac-dye for our feet and for the tips of our nails! (9)
One woman spoke to him with affection, saying:
"Make for me on my cheeks and breasts a row of leaf-designs enriched with various wonderful and variegated colors.
Having observed their state of intoxication, he made this inference in his mind. (10–11)
The all-pervading Lord Mādhava, whose nature is self-willed, vanished along with Rādhā in an exceedingly secluded place; there, out of joy,
he engaged in amorous pastimes in various ways and for various durations.
On every delightful mountain, in every uninhabited island,
on every bank of rivers devoid of all living beings,
at the sacred cow-pen, on the Jewel Mountain, and also on the shore of the Ganges at the ocean’s edge. (13–14)
On Mount Kālinda and Pulinda, at Mandira and Gandhamādana; in Manohara, in the Kundavana forest, and on the lotuses of the Kāverī’s banks (15);
in the Supuṣpita flower garden growing on the sands of the Puṣpabhadrā.
Having enjoyed himself everywhere and having assumed the guise of Rādhā,
he went to the delightful valley of Malaya, fragrant with sandalwood breezes;
there, having prepared a bed of flowers, he sported with her.
From the intense enjoyment of bliss, Rādhikā fell into a swoon; with her body covered in horripilation, she drew Govinda to her breast. Seeing her unconscious, with her heavy hips and breasts, Kṛṣṇa—
He restored consciousness to her, who was disarrayed in dress, afflicted by passion, naked, and with loosened locks; placing her languidly upon his chest,
he clothed Rādhā in garments and a girdle.
With her left hand, she fashioned a braid with a slight curve,
adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers and entwined with *kunda* blossoms.
She then applied a beautiful vermilion mark (*sindūra-tilaka*) upon her forehead.
With joy, she drew a variegated leaf-design on her cheeks and breasts;
she also marked her lotus-feet with nail-marks stained with red lac.
With her own nails, she fashioned artificial lotuses upon her hips and chest.
Then, having risen, he went together with her to a lake that was resplendent with rows of various kinds of lotuses,
filled with water as clear as pure crystal, and enchanting to the mind. (24)

It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, resounded with the cries of water-fowls, and served as a dwelling for bees greedy for honey; it was born from beautiful lotuses and was indeed constantly made resonant by the sweet, soft notes of the *cāruṇa* birds. (25)
Having bathed there, he indeed engaged in water-sports with her.
With joy, she gave water to Rādhikā, and Mādhava gave it to her.
Then Mādhava himself took a thousand-petaled lotus.

He gave one to Rādhikā and kept one for himself. (28) Having offered his own body to Rādhikā, the Lord of Rādhikā anointed her with the desired liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
(29) Then, proceeding along with her, he saw a banyan tree ahead.
With its extremely lofty tips and exceedingly wide branches,
it was surrounded by shade for a distance of one yojana at its base;
there Govinda dwelt in the vicinity of a grove of ketaka trees.

In a place made fragrant by a pleasantly cool breeze scented with flowers, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, filled with great joy, spoke for a long time about the wonderful, secret, ancient, and primordial Purāṇa to Rādhikā.
In the meantime, he beheld there the bull among sages approaching;
and seeing him with a serene face and eyes,
yet not having seen in his heart the form of the Lord, the Supreme Self.
He saw him who had desisted from meditation and was looking right outside;
he whose every limb was crooked, who was dark-complexioned, whose garment was the quarters of space, who was named Aṣṭavakra, who wore matted hair, and who blazed with the splendor of Brahman. (35)
Vomiting fire from his mouth, appearing like a mass of ascetic heat risen up;
"Aha! Is this perhaps the splendor of Brahman itself, manifest here in bodily form—tranquil yet supremely radiant, with long nails and beard? (36–37)

Seeing Rādhā laughing— she who was filled with devotion, her hands joined in *añjali*, frightened, and her neck bowed in prostration— Mādhava restrained her and described the power of that great-souled lord of sages.
Then, having prostrated before Govinda, that bull among sages offered praise with that hymn which had formerly been given by the high-souled Śaṅkara. Aṣṭāvakra said:
O You who transcend the qualities, the substratum of qualities, the seed of qualities, and the essence of qualities;
O Lord of those possessing qualities, the seed of all possessors of qualities, the abode of qualities—salutations be unto You!
O You whose nature is perfection, the Lord of perfection, the seed of perfection, the one higher than the highest! 40.
Salutations to the Guru of the Siddhas, the sovereign lord of the qualities of accomplishment and supernatural powers.

(41) O seed of the Vedas, knower of the Vedas, O Vedin, best among those who know the Vedas; O Lord whose form is unknown even to the Vedas, O Lord of the command of the Vedas, salutations be unto you! (42)
O Brahmā, Ananta, Īśa, Śeṣa, Indra, and sovereign lord of Dharma and the rest;
O All, Lord of all, Lord of Śarva, whose form is the seed—salutations be to you!
O Prakṛti, O Prākṛta, O Prajña, O Lord of Prakṛti, O Supreme beyond the supreme!
O tree of saṃsāra, whose seed and fruit are You; homage be to You!
O Lord of the seeds of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; O cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
O seed of the great Virāṭ-tree, O Lord of Rādhikā; homage be to You!
Oh! He whose three trunks are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
whose branches and sub-branches are the Vedas and other scriptures, and whose flowers are the ascetic penances;
he is indeed the very sprout of primordial nature (prakṛti), while worldly existence is merely its fruitless state. (46)
O support of that, O supportless one, O support of all—homage be to you!
O you whose form is splendor, O formless one, who are both directly perceived and beyond inference;
O you who are most directly perceived in every form, O you who consist of your own will—homage be to you!
Having spoken thus, that best of sages prostrated at their lotus feet and,
right before their very eyes, gave up his life through yoga;
his body then fell there, close to their lotus feet.
That splendor arose, resembling a blazing crest of fire;
rising to the height of seven palm trees, it fell down,
and after circling around repeatedly, it dissolved into the lotus feet.
Whoever recites this hymn composed by Aṣṭāvakra upon rising in the morning attains supreme liberation and final beatitude; of this there is no doubt.
O Nārada, for those seeking liberation, this king of hymns is dearer than life itself.
"Indeed, in ancient times, Hari gave [it] to Śaṅkara in Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Episode of the Liberation of the Sages," in the Nārāyaṇa section of the *Śrīmad-Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa*.
Nārada said:
"O Great Sage, O Brahman, what wonderful secret have you heard?
What did Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, do when the sage had died?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing the sage dead, Kṛṣṇa prepared to perform the funeral rites;
placing the body upon his chest, he wept aloud like a mortal man.
Embracing him with both arms, he crushed him, overwhelmed by excessive delusion.
A mass of ashes emerged from the corpse due to the friction against his vajra-like limbs.
That body of the Great-Souled One was devoid of blood, flesh, and bone;
O Sage, he remained without food for sixty thousand years. (3–4)
The blood, flesh, and bones were consumed by the blazing fire of his stomach—
[the fire] of one who was devoid of external knowledge yet whose mind was fixed on the lotus feet of Hari.
Having fashioned a funeral pyre from sandalwood, Madhusūdana [prepared it].
Having performed the fire-rite, he remained right there out of grief.
He placed the fire upon the funeral pyre after laying wood over the corpse;
and when the pyre was ablaze, the lord fell into a swoon for a moment.
When his body was reduced to ashes, kettledrums resounded in the sky;
and lo, at that very moment, a rain of flowers fell from the heavens.
In the meantime, there [appeared] one fashioned from the essence of jewels.
And a chariot that moved as fast as thought, adorned with garments, garlands,
and trappings, appeared before Hari from Goloka— beautiful, accompanied by excellent associates who were like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself. (9–10)
Quickly descending from their chariot, all those foremost attendants of Hari,
who were identical in appearance, bowed down to Rādhikā and her Lord,
and having prostrated before the lord of sages who had assumed a subtle body, they paid him homage.
Having placed that body upon the chariot, they went to the supreme Goloka.
When the lord of sages had departed for Goloka, that virtuous woman, who delighted in Vṛndāvana, was filled with wonder and questioned the Lord of the Universe.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"O Lord, who is this best of sages? His body is composed of all [the elements], yet he has the form of an extremely short person; he is most radiant, yet utterly contemptible. (14)
Or how did the ashes issue from his body—what a marvel!
For that splendor, which was like fire, vanished directly into the lotus of your feet.
Seated upon his chariot, the meritorious one immediately went to Goloka.
"O Lord, tell me quickly the entire explanation of why you, who delight in your own self, wept, and for what reason you performed such an act of hospitality with eyes filled with tears. (16–17)
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, Madhusūdana smiled and began to relate a story that had occurred in another age.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O beloved, the secret concerning Aṣṭāvakra is renowned everywhere;
later, in due time, you shall hear it from the mouths of the wise in the course of conversation.
Even Aṣṭāvakra, the lord of sages, is famous throughout the three worlds.
If these three worlds were filled with his fame from birth—having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, Hari’s beloved wife became despondent;
her throat, lips, and palate parched, she spoke sweetly with great effort. (20–21)
Rādhikā said:
If the mind of one who is thirsty has not been satisfied by the ocean of nectar, will that person become satiated by drinking the water from a cow’s hoofprint? || 22 ||
"You are the Lord of the Vedas, of the speakers of the Vedas, of the Ordainer, and of Janaka;
you are Mahāviṣṇu. Who else is there who speaks beyond you?
(23) Having heard these words of Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa indeed became delighted.
He spoke this secret, most wonderful mystery that is to be guarded.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall relate an ancient history.
By hearing or reciting [this], all one's sin is destroyed.
From the navel-lotus of Mahāviṣṇu was born the Creator of the worlds;
he arose from a portion of me and by a fraction of my power within the three worlds flooded with water.
In ancient times, four sons were born from the mind of Brahmā;
all were devoted to Nārāyaṇa and blazed with the splendor of Brahman.
They were like five-year-old children, naked and as if ignorant.
Devoid of external knowledge yet proficient in the reality of Brahman—Sanaka, Sananda, the third, Sanātana, and the venerable Sanatkumāra; these indeed are the four. (28–29)
The Creator of the world said to them, "O sons, perform the work of creation.
They did not abide by their father's word; they departed for penance unto me. And the Ordainer became despondent when his sons had gone.
If a son were to become a source of sorrow for his father by speaking ill of him; [then consider this:
With his knowledge, he fashioned sons from his own limbs who were rich in asceticism, learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras,
Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Voḍhu, Kapila, Āsuri, Kavi,
Śaṅku, Śaṅkha, Pañcaśikha, and Pracetas— these were those whose wealth was their asceticism. (33)

Having performed austerities for a long time, they created the world by his command. All of them, now possessing wives, became intent on carrying out the cycle of worldly existence; and all those ascetics had sons and grandsons.
Let there be much discourse concerning the glorification of the lineage of the sages—
charming and of a meritorious nature— but listen now, O beautiful one, to the subject at hand.
The illustrious Asita, the son of Pracetas, was a preeminent among sages.
Together with his wife, he performed austerities for a thousand divine years.
No son was born to him, and he prepared to give up his life.
Then, an incorporeal voice arose to awaken him.
"Why do you abandon your life? Go into the presence of Śaṅkara!
Having received the mantra from the mouth of Śaṅkara, accomplish your goal;
the Goddess who presides over the mantra will immediately appear before you in person. (39)
"By the boon of your chosen deity, you shall certainly have a son.
Having heard this account, the brahmin went into the presence of Śiva,
to the stainless world of Śiva, which is inaccessible even to yogins.
Accompanied by his wife, the yogi Asita, with palms joined in reverence and his neck bowed low in devotion, praised the guru of yogis.
(42) Asita said:
O Teacher of the World, salutations to You, the Auspicious One and the Bestower of auspiciousness.
Salutations to the Lord of Yogins, the Lord of teachers, and the Guru of gurus.
O Destroyer of the cycle of death and worldly existence, who assumes the very form of Death itself!

O Lord of Death, O Seed of Death, O Conqueror of Death, salutations be unto You! (44) O You who assume the form of Time, O Cause of those who reckon Time, O Lord of the Time of Time, O You who transcend Time, O Time of the Time of Time, salutations be unto You! (45)

Salutation to the one who transcends the qualities (*guṇātīta*), the substratum of the qualities (*guṇādhāra*), the seed of the qualities (*guṇabīja*), and whose nature consists of the qualities (*guṇātmaka*).
Salutation to the Lord of the possessors of qualities (*guṇīśa*), the seed of the possessors of qualities (*guṇināṃ bīja*), and the teacher of the possessors of qualities (*guṇināṃ guru*).
(46) O you whose very form is Brahman (*brahmasvarūpa*), the knower of Brahman (*brahmajña*), and who are intent upon the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*).
"O Seed of Brahman, obeisance to you who are the very nature of the Seed of Brahman!
(47) Having thus praised Śiva and bowed to him, the lord of sages stood before him, his eyes filled with tears for the distressed like a mother cow, and his body covered in horripilation. (48)
Whoever, filled with devotion, should recite this hymn composed by Asita for one year while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) dedicated to the high-souled Śaṅkara,
shall indeed obtain a Vaiṣṇava son who is wise and long-lived.
One may become wealthy or poor and even suffer; one becomes mute or a scholar.
One who has no wife obtains a wife of virtuous character and devotion to her husband.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at last into the presence of Śiva.
In ancient times, this supreme hymn was given by Brahmā to Pracetas;
and by Pracetas, it was given to his own son, Asita.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: [52]
Having heard the sage’s hymn of praise, Lord Śaṅkara himself,
who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke to Brahmā’s son, his own devotee.
Śaṅkara said:
"Be firm, O best of sages; I know your desire.
A son shall truly be born to you, equal to me and born of my own portion.
I shall grant you an incomparable mantra, which is very difficult for all to obtain. (54)
Having spoken thus, he gave you the sixteen-syllable mantra,
as well as the hymn of praise, the ritual for worship, and the most wonderful armor (kavaca),
along with that named Saṃsāravijaya, preceded by the rite of preliminary purification (puraścaraṇa).
"May the desired goddess become manifest in order to grant me a boon.
Having spoken thus, Rudra ceased; having bowed to him, he departed.
That Asita then chanted the supreme mantra for a hundred years.
O virtuous lady, having appeared before him in person, you formerly granted him a boon:
"A son shall truly be born to you, a son who is a possessor of great knowledge.
Having bestowed this boon, you departed for Goloka, into my presence.
In due time, a son was born to him by a portion of Śiva;
he was named Devala, devoted to Brahman, and as beautiful as Kandarpa.
With joy, [the sage] took the daughter of King Suyajña, Ratnamālāvatī.
He married that Sundarī, who was beloved by all;
and for a hundred years, he, being skillful and preeminent in the art of lovemaking, took his pleasure with her in various places and in private.
In the course of time, that bull among sages became dispassionate;
having renounced all pleasure, the most righteous one, remembering Śrī Hari,
rose from his bed at night, detached and rich in asceticism.
He went to the lovely Gandhamādana mountain for ascetic practice.
And his beloved wife, a virtuous woman, having abandoned sleep and not seeing her husband,
lamented intensely out of grief, consumed by the fire of separation.
Rising up and sinking down, she wept aloud again and again;
her mind at that time became like grain in a heated pan.
Having abandoned all food, the beautiful woman gave up her life.
Her son performed for her the funeral rites and other duties.
That sage, my devotee with his senses conquered, practiced austerities in a cave on Mount Gandhamādana for a thousand divine years.
Rambhā, who was skilled in the arts of adornment, beheld him by divine grace—
he was exceedingly beautiful and serene, as handsome as Kandarpa himself.
And she, having approached him in a secluded place, spoke to him.
Having carefully assumed an attire that enchants the minds of the three worlds,
Rambhā said:
"O virtuous one, listen to my words, which are so captivating to lovers."
Abandoning that harsh [world], enjoy me in secret, for I am the bestower of happiness.
You are the most excellent among suitors on this earth, and I am a maiden of noble form choosing my own husband;
the first union of a clever man with a clever woman is difficult to attain.
O Sage, the kings in Bhārata perform sacrifices for the sake of heaven and for the purpose of enjoying celestial pleasures; we, however, are the very essence of such enjoyment.
[Our] pair of breasts, my thighs, and my beautiful lotus-face— 73.
Who would not find happiness upon seeing her with a smile and a play of her eyebrows? (74) The essence of pleasure is the delight of women, which even sages long for;
the enjoyment of pleasure by those who relish it is exceedingly difficult to obtain in solitude. (75)
Whether he be a god, a human, a gandharva, or even a rākṣasa,
he who is deceived by passion regarding Rambhā would remain unknowable even in the midst of women’s pleasures.
He who has conquered his senses would not fail to enjoy his beloved when she approaches him in secret.
He shall certainly dwell in Kumbhīpāka for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Truthfully, he becomes subject to death by her curse;
yet, due to the curse of Mohinī, he remains unslayable by anyone in the three worlds. || 77–78 ||
Just as a wanton woman looks upon the man who has abandoned her for another,
she does not look with such anger upon her husband, her sons, or her kinsmen, even if they are her slayers.
The wanton woman knows her paramour to be the most beloved of all.
If she is abandoned by him, that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall indeed slay him;
for she is a wanton woman, destined in every birth to be among violent creatures, among those who kill the nine [classes of beings], wicked, eternally devoid of compassion, and of evil end.

"Abandon your meditation, O best of sages; enjoy this fruit of your asceticism, and taking me, who have come to you in secret, grant me long-lasting happiness. Having heard Rambhā’s words, he spoke to her, overwhelmed with fear.
[It is] beneficial, true, the essence of policy, and bringing about happiness in the end.
Devala said:
Listen, O Rambhā, I shall proclaim the supreme speech, the essence of the Vedas.
Truth is appropriate for the family dharma of ascetic Brahmins.
This is the duty: at the proper time, a twice-born man who delights in his own wife is always honored everywhere, both in this world and in the next. (84–85)
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, if he is devoted to another’s wife,
Lakṣmī becomes enraged and departs from his home, even though he has not failed to worship her.
In this world he is utterly censurable, and everywhere he is disqualified from performing his own duties.
Furthermore, he shall dwell in the Andhakūpa hell for as long as a hundred years.
A householder should accept a woman who has approached him, not an ascetic;
in rejecting amorous women, the householder incurs fault, becoming a partaker of curses and a partaker of sin.
Even Brahmā, the creator of the world, was not dispassionate and remained possessed of a wife. There is no fault in renunciation for us who have already abandoned our women;
yet he who, having abandoned his own wife, takes another's woman [commits a sin]. (89)
For one who is dead while living, there is a loss of fame, wealth, and lifespan. (90) For him who possesses no fame on earth, his life is fruitless.
Of what use are great prosperity, sovereignty, or happiness to an ascetic? (91)
"What need have you for me, an old man devoid of desire?
O beautiful one, look at this youth, handsome and well-attired!
Having heard these words, the foremost of the Apsarases became enraged.
Trembling and with her lower lip quivering, she spoke these words to him once more.
Rambhā said:
"O you who possess the luster of the beautiful campaka flower, as handsome as Kandarpa himself!"
Through the power of her asceticism, she is radiant, well-attired, and esteemed by women.
"Without you, whom else shall I go to? Or what man is there who is more devoted than you? Abandoning you, what woman—especially one as passionate as I—could continue to live? (94–95)
"O best of Brahmins, unite with me quickly, for I am constantly consumed by the fire of desire.
Just as Rambhā was devoured by the elephant, let my passion perish through you;
otherwise, O foremost of those who know the Vedas, I shall utter a curse."
"Either take me, or this terrible curse, or seize it quickly!
For my life-breaths are consumed, my mind is burnt, and my very self is scorched;
thus, may it attain the state of extinction through drinking the nectar of fresh erotic sentiment. (97–98)
Whomever one who is afflicted by internal suffering curses with certainty,
even the Creator, the Lord of the World, is not able to annul that curse.
(99) Having heard the words of Rambhā, the twice-born became absorbed in meditation.
Remaining silent, she said nothing; then, out of anger, she cursed him:
"O crooked-minded Brahmin, may your body be misshapen in all its limbs, resembling collyrium in appearance, and devoid of beauty and youth."

"May my ancient asceticism, which has become utterly deformed in appearance and is censured throughout the three worlds, be instantly destroyed— this is certain. Having spoken thus, the unchaste woman, out of desire, departed for the world of Kāma.
Before long, the Lord of Sages no longer beheld the footprints of Hari;
indeed, he became deeply distressed by the separation from that lotus-foot.
Seeing his own body transformed and deprived of its former merit, he was overcome with grief. (3–4)
Having prepared a fire-pit, he was intent on giving up his life out of grief;
I saw him and, having granted him a boon and awakened him through divine knowledge,
I comforted him with affection, whereupon he became peaceful.

Having seen the eight limbs and the curved [features] of the great sage, I quickly gave him the name "Aṣṭāvakra" out of curiosity. Having come here from the valley of Mount Malaya in haste at my word, [he has arrived]. (6–7)
For sixty thousand years he performed supreme austerity.
At the conclusion of his penance, O beloved, my devotee was united with me by me.
Even when everything has perished in the universal dissolution, my devotee does not perish.
After a very long time, due to his asceticism and the blazing fire of his internal digestion,
the interior of the sage— who had abandoned all food— became filled with ashes. Then,
O beloved, I came to the valley of the Malaya mountain for the sake of that sage.
"Among those devoted to me, there has never been nor will there ever be another like Aṣṭāvakra.
Such was this sage, the great-grandson of Brahmā, who was established in austerity.
Yet, due to the curse of a harlot, he became devoid of parts (niṣkala), just as Brahmā was rendered unworthy of worship in former times."
Thus has been told everything—the secret of the Great-Souled One—which bestows happiness, merit, and is profound. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Question of Rādhā," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Lord, what a wonderful and most enchanting account I have heard!
Now I wish to hear the cause of Brahmā’s curse. (1)
"How could he who is the creator of the three worlds and the bestower of the fruits of austerities have become unworthy of worship due to the curse of an unchaste woman?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the Manvantara of Raivata, Sucandra was the preeminent among kings;
he was an ascetic, a supreme Vaiṣṇava, a man of knowledge, and most righteous.
O my beloved, while formerly performing penance, he came to me.
And in this delightful Malayadroṇī within the land of Bhārata,
that lord of kings performed austerities for a thousand years.
Through the rigorous penance of that ascetic, his body became worn away.
Seeing his body covered by an anthill, the Creator, a treasure-house of compassion,
came to that secluded place of penance to grant him a boon.
[6] With the water from his water-pot and with the water arising from my own body, [he sprinkled it].
The knower of yoga sprinkled him with the mantra given by me.
Rising up at the touch of the water from the ascetic’s jar,
the king himself bowed with devotion to the Creator of the worlds standing before him.
To that king who was bowing before him, the Lotus-born One said:
"Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, whatever is desired in your heart.
Having heard those words of his, he chose a boon that was supreme beyond the supreme.
"By my grace, Brahmā granted him his desired boon: devotion to my very feet and service unto me alone. And he stood before him, possessing a splendor equal to that of the god of love.
In the meantime, the king beheld an excellent chariot descending from the sky,
possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns;
it shone intensely, its splendor pervading everything and all ten directions.
It was fashioned from the finest essence of the king of jewels and endowed with a hundred wheels;
it was constructed of priceless gems, radiant with various ornamental jars, and resplendent with networks of pearl, ruby, and diamond garlands. (13–14)
It was exceedingly beautiful, radiant with mirrors of fine jewels,
adorned with divine garments and millions of white chowries,
and graced by clusters of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers. 15.
It was mind-moving and most wonderful, adorned with various colorful paintings (16).

It was surrounded by divine attendants, decorated with jewel ornaments, four-armed, dark-complexioned, radiant, and in the full bloom of youth (17). They were dressed in yellow garments and anointed with sandalwood and aguru paste.
Seeing the gods stationed upon their chariots, the king bowed with joy;
suddenly, a rain of flowers fell upon his head. In heaven, kettledrums resounded and enchanting cymbals rang out.
The sages, the ascetics, and the perfected ones offered blessings with joy;
all the gods, overflowing with delight, praised the king.
And the king, having meditated upon his attendants, assumed their very form.
Placing him upon their chariot, his attendants led him away and went to my abode.
Having become one of my own attendants, he remained in my presence.
Then Mohinī saw Brahmā departing for his own palace.
In that delightful flower garden, by the breeze scented with flowers and sandalwood,
she was instantly bewildered upon seeing him, for she had been consumed by the fires of passion.
Beholding him, the woman with the curved eyes protected her face with a smile.
Wearing a dot of vermilion along with a dot of musk,
possessing the beautiful hue of a campaka flower, eternally fixed in the bloom of youth,
she has broad hips and full buttocks and breasts. (24–25)
Her face captivated by the brilliance of the full moon’s rays in autumn, she was clothed in fine garments and adorned with jeweled ornaments;
she was capable of enchanting the three worlds by her mere playful side-glances. (26)

Exceedingly passionate, always walking with the slow gait of a lordly elephant, her entire body covered in horripilation, she fell into a swoon on the path. Having gazed intently at her, Brahmā departed, remembering Śrī Hari. (27–28)
He, delighting in the Self and having conquered his senses, did not undergo any transformation;
he reached the world of Brahmā, and Brahmā, the lord of the worlds, [honored him]. And that unchaste woman, her consciousness destroyed, became filled with desire.
Day and night, contemplating the Four-faced One in both dream and waking states,
the sovereign lady forgot her paramour entirely and abandoned Hari.
Whether rising up, staying still, or lying down for a moment, she remained focused on him.

Just as grain in a heated pan tosses about, so did he on that path. In the meantime, Rambhā, the most skilled among the Apsarases, was traveling along that same road toward the world of Kāma with her desires fulfilled. (32)
Seeing her companion there with her throat, lips, and palate parched, she understood her intention by her expression; then, smiling, she questioned her.
Rambhā said:
"How is it that you are such as this, O enchantress of the minds of the three worlds?
Speak quickly, O illustrious one! If you are Rambhā, regain your senses.
With desire for whom do you go toward your beloved?"

The unchaste woman possesses all good fortune; we are not guardians of our families. All beings in the three worlds are preoccupied with the pleasure of the senses. Since life departs at the appointed time, what shame is there for those who live? (36)
And there is no one in the three worlds dearer than oneself.
That affection which exists for a beloved, a child, or one’s own kinsman is rooted in oneself;
indeed, as long as the connection with oneself persists, so long does that affection remain toward them. (37–38)
For those whose minds are constantly fixed upon certain things, their very lives depart with them.
O beloved, behold me as I go to the world of desire with longing;
look upon me together with my friend and go to that lover with your mind.
Having tied your waist-knot and arranged your hair, and having assumed your desired attire,
O enchantress, cast that delusion which is the seed of the sages' infatuation.
O illustrious lady, speak words that are pleasing to the heart.
One should protect oneself and one's influence regarding women in the three worlds;
furthermore, one's own intentions during sexual union must never be disclosed—except to a beloved husband who is devoted to one, or to a companion who is upright. (42)
Therefore, O beloved of my beloved, one's heart's words should be disclosed with effort;
otherwise, they lead only to ridicule or even to death.
Having heard her words, she smiled and was deeply abashed.
And he told her what was pleasing to the heart, by which cause such a fate had come to pass. Mohinī said:
"O Rambhā, as long as the four-faced one was seen by me in a secluded place... (44–45)
My mind has been scorched for so long by the constant fires of the god of love;
food was not given to myself, for it did not please me in the meantime. I do not know the rising of either the moon or the sun.
Now there is no longer any difference for me between waking and dreaming.
(47) My life-breaths await her embrace alone;
having found her for even a moment, they will not depart for long, O beloved, and not otherwise. (48)
And by the clusters of flames of passion, my body, which had previously been like gold,
has now become like a scorched mountain due to lack of food;
I am unable to walk or stand, and I am intent on making my bed.
"Fie upon this class of unchaste women, and especially upon me!
Tell me, Rambhā, what means shall I employ now?
Shall I cast away my shame, or my body—what of these two?"
Having heard the words of Mohinī, the best of the Apsarases laughed and spoke to her words that were beneficial, prudent, strategic, and a cause for auspiciousness.
Rambhā said:
"Truly so! O blessed lady, this is indeed the cause of your welfare.
I shall remove all of it; hear the means and cast away your fear.
Having assumed an unprecedented disguise, first propitiate the God of Love. (53)
Go there yourself with him and delude him, O beautiful woman!
Who is capable of conquering that Lord, the foremost among those who have mastered their senses, who is the very essence of Nārāyaṇa himself, without the aid of desire? (54–55)
"O deluder, perform austerities and worship Kāma; go to Puṣkara.
That lord of women, who is compassionate, will immediately appear before you in person.
Having spoken thus to her, that foremost of apsarases [sent her] to the presence of Kāma.
She went for the sake of pacifying her senses, and she went to Puṣkara.
Having performed austerities at Puṣkara and having attained her desire, the enchanting woman went together with him to the stainless world of Brahmā.
And seeing the lotus-born Brahmā situated in a solitary place,
Mohinī stood before him and began to enchant him;
for a moment she danced with beautiful limbs, and for a moment she sang.
This music, connected with me, is the enchantment of the hearts of my devotees.
(60) Having heard her desired music, the Creator of the worlds, his entire body covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears, was overcome by a swoon. (61)
Seeing the charming four-faced one, Mohinī, her mind filled with joy,
playfully displayed her true nature and the extent of her arts;
she revealed her own form, preceded by a smile and a contraction of her eyebrows.
What shame is there for one in this world whose consciousness is struck down by desire?
(63) Having understood her state of mind, Brahmā bowed his face and became silent;
having bestowed that gift upon her, he desisted while remembering Śrī Hari. (64)
Having understood the disposition of Brahmā, her throat, lips, and palate parched,
she— her efforts frustrated— praised Kāma, the excellent bestower of desires.
(65) Mohinī said:
The most excellent of all the senses, the mental portion that is a fragment of Viṣṇu,
that very thing which is the seed of actions— O you who have arisen therefrom, salutations to you!
For the Lord Maheśvara himself is the Self, whose nature is knowledge.

Salutations to you, O Brahman, creator of the world; salutations be to you, O source from which that [world] arises. (67) Salutations to you, the creation within all bodies, and the vision even of yogins;
O world-attainer, difficult to propitiate, difficult to restrain—salutations to you. (68)

O All-Conquering One, Conqueror of the World, O Living One, Enchanter of the Living! O Seed of Rati, Lord of Rati, Beloved of Rati, homage be unto You! (69) O Eternal Abode of Women, Whose Beloved is dearer than life itself!
O You who have women as Your vehicle, women as Your weapon, and women as Your bond— homage be to You!
O Supporter of all forms whose purpose is to be accomplished by Your consort, O Abode of Virtues,
O Companion of the fragrant breeze, O Friend of Spring— homage be to You!
O you who provide the constant foundation for the womb, who increase the longing upon seeing women,
and who bring an end to the lives of the clever and the separated— homage be to you!
For those toward whom you show no mercy, misfortunes arise and their knowledge is destroyed.
O ocean of compassion, salutations to you who, with ease, [remove] the seeds of obstacles to the penances of ascetics;
salutations to you who are capable of making the minds of the liberated possessed of their desires. (73–74)
"O you who are to be accomplished through austerity and always to be propitiated, composed of the five elements,
whose support is provided by the five senses— O Five-Arrowed One, salutations to you!
Having spoken thus in her mind before the Creator, she became known as Mohinī.
She ceased speaking, her face bowed, and became absorbed in meditation.
This enchanting hymn was spoken at the end of the midday rite;
formerly, it had been given by Durvāsas to Mohinī on Mount Gandhamādana.

Its waters are always like milk, and it possesses exceedingly lofty waves.
From Vaikuṇṭha she came to the world of Brahmā, and from there she arrived in heaven.
From heaven, she joyfully descended to the earth by way of the Himalayas;
that stream, known as the Alakanandā, was then mixed with the salt-water ocean.
Resembling pure crystal and possessing great velocity,
she takes the form of fire in order to burn the dry fuel of the sins of the wicked.
Oh, she bestows the liberation of nirvāṇa upon those born of the lineage of Sagara!
And that excellent water, which leads to Vaikuṇṭha and serves as a staircase,
is for this reason offered first at the feet and then into the mouth of the virtuous whose nature is merit at the time of death. (28–29)
Having ascended the steps of the Gaṅgā, the virtuous go to the state free from affliction;
having transcended even up to the world of Brahmā, they proceed seated upon chariots, free from all calamity.
If, however, by some past fate or due to previously committed sins, one has already sunk [into the depths], [then...]

They rejoice in the abode of Hari for a period of years equal to the number of hairs on their bodies. Then, for those who maintain the array of time (the cosmic cycle), there will certainly be an experience of both merit and sin in a very short time.
Then, having obtained birth in the home of the meritorious in Bhārata and having attained unwavering devotion, they become the very form of Hari.
If, by fate, Śūdras carry the bodies of deceased twice-born men, [they likewise attain this state].
Their stay in hell lasts for a period measured by the falling of a single footstep;
thereafter, she who takes the form of Hari assists them,
and being full of compassion, she grants them liberation in due course.
Having caused one’s birth to take place in the home of the meritorious in Bhārata,
one certainly receives a place in Vaikuṇṭha within three births.
Furthermore, he who performs the pilgrimage and goes to bathe in the pure waters of Sureśvarī [attains the same].
And he certainly rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as many years as there are particles of dust in his footprint.
(37) If a man who is defiled by impurity should bathe upon reaching the Gaṅgā even incidentally, he is liberated from all sins, provided that he is not tainted again. (38)
In the Kali age, her [the Goddess’s] presence shall remain in Bhārata for five thousand years.
Alas, what power can there be in the Kali age while she is present?
In the Kali age, my image [shall remain] for ten thousand years.
The ancient [sacred sites] remain, so what power does the Kali age have there?
That stream which flows to Atala is known as Bhogavatī;
it is ever like the foam of milk and possesses exceedingly great velocity. (40–41)
It is a constant mine of priceless jewels and supreme gems;
on its banks, Naga maidens of perpetual youth sport,
and the Goddess herself constantly encircles Vaikuṇṭha.
It is one thousand yojanas in width at its base and one hundred thousand yojanas in length.
O my daughter, there is no destruction for her even at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya).
Her divine shore is exceedingly beautiful and a source of various jewels.

Thus has been told everything regarding the merit-bestowing birth of Jāhnavī, as well as the remedy for Brahmā and the subjugation of Mohinī; now hear [the rest]. Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Account of the Birth of Jāhnavī," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Nārāyaṇa spoke again to Brahmā out of compassion:
"Having seen that Gaṅgā, they all considered her to be my own Māyā. (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Arise and go; may it be well with you, O Four-faced One.
Having bathed here, though you have been cursed, become purified by my command. (2)
O Sage, although all the sacred waters of the Lord of Viṣṇu constantly desire your touch because you are yourself pure and true,
nevertheless, you have been released from the curse here due to your slighting of Prakṛti.
And egoism is the seed of all sins and inauspiciousness for everyone.
(4) Go quickly to Goloka, my supreme abode;
there you will find Bhāratī, who is a portion of Prakṛti and the bestower of auspiciousness. (5)
"O auspicious one, resort to Prakṛti, who is the very nature of the seed of creation!
Alas, you have now performed penance until the end of the kalpa!
No one accepts your mantra due to the curse of a prostitute."
Whatever else there may be in the worship of other deities, that shall become your own worship.
You alone are the creator of the worlds, one who delights in the Self, and the beloved;
you possess all forms and are the object of worship everywhere within all bodies.

Then, at my command, Brahmā, the preceptor of the world, bathed in the waters of the Ganges and quickly departed for Goloka after bowing down to me. All those gods and sages likewise went joyfully to their own abodes.
Singing my exceedingly pure glory again and again,
Vidhi came to Goloka and approached the virtuous Bhāratī,
the presiding deity of all sciences, who had been produced from the lotus of my mouth. || 10-11 ||

Having obtained Vāgīśvarī, Brahmā himself was filled with joy; the all-pervading Lord himself sanctioned the operation of the weapons of desire. Then, having come and bowed to me, he attained the one who deludes the three worlds.
The Blessed One sported in various most secluded places.
Having enjoyed himself for a very long time, the Creator himself ceased;
he then spoke thus to Vāgīśvarī: "You indeed are Brahmā through your own action."
"O beautiful one, look at this youth, who by his own karma is virtuous, worthy of honor, and possessed of eternal youth; he is the very embodiment of your own past actions.
The union of a clever woman with a clever man shall be full of merit. (15)
"I am afflicted by old age, aged, a poor ascetic, a Vaiṣṇava, and a twice-born.
Being dependent and subject to another's will, what pleasure could I find in unchaste women?
Having said this, he returned once more to his own abode in the world of Brahmā.
Residing in the world of Brahmā, they beheld that goddess with great curiosity—exceedingly beautiful, charming, fair-complexioned, and smiling;
her face like the cool-rayed autumn moon and her eyes like autumn lotuses. (18)
Her sprout-like lower lip was radiant, eclipsing the glow of a ripe bimba fruit; she was enchanting with a row of teeth that surpassed a string of pearls;
she was adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets;
and she shone at the roots of her ears with a pair of jeweled earrings.
Her chest was made radiant by a necklace of the finest essence of jewels;
she wore a fine garment of fire-purified silk; she was in the bloom of youth, exceedingly beautiful, with full hips and breasts. (21–22)

Holding a lute and a book in her hands, and displaying the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā), the excellent Bhāratī— having performed the ritual purification (nirmañchana)— joyfully brought about the supreme auspiciousness and ushered Brahmā into the city. (23)
Brahmā sported with her day and night, constantly immersed in the joy of supreme pleasure. This is hidden in all the Purāṇas; what more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of the Lord of Prāṇa, the Supreme Goddess laughed and again questioned him out of curiosity regarding her mind in the past. (26)
Śrī Rādhikā said:
Why did Brahmā not accept the prostitute who had approached him of her own accord?
Is he not the giver of fruits for actions performed in secret on the field of karma? (27)
"Indeed, there is a great fault in abandoning a woman who has presented herself;
knowing this, how could the divine Creator have abandoned Mohinī?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, Madhusūdana smiled and spoke to the Supreme Goddess concerning the events of the Pādma-kalpa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall relate the desired ancient account;
though it is unspeakable, to be kept secret, and censured by the great.
Once, the Creator was impelled by me to create living beings.
He mentally created sons blazing with the splendor of Brahman:
Sanaka, Sananda, the unsurpassed Sanātana,
Sanatkumāra, Voḍhu, Kavi, and the powerful Pañcaśikha.
The father spoke to those who were born of my lineage—Asita, Kapila, and Siddha—who were naked and five years of age, saying, "Create progeny.
But they disregarded their progenitor and impeller, their father. (33)
Devoted to my worship, they quickly departed to perform austerities.
Then the Creator of the World, being enraged, again produced eleven excellent sons, the Rudras, who were weeping and possessed of terrifying forms. (34–35)
Having applied himself with vigor to that [yoga], the yogi, delighting in his own self, meditated upon me within his own body and again created sons through yoga:
Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Aṅgiras. (36)
Having created Bhrigu, Atri, Pulastya, Dakṣa, and Kardama,
as well as Marīci, and having appointed them to create progeny,
he, with a joyful mind, produced a son and one daughter.
The son of the lustful Kṛṣṇa became Kāmadeva.
A sixteen-year-old daughter, adorned with jewel ornaments, [was there].
That Creator spoke to his son, who stood before him, blazing with splendor.
"Difficult to restrain, a portion of my own power, delighting in his own self, and enchanting.
(40) Brahmā said:
"And you were joyfully created for the sake of the sport of the male and female."
Through the application of joy, you shall effect the empowerment of all.
[It is] the cause of delusion, agitation, and the paralyzing of seeds;
it is the seed of madness, the blazing [fire], and that which perpetually robs one of consciousness.
"Taking these arrows given by me, perform the act of total delusion (*saṃmohana*).
By my boon, O child, become one who is difficult to resist throughout all existences.
Having thus spoken and given the arrows, the Creator of the World was filled with joy.

Seeing this, he spoke to his daughter, being prepared to bestow a boon. In the meantime, Kāma, having reflected in his mind upon their counsel and intending to perform a trial of weapons, discharged his arrows at Brahmā.
Pierced deeply by arrows purified with mantras— which were difficult to resist— and by the mere remembrance [of them],
the great yogi fell unconscious, his mind struck.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, he beheld a maiden before him.
He set his mind upon enjoying her, but the virtuous woman fled in fear.
Seeing her father running behind her, deprived of his senses, she quickly sought refuge with her ascetic brothers. (47–48)
Having placed him nearby, they spoke with anger to their father these supreme words,
which were beneficial, true, declared in the Vedas, and the essence of political ethics.
The sages said:
"Alas! O Creator of the World, what is this most despicable deed of yours? Why do you perform such conduct as is practiced only by the base?
The virtuous always regard the wife of another as they would their own mother. (50)
Those who have conquered their senses are to be honored everywhere, both here and in the next world.
You yourself are the author of the Vedas, yet you desire to enjoy a maiden;
and it is heard in the Vedas that a maiden is included among the ranks of mothers.
The wife of one's guru, the wife of a king, the chaste wife of a brahmin;
the wife of one's brother or son, the wife of a friend, and her mother (53);
likewise the mother of one's parents, the wife of one's brother, one's mother-in-law, and one's own daughters.
His mother, her co-wife, his sister Surabhi,
the wife of his chosen deity, the nurse who provides food,
the nurse who carries him in her womb, and the beloved one who protects him from fear by her own name. (54–55)
These, ordained by the Vedas, are remembered as the mothers of all;
and among all of them, there is no deficiency whatsoever.
The giver of a daughter, the giver of food, the giver of knowledge, and the giver of fearlessness— [these are the four types of givers].
The one who gives birth, the one who imparts the mantra, the eldest brother, and the fathers are remembered as gurus.
Those fools who carry these persons— who are indeed their own progenitors—
on their heads, are cooked in hell for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Having cast them into a blind well from afar, the servants of Yama constantly inflict beatings upon them and force them to drink excrement.
You alone are the creator of the universe and indeed the punisher of Yama himself.
"We are the creators of the worlds; therefore, you take this maiden [from us].
Go far away from our presence, O you whose mind is afflicted by passion!
We are indeed capable of reducing Janaka to ashes."
The wise ought to forgive thousands of faults in their teacher;
those who know the principles of policy destroy him who harms them all, even if he be their own teacher—provided he seizes their entire property, curses them, and is cruel. (62)
The virtuous do not revile him; rather, they bow down with their own devotion.
But those who hate and revile the Guru, who is the beloved deity and supreme, are cooked in the Andhakūpa hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
"Agitated by the beatings of Yama, they constantly consume excrement,
and they are bitten day and night by insects the size of mustard seeds.
Having spoken thus, the sages bowed at his lotus feet.
Everything certainly becomes pacified by divine power when the mind is tranquil. (66) All the sages turned their faces upward toward their own duties.
Brahmā, out of shame, prepared himself to cast off his body. (67)
Having pierced the six wheels through yoga and restrained all the vital breaths,
he brought them to the aperture of Brahmā and released them by his own path;
then, remembering Śrī Hari with his mind, he offered salutation.

"O Lord, my mind shall not even slightly covet the property of another. Having fixed this single thought in his heart—that for the illustrious, infamy is a greater suffering than the loss of life—Brahmā dissolved into Brahman. (69–70)
Seeing her father dead and lamenting him repeatedly and intensely,
the maiden abandoned her body through yoga and merged into Brahman.
O best of sages, having seen both her father and her sister dead, [she acted likewise].
Having lamented, they remembered Śrī Hari, who delights in his own self, out of anger.
Then Nārāyaṇa, a portion of myself, arrived quickly out of compassion and restored Brahmā to life through the knowledge of Brahman, as well as that daughter of his.
Seeing Hari before him, Brahmā chose his desired boon:
"May there be eternal, unwavering, and undying devotion at Your feet.
Seeing Brahmā dejected, the Treasure of Compassion spoke to him: 74.
This awakening discourse is true, the essence of ethics, and captivating.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Brahmin; I shall now speak, having lifted up my face.
Abandon, O Lord of the World, this shame that takes the form of a fever in the heart.
(76) Whether it be good fame or ill repute, whether well-established or a source of affliction, it comes to both the base and the great solely through their own actions. (77)
For all people, one's own action is more powerful than all others;
therefore, the virtuous always perform good deeds continuously.
Some, however, root out all actions whatsoever.
Having experienced the full consequences of past actions, those whose minds are fixed on the lotus feet of Hari will certainly feel shame for their evil deeds;
from virtuous deeds, however, comes firm standing everywhere and stainless fame. (79–80)
O Creator, over time, the body, strength, beauty, fortune and misfortune, fame— which consists of the three qualities— as well as delusion and ill-repute,
debts, wounds, and slander of living beings all pass away through the power of time. (81)
Those two previously mentioned [objects] belong to the great ones, and never any other. 82.
Constant ill-repute dwells in the wives and possessions of others;
therefore, the virtuous do not seize them, as they are the cause of their own suffering. 83.
"Remember me within your Brahman-consciousness and make me your own object of focus;
then your restless mind will no longer be drawn toward the things of others.
Furthermore, my Māyā in the form of women is the deluder of all. (84)
He who delights in his own Self constantly creates delusion through his divine play.
In a place that is merely the locus of various mudrās, the passionate man finds constant pleasure;
yet [that place is] a lump of flesh called a breast, a lip which is a dwelling for saliva and is impure.
