Their hips, faces, and breasts are always the abode of the god of love;
therefore, the virtuous, who fear unrighteousness, do not look upon them.
What dharma, what fame, what standing, and what austerity can they possess?
What wisdom, what knowledge, or what generosity can there be for one whose mind is set on another’s wife?
In this world there is infamy and suffering, and in the next world there is dwelling in hells;
moreover, they suffer blows and beatings, and are devoured by worms.
Considering pleasure to be the seed of suffering, the deluded, due to the fault of fate,
constantly and joyfully engage in the pursuit of another's wife.
The best always [seek] the lotus feet of my state, while the middling always [seek] virtuous action.
The base always remember with delight the pursuit of another's wife.
Misfortune is constant for one whose mind is set upon the possessions of others—especially upon the wives of others, gold, and lands. (91–92)
He who, upon seeing another's wife by chance, desists while remembering Hari;
and he who, having seen another's gold, becomes pure by washing his hands;
such virtuous men are never attached to their own wives out of lust.
Out of fear of consumption, disease, loss of knowledge, and public reproach,
ascetics remain fixed in their austerities, scholars in their reflections on the scriptures,
yogis in their meditations on yoga, and those learned in the Vedas in the meaning of the Vedas. (94–95)
Householders are to be directed toward the service of their husbands and domestic duties;
those who enjoy sense-objects are to be directed toward me, my devotees, and my service.
These, being thus appointed to these tasks, are praised in assemblies. (96)
By the very practice of what is declared in the Vedas, those who act contrary to it are censured.
O Creator, all people always and eternally praise one who walks the path of the righteous;
even plowmen censure one who follows a wicked path.

"From this day forward, by my boon, your mind shall not dwell upon the wives of others nor upon the possessions of others while you live. Perform what is pleasing to me by remaining outside my domain as granted by me. 99.
O Brahmin, let there be born to me a daughter who, by meditating upon my lotus feet—which destroy all obstacles—shall become the beloved of Kāmadeva;
let her be named Rati, the presiding deity of passion, who must be abandoned [by him]. (100–101)
Having spoken thus and consoled Brahmā, the Lord of Kamalā,
whose delight is in Vṛndāvana, departed for eternal Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
By this very same discipline, Brahmā abandoned Mohinī; how then did he become unworthy of worship due to the curse of an unchaste woman? 1.
How did the Lord of Kamalā bring about his humiliation?
Tell me, for you are yourself the Lord of all and the seed of everything.
(2) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Rāseśvarī, the Lord of Rasikas smiled and began to relate that secret history to her. (3) Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having performed penance for a long time and obtained an excellent boon from me,
Brahmā became the Creator after fashioning various kinds of creation;
he is the bestower of the fruits of all austerities and the sovereign Lord who ordains the instruction of all.
Having realized himself to be the Lord, he indeed became possessed of great pride.
Thinking, "In all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), there is no elevation greater than pride," I brought about the destruction of Brahmā's arrogance.
"Whosoever may possess pride within the cosmic eggs as being higher than the highest—
the All-Self, having recognized all, am indeed their punisher.
I have heard that in the beginning, the pride of Brahmā was crushed to dust by me."
O beloved, listen as I describe in order the shattering of the pride of Śaṅkara and Pārvatī, as well as that of Candra, Ravi, Vahni, Durvāsas, and Dhanvantari. (8–9)
"O beloved, for those— whether small or great— who possess pride,
I shall reduce them to powder in such a manner.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, her throat, lips, and palate parched,
Rādhā, trembling and overwhelmed with fear, inquired with great effort.
(11) Śrī Rādhikā said:
By whose power did that great arrogance arise?
By what power was it previously shattered by you?
O Lord of my life, O crusher of the pride of all, please tell me.
The giver of pride, the giver of fear, the Lord who is the sole cause for the granting of life.
(13) Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
By whom was heard that which reduced the pride of Brahmā, the creator of the three worlds, to dust?
O Rādhā, listen to others as well; I shall tell them to you through Vyāsa:
He who is Śiva himself, a portion of my own self, and the destroyer of the worlds—he is equal to me in splendor, complete in knowledge, and in virtue. (14–19)
He whom yogins meditate upon is the Guru of the lords of yogins;
he is the very nature of the bliss of knowledge. Listen, O beloved, to his narrative, [he who] performed austerities day and night for sixty thousand yugas.
Having become filled with a portion of my own power, the Lord became equal to me.
By virtue of his austerity and splendor, he became a perpetual mass of radiance,
possessing the brilliance of ten million suns and serving as a wish-fulfilling tree for his devotees.
And after meditating upon that splendor for a long time,
the lords of yogis behold within it a most beautiful form—
resembling pure crystal, with five faces and three eyes. (19)
Holding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, clad in excellent tiger-skin garments, he was reciting the mantra to his own Self by means of his own self with a rosary of white lotus seeds;
his face was bright with a slight smile, his crest was adorned with the moon, and he was the Supreme beyond the supreme. (20–21)
Joyfully bearing a mass of matted locks with a golden luster upon his head,
he was peaceful, beautiful, and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees throughout the three worlds.
Then, recognizing him as his own Lord and the giver of all prosperity— 22 —
The wish-fulfilling tree grants everything desired to everyone;
likewise, the Lord of Boons, having granted whatever boon each person desired,
became filled with pride through his own divine play, though he is one who finds delight in his own self.
And once, the Daitya Vṛka performed severe penance at Kedāra for one year, day and night;
and the Treasure of Compassion, out of mercy, went to his presence constantly. (25)
The asura did not accept the boon he desired to grant.
At the end of the year, Śaṅkara himself remained perpetually before him;
bound by the noose of devotion, the granter of boons was unable to depart even for a moment.

The Daitya did not accept any sovereignty, any supernatural power, worldly enjoyment, liberation, or even the state of Hara from the wielder of the trident on any side. Seeing him meditating upon that lotus-foot, Maheśvara was struck with fear.
Overwhelmed with love, he wept for one who was motionless and made no request.
Due to his excessive weeping, his meditation was indeed broken;
he beheld before him the manifest giver of all prosperity. (29–30)
When the lord of the Daityas chose a boon through his illusory power with great devotion, Śiva placed his hand upon the demon's head, saying, "This shall become ashes.
Having said "Om," as the deity departed, that bull among Daityas rushed after him.
Mṛtyuñjaya, overwhelmed by terror, fled from the fear of death. His hand-drum fell, as did his beautiful tiger-skin. Naked, he fled toward the ten directions out of fear of the Dānava. (32–33)
Out of compassion, he who is affectionate toward his devotees does not kill even such a person;
and a virtuous man never follows the path of the wicked.
Even virtuous men will kill a servant, a son, or anyone else—except for a beloved wife—even if she herself kills them. (34)
And Śiva, unable even to awaken his own self, out of compassion, 35.
perceiving his own death and being terrified, became free from egoism;
repeatedly remembering me, O blessed lady, he went to me alone for refuge. 36.
Seeing him approaching his own hermitage with his throat, lips, and palate parched, muttering "O Hari, save me! Save me! while overwhelmed by fear, that Daitya was placed near him and awakened by me.
Questioned, he related the entire account to me in due order.
Then, by my command, the asura was swiftly deceived by illusion;
placing his hand upon his own head, he instantly turned to ashes.
Then the Siddhas, the lords of the gods, the lords of the sages, and the Manus praised me with joy and great devotion; and Śiva, overcome with shame, became humbled,
his pride was crushed to powder, and he attained enlightenment through my instruction.

"The Giver of Boons grants a boon; therefore, I am indeed Śiva, who is to be awakened. Then Rudra, filled with pride, thinking in his mind that he was the destroyer of all worlds, resolved to slay the formidable Tripura.
Thinking, "Who is this Daitya? and considering him to be like a moth, he went to the battle, casting aside the trident given by me and my supreme armor.
The combat continued for a long time, day and night, for one full year.
At that time, no one was able to defeat the other; the two were equals in battle.
O beloved, having placed his feet upon the earth, the lord of the Daityas rose up very high by means of his illusory power (māyā) to a height of fifty crore yojanas.
The Lord of the World, Śaṅkara, quickly rose up to slay the Daitya.
A battle took place there for one month in that desolate place.
The powerful Asura cut through the weapons and the bow of Śaṅkara.
The lord of the Daityas shattered the chariot, the bow, and the weapons received from Śaṅkara.
In his great wrath, Rudra struck the lord of the Dānavas with his fist;
by that blow of his thunderbolt-like fist, the latter immediately fell into a swoon.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, that bull among the Dānavas, out of rage,
lifted up the reclining Śiva and cast him down upon the ground.
When Rudra had been thrown from his chariot, the gods and celestial sages were struck with fear.
They praised me, saying again and again, "O Kṛṣṇa, protect us!
Hara, free from fear though facing a cause for fear, called upon me alone and,
in that crisis, praised me with devotion using the hymn granted by me.
Then, quickly assuming the form of a bull by means of my partial incarnation (kalā),
I seized the wide-striding Śaṅkara as he lay asleep with my two horns;
I then gave him my own armor and my trident that crushes enemies.
Having reached that place of the Danavas, which was situated very high and without support,
Hara struck Tripura with the spear given by me.
Then, filled with shame, he praised me alone, the destroyer of his pride.
The lord of the Daityas fell instantly, reduced to powder upon the earth.
All the gods and sages joyfully praised Śaṅkara. Then the omnipresent Lord Śaṅkara abandoned the pride that was the seed of obstacles.
His nature is knowledge and bliss, and he is untainted by all actions.
Therefore, I carry that beloved one in the form of a bull;
there is no one dearer to me than Śiva in the three worlds.
Brahmā is my very nature as the mind; Maheśvara is my nature as knowledge.
The divine Durgā is my intellect, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti.
Those powers such as sleep and the rest are all the various manifestations (kalās) of Prakṛti.
She who is the presiding goddess of speech is Sarasvatī herself.
The lord of the Gaṇas, in the form of Harṣa, is the presiding deity of my welfare.
The supreme reality is Dharma himself, and the fire-god Agni is my devotee.
You are the presiding goddess of all sovereignty for me and for all the inhabitants of Goloka;
you are the presiding goddess of my life-breath, and you are always superior to my very life.
The cowherd girls are but your portions (kalās), and for that reason they are dear to me.
The cowherds born from my pores are all the inhabitants of Goloka;
the sun, whose nature is splendor, is known as my vital breaths,
and Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, and the earth are born from my excretions.
The great void is mine; Madana is born from my mind.
Indra and all the other gods have arisen from minute portions of my own power.
Indeed, these—the Great Principle (Mahat) and the rest—are the seeds of creation.
I am the seed-form of all, the Self itself, independent and without support. The individual soul (jīva) is my reflection, the one authorized for the experience of karma.
I am the witness, devoid of desire, and not an enjoyer in any actions.
"This body of mine, which exists for the sake of devotion and meditation, belongs to one who is composed of his own will.
I am both Prakṛti and Puruṣa; I alone am the Supreme beyond the supreme.
O Rādhā, thus has been told this [account] that removes the pride of Śiva.
"And hear from me the seed of creation, which releases the pride of Pārvatī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
To Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and Lord, who had spoken thus—
The goddess Rādhikā asked about her secret desire. Śrī Rādhikā said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all truths, seed of all, eternal one!"
Speak to me my desired question, which shall shatter all doubts.
Śaṅkara is the presiding deity of all knowledge and the knower of all principles;
the Lord is the conqueror of death, the time of time, and great like you.
How is it that the Lord of Gods has limbs of cosmic splendor, five faces, and three eyes;
that he is naked, wears matted locks, and is adorned with a multitude of serpents;
and that he wanders about on a bull, having abandoned his excellent vehicle? (72)
Why does he not wear ornaments fashioned from the finest jewels?
Having cast aside garments purified by fire, he wears a tiger skin;
and having abandoned the *pārijāta* tree, he wears the *dhattūra* flower. (73–74)
There is no desire for a jeweled crown; there is supreme delight in matted locks.

Having abandoned the divine world, the Lord’s longing is for cremation grounds. (75) Having renounced sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and fragrant flowers, his longing is for bilva leaves, bilva wood, and its ointment. (76)
"I wish to know this; O Lord, tell it in detail.
O Master, my curiosity and the longing of my heart to hear it increase.
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, Madhusūdana smiled.
Having placed Rādhā upon his chest, he began to tell a story.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"After performing austerities for sixty thousand yugas, Maheśvara..."
Pūrṇatama ceased [speaking], having meditated upon me with a joyful mind.
In that interval, he beheld me standing before him—
possessing exceedingly beautiful limbs, a youth, and dark-complexioned beauty.
Having beheld that unsurpassed form, which was beyond description, the Three-Eyed One did not become satiated with his two eyes;
thinking in his mind, "I am gazing without blinking," he remained thus. (81)
Due to the excess of his devotion, the great devotee wept, overwhelmed by love.
The thousand-faced Ananta, the fortunate one, and the four-faced Brahmā, having beheld [the Lord] with many eyes, praised Him with many mouths. (82–83)
"What shall I see, or what shall I praise, having obtained such a protector?"—
thus she thought again and again in her own mind, seeing him fourfold through his single face and two eyes, both in Śaṅkara and in the ascetic woman. 84.
That [face] became a fourth, making five together with the eastern one.
Each individual face shone with three eyes each;
therefore, he came to be known by the names Pañcavaktra (Five-faced) and Trilocana (Three-eyed).
Śiva’s affection for me increased through my hymn of praise,
and because of that, he came to possess many eyes;
for the eyes of him whose nature is Brahman are themselves of the nature of his qualities.

Understand that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are its causes. Beholding with a gaze consisting of the *sattva* portion, Śambhu protects those characterized by *sattva*; with the *rajas* portion, those characterized by *rajas*; and with the *tamas* portion, those characterized by *tamas*. Subsequently, from the eye of Hara situated on his forehead, which consists of *tamas*—
At the time of dissolution, fire shall manifest from the Destroyer in a state of wrath;
ten million tālas in height and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns, with long flickering flames, that Lord is capable of burning the three worlds. (90–91)
That omnipresent Lord, whose body is composed of the ashes of the funeral rites of Satī,
wears her garland of bones and her ashes out of a spirit of love.
Although the Lord delights in his own self, nevertheless, for a full year—
Taking the skull of Satī, he wandered here and there and wept.
Wherever it fell upon each of her limbs,
there arose a Siddha-pīṭha that grants the perfection of mantras.
Then, O Rādhikā, having reduced him to nothing but a corpse and placing him upon his chest, Śaṅkara fell down unconscious at that field of perfection (siddhikṣetra).
Then, having gone to Maheśa and taking him onto his lap, he awakened him.
I gave him the supreme, divine truth that removes all sorrow.
Then Śiva, being well-pleased, departed for his own world;
and in due course, through another form, he regained his beloved Satī.
By virtue of his bearing divine garlands, there is no desire in the eternal, supreme Lord.
Even today, through discernment, he wears matted locks from the time of his ascetic penance;
yet the yogi has no desire for the grooming of hair or for the adornment of his own body.
He is equal toward sandalwood paste, mud, a clod of earth, and a sovereign jewel.
The serpents, who were enemies of Garuḍa, sought refuge with Śaṅkara;
out of compassion, He bears those very same ones upon His own body as they have come for refuge. (99–100)
I am the bull-form vehicle; another is incapable of bearing that burden.
Formerly, during the destruction of Tripura, he was born from a portion of my own energy.
[He brought] the Pārijāta and other flowers, fragrant scents, sandalwood, and so forth.
Having thus entrusted [everything] to me, he never has such attachment to those things:
to the *dhattūra* flower, nor to the application of *bilva* leaves, nor to fragrant yet scentless substances, nor to the tiger skin beloved by yogis. (2–3)
His mind is not set on the divine world, nor on a celestial couch among the people;
rather, he meditates upon me day and night in the cremation ground, in utter solitude.
Śiva regards all things equally, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
My mind is immersed here in this form that is beyond description.
Even by the falling of Brahmā or the wielder of the trident (Śiva), but a single moment would pass;
nor do I know the measure of its lifespan—what scripture could describe it?
Śaṅkara wields the trident that conquers death, which is equal to my own splendor.
Without me, no one is capable of defeating that Śaṅkara.
Śaṅkara is my Supreme Self; the auspicious Lord is dearer to me than even my own life-breaths.

O Tryambaka, my mind is forever fixed on you; no one other than you is dear to me. (8) The multitude of cosmic eggs, ever shrouded by my *māyā*, trembles before Hara; yet it is not capable of deluding him. (9)
I do not dwell in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor upon your chest; I am forever bound by the noose of love within the heart of Sadāśiva.
By this son born of his own essence, Śaṅkara [is honored] with five faces.
He constantly sings my song; therefore, I am in his presence.
Indeed, that yogi who, by the mere play of a frown, is capable of creating and destroying a multitude of universes through yoga—there is no one superior to Śaṅkara.
He who, by the play of a mere frown of his eyebrows, can through divine knowledge create or destroy death, time, and all else—there is no devotee wiser than Śaṅkara.
[To him belong] my devotion, service, liberation, and all riches. (13)
He alone is capable of bestowing all success; there is no giver other than Śaṅkara.
Indeed, he who chants my name day and night with fivefold speech, and who constantly meditates upon my form—there is no devotee superior to Śaṅkara. (14–15)
"I am Sudarśana, and we are equal in splendor to Śambhu.
Brahmā is the creator through yoga, yet he is not our equal in splendor.
Thus was the entire stainless glory of Śaṅkara recounted.
"Nevertheless, do you wish to hear further of his humiliation?

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise of Śaṅkara by Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"O destroyer of doubt, tell me: why is it not considered praiseworthy for the all-pervading Lord, the Master of All, the Great Soul who has become thus, to have remnants of food?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate an ancient history which is like a blazing crest of flame for burning the fuel of sins. Once, Sanatkumāra went to Vaikuṇṭha.
The twice-born saw the Lord Nārāyaṇa having finished his meal;
he prostrated with devotion and joy and praised him with profound hymns.
Being pleased, the Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, gave him the remnants of the food.
Upon merely arriving there, he ate some food right then and there;
he also set aside a portion, difficult to obtain, for his kinsmen to eat.
And that which was given at Siddhāśrama to the trident-bearing Guru—
And through the intensity of his devotion, all that was enjoyed by him merely upon being attained.
Having consumed that most difficult thing to obtain, he danced, overwhelmed with love;
his entire body marked with horripilation, his eyes filled with tears, and filled with joy.
Singing my virtues with devotion from his five mouths, Su-kaṇṭha, absorbed in a particular musical mode (*rāga*) and beautiful in its rhythmic measure (*tāla*),
dropped the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), the horn, and the tiger-skin from his hands.
Having himself fallen down and then weeping, he indeed fell into a swoon;
with his mind one-pointed, meditating upon that exceedingly beautiful form,
he beheld me situated within the thousand-petaled lotus of his heart.
In the meantime, Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of the afflictions of distress, arrived quickly with joy, her face and eyes radiant with grace.
Seeing him weeping, unconscious, and prostrating out of devotion, [she approached]. (11)
Laughing, she asked about the news of the trident-bearing youth.
With palms joined in reverence, the youth told her everything.
Upon hearing this, the goddess, her lower lip quivering, became enraged at Śiva.
As the goddess rose up to curse her, the three-eyed Lord awakened her with various words and praised her with palms joined in reverence. Having heard that captivating hymn, Śivā did not curse Śiva.
That wheel became defiled by his leavings and was unfit to be eaten even by the wise.
(15) Neither the power of people, nor their asceticism, fortune, or splendor [avails them];
even the Destroyer of the Entire Universe trembled out of fear of Pārvatī. (16)
The Mother of the World, the progenitor of the Gaṇas, her eyes like red lotuses, spoke these supreme words, the very essence of policy, with anger:
"Alas! Such is the power of asceticism and the luster of those who live by their own splendor! (17)
The daughter of the mountain trembled before him, the destroyer of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
Pārvatī said:
"You are the nourisher and protector of the worlds, and especially mine."
The speaker of the four Vedas, the progenitor himself, the all-pervading Lord,
the bestower of liberation upon devotees, and the giver of all prosperity—
if you practice such wicked policy, who indeed will protect the Dharma? (19–20)
I am always to be protected by you and nourished as your devoted servant;
yet, due to the fault of my past actions, I have been deprived of eating the *nirmālya* (remnants) of Śiva.
A certain thing is purified by gold, and another substance by air.
By the mere washing away of a little [impurity], everything is purified through offering to Viṣṇu.
All the deities, the ancestors, and likewise guests should be worshipped with food offered to Viṣṇu; this is the settled conclusion in the Vedas. (22–23)
That which is not offered and is unfit for consumption becomes the *naivedya* (food offering) within the belly of Hari.
He who, having renounced [worldly desires], partakes of it with devotion shall become a foremost attendant (*pārṣada*) of the Lord.
Among all things, this is nectar—the essence of all that is desired, and exceedingly difficult to attain.
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of food offered to Viṣṇu.
Alas, that nectar-like food offering of Hari alone makes one equal to Hari; it destroys untimely death and deludes the foolish. (25–26)
He who, having associated with the virtuous, partakes of that food offering by chance,
obtains the fruit of ascetic penance for sixty thousand years.
And he who, being a devotee, always eats with devotion after having offered it to Hari.
Or what penance will he perform? He is equal to Hari in splendor.
Previously, I heard from your own mouth in Puṣkara, in the assembly of sages:
"I am the ordainer of the Vedas; am I not capable of speaking? (28–29)
"O Lord, after performing austerities for a very long time, you were obtained by me as my master.
O Lord, how have I been deceived by you through the grace of Viṣṇu,
since you have not now given me the food offering (naivedya) belonging to Viṣṇu?"
Therefore, O Maheśvara, accept this very fruit from me.
From this day forward, those people who consume your *naivedya* (offering) shall indeed become dogs for one birth in Bhārata.
Having spoken thus, Mother Pārvatī wept before the Lord.
Her gaze fell upon his throat, and he became blue-throated (Nīlakaṇṭha).
Then Śiva, out of devotion, respectfully placed Śivā upon his chest.
He indeed dispelled that injury to his pride with a hymn and with humility.
Wiping the tears from his eyes again and again with his hand,
he consoled him with various charming words of prudent counsel.
And that queen, being thoroughly satisfied, said to her husband:
"I shall cast off this body if it is without the *naivedya* offering of Hari;
for He constantly sustains this body of yours, which increases your good fortune. (36)
How can I carry this body, devoid of fortune?
Your unprecedented offering, which removes birth, death, and old age, has been rendered defiled;
therefore, look, I shall cast off this body. (37–38)
"O Lord, whatever is offered upon the *liṅga* is indeed unacceptable;
however, it becomes perfectly pure for him if it is mixed with the *naivedya* of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus, that goddess prepared to cast off her body.
Terrified, Hara praised her in her presence and accepted [the boon].
Śaṅkara said:
"Be firm, O Great Goddess Caṇḍikā, Mother of the World!"
O beautiful one, you ought to forgive all my transgressions.
Show mercy toward me, your servant, who has been purchased by your ascetic power.
O Eternal One, you who are the seed-source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Oh, O beloved of the Lord of Goloka, who transcend the qualities yet abide in that which is beyond qualities;
whose very nature is all-pervasive power; who are eternally His companion;
who possess both form and formlessness; who are eternal and composed of Your own will! 43.

Out of compassion, O Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), enchanting one whose nature is the seed of all things, O Goddess who bestows all perfections, who grants liberation, and who grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa— reside right now within my breast, which belongs to that very All-pervading Lord.
"Only the will of Śrī Hari is sufficient; I am not even capable of granting this.
Therefore, having abandoned the body, go to the Nirguṇa state within the Nirguṇa.
Having spoken thus, Candraśekhara stood before him.
She became exceedingly gracious and bowed down to Hara, the Supreme.
(47) Thus was this hymn to Pārvatī composed by Śaṅkara in the past;
whoever recites it, even when seized by calamity, is liberated from fear. (48)
There would be a breach of friendship, whereas previously there was great affection between them;
yet Pārvatī, being well-pleased, would not abandon his abode.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard the promise of her Lord, she became exceedingly pleased.
By the command of Śaṅkara, she went quickly to the celestial river (Gaṅgā) for the purpose of bathing.
Having bathed and worshipped with devotion that fragrant and supreme [deity] who is beyond the guṇas...
He quickly prepared the sweet foods and side dishes that had been set forth.
Having bathed and worshipped the eternal Brahmajyotis,
Śiva praised me alone, who am situated within his heart, with supreme devotion.
Having gone there, Pārvatī ate everything, gave him his heart's desire, and received the food offering (naivedya);
then, filled with joy, she returned to your presence along with her husband, eating the remnants. || 53 ||
He praised Śaṅkara with devotion and prostrated himself again and again.
(54) Thus, O Queen of the Gods, everything you asked has been told:
the reason why the *nirmālya* of Śaṅkara was cursed. (55)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Episode of the Curse for Wearing Śiva’s Offerings," in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Goddess, you have heard of the shattering of the pride of Śaṅkara, the teacher of the world.
Now hear from me the liberation of Durga from her pride.
Having manifested through the splendor of all the gods, the Mother of the World assumed the form of a lovely and enchanting woman. 1–2.
Having slain the lords of the Dānavas, she protected the host of the gods.
Then the Goddess took birth from the womb of Dakṣa’s wife. That Goddess grasped the Pināka-wielder as her means for accomplishing the welfare of the gods.

The virtuous woman served her husband with constant and supreme devotion. Yet, due to the turn of fate, there arose in the past, within the assembly of the gods, a hostility toward Śiva on the part of the divine Dakṣa—a hostility that was truly without cause. (4–5)
Then Dakṣa, having returned from that [sacrifice] in a state of anger, performed another sacrifice;
there he made a proclamation to everyone except Śaṅkara. All the deities, accompanied by their wives, arrived at Dakṣa’s abode.
Accompanied by his retinue, Śaṅkara did not come out of anger and pride.
Satī, out of delusion, tried diligently to awaken her husband,
yet she herself, being fickle, was unable to move him.
She came to her father’s house out of pride, even without his permission.
By his curse, her pride was indeed shattered;
for her father did not even exchange a word with her.
And having heard the censure of her husband, she abandoned her body out of pride. (10) Thus, O beloved, has been narrated the relinquishing of the pride of the Satī;
now hear of her subsequent birth and the constant breaking of her pride. (11)
The virtuous woman quickly obtained birth in the womb of the mountain’s wife. Śiva, out of devotion, took her funeral ashes and bones;
he made a garland of the bones and anointed his body with the ashes.
Remembering Satī again and again with love, and beholding her over and over, Menā gave birth to that goddess who was exceedingly beautiful;
indeed, there is no comparison for her anywhere in the creation of the Creator. Born of virtue, she possesses all virtues and bears every form.
And all the wives of the gods do not equal even a sixteenth part of her.
She grew like the digit of the moon in the bright fortnight;
and day by day, she reached the full bloom of youth while in the mountain dwelling.
And a voice from the sky addressed that Mother of the World:
"O Śivā, you shall obtain auspiciousness through severe penance;
yet, without the Lord, you shall not indeed attain the state of being conceived in a womb. (17)
Having heard this, she stood there laughing, proud of her youth:
"How is it that he who carries my ashes and bones from a previous birth does not take me as his wife upon seeing me grown up in this life? (18–19)

How could he, who was consumed by grief for me and wandered through the universe, not take me upon seeing me, most beautiful of all? He, the ocean of mercy, who destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice for my sake—how could he not accept me? (20)
How is it that he does not accept me as his wife in birth after birth?

For whoever was the wife of whom, and whoever was the husband of whom, in the past from of old—how could there be any separation between them in this world? Their union would not be otherwise. (21–22)

Thinking herself superior in her own intelligence, that virtuous woman did not perform penance, nor did she recognize him as the Lord, considering him merely a repository of all physical qualities. Among all beautiful women, she thought, "There is no one more beautiful than I. (23)
Thinking thus in her heart, Śivā did not perform penance out of pride:
"A man is captivated by the beauty, youth, and attire of his own wives;
yet Śiva, merely by hearing of me, desires me even without penance. (24–29)
Thinking thus in her heart, the Daughter of the Mountain remained in the home of Himavat,
perpetually intoxicated with play day and night in the midst of her constant companions.
In the meantime, a messenger quickly arrived at the assembly of the Lord of Mountains.
Approaching him with his hands joined in reverence, he spoke sweetly before him:
The messenger said:
"Arise, arise, O Lord of Mountains! Go to the vicinity of the imperishable banyan tree."
Mahādeva, whose vehicle is the bull, arrived with his retinue.
Having offered the madhuparka and other honors, with his neck bowed low in devotion, he said:
"O Lord of Mountains, perform the worship of that Indra of gods who transcends the senses. (28–29)
The very nature of perfection, the Lord of Perfection, the teacher of the lords of yogis;
the conqueror of death, the death of time, the eternal light of Brahman;
the nature of the Supreme Self, both with attributes and without attributes, the all-pervading.
Bearing a stainless body for the sake of his devotion and meditation, the Lord [remained there].
(31) Having heard the words of the messenger, the Mountain, filled with joy, rose up;
taking the madhuparka and other offerings, he went into the presence of Śaṅkara. (32)
Having heard the words of the messenger, the goddess, her face and eyes radiant with joy, thought thus in her heart: "For my sake, Maheśvara has arrived.
She assumed an incomparable appearance and put on exquisite garments.

He fashioned for Śaṅkara ornaments made of the finest essence of jewels, a captivating jewel-necklace, and a garland of *pārijāta* flowers combined with sandalwood; indeed, he considered that garland to be truly enchanting. (34–35)
Seated upon that jeweled lion-throne, she beheld her face in the mirror—
adorned with a spot of musk along with a dot of vermilion,
and possessing a pair of slightly reddened eyes anointed with pure collyrium. (36)
Like a stainless midday sun surrounded by rows of bees, his pair of very tender lips was suffused with the red hue of betel;
exceedingly beautiful, they were like lovely, ripe bimba fruits. (37–38)
And his cheeks were resplendent with the luster of jeweled earrings, like the peak of Mount Sumeru blazing at sunrise;
he was utterly indescribable and captivating with his rows of teeth. (39)
Like a cluster of pearls with water at the onset of the rainy season,
adorned with elephant-pearls and a most beautiful, excellent nose;
as splendid as Mount Meru graced by the stream of the celestial river.
Like a fresh rain-cloud adorned with rows of cranes, he was endowed with the weight of a braid of hair entwined with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
he possessed the luster of molten gold and shone brilliantly upon his beautiful chest. (42)
Her pair of breasts, anointed with necklaces of the finest jewels and perfumed with musk and saffron,
possesses the lovely hue of a beautiful campaka flower; they are enchanting,
resembling jujube fruits, and adorned with charming nipples.
The waist was captivating, slender, and radiant with its deep navel;
the abdomen was exceedingly beautiful, charming, and perfectly rounded.
His pair of thighs were as enchanting as they were uniquely surpassing the plantain stalks. (45)
Her abode of desire was very firm and concealed by a silken garment;
her pair of feet, which eclipsed the luster of land-lotuses, were captivating,
adorned with jeweled anklets and decorated with perfected lac-dye.
Wearing jeweled anklets that imitated royal swans,
adorned with ornaments made of the finest essence of gems fashioned by Viśvakarman,
her hand was exceedingly tender, beautiful, and possessed the luster of gold.
Adorned with ornaments of gems, bracelets, armlets, and conchs;
bearing a fine jewel-mirror and a radiant play-lotus;
and wearing an incomparable, most beautiful gem-studded ring. (49–50)

Having beheld his incomparable form, she meditated upon Śaṅkara, the Lord; with her mind she constantly distinguished the lotus-feet of her husband above her father, mother, kinsmen, virtuous women, and brothers. (51) She [then thought of] her father, mother, relatives, the assembly of virtuous women, and her brother.
In that interval, she remembered nothing at all except Śiva.
Then the Lord of Mountains beheld there the Moon-crested One,
rising with a smile from the beautiful sandy bank of the celestial river.
Wearing a consecrated garland and chanting my name, he shines with a mass of matted locks endowed with the luster of molten gold;
mounted upon a bull, holding a trident in his hand, and resplendent with all ornaments. (54)
He has a serpent as his sacred thread and is adorned with ornaments of snakes;
he resembles pure crystal, wears a tiger skin, and is supreme.
His limbs are decorated with holy ashes, he wears a garland of bones, and he is clothed only by the directions.
He beheld Rudra with five faces and three eyes, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, blazing on all sides with the luster of Brahman;
to Śiva’s left was Mahākāla, and to his right was Nandikeśvara.
[He saw] bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, brahmarākṣasas, vetālas, and kṣetrapālas, as well as Bhairavas of terrible prowess;
and Sanaka, Sananda, Kumāra, and Sanātana. (58–59)
Jaigīṣavya, Devala, Kāṇāda, Gautama, as well as Pippalāda, Kaṇakhana, Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Kaṭha,
Jājali, Karakha, Karṇa, Lomaśa, and Sūryavarcas.
Having bowed to Kātyāyana, Pāṇini, Śaṅkha, Durvāsas,
Śātātapa, Pāribhadra, Aṣṭāvakra, and Marudbhava—
these being the foremost— he, the Mountain, prostrated himself before Śiva.

Prostrating himself upon the ground like a staff with his palms joined in reverence, he then took hold of his lotus feet with profound devotion; with eyes brimming with tears and his body covered in horripilation, he bowed down to him. (63)
With this hymn, Dharmadatta praised the Supreme Lord.
When the day of Brahmā had passed and the solar eclipse at Puṣkara had occurred, Himālaya spoke:
Himālaya said:
You are Brahmā, the creator; you are Viṣṇu, the protector.
You are Śiva, the infinite bestower of auspiciousness and the agent of universal dissolution.
You are the Lord, transcending all qualities, eternal, and whose form is light.
You are the primordial nature, the lord of nature, the one born of nature, and that which transcends nature.
You assume various forms for the sake of meditation by your devotees;
you manifest whatever form in which they find delight. (67)
You are the sun, the progenitor of creation and the support of all splendors;
you are the moon, the protector of the crops by means of your constant cool rays.
You are the wind, you are Varuṇa, and you are the fire that consumes everything.
You are Indra, the king of the gods, as well as Time, Death, and Yama;
you are the conqueror of death, the death of death, the one who ordains time, and the ender of Yama.
You are the Veda, the creator of the Vedas, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
You are the progenitor of the wise, and you yourself are a wise man, the preceptor of the learned.
You are indeed the mantra, you are the recitation, you are the austerity, and the bestower of its fruit.
You are speech, you are the presiding deity of speech, you are its performer, and you are yourself its teacher.
"Aha! O seed of Sarasvatī, who here is capable of praising you?
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Mountains stood holding Śiva’s lotus feet;
there Śiva remained, having awakened him and descended from his bull.
The man who recites this highly meritorious hymn at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and from the fears within the ocean of existence.
If one should recite it for a single month, even a childless person obtains a son.
One bereft of a wife shall obtain a virtuous and most charming spouse;
he shall certainly and suddenly recover an object lost for a long time.
One fallen from his kingdom shall regain his kingdom through the grace of Śaṅkara.
In a prison, in a cremation ground, when overwhelmed by enemies, or in extreme distress;
in deep water, amidst a great flood, in a wrecked ship, or in despair;
in the midst of battle, in great fear, or surrounded by predatory beasts—(in these situations, one should remember the mantra). 77–78.
By praising [him], one is liberated from everything through the grace of Śaṅkara.
(79) Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having thus offered praise, the Himālaya mountain, having received permission and being honored by all, dwelt at a distance in front of Śaṅkara as he resided there;
he offered him the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors with devotion.
Then he worshipped the sages and the attendants of Śaṅkara. At that time, Menakā, having arrived there with a host of women,
beheld Śaṅkara, the moon-crested one, seated at the foot of the banyan tree.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile,
he sat upon a tiger skin in the midst of a host of sages, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
like the radiant king of stars [the moon] in the sky among the constellations.
His form was supremely gladdening, resembling ten million Kandarpas;
having abandoned the state of old age, he possessed fresh youth.
He was exceedingly beautiful, charming, and a thief of the hearts of women. (5–6)

He is Mahāviṣṇu to the Vaiṣṇavas, Sadāśiva to the Śaivas, the very nature of Śakti to the Śāktas, and the form of Sūrya to the Sauras— just as a son is to virtuous women who are afflicted by desire for their lover. (7)
He is the very nature of Time, the protector of the virtuous and the destroyer of the wicked.
He is equal to the Death of Time, the death of Death itself, and terrifying to behold.
His beautiful garment was a tiger skin, and his sandalwood paste was ash.
The serpents are his beautiful garlands; the musk is the radiance of his poison.
His matted locks contain lovely crests, and the moon serves as sandalwood paste for his forehead.
The most exquisite garland of *mālatī* flowers is the captivating stream of the Gaṅgā.

A garland of bones, a garland of jewels, a dhattūra flower, and a beautiful campaka—these five, unified as a single five-faced form, were adorned with a pair of lotus-eyes. Resplendent like the full moon of autumn, it shone most brilliantly, surpassing even the bandhujīva flower; its upper and lower lips were enchanting.
The white moon and the lordly bull, along with Bhūta and the others, were like dancers;
O Maheśvarī, they all immediately performed a circumambulation of Maheśa.
Having thus beheld the form of Śiva, Menā became truly delighted. (13–14)
Some, devoid of blinking and their hair standing on end with desire,
became truly overcome by intense passion, while others fell into a swoon.
Some, having censured their lovers, praised Maheśvara.
Some embrace him with their minds full of longing;
another, out of desire, joyfully performs a mental kiss, thinking:
"Surely we shall fulfill our passion within the ocean of love."
"If he were our husband only in the next world, then fame would be ours;
but what shall we do with such lovers in this very life?
Enough of them!"—thus some women spoke as they gazed upon him for a long time.
Some, having seen Śiva, slightly covered their faces with their garments;
smiling and with sidelong glances, they looked at him again and again, saying:
"We shall not go home; we shall go into the presence of Śiva. (19–20)
"Day and night we shall joyfully behold the face of the autumnal moon;
we shall no longer undergo worldly existence, but enter the sacrificial fire.
Thus some women speak, saying, "Śiva shall be our Lord."
"Aho! How fortunate is Durgā, whose birth in Bhārata is so praiseworthy!"—thus some spoke, saying, "He whose lord is this Śiva. Seeing Śiva, Menā returned home with them in great joy. (22–23)

Having fully worshipped Śiva and bowed down, the Lord of Mountains went to his own home. Having deliberated in private with Menā, the Lord of Mountains dispatched Durgā to the presence of Śiva for the sake of Śiva. (24)

Having prepared a captivating disguise together with her friends, Pārvatī, filled with love and joy, went into the presence of Śiva. Seeing Śiva, peaceful and with a gracious face and eyes, Śivā [was moved]. (25–26)

Having performed seven circumambulations, she bowed down with a smile. To him who was single-mindedly devoted, virtuous, peerless, and the best among the wise, she gave this blessing: "O beautiful one, may you obtain a handsome husband. (27)
O auspicious mistress, your good fortune shall be constant;
O virtuous one, you shall have a son equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities.
O Mother of the World, supreme worship shall be yours throughout the three realms.
And in all the cosmic eggs, become supreme among all beings!
Since you have performed seven circumambulations and bowed with devotion, O beautiful one, I am pleased with you for seven lifetimes; receive the fruit thereof.
"Whatever the degree of faith one has in a sacred ford, a beloved deity, a preceptor, a mantra, or likewise a medicinal herb,
such indeed shall be their success.
Having said this, Śaṅkara quickly [merged] me into the supreme Brahman-light.
Having assumed a yogic posture upon a tiger skin, the Lord of Yogis meditated.
The Goddess, having washed her feet, drank the water from his feet;
with devotion, she performed the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) using a cloth purified by fire.
He indeed presented a beautiful jeweled lion-throne fashioned by Viśvakarman and other artisans;
he offered unprecedented food offerings placed in a bronze vessel,
and he gave water for the feet consisting of the waters of the Mandākinī.
He offered fragrant sandalwood paste, beautiful musk, and saffron, as well as a garland of *mālatī* flowers upon his neck, which was as lovely as poison;
then, with devotion, he performed worship and rained down flowers for his satisfaction. (36)
He offered sweet honey situated in a golden vessel;
a hundred jewel-lamps and excellent incense on all sides;
garments difficult to obtain in the three worlds, and a golden sacred thread (yajñopavīta). || 37–38 ||
Pārvatī gave fragrant, cool water for drinking,
as well as an exceedingly beautiful and charming ornament made of the finest jewels,
and the rare wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) endowed with golden horns.
Having offered bathing water from sacred fords, delightful betel leaf,
and the sixteen modes of worship (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), he prostrated again and again.
Having worshipped the Wielder of the Trident with devotion, he went daily to his father’s house.
Maheśvara Indra heard of the goddess from the mouths of the Apsarases;
having heard this news, Śunāsīra danced, filled with joy.
In haste, he summoned Kāmadeva through a messenger.
By Indra’s command, Kāmadeva went to Amarāvatī;
he dispatched him quickly to where Śiva and Śivā were.
Equipped with his five arrows, the five-arrowed god departed.

There, Madana went and beheld the all-pervading Lord Śiva, who was accompanied by Śivā; he was serene-faced, glorious, and endowed with power. He was peaceful, the beloved of the three worlds, and possessed a gracious countenance and eyes. (45)
Kāma, standing in the intermediate space and holding his bow with an arrow,
joyfully discharged an irresistible and infallible weapon at Śaṅkara.
That weapon, though infallible, became futile against the Supreme Self.
Like the sky, unstained within the unstained Supreme Self;
and as his weapon became futile, Manmatha was seized by fear.
Standing before him and beholding the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya, he trembled.
Overwhelmed by fear, Kāma remembered the thirty gods, Śakra and the others.
All the deities arrived, trembling from the wrath of Śambhu,
and they offered praise to Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty, with a hymn of praise.
As the gods offered praise, that fire born of Śambhu— emitting the flame of his anger from his eye in the forehead,
blazing with upward-pointing crests like the fire at the end of an aeon— flared up intensely.
Leaping into the sky and whirling about, he fell back to the surface of the earth;
spinning again and again all around, he fell upon Madana.
In an instant, Kāma was reduced to ashes by the wrath of Hara.
All the deities were despondent, and Pārvatī, her face bowed down,
lamented profusely before Hara.
All the deities, trembling with fear, offered praise to the moon-crested Lord.
All the gods spoke to Rati and wept again and again:
"O Mother, take some of this ash and abandon your fear;
we shall restore him to life, and you will regain your beloved once more. (55)
On that day when Hara’s anger had been dispelled and he was well-pleased,
Pārvatī, having witnessed the lamentation of Rati, fell into a swoon;
she then praised the moon-crested Lord, who transcends the senses and is beyond all qualities.
Leaving the weeping Pārvatī, Śiva departed for his own abode;
immediately thereafter, the pride of Pārvatī was dispelled right there,
and the daughter of the mountain abandoned her arrogance regarding her beauty and youth.
She felt shame before her circle of friends to show her face. And all the gods, having consoled Rati,
bowed down to Rudra like a staff, their minds agitated by grief, and went to their own abodes.
Having praised and wept out of grief and fear, Rādhikā, longing for her desire,
went to her own abode, leaving Rudra with eyes reddened by anger.
Pārvatī, however, did not go to her father’s house due to her shame.
Though being restrained by her female companions, she went to the forest for asceticism.
Her attendants followed after her, overwhelmed with grief.
Though being restrained by her mothers, she [went] to the forest on the bank of the celestial river (Svarṇadī).
Having performed austerities for a very long time, she attained the Three-eyed Lord;
and by the boon of Śaṅkara, Rati regained Madana.
Thus has everything regarding the removal of Pārvatī’s pride been told.
"O Rādhā, what more do you wish to hear regarding her secret conduct? (65).
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"Oh, how wonderful and unprecedented is this conduct! What have I heard, O Lord?
It is beautiful, nectar to the ears, profound, and the cause of knowledge.
Neither the specific details nor the summary have been heard, nor is the full expansion desired."
Now I wish to hear; tell me in detail, O Lord:
what various severe austerities did Pārvatī herself perform?
Having obtained which boon, or in what manner, did she attain Maheśvara?
In what manner did Rati restore Manmatha to life?
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, describe the marriage of Pārvatī and Śiva, as well as their private union which liberates sinners from their sins. (4)
O ocean of compassion, let the liberation from suffering for those who are afflicted be told.
(5) O Kṛṣṇa, there is a great curiosity to hear the account of the couple’s separation, the wife’s burning pain in her ears, and their subsequent reunion. (6)
The flame of fire and the flame of poison may be endured, as well as the flames of women;
yet the flame of separation from one's husband or wife cannot be endured for even a moment.
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, he was struck with wonder, his face agitated with alarm.
With a grieving heart, he began to speak at length:
"Rādhā is unable to hear these words concerning the separation from her husband;
what will become of her when our parting lasts for a hundred years? (8–9)
Having thus reflected in his mind, the Lord of Māyā, endowed with Māyā,
that ocean of mercy, out of compassion, prepared to recount the narrative.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā, who are dearer than life; O beloved of my life, listen!
O Goddess presiding over life, O Mistress of life, O support of life, O enchanting one!
When Rudra had departed from the foot of the banyan tree, Pārvatī went away to perform ascetic penance. (11)
Again and again she was restrained by her mother and father; nevertheless,
having gone to the bank of the celestial river (Svarṇadī), she joyfully bathed three times a day and,
with delight, recited that mantra which had been entrusted to her by me.
For one full year, the Mother of the World, through her own devotion, performed severe penance without food;
and in the summer, she remained surrounded by a blazing fire day and night.
Having performed [her rites], she set out into their midst, continuously chanting the mantra.
Śivā, having assumed a yogic posture in the cremation ground during the rains, saw a rock and became drenched by a stream of water. 15–16.
She constantly set out with devotion into the midst of cold waters during the fierce frosts of autumn,
remaining without food while the quarters were shrouded in mist.
Having spent a full year in this manner, Satī still did not obtain Śaṅkara.
Having prepared a fire-pit out of grief, she prepared to enter it. Seeing her entering the fire-pit, emaciated by her ascetic penance, Śiva, the ocean of compassion, approached her out of pity.
Extremely dwarfed, a child, in the form of a Brahmin, blazing with his own splendor,
joyful in mind, carrying a staff and an umbrella, wearing matted locks,
clad in a white sacred thread and white garments, and smiling. (20)
Wearing a garland of white lotus seeds and a radiant tilaka mark, she too, upon seeing the boy in that secluded place, spoke with affection;
completely overwhelmed by his splendor, she herself abandoned her ascetic penance. (21–22)
"Who are you? she asked the child standing before her, desiring to embrace him in her mind with the utmost reverence. Having heard the question, the Supreme Lord, the Son of the Mountain, smiled.
He spoke most sweetly, like nectar to the ears, to the Goddess.
Śaṅkara said:
"I am a young brahmin boy, an ascetic who goes wherever he pleases."
"Who are you, O beautiful one, performing penance in this vast wilderness?
Tell me, in whose family were you born, whose daughter are you, and what is your name? For what reason do you perform penance—you who are the bestower of the fruits of asceticism? (25–26)
"O lotus-eyed one, are you perhaps a mass of ascetic power (tapas) personified, or are you performing penance for the sake of instructing the world?
Or are you the Sovereign Primordial Nature (mūlaprakṛti), whose very essence is splendor? (27)
Having assumed a physical form for the sake of being meditated upon by devotees, you took birth in Bhārata;
or rather, are you Lakṣmī, the eternal embodiment of prosperity in the three worlds, who has come into the presence of the Creator to protect the worlds? (28–29)
Or are you Ambikā, the goddesses of the gods themselves in embodied form;
or are you Sāvitrī, who has come by her own will to take birth in Bhārata;
or are you the presiding deity of passion, Sarasvatī herself in person? (30)
I have taken birth in Bhārata by my own will to manifest all branches of knowledge.
Among these, who are you? I am not able to discern that. O auspicious lady, whoever you may be, please be well-pleased with me.
When you are pleased, the Supreme Lord is pleased;
when the devoted wife is satisfied, Nārāyaṇa himself is satisfied.
When the divine Nārāyaṇa is satisfied, the three worlds are forever satisfied.

"Just as when the roots of a tree are watered, the branches are likewise moistened, O beloved," [said the child]. Having heard those words of the child, the Supreme Goddess laughed and spoke these beautiful words, which were nectar to the ears.
Pārvatī said: "I am not Lakṣmī, the source of the Vedas, nor the presiding deity of speech. My current birth is as the daughter of the mountain in Bhāratavarṣa.
In a former birth, I was Satī, the beloved of Śaṅkara, born in the house of Dakṣa."

"O twice-born one, having abandoned my body through yoga due to the reproach of my father and husband, I attained Śaṅkara in this life by virtue of my merit. Having cast me aside and reduced Manmatha to ashes, he departed. (37–38)
When Śaṅkara had departed, due to the heat and out of shame before my father’s house,
my mind turned toward performing penance on the bank of the celestial river (Svarṇadī).
Having performed severe penance for a very long time, [I attained] my beloved of life.
"Having seen you and being unable to enter the fire, I stood still for a moment.
O Brahmin, fulfill your own desire and attain your unfulfilled wish for the attainment of Hara; go now, I shall enter the fire which resembles the flames of the fire of universal destruction."
In whatever birth I may obtain a life, may I attain supreme Śiva— in every birth— my beloved, my lord, who is dearer to me than life itself.
For all beings indeed desire a birth that allows them to obtain their own beloved.
That birth was heard of in the Vedas by all for the sake of obtaining a husband:
"For whatever husband was previously destined for them, he shall be theirs in every successive birth; and whatever woman is firmly devoted to whom, she shall belong to them birth after birth. (43-44)

"Without obtaining that body here, and having performed most terrible austerities and the rites for desired objects in a fire-pit, I shall obtain him in the next world. Having spoken thus, Pārvatī entered into that [fire] before him.
O Supreme Goddess, as Pārvatī was repeatedly forbidden by the Brāhmaṇa before her, the fire into which she was entering suddenly became,
through her ascetic power, as cool as sandalwood.
Having stood for a moment within that space, Śiva again suddenly questioned Śivā as she was flying upward, O delighter of Vṛndāvana. Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O blessed lady, alas for your asceticism! Indeed, nothing at all has been realized.
Your body has not been consumed by fire, nor has your desired goal been attained.
You merely wish to make your husband auspicious and of a virtuous form. (49)
Having made the bodiless one your husband, what could you possibly desire?
O lady of pure smiles, if you wish for a husband who is a destroyer—if what woman would desire a lover who is the cause of universal destruction? (50–51)

"O Goddess, if you desire liberation, having made your beloved take his true form, you shall be the bestower of universal liberation; thus, your asceticism will not be in vain. Furthermore, Śiva is present in Maṅgalā for the sake of liberation, and he is not seen as a destroyer."
Furthermore, no other meaning for the word "Śiva" has been established in the Veda.
O beautiful one, if you desire that Rudra as the agent of destruction—the one who causes fear to all the worlds—you shall obtain him in union. (53–54)
There will be no liberation for you, nor the service of the gods that you desire.
The remembrance of Hari is unfailing and always bestows all auspiciousness.
Go quickly to your father’s house; there you shall behold Śaṅkara.
"By my blessing and by the fruit of your own austerities, [this] which is very difficult to attain," having spoken thus to Pārvatī, the brahmin vanished right there.
Durgā went to her father’s house, saying, "O Mahādeva! (56–57).
Upon hearing of Pārvatī’s arrival, Menakā and Himālaya,
overwhelmed with joy, set forth placing a divine vehicle at their head.
O Rādhikā, they placed auspicious jars upon the royal highway.
[It was] endowed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, fruits, and branches;
[it was] surrounded on every side by clusters of plantain trunks, provided with *rasāla* sprouts tied together with silk threads. (59–60)
Accompanied by groups of women with sons who held lamps in their hands,
and filled with Brahmins of great merit, sages, and celibate students, all provided with parched grain, rice, dūrvā grass, fruits, and flowers. (61)
It was graced by female actors and dancers, as well as lordly elephants;
it was joined by officiating priests who made auspicious sounds, holding beautiful garlands of *mālatī* flowers in their hands—men who were skilled and highly praised. (62–63)
Amidst various kinds of musical instruments resoundingly echoing with the blast of conchs,
and having entered the city— which was made beautiful by vermilion powder and thick with the liquid paste of sandalwood— Durgā beheld her parents before her.
Extremely serene, they ran forward, their hair standing on end with tears of joy.
With a gracious countenance, the Goddess prostrated before them along with her attendants. Then, having united with her, they both placed their hands upon her chest and bestowed their blessings.
Crying out "O child! O child! while overwhelmed with affection and weeping, they then placed her upon the chariot and departed for their own abode.
The women performed the ritual purification, and the Brahmins offered their blessings.
The lord of mountains gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas and the bards;
he caused auspicious rites to be performed and had the Vedic texts recited.
Thus, the two of them remained in their own palace together with their daughter. (68–69)
Indeed, with their minds overflowing with joy, the two of them dwelt happily in that abode.
And once, the mountain went to the celestial river (Svarṇadī) to perform austerities;
meanwhile, he lived joyfully in the courtyard together with Menakā’s daughter.
In the meantime, a certain monk and a dancer who was a fine singer suddenly arrived joyfully in the presence of Menakā. He held a horn in his left hand and a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his right.

Having adorned his limbs with ashes, appearing exceedingly aged and afflicted by extreme old age, with a hump on his back, dressed in red garments, and possessing a beautiful throat, he was most enchanting;
having performed a captivating dance, he sang the recounting of my virtues. (73)
He sounded his horn and likewise played the *ḍamaruka* drum for a moment.
The citizens—boys, girls, overwhelmed with joy, as well as the elderly, the young men, groups of young women, and aged matrons—all arrived. (74–75)
Having heard that beautiful song joined with the notes of the *sutāna* scale,
they all suddenly became bewildered and fell into a swoon.
Durgā, having reached a state of fainting, beheld Śaṅkara within her heart.
The supreme one, wielding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, wearing a tiger skin;
adorned with sacred ash, beautiful, wearing a perfectly pure garland of bones;
his face bright with a slight smile, exceedingly gracious, and three-eyed. (77–78)

Seeing Hara standing within her heart— the beautiful one with the moon as his crest, five-faced, with a garland in his hand, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, and saying "Choose a boon"— she bowed to him mentally.
She chose this boon in her mind: "May you become my husband.
Having granted this to him, Śiva vanished.
Not seeing him, Durgā regained consciousness in her heart once more.
Opening her eyes, she beheld before her a mendicant who was singing;
and Menakā, from that dance and song of the mendicant,
went forth to give him jewels placed within a golden vessel.
The mendicant begged for alms from that Durgā and accepted no other;
then, out of curiosity, he prepared to perform a dance once more. Hearing those words, Menā became enraged and was filled with astonishment. (83–84)
She rebuked the mendicant and told him to go outside:
"He is the wife of Śiva, the Supreme Soul and Lord of the three worlds;
send this eloquent man far away as he makes this request. (85)
In the meantime, having performed his penance, the mountain returned to his own abode.

There he saw before him a charming mendicant standing in the courtyard, who had performed the worship of Nārāyaṇa on the beautiful bank of the Gaṅgā; his mind was distressed by the grief of separation from meditation upon that deity’s form.
Having heard this news from the mouth of Menā, he laughed and grew enraged.
He gave an order to his servant to cast the mendicant outside—[the mendicant] who was as difficult to touch as the sky and blazing with his own splendor. (88–89)
Unable to go near him, he was not able to cast [the weapon] outside;
at that moment, the Mountain beheld a supreme mendicant with beautiful four arms, wearing a crown and earrings, and clad in yellow garments. (90)
Well-attired, beautiful and dark-complexioned, with a slight smile and captivating;
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, he is ever-eager to bestow grace upon his devotees. Whatever flower is offered at the time of worship to the wielder of the mace— 91–92.
Śaila beheld all of that— the incense, the lamp, and the charming food offering— that had been given upon the body and head of the mendicant, as it stood before him. (93)
For a moment he beheld the two-armed one, who held a flute for his sport;
a youth in the guise of a cowherd, smiling and darkly beautiful;
with a crest of peacock feathers and adorned with jewel ornaments. (94–95)
For a moment, he beheld Śaṅkara, whose entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with a forest garland, pure, moon-crested,
holding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, and clad in a tiger skin as his garment. (96)
His body was radiant and stainless, adorned with a garland of bones;
he wore a sacred thread made of serpents and bore matted locks like molten gold.
Holding a hand-drum and a horn in his hands, he was most praiseworthy and captivating to the mind. (97–98)
He was chanting the name of Hari with a rosary of white lotus seeds;
his face was bright with a slight smile, and he was intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees.
Blazing with his own splendor, he had five faces and three eyes.
For a moment he beheld the four-faced Creator of the worlds,
chanting the name of Śrī Hari with a rosary of clear crystal;
for a moment he beheld the form of the Sun, consisting of the three qualities.
He beheld him as exceedingly intense, blazing with the splendor of Brahman; at one moment he saw him in the form of fire, flaming with supreme brilliance,
and at another moment he indeed beheld him in the form of the moon, producing delight.

For a moment, he beheld the Supreme, whose nature is light, formless and stainless, untainted, desireless, and the very essence of the Paramātman; thus he saw the Supreme, who consists of His own will and assumes manifold forms. (3–4)
With tears of joy and his hair standing on end, the mountain prostrated before him like a staff.
Having circumambulated him with devotion and bowed down again and again,
he leaped up, filled with joy, and beheld him once more.

Seeing that true mendicant, who bore various forms, the Lord of Mountains was made to forget all that by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu. Then the mendicant begged alms from him, keeping his begging bowl at his side. (6–7)
Clad in red garments, with a horn and a variegated *ḍamaru* drum in his hand,
the mendicant was eager to seize Durgā, and never anyone else;
yet the Lord of Mountains, deluded by the *māyā* of Viṣṇu, did not accept her.
The monk accepted nothing and vanished right there.
Then, O beloved, knowledge arose in both Menakā and the Mountain:
"Aha! We have seen the Lord of the World today, as if in a dream."
Having deceived us two, Śiva and myself, the Lord went to his own abode.
Seeing their devotion to Śiva, all the gods were concerned;
Indra and the others devised a stratagem for the protection of Mount Sumeru.
If Śaila bestows his daughter upon him with single-minded devotion,
he will certainly attain immediate liberation in Bhārata.
If [Śaila], the repository of infinite jewels, abandons the earth, it too shall depart.
The earth named Ratnagarbhā will certainly become false;
having abandoned her state as an immobile being and assumed a divine form,
she will give her daughter to the Wielder of the Trident and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Through his divine play, he will indeed attain a form identical to that of Nārāyaṇa;
having attained the status of an attendant, he will become a servant of Hari.
A daughter equal to ten ponds [in merit] is given by him to a Brāhmaṇa.
To one who knows the Vedas, who is pure, who does not accept gifts,
who performs the twilight prayers, sacrifices, and the recitation of the Vedas, and who speaks the truth—
to such a person this girl has been given, yielding the fruit of ten ponds. (17)
Having given [this] to a virtuous Brahmin who performs the three daily rites, speaks the truth, maintains a household, and knows the Vedas, it yields excellent fruit;
yet it is not for a twice-born priest who has taken another's wife. (18–19)
A daughter who grants only half the fruit [of her gift] is said to be given to one who is deceitful, or to one who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā),
or even to one who is devoid of the Gāyatrī at all times of the twilight prayers;
likewise, she who is given to one born of a Vaiśya is remembered as granting only half the fruit.

Having given [her] to a sinner, to one born of the Śūdra caste, to one born of the Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya castes who is equal to a Caṇḍāla— that maiden brings about hell. [But she should be given] to a learned Brāhmaṇa who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and a speaker of truth.
That which was given to one who has conquered his senses yields the fruit of twenty ponds;
having assumed a divine form for sixty thousand years,
if it is given to such a person, he rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.

Having given a maiden of virtuous character to either Śiva or Viṣṇu, one will indeed become the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa; this is heard in the Vedas. When a devotee of Viṣṇu gives a maiden for the pleasure of Viṣṇu, [he attains that state].
"He shall surely obtain the state of being Hari’s servant and the birth of a Brahmin.
Having reflected thus and held a consultation, O beloved, all the gods set out toward the home of Himālaya to dispatch their preceptor.
Having gone and bowed to their preceptor, they all made this representation:
"Go to the home of Himālaya and utter insults against the wielder of the trident;
without the Pināka-bearer, Durgā will choose no other as her husband. (27–28)
Having given his daughter against his will, he shall quickly obtain the fruit [of his merit].
Let the Lord of Mountains go at his own time; for now, let him remain on earth.
And you yourself must protect this land of Bhārata, which is the repository of infinite jewels.
Having heard the words of the gods, he placed his hands over his ears;
remembering "Nārāyaṇa," his own teacher, he did not accept [the challenge].
And having rebuked the host of gods again and again, he spoke. (130–131)
He was a knower of the Vedas and Vedānta and a great devotee of Hari, the Lord.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O gods, who are intent on achieving your own ends, listen to my truthful words. (32)

Those sinners who revile the essence of ethics as declared in the Vedas—which brings about happiness in the end—and those who revile the devotees of Hara and Keśava, as well as the gods on earth (the brahmins), their own guru, and devoted wives; 33. [they go to hell].
Likewise, those gods who have created rival monks, fellow celibates, or the seed of creation,
are cooked in the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure;
they lie day and night amidst phlegm, urine, and excrement.
Devouring them, swarms of insects make a sound as they eat those cowards who revile Brahmā, the creator and teacher of the worlds,
as well as Śiva, the foremost of the gods, and Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī. (36)
Those who [neglect] the Gītā, Tulasī, the Gaṅgā, the Vedas, and the Mother of the Vedas (Sāvitrī);
the vow, austerity, worship, the mantra, and the preceptor who bestows the mantra—
they indeed cook in the Andhakūpa hell for half of their allotted lifespan, O Aho!
And those who, having equated Hṛṣīkeśa with other gods, revile him, are devoured by swarms of serpents and cry out incessantly.
[This applies to those who revile] the Purāṇa which bestows devotion to Viṣṇu and is superior even to the Vedas.
Rādhā, the cowherd girl born from his body, and those brāhmaṇas who were always honored by him—
those gods are cooked in a pit for a duration equal to the lifespan of the Creator.
They remain with their faces downward and legs upward, entwined by swarms of serpents.
Devoured by worms of hideous form that resemble snakes,
they are exceedingly distressed and terrified, crying out incessantly.
Agitated, they surely devour phlegm, urine, and excrement.
And the enraged servants of Yama cast flaming torches into his mouth;
having threatened him at the three junctions of the day, they inflict blows with staffs.
They force him to drink urine and, out of fear, make him thirst with their strikes.
Then, in order to create the world again at the beginning of another kalpa, the Lotus-born One said that there would be a remedy for them:
"Indeed, having reviled Śiva, the gods shall go to hell. (45)
"O sons, you wish to do this very favor for me.
Dakṣa, though impelled by Brahmā and having given his daughter to the wielder of the trident, did not attain supreme sovereignty because he was a reviler of Hara. (46–47)
By giving his daughter against his will, he obtained the fourth merit;
oh, having abandoned the state of *sārūpya*, he obtained the inferior heaven!
O gods, let someone among you go to the mountain-dwelling.
Let him diligently fulfill the will of the Lord of Mountains;
having given his daughter against his own will, let him dwell happily in Bhārata.
By giving his daughter to him with devotion, he will certainly attain liberation. (49–50)
Afterwards, all the Seven Sages, taking Arundhatī with them,
will go to Dhruva’s house and inform Parvata;
Durgā will choose no other suitor than Pinākin (Śiva).
"Without his own desire, he will give his daughter to him at the command of his son.
Having thus related everything, "O gods, go to the temple," the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) quickly departed for the celestial river (Gaṅgā) to perform penance.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then the gods, having deliberated together, went into the presence of Brahmā.
All of them made a petition to Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds.
The gods said:
"In your creation, Himālaya, the creator of the world and the repository of jewels, [is situated]."
If he attains liberation, how could the earth not be filled with jewels?
By giving his daughter to the Wielder of the Trident with devotion, the Lord of Mountains himself will attain a form identical to Nārāyaṇa; of this there is no doubt. (2–3)
"Having censured him, you must instill doubt in his mind.
O Lord, there is no one else capable of this task except for you; go to the mountain abode.
Having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā himself spoke to them:
This speech, the essence of political wisdom and the supreme nectar for the ears.
5. Brahmā said:
O children, I am not able to perform the extremely difficult task of censuring Śiva.
He sends forth the Lord of Beings, who is the form of the destruction of prosperity and the seed-form of calamities. He subjects himself to self-reproach;
for while reproaching others leads to ruin, reproaching oneself leads to supreme glory.
O beloved, having heard the words of Brahmā and having bowed to him,
the gods went quickly to Kailāsa and praised Śiva.
They all made their petition to Śaṅkara, the abode of compassion.
Having consoled them and smiling, he went to the foot of the mountain.
(9) All the gods rejoiced and quickly returned to their own abodes.
Success in one's desires brings constant joy, while failure increases suffering. (10)

Then Śaila, accompanied by Pārvatī and surrounded by his circle of kinsmen, sat down in the midst of the assembly, filled with joy. In the meantime, Śiva himself appeared there in the form of a brahmin.

He arrived suddenly, with a serene face and eyes, wearing a staff, a parasol, and long robes, and bearing an excellent tilaka. He held a crystal rosary in his hand and wore a śālagrāma stone around his neck. (12–13)
Upon seeing him, Himālaya rose up with his retinue;
out of devotion, he prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before that unprecedented guest.
Pārvatī also bowed with devotion to the Lord of her life, who was in the form of a brahmin.
The wise man offered a blessing to everyone with affection.
(15) The Brāhmaṇa himself quickly sat upon the seat provided by Śaila;
he accepted the madhuparka and all other offerings with affection. (16)
The mountain inquired after the welfare of the brahmin and asked, "Who are you?
The lord of brahmins then spoke everything with reverence to the lord of mountains. (17) The brahmin said:
Relying on the occupation of a watchman, I wander upon the surface of the earth.
By the grace of my guru, I am able to travel as fast as thought, go everywhere, and am all-knowing.
I have learned that you wish to give your daughter to Śaṅkara.
To him who is equal to a lotus, divine, and whose lineage and conduct are unknown;
to him who is without support, without attachment, formless, and devoid of qualities;
to the one who frequents cremation grounds, the lord of all beings, and the yogin. (19–20)
To the one clothed in the directions, whose body is the serpent, and who is adorned with ashes; to the one whose very form is a snake-catcher, and who is the slayer of Time (Kāla);
to the one whose death is unknown, who is unknowable, who is without protector, and who is without kin—O Bhava! (21)
To the one who bears a mass of matted hair like molten gold, and yet is penniless;
to the one whose age is unknown, who appears exceedingly old, and who is changeless;
to the refuge of all, who wanders as a mendicant wearing a serpent as a necklace. (22–23)
"Understand that Nārāyaṇa, born of noble lineage, is the best among the wise;
he is the fitting recipient for your act of giving Pārvatī.
Upon merely hearing this, the great people will have smiling faces. (24)
"You are the lord of the mountain of a hundred thousand peaks, yet you have not a single kinsman.
Quickly and with great effort, inquire about your kinsmen; ask them all diligently, O friend, regarding everything except Pārvatī. (25–26)
"Medicine never pleases a sick person; rather, unwholesome food always appeals to them.
Having said this, the brahmin quickly bathed, ate, and filled with joy, went peacefully to his own home, O delighter in the pastimes of Vṛndāvana.
Having heard the words of the brahmin, Menā spoke to Himālaya with eyes full of tears and a heart burning with grief.
Menā said:
"Listen, O Lord of Mountains, to my words which bring about happiness in the end.
Ask these best of mountains [on my behalf]: 'I will not give my daughter to him.
I shall renounce all sensory objects and consume poison itself. (29–30)
