"See, I shall go to the terrible forest, having bound Ambikā by the neck!
Taking Pārvatī, Menā went in anger to her chamber;
abandoning food and weeping, she made her bed upon the ground.
In the meantime, Vasiṣṭha arrived there together with his brothers;
afterwards, Arundhatī also joined them.
Having bowed down to all of them, the mountain offered them golden lion-thrones.
Having offered the sixteen types of service, he worshipped with devotion.
And the sages sat comfortably on easy seats in the midst of the assembly.
Arundhatī went quickly to where Menā and Pārvatī were.
Having gone there, she saw Menā lying unconscious with grief.
The virtuous Arundhatī spoke these sweet and beneficial words to her, who was now attentive. Arundhatī said:
"Arise, O virtuous Menakā! I am Arundhatī in your house.
Know me to be the mind-born daughter of the ancestors and the bride of Vidhi.
Hearing the voice of Arundhatī, Menakā rose up quickly.
Having bowed her head, she spoke to her who was like a lotus in splendor.
Menakā said: "Aha! What is this merit of ours today, we whose births are so virtuous? (37-38)

"The bride, the wife of the Creator of the world, [resides] in my home, that of Vasiṣṭha. Having spoken thus in haste—"This very house is yours, and I am your servant"—the sovereign lady of the world's creator arrived through her great merit. (39)
Having offered water for the feet, he seated that virtuous woman upon a golden throne.
He fed her with sweet food and ate together with the maiden. For the sake of Śiva, he also instructed Menakā in the principles of conduct.
In connection with Arundhatī, they also discussed the arrangements for matrimonial alliances.
Then the sages and the lord of mountains [Vasiṣṭha] instructed him with supreme words on the essence of political ethics, explaining the various arrangements for alliances as the occasion arose. (42)
The sages said:
"O Lord of Mountains, hear our words which bring about auspiciousness.
Give Pārvatī to Śiva; become the father-in-law of the Destroyer."
"Exert yourself quickly to awaken the Lord of Gods, who does not ask for anything,
for the sake of destroying your doubt regarding the rite of union with Brahmā.
Śaṃkara, the best of yogis, has no desire for union with a wife."
"O Lord, at the request of Brahmā, he will accept your daughter;
having made this promise to you at the conclusion of his penance,
that lord of yogis will perform the marriage for two reasons."
Having heard the words of the sages, Himālaya laughed and,
though somewhat afraid, spoke with great humility.
Himālaya said:
Indeed, I do not see any royal paraphernalia whatsoever belonging to Śiva—neither any hermitage, nor sovereignty, nor even his own kinsmen or relatives.
He would not deign to give a daughter to a yogi who is so utterly detached. (48)
"You are the sons of the Creator; speak the truth with certainty.
(49) If a father gives his daughter to an unsuitable son—whether out of time, greed, fear, or delusion—he shall go to hell for a hundred years. (50)
"I will certainly not give my daughter to the wielder of the trident of my own accord;
O sages, let that arrangement be made which is appropriate.
Having heard these words of Himālaya, Vasiṣṭha, the son of Vidhi, [spoke].
A knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, intent on proclaiming what is declared in the Vedas;
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Mountain, there are various kinds of speech, both worldly and Vedic."

The knower of the scriptures understands everything through the eye of stainless knowledge. An enemy speaks what is untrue, harmful, and pleasant to hear at present; though it may seem well-reasoned, it is never beneficial.
Producing joy at first sight and bringing happiness in its ultimate result,
the compassionate one, devoted to righteousness, indeed instructs his kinsman—
[that teaching] which, by the mere hearing of it, is equal to nectar and brings happiness at all times.

"O Mountain, that which has truth as its essence, which is beneficial, the best of speech, and desired—such is the threefold [speech] described in the treatises on ethics (nītiśāstra). Among these three, tell me: which desired statement shall I speak? (56–57)
And Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty gods, was devoid of external prosperity;
his mind was entirely immersed in the oceans of the knowledge of reality.
The attainment of worldly delusions is as fleeting as the splendor of lightning.
What desire can there be for the Lord, who is eternally blissful and delights in his own Self?
(59) A householder gives his daughter to one who possesses royal wealth;
yet by giving his daughter to an enemy, the father becomes a slayer of his own child. (60)
Who would say that Śaṅkara is miserable when Kubera is his servant?
For he is indeed capable of creating and destroying the universe by the mere play of a frown.
He is the attributeless Supreme Self, the Lord who transcends primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is the Lord of all, yet untainted; yet he is tainted within all living beings.
He is the one [agent] in creation and dissolution; he is everything in the act of creation.
He is both formless and possessed of form, the omnipresent one who is himself composed of his own will.
The Lord, who in the act of creation assumes a threefold form—
the one called Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— which brings about creation, preservation, and dissolution:
Brahmā resides in the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), and Viṣṇu makes his abode in the Ocean of Milk.
Śiva, the dweller of Kailāsa, and all other manifestations of Kṛṣṇa;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself has become twofold, as two-armed and four-armed.
The four-armed one resides in Vaikuṇṭha, while he himself is two-armed in Goloka. (65–66)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are portions (aṃśa) of that God;
some gods are his parts (kalā), and others are even parts of those parts (kalāṃśa). Kṛṣṇa, intent upon creation, likewise brought forth Prakṛti there.
Having created her, he indeed deposited his seed into her womb.
From that, a child was born, and within him was the Great Virāṭ.
He is to be known as Mahāviṣṇu, who is a sixteenth part of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Brahmā was born from the lotus at the navel of that very one who reclines upon the waters;
Śaṅkara, the moon-crested creator, was born from his forehead;
and Mahāviṣṇu, as well as Viṣṇu himself, were born from his left side. (70)

O Mountain, all natural beings, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest, are manifestations of Prakṛti born from Kṛṣṇa. Prakṛti assumes a fourfold form through her portions and digits for the sake of playful creation in manifold ways. (71–72)
Rādhā herself, the sovereign of the Rāsa dance, was born from the left side of Kṛṣṇa;
Vāṇī herself, the presiding deity of musical passion, was born from his mouth;
and Lakṣmī, the embodiment of all prosperity, was born from his chest. (73)
Śivā manifested her presence within the splendors of the gods;
having slain all the Dānavas, she bestowed prosperity upon the deities. Having obtained birth in another Kalpa from the womb of Dakṣa’s wife... (74–79)
Known by the name Satī, she attained Śiva; Dakṣa gave her to him.
Having heard the censure of her husband, she abandoned her body through yoga.
Menakā, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, is your wife.
She was born from his lap into his womb; she is the Mother of the Universe.
O Mountain, in birth after birth, she is Śivā, the wife of Śiva.
In kalpa after kalpa, she is the supreme mother of the wise, existing in the form of the intellect.
She remembers her past lives, is all-knowing, the bestower of perfection, and the very embodiment of accomplishment.
Śiva himself devoutly wears the ashes from her funeral pyre upon his bones.
O Bhadra, give this girl of your own free will; give her to Śiva.
Or else she herself will go to her beloved’s place and see him. Whichever woman was the beloved of a man in a previous life, she attains that dear one;
and no one is able to violate the decree of Prajāpati.
Śambhu, who delights in his own self and knows the ultimate reality, was not eager for marriage.
All the gods, oppressed by the one named Tāraka, praised him.
Seeing the affliction of the gods, the omnipresent Lord was entreated by Brahmā.
Out of compassion, the merciful one quickly accepted [the request] in the assembly of the gods.
Having made his vow and beholding your daughter's immeasurable suffering, that lord of yogis,
appearing in the form of a brahmin, came to the place where she was performing her penance.
Having comforted her and granted a boon, he went to his own abode.
Upon hearing that, all the gods, headed by Śakra, arrived with joy;
as did the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, and Dharma at that very moment.
All the sages, seers, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas—
there, by all those who were filled with joy and engaged in deliberation,
we were quickly dispatched so that Arundhatī might be freed from her debt. (86–87)
My joy in awakening you increases ever greatly;
a virtuous deed has been accomplished that brings happiness at all times.
O Lord of Mountains, if you do not grant Śivā to Śiva of your own free will, [it will lead to disaster]. 88.
And a marriage shall take place by the power of destiny;
the Lord who has Nārāyaṇa as his companion will arrive, having placed the most excellent of the gods upon a chariot made of the finest jewels. (89–90)
To her, Śiva granted a boon at the site of her ascetic penance— [to her] who was the most excellent among the lords of yogis, the teacher of teachers to the wise,
devoid of beginning, middle, and end, immutable, unborn, and supreme.
For that which is promised by the Lord can never be difficult to obtain or fruitless. (92) From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, everything is perishable and unstable.
Oh, how inviolable is the promise of the virtuous; it is indestructible! (93)
Maheṃdra alone effortlessly severed the wings of the mountains;
Pavana likewise playfully shattered the peaks of Meru.
O Himālaya, who else among the mountains could be warriors against the gods?
Driven by the winds, they will fall into the oceans in an instant.
O Lord of Mountains, if all one's wealth perishes for the sake of a single purpose, it is better to give that away to protect everyone—except for one who has come for refuge. (95–96)
Those who know the principles of ethics understand that for the sake of protecting one who has sought refuge, one ought to give even one’s life, as well as one’s sons, wife, and all wealth.
O lord of kings, Anaraṇya gave his own daughter to the brahmin.
Released from the Brahmin’s curse, he protected all his prosperity.
People learned in the treatises on statecraft quickly enlightened him—he who was submerged by the Brahmin’s curse, devoted to the Brahmins, and deeply distressed. (98–99)
"O Lord of the Kings of Mountains, by giving your daughter to Śiva,
you alone shall protect all your kinsmen and bring even the gods under your control.
Having heard Vasiṣṭha’s words, the Lord of the Mountains laughed.
With a grieving heart, he asked about the news of the king.
Himālaya said:
"O Brahmin, from whose lineage did this lord of kings, Anaraṇya, arise?"
"And how did he protect his entire prosperity after giving away his daughter?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"That lord of kings, Anaraṇya, was born in the lineage of Manu."
Long-lived, virtuous, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and one who had conquered his senses—
Svāyambhuva Manu, the son of Brahmā and most righteous, formerly ruled the kingdom righteously for seventy-one yugas. (103–104)
Then, accompanied by Śatarūpā, he went to Vaikuṇṭha;
having attained the proximity of Hari’s service, he became His servant.
After that, he himself became the great Svārociṣa Manu.
O Mountain, when Svārociṣa had passed away, the most excellent Manu appeared;
when Uttama had departed, the righteous Tāmasa became Manu.
Then, in this world, Raivata arose as Manu, the best among the wise.
From him, Cākṣuṣa is to be known; Śrāddhadeva is the seventh.
Sāvarṇi is to be known as the eighth, the great son of the illustrious Sun.
In ancient times, there was a king named Suratha on earth, born of the lineage of Caitra.
The ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi; the tenth is Brahmasāvarṇika.
The eleventh, the best of Manus, is called Dharmasāvarṇi.
After him is Rudrasāvarṇi, a devotee of Viṣṇu who has conquered his senses.
Tatpara, Devasāvarṇi, and then Indrasāvarṇika—
thus, O friend, the fourteen Manus have been described.
When these had passed away, a day of Brahmā occurred.
Listen to me for the entire account of Indrasāvarṇi.
The most excellent of Manus, a righteous devotee of the Wielder of the Mace (Viṣṇu),
ruled his kingdom according to dharma for seventy-one yugas.
Having given the kingdom to Surendra, he went to the forest for asceticism.
The son of Surendra was the illustrious and very powerful Śrīniketu.
His son was the great yogi Purīṣataru.
His son was the exceedingly radiant one known as Gokāmukha (15).
Vṛddhaśravas was his son, and his son was Bhānu. Puṇḍarīka was his son, and his son was likewise Jihvala (16).
The son of Jihvala was Śṛṅgin, and his son was Bhīma.
His son was Yaśaścandra, who surpassed even the moon with his fame.
The virtuous gods constantly sing of his stainless glory.
His son was Vareṇya, and Purāraṇya was his son.
His son was the righteous and illustrious Dharāraṇya.
His son was Maṅgalāraṇya, an ascetic and the best among the wise.
That best of kings, being childless, went to Puṣkara for asceticism.
Having performed penance for a very long time and having obtained a boon from Maheśvara,
he indeed received a Vaiṣṇava son, Anaraṇya, who had conquered his senses.
Having given the kingdom to him, he went to the forest for asceticism.
Anaraṇya, the best of kings and lord of the earth with its seven continents,
performed a hundred sacrifices with Bhṛgu as his domestic priest.
Considering the status of Śakra to be empty and perishable, the wise one did not quickly accept it;
for Śakra was conquered by him with ease, and Bali was likewise conquered with ease.
Indeed, the lords of the Dānavas were defeated by his own blazing splendor.
O Himālaya, that king had one hundred sons;
he also had one daughter, beautiful and charming, equal to Padmā who dwells in the lotus.
That maiden reached the bloom of youth while remaining in her father’s palace.
The lord of kings dispatched a messenger for the bridegroom.
Once, Pippalāda, eager to go to his own hermitage,
saw a Gandharva in a secluded place where he was performing austerities.
Seeing him with his mind immersed in women within the ocean of the erotic sentiment,
intoxicated by lust, and unconscious of day or night,
that tiger among sages himself became filled with desire. (27–28)
Then, with his heart deeply wounded, the lord of sages reflected upon taking a wife;
once, while going to bathe in the Puṣpabhadrā river,
he beheld a young woman named Padmā, as beautiful as the goddess Padmā herself.
The sage asked the people standing nearby, "Who is she, and to whom does she belong?
The people made their report: "She is Padmā, the daughter of Anaraṇya.
Having bathed and worshipped his chosen deity, Rādhikeśvara, the sage [proceeded].
The lustful king went to the courtyard of Anaraṇya’s assembly hall for the purpose of begging.
Upon seeing the sage, the king quickly prostrated himself, overwhelmed with fear.
Having offered the madhuparka and other honors, he worshipped him with devotion.
Having accepted everything out of desire, the sage requested the maiden.
The king became silent, unable to say anything in reply.
The sage requested him again, saying, "O King, give me the maiden."
"Or else, I shall reduce everything to ashes in an instant.
O Sage, all the attendants were overwhelmed by the sage's splendor;
and the king, along with his followers, wept upon seeing the old man afflicted by decrepitude.
All the queens wept, not knowing what ought to be done.
The chief queen, the mother of the princess, overwhelmed with grief, fell into a swoon.
Then the wise minister, learned in the treatises of political ethics, sought to console the king.

O King, you must give away the queen, the princes, and the daughters—who possess the highest conduct—either today or at the end of the day; to whom else but a supreme Brahmin should you give them? Or to what other person? 38.
I see no worthy recipient other than a Brāhmaṇa in the three worlds.
(39) By giving your daughter to the sage, protect all your prosperity;
for on account of a royal maiden, all prosperity may perish. (140)
"He protects everyone, yet having abandoned all, he does not protect him who has come for refuge.
Having heard these words of the wise man and lamenting again and again,
the king indeed gave his daughter, adorned with ornaments, to the lord of sages.
Taking his beloved, that sage went joyfully to his own abode.
The king, abandoning everything, departed for asceticism out of grief.
And Sundarī gave up her life due to the sorrow for her husband and her daughter.
The sons, grandsons, and servants fell into a swoon without the king.
Anaraṇya, having performed austerities while meditating on the Lord of Rādhikā,
and having served the Lord of Goloka, departed for Goloka.
The king’s eldest son became renowned and protected all the subjects on the face of the earth like his own children.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa," within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa. 41.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then the daughter of Anaraṇya served the sage with devotion through her actions, mind, and speech, just as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa. (1)

Once, on the road, Dharma, assuming the form of a king through his illusory power, beheld the virtuous Satī as she was smiling while going to bathe in the celestial river (Svarṇadī). He was seated in a beautiful chariot of jewels and adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Possessing the splendor of fresh youth and a radiance equal to that of Kāmadeva, the Lord,
having seen that beautiful and charming woman, spoke through his illusory power (māyā) in order to ascertain the inner reality of that sage’s wife. (3–4)
Dharma said: "O beautiful one, like Lakṣmī herself, worthy of a king, enchanting, in the full bloom of youth, O passionate woman of enduring youth! (5)
You do not shine in the presence of this old man afflicted by old age;
you shine upon the chest of a king, anointed with sandalwood and aloe.
[A Brahmin] devoted to austerities, a knower of truth, is now facing death.
"Leaving him aside, O King, behold the lord of kings, a hero in pleasure, afflicted by love.
One attains beauty from the merit of a previous birth;
may all that become fruitful through the embrace of a connoisseur. (7–8)
"O beloved, make me your servant— I who am skilled in the science of love and the lover of a thousand beauties— and I shall abandon even them.
[I shall dwell] on mountain after mountain, in delightful, waterless, and uninhabited places."
In a flowering garden, with the fragrant breeze of blossoms;
in Malaya, in the sandalwood forest, with the lovely breeze of sandalwood— I shall sport with you, my beloved, according to my desire.
"I am capable of bringing peace to one consumed by the fever of desire.
Sport with me and make this birth fruitful.
Having spoken thus, he descended from his own chariot.
To him who was eager to seize her hand, that devoted wife spoke. Padmā said:
"Go far away, go far away, O most sinful one, lowest of kings!"
If you look upon me with lustful desire, you shall instantly turn to ashes.
(14) Abandoning Pippalāda, the best of sages, whose body is purified by austerity, I shall instead resort to you, who are conquered by women and addicted to pleasure. (15)
By the mere touch of one conquered by women, all merit perishes.
There is no sinner on earth more sinful than one who is conquered by women.
And it is because of this that you speak to me and my mother, having assumed a female form.
"By that curse of mine, there shall be destruction at that time.
Having heard the Satī’s curse, Dharma abandoned his royal form;
assuming his own true form, the Lord of Gods, trembling, spoke to her.
Dharma said: "O Mother, know me to be Dharma, the teacher of the teachers of those who know dharma; O virtuous lady, I am one who always regards the wives of others as my own mother. (19)
"I have come into your presence to understand your inner thoughts;
yet, though I know your minds, I am impelled by destiny.
O virtuous lady, my subduing of you was not improper, but was entirely appropriate. (20)
Instruction was fashioned by the Lord for those who have strayed onto wrong paths.
To that Kṛṣṇa—who is capable of making one understand one's own duty (dharma), of measuring time, and of ordaining the Creator—be my salutation. (21–22)
Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa, the all-pervading Lord, who at the proper time is capable of withdrawing even Bhava, the Destroyer; who effortlessly creates the Creator;
and who is able to turn an enemy into a friend, or bring about great affection and strife. (23)
Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa, who is capable of creating and likewise destroying that very same world;
salutations to you, that Kṛṣṇa, who is able to bestow curses as well as all joys, sorrows, and boons, and who indeed ordains both prosperity and adversity.

Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa by whom Prakṛti was created and Mahāviṣṇu was manifested, and by whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others were brought forth. Salutations to him by whom milk was made white and water was made cool in the past.
Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa, by whom even the fire was made to burn;
salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa, who have arisen as supreme splendor, whose form is light itself, who are the embodiment of the highest qualities yet are devoid of all material attributes. 27–28.
"Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa, who is everything, the seed of all, the inner self of all, and the very nature of all kinsmen.
Having spoken thus, Dharma, the teacher of the world, stood before her.
Recognizing him, that virtuous woman spoke suddenly, O Parvata.
Padmā said:
"You alone are the dharma of all beings and the witness of all actions."
The all-pervading Self, the omniscient knower of all principles, dwells within all internal spaces.
Why do you mock me, your servant, by asking how I might know your mind?
O Brahman, whatever offense was committed against me for your sake has been done. (31–32)
"And you, O Lord, were cursed by me out of ignorance, due to my feminine nature and in a fit of anger.
I am now reflecting upon what the remedy for that might be.
Even if this sky, all the directions, and the winds were to perish,"
Nevertheless, the curse of that virtuous woman can never be nullified.
If you were to perish, then the destruction of creation itself would follow.
Though I am thus bewildered as to what ought to be done, I nevertheless speak to you. (34–35)
O King of the Gods, you shine at all times, day and night, with the truth complete in its four quarters, like the moon on a full-moon night.
O Blessed One, however, there shall be a diminution of one quarter of your truth during the Tretā age.

O All-pervading Lord, two feet will remain in the Dvāpara age, and a third in the Kali age. At the end of the Kali age, even that remaining foot of yours will be concealed; when the Satya age returns once more, you shall become complete again.
O Lord, you are all-pervading in Truth, and in some measure even in others; hear as I describe the places where you have a dwelling and support:
among all Vaiṣṇavas, among ascetics, and among celibate students. (39)
Among women devoted to their husbands, among the wise, among forest-dwellers and mendicants;
among kings of virtuous character, among true members of the Vaiśya caste, among Śūdras who serve the twice-born, and among those established in the company of the good. (40–41)
O Dharmarāja, you shine forth eternally complete within these;
for in every age, the most meritorious people take them as their support—
namely, the Aśvattha, Vaṭa, and Bilva trees, as well as Tulasī and sandalwood.
You are present in the grounds for initiation, examination, oaths, assemblies, and cow-paddles;
in marriages, in flowers, and in trees;
in temples, at sacred fords, and constantly in the homes of the virtuous. (43–44)
In the hearing of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, in waters, and in assemblies;
in places where the qualities and names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are uttered, and in the context of Vedic songs;
in places of vows, worship, austerity, logic, and sacrifice; and in the presence of witnesses.
For you see that [the quality] exists only in cows and in cow-pens;
by that, there will be a thinness (kṛśatā) in those places and in their dharma.
Listen now to what this thinness is in other things, and what is inaccessible.
In all cases of unchaste women, in the houses of those who kill men,
among those who kill men, among the base, the foolish, and the wicked;
and among those who seize the wealth of deities, teachers, brahmins, and those worthy of protection.
Among those who are non-existent, among rogues, thieves, and places of sensual pleasure;
in the arenas of gambling, wine-drinking, and quarrels;
and among those devoid of the Śālagrāma stone, holy men, sacred fords, and Purāṇas.
In disputes involving affection for bandits, in the shadows of palm trees filled with pride,
among those who live by the sword, those who live by ink, those who sacrifice for the gods, and village priests; among those who ride bulls, goldsmiths, and those who subsist on violence— (51)
[One should not look] at women who revile their husbands, nor at men who are enslaved by women;
nor at twice-born men who are devoid of initiation, the twilight prayers, and devotion to Viṣṇu;
nor at those who sell their own daughters or sell their own wives. (52–53)
O Lord, [the same applies] to those who sell Śālagrāma stones, sacred texts, or land;
to those who betray friends, the ungrateful, and those who destroy truth and trust;
and even to those men who kill the distressed who have come for refuge or those who have sought shelter.
[The king should punish] those who are constantly habituated to false speech, as well as those who encroach upon boundaries;
those who give false testimony out of desire, anger, or greed;
and those who are devoid of meritorious deeds or who act in opposition to meritorious deeds. (55–56)
"O Lord, you have no right to remain among these censurable ones.
At that very moment, my word also became true for you:
'I shall go to serve my husband; go, dear father, to your own home. (57)
To the virtuous woman who had spoken thus, the illustrious son of Vidhi, with a gracious countenance and exceeding humility, spoke these words. Dharma said:
"You are blessed; you are devoted to your husband; may you have perpetual well-being!
(59) Accept a boon, for I shall grant it to you, O lady who has saved me!
May your husband become young again, O maiden, and a hero in the art of love. (60)
O virtuous daughter, may he be handsome, endowed with good qualities, and eternally possessed of stable youth;
may you be endowed with supreme sovereignty and remain forever youthful.
O daughter, may he live a long life, surpassing even Mārkaṇḍeya.
From Kubera you shall possess wealth, and from Śakra you shall possess sovereignty;
devoted to Viṣṇu and equal to Śiva, you shall be a supreme Siddha through Kapila.
May you be endowed with the good fortune of a husband for as long as you live.
"O virtuous lady, may your homes be superior even to the palace of Kubera.
You shall be the mother of ten sons who are virtuous, long-lived, and even more distinguished than your own husband; of this there is no doubt. (64)
Having spoken thus, O Parvata, Dharmarāja stood still.
She, having circumambulated him and bowed down, went to her own home.
Dharma, having pronounced a blessing upon her, departed for his own abode.
In every assembly, he praised her for her devotion to her husband.
She constantly took delight in secret with her youthful lord.
Afterwards, she became the mother of a virtuous son who surpassed even her husband in his qualities.
O Lord of Mountains, you have related this entire ancient history.
Anaraṇya protected all his wealth by giving away his daughter;
likewise, you yourself gave your daughter to the Lord of All. (68–69)
Protect all your kinsmen and your own entire prosperity. When seven days have passed, at a rare and exceedingly auspicious moment,
when the lord of the ascendant is situated in the ascendant and the Moon is accompanied by its own son (Mercury).
It rejoices when the moon is joined with Rohiṇī, pure, and when the stars are clear (71).
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Monday free from all defects,
when it is aspected by all auspicious planets and devoid of inauspicious ones (72).
O bestower of excellent offspring, O giver of supreme conjugal felicity to the husband, O granter of non-widowhood and happiness in birth after birth,
O Supreme Being beyond the highest, O bestower of the uninterrupted flow of intense love! 73.
"O Parvata, having given your daughter to the God, become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
[Give] the Mother of the World, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the Sovereign,
whose form is light, and who is worshipped by all the gods, to the Father of the World."
In a former kalpa, she manifested for the protection of the gods—
a mass of splendor belonging to the hosts of deities, blazing through the ten directions.
By her own radiance, some Daityas were consumed, while others fled.
O Lord of Mountains, some were reduced to ashes upon the earth;
some entered caves, and some fell into a swoon.
Others, placing grass between their teeth, sought refuge in the Goddess.
Some hurled their weapons, while others were rendered motionless;
some, having fought for a long time in battle, went to the healthy realm of heaven.
By her grace, those gods became free from enemies.

By the command of Kṛṣṇa, she became the daughter of Dakṣa at the end of the kalpa. And Dakṣa, according to the prescribed rites, gave the goddess to the wielder of the trident (Śiva) during my father’s sacrifice, amidst the assembly of the gods, by divine decree. (80–81)
A great quarrel broke out with that wielder of the trident, O Mountain;
and having paid homage to Brahmā, the three-eyed Lord departed in anger.
And Dakṣa, along with his attendants, being enraged, then went to his own abode.
Out of anger, Dakṣa, having gathered all the necessary materials, performed a sacrifice;
yet, out of malice, he gave no share of the sacrifice to the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
Seeing this, Satī became enraged, her eyes turning red, and she addressed her father.
Having rebuked him severely with a grieving heart,
she rose from the place of sacrifice and went into the presence of her mother.
She, who knows the three periods of time and is higher than the highest, spoke of what was to come.
He also saw the destruction of the sacrifice and so forth, as well as the humiliation of his father;
the flight of the gods from the site of the sacrifice toward the Lord of the Mountains (Śiva), and likewise the departure of the sages, the officiating priests, and the mountains. (86–87)
The victory of Śaṅkara’s armies and his own imminent death;
wandering out of grief with a mind distressed by separation from her husband;
the creation [of the world] and the awakening of the "essence of the eyes" (the sun) from Janārdana.

Having told her everything—including the attainment [of Buddhahood] through a different form of embodiment, his dwelling in that state which is equal [to his own], and his other future activities—she departed. Though forbidden by her mother and sisters, she remained sorrowful. (89–90)
Through the yoga of non-perception, she became a perfected yoginī for all;
having gone to the bank of the Jāhnavī, and having remembered and worshipped Śaṅkara,
that beautiful woman abandoned her body after remembering his lotus feet.

He entered the body situated in the valley of Gandhamādana, by which he had formerly destroyed the entire race of the Daityas. All the gods, being greatly amazed, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
The armies of Śaṅkara, having destroyed the sacrifice of the country and having brought about the defeat of all, departed in great distress;
they quickly related the entire account to the Lord.
Having heard the news, the Destroyer (Śiva), surrounded by all the hosts of Rudras,
went to the bank of the celestial river where the body of the Goddess lay.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Satī’s Body," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Mahādeva beheld Durgā, the enchanting embodiment of Satī, whose face was like a fresh lotus, as she lay upon the bank of the Jāhnavī. 1.
Seeing her holding a rosary that shone like refined gold,
blazing with splendor, and wearing white garments—
seeing the body of Satī, he was consumed by the fire of separation.

And yet, that embodiment of the mass of ultimate truths fell into a swoon. 3. The powerful grief for his wife afflicted him—the one who delights in his own Self, the Supreme beyond the supreme, the seed of the Vedas, and the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis. 4.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, the three-eyed Sthāṇu, who is like another immovable pillar, gazed upon her lotus-like face;
he was full of tears, exceedingly dejected, yet the refuge of the distressed. (5)
And he, who removes the wretchedness of the miserable, uttered these supreme words.
Śaṅkara said:
"Arise, arise, O blessed one, O virtuous lady, O mistress of my life, O beloved!"
"I am Śaṅkara, your master; behold me, who have come near to you.
I am Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness, the embodiment of all prosperity, and the giver of spiritual attainments.
I am the Self of all and the Lord of all, yet without you, I am like a corpse. (7–8)
I am capable only when together with you, whose very nature is power;
deprived of power, I am like a corpse, motionless in all actions.
And he who does not know power, being devoid of knowledge, censures it.
"It is fitting for a wise man to abandon that [which is harmful]; why then, O beloved, do you abandon me?
You are yourself Brahmā, you are yourself Viṣṇu, and we are your very essence (sādhya). Speak something like nectar, with a smile and a sidelong glance. (10–11)
Sprinkle me, who am scorched by the sight of your sweetly deceptive glance!
Seeing me from afar, you quickly speak to me affectionately with a smile;
why do you not speak to me now, though I lament, as if still angry? (12)
"O you who are dearer than life, arise! Do you not see me weeping?
O beautiful one, you ought not to depart, abandoning our very lives.
O Mother of the World, arise, O support of life, O Supreme beyond the supreme! (13–14)
"O devoted wife, arise! Why do you not attend to me today?
O daughter of Śruti, having recognized this, how can you cause the breaking of my vow?
Having spoken thus, he was afflicted by the pain of separation from his beloved's lifeless body.
Placing her upon his chest and embracing her, Śaṅkara kissed her again and again. Having pressed his lower lip to her lower lip and his breast to her breast,
and having embraced her repeatedly, he fell once more into a swoon.
Regaining his composure, the teacher of teachers among the wise rose up swiftly from his grief and ran like one insane across the seven continents,
the seven oceans, and the golden Lokāloka mountain. (18)
The wise one wandered as if deluded, having placed Satī upon his chest,
on the slopes of Mount Śataśṛṅga and in Bhārata within Jambūdvīpa;
in a very secluded spot at the Akṣayavaṭa, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, and by the shore of a river.

Having cried out "O virtuous one! he himself wept aloud; by the tears from the eye of the Three-eyed Lord, a lake was formed. That eye and the lake became known as the place for the asceticism of sages.
That enchanting holy ford (puṇyatīrtha) is two yojanas in extent;
O Mountain, by bathing there, men shall not undergo rebirth.
Even the sin committed over a hundred lifetimes is destroyed by the mere act of bathing.
Having abandoned that human form, men go to the abode of Hari.
There, having abandoned weeping, that great yogi, his mind distressed by separation, wandered the earth for a full year. (24)
O Lord of Mountains, with the limbs and minor members fallen from Satī, a collection of Siddha-pīṭhas arose that grants all desires.
And Mahādeva, having performed the purificatory rites for the remaining limbs, [established them]. || 25–26 ||
Having fashioned a garland of bones, he made it an ornament for his neck;
and with devotion, he constantly applied that ash as an ointment to his body.
Saying, "You are the mistress of my life," he fell into a swoon once again.
The self-born one forgot the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Self;
delighting in his own self and having all desires fulfilled, he remained motionless due to the fever of separation.
While he was lying near the great mountain at the foot of a banyan tree— 28–29.
Having seen this, the gods, filled with wonder, gathered in the presence of Śiva;
and the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Padmā, arrived together with his attendants in a chariot of jewels. (30)
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments, wearing yellow garments, and possessing four arms;
with a slightly smiling and serene countenance, he is decorated with a forest garland.
Brahmā, Śeṣa, Dharma, all the gods, and the great sages [are present]. (31–32)
Having prostrated before you in the assembly of the Lord, O Beloved of Lakṣmī,
Śrī Hari— the knower among knowers and the teacher of sages— having placed the unconscious Śaṅkara upon his chest, awakened him as he wept. (33)
The Blessed Lord said: O one who delights in your own Self, understand this; hear my words, which are beneficial, the essence of the inner self, and the cutter away of suffering and grief. (34)

Although you possess the seeds of all internal sciences, are a treasury of knowledge, and are the ordainer of the Creator’s rites—indeed, though you are omniscient and the very method of Brahmā—I nevertheless instruct you.
For even an ignorant person is capable of enlightening a wise man when his life is in peril. (35–36)
All worldly transactions among all people in the worlds exist [only through this].
All the qualities (guṇas) resting upon Māyā are the causes of pleasure and pain.
The powerful Māyā of Viṣṇu overpowers that which is joined with the qualities.
O Śambhu, O Lord, suffering, grief, and fear arise during an ill-fated day;
once that has passed and a fortunate day has arrived, from where would those [sorrows] come?
Joy and the pride of sovereignty increase continuously during that [fortunate time]. (38–39)
The wise count all these as being like dreams.
O Mahādeva, eternal seed of knowledge, grant me wisdom! May you be blessed; awaken your consciousness, and you will certainly attain Satī.
Likewise, coolness never leaves water, nor does burning heat leave fire;
O Śiva, light [never leaves] the sun, fragrance the earth, and likewise Satī [never leaves] you, O Śiva.
Having heard these words, "O Śailā," she spoke somewhat to Hari.
Having opened his eyes, the Three-eyed One said, "Listen!
The Three-eyed One spoke: "Who are you, who are of the nature of splendor? And who are these [beings] in your presence? (43)
"What is your name, and what are the names of these [others]? Who is Satī?
Who am I, and who are you? Tell me, from where have you servants come?
Where will you go, where shall I go, and tell me, where are these people going? (44)
O Mountain, having heard the word "Hari," he wept along with his attendants.
He drenched the three-eyed Lord with the tears from his own eyes as he was weeping;
indeed, there, by the falling of the tears from the eyes of Hari and the three-eyed Lord, [the fire was extinguished].
There, to the west of the Sunset Mountain in Bhārata, near the Akṣayavaṭa tree, there was a sacred site— the best of lakes, purifying the world—
a place for ascetics where penance flourishes and which serves as the seed of liberation. (47)
Then Hari spoke again quickly concerning the supreme self and Hara,
while all the gods and the sages of sublimated vital energy were listening.
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, O Śaṅkara, eternal bliss of knowledge, I shall speak:
O treasury of knowledge, O one higher than the highest, you have forgotten [this] due to sorrow.
In every birth, fair days and foul days indeed constantly occur. (49–50)
For all ordinary beings, pleasure and pain reside within their seed;
from pleasure arises joy, pride, and reckless valor;
as well as passion, the desire for power, and constant aversion. (51)
From suffering, from grief, and from agitation, fear constantly arises.
O Maheśvara, all these are destroyed when the seed is destroyed.
O Bhava, both fair days and foul days arise from all actions.
That action is to be accomplished through austerity, as is action that is auspicious or inauspicious;
austerity is to be accomplished through one's inherent nature, and that nature arises from habitual practice.
Superimposition is to be accomplished through association, and association arises from merit.
The mind is the seed of merit, and it is also the fickle seed of sin.
O Śambhu, the mind is my own portion, preceding all the senses. I am the progenitor of all, and you, the intellect, are Brahmā, the Lord.
Brahman is one, yet its manifestation as distinct forms is continuous due to the differentiation of qualities.
O Śiva, that Brahman is a manifold reality, both with qualities (saguṇa) and without qualities (nirguṇa).
That which rests upon Māyā is with qualities; that which transcends Māyā is without qualities.
The Blessed Lord consists of His own will and transforms Himself according to His desire.
His power of will is primordial nature (prakṛti), eternal, the constant source of all things. Some indeed declare that there is only one, the eternal Brahman-light.
Some say that Brahman is twofold, preceded by *prakṛti*. Listen to those who say that there is one [Brahman] which is superior to both *māyā* and *puruṣa*;
from that [one], those two come into being, and that Brahman is the cause of all. (60)
And yet, the one supreme Brahman becomes twofold by its own will. (61) The power of will is Prakṛti, the eternal source of all powers;
therein [is] the unchanging, possessed of attributes (saguṇa), the support of all, the eternal. (62)
The Lord of All, the Witness of All, exists everywhere as the bestower of fruits.
O Śambhu, the body is of two kinds: the eternal and the material.
The eternal is devoid of destruction, while the material is always perishable.
"O Blessed One, neither you nor I possess a permanent body.

Those who are born from our portions—Rudra and the others—are of the nature of *prakṛti* and have no fixed form; they are your portions appearing as Rudras and my portions appearing in the form of Viṣṇus."
My form is likewise twofold: two-armed and four-armed.
In Vaikuṇṭha, I am four-armed along with Padmā and my attendants;
in Goloka, I am two-armed along with Rādhā and the gopīs.
Those who speak thus maintain that there are two primary principles in their doctrine:
the Puruṣa, who is eternally constant, and the sovereign Prakṛti, who is also eternal. O Śiva, these two are always joined together; they are the parents of all.
Possessing bodies or bodiless, they assume every form by their own will.
Just as the preeminence of the Puruṣa is always [equal] to that of Prakṛti,
O Śambhu, if you desire Satī, then offer praise to Prakṛti.
That hymn which was joyfully given by you to Durvāsas in the past—that divine hymn proclaimed in the Kaṇva recension—worship with it the Mother of the Universe.
May there be the destruction of your sorrow; may all be auspicious through my blessing, O Śiva!
"May the fever of separation from women, which is a cause of great ruin, go far away!
Having spoken thus to the Lord of the Mountains, the Lord of Lakṣmī ceased;
then Maheśvara began to offer praise to Prakṛti.
Having bathed and bowed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Brahmā with devotion, with palms joined in *añjali* and his body covered in horripilation, Maheśvara said: 73. Maheśvara said:
Oṃ, salutation to Prakṛti; this is the mantra:
"O Brāhmī, you who are the very nature of Brahman, be gracious to me, O Eternal One!
You who are the nature of the Supreme Self and whose form is supreme bliss! (74)
O auspicious one, bestower of auspiciousness, O Durgā, slayer of the difficult, destroyer of the difficult!
You who are the very form of the boat, you who are ancient—be gracious to me in the ocean of worldly existence.
O you whose nature is all things, sovereign of all, you whose nature is the seed of all!

O support of all, O you who possess all knowledge, be gracious to me, O bestower of victory! O you whose form is every auspiciousness, O giver of every auspiciousness, O support of all that is auspicious, be gracious, O you who are all-auspiciousness! (76–77)

O you who are sleep, drowsiness, patience, and faith; O you whose nature is contentment and nourishment; O you who are modesty, intelligence, and the form of wisdom; O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, be gracious!
O you whose nature is the Vedas, the cause of the Vedas, and the giver of the Vedas!
O Mother of the Vedas, who embodies all the limbs of the Veda, be gracious to me!
O Dayā (Compassion), Jayā (Victory), Mahāmāyā (Great Illusion), O Mother of the World, be gracious!
O Kṣānti (Patience), Śānti (Peace), Sarvāntā (End of All), you whose nature is hunger and thirst!
O Lakṣmī on the lap of Nārāyaṇa, O Bhāratī on the chest of the Creator;
O Mahāmāyā on my own lap, O Viṣṇumāyā, be gracious to me!
O you whose nature consists of the divisions of time such as Kalās and Kāṣṭhās, O you who are the very form of day and night! 81.
O Goddess who grants transformation, be gracious, O you who are compassionate toward the wretched!
(82) O Rādhikā, the cause of all powers, upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa;
O auspicious one, superior even to Kṛṣṇa’s own life-breath, be gracious, O you who are worshipped by Kṛṣṇa! (83)
O you who are the very essence of glory, the cause of glories, and the bestower of glory;
O you who are the embodiment of all goddesses and the one who assumes the form of a woman;
O you who exist in the form of every beloved woman—be gracious to me with even a fraction of your power.
O auspicious one, whose very nature is every perfection and who bestows all perfections, be gracious!
O supreme bliss, the cause of all riches, be gracious!
O you who are worshipped by the illustrious, be gracious, O treasure-house of glory! (85–86)
O Support of all worlds, O Vasundharā, the repository of jewels;
O you whose nature encompasses the moving and the unmoving, be gracious to me without delay!
87 O you whose nature is Yoga, Sovereign of Yogins, Bestower of Yoga, Cause of Yoga!

O Goddess, sovereign of yoga, be gracious, O Siddhayoginī! O you whose very nature is all perfections, O bestower of all perfections! O Sovereign of Siddhas, the cause of all perfections, be gracious to me! (88–89)
O Maheśvarī, regarding the differences of opinion in the exposition of all the scriptures,
O Supreme Goddess, forgive all that has been said concerning knowledge.
Some say that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are predominant.
Regarding this duality of opinion, some wise ones understand it as a difference in interpretation:
[The Lord] saw that lotus-born one situated at the navel-region of Mahāviṣṇu, while the two great Daityas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were prepared to slay him with ease. (91–92)
Seeing Brahmā offering praise in order to protect him in the past,
Govinda awakened [him] for the sake of the destruction of those two.
And through devotion to you, Nārāyaṇa slew those two great asuras.
The Lord of All is with you, but he is helpless without you.
O Goddess of the Gods, in former times during the battle of Tripura, when I had fallen from the sky, I was protected by you together with Viṣṇu. || 94–95 ||
"Now protect me, O Sovereign, who am consumed by the fire of separation!
O Supreme Goddess, redeem me with the merit of beholding your own self!
Having spoken thus, Śambhu ceased and beheld her stationed in the sky.
With joy, [he beheld] that goddess seated upon a chariot made of the essence of jewels, possessing a hundred arms,
radiant with the luster of molten gold, adorned with jeweled ornaments,
her face bright with a gentle smile— the virtuous mother of the worlds. (97–98)
Seeing her, he, overcome by the pangs of separation, quickly praised her once more;
weeping, he announced his suffering born of that separation, and showed her the garland of bones and the ashes adorning his body. (99)
Having offered many concessions, he gratified Sundarī.
Then Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Dharma, Śeṣa, and the celestial sages,
saying "May Śiva protect you, O Sovereign Lady," praised the Eternal One.
At that moment, she became completely satisfied by their hymn of praise.
The beloved of her life spoke with compassion to Śambhu, the lord of her life. (2) Prakṛti said:
"Be firm, O Mahādeva; you are dearer to me than life, O Lord.
You are my very self, the master of yogis, and my sovereign in birth after birth.
Having obtained birth from the consort of the King of Mountains, O Maheśvara..."
"I shall become your wife; release your fever of separation.
Having spoken thus and consoled Śiva, she vanished. The gods, their necks bowed with shame, departed after having consoled him.
With his inner soul filled with joy, Giriśa departed for Kailāsa;
abandoning the fever of separation, he quickly began to dance together with his attendants.
Any man who recites this hymn composed by Śiva with natural devotion—
In birth after birth, he shall never suffer separation from his beloved;
having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the abode of Śiva.
He attains virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation—of this there is no doubt. (108)

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Śaṅkara’s Grief," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Himālaya, together with his attendants, [acted accordingly].
Filled with wonder, Pārvatī herself laughed along with her wife.
And Arundhatī enlightened the distressed Menā;
she [Arundhatī] caused her, who was fasting and weeping, to abandon her grief through joy.
Having fed Arundhatī, he enjoyed the finest delicacies;
with a joyful heart, he performed every auspicious rite.
Then, O beloved, having gathered all the necessary provisions by the command of Vasiṣṭha, he prepared for the journey.
He dispatched a letter with great haste to various places. Then he sent forth an auspicious letter to Śiva and prepared various kinds of external offerings.
O beautiful one, he indeed constructed mountains of rice and of flattened grains (pṛthuka),
as well as ponds of oils, clarified butters, and curds;
likewise, there were [heaps] of jaggery, seats, and milk.
Furthermore, O Sage, there were fresh butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*), salts,
sweets (*laḍḍuka*), sugar-candies (*śarkarā*), and likewise *svastika* confections;
these were made from flour such as barley-meal and cooked in ghee.
Having prepared various kinds of garments that are purified by fire,
as well as great jewels, corals, gold, and silver—
these materials, O Lord of Mountains, according to the prescribed ritual— 9.
On that very auspicious day, they began to perform the auspicious rites. The women of the mountains had Pārvatī undergo the purificatory sacraments;
having bathed her, they quickly dressed her in a pair of garments. (10–11)

Having dressed her in beautiful attire and adorned her with jewel ornaments, they held up a mirror provided with dūrvā grass and unbroken grains (akṣata). They also applied lovely red lac-dye to the toes and soles of her feet.
They fashioned a beautiful leaf-design upon her cheek and applied bright collyrium to her eyes. They arranged her braid, encircled with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
she was charming, with a lovely face and adorned with a silk thread. (13–14)
In the meantime, O Rādhā, the lords of the gods arrived there,
having brought the three-eyed Lord seated upon a jeweled vehicle;
Śaila then addressed the lords who were provided with all necessary offerings.
He dispatched the mountain-dwellers and also honored the Brahmins. He had a courtyard constructed, adorned with plantain pillars that were bound with silk threads and decorated with mango sprouts.
With water-filled jars adorned with fruits and sprouts,
and provided with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and beautiful flowers,
and further graced with garlands of jasmine, it was exceedingly enchanting. (18)
Having seen the supreme Lord of the gods, Himālaya prostrated himself.
He urged his servants to bring forth a jeweled lion-throne.
Indeed, the Blessed Nārāyaṇa dwelt there together with his attendants.
Quickly descending from the son of Vinatā, the four-armed Lord was attended by four-armed attendants adorned with jewel ornaments,
who held jeweled caskets and white chowries.
Being praised in that assembly by the best of sages and the best of gods,
with a face brightened by a slight smile and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees,
Brahmā dwelt in his presence together with the hosts of deities.
Sages and seers were dwelling together on that auspicious ground.
In the meantime, Śambhu, descending from his chariot,
stood upon a jeweled throne and beheld the mountain-dweller.
The women of the city of the mountain king gathered to see Śiva—old women, children, and young maidens adorned with garments and ornaments;
some held collyrium in their hands, and others held garments. || 25–26 ||
Some held vermilion in their hands, and some carried combs;
some were adorned with only half their attire, while others were not adorned at all;
some were entirely without ornaments, and some were adorned with every kind of jewelry.

Having arrived, they all stood together with smiles in the mountain abode—charming ṛṣi-maidens, celestial maidens, and nāga-maidens; the daughters of gandharvas and mountains, and princesses, had all assembled there. (28–29)
All the divine Apsarases, led by Rambhā, were present;
Menā, together with her groups of daughters, beheld the excellent Śaṅkara, who possessed the hue of a beautiful Campaka flower, had one face, and three eyes. (30)
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, adorned with jewel ornaments,
beautified by sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and lovely saffron,
graced with garlands of *mālatī* flowers, and radiant with a crown of excellent gems. (31–32)
He was exquisitely adorned with a pair of wonderful, priceless garments that were peerless, extremely fine, and brilliant like fire;
he held a jeweled mirror in his hand, and his eyes were brightened by collyrium.
Completely enveloped in every radiance, it was exceedingly beautiful;
exceedingly youthful, its limbs adorned with lovely ornaments; bearing an incomparable and supreme form by the command of Nārāyaṇa. (34–35)
The eternal light of Brahman, whose nature is Yoga, the Lord of Yoga, the Guru of the lords of yogis, consisting of His own will, transcending the qualities (guṇas),
though formless, assumes infinite forms through the differentiation of the qualities. 36.
He is the deliverer of those dwelling in existence, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
the support of all, the seed of all, the Lord of all, and the life of all;
he is the form of the witness, devoid of desire, supreme bliss, and imperishable. (37–38)
Having seen her son-in-law—who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, the primordial of all, and the embodiment of all forms—Menā, filled with joy, abandoned her grief.
And the young women praised her, saying, "Blessed, blessed is that virtuous woman! (39)
Some young maidens said, "Durgā is truly fortunate. Some amorous women, paralyzed by desire, became silent and said,
"No bridegroom has been seen by us within the range of our knowledge."
Some remained without blinking, while others fell into a swoon;
some censured their own husbands, and others acted according to their own desires.
Some wept with deep emotion, their bodies covered in horripilation.
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced;
and upon seeing the form of Śaṅkara, all the deities were overjoyed. Various kinds of musical instruments, both beautiful and sweet, [resounded].
There, indeed, the musicians played with various instruments.
In the meantime, Durgā, who was moving within the inner apartments of the mountain,
brought outside a jeweled altar-platform upon which sat a seat of excellent gems.
Adorned with dense drops of musk and thick dots of vermilion,
shining like beautiful sandalwood and the moon, radiant upon the surface of her bowed forehead,
and her chest embellished by a necklace of the finest essence of gems. (46–47)

To her, whose eyes had been granted by the Three-Eyed One and were thus unimpeded, whose face was endowed with a very gentle smile, who cast sidelong glances, and who was enchanting; adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and gem-studded bangles;
entwined with jeweled cords, and made resonant by tinkling anklets—(48–49).
She was beautifully adorned with a pair of garments rich in priceless and incomparable embroidery;

her lovely cheeks were made radiant by two earrings of excellent gems. Her row of teeth shone, eclipsing the luster of the finest jewels, while she held a jeweled mirror in one hand and twirled a play-lotus in the other. Her limbs were anointed with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron.
All were filled with joy upon seeing her, the primordial one of the world and the mother of the universe. (92) The three-eyed Lord, filled with delight, beheld her with the corner of his eye;
seeing her entire form as Satī, he abandoned the fever of separation. (53)
Śiva forgot everything else, his mind being entirely absorbed in Durgā;
with all his limbs covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears of joy.
In the meantime, the Mountain, together with his family priest, was overjoyed.
He chose that boon [for her] with garments, sandalwood paste, and ornaments;
with devotion, he offered water for the feet and other honors, along with garlands and divine, fragrant, and enchanting perfumes.
Then, quickly, he performed the formal gift-giving ceremony for her with Vedic mantras.
O Rādhikā, he gave him wedding gifts consisting of various jewels,
beautiful vessels fashioned from exquisite gems,
a hundred thousand cows, and thousands of lordly elephants.
Filled with joy and free from fear, he gave thirty lakhs of horses equipped with jeweled blankets and goads,
as well as a lakh of devoted female servants adorned with excellent jewels. (58–59)
And a hundred young brahmin students resembling the brother of Pārvatī,
and a hundred beautiful chariots constructed from the finest essence of jewels—
uttering "May it be well," Śaṅkara [gave these] to Pārvatī along with her belongings.
With a joyful mind, he accepted with effort the daughter offered by the mountain;
having given his daughter, Himālaya performed that ritual of dismissal.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he praised [Śiva] with the *Tātra* hymn spoken at midday.
Himālaya said:
Be gracious, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, O savior from the ocean of hell!
O embodiment of the self of all, O Lord of all, O you whose form is supreme bliss! (63)
O ocean of virtues, O one who transcends qualities, O you endowed with qualities, O Lord of the hosts!
O seed of all qualities, O highly fortunate one, be gracious, O best among the virtuous!
(64) O support of yoga, O embodiment of yoga, O knower of yoga, O cause of yoga!
O Lord of Yogis, seed of yogis, be gracious, O Teacher of yogis!
O sole cause of the dissolution of the dissolution and of all beings,
seed of creation at the end of dissolution, be gracious, O Protector!
O cause of creation and dissolution during the terrible time of withdrawal;
O you who are difficult to restrain, difficult to propitiate, yet quickly pleased—be gracious to me!
O you whose nature is Time, Lord of Time, and bestower of fruits within Time!
O destroyer of Time by means of the seed-syllable of Time, be gracious, O protector of Time!
(68) O you whose nature is Śiva, giver of auspiciousness, seed of Śiva, refuge of Śiva;
O you who have become Śiva, the life-breath of Śiva, be gracious, O supreme refuge! (69)
Having thus offered this praise, Himālaya became silent.
All the gods and sages lauded the Lord of Mountains.
Any self-controlled man who recites this hymn composed by Himālaya—
"O Rādhikā, Śiva will certainly grant him his desire.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Bestowal upon Pārvatī," in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Then, having established the fire according to Vedic injunctions, the Lord performed a sacrifice right there, having seated Pārvatī at his left side. When the sacrifice had been completed according to the rules, he gave sacrificial fees to the Brahmin.
Śiva [bestowed] one hundred gold pieces upon the one who delights in Vṛndāvana.
(2) Then, having brought a lamp, the women of the city of Śaileśvara performed auspicious rites; and the couple, having reached their home, (3) [proceeded].
Having joyfully raised shouts of victory and performed auspicious rites such as the ceremonial sprinkling (*nirmañchana*), the throngs of amorous women—
smiling, casting side-long glances, and their bodies covered in horripilation—
entered the bedchamber and beheld [him].
Śaṅkara, rich in form and attire, adorned with jewel ornaments;
his body anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
his face bright with a slight smile, captivating with side-long glances. (5–6)
Adorned with an unprecedentedly subtle attire and decorated with a dot of vermilion,
possessing the lovely hue of a *campaka* flower and beautiful in every limb,
he was in the bloom of fresh youth and captivated the minds of the lords of sages.
Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, Jāhnavī, and Rati;
Aditi, Śacī, Lopāmudrā, and Arundhatī;
Ahalyā, Tulasī, Svāhā, Rohiṇī, and Vasuṃdharā. (8–9)
Śatarūpā, Saṃjñā, and sixteen virtuous women—
divine maidens, nāga maidens, and captivating daughters of sages—
whoever was present there, who would be capable of numbering them all? (10)
When they had offered him a jeweled throne, Śiva sat there with joy.
Then the goddesses spoke to him in turn with sweet words like nectar.
Sarasvatī said:
Having now attained her who is dearer than life, O Mahādeva,
abandon your distress with joy upon seeing the moon-like face of your beloved, O lover;
spend your time, O Lord of Time, always preceded by constant union.
"By my blessing, there shall never be a separation between you at any time.
Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord of Gods, casting aside shame, place the virtuous woman upon your own chest."
"Stay for now; what shame is there when life itself departs without you?
Sāvitrī said:
"O Śambhu, having first fed Satī, feed me quickly; do not be distressed."
Then, having sipped water, give her betel-leaf with camphor with devotion.
Jāhnavī said:
O woman, taking hold of a golden comb, brush the hair.
For a woman in love, there can be no happiness greater than the good fortune of her husband.
Rati said:
"O Lord, having taken Pārvatī, who is so fortunate and exceedingly difficult to obtain..."
"How is it that my lord of life has been reduced to ashes for no selfish purpose?
O All-pervading One, you satisfy desire at will within yourself;
therefore, cast far away this torment of mine caused by our separation. (17–18)
"O Ocean of Compassion, although you know all the suffering caused by the separation of husband and wife,
nevertheless my beloved has been reduced to ashes through your wrath.
Having spoken thus, she then gave him the ashes of Kāma tied in a knot.
He wept before Śambhu, crying out, "O Lord of Lords!
(20). Hearing that weeping, Hari—the ocean of compassion—along with Brahmā and the gods headed by Dharma, went to the dwelling of Śiva (21).
Having seen Nārāyaṇa, Dharma, Brahmā, and the gods as well, he rose swiftly from his seat and said, "Carry out my command! (22).
Having heard Śaṅkara’s words, Hari himself spoke to him.
Saying, "O Rudra, please bring him back to life," he departed quickly.
The goddesses spoke many words with great humility;
then, having seen the wielder of the trident in a state of wrath, Smara emerged from the ashes. (23–24)

Having seen him, Kāma bowed to Maheśvara, who possessed that very form and appearance, smiling and holding his bow and arrow. Having prostrated before Śaṅkara and offered praise according to the scriptures, Kāma [stood there]. (25)
Having gone outside and bowed to Hari and the gods, he spoke to them.
After conversing with him as they pleased, the gods bestowed blessings upon him.
"Who can ward off protection, destruction, or prohibition when their time has come? (26–27)
Then Śaila, with devotion, fed all the gods, headed by Nārāyaṇa, and diligently provided them with beds. Then Śambhu, having placed Pārvatī on his left side in the bedchamber, [rested].
Filled with joy, he fed him sweet foods together with her.
When Śiva had finished eating there, Aditi, the mother of the gods, herself spoke these charming words with great affection and a smile, O Rādhā. (29–30)
Aditi said:
"O Śacī, at the conclusion of the meal, offer water to Śambhu for the sake of purification.
Out of affection for me, quickly provide it with love for the couple. (31)
Śacī said:

"For whose sake you lamented, placing the corpse upon your breast, and who wandered the earth out of delusion—by the power of Time, he has now attained that state of being a virtuous woman (satī). (32)
Arundhatī said:
"Although Menā was unwilling to give her to you, she has been given by me to you. You ought to instruct her in various ways and show her affection. (33)
Ahalyā said:
"O Lord, having cast off his old age, he has now become exceedingly youthful;
therefore, Menā intends to bestow her daughter upon you. (34)
Tulasī said:
Satī was abandoned by you, and Kāma was burnt away in the past;
O Lord, why then has Vasiṣṭha now been sent away? (35)
Svāhā said:
"O Mahādeva, be firm now regarding the words of women;
there is a custom in marriage where city women possess boldness. (36)
Rohiṇī said:
"O you who are expert in the science of love, fulfill the desire of Pārvatī;
as a lover yourself, cross over the ocean of desire for those who long for it. (37)
Vasundharā said:
"A man of pleasure is certainly not satisfied without the objects of enjoyment, for he is afflicted by hunger.
O Śambhu, it is fitting for a wife to do that by which satisfaction may be attained. (38)
Saṃjñā said:
"O omniscient one, you know the state of women afflicted by desire;
yet, O Śambhu, Satī did not recognize her own husband when they were united. (39)
Śatarūpā said:
"Quickly send Śaṅkara forth with affection along with Pārvatī;
having prepared a jeweled lamp, betel, and a bed in a secluded place. (40)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard those words of the women, Śiva himself spoke to them—he who is changeless, the Blessed Lord, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis. (41)
Śaṅkara said:
O goddesses, do not speak such words in my presence;
you are the virtuous mothers of the worlds—how can there be fickleness toward one's own son? 42.
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, the celestial women became ashamed;
in their agitation, they remained silent like figures in a painting.
Having eaten the sweets and sipped water, the Blessed One was filled with joy.
Accompanied by his wife, Śambhu partook of betel-leaf with camphor.
Seated upon a beautiful jeweled throne offered by Menā,
he, filled with joy, beheld the dwelling chamber.
It blazed with the splendor of hundreds of flaming jewel-lamps;
it was strewn with jeweled vessels and jars, adorned with pearls and rubies,
enriched by the beauty of jeweled mirrors, and decorated with white chowries.
It was endowed with sandalwood and agallochum, provided with flower-beds,
and filled with various wonderful and diverse designs; it was fashioned by Viśvakarman,
inlaid with the finest gems, and adorned with excellent diamonds.
In some places it was as enchanting as the Vaikuṇṭha created by the gods;
in some places it was Vṛndāvana with its groves and forests, and in some places the circle of Rāsa-dance. In one place it was Kailāsa, and in another the palace of Indra.
Having seen this marvel, Mahādeva became truly gratified.
(50) Then, O beloved of my life, the time of dawn arrived;
people began to play various kinds of musical instruments. (51)
All the gods arose, prepared and full of haste;
mounting their respective vehicles, they were ready to go to Kailāsa.
Having arrived at the chamber of rest by the command of Nārāyaṇa, Dharma [remained there].
The yogi spoke to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Yogis, in a manner appropriate for the occasion. Dharma said:
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you, O Lord of the Pramathas!"
"Perform a pilgrimage to Mount Mahendra together with Pārvatī, while remembering Hari.
Having heard these words of Dharma, Śaṅkara, accompanied by Pārvatī,
undertook a pilgrimage to Mahendra, which is a place of delight for Vṛndāvana.
While Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, was setting out on his journey together with Pārvatī,
Menā, having wept aloud, spoke to him, the ocean of compassion.
Menā said:
O ocean of compassion, having shown mercy, you will protect my daughter;
the Lord, who is easily pleased, will forgive her thousands of faults.
In birth after birth, this daughter of mine shall be devoted to your lotus feet.
In dreams and in waking cognition, there is no memory [of anything] except for the Lord Mahādeva.
Merely by hearing of devotion to you, one becomes filled with tears of joy and horripilation;
through censure of you, O Mṛtyuñjaya, one becomes silent as if dead. (58–59)
Thus addressed, Menakā quickly returned there;
Himālaya then wept aloud, placing his daughter upon his breast, crying out, "Where are you going, my child? and leaving Himālaya desolate.
"Remembering again and again that multitude of attendants, my mind is clearly rent asunder.
Having spoken thus and having offered Śivā to Śiva,
the lord of mountains, together with his son, wept aloud again and again.

And the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, that ocean of compassion, himself awakened everyone through the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) out of his grace. Pārvatī bowed with devotion to her mother, her father, and her guru.
And by means of her illusory power, Mahāmāyā wept loudly again and again. At the very sound of Pārvatī’s weeping, all the women wept;
and all the sages and gods, together with their wives and their attendants, certainly did likewise. (64–65)
Those gods, resting upon Lake Mānasa, went swiftly to Kailāsa;
in half a muhūrta, they joyfully reached the abode of Śaṅkara.
Seeing that he had departed, the wives of the gods and the wives of the sages quickly followed.
They arrived joyfully for the auspicious rite, bringing lamps:
Vāyu’s wife, Kubera’s beloved, Śukra’s beloved, Tārā the wife of the preceptor of the gods, and likewise the wife of Durvāsas. (67–68)
Atri’s wife Anasūyā, as well as the wives of the Moon, thousands of celestial maidens, Nāga maidens, and sage maidens—[there was] a multitude of countless beloved women;
who is capable of numbering them? (69)
And they led the couple into their own residence;
they seated the Goddess upon a beautiful jeweled throne. Śiva joyfully showed that virtuous woman his former abode.
"O Smara, since you departed from this house for your father’s abode, you have now become the daughter of the Mountain; formerly, however, you were the daughter of Dakṣa.
Since you remember your past lives, I shall remind you constantly; tell me if you recall it. (72)
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, that virtuous woman (Satī) spoke with a smile:
"O Lord of my life, I remember everything; please remain silent.
Then Śiva prepared a collection of various delightful materials.
He caused the gods, headed by Nārāyaṇa, to eat.
Having eaten and being adorned with various jewels, all those gods,
together with their wives and their attendants, departed after bowing to the moon-crested Lord.
Śaṅkara himself bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā; they both embraced him, offered him their blessings, and departed. Then Śaila and Menā summoned Maināka. (76–77)
"Bring Pārvatī and Śaṅkara quickly, may you be blessed, O son! Having heard their words, he went swiftly to the abode of Śiva and returned after bringing Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord.
Upon hearing that Pārvatī was arriving, the boys and girls,
as well as the old women and young maidens, and even the mountain itself, ran forth with joy.
Menā, along with her two sons and her daughter-in-law, also ran out with a smile.

And the Himalaya, filled with joy, ran after his daughter. Having descended from her chariot, the goddess, delighted and immersed in an ocean of bliss, prostrated before her mother, father, and preceptor. (81)
Embracing Pārvatī, Menakā was overwhelmed with joy;
and Himālaya, delighted, felt as if his very life-breaths had returned.
Having settled his daughter in his own home, he presented her with a throne of jewels.
With joy, he offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors to the Trident-bearer and his attendants.
Then the Moon-crested Lord, together with his attendants and his wife, remained in the house of his father-in-law,
constantly worshipped with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Thus, O Rādhā, has been narrated the auspicious marriage of Śaṅkara. It produces joy even from sorrow. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Śaṅkara," in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Rādhikā said: Kāma had been dead for a very long time, yet he was restored to life by Śaṅkara.
Having regained her beloved once more, what did Rati do, filled with joy? (1)
For women, the separation from their own husband is more difficult to endure than death;
yet, reunion with the husband is a supreme happiness that is exceedingly rare.
Having obtained Satī for his companion during the auspicious rite, Śiva—

Filled with joy, what did he do after being separated from his beloved for so long? (3) For men, separation from a wife is more difficult to endure than all other sorrows; yet, reunion with her is a happiness greater than the gift of life itself. (4)
Rati was separated from her husband, and Śiva was long separated from his wife.
When both were reunited with their respective partners, what happiness did they find?
(5) I wish to hear this; my curiosity is great.
Out of compassion, O best of the wise, O Lord, relate the story without omission.
[Tell us] of the union of Śakti and Śiva, and thereafter of Rati and Manmatha;
it removes the grief of those who hear it and is the cause of all auspiciousness.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Rādhikā ceased, smiling.
Hearing those words, Kṛṣṇa also smiled and spoke to her. 8.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having regained her deceased Kāma, that woman, afflicted by desire and longing for love, brought him back to her own abode from the wedding hall of Hara. Alas! (9)
Eager for dalliance with her lover, Rati joyfully and with great effort had her own maids prepare various fine garments for herself and her husband.
But Kāma, the author of the treatises on love, perceived her state of mind.
Having mounted the jewel-chariot, he departed from his own abode for the forest.
On every mountain, in every most beautiful valley, by every river and every stream,
on every island and at every ocean shore, and in every enchanting flower garden— 11–12.
On a heap of golden earth at the foot of a banyan tree in a most secluded place,
on the banks of a river, and in a flowering forest of *puṣpaka* trees (13),
which resounds with the humming of bees and the songs of male cuckoos.
Filling the air with fragrant breezes and scattering sprays of water, she— oh, what a wonder!— aroused passion in the hearts of sentient beings through various modes of artistic expression. 14–15.
For a full hundred divine years he took delight with Vāmā;
day and night, ever attached and filled with joy, he was not aware of the passage of time. And the two of them remained right there, constantly attached and filled with joy.
Skilled in the science of love, she took no pleasure in the cessation of lovemaking;
she abandoned the grief caused by her husband’s absence with joy.
Who, having obtained a stolen jewel, would ever wish to let it go for even a moment? (17–18)
Thus has everything been told regarding the causes of the joy and the torment [of love].
O Rādhikā, hear now of the incomparable *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) of Śakti and Śiva—this supreme wonder, desired by those who hear it, which is nectar for the ears. 19.
It removes all distress, bestows happiness, grants merit, and is auspicious.
(20) While dwelling with Pārvatī in his father-in-law’s house, Śaṅkara, having obtained her permission, went to the forest for the sake of sport. (21)
Having mounted a chariot made of jewels, adorned with the finest gems,
inlaid with precious stones, and fashioned by Viśvakarman;
[he traveled] to Śataśṛṅga, Suvasana, Malaya, and Gandhamādana.
In Nandana, Puṣpabhadraka, Pāribhadra, and Bhadraka;
in Pulinda, Kalinda, Puṇḍra, Piṇḍāraka, and Andhaka;
in every most delightful forest, and on every shore of the oceans.
Near the western mountain, at the base of a banyan tree on a charming slope—
where the virtuous Satī had performed her penance after abandoning Śiva—
in various secluded spots, free from beasts and birds. (25)
He wandered with Vāmā, going wherever his heart desired.
Wherever he led Śivā and roamed the surface of the earth, Śambhu, filled with joy, showed her all of it. (26–27)
Having constructed the monastery for a very long time, the minds of those two were not yet satisfied;
then the Father of the World began a great drama lasting a thousand years.
Transcending illusion, the Lord of supreme illusion became attached to illusion through his own power of māyā. (28)
The yogin, who brings about the end of time, did not perceive the passing of time as he dwelt in bliss;
there was no exhaustion for either the power (śakti) or the possessor of power (śaktimant), as they abandoned all the suffering born of their mutual separation. (29–30)

With minds deeply attached to pleasure, their limbs bristling with horripilation, fainting from the arrows of love, reclining upon a bed of flowers— (31)— they were naked, engaged in the enjoyment of bliss, and conversant with the rules of the science of erotics.
With their bodies mangled by wounds from blows of nails and teeth,
anointed with drops of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and vermilion,
their braided hair-crests loosened and their flower-garlands torn asunder; (32–33)
O beautiful one, as they engaged in play amidst the sounds of their garments, anklets, bracelets, bangles, and earrings,
they lay upon a bed of flowers, shedding profuse tears. (34)
By the constant play and curiosity of those two who were equal in splendor, the earth, already burdened by the weight of the two world-sustainers, was overcome by that further load;
she split asunder and trembled along with her mountains, forests, and oceans. (35–36)
And by the weight of those two, the earth was overcome by its burden;
for Śeṣa was oppressed by that weight, and the Tortoise was likewise afflicted by their burden.
