By the very weight of the Tortoise, the winds—the support of all—were also overwhelmed.
All living beings were struck with great agitation and paralyzed;
when the vital breaths were thus paralyzed, the three worlds were overwhelmed by fear,
and all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, went to Vaikuṇṭha for refuge.
They all made their report at the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa spoke to the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Creator, the time for the destruction of passion has not yet arrived.
The task ordained by Time has been accomplished in accordance with its proper season. When the thousand years are complete, he will cease of his own accord.
Who is capable of creating a separation between Śambhu and his beloved?
He who, by some means, causes the interruption of the pleasure of a man and woman, shall experience the separation from his wife in birth after birth. (42–43)
That sinner goes to the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred thousand years;
in this world, he shall be one whose knowledge is lost, whose fame is destroyed, and who is devoid of prosperity.
[He] made this Śakra, who was united with Rambhā, cease from sexual union.
The great lord of sages, Durvāsas, became separated from her wife;
having obtained another woman and served the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for a thousand divine years, he abandoned the fever of separation.
The great seer Gautama caused the moon, together with Rohiṇī, to cease from sexual union; indeed, he suffered the loss of his wife. Later, having propitiated Śiva at Puṣkara, he regained Ahalyā.
And for a thousand divine years, he abandoned the fever of separation.
On a day when the sage was absorbed in his own wife in the lonely forest,
he took the son of Brahmāṇḍaka and, out of anger, rendered him motionless.
In another kalpa, he experienced the loss of his son once again;
yet, by serving Śiva and regaining his son, he abandoned all despondency. Hariścandra likewise [suffered] when he saw the plowman united with a low-caste woman.
He restrained him while he was motionless in that desolate place; hear now the fruit of that.
Viśvāmitra, the great seer, formerly struck him with ease, causing him to fall from his fortune, kingdom, and wealth. (51–52)
Then, having propitiated Śiva, the bestower of all prosperity,
he went immediately with his attendants to Vaikuṇṭha, my abode—
along with that best of brahmins, Ājāmila, who had been united with a low-caste woman.
Some of the gods did not restrain him out of fear;
and when his experience of the fruits of his karma was completed, that devotee of mine was indeed released.
By the mere remembrance of my name, he came to my abode.

Everything is to be accomplished through *niṣeka*, and *niṣeka* is powerful in its application; I am the bestower of the fruit of *niṣeka*. By whom can *niṣeka* be obstructed? For a thousand divine years, I performed the act of union with Śambhu.

But Maheśvara, the bestower of the fruits of the *niṣeka*, having gone there after a full thousand years, will certainly bring about that accumulation of the fruits of the *niṣeka* by means of which his seed shall fall upon the earth. (57–98)
"In that regard, Skandaka shall become a provider of food through his vigor.
I am always of an auspicious nature; what fear can there be for you while I am present?
Now, O Blessed One, go home along with your own attendants."
"May Śambhu enjoy union with Pārvatī in a secluded place.
Having spoken thus, the beloved of Kamalā quickly went to his inner apartments;
the gods returned to their own abodes, and Śiva remained composed, intent on the pleasure of love.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, who was smiling and casting sidelong glances, Kṛṣṇa went with her to a secluded sandalwood grove. 62.

Extremely secluded, delightful, and made fragrant by the breeze, it was filled with flower gardens; there he indeed took his pleasure, amidst beds strewn with flowers and hearing the warbling of cuckoos. (63)
Amidst the enchanting humming of female bees,
she was completely overwhelmed with bliss by the mere act of Kṛṣṇa’s union;
and Kṛṣṇa, for his part, was intensely swooned by the mere touch of Rādhā’s body.
O sage, Rādhā and the Lord of Rās remain there united, motionless in the midst of supreme passion. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus, whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this auspicious deed—
O Nārada, never shall there be a separation from his kinsmen;
even when submerged in a great ocean of grief due to a rift between son and wife,
he will certainly obtain [peace] within a month upon hearing [this account] from my devotees and kinsmen.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the great sage, the son of Dharma, ceased;
then the celestial rishi, filled with curiosity, began to question him again. (69)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Auspiciousness," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
Then, during the course of their play, what did Rādhā ask the all-pervading Lord Hari?
"O ocean of compassion, please tell me—what story did He relate?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Rising from His blissful enjoyment, Hari placed Rādhā before Him.

He dwelt at the foot of a beautiful banyan tree in a valley of the Malaya mountains. Rādhā, with a smile, questioned him regarding that most enchanting and secret account of the humbling of Indra’s pride, which was as beautiful as the Vedas.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
I have heard of the glory of the Trident-bearer and his defeat of the pride of the gods;
likewise, I have heard of Pārvatī’s defeat of pride and, oh, their marriage! (4)
"Now, O Hari, I wish to hear of the humbling of the pride of Hari;
O Teacher of the World, tell me also of the others in due order.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O beautiful lady, listen to this matchless and lovely nectar for the ears, renowned throughout the three worlds, concerning the shattering of the pride of the Lord of the Gods.
Long ago, the performer of a hundred sacrifices (Indra), out of arrogance, having performed a hundred sacrifices with joy...
He became the presiding lord of all the gods, endowed with prosperity.
Day by day, his sovereignty increased through the fruit of his ascetic penances.
Bṛhaspati then caused him to undergo initiation, providing him with prepared food.
He recited the great mantra at Puṣkara for a hundred years.
He became perfected in mantra and his desires were completely fulfilled. Yet, though he had attained the nature of Brahman, that fool did not recognize it.
She cursed him, and he received a curse from his own preceptor due to excessive anger.
Once, his intellect impaired by the curse of Prakṛti, he saw his preceptor in his own assembly; though he rose up, he did not bow with joy. (10–11)
Then Bṛhaspati, out of anger, did not remain in his home;
he did not stay near Tāraka but went to the forest for asceticism.
Dejected, he thought in his mind: "May the fortune of Hari depart."
Then Śakra, having formed a plan, thought, "Where has my lord gone?
Having said this, he rose swiftly from his seat and went into the presence of Tāraka.
Bowing with devotion to his mother, with shoulders bent and palms joined in *añjali*, he stood before her.
Having made this entire report, she wept aloud again and again.
Seeing her son’s weeping, Tārakā wept intensely:
"Child, go home; you shall not see your preceptor at this time. (15)
"Having reached your teacher at the end of this stormy day, you shall regain your fortune once more.
Now, O fool of evil intent, experience the fruit of your actions!
When the day is overcast, one finds fault with one's teacher; when the day is bright, one offers him praise. (16–17)
"O Śakra, a fair day or a foul day—these are the causes of happiness and sorrow.
Having spoken thus, the devoted goddess Tārakā ceased speaking.
Śakra then went to the most enchanting celestial river (Svarṇadī) for the purpose of bathing.
There he beheld the beautiful Ahalyā,
the beloved wife of Gautama, who was broad-hipped, smiling, and casting sidelong glances as she was cleaning herself;
and having seen her, with her ample hips and her enchanting pair of breasts.
Beholding her, Śakra, deluded by passion, lost his senses. Regaining consciousness, O Goddess, he left the bathing place,
assumed the form of her husband, and went into her presence.
Having gone there, he, afflicted by love, pulled her toward him as she wore a soft garment;
he then engaged in various most enchanting amorous acts. The sage’s beloved fell into a swoon from passion and was overcome by drowsiness.

Motionless from the enjoyment of bliss, the lord of the thirty gods was also motionless. In the meantime, having arrived after performing austerities, the lord of sages saw the couple in their home, both of whom were intent on sexual union.
Seeing this, the sage became enraged like a blazing fire;
with intense fury born of his supernatural knowledge, he shattered the moment of sexual union.
Śakra, having regained consciousness and beheld that bull among sages, [was struck with fear].
Out of fear, Kāla held the lotus-foot [of the Lord];
with his face and eyes red with anger, Gautama spoke words of policy to the God who had prostrated at his feet out of dread and had come for refuge. (27)
Gautama said:
"Fie on you, O Indra, best of gods, son of Kaśyapa, and wise one!
How can such a mind as this belong to you, the great-grandson of the Creator of the worlds?"
Your maternal grandfather was Dakṣa himself, and your mother Aditi was devoted to her husband.
One’s inherent nature is achieved through action, yet it may obstruct the dharma of one’s lineage;
having understood the Veda, you, though a man of knowledge, are greedy for birth on account of your past actions.
"And let there be a thousand vaginas upon your body here;
for a full year, may you constantly experience the odor of a vagina.
Then, by propitiating the Sun, your vagina shall become an eye."
"O fool, because my mistress was treated wickedly by you,
fall now from your prosperity through my curse and the anger of your preceptor.
O fool, it is only out of regard for your guru that your life-breaths have not been taken away."
"O radiant one, O god, rise up, rise up! O Lord of the Devas, go, my child, to your own abode, for fear of causing a rift among our kin.
Whatever occurs, whether auspicious or inauspicious, all that arises from karma. (34)

Having gone to Puṣkara at the word of the Great Lord of Sages, Śakra performed worship with devotion and indeed practiced asceticism. Then the bull among sages spoke to Ahalyā, who was prostrate at his feet.
"Go to the forest and remain there for a long time, having fashioned a stone image [of yourself].
O beloved, Śakra lusted after me though I was unwilling; I know all this. Likewise, O lowest of women, go away; I am not to be enjoyed by you, as I am already enjoyed by another."
"O Ahalyā, listen to the means by which semen that enters the womb—whether intentionally or unintentionally—due to destiny [is purified].
If it was unintentional, she is not defiled; she becomes pure through expiation. (38–39)
She must be abandoned through the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; she is purified by the experience of [the fruits of] karma.
She has no entitlement to the ancestral rites (pitṛpāka), the divine rites (daivapāka), or to worship.
For sixty thousand years, she goes to the Kālasūtra hell.
Having exhausted sixty thousand years of her own karma, she, at the command of her master, bowed down to him in fear;
crying out "O Lord! O Lord! while weeping, she entered the forest.
Having enjoyed pleasures for sixty thousand years,
the beloved of the sage became instantly purified by the touch of Śrī Rāma’s feet.
The wife of the sage assumed a form that enchanted the three worlds.
Having reached Sundarī, the sage went into the presence of Gautama. (44) Now, O beautiful one, hear the supreme account of Śakra;
having clothed myself in that which destroys sin and is the seed of merit, I shall relate it to you. (45)
And once, due to his teacher’s anger and his contempt for Prakṛti,
the mindless Śakra incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin;
abandoned by his teacher, seized by fate, and oppressed by the Daityas, he [fell].
Terrified, he went for refuge to Brahmā, the preceptor of the worlds.
By his command, Viśvarūpa was made the family priest.
There, Hari became full of trust, his intellect having been deluded by fate.
Having discerned the intention of the grandson of the Daitya,
the wise one [Viṣṇu] effortlessly severed his head with a sharp arrow.
Upon hearing this, Tvaṣṭṛ, the father of Viśvarūpa, was instantly incensed.
Having said, "O enemy of Indra, prosper!", he performed a sacrifice.
From the sacrificial pit arose the great asura named Vṛtra;
out of anger, he effortlessly brought about the subjugation of the gods.

Śakra, the crusher of the Daityas, fashioned a most formidable vajra from the bones of the Great Sage and struck Vṛtra, the thorn of the gods. The sin of Brahmin-slaughter then pursued Śunāsīra, who was deprived of his senses.

Clad in red garments and wearing the attire of Vṛtra’s wife, she stood seven palm trees in height; with her throat, lips, and palate parched, and teeth as large as plowshafts, she struck him with great terror. (53–94)
Running after him as he fled, the powerful woman,
sword in hand and devoid of mercy, pursued the unconscious man with great speed.
And Indra, beholding that terrible sight, repeatedly called to mind the words of his preceptor.
She entered Lake Mānasa by means of a fine thread of lotus fiber. (56) There she was unable to proceed further due to the curse of Brahmā;
she remained upon the branch of a banyan tree near the shore of the lake. (57)
Then, King Nahuṣa became the lord of the three worlds.
Being the strongest, he demanded Śacī from the gods, even though they were weak.
Hearing this, Śacī was greatly terrified and went to Tārakā for refuge.
Tārā, having rebuked her own husband, protected the wife of the servant;
and Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, having consoled Śacī, went joyfully to that lake.
He summoned Śunāsīra, who was distressed and deprived of his senses.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Arise, arise, O child! Why do you fear while I am present?
Listen to the voice of your lord himself and cast away your fear."
Having recognized the voice of Bṛhaspati, Hari, the lord of all perfections,
abandoned his subtle form and assumed his own true form.
Rising up immediately, agitated, he [approached] that preceptor who possessed the splendor of the sun.
Seeing him fallen at his lotus feet, weeping and overwhelmed by fear, he— himself filled with joy and having abandoned all anger— bowed down with great affection.
Placing the other upon his chest out of love, he too wept, overwhelmed by affection.
The Lord of the Thirty-three Gods praised the joyful Vākpati as he wept,
with palms joined in reverence, his hair standing on end, and his neck bowed low in devotion.
Indra said:
Forgive this fault, O Blessed One; have mercy, O Treasure of Compassion!
(65) A true Lord never takes to heart the transgressions of his servants, whether toward his own wives, his disciples, his servants, or his sons. (66)
Whether weak or strong, who is unable to inflict punishment?
Among the thirty-three gods, I am but a simple Devaka;
yet, O best of deities, by your grace and through your compassion, I have been brought to growth.
"You are capable of withdrawing everything; who else, even I, am like an insect?
You are the grandson of the Creator himself and are yourself capable of creating again.
Having heard this praise of his, the Guru himself was deeply gratified.
With a serene face and eyes, he spoke these words with affection.
The Guru said:
"Be steadfast, O highly fortunate one; attain unwavering prosperity."
"Having attained supreme sovereignty, four times greater than before,
go to Amarāvatī, my child, and rule the kingdom, O Purandara!
With your enemies slain through my grace, go and see the virtuous Śacī."
Having spoken thus, that preceptor, prepared to depart along with his disciple,
beheld before him the terrible and most unbearable sin of Brahman-slaughter.
Seeing it, Śakra became greatly terrified and went to that preceptor for refuge.
Bṛhaspati, greatly terrified, called to mind Madhusūdana.
In that interval, an incorporeal voice arose there;
it was brief in syllables yet rich in meaning, and Bṛhaspati heard it.
It is named *Samsāravijaya*, the destroyer of all that is inauspicious.
(75) Having heard these words, O Rādhikā, [the Lord] said, "Protect the disciple now!
Then, he who is affectionate toward his disciples gave his own armor (*kavaca*) to the disciple. (76)
And he reduced her to ashes with ease by a mere *huṃkāra*. Then, taking his disciple, he went to that Amarāvatī and saw it shattered and destroyed by the enemy at the word of the Guru.
Hearing of her husband’s arrival, Śacī, with a heart full of joy,
bowed with devotion to her elder and prostrated before her own beloved.
O dear one, hearing of Indra’s approach, the gods assembled together.
The sages and seers, their minds choked with joy, prepared to perform a hospitable reception. The architect constructed Amarāvatī for a full hundred years. (79–80)
Richly adorned with various jewels and fashioned from the finest of gems, that enchanting and incomparable palace was such that even Hari was not satisfied with it;
Viśvakarmā could not leave the house without [the Lord's] command. (81)
With a mind of extreme agitation, he went for refuge to Brahmā.
Having understood his intention, Vidhi himself said to him:
"Only upon the exhaustion of your karma shall it come to pass tomorrow."
Having heard those words, the artisan quickly reached Amarāvatī;
Brahmā went to Vaikuṇṭha and, having prostrated, spoke to his mother.
Hari, having consoled Brahmā, sent him back to his own home.
Assuming the form of a brahmin, he came to Amarāvatī (85).
Carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in white garments, and wearing a brilliant tilaka (86),
he was very short in stature, with white teeth, smiling, and exceedingly handsome.
Though very young in age, he was wise through the growth of his intellect;
he was himself the creator of the Creator and the bestower of all prosperity.
Rising at the gate of Indra, he spoke to the doorkeeper.
"Announce this at the gate of Brahmā: 'I have come quickly to see you.
Having heard these words, he (the gatekeeper) made him known at the gate.
And he, arriving quickly, beheld the young Brahmin.
Surrounded by throngs of boys and girls, laughing with great enthusiasm and accompanied by smiles and radiant splendor,
Hari bowed with devotion to that Lord Hari who had assumed the form of a child.
Hari, who is affectionate toward his devotees, joyfully bestowed a blessing upon him.
Having offered the madhuparka and other honors, Śakra performed worship for him and asked the brahmin boy, "Tell me, why have you come? (91–92)
Having heard the words of Indra, the young brahmin,
the preceptor of the preceptor of Bṛhaspati, spoke to him in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
(93) The brahmin said:
I have come to see you and to ask the question I desire:

having heard of the marvelous and wondrous construction of the city, O Hari, for how many years were you resolved upon its creation? (94) And according to your intention, how long will it take for the construction to be completed?
How many such creations will Viśvakarman ever fashion?
No Indra has ever fashioned a creation of this kind;
even the supreme Viśvakarman is not capable of such a perfect creation.
Having heard the boy’s words, that lord of the gods laughed; and being exceedingly intoxicated with the pride of his prosperity, he questioned the boy again:
"Have you seen or heard of a multitude of Indras?"

"O child, tell me now: how many kinds of Viśvakarman are there? Having heard Śakra’s words, the young brahmin smiled and spoke to him these words, which were pleasing to the ear and like nectar: 98–99. "O child, tell me now: how many kinds of Viśvakarman are there? Having heard Śakra’s words, the young brahmin smiled and spoke to him these words, which were pleasing to the ear and like nectar.
The Brahmin said:
"O dear one, I know Kaśyapa, your father, the lord of creatures (Prajāpati), as well as the sage named Marīci, who is a treasure-house of asceticism. 100.
Having praised that Lord Brahmā, who was born from the lotus of Viṣṇu’s navel,
and having praised that Viṣṇu, the protector endowed with the supreme quality of goodness (sattva),
[he described] the dissolution as a single ocean, devoid of beings and terrifying.
O Śakra, how many kinds of creation are there? How many kinds of kalpas and eternal principles (dhruva)?

How many kinds of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) are there? How many kinds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are there? And among these cosmic eggs, how many Indras are there, and who is capable of going [to them]? (2–3)
O Lord of the Gods, even if there were a number for the dust particles on the earth,
the wise know that there is nonetheless no such number for the Śakras.
The lifespan and the tenure of office of a Śakra last for seventy-one yugas.

When twenty-eight Śakras fall in a single day and night of Brahmā, the lifespan of that Brahmā is measured at exactly one hundred and eight years. What, then, is the number of these lords of the gods? There is no end to their number, nor even to that of Brahmā.

Wherein the number of cosmic eggs exists, and where indeed are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara? Within the pure water arising from the pores of Mahāviṣṇu’s skin, there is a boat made of artificial material, just as there is one within a cosmic egg. 7.
Thus, by the measure of a single hair, there exist innumerable cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
And within each cosmic egg, how many gods are there who are indeed equal to you?
In the meantime, Puruṣottama beheld [them] there.
And having observed in succession that swarm of ants extending for a hundred bow-lengths, the young brahmin laughed loudly;
yet he said nothing, remaining silent and profound like a sage accompanied by his attendants.
Seeing the laughter and hearing the verse of the Brahmin and the boy, Indra was greatly astonished.
With his throat, lips, and palate parched, he questioned the Brahmin once more.
Indra said:
"Why do you laugh at me, the best of Brahmins? Tell me the reason quickly.
Or who are you, disguised by your power of illusion (māyā) in the form of a child, though you are an ocean of virtues?
Having heard Indra's words, the young Brahmin spoke to him.
The essence of internal policy, the seed of knowledge, most excellent and supreme.
(13) The Brahmin said:
A swarm of ants was seen; the hidden cause of this [was revealed]. (14)
Do not ask me about that seed of sorrow which is the cause of your other ignorance—
the unsurpassed lamp of knowledge that cuts down the root of the tree of worldly existence for those caught in saṃsāra, and which dispels the darkness of nescience. (15)
"Hidden within all the Vedas, difficult even for the Siddhas to attain,
equal to life itself for yogins, and the shatterer of the deluded ego"—
having said this, that bull among the twice-born remained there with a smile.
Again Śakra, his throat, lips, and palate parched, questioned him.
Śakra said:
"Speak quickly, O brahmin boy, of the ancient lamp of knowledge."
"I do not know who you are, O child; you are a mass of knowledge incarnate.
Having heard Indra's words, Janārdana, in the form of a brahmin, began to speak of that knowledge which is very difficult even for the lords of yogis to attain. (18–19)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Śakra, each individual ant was created by me one after another;
through their own karma, O Śakra, they all became like Śakra in the abode of the gods."
Now, by means of their actions, all [beings] gradually attain the birth of various creatures in past times,
such as the ant species;
yet those who live by [righteous] action go to the stainless Vaikuṇṭha.
By action one reaches the world of Brahmā and by action the world of Śiva;
by one's own action one reaches heaven, the abode of heaven, and the netherworld (pātāla);
and by action one reaches the terrible hell, which is the sole cause of suffering for oneself.
By one's own action, [one enters] the womb of a sow; by action, the life of a lowly creature.
By action, [one becomes] the wife of cattle; by action, the female of birds.
And by one's own action, [one attains] the birth of an insect and the state of being a tree. (24–25)
By one's own action one becomes happy or miserable, a master or a servant;
by action one attains the status of a Brahmin, and even divinity through one's own action;
by one's own action one becomes a ghost, and the state of Brahmahood likewise through one's own action. (26)
Through karma one is afflicted by disease, and through karma alone one is exceedingly beautiful;
through karma one is deprived of limbs, and through karma one has redundant limbs.
By the thread of karma, the Ordainer is the giver of fruits to all living beings. (27–28)
Karma is accomplished through its own nature, and nature subsists upon habituation.
Thus has been declared all this supreme discourse on the inner self;
it bestows happiness, bestows merit, is the very essence, and is the means of crossing over the ocean of hell.
O Lord of the Gods, this entire cycle of existence, including all that is mobile and immobile, is like a dream. Death stands upon the head of everyone through the power of time;
and for all living beings, both the auspicious and the inauspicious are like bubbles upon the water.
"O Śakra, one who is not possessed by [ignorance] never wanders there; the wise man remains thus.
Having spoken these words, the brahmin stood there with a smile.
The Lord of the Thirty-three was struck with wonder, yet he did not hold himself in high esteem.
In the meantime, the lord of sages arrived swiftly—
he was a great yogi, exceedingly aged and eminent in both knowledge and years,
wearing a black antelope skin and matted locks, and bearing a radiant tilaka.
He bears a circle of hair upon his chest and a tuft on his head;
everything situated in the middle [of his body] is clearly somewhat uprooted.
Having arrived, he stood between the two like a pillar.
Seeing the Brahmin, Mahendra bowed down, filled with joy.
Having offered the *madhuparka* and other honors, he worshipped him with devotion.
He inquired after the welfare of the Brahmin and again showed him due humility. (36–37)

With joy and great respect, he honored him with the hospitality due to a guest. Together with that brahmin boy, he engaged in conversation and spoke of his supreme desire in its entirety, with humility. (38)
The boy said: "O Brahmin, from where have you come? Tell me, what is your name? What is the reason for your arrival here, and for what purpose do you dwell here? (39)
"How is it that there is a mat upon your head and a circle of hair upon your chest?
O Sage, why is the middle part of your body so exceedingly high and slightly uprooted?
O Brahmin, if you have compassion for me, please explain everything after removing [your disguise]."
"All this is most wonderful; I have a great curiosity to hear it. Having heard the words of the child, the great sage joyfully related his entire history before Śakra.
The sage said: "O Brahmin, because my life is short, I have not built a home anywhere; nor have I married. Now, I subsist on alms. (43)

"Lomaśa" is my name, and the reason for it is the sight of a brahmin. Listen now to the cause for the circle of hair on my chest and the tuft of hair on my head, which serves to alleviate the heat of the sun. (44)
It brings fear to those caught in worldly existence and generates supreme discernment.
(45) O Brahmin, for every single fall of Indra, there is the plucking out of one hair from the circle of hair upon my chest; this is the measure of the duration of my life. (46)
The hairs produced by him stand upright in the middle.
My death has been ordained for Brahmā at the end of two *parārdhas*.
O Brahmin, there are innumerable ways of dying, and even those who have died will die again.
What need is there for a wife, a son, or a home?
Even the blink of an eye of Hari occurs at the falling away of Brahmā;
therefore, I meditate incessantly upon His incomparable lotus feet.
Service to Śrī Hari is difficult to attain; devotion is more exalted than liberation.
All lordly power is like a dream and is an obstacle to that devotion.
This supreme knowledge was bestowed upon me by my guru, Śambhu.
"Without devotion, I do not accept the fourfold [liberation] beginning with *sālokya*.
Having spoken thus, that sage went into the presence of Śiva;
and Hari, in the form of a child, vanished right there.

Indra, having seen it as if in a dream, was struck with wonder there. He realized that even in the case of supreme sovereignty, there is only thirst for wealth, and no actual fulfillment. Then Śatakratu, having summoned Viśvakarman, spoke kindly to him.

Having given jewels and honored him, he sent him home. Having entrusted everything to his son, the discerning man, desiring liberation from decay, prepared to go for refuge, abandoning Śacī and the splendor of the kingdom. (54–55)
Seeing her beloved husband, the discerning one, with a grieving heart,
Śacī, afflicted by sorrow and trembling with fear, went for refuge to her teacher.
Having made a full report of everything, she brought Bṛhaspati there.
That lovely woman awakened Śakra by means of the essence of political ethics (nītisāra);
having herself joyfully composed a specific treatise of the Guru, imbued with the flavor of the joys of a married couple, she taught it to him with delight. (57–58)
The sage, the lord of speech, instructed him in the specific scriptures.
He then ruled the kingdom in Vṛndāvana, which delights the mind.
Thus has been told everything regarding the removal of Indra's pride.
O Goddess of the gods, the shattering of [Brahmā’s] pride was witnessed directly at Nanda’s sacrifice.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled “The Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā,” within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa. 47.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"You have related to me the breaking of the pride of Lord Hari, which I have heard.
Now I wish to hear, according to the truth, about the breaking of the pride of the Sun as well. (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Once, after the sun had risen, it went to its setting.
Then the two lords of the Daityas, Mālī and Sumālī, prepared themselves to emit radiance. 2.
Intoxicated by the great pride born of their perfection and by the boon of Śaṅkara,
O beautiful one, the sun became enraged that the night would not end because of their radiance,
and he struck them effortlessly with his own trident.
Struck by the sun-weapon, they both fell unconscious upon the surface of the earth.
(4) Then Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, perceiving the distress of his devotees, arrived and restored them to life through his great wisdom. (5)
Having bowed with devotion to Śiva, the two of them went to their own abode.
And Mahādeva, blazing with rage, rushed forth to slay the Sun.
Seeing Hara, the agent of destruction, desiring to kill him, Ravi—
Fleeing in fear, he went to Brahmā for refuge. And Mahādeva, the end-maker of Time and the ordainer of the Ordainer, rushed in wrath toward Brahmā’s abode, raising his trident exceedingly high.
Seeing Hara enraged, Brahmā, the lord of the worlds, praised the Supreme Lord with four faces using a hymn declared in the Vedas. (9) Brahmā said:
Be gracious, O slayer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; the sun has come to me for refuge.
O Teacher of the World, at the very commencement of creation, he was created by you alone.
O easily-pleased one, O illustrious one, be gracious, O you who are kind to your devotees!
And out of compassion, O ocean of mercy, protect me, protect me day and night!
(11) O Blessed One, whose nature is Brahman, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
having yourself created the sun, you now desire to destroy it yourself. (12)
Brahmā himself, Śeṣa himself, Dharma, Sūrya, and Hutāśana;
Indra, Candra, and the other gods—all are afraid of you, O Supreme beyond the supreme.
The ṛṣis and munis, whose wealth is their austerity, likewise serve you.
"You are the bestower of the fruits of austerities; you are austerity; you are the fruit of austerities.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā brought Sūrya with devotion and affectionately presented him to Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward the distressed.
Having bestowed that blessing upon him and bowed to the Creator, Śambhu, the ordainer of the universe,
with a gracious countenance, departed joyfully for his abode.
Thus, the man who recites this hymn composed by the Creator during times of distress—
The frightened one is liberated from fear; the bound one is released from bondage.
At the king’s gate, in the cremation ground, or when a ship has foundered in the great ocean—by the mere recollection of this hymn, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. (17–18)

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā," within the "Dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada" in the "Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa" of the glorious *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having bowed to Brahmā, Sūrya, filled with joy, [proceeded] by his command.
The radiant one, whose nature consists of the three qualities, affectionately established the code of conduct.
Now, listen attentively to the narrative of Agni—
this supreme nectar for the ears, which is to be kept secret within the Purāṇas.
Once, Agni prepared to reduce the three worlds to ashes;
making his terrifying flame a hundred palm trees in height,
he became agitated and enraged due to the cause of Bhṛgu’s curse.
Considering himself to be powerful and regarding another as insignificant compared to himself,
in that interval Viṣṇu arrived with effortless ease;
standing before him, he seized that burning power of the fire.
Assuming the form of a child through his illusory power (*māyā*), Janārdana spoke to him with a smile, acting with humility and with his neck bowed low in devotion. (6) The child said:
"Why are you angry, O Blessed One? Tell me the reason;
you are preparing to reduce the three worlds to ashes for no purpose.
You yourself were cursed by Bhṛgu; now bring about Bhṛgu’s subjugation."

You ought not to reduce the three worlds to ashes for the sake of a single offense. The universe was created by Brahmā, its protector is Hari himself, and the Lord Rudra is its destroyer; such indeed should be the sequence.
"Therefore, while Śaṅkara, the Lord, stands ready to reduce you to ashes,
defeat Hari, who is your protector, and carry out your destruction quickly!
Having spoken thus, the young Brahmin boy [cast] a reed-arrow that stood before him.
Taking the extremely dry wood in his hand, he joyfully gave it to him to burn.
Seeing the fire with its dry fuel, licking [the wood] and terrifying,
it enveloped the brahmin with its crest of flames, as a cloud covers the moon.
Seeing that neither the dry leaf nor even a single hair of the child had been burned,
Agni was filled with shame; standing motionless before the child,
he humbled his pride and vanished from sight.
Vahni, having withdrawn his own form, departed for his own abode like one who is terrified.
(14) The crushing of Vahni’s pride has been told; indeed, you desire to hear further—the ever-fresh narrative concerning the removal of the pride of the gods. (15)
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Lord, tell me in due order of the destruction of the pride of the remaining [demigods].
At the end of this stream of nectar-like stories, who on earth would not be satiated? (16)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Rādhikā, the Lord, the Master, smiled and began to relate the ancient and delightful narrative. 17.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Removal of Agni’s Arrogance," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O beloved, listen as I relate the humbling of Durvāsas’s pride.
Due to the yoga of the Great Sage and because he was a portion of Rudra possessed of supreme splendor,
once Āmbarīṣa, having performed the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata),
began the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) after having fed many twice-born brahmins.
In the meantime, a sage arrived there in person;
afflicted by hunger and thirst, he was entirely devoted to the vow of Viṣṇu.
He said to the king, "O illustrious one, feed me."
Out of devotion, the king gave him excellent food resembling nectar.
(4) Seeing the milk-rice mixed with hair, he prepared to curse the king;
cutting off a lock of hair from his head, he placed it upon the ground. (5)
Emerging from the midst of his matted locks, resembling a blazing crest of fire,
a man seven *tāla* trees in height and the destroyer at the end of the dissolution,
was intent on killing the king, the best of monarchs, out of anger. (6)
All were trembling with fear, their throats, lips, and palates parched.
(7) Greatly terrified, the king remembered my lotus feet;
by the mere act of remembrance, all obstacles were indeed pacified. (8)
In that interval, the Sudarśana discus, irresistible and equal to my own splendor, resembling the radiance of ten million suns,
suddenly appeared in the midst of the assembly, whirling about.
Having cut down the magical man (*kṛtyāpuruṣa*), he rushed toward that bull among sages.
Having caused the entire earth—including its mountains and oceans—to revolve as if it were a supreme golden ground, he again rushed toward that sage. (10–11)
As he was running with disheveled hair, terrified, cowardly, and distressed,
[the Lord], eclipsing the sun with his splendor and casting forth supreme radiance,
[reached] Kailāsa, the sevenfold group [of worlds], and the healthy realm of Brahmā.
Having wandered about, the best of brahmins went for refuge to Vaikuṇṭha.
He saw that preeminent brahmin falling at his lotus feet;
and out of compassion, that ocean of mercy granted the brahmin fearlessness.
By the very boon of Nārāyaṇa, the twice-born became free from fever;
having praised Hari once more, he returned to the king’s palace by his command.
Having approached the lord of sages, the king fed him with milk-rice (pāyasa).
He himself, together with his wife and kinsmen, performed the breaking of the fast.
Having offered blessings to the king and finished his meal, the brahmin returned to his home.
"The wheel has been set in motion by me for the protection of my devotees. (16–17)
All perish at the time of dissolution, but my devotee does not perish.
All the gods are my vital breaths, yet my devotees are dearer to me than my own life.
You are Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Sāvitrī, or Sarasvatī.

Brahmā, Śambhu, Ananta, Dharma, as well as the brāhmaṇas, the cowherd women, and the cowherds—all these are most dear to me. Yet, those who possess supreme devotion are dearer than them; there is nothing dearer to me than my devotees.
Having given the Sudarśana discus for the protection of my devotees, nevertheless, I have no confidence; O Goddess of the gods, I shall go there myself to see it,
for I have heard from you of Durvāsas’s humbling of pride.
"Command me, O illustrious one; what more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"O Teacher of the World, tell me of the shattering of Dhanvantari’s pride."
"This is a secret from the Purāṇas, yet I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having heard Rādhikā's words, Madhusūdana laughed."
He began to relate an ancient tale, delightful to hear.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Humbling of Durvāsas's Pride," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The Lord Dhanvantari himself, a great portion of Nārāyaṇa,
arose in ancient times from the great ocean during the churning of the sea.
He was proficient in all the Vedas and an expert in mantras and tantras.
For he was a disciple of Vainateya and a grand-disciple of Śaṅkara. O Goddess, having gone to Kailāsa with a thousand disciples, he saw on the path the terrifying Takṣaka licking his lips. || 2-3 ||

Seeing him thus approaching in a rage to devour [the snake], surrounded by *lakṣaṇa* serpents, resembling a trident, and overflowing with virulent poison, the deceitful disciple of Dhanvantari seized the formidable Takṣaka and laughed. (4)
Having caused it to yawn by means of a mantra, he rendered it free of poison.
He then seized the priceless jewel situated upon its head;
having whirled it with his hand, he cast it far away.
Takṣaka stood motionless on that path as if dead.
The attendants went to the presence of Vāsuki and reported this;
having heard it, Vāsuki blazed up with extreme anger.
He dispatched innumerable serpents of virulent poison,
as well as five eminent and skilled generals at the head of the serpent army:
Droṇa, Kālīya, Karkoṭaka, Puṇḍarīka, and Dhanañjaya.
All the *nāgas* assembled where Dhanvantari himself was present.
Upon seeing the countless *nāgas*, the groups of disciples were seized with fear;
by the wind from the *nāgas*' sighs, all the disciples became as if dead. (10)
Motionless and devoid of consciousness, they lay upon the surface of the earth.
Then the venerable Dhanvantari, remembering his preceptor, restored his disciples to life by raining down nectar and through the power of mantras.

Having caused his disciples to perform the ritual of intent (*cetanā*), the Teacher of the World rendered the swarm of snakes, fierce with poison, motionless by means of mantras. All of them became paralyzed; having been thus rendered inert, they were as if dead. (13)
O Goddess, no one among the Gaṇas was able to give any news from there.
Vāsuki, who is omniscient, perceived the entire crisis;
he summoned his sister Jagadgaurī, who is the embodiment of knowledge. (14–15)
Vāsuki said:
"O Manasā, come hither and protect the Nāgas from this extreme peril;
O illustrious one, you shall receive worship throughout the three worlds. (16)
Having heard the words of Vāsuki, the maiden, standing bowed with humility, laughed and spoke these words that were like nectar;
thus spoke Manasā.
"O Lord of Nagas, hear my words: I shall go forth to the battlefield.
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, I shall act as is appropriate, relying on destiny.
I will destroy that enemy upon the field of battle with ease."
Who is capable of protecting him whom I shall slay?
(19) Even if Brahmā and the other gods should arrive upon the field of battle, nevertheless I shall conquer your enemy; of this there is no doubt. (20)

My guru was the blessed Śeṣa, who bestowed upon me a perfected mantra of Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the worlds, which is most wonderful. I wear around my neck that supreme armor, the auspiciousness of the three worlds. (21)
Having reduced saṃsāra to ashes, I am capable of creating it anew.
In former times, I was a disciple of the blessed Lord Śambhu in the mantra-śāstras;
and out of compassion, the omnipresent Lord bestowed upon me great knowledge.
"I certainly do not count Garuda as a disciple of Śambhu;
nor do I count Dhanvantari, who is but one among his disciples. Having spoken thus, she departed alone in anger, abandoning the hosts of serpents.
Having bowed to Śrī Hari, Śambhu, and Śeṣa with a joyful heart,
that goddess, her eyes reddened with anger, arrived in wrath at the place where the divine Dhanvantari stood with a gracious face and gaze. (25–26)
By a mere glance, Sundarī restored them all to life;
with a poisonous gaze, she rendered the disciples of her enemy motionless.
The venerable Dhanvantari, however, was an expert in the science of mantras.
The Lord was unable to raise him up despite his efforts with mantras.
Seeing Dhanvantari, the Goddess, the Mistress of the Gods, quickly spoke with a smile; full of pride, she addressed him with many meaningful words. (28–29)
Manasovāca said:
"O Siddha, you know the meaning of mantras, the art of mantras, the breaking of mantras, and great medicinal herbs; tell me, for you are a disciple of Garuḍa. (30)
"Both I and Vainateya are the renowned disciples of Śambhu. Listen, Dhanvantari: for a very long time, during an auspicious kalpa, [I remained there].
Having said this, the Mother of the World brought forth a lotus from the lake.
Having charged it with mantras, he hurled it in his wrath.
Seeing the lotus flower approaching, resembling a blazing crest of fire, Dhanvantari reduced it to ashes with his breaths. (32–33)
And Dhanvantari, seeing that, laughed and with ease reduced it to ash using a handful of dust accompanied by mantras;
then the Goddess seized a spear (śakti) possessing a brilliance equal to the summer sun.
Having empowered it with mantras, he hurled that spear at the enemy.
Seeing that spear blazing intensely,
Dhanvantari himself effortlessly severed it with a trident given by Viṣṇu.
Seeing that power rendered futile, the Goddess blazed with rage.
She seized a terrible, unerring, and formidable serpent-noose,
which was joined by a hundred thousand serpents and consecrated with perfected mantras.
In his wrath, he hurled [the weapon] which possessed a luster like that of Time, the Destroyer;
and Dhanvantari, seeing the serpent-noose, smiled with joy and quickly called to mind Garuḍa, the lord of birds, who arrived at once. (38–39)
Seeing that the serpent-weapon had arrived, Garuḍa, whose vehicle is the horse,
quickly seized it with his beak and, being long hungry, devoured it.
Seeing the serpent-weapon rendered fruitless, she (the goddess) became exceedingly red-eyed with rage.
O beloved, he took up a handful of ash previously given by Śiva;
and seeing that handful of ash purified by mantras as it was being cast forth,
as if driven by the wind of his wings, he placed his disciple behind him and threw it.
Seeing the handful of ashes cast away, the Goddess became enraged;
she herself seized an infallible trident to slay Dhanvantari—that trident given by Śiva, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns. (43)
A spear of unfailing power, possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction, appeared among the worlds.
Then Brahmā and Śambhu likewise arrived at the field of battle for the protection of Dhanvantari and for the subduing of the bird.
Having seen Śambhu and Brahmā, the lord of the worlds,
Gaurī of the universe bowed with devotion to those two very ones;
so too did the wielder of the trident, Dhanvantari, and Garuḍa bow down to the lords of the gods.
He praised them with supreme devotion, and they both bestowed blessings upon him.
Brahmā, out of joy and desiring the welfare of the worlds, spoke sweet and beneficial words to Dhanvantari for the sake of honoring Manasā.
Brahmā said:
"O highly fortunate Dhanvantari, you who are proficient in all the scriptures, my mind does not find even a battle with you to be equal; indeed, in my opinion, there is no equality between us. (49)
"O Lord of the Gods, with this trident bestowed by Śiva, which is irresistible in every respect,
I am capable of reducing the three worlds to ashes.
Having performed meditation according to the Kauthuma branch with devotion and a concentrated mind," ||| 50 ||
Having offered the sixteen types of service, perform the worship of the Goddess.
You should offer praise with the hymn spoken by Āstika;
and being well-pleased in her mind, she will grant you a boon.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Śiva gave his consent; and Vainateya, with great affection, exhorted him with diligence. Having heard their words, he bathed, became pure, and adorned himself.
Having appointed the priest to perform the ritual, he prepared himself to offer worship.
Dhanvantari said:
"Come here, O Gaurī of the world; accept my worship."
O daughter of Kaśyapa, you were worthy of worship in the three worlds from of old.
O Goddess, having assumed the form of Viṣṇu, you have conquered the entire universe;
therefore, you did not employ your weapons upon the fields of battle.
Having spoken thus, he became self-restrained, his neck bowed in devotion;
taking a white flower, he prepared himself for meditation upon her who possesses the luster of a beautiful campaka flower and is enchanting in every limb. (57)
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, adorned with fine garments, graced by the beauty of her exquisite braided hair, and decorated with jeweled ornaments;
the Goddess who bestows fearlessness upon all and is ever-eager to show grace to her devotees. (58–59)

I worship the supreme Goddess Nāgeśvarī, who bestows all knowledge, who is peaceful, who is proficient in all sciences, and who is borne by the lord of serpents. Having meditated thus and offered a flower accompanied by various substances, [one should proceed].
Having offered the sixteen types of service, O beloved, he worshipped her;
with his body covered in horripilation, he composed a hymn with great effort,
joining his palms in reverence and bowing his neck in devotion.
Dhanvantari said:
Salutations to her whose very nature is perfection; salutations again and again to the bestower of perfection.
Salutations to the daughter of Kaśyapa; salutations again and again to the giver of boons. (63)

Salutations to the daughter of Śaṅkara; salutations again and again to Śaṅkarā. Salutations to you, O rider of serpents; salutations again and again to the sovereign of the Nāgas. Salutations, O mother of Āstīka, the mother of the worlds and of me.
Salutations to the cause of the universe, salutations to the wife of Jaratkāru.

Salutations to the sister of the Nāgas, and salutations again and again to the Yoginī. Salutations to the one who has long practiced austerities, salutations again and again to the bestower of happiness.

"Salutations to her whose form is asceticism; salutations again and again to the bestower of fruits. Salutations again and again to the one of virtuous character, the chaste woman, and the peaceful one.
Having spoken thus, he bowed down with devotion and great effort.
The goddess, being pleased, granted the boon and quickly departed for her own abode.
Brahmā, Rudra, and Vainateya returned to their respective dwellings,
and the blessed Dhanvantari also went to his own palace.
The nāgas, adorned with rows of hoods, departed full of joy.
Thus, I have related to you in its entirety this king of hymns;
and Āstīka, filled with devotion, performed the ritual for his mother according to the prescribed injunctions.
Then Jagadgaurī was pleased with that bull among sages, her son.
Whoever recites this highly meritorious hymn with devotion, for him and his lineage there is no fear of serpents; of this there is no doubt. (71–72)

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Victory of the Mind Intending to Break the Pride of Dhanvantari," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
You have heard the account of the breaking of the pride of all [the gods].
For both the small and the great, it has already been accomplished; of this there is no doubt. Now arise and go to the forest of Vṛndāvana.
O beautiful one, I shall soon behold the gopīs who are afflicted by the pain of separation.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words, the proud mistress of the connoisseurs spoke to Kṛṣṇa: "O Lord, take me with you; I am not able to go. 3.
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, Madhusūdana smiled and,
saying "Come, mount upon me," he vanished from sight.
Rādhā, who travels by mind alone, wept for a moment.
Having searched for her here and there, she went to the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Weeping and overwhelmed by grief, she entered a grove of sandalwood trees.
There she saw the gopīs, afflicted by sorrow and agitated by fear.
With copper-colored faces and eyes full of longing, they wandered through the entire forest, crying out "O Lord! O Lord! while fasting and filled with agitation;
seeing them, Rādhikā became distressed by the prospect of their love being severed.
She related the account of her wanderings in the Malaya mountains and so forth.
And together with them, Rādhā, distressed by separation, wept, crying out "O Lord!
O Lord! and lamenting again and again.
Having reviled Kṛṣṇa, she threatened him in anger for a moment;
then, in a fit of rage, they all prepared to cast off their bodies for a moment.
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa was there in that sandalwood grove.
He revealed himself to Rādhikā and the assembly of gopīs.
Seeing her lord, Rādhā, along with the cowherd women, was filled with joy;
smiling, she ran toward him, her body covered in horripilation.
Quickly embracing Kṛṣṇa, the proud woman angrily snatched away his flute;
having broken his garland and his yellow garment, she then put on the beautiful cloth and garland herself. (13)
Delighted by his flute of diversion, she who finds delight in Vṛndāvana anointed him with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron;
gazing repeatedly at his face, she kissed it with the utmost reverence. (14–15)
At one moment he threatened him, and at another he offered praise;
at another moment, with joy, he gave him betel-leaf and camphor.
Then all the cowherd women wept, overwhelmed with love.

They reported everything: their own suffering born of separation, the abandonment of their bodies, their bathing, the renunciation of their food, and their constant wandering day and night from forest to forest. (17–18)
For a moment they rebuked him, and for a moment they joyfully offered hymns of praise;
for a moment they gave him ornaments, and for a moment sandalwood paste.
Some said continuously, "Look upon this thief of our life-breaths and protect us! (19)
"Furthermore, you must never act in this manner," said some. Others said in their midst, "Bind him quickly with the heart-cord of love. (20–21)
Some said, "This man does not exist; there has never been any perception of him. Others said, "Look, look! With effort, behold this thief of consciousness!
Still others, out of anger, said, "This man is cruel, a slayer of men!"
Nor did she ever say to me, "O Nārada, do not speak of this," nor did she forbid it.
Out of curiosity, those gopīs would wander with Kṛṣṇa through whatever secluded and beautiful forests there were. (23–24)

Thus, having placed their Lord in their midst, all those cowherd girls went into the interior of the forest where the most beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala was located. Having gone to the Rāsa dance, that Lord of Rasikas sat upon a golden throne.
Just as the moon shines in the sky at night together with the hosts of stars,
so Janārdana, having assumed various forms here along with them,
again engaged in enchanting play with those amorous women.
Himself taking Rādhā by the hand, he, afflicted with love, ascended the pleasure-palace previously described,
which was constructed by Viśvakarman and rendered fragrant,
anointed with sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron. 28.
There, upon a bed of *campaka* flowers, he slept with her;
being an expert in the science of love, the lustful and curious man engaged in various kinds of amorous dalliance and play with his beloved.

O sage, their amorous dalliance there continued for a very long time; their delightful passion was so intense that there was no moment's pause between them. Thus Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa remained there, eager for the aesthetic rasa.
Those forms of Kṛṣṇa remained in amorous union with the gopīs.
Nārada said:
The wise know that one should first utter the name of Rādhā and afterwards that of Kṛṣṇa.
"O beloved of your devotees, tell me the cause for this devotion of mine.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen as I describe the threefold cause for this."
Prakṛti is the mother of the world, and Puruṣa is the father of the world.
(34) The mother of the three worlds is a hundred times more venerable than the father.
The names "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa" and "Gaurī-Īśa" have been heard by me from the Vedas. (35)
"Kṛṣṇa-Rādhā-Īśa-Gaurī"—such a name has never been heard in the world. Be gracious, O Moon of Rohiṇī; accept this *arghya* from me.
O Bhāskara, accept this *arghya* offered by me together with Saṃjñā.
"Be gracious, O Beloved of Kamalā; accept my worship.
(37) Thus it is seen in the Kauthuma Sāmaveda, O best of sages. Merely by the utterance of the word "Rā," Mādhava becomes expanded with joy. (38)
After pronouncing the word "dhā," one indeed runs away in agitation.
O Sage, if one first utters the *puruṣa* and afterwards utters the *prakṛti*,
he becomes a killer of his mother upon the transgression of the Vedas.
In the three worlds, Bhārata is blessed, a field of action that bestows merit;
even more so than that is the meritorious Vṛndāvana, [sanctified] by the dust of Rādhā’s lotus feet.
For sixty thousand years, Brahmā performed austerities there.
"For the sake of attaining the dust of the lotus feet of Rādhikā.

(41) Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāsa Dance of Rādhā and Mādhava," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said:
When the full dance had concluded, what did the Lord of the World do?
What secret occurred thereafter? You ought to tell us that.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having concluded the *rāsa* dance, and being accompanied by the Mistress of the *rāsa* (*rāseśvarī*) within that *rāsa*,
he himself, as the Lord of the *rāsa* (*rāseśvara*), then went to the sandy bank of the Yamunā. Having bathed there and drunk the pure water from the stainless waters, [he remained].
Together with the cowherd girls, he engaged in water-sports.
Then the Blessed One went to Bhāṇḍīra with Rādhā,
while the cowherd girls returned to their own homes, distressed by separation.
He sported in secret at Bhāṇḍīra in the Mālatī grove,
eager for dalliance upon a delightful bed of Mālatī flowers. Having finished his play there, he went to the Vāsantī forest.
There, in the most enchanting springtime, the Lord of the Rāsa danced;
having enjoyed himself right there, he went to the sandalwood forest, his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, taking hold of one who was likewise anointed with sandalwood. (6, 17)
On a delightful sandalwood couch, amidst tender sandalwood sprouts,
he sported with her when the full moon had risen.
Having enjoyed his pastime right there, he went to the campaka grove.
And the Sovereign Lady took her pleasure upon a delightful bed of *campaka* flowers.
Having finished her dalliance right there, the Lord went to the lotus grove,
to a most enchanting bed strewn with lotus petals.

There, together with Padmā, the foremost of women, he enjoyed pleasant pleasures with the cool lotus-breeze and fell asleep with her. Having abandoned sleep, the Lord of Sleep beheld his beloved lying fast asleep.
Seeing her lying upon a bed of lotuses, enjoying only the pleasure of rest,
her face moist with perspiration and surpassing the autumnal moon—
her vermilion completely faded and her thick kohl vanished; (12–13)
With the redness of her lips faded and the decorative leaf-patterns on her cheeks erased,
with the mass of her braided hair disheveled and her lotus-eyes closed,
she was adorned with a pair of priceless jeweled earrings. (14)
Mādhava,

who is affectionate toward his devotees, out of love performed the cleansing of her face with devotion, using a fine cloth purified by fire and adorned with pearls from the tusks of a lordly elephant. (15–16)
Having groomed her hair and fashioned it into a braid, Hari adorned her with a profusion of *mādhavī* and *mālatī* garlands;
she was beautiful-faced, captivating, and her braid was secured with a jeweled silk thread. (17)
She gave her a forehead mark of vermilion (sindūra-tilaka) that was exceedingly circular, beautifully adorned with kunda flowers, and bright with sandalwood paste below;
it was further graced on all sides by a drop of musk. || 18–19 ||
He applied decorative leaf-patterns, variegated and colorful, upon her two cheeks;
with devotion, he offered collyrium that made her lotus-eyes radiant. Out of deep affection for Rādhā, he also applied red dye to her lips.

And Vaikuṇṭha placed upon him a pair of ear-ornaments that were exceedingly pure, (21) as well as a necklace of priceless gems, radiant upon his pair of swelling breasts, and adorned with rows of jewels, which he placed around his neck. (22)
He clothed her in a divine, priceless garment, purified by fire and adorned with every kind of jewel; he perfumed that robe with musk and saffron,
and placed upon her two feet anklets resplendent with gems.
With devotion, he applied red lac to the nails of her toes;
he performed service for her who is worthy of service, she who is to be served by the virtuous of the three worlds.
Oh, how [she was honored] with a white chowrie through the intense devotion of her servant! 24–25.
The best among those who know all things, a knower of awakening and an expert in the science of love,
awakened the passionate woman and took her onto his chest;
out of love, he gave her an auspicious mirror made of fine gems.
And for the sake of beholding her beautiful attire and to polish her moon-like face,

Hari placed upon the cheek of that woman endowed with good fortune a garland fashioned from various flowers— never-fading and sprinkled with sandalwood paste— as a token of his own auspicious favor. (27–28)
Then, with a heart full of love, the beloved applied fragrant sandalwood paste, smeared with musk and saffron, to all the limbs of his beloved.
Furthermore, he gave her a flower of the Pārijāta tree that had been presented in secret by Brahmā.
O Nārada, he gave that pure, divine, thousand-petaled, and radiant lotus—which had been given by Śiva in private—to Kabarī and Lalitā; he placed it upon their right hands. (30–31)
In private, Dharma gave her the supreme of jewels, the Kaustubha gem, for her great pleasure; he also gave her,
in that secluded place, wine contained in a jeweled vessel, which had been given by the Aśvins.

For her to drink, he gave that supreme beverage which causes the intoxication of desire. (33) For her great pleasure, he gave her flowers such as *mālatī*, *mādhavī*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, and *campaka*, placed in vessels of fine jewels. (34) He also gave her betel leaf, exceedingly rare and well-prepared with camphor and other ingredients.
Knowing the proper time, he caused his beloved to consume that which is most difficult for all in the worlds to obtain, fashioned by the Lord of Speech (Brahmā),
unsurpassed and priceless, and bestowed by Varuṇa in a secluded place. (35–36)
Out of curiosity, she clothed the naked woman with a garment that was exceedingly fine, incomparable, offered with devotion, and radiant;
it was adorned with pearls from the tusks of the lordly king of elephants, presented by the King of the Gods. (37)
He gave her a beautiful nose-ornament for her great pleasure. In the meantime, sixty well-established gopīs, headed by Suśīlā, who were the virtuous companions of Rādhā, arrived there.
With sixty-six crores of gopīs, their minds filled with joy,
they followed by the footprints of their beloved as he carried his dear one.
Some held sandalwood paste in their hands, while others were bearers of yak-tail whisks.
Some held musk in their hands, and some held garlands;
some held vermilion, and some held combs;
some held red lac-dye in their hands, and some held garments.
Some held mirrors in their hands, while others, the most excellent, bore vessels of flowers;
some held play-lotuses in their hands, and some held garlands;
some held wine in their hands, and some were carriers of ornaments.
Some held cymbals in their hands, while others carried mṛdaṅga drums;
some held instruments for producing notes, and some held vīṇās in their hands.
Passionate with the thirty-six musical modes, they assumed the forms of gopīs.
Having come from Goloka to Bhārata together with Rādhā,
some sang and others danced upon their arrival;
some performed service for Rādhā with white chowries.
Some joyfully massaged the feet of the Goddess,
O great sage, while another offered betel nut for her to chew.
Thus, filled with curiosity, he remained in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana.
Accompanied by the gopīs and resting upon the chest of Rādhā,
Mādhava set forth; for a moment he drank sweet wine with his beloved,
for a moment he chewed betel, and for a moment he joyfully fell asleep.
For a moment he indulged in amorous pastimes in a palace fashioned of jewels;
for a moment he engaged in water-sports in the waters of the Yamunā.
Thus, O child, has the Rāsa-dance of Hari been described—how wonderful!
Of the Self who consists of His own will, who is most perfectly full,
who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), who is independent, the supreme Lord of primordial nature (prakṛti),
and the transcendent Lord of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest. (52)
The secret of Kṛṣṇa’s birth and His desired childhood sports have been told; the deeds of His youth have also been described. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Rāsa Dance," in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Nārada said: O best of sages, what further secret occurred after this? How did the Blessed One go from Nanda’s house to Mathurā? (1)
How could Nanda maintain his life-breaths after the separation from Hari?
Or how could Yaśodā and the cowherd women, whose minds were entirely fixed on Kṛṣṇa? Indeed, Rādhā does not live even for the duration of a single blink of an eye.
How did that queen sustain her life-breaths without the Lord of her life?
(3) And how did those cowherds who were attached to him forget such a kinsman in Vraja, regardless of their beds, seats, or enjoyments? (4)
"Having gone to Mathurā, what various deeds did Śrī Kṛṣṇa perform?
You ought to describe them, up until his ascension to heaven.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Kaṃsa performed a sacrifice, and having been invited to the bow-sacrifice,
the Blessed One went there at the invitation of that king. The king then dispatched Akrūra, who was dear to the Blessed One.
Urged by the king, Akrūra went to Nanda’s abode and,
taking Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with his companions, departed for Mathurā.
O sage, having reached glorious Mathurā, Kṛṣṇa slew the king.
He slew the washerman, Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, and the elephant;
he, the kinsman of his kin, brought about the deliverance of his parents and his relatives.
Having engaged in amorous play with Kubjā out of curiosity, [he performed these deeds].
And the Lord of the Gopīs sent him to Goloka;
out of compassion, Viṣṇu brought about the liberation of the garland-maker,
and through His grace, He enlightened the Gopīs by means of Uddhava.
Then, having been brought there, the Blessed One went to the city of Avantī;
there he undertook the acquisition of knowledge from his preceptor, the sage Sāndīpani.
Then, having conquered Jarāsaṃdha and slain the lord of the Yavanas, [he returned].
And he installed Ugrasena as king according to the prescribed rites.
Having gone to the vicinity of the ocean and constructed the city of Dvārakā,
he defeated a multitude of kings and carried off the queen Rukmiṇī.
Having slain King Naraka in a fierce battle, he performed the marriage rites with Kālindī, Lakṣmaṇā, Śaibyā, Satyā, the virtuous Jāmbavatī, Mitravindā, and Nāgnajitī. (15)
He established a pleasure grove for his sixteen thousand wives;
he sportingly defeated Śakra and carried off the Pārijāta tree;
and having conquered the moon-crested Lord Śiva, he severed the hands from Bāṇa.

Having secured the liberation of his grandson and returned again to Dvārakā, he revealed himself to the people in every house. And while Vasudeva was engaged in yoga during the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), [he appeared].
And there he beheld Rādhikā, the goddess presiding over the vital breath (prāṇa).
When a full hundred years had passed and Sudāmā was released from his curse,
he went once again with her to the holy forest of Vṛndāvana.
Furthermore, for fourteen years,
the Lord of the World performed the *rāsa* dance with her in the holy land of Bhārata at the *rāsa* festival;
and having returned to the house of Nanda, He remained there for a full eleven years.
In Mathurā and Dvārakā,
the omnipresent Lord of vast prowess performed the removal of the earth's burden for a full hundred years,
O Sage; thus, at twenty-five years of age, he had completed more than a hundred years [of his earthly manifestation].
Remaining on earth, the Ancient One departed for Goloka;
he granted to Yaśodā, Nanda, and the wise Vṛṣabhānu,
as well as to Rādhā’s mother Kalāvatī, liberation through proximity to him.
Out of curiosity, Rādhikā and the gopīs [acted] together with Kṛṣṇa;
yet, in every age, they have firmly bound the bridge of dharma as declared in the Vedas.
Thus, O great sage, everything has been told to you in brief.
The delightful life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa bestows the fruits of the four aims of human existence.
Everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is indeed perishable.
Therefore, joyfully worship that Supreme Bliss, the delighter of Nanda.
The Supreme Brahman, the Paramātman, the Lord, who consists of His own will;
the supreme, immutable, unmanifest one, whose form is for the grace of His devotees;
who is truth, eternal, independent, the Lord of all, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). (28–29)
"Devoid of qualities, devoid of effort, formless, and stainless.

(30) Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā," within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada in the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa. May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The first half is complete.
May it be auspicious!
