Oṃ tat sad brahmaṇe namaḥ.
The Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa composed by the illustrious sage Dvaipāyana.
Now begins the latter half of the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa. Om, salutations to that Brahman which is Tat-Sat.
The Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa composed by the venerable sage Dvaipāyana.
Now begins the latter half of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
He alone is the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person and the Self of all;
he is difficult to propitiate yet easily accomplished, the one to be worshipped by all, and the bestower of happiness.
He is exceedingly easy to attain for His own devotee, yet truly unattainable by the non-devotee;
He is eternally visible to His own devotee, yet invisible to the non-devotee.
His conduct, His actions, and even His very heart are difficult to comprehend.
All are bound by his māyā and deluded by that which is difficult to overcome.
Out of fear of him this wind blows; the supportless tortoise supports itself [in space], and out of fear of him the tortoise constantly supports Ananta.
O Nārada, Śeṣa supports the entire universe out of fear of whom;
and from but a single portion of the head of that thousand-headed Puruṣa,
the earth— consisting of seven continents and joined with the seven oceans— is sustained.
Together with mountains and forests, there are exactly seven netherworlds (pātālas),
as well as the various seven heavens including the world of Brahmā.
Thus, the triple-world universe is proclaimed to be artificial.
Out of fear of whom the Creator fashioned the various creations,
and likewise the great Virāj with its countless pores of the skin;
out of fear of whom he ordains all things, upon whose food he subsists, and whom he indeed meditates upon.
Viṣṇu, the ocean of compassion, protects the world out of fear of him;
Kālāgnirudra, terrified of him, [causes] Time to withdraw all creatures;
and Mahādeva, the conqueror of death, meditates upon him out of fear of him.
Though possessing the six qualities and the [eight] attachments, he is always dispassionate and detached.
Out of fear of him the fire burns; out of fear of him the sun shines;
out of fear of him Indra sends down rain, and Death moves among living beings.
Out of fear of whom Yama, the punisher, and Dharma himself hold even the sinner in check;
out of fear of whom the earth supports the worlds of moving and unmoving beings;
and out of fear of whom Prakṛti brings forth the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest in the act of creation. (12–13)
"O son, who indeed knows his intention, which is so difficult to comprehend?
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara do not know his power.
How then can I, my child, of very dull intellect, know his conduct?"

How did he go to Mathurā, abandoning the forest of Vṛndāvana? How did the son of Nanda abandon the gopīs, his beloved Rādhā who was dearer to him than life, as well as Yaśodā, his kinsmen, and Nanda? || 15–16 ||
He is the destroyer of pride and the bestower of pride; he is the eternal giver of everything to all.
Yet, due to the cause of Sudāmā’s curse, he broke the pride of Rādhā.
For others, the attainment of Brahman occurs through the power of their own contemplation.
Thus the lotus-born Brahmā engaged in some reflection.
Long ago, the all-pervading Lord Mahāviṣṇu brought about the shattering of the pride of Brahmā, as well as that of Viṣṇu, Śeṣa, and Śiva.
And [he saw] Dharma, Yama, Sāmba, the Moon and the Sun,
Garuḍa, Agni, and likewise his guru Durvāsas;
as well as the gatekeeper Bhakta, Jaya, and Vijaya.
Of the gods and the asuras, of you and Kāma and Śakra;
likewise of Lakṣmaṇa, Arjuna, Bāṇa, and Bhṛgu;
of Sumeru, the oceans, Vāyu, and Varuṇa.
And of Sarasvatī, Durgā, Padmā, and Bhū; likewise of Sāvitrī, Gaṅgā, and Manasā;
and of the goddesses presiding over the vital breaths, who are dearer even than life itself. (23)
What need is there to mention others, when even Rādhā, who is dearer to him than his own life, [is surpassed]?
He humbled the pride of all and bestowed grace upon them;
he is the creator, the destroyer, the protector, and the sustainer of the Creator himself in every respect. (24–25)
Even Śaṅkara, with his five faces, is not able to praise him;
nor is Vidhātā, the creator of the worlds, with his four faces, able to praise him.
Oh, even Ananta, with his thousand mouths, is not able to praise him! (26)
Even Viṣṇu himself, the all-pervading Janārdana, is not able to praise him;
nor even Mahāvirāṭ is capable of praising that Supreme Lord,
before whom Prakṛti trembles in the presence of that Supreme Self.
Sarasvatī has become tongue-tied to praise that Supreme Lord,
whose majesty even the Vedas do not know, O Nārada.
Thus, O Brāhmaṇa, has the power of the Supreme Self been described.
"And what more do you wish to hear regarding the attributeless Kṛṣṇa?

(30) Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled 'The Description of the Power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,' in the latter half of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and [Brahmā].
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter.
Nārada said:
O Brāhmaṇa, what unprecedented, secret, and most wonderful thing have you heard— the blessed account of the infinite deeds of the infinite Acyuta?
How did that Kṛṣṇa bring about the destruction of the pride of Mahāviṣṇu, or how did he do so for others? Oh, you ought to tell me that!
Indeed, the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is exceedingly sweet to hear.
Then, from the mouth of the poet, there emerged a poem exceedingly sweet and beautiful.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"And the ego of Mahāviṣṇu arose suddenly."
"I am the Lord, and all the various worlds are indeed within my every pore.
(4) Having become Saṃhārabhairavī, she swallowed him effortlessly;
and when he remained with only his head left, she bestowed her grace upon him. (5)
Being meditated upon with his whole being and praised, that treasury of compassion restored that body, which had been terrified, to its former state of perfect health.
O Brahmin, pride then suddenly arose in Brahmā, thinking, "I am the Creator."
"I am the sustainer of the three worlds; I am the creator, I am the Lord himself.
(7) "There is no one superior to me who is worshipped, nor anyone superior to me who has conquered his senses.
Having formed such thoughts in his mind, he indeed became filled with great pride. (8)
At that very moment, he showed him that assembly of Brahmas dwelling near himself in Goloka before the Lord—
some with four faces, some with five, some with six, and even more than that. (9)
He saw that [the universe] had a hundred mouths, each containing a multitude of cosmic eggs,
and that it was desiring to abandon its own body out of playfulness, with its neck bowed in shame.
Then the ocean of mercy, out of compassion, bestowed his grace upon him once again.
In due course, through Mohinī, he rendered him unworthy of worship;
having shown him his own daughter, he indeed made him full of desire, and then,
through Śiva, he brought about the shattering of that pride.
Out of shame, he abandoned his body and assumed another;
then the Lord of Brahmā again made that Brahmā worthy of worship.
The eternally blissful one of great wisdom bestowed knowledge upon him.
Viṣṇu conceived the pride [of thinking], "I am the Lord, the protector of the world.
When he had thus forgotten his true self, Kṛṣṇa brought it to an end at the birth of Rāma.
Śeṣa likewise became arrogant, thinking, "I support the entire universe. (14–15)
He caused that pride to be ground to dust by means of Garuḍa.
Once, O Sage, Garuḍa— the vehicle of Kṛṣṇa— was worshipped by the Nāgas,
but he was not worshipped by Śeṣa due to his own arrogance in the past.
Out of anger, Garuḍa conquered that high-minded Ananta;
however, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, brought about his liberation.
And Śiva himself, due to his own pride, did not perform the marriage ceremony.
Having done that, he caused delusion through his illusory power (māyā) by means of a woman;
then he again carried off his wife, the highly virtuous daughter of Dakṣa.
For a year, Śaṅkara held her body in his lap and grieved for it.
He wandered through various places, weeping again and again out of grief.
Having joyfully regained that same Satī, Pārvatī, in another birth,
Śiva— having been cursed by Dakṣa— forgot his own spiritual knowledge once more.
Furthermore, he quickly reminded him through the son of Aṅgiras:
"In ancient times, Śambhu, accompanied by his chariot, was impelled against Tripura;
having slain the Daitya through Śiva, he made him the enemy of Tripura. (22)

Śambhu, the ocean of compassion, being himself the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), made a promise to grant every boon to everyone. Then the demon Vṛka, having performed his ritual observances, chose a boon from the Lord.
"If I place my hand upon your head, you shall be reduced to ashes in an instant.
The Lord of the worlds said, "Your desire shall be fulfilled.
Having thus obtained this boon from Rudra, [the sage] followed the omnipresent Śaṅkara as he departed.
He rushed forward in haste to place his hand upon [Śiva’s] head;
but Śambhu, being utterly terrified, went for refuge to Hari.
And the Blessed One, for the sake of Śiva, reduced the Daitya to ashes.
In ancient times, during a battle with arrows, the Lord rendered Śiva— who was engaged in combat—
motionless by playfully employing the *jṛmbhaṇa* (yawning) weapon.
[Likewise,] he [confronted] Śambhu who had arrived at Dakṣa’s sacrifice through deceitful play.
The Blessed One restrained him by placing his hand upon his throat.
Cursed through the mediation of Kedārakanyā, Dharma, though a supreme deity,
became exceedingly emaciated and terrified, like the moon on the new-moon night.

Then, at the end of her curse, that truth indeed became full. It became three-quarters during the Tretā age, two-quarters during the Dvāpara, and one-quarter during the Kali age; furthermore, at the end of the Kali age, it undergoes destruction once more.
At that time, when the Satya Yuga began, he became full once again;
however, in accordance with the sequence of the yugas, he gradually underwent decline once more. (32–33)
Yama, due to the curse of Māṇḍava, entered a Śūdra womb;
then, at the end of a hundred years, he became pure once again.
Sāmba, due to the curse of his stepmother, became afflicted with oozing leprosy.
Then, having performed the Sūryavrata, he became pure once again.
And Candra, out of the intoxication of pride, carried off the wife of his preceptor;
his pride was shattered, and he became afflicted by consumption.
Out of pride in his splendor, Sūrya went swiftly toward the mountain to slay the servant of Śaṅkara, a Daitya named Sumālī,
who made the region of the Sun radiant day and night.
Terrified by the Sun, the Daitya sought refuge with Śaṅkara.
Upon seeing the Sun, Śaṅkara seized his trident;
and seeing the wielder of the trident, O Sage, the Sun fled in fear. (38–39)
In Kāśī, the wielder of the trident struck the Sun with his spear;
having fallen into a swoon from that spear, the king of Kāśī’s pride was shattered.
A dense darkness suddenly seized the surface of the earth.
The great god Āśutoṣa restored him to life at that very moment.
Though filled with shame and fear, Sūrya praised Śaṅkara;
and having bestowed his blessing upon him, the ocean of compassion, being pleased, departed for his own abode.
In ancient times, the Lord effortlessly shattered the pride of Garuḍa,
as well as that of Śiva’s bull, even though it was impelled by [Śiva’s] breaths.
Furthermore, in the past, he placed Śiva upon his back as he was approaching Vaikuṇṭha.
Having arrived with devotion to behold the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa—
[he who had become] Vahni (Fire), who became a consumer of all things due to the curse of Bhṛgu,
and Darpa (Pride), who was reduced to ashes because of his teacher’s wife Hiraṇā— [the Lord spoke]. (44–45)
Indeed, the pride of Durvāsas was humbled by Ambarīṣa through Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus, which is difficult to withstand.
He likewise brought about the subduing of the pride of both Jaya and Vijaya.
And just as Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Nṛsiṃha even though he had fallen from Vaikuṇṭha under the pretext of a Brahmin’s curse,
so too was Hiraṇyākṣa slain effortlessly by the Boar in the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa were slain by the arrows of Rāma at the request of Brahmā in another birth; likewise,
Śiśupāla was indeed slain effortlessly by the arrow of Kṛṣṇa.
And Dantavakra, in this very completed birth,
suddenly brought about the shattering of the pride of the gods through the agency of the Daityas,
and [the shattering] of the Asuras through the agency of the gods, by means of their mutual hostility.
Through the agency of the ritual, he brought about the shattering of your pride;
for in former times you were Nārada, the son of Prajāpati,
who subsequently became a Gandharva and then, in due course, the son of a Śūdra woman by virtue of his father’s curse.
Then, once again, by the grace of the Lord, Nārada now became filled with the pride of desire,
thinking, "The universe is to be accomplished by me.
He reduced that negligent one to ashes through Hara.
Once again, having shown him favor, he restored him to life with ease;
for that devotee was his exclusive follower, and thus he did not employ the weapon [against him].
He also brought about the shattering of the pride of the arrogant Lakṣmaṇa.
O Nārada, having been struck in battle by the trident of Śaṅkara hurled by Rāvaṇa,
he was restored to life again by means of a hymn of praise to Rāma;
for he himself had forgotten Viṣṇu due to the curse of Brahmā.
In ancient times, with his unerring axe as a weapon, he brought about the humiliation of Kārtavīryārjuna and the son of Jamadagni;
and [he acted] upon the death of a brahmin’s son and the abduction of the two Kṛṣṇas’ wives.
In battle, together with Karṇa, he shattered the pride of Pārtha;
and at the abduction of Bāṇa’s daughter, the Lord cut off his arms;
and at Bhṛgu’s sacrifice, during Dakṣa’s ritual, he brought about the destruction of [Dakṣa’s] pride.
In ancient times, while Parśurāma and Rāma were traveling on the road,
the Lord shattered their pride in battle through [the agency of] Rāma;
and he caused the peak of Mount Sumeru to become a bee through [the agency of] Vāyu.
He brought about the shattering of the pride of the oceans by consuming them through Agastya;
and in the past, when his son had died due to the premature destruction of creation,
he shattered the pride of the wrathful Vāyu as well.
During the expedition for the abduction of Uṣā and Hari’s arrival at Dvārakā,
he cursed Bāṇa and Varuṇa on account of the cows;
and in a quarrel with Gaṅgā, he spoke harsh words in the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
He abandoned Sarasvatī and shattered her pride;
having abandoned the haughty Durgā on Himālaya, the omnipresent Lord Śambhu reduced Kāma to ashes and departed for ascetic penance.
That goddess felt shame, and he shattered her pride;
she went to perform penance for the sake of attaining Viṣṇu and Śiva.
Having performed penance for a very long time in Bhārata, by the grace of Viṣṇu, that goddess—
She made Śambhu her eternal Lord, the Blessed One.
Endowed with great good fortune, she became the beloved of Śaṅkara;
among all the goddesses in the universe, she was worthy of worship, salutation, and praise by the gods.
O great sage, that Mahālakṣmī became possessed of pride;
in former times, the goddess had been defeated by Jaya and Vijaya.
Yet, as she was entering the door of the Lord, she granted the desired object to her devotee.
She was indeed barred from the door by that gatekeeper;
then that high-born lady, possessed of great self-respect,
remembering the lotus feet of Hari, prepared to cast off her body in response to the insult she had suffered.
Then Brahmā, Maheśa, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Bhāskara,
Candra, Kāmadeva, Vaiśvānara, Dhaneśvara,
the Ṛṣis, the Munis, and the Manus who destroy obstacles [were present].
In former times, Mahendra, Varuṇa, Jagatprāṇa,
and Hutāśana approached Rudanta before Padmā and praised Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti.
The gods said:
"Forgive us, O Blessed Mother, O you whose nature is forgiveness, O Supreme One beyond the supreme, whose form is pure being, and who are entirely free from anger and other such passions. (76)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, you are the peerless ideal among all virtuous goddesses;
without you, the entire world is as if dead and devoid of purpose.
You are the embodiment of all prosperity, possessing every form for all beings.
You are the presiding goddess of the Rāsa dance, and all women are but portions of you.
On Kailāsa you are Pārvatī, and in the Ocean of Milk you are the Daughter of the Sea. In heaven you are the Fortune of Heaven, and on earth you are the Fortune of Mortals.
In Vaikuṇṭha you are Mahālakṣmī, the goddess of the gods; Sarasvatī;
Gaṅgā; and Tulasī. And in the forest of Vṛndāvana, you are Vṛndā. You are Rādhikā herself, the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath in Goloka.
In every *rāsa* you are the Mistress of the *rāsa*, and in the forest of Vṛndāvana you are Vṛndā.
You are the beloved of Kṛṣṇa at Bhāṇḍīra, and Candrā in the sandalwood grove.
At Virajā you are in the campaka forest, and at Śataśṛṅga you are Sundarī.
Padmāvatī was in the lotus grove, Mālatī in the jasmine grove, Kṛndadantī in the *kunda* grove, and Suśīlā in the *ketakī* grove.
You, O Goddess, are Kadambamālā even in the *kadamba* forest. (83)
"Royal fortune shall be in the royal palace, and domestic fortune in every house.
Having spoken thus, all the deities, sages,
and Manus wept with downcast faces, their throats, lips, and palates parched.
Thus, whoever rises early in the morning and recites this meritorious and auspicious hymn to Lakṣmī composed by all the gods, shall certainly obtain everything.
One without a wife obtains a modest and virtuous daughter as a wife.
A man without a son obtains a son who is virtuous, beautiful, charming, exceedingly sweet-spoken,
possessed of sons and grandsons, pure, of noble birth, tender, excellent,
and a devotee of Viṣṇu who lives for a long time. (87–88)
One endowed with supreme sovereignty, possessed of knowledge, and renowned shall regain it;
one fallen from his kingdom shall obtain a kingdom, and one fallen from prosperity shall obtain prosperity.
One whose kinsmen have been slain shall find kinsmen, and one who has lost his wealth shall obtain wealth.
One devoid of fame shall obtain fame, and one shall certainly attain a firm standing.
This hymn bestows all auspiciousness, destroys grief and torment, constantly produces joy and bliss, and grants dharma, liberation, and friends. (90–91)

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn to Lakṣmī," within the Description of the Lord’s Qualities, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, having heard the praise of the gods and having ceased her weeping, Satī, being well-pleased by their hymn of praise, spoke to them.
Mahālakṣmī said:
"I do not cast off this body now out of anger, nor out of world-weariness;
having reflected thus in my heart, O gods, let this be heard. (2)
In whom— who is peerless, great, equal toward all, devoid of qualities,
the self of all, and eternally blissful— there is equality between a blade of grass and a mountain;
and he who, by the mere play of a frown, is capable of creating a hundred thousand Lakṣmīs.
If there is equality between a servant and a woman, what purpose is served by serving him?
Now I am the principal wife of that man, yet I am treated with indifference by the gatekeeper;
I am not even desired by his servant’s servant, though he is fully occupied.
"O Mistress, I, being unfortunate, shall give up my life;
having made an offering into the fire, let it be well as it was before.
That woman who is unfortunate toward her husband is unfortunate in every respect. (6)
For her, there is no happiness in sleeping or eating; her life is in vain.
For her who has no love for her beloved, her birth is meaningless. Is it then in a son, wealth, beauty, prosperity, or even youth? (7–8)
She who has no devotion for her husband— who is beloved by all and supreme—
is impure, devoid of dharma, and excluded from all sacred rites.
For the husband is her kinsman, her refuge, her sustainer, her deity, and her very guru.
The master is superior to everything else, and there is no one superior to the master.

O gods, for foolish women, the father, mother, son, brother, and even a distressed man who can give this wealth, as well as the master who gives away all his possessions, are merely objects of attachment. (10–11)

For only a certain woman knows her husband—she who is a great virtuous wife, born of an excellent lineage, well-behaved, and a protector of the family. But she who is born of an inferior lineage, ill-behaved, and devoid of dharma [does not]. (12)
Corrupt in speech and corrupt in her womb, she reviles her husband out of anger.
(13) That woman who hates her husband—who is the highest of all and a guru equal to Viṣṇu—is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. (14)
Vows, fasting, charity, truth, merit, and long-standing austerity—
all these are reduced to ashes and rendered useless for a woman who is devoid of devotion to her husband.
Therefore, I shall not say anything harsh to my husband, my lord.
"Due to the faults of my servants, I shall certainly give up my life for the sake of my lord.
A great virtuous woman should not speak harshly to her husband even when he is at fault;
if she is unable to endure it, she may lawfully abandon her life. (16–17)
Service to the husband is the vow of women; service to the husband is the supreme austerity.
Service to the husband is the highest dharma; service to the husband is the worship of the gods.
Service to the husband is the highest truth, as well as the practice of charity and the visiting of sacred fords.
The Lord consists of all the gods; he is pure and consists of all the gods.
Janārdana is the husband whose form is composed of all merit.
She who always eats the remnants of her husband’s meal and drinks the water from his feet is a virtuous wife.
"The deities always desire the sight and the ritual touch of her;
therefore, all sacred fords purify even sinners from their evil.
Having spoken thus, the great virtuous woman wept again and again.
Brahmā, filled with fear and with his neck bowed in devotion, spoke.
Brahmā said:
"There will be no good fortune for either Jaya or Vijaya."
Those two fools were not cursed by you because you were afraid of offending your beloved.
O virtuous lady, if one who is most righteous had not forgiven an offender through patience, his total destruction would have been certain; do not delay, O Satī! (23–24)
If you are unable to curse him and not empowered to inflict punishment,
yet Dharma inflicts punishment upon a man who has committed an offense—
then forgive everything, O Māriṣa, and go to the presence of your beloved.

"And having appointed me, who am devoted to your master, to the work of plowing," (26) having spoken thus and placing her at the forefront, the Lord went quickly to Vaikuṇṭha along with the gods and the great sages to praise Vaikuṇṭha. (27)

Having gone there, the four-faced Brahmā, the preceptor of those who know the four Vedas, praised the protector of the world, whose seat is the lotus, with his four faces. Having heard the praise of Brahmā and seeing Lakṣmī standing before him, [he was pleased].
To her as she was weeping with a downcast face, the Lord of Kamalā spoke.
The Blessed One said: "I know everything; I am the omniscient one, the soul of all, and the protector of all."

I am the teacher of all and the primordial cause of all, born from the lotus. My equanimity extends toward my devotee, my wife, and my kinsman alike; yet, in particular, my devotee is even dearer to me than my own wife.
Your two sons, who are my devotees and gatekeepers, are formidable destroyers;
forgive me for my offense against them, for they are full of devotion.
One who is filled with devotion to me, even if powerful, does not fear the Daityas.
"Protected by my discus, he is intoxicated by the honey-wine of devotion.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds placed Lakṣmī upon his chest,
summoned Dvāraṇaka, and said this very thing to him as well.
"Do not fear, my child; remain at ease. What cause for fear is there while I am present? And who is the punisher of those devoted to me? Go, my child, to your own abode.
Having spoken thus, O great sage, the Blessed One ceased speaking there.
The gods departed for their own abodes after bowing down to the Lord of the Universe.
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, the gatekeeper,
his entire body bristling with horripilation and his neck bowed in devotion, spoke to him.
Jaya said:
"With my mind solely absorbed in meditation upon the lotus-feet of yours, O Lord, I fear neither the gods, nor Lakṣmī, nor even the hosts of great sages. (38)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of Lakṣmī through Dispassion," in the *Śrī-Brahma...* [Mahāpurāṇa], within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and [Kṛṣṇa].
Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Pṛthivī (the Earth) became arrogant, thinking, "I alone am the support of the serpents.
Her lord, Pṛthu, destroyed that pride of hers.
Sāvitrī also became arrogant, thinking, "I alone am the mother of the Vedas."
In due time, he caused the disappearance of her and her sons.
Gaṅgā became filled with pride, thinking, "I am the one who bestows liberation.
Then the Lord of the worlds took away that pride through the Jahnu-dvāra.
O Sage, in ancient times, through the gateway of Durgā, he carried away Kṛṣṇa with his mind full of pride;
when Kṛṣṇa had reached Virajā, he rebuked him out of anger as he was entering the cave of Rāsa,
which was being blocked by the gopīs.
And she was struck with canes by the gatekeepers out of pride.
(5) Rādhā was indeed cursed by her own devotee Sudāmā;
suddenly cast down by the Lord, she came from Goloka to the earth. (6)
O Nārada, Kṛṣṇa was born of Vṛṣabhānu’s wife Kalāvatī;
out of devotion to him and under the pretext of fear of Kaṃsa,
he came to the house of Nanda, and for that reason, I am called the Delighter of Nanda.

"The Lord of the World went again to Mathurā for the sake of fulfilling Sudāmā’s desire to break his curse," so said the Lotus-born One. "O Nārada, who indeed knows His other underlying intention? (8–9)
"How was he born when Mathurā and Gokula were united?
Thus everything has been told; hear the rest. [Thus spoke Nārada. "Hear how that delight of Nanda went to Mathurā from Nanda's home."
Nanda and Yaśodā fell into grief by the power of fate;
so too did the cowherds, the cowherd women, and the cows in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
In forest after forest, what wild creatures were there that did not know something of this? || 11-12 ||
O Sage, having abandoned even the delightful forest and its wild regions, that beautiful woman wandered from forest to forest, from cremation ground to non-cremation ground;
and for a moment, she wandered, losing her senses, having left the village behind.
Deprived [of him] in an instant, she prayed for him at every moment.
(14) Moment by moment she sighed, reflecting for a moment; for a moment she entered the bed, and for a moment she stood up and remained there. (15)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus has everything been told, which shatters the pride of all;
and the destruction of Indra’s pride has been related in detail, O son of Niśā,
as he fell from his excellent jeweled lion-throne in the assembly hall out of arrogance.

Seeing his own guru, Bṛhaspati, who was most devoted to Brahman, he did not rise. The guru, extremely enraged and intent on taking revenge for this insult, departed; nevertheless, out of compassion and affection for his duty, he did not curse him.
Without a curse, that ladle was indeed reduced to powder;
for even if another does not curse due to righteousness or out of affection, a great sin [is incurred],
yet O Nārada, righteousness bears fruit for him and destroys that [evil].
For when a righteous man, out of anger, curses one who is violent and guilty, [the following occurs]:
the destruction of the guilty one takes place, but the dharma of the righteous man is destroyed.
By that unrighteousness, Indra indeed incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Terrified, he abandoned his own kingdom and went to the lake;
there, upon the lotus stalks of the lake, he made his dwelling.
Unable to go to Viṣṇu’s Puṇya-sarovara, he remained there.
It is the most excellent place of penance for ascetics in Bharatavarṣa.
Those who know the ancient lore proclaim that very place to be the sacred site of Puṣkara.
Seeing Hari deprived of his kingdom, the king, a devotee of Hari, [acted].
The righteous one named Nahuṣa forcibly seized that kingdom upon seeing Śacī— of beautiful limbs, childless, and lovely—
as she was going toward the celestial Gaṅgā with a grieving heart.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with jewel ornaments,
very delicate, possessing beautiful teeth, and speaking as a great virtuous woman— to her,
King Indradyumna fell into a swoon through the power of desire and youth.
Standing before him, he spoke with great humility like a servant.
Nahuṣa said:
"The course of destiny is manifold and difficult to comprehend, even for the wise."
Such is the woman of one who is greedy for the female organ and lusting after another’s wife; such is the beauty of one whose mind is fixed upon the wives of others.
And in her presence, what is Rambhā, what is Urvaśī, and what is Tilottamā?
Or Menā, or Ghṛtācī, or Ratnamālā, or Kalāvatī;
Kālikā, Sundarī, Bhadrāvatī, and likewise Campāvatī—
these and other apsarases do not equal even a sixteenth part of her.
"Having abandoned this one, how can a fool, dull-witted as he is, go to another?
He who has been chosen by us and by her is certainly equal to a slave.
O lady of beautiful hips, accept me; be well-pleased with your servant."
Just as Rādhā shines upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa in Goloka;
as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī do upon the chest of Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha;
and just as Brahmāṇī does upon the chest of Brahmā in the world of Brahmā.
Just as the Great Virtuous One (Mahāsādhvī) resides upon the chest of Dharma,
or as Lakṣmī dwells upon the chest of Ananta in the depths of Pātāla;
just as Puṣṭi resides in Gaṇeśa, and Devasenā in Kārttikeya.
As Varuṇānī is to Varuṇa, as Svāhā is to the Consumer of Oblations (Agni),
as Rati is to Kāmadeva, as Saṃjñā is to the Maker of Day (the Sun),
as the wife of Vāyu is to Vāyu, and as Rohiṇī is to the Moon; || 21–22 ||
Just as Aditi was the mother of the gods and your mother-in-law to Kaśyapa, as Menā was the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs on Himālaya,
as Lopāmudrā was to Agastya, and as Tārā was to Bṛhaspati; || 23 ||
O beautiful one, just as Devahūti was to Kardama, Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha,
Śatarūpā to Manu, and Damayantī to Nala,
so may you, through your good fortune, abide upon my breast.
As a lord, I am capable of effortlessly felling thousands of Indras;
yet this woman desires a paramour who is more powerful than her own husband.
Even though Mount Sumeru is a formidable and secluded place, she seeks it out as a secret spot.
Or else, in the delightful Malaya mountain, fragrant with the breeze from the sandalwood trees; or in the Viśrambhaka forest, or in the beautiful Nandana grove;
or near Mount Śataśṛṅga, on the banks of the Puṣpabhadrā river.
In the waters on the banks of the Godāvarī, near a cool breeze;
on the delightful bank of the Campāvatī river, in a beautiful grove of campaka trees;
in a cremation ground, in a most terrifying cremation ground, and in a lovely, utterly secluded forest. (29)
On every mountain, in the most secluded caves, and in the forests;
on every island, in inaccessible fortresses, by every river and stream;
and on the delightful shores of the ocean, devoid of all living beings.
The union of a clever woman with a clever man in a secluded place is blissful—
upon a bed of flowers and sandalwood, anointed with flowers and sandalwood.
Taking me, who am likewise anointed with flowers and sandalwood, grant me delight.
"O Goddess, by the boons of Brahmā, O auspicious lady, make me your husband— one who is free from old age and death, eternally possessed of stable youth,
well-attired, handsome, steadfast, and proficient in the science of love. (33–34)

[He is] one whose face is like the full moon of autumn, born of the lunar dynasty, who abandoned Urvaśī when she arrived on earth, and who was entreated by her. "I have no desire for the wives of others; yet my mind has become greedy upon seeing you."
I have abandoned my own wives, who were adorned with jewel ornaments.
(36) Now, having protected all of them and made them my female slaves, O Vahānana, I shall give to you the necklace of the finest essence of jewels that belongs to Varuṇa. (37)
"O Goddess, having conquered Varuṇa in battle with the exceedingly powerful Brahmāstra,
and having defeated the utterly weak Vahni after winning a pair of garments purified by fire,
I shall give them to you this very day; command me, for I am at your service."
"O beautiful one, having conquered the gods, I shall give to the Mother of the Gods two earrings fashioned from the essence of the finest jewels,
as well as a pair of armlets made of exceedingly priceless gems."

"Today itself, having defeated Candra— who is afflicted by consumption, exceedingly emaciated, and my own ancestor from former times— I shall give him to Rohiṇī, who is otherwise so difficult to obtain;
or else, being afraid, he will grant him to me out of compassion without a fight."

"Having made a request of Maheśvara— who is easily pleased by praise, the lord of devotees, compassionate, and the fulfiller of desires— I shall today give to Pārvatī this pair of anklets fashioned from priceless jewels. (42-43)

O auspicious one, O beloved, having fought a most difficult battle with Gaṅgā today, I shall give you a pair of armlets fashioned from priceless jewels— supreme wish-fulfilling trees that bestow all prosperity.
O beautiful one, today I shall give you a charming pair of bracelets for the arms, lovely like the wife of the Sun, fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems;
and also a mirror, exceedingly pure, fashioned from priceless jewels. (45–46)
"O beautiful one, having conquered Kāma with ease, I shall grant you the desire of the wife of Kāma; and I shall give you the unfading play-lotus of Kamalā.
Having made a request and having praised the Lord of Kamalā, I shall bestow it upon you."

As the boy wept in great fear, the guru took him joyfully upon his chest.
Having performed for him the Soma sacrifice and the Pragamya rite for the sake of his heart's desire, [he bestowed the Veda].
The Guru seated him upon a beautiful jewel-encrusted lion-throne (51).
He bestowed upon him supreme sovereignty, four times greater than that of his predecessor.
And all the gods, having arrived, performed service for him with great joy (53).
"Thus has been told, O child, the shattering of Mahendra’s pride and the protection of Śacī’s virtue. What more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
O best of sages, tell me the procedure for the Soma sacrifice;
how did the Guru cause it to be performed, and what is its supreme fruit?
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, it pacifies the sin of killing a Brahmin and yields the fruit of a Soma sacrifice;
for one year the sacrificer drinks the Soma creeper,
and for one year he joyfully partakes of its fruit, and for one year he drinks water.
This vow lasts for three years and destroys all sins.
He who has stored enough grain for three years— or even more— for the sustenance of his dependents, is worthy to drink the Soma.
"O Sage, neither the great king nor Dēva is capable of performing this sacrifice;
for this sacrifice requires abundant food and vast sacrificial fees.
Thus [ends] the section on the Breaking of Indra’s Pride in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
The sixtieth chapter, titled "The Narration of Śakra’s Liberation.
Now begins the sixty-first chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus I have related to you a portion of the humbling of Indra’s pride;
hear now another secret account, O Brahmin, with full attention.
Long ago, having performed the churning of the ocean and having drunk the essence of nectar, [the gods]...
Having conquered the hosts of Daityas, he indeed became exceedingly arrogant.
Then Kṛṣṇa, through the agency of Bali, shattered the pride of Śakra.
Those gods, led by Indra, were deprived of their prosperity.
Then, by the power of Bṛhaspati’s hymn and Aditi’s vow,
the all-pervading Lord Vāmana was born of Aditi through a portion of His own essence.
Having made a request, that treasure-house of compassion, out of mercy, [bestowed] the kingdom upon Bali.
He bestowed that prosperity upon Mahendra and the gods as well. O Sage, in former times at the end of a kalpa, the powerful Duvasīpa again took away that glory of Indra through his power.
Out of compassion, the merciful one, who is affectionate toward his devotees, gave her back again;
yet once more, that illustrious Durmada carried off the beloved wife of Gautama.
Then, by the curse of Gautama, he became one whose limbs were shattered.
In former times, Indra suffered agony from the pain in his own body;
seeing him then, the sages and the Manus laughed aloud,
and all the gods were ashamed, for Bṛhaspati was like one who was dead.
Then, having performed penance for a thousand years in the presence of the Sun in former times,
that Śakra became the thousand-eyed one by virtue of a boon from the Sun.
That supreme collection of eyes of Indra took on the form of a dark spot.
And just as the moon acquired its spot from the abduction of Tāṇḍakā.
Nārada said:
"O Brahmin, by what means did he carry off the beloved wife of Gautama?"
And [tell me of] Mahāsatī Samahalyā, who is worthy of worship and the protector of the world;
[and of] the highly fortunate Śuddhāśā, who is stainless and a portion of Kamalā.
I desire to know this; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas. (12–13)
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, during a pilgrimage to Puṣkara on the occasion of a solar eclipse, Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, beheld Ahalyā who had arrived there.
Smiling beautifully, lovely to behold, peaceful, and with full, firm breasts—
Indra fell into a swoon at the mere sight of her at that very moment.
Then, on another day, having seen her on the bank of the Sandākinī river—
Seeing her alone, smiling, bathing naked yet bashful,
Hari beheld her hips and her exceedingly full pair of breasts;
afflicted by desire, he fell into a swoon and lost his consciousness once more.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, the lustful one went to her side and spoke with gentle words and humility to that devoted wife.
Mahendra said:
Oh, what virtues! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fresh youth!
Oh, how your facial splendor mocks the autumnal moon!
Oh, what a sidelong glance—crooked and yet captivating the hearts of men! (19)
Ah! What a gaze, which releases the splendor of a lotus!
(20) What a lovely gait, which puts to flight the *kañjana* birds!
Oh, what exceedingly sweet speech, more difficult to obtain than nectar! (21)
"Ah, what is this woman with such broad hips, the support of desire, so enchanting?
She grants every wish to the lustful and deludes the mind of even a sage.
Her thighs are exceedingly firm and full, rivaling the beauty of plantain trunks. (22)
Oh, how round is the pair of your hips, like the orb of the moon!
(23) Your pair of breasts is endowed with beauty, resembling a pair of *śrīphala* fruits;
they are exceedingly high, very firm, and enchanting to the minds of the three worlds. (24)
Aha! What austerity did Gautama, whose wealth is penance, perform, that by its very fruit he obtained this excellent, beautiful woman with lovely teeth?
Having served the eternal Durgā, the primordial Prakṛti, the illusory power of Viṣṇu.
And he obtained such a lotus-like Lakṣmī, who was like Lakṣmī herself—
extremely delicate, with a beautiful face, a woman with a lotus-like countenance, pure, with lovely teeth, youthful, and possessing the proportions of the middle of a banyan leaf.

I know that you are skilled in the science of love (*kāmaśāstra*) and capable of protecting [women]; yet, O Moon, does Gautama know either Kāma or a lover? Those experts in the science of love always praise me.
"Urvaśī and the other Apsarases praise me constantly.
O fair-faced one, having made Śacī your servant, I shall give her to you;
take the vast splendor of the three worlds and abandon Gautama. (29–30)
Unlearned in the science of love, weak, and ascetic; unfit for sexual union, free from desire, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa—
such was he whom the unskilled Creator joined with one to whom he was unsuited.
"Such a lovely and amorous woman as this he gives even to an ascetic.
Having spoken thus, Śakra, the lustful one, fell at her feet with clay.
To him, the great virtuous lady spoke what was appropriate and in accordance with the Vedic injunctions.
Ahalyā said:
"Due to the misfortune of Brahmā, and of the ascetic Marīci,
and due to the misfortune of Kaśyapa as well, you have been born as a son with a sinful mind."
Of what use is the muttering of prayers, asceticism, silence, or religious vows; of what avail is the worship of gods, pilgrimage sites, or sacred waters—to him whose mind has been stolen by women?
The form of woman was fashioned in creation to delude the minds of those possessed by desire.
Otherwise, creation would not have come into being; therefore, by his ancient command, he [created] everything:
the casket of illusion, the bolt upon the path of dharma for men, the obstacle to ascetic practices, and the supreme refuge of vices. (36–37)
For those bound by the fetters of karma, it is known as a harsh shackle;
it is like a lamp to moths and a hook to fish.
At its commencement, it is like milk on the surface and honey in taste, yet it is a swelling of poison.
In its transformation, it is the seed of suffering and the very staircase to hell. (39) The sages, Sanaka and the others, did not perform marriage even though they desired it;
for those whose minds are set upon the wives of others, everything is fruitless. (40)
"O Śakra, the pursuit of another's wife brings misfortune even in this world,
and in the next, it bestows a terrible hell upon the lustful man.
Having spoken thus, the great virtuous woman abandoned that lustful man.
The wife of Gautama quickly returned to her own home.
She related everything to the ascetic Gautama;
that sage stood there laughing and censuring Mahendra.
Once Gautama went quickly to the abode of Śaṅkara;
there, Śakra, in the form of Gautama, had sexual union with her.
Knowing everything, the Omniscient One arrived at the door of the temple.

The bull among sages saw Mahendra departing, and he beheld Ahalyā naked in private, her hips and breasts full. The sage cursed Śakra, saying, "May you have the mark of the female organ upon your body! (45–46)
In his anger, he cursed his weeping wife, who was overwhelmed by fear, saying:
"And you shall become a stone in the great forest.
Then Śakra, his mind solely intent on shame, departed for his own home.
Emaciated by grief and terrified, she spoke sweetly to her husband:
Ahalyā said:
"O righteous one, why do you abandon me and this faultless servant?"
"And you, the best among those who know the Vedas, deliberate according to dharma.
Gautama said:
"I know you to be pure of mind, observant of excellent vows, and devoted to your husband."
Nevertheless, I shall abandon you, even though you bear the prowess of another;
for a beloved woman who is enjoyed by another is impure in all ritual acts.
A great fool who would unite with her would dwell in hell for an entire kalpa.
Food is excrement and water is urine; it is certain that [the body] is for the enjoyment of others.
One who touches her destroys the merit previously acquired.
Even if she does so unintentionally, a woman is not defiled by a lover.
A wicked woman certainly becomes virtuous when it comes to the act of self-willed amorous play.
Having regarded Śakra as your husband and having enjoyed pleasure and delight in the home, you later attained knowledge upon seeing me; now listen! (53–54)
"Go, go to the great forest and become like a stone.
By the touch of Rāma’s toe, you shall be instantly purified.
Through that merit, you will attain me and return once again."
"Go, my beloved, to the great forest," he said, and departed for asceticism.
Thus has all this been told, O Sage, which shattered the pride of Mahendra; and by the grace of the Lord, she regained her fortune once again.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Kṛṣṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the sixty-second chapter.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, in what manner did Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
himself effect the liberation of Gautama’s wife, and in which age did it occur?
"O illustrious one, relate in brief the enchanting and bliss-bestowing incarnation of Rāma; I have a great curiosity to hear it. Nārāyaṇa said:
Requested by Brahmā, Viṣṇu himself was born from Daśaratha; the Blessed One appeared in Kausalyā during the Tretā age, endowed with clay [as an image],
and Bharata, equal to Rāma in virtue, was born from Kaikeyī.
And Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, an ocean of virtues, were born of Sumitrā.
Then, sent by Viśvāmitra, the illustrious Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa,
set out for the beautiful city of Mithilā for the purpose of obtaining Sītā.
Seeing a woman in the form of a stone on the path, Rāma,
the Lord of the World, questioned Viśvāmitra regarding the cause.
Having heard Rāma’s words, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic—
There, the most righteous one spoke the entire secret;
having heard that cause from his mouth, Rāma, the purifier of the world,
touched her with the tip of his toe, and she became a lotus-lake.
Having offered a blessing to Rāma, she departed for her husband’s palace;
having obtained his wife, Gautama gave him auspicious blessings.
And Rāma, having gone to Mithilā, [performed] the breaking of Śiva’s bow.
And he performed the marriage with Sītā, O Nārada.
Having celebrated the wedding and slain Bhṛgu’s pride, the lord of kings returned to the beautiful city of Ayodhyā amidst games, festivities, and auspicious rites.
The king, having shown due respect, desired to make his son the sovereign;
he quickly brought water from the seven sacred fords from the foremost of sages,
and performed the consecration (*adhivāsa*) of Śrī Rāma, who was endowed with every auspiciousness.
And having seen Bharata, Kaikeyī, overwhelmed with grief, requested from the king the boon she had previously agreed upon:
that Rāma go into exile in the forest and that Bharata receive the kingship. (13–14)
Deluded by love, the great king did not wish to grant the boon;
out of fear for righteousness and truth, the wise Rāma spoke to the king.
(15) Śrī Rāma said:
Whatever merit a man obtains by the gift of a hundred ponds,
he certainly obtains even more than that by the gift of a single step-well (vāpī).
Whatever merit a man obtains by the gift of ten step-wells—
And one obtains even greater merit than that from the gift of a daughter.
O lord of men, the merit that a man obtains by the gift of ten daughters, he obtains even more than that by means of a single sacrifice. (17–18)
Whatever merit a person who performs virtuous deeds gains from a hundred sacrifices,
he gains even more than that by the sight of his son’s face.
(19) A man gains whatever merit comes from seeing a hundred sons [by beholding him].
The virtuous man surely obtains that merit by speaking the truth.
Indeed, there is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, and no god superior to Keśava.
There is no kinsman superior to Dharma; there is no wealth superior to Dharma.
Who indeed is dearer than Dharma? Therefore, protect Dharma with effort.
My son, when one's own Dharma is protected, there is constant auspiciousness everywhere.
Bringing fame, a firm foundation, majesty, and supreme honor—
having abandoned the pleasures of home for fourteen years, I shall wander and dwell in the forest in accordance with dharma, for the sake of upholding your truth.
Having made a truthful oath, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he who does not fulfill it indeed reaches the end of his life as ashes;
he is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
"Then that man shall become mute and suffer from skin disease for seven births.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Rāma, having fashioned a *kalkala* garment and matted locks,
departed for the great forest together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
O Sage, out of grief for his son, the great king abandoned his own body;
and to protect his father’s truth, Rāma wandered through the forest.
After some time, in the great wilderness, [he encountered] the sister of Rāvaṇa.
Wandering in the terrible forest with her husband out of great curiosity,
that unchaste Rākṣasī, afflicted by passion, then beheld Rāma;
with all her limbs bristling with horripilation, she fell into a swoon from the god of love.
Approaching Śrī Rāma, she who was possessed of youthful beauty, exceedingly mature, and intoxicated by passion, spoke with a smile. Śūrpaṇakhā said:
31. Śūrpaṇakhā said:
"O Hiraṇyakeśa, O Dhanashyama, O Abode of Beauty, endowed with beautiful ears!
Accept me, a woman devoted to you through *māyā*, in this secluded place.
Having heard Shurpanakha’s words, the righteous one recalled his duty (*dharma*).
And Narada, fearing for the child, spoke these words to the charioteer.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O mother, go with your wife to my younger brother, who is without a wife."
"He would suffer if he were to resort to another beloved woman, or else he would find a dwelling of happiness.
Having heard Rāma’s words, he went joyfully to Lakṣmaṇa;
there he beheld Lakṣmaṇa, peaceful, handsome, and endowed with auspicious marks.
"O fortunate one, accept me! he said again and again.
Hearing those words, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to her out of curiosity.
Lakṣmaṇa said:
"O fool, having abandoned Rāma, the Lord of All, you desire a servant!
Sītā is my wife and a servant, and I myself am a servant of Sītā.
Become a co-wife to Sītā; go to Rāma, my master! (37)
"O virtuous one, I shall become your son, just as [I am] Sītā’s.
Hearing these words of Lakṣmaṇa, her mind carried away by passion,
the deluded woman— her throat parched and palate dry— spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
Śūrpaṇakhā said:
"O fool, if you reject me who have come to you of my own accord out of desire, there will be no doubt that ruin shall befall both of you. (40)
Brahmā, having abandoned Mohinī, became unworthy of worship by all; and Dakṣa, due to the curse of Rambhā, became one whose head was that of a goat.
And the physician of the gods (Dhanvantari), due to the curse of Urvaśī, was deprived of his share in the sacrifice.
O Lakṣmaṇa, Kubera was deprived of his beauty by the curse of Menā;
Kāma was reduced to ashes by Śiva due to the curse of Ghṛtācī;
and Bali indeed fell from his kingdom because of the curse of Madālasā.
By the curse of the mendicant woman Keśī, Bṛhaspati had his wife taken away;
likewise, by my curse, Rāma shall have his wife taken away.
[Though] she was in the prime of youth and overcome by passion, his wife approached him of her own accord.
One who fears unrighteousness should not abandon the sacred learning heard at the midday sacrifice;
having abandoned it here, one is swallowed by [the consequences] while drinking [the fruits of life], and in the next world, one goes to hell.
Having heard the words of Śūrpaṇakhā, Lakṣmaṇa [replied] with half a moon.
He effortlessly severed her nose with a razor-sharp blade.
Her powerful brother, Khara-dūṣaṇa, also fought;
accompanied by his army, he went to the abode of Yama by means of Lakṣmaṇa’s missile.
Seeing that fourteen thousand Rākṣasas, along with Khara and Dūṣaṇa,
had perished, Śūrpaṇakhā rebuked Rāvaṇa;
having reported everything, she then departed for Puṣkara.
Having performed difficult penance, she obtained a boon from Brahmā.
Seeing that ascetic woman fasting in such a manner, O Nārada, the omniscient one, who is an ocean of compassion, perceived her intention and spoke. (50–51)
Brahmā said:
Without having obtained Rāma, who is difficult to behold, you are performing a penance that is hard to accomplish;
[you disregard] Lakṣmaṇa, the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, who is the very embodiment of dharma.
"O lovely-faced one, you shall obtain in another birth as your husband the Lord who transcends Prakṛti and is the sovereign of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā joyfully departed for his own abode.
She cast off that body in the fire and became a hunchbacked woman.
Then, at the words of Śūrpaṇakhā, the lord of the Rākṣasas, a master of illusion whose body trembled with rage, seized Sītā by means of his magic power.

O sage, not seeing Sītā, Rāma fell into a swoon for a long time; his brother restored him to consciousness through spiritual discourse. Thereafter, he wandered through the dense forest, the mountain, the cave, and the river.
O Sage, afflicted by grief day and night, the lord Rāma searched for a long time through the hermitages of the sages; not seeing Jānakī,
the powerful master himself formed a friendship with Sugrīva.
Having slain Vālin with his arrows, he effortlessly bestowed the kingdom upon his friend Sugrīva in order to fulfill his promise. Then the lord of monkeys dispatched messengers everywhere.
Śrī Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, remained in the palace of Sugrīva.
He gave a beautiful jeweled ring as a boon to Hanumān,
and [gave] an auspicious message to Sītā, which was the cause of her sustaining her life.
Having affectionately embraced him and offered his own most rare foot-dust, he dispatched him toward the excellent southern direction;
thus Hanumān departed for Laṅkā for the purpose of searching for Sītā.
Having received his message from Rāma, the son of Rudrakalā departed.
In the Aśoka grove, he beheld Sītā, emaciated by grief,
fasting, and exceedingly thin, like the crescent of the moon on the new-moon night.
She was constantly chanting "Rāma, Rāma" with devotion,
bearing a mass of matted hair resembling molten gold,
and meditating day and night upon the lotus feet of Śrī Rāma.
Having seen her—pure in intention, virtuous, firm in her vows, and devoted to her husband;
endowed with the marks of Mahālakṣmī, blazing with her own splendor;
the giver of merit for all sacred fords; the protectress of the world. (66–67)
Having prostrated before his mother and seeing her weeping, the son of the Wind-god,
filled with joy, gave her Rāma’s jeweled ring.
Seeing her and clasping her lotus-like feet, the virtuous one wept.
Hanumān delivered Rāma’s message, which was the very life-preserver for Sītā. Hanumān said:
"Beyond the ocean, Śrī Rāma stands ready for battle along with Lakṣmaṇa."
And the powerful monkey Sugrīva became a friend to Rāma.
Having slain Vālī, Rāma bestowed upon his friend Sugrīva a kingdom free from all thorns, as well as the wife of Vālī whom he had previously taken.
Sugrīva has also rightfully undertaken your rescue,
and all the monkeys have departed for the purpose of searching for you.
O lotus-eyed one, having received auspicious news from me, [he has set out].
Having crossed the deep ocean, he will return before long.
Having slain the wicked Rāvaṇa, along with his sons and kinsmen, he will, in no time at all, O Mother, effect your liberation. (73–74)
"O Mother, by your grace, today I shall fearlessly reduce jewel-encrusted Laṅkā to ashes; look on with a smile!
O lady of virtuous vows, I now behold Laṅkā as being no more than a mere monkey’s cub."
I am capable of effortlessly destroying the ocean as if it were mere urine, the earth as if it were a single bowl,
and Rāvaṇa along with his army as if he were a swarm of ants—
all within half a moment. (76–77)
"In order to protect Rāma’s vow, I shall not kill you for now.
Be at ease, O illustrious one; cast away your fear, O my mistress.
Having heard the words of Pānara, she wept aloud again and again.
Terrified, Sītā, devoted to her husband Rāma, spoke these words:
"O, does my Rāma still live, having emerged from the terrible ocean of my grief? (79–80)
Is my lord, the master who brings joy to Kausalyā, well?
And how is he now—his body emaciated, yet the very life of Jānakī?
What food does my beloved, who is dearer to me than my own life, eat?
Is it true that even beyond the ocean, Sītā’s husband himself is well?
Is it true that which lord, though armored for battle, has not been destroyed by grief?
Does he perhaps remember me, his sinful wife, who has become the very embodiment of suffering?
How much suffering did that lord of mine endure for my sake?
Formerly, the necklace was not placed upon his neck, being kept aside during our lovemaking.
Now, however, there is an ocean of a hundred yojanas between us.
Shall I behold that Lord Rāma, an ocean of compassion?
(85) He who is beloved, peaceful, exceedingly righteous, and devoted to dharma—shall I once again perform service at the lotus feet of the Lord? (86)
The life of a foolish woman deprived of her husband’s service is in vain.
Does even my son by Dharma, Lakṣmaṇa, truly live?
He is immersed in an ocean of grief for me, his pride shattered, being without me.
The foremost among heroes, righteous, god-like, and a lord of gods—
will I truly see that Lakṣmaṇa, ever armed, the younger brother of a noble master, whose very character is dharma? (88)
"Out of love greater than for his own life, he is blessed and the very embodiment of merit.
(89) Having heard these words and given a favorable reply, O Sage, he effortlessly reduced that Laṅkā to ashes. (90)
Then the monkey, the son of the Wind, restored consciousness to her and proceeded with ease and speed to where the lotus-eyed one was;
he related the entire account of his mother’s situation to him.
Having heard the auspicious account of Sītā, Rāma wept.
O Nārada, Lakṣmaṇa and Sugrīva also wept loudly;
all the monkeys, together with their armies and prowess, likewise wept.

Having constructed a bridge, the joy of the Raghus, accompanied by his army and his younger brother, quickly marched toward Laṅkā, fully prepared, O Nārada. Having waged war, Rāma slew Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen.
O Brahmin, O lady of auspicious gaze, he brought about the liberation of Sita;
and having placed the truth-devoted Sita upon the Puṣpaka vehicle,
he quickly departed for Ayodhyā amidst sports, festivities, and auspicious rites.
The Blessed One took Sītā upon his chest and sported with her;
at that very moment, both Sītā and Rāma abandoned the flames of separation.
Rāma became the lord of the seven islands upon the surface of the earth.
The entire earth became free from mental anguish and physical disease.
Rāma’s two sons, Kuśa and Lava, were likewise righteous. Through their sons and grandsons, there arose kings born of the Solar dynasty.
Thus, O child, I have narrated to you the auspicious life-story of Śrī Rāma;
it bestows happiness, grants liberation, is the very essence, and is a boat for reaching the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Life-Story of Śrī Rāma," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the sixty-third chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: Then Kaṃsa, having reflected thus and having seen that very evil dream, [acted accordingly].
Agitated, greatly terrified, abstaining from food, and devoid of all interest,
he summoned his son, friends, the circle of kinsmen, relatives, and the family priest into the midst of the assembly and, being deeply distressed, spoke to them. (1–2)
Kaṃsa said:
"O wise ones, all my kinsmen and priests, listen to that terrifying bad dream which I beheld at midnight."
Wearing a garland of red flowers and red sandalwood paste,
she bore a sharp sword, a red garment, and a terrifying skull-bowl;
by her very nature, she possessed a loud, boisterous laugh, a flickering tongue, and was fearsome.
An exceedingly old woman with a dark body dances in my city.
(5) With disheveled hair and a severed nose, she is dark-complexioned and fond of dark-colored garlands;
that widow, a great Śūdra woman, desires to embrace me. (6)
Wearing a piece of soiled cloth and possessing coarse hair,
she placed a powder-mark upon her cheeks against my chest;
O Satyaka, they were black in color, ripe, and torn and broken.
Making constant sounds like falling palm fruits,
he— wearing tattered rags, deformed in appearance, a barbarian with coarse hair—
gives me for ornamentation broken and worn-out cowries.
Greatly enraged, the divine woman, though chaste and possessed of husband and sons,
broke the full water-jar while cursing him again and again;
she also [broke] a garland of unfading *amoda* flowers, which had been smeared with red sandalwood paste.
The Brahmin, being greatly enraged and having uttered a curse, shall bring misfortune.
For a moment there shall be a rain of coals, for a moment a rain of ashes, and for a moment a rain of blood; this shall happen in my city again and again. (11–12)
I see a monkey, a crow, a dog, a bear, a boar, and a donkey—
of hideous form and making a harsh sound. I see a heap of dry wood and unsoiled soot.
At the time of sunrise, she had torn the monkeys' nails;
she was dressed in yellow garments, anointed with white sandalwood paste, wearing a garland of *mālatī* flowers, and adorned with jeweled ornaments. (14–15)
Holding a play-lotus in her hand and adorned with a dot of vermilion,
that virtuous woman, having cast a curse upon me in her anger, departs from my palace.
She is followed by terrifying men with disheveled hair, carrying nooses in their hands.
I see my city utterly desolate and exceedingly parched;
in every house, I see naked women with disheveled hair dancing, always appearing with smiles yet possessing most hideous forms. (17–18)
With her nose cut off, a widow, a great Śūdra woman, naked— she,
most terrifying, makes me anointed with oil.
And [there were] naked women, covered in ashes, possessing extinguished embers.
At the time of early dawn, I see various [beings] with smiles;
I also see a wedding, enchanting with dance and song,
and men wearing red garments with red hair-tufts.
I always see a man vomiting blood, dancing naked and grotesque, running and lying down, and smiling. And I see the orbs of the moon and sun in the sky seized by Rāhu.
O kinsmen, at one and the same time I behold a universal devouring;
O priest, I behold the falling of meteors, comets, earthquakes, the upheaval of the kingdom, violent winds, and great portents.
I see great trees with severed trunks whirling in the wind,
as well as fallen mountains upon the surface of the earth; and I see a naked man with a severed head, dancing and standing tall.
I see a terrible garland-maker with a shaven head in every house. I see the entire hermitage burnt, filled with ashes and heaps of charcoal, and everywhere I see everyone crying out in lamentation.
Having spoken thus, the king ceased on the floor of the assembly hall.
Having heard his own dream, Dṛṣadvatī and her kinsmen sighed deeply;
and the priest Satyaka immediately lost consciousness.
O Nārada, perceiving the destruction of Kaṃsa as he was performing the sacrifice,
the group of women, as well as his father and mother, wept out of grief;
they felt that the hour of his own destruction had immediately arrived.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of Kaṃsa’s Dream of Sorrow," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the sixty-fourth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having conducted a thorough investigation of everything, Satyaka, the domestic priest,
who was wise and a disciple of Śukra, spoke these beneficial words to him, O Sage.
Satyaka said:
"Abandon your fear, O illustrious one! What fear do you have while I am present?
Perform a sacrifice to Maheśvara, which destroys all misfortunes.
This sacrifice is named Dhanurmakha; it abounds in food and involves many sacrificial fees."

It is the destroyer of evil dreams and the eradicator of fear from enemies. (3) It is the shatterer of these three kinds of intense portents—those arising from the self, those from the divine, and those from other beings—and the increaser of prosperity. (4)
When the sacrifice was completed, Śambhu granted him the boon that removes old age and death;
he became the manifest bestower of all prosperity.
And in former times, the exceedingly powerful Bāṇa performed this very sacrifice.
Nandi, Paraśurāma, and Bhalla, the best among the strong—[these were his attendants].
In ancient times, Śiva gave this bow to Nandīśvara;
having become perfected through sacrifice, that righteous one gave it to Bāṇa.
Having performed a sacrifice at Puṣkara, the great Siddha gave it to Rāma;
and Paraśurāma, a treasure-house of compassion, gave it to you out of grace,
O King— a weapon measuring a thousand cubits in length and exceedingly hard.
Ten cubits in height and fashioned by the will of Śaṃkara, it was the bull of Paśupati, difficult to be borne even by a suitable vehicle;
and all were unable to break it, except for the god Nārāyaṇa. (9–10)
In this sacrifice, perform the worship of the bow before Śaṅkara;
quickly do so for the sake of auspiciousness, and extend invitations to all.
O lord of men, if the breaking of the bow should occur during this sacrifice—
The destruction of the sacrificer will occur, there is no doubt.
When the bow is broken, the sacrifice is certainly ruined.
And when the rite is unaccomplished, who here can bestow the fruit?
O high-minded one, Brahmā was at the base of the bow, Nārāyaṇa himself was in the middle, and Mahādeva, of fierce majesty, was at the tip;
for that excellent bow was made of three parts and inlaid with precious gems.
Its cause was obscured by the rays of the midday sun in the heat of summer.
It was impossible even for the infinite and mighty Kārttikeya to bend it, let alone the Sun; what then can be said of anyone else, O King? (15–16)
In ancient times, Tripurāri joyfully destroyed Tripura with this [weapon];
therefore, O you who are worthy of auspiciousness, celebrate a great festival freely and without fear.
Having heard these words of Matyaka, the enhancer of the Lunar dynasty [acted].
Kaṃsa spoke to him who was always seeking his welfare in all matters.
Kaṃsa said:
"In the house of Vasudeva was born my slayer, the destroyer of the Kuru race."
The delighter of Nanda grew up at his ease in the house of Nanda.
The powerful boy slew my heroic kinsmen, the highly skilled ministers, and my sister, the pure Pūtanā. (19–20)
The increaser of strength held up Govardhana with the tip of his hand and brought about the defeat of the heroic Mahendra.
He revealed to Brahmā his own form as Brahman, which encompasses all that is moving and unmoving.
With joy, he created a herd of artificial calves.
"O Satyaka, devise a plan to kill that very bull;
for without him, I have no enemy here upon the face of the earth."
Neither in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor indeed in the three worlds,
are there any truly virtuous kings who are my kinsmen everywhere.
Even Brahmā is a great ascetic, and Śaṅkara himself is an ascetic.
Viṣṇu is omnipresent, the soul of all, the eternal one who perceives with equanimity.
(25) Having slain the son of Nanda, I shall be honored throughout the three worlds;
I shall become a great sovereign, the lord of the seven continents. (26)
Having slain Śakra in heaven— him who was weak and defeated by the Daityas—
I shall become Mahendra; and having conquered the Sun there,
as well as the Moon who is afflicted by consumption, [I shall restore] my own ancestral forefather.
"I shall certainly conquer Vāyu, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Yama.
Go quickly to Nanda’s cowherd settlement and bring here at once Nanda, the delighter of the Nandas, as well as his powerful brother Bala. (28–29)
Having heard Kaṃsa’s words, Satyaka spoke to him words that were beneficial, truthful, the essence of policy, and highly appropriate for the occasion. Satyaka said:
"O highly fortunate one, dispatch either Akrūra, or Uddhava, or even Vasudeva, to the desired Nanda-vraja.
Having heard Satyaka’s words, he remained there in that assembly.
And he spoke to Vasudeva, who was seated upon a golden throne.
Kamsa said:
"You are a knower of reality and an expert in the treatises on ethics; you are skilled in the means [of policy]."
"O friend Vasudeva, go to Nandavraja, the abode of Vasudeva’s son.
Quickly bring Vṛṣabhānu, Nanda, Balarāma, the delight of the Nandas, and everyone dwelling in Gokula here for this sacrifice. (33–34)
"Taking this letter, let the messengers go forth in the four directions with joy to present their petition to all the kings and the hosts of sages.
Having heard the king's words, [the messenger’s] throat, lips, and palate became parched.
O Brahmin, he spoke these words with a heart full of resentment.
Vasudeva said:
"O Indra among kings, it is now my duty to go there."
To inform Nandavraja, or Nanda, the delight of the Nandas:
"If the son of Nanda has arrived for your great festival sacrifice, there will inevitably be a conflict between him and you. (37–38)
"Having brought him here, I shall have him joined [to his body];
thus it will not be well for me, nor indeed for you, O gentle one, for everyone will say that he died while being carried by his father. (39) Kṛṣṇa, everyone will say that he is dead.
Vasudeva, through his son, shall indeed slay the king.
(40) Either one of the two will meet with immediate death;
the heroes shall fall, for there is no war that is without its spoils. (41)
Hearing Vasudeva’s words, the lord of kings, his eyes reddened like mud, seized his sword and set out to kill him;
but at that very moment, crying out "Alas! Alas!", he restrained his son.
O Sage, Ugrasena was exceedingly powerful, O Great King;
and Vasudeva, overcome with anger, departed from his own seat for his home.
The king then dispatched Akrūra to go to Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
He dispatched messengers quickly in every direction; all the sages arrived, as did the king with his retinue,
all the world-protectors, the gods, and the ascetic brahmins.
Sanaka, Sananda, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha;
the venerable Sanatkumāra, blazing with the splendor of Brahman; as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Paila, Sumantu, and Sanātana. (46–47)
Pulaha and Pulastya, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Atri, Cyavana,
Bharadvāja, Vyāsa, Gautama, and Parāśara.
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Saṃvarta, and Bṛhaspati;
Kātyāyana, Yājñavalkya, Uttaṅka, and likewise Saubhari;
Parvata, Devala, Jaigīṣavya, and Jaimini.
Viśvāmitra, Sutapas, Pippala, Śākaṭāyana, Jābāli, Jāṅgali, Piśali, and Śilālika; Āstauka, Jagatkāru, and likewise Kalyāṇamitraka. (51)
Durvāsas, Vāmadeva, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vibhāṇḍaka,
Pathi, Kavi, Kaṇāda, Gauśika, Pāṇini, Kautsa, Adyamārṣaṇa, Vālmīki, and Lomaharṣaṇa. (52–53)
Mārkaṇḍeya, Mṛkaṇḍu, Paraśurāma, Sāṃkṛti, Agastya, Vānta, and other sages, O sage,
along with their disciples, their sons, and ascetic Brāhmaṇas.
Jarāsandha, Dantavakra, the deceitful lord of Draviḍa,
Śiśupāla, Bhīṣmaka, Bhagadatta, Mudgala,
Dhārtarāṣṭra, Dhūmakeśa, Dhūmraketu, and Śambara.
Śalya, Satrājit, Śaṅku, and other kings of great strength;
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the teacher Kṛpa, and the mighty Aśvatthāman;
as well as Bhūriśravas, Śālva, Kaikeya, and likewise the king of Kośala.
The great king addressed everyone as was appropriate,
and Satyaka chose an auspicious moment for the day of the sacrifice.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Account of Kaṃsa’s Sacrifice," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada.
Then the sixty-fifth chapter.
Nārada said: Having heard the words of Kaṃsa, Akrūra, the best among the righteous, [acted].
And he, being tranquil and with a joyful mind, spoke calmly to Uddhava.
Akrūra said:
"Today the night has dawned auspiciously for me; it has become a blessed day."
The preceptors, the Brahmins, and the gods were surely pleased with me.
The merit accumulated by me over ten million births has presented itself to me of its own accord;
whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, had arisen for me, it has now come to pass.
He severed the shackles of bondage with which I was bound by my own karma;
released from the prison of saṃsāra, I go to the abode of Hari.
And I have fulfilled the purpose of my friend Kaṃsa, who acted out of anger despite his wisdom.
The god’s anger toward me has indeed become equal to a boon.
O King of Vraja, I shall now go to Vraja to collect [the taxes];
I shall behold the Supreme One, worthy of worship, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like blue lotuses, adorned with yellow garments shining upon his waist;
his limbs either greyed by dust or anointed with sandalwood paste. (7)
Or perhaps I shall see his smiling limbs anointed with fresh butter;
or perhaps him playing his enchanting flute for diversion;
or perhaps him tending the herd of cows here and there. (8–9)
Whether he is staying, moving, or lying down, what is his state of sleep? Having clearly perceived this today, O auspicious one, [know that] this is a favorable moment—
for those such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva meditate upon his lotus feet.
For even Ananta, whose form is infinite, does not know his limit;
the gods and the virtuous do not constantly know his power;
and at his praise, the goddess Sarasvatī herself becomes paralyzed with fear.
The maidservants appointed by her are the great Lakṣmīs who are themselves marked by fortune; and from whose lotus feet Gaṅgā has issued forth, she who is the essence of existence and Rūmiṇī.
She removes birth, death, old age, and disease, and is superior to the three worlds.
By both seeing and touching her, she destroys the sins of men.
She whose lotus feet are meditated upon is Durgā, the destroyer of difficulties;
she is the Goddess, the Mother of the three worlds, the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti), and the Sovereign.
Within the pores of the hair of that Great Viṣṇu,
who is more massive than the most massive, there exist all the countless and diverse [universes] of him who is the Lord of All, and he is but a sixteenth part of Him.
O friend, I am going to see Him who has assumed an illusory human form—
He who is the inner self of all, the omniscient one, beyond primordial nature,
whose very essence is the light of Brahman, and whose body is manifested for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees. (17–18)
He is devoid of qualities, devoid of effort, devoid of worldly joy, and without support;
he is the supreme, the supreme bliss, the blissful one, the delighter of Nandana;
he consists of his own will, is higher than all, the seed of all, and eternal.

The yogis constantly declare that they meditate day and night upon the Child (Śiśu). For a thousand Manvantaras, the lotus-born Brahmā, emaciated and abstaining from food, performed austerities upon the lotus in the ancient age for the sake of the Padma-kalpa.
"Perform penance once more, and then you shall see me.
He heard this voice, yet even so, he did not see him.
Having performed penance for that same duration once again, he obtained a boon and beheld him.
O Uddhava, today I shall behold such a Supreme Lord;
formerly, Śambhu performed penance for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā,
and there he beheld Him within the sphere of light in Goloka.
He attained the supreme and most excellent truth of all, the perfected truth of "mine" (mamātattva),
and achieved pure, supreme devotion at his lotus feet.
And he, who is affectionate toward his devotees, made that devotee equal to himself.
O Uddhava, today I shall behold such a Supreme Lord,
before whom Ananta performed endless penance with devotion toward the Supreme Soul, remaining without food until the fall of a thousand Indras, his belly emaciated. (26–27)
Then the Lord granted him knowledge equal to his own,
saying, "You shall behold such a Supreme Lord.
And he performed that austerity which lasted until the fall of a thousand Indras.
Then he became the witness of all righteous deeds and all actions;
he is the teacher and the giver of fruit for men in this world through whose grace [all things occur]. Oh, how wonderful! I shall behold such a Lord of All.
Twenty-eight Indras pass in the time it takes for one [day] to fall;
in this sequence, months and years constitute the lifespan of Brahmā, which is one hundred years.
A day of that Brahmā is such that, in its mere blink of an eye, his own passing occurs.
One shall behold such a Supreme Self... (32). Just as there is no countable number of Brahmās due to the dust of the earth, so too is the bondage of all worlds; its support is the Great Virāṭ. (33)
All the Viśvas, and each individually— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others; the sages, the Manus, the Siddhas, human beings and so forth, along with all things moving and unmoving—
[are such that] that which is a sixteenth part of Him is the Virāṭ, who is created and destroyed by way of His divine play.
"I shall behold such a Teacher of all...
(35). Having spoken thus, Akrūra, his body covered in horripilation, fell into a swoon; with eyes full of tears, he meditated upon His lotus feet. (36)
Filled with devotion, he repeatedly remembered the lotus feet [of Kṛṣṇa];
and having performed a circumambulation of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
Uddhava embraced him and praised him again and again.
He departed quickly for his home, and Akrūra also went to his own residence.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Excess of Akrūra’s Joy," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the sixty-sixth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, in the *rāsa* dance, the Lord of the *rāsa* himself was joined by the Queen of the *rāsa*.
And he took delight with her, being exceedingly eager for amorous play. (1) Rādhikā fell asleep from the mere act of enjoying pleasure;
having seen a dream, she arose and spoke dejectedly to her beloved during the day. (2)
Rādhikā said:
"O Lord, come here! I shall place you upon my own breast.
As for what the Creator will do in the end, I do not know. (3)
Having spoken thus, that illustrious lady, having placed her beloved upon her breast,
related the evil dream with a heart tormented by grief.
Rādhikā said:
O Lord, while I was seated upon a jeweled throne and holding a jeweled parasol,
the brahmin Ruṣaṭa seized that very parasol from me.
[This occurred] over the ocean, which was like collyrium in appearance, most terrible, and difficult to cross.
And he drove me, so weak, into that deep [water].
There, in that current, afflicted by grief, I wandered again and again;
I was overwhelmed by the force of great waves and beset by crocodiles.
"Save me! Save me! O Lord, thus I speak to you again and again.
Seeing no one else, I, seized by great fear, offer this prayer to the God.
