O Kṛṣṇa, as I sink there, I behold the orb of the moon.
And I saw it falling from the sky in a hundred fragments onto the surface of the earth. And in another moment, I saw the orb of the sun falling from the sky;
having struck the surface of the ground, it became four fragments.
And at one and the same time, I saw in the sky the orbs of both the moon and the sun,
appearing intensely like black collyrium and entirely eclipsed by Rāhu.
And in the next moment, I beheld the radiant splendor of Brahmā.
In anger, he broke the jar of nectar resting on his lap.
And in another moment, I saw a Brahmin greatly enraged,
seizing and leading away a man from my very eyes.
O Lord, the handle of my play-lotus fell from my hand;
suddenly, along with its stalk, it was shattered into pieces.
And the mirror made of the finest jewels also suddenly fell from my hand.
Stainless and resembling collyrium, his body became broken into fragments.
My necklace of precious gems, having snapped from my chest,
fell to the surface of the earth like an exceedingly faded lotus.
All the puppets on the palace roof dance and laugh;
they clap their hands, sing, and weep from moment to moment.
A large black wheel revolves repeatedly in the sky.
I saw him falling and leaping about, appearing terrifying. That Puruṣa, the presiding deity of my life-force, emerged from within me and said, "O Rādhā, grant me leave; I am departing. (18–19)
"A dark-complexioned image embraces and kisses me; I see her now wearing black garments. O beloved of my life, having seen this very contrary sight, [I am distraught].
My limbs dance, and my vital breaths tremble;
they weep out of grief and drag my mind into agitation.
"What is this? What is this, O Lord? Tell me, O best among the knowers of the Vedas! (21–22)
Having spoken thus, the goddess Rādhikā— her throat, lips, and palate parched,
terrified and consumed by grief— fell at His lotus feet.
Upon hearing the dream, the Lord of the World placed the goddess upon His own chest.
At that moment, she awakened him through internal yoga.
And having attained stainless knowledge, the goddess dispelled his grief;
she made the Lord peaceful and placed her beloved upon her own breast.

Thus [ends] the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Rādhā’s Sorrow," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa*, within the Great *Śrīkṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa*, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the sixty-seventh chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing Māminī distressed by separation, Kṛṣṇa, the enchanter of desire, took her upon his chest and went to the pleasure-lake.
Rādhā, the queen of the sovereign of kings, shone upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest.
O Sage, like lightning in a cloud or a river in the sky,
that ocean of compassion took delight with Ramā and Kṛpā;
just as a ruby is set between two gems of gold and sapphire respectively.
On a couch fashioned from jewels, constructed from the essence of the finest gems,
while jewel-lamps were blazing, he was adorned with jeweled ornaments.
Out of curiosity, he engaged in the play of the dance (*rāsa*) with her who was likewise adorned with jeweled ornaments.

Immersed in the beautiful *Rasaratnākara*, the Lord of Rasikas, Rādhā—the Queen of the *rāsa*—spoke to the Lord of Rāma. When their amorous play had ceased and her desire had subsided, she said: (5–6)
Rādhikā said: "O Lord, I am blossomed by you; without you, I am withered as if dead.
Just as a multitude of great medicinal herbs shines at dawn when the sun has risen. (7)
Like the flame of a lamp at night, I am with you; yet without you, day by day I wane like a digit of the moon during the dark fortnight.
Upon your chest, my radiance was equal to the light of the full moon.
Abandoned by you, I have died instantly, like the digit of the moon on the new-moon night (kuhvāṃ).
With you, I was like a blazing flame of fire fed by an offering of clarified butter;
without you, I am extinguished, like a lotus in the cold season.
Seized by the fever of anxiety and old age, I am as I am even now that you have departed;
I am like the earth when the sun has set and the moon is swallowed by darkness.
Deprived of you, my dress, beauty, youth, and consciousness have all fallen away.
Tārāvalī has fallen away, like the sun’s daughter at the rising of the sun.
You alone are the self of all, and especially my lord;
just as the body is abandoned by the self, so am I without you.
You consist of the five vital breaths for me, and I am dead without you;
the eyes are like sockets without sight, and sight is like a puppet without the eyes.
Just as a canvas is rendered meaningful by a painting, so am I with you.
Deprived of you, I am like the earth covered with grass—unadorned. O Kṛṣṇa, with you I am like a clay figure painted with colors;
without you, washed by water, I am as formless as a plain earthen vessel.
The splendor of the cowherd women is enhanced by you, the Lord of the Rāsa dance;
and the golden necklace shines along with the white gem.
O King of Vraja, together with you, these royal ladies truly reign as queens.
Just as the host of stars shines in the sky by means of the moon, O son of Nanda, so does the splendor of Yaśodā shine because of you;
just as a row of trees shines with its branches, fruits, and trunks. (18–19)
O Lord of Gokula, by you the splendor of the inhabitants of Gokula is enhanced,
just as the entire circle of worlds is graced by a great king.
O Lord of the Rāsa dance, even the beauty of Rāma is rendered enchanting by you.
It shines like Amarāvatī in heaven under the rule of the King of the Gods.
You are the splendor, the lord, and the refuge of the trees of Vṛndāvana,
and for all other forests as well, you are like the powerful lion.
Without you, Yaśodā is submerged in an ocean of grief;
unable to find her calf, Murārī cries out in agitation.
Nanda’s life-breaths tremble and his mind is consumed with sorrow. (23)
"Without you, [I am] like a heap of grain in a heated vessel.
Having spoken thus with supreme love, as she fell at the feet of Hari,
the All-pervading Lord again enlightened her through spiritual instruction alone.
The great yogi within is the cause for the total destruction of delusion,
just as an axe with a sharp edge is for trees, O Nārada.
Nārada said:
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me of the great internal yoga and the cutting away of the grief of the worlds; I have a great curiosity to hear it. Nārāyaṇa said:
The internal great yoga is not known even by the yogis;
yet Hari himself knows it in all its various forms.
And the Lord of Rādhikā knows some portion of that very internal yoga within the world of cows.
O Sage, being well-pleased, he related [the story] of the Enemy of Tripura to him who was performing penance until the fall of a thousand Indras— him who is the Lord,
the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, the eldest, and the most excellent among ascetics. (29–30)
Having performed difficult austerities at Puṣkara and Padma-like penance at Pādma, the Lotus-born One saw him; Kṛṣṇa spoke something to that god with reverence:
"O you whose belly is emaciated by harsh [asceticism] for as long as a hundred Indras have fallen."
Motionless and with his bones as his only strength, that treasury of compassion, out of pity, [rescued him].
Long ago, in the land of Siṃha, my father—who was the best among the righteous—having performed emaciating penance for a period bounded by fourteen Indras, [attained] Dharma. (32–33)
The treasure-house of compassion, out of pity, recited some portion of the Ātmopaniṣad;
and he spoke to me, who was performing penance under the shade of a Śata-indra tree, as well as to Sanatkumāra, who had been performing supreme penance for a very long time. (34)
Nārada spoke something to the ascetic Kapila,
who had been performing penance for a long time on the Himālaya mountains,
and who was performing a certain difficult austerity at Puṣkara and Bhāskara.

The Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees and a treasure-house of compassion, spoke thus with loving-kindness to Prahlāda, Durvāsas, Bhṛgu, and that hidden devotee while they were on the beautiful sporting-lake. What did that ocean of mercy say?
Listen as I relate that [event] concerning Rādhikā, who was afflicted by grief.
Seeing the connoisseuress of rasa distressed, the teacher of yogis took her upon his chest and spoke certain spiritual words to that yoginī. (38–39)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O beloved, you who remember your past lives, how can you forget yourself,
as well as all the events of Goloka and the very curse of Sudāmā?
"O noble lady, due to a curse, there will be a separation from you for a few days;
however, we two shall meet again.
I shall once more go to that Goloka, my own abode. (41)
Having gone there with the cowherd women and the cowherds who dwell in Goloka, I shall now speak to you something concerning the supreme self;
listen. It is the destroyer of grief, the giver of joy, the essence, and the bestower of mental happiness.
I am the inner self of all, untainted by any actions; though present within all things, I am unseen everywhere. Just as the wind moves through all places and within all objects, so do I.
And yet I am not smeared [by action], for I am likewise the witness of all deeds.
The individual soul (jīva) is my reflection, present everywhere among all living beings;
it is always the enjoyer of good and evil, and the agent of actions.
Just as the reflection of the moon and the sun appears only in moving jars,
yet when those jars are broken, that reflection merges back into those two alone;
so too, O beloved, the individual soul (jīva) remains joined to me at the time when living beings have died.
And we two exist eternally within all living beings.
I am the substratum and the supported, the effect and the cause, even without [external] instruments.
O beautiful one, all material objects are perishable.
In various places, some of my portions manifest as superior, while others are indeed inferior; some are gods who are my partial incarnations (aṃśas), and some are gods who are my portions (kalās).
Some are portions of portions (kalāṃśas), and some are even portions of those portions (kalāṃśāṃśas).
My own subtle Prakṛti is fivefold in her manifestations:
Sarasvatī, Kamalā, Durgā, you (the Earth), and she who is the mother of the Vedas.
All the gods who possess embodied forms are of this same primordial nature.
I am the Self, the eternal possessor of a body, acting in accordance with the meditations of my devotees.
O Rādhā, those who are of the nature of *prakṛti* have perished in the dissolution of *prakṛti*.
I alone existed in the beginning, and even afterwards, I alone exist.
Just as there is never any difference between whiteness and milk,
so too it is certain that no difference shall ever exist between you and me.
I am the Great Virāṭ, within whose body-hairs all the worlds reside.
In that [creation], you are a great portion, and by your own portion you are his beloved;
I am the small Virāṭ in the creation from whose navel-lotus the universe arises.
O virtuous lady, this [world] resides within a single pore of Viṣṇu’s skin, and I too reside there as a portion.
You and Bṛhatī are his two wives, both fortunate in their own abodes.

Furthermore, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all the other gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, are each his individual portions; they are his partial incarnations (aṃśas) as well as my own emanations (matkalās).
O Goddess, all moving and non-moving beings exist by a minute fraction of a fraction of my own power.
In Vaikuṇṭha you are Mahālakṣmī, and there I am the four-armed one;
and that realm is outside and above the universe, just like Goloka.
You are Sarasvatī in truth, and Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā;
(60) you are Śivā in the world of Śiva, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti;
having destroyed all difficulties, you are Durgā, the destroyer of all misfortune. (61)
She alone was the daughter of Dakṣa, and she alone was the daughter of the mountain;
thus Pārvatī rests upon the chest of Śiva on Kailāsa as his auspicious consort.
By your own portion, you are the daughter of the ocean on the chest of Viṣṇu in the Milky Ocean.
And by my own portion, I created Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
and you, Lakṣmī, Śivā, Dhātrī, and Sāvitrī, each separately.
And in Goloka, you are yourself Rādhā, and in the Rāsa dance, you are eternally the Mistress of the Rāsa (Rāseśvarī).
O Vṛndā, you who were Virajā on the banks of the Virajā in the beautiful Vṛndāvana,
have come to the holy land of Bhārata by the curse of Sudāmā,
O beautiful one, in order to purify both Bhārata and the forest of Vṛndāvana.
By a minute fraction of a fraction of Your power, all women in the universe are You;
whatever woman there is, she is You, and whatever man there is, he is indeed I.
And by a fraction of My power, I am Agni, and You are Svāhā, my beloved, who possesses the power of burning.
I am capable only with you; without you, I am not able to burn.
I am the Sun among luminous bodies, and you are my radiance by your very portion.
You are Saṃjñā, and through you I shine; without you, I possess no luster.
I am the moon by my digit, and you are its splendor, Rohiṇī.
Manohara is with you, yet you are not merely Sundarī.
I am Indra by my digit, and you are Śacī, the Fortune of Heaven.
Together with you, the king of the gods was possessed of splendor; without you, he was shorn of his glory.
I am Dharma, and you are a portion of him, while you yourself are the embodied form of righteousness.
Without you, who are the very act of dharma, I am not capable of performing righteous deeds.
I am the sacrifice through my portion, and you are the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) through your own part. Together with you, I bestow the fruit [of action], but without you, I am devoid of purpose.
Through my portion I am the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), and you, being virtuous, are the Svadhā offering through your own part.
I am sufficient for the offering of oblations to the ancestors, yet I am never sufficient without you.
I am the Puruṣa and you are Prakṛti; I am not a creator without you.
You are the form of the year, and I am the Lord together with you.
Endowed with Lakṣmī by you, O Lakṣmī, and likewise destitute of fortune without you;
just as a potter is unable to fashion a jar without clay,
so too am I and Śeṣa [unable] without you, who are the Earth through a portion of yourself, a part of your own self.
O beautiful one, I carry you upon my head—you who are the receptacle of grain and jewels;
you are beauty, peace, prosperity, and virtue incarnate.
You are contentment, nourishment, forgiveness, modesty, hunger, thirst, supreme compassion, and the highest mercy.
Sleep, faith, lassitude, fainting, humility, and action—[these are your forms].
You are embodied as form, as devotion, and as the physical body of all embodied beings; you are always my support, and I am your very self; we are mutually one another.
"Just as you are, so am I; we two, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, are equal.
Indeed, O Goddess, creation could not come into being without one of the two.
Having spoken thus to Rādhā, his beloved who is dearer to him than life, the Supreme Self—
Having placed him upon his chest, he was well-pleased and awakened him, O Nārada.
And he became engaged in play within the jeweled palace;
likewise, the lover was with Rādhā, the amorous woman.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Discourse on Spiritual Yoga by Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the sixty-eighth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having finished his play and arisen from the bed of flowers, the Ancient One immediately awakened her who was sleeping like his own life-breath;
he wiped her face with the hem of his garment, making it stainless.
Madhusūdana spoke sweetly and peacefully to the peaceful one.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhā, O Queen of the Rāsa, O lady of pure smiles, stay for a moment!"
Go to Vṛndāvana, or go to Vraja, O Queen of Vraja! O Goddess presiding over the Rāsa, perform the Rāsa dance for a moment in the Rāsa arena.
Just as there are village deities in every single village everywhere, [so be you in every place].
"O beautiful one, go for a moment with your dear friends to the sandalwood grove, or to the campaka forest; or else stay here.
For a moment I shall go home, as I have an important task to attend to."
"O beloved of my life, grant me a moment of leave with affection.
(6) You are the presiding deity of my life-breaths, and my life-breaths abide in you.
O dear one, where is a living being capable of remaining after having abandoned his life-breaths? (7)
My mind is eternally fixed on you; my worldly attachment belongs to you.
There is no one dearer to me than you; you alone are dearer to me than Śaṅkara.
It is true that Śaṅkara is my life-breath, and you, O virtuous lady, are dearer to me than my life-breath.
Having spoken thus and embraced her, the Blessed One prepared to depart. (9) Knowing of Akrūra’s arrival, the omniscient one, the provider of all means,
the self and protector of all, and the performer of every benefit— (10)
Seeing him departing thus, eager and with a distracted mind,
the goddess Rādhikā spoke with a heart in anguish.
Rādhikā said:
O Lord, most beloved of my lover, the best among those dear to me!
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Ramā, O Master of Vraja, do not abandon Vraja!
Now, O Lord of my life, I see you with a troubled mind.
Upon your departure, my love and my very good fortune have departed as well.
Where are you going, abandoning me in this deep ocean of grief—me, distressed by separation, wretched, and having sought refuge in you alone? (13–14)
I shall not return home again; I shall go to another forest, singing "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" day and night.
Or rather, I shall not go to the wilderness; I shall go into the ocean of desire.
There, having fulfilled your desire, I shall cast off this body.
Just as space, just as the self, and just as the moon or the sun,
so shall you go to my side, bound to the hem of my garment.
Now you depart, having cast me into despair, O you who are compassionate toward the wretched! It is indeed not fitting to abandon me, a miserable woman who has come to you for refuge.
(18) You whose lotus feet are meditated upon by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.

O envious one, how could I have known you, who were wearing the guise of a cowherd through your illusory power? O Lord, forgive whatever misconduct I have committed, the thousands of offenses I have made, and whatever was spoken out of my sense of being your wife and my pride. (19–20)
My pride has been ground to dust and my desire has vanished;
what else can I tell you to make you understand my own good fortune?
Having learned this from the mouth of Garga and having heard it, I was bewildered by your illusory power.
I am unable to speak to you because of love or the bonds of devotion.
(22) If you depart, abandoning me, you will become defiled;
your sons and grandsons shall perish by the fire of Brahma’s wrath. (23)
"Without you, my beloved of life, I consider a single moment to be a hundred ages;
O Lord, how could I sustain my life for a hundred years after abandoning you?
Having spoken thus, Rādhikā fell from her seat onto the surface of the earth.
O Sage, she suddenly fell into a swoon and lost consciousness.
Seeing her thus unconscious, Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, restored her senses out of pity and took her onto his chest.
He consoled her in various ways with methods for shattering grief;
nevertheless, she of the pure smile was unable to abandon her sorrow.
For the loss of ordinary objects leads only to the sorrow of men.
And where can the separation between the body and the self lead to happiness?
(28) On that day, the Lord of Vraja did not go to Vraja;
rather, he went with Rādhā to the vicinity of the pleasure-lake. (29)
Having gone there, he again engaged in play with her;
the Queen of the Rāsa dance joyfully abandoned the flame of shame during the rāsa.
Adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste, that Rādhā was together with her Lord.
And Nārada remained in seclusion upon a couch of flowers and sandalwood.

(31) Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Rādhā’s Sorrow," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, concerning the arrival of Nārada.
Now begins the sixty-ninth chapter.
Nārada said: Tell me what further secret there is concerning Rādhā and Keśava;
you ought to explain that to me, for its true nature is hidden and not clearly manifest.
Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare a most wonderful secret,
which is to be concealed even among the Vedas and Purāṇas by those who know the ancient lore.

Furthermore, the Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is full of desire, all-pervading, and composed of His own will, took delight with Ramā; He, the skillful one, with her who was likewise skillful, just as a beautiful woman takes delight with a wife endowed with the power of the sixty-four arts. (3)
She was skilled in the treatises on love (*kāmaśāstra*), clever, and the sovereign of connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*).
She was adept in the playful arts of passion (*śṛṅgāralīlā*), eternally desirous, and full of longing.
Among beautiful women, she was the most beautiful, possessing a youth that remained forever firm.
The mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, auspicious, venerable, and proud;
a disciple of Śambhu, endowed with wisdom, and living for the end of a hundred kalpas;
skilled in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and proficient in the methods of yoga.
The virtuous and renowned Siddhayoginī assumed various forms.
Her daughter, the goddess Rādhikā, who was like a mother yet full of desire, being of excellent character, displayed various emotions toward her husband. (7–8)
Eager for the aesthetic delight of love (*rāmarasa*), he engaged in the *rāsa* dance together with that distinguished woman, manifesting the sixty-four arts of amorous passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
Her hips were marked by the tips of his fingernails, and her breasts bore the wounds of his claws.
The Goddess of Sleep approached her, whose sandalwood paste and vermilion were washed away, whose braid was disheveled,
who was virtuous yet immersed in the bliss of sexual union, naked and fainting from grief,
her body covered with horripilation like a serpent.

Seeing her asleep, Kṛṣṇa— the ocean of mercy, the master of illusion, and the Lord of Māyā— out of compassion and for the instruction of the world, wept through his illusory power. Placing Rādhā upon his chest, he kissed her again and again.
And he dressed his beloved, the presiding deity of his life-breaths, who had bathed her eyes with tears,
in two garments that were purified by fire, exceedingly fine, priceless, and difficult for the entire world to obtain. (13–14)
And he gave her a *kabari* [turban] and saffron-sandalwood paste;
upon her body and neck, he placed a priceless necklace made of jewels.
He also applied vermilion (*sindūra*) upon her pure forehead, below the parting of her hair.
She fashioned a *padmaka* mark on her cheek, shaped like a pomegranate flower and adorned with drops of sandalwood paste, variegated with many diverse patterns;
and she placed upon his lotus-feet anklets resplendent with jewels. (16–17)
The Lord also applied beautiful red lac to the nails of her toes. As she was overcome by sleep and radiant in various fine garments, he again passionately embraced her as he desired.
And again, having kissed her and placed her upon his own chest,
the Lord of the worlds, distressed by separation from his beloved, fell asleep.
In the meantime, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [arrived] in that forest.
He arrived together with Śiva, Viṣṇu, and other gods, as well as the lords of sages.
Having arrived, he bowed his head in salutation and, with palms joined in reverence, praised the all-pervading Lord, who is most perfect, with hymns from the Sāmaveda. (21–22)
Brahmā said:

Victory, victory to you, O Lord of the universe, whose feet are worshipped; O one devoid of qualities, formless, composed of your own will, who bestows grace upon devotees, and whose form is eternal! (23)

O Lord who appeared in the guise of a cowherd through Your power of illusion, O Master of Illusion, O One of beautiful form and virtuous character, O Peaceful One, O All-Enchanting One, O Self-Controlled One, O You whose bliss of knowledge is absolute, O Supreme beyond the supreme, O Being beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*), O Form of the inner self of all, O Untainted Witness, O Manifest and Unmanifest One, O Stainless One, O Remover of the world’s burden, O Ocean of Compassion, O Swallower of the river of sorrow, O Dispeller of the fear of old age, death, and other evils, O Protective Cage, O Bestower of grace upon devotees, O Lover of devotees, O Wealth accumulated by devotees—*Oṃ*, salutations be unto You!
(24) Having thus spoken for the sake of pleasing the presiding deity of the serpent...
He spoke this again and again and indeed fell into a swoon.
(25) Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this hymn composed by Brahmā, they will certainly attain their desired success from serpents; of this there is no doubt. (26)
A sonless man obtains a son; one bereft of a beloved regains his beloved;
a pauper obtains truth and most perfect wealth.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he shall at the end attain the service of Hari.
He attains unwavering devotion, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain even for liberation.
Having praised the Creator of the worlds and having bowed down again and again, he rose up very slowly and spoke once more with devotion. (28–29)
Brahmā said:
Arise, O Lord of the gods of gods, O cause of supreme bliss!
O delighter of Nanda, O joyful one, O eternal bliss; salutations be unto you! (30)
O Lord, go to the home of Nanda and abandon the forest of Vṛndāvana;
remember the curse of Sṛdāmā, which binds you for a hundred years.
Due to the obstruction caused by the curse of your devotee, O beloved, abandon your wife for a hundred years.
Furthermore, having regained her, you shall go to Goloka.
O Lord, having gone to your father’s house, behold Akrūra who has arrived—
your venerable uncle, a guest worthy of honor, blessed, and a Vaiṣṇava, O Master.
Go now with him to the city of Mathurā;
O Hari, break Śambhu’s bow and shatter the host of your enemies.
Slay the evil-minded Kaṃsa, awaken your father, and enlighten your mother.
The manifestation of Dvārakā and the removal of the earth’s burden;
O Lord, the burning of Vārāṇasī and the abode of Śakra;
the yawning of Śiva in battle and the severing of Bāṇa’s arms. (35–36)
O Lord, [perform] the abduction of Rukmiṇī and the slaying of Naraka;
take the hands of sixteen thousand women in marriage.
Abandon your beloved who is as dear as your own life; O Lord of Vraja, go to Vraja!
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you, before Rādhā awakens.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, together with Indra and the hosts of gods, as well as Śeṣa and Śaṅkara, departed for the world of Brahmā.
And the deities showered a rain of flowers and sandalwood upon Kṛṣṇa with love and devotion, and an incorporeal voice arose:
"Slay Kaṃsa as is fitting, and effect the liberation of your own parents."
"O Nārada, thus indeed bring about the destruction of the burden of the land of the Kurus.
(41) Having heard these words of his, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, left the divine Rādhā and rose up very slowly. (42)
Hari went a short distance away, looking back again and again;
he stood for a moment near his dwelling in a grove of sandalwood trees. Abandoning her sleep, Rādhā rose from her own bed.
Not seeing her peaceful, beloved, and life-cherished Hari, she cried out:
"Alas, O Lord, lover, dearest one, master of my life, beloved of my life, thief of my breath, most dear one! Where have you gone? (44–45)
Having searched for a moment, she wandered through the Mālatī grove;
she sat for a moment, stood up for a moment, and slept upon the ground for a moment.
She wept for a moment with great intensity and lamented again and again.
"Come, come, O Lord!"— having spoken thus again and again,
she fell into a swoon from the torment of the fires of separation;
and covered by the grass upon the ground, she fell down as if dead.
O Brāhmaṇa, hundreds of thousands of gopīs arrived there;
some held chowries in their hands, and others carried liquid sandalwood paste.
In their midst, the beloved Līlā placed Rādhā upon her own chest.
Seeing her beloved as if dead, she wept, overwhelmed with love.
Placing a lotus petal wet with water upon the mud,
she laid down Rādhā, who was motionless and like one deceased.

Having arrived there, Kṛṣṇa beheld that very woman, dearer to him than life itself— she who was served by the gopīs with beautiful white chowries, anointed with sandalwood paste, and dressed in smooth garments. (52)
O Nārada, although he was restrained by the most powerful gopīs,
the ocean of mercy approached Rādhā— who had been led away like an offender being punished by the king’s soldiers— and took her upon his lap.
She caused her to regain consciousness and awakened her with various means of awakening.
Having regained consciousness, the goddess beheld her beloved, who was as dear to her as life itself. The goddess became firmly composed and cast off the fever of separation.
That beloved woman performed the desired embrace of his limbs;
Madhusūdana engaged in various forms of amorous dalliance. Placing Rādhā upon his chest, he rested upon a bed of jewels.
Ratnamālā, a clever friend of Rādhā who is honored by all,
spoke sweetly to Kṛṣṇa words that were the essence of ethics and unsurpassed.
Ratnamālā said:
Listen, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall declare that which brings happiness in the end—
beneficial, true, the essence of ethics, and the cause of affection between husband and wife.
It is esteemed in the treatises on love, in ethics, and in the Vedas and Purāṇas.
It is praiseworthy among worldly activities and brings about great renown.
(60) Among women, a mother is dear; among kinsmen, a brother is dear;
beyond that, a son is dear; and from a son alone, a husband is dear. (61)
To virtuous women, a husband who is esteemed by the righteous is dearer than a hundred sons;
indeed, for those who are connoisseurs and refined, there is nothing dearer than a husband.
If the husband is himself refined, he brings happiness to those who are refined.
Otherwise, a wicked person is indeed like poison and is truly treacherous. O child, in this false cycle of existence, the mutual affection between husband and wife,
as well as their equality toward one another, is the desired good fortune.
Wherever there is discord between husband and wife, there is indeed misfortune; their life is utterly fruitless. Furthermore, division from a good husband is the supreme sorrow for women.
Life is the seed of the torment of grief, and it is even more subject to death [than life itself].
Whether in sleep or in waking, the husband is the life-breath of women;
indeed, the husband alone is the teacher for women in this world and in the next.
When you, her protector, had departed from her, Rādhikā fell into a swoon and suddenly collapsed upon the ground covered with grass.
I then placed excellent, cool water into her mouth.
Then her breath returned, as did her consciousness and her childhood innocence.
For a moment she says, "O Lord! O Kṛṣṇa! for a moment she calls out to her friend;
for a moment she weeps in deep anguish, and in that very instant she falls into a swoon.

Rādhikā’s body was scorched by the fires of separation; like a heated iron rod, it was untouchable and resembled fire itself. Whether in dream or waking, by night or by day, at home or in the forest— (71) —[it remained thus].
Whether in water, on land, or in the atmosphere, during the rising of the moon or the sun,
there is no difference in Rādhā’s perception; she, whose form is as inert as a corpse,
remains constantly situated in her place, beholding the entire world as permeated by Viṣṇu.
Having fallen upon a bed made of lotus petals still wet with water amidst the glossy mud,
she, distressed by separation, lay down to sleep;
though she had been constantly fanned by her dear friends with white chowries.
Drenched with sandalwood paste and covered with smooth garments, the mud attained dryness at the mere touch of Rādhā’s body;
even the glossy lotus petals were reduced to ashes in an instant. (75–76)
The sandalwood became dry, its color resembling that of the campaka flower;
O Hari, the hair took on the appearance of collyrium in hue.
The beautiful drop of vermilion instantly turned black.
Her dress, her grace, her charm, and her play were all abandoned.
Then, seeing her [in that state], Ratnamālā went to the presence of Kṛṣṇa and spoke these sweet words, which were supremely beneficial for Rādhā. (78–79)
Ratnamālā said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Beloved of Kamalā, my friend will surely give up her life very soon through separation from you, if you do not return. (80)
"O Kṛṣṇa, having reflected with your mind, do that which has been proposed,
so that there may be no sin of killing a woman, O expert in ethics.
Having heard the words of Ratnamālā, Mādhava smiled and said:
Beneficial, truthful, the essence of policy, and bringing about happiness in the end. (82) The Blessed One said:
"O beloved, although I, as the Lord, am capable of annulling the conception,"

Nevertheless, I am not able to disregard the established order regarding the jewels; therefore, I do not act [otherwise]. (83) Furthermore, within all the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), the boundaries have been established by me.
By means of those [boundaries], the sages, gods, and humans perform their respective duties. (84)
"O beautiful one, due to Sudāman’s curse, a separation of one hundred years shall indeed occur for us two, husband and wife; O slender-waisted one,
there will also be a separation from me during her waking state."
"Through my boon, there shall be constant union with her even in dreams.
An internal [realization] has been granted by me, and the cutting away of grief will occur.
Inform Rādhā—blessings be upon you—and I shall go to the abode of Nanda. (86–87)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds departed for the abode of Nanda;
and the throngs of his beloveds, O Nārada, awakened Rādhikā.
Having gone home, he bowed to his father and likewise to his mother.
The mother placed fresh butter upon his lap;
he chewed the betel leaf given by his mother and drank cool water.
There, the Lord of the worlds dwelt in the presence of his mother.
He was served by all the hosts of cowherds with white chowries;

they joyfully offered him garlands, sandalwood paste, and betel-nut. Thus ends the [chapter on] the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma... Mahā... Śrī Kṛṣṇacaritra, as narrated by Nārada.
The sixty-ninth chapter.
Now begins the seventieth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Akrūra, having returned to his own quarters after being sent by Kaṃsa,
prepared his bed upon a couch after eating excellent, delicious food.
He chewed betel-leaf with camphor and drank scented water.

He fell into a pleasant sleep, arising from the mere enjoyment of comfort. Then, at the time when the night was nearly over, being free from all afflictions and the like, he beheld an auspicious dream in accordance with the ancient scriptures.
Free from disease, with hair tied up, endowed with a pair of garments,
sleeping on a comfortable bed, very affectionate, and devoid of anxiety and sorrow;
[he beholds Him] who is of youthful age, dark-complexioned, two-armed, and holding a flute.
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland (vanamālā),
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste and beautified by garlands of jasmine (mālatī),
he was further embellished with ornaments worthy of the finest jewels and gems.
O Sage, he first beheld two infants of such a nature: one with a crest of peacock feathers and a smiling lotus-eyed countenance;
then he saw a beautiful, virtuous woman who possessed both a husband and sons.
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with jewel ornaments,
holding a blazing lamp in one hand and a handful of white grain in the other, she is excellent;
her face resembles the autumn moon, and she is auspicious, smiling, and granting boons.
Then he saw a brahmin pronouncing auspicious blessings,
a swan upon a white lotus, a horse, and a lake;
and he beheld a beautiful, auspicious tree, variegated, laden with fruit, and in full bloom.
[One should visualize] a mango tree, a neem tree, a coconut tree, a *guru* tree, an arka tree, and a plantain tree;
[and one's own self] as a white serpent biting [them], situated upon a mountain, standing upon a tree, mounted upon an elephant, and seated upon a boat or a horse. (11–12)
He saw him playing the lute and eating milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
as well as his desired food mixed with curd and milk served upon lotus leaves;
yet he also saw his body covered in worms and excrement, weeping and then deluded.
[One should visualize] one's own self as holding white grain and flowers, momentarily smeared with sandalwood paste,
situated upon a palace and standing in the ocean, reddish in color,
mangled and pierced, with limbs wounded and covered in fat and pus. (14–15)
Then he beheld silver, bright gems, and gold; pearls, rubies, and precious stones; auspicious water from full jars;
a fragrant cow with her calf, a lordly bull, and a peacock.
A parrot, a crane, a swan, a hawk, and a wagtail;
betel, flower garlands, a blazing fire, and the worship of the gods;
an image of Pārvatī, an image of Kṛṣṇa, and the Śiva-liṅga. (17–18)
Having seen in a dream a Brahmin woman, a child, a well-ripened harvest,
a sacred site, a lord of kings, a lion, a tiger, a guru, and a god,
he arose and performed his desired daily rites.
He related the entire account to Uddhava. Having received Uddhava’s command and performed the worship of his guru and the gods,
O Nārada, he set out on his journey while meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his mind.
And on the very path before him, he beheld auspicious signs worthy of blessing, bestowing good fortune,
granting the fruits of one's desires, delightful, and indicative of prosperity:
on his left, a linga of Śiva, a female jackal, a full water-pot, a mongoose, and a blue jay.
A virtuous woman accompanied by her sons, adorned with divine ornaments;
white flowers, garlands, grain, and an auspicious wagtail;
a blazing fire in the south, as well as a Brahmin, a bull, and an elephant. (23–24)
A calf, a cart, a white horse, a royal swan,
a courtesan, a garland of flowers, a banner, curd, milk-rice,
a jewel, gold, silver, pearls, rubies, and whatever else is desired. (25)
Wine, meat, sandalwood, honey-wine, and excellent clarified butter;
the black-spotted deer, fruit, parched grain, cooked food, and likewise a mirror;
a variegated celestial chariot and a brilliantly radiant image. (26–27)
He heard the auspicious sounds of white lotuses, a forest of red lotuses, conch shells, *cilla* birds,
*kīraka* birds, cats, mountains, clouds, peacocks, parrots, and cranes;
as well as the sounds of conch shells, cuckoos, and musical instruments.
Having seen such auspicious sights and heard the various melodies of the Kṛṣṇas, the sound of "Hari," and the shouts of victory, his mind was filled with joy;
remembering Hari, he entered the holy forest of Vṛndāvana. (29–30)
He beheld before him the delightful and desired circle of the rāsa dance, perfumed by the breeze carrying the scent of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and flowers,
and resplendent with auspicious jars and plantain trees.
It was adorned all around with clusters of mango sprouts variegated with silk threads (32),
and it was constantly beautified by three crores of jewel-palaces made of rubies, which were themselves worthy of being beautiful (33).
Having beheld Vṛndāvana, which shines with hundreds of millions of delightful bower-cottages, he proceeded some distance further.
He then saw before him the most excellent and beautiful Nanda-vraja.
It was supreme, resembling Vekuṇṭha, the auspicious abode of Vaikuṇṭha;
it was provided with jeweled staircases, resplendent with jeweled pillars,
enriched with various wonderful paintings, and adorned with excellent jeweled bracelets.
Inlaid with the finest gems and fashioned by Viśvakarman,
he entered the royal gate through a path visible at the entrance;
it was richly adorned with networks of jewels and banners, and embellished with pearls and rubies.

Abounding in the splendor of jeweled mirrors, variegated with diverse inlaid gems, (the city) was adorned with jeweled streets and auspicious with jars filled with auspicious substances. Upon hearing of Akrūra’s arrival, Nanda and the others were filled with joy. (38–39)
Accompanied by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and joined by Vṛṣabhānu and others, he went forth to follow [the departing bridegroom], placing the courtesan at the head of the procession,
with a full water-pot and a lordly elephant carrying white grain leading the way.
Having respectfully received a black cow, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for the feet, a jeweled seat, and other offerings,
Nanda— accompanied by his attendants and the child, peaceful, smiling, humble, and filled with joy— stood before him. (41–42)
Seeing the highly fortunate Akrūra, he quickly gave him an embrace;
all the cowherds bowed their heads in salutation and received his blessing.
O Sage, a meeting took place between them, full of mutual virtues.
And Akrūra placed Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, one after the other,
upon his lap; with his body covered in horripilation, his eyes filled with tears, and overflowing with joy, he— having achieved his purpose and fulfilled his desire— kissed them on both cheeks.
For a moment he beheld Kṛṣṇa, two-armed, dark and beautiful,
clad in yellow garments and adorned with garlands of jasmine;
his entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, and he was the supreme, excellent bearer of the flute.
He beheld for a moment the all-pervading Lord, who is praised by Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, and other lords of sages such as Sanaka,
and who is gazed upon by the cowherd girls; he was most full,
seated upon his lap, smiling, and possessed of four arms.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, adorned with a forest garland,
and attended by his attendants Sunanda, Nanda, and Kumuda;
served by hosts of Siddhas bowing in devotion, he is the Supreme beyond the supreme.
For a moment he beheld that god with five faces and three eyes;
resembling pure crystal, adorned by the lords of serpents,
naked, the supreme Brahman, with ashes upon his limbs and matted hair.
For a moment he was a yogin, supreme and devoted to meditation, holding a rosary;
for a moment he was the four-faced Brahmā, the best among the wise and established in contemplation;
and for a moment he was the very embodiment of Dharma, and for a moment the form of Śeṣa.
At one moment he has the form of the sun, the eternal embodiment of light;
at another moment he is rich in supreme beauty, surpassing ten million Cupids,
desirable to women, amorous, and united with desire.
Seeing the infant in such a state, O Nārada, she placed him upon her breast on a beautiful jewel-encrusted lion-throne given by Nanda.
With her body covered in horripilation, she circumambulated him with devotion.
Having bowed his head to the ground, he praised Puruṣottama.
Akrūra said: "Salutations to the one whose form is the cause, whose nature is the Supreme Self."
Salutations again and again to the Lord of all the universes;
to the Supreme Lord beyond primordial nature, and even higher than the highest.
Salutations to the one who is devoid of qualities, free from desire, formless, yet the very embodiment of his own true nature.
To the one who possesses the nature of all gods, and to the lord of all gods;
to the supreme god of all gods, whose form is the primordial source of the universe;
and to the one who consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva within all beings that are beyond doubt.
Salutations to the one whose own nature is the primordial seed-syllable, who possesses the universal form of that Lord;
salutations to the Lord of the cowherd women, who takes the form of the Lord of Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to the Lord of the hosts of gods, salutations again and again to the Lord of Rādhā.
To him whose form is Rādhā’s lover, and who himself assumes the form of Rādhā;
to him who is worshipped by Rādhā, and who is dearer to her than her own life-breath;
to him who is to be attained through Rādhā, and who is the most beloved deity presiding over Rādhā.
Salutations to You, the supreme deity of Rādhā’s life-breath, whose form is the universe;
salutations to the one praised by the Vedas, who embodies the knower of the self and the Vedas, the omniscient one.
Salutations to You, the presiding deity of the Vedas, the seed of the Vedas.

Salutations again and again to the Great Viṣṇu, the Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, in whose hairs all things— both numbered and unnumbered— reside eternally; salutations to Him who is Himself the form of primordial nature (prakṛti) and who is both transcendent and immanent within that nature.
Having thus offered praise to the one whose form is both primordial nature and the Lord, and who is both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, he fell into a swoon upon the floor of the assembly hall.
He suddenly fell to the ground, and then he beheld the Lord once again.
Seeing the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign, who exists both outside and within the heart;
who is dark-hued on all sides, who dwells in the universe and is indeed the universe itself;
and seeing Akrūra unconscious, Nanda looked upon him with great reverence.
O Nārada, he seated him upon a beautiful jeweled throne and asked about the entire account: "What indeed have you seen?
He then fed him sweet food and repeatedly inquired after his welfare.
Akrūra related the desired account of Kaṃsa’s conduct and the departure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa for the sake of liberating their parents.
Whoever recites this hymn composed by Akrūra with a well-concentrated mind, [attains the highest goal].
One without a son obtains a son; one without a wife obtains a beloved; the poor man acquires wealth; and one without land obtains fertile earth.
One whose children have perished gains offspring, and one who lacks stability attains firm standing. (72)
Even one who is infamous effortlessly attains vast renown.
Then, at the proper time, with his mind supremely delighted, he fell asleep upon a beautiful bed of *campaka* flowers, having placed Kṛṣṇa upon his own chest.
Rising early in the morning and having quickly performed the unsurpassed fire-ritual (*agnikārya*),
he placed Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the lords of the universe, upon his own chariot;
[he also offered] the fivefold products of the cow and various other very rare substances.
Vṛṣabhāna, Nanda, Sunanda, and Candrabhānaka;
and various kinds of musical instruments, such as the mṛdaṅga, muraja, and others; as well as the paṭaha, paṇava, ḍhakkā, dundubhi, and ānaka. (76–77)
Nandagopa, the lord of Vraja, joyfully played the *sajjā*, the *saṃnahanī*, the *kāṃsyapaṭṭa*, the *mardala*, and the *maṇḍavī*.
And hearing that music, the gopīs [learned] of the departure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa standing upon his chariot, they approached him, oppressed by anger.
O twice-born one, though all were forbidden by Kṛṣṇa, they were incited by Rādhā;
with playful ease, they shattered the Lord’s chariot with the stamping of their feet.
There, while all the cowherd leaders raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!", the powerful women went forth, placing Kṛṣṇa upon their own breasts;
one woman, out of anger, rebuked that cruel Akrūra.
Some, having tied a cloth around his neck, departed from there;
another struck him with her hand and its bracelet,
and having stripped him naked, O Sage, she caused that garment to fall away.
Seeing Akrūra with all his limbs wounded and mangled,
Mādhava went to the side of Rādhā and again enlightened her through spiritual yoga and respectful humility. (84)
He awakened Akrūra, and he awakened her again.
Hari saw before him a divine chariot sent forth by Sanātana, which had descended from the sky and was adorned with variegated cloths. (85–86)
Having seen that [palace], which was inlaid with the finest jewels and fashioned by Viśvakarman, the Lord of the World went to the abode of his mother.
Having eaten, drunk, and slept comfortably, the Blessed One remained there together with his kinsmen.
He remained there, honored by the lords of sages, Indra, Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa.
O Nārada, all the gopīs, their minds filled with supreme joy, slept upon a beautiful bed of flowers together with Rādhā.
And all the people residing in Gokula were filled with bliss;
some cowherds danced, while others were intent upon music.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Episode Concerning the Cowherd Women," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the seventy-first chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: While Rādhikā was asleep and the gopīs were also sleeping...
On a bed of flowers and sandalwood made fragrant by the breeze,
when the third watch of the night had passed and at an auspicious moment,
during a favorable conjunction of the moon and the lunar mansions, and endowed with the *amṛta-yoga*.
When the ascendant was conjoined with and aspected by benefic planets,
and was free from the evil defects associated with malefic planets,
Yaśodā awakened [the child] and caused auspicious rites to be performed. (3)
Hari himself arose and consoled his kinsmen.
Fearing Rādhikā, he prohibited the music,
even though he was the independent creator of the universe, its protector, and its sustainer, acting as if he were subject to her will.
Having washed his two feet and put on two clean garments,
he sat in a consecrated place smeared with sandalwood paste and other substances.
[The vessel] was prepared with sandalwood and the like, and provided with fruits and sprouts.
Having placed a full water-pot to his left, and fire and a Brahmin to his right;
likewise, a woman with her husband and sons, a lamp, and a mirror in front;
as well as a very glossy blade of dūrvā grass, flowers, and auspicious white grain.
Having taken what was given by his guru, he placed it upon his head;
he saw that the honey-wine (mādhvīka) had become silver, the curd gold, the sandalwood paste an ointment, and the flower garland placed around his neck [transformed]. (9)
With devotion, he paid homage to the assembly of gurus and the brahmins.
With supreme respect, he listened to the sound of conch shells, the recitation of the Vedas, music, the auspicious eightfold hymns, and the delightful benedictions of the brahmins.
Having meditated upon that auspicious form which bestows auspiciousness everywhere,
the Lord placed his beautiful right foot, which was his own very embodiment.
Holding the left side of his nose with his middle finger, the All-pervading One—
Having fully expelled the breath through the right nostril, Nandananda then went to the excellent courtyard of Nanda;
he was full of joy, supreme bliss, eternal, and everlasting. (13–14)
He is eternal, yet appearing as both eternal and non-eternal; his essential nature is eternally radiant, and his form is eternal.
He possesses eternal limbs, is the eternal Lord, and is expert in eternal duties.
His appearance is eternally fresh, and his youth is eternally renewed.
His attire is ever-new, and he is ever-new in age;
his conversation is ever-new, and his love is ever-new.
His attainment is ever-new, and his good fortune is ever-new. (16–17)
His speech is as sweet as the essence of nectar and is eternally fresh;
His state is eternally fresh, and those who are devoted to Him are eternally fresh.
Having repeatedly stood upon this courtyard, the Lord of Māyā, endowed with Māyā, [remains here].
In that exceedingly beautiful place, he became very affectionate, yet intent on departing.
[The garden was] filled with clusters of plantain trunks accompanied by mango sprouts,
beautifully arranged and well-crafted, bound together with silk threads.
There, Kṛṣṇa himself stayed together with Akrūra and his kinsmen, in a place inlaid with rubies fashioned by Viśvakarman and beautifully adorned with sandalwood paste mixed with musk and saffron.
He was embraced on his left side by Yaśodā and by Māyā;
he was embraced on his right side by Nanda, who was filled with joy;
he was addressed by his kinsmen, and kissed by his father and mother.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Auspicious Departure of Nārada," in the latter part of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great [Purāṇa], the Glory of the Birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Now begins the seventy-second chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O sage, Kṛṣṇa, having bowed to his preceptor and departed from the camp,
ascended his celestial vehicle and went to the auspicious city of Mathurā.

Having conquered the beautiful and enchanting city of Indra, which was endowed with splendor and inlaid with the finest jewels and fashioned by Viśvakarman, he entered the lovely Mathurā together with the hosts of Akrūra.
It shone, resplendent with priceless jeweled jars;
it was encircled by hundreds of excellent, beautiful royal roads,
refined with moon-shaped gems of lunar essence.
It was adorned with hundreds of market-streets fashioned from various excellent gems,
graced by eminent merchants endowed with meritorious goods,
and beautified on all sides by thousands of lakes.
It was adorned by throngs of lotus-like women who resembled pure crystal, were radiant with rubies,
and were enriched with ornaments of precious gems;
they possessed perpetual youth and were supreme, being devoid of even a blink of an eye.
With faces turned upward and syllables [of praise] on their lips, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa;
with playful movements of their eyebrows and eyes that were perpetually flickering;
ever filled with desire, they possessed full hips and breasts.
[It was filled] with those of delicate limbs, with slender waists, and skilled in the delights of love;
it was adorned with tens of millions of vehicles fashioned from jewels,
and with women decorated with ornaments and variegated paintings.
It was endowed with various kinds of splendor through thirty million flower gardens,
which were filled with various blossoming flowers that delighted the slayers of Madhu;
these were joined by bees, greedy for honey and filled with joy, who were united with the sweetness of spring honey.
It was filled with swarms of female bees intoxicated by honeyed wine;
it was difficult for hosts of enemies to traverse due to its various kinds of fortifications;
and it resounded with the cries of guards who were constantly experts in the science of protection.
It was joined with three-storied towers and was exceedingly beautiful,
fashioned indeed by Viśvakarman with various excellent jewels.
Having seen Mathurā in such a state, the lotus-eyed one—
On the road he saw that hunchbacked woman, aged, exceedingly wretched, and extremely miserable;
walking with the aid of a staff, she was deeply bent and possessed of sagging folds of skin;
parched and deformed in appearance, yet she bore an ointment of sandalwood paste. (15–16)
O Nārada, upon merely touching him who was smeared with musk and saffron,
fragrant with honey-like scent, rich in fragrance, and most enchanting,
the elderly woman looked at the peaceful Lord, the beloved of Śrī, and smiled. (17)

Having suddenly prostrated with her head before Him— the one endowed with glory, the abode of Śrī, the seed of Śrī, and the sanctuary of Śrī— she, bowing low with devotion and palms joined in reverence,
applied sandalwood paste to His dark and beautiful body.
With golden vessels in her hands, she touched the limbs of Kṛṣṇa and his attendants; having performed a circumambulation of Kṛṣṇa, she bowed down again and again.
By the mere sight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she became endowed with splendor.
Suddenly, there appeared a woman as beautiful as Śrī, lovely in form and youth.
(21) Clad in garments of pure white silk and adorned with jewel ornaments, she was like a blessed and captivating maiden of twelve years. (22)
With bimba-like lips, smiling, dark-complexioned, and resembling molten gold;
with beautiful hips, lovely teeth, and breasts like bilva fruits;
she shone, adorned with a magnificent necklace fashioned from priceless gems.
Moving with the gait of the king of elephants, adorned with jeweled anklets,
she bore a mass of braided hair encircled by garlands of *mālatī* flowers, which was protected on her left side and possessed a beautiful, rounded shape. (24–25)
Wearing a dot of vermilion in the shape of a pomegranate flower,
with a dot of musk above it along with half-moon-shaped dots of sandalwood paste,
and holding a shining mirror in her hand— she is highly praised for acts of love.
She chose Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the corners of her restless eyes.
(27) Śrīvāsa, having consoled her, went to another supreme place;
she, having fulfilled her purpose, went with love to the abode of Padmā [Lakṣmī]. (28)
He beheld his own abode, which was like the palace of Pādyālayā; it was fashioned from the finest essence of excellent jewels and constructed with jeweled couches.
It shone, illuminated by rows of radiant jewel-lamps.
It was resplendent on all sides with rows of jewel-mirrors (30).
It was surrounded by female attendants carrying vermilion, garments, betel, white chowries, and garlands, as well as by throngs of male servants (31).
Having gone there and eaten delicious food with great joy,
she slept upon a jeweled couch attended by her maidservants;
she partook of betel-leaf mixed with camphor, musk, and saffron.
The virtuous woman placed sandalwood upon her own bed for Hari;
she also set near him a pair of jasmine garlands, water scented with camphor and other fragrances,
cool and sweet water, and delicious food.

O sage, she who was longing for him, constantly perceived the world as being entirely composed of Kṛṣṇa; with her actions, mind, and speech, she meditated upon the feet of Hari, as well as upon Hari’s arrival and his enchanting moon-like face. (35)
He possessed the playful charm of ten million Cupids, was devoted to love, and was full of desire.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa saw that captivating florist, carrying a multitude of garlands, as he was walking toward the royal palace. (36–37)
He too, having seen the Beloved of Śrī, prostrated himself with his head upon the ground and offered a multitude of garlands to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
Kṛṣṇa granted him a boon: the state of being His servant, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Taking the garland, the excellent suitor set out upon the royal road.
There he saw a washerman carrying a bundle of clothes; he was arrogant, powerful, and constantly intoxicated by his youth. (39–40)
O great sage, Kṛṣṇa requested a garment from him with humility;
however, he did not give him the garment and spoke to him harshly:
"This garment, which is very difficult to obtain, is suitable for cowherds like you. (41)
O fool, O lover of the cowherd folk!
Having taken the daughters of the cowherds, O lecherous libertine, you engaged in your dalliances there in the forest of Vṛndāvana, which was then without a king. (42–43)
"And there was no such deed for King Kaṃsa to follow in this matter;
here stands the lord of kings, the punisher of the wicked, right at that moment.
Having heard the words of the washerman, Madhusūdana laughed.
Baladeva, along with Akrūra and the group of cowherds, laughed.
Having struck him with his palm, Śrī Kṛṣṇa seized the bundle of clothes; thus, together with his companions, he put on the garment.

And the king of washermen, having assumed a divine body— eternally endowed with youth, excellent, and removing both old age and death— departed on a jeweled vehicle surrounded by a retinue of attendants. (47)
Clad in yellow garments, smiling, and darkly handsome, he too became an attendant among the attendants in Goloka;
self-controlled, he constantly remembered Kṛṣṇa’s arrival there. (48–49)
Although the sun had set, Akrūra went to his own home;
and having obtained Kṛṣṇa’s permission, Kṛṣṇa also went to the house of a certain Vaiṣṇava weaver who was destitute.
Accompanied by Nanda, together with Ānanda, and joined by Baladeva and others,
that devotee bowed down and worshiped the Abode of Śrī.
He granted him his own state of servitude— a boon difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to attain.
Having eaten the finest sweet food, they all slept upon the couch;
that hunchbacked woman also obtained sleep, and the Lord of Sleep (Viṣṇu) too went there with joy.
Having gone there, he saw the hunchbacked woman sleeping on the bed of jewels.
Surrounded by groups of maidservants like the beautiful Kamalā,
Kṛṣṇa awakened her, even though the maidservants were still asleep.
The Lord of the World spoke to that virtuous woman, the beloved of the Lord of the World.
The Blessed Lord said: "O illustrious one, abandon sleep; O beautiful lady, bestow your grace.
In former times, you were Śūrpaṇakhā, the sister of Rāvaṇa. (56)
"O beloved, you performed penance for my sake at the time of Rāma’s birth.
By the power of that penance, enjoy me as your husband at the time of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s birth.
Now, having united with me in happiness, go to my abode."
"And Goloka is most difficult to attain, the supreme remover of old age and death.
Having spoken thus, Śrīnivāsa placed her upon his chest,
stripped her naked, and kissed that amorous woman as he adorned her with love.
Smiling, yet bashful from their first union, she kissed Śrī Kṛṣṇa on the cheek; he held her to his chest just as Kamalā does.
For the couple, both experts in the arts of love, there was no end to their dalliance.
O Nārada, various kinds of amorous play took place there.
The Blessed One wounded her pair of breasts and hips with his sharp fingernails, and bit her excellent lower lip with his teeth.
At the time of the night's end, he performed the act of procreation;
through the enjoyment of their mutual pleasure, Sundarī fell into a swoon.
There, languor came upon her as she lay upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest.
She perceived neither day nor night, heaven nor mortal earth, water nor land.
(64) And the night became a beautiful dawn; yet the lord of the night grew dim, as if out of shame at his husband’s transgression. (65)
Then a chariot fashioned from jewels arrived from Goloka;
holding her divine body, he went to that world [with her].
She was as pure as fire, possessed a beautiful form, and was adorned with jewel ornaments.

O sage, she became a cowherd girl there with a face like the moon, possessing the luster of molten gold and eternally free from birth and other such states. And how many cowherd girls became her attendants?
The Blessed One also, having stayed there for a moment, went to his own abode, where Nanda and the Joy of Nanda were full of delight.
Then, during the night, Kaṃsa was overwhelmed with fear while asleep.
He beheld a most painful and evil dream that portended his own death.
O Sage, he saw the sun fallen from the sky onto the earth in four fragments;
he saw the orb of the moon fallen from the sky onto the earth in ten fragments.
Men of deformed appearance with ropes in their hands and naked;
a widow, the wife of a Śūdra, and a naked woman with a severed nose;
laughing, wearing a cosmetic mark of powder, and having high hair that is white and black.
Holding a sword and a skull-bowl in her hands, with a flickering tongue,
she is adorned with a garland of severed heads; [she rides] a donkey, a buffalo, a bull,
a bear, a boar, a crow, a vulture, a crane, and a monkey.
A dustless dog, a crocodile, a jackal, a heap of ashes, a pile of bones, a palmyra fruit, hair, and an abundance of cotton;
a extinguished ember, a skull, and a corpse resting upon a funeral pyre. (75)
The wheel of a potter, oil-pressers, and coin-minters; a crooked cowrie shell;
a cremation ground, burnt wood, dry wood, a thorn, and grass;
a moving headless trunk, and a shouting severed head—[these are inauspicious]. (76–77)
A burnt site with ashes, a pond devoid of water, scorched fish, iron, a forest consumed by fire,
a man suffering from oozing leprosy, a low-born man, one who is naked, and one whose hair has been shorn. (78)
Seeing such a brahmin who was excessively angry and cursing his guru,
as well as a mendicant, a yogi, and a Vaiṣṇava man who were likewise exceedingly enraged,
he rose up and spoke to his mother.
We had a palanquin prepared for his father, brother, and wife—who were weeping and overwhelmed with love—and placed them upon it; we also had the elephant stationed there.
Furthermore, we had the army of wrestlers and the combatants perform auspicious rites.
He caused a meritorious, auspicious, and propitious assembly hall to be constructed.
With great effort, he appointed a priest skilled in yoga.
Holding a remarkable sword, he stayed upon a beautiful couch.
He deployed warriors skilled in combat into the fray;
he settled the lords of kings, as well as Brahmins and great sages.
And the Brahmins [settled] circles of friends who were most righteous and skilled in battle.
Then Govinda arrived there with Rāma, O Nārada;
he effortlessly broke the middle of Maheśa’s bow,
and by its sound, Mathurā indeed became deafened.
Kaṃsa fell into despair, while the son of Devakī attained joy;
having entered the midst of the assembly and slain the elephant-athlete, the Yogi beheld that Lord, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign. (87)
Just as he resides within the lotus of the heart, so too does he exist externally;
in the form of a sovereign king, he is the ruler who wields the rod of punishment over kings.
Just as a father and mother [protect] an infant with milk on its face, one who is still blind to the breast.
The amorous women saw him as possessing a beauty that surpassed even the playfulness of ten million Cupids;
Kaṃsa saw him as the personification of Death, his kinsmen as their enemy,
the wrestlers as the bringer of death, and the Yādavas as one equal to their own life-breath.
Having paid obeisance to the sages, the brahmins, his father, mother, and guru,
he went toward Mañcakāmyā, taking Sudarśana by the hand.
Seeing his devotee, the friend of devotees and ocean of mercy, out of compassion—
O Sage, having dragged Kaṅka from his bed, he killed him with ease.
Then the king beheld the entire universe as being supremely composed of Kṛṣṇa,
and before him, a chariot made of jewels and adorned with necklaces of diamonds.
Having assumed a divine form, he went to the realm of Viṣṇu;
O Sage, his effulgence entered the supreme lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Having returned, he honored the brāhmaṇas and gave them land.
He gave the kingdom and the royal parasol to the wise Ugrasena. He became the lord of kings, born of the Lunar dynasty.
Kaṃsa’s mother, his wife, and his father all lamented.
"O Indra among kings, grant an audience to your kinsmen, your mother’s kin, your sister, and your brother’s wife! Arise upon your royal throne!
Protect the kingdom, protect your wealth, your kin, and your army! (97)
"Where are you going, O one of great strength, abandoning us who are without a protector?
He who, as a mere play, creates the entire universe—countless and extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—and who is the support of all things moving and unmoving. (98–99)
Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, Dharma, the Sun, Gaṇeśvara,
the host of great sages, and the Lord of the Gods meditate upon Yama day and night.
Kṛṣṇa praises him whom the Vedas laud, while Sarasvatī praises him in fear.
He whom Nature, being delighted, praises—He who is beyond Nature, though appearing as Nature; who consists of His own will, is devoid of effort, free from qualities, and stainless;
the Brahman higher than the highest, the Supreme Self, the Lord. (101–102)
He is the eternal light by nature, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon devotees;
he is eternal bliss, eternally present, and his form is eternally imperishable.
Indeed, that Blessed Lord has descended for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden.
The Lord of Māyā, the Master, assumes the guise of a cowherd boy through his illusory power.
(104) He who is the Lord of all destroys whomsoever [he will]; what man can protect him?
He who is the Soul of all protects whomsoever [he will]; no one can slay him. (105)
Having spoken thus, O great sage, everyone fell silent;
he fed the brahmins and gave them all his wealth.
Then the Blessed One, the soul of all, went into the presence of his father.
And with his mind, he released the iron shackles from the two of them.
He prostrated like a staff upon the ground before his mother and father;
then, with his neck bowed in devotion, the lord of gods praised them with piety.
The Blessed Lord said:
That man who does not support his father, mother, teacher, or the one who gave him knowledge and mantras for as long as he lives is impure. (109)
Among all those worthy of worship, the father is the venerable and great preceptor;
yet the mother is a hundred times more so than the father, because she bears and nourishes the child in her womb.
Furthermore, the mother is like the earth and is the one who desires the welfare of all.

On this earth, there is no kinsman superior to a mother for anyone. (111) One who bestows knowledge and mantras is more venerable than a mother; indeed, according to the Vedas, there is no one else in the world more worthy of salutation or worship than him. (112)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balabhadra bowed down; O Sage, their mother and father both affectionately took them onto their laps. Then he fed the Brāhmaṇas with the finest sweet foods.
With joy, he gave the Vasu and the collection of Vasus to the Brāhmaṇas.

(114) Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Killing of Kaṃsa and the Liberation of Vasudeva and Devakī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma... Mahā... Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa... [concerning] Nārada’s narration.
Now begins the seventy-third chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: Then Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma joyfully consoled their father Nanda, who was afflicted by grief, with divine discourses on spiritual matters and the like.
To him who was weeping loudly, motionless, and distressed by the loss of his son,
the Lord of the World gave that most excellent jewel and spoke as follows. The Blessed One said:
Understand this with joy, O Nanda; abandon sorrow and attain delight.
Accept the knowledge given by me, which was formerly bestowed upon Brahmā.
Whatever has been given for the sake of drying up [the world] has been given to Gaṇeśa and Īśvara.
To Dineśa, Munīśa, and Yogīśa at Puṣkara:
|| 4 || Who is whose son? Who is whose father? Who is whose mother? And from where does anyone come?
They enter and exit the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) solely by virtue of their own performed actions (karma). || 5 ||
A living being is born according to its karma and according to the distinctions of place;
by virtue of karma, some being is born among the wives of the lords of yogis, among the wives of brahmins, among kṣatriyas, among vaiśyas, or in the wombs of śūdras. (6)
Some among the animal wombs, and some among the wombs of beasts and the like— 7—
all these, by my very *māyā*, are full of joy in sense objects,
yet they are despondent at the time of casting off the body and at the separation from kinsmen. 8.
The loss of progeny, land, wealth, and so forth is worse than death;
yet the fool is constantly [distressed by it], while the wise man is not joined with such grief.
My devotee, endowed with devotion, worshipping me, and having conquered his senses— || 9 ||
A devotee of my mantra, intent on service to me and pure—
through fear of me this wind blows, the sun shines eternally,
the moon and Mahendra shine, and he rains at the proper time. (10–11)
Fire carries [the heat] and death indeed moves among living beings;
the tree bears flowers and fruits in due time.
The wind is without support, and the belly is supported by the wind.
And Śeṣa has the tortoise as his support, and the mountain has Śeṣa as its support.
The seven netherworlds (pātālas) indeed rest upon that [mountain] in successive layers.
Consequently, the water is motionless, and the earth rests upon that water.
The support of the seven heavens and the earth, the circle of light that is the abode of the planets,
the supportless Vaikuṇṭha which is superior to the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas),
and even beyond that is Goloka, fifty million yojanas away.
It was elevated and without support, fashioned from the essence of jewels;
it had seven gates, seven essences, and was provided with seven moats;
it was endowed with a hundred thousand walls and accompanied by the river Virajā.
It was encircled by a beautiful mountain of jewels with a hundred peaks;
one of its radiant peaks measured ten thousand *yojanas*,
while the mountain itself rose up to a height of a hundred *koṭis* of *yojanas*.
Its length is a hundredfold, and its circumference is one hundred thousand yojanas.
Right there, the Rāsa-maṇḍala extends for ten thousand yojanas;
it is fashioned from priceless jewels, circular, and like the orb of the moon.
It was surrounded by a blossoming *pārijāta* grove,
as well as by thousands of *kalpa* trees and hundreds of flowering gardens;
it was further graced by various kinds of beautiful flowering trees in full bloom.
It was a palace with three million jewels, guarded by hundreds of thousands of cowherd women;
it was provided with jewel-lamps and furnished with jeweled couches,
endowed with various objects of enjoyment, and surrounded by hundreds of excellent ponds.
Endowed with a lake of nectar and possessed of all objects of desire,
he is skilled in describing the dimensions of the abode of Goloka;
neither any learned man nor even a knower of the Vedas knows the Lord of Vraja.
The supreme abode of Rādhā was beautiful, charming, and delightful, adorned with thirty million palaces fashioned from priceless jewels;
it was radiant with jars of priceless gems and mirrors of precious stones. (25–26)
It shone with rows of the luster of priceless gems,
and was adorned with various wonderful and variegated white chowries;
it was set with rubies and pearls, and endowed with settings of diamonds.
It was graced with jewel-lamps and made beautiful by jeweled stairways;
it shone with rows of couches adorned with priceless jewel-leaf ornaments, and was further embellished by three variegated panels inlaid with priceless jewels. (28–29)
It was provided with three moats and three difficult-to-access gates,
joined by sixteen enclosures (kakṣās) at each interval between the gates;
and it was manned here and there by sixteen lakhs of gopīs stationed for duty.

The excellent inner chamber was filled with a multitude of Rādhikā’s handmaidens, who wore garments as pure as fire, were adorned with jewel ornaments, possessed a complexion like molten gold, and were graced by hundreds of moons. (31–32)
The courtyard was exquisitely beautiful, fashioned from priceless jewels, and graced by clusters of pillars made of priceless gems.
It was further adorned with auspicious jars of jewels, filled with fruits and sprouts. (33)
It was joined with jeweled pedestals and adorned with desired pearl ornaments;
oh, it was beautified by exquisite mirrors made of priceless gems! It was the most excellent house among dwellings, constructed from priceless jewels. (34–35)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and served by millions of cowherd girls, she is enriched with the splendor of ten million full moons and resembles a white campaka flower;
she is adorned with ornaments fashioned from priceless gems.
Wearing garments of priceless jewels and holding a jeweled mirror,
she carries a beautiful jewel-lotus in her right hand and a most enchanting, vermilion mark shaped like a pomegranate flower in her left hand. (37–38)
She was beautifully adorned with desired drops of sandalwood paste and musk, bearing a mass of braided hair decorated with *mālatī* garlands;
she was the enchanting creation of the left half of the lords of sages. (39)

In such a state, Rādhā was there attended by the gopīs on all sides— gopīs who were her equals, holding white chowries in their hands and adorned with ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels. || 40–41 ||
She who is the presiding deity of my life-breath, the most excellent and best among goddesses,
she who was the daughter of Sudāman has now become the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu due to a curse;
for her separation from me shall last for one hundred years.
"O Father, by that you shall effect the removal of the earth's burden.
Then, together with her, with Yaśodā, and also with the cows and the gopīs, I shall certainly go to Goloka. (43–44)
"Thus you shall speak joyfully to Nanda and Yaśodā, along with Vṛṣabhānu, his wife Kalāvatī, and their kinsmen:
'O illustrious one, abandon your grief; go to Vraja together with the inhabitants of Vraja.'"
I am the Self and the witness, untainted among all living beings.
It is universally agreed that the individual soul (jīva) is my reflection;
and while Prakṛti is a modification of me, I myself am that very Prakṛti. || 46–47 ||
Just as whiteness is in milk, and there is no difference between the two;
just as coldness is in water, and burning power is in fire;
just as sound is in space, so too, O King, is fragrance in the earth. (48)

Just as there is beauty in the moon and radiance in the sun, and just as there is light in a lamp, so too am I the Self together with Rādhā. Abandon the notion that I am a gopī; [abandon] the idea of being my son toward Rādhā.
I am the power of all, and she is Nature, the sovereign.
Listen with joy, O Nanda, to my glory-bringing majesty,
which was formerly described by me to Brahmā, whose birth is manifest, my dear.
I am Kṛṣṇa among the gods, manifesting myself with two arms in Goloka;
I am four-armed in Vaikuṇṭha, and I am Śiva himself in the world of Śiva.
In the world of Brahmā I am Brahmā, and I am the Sun among the luminous bodies.
Among purifiers I am the fire, and among liquids I am water;
among the senses I am the mind, and among those that move swiftly I am the wind.
Among the dispensers of punishment I am Yama, and among reckoners of time I am Time.
Among letters, I am the letter *a*; among Sāman chants, I am the Sāman itself.
(55) Among the fourteen Indras, I am Indra; among the wealthy, I am Kubera. Among the lords of the directions, I am Īśāna; and among the pervasive, I am the sky. (56)
I am the inner soul within all living beings, the Brāhmaṇa among the stages of life (āśramas),
and the priceless jewel among riches, difficult to obtain at all times.
Among luminous things I am gold, and among gems I am the Kaustubha itself.
Among the Vaiṣṇavas I am Kumāra; among the lords of yogis, I am Gaṇeśvara.
Among flowers I am the Pārijāta; among sacred fords, I am Puṣkara itself.
Likewise, among objects worthy of worship I am the Śālagrāma, and among leaves, I am the Tulasī.
Among generals I am Skanda; among archers I am Lakṣmaṇa;
among lordly kings I am Rāma; and among the stars I am the Moon.
Among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons I am Mādhava.
Among the days of the week, I am Sunday; among the lunar days, I am the eleventh (Ekādaśī).
Among those who endure, I am the Earth; and among kinsmen, I am the Mother.
Among things to be eaten, I am nectar; and likewise, among products of the cow, I am clarified butter (ghee).
Among trees, I am the Kalpavṛkṣa; among wish-fulfilling cows, I am Surabhi;
among rivers, I am Gaṅgā, who destroys committed sins.
Among the learned, I am Vāṇī; and likewise, among mantras, I am the Praṇava.
