Among the sciences, I am the seed-form; among crops, I am the grain itself. Among fruit-bearing trees, I am the Aśvattha; among teachers, I am the giver of mantras himself. Likewise, among the lords of progeny, I am Kaśyapa; and among birds, I am Garuḍa. (64–65)
I am Ananta among the Nāgas and the sovereign of men;
among the Brahman-sages I am Bhṛgu, and among the divine sages I am Nārada.
Among the royal sages I am Janaka, and likewise, among the great sages I am Śuka.
Among the Gandharvas I am Citraratha; among the Siddhas, the sage Kapila.
Among the intelligent I am Bṛhaspati, and among poets, Śukra himself. Among the planets I am Śani, and among artisans, Viśvakarman.
Among deer I am the king of beasts; among bulls, the vehicle of Śiva;
among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among meters, I am the Gāyatrī. Among all the Vedas and scriptures, I am the Vedas; and among aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa.
Urvashi is the foremost among the Apsarases, just as the ocean is among bodies of water;
Sumeru is the foremost among mountains, and the Himalaya among those rich in jewels;
and Durga is the foremost among all goddesses, just as Kamalalaya (Lakshmi) is among the Prakritis.
Śatarūpā is the foremost among women, and Rādhikā is the foremost among those dear to me;
Sāvitrī is certainly the foremost among virtuous wives, and she is the Mother of the Vedas.
Prahlāda is the foremost among the Daityas, and Bali himself is the foremost among the most powerful.
The venerable sage Nārāyaṇa was the foremost among the wise;
Hanumān among the monkeys; Dhanañjaya among the Pāṇḍavas; and Droṇa alone was the foremost among the daughters of the Nāgas and the Vasus by virtue of his mind.
Among clouds I am the rain-cloud, and among ages I am the Kali-yuga, O Bhārata;
among lovers I am Kāmadeva, and among lustful women I am Rambhā.
And among worlds I am Goloka, the most excellent, transcending all.
Among the Mātṛkās I am Peace, and among beautiful women I am Rati;
among witnesses I am Dharma, and among the watches of the day I am the twilight.
Among the gods I am Māhendra, and among the Rākṣasas I am Vibhīṣaṇa.
Among the Rudras, I am Kālāgnirudra; among the Bhairavas, I am Saṃhāra;
among conch shells, I am Pāñcajanya; and among limbs, I am the head.
Among the Purāṇas and Sūtras, I am the excellent Bhāgavata.
Among the Itihāsas I am the Bhārata, and among the Pañcarātras I am the Kāpila [system].
Among the Manus I am Svāyambhuva, and among the sages I am Vyāsadeva. I am Svadhā among the wives of the Pitṛs, and I am Svāhā among the beloved wives of the Vasus.
Among sacrifices, I am the Nājasūya; among the wives of sacrificers, I am the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Among those skilled in weapons and missiles, I am the great Rāma, son of Jamadagni. Among the reciters of the Purāṇas, I am Sūta; among those possessed of political wisdom, I am the sage Aṅgiras.
Among vows, I am the vow of Viṣṇu; among strengths, I am divine power alone.
Among herbs, I am dūrvā grass; among blades of grass, I am the kuśa grass. Among religious acts, I am truth; and among vessels of affection, I am a son, O dear one.
Among enemies, I am disease; likewise, among diseases, I am fever.
Among those devoted to me, I am known as my own service; and among boons, I am considered the best.
Among the stages of life, I am the householder; and among the discerning, I am the renunciant.
I am Sudarśana among weapons, and I am skillfulness among auspicious blessings;
I am great knowledge among sovereign powers, and dispassion toward pleasures; I am pleasant speech among things that cause joy, and the gift of one's own self among gifts.
Among accumulations, I am the practice of Dharma; among actions, I am the worship of Me.
Among severe austerities, I am austerity itself; and among fruits, I am liberation alone.
Among the eight supernatural powers, I am the power of irresistible will (prākāmya); and among cities, I am the city of Kāśī.
Among cities, Kāñcī is so; and that region where a Vaiṣṇava resides is likewise.
Among all gross substrates, I alone am the great Virāṭ;
and among all subtle things in the universe, I am eternally the supreme atom.

Of physicians, he was the two sons of Aśvinī; among medicinal herbs, he was the elixir (rasāyana); of those who know mantras, he was Dhanvantari; of those who cause the destruction [of enemies], he was Viṣāda;
of melodies, he was Meghamallāra; and among his beloved women, he was Kāmoda. (90)
Among my attendants, Śrīdāmā is I; among those who follow me, Uddhava is I.
Among domestic animals, I am the cow; and among forests, I am the sandalwood tree. Among the pure, I am the one sanctified by sacred fords (tīrtha); and among those free from fear, I am the Vaiṣṇava.
Indeed, there is no living being higher than a Vaiṣṇava, nor one who is a worshiper of my mantra.
I am in the form of the sprout within trees; I am the form within all things.
I abide eternally in all beings, and all abide in me.

Just as fruits exist in a tree and a sprout exists within those fruits, so too am I the form of all causes, yet there is no cause higher than Me. I am the sovereign of all; indeed, there is no lord even over Me, for I am the cause of all causes.
The wise declare that all seeds exist within all things;
yet sinful people, deluded by my *māyā*, do not know me.
They are possessed by sin, possessed of evil intellect, and deceived by fate.
I am the self of all living beings; I am their master, yet I am not honored by them myself. Wherever I am, there are my powers, and likewise hunger, thirst, and the rest.
When I depart from the human body, they likewise depart like followers.
"O Nanda, father of Vraja, having understood this knowledge, go to Vraja;
and speak of that Rādhā, Yaśodā, and the very nature of knowledge.
Having thus understood the knowledge, the Lord of Vraja departed together with his followers.
Having gone there, he spoke to those two excellent women.
And they all abandoned their grief through that great knowledge, O Nārada,
even though Kṛṣṇa is untainted, the lord of Māyā, yet engaged with Māyā.
Urged by Yaśodā, Nanda returned and praised Mādhava, the son of Nanda who is supreme bliss,
with a hymn from the Sāmaveda that had been composed by Brahmā in ancient times. (102)
Standing before his son, he wept again and again.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Liberation of Nanda and Others," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada’s arrival.
Now begins the seventy-fourth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: Śrī Kṛṣṇa is supreme bliss, the most perfect Lord, the Supreme Soul, the highest, and the one who bestows grace upon His devotees. (1)
The Lord, who removes the burden of the earth, who is beyond the material nature (prakṛti),
and who is higher than the highest, was worshiped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa.
Delighted upon hearing Nanda’s hymn of praise, the Lord of the universe spoke to him.
As he was coming from Gokula, distressed by the fever of separation, the Blessed Lord said:
"Go to Nanda's settlement, O Nanda; abandon your grief and delusion regarding this world."
Listen to the supreme truth, the highest knowledge, which cuts through the knot of sorrow.
(4) Air, earth, space, water, and fire as the fifth—these five elements are declared by the collections of Vedic scriptures to be eternal. (5)
O dear one, for all embodied beings, the body is composed of the five elements;
it is a false delusion, artificial, and permeated by illusion like a dream. The five elements constantly assume the form of a body for all of them.
That recognition takes the form of illusion and convention; it is of the nature of delusion.
(7) Who indeed belongs to whom, O dear one? What woman belongs to whom as a husband?
For all beings, there is constant wandering through many births due to their karma. (8)
By action a living being is born, and by action alone it perishes;
through action one encounters happiness, suffering, fear, and grief.
For whom is there birth in the heavens, and for whom in the abode of Brahmā?
In whom [is it] among Brahmins, or in whom among Kṣatriyas; or in whom among Vaiśyas and Śūdras?
(10) Or in whom among those who are very low, or in whom among worms and excrement?
Or in whom among beasts and birds, or in whom among small creatures? (11)
O dear one, all wander again and again due to their own karma;
however, my devotee, who is always dear to me, renders karma rootless.
Truth, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—these constitute the four ages.
At the end of the age, there is the destruction of twenty-five thousand Manus.
The maximum lifespan of a Manu is established as equal to that of Mahendra.
The passing of fourteen Indras is said to constitute one day of Brahmā.
Thus has the night been measured and determined by those who know time;
thus have the months and the year been precisely fixed.
And the supreme lifespan of Brahmā has been established as one hundred years.
This time, at the dissolution of Brahmā, is but a mere moment for me.
Everything in the universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has been created by me.
I am the Truth, the Supreme Self, whose form consists of grace toward my devotees.
A true devotee of my mantra, having cast off his body upon this earth,
shall indeed go to Goloka, having severed his ancient karma.
Even when the countless Brahmās pass away, there shall be no falling for him.
He constantly assumes his own body, which destroys birth, death, and old age.
O Nanda, no inauspiciousness exists anywhere for my devotees;
that Sudarśana protects them perpetually on all sides.
For I am more powerful than your son; I have been meditated upon by you, while he has not.
I alone am his master, and neither my father nor my mother is his master.
Abandoning the notion that he is your son, worship me, who am the form of Brahman.
O Brahmin, go yourself to Goloka, which is free from the fetters of the mind.
Go to Yaśodā, the cowherd woman, and the hosts of cowherds;
with all those people, cast off your grief and return to your own abode.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One ceased speaking in the assembly.
Then Nanda, overflowing with bliss, questioned him once again.
Nanda said:
"Tell me the worldly knowledge by which I may attain your state;
I am deluded, O Supreme Bliss, for you are the progenitor of the Vedas.
Having heard these words of Nanda, the omniscient Lord himself—
"Tell me the daily ritual (*āhnika*) which has indeed not been heard by the Vedas.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Nanda and Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī Brahma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma Khaṇḍa*.
Now begins the seventy-fifth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Nanda, I shall proclaim most wonderful knowledge.
It is to be well-guarded, rare even in the Vedas and Purāṇas.
(1) For there can never be trust in women who are unchaste, who are like bolts barring the path to liberation, and who are mere delusions and illusions. (2)
O Lord of Vraja, among women who are unrighteous toward devotion to Hari— whether they are hostile, conciliatory, or merely the seed-forms of destruction—
one should always rise at dawn and cast off the garments worn during the night.
Having meditated with his mind upon his chosen deity in the heart-lotus and the supreme Guru in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
the wise one, having performed the morning rites with firm resolve,
bathes in pure waters.
The devotee, who cuts away his karma, forms no worldly resolve;
having bathed and performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), he remembers Hari and returns toward his home.
Having washed his feet and put on two clean garments, he should enter.
Worship me alone as the Supreme Self, the cause of liberation.
[Do so] especially in a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, an image, or even in water;
likewise in a Brahmin, a cow, and in one's gurus.
In a water-clock, an eight-petaled lotus, or a vessel made of sandalwood,
one should perform the invocation everywhere using water.
Having meditated upon me through meditation corresponding to the mantra, the observer of the vow should worship me.
One should devotedly offer the sixteen types of ritual articles with the root mantra.
One should worship the five cowherds: Śrīdāman, Mudāman, Vasudāman, Vīrabhānu, and Śūrabhānu. (10–11)
My attendants Sunanda, Nandaka, Kumuda, and Sudarśana;
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Rādhā, Gaṅgā, and Vasundharā;
as well as the Guru, Tulasī, Śambhu, Kārttikeya, and Vināyaka.
The wise person should worship the nine planets and the guardians of the directions all around (verse 13).
Having first worshipped the six deities who ward off obstacles,
he should worship Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā (verse 14).
One should worship the gods fashioned in the Śruti, who bestow liberation and sever the bonds of karma;
Gaṇeśa for the destruction of obstacles, and the Sun for the destruction of disease.
One should worship Agni for the sake of attainment; he will certainly become pure and peaceful.
The wise person should worship Viṣṇu for the sake of liberation, Śaṅkara for the sake of bestowing knowledge,
and Pārvatī for the sake of intelligence and release.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should recite one's own hymn of praise and the armor-verse (kavaca).
Having bowed to and fully worshipped the Guru, one should thereafter bow to the Deity.
Having performed the *āhnika* and worshipped as prescribed according to one’s inclination,
one should perform these duties enjoined by the Vedas for the purification of one's own self.
A wise man should not look upon excrement, which is the very nature of the seed of disease (19).
He should also avoid urine, which is the seed of disease and a supreme cause of hell;
and he should avoid the male organ and the female womb, which bestow sin, suffering, disease, and poverty (20).
The broad face, the breasts, the sidelong glances, and even the laughter of women—
these are the seeds of destruction and the constant cause of calamities.
One should avoid the enjoyment of one's own wives during the day and refrain from private conversation with them.

One should not look at the sky with only one pupil visible due to the fear of disease; this is the cause of ailments for the eyes and likewise for the ears. If, by chance, one sees such a sight, one should remember Hari and recite the name of Nārada seven times.
One should not look at the sun or the moon at the time of setting, for that is a cause of disease.
One should not look at the moon when it is eclipsed or partially risen, for that is a cause of disease.
Furthermore, having seen the sun or the moon reflected in water, a person shall incur grief.
One should not engage in excessive sexual intercourse, for it is the cause of the severance of one's kin.
(25) One should not share a bed, a dwelling, a meal, or travel with a sinner; all such things are signs of impending ruin. (26)
Through conversation, physical contact, sharing a bed, a seat, or food,
the wicked certainly spread about like a drop of oil upon water.
One should not go near predatory animals, for they are a cause of suffering.
One should not associate with a wicked person, for it is a cause of sorrow.
(28) One must never commit violence or cause harm toward Brahmins, cows, and especially Vaiṣṇavas; such acts are the cause of total destruction. (29)
One should not seize the wealth or property of gods, temples, Brahmins, or likewise of Vaiṣṇavas; for that is the cause of total destruction.
Whoever seizes the property of a Brahmin, whether given by himself or given by another, [incurs great sin].
For sixty thousand years he is born as a worm in excrement;
for a thousand crores of years he is a vulture; for a hundred births he is a pig;
for a hundred births he is a beast of prey; and for seven births he is a rhinoceros.
For seven lifetimes he becomes a horse, for five lifetimes a crocodile,
and for a hundred lifetimes he is certainly a worm in the womb of unchaste women;
furthermore, O Nārada, for a hundred lifetimes he becomes a worm in their sores.
For seven births he was a lizard, for seven births an ass;
for seven births a cat, and for three births a mongoose;
he was Uccaiḥśravas for a hundred births, and likewise a donkey.
He was a cruel serpent and a tiger for seven births;
a buffalo for seven births; a frog for a hundred births; and a goat for seven births.
He was a bear for a hundred births and a jackal for a hundred thousand births.
Then, by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one certainly becomes a leech;
and for a hundred years, those sinners who, having designated a gift for a Brahmin, do not give it at that very moment, are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
When one night has passed, that gift becomes twofold;
in a month it is said to be a hundredfold, and in two months a thousandfold.
But when a year has passed, that donor shall go to hell.
The fool is not given by the giver, nor does he beg as a recipient.
Both of them go to hell; the giver shall become afflicted with disease.
By committing violence against Brahmins, one will certainly suffer the destruction of one's lineage.
One who departs having abandoned wealth and fortune shall become a beggar;
he who, upon seeing the Lord Brahmā, does not bow down shall experience the grief of hell.
He who does not practice devotion to his guru shall experience the grief of Raurava.

That foolish woman of wicked conduct who does not behold her own husband as the form of Hari, having uttered threats against him, will certainly go to the Kumbhīpāka hell. By threatening with words she becomes a crow; by striking him she becomes a pig.
Through anger one becomes a serpent; through pride, one becomes a donkey;
through harsh speech, a dog; and through looking upon poison, one becomes blind.
A devoted wife, however, shall certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha together with her husband.
Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇapati, Sūrya, a brāhmaṇa, and a Vaiṣṇava—[these he should not revile].
That fool who reviles Viṣṇu shall go to the Mahāraurava hell.
Likewise, [he who reviles] his father, mother, son, virtuous wife, or teacher [shall go there].
Having reviled a helpless sister or daughter, one shall go to hell.
Those born of the *kṣatriya*, *vaiśya*, or *śūdra* castes who are devoid of devotion to Brahmins,
and those devoid of devotion to Hari, will certainly be cooked in Naraka.
Those who lack devotion and those who are unchaste young women are the lowest of men.
But those Brahmins who consume the water of the Śālagrāma and the remnants of Viṣṇu’s offerings purify a hundred generations of men on this earth.
A twice-born man who, being pure, eats meat after having duly honored the ancestors and the gods is blameless;
however, he who eats meat in vain shall go to the Mahāraurava hell.
And a twice-born man who has eaten fish out of desire must observe a fast.
Then one should perform an expiation and observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
O Nanda, that Brahmin who, weak in knowledge, eats fish out of desire,
remains perpetually impure and destroys his previously acquired merit.

He who eats the remnants of Viṣṇu’s meal and abstains from fish and meat certainly obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step. Those who observe the Ekādaśī fast and the Kṛṣṇa-janmāṣṭamī vow [attain the same].
They are liberated from the sins committed in a hundred births; there is no doubt about this.
Whatever misdeeds were committed in childhood, in youth, in old age, or in middle age, they reduce them all to ashes.

He who eats on the day of Ekādaśī while observing the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī vow undoubtedly incurs the sins produced by the three worlds. There is no restrictive rule for one who is ill, nor for the elderly or the young.
By giving double the amount of food to a Brahmin, one becomes pure.
He who eats on the night of Śivarātri or on the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī,
despite being capable of fasting, shall go to the Mahāraurava hell.
On the new moon, the full moon, the saṃkrānti, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days,
a man becomes born into the womb of a caṇḍāla by consuming oil and meat with a woman. Likewise,
[one becomes so] by eating fish, meat, and lentils from a bell-metal vessel.
One should avoid eating ginger and red leafy vegetables on Sundays;

otherwise, O Lord of Vraja, one goes without doubt to the Kumbhīpāka hell, as well as for consuming the food of a menstruating woman, the food of a prostitute, or the food of one who has drunk liquor.
The Brahmin who eats by chance from the food of a *viḍbhojī* will certainly become a *viḍbhojī* himself;
whatever ritual act he performs during that day, he shall not partake of its fruit.
He remains perpetually impure, and his period of birth-impurity lasts until his body is reduced to ashes.
A woman who goes to four men should be recognized as a prostitute.

(64) Furthermore, there shall be no eligibility for the ancestors or the gods regarding the food of those who sacrifice for an entire village, nor the food of those who eat at a Śrāddha ceremony performed by a Śūdra. (65)
Having eaten [the food of those who eat at a Śrāddha], the twice-born go to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure,
if they eat that food on the day of a Śrāddha for Śūdras;
they are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a hundred Brahmās.
He who, having been permitted by a Śūdra, eats elsewhere on the day of a Śrāddha ceremony,
should be known as a drinker of liquor, excluded from all religious duties.
[Likewise excluded are] one who lives by the sword, one who lives by ink, a temple-priest (Devala), and a bull-driver.
That twice-born man who burns the corpse of a Śūdra or who is the husband of a Śūdra woman should be excluded like a Śūdra; his food is equal to excrement in the eyes of the virtuous.
He who does not attend upon the morning twilight and he who does not worship the evening twilight [is likewise excluded].
He should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born like a Śūdra.
One who neglects the *saṃdhyā* is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever work he performs during the day, he shall not partake of its fruit.

And a Brahmin who worships Vāmamantras shall go to hell. A wise man should not discharge feces in the middle of a river, in a pit, at the root of a tree, near water, in the presence of a deity, or in a field of grain.
O Lord of Vraja, one should not take earth dug up by anthills or mice, nor earth from within water,
nor that which remains after purification, nor earth from a house used for smearing, nor earth containing living creatures or ants, nor earth turned up by a plow. (73–74)

O Nanda, one should avoid all these types of earth when performing purification: that which has risen from a water-trough, likewise that which has risen from a field of grain, that which has risen from the root of a tree, and likewise that which has risen from the bed of a river.
A woman who destroys a pumpkin-gourd and a man who extinguishes a lamp shall be diseased for seven births and remain poor birth after birth.
[One should not touch] a lamp, a Śiva-liṅga, a Śālagrāma stone, or likewise a gem.
Having cast upon the ground an image, a sacrificial thread, gold, a conch shell,
a diamond, as well as pearls, cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter,
and the water from a Śālagrāma stone, one should descend below.
Poor, wretched, leprous, lacking lineage, and even without a wife;
deprived of land, deprived of progeny, and deprived of kinsmen; despicable;
blind, lame, dwarfish, crippled, or indeed lacking limbs. (79–80)

He who abandons these on earth shall indeed become a sinner by degrees; he who indulges in sleep or sexual union with women during the day or at the two twilights shall be diseased for seven births and remain poor for seven births.

He who performs the cleansing of his teeth once the Lord of the World has risen—how can such a most sinful person say, "I worship Janārdana"? [Nor should he do so] with earth, ashes, cow-dung, cow-urine, or even with sand. (82–83)
Having made a *liṅga*, one who worships it even once shall dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas;
by worshipping it a thousand times, he too obtains his desired fruit.
And he who worships it a hundred thousand times certainly attains the state of Śiva.
The Brahmin who worships the Linga shall become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
A Brahmin devoid of the worship of Śiva shall go to hell.
Those men who revile Śiva, my most beloved, who is worshipped by me, [shall likewise suffer]. (85–86)
They are cooked in hell for as long as a hundred lifetimes of Brahmā,
even if a single grain of sand or a single hair has been offered to a Śiva-liṅga.
That great sinner shall become a Yavana [barbarian] because of that grain of sand or hair.
The term *kṣudra* may mean "miserly," "poor," "wretched," or "disease," as well as when used in a derogatory sense. (88) Among all things, the loss of honor occurs; one is born into low wombs.
Among all those who are worthy of affection, O Brahmā, I am dear to me. (89)
Lakṣmī is always dear to Brahmā and resides upon his chest;
Rādhā is dearer than she, and my devotees are dearer than she. Śaṅkara is dearer to me than those, and there is no one dearer to me than Śaṅkara.
"Mahādeva! Mahādeva! Mahādeva!"—thus the speaker cried out.
Afterwards, being fully satisfied by the longing to hear His name, he said:
"My mind is rooted in devotion, and my life-breaths are certainly centered on Rādhā. (91–92)
My self is Śaṅkara’s abode, and Śiva is dearer to me than life itself;
the primordial Śakti is Nārāyaṇī, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
And by her, as well as by whom [I am sustained], I bring forth the creation and the deities beginning with Brahmā.

That by which the universe is conquered and by which creation is brought forth—without which the world does not exist—that [power] has been granted by me to Śiva. It is compassion, sleep, hunger, satiety, thirst, faith, forgiveness, and fortitude. (94–95)
She is indeed the presiding deity of contentment, nourishment, peace, and modesty;
she is Mahālakṣmī in Vaikuṇṭha, the virtuous Rādhikā in Goloka,
Lakṣmī in the mortal world, and that very Satī who was the daughter of Dakṣa in the Ocean of Milk.
She is Durgā, the daughter of Menakā, the destroyer of the misfortune of the Daityas.
She is Durgā, the Fortune of Heaven, present in every house of Śakra and the other gods;
she is Vāṇī, she is Sāvitrī, the presiding deity of knowledge.
In fire, it is the power of burning; in the sun, the power of radiance;
in the full moon, the power of splendor; and in water, the power of coolness.
It is the power that produces crops and the power of support within the earths. (99)
She is the power of Brahminhood among the Brahmins, and the power of the gods among the deities;
she is the asceticism of the ascetics, and the household deity of the householders;
she is the power of liberation for the liberated, and she is the hope of the worldly man.
The power of devotion of my devotees always bestows devotion upon me;
she is the royal fortune of kings and the attainable form of wealth for merchants.
She is the essence of the three Vedas and the savior across the oceans of worldly existence.
Among the virtuous, she is the form of the intellect that perceives the real; she is the nature of the power of intelligence (medhā).
She is the power of exposition in the Vedas and the scriptures, and the power of generosity in givers.
Among the Kṣatriyas and others, she is devotion to Brahmins, and among chaste women, she is devotion to their husbands. (103–104)
Such is the power as it was given by me to Śiva.
Thus everything has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Whatever question you ask me, I shall explain all of that to you. (105)
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Conversation between Nārada and Yaśodā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the seventy-sixth chapter.
Nanda said:
O Lord of All, tell me all of this, for my curiosity to hear it is great: by the sight of whom does merit accrue, and by the sight of whom does sin? (1)
The Blessed Lord said: Upon seeing noble brāhmaṇas, sacred fords, and Vaiṣṇavas,
a man becomes as one who has beheld the images of the deities and bathed in sacred waters.
With devotion toward the sight of the sun, and likewise toward the sight of those possessed of wisdom;
and similarly toward renunciants, ascetics, and students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins);
with devotion toward cows, the sacrificial fires, and especially toward one's teachers.
Of lordly elephants and lions, and likewise of white horses;
of parrots and cuckoos, and likewise of wagtails; of swans and peacocks, of blue jays and conch-birds. (4–5)
Likewise, [the sight of] cows accompanied by their calves, *aśvattha* trees, men who have wives and sons, those traveling on pilgrimage,
lamps, gold, and especially jewels.
O noble-minded one, the sight of pearls, diamonds, rubies, tulasī, and white flowers destroys sin.
So too do fruits, white grains, ghee, curd, and honey. (7–8)
O King of kings, by seeing a full water-pot, parched grain, a mirror, water,
and a garland of white flowers, a person obtains merit. [Likewise] by seeing yellow pigment, camphor, silver, and a lake.

Having seen a flower garden and blossoming flowers, O Puṣya... || 10 || Having seen the moon of the bright fortnight, as well as nectar, sandalwood, musk, and saffron, O Nanda, [one obtains] merit. || 11 ||
Having seen a banner, an inexhaustible banyan tree, a tree risen from a deity, an auspicious temple,
a divine pool, and likewise a place where deities dwell, a divine staff, and a fragrant breeze— [one attains] merit. (12)
Upon seeing a conch shell and a drum, one immediately gains merit...
(13) Upon seeing parrot feathers, coral, silver, crystal, the roots of *kuśa* grass, clay from the Gaṅgā, *kuśa* grass, and copper, one gains merit... (14)
Having seen a pure Purāṇa manuscript, a Viṣṇu yantra with its seed-syllables, glossy dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, a gem,
the perfected mantra of ascetics, a muslin cloth, and the skin of a black antelope— [one obtains] merit... (15).

Having seen a sacrifice or a great festival, that man obtains merit. Having seen cow urine, cow dung, milk, the dust raised by cows, a cow-pen, a cow’s footprint, or a field filled with ripened grain, one certainly obtains merit.
A beautiful, youthful lotus-woman, dark-complexioned and well-proportioned like a banyan tree,
elegantly dressed, wearing fine garments, and adorned with divine ornaments—
the courtesan Kṣemakarī— [and] fragrance, excellent durvā grass, unbroken rice, and grains.

Upon seeing *siddhānna* and *paramānna*, a person gains merit. (19) On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, by worshipping, beholding, and bowing before the auspicious image of Rādhikā, one brings about the destruction of rebirth. (20)
Likewise, on the auspicious eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina at Hiṅgulā,
one experiences rebirth upon seeing the image of Śrī Durgā;
and by beholding Viśvanātha at Kāśī on Śivarātri.
Having observed a fast and performed worship, he makes his birth [fruitful].
|| 22 || On the day of Janmāṣṭamī, the devotee, having seen me as Bindumādhava, bows down, performs worship, and makes his birth [fruitful]. || 23 ||
In the month of Pauṣa, during the bright fortnight, wherever a man beholds an image of Padmā and performs [this rite], he shall experience seven births;
his sons and grandsons shall become lords of wealth. (24)

Having observed the fast on Ekādaśī and bathed at dawn on the twelfth day, one who beholds Annapūrṇā in Kāśī effects the destruction of rebirth. On the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra, in the merit-bestowing land of Kāmarūpa, [one should likewise act]. || 25–26 ||
Having seen and bowed to Bhadrakālī, one makes [their] birth... And on the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī, having fully worshipped, bowed to, and seen Rāma in Ayodhyā, one makes [their] birth... (27)

Having fasted and bathed at Puṣkara, or perhaps at Badarikāśrama, and having worshipped and beheld me alone, one makes their birth fruitful. And he who offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Viṣṇupada and worships Viṣṇu... [28–29]
He brings about the rebirth of his ancestors and of himself...
if he performs the tonsure at Prayāga and offers gifts;
and having fasted in the Naimiṣa forest, he brings about the rebirth... [of his ancestors].
Having achieved perfection, he enjoys the jujube fruit at Badarikāśrama.
O Nanda, having seen my own likeness, he takes birth...
[and sees] me as Govinda, moving about in the holy Vṛndāvana.
Having seen [Me], having worshipped and bowed down, the devotee effects his rebirth...
Having seen Me alone, Madhusūdana, upon the couch in the month of Bhādrapada, and having worshipped and bowed down, the devotee effects his rebirth... (33)
And the man who, in the Kali age, shall behold the Lord of the World seated upon His chariot,
having worshipped and bowed with devotion, makes his birth fruitful.
(34) One should perform a ritual bath at Prayāga during the transit of the sun into its northern course.
Having worshipped and bowed down to me alone, he effects his birth... (35).
And on the full moon day of Kārttika, having beheld my auspicious image, having fasted and performed worship, he effects his birth... (36).
Near the Candrabhāgā river, at midday, the wise person should bow to me;
having seen me there with Rādhā, one brings about the end of rebirth.
At Rāmeśvara on the Setubandha, on the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha...
Having approached, seen, and worshipped him, he effects his birth... (38).
In heaven, the Vidyādharas dance again and again at night;
Vibhīṣaṇa also comes to that Lord in order to offer obeisance. (39)
At night, the Kinnaras and Gandharvas sing enchanting songs for that Lord Mādhava, who comes to offer his salutation;
having seen the Moon-crested One, the Lord of All, manifest as Spring itself.
One becomes liberated while living and at the end departs for the abode of Hari.
Having fasted, seen, and worshipped the Lord of the Wretched, the Sun, at Koṇārka during the northern transit of the sun, one makes [his] birth... [fruitful]. (41–42)
In Kṛṣikoṣṭha, Suvasana, Kalarvika, Vasundharā, Vispandaka, Rājakoṣṭha, Nandaka, and Puṣpabhadraka—
having beheld there the image of Pārvatī, as well as Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśvara.
Having seen Nandin, the benefactor of Śaṅkara, one brings about the destruction of rebirth.

(44) Having fasted, having worshipped in the morning, having seen [him], and having offered praise while bowing in the hymn of praise, and having broken the fast by consuming curd, one brings about the destruction of rebirth. (45)
Having fasted at Trikūṭa, Maṇibhadra, and in the vicinity of the western ocean,
and having eaten curd after beholding me, one shall attain liberation.
[Likewise] before my own images and images of Pārvatī.
Having renounced his life and having performed worship, he undergoes birth... (47).
Having constructed a temple for Śiva and Durgā, and especially one for me, and having established an image of Śiva, he undergoes birth... (48).
Having established a flower garden, a sacrificial post, a bridge, a moat, a lake,
and having performed the installation of a Brahmin, one effects [the purpose of] birth.
Yet the Vedas and Purāṇas do not state that the fruit [of these acts] is the establishment of a Brahmin.
The virtuous sages, the gods, the brahmins, and others know [this], O Father.
(50) The particles of dust of the earth may be counted, and the drops of rain may be counted;
yet even the Creator cannot calculate the fruit of establishing a brahmin. (51)
By making this the means of subsistence for a brāhmaṇa, a man becomes liberated while living;
he attains unshakable prosperity and, in the end, the fourfold liberation.
He shall obtain devotion as my servant and rejoice for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha.
Indeed, there shall be no rebirth for him, just as there is none for Me, the Supreme Self.
He who gives away a beautiful eight-year-old maiden,
having honored her with all ornaments, shall obtain the fruit of the gift of Durgā.
Beholding all that leads to heaven and being honored in the worlds of Brahmā, he attains my service and rejoices for a long time in Vaiṣṇava-loka.
By witnessing the marriage ceremony, one obtains the fruit of giving ten million gold coins.
In this way, one goes to heaven; likewise, one attains stable prosperity even in this world.
He who, upon seeing a very learned man who is protectorless and poor, performs his marriage, certainly attains liberation. (56–57)
Whoever offers an umbrella and sandals to a Śālagrāma stone or to a woman with devotion on an auspicious day shall obtain the fruit of the gift of the entire earth.
Furthermore, it is heard in the Vedas that by the gift of an elephant, one enjoys [the merit] for as many years as there are hairs upon its body.

One who gives a lordly elephant possessing four virtues rejoices in my abode. O Father, half the merit of a white horse is obtained by giving a conscious being, and one obtains a fruit equal to that of a gift of black cows by giving an elephant.

The fruit of giving land is equal to that; half of it is obtained from the gift of an ordinary cow, and one obtains the fruit of the earth from the gift of cows that have calved for the first time. By the gift of land, one gains a residence in my own abode for as many years as there are particles of dust in the gift.

By the gift of knowledge there is great merit, and one rejoices for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha. One obtains prosperity through the gift of gold, and kingship through silver. The fruit of the gift of food is a house; how could I know what is heard regarding the gift of water? (62–63)
One obtains the fruit of all possible gifts by feeding a Brahmin.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
In this matter, there is no examination of the recipient’s worthiness, nor is there any restriction regarding the time.
In the gift of food, there is auspicious merit for the giver, provided the recipient is free from sin.
The gift of food on earth is blessed, as it leads to Vaikuṇṭha. He who gives clothing to a poor Brahmin who has a family [is likewise blessed]. (65–66)

Having given clothing, thread, a man-measure of grain, or a lamp made of iron provided with a golden wick, one rejoices for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha, as well as in the most beautiful world of the Moon and likewise in the world of Varuṇa. (67)
He offered a lamp of ghee to Hari, the Supreme Soul.
Neither darkness, nor his home, nor the messengers of Yama, nor Yama himself does the donor behold; he goes instead to my abode.
Having indeed given [a seat] to a Brāhmaṇa, one does not go to the torments of Yama;
for a thousand divine years, one rejoices in the abode of Śakra.
One obtains a seat in heaven in accordance with the quality of the object given.
In the case of the highest [quality], one obtains [the fruit] for a hundred thousand years, and in other cases, half of that.
(71) By offering betel-leaf, one attains enjoyment in heaven for a hundred years.
By the gift of garlands, one goes to a beloved heaven, in accordance with the quality of the material. (72)
One obtains the fruit of the gift’s result as heaven; there is no doubt in this matter.
By the gift of an ordinary bed, one goes to heaven for a hundred years.
In an excellent [bed], it is fourfold; in one endowed with all characteristics, it is a hundred thousandfold.
If a house is given to one who is destitute and highly learned, he is honored right here for a human year and in the world of Śakra. Seeing a hungry Brahmin, food is given to him. (74–75)
One attains imperishable glory that increases one's sons and grandsons.
O Lord of Vraja, go now to Vraja; wander upon the land of Vraja, O Lord of Vraja! Go, feed the Vipras, and wander everywhere throughout Vraja.
O child, in every cow-pen free from turmoil, O child,
in every cow-pen, and in every settlement of cows crowded with those who were distressed—
in every such place, O Nanda, this has been told to you for your joy and for the increase of merit.
The vision of auspicious dreams is meritorious, provided one does not speak of what is base.

Having avoided one who is of the Kāśyapa lineage, one who is unfortunate, base, an enemy, ignorant, or a stranger, one should speak to a Brahmin on the day, avoiding the night, even if he is a mediocre scholar. (78–79)
By mentioning a deity in a temple, or even the Aśvattha, Tulasī, or Vaṭa tree, one obtains double the merit; by not disclosing it, one obtains fourfold.
Upon seeing a good dream, a wise person obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
One shall obtain wealth, riches, a wife, land, sons, and progeny;
one attains liberation, supreme sovereignty, and everything desired.
Thus has it been told, my dear; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Conversation between the Blessed Nārada and Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the section concerning the Birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Now begins the seventy-seventh chapter.
Nanda said:
By what dream does what merit arise, and by what does liberation and happiness come to be?
O Lord, tell me all that—whatever auspicious dreams there may be. (1)
The Blessed Lord said: Among the Vedas, the Sāmaveda is praised for all ritual acts;
likewise, within the beautiful Puṇyakāṇḍa of the Kaṇva recension.

O dear one, listen as I relate all of that which is auspicious, as well as the bad dreams that constantly yield the fruits of merit. I shall proclaim this chapter on dreams, which bestows manifold meritorious rewards.
Having heard this chapter on dreams, a man obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
A dream seen in the first watch of the night yields its fruit within a year;
in the second, within eight months; and in the third, within three months.
In the fourth case, a dream occurring within half a month yields its own fruit;
even a dream seen at the description of dawn yields its fruit within ten days.
A morning dream also yields its fruit if one is awakened at that very moment.
Whatever is seen during the day in the mind, all that one will certainly obtain. (7) A man afflicted by anxiety or disease sees a dream;
all that, O dear one, becomes fruitless and surely passes away—of this there is no doubt. (8)
One who is mute, oppressed by urine and feces, or agitated by fear;
one who is naked or has disheveled hair—such a person shall not obtain the fruit born of the dream.
And if, having seen a dream, one who is sleepy falls back into sleep, [the dream is likewise fruitless].
If one speaks while utterly deluded at night, one will not obtain the fruit born of dreams.
Having spoken [thus] regarding the Kāśyapa lineage, one certainly incurs misfortune;
in a low state one goes to a miserable rebirth, and in a base state one encounters disease.
One encounters fear from an enemy and strife with a fool;
there shall be loss of wealth through a woman, and danger from fire at night.
One finds sorrow in sleep and the desired fruit with a wise man. (12)
O Kāśyapa, a wise person should not disclose a good dream; go [and keep it secret].
O Lord of the Herd, this applies likewise to dreams of cows, elephants, horses, palaces, mountains, and trees.
Ascending [a vehicle], the giving of wealth, eating, weeping,
receiving a lute, and touching land rich in crops—
when one is pierced by a weapon or missile, or likewise by a wound or a worm.
Even if one is joined with the *viṣṭi* asterism and blood, one shall become wealthy.
(16) He who, even in a dream, obtains a wife by approaching a woman who should not be approached, shall drink semen while drenched in urine and shall enter hell as well. (17)
If one enters a red city or drinks the ocean of nectar,
one receives auspicious news and obtains abundant wealth.
One also beholds an elephant, a king, gold, a bull, and a cow.
Upon seeing a lamp, food, fruit, a flower, a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a banner,
a family, a full water-pot, a brahmin, fire, flowers, betel, or a house, one obtains extensive fame and prosperity. (19–20)
Upon seeing white grain, a river, or a courtesan, one shall obtain prosperity;
and upon seeing cow’s milk or ghee, one shall acquire wealth and the riches of merit.
(21) [Likewise,] milk-rice on a lotus leaf, curd, milk, ghee, and honey—
Having eaten sweet food and a *svastika* cake, one will certainly become a king.
(22) If a man eats the flesh of birds or humans, he obtains great wealth, auspicious news, and his desired fruit. (23)
Having obtained either a parasol or sandals, he goes to obtain grain;
and whatever sharp sword he receives shall likewise become so.
He who crosses over with ease shall indeed become preeminent.

And having seen a tree bearing fruit, one certainly obtains wealth. Indeed, he who is bitten by a serpent shall obtain profit from that very act. Having seen the sun or the moon in a dream, one is liberated from disease and bondage.
If one sees a mare, a hen, or a female curlew as one's wife in a dream, one will certainly obtain a spouse.
He who dreams of being bound with fetters will attain high status and obtain a son.
If one eats curd-rice or milk-porridge on a lotus leaf by a riverbank [in a dream], [one will attain prosperity].
And that king shall likewise become one whose lotus-feet are shattered.
(28) If he sees a leech, a scorpion, or a snake, he shall obtain wealth, a son, victory, or renown. (29)
If one is afflicted by horned animals, fanged beasts, boars, or monkeys,
it shall certainly be that the king will become established and obtain abundant wealth.
[One may also find] fish, meat, pearls, conch shells, sandalwood, and diamonds.
He who sees vast wealth at the end of a dream shall obtain riches;
having consumed liquor, blood, or gold, he shall obtain wealth;
and having seen an image or a Śiva-liṅga, he shall obtain victory and wealth.
Seeing a *bilva* tree laden with fruit and flowers, or a mango tree, one shall obtain wealth;
seeing a blazing fire, one shall obtain wealth, intelligence, and prosperity.
Seeing an *āmalaka*, a *dhātrī* fruit, or a blue lotus, there shall be the arrival of wealth.
Whatever one gives to deities, brahmins, cows, ancestors, or ascetics in a dream, that shall indeed come to pass. Women wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, [appear].
For one whom they embrace in a dream, prosperity and happiness come from every side.
(35) For him who embraces in a dream a woman wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents, well-being arises. (36)
All white things are praised, provided they are devoid of ash, bone, or cotton;
all black things are strictly censured, with the exception of cows, elephants, horses, Brahmins, and deities.
A celestial woman accompanied by a smile, O Brahmins, adorned with ornaments and garlands—
He whose temple he enters certainly attains what is dear to him.
And in a dream, the god Brahmā appears as a Brāhmaṇa, or a divine maiden as a Brāhmaṇī;
or else it is a Brāhmaṇa or a Brāhmaṇī who is contented, smiling, and virtuous.
To whomever it grants its fruit, he shall become his son;
and whatever auspicious blessing the Brahmins bestow upon him in a dream,
that shall come to pass for him, and he shall certainly attain sovereignty.

O best of the twice-born, Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, and Brahmā enter the hermitage of that person whose home He visits with full satisfaction. His prosperity becomes abundant, as does his auspicious and extensive fame.
At every step he shall find happiness and attain equal honor;
even if he should unexpectedly smell a fragrant scent in a dream,
he shall obtain land and a devoted wife.
If an elephant, having taken something with its trunk, should place it upon one's head, the acquisition of a kingdom will certainly be his; this is the opinion found in the Śruti.
Furthermore, O Vraja, if a gratified Brahmin embraces one in a dream—
Even he who merely bathes at a sacred ford (tīrtha) shall certainly be endowed with prosperity.
O twice-born one, that meritorious person to whom the Brahmin gives a flower in a dream shall be victorious,
renowned, and happy on earth.
And in a dream he beholds sacred fords and houses made of gold and jewels.
Such a man shall be victorious, wealthy, and one who bathes at sacred fords.
Furthermore, in a dream someone gives a full water-pot to another.
He shall obtain a son or attain great prosperity. That man into whose hand a beautiful woman comes, carrying either a *kuḍava* or an *āḍhaka* measure [of grain],
will certainly attain fortune (*lakṣmī*).
O twice-born one, if a divine woman should enter a man's house and void excrement there,
he shall obtain wealth and his poverty shall depart;
likewise, when a Brāhmaṇa arrives at a man's home accompanied by his wife.
Whether it be Śambhu with Pārvatī, or Nārāyaṇa with Lakṣmī,
or even a Brāhmaṇa or a Brāhmaṇī, they are presented to him in a dream;
or even a handful of flowers or grain— his prosperity flows forth in every direction.
O Vraja, if a Brahmin gives a pearl necklace, a garland of flowers, or sandalwood in a dream, one shall obtain all prosperity.
[Likewise, if he gives] yellow orpiment, a banner, turmeric, or a stalk of sugarcane. (53–54)

If one obtains prepared food in a dream, his prosperity shall be complete. Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa or a Brāhmaṇī who places an umbrella or another white cloth upon one's head, that person shall become a great king.
In a dream, a man standing on a pillar, adorned with white garlands and unguents, eats curd or milk-rice there; or he may become a king.
Furthermore, in a dream, a Brahmin or a Brahmin woman gives him nectar and curd.

To whomsoever this praiseworthy vessel belongs, he too shall certainly become a king. Furthermore, if an eight-year-old maiden adorned with jewel ornaments should appear pleased to one in a dream, he shall become a poet-scholar.
And she who gives a book in a dream to a meritorious person—
(59) he shall become world-renowned, a lord among poets, and a sovereign of scholars;
or she who teaches him in a dream, just as a mother does her son— (60) [he shall likewise become so].
Even that son of Sarasvatī is not a scholar who is more devoted than he;
for he is like a father who would have a Brahmin teach [the text] with great care and,
out of affection, bestow the manuscript upon him, and such a person shall become equal to the virtuous.
He obtains the book either in a dream, on a road, or wherever else it may be.
He becomes a scholar, illustrious, and renowned upon the earth.
If a Brahmin bestows a great mantra upon another Brahmin in a dream, [he attains these qualities]. (62–63)
That wise man shall become wealthy, virtuous, and highly intelligent.
If, in a dream, he gives a mantra or a stone image to someone,
O Brahmin, that person shall attain the perfection of the mantra.
Upon seeing a single Brahmin or a multitude of Brahmins, one should bow and receive their blessing.
Such a person may even become a lord of kings or a poet-scholar;
to whomsoever a Brahmin might bestow land filled with white grain. (65–66)
Even in a dream, that lord of the earth shall be fully satisfied;
having placed a brahmin upon a chariot in his dream, he shall show him various heavens.
He shall become long-lived, and the increase of his wealth shall be certain.
To that brahmin to whom a satisfied brahmin gives his daughter,
he shall always become wealthy in dreams and a lord of the earth himself. He who sees a lake, or the ocean, or a river or stream in a dream— || 69 ||
By seeing a white mountain with white peaks, one shall obtain prosperity;
whoever sees a dead person in a dream shall become long-lived.
The healthy shall become ill, and the suffering person shall become happy.
A divine woman declares, "You shall be my lord.
Having seen this in a dream, he shall certainly become a king.
Or, having seen Kālikā in a dream, he obtains a crystal rosary.
He shall certainly obtain the rainbow and Indra’s thunderbolt as his firm support;
and the Brahmin who says in a dream, "Become my servant," having attained a golden countenance and devotion to me, shall indeed become a Vaiṣṇava. (73)
In my dream, the Brahmin was Hari, Śambhu, and the Brahmin woman was Kamalā, Śivā, Śakrā, the Mother of the Gods, Jāhnavī, or Sarasvatī;
she was a young girl wearing the guise of a cowherd girl—she was my Rādhikā. (74–75)
And this boy, the cowherd’s son, has been revealed by those who know dreams.
O Nanda, this auspicious dream, which is the cause of merit, has been told to you. What else do you wish to hear? What more shall I tell you? (76)
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Account of the Auspicious Dream," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa, [spoken by] Nārada.
Now begins the seventy-eighth chapter.
Nanda said:
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the worlds, I have heard an auspicious dream, which is the essence of the Vedas, the essence of ethics, and both worldly and Vedic in nature. (1)
Now I wish to hear, O child, about those whose sight is sinful, or in which action it occurs; you ought to tell me that.
[And] the word spoken in the Vedic scriptures, as well as those who follow the Vedas.
The worlds, being greatly distressed, likewise desire to hear [this] from your mouth.
You are the progenitor of the Vedas and of the virtuous followers of the Vedas,
as well as of the gods beginning with Brahmā, of the sages, and of the worlds themselves.
The nectar of your words, which serves as authoritative proof, has been heard from your lotus-like mouth;
by that, my body, which was burning from the separation from my child, has been consecrated.
[5] That lotus-feet of yours, which grant the fruit of all desires, appeared even in my dream as a refuge.
Even Brahmā and the other gods do not see that which has today come within the range of my vision.
Beyond this, where shall I, a sinner, behold your lotus feet?
My body, a vessel for excrement and urine, is bound by its own past actions.
"O child, when will such a day come for me—
a sinful man— as to have a conversation with you, the Lord who is the master of Brahmā and the other gods?
Have mercy, O Lord of Mercy, and forgive my fault."
And whatever misconduct was committed by me out of the notion that you were my calf, O Maheśvara—
[for] Brahmā, Īśa, Śeṣa, and the sages meditate upon your lotus feet,
at whose praise Sarasvatī and Śruti themselves would fall into a state of dullness.

Having spoken thus, Nanda, joyless and overwhelmed by grief, fell into a swoon after weeping, distracted by the separation from his son. The Lord Kṛṣṇa, filled with alarm, diligently endeavored to restore him to consciousness.
The Lord of the World bestowed upon him the supreme spiritual knowledge.
The Blessed One said: "O Nanda, best among fathers, most excellent of all, Lord of Vraja!"
Perform auspicious volition and listen to the supreme knowledge.
(13) This supreme spiritual knowledge is very difficult for even the wise to attain;
though it is to be kept secret in the Vedas and Śāstras, I shall bestow it upon you alone. (14)
Listen, O Nanda, with joy and with a well-composed mind:
that through the practice of which birth, death, old age, and disease do not arise.
Be firm, O Great King; O Lord of Vraja, go to Vraja.
Having attained knowledge, he is ever-blissful and freed from grief and delusion.
(16) He perceives the entire cycle of existence, including all moving and non-moving beings, as being like bubbles on water;
at dawn it is seen to be as false as a dream, and its sole cause is delusion. (17)
And the human being, composed of the five elements, has as its cause false, artificial, and constructed fabrications;
through illusion and the perception of reality, he comes into existence.
Enveloped by desire, anger, greed, and delusion in all his actions, he exists. (18)
Constantly deluded by māyā, devoid of knowledge, and weak;
enveloped by sleep, lethargy, hunger, thirst, exhaustion, lack of faith, and lack of compassion; and further encircled by shame, tranquility, fortitude, nourishment, and contentment—(19–20).
Attached to the mind, intellect, and volition, together with the vital breath, knowledge, and the self, as well as all the gods— just as a tree is surrounded by crows—
I am remembered as the Self, the Lord of All, whose nature is universal knowledge. (21)
The mind is Brahmā, and the eternal intellect is Prakṛti.
Viṣṇu is the vital breaths, and that consciousness is Padmā as the presiding deity.
When I am present, all remain; when I have departed, they too have gone.
Without us, the body certainly falls immediately;
composed of the five elements, it dissolves into those five elements at that very moment.
Its form, consisting of names and conventions, is fruitless and a cause of delusion.
Grief belongs to the ignorant, my dear; for those who possess knowledge, nothing [of this nature] exists.
Sleep and the other powers are all the constituent parts (kalās) of Prakṛti.
Greed and the other unrighteous tendencies, with egoism as the fifth, likewise [arise from it]. (25–26)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the three qualities, beginning with sattva.
Śiva is of the nature of knowledge, light, and the self; I am the attributeless (nirguṇa).
When I enter into primordial nature (prakṛti), then I am remembered as possessing qualities (saguṇa).
The objects of the senses, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, possess qualities;
likewise, Dharma is a portion of Me, as are the subject, Śoṣa, Sūrya, and the Moon.
In this way, all the gods, including the sages, Manu, and the rest, are portions of My true creative power (satkalā).
Having entered all bodies, I am untainted by all actions.
My devotee is liberated while living, a remover of birth, death, and old age;
he is the lord of all perfections, illustrious, renowned, learned, and a poet. (30)
The thirty-fourfold perfected one is the remover of all karmas;
I myself approach that self-perfected one, for the devotee desires nothing else.
The twenty-two-fold perfected one is the cause for accomplishing spiritual attainments.
"O Nanda, listen from my mouth and receive this perfected mantra:
Aṇimā (minuteness), laghimā (lightness), prāpti (attainment), prākāmya (efficacy), mahimā (greatness),
īśitva (lordship), vaśitva (control), and likewise kāmāvasāyitā (the power to resolve desires at will)."
Hearing from afar is indeed [the power of] entering another's body (34). Traveling by means of the mind is indeed the desired state of omniscience.
Furthermore, there is the stopping of fire, the stopping of water, and long life itself (35).
The paralysis of wind, as well as the suppression of hunger, thirst, and sleep;
the emanation of multiple bodies, perfection of speech, the bringing back of the dead, and the desired [powers];
the creation of worlds and the drawing in of the vital breaths. (36)

Oṃ, svāhā to Madhusūdana, the Lord of all lords, the destroyer of all obstacles! (37) This mantra is profoundly secret; it is a wish-fulfilling tree for all. It is proclaimed in the Sāmaveda as the bestower of all accomplishments upon those who have attained perfection. (38)
By this [mantra], yogins, perfected beings, lords of sages, and likewise gods [attain success];
for the virtuous, the perfection of the mantra occurs simply through a hundred lakhs of recitations.
If one, devoted to sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), should recite it in the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa, [the result is certain].
Go, my dear father, and perform your recitations at Kāśikā and Maṇikarṇikā.
Listen: in the four regions beneath the waters of the Nārāyaṇa-kṣetra, Nārāyaṇa alone is the Lord; there is never any other Lord here.
And here, when the world has passed away, knowledge indeed becomes his very form;
even without vows or mantras, he is liberated while living—of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Vraja, make Vraja pure; go to Vraja, go to Vraja!
O dear one, listen as I describe the evil that exists in his very sight:
it is a bad dream, the seed of sin, and a cause of obstacles alone;
it is like killing a cow or a Brahmin, or being ungrateful and likewise crooked. (43–44)
One who destroys the gods, one who kills father or mother, a sinner, a destroyer of all dwellings,
a giver of false witness, one who deceives guests,
a village sacrificer, and likewise one who steals the property of gods or Brahmins.
One who fells an *aśvattha* tree, a wicked person, one who reviles Śiva and Viṣṇu, (46) likewise a twice-born man who is uninitiated, lacks proper conduct, or omits the twilight prayers;
a temple-priest, one who drives an ox-cart, and a cook for Śūdras; (47)
One who burns the corpses of Śūdras, one who eats the food at a Śūdra’s funeral rite (śrāddha), one who is without a husband, one whose nose has been cut off, one who reviles the gods and Brāhmaṇas,
one who lacks devotion to the Goddess, and one who is devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu.
A Śūdra woman, a widow, a Cāṇḍāla woman, or an unchaste woman;
one who is constantly angry, a wicked person, one burdened by debt, one born of an adulterer, a thief, a liar, and one who has abandoned those who have sought refuge. (49–50)

One who steals meat, a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who has sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Śūdra, a twice-born man who is a usurer, one who approaches a woman who should not be approached, a wicked man, and the lowest of men among the four castes— [these are to be avoided].
One's mother, a co-wife's mother, a mother-in-law, a sister, a daughter;
the wife of a guru, the wife of a son, the beloved and virtuous wife of a brother; likewise, a maternal aunt, a paternal aunt, and the beloved wife of a nephew. (52–53)
The wife of a maternal uncle, a newly married woman, the wife of a paternal uncle who is menstruating,
and the daughters of one's father and mother— these eighteen are recorded in the Sāmaveda as women not to be approached (agamyā), O assembly of the virtuous, and they must be protected.
Upon seeing and touching these, a man incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Therefore, having seen them by fate, one should look at the sun and remember Hari;
for if they see them out of desire, they indeed become censurable.
Therefore, O Lord of Vraja, the virtuous do not look [at the sun], fearing a curse;
even the wise do not look at the radiant sun when it is seized by Rāhu.
When Jupiter is in the eighth or seventh house, and the Sun is in the tenth house, [this occurs].

When the moon is in the birth asterism, in the eighth house, or even in the fourth house (58), they do not see the trembling moon and sun with all their constituent parts. In the month of Bhādrapada, during both the bright and dark fortnights, the moon is neither desired nor visible. (59)
On the fourth day, the moon has risen, yet it is abandoned by the wise;
for the moon’s theft of the stars—a stain most difficult to remove—is ever present.
O Nanda, look! Out of desire, she gives herself to him.
If a man unintentionally sees [a corpse], he should drink water consecrated with mantras.
Then he becomes immediately pure and stainless upon the earth.
"The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavat. (61–62)
"O delicate one, do not weep; for this Syamantaka belongs to you.
With this mantra, the virtuous man should certainly drink the purified water.
Thus everything has been told to you; I shall tell you more besides. (63)
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Conversation between the Blessed Nārada and Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa within the glorious Mahā-... Śrī Brahma-purāṇa.
Now begins the seventy-ninth chapter.
Nanda said:
O Lord of the World, how is it that the sun or even the moon is seized by Rāhu?
And why is the moon undesirable on the fourth lunar day of both the dark and the bright fortnights in the month of Bhādrapada? (1)
"You are the progenitor of the Vedas; whom shall I ask in your absence?
Even the most discerning scholars do not know that which is secret within the Vedas and Purāṇas.
Having heard those words, he spoke this reply: (2)
The Blessed One said: This statement is untrue and is even forbidden by the Vedic scriptures.
Forgive me, O Nanda; may it be well with you; ask me another question. (3)
"O dear one, wise men should not disclose confidential words;
for when disclosed, obstacles arise for the virtuous and a vulnerability is created by fate.
Nanda said:
"Speak, O Lord of the World; do not deceive your devotee!
Even though the two Lords of Gods are invisible, they are being eclipsed by Rāhu while bestowing prosperity. The Blessed One said:
Listen, Nanda, I shall relate this ancient narrative,
by hearing which a man becomes stainless and as one who has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas). Whatever sin a man incurs by merely looking upon an evildoer—
By merely hearing this narrative, it shall be reduced to ashes.
Once, Jamadagni, filled with great curiosity and accompanied by Reṇukā, went joyfully to the bank of the Narmadā. (7–8)
He sported with her on the secluded bank of the Narmadā—
a beautiful woman, newly married, endowed with fresh youth,
well-attired, smiling sweetly, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (9)
With her body bent by the weight of her breasts and the weight of her hips, she was slow-moving;
she was incomparable among beautiful women, with the complexion of a white campaka flower,
possessing a face like the full moon and endowed with side-long glances.
Go to her who wears exceedingly fine garments, who is afflicted by the arrows of love,
and who has fainted from the enjoyment of her entire body being covered in horripilation.
[Go] to that delightful place filled with male cuckoos and resounding with the humming of bees.
In that auspicious place, filled with fragrant breezes and provided with couches of flowers,
the Sun himself spoke to the sage, whose body was smeared with sandalwood paste, who wore garments and garlands, and who was immersed in the great delight of amorous play.
He was the great-grandson of Brahmā, the creator of the Vedas and the protector of the world;
he was ever pure and thoroughly proficient in the duties prescribed by the four Vedas.
He was the author of the Vedāṅgas, a knower of dharma, the most excellent among those who know the Vedas.
He was a great ascetic, radiant, a celibate student, and firm in his vows.
Furthermore, another learned man, having studied the scripture spoken by those like you, declared:
"Dharma is that which is ordained by the Vedas; adharma is its opposite. (16–17)
How could one who knows the Dharma abandon it by delighting in unrighteousness?
Moreover, the Veda specifically speaks of the fault of sexual intercourse during the day.
I am the witness of those who follow the Dharma; for that reason, I tell you this.
Having heard the words of Sūrya, the twice-born abandoned sexual intercourse.
Seeing before him the radiant god Sūrya in the form of a brahmin, he—
his face flushed with anger and shame— spoke to Sūrya.
There, the virtuous Reṇukā, feeling ashamed, adjusted her garments.
Jamadagni said: "Who are you, imagining yourself a scholar? There is no scholar other than you."
"I am a disciple of the venerable Bhṛgu, and you are that of Kaśyapa.
I know the four Vedas, which define dharma and adharma;
for dharma is that which is established by the Vedas, while adharma is its opposite."
An ignorant man is perpetually deluded by his own actions;
yet this is no fault for those who are more powerful, just as fire consumes everything it touches.
You, others, the Dharma, and all witnesses of one's deeds [bear witness].
For your son is always a giver of fruits and a knower of the scriptures.
(24) You are indeed not the instructors of the Vaiṣṇavas, nor of us;
for those who are devotees of Vāsudeva, no inauspiciousness exists anywhere. (25)
Lord Hari’s Sudarśana discus eternally protects the Vaiṣṇavas;
so too do the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, Brahmā, and Śaṅkara.
Yama is our ruler, as are you indeed, O Divākara.

"O Prince, we are free to go wherever we please; we are in our own place. I am capable of reducing Yama, as well as all the gods beginning with Mahendra and Sūrya, to ashes in an instant, as if in mere play. (27–28)
"Who are you, a preacher of dharma to me? Go back to your own place!
My teacher, however, is the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Today, in this secluded place, you have caused a disturbance to my aesthetic rapture (rasa). (29)
"O sinful one, you shall become visible to me like Rāhu when eclipsed.
All those clouds that come to see you will be driven far away; likewise, they will be scattered by the wind and leave you concealed. (30–31)
"By your own splendor, through your arrogance, you shall have your radiance destroyed;
covered by clouds with diminished luster, may you become eclipsed by Rāhu.
Having heard these words of the Brāhmaṇa, the Blessed Sun himself—
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he praised the bull among sages.
Bhāskara said:
"O knower of dharma, all [beings] are inviolable; they are blessed, worthy of honor, and held in high esteem."
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, Brahmā himself the sovereign,
the Gaṇeśas, Śeṣa, and the eternal Dharma—
all these praise Brahmā, as does Janārdana in the form of a Brahmin.
O Brahmin, he who is granted by a Brahmin is like us;
O twice-born one, we are all gods with two mouths—the sacrificial fire and the Brahmin—and the Brahmin is the superior one.
Therefore, forgive us; you are a pure Vaiṣṇava, so practice your own duty.
"Those in whose hearts Janārdana dwells have directed their wrath toward the Vaiṣṇavas.
We have honored the Brahmins, while you have honored the gods;
O twice-born one, this conduct of yours is a vessel for mutual affection. (37–38)
"May you become one who has been cursed by me, just as I have been cursed by you!
Otherwise, O Sun, people will say of me that I am devoid of luster;
O Lord of the Twice-born, you shall be defeated by a Kṣatriya. (39)
"And your death shall come by the weapon of a Kṣatriya.
Having heard the words of Sūrya, the Brāhmaṇa became enraged once more;
with his face flushed red, he cursed him: "May you be defeated by Śambhu! (40–41)
Having learned of the quarrel between the two,
Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, himself arrived together with Kaśyapa.
Upon arriving, Brahmā enlightened the terrified Bhāskara.
And [he spoke] to the best of sages, the knower of dharma, who is the teacher of the teachers of dharma-knowledge.
Brahmā said:
"Forgive me, O Bhāskara; you are Nārāyaṇa himself."
"O Brahmins, you are always to be protected by me and are never to be slain. I shall bring an end to this terrible curse of yours;
I have come here terrified, having been sent from there by Bhṛgu."
"I am clearly impelled by Kaśyapa and Marīci.
Be at peace, O best of those who protect the gods; you are the witness of all actions.
O Brahmā, on some day, remain there for some moment."
You will be covered by thick clouds, yet you will be released immediately.
During years of deficient or excessive rain, you will be seized by Rāhu;
therein, you will be invisible to some, but visible to someone through their merit.
Otherwise, you would be visible as a field of merit on earth at all times;
and upon seeing and bowing to you, all people would become free from sin.
[49] [Furthermore, one should avoid birth in the seventh, eighth, sixth, twelfth, fourth, or tenth house.]
At the time of your birth-star (janmarkṣa), you will become invisible to men due to your death.
At the time of setting when the sky is covered by clouds, or when the sun is at midday in the water, or when it has half-risen, you will be visible only to the wicked.
On account of your wife— meaning, with your wife as the cause—
you will have your vital energy destroyed by your father-in-law and your brother-in-law.
Otherwise, your consciousness would not have been able to endure your splendor.
"And in the battle between Mālī and Sumālī, you were defeated by Śambhu.
Having spoken thus, he addressed the Brahmin Sūrya:
"Go, humble, overcome by the curse, ashamed, and provoked to anger! (53–54)
"O Brahmin, go to the dog's house; go, my child, as you please!
By your splendor, the world shall be reduced to ashes in an instant.
The sun is to be protected by you, and you are eternally [protected] by the sun. (55)
There will be a mutual relationship between you two, one of worshipper and worshipped, and of the nourished and the nourisher.
You shall be defeated by the Kṣatriya Haryaśva, that is, Kārtavīryārjuna; there is no doubt that the twice-born man, having been overcome, will die. (56–57)
"Formerly, none of your past deeds were ever thwarted.
And Nārāyaṇa himself, as a portion of his own self, shall become your son.
Twenty-one times he shall rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas."
"Death shall become the seed of your fame upon the surface of the earth.
Having spoken thus, O Lord of Vraja, Brahmā went to his home;
Jamadagni and Bhāskara also departed for their own abodes.
Thus, O dear one, has been told this meritorious narrative,
by which reason the sun, seized by Rāhu, becomes invisible;
and how the moon rises on the fourth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada, both during its bright and dark fortnights.
Listen to the reason why he became invisible and his form vanished.
O father, in the past, Rāhu was seized by me and cursed;
I shall tell you this entire ancient story.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and the Blessed Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the eightieth chapter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, Tārā, the wife of her preceptor, was endowed with fresh youth; she was adorned with ornaments of jewels and dressed in excellent, fine garments. (1)
She possessed beautiful hips, was smiling, lovely, charming, and most captivating;
her braid was exceedingly delightful, adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers.
Along with a drop of musk, there were beautiful drops of sandalwood paste.
Shining with a drop of musk upon her forehead, she was adorned by the tinkling anklets fashioned from the finest essence of gems;
she possessed beautiful curved eyes, was dark-complexioned, and was radiant with lovely, well-applied collyrium. (3–4)
She was enchanting with rows of teeth as beautiful as pearls of exquisite luster;
her lovely cheeks were radiant with a pair of jeweled earrings.
This young woman, peerless among all who desire love, moved with the slow, majestic gait of a lordly elephant.
She was very delicate, moon-faced, the support of desire, and full of longing.
(6) Having bathed on the banks of the celestial Mandākinī, wearing beautiful and smooth garments, she meditated upon the feet of her guru while intent on returning to her own home. (7)
O Vraja, having seen her entire form, the Moon, afflicted by the arrows of the God of Love, lost his consciousness on the fourth day of the month of Bhādrapada.
Regaining his awareness in an instant, the powerful lover remained seated upon his chariot.
Taking Tāraka by the hand, he caused him to mount the chariot.
Intoxicated with passion, he embraced that lovely woman and kissed her. As he was intent on engaging in amorous dalliance, the preceptor’s wife spoke to him: (9–10)
Tārakā said:
"Leave me! Leave me, O Moon, you disgrace to the lineage of the gods! I am the wife of my guru, a Brahmin woman devoted solely to her husband! (11)
In having sexual intercourse with the wife of one’s guru, there shall be the sin of a hundred brahmin-murders.
If she is the wife of a guru or the wife of a brahmin and is devoted to her husband,
by having intercourse with her, one incurs the sin of a thousand brahmin-murders.
"You are my son and I am your mother; exercise fortitude, O Lord of the Gods! Shame on you! Upon hearing this, the Preceptor of the Gods will reduce you to ashes.
You are dearer to my master than a son, and you are his beloved disciple. (13–14)
"Protect your own duty, O most wicked one! Do not abandon me, your mother, in this way. I shall inflict the punishment of killing a woman upon you if you take her by force.
[15] Thus, disregarding Tārā’s words, he prepared to enjoy her.
Free from desire and devoted to her husband, Tārā cursed him in anger:
"May you be eclipsed by Rāhu, may you be swallowed by the clouds, and may you become visible only to the sinful!
You shall be marked with a stain and seized by consumption; of this there is no doubt. (16–17)
Having then swiftly cursed Candra, she cursed Kāmadeva:
"By some radiant being, you shall be reduced to ashes.
And Candra, having taken Tārā and enjoyed her company, departed.
Taking her onto his lap, he departed with her weeping and overcome by grief.
[He went] from secluded to secluded spot, from delightful mountain to delightful mountain,
and from charming bank to charming bank of lakes, streams, and rivers.
In a flower garden beautifully blossomed and filled with the songs of bees and cuckoos,
he took delight with Rāmā upon a lovely couch of flowers.
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, the god was devoted to drinking honey-wine.
Attached to the enjoyment of pleasure, he did not perceive day or night.
[He dwelt] in Malaya, in the forest of Malaya, joined by the Malaya breeze;
in Syandana, in the sandalwood grove, near the western ocean.
On Mount Trikūṭa, at the foot of a banyan tree, there by the Moon Lake,
upon a very beautiful lotus leaf smeared with sandalwood paste;
in a most lovely campaka grove, honored by the campaka-scented breeze.
On the ground of milk-ocean and gold, at the mountain of Krauñca-gold,
on the jewel-mountain made of gems, beautiful with jeweled palaces, and adorned with a flood of rubies and pearls and necklaces of diamonds. || 25–26 ||
In that beloved place of divine sport, adorned with beautiful garments and richly decorated with variegated patterns, and graced by white chowries, mirrors, and jewel-lamps; there,
accompanied by Varuṇānī, he drank the wine Vāruṇī.
Where Varuṇa delights, there he took pleasure with her—
in the purifying Pavana garden, by the breeze from the *parijāta* tree, enchanted by its fragrance, and upon the stainless shore of the Ratnamālā river. (28–29)
On Mount Ṛkṣa, in the forest of Kalpavṛkṣas, at the hermitage of Vahnipriyā,
he drank the milk of the Kāmadhenus on the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Vahni joyfully gave him a pair of garments purified by fire.
Varuṇa [offered] a garland of jewels, and Samīraṇa a dancing parasol.
Having seen the preceptor of the Asuras who had arrived from the house of Bali,
Candra bowed down, spoke everything, and sought refuge with him.
Śukra, who was indifferent to worldly ties, most excellent among sages, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, awakened him with words endowed with political wisdom.
Śukra said:
Listen, my child, I shall speak: give the *tārakā* (the saving star) to the Guru;
it should indeed be given by Śambhu to his virtuous son, and by Brahmā to his grandson—O Lord of Night, it should be given to him who is honored by the gods.
"O Moon, quickly go for refuge to her who is dear to him; give that which is dear to her.
Abandon the wife of your preceptor, who is equal to a mother, at my word. Bring about the destruction of your sin, for the cessation of evil is of great fruit. (35–36)
By forcibly seizing virtuous wives of gurus,
a person incurs the sin of a thousand killings of Brahmins and is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a hundred Brahmās.
O God, there is equality between a blade of grass and a mountain in the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
