Who are you, O child, in the place of Hari? There is the experience of karma for Brahmā.
All living beings in this world are of three kinds, having taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Abduction of Tārā," in the *Nārada-nārāyaṇa-saṃvāda* within the *Bhagavan-nanda-saṃvāda*, in the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Brahma-mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-janma-khaṇḍa*.
Now begins the eighty-first chapter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the meantime, Śukra beheld Surakṣeṇī approaching through the path of the sky, bearing weapons and missiles for battle;
she was accompanied by thirty million banners and one billion great chariot-warriors.
There were a hundred koṭis of lordly elephants, and chariots four times that number;
horses were four times that [number], forming a most formidable host, and the multitude of foot soldiers was six times the number of the horses. (2–3)
Likewise, there were five hundred thousand musical instruments such as the *dundubhī* drums;
three hundred thousand *paṭaha* drums; and two hundred thousand *ḍiṇḍima* drums.
On Airāvata he established Mahendra, and on Śvetāśva, Dharma.
Kubera, Varuṇa, Vahni, and likewise Pavana seated upon his chariot;
Yama mounted upon his buffalo, and Divākara stationed upon his chariot;
Īśāna seated upon the king of bulls, and Ananta whose vehicle is the serpent.
Having seen the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,
as well as the munis liberated while living, whose splendor was like that of the sun and who were full of desire,
Śukra became fearless and comforted the Moon.
O Lord of Vraja, he summoned a twice-as-large army of the gods.
There, on the bank of the river Ratnamālā, in the hermitage dear to the Fire-god,
the Daitya army remained on the shore of the holy Ocean of Milk.
In the meantime, Śuka beheld on the shore of a nearby lake,
in a holy hermitage at the Akṣaya-vaṭa tree,
Śaṅkara— the benefactor of all— arrived from the celestial army and mounted upon his bull.
Wearing a tiger-skin garment and bearing the trident of Triśalā, he is the most excellent one.
He is the supreme embodiment of splendor, whose form exists for the grace of his devotees;
he is the bestower of all prosperity, the omniscient cause of all things. (11–12)
The Lord of all, worshipful by all, the embodiment of all oblations, the eternal one,
solely devoted to the protection of the distressed and the afflicted who have come for refuge—
the Supreme Self, smiling and blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Terrified, he suddenly rose and bowed at His lotus feet.
The Supreme Lord, being well-pleased, bestowed auspicious blessings upon him and respectfully seated him upon a jeweled throne.
Then, in that interval, he beheld before him that Brahmin,
peaceful and appearing like the Creator himself, seated upon an excellent chariot of jewels,
clad in garments as pure as fire, and adorned with garlands of gems.
He is gracious, beautifully smiling, pure, and the supreme Lord of the worlds;
the bestower of the fruits of actions, the embodiment of austerity for those who practice penance, the progenitor of the Vedas, the source of the Vedas, lovely and captivating to the mind. (17–18)

Then, with palms joined in reverence and trembling with fear, he bowed down to the Lord of the Gods. Out of devotion, he seated him upon a beautiful jeweled throne and performed worship with devotion at the lotus-feet of both.
"It is not appropriate to inquire after their welfare or their well-being.
(20) O Nanda, the Creator of the worlds, who is highly esteemed by Śiva, spoke with great effort to Śakācārya, who was standing before him, regarding Sunīti. (21)
Listen, Śukra, son of the Moon, for I shall declare to you a policy that causes shame to the three worlds and is outside the Vedic tradition:
[to approach] a chaste wife of one's guru, who has bathed and is facing her home at night. (22)
Having taken hold of him, he has now sought refuge in you despite his sins.
O child, behold the assembled army of the gods ready for battle;
Śambhu and I have both come here to your presence for that purpose.
Śambhu said: "O Brahmin, bring the Moon here if you desire your own welfare;
I shall destroy the head of that sinner with my trident."
"Otherwise, I shall annihilate all the Daityas in an instant.
O twice-born one, when I am enraged, who could be the protector of the Daityas?
Right now, with the Pāśupata and Vāyu weapons, I shall [destroy them]."
"And I shall effortlessly destroy the host of enemies of the Suras. Durvāsas is a portion of myself; his preceptor is the sage Aṅgiras.
Due to their mutual relationship, he is both my preceptor’s son and my own preceptor. (27–28)
The radiant Bṛhaspati was capable of reducing him to ashes,
yet out of compassion, he did not do so because of his beloved disciple.
In the past, having seen Utathya’s wife, he took pleasure with her according to his own desire.
Due to the curse of that very lord, his beloved wife Satī has been seized by another.
Give me back Tārā, the captivating daughter-in-law of my preceptor’s son;
and [punish] Candra, my enemy, who abducted the wife of his brother.
If a lord does not protect one who has come for refuge and is miserable and distressed,
he shall be cooked in hell for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
In this matter, I have no hesitation regarding one who has come for refuge, however sinful he may be.
"Whosoever seeks refuge with a sinner becomes a sinner as well; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O tiger among brahmins, cast out that sinner who has violated his mother, along with Tārā and the virtuous woman, from your own hermitage."
Śukra said:
"Among the gods, the asuras, and all the worlds, you alone are the Lord and the ruler; who indeed can rule over the gods and asuras?"
Having rendered assistance to the gods, how will you slay the Daityas?
And what manliness is there in the host of Daityas for the Destroyer of all the worlds?
You are the supreme light, Brahman itself, both with attributes and without attributes.
Due to the distinction of qualities, there is a distinction of forms consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Lord, at the gateway of Bali, you yourself, mace in hand, were present;
and by your very play, even Śrī was bestowed by you upon that Indra.
Forgive me, O Blessed Śambhu; Hara, withdraw your anger!
What manliness is there in your harming even a Brahmin?
As long as I live, I will not surrender the moon with my body.
[Protect] those who have come for refuge, the wretched, the afflicted, the modest, and those joined with sin.
(40) And I, O Śaṅkara, go for refuge at your lotus feet.
O All-pervading Lord, act as is appropriate, and likewise for the entire world. (41)
Having heard the words of Śukra, the blessed Lord Śiva was pleased and said to the Lord of Night: "Bring him here; let there be auspiciousness.
In the meantime, the omnipresent Brahmā, having enlightened the poet (Śukra), [acted].
"Bring the Lord of the Night (the Moon) together with the stars and go to Vraja.
He then offered him at the lotus-feet of Śambhu;
and Śambhu, filled with affection, placed him upon his chest.
He gave him the dust of his feet and rendered him sinless;
placing his hand upon his head, the compassionate one granted him fearlessness.
Having bathed him in the Ocean of Milk, Śaṅkara purified him through expiation.
Accompanied by Brahmā, he made the Moon pure and free from sin.
That lord of yogis, through his yogic power, divided the Moon into two parts;
he kept one half upon his forehead, while the other half remained before Brahmā.
For this very reason, Mahādeva became the moon-crested one;
there, in the assembly of the gods, the moon was ashamed because of its spot.
Out of shame, and through his own yogic power, he abandoned his body.
And that body was entrusted by Brahmā to the Ocean of Milk (49).
And Atri wept on the shore of the Ocean of Milk with piteous grief;
O Vraja, his eye-water fell into the water. (50)
Therefore, Candra became free from sin in the assembly of the gods.
Brahmā and the Lord Śambhu performed his consecration.
Mahādeva spoke to him fearlessly in the assembly of the gods: (51)
Mahādeva said:
"Go to your own abode, my son, and rule your realm with joy;
later, however, you shall be seized by consumption due to her curse."
"Kubera was able to render the curse of the devoted wife (pativratā) futile on this earth;
furthermore, by my blessing, there shall be a remedy for the consumption (yakṣman).
This is because on the fourth day of the month of Bhādrapada, an injury was committed against the preceptor’s wife. (53)
Therefore, my child, on that day [and] in age after age, one remains invisible to the wicked. (54) Action that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Whatever action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—has been performed must necessarily be experienced. (55)
"O child, by the abandonment of the body, the experience of karma is not destroyed;
through expiation there is no doubt that it will indeed be cast off.
O child, the stain upon the lunar orb was caused by the abduction of Tārā."
"In every age, you shall take the form of a deer and be marked with a spot.
Listen to my words here and come, O Tārakā, devoted wife!
Speak the truth, my dear: whose embryo did you abandon, and how have you become pure?"
"A virtuous woman who is forced against her will by a paramour is not defiled;
however, she who does so out of desire goes to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Tārā spoke these words to Brahmā with a smile regarding the embryo of Candra.
All the deities, Śambhu, and the hosts of sages laughed,
O Lord of Vraja. Bṛhaspati then gave Tārā to his ashamed preceptor and, taking that devoted wife with him, went to his own home.
Having taken the beautiful son born of her, who possessed a golden luster,
she departed after offering salutations to Candra, Brahmā, and Śivā.
The gods, the sages, Śambhu, and the lotus-born Brahmā also departed.
Śukra, accompanied by the Daityas, departed for his own home filled with joy. (63) O Nanda, this auspicious narrative that bestows merit has been told to you.
By hearing this, a person becomes free from sin and stainless. (64)
It is auspicious, bestowing fame and long life, the supreme bringer of all prosperity, the dispeller of sorrow, the creator of joy, and a blessing in every respect.
(65) Abandon your grief; always rejoice! Return home, O Lord of Vraja.
Tell everything to Yaśodā, my own mother, and to the assembly of cowherd women.
You shall awaken all those women who are overwhelmed by grief;
being filled with joy through the knowledge imparted by me, remain forever so.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Recovery of Tārā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the eighty-second chapter.
Nanda said:
"O highly fortunate one, I have heard everything; O Lord, tell me about the bad dream.
The Blessed One said to him, "Listen," and these were his words.
(1) The Blessed One said:
If one laughs out of joy in a dream and sees a wedding, dancing, singing, or something desirable, his misfortune is certain.
He whose teeth chatter and who sees them moving [in his sleep]— [his misfortune is certain]. (2)
He shall suffer loss of wealth as well as bodily affliction.
(3) Furthermore, he who travels toward the southern direction while anointed with oil, or mounted upon a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo, will meet his death; of this there is no doubt. (4)
If, while sleeping, he sees a hibiscus flower, an aśoka, or a karavīra in his ear,
or if he sees oil and salt, there will be misfortune for him.
Likewise, [he who sees] a naked woman, a black woman, one with a severed nose, or the widow of a śūdra.
Upon seeing a cowrie shell or a palm fruit in a dream, one may fall into grief. If one sees an angry Brahmin or a Brahmin woman filled with wrath,
misfortune shall befall him, and Fortune will certainly depart from his home.
Upon seeing forest flowers, red flowers, a well-blossomed *palāśa* tree,
cotton, or white cloth, one shall experience sorrow. Likewise, upon seeing a woman wearing black garments who is singing and laughing...
Upon seeing a black widow, a man shall meet his death.
Where the deities dance, sing, and laugh, and where they clap their hands and run, there the body of that person shall perish.
If one sees vomit, urine, or feces, or a physician, silver, or gold—
either in person or in a dream— one’s life will last for ten days.
[One who sees] a woman wearing black garments, adorned with black garlands and unguents...
He who embraces [someone] in a dream will meet his death.
He who sees a dead child, a shaven head, or the bones of a deer or a man, as well as a garland of bones, will certainly encounter misfortune. (12–13)
He who would mount a chariot yoked with donkeys and camels alone—even while situated upon it, death itself remains awake; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, one should rub [the body] with clarified butter, milk, and honey.
Even with buttermilk or molasses, his suffering is certain.
(15) He who embraces in a dream a woman wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents, will certainly suffer from disease. (16)
Upon seeing fallen nails, kings, extinguished embers, ashes, dust, or a funeral pyre, one surely meets with death.
Likewise, [seeing] a cremation ground, dry wood, grass, or iron [brings the same]. (17)

Upon seeing a *śamī* tree, or even a black horse, one will certainly experience sorrow. (18) Seeing a sandal, a red plank, a garland of flowers, or something terrifying, or seeing black gram, lentils, or green gram, one will immediately incur a wound. (19)
A bracelet, a lizard, a crow, a bear, a monkey, or an ox;
pus, bodily excrement—in a dream, these are solely causes of disease.
A broken vessel, a wounded person, a Śūdra, and a leper suffering from skin disease.

Having seen in a dream one wearing red garments, one with matted hair, a boar, a buffalo, or a donkey; or seeing pitch-black, most terrible darkness, or a terrifying living corpse— one will certainly meet with misfortune regarding the female organ and the male organ.
Upon seeing a messenger of Yama who is fearsome, wearing ill-fitting garments and having the appearance of a barbarian,
with a noose in hand and a noose as his weapon, a man meets his death.
[This applies even to] a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇī, a young girl, a boy, a son, or a daughter.
If one sees [these] and utters lamentations out of anger, one shall incur suffering.
Seeing a black flower, its garland, grain, one bearing weapons or missiles,
or a barbarian of deformed appearance, one will certainly meet death.
Seeing one who has given up their life-breath or is dead, one certainly meets with death;
indeed, whoever wears [images of] fish and so forth, the death of that person's brother is certain.
[One should avoid] instrumental music, dancing, singing, a singer, and those dressed in red garments.
Seeing that drum being beaten, one will certainly experience suffering.
Seeing a severed headless trunk, or a deformed body with disheveled hair, or one dancing while scattering [dust], a man shall meet his death. (27–28)
Whether he is dead or she is dead, if in a dream one is embraced by a terrifying black barbarian woman (mlecchā), his death is certain. Furthermore,
for those whose teeth are broken and whose hair indeed falls out, [death is certain].
He shall suffer loss of wealth or physical affliction of his own body.
(30) If horned animals or even fanged beasts, as well as children or men, attack him in a dream, he shall have fear of the royal court. (31)
Seeing a tree with its branches severed falling, a shower of stones, chaff, or razors, red embers, or a rain of ashes, one shall experience suffering.
Likewise, seeing a house, a mountain, or a terrifying comet falling. (32)
Or seeing the trunk of a tree broken, one shall experience suffering.
(33) He who falls to the ground in a dream from a chariot, a house, a mountain, a tree, a cow, an elephant, a horse, or from the sky, for him misfortune is certain. (34)
They fall headlong into pits filled with ashes and charcoal, and into alkaline pits and powders; for them there is no doubt of death.
Furthermore, a wicked person forcibly seizes the parasol from one's head.
The destruction of his father, or of his preceptor, or even of the king, shall occur.
From whosever house a fragrant cow, accompanied by her calf, departs in terror,
from that sinner both prosperity and the earth itself depart.
Whomever the messengers of Yama, along with the Mlecchas, seize and depart having bound him with a noose— his death is certain.
Whether it be an astrologer, a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇī, or likewise a Guru.
If one who is deeply enraged utters a curse, misfortune will certainly befall him.
(39) Furthermore, if crows, roosters, or even bears descend upon and alight on a person's body while he is in opposition [to them], his death is certain; of this there is no doubt. (40)
If in a dream buffaloes, bears, camels, boars, and donkeys run toward someone while enraged, that person will certainly become ill.
He who offers oblations of red sandalwood wood smeared with ghee [is likewise affected].
By that [recitation] of a thousand Gāyatrīs, peace is ordained.
Indeed, he who worships this Madhusūdana with devotion a thousand times shall become free from sin;
even a bad dream shall become a good dream.
Acyuta, Keśava, Viṣṇu, Hari, Satya, Janārdana,
Haṃsa, and Nārāyaṇa— this indeed is the auspicious eightfold name.
One who, being pure, wise, and facing the east, recites this ten times, [attains the highest goal].
He shall become free from sin, and even an evil dream shall turn auspicious.
[One should worship] Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Mādhava, Madhusūdana, Hari, Narahari, Rāma, Govinda, and Dadhivāmana.
Whoever recites these ten auspicious names with devotion,
having recited them a hundred times endowed with faith, shall attain freedom from disease.
Indeed, he who recites them a hundred thousand times will certainly be liberated from bondage.
Having recited it one million times, even a woman who has long been barren shall give birth;
by eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remaining pure, one who was poor shall become wealthy.
And having recited it ten million times, a man becomes liberated while living.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇapati, Kārttikeya, and the Sun;
to Dharma, Gaṅgā, Tulasī, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
Whoever, having bathed in water, should recite these auspicious names—
He shall obtain his desire, and even an evil dream shall become auspicious.
*Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the destroyer of past misfortunes, svāhā.* This seventeen-syllable mantra is indeed a wish-fulfilling tree for the worlds.
Being pure, by reciting it ten times one becomes free from bad dreams and attains happiness;
indeed, by reciting it a million times, men achieve perfection in the mantra.
One whose mantra is perfected obtains all perfections and whatever is desired.
One should recite "Oṃ, obeisance to Mṛtyuñjaya, svāhā" one hundred thousand times, ending with *svāhā*.
Upon seeing death in a dream, a man shall attain a lifespan of a hundred years.
Having turned toward the northeast, he should disclose the dream to a wise person.
One should not disclose a dream to one who belongs to the lineage of Kāśyapa, to one in a low or miserable state, to one who reviles gods and brahmins, nor to one who is foolish or ignorant.
[One should disclose it] to an Aśvattha tree, to an astrologer, to a brahmin, or to the seats of the ancestors and the gods.
One should disclose one's daytime sleep to a noble person, a devotee of Viṣṇu, or a friend.
(57) Thus has been narrated to you this meritorious account, which destroys sin, brings wealth, fame, and long life. What more do you wish to hear? (58)
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Nārada and Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the eighty-third chapter.
Nanda said:
"O son, you are the cause of the Vedas and of Brahmā and the others.
Tell me everything—may prosperity be yours—for whom else may I inquire in your absence?"
Indeed, that which is the duty of the Brahmins, and the duties of those belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes;
the duty of renunciants, of ascetics, and of celibate students (brahmacārins);
[and] the duty of Brahmins, of widowed women, and of virtuous Vaiṣṇavas—[all this he explained].
You ought to explain all of that concerning devoted wives;
specifically, regarding householders and their wives, disciples, sons, and daughters in relation to their fathers and mothers. (3–4)
O Lord, how many kinds of women are there, and how many kinds of devotees?
How many kinds of universes are there, and what is the nature of the mouth?
What is eternal and what is artificial? Tell me all of this in due order. (5)
The Blessed Lord said: A brahmin who is always purified by the twilight prayers performs service to me;
he constantly partakes of my grace and never eats without first offering it to me.
Food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu is excrement, as is water;
yet the Brāhmaṇa who eats the remnants of Viṣṇu’s grace is liberated while living.
He is constantly devoted to austerity, pure, peaceful, and a knower of the scriptures.

The righteous man, resorting to the sacred sites of the vow and engaged in various forms of study, takes up the mantra of Viṣṇu and performs service to his guru; having received the guru’s permission, he thereafter becomes a householder. (8–9)
One should offer the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor for his constant worship;
the nourishment of one's gurus must always be performed—of this there is no doubt.
Among all those worthy of veneration, the father alone is the greatest guru.

A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father; a deity is a hundred times more venerable than a mother. A teacher of the mantras and a teacher of the tantras is four times more venerable than the gods.
And the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the Guru, the manifest Īśvara himself.
It is heard in the Śruti that the offering is given to him as "to the deity";
yet one's own guru is the direct enjoyer, being himself Janārdana.
The guru is Brahmā, the guru is Viṣṇu, and the guru is indeed Śiva himself.
All the gods always reside joyfully in the guru.
When the guru is pleased, Hari is pleased; and when he is pleased, the deities are pleased.
A guru will never fail to show affection toward his disciples as if they were his own sons.
He incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and eats without having offered a blessing;
yet a Brahmin devoted to his own duty is always pure. A Brahmin who serves Viṣṇu is always pure, while any other is always impure.
A Brāhmaṇa who drives oxen and a cook for Śūdras;
a Brāhmaṇa who serves as a temple-priest (devala), one who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and one who is weak;
a Brāhmaṇa who sleeps during the day and eats food at a funeral rite (śrāddha) performed by a Śūdra. (17–18)
Those twice-born ones who burn the corpses of Śūdras are equal to Śūdras;
yet, having performed the worship of the Śālagrāma with its great mantra according to the prescribed rite,
they eat the remains of the food offering and likewise drink the water from His feet.
Having drunk the water from Hari’s feet, a person becomes one who has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrtha).
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. He has effectively bathed in all holy places and is initiated into all sacrifices.

O Vraja, the water of the Śālagrāma stone possesses ten times the merit of the Ganges' water for one who performs an ablution with it. And that brāhmaṇa who eats [the remnants] daily is liberated while living and becomes equal to the gods.
The daily duty of the brahmins is the eating of the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu.
With effort, they perform his worship and the drinking of the water used for that worship;
and with devotion, they perform my own worship constantly at the three junctions of the day.
O dear one, that twice-born man who observes the vow and does not eat on the eleventh day, on the anniversary of my birth,
on Śivarātri, and on the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī,
is indeed liberated while living.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist upon the earth, they are all present in his feet.
By drinking the water from a Brahmin’s feet, a man becomes one who has bathed in all sacred fords.
As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from a Brahmin’s feet, [so long does that merit endure].
During that time, the ancestors drink water from lotus-leaves;
and he who eats by the grace of Viṣṇu makes the earth pure.
Indeed, that twice-born one is liberated while living, as are both sacred fords and men.
He has bathed in all sacred fords and shall obtain the fruit of religious vows;
at every step he certainly gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Purified like fire and wind, he is equal in splendor to the sun.
He does not see the messengers of Yama nor Yama himself even in a dream;
he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha as an attendant together with Hari. Indeed, there shall be no downfall for that brāhmaṇa who serves Hari.
A twice-born man who worships the mantra of Viṣṇu is indeed a Vaiṣṇava;
a wise Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa is truly no higher than him.
Whether it be as declared in the Vedas, the Purāṇas, or the Tantras.
Manu is pure.
(33) Having grasped that through inquiry, he becomes a devotee of Śiva, Śakti, or Viṣṇu;
for him into whose ear this mantra of Viṣṇu enters from the mouth of the Guru. (34)
The wise declare that [initiation] to be the great purifier of Viṣṇu;
by the mere reception of the mantra, a person becomes liberated while living.
Having shattered the entire universe, he shall surely go to the abode of Hari.
A devotee should rescue seven ancestors, seven descendants, and seven beginning with his maternal grandfather (mātāmaha), as well as his uterine brothers, their mothers, and their mothers’ mothers;
he should perform this in the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa, preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite. || 36-37 ||
O Lord of Vraja, by the mere reception of this mantra, one may effortlessly uplift a thousand men;
through the performance of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), one may uplift a hundred men for each [mantra].
An exclusive Vaiṣṇava indeed may uplift a hundred thousand men.

(39) He whose ritual actions are directed toward the station of Viṣṇu and whose resolutions are turned away from the external world; who regards the twice-born, the gods, and my own life-breaths as himself; such a devotee is dearer to me than life itself. (40)
Among all beloved objects, none is dearer to Me than My devotee.
Having seen a Guru who is more radiant than the sun and capable of protecting one everywhere, one should receive initiation from him;
therefore, let the wise person become such. (41)
One should never receive a mantra from a guru who is deficient in age, deficient in knowledge, likewise deficient in learning, or deficient in caste.
One should never receive a mantra that is impaired by being contrary to the meaning of the scriptures.

One should never receive the mantra from a fool, from one who lacks the stages of life (āśrama), nor from a father; likewise not from a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), a sick person, one lacking a lineage, or one lacking a wife; and likewise not from one whose mantra has been cast out by another mantra.
One should not receive the Viṣṇu-mantra from one devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu;
nor should one receive it from a Śaiva or a Śākta, but rather from a Vaiṣṇava twice-born.
Likewise, one should not receive it from one deficient in age, for that leads to a short life, nor from one lacking knowledge, for that results in a lack of learning.
From one devoid of knowledge, one becomes deluded; from one devoid of caste, there shall be ruin.
From a fool, one immediately becomes a fool; from falling away from one’s own stage of life (āśrama), one becomes miserable.
Furthermore, there is loss of reputation for the father, and likewise death for the renunciant (saṃnyāsī).

One who is afflicted by disease is equal to one who is diseased; one who is without lineage is equal to one who lacks a family line; even one who is without a wife is equal to one who is bereft of a woman; and, O Guru, one who is cast out by mantras is equal [to others].
Furthermore, a man who lacks devotion is equal to one who is devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu.

If one adopts [the practices] from the Śaivas or the Śāktas, devotion to Hari does not increase. (49) A pure Vaiṣṇava Brahmin is the one empowered to give cooked food; any other person is incapable of giving cooked food to Hari. (50)
From the utterance of the syllable *Oṃ*, from burnt offerings (*homa*), from the worship of the Śālagrāma stone,
and from the gift of cooked food to me— that is, to a Brahmin— anyone other than such a person shall go to a low state.
A wise man should not learn the mantra from one who is indifferent or from one whose conduct is far removed [from the prescribed rules].
If, by chance, he should take [meat], he will certainly become destitute of wealth.
(52) The food of Brahmins should always be sacrificial, fit for oblation, and free from meat.
By renouncing meat, one becomes like the sun in splendor. (53)
Cooking should always be performed using fresh utensils;
otherwise, they should be discarded by the wise after a period of one fortnight.
Having thoroughly purified the place and completed the cooking, the worshiper—
In a consecrated place, a Brahmin, having given with devotion to me [the food],
then partakes after having offered it respectfully to another Brahmin.
If he eats without having first offered it, that twice-born man becomes a drinker of liquor.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, during periods of impurity due to death or birth,
or when touched by an impure person, one should immediately discard the vessel used for cooking. Likewise, having handled roasted goods or cooked food, one should wash both garments.
Having washed his feet, he should eat in a place that has been purified.
(58) Twice- born men must not eat a second meal while the sun is still up;
that act becomes fruitless, and having eaten thus, one goes to hell. (59)
On the day of a śrāddha, one should avoid travel, fighting, the riverbank, eating a second meal, and sexual intercourse; being self-controlled, one should eat only sacrificial food (haviṣya).
One should give a vessel to a twice-born man who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and is wise.

One should never give [the gift] to the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, nor to one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras, nor with effort to one who neglects the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), nor to a wicked person, nor to one who uses an ox as a vehicle, nor to a seller of semen, nor to a temple-priest (*devala*). (61–62)
Giving a gift to these [unworthy] Brahmins leads one to hell.
Having engaged in sexual intercourse on the same day as having eaten from a worthy recipient (pātra), one shall go to hell.
O dear one, the seller of a daughter is the most sinful of all.
He who takes a pledge and then fails to deliver it shall go to the Mahāraurava hell.
For as many years as there are hairs on the body of the maiden, he, along with his ancestors,
his son, and even his domestic priest, is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Therefore, a wise person should give his daughter in marriage to a worthy recipient;
he should never treat Brahmins like Shudras, nor should he act in such a way toward their lineage. O Lord of Vraja, the duty of the Brahmin-Vaiṣṇavas has thus been declared.
And as it has been stated by the four Purāṇas as well as by the Śrutis:
the worship of the twice-born, as well as the worship of Nārāyaṇa, the protection of kingdoms, and likewise fearlessness in battle—these are the duties of Kṣatriyas. (67–68)
Constant giving to Brahmins, the protection of those who have come for refuge,
and the nurturing of subjects as if they were one's own children when they are suffering;
proficiency in weapons and missiles, and valor indeed in battle.
He should perform austerities and religious duties with joy and diligence.
He should always protect the learned man who is knowledgeable in ethics and the sciences,
and he should constantly employ him in the midst of the assembly together with virtuous men.
One who is illustrious and powerful should always protect with diligence the fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
When challenged to battle, he should never turn away from giving.
Or he who would give up his life in battle, for him there is heaven and glory.
For Vaiśyas as well, [the duties are] trade, lordship over agriculture and cattle-rearing,
the worship of Brahmins and gods, giving gifts, austerity, and the observance of vows.
The constant worship of Brahmins is ordained as the duty of a Śūdra.
If he engages in agriculture or seizes their wealth, that Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
for a thousand million births he becomes a vulture, and for a hundred births a pig.

A Śūdra who steals the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa becomes a beast of prey for a hundred births. That sinful Śūdra who approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman or his mother is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the lifespan of a Brahmā.
In the Kumbhīpāka hell, he is devoured day and night by serpents in boiling oil;
and due to the beatings of Yama, he utters distorted cries.
Thereafter, that sinner shall be born as a Cāṇḍāla for seven lifetimes.
For seven births he becomes a snake, and for seven births a leech;
for a thousand million births he is born as a worm in excrement,
and for seven births he becomes a worm in the womb of unchaste women.
Pride is a worm that festers within the wounds of sin; such a transgressor wanders through seven births, transmigrating from womb to womb, never again to be born as a human being.
Now, listen from my own mouth to the dharma of those who have renounced the world.
Merely by taking up the staff, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa.
Having burnt away his past karmas, he cuts through future karma;
he meditates upon me and indeed comes to my abode. (82–83)
By the touch of the feet of renunciants, the earth is immediately purified;
O Vraja, just as sacred fords purify instantly upon the arrival of a Vaiṣṇava.
And by the touch of a renunciant, a man becomes free from sin.
By feeding a renunciant (saṃnyāsin), one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By bowing to him and seeing him with devotion, one obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice.
The fruit for renunciants is equal to that for ascetics (yatins) and students (brahmacārins).
In the evening, the mendicant (*saṃnyāsī*), being hungry, goes to the houses of householders;
whether it be good food or poor food, he should never reject what is given by them.
He should not beg for sweet delicacies, nor should he harbor anger.
One should not accept wealth, remaining with but a single garment and free from worldly desire.
Equal toward cold and heat, and devoid of greed and delusion,
one should stay there for a single night and depart for another place in the morning.
Having engaged in the pride of vehicles, having seized the wealth of householders,
and having built a house, a householder falls away from his own beautiful dharma.
And he who, having practiced agriculture and trade, adopts a base livelihood— || 90 ||
That renunciant, having abandoned his conduct, would fall away from his own duty (svadharma).
Even if he performs actions that are either inauspicious or auspicious, he will be cast out from his own duty and indeed become an object of ridicule. (91–92)
A Brahmin woman who is bereft of her husband and remains ever free from desire should eat but one meal at the end of the day, always subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
She should not wear divine garments, nor scented substances, nor high-quality oil.
Having abandoned garlands, sandalwood paste, and ornaments such as conch-shell bangles and vermilion, she should always wear soiled garments and constantly remember Nārāyaṇa;
and she should likewise perform service to Nārāyaṇa at all times.
She constantly utters his name and not out of devotion to any other;
she always regards that man as equal to her own son according to dharma. O Vraja, she would not eat sweet food nor would she display any luxury.
One must not eat on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), on the day of Kṛṣṇa’s birth (janmāṣṭamī),
on the ninth day of Śrī Rāma, on Śivarātri, on the Pavitrā, on the Aghorā, on the Pretā, and during lunar and solar eclipses. (97–98)
Having abandoned fried food, one should eat only what is most excellent;
for widows, ascetics, celibate students,
and renunciants, betel-leaf is declared in the Śruti to be equal to meat and liquor.
Red leafy vegetables, lentils, the citron fruit, and the parṇa-leaf;
likewise, the round-shaped bottle-gourd—these must be avoided by them.
A widow who sleeps on a couch causes her husband to fall [from heaven]. (100–101)
Having mounted a vehicle, a widow shall go to hell. She should not perform the grooming of her hair nor the grooming of her body;
she should keep her hair in braids or matted locks, and undergo a shave only at a sacred pilgrimage site.
One should not perform an oil massage, nor look at a mirror,
one’s own face, other men, a journey, a dance, a great festival,
dancing, singing, or a well-dressed, auspicious man. (103–104)
One should listen to the dharma of the virtuous as set forth in the Sāmaveda; understand also the supreme ultimate truth, which I shall declare to you:
teaching, meditating, and the nurturing of disciples.
Constant service to the gurus, as well as the worship of the two deities;
proficiency in the scriptures of the Siddhānta, meditation, and self-satisfaction; pure exposition and the continuous study of the texts. (106–107)
Inquiry for the sake of purifying one's own state is sanctioned by the Veda;
likewise, the practice of the meaning of the scriptures must be performed by oneself alone.
Proficiency in the daily rites for the gods and the observance of the Vedas are desired.
O Lord of Vraja, learn now that dharma which belongs to devoted wives: the consumption of what is prescribed by the Vedas and the constant practice of purifying conduct.
Out of perpetual longing for their husband, they ever desire the water from his feet. (109–110)
One should always eat with a spirit of devotion by his permission;
having diligently abandoned vows, asceticism, and the worship of other deities, one should perform service to his feet, offer praise, and seek to please him. (111)
A virtuous woman should never perform an action without his permission.
A virtuous woman constantly meditates upon her beloved Nārāyaṇa as supreme; she avoids the faces of other men and even the sight of well-dressed strangers.
A woman of virtuous vows never attends grand processions, festivals, dancing, singing, or the playful sports of others;
she eats only that which her husband regularly consumes. (114)
O woman of noble vows, she should not abandon his company even for a single moment. A devoted wife should not offer a retort to her husband;
being pure, she does not give way to anger even when struck by him in a fit of rage.
She should feed her beloved husband when he is hungry and give him drink and food.
She should not wake him while he is sleepy, nor should she urge him toward labors.
A virtuous wife should show a hundredfold more affection for her sons than for her own children.
The husband is the kinsman, the refuge, the supporter, and the deity of women of noble family.
(118) Beholding her beloved, who is like nectar, the beautiful woman looks upon him with a smiling face, making an effort through her devotional disposition. (119)
A virtuous woman may uplift a thousand men,
and the husband of devoted wives is liberated from all sin. By the power of the vow of those virtuous women, there is no further experience of the fruits of their past actions.
Together with her, he rejoices without effort in the abode of Hari.
Whatever holy places exist upon the earth, they are all contained within the feet of a virtuous wife; the splendor of all the gods and sages likewise resides in virtuous wives. (121–122)
Go, O Vraja! All the austerity of ascetics and whatever fruit belongs to those observing vows—all that, as well as the fruit of giving for those who bestow gifts, is perpetually present within them.
Nārāyaṇa himself, Śambhu, and even the Creator of the worlds [reside there].
All the gods and sages were constantly terrified of those two.
By the dust of the feet of virtuous women, the earth was instantly purified;
by bowing down to a woman devoted to her husband, a man is released from sin.
That devoted wife, ever possessed of great merit, was capable by her own splendor of reducing the three worlds to ashes in a mere instant.
The husband of virtuous women is righteous, and their son is indeed free from fear.
Indeed, he has no fear whatsoever, neither from the gods nor even from Yama.

Born in the home of those possessing the merit of a hundred lifetimes, she is a devoted wife; her father, the progenitor of that devoted wife, is likewise purified and liberated while living. (127–128)
A virtuous wife, having risen at dawn and discarded her night-garments,
bows to her husband and joyfully offers him praise.
Then, having performed her household duties, she bathes and puts on two clean garments.
Having taken white flowers, she should worship her husband with devotion.
Having bathed him with very pure and stainless water,
she should joyfully give him a washed garment and wash his feet.
Having seated [the deity] upon the throne, having applied sandalwood paste to the forehead,
having performed the anointing of all limbs, and having also placed a garland around the neck,
[one should worship] with substances of enjoyment resembling nectar, using a mantra declared in the Sāmaveda.
Having worshipped her beloved with devotion and having praised him, she should bow down with joy.
(133) With this very mantra—*Oṃ namaḥ kāntāya śāntāya sarvadevāśrayāya svāhā*—she should offer flowers and sandalwood paste. (134)
Having offered water for the feet, the arghya offering, incense, lamps, clothing, excellent food offerings,
pure and well-scented water, and fragrant betel leaf,
one should recite whatever hymn has been composed or is to be recited.
Oṃ, salutations to the beloved one and to the husband, who has the nature of the moon upon his head.
Salutations to the peaceful one, to the self-controlled one, and to the refuge of all the gods.
Salutations to him whose nature is Brahman, and to him who is the supreme life-breath of Satī.

Salutations to you who are worthy of homage and worship, the support of the heart; salutations to the presiding deity of the five vital breaths and the pupil of the eye. Salutations to the support of knowledge, the embodiment of supreme bliss for [your] consorts.
The Lord is Brahmā, the Lord is Viṣṇu, and the Lord alone is Maheśvara.
O Lord who is the support of the attributeless and whose form is Brahman, salutations be unto You!
O Blessed One, forgive whatever fault has been committed through knowledge or ignorance.
O Lord who binds his wife, O ocean of mercy, forgive my fault as a servant!
This hymn of great merit was composed at the beginning of creation by Padmā, Sarasvatī, Dharā, and Gaṅgā; [recite it] in Vraja from now on.
In former times, it was performed by Sāvitrī for Brahmā,
and also constantly by Pārvatī with devotion for Śaṅkara on Kailāsa;
and in the past, it was performed by the wives of the sages and the gods.
This hymn brings auspiciousness to all women devoted to their husbands. Whether it be a man or a woman, any devoted wife who hears this highly meritorious hymn obtains all her desires.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth obtains wealth.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
Furthermore, a devoted wife, having offered praise, shall obtain the fruit of bathing at sacred pilgrimage sites.

O Lord of Vraja, she partakes of the fruit of all her austerities and vows after having praised and bowed down to Him with His permission. The dharma of devoted wives has been told; now listen, O Vraja, to that of householders. (147)
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and the Blessed Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the eighty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
The householder constantly performs the worship of the twice-born and the gods, as well as the practice of his own duty;
indeed, all the gods and others always fulfill the expectations of householders. (1)

And a householder who fails to honor his guests is always impure. At the time for ritual acts and at the time for receiving guests, the ancestors and the deities all come to the householder like cows to a watering hole.
In the evening, a hungry guest arrives with effort;
having received honor and offered blessings, he departs from the householder's home.
By failing to perform the worship of the guest, the householder becomes a sinner.
He incurs the sin produced by all the three worlds; of this there is no doubt.
(5) From whose house a guest departs with his hopes frustrated, his ancestors, the gods, and likewise the sacrificial fires [are likewise disappointed]. (6)

Householders who do not honor a guest become equal in fault to those who kill women, those who kill cows, those who are ungrateful, and Brahmins who violate the teacher’s bed; thus, guests depart from their homes disappointed.
Having bestowed his own sin upon others and taken their merit, he departs.
Therefore, having performed service to all and having supported those who are to be maintained, one who possesses auspicious intent and knows the Dharma eats afterwards. (8–9)

He whose mother is not at home and whose wife is likewise unchaste should go to the forest; for him, the home is more painful than the forest. That wicked woman always hates her husband and looks upon him as if he were poison.
She never gives him food and constantly reviles him;
though he is honored like a sage, that most wicked woman always treats him with contempt as if he were mere straw. (11–12)
Burnt by the fire of harsh words, he lives as if dead;
yet, having obtained a wife born of a wicked lineage for the duration of his life, listen to the virtuous conduct of housewives as it is heard in the Śruti. (13)
The housewife, devoted to her husband and honored by gods and Brahmins,
should rise early in the morning and, having purified herself and paid homage to her husband as a deity, should provide auspicious offerings in the courtyard with cow dung and water. (14–15)
Having performed her household duties and returned home after bathing,
the virtuous woman should bow to her husband— the god among brahmins— and worship the deity of the home.
Having completed her domestic tasks and having fed her husband, the virtuous woman [should proceed].
Having honored the guest, the virtuous woman eats herself with ease.
(17) The father is honored by his sons, and the teacher is honored by his disciples;
both son and disciple perform their duties at his command like servants. (18)
A son or a disciple should not urge their father or teacher toward any actions;
rather, one should constantly offer everything to the father and the teacher.
One should never, at any time, conceive of the teacher or the father as a mere human being.
And having formed the notion that she is a mere human woman, one will certainly incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
One should worship one's mother with devotion, and likewise even more so one's father;
and one should worship the supreme teacher of one's mother with the application of devotion.
The father, mother, teacher, wife, disciple, son, and even one who is always incapable,
as well as the helpless sister and maiden and the beloved of the teacher— these must always be supported.
Thus, O dear one, has the supreme dharma for all been declared.
The female species is indeed pure by nature, and all of them are devoted to their husbands. (23) Originally, all castes were created as a single kind by Brahmā;
they are all portions of Prakṛti, pure and superior even to the learned. (24)
Indeed, that Dharma fell into decay due to the curse of Kedārakanyā. Then, out of anger, the Creator fashioned a female Kṛtyā.
In ancient times, the Brahmā created three types of Kṛtyā women.
Go forth! There are three types of women: the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
(26) The superior woman is devoted to her husband and possesses some degree of virtue;
even at the cost of her life, she does not commit adultery, which brings dishonor. (27)
She should worship the gods, the twice-born, and guests just as she does her husband;
she observes vows and fasts, and performs all forms of worship.
Protected with diligence by her teacher, she would not consort with a lover out of fear.
She may be artificial or mediocre, yet she serves her husband according to her means. (29) There is no place, there is no moment, and there is no man who makes a request;
therefore, O Nanda, their virtue arises from that very circumstance. (30)
She is base, supreme in wickedness, and born of an utterly ignoble lineage;
she is unrighteous in character, ill-behaved, foul-mouthed, and prone to quarreling.
She constantly reviles her husband and always consorts with a paramour.
She gives what is painful to her beloved and views him as if he were poison.
By some stratagem, she destroys her charming lover—him who is most righteous, most excellent, and most venerable on the face of the earth. (32–33)
Out of lust, that most wicked woman looks upon her lover as equal to Kāmadeva;
with a favorable glance and a sidelong look, she regards him joyfully like an arrow.
Having seen a well-dressed young man—a boar of passion—[she is filled with desire]. (34)
The vulva of lustful women becomes constantly moist.
She does not give food to her husband but speaks incessantly with poisonous words; she constantly contemplates unrighteousness and takes supreme delight in her paramour. (35–36)

Though she was scolded by her elders and guarded by a hundred men, she nevertheless continued to consort with her lover; she could not be restrained even by the king. There was nothing dear to her, for everything was done merely out of necessity.
Like cows in the forest seeking fresh grass again and again,
her affection is like a flash of lightning in water or a line drawn upon it;
joined with unrighteousness, she constantly speaks deceitfully, as is certain.

Her mind was not fixed on vows, austerity, or dharma, nor on domestic duties; it was not directed toward her teacher or the gods, but was fickle and affectionate only toward her lover. Furthermore, I have related the threefold discourse concerning the female species.
"Listen now to the characteristics of the three kinds of devotees.
(41) A devotee who delights in sleeping on a bed of grass, having abandoned the causes of worldly pleasure, should fix his mind upon the chanting of my names and qualities. (42)
He who exerts himself and worships my lotus feet with a spirit of devotion— for him,
who is free from selfish motives and devoid of worldly intentions, the gods do not even desire any supernatural power (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* or other desired boons. (43)
Neither the state of Brahmā, nor immortality, nor the status of a god— a source of happiness—
nor even the fourfold attainment beginning with *sālokya*, nor the liberation of *nirvāṇa*, nor the drinking of nectar, do they desire without servitude (*dāsya*). (44–45)
They desire unwavering devotion to me, even though it is incomparable;
there is no distinction between male and female among all living beings,
O Lord of Vraja, for those who are Siddhas, Ishvaras, and the most excellent.

Having conquered enemies such as hunger, thirst, sleep, greed, and delusion, these sky-clad ones meditate upon me day and night. O Nanda, you are the best among my devotees; now hear about the intermediate and other [levels].
The householder, unattached to actions and pure by virtue of his prior practice,
constantly performs the cutting away of past karma;
free from mental constructs, he does not perform further action even with effort.
"Everything whatsoever belongs to Kṛṣṇa; I am not the doer of action.
One should constantly contemplate thus through deed, mind, and speech.
He whose devotion is deficient is himself deficient, and he is merely materialistic according to the Śruti. (50–51)
One does not see Yama or a messenger of Yama even in a dream;
one who was previously devoted [to the practice] may deliver a thousand men, one of middling devotion a hundred men, and an ordinary person a fourth part of that. (52)
O dear one, by your command, the three types of devotees have been described.
Now listen with attention to the narrative of the construction of the universe;
for it is through diligent effort that devotees understand the purpose of the universe's creation.
The sages and the virtuous gods know only a little through suffering;
Brahmā, Ananta, and Maheśvara know the entire universe and all its objects. 55.
Dharma, Sanatkumāra, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Kapila, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī,
the Vedas, the Mother of the Vedas, and the omniscient Rādhikā herself.
These [beings] know the purpose of the universe; no one else knows it at all.
And for the sake of their diversity, even all the wise are unable to fully comprehend them.
Just as the self and the eternal ether are [eternal], so too are the ten directions eternal.
Just as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is eternal, so too is the sphere of the universe (*viśvagolaka*);
and just as Goloka is eternal, so indeed is Vaikuṇṭha.
Once, while I was eternally performing the *rāsa* dance in Goloka, [the following occurred].
And from his left side there appeared a young girl of sixteen years;
she had the complexion of a white campaka flower and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon.
She was exceedingly beautiful, a lovely woman who was the most excellent among all women.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, her limbs tender and captivating,
she was clothed in garments as pure as fire and adorned with jeweled ornaments;
she was like a row of clouds beautified by a flight of cranes.
Resplendent with partings of hair shining with drops of vermilion, beautiful spots of sandalwood paste, and dots of musk;
radiant with the smooth, brilliant rays of ornaments fashioned from priceless gems. (63–64)
Resplendent with her beautiful cheeks adorned by various and most wonderful paintings;
beautified by a nose-pearl that surpassed the beak of the king of birds (Garuḍa);
and decorated with ornaments of pearls shed from the temples of lordly elephants.
Her rows of teeth were as enchanting as pearls released from a mother-of-pearl shell;
she was most excellent, with lips like the ripened bimba fruit that surpassed all ornaments; her face was a constant reproach to the full moon, and her eyes put the lotus to shame. (67–68)
Resplendent with beautiful kajjala-like pigment, freshly applied and resembling the black antelope;
radiant with armlets and bracelets fashioned from priceless gems;
and brilliant with a pair of conch shells [held in her hands] and rows of the finest sovereign jewels. (69)
Adorned on her fingers with these jeweled rings, she was graced by fingers as if dripping nectar;
beautified by the king of kings among jewels, she was made radiant by tinkling anklets;
and her toes were made to shine by rows of jeweled bands.
Resplendent at the base of her feet with the beautiful glow of red lac,
that lovely woman with beautiful eyes and the gait of a lordly elephant—
she, a charming lady eager for dalliance, beheld me with a sidelong glance.
Having come together in the *rāsa*, that beautiful woman stood before me;
therefore she is called Rādhā by those who know the truth and is worshipped by them.
Her nature is one of great joy, and for that reason she is the Sovereign Nature (*prakṛtir īśvarī*).
She is capable in all undertakings; therefore, she is proclaimed as Śakti.
She is the support of all, the form of all, and worthy of auspiciousness from every side.
Because she is skilled in bestowing all auspiciousness, she is Sarvamaṅgalā.
In Vaikuṇṭha she is Mahālakṣmī; in her different manifestations, she is Sarasvatī.
Having given birth to the Vedas, she is eternally known as Vedamātā (the Mother of the Vedas). She is Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and the nurse of the three worlds.
Having formerly withdrawn the fortress, she is celebrated as Durgā;
having manifested in the past from the splendor of all the gods, she is Satī.
Therefore, she should be known as the primordial Prakṛti, the crusher of all Asuras.
She is the embodiment of all bliss, she who is full of joy, and the destroyer of suffering and poverty.
She bestows fear upon enemies and removes the fear of her devotees.
She is the daughter of Dakṣa, Satī, and she who was born from the mountain—Pārvatī.
She is the very nature of the support of all; by one portion she is the Earth, by one portion Tulasī, by one portion Gaṅgā, and by one portion all women.
O dear one, it is by that power (śakti) that I create the universe again and again.
O dear one, having seen her standing in the midst of the rāsa dance, my play with her continued for a very long time,
indeed until the end of a hundred Brahmās.

In that circle of the *rāsa* dance, a mass of dharma flowed forth from those two, consisting of supreme wonder, curiosity, and great, desired passion. From that was born the enchanting Lake of Names and Forms (*Nāmākāra-sarovara*).
A stream of dharma fell downward with great force upon the cosmic sphere;
and the entire sphere of the universes became filled with water.
O Lord of Vraja, in the beginning, everything was filled with water and devoid of creation.
At the conclusion of the erotic rasa, I performed the act of impregnation upon her.
Rādhā bore that embryo for as long as a hundred Brahmās; at the end of that time, she gave birth to a most wonderful child.
Seeing him, the Goddess became enraged; she wept and despaired.
She pushed him down into the cosmic egg with her foot.
O dear one, that great Virāṭ, the support of all, fell into the water.
Having seen her offspring situated in the water, she was cursed by me in the past. O Lord, due to my curse, she was previously childless;
therefore, Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī were born from her in succession.
Those four were fully developed and certainly gave birth;
O Lord of Vraja, other goddesses and beautiful women also gave birth there,
whose origins are from a portion (kalā) of her, or even from a fraction of a fraction (kalāṃśāṃśa).
By that infant, who was the locus of a portion [of the Supreme], the great Virāj was born.
He drank the nectar from my thumb which I had given him;
and he lies in the water in the form of a stationary being due to his own karma.
By the power of yoga, his pillow, water, and bed,
as well as the pits filled with water within his body hairs, are all continuously present.
Within each of these, the minor Virāṭ lies down in succession.
A thousand-petaled lotus was born from the navel of the Subtle One (Kṣudra).
Therein was born the excellent Brahmā; therefore, he is known as Kamalodbhava (the Lotus-born).
Having manifested there, that Creator (Vidhi) became overwhelmed by anxiety.
"Why was my body [there]? Where were my mother, my father, or my kinsmen?
For three hundred thousand divine years, he wandered within the lotus.
Then, for five hundred thousand divine years, he remembered me through his ascetic penance."

Then, within a lotus, he chanted the mantra given by me for seven hundred thousand divine years, self-controlled, restrained, and pure. Having then received a boon from me, he, the creator, brought forth creation.
Through Māyā, within every universe, there are those whose nature is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
the guardians of the quarters, the twelve Ādityas, and also the eleven Rudras;
the nine planets, the eight Vasus, and likewise thirty million gods.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
the Bhūtas and others, as well as the Rākṣasas—indeed, all that is moving and unmoving;
all the various emanations and the seven heavens in their proper order. (101–102)
The earth, consisting of seven continents and joined by the seven oceans,
together with the golden ground and likewise the region of darkness;
the seven netherworlds (pātālas) and the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are all composed of these very elements.
O Lord of Vraja, every single moon and sun, as well as the sacred field of Bhārata,
and all the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā everywhere— these are equal in number to the pores of the skin of Mahāviṣṇu, one by one. (104–105)
For indeed, all these worlds are as numerous as they are, and certainly incalculable.
Above all these worlds is Vaikuṇṭha, which is without support.
Even the Vedas, created by my will, are unable to describe it.
It is certainly not seen by bad yogīs nor by those who are not devotees.
Above that is Goloka, fifty crores of yojanas in extent; it is a wonderful supreme abode, supported by the wind. (107–108)
Exceedingly beautiful in its construction, eternal in form by my will,
it is joined by the mountain Śataśṛṅga, the meritorious Vṛndāvana,
the assembly of gods, and the river Virajā. (109)

O Vraja, it is free from dust, ten million yojanas in width, and its circumference is a hundred times that length; it is supremely auspicious, adorned with heaps of priceless jewels, diamonds, and rubies. (110–111)
There, in every mansion, were enchanting structures fashioned from priceless gems, including countless *kaustubha* jewels and others;
and there was a captivating rampart, the like of which had never been seen even by Viśvakarman.
The circle of the rāsa dance was surrounded by gopīs and throngs of cowherds, by wish-fulfilling cows,
by countless kalpa-trees and pārijāta trees, and by millions of lakes and flower gardens. (113–114)
It was surrounded by hundreds of millions of cowherd dwellings, which were themselves encircled by other dwellings;
these were provided with jeweled lamps and furnished with beds of flowers,
filled with the fragrance of scented sandalwood and blended with musk and saffron.
It was provided with articles for play and enjoyments, scented betel leaves, perfumed waters,
fragrant and delightful incenses, garlands, jeweled mirrors,
and was constantly guarded by protectors and thirty million maidservants of Rādhā. (116–117)
It was further surrounded by troops in due order, adorned with priceless jewel-ornaments and garments purified by fire, and accompanied by lordly elephants endowed with auspicious marks;
they were possessed of incomparable forms and the fullness of fresh youth.
Go to that delightful, circular place, which resembles the orb of the moon;
it is fashioned from priceless jewels, extends for ten yojanas, and is adorned with excellent musk, saffron, and fragrant sandalwood. (119–120)
It was covered with auspicious jars filled with fruits and sprouts,
with curd, parched grain, leaves, glossy dūrvā grass shoots, and fruits;
and with countless, enchanting plantain trunks of Śrī Rāma.
It was adorned with smooth sandalwood sprouts bound with silk threads, with garlands clinging to the sandalwood, and with ornaments;
it was fashioned from priceless jewels, possessed a hundred peaks, and was enchanting. (122–123)
Its height is one *koṭi* (*yojana*) and its length increases a hundredfold;
it measures fifty *koṭi* *yojanas*, the size of a mountain ridge.
It is exceedingly beautiful, indescribable even by the Vedas.

Like a beautiful wall surrounding that Goloka world, it was lovely and encircled on all sides, adorned with strings of pearls. Therein lay the delightful Vṛndāvana, graced with sandalwood trees. (125–126)
It was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), *namya* trees, and *mandāra* trees, as well as with *kāmadhenu* cows;
it was beautified by enchanting flower gardens rich in splendor,
by delightful pleasure-lakes, and by most charming pleasure-palaces.
It was exceedingly beautiful, situated in a secluded place suitable for the *rāsa* dance,
protected by countless charming guards and throngs of *gopīs*, and was a forest three hundred thousand *yojanas* in circumference, circular in shape on all sides. (128–129)
Resounding with the humming of bees and accompanied by the warbling of male cuckoos,
there stands a delightful, imperishable banyan tree, vast and extensive in its secret majesty.
It rises a thousand yojanas high and extends four times that distance in every direction.
He was a wish-fulfilling tree for the gopīs, bestowing the fruits of all their desires;
he was surrounded by three hundred thousand maidservants of Rādhā engaged in play, and [he was cooled] by the cool breeze blowing from the banks of the Virajā river. || 131–132 ||
Adorned with flowers, gentle, pure, and fragrant,
she who delights in Vṛndāvana sports there with countless throngs of maidservants;
that Rādhā is the presiding deity of my very life-breath.
This very daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, now [present] in Vraja by the curse of Śrīdāmā,
is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, by the lords of the Siddhas, and by the lords of the Munis—
[worshipped] for her perfected qualities, strengths, intellect, knowledge-yoga, and learning. (134–135)
"O dear one, in every respect she is worthy of worship, a beloved like unto the virtuous.
Thus has the description of the universes been told, O Nanda, appropriately and in brief. What more do you wish to hear? 136.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Blessed Nārada and Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the eighty-fifth chapter.
Nanda said:
O highly fortunate one, tell us now regarding the four castes, what is fit and unfit to be eaten,
the ripening of the actions of all living beings,
and the ultimate cause of all causes.
"To whom else but you, the eternally perfect Lord, shall I inquire?
(2) The Blessed One said: "I shall explain what is fit and unfit to be eaten for the four castes, as is appropriate."
O dear one, listen to what is declared in the Vedas; hear it with careful attention.
(3) The drinking of milk from an iron vessel, cow-derived prepared food, fried items and the like, flour, molasses, and likewise coconut water—(4)
Manu declared that whatever fruits and roots there may be are edible;
however, burnt food and heated *sauvīra* (sour gruel) are inedible, as ordained by Brahmā.
Coconut water kept in a bronze vessel and honey kept in a copper vessel [are likewise inedible].
All products of the cow kept in a copper vessel— except for liquor and clarified butter—
as well as drinking milk from a copper vessel while impure, eating clarified butter while impure,
and drinking salted milk, are equivalent to the immediate consumption of beef. (6–7)
Honey, molasses, ghee, oil, and likewise jaggery are not to be eaten;
similarly, ginger combined with jaggery is considered inedible according to the Vedas.
Likewise, water remaining after one has drunk it, and radish during the month of Māgha, are forbidden.
A wise man should always renounce recitation and similar practices while lying down.
(9) A wise man should certainly renounce eating twice during the day, as well as eating at the two twilights, and eating during the remainder of the night. (10)
Water, milk-rice, powder, clarified butter, and salt;
a svastika-shaped cake, molasses, milk, buttermilk, and likewise honey;
and food passed from hand to hand, as well as beef—these are [forbidden]. (11)
Camphor kept in a silver vessel is considered inedible according to the Vedas.
(12) If the server touches the eater, that food is considered inedible for everyone; this is the consensus of all. (13)
Of mongooses, gaṇḍakas, buffaloes, and birds;
of snakes, boars, and especially donkeys;
and of cats, jackals, and cocks, O Lord of the Herd. (14)
The flesh of tigers and lions must always be avoided by men;
likewise, that of aquatic creatures, crocodiles, hyenas, frogs, crabs, and cucundrats is certainly forbidden. (15–16)
In the Kali age, there shall be no eating of the flesh of cows, yaks,
elephants, horses, humans, or even of Rākṣasas;
nor [shall there be the eating of] gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, or ants.
O Lord of Vraja, on other occasions as well, the meat of those forbidden in both the world and the Veda is prohibited—
namely that of monkeys, bears, and likewise śarabhas,
as well as the meat of musk deer and donkeys. (18–19)
The milk, curd, and ghee of the queens are not to be eaten;
likewise, the *svastika* cake and fresh butter there belong to the Brahmins.
The flesh of the horse Ucchaiḥśravas, as well as its milk and other products, is likewise [forbidden].
Furthermore, among the four castes, it is heard in the Śruti that certain things are not to be eaten:
ginger is inedible for everyone on the day of the Sun (Sunday), as is stale food,
moving food, and the milk of Brahmins.
Among the four castes as well,
eating the food of one who lacks a protector (avīra) is equal to liquor and even more than eating cow's flesh.
That food of one lacking a protector, which a Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge eats, [is likewise condemned].

Manu declared that for such a person, the worship of ancestors and deities is fruitless. Fish is forbidden as food for Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas; it is likewise certainly forbidden for others on the five sacred festival days (parvan).
And meat that remains after offerings to the ancestors and gods is not considered spoiled;
yet Manu declared that on the five parvan days, it must be avoided by everyone.
Likewise, salt and oil that have not been consecrated are indeed unfit for consumption.
Food that has been consecrated by fire is pure for all as a side dish.
Ghee or water held in a single hand is considered unfit for consumption by everyone.
That which is turbid, infested with insects, or even if it appears perfectly clear and stainless [is likewise unfit]. (27–28)

It is unfit to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas, and especially by Vaiṣṇavas; it is not to be offered to Hari, nor to ascetics or celibate students. Likewise, honey mixed with ants, as well as cow's products [such as milk] and molasses, are forbidden.
O dear one, it is heard in the Śruti that no matter what substance it may be, it is not to be eaten.
That which is eaten by birds, that which is eaten by insects, that which is eaten by dogs, as well as ripe fruit,
that which is eaten by crows, and indeed all such substances are forbidden as food.
Food cooked in ghee or oil, sweetmeats, or anything prepared by a Śūdra are unfit for Brāhmaṇas to eat; likewise, the seat used by a Śūdra is forbidden. One should abandon all impure water and food.
On the day following the end of the period of impurity, one is indeed pure; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Vraja, you have described according to your knowledge the ripening of karmas—which is difficult to master and sanctioned by the Vedas—as well as what is fit and unfit to be eaten.
O Father, listen as I relate the fourfold doctrine taught in sequence within the four Vedas; it is the very essence of them all.
Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas if it has not been experienced.
One must necessarily experience the results of the actions one has performed, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious.

(36) Even with the assistance of sacred fords and the gods, as well as by means of the human body and its manifold manifestations, there is only a slight degree of help available in every respect. (37)

O dear father, penances performed with a mind certainly turned away from Me do not purify one, just as rivers cannot cleanse a jar of liquor. Indeed, human beings are not purified by meritorious penance.

O Lord of Vaiśyas, whether through every possible effort, by means of charity, or even through yoga, there is no destruction of any action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—without its being experienced. Through experience one attains purification; from that, liberation comes to human beings. (39–40)
An evil deed committed does not perish by means of a good deed,
nor does a good deed committed perish by means of an evil deed.
[This is not overcome] even by sacrifice, austerity, religious observance, or fasting.
By bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), by giving gifts, by recitation (japa), and by observances;
by circumambulating the earth, by listening to the Purāṇas, by meritorious instruction, and by the worship of the guru and the gods. (42–43)
By the very performance of one's own duty, by honoring guests,
and especially by honoring and feeding the Brahmins—
whatever is offered to a Brahmin is obtained in its full form.
That gift is the seed-form and Brahmā is the field-form.
O dear one, by a single action a human being attains heaven;
yet by that same action one does not attain liberation—only through service to me.
One goes to heaven by good deeds alone, and to hell by evil deeds.
From that [evil], one undergoes illness and birth in a contemptible womb; thereafter one becomes pure.
He who kills a cow or commits an offense against Brahmins out of desire is guilty of a minor sin (upapātakin).
He becomes a venomous serpent for as many years as there are hairs on a cow’s tail;
he is devoured by that serpent, and due to its poison,
he remains thirsty, tormented, without food, and emaciated.
Then, rising from that pit, he becomes a cow shedding hair for a year;
thereafter, for a hundred thousand years, that man becomes a leper and a Cāṇḍāla;
at that time, indeed, by his own karma, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa afflicted with leprosy.
Having fed one hundred thousand Brahmins, he shall become pure and free from disease.
For a Kṣatriya, half of that [penance] applies even if done intentionally; for one unintentionally, half of that; and for a Vaiśya, half of that again.
A Śūdra who kills a cow incurs half of that sin; of this there is no doubt.
Once purified by penance, he experiences only the remainder of his karma.
In the case of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), he incurs a fourth part of the sin; of this there is no doubt.
And the sin of those who kill cows, as well as that of Brahmins, is fourfold.
O Brahmin, whether it be a Brahmin or anyone else, they partake of the sin;
this should be understood according to the sequence [of the offenses], whether committed intentionally or unintentionally.
The atonement for this birth and its karma is indeed disease; there is no doubt.
For a year, he becomes a cow-killer and the cow itself [becomes his victim]; this is certain.
And for those who commit these fourfold sins, the killer of a Brahmin shall become a worm in excrement.
Then he becomes a barbarian (mleccha) for four times that number of years.
After that, O Brahmin, he becomes blind for four times the duration of the previous period.
By feeding four hundred thousand Brahmins, he shall become pure.
Even he who is possessed of sight and renowned shall fall from his status due to a heinous crime;
he who kills a woman, or commits such acts against the four castes, is a perpetrator of a most grievous sin.
He shall reach the Kālasūtra hell for a duration equal to the number of hairs on a woman's body.
There he is devoured by worms, deprived of food and filled with agony.
For that many years, the sinner remains in that world;
thereafter, by the power of his karma, he becomes a sinful man afflicted by consumption.
If one should feed a hundred thousand million Brahmins for a hundred years,
then that learned Brahmin, purified and restrained in austerity,
might consume a small remnant of his sin; yet through the gift of gold, he becomes pure.
The great sinner who destroys a fetus attains the face of a female dog for a hundred years;
and for another hundred years, he shall certainly become a horse,
tormented by sharp weapons.
Then that Vaiśya becomes sinful through his actions involving wealth;
however, by the gift of gold for fifty years, he becomes pure.
Thereafter, even though born of his own [low] lineage, he becomes a healthy and pure Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa who slays a Kṣatriya, or a Kṣatriya who does so outside of battle,
undergoes the ordeal of the heated spike for a thousand years;
he is boiled in molten iron and utters cries of agony.
Then he would become a rutting elephant for a hundred years;
then a Śūdra afflicted by blood disorders for a hundred years.
And then, through the gift of an elephant, that twice-born man was liberated from his disease.

One who kills a Vaiśya and a Vaiśya himself, as well as one who kills a Śūdra and a Vaiśya, (69) and likewise one who kills a Vaiśya and a Śūdra—these certainly incur equal sin. Furthermore, they enter the Pit of Worms for a hundred years. (70)
Then, O wicked one, you shall become a Kirāta and be devoured by worms;
for a hundred years, moreover, you shall be afflicted with the disease of worms.
Thereafter, possessed of a weak digestion and full of wretchedness, go forth as a Brāhmaṇa.
For up to fifty years, he remains weak with a thin belly;

liberation comes through disciplined practice at a sacred ford and by the gift of a horse. This applies even to one who has killed a Śūdra or a Brāhmaṇa, whether intentionally or unintentionally. (72–73)
By reciting the Sāvitrī ten thousand times, one becomes pure; by half that number, one is likewise purified.
Even a man of the four castes who has killed a dog, or one cursed by Śambhu, shall attain Raurava for a full hundred years.
Then he shall become a cock for sixteen years;
thereafter, having been devoured by a dog, the brahmin shall become pure.
He shall also become pure by bathing in the Gaṅgā and by the gift of gold.
A four-caste man who kills a cat becomes pure by bathing in the Gaṅgā;
by giving six palas of salt to a brāhmaṇa, he is liberated from [that sin].
Having killed snakes marked with my foot, a four-caste man [is likewise purified].
He will certainly incur the fourth mortal sin, that of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā).
Furthermore, tormented by agony and mangled by a sharp edge, he shall spend a hundred years in the Asipatra hell.
Then he becomes a snake and a *ḍuṇḍubha* for five years;
struck by a man, he suffers in misery and is tormented by death.
Then that man becomes a sinner, afflicted by fever and indeed weakened.
By his own karma, he dies within five years.
The killer of horses, the killer of elephants, and the sinner against the four castes likewise dies within five years by his own karma.
Then, O Lord of Vraja, he becomes an elephant or a horse for twenty years; thereafter, he will certainly become a Śūdra. Arrogant and afflicted by disease, he is liberated by the gift of silver.
By feeding a hundred Brahmins, one shall become pure.
By the very act of killing small creatures, a man becomes a small creature himself;
for a hundred years he shall suffer from minor ailments, and only thereafter will he overcome them.
O Lord of Vraja, the virtuous must always show compassion even toward predatory creatures; for there is no fault in the act of killing when it is committed by those who are naturally predatory.
One who destroys an *aśvattha* tree incurs a sin equal to one-fourth of that of killing a Brahmin.
And he incurs sin, dear one, and will certainly go to the Sword-Leaf Hell (Asipatravana).
There, cut by even a sharp weapon day and night for a full hundred years, he experiences supreme torment. (87–88)
