Then he becomes a *śālamali* tree for one hundred thousand years;
thereafter, he becomes a *śūdra*, with maimed limbs and afflicted by disease.
Then, until the end of his life, he will certainly become a *vipra*.

One afflicted by wounds or disease is liberated through the gift of gold. Likewise, one who gives false testimony, the ungrateful, the excessively ungrateful, the betrayer of trust, the slayer of friends, and the stealer of Brahmins' wealth [are likewise purified]. (90–91)
One who eats food at a *śrāddha* ceremony for *Śūdras*, one who burns the corpses of *Śūdras*,
a cook for *Śūdras*, and one who commits the sin of driving a bull— these, as well as a washerman and a temple-priest (*devala*), are likewise great sinners. (92)
He goes to Kumbhīpāka for a thousand years;
there he is scorched day and night by boiling oil,
pierced and tormented in every way by living creatures.
For ten million births he becomes a vulture, for a hundred births a boar, and for a hundred births a beast of prey; thereafter he becomes a Śūdra afflicted by disease.
Furthermore, for fifty years he remains possessed of sluggish digestion and fever.
By giving one hundred palas of gold, he shall certainly become pure.
A man who steals garments, a stealer of cow-products, a stealer of silver or pearls, and one who misappropriates the property of a Śūdra [are likewise purified]. (96–97)
One will certainly become a crane for a thousand years; likewise,
having consumed urine and excrement,
one becomes a Śūdra for a hundred years, O Vraja.
Afflicted by leprosy and fallen from his status as a sinner, he shall thereafter become a Brāhmaṇa still possessed of the remnants of that leprosy;
by the gift of six *pala* of gold, he is purified and released from the disease. (99–100)
Furthermore, one who steals vegetables, as well as one who steals fruits,
and a Yakṣa who steals the belongings of Līlā,
shall certainly become a blue jay for a hundred years upon being born on earth. (101)
Then he would become black-complexioned and a Śūdra on the land of Bhārata. Then, even if he were born with an extra limb as a Brāhmaṇa,
having once again become a twice-born through rebirth, he is liberated by feeding Brāhmaṇas.
One who steals cooked food will certainly be born as an animal;
he whose scrotum is smeared with fragrance and whose name is Musk (kastūrī) shall become a deer for seven births and thereafter become musk-deer.
Then, in one birth, he becomes a Śūdra afflicted with flowing leprosy in that life.
Thereafter, still joined with the remnants of his disease, he becomes emaciated.
By the gift of six *pala* of gold, he is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (105–106)
One who steals grain shall be miserable and wretched for seven lifetimes;
having fallen into a pit of excrement for a hundred years, he is released only with great terror.
A man who steals gold becomes a leper and falls from his caste.
He who accepts a gift of gold goes to the Viṭkuṇḍa hell.
Having consumed excrement there day and night for a hundred years,
he subsequently becomes a Śūdra hunter, afflicted by the disorder of blood.
Having experienced the sin of that birth, the Brāhmaṇa shall become so again;
freed from disease and anger, he is liberated through the gift of gold.
And one who approaches those women who should not be approached goes to the previously mentioned Raurava hell.
He shall dwell for an incalculable number of years in the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell;
thereafter, he shall become a worm in the wombs of unchaste women for a thousand years,
and then a dung-worm for a hundred thousand years.
From that he becomes one born as an animal, and from that, a small insect; thereafter he becomes a mleccha caste, and then an outcaste śūdra;
subsequently he becomes a brahmin afflicted by disease and a eunuch.
Furthermore, by becoming a brahmin and wandering among sacred fords (tīrtha),
he gradually becomes pure and is freed from the sin of his lineage;
having fed one hundred thousand brahmins, he becomes pure and obtains a son.
A person filled with anger becomes a donkey for seven births;
a person obsessed with quarreling becomes a crow for seven births.
One who accepts a *śālagrāma* stone will certainly go to the *kālasūtra* hell.
Then, for a hundred years, he becomes a sparrow;
a thief of iron becomes a cuckoo, a thief of ink becomes a parrot, a thief of collyrium becomes a [cuckoo], and a thief of sweets becomes a worm. (117–118)
One who hates brahmins or hates one's guru shall become a worm in the head.
And having enjoyed an unchaste woman out of lust, O dear one, one shall go to the Raurava hell;
thereafter, one becomes a useless worm for a hundred years.
Furthermore, for seven births thereafter, she shall be a widow and then barren;
she shall become untouchable and degraded in caste, and her nose shall be successively cut off.
By stealing substances of a red color, she shall be afflicted with blood-related diseases.
One devoid of right conduct becomes a barbarian; a violent person becomes lame.
One who has not received initiation becomes humpbacked, one of evil vision becomes one-eyed, and one who is full of egoism becomes earless and deaf for reviling the Vedas. (122)

One who steals speech becomes mute; a violent person becomes hairless. A speaker of falsehood becomes beardless; one who utters harsh words becomes toothless. One who steals the truth becomes devoid of a tongue; and even a wicked person who steals [another's] limbs becomes fingerless. (123–124)
The thief of books shall certainly become a fool afflicted by disease;
the stealer of horses and its thief shall pass urine mixed with saliva. Having remained so for a hundred years, he shall certainly become a horse.
An elephant-thief who seizes elephants shall remain for a thousand years in the Viṭkuṇḍa hell;
thereafter he becomes an elephant, and after that, a Śūdra.
Furthermore, one who slaughters a goat at a non-sacrificial rite, or one who accepts a goat from a thief, [shall likewise suffer]. (126–127)
Having remained in a pit of pus for a hundred years, he becomes a caṇḍāla;
then that man becomes a goat for a full year,
after which, when cut by the weapon of an enemy, he is released as a twice-born brahmin.

One who steals what has been given, having made a verbal promise of marriage but then taking it back again, shall be born in the womb of a barbarian; having experienced hell, he shall go there once more.
He who eats sweet food all alone will certainly enter the Kālamūtra hell.
Having remained there for a hundred years, one then becomes a bat for a thousand years;
at that time, there is one birth as a fly and one as an ant.
There is one birth as a bee and one birth as a honey-bee.
One birth as a *varala* and one birth as a *daṃśa*;
one birth as a *maśaka* and one birth as a *pūtika* is recorded;
and one birth as a bedbug (*talpakīṭa*)—then he will certainly become a *śūdra*. (132–133)
Then the twice-born man, possessed of the notion of non-existence and afflicted by disease, shall be liberated.
A thief of oil becomes an oil-maker for three births;
then, with a wicked mind, he becomes a goldsmith for one birth. (134)
One who steals gold from a person of faith becomes a merchant of gold and remains in the Pit of Darkness for a hundred years;
for one birth he shall be of depraved conduct, and for one birth he shall be a thief. (135–136)
While residing in the womb, the scribe did not eat his mother’s flesh;

yet he lacked compassion there solely due to the absence of teeth. O Lord of Vraja, the goldsmith, the gold merchant, and the scribe— [The verse continues: ...are all born from the seed of the Creator (Brahmā). Just as the Creator is the father of all beings, so too is the scribe the father of all castes. O King, the scribe is the father of the four varṇas, and the goldsmith is the father of the three varṇas. The gold merchant is the father of two varṇas, and the washerman is the father of one varṇa. The leather-worker is the father of the Śūdras, and the butcher is the father of the outcastes. The barber is the father of the low-born, and the potter is the father of the base. The fisherman is the father of the fishermen, and the hunter is the father of the hunters. The weaver is the father of the weavers, and the dyer is the father of the dyers. The oil-presser is the father of the oil-pressers, and the liquor-seller is the father of the liquor-sellers. The betel-seller is the father of the betel-sellers, and the grain-measurer is the father of the grain-measurers. The astrologer is the father of the astrologers, and the physician is the father of the physicians. The musician is the father of the musicians, and the dancer is the father of the dancers. The storyteller is the father of the storytellers, and the bard is the father of the bards. The actor is the father of the actors, and the mime is the father of the mimes. The juggler is the father of the jugglers, and the sorcerer is the father of the sorcerers. The thief is the father of the thieves, and the rogue is the father of the rogues. The gambler is the father of the gamblers, and the drunkard is the father of the drunkards. The liar is the father of the liars, and the slanderer is the father of the slanderers. The cheat is the father of the cheats, and the deceiver is the father of the deceivers. The oppressor is the father of the oppressors, and the tormentor is the father of the tormentors. The cruel is the father of the cruel, and the wicked is the father of the wicked. The impure is the father of the impure, and the unclean is the father of the unclean. The ungrateful is the father of the ungrateful, and the faithless is the father of the faithless. The atheist is the father of the atheists, and the heretic is the father of the heretics. The hypocrite is the father of the hypocrites, and the pretender is the father of the pretenders. The false ascetic is the father of the false ascetics, and the false devotee is the father of the false devotees. The false mendicant is the father of the false mendicants, and the false monk is the father of the false monks. The false priest is the father of the false priests, and the false teacher is the father of the false teachers. The false king is the father of the false kings, and the false minister is the father of the false ministers. The false friend is the father of the false friends, and the false relative is the father of the false relatives. The false guest is the father of the false guests, and the false host is the father of the false hosts. The false servant is the father of the false servants, and the false master is the father of the false masters. The false witness is the father of the false witnesses, and the false judge is the father of the false judges. The false lawgiver is the father of the false lawgivers, and the false punisher is the father of the false punishers. The false protector is the father of the false protectors, and the false refuge is the father of the false refuges. The false shelter is the father of the false shelters, and the false support is the father of the false supports. The false foundation is the father of the false foundations, and the false pillar is the father of the false pillars. The false beam is the father of the false beams, and the false roof is the father of the false roofs. The false wall is the father of the false walls, and the false door is the father of the false doors. The false window is the father of the false windows, and the false lattice is the father of the false lattices. The false floor is the father of the false floors, and the false ceiling is the father of the false ceilings. The false step
Among men on this earth, those two are rogues devoid of compassion;
their hearts are like the edge of a razor, and they possess no regard for others. Among hundreds, there might be some virtuous person, but neither of those two is such a one.
O dear one, for the sake of one’s own welfare, one should not place trust in those who are clever-minded, devoted to Śiva, learned in the scriptures, and whose minds are fixed on dharma—
provided they are boundary-seizers, wicked, thieves of land, or violent. (140)
One who seizes land that has been given will certainly go to the Kālasūtra hell.
Remaining there for sixty thousand years, afflicted by hunger and nakedness, he then emerges from those very places and is born as a worm in excrement. (141–142)
From that, one becomes a wicked Śūdra for one birth, and thereafter becomes pure.
Therefore, a wise person should be diligent and strive with effort through various forms of knowledge. Furthermore, one who steals dyed cloth becomes a red insect for one birth.
Then that Śūdra shall take one birth, after which he becomes a pure Brāhmaṇa.

A man who neglects the three daily junctions (saṃdhyā), who goes to sleep at dawn, who sleeps during the junction times, who sleeps during the day, or who steals the sacred thread (yajñasūtra)—[these likewise fall]. 144–145.
One who performs the twilight prayers while impure, one who reviles the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,

and a twice-born man who opposes them or has fallen through three births— such a person is barred from the path to heaven. Furthermore, a Śūdra who commits adultery with a Brāhmaṇa woman will certainly go to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
There, tormented, he is cooked for three hundred thousand years;
scorched day and night in a dreadful, boiling oil,
that sinner against unchaste women thereafter becomes a worm in the womb of prostitutes.

For sixty thousand years his food shall be that very excrement; thereafter, he becomes a Caṇḍāla for a hundred thousand births in succession. Then he becomes a Śūdra afflicted with leprosy for one birth, and after that, he becomes pure.
That brahmin, though remaining with a remnant of disease, becomes pure through wandering to sacred fords (tīrtha).
And that man who offers impure food as an oblation (naivedya) to a god in an improper place, such as one worshipped by non-believers, becomes an unworthy śūdra. (150–151)
By worshipping a royal linga with hair upon it, one becomes a Yavana;
by worshipping one that is weak, one becomes blind; and by worshipping one that is contemptible, one becomes contemptible.
Furthermore, such a person becomes physically deformed, impoverished, and afflicted by disease. (152)
And through lack of faith, the fruit is similar to the creation itself.
(153) Having fashioned a linga even from clay, ashes, cow-dung, or sand, and having worshipped it but once, one shall dwell in heaven for the duration of a kalpa. (154)
Then, by worshipping one hundred lingas, one becomes a learned brahmin, a possessor of great wisdom, and a sovereign of the earth;
and by worshipping them a thousand times, one certainly attains that fruit as well. (155)
Having dwelt for a very long time in heaven, he shall become a lord of kings in the land of Bhārata.
For ten thousand [offerings] he becomes their master, and for a hundred thousand he becomes a sovereign of the earth.
Through worship with extreme devotion, one shall obtain even a greater fruit than this.
Through bathing at sacred fords, through giving gifts, through feeding Brahmins,
and through the worship of Nārāyaṇa, as well as by means of action,
one born of the Brahmin caste becomes a learned Brāhmaṇa through superior austerity.

A wise man, a brahmin, and a devotee of Viṣṇu who has conquered his senses is born upon the land of Bhārata through the merit of many births. By the mere touch of his feet, the earth is instantly purified.
Holy places become holy through those who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and through Vaiṣṇavas;
it is heard in the Śruti that they purify even a thousand of their own men.
Even a Brāhmaṇa who is difficult to treat is born as a physician due to his past sin.
Likewise, one who is difficult to treat as a physician [is reborn as] a snake-catcher for three lifetimes.
One who is exceedingly cruel, of wicked conduct, and a hater of gods and Brahmins shall become a crooked serpent for a thousand years. (162–163)
And she who is a female messenger for those who are lustful after unchaste women, O Vraja,
shall remain in Kālamūtra for a hundred years and then become a lizard.
Having been a lizard for one birth, she shall then be a deer for three births.
For one birth he becomes a buffalo, and for one birth he becomes a wild cat;
for one birth he is a rhinoceros, and for three births he is a jackal—having despoiled another's tank and given away its crops. (165–166)
That Brāhmaṇa who, being greedy for fish, eats meat in vain, shall become a crocodile and a tortoise for three births;
and he who eats meat that has not been given shall become a fish and a deer.
And having experienced that sin for a thousand years,
O dear one, he becomes purified through the exhaustion of his karma and shall become a Brahmin once again.
However, a Brahmin who neglects the Ekādaśī fast falls from his status.
By giving double the amount of food, one is released from that sin. And that base man who eats on my birthday—he too consumes the sin produced by the three worlds; of this there is no doubt.
Having experienced all of hell, one subsequently falls into the state of a Caṇḍāla.
(171) Likewise, on the occasion of Śivarātri and on the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī, one who is unable to observe a fast should partake of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna). (172)
Then, being incapable and weak, one should also feed Brāhmaṇas;
having performed my meritorious great festival, one becomes pure from sin. Therefore, the chanting of my names should be performed with effort.
By eating at night on the new moon day, one becomes a vulture for a thousand million lifetimes, a pig for a hundred births,
and a beast of prey for a hundred births;
likewise, a twice-born man who is uninitiated becomes a conch-shell and a chilla-bird.
He shall become a parrot;
and a twice-born man who does not marry shall certainly become a royal swan.
One who steals variegated garments shall become a peacock for three births.

One who steals a leaf of fire becomes a kāraṇḍava bird for a long time; one who steals an image of the gods remains blind for seven years, becoming impoverished, afflicted by disease, deaf, and hunchbacked. (177)
The great fool who consumes women, oil, honey, or meat on a Sunday or during the five festival days (parvan) will certainly go to Vajradaṃṣṭra; as a sinner,
he shall remain there in suffering for a thousand years.
Thereafter, one becomes a barbarian and a *cāṇḍāla* for seven births;
then, freed from disease, one becomes a *śūdra*, and thereafter a pure *brāhmaṇa*.
Therefore, one who fears unrighteousness should not eat [the forbidden] in Bhārata with any effort.
That lowest of men who, upon seeing a Brāhmaṇa or a deity, does not bow down, shall remain impure as a Yavana for the duration of his life;
likewise, he who does not rise to greet a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived [remains so]. (181–182)
He will certainly become a slayer of a Brahmin for seven births;
a hater of Śiva becomes a cock for seven births, as does Devala.
One who is weak in knowledge destroys the worship of the ancestors and gods prescribed by the Vedas.
That sinner goes to Narama for a thousand years.
After that, having experienced Raurava, he becomes a crow at a sacred ford for three births, and for three births he becomes a jackal; O Vraja, he eats a corpse at a sacred ford.
Throughout three births, he shall be a protector of corpses at sacred fords;
by his actions, he is a sinner who takes the toll from the dead.
Having performed the daily worship of the gods, he is a hypocrite weak in knowledge.
He who does not worship his guru with devotion and does not give him food shall become a miserable man, a sinner cursed by the gods;
though he performs the daily worship of the deities, he is a hypocrite whose knowledge is weak. (187–188)
That wooden being who commits treason against the gods does not obtain the fruit of his merit;
and he who extinguishes the lamp becomes a firefly for seven births. Furthermore, one who is excessively greedy for fish and eats what is not an offering [to the deity] [suffers likewise].
He shall become a fish, a deer, and a cat for seven births.
A stealer of a cow becomes a pigeon; a stealer of a garland, a bird;
a stealer of grain, a sparrow; and a stealer of meat, an elephant. (190–191)

In seven births he shall be a poet who strikes at the learned, a croaker (*māṇḍraka*), and a village Brahmin who is a bad poet; in seven births he shall be a mongoose (*nakula*). For one birth he shall be a leper, and for three births a lizard (*kṛkalāsa*).
One birth as a *varaḷa*, then as a tree and an ant;
thereafter as a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, and likewise a Brāhmaṇa—such is the human being of the four castes who sells his daughter. (193–194)
He immediately goes to the Tāmisra hell for as long as the moon and sun exist;
thereafter, he becomes a hunter and a seller of meat. After that, he will subsequently become a sick man, just as he was in his previous birth.
A Brahmin who sells my name will certainly never be liberated.
Furthermore, in the world of mortals, even the mere remembrance of my name does not exist for him. 196.
Thereafter, being weak in knowledge, he shall take one birth in the womb of a cow (197).
Then he becomes a goat, then a ram, and for seven years a buffalo;
then he becomes a human being who is a great wheel-bearer, crooked, and devoid of dharma (198).
For seven births he shall be an oil-presser and likewise a potter;
he who speaks false slanders and reviles the gods and Brahmins shall become a goldsmith and a washerman for seven births.

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are contemptible and devoid of purity—200—their birth shall likewise be in the womb of Mlecchas for ten thousand years. Furthermore, he will be excessively greedy for women, lustful, and always devoted to women. 201.
He who lustfully gazes upon the hips, breasts, or face of women will immediately be seized by consumption and shall become a eunuch even in the next world. Furthermore,
he who does so shall become blind and a eunuch in the hereafter as well.
A Brahmin who performs malevolent magic, a violent person, or one weak in knowledge,
likewise goes to the Andhatāmisra hell for ten thousand years.
At that time, even an astrologer who is of wicked mind and a first-rate giver [of such things] undergoes the same fate.
Then, through the enjoyment of the fruits of his actions, that Śūdra shall likewise become a Brāhmaṇa;
yet, out of greed, he speaks falsely regarding his knowledge of the scriptures and astrology.
He will certainly become a Jyeṣṭhī monkey for seven births.

Through the austerity of many births, one may become a Brāhmaṇa in Bhārata. One who possesses sound intellect and is exceedingly righteous is a Brāhmaṇa; one devoid of dharma is a sinner. A Brāhmaṇa devoted to his own duty is superior even to the sacrificial fire. (206–207)
He is pure and exceedingly radiant; therefore, the gods are always afraid of him.
Just as Gaṅgā is among rivers, Puṣkara among sacred fords (tīrthas), Kāśī among cities, and Śaṅkara among the wise, [so is he]. 208.
And as the Vedas are among scriptures, as the Aśvattha is among trees,
(209) as fasting is among penances and religious observances,
so too among all castes, the Brāhmaṇas alone are the most excellent. (210)
When sacred fords and meritorious vows have fallen into neglect,
the pure dust from the feet of Brahmins is the destroyer of the disease of sin;
their auspicious blessings are the cause of all well-being.

This, O dear one, has been told to you—the ripening of karmas, alas!—exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was understood; understand that in its entirety. And having heard this ripening of dharma, [give] gold to the reciter.
One should give him silver, clothing, and betel-leaf;
one should immediately bestow a hundred pieces of gold and a herd of cows.
Out of love for me, one should also give silver, clothing, and betel-leaf to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Bhagavān and Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the eighty-sixth chapter.
Nanda said:
In the context of the maiden of Kedāra, the glorification of [her] deeds was told.
O Lord, please speak at length regarding that, in connection with the female *kṛtyā* weapons.
Who indeed was that maiden of Kedāra, or who was the sovereign of Kedāra?
"Whose lineage was his birth in? You should explain that to me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In former times, there was a son of Brahmā named Manu Svāyambhuva."
His wife was Śatarūpā, blessed and the most venerable among women.
They had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda;
and the son of Uttānapāda was the highly illustrious Dhruva. (3–4)
His son was Nandasāvarṇi, and Kedāra was his offspring. The illustrious Kedāra, a devotee of Viṣṇu himself, was the lord of the seven islands.
For the sake of his protection, the Sudarśana [discus] appeared in the assembly of the virtuous.
A hundred thousand pure cows, adorned with golden horns,
were given by Varuṇa; likewise, garments purified by fire,
a hundred thousand pieces of gold, and the earth abounding in all kinds of crops were bestowed.
Jewel-gems, pearls, and likewise supreme diamonds;
a hundred thousand rubies, horses, and elephants;
silver, coral, sweetmeats, and an excellent mountain of a hundred grains.
Day after day he gave jeweled ornaments to the Brāhmaṇas;
every day he fed one million Brāhmaṇas.
The king gave vessels for water and food made of gold.
With joy, he gave to the Brahmins golden sacrificial threads, excellent finger-rings, and seats made of gold and jewels; and he provided a hundred thousand Brahmins with the royal cook. (11)
And two hundred thousand brahmins were appointed as servers.
There were enchanting streams of ghee, streams of honey, streams of curd,
streams of molasses, and streams of milk, which were constantly desired according to one's prayers.
From morning until the twilight rites, he likewise provided meals for the Brahmins,
as well as appropriate gifts of wealth to the distressed and the mendicants.
The king, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses, subsisted on fruits and roots.
Having offered everything to me, he chanted my name day and night.
(15) Once, the cook said to that lord of kings: "Ten lakhs [of brahmins] have arrived for the meal of the twice-born. (16)
"O Lord, tell me, let the Brahmins eat coarse food today;
indeed, O King, let those Brahmins consume it with soup and other condiments.
Furthermore, the king's jurisdiction extends for four yojanas."
The king who possesses ten times those qualities is indeed a Maṇḍaleśvara.
A king possessing ten times those [qualities] is proclaimed a Rājendra.
Five hundred thousand Rājendras always gather in the assembly at Kedāra.
He offered to Kedāra the priceless jewel-maṇikya, the pearl-oyster, the lord of gems, the elephant-jewel, and the horse-jewel.
Those born from the sacrificial pit, produced by a portion of Kamalā—
Wearing garments as pure as fire and adorned with jewel ornaments, that lotus-eyed maiden, the most excellent of loving women and full of desire, said to the king:
"O Great King, I am your daughter. (21–22)

Having honored her with devotion and having entrusted his wife to her care, the king remained there. She, recognizing her mother and father, and having offered them great reverence, went to the beautiful Puṇyavana forest to perform austerities near the Yamunā.
Because it was a forest for that penance, it is therefore remembered as Vṛndāvana.
By means of her austerity, she chose me as her most excellent boon;
Brahmā granted her the boon: "In the future, you shall behold Kṛṣṇa."
Once, while she was dwelling on the bank of a river, smiling,
reclining upon a bed of flowers, and adorned with jeweled ornaments,
Brahmā went there to test that most beautiful and virtuous woman.
In seclusion, she beheld a supreme young man:
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with jewel ornaments, smiling, amorous, beautiful, and desired by women. (27–28)
Like a sixteen-year-old youth with a golden luster, possessing the grace of ten million Cupids, the excellent one was clad in no garments;
his face was like the full autumn moon, and his beautiful eyes were like autumn lotuses. (29)
Seeing him, she rose up and welcomed him into her presence;
with devotion, she offered him worship and joyfully gave him fruits and roots.
Having offered him fragrant water, she bowed down, filled with great delight.
Having accepted the worship, the Lord, appearing in the form of a brahmin and blazing with spiritual luster, spoke to her with joy and respect:
"Go to him who is desirable to women full of passion, yet difficult for chaste wives to attain. (32)
Dharma said: "Whose daughter are you, O enchanting one, and what is your name? What are you doing here in secret? You ought to tell me that. (33)
"For what reason do you practice austerities, or what do you desire, O beautiful one?
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever is wished for in your heart.
Vṛndā said:
"O Brahmin, I am Kedārakanyā, Vṛndā, who dwells in Vṛndāvana.
I perform penance in solitude and meditate upon Hari as my husband.
If you are capable of granting it, give me the boon I desire. (35)
"If you are incapable, then go; what is the use of your questioning, O Brāhmaṇa? Dharma said:
"The Supreme Self, the Lord, is free from desire and inconceivable."
He is devoid of qualities and formless, yet his very form exists to bestow grace upon his devotees.
Who but Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī is capable of being the wife of such a Lord?
The four-armed Hari, the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha, has two wives. (37–38)
In Goloka, he is two-armed, with the divine flute to his face,
dressed as a youthful cowherd, and the most perfect of all;
his wife is Rādhā herself, the Great Lakṣmī, higher than the highest.
The supreme one, whose nature is Brahman, constantly worships the Supreme Lord, the Ātman— tranquil, most beautiful, dark and handsome,
possessing a fair form that puts to shame the beauty of ten million Cupids. (40–41)
He is adorned with ornaments of priceless jewels, truth personified, eternally embodied, clad in yellow garments, beautiful, and the bestower of all prosperity.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa exists in two forms: as the two-armed and the four-armed.

In Vaikuṇṭha he is four-armed, while in Goloka he himself is two-armed. A single blink of Vṛndā is equal to the fall of Brahmā; and with twenty-five thousand such blinks, there occurs the fall of Indra.
Fourteen periods of Indra’s time constitute a day of Brahmā;
his night is of equal duration, O Creator of the worlds as well.
Thus, thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year.
Thus, O you who are intent on awakening, understand that his lifespan is a hundred years;
yet Sanaka and the others serve him until the end of their lives, even for millions upon millions of kalpas— for that All-pervading Lord is not to be attained by such means alone.
Even Śeṣa, who possesses a thousand mouths, serves him day and night with devotion while constantly chanting, for hundreds upon hundreds of millions of kalpas;
yet he, the benefactor who is higher than the highest, is difficult to propitiate and cannot be easily attained.
In birth after birth, Brahmā should worship Him who is the very nature of Brahman.
With his four faces, he constantly and eternally praises the Sanātana;
He is the one beyond description in the Veda, the Creator of the Vedas, and the Ordainer (Vidhi).
He is the ordainer, the giver of fruits, and the bestower of all prosperity;
for that Blessed One, the ender of even the Destroyer of Time, cannot be accomplished [as an object].
He is the agent of the dissolution of the worlds through his power in the form of Rudra.
He praises her with five faces; what need is there to mention anyone else?
Listen, O Vṛnda: there is no one dearer to the Blessed One than she who is devoted to him.
Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, is the very embodiment of all powers. (52–53)
She is the supreme sovereign, the primordial nature whose essence is Brahman;
she is Nārāyaṇī, the illusory power of Viṣṇu, Vaiṣṇavī, the eternal one. By her māyā, the world is deluded and perpetually wanders within that which is impermanent.
This Vṛnda praises this God with devotion day and night;
and this six-faced Gajavaktra praises Him with devotion according to his own capacity.
Gaṇeśa meditates upon Him, and His worship comes first of all.
The Blessed One is the Lord of all gods and the teacher of teachers for the wise.
Among the lords of the Siddhas, the lord of the gods, the lord of the moon, and the teacher of the wise—there is no scholar greater than Gaṇeśa; and Gaṇeśa is the sovereign of the deities.
Even the supreme goddess Sarasvatī is unable to praise him;
day and night, Padmā serves his lotus feet with devotion.
By his sidelong glance, the entire universe becomes the most perfect Śiva.
Out of fear of him this wind blows, out of fear of him the sun shines;
Indra pours down rain, Agni burns, and Death moves among living beings.
The earth, the supporter of all, dwells [in submission] because of his service.
O beautiful one, even the prosperous and immovable mountains were struck with fear by him.
By service to his lotus feet, that Gaṅgā became the essence of all holy fords— purifying, bestowing liberation, and the goddess who sanctifies the worlds.
The goddess Tulasī is purifying through the mere remembrance and service of whom;
and by whose majesty the nine planets and the guardians of the quarters are struck with fear.
And throughout all the cosmic eggs, those who consist of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva [are likewise subdued].
There were others who were various lords of the gods, as well as Śeṣa and the other sages;
some were of the nature of *kalās* (parts), and some were of the nature of *aṃśas* (portions);
some were *kalā-aṃśas* (sub-portions) of Kṛṣṇa, and some were [parts] of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
"O auspicious lady, you desire as your husband the Lord who is beyond material nature;
yet Rādhikā is attainable by me alone in Goloka, never by anyone else.
O highly fortunate one, worship me, the sovereign of kings, as your husband."

And you shall be powerful against the gods and the Daityas, O fair-faced one. Whatever joys exist indeed within the three worlds, O auspicious lady, enjoy them all by my grace; of this there is no doubt.
And on the far shore of the seven seas, there is a beautiful and excellent golden city built by the Creator for the sport of the gods.
Go there; may you be blessed, and enjoy yourself with me, O Rāma.
Go to Mahendra’s beloved forest, which is filled with flowering gardens;
go to golden Laṅkā, adorned with various jewels. Go right there—may it be well with you—and enjoy yourself. (70–71)
Go to Vispandaka, Suvasana, Nandaka, and Puṣpabhadraka;
may it be well with you, enjoy yourself there.
Or else go to the cave of Sumeru or the enchanting Ocean of Milk.
Go right there—may it be well with you; take your delight... (73).
To Satyaloka, to Brahmaloka, the delightful abode, the secret place; go right there—may it be well with you; take your delight... (74).
In Malaya is a delightful abode, constructed from the finest essence of jewels,
perpetually fragrant and purified by the sandalwood breeze. There,
too, are lovely *mālatī*, *yūthikā*, *ketakī*, and *mādhavī* flowers.
Exceedingly enchanting with the fragrance of beautiful campaka flowers,
and filled with the sweet sounds of cuckoos and bees—
go there, may you be blessed; it is delightful.
Among these— the worlds of Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama,
the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), Agni, Dharma, and likewise the Moon—
choose whichever world you desire.
Go to that very place—may it be well with you—enjoy yourself... 79. To Ratnadvīpa, Maṇidvīpa, and the beautiful Candrasarovara; go to that very place—may it be well with you—enjoy yourself... 80.

Having spoken thus, as he was departing to enjoy himself, that princess, her face and eyes flushed with anger, spoke deceitfully—not for the sake of a genuine investigation, but to demonstrate her own chastity: "Go! (81) she said.
"It is beneficial, truthful, endowed with yoga, conducive to dharma and wealth, and brings fame.
Vṛndā said:
"Be steadfast, O illustrious one; you are the best among the castes of Brahmins."
For Brahmins, austerity is the root, as are truth, the Vedic vows, and fortitude.
(83) But for the unrighteous, consorting with the wives of others is their very nature;
indeed, O Brahmin, through unrighteousness alone the wicked man perceives misfortunes. (84)
Then, while the rival prospers, he who remains rooted in that state perishes;
for it is certain that by the forceful violation of women devoted to their husbands, one immediately becomes a violator of his mother and incurs the sin of a hundred murders of Brahmins. (85)
He is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell as long as the moon and sun endure;
scorched in vessels heated with oil, he does not die because of his subtle body (sūkṣmadeha);
and he is struck on the head by the messengers of Yama with iron clubs.
Momentary pleasure leads to long-lasting suffering and is the cause of total ruin; a righteous man never desires the act of approaching one who should not be approached.
"Forgive me, go, may it be well with you, O Brahmin weak in wisdom."
Just as an insect inevitably falls upon seeing the flame of a lamp;
just as a greedy fish sees bait on the tip of a hook, or as a hungry eater consumes food smeared with poison. (89–90)
A wicked man grasps what is wicked, like a jar of poison with milk on its surface;
likewise, having seen the charming lotus-faces of other men's wives,
the deluded libertine takes hold of the seed of his own destruction through infatuation.
The face of women is beautiful, and their pair of hips is captivating.
Yet the vulva is the support of lust, the seed of destruction, and the very site of unrighteousness;
it is a pit of hell, filled with saliva and urine. (92–93)
Stinking, sinful, and the cause of Yama’s rod of punishment,
just as the *liṅga* enters into the wombs of women who are of sinful birth,
so too does the male enter into the Raurava hell age after age.
"Having seen this secret and this calamity, you wish to violate me!
Right here are all the gods, the world-protectors, and the Brahmins; and Dharma, blazing brightly, is the witness and the judge of all actions. (95–96)
Yama, the wielder of the rod of punishment, was himself established by Hari;
and Kṛṣṇa himself is the righteous-souled Maheśvara, whose form is knowledge.
Durgā is the intellect, Brahmā is the mind, and likewise the gods are the senses.
O twice-born one, witnesses of all actions abide within all living beings. Where is there anything hidden or secret from the Knower of Brahman, O you who are weak in wisdom?
Forgive me; go, may it be well with you, for the twice-born are not to be slain.
"I am capable of reducing you to ashes; go, my child, as you please.
One hundred and eight yugas have passed for me in ascetic penance.
I have no lineage, nor do I have a father or a mother."
"O twice-born one, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the inner self of all, protects me.
Dharma, established by Kṛṣṇa, also protects me constantly. Likewise, the Sun, the Moon, the Wind, and the Fire [protect me]. (101–102)

Brahmā, Śambhu, and the Blessed Goddess Durgā protect me always—He by whom the swans were made white and the parrots were made green; He by whom the peacocks were made variegated; He shall grant me protection.
All the gods are the protectors of the helpless, the young, and the aged.
Dharma will never abandon me, for it always regards me as a woman.
"O child, leave me, your mother, and go wherever you please."

Having spoken thus, that goddess stood there like the earth, neither approaching to enjoy him nor departing through awakening. And out of anger she cursed him, saying: "O blind Brahmin, become subject to destruction!"
"O you of evil conduct, perish! O most sinful one, perish!
[107] Then the Sun himself, having cursed him, restrained him with great effort.
In the meantime, O dear one, the Lords of the World appeared right there. [108]
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other lords of the gods arrived, utterly terrified;
seeing Dharma in the form of a digit, they wept, holding him—extremely emaciated and frightened like the moon on the new-moon night—in their laps. (109)
"Go, for he is motionless, soiled, and scorched by the fire of Satī’s anger.
Śrī Bhava said:
"Forgive him, O Vṛndā, my devotee who removes birth, death, and old age!"
“O Dharma, O devoted wife, revive my devotee and protect him!
(111) Brahmā said: “Indeed, without Dharma, this entire world became filled with darkness.”
The moon and the sun trembled, as did Śeṣa and the earth.
Mahādeva said:
"O beautiful one, the entire world has perished because of the absence of dharma."
"Revive the Dharma; may it be well with you, and may there be auspiciousness for you, O lady of beautiful countenance.
Sūrya said:
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever is desired in your heart."
"Revive Dharma—blessings be upon you—and protect the creation, O devoted wife!
Ananta said:
"How do you practice Dharma through austerity, and why do you mock Dharma?"
"Revive Dharma—blessings be upon you—and let all Dharma be yours.
Candra said:
"Dharma, assuming the form of a twice-born, has come here to test you."
"Urged by Brahmā and yet free from fault, he was struck down.
Mahendra said:
"O King, dharma is attained through austerity, and the fruit of dharma comes through dharma."
"And how can there be fruit from austerities if dharma has gone to destruction?
Varuṇa said:
"O most virtuous one, revive dharma; protect the eternal dharma."
"The action of those who perform rituals is fruitless without dharma, as is the conduct of the unrighteous.
Pavana said:
"O auspicious one, purify the world; restore dharma now!"
"When dharma is destroyed, your unprecedented ascetic merit will perish.
Vahni said:
"And you have come to Bhārata in order to perform the acquisition of your own dharma."
"You destroy the Dharma through ignorance; revive it once more, O beautiful one!
Yama said:
"O lovely-faced one, I am capable of performing the rites prescribed in the Vedas for all beings."
"O Dharma, grant the fruit [of our merit] through your compliance with the Law; revive us quickly!
(121) Having heard the words of the gods, the devoted wife rose up;
having paid homage to the lords of the gods, that ascetic woman spoke to them. (122)
Vṛndā said:
"O gods, I did not recognize that he was a brahmin in the form of Dharma. Out of anger, I destroyed him, who had come to embrace me. (123)
"By your grace, I shall surely restore Dharma to life.
Having spoken thus, O Lord of Vraja, that Vṛndā said:
"If my austerity is true, and if my worship of Viṣṇu is true," ||| 124 ||
By that merit, may this twice-born man here immediately become free from his fever.
If my vow is true and my asceticism is pure and true, by that merit and by that truth, may the twice-born man [become... (125–126).
If Nārāyaṇa is real, the soul of all, with an eternal form,
and if Śiva is real as the essence of knowledge, then the twice-born is... If Brahmā is real, and those gods are real, and if Prakṛti is supreme—
"Sacrifice is truth, austerity is truth, the twice-born is [truth]... (128).
Having spoken thus, Vṛndā placed Dharma upon her lap;
and seeing him in that beautiful form, the virtuous woman wept out of compassion. (129)
In the meantime, Mūrti, the wife of Dharma, overwhelmed with grief,
fell at the feet of Viṣṇu with her head bowed and spoke thus.
Mūrti said:
O Lord, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, have mercy!
O Jagannātha, full of grace, quickly restore my beloved to life!
For that woman who is deprived of her husband is a sinner in the ocean of worldly existence.
Just as the eye is absent from the mouth, and as the body is devoid of life; (so too are others limited).

For a father gives only a limited amount, a brother only a limited amount, a son only a limited amount, a kinsman only a limited amount, and a mother only a limited amount; but the lord, the husband, is the giver of everything.
Having spoken thus, that goddess remained there and wept.
Then the Blessed Lord, the soul of all, who is beyond primordial nature, spoke to Vṛndā.
The Blessed Lord said:
"You have obtained this lifespan through austerity, as long as the lifespan of Brahmā. Give that very life to Dharma and go to Goloka, O beautiful one.
With this body and through further austerity, you shall obtain me later."
O fair-faced one, having later come to Goloka during the Vārāha-kalpa,
you shall become Rādhā’s shadow as the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu;
and Rāyaṇa, a portion of My own energy, will take you in marriage.
And you shall obtain me in the *rāsa* dance along with the gopīs and Rādhā;
for when Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, was [born] due to the curse of Śrīdāmā,
she alone was the real Rādhā, while you were her shadow-form.
At the time of the wedding, King Nārāyaṇa will take both you and Chāyā.
Having given you away, the real Rādhā will become invisible;
and the deluded ones will perceive her as being Rādhā herself.
And in Gokula,
the cowherds do not see the lotus feet of Rādhā in their dreams;
yet Rādhā herself is in my lap, the beloved of the King of Kings.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu, Sundarī granted him long life.
Pūrṇadharma arose, resembling molten gold;
more beautiful than before and endowed with splendor, he bowed down to the Supreme beyond the supreme. (142)
Vṛndā said:
O gods, listen attentively to my words, which must not be transgressed;
indeed, my word shall not be false—heed it well. (143)
"May there be destruction!"—these words were spoken by me out of fear of his anger.
But the Sun restrained me from speaking them again for a third time.
And this [truth] is as complete now as it was before.
In the Tretā age, this Dharma stands on three feet; likewise, in the Dvāpara, it has two feet;
and in the first part of the Kali age, O Hari, it has one foot.
In the remainder of the Kali, it is reduced to a sixteenth part, yet at the end of the Kali, it returns to its former state as in the Satya age.
Because it emerged from my mouth three times, there was consequently a gradual waning;
and when it was repeated in the mind, Bhāskara (the Sun) restrained it.
By that very same discharge, this [Moon], consisting of digits, remained as a mere remnant.
Thus cursed, he remained fixed in that fortress for the remainder of the Kali age; so it was certain.
In the meantime, O Nanda, the deities beheld a chariot arriving with speed from Goloka—exceedingly beautiful and auspicious. (148–149)
It was fashioned from priceless jewels,
adorned with necklaces of diamonds, and embellished with gems, rubies, pearls, garments, white chowries, and beautiful ornaments such as mirrors for the breasts. (150)
Having bowed to Hari, Hara, Vṛndā, Brahmā, and all the deities, she ascended her chariot, beheld Goloka, and departed. The gods also went to their own abodes. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and the Blessed Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma... Mahā... Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the eighty-seventh chapter.
Nanda said:
Even the Vedas themselves are not capable of knowing you, the Lord of the Vedas; nor are the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa, nor likewise the sages, Siddhas, and others.
Great curiosity has arisen in me to know who you truly are.
"O Lord, tell me all that regarding the true nature of your own self in this solitary place.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"In the meantime, O lords of sages, [they came] there to see Kṛṣṇa."
They arrived suddenly, O child, blazing with the splendor of Brahmanic power:
Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Durvāsas, and Kaṇva. (3–4)
Kātyāyana and Pāṇini, Kaṇāda and likewise Gautama;
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
Kapila, Āsuri, Vāyu, and likewise Pañcaśikha.
Viśvāmitra, Vālmīki, Kaśyapa, and Parāśara;
Vibhāṇḍaka, Marīci, the two Śukras, Atri, and Bṛhaspati;
likewise Gārgya, Vātsya, Vyāsa, and Jaimini. (6–7)
Mitavāk, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Yājñavalkya, and Śuka;
Saubhari, Śuddhajaṭila, Bharadvāja, and Subhadraka;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Lomaśa, Āsuri, and Viṭaṅkaṇa.
Aṣṭāvakra, Śatānanda, Vāmadeva, Bhāsuri, Saṃvarta, Utathya, Nara, and I myself, Nārada;
Jābāli, Paraśurāma, Agastya, and Paila as well. (9–10)
Yudhāmanyu, Gauramukha, Upamanyu, Śrutaśravas,
Maitreya, Cyavana, and the sage Vararuci—
seeing them, he rose up suddenly and, with palms joined in reverence, paid his respects.
He respectfully seated them upon beautiful lion-thrones;
he honored them according to tradition, beginning with inquiries after their welfare.
Having conversed with one another, Kṛṣṇa sat down in their midst.
In the meantime, O child, Kṛṣṇa beheld a mass of splendor;
those sages also saw it blazing intensely in the sky.
Within that splendor, he saw a boy with the luster of gold.
O Nārada, just like a beloved five-year-old naked child, he suddenly appeared in the midst of the assembly. Seeing him rising up so suddenly, the preeminent sages [were amazed]. (15–16)
All the sages bowed down, and Śauri also prostrated before him; having looked upon him with a smile and affectionate eyes, and having employed appropriate courtesy with respect,
he (Balarāma) offered blessings to everyone and sat together in the assembly.
And he spoke to them and to Śauri, the eternal Blessed One.
Sanatkumāra said:
"May it be well with you, O sages; may the desired fruit of your constant austerities be attained."
The inquiry after the welfare of Kṛṣṇa, the seed of auspiciousness, has been rendered fruitless.

At present, however, there is well-being for you, as well as the vision of the Supreme Self, due to the grace of the devotees, even though He is beyond both material nature and the physical body. (19–20)
"By the splendor of this one who is beyond qualities, devoid of effort, the seed of all,
and who has now manifested solely to remove the burden of the earth," Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Even for those who possess bodies, the inquiry after welfare is desired.
Therefore, O Brahmin, why is it that the inquiry after my welfare does not exist?
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Lord, since auspicious and inauspicious [results] constantly arise within this material body,
it is useless to ask about Śiva regarding that eternal body which is the seed of well-being.
The Blessed One said:
"Whosoever bears a physical form is considered to be composed of primordial matter (prakṛti). O Brahmin, no body exists apart from that eternal primordial matter.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those bodies arising from drops of blood are known as being composed of *prakṛti*.
How can the Lord of *prakṛti* have a body made of *prakṛti*, he who is himself the Blessed One, the source of all seeds and the beginning of all? (25)
Having established the primary, imperishable seed of all incarnations—
which is eternal, true, and ancient— the Vedas declare it to be the primary, imperishable seed whose nature is light. (26–27)

"O Lord, the Vedāṅgas as well as those who know the Vedas declare that through Māyā he possesses qualities (saguṇa), while as the Lord of Māyā he is supreme and devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Now that I am Vāsudeva, whose body is resplendent with red and yellow [garments],
O Brahmin, why do you not ask the intended question concerning Śiva?
Sanatkumāra said:
He who is the abode of all, the dwelling place of everything, and whose every hair-pore contains the universe—
he is the God, the Supreme Brahman, proclaimed as Vāsudeva.
That name "Vāsudeva" is found in the four Vedas.
It is seen in the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and in the accounts of pilgrimages and the like.
Where in the Veda is your body, which relies on red seed, described?
The sages are witnesses, as indeed is Dharma everywhere.
"My witnesses are now the Vedas, the sun, and the moon.
Bhṛgu said:
"You alone speak the truth, O foremost of Vaiṣṇavas."
"Welcome; all is well. For what reason have you come here? Sanatkumāra said: "Listen, all you sages; listen now, O Kṛṣṇa."
"Aha! By what cause have you come here so very swiftly? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, for what purpose have you come here?"
"You know everything; you alone, O Omniscient One, are the best among the wise.
(36) Sanatkumāra said:
"O Blessed One, you are blessed and forever worthy of honor even by the worlds."
"You are the Lord of all lords; there is nothing beyond you in the entire universe.
(37) Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O lord of the twice-born, among sacrifices, vows, and ascetic practices..."
"I am the constant giver of fruit along with the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās)," he said.
Having heard this, the prince went swiftly into the forest;
considering those words to be a marvel, he restrained them as well.
The sages said:
O lord of the Siddhas, O highly fortunate one, O compassionate Kumāra!
What was that suspicious story told in the presence of the Blessed Kṛṣṇa?
"O son, what wonder have you seen, or has anything been heard by you anywhere?
Having made it very extensive, you ought to tell it to us.
In the meantime, Brahmā and Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī, [arrived].
Ananta, Dharma, Śrīsūrya, and Niśākara;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the guardians of the quarters, and other deities—
Śrī Kṛṣṇa suddenly rose and greeted each of them individually.

And a conversation took place between the twice-born and the god.
The prince, radiant as gold, sat upon a seat in the midst of the assembly and began to speak in the presence of the twice-born and the gods:
"I went to Goloka, but I did not see the Lord of Rādhikā."
Then he went to Vaikuṇṭha, but the four-armed Lord was not there. Then he went to the Ocean of Milk, but Hari himself was not there.
Exhausted and despondent, he bathed on the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
In the midst of vast sands, a tortoise a hundred yojanas long was seen there— terrified, trembling, suffering, and parched.
He was rescued by Rāghava and by the high-souled Mīna.

When I said, "You are blessed," he replied, "I am not blessed. "The Ocean of Milk is blessed," he said, "for in it dwell creatures such as I, and even those greater than I, O great sage, in numbers beyond counting. (49–50)

Then, having gone to Dharmālaya and not having seen the Lord of the World,

When this was said, the Blessed One declared the cause of everything: "A sacrifice that is devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) yields no fruit; a sacrifice is destroyed by the absence of dakṣiṇās. If the dakṣiṇā intended for a Brahmin is not given at that very time," [then the sacrifice fails].
When one night has passed, that gift becomes twofold;

Having fallen into a pit of urine for a thousand years,
that sinner, afflicted by disease, then attains the state of a *cāṇḍāla*.
[This occurs] when the giver does not bestow the gift, and the receiver does not accept it.
Both of them reached hell for a thousand years—
the sacrificer, who was a Cāṇḍāla, and his priest, who was a Brāhmaṇa;
both of those sinners were afflicted with disease as the fruit of their actions.
All the gods and sages laughed and were filled with wonder;
Nanda was struck with amazement and abandoned his paternal affection for his son. Overcome by grief and devoid of shame, he wept in the midst of the assembly.
"Abandon this delusion," saying this, Pārvatī enlightened him.
Nanda said:
"Just as a priceless ruby might be found in the house of one of low birth..."
O Lord of gods, because of that [deception] you remained there, and thus I have been cheated, O Master.

I shall not go back again to my home in Gokula on the banks of the Yamunā.

all that belongs to Yaśodā and to the presence of the cowherd girls.
What more shall I say? [I speak of] Yaśodā and her beloved Rādhikā.
"O, tell me, what shall I say to this flood of children who are the vessels of my love?
Having spoken thus in the midst of the assembly, Nārada fell into a swoon;

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Conversation between the Blessed Lord and Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the eighty-eighth chapter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Be conscious, O dear one! Be conscious, O dear one!
All of saṃsāra, including the moving and the non-moving, is like a bubble on the water.
Abandon delusion, O illustrious one; praise the supreme Māyā."
The supreme form of Brahman, the destroyer of all delusion,
the bestower of liberation, the highly fortunate and eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu;
during the terrible slaughter of Tripura, in that great battle filled with fear— 2–3.
O Nanda, listen here in this assembly to this king of hymns, which bestows all desires and cuts through all delusions—a hymn by which Sambhu slew that Daitya. I shall now impart it to you. 4.
Nanda said:
For the destruction of all obstacles, for the pacification of suffering, for prosperity and fame, and for the accomplishment of the desires of men. (5)

it is supreme, the destroyer of misfortune, secret, and very difficult to obtain.
O You who are kind to Your devotees!
"You are the progenitor of the Vedas, devoid of qualities, and higher than the highest.
The Blessed Lord said:

For the sake of destroying all obstacles and severing the bonds of delusion,

Seeing Śiva seized by the enemy, he spoke to Brahmā;

(11) Urged by Hari, O Lord of Gods, I speak to you;
for who indeed is capable of conquering anyone without the assistance of Śakti? (12)
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Śaṅkara remembered Durgā;
with palms joined in reverence, his neck bowed low in devotion, he bathed, washed his feet, and put on two clean garments. (13)
Having sipped water for purification, holding *kuśa* grass in his hand, and being pure while recollecting Viṣṇu—
Mahādeva said: "Protect, protect me, O Great Goddess Durgā, destroyer of misfortune!"
O you who are full of compassion for me, your devoted and attached servant, when I am seized by enemies!
O Viṣṇumāyā, O highly fortunate one, O Nārāyaṇī, O eternal one;
O supreme one whose nature is Brahman, O you whose nature is perpetual bliss! 15–16.
And you, O Mother of the world, are the mother of the gods beginning with Brahmā;
through your qualities, you are both the agent of dissolution and the formless one beyond all qualities.
By means of *māyā*, you are the Puruṣa, and by means of *māyā*, you yourself are Prakṛti.
Of those two, O Eternal One, you bear the Supreme Brahman as your supreme form.
You are the mother of the Vedas, the Sāvitrī who is higher than the highest;
and in Vaikuṇṭha, you are Mahālakṣmī, the embodiment of all prosperity.
In the Ocean of Milk you are the Fortune of mortals, the beloved of Him who reclines upon Śeṣa;
in the heavens you are the Fortune of heaven, and on earth you are the Royal Fortune.
In the netherworld (pātāla) you are the Fortune of the Nāgas and others, and in homes you are the household deity.
You are the very essence of all crops, the bestower of all sovereignty.
You are the Goddess presiding over passion (Rāga), and you are Sarasvatī of Brahmā.
You are the presiding deity of the vital breaths (prāṇas) of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
In Goloka, Rādhā herself resides upon the chest of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the goddess Dṛndā presides over Goloka in the forest of Dṛndāvana;
she is the delightful one in the circle of the Śrī Rāsa dance, finding her delight in Vṛndāvana. (23)
You are the presiding deity of Śataśṛṅga, and by name you are Citrāvalī.
In this kalpa and in other kalpas, you are the daughter of Dakṣa and the mountain-born Pārvatī;
you are Aditi, the mother of the gods, and the Earth, the support of all.
You alone are Gaṅgā, you are Tulasī, and you are Svāhā and Satī.
By a mere fraction of a fraction of a portion of You, all the wives of the gods and other beings exist.
O Goddess, You possess the form of a woman, the form of a supreme man, and You are also the neuter.
Among trees, you are created in the form of creepers and in the form of sprouts;
in fire, you are the power of burning, and in water, you are the nature of coolness;
in the sun, you are the nature of brilliance and the nature of radiance at all times.
She is of the nature of fragrance on earth, and of the nature of sound in space;
she is certainly of the nature of splendor in the moon and in the multitude of lotuses.
In creation she is the very form of creation, and in preservation she is the protectress.
You are the great pestilence at the time of universal destruction, and you are the water in the form of water.
You are hunger, you are compassion, you are sleep, and you are thirst; you are the embodiment of intellect.
You are contentment, you are nourishment, you are faith, and you yourself are forgiveness.
You are peace yourself, you are delusion, you are beauty and fame;
you are modesty as well as illusion, whose nature is both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
You are the embodiment of all powers and the bestower of all blessings.
In the Veda you are declared to be ineffable; no one at all knows you.
O Sovereign of the Gods, even the thousand-faced one is not able to praise you;
the Vedas are not capable, nor is any wise man, nor is Sarasvatī herself able [to do so]. (33–34)
Neither the Creator himself nor the eternal Viṣṇu is capable [of this]. O Maheśvarī, terrified in battle, what can I praise with my five faces?
Have mercy, O Mahāmāyā; bring about the destruction of my enemies.
Having spoken thus with compassion as he lay fallen on the battlefield in his chariot,
Durgā appeared, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
impelled by grace from Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.

Mahādeva said:

The Blessed Lady said:

In that interval, Viṣṇu indeed assumed the form of a bull.

Śiva, having taken up his weapon and meditated upon Viṣṇu and Maheśvarī, swiftly struck Tripura; it fell to the surface of the earth.
The gods praised Śaṅkara and rained down a shower of flowers.

In the meantime, O dear one, [I shall recite] this unsurpassed king of hymns,

It removes sorrow and suffering, and is the supreme bestower of all success.
By reciting this king of hymns, even a woman who has long been barren gives birth;
the miserable one is released from bondage, and the fearful one will certainly be freed from fear. (51–52)
The sick person is liberated from disease, and the poor man shall become wealthy;
one does not die even when immersed in the midst of a forest fire, nor does one sink when aboard a boat in the great ocean.
One who is seized by bandits, seized by serpents, or beset by predatory beasts [is likewise saved].
O lord of Vaiśyas, by means of this hymn, a man indeed attains auspiciousness.
Just as a gem is among radiant objects, as the twice-born is among the stages of life (āśramas), as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and as the Praṇava is among mantras; || 54–55 ||

Just as Śambhu is among the wise, Gaṇeśvara among the Siddhas;

has been given by me to you, my dear, who are as dear to me as my own life; go now.

"What qualities and defects will exist in the remainder of the Kali age?

(20) Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Conversation between Nārada and the Blessed Nanda," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the ninetieth chapter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Nanda, I shall joyfully relate to you that delightful and most sweet narrative, refined within the Purāṇas, which pertains to the mind. (1)
In the Kṛta Yuga, the Dharma is most complete, as are those who act according to the Dharma;
truth is most complete, and compassion is most complete.
Furthermore, the four Vedas themselves possess an exceedingly radiant form.
The auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*), as well as the *Purāṇas*, the *Itihāsas*, and the *Saṃhitās*;

All those brahmins, knowers of the Vedas, meritorious and ascetic, meditate upon Nārāyaṇa and mutter His mantra. The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and the four castes who are Vaiṣṇavas [do likewise].

Śūdras shall be servants to Brāhmaṇas and devoted to truth and righteousness. (6) Kings shall indeed be righteous and intent upon protecting their subjects; O sages, they shall take only a sixteenth part as tax from the people. (7)
The Brahmins were free from taxes and worthy of worship, moving according to their own will;
the earth was overspread with all kinds of crops and served as a repository for jewels.
The disciples were devoted to their gurus, and likewise the sons were devoted to their fathers.
The women were devoted to their husbands and dedicated to the vow of fidelity.
All engaged in sexual union only during the proper season; none were lustful for women, nor were they lecherous.
There was no fear of bandits or thieves, nor were there any adulterers there.
The trees were laden with fruit, and the cows yielded abundant milk.
All people were strong, tall, and endowed with beauty. Some meritorious ones possessed a lifespan of one hundred thousand years and were free from disease.

Just as Brahmins are devotees of Viṣṇu, so too are those of the three other castes who serve Viṣṇu (12). Likewise, rivers and streams are constantly full of water, and mountain caves are likewise [full]. The four castes are purified by sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and the twice-born are purified by austerity (13).
The three worlds shall all be purified in mind and free from the wicked;
filled with noble fame, glorious, and endowed with auspiciousness.
At all times and on every lunar day, the ancestors and the deities [shall be satisfied].
At all times, guests were honored in every house;
they belonged to the three [upper] castes, were devoted to the Brahmins, and were intent on feeding the Brahmins.
The mouth of a Brahmin is a field that is neither saline nor thorny.

Through the glorification of Nārāyaṇa, they were filled with joy during that festival; and all people had no enemies, but were instead seekers of the welfare of all. No one praised themselves; rather, everyone was eager to recognize the virtues of others. (17)
There, neither gods nor twice-born ones, nor learned men, were detractors;
there were no foolish men or women, nor were there fools among the wise.
In that land of truth, no people were miserable, for it was a palace of jewels for everyone.
It was endowed with heaps of jewels such as gems, rubies, and gold;
there were no beggars, no those afflicted by disease, and everyone was free from sorrow and filled with joy.
Indeed, there were no men or women whatsoever who were devoid of ornaments.
There were no sinners, no rogues, none afflicted by hunger, and none who were contemptible;
all living beings were free from old age, eternally established in youth,
devoid of mental anguish and physical disease, and their embodied forms were free from all defects.

The dharma that was indeed taught in the Satya Yuga consisted of truth, compassion, and so forth; in the Tretā it is diminished by one quarter, and in the Dvāpara it is likewise reduced to half of the truth.
In the first [age] of the Kali, it is reduced by another quarter, becoming extremely thin and weak.
O Vraja, the sprout of wicked bandits and thieves will arise.
Some will be devoted to unrighteousness; likewise, there will be cowherds who are fearful, as well as harlots who are fearful and those who violate the wives of others who are fearful. (24–25)
There will be constant fear for those who are righteous, and those who are unrighteous will tremble.
Kings will take delight in very little dharma, and the twice-born will take delight in very little Veda.
Some will take delight in vows and duties, yet all will act according to their own whims.
As long as sacred fords endure, as long as holy men endure,

O dear one, although the Kali age is a repository of faults, it has one great virtue:
merit arises from the mind, for there is no evil deed performed [therein]. O dear one, when one goes to sacred fords and the like, even a portion of one's dharma may be lost.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "In the Kali age, Hari remains upon the earth for ten thousand years."
The images of the gods, the scriptures, and the Purāṇas are to be worshipped;
(32) even half of that are the sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, this is well-established;
half of that again are the village deities and the Vedas, even for the learned. (33)
O Father, at the end of that Kali age, unrighteousness will be rampant;
the four castes will indeed become a single caste.
There will be no marriages purified by mantras, nor truth, nor forgiveness.
Constantly devoted to taking women as their own, with vulgar conduct as their primary concern;

lacking the sacrificial thread and the sectarian mark (tilaka) at all times, these members of the Brahmin lineage have abandoned the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and the scriptures, even though they were learned in them. (35–36)
Everyone ate everything together, disregarding all rules of conduct; people devoured what was forbidden to eat, and the four castes became licentious.
Among women, there was no chaste wife; in every house, there was only a wanton woman.
She makes threatening gestures toward her beloved, who trembles like a servant.
Having given sweet food, betel, clothing, and sandalwood to her paramour, O Father, she does not give even food to her distressed husband. (38–39)
The father was reviled by his son; the teacher was reviled by his disciple.
The king was struck by his subjects; the subjects were oppressed by the king. The virtuous were tormented by bandits, thieves, and the wicked.
The earth will be devoid of crops, and wealthy men will be devoid of milk.
(41) There will be no ghee or butter in milk that contains very little milk;
all people will be devoid of truth and will constantly speak falsehoods. (42)
Brahmins devoid of purity, twilight rituals, and scriptural knowledge; those who drive bulls; cooks for Śūdras; and those who cremate the dead for Śūdras;
those constantly devoted to Śūdra women; and Śūdras devoted to the wives of Brahmins. (43)
The cooks shall eat the food of that Brahmin;
lecherous Shudras shall seize his mother’s superior wife.
And a servant, having slain the king, shall himself become king.
A woman, having killed her husband out of lust, will enjoy a paramour out of curiosity;
and a son, having killed his father, will himself become king.
All will be devoted to their own whims, intent only upon their genitals and bellies.
Those who are hunchbacked, afflicted by disease, contemptible, or dressed in tattered rags; those whose mantras have been corrupted or smeared, and those who practice false mantras;
those who are of low birth, those who are preceptors lacking in age, and those who are revilers. (47–48)
Even kings, barbarians, and Yavanas who revile the Dharma joyfully uproot the good reputation of the virtuous;
they do so constantly toward their ancestors, gods, the twice-born, and guests. (49)
There is no worship of the gurus, nor the honoring of parents or women;
there is respect for female kinsmen and constant devotion to women, O Father. A thief who steals from noble families and the property of Brahmins and gods— || 50-51 ||
Driven by greed and out of curiosity for the practices of the age, they carry themselves with pride;
the entire world is bereft of divine shrines and agitated by fear.
Due to the constant defects of the Kali age, it is without a king, ill-governed, and perpetually troubled.
Men will be hungry, poorly clothed, impoverished, and afflicted by disease.
Indeed, the lord of kings, Ghaṭeśvara—the overseer of the water-jar—will be like a mere cowrie-shell.
Likewise, people will be as small as the thumb of an old man, and trees will be like potherbs.
Of palmyra palms, coconuts, and likewise jackfruit trees—their fruits are like mustard seeds; beyond that, it is even more minute.
[This is] by means of a water-vessel, a grain of rice, and likewise a thread.
The entire residence was devoid [of splendor], with its houses left unadorned (56).
It was enveloped in smoke, bereft of lamps, and shrouded in darkness.
All the people there were sinful and terrified by the fear of predatory beasts (57).
All were possessed by strife; the unchaste women were lovers of quarreling.
There were no beautiful women who were not lustful, nor were there any men who were handsome.
The rivers, streams, caves, ponds, and lakes—
Those devoid of water-lotuses, as well as those devoid of water and wealth;
women deprived of offspring, yet lustful and joined with paramours;
all those who cut down the *aśvattha* tree, and the earth devoid of trees. (59–60)

Trees were devoid of fruit, branches were stripped of their trunks, and fruits lacked sweetness; so too were the foods and the waters. Men were harsh of speech, merciless, and bereft of righteousness.
At the end of that [age], O Lord of Vraja, twelve suns will consume all human beings and all creatures with heat and heavy rain;
the earth will remain as nothing more than a mere memory.
When the Kali age has passed, the earth will become a field of merit (*kṣetra*) again, just as it is when the rains arrive;
and the practice of truth (*satya*) shall indeed prevail once more in due course.
Thus everything has been told; go now, my dear son, to Vraja in happiness.
I am but a child with a mouth full of milk; what can I say to you, my son? [Yet I offer:
fresh butter, ghee, milk, curd, and seasoned buttermilk;
auspicious *svastika* cakes fit for virtuous rites, and sweetmeats like nectar. (65–66)
Whatever sweet substance was consumed by force for the sake of the ancestors or the gods—all that was done through the crying of children; crying is the strength of children.
Therefore, forgive this offense of mine; such is the fault of children at every step.
"You are my father, and I am your son; Yaśodā is my mother.
Tell Yaśodā and Rohiṇī about my jesting.
Everything was heard by the boy from their mouths; I am indeed that very person," thus he spoke as desired.
You shall proclaim all of that to every resident of Gokula:
Time brings about the union of kinsmen with their kin;
Time effects separation, discord, and even affection.
Time brings about creation, and Time effects preservation.
Time creates with joy; Time destroys all beings.
It brings forth pleasure, pain, fear, grief, old age, death, and birth.
Everything is brought about by Time alone according to the force of past actions; everything, my dear, is created by Time—do not fall into amazement.
Where did you come from? You are a Vaiśya in Gokula, while Nanda is a king and a lord of Vaiśyas.
"How is it that Vasudeva’s son is here and I am in Mathurā?
Alas! My father was brought to your house because he was afraid of Kaṃsa.
You are the father beyond the father, and you are indeed the mother beyond the mother. (74–75)
"O Lord of Vraja, by the knowledge given by me and by Pārvatī, abandon your delusion, O illustrious one; go, dear child, home in happiness.
Nanda said:
O dear one, remember Vṛndāvana, which is delightful, meritorious, and a place of great festival; remember Gokula, Gokula—the beautiful and charming bank of the Yamunā;
and remember the most enchanting Rāsa-maṇḍala, so dear to you, where the women gather.
O son, why do you not remember Gopālikā, the cowherd boys, Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, and your beloved Rādhikā, who is dearer to you than life itself? O child,
go to Gokula just once for a few short days.
Having spoken thus, Nanda took Kṛṣṇa onto his lap;
overcome with grief, he drenched him with tears filling his eyes.
Out of delusion, he pressed him to his chest and kissed both of his cheeks.

Filled with joy and supreme bliss, the Blessed One spoke to him. Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Conversation between the Blessed Nanda and Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Brahma Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the eighty-ninth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Union occurs through the act of impregnation, or by means of that [act], separation may occur."
"By whom can his arrival in an instant and his subsequent conception be prevented?
(1) Furthermore, Uddhava will speak regarding the purpose of his coming and going;
I shall dispatch him quickly, and from that you will learn [the truth], O Father. (2)
Having gone there, he will awaken Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, Gopikā, the cowherd boys, and that Rādhikā who is dearer to him than life itself. In the meantime, Vasudeva and Devakī were there.
Baladeva, Uddhava, and likewise Akrūra arrived in haste.
Vasudeva said:
"O Nanda, you are powerful, wise, and my true kinsman and friend."
"Abandon your delusion and go home, my child; he is yours just as he is mine.
O kinsman, Mathurā is far from Gokula, yet there is no distance for you.
O Nanda, during this great festival of eternal bliss, you shall see your son."
Devakī said:
"O Nanda, it is certain that this son belongs to us just as much as to you; for what reason does his body appear so languid and marked by grief? (7)
"Having stayed happily in your palace for eleven years with all your strength,
how will you become overwhelmed by grief in so few days?
Stay for some more days with your son in Mathurā."
Behold the one whose face is like the full moon; make your birth fruitful.
(9) The Blessed Lord said:
Go, O Uddhava; may there be well-being and that which is dear to you shall come to pass.
Filled with great joy, go to Gokula and awaken Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, their mother,
the assembly of cowherd boys, Rādhikā, and the multitude of gopīs by means of the spiritual instruction given by me, which cuts through all sorrow.
"Let Nanda remain with joy at my mother's command, free from sorrow;
you shall report Nanda’s conduct with humility to Yaśodā.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, along with his father, mother, and Balarāma—
Together with Akrūra, he quickly went into the inner apartments of the house.
O Nārada, having stayed for the night in Mathurā,
Uddhava departed swiftly at dawn for the beautiful forest of Vṛndāvana.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue with Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Brahma-mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Śrīkṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa*.
Now begins the ninety-second chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:

Impelled by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he was filled with joy; having prostrated before Gaṇeśvara, he meditated in his mind upon Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and that Great Lord, the Master of the Quarters. (1)
And Uddhava, seeing these signs indicative of auspiciousness, began to sing.
He heard the sound of kettledrums, the ringing of bells, and likewise the blare of conchs;
he heard the word "Hari," songs, and the sound of auspicious music.
A virtuous woman with sons, a lamp, a garland, a mirror,
a full water-pot, curd, parched grain, and fruit;
durva grass shoots, white grain, silver, gold, and honey.
A multitude of Brahmins, a black antelope, a bull, clarified butter,
fresh meat, a lordly elephant, a king of men, a white horse,
a banner, a mongoose, a blue jay, white flowers, and sandalwood. (5–6)
Having thus seen this auspicious sight on the road, he reached the forest of Vṛndāvana.
He beheld before him the imperishable Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa tree—
a lush-leaved, crimson-hued, merit-bestowing, and longed-for sacred site.
Having consoled those well-dressed children, adorned with jewel ornaments, who were crying out "O Balarāma! O Kṛṣṇa!
while overcome with grief, he entered the city with joy and proceeded a great distance.
He beheld Nanda’s camp, fashioned by Viśvakarmā, constructed of jewels and gems— pearls, rubies, and diamonds—
beautifully adorned, and provided with excellent jeweled water-pots.
Having seen the gate, which was variegated and richly adorned with diverse decorations, he entered it.
