Quickly alighting from his chariot, he stood joyfully in its courtyard.
Yaśodā and Rohiṇī immediately asked after his supreme welfare.
With joy he offered a seat, water, a cow, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
"Where is Nanda? Where are Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa? Tell me the truth, O Uddhava! Uddhava related everything in due order, all being well.
Together with Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, Nanda will come with great joy,
though somewhat delayed, until the time of Kṛṣṇa’s initiation ceremony;
he will do so after having duly ascertained the truth regarding your welfare.
"O Yaśodā, listen now: I shall go to Mathurā.
Upon hearing these auspicious words, Yaśodā and Rohiṇī were filled with joy;
they gave the brāhmaṇa jewels, gold, and his desired garments.
He fed Uddhava with sweet food that was like nectar;
he gave him the finest jewels, gems, and diamonds;
and likewise, he had various kinds of auspicious musical instruments played.
He fed the Brahmins and caused auspicious rites to be performed;
he had the Vedas recited with supreme joy,
and through the mediation of the Brahmins, he worshipped Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord.
With various offerings and oblations, with flowers, incense, and lamps;
with sandalwood, garments, betel, honey, cow products, clarified butter, and so forth,
he worshipped Bhavānī, the deity of the illustrious Vṛndāvana forest.
O Sage, with sixteen types of ritual offerings, various substances, and powerful oblations;
having taken one hundred pure buffaloes, one thousand pure goats,
and ten thousand pure rams, along with five additional suitable items.
For the sake of Kṛṣṇa’s welfare, he quickly gave a hundred pieces of gold and a hundred cows as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇas;
and he honored Uddhava with great respect again and again.
Having consoled Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, the cowherd boys,
the elders, and all the cowherd women, they proceeded to the circle of the rāsa dance.
There he beheld the beautiful rāsa dance, circular like the orb of the moon.
It was adorned with hundreds of pillars of auspicious plantain trees (26),
joined with smooth garments and sprouts of sandalwood,
and graced with clusters of beautiful garlands fastened with silk threads (27).
Adorned with curds, parched grain, fruits, silken cloths, flowers, and even sprouts of dūrvā grass,
and refined with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
it was carefully enveloped and guarded by thirty million gopīs.
It was closely surrounded by three hundred thousand beautiful and charming pleasure-pavilions,
and encircled by a hundred thousand cowherds who were apprehensive of Kṛṣṇa’s arrival;
having kept the Yamunā to his right, he proceeded to the Mālatī grove.
Having circumambulated a grove of sandalwood, campaka, and yūthikā trees, as well as a forest of ketaki and mādhavī,
and a woodland of bakula, vañjula, and aśoka trees.
Likewise, there were groves of *mallikā*, *palāśa*, and *śirīṣa* trees;
as well as forests of *dhātrī*, *kāñcana*, and *karṇikā*; and similarly, woodlands of *nāgeśvara* and *lavaṅga*.
And there was a forest of *śāla* and *tāla* trees, as well as a forest of *hintāla* trees; a charming grove of *panasa*, *rasāla*, and *lāṅgalī* trees;
and a delightful grove of *mandāra* trees—which he quickly passed on his left.
Having beheld the delightful Kunda grove and reached the Madhuka forest,
it was filled with the sweet songs of male cuckoos and resounded with the honeyed humming of swarms of bees.
Surrounded by wild trees, it was a desirable repository of honey-wine,
made fragrant by the wind carrying the scent of forest flowers.
Having seen that [place] now along the royal road as described by Yaśodā.
He went quickly and without agitation to the secret Badarī forest (38),
as well as to the grove of śrīphala, nimba, and nāraṅga trees,
and to the woodland of lotuses, karavīras, and tulasī plants (39).
Having seen a desired, well-ripened fruit of a reddish hue,
he placed it to his left and entered the plantain grove.
In that exceedingly secluded and beautiful place, he beheld the hermitage of Rādhikā.
It had a wall made of the finest jewels, surrounded by moats and fortifications;
it was inaccessible to enemies yet easily accessible and pleasant for friends, with its secret pathways guarded by protectors. (41–42)
It was fashioned by Viśvakarman, richly adorned with various wonderful and diverse designs,
supremely radiant with necklaces of the finest gems, pearls, rubies,
and diamonds; it was constructed from the essence of the best jewels and beautifully graced with jeweled pillars.
It was enchanting with palaces joined by stairways of jewels;
it was inlaid with priceless gems, adorned with water-pots,
and decorated with banners of cloth as pure as fire.
He beheld the main gate, preeminent with mirrors of fine jewels, adorned with white chowries, and fitted with jeweled door-panels;
and above the gate, the wonderful and beautiful forest of Vṛndāvana.
The delightful Kadamba forest, the theft of his garments and other such events,
the most beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala fashioned by Viśvakarman,
and the various jeweled huts filled with cowherds and cowherd-maidens— [all these were manifested]. (47–48)
Seeing that gate ahead, which was guarded by millions of charming cowherd girls with canes in their hands—
guards who were limitless, joyful, powerful, and always acting according to their own will—
he leaped over it and proceeded.
Having leaped over the second gate, he reached the fourth gate, which was more excellent than that and distinct from everything else;
thereafter, he beheld the fifth gate, wondrous and supreme. (50–51)
And he proceeded to six gates that were everywhere most beautiful;
there was the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, a captivating mural on the wall,
as well as the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu and a constructed Rāsa-maṇḍala.
And the sporting in the waters of the Yamunā, fashioned by Viśvakarman;
and the sixth door, guarded by a thousand gopīs adorned with ornaments made of the finest essence of jewels. (53–54)
With a staff made of the seven precious gems and adorned with diamonds,
and wearing necklaces of sapphire, pearl, ruby, and diamond,
Mādhavī— she who was preeminent among them— then questioned Śiva.
Uddhava gave all the replies in due order (56).
Having gone there, he informed the group of Rādhā’s dear friends.
That Mādhavī, greatly delighted, joyfully established him there (57).
Having heard the auspicious news from the circle of Rādhā’s dear friends,
and having sounded conchs along with the resonance of bells, mṛdaṅgas, and paṭahas,
they quickly performed the ritual purification for their beloved Uddhava who had arrived.
Delighted, she caused her to enter the most excellent inner chamber. Having gone into that supreme palace constructed of priceless jewels,
she saw Rādhā before her, resembling a digit of the moon on the new-moon night.
She had eyes like well-blossomed lotuses; she lay there, fainting from grief, weeping with a tear-stained face, her ornaments cast aside.
Motionless and abstaining from food, she wore earrings of golden hue.
With her lips and throat parched and emitting faint sighs,
the devoted Uddhava, his entire body bristling with horripilation, saw her and bowed down with his neck bent low in devotion. (62–63)
Uddhava said:
I bow to the lotus feet of Rādhā, which are worshipped by the multitude of gods beginning with Brahmā;
by the mere chanting of whose glory the three worlds are purified.
Salutations, repeated salutations, to Rādhikā, the dweller of Gokula; salutations to Candrāvatī, the dweller of Śataśṛṅga;
salutations to Vṛndāraṇyā, the dweller of the Tulasī grove.

Salutations to the Dwellers of the Rāsa-circle, to the Sovereign of the Rāsa, ... (66) । Salutations to Vṛndā, who dwells on the banks of the Virajā, ... । Salutations to Kṛṣṇā, who sports in Vṛndāvana, ... (67) ।
Salutations to her who is dear to Kṛṣṇa and to Śāntā; salutations to her who dwells upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest and to his beloved. Salutations to Mahālakṣmī, the resident of Vaikuṇṭha.
And to Sarasvatī, the goddess presiding over knowledge, [salutations]... (69) And to Kamalā, the supreme goddess of all sovereignty, [salutations]...
And to Padmā, the beloved of Padmanābha, [salutations]...
(70) And to the Mother of Mahāviṣṇu, the primordial Parā, [salutations]...
Salutations to the daughter of the ocean and to her who is the mark of mortals... (71). Salutations to the beloved of Nārāyaṇa and to Nārāyaṇī...
Salutations be to Viṣṇu’s Māyā and to Vaiṣṇavī... (72).
Salutations to her whose nature is Mahāmāyā, the source of all prosperity; salutations to her who is auspicious in form, the embodiment of well-being;
salutations to the Mother of the four Vedas, Sāvitrī.
Salutations to her whose form is intellect, the giver of knowledge...
(74). Salutations to Durgā, the goddess who destroys difficulties...
In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, [she appeared] joyfully within the splendors of all the gods... (75).
Salutations to her who is both produced by empowerment and primordial nature;
salutations to Tripurā, the destroyer of the three cities. Salutations to her who is beautiful among the beautiful and yet devoid of qualities.
Salutations to her whose nature is sleep, who is beyond all qualities...
77. Salutations to the daughter of Dakṣa, salutations to the Truth...
Salutations to the daughter of the mountain, and to Pārvatī... 78.
Salutations, salutations to the ascetic woman, and to Umā... Salutations to her whose nature is fasting, and to Aparṇā...
Salutations to Gaurī, who sports in the world, and to Gaurī... 79.
Salutations to Māheśvarī, who dwells on Kailāsa... 80. Salutations to Nidrā (Sleep), Dayā (Compassion), and Śraddhā (Faith)...
Salutations to Dhṛti (Fortitude), Kṣamā (Forbearance), and Lajjā (Modesty)... 81.

Salutations to her who is thirst, whose nature is hunger, and who sustains existence; salutations to Mahāmārī, whose form is destruction. Salutations to her who is fear and who is fearlessness, and who bestows liberation.
Salutations to Svadhā, to Svāhā, to Śānti, and to Kānti... (83). Salutations to Tuṣṭi, to Puṣṭi, and to Dayā...
Salutations to her whose nature is Nidrā, and to Śraddhā... (84).
Salutations to Lañjā, whose nature is hunger and thirst;
salutations to Dhṛti, Kṣamā, and Cetanā... Salutations to Sarvamātṛ, who is the embodiment of all powers... 85.
To her whose nature is burning in fire, and to Bhadrā... (86).
To Śobhā and the full moon, and to the autumn lotus... (87).
O Goddess, there is never any difference between them, just as there is none between milk and whiteness. (87)
Just as between fragrance and the earth, just as between water and coldness,
just as between sound and water, and just as between light and the sun;
so too, in the world, in the Veda, and in the Purāṇas, is it with Rādhā and Mādhava.
"O virtuous lady, form a resolve; give me an answer, O wise one.
Having spoken thus, Uddhava bowed down there again and again. Whoever recites this hymn composed by Uddhava with devotion, [attains the supreme goal]. (89–90)
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari. There shall be no separation from kinsmen, nor disease, nor most terrible grief.
A woman whose husband is away shall regain her beloved; one who has caused a breach with his wife shall regain his dear spouse.
One without a son obtains sons, and one without wealth obtains wealth.
One who lacks a realm shall obtain a realm; one bereft of progeny shall obtain progeny.
The sick are freed from disease, and the bound are released from bondage.
The fearful are freed from fear, and the distressed are freed from calamity. (93)
One of obscure fame becomes highly renowned; a fool becomes a scholar.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Rādhā" by Nārada, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma... [Mahāpurāṇa] Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the ninety-third chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard Uddhava’s hymn of praise, Rādhikā regained her consciousness;
beholding the form of Kṛṣṇa, she spoke to him, overcome with grief.
Rādhikā said:
"O child, what is your name? By whom have you been sent?
From where have you come? Tell me, for what reason have you arrived? (2)
With your dark form and all your limbs, I consider you an attendant of Kṛṣṇa;
tell me now of the welfare of Kṛṣṇa, the boon-bestowing god.
Tell me also, for what reason does Nanda remain right there?
Sovinda will come to the beautiful forest of Vṛndāvana. (4) Again I shall behold his auspicious face, like the full moon;
again I shall sport with him in the circle of the rāsa dance. (5)
"I shall sport again in the water with my friends,
and once more I shall apply sandalwood paste to the body of the Glorious Nandana.
Uddhava said:
"O fair-faced one, my name is Uddhava; I am a Kṣatriya.
Sent by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, for the purpose of bringing auspicious news, I have come into your presence as an attendant of Hari. (7)
"May there be well-being for Kṛṣṇa, for Baladeva, and now for Nanda.
Rādhikā said:
"That bank of the Yamunā exists; that fragrant breeze exists."
Now, the very root of his playful kadamba trees has been destroyed.
Yet, there remains the auspicious and beautiful Vṛndāvana, which is desired;
there is the warbling of male cuckoos and a couch anointed with sandalwood paste.
There was the fourfold food and beautiful honey-wine;
likewise, there was the most wicked Manmatha, whose end is terrible and who bestows suffering.
And those jewel-lamps were blazing in the circle of the Rāsa dance.
There is indeed a pleasure-chamber fashioned from the finest of gems;
there is a host of cowherd maidens, and the full moon shines resplendent.
There is a couch strewn with fragrant flowers and anointed with sandalwood paste. (12–13)
Betel-leaf fit for the enjoyment of pleasure, well-prepared with camphor and other ingredients; fragrant garlands of *mālatī* flowers; white chowries and mirrors;
a captivating pearl necklace set with rubies and diamonds; and sandalwood paste smeared with musk and saffron, filling its vessel. (14–15)
There is a delightful grove of various trees, a beautiful lake for sporting, fragrant flower gardens, and enchanting rows of lotuses;
yet, how can my lord of life possess all such splendor? (16)
"Alas, Kṛṣṇa! Alas, Lord Rāma! Where are you, O beloved of my life?
(17) Where is the offense of this servant, for a servant's fault occurs at every step?
Having spoken thus, that goddess again fell into a swoon. (18)
Uddhava again caused her to regain consciousness;
seeing her, that bull among Kṣatriyas considered it a supreme marvel.
She was constantly attended by seven female companions with white chowries.
She was served by three hundred thousand gopīs who were very dear to her,
and she was surrounded day and night by ten billion gopīs;
one held kohl in her hand, another held excellent garlands, and yet another [held other offerings].
One woman stood with sindūra in her hand, another held gorocanā;
one stood holding a vessel of sandalwood paste in her hand,
another held a mirror, and yet another carried a box of saffron.
One woman indeed carried there a desirable vessel of musk;
another stood holding a campaka flower-vessel in her hand,
filled with sweet honey, yet overcome with grief.
One stood waiting, holding fragrant oil; another carried betel-leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other aromatics;
and another stood holding clear water that had been perfumed.
One woman guards a play-doll richly adorned with paintings;
another carries a ball, and yet another a jeweled ornament.
One woman carefully protects a priceless garment purified by fire.
One woman, having taken an offering of food, moves about;
another fashions a desired garland for the purpose of arranging her hair.
Another stands before [him] holding a comb.
One woman carries *yāvaka* in her hand, and another joyfully carries *dhātrī* juice;
even from afar they proceed in this manner, while yet another stands about, trembling with fear.
One praises out of fear, and another weeps from grief.
A certain clever woman tried to awaken her who was thus afflicted by separation;
another, herself tormented by heat, placed her upon a charming, smooth bed,
or on a beautiful, smooth lotus petal, in order to alleviate the burning pain.
Seeing her in such a state, Uddhava spoke again with humility and as if out of fear, words that were very dear to her and like nectar to the ears.
Uddhava said:
I know you to be the Goddess of the gods, the sovereign, most affectionate, and a perfected yoginī;
the embodiment of all powers, the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the supreme mistress.
You are the beloved of Goloka who descended to the earth due to the curse of Śrīdāmā.
The Goddess who dwells upon His chest, whose life is dearer to Him than His own—
O Goddess, listen, for I shall tell you the auspicious and desired news that is deeply heart-warming and shared with her friends. (34–35)
For her who was scorched by the forest fire of suffering, she is like a rain of nectar;
for her afflicted by the disease of separation, she is an auspicious elixir.
There dwells this Nanda, ever joyful and well-contented.
And having been invited by Vasudeva until the time of Kṛṣṇa’s initiation ceremony,
that Nanda, filled with supreme bliss, will come to Gokula with great joy, taking Kṛṣṇa along with Balarāma for the auspicious rites accompanied by all their limbs.

Having arrived and joyfully prostrated before his mother once more, Kṛṣṇa will return at night with delight to the sacred forest of Vṛndāvana. O virtuous lady, before long you shall behold the lotus-face of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
And you shall now abandon all the sorrow of separation.
Be firm, O mother; cast off this most terrible grief.
Joyfully donning beautiful garments purified by fire, remain steadfast.
Take these ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels;
take this smooth sandalwood paste blended with musk and saffron.
Adorn your hair with a garland of jasmine flowers and perform its decoration.
"O auspicious one, dress yourself beautifully and apply decorative leaf-patterns on your cheeks.
Place a dot of vermilion at the parting of your hair, mixed with musk and sandalwood paste.
Make your feet dyed with lac and adorned with ornaments of red resin. (43–44)
"Stay! Arise! Sit upon this excellent lion-throne of jewels.
O virtuous lady, abandon this bed of mud-stained lotuses along with your grief.
With a pure mind, enjoy the sweet honey of Kṛṣṇa. (45)
Refined speech, fragrant water, and well-scented betel;
on a most enchanting couch fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems,
draped with excellent silken cloths and adorned with garlands of jasmine— 46–47.
It was endowed with fragrances such as musk, jasmine, campaka, and sandalwood;
it was adorned all around with garlands of *mālatī* flowers and strings of pearls;
and it was embellished with beautiful *maṇīndra*, pearl, and ruby gems.

O Queen of Gods, who are always served by the gopīs, lie down upon this bed provided with flower garlands and pillows, worthy of auspicious rites and filled with joy. May your beloved circle of friends, together with the white-clad celestial maidens, perform service for you constantly.
"O charming one, the devotees of the gopīs [long for] service to your lotus feet upon a most beautiful couch fashioned from the finest jewels.
Having spoken thus, O sage, he became silent once again.
Having bowed at her lotus feet, which are worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā,
the virtuous Rādhikā, smiling, listened to Uddhava’s words and gave him a wedding gift: a ring made of the finest gems.
Priceless, beautiful, and charming, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
visible to the eye, yellow in color, and brilliantly radiant like a magnificent lamp.
This unprecedented [jewel] was given by Kṛṣṇa with fire in the Rāsa-maṇḍala.
A pair of jeweled earrings fashioned from priceless gems;
all desired ornaments crafted from priceless gems;
a pair of garments purified by fire, with a necklace fashioned of jewels.
In former times, Varuṇa gave to Kṛṣṇa with great affection a most enchanting necklace fashioned from diamonds;
and Śrī Sūrya gave to Śrī Kṛṣṇa the Syamantaka jewel.
The nuptial gift (kaulautuka) which was formerly given to him by Hari,
and the excellent jeweled throne which was given by Mahendra— that was joyfully bestowed upon him with affection by the goddess Rādhā. || 58–59 ||
The charming jewel-parasol, fashioned from the essence of the finest gems, adorned with pearls, rubies, and strings of diamonds,
was ever variegated with a wonderful lotus made of diverse jewels. (60)

It was adorned on all sides with other mirrors fashioned from jewels. That [mirror] which was given with affection by Brahmā to Hari in the circle of the rāsa dance was then given there with great joy by Rādhā to Uddhava.
That very same rosary of *japā* flowers, fashioned by a master jeweler and adorned with the finest gems— which had been consecrated and given long ago by Śambhu—
was then bestowed upon him; it was priceless, merit-bestowing, and auspicious.
She gave him the exceedingly beautiful Candrakānta jewel, which removes birth, death, old age, and disease; it was lovely, bestowed by Candra, well-adorned,
and as radiant as the full moon— she gave that [jewel] to him as she gave Candrāvalī.
A pure, inexhaustible honey-vessel filled with honey,
which was given according to dharma by his beloved to Hari;
and a golden water-vessel for food, fashioned from gold.
He gave sweet food and supreme rice, most delicious and pleasant;
having caused them to eat, he quickly gave betel-leaf scented with camphor and other fragrances, as well as garlands and very smooth sandalwood paste.
And he bestowed auspicious blessings and the most excellent boon desired by him:
the knowledge which had been granted by Kṛṣṇa in Goloka within the circle of the Rāsa dance,
as well as the steady Goddess Kamalā for a period of one hundred generations of men.
[He bestows] pure, fame-bestowing knowledge, as well as stainless glory and renown;
all perfections, service to Hari, and unwavering devotion to Hari;
the status of being a preeminent attendant, and [the attainment of] being an attendant of Hari. (70–71)
Having granted this boon and rising up filled with joy,
he donned two garments as pure as fire, priceless jewel-ornaments,
a necklace of diamonds, and a captivating string of gems.
Sindūra, collyrium, flower garlands, and well-polished sandalwood paste—
having joyfully worshipped him who was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, already worshipped by others,
she surrounded him with ten million gopīs who were filled with delight.
Having the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to a hundred moons, Rādhikā said:
"Will Hari truly come? Tell me the truth, speak without guile."
Speak the truth, casting aside fear; speak the truth in this noble assembly.
A large pond is better than a hundred wells; a sacrifice is better than a hundred ponds;
a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; indeed, truth is better than a hundred sons.
For there is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood. (77) Uddhava said:
"O beautiful one, Hari will surely come; you will surely see him."
"Surely you will cast off your distress upon seeing the moon-like face of Hari.
O illustrious lady, by my sight your fever of separation has departed;
having enjoyed the happiness of various pleasures, abandon this insurmountable anxiety. (78–79)
"I shall set out for Madhupurī and, having gone there, awaken Hari; once that is accomplished, he will perform whatever other task remains.
Grant me leave, O Mother; I am going into the presence of Hari."
"I shall relate all that account of yours to you exactly as it happened.
Rādhikā said:
"O child, when you go to the most enchanting Mathurā..."
Listen to a certain tale of sorrow; stay, my child, remain firm!
(82) You will not forget me, who am distressed by the fever of separation.
You will tell my beloved and you will certainly send him away. (83)
What wise man truly knows the state of the minds of women? Based on some scriptural authority, one merely offers a description.
Even the Vedas are not able to speak of them; what then can the other scriptures say?
"I shall tell you everything, my son, and you shall speak of Kṛṣṇa.
To me there is no difference between home and forest, nor between beasts and men;
what is water, what is a dream, and what is ignorance, day or night? (85–86)
I did not even know myself, nor the rising of the sun and moon;
yet, having obtained for a moment news of Hari, my consciousness returned to me.
I beheld the form of Kṛṣṇa and heard the sound of his flute.
Abandoning family, shame, and fear, I contemplate the feet of Hari;
having attained the Lord of all the worlds, who is beyond primordial nature, I have come to know through my knowledge that the Lord of the Gopas cannot be known by means of *māyā*. (88–89)
"Even the Vedas, Brahmā, and the other gods meditate upon whose lotus feet;
how could he have been rebuked by me? This is my truth. [Yet] through service to his lotus feet, or even by the mere mention of his qualities..."

Because that moment was spent in devotion to Him—meditated upon through meditation and worship—all auspiciousness, joy, and long life became firmly established therein. Furthermore, there was constant distress in the heart at the thought of separation from Him. (91–92)
O Uddhava, such delight in play shall not happen for me again,
nor shall there be such fortune of love or union with Him in solitude;
therefore, I will not go to Vṛndāvana to be in His company again.
I shall not offer sandalwood paste upon the chest of the Joy of the Nandana grove;
I shall not give him a garland, nor shall I behold his lotus-like face. I shall not visit the groves of *mālatī*, *ketakī*, and *campaka* flowers. (94–95)
Once again I shall not go to the beautiful circle of the rāsa dance; I shall not go to the lovely sandalwood forest where Hari dwells. Once again I shall not go to Malaya, that temple of jewels.
The delightful and secret grove of Mādhavī creepers, the forest of Madhuka trees;
the beautiful sandalwood forest, the clear Candrasaras lake, the Vispandaka divine forest, Nandana, and Puṣpabhadraka. (97–98)
I shall not go again and again with the deer toward Bhadraka.
Where is that lovely, blossoming *mādhavī* creeper in the month of Mādhava?
Where has the *mādhavī* night gone, where is the spring (*madhu*), and where indeed is Mādhava?
Having spoken thus, Rādhā meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa;
falling once more into a swoon, she wept, her body covered in horripilation.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter of the *Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Nārada-nārāyaṇa-saṃvāda*, within the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa*, in the *Uttara-bhāga*, in the *Rādhoddhava-saṃvāda*.
Now begins the ninety-fourth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, Uddhava was struck with wonder and experienced great fear.

He caused her to perform a conscious act and spoke to her as if she were dead. Recognizing her devotion and seeing that virtuous woman of great fortune, he considered himself to be merely one among his devotees and regarded the entire world as insignificant.
Uddhava said:
"Be conscious, O auspicious one, Mother of the World; salutations to you!
You shall now behold all that was formerly done by Kṛṣṇa."
From you the universe is pure, and by the dust of your feet the earth is most holy;
your face is sacred, and the cowherd women are meritorious.
The worlds sing only of you with songs and auspicious hymns.
And the gods, as well as Sanaka and the others, constantly [proclaim] your glorious fame—
which removes committed sins, is meritorious, is the pure worship of sacred fords,
bestows devotion to Hari, is auspicious, and destroys the multitude of all obstacles.
You alone are Rādhā; you are Kṛṣṇa; you are the Supreme Person and the Supreme Nature.
There is no difference between Rādhā and Mādhava, neither in the Purāṇas nor in the Śruti.
Having seen Rādhikā unconscious, he placed her upon his lap.
The gopī Mādhavī, standing before Rādhā, said:
(8) Mādhavī said: "What indeed is the form or the excellent attire of the thief Kṛṣṇa?"
What is happiness? What is sovereignty? Or what is unsurpassed honor? (9) What is that heroism? What is lordship? Or what is invincible valor?
What is accomplished? What is renowned? Or what is equal to the highest virtue? (10)
From where did you come here, and where have you gone again?
This child, dressed as a cowherd, is surely not a prince; he is a man.
O auspicious lady, do you remember the cowherd who is the delight of the Nandana grove?
Who is dearer to oneself than one's own self? Therefore, protect yourself with effort. (12) Fie on you, O Rādhā, so utterly shameless! Your very life is in vain;
you bring about the destruction of the good reputation of the world’s young women. (13)

O friend, women must conceal themselves; for when they are fully exposed, their own reputation is destroyed. Therefore, with effort, ensure that your eyes are worthy of being directed [only] toward walking about. Furthermore, concealing your inner state of passion, cultivate a state of mind [of composure].
Indeed, O Goddess of the Suras, there is no such thing as innate enmity among enemies or friendship among friends.
One becomes an enemy solely through the exigency of affairs, and a friend through action.
A wise person should accomplish their own purpose; to let one's purpose perish is folly.
O Rādhā, who is dear to whom, and who indeed is unpleasant to whom?
Knowing the task and the proper time, the virtuous always act accordingly.
A thief of wealth is an enemy, and one who takes away life is even worse than that.
Listen to the characteristics of enemies: they speak harshly and inflict suffering.
Having cast you out from your own family and abandoned you to an ocean of grief, that cruel and ruthless man has departed, seizing both your consciousness and your life-breaths. (18–19)
"What, what do you remember, O foolish woman? Indeed, abandon this most cruel grief!
Protect yourself with effort; for who is dearer than one's own self?
Padmāvatī said:
You have said it all: near the waters of the Yamunā, there is no pleasure for one devoid of passion; for women, there is no happiness in a lover, O dear one.
A flash of lightning in the water, a line drawn upon the surface, and the affection of the wicked—these are all alike fleeting.
One should have no great trust in the treatises on statecraft (*nīti*), nor in wicked people.
(22) When, oh, you beheld Hari’s face upon the bank of the Yamunā—smiling and casting sidelong glances—and then again concealed it; (23)
Again and again you gazed [at him], yet you abandoned that conscious being;
leaving home, the fear of your elders, and the auspicious words of your friends,
you constantly meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, and likewise neither food nor life itself.
"Where is Kṛṣṇa? He is in Mathurā, and you are somewhere in the plantain grove.
(25) If you give up your life now, he will not appear;
O beautiful one, if you preserve yourself, you shall see him in due time. (26)
Candramukhī said:
"All auspiciousness, happiness, and prosperity endure for a long time through past deeds; likewise, suffering, grief, misfortune, and even success in the present arise from past deeds.
This is so even in Bhārata, the land of merit, the most excellent and desired of all places. (27)
"By her ascetic penance, she shall obtain Hari, the beloved who transcends primordial nature (prakṛti), as her husband.
Nevertheless, her body is now being scorched by the arrow of desire.
How can the moon, or spring, or both Madhu and Mādhava, be her enemies? (28–29)
That Manmatha was once again consumed by Śaṅkara;
Rāhu may swallow the moon and likewise vomit it up again;
and Madhu, out of grief for his friend, gave up his life and went to Yama.
To me, the ocean of nectar and the moon are like an ocean of poison;
fine clothing is like a blazing fire, sandalwood paste is like an oblation of ghee, and even the fragrant breeze would constantly burn my limbs. (31–32)
"Behold, my friend has given up all food; look, she breathes and lives!
O joy of the Kurus, offer praise to Kṛṣṇa with your own mouth.
By the mere remembrance of his name and by hearing of his virtues," [she is restored].
And by that auspicious news, consciousness may suddenly arise.
Śaśikalā said:
"O Mādhavī, do you know Kṛṣṇa as the Self, the Lord?"
That lotus-foot, desired by the gods, which Brahmā and the other deities as well as the four Vedas themselves meditate upon with constant devotion;
that [Lord] who is Padmā, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Ananta, and Maheśvara.

That which the lords of perfected beings (*siddha*), the lords of sages (*muni*), and likewise the gods do not know—how could there be a form for the Self of All, who is devoid of qualities? How could there be qualities for him? (37) And that which was spoken by Satya is indeed true and appropriate;
it bears what is captivating for the removal of the earth’s burden. (38)
A form that is blissful, exhilarating, and delightful, an embodiment of grace toward devotees; an indescribable beauty that captivates the hearts of people;
possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids, an abode of divine play, auspicious and imperishable. (39)
The supreme Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, who is ever detached, bears with devotion upon his head the sweet honey of whose lotus feet is the water of the Mandākinī;
he constantly performs the glorification of the one whose fame is that of a sacred ford.
For a moment he dances with devotion and sings with five faces;
having cast off food, ornaments, and clothing, he is naked as the sky.
Meditating upon the pure and stainless Brahman, whose nature is the light of consciousness, ||| 42 ||
Indeed, Brahmā passes his life through austerity and service;
so too does Śeṣa, Sanatkumāra, and the assembly of Siddhas who are knowers of yoga.
Suśīla said:
Even a hundred times a hundred desires would not be enough to describe him;
by whom could the Moon, Aśvinīkumāra, or Śiva be counted among those of such beauty?
And throughout the countless universes, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
The sages, men, perfected beings, devotees,
and the virtuous constantly meditate upon the lotus feet of that Self which is indeed beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).
Neither the Vedas nor Sarasvatī are able to praise that Lord.
Stupefied and terrified, she sought forgiveness through praise;
even the thousand-faced one trembled incessantly at the hymn.
Brahmā, the progenitor of the Vedas, was himself the lord of that very hymn.
Mādhavī reviles that Truth, the Eternal Lord.
The assembly has become impure; the life of the gopīs is in vain.
Among them, only the meritorious woman’s grief will undoubtedly perish.
Hari held up Mount Govardhana with his left hand, just as he had worn the jewel-garland;
what then is the valor of that [other] father of the worlds? (51)
The king of the Daityas is capable of shattering a thousand mountains,
yet Hari is able to destroy a hundred thousand of them with mere ease.
It was by a portion of his very essence that the Lord Viṣṇu was born as the Boar.
And he effortlessly lifted up the earth with the tip of his tusk.
(53) There, upon the surface of the earth, were thousands of mountains, as well as innumerable Daityas and likewise heroic warriors. (54)
"By that very same karma, O friend, he possesses neither valor nor manliness,
neither fame nor praise, in every respect and by his very self.
Pārijātā said:
And the earth with its seven islands, together with its mountains, forests, and oceans,
including the golden ground— the beautiful support of all—
O beloved, as well as the various seven heavens up to the world of Brahmā.
And there are seven Pātālas, diverse and beautiful.
By these [elements] the universe, the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), was fashioned by Brahmā;
it is thus situated within a single pore of Mahāviṣṇu like a minute atom.
As many hairs as he has, so many are all these worlds; yet he himself is but a sixteenth part of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
(59) How could even a gluttonous cowherd girl, or Mādhavī, know His fame, purity, or incomparable greatness? (60)
Mādhavī said:
"The foolish Gopīs speak without understanding what I have said.
O Uddhava, listen to my auspicious words as they were spoken by me. (61)
By His own will, Viṣṇu possesses attributes; by His own will, He becomes devoid of attributes.
For the removal of the earth’s burden, the all-pervading Lord became a child dressed as a cowherd.
If the Vedas, Purāṇas, Siddhas, and holy men [speak] continuously...
Even Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa do not know that Lord;
how then could I, a foolish cowherd girl who merely devours food, know Him?
Nevertheless, O child, let my words be heard as true this very moment.
What is the indefinable form of Hari—his heroism, fame, strength, valor, dress, perfection, or whatever other quality he may possess?
For he is composed of his own will and is currently endowed with attributes. (65)
And how can that qualification be indescribable?
For Viṣṇu, who is devoid of qualities and lacks a body, what can possibly exist as his own self? And what can be said regarding his form and other such attributes? (66–67)

"This great fool reviles me, yet she does not understand my words. What does this fool know of that Truth which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—the Supreme Light, the Supreme Self, the Lord? (68)
He is inexpressible and possesses a form that bestows grace upon his devotees.
(69) That supreme Lakṣmī, the mother of the three worlds, serves at his lotus-feet, trembling and afraid, constantly out of fear like a maidservant. (70)
And Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the primordial Prakṛti,
eternal and of the nature of Brahman, stood on the right side, terrified;
and the supreme goddess Sarasvatī was likewise paralyzed with fear.
The Vedas are not able to praise Him; how then can they praise the Supreme Lord?
(72) Having heard those words of theirs, Uddhava was overwhelmed with devotion;
his entire body bristling with horripilation, he wept and fell down. (73)
Having attained a state of trance through devotion and having meditated upon that Supreme Lord, he considered himself insignificant; and out of devotion, he spoke to the gopī.
Uddhava said:
Blessed and glorious is Jambudvīpa, the most enchanting of all continents,
wherein lies Bhāratavarṣa, which bestows merit and auspiciousness;
it is the desired place of trade for merchants, created by their own meritorious deeds.
Having performed great merit here, one enjoys auspicious fruit elsewhere.
Blessed indeed is Bhārata-varṣa—bestowing merit, granting auspiciousness, and most excellent;
it is supremely pure, sanctified by the dust of the lotus feet of the gopīs. (76–77)
Even more blessed than those is another woman among the women of Bhārata,
who constantly beholds the lotus feet of Rādhā, which bestow great merit.
For sixty thousand years, Brahmā performed penance for this.
For the sake of obtaining the dust of Rādhikā’s lotus feet—[there resides] Rādhā, the supreme resident of Goloka who is dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life;
yet there, by the curse of Śrīdāmā, she has now become the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu. (79–80)
Whatever devotees of Kṛṣṇa there may be, including the gods such as Brahmā and others,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of Rādhā and the gopīs.
And Maheśvara, the lord of yogīs, truly understands devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Rādhā, the gopīs, the gopas, and those who dwell in Goloka;
Sanatkumāra to some extent, as does Brahmā when he is a subject of experience;
and the Siddhas and devotees certainly know only a small portion. (82–83)

I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, since I have come to Gokula and obtained unwavering devotion to Hari from the gopīs and my elders. I shall not go to Mathurā, nor shall I engage in the glorification of the fame of sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having become a servant, I shall listen [to their teachings] throughout birth after birth for the sake of the gopīs.
There is no devotee of Hari, the Supreme Self, greater than the gopīs;
nor do others possess such devotion as that which the gopīs have attained.
Kalāvatī said:
"I am Menā Kalāvatī, the blessed mental daughter of the Pitṛs. We three sisters wander upon the surface of the earth. (87)
Blessed is Janaka’s wife, the devoted Sītā’s mother;
blessed is Rādhā, who was not born from a womb, and I too am not born from a womb.
Due to the curse of Śrīdāmā, Rādhā became the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu on earth.

Due to the curse of Sanatkumāra, we ourselves [reside] upon the surface of the earth. Out of devotion, the three of us sisters went to the beautiful Ocean of Milk, to the enchanting Śvetadvīpa, in order to behold Viṣṇu.
Out of anger, he did not rise to greet him and instead cursed him;
for the venerable Sanatkumāra is the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogins.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Stay on the earth as fools, and you shall not go to heaven again, having become fond of mortal beings due to the cause of egoism. Then,
being pleased, the Lord of the Twice-born granted a boon to each one once more.
"Let your eldest daughter become the beloved wife of Viṣṇu, of Vaśa, of Śaila, and of Himādhāra; she shall indeed become Pārvatī. And let her be the blessed beloved of the yogin Janaka."
His daughter, Mahālakṣmī, will become the goddess Sītā;
she is the youngest sister of Kalāvatī, the daughter of the Vaiśya Vṛṣabhāna, a preeminent among yogis and a disciple of Durvāsas. (95)
At the end of the Dvāpara age, she will become a beloved and virtuous wife in Gokula.
Rādhā, the daughter of Kalāvatī and a resident of Goloka, will come to be there due to the curse of the cowherd Śrīdāma; of this there is no doubt.
The Lord, for the sake of relieving the burden of Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa,
will come to the earth and to the holy land of Bhārata.
Out of curiosity, Vṛṣabhānu, together with his daughter Kalāvatī, [will also go].
Liberated while living, he will go to Goloka; of this there is no doubt.
And that blessed woman, along with Sītā, will go to Vaikuṇṭha.
By the boon of Pārvatī, Menakā became a perfected yoginī.
At the end of the eon, he rejoices for a long time like Lakṣmī in the world of Viṣṇu.
Without adversity, whose greatness could arise, and where?
When suffering has passed away through one's actions, happiness—which is difficult to attain—shall prevail.
Formerly, we were the daughters of the Pitṛs, sporting in the enjoyments of heaven;
yet, by the boon of the Brahmin through the vision of Viṣṇu, we became equal to Lakṣmī,
and our karma was exhausted through that vision of Viṣṇu.
By that intense merit, he obtained a vision of the Kumāra;
there, from the mouth of the Kumāra, he heard the knowledge that is most difficult to attain,
concerning Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as the perfected beings (siddhas) and the worlds.
The Lord, the Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond material nature, devoid of qualities, free from desire, supreme, consisting of His own will, and most excellent— [to Him].
(105) Tulasī said:
In all living beings, the gods indeed abide individually: Prāṇa is Viṣṇu, the mind is Brahmā, and consciousness is the presiding deity of all powers, whose form is intellect (buddhi). (106)
Śambhu is the very nature of knowledge, and he himself is Dharma and Puruṣa.
He is the attributeless Supreme Self, that Brahman who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
He alone is Kṛṣṇa, the witness even of the actions of all living beings.
The individual soul (*jīva*), which is its reflection, is the enjoyer of pleasures and pains.
The sun and moon are in the two eyes, and Sarasvatī is in the tongue. The earth is always in the skin, and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) are in the two arms. (109)
O serpent, even those who serve you in the form of attendants are dear only to themselves; all living beings depart for their own sake,
just as followers seek out human bodies within the assembly of worldly existence.

Therefore, the virtuous always and continuously worship the Self with their whole being; and the yogis joyfully meditate upon Him with supreme devotion. How could there be concealment of action for those whose actions have the [Self] as their witness? (112)
The Inner Controller and Kṛṣṇa move about with joy.
Kālikā said:
"Men are of three kinds—children, the elderly, and the young."
And if the gods and others who have attained perfection all know Him as the Supreme.
Uddhava said:
Now it is proper for a wise man to awaken Rādhā, who has fainted.
In this matter, O Uddhava, reasoning is paramount; awaken it within yourself.
Be mindful, O auspicious one, Mother of the World; know me as the servant even of the servant of that devotee of Kṛṣṇa who has arisen [for your sake]. (115–116)
"O mother, show me favor; I shall go to Mathurā once again.
I am not independent, being dependent on another, like a wooden puppet.
I am constantly under the control of my driver, just as a bull is subject to its master. (117)
Thus, O Mother, it is certain that the entire world belongs to the Lord of the World.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Uddhava concerning Rādhā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the ninety-fifth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Uddhava and regained her composure, Rādhikā rose upon her excellent jeweled throne and spoke.
The goddess, her heart tormented with grief, spoke sweetly,
while being served with devotion by seven gopīs holding white chowries.
Rādhikā said:
"Go to Mathurā, my child, and do not forget me; remember us.
Even because of this, there shall be no further unrighteousness for you in the ocean of worldly existence.
Having gone there, now relate all my words."
"Quickly bring my Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Bliss!
Among all women born as females, having obtained such a husband, who else but me could have experienced such separation? Who indeed is more miserable than I? || 4-5 ||
"What awakening will you give me? I have nothing worthy of being awakened.
O Uddhava, for embodied beings, the body is fruitless without the Self.
[Yet] with true affection, there is good fortune and ever-fresh dignity. (6)

I constantly remember with my mind that love which is exceedingly difficult to attain, the secret of our new union; no other thought dwells in my heart. Forsaking sleep at night, this remembrance only increases my grief.
"O child, lift me up, for I am surely submerged in an ocean of grief.
For men, the fruit of bathing at a sacred ford comes through the granting of life and liberation;
yet I am unable to awaken my mind, which is difficult to restrain. (9)

I meditate upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. As I repeatedly remember His qualities, His majesty, my joy, the ocean of love, and His auspicious beauty, my mind is not steady but restless.
Among all the young women in the worlds, who else possesses such sorrow?
And who, other than me, knows the pain of separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa?
Sītā knows something of it, and I too know what has been ordained by fate.
"Among all women in the three worlds, there is no one as wretched as I, who am devoted to my husband.
O son, who could possibly believe my words after hearing of my mental anguish? Or among young women, whose sorrow could ever be equal to mine? (13–14)
Among women, there has never been, nor will there ever be, one equal to Rādhikā;
though she was once afflicted by sorrow and tormented by separation, she is now radiant with happiness and good fortune.
Having obtained as her husband the wish-fulfilling tree, the Lord of the worlds, [she shines].
I have been deceived by the merciless and sinful Creator.
My life, my birth, my very affectionate eyes, and my mind have become fruitful through the sight of the moon-like face, the form, and the attire of his lotus feet. (16–17)
Merely by hearing his name, the five vital breaths are thrilled;
by his mere remembrance, they blossom forth and the self becomes truly affectionate.
And he who touched her during the act of love became famous throughout the three worlds.
O child, whether in conversation or in prosperity, how could I forget that Lord?
He who possesses a form that brings victory over the three worlds and embodies virtue itself—he by whom Brahmā was created has not been created by Brahmā. (19–20)
To him, the ordainer of destiny and the bestower of all prosperity, more tranquil than the wish-fulfilling tree, the beloved of Lakṣmī, and captivating to the mind;
to the Lord of all, the seed of all, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign. (21)
Or by what perfection, my dear, do I forget my husband?

He for whom neither the moon, nor the god of love, nor even the twin Aśvinīkumāras are worthy of comparison; he with whom the quarters of the sky share no equality in their qualities. Even Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu meditate upon his lotus feet.
Or by what accomplishment, my dear, could I forget that Lord?
Even those who behold His incomparable and captivating form in a dream abandon everything else and meditate upon Him day and night. (24–25)
By virtue of his merit, the mountain flowed like water, dry wood became liquid,
the dead tree budded, and the wind was brought to a standstill;
even the sun and the ocean were halted through the power of his devotion.
O son, by what perfection could I forget that beloved Catas?
Out of fear of whom this wind blows, out of fear of whom the sun shines, Indra rains, Agni burns, and Death moves among living beings. (27–28)
Out of fear of whom even fruit-bearing trees blossom at the proper time;
whom the oceans, the planets, the sages, and the gods regard as their own domain—
he is the Time of time, the destroyer of the destroyer, and the Lord of the creator.
He is self-dependent, independent, and is himself designated as the Self.
By what prosperity, O devotee, could I forget that Lord?
There is no awakening regarding His distinction by which a wise one might awaken me.
Neither Sāvitrī nor Sarasvatī is able to awaken me;
neither the Vedas nor the Vedāṅgas, nor who are the virtuous ones, nor who are the gods?
Even the thousand-faced Ananta and Brahmā, the progenitor of the Vedas.
Neither Śambhu nor the Gaṇeśas [know it], for he is the teacher of the lords of yogins.
(33) The movement of stability must be contemplated; how can there be movement where the path is empty?
Everything—pleasure and pain, the auspicious and the inauspicious—is to be accomplished by time. (34)
That time is difficult to ward off, and in the worlds, everything is subject to time.
Arise, my child, and go happily to the enchanting Mathurā.
Abandoning the speech of Vraja, you are eager to depart.
"A long separation from Kṛṣṇa leads only to suffering and not to happiness.
(36) Behold His moon-like face, which removes birth, death, and old age!
Having heard these words of Rādhikā, Uddhava wept bitterly.

Seeing Rādhikā weeping, distressed by the separation from her kinsmen... [Thus ends] the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rādhā and Uddhava," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the ninety-sixth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Uddhava was about to depart;
he was bowing his head at the lotus feet of Rādhā, his body covered in horripilation.
The gopī Mādhavī, overwhelmed with love, spoke while weeping,
as did her devotee, who was crying out loudly, distressed by the separation from Rādhā. (2) Mādhavī said:

O Uddhava, listen; I shall speak. Wait for a moment as is appropriate, for I shall impart that supreme, secret knowledge which you desire in your mind—knowledge exceedingly rare among the Purāṇas and Vedas, and worthy of being kept hidden. (3)
"O illustrious one, ask a question concerning Rādhikā, the mother of the three worlds.
Having spoken thus, that queen of the gopīs sat in the assembly;
and Uddhava also spoke sweetly to the peaceful Rādhikā.
Uddhava said:
A living being comes alone into existence and departs alone again and again;
following his own past actions, the person experiences the fruits of his deeds.
A living being is born through karma and through karma alone it perishes;
pleasure, pain, fear, and grief are encountered solely by means of karma.
A living being experiences enjoyment throughout various states of existence according to the remainder of its past enjoyments.
Furthermore, through the experience of karma, one comes and goes again.
(8) O virtuous lady, whatever gems or other things have been given to me by you do not go along with me; what use are they to me? (9)
O Goddess, in crossing the ocean of worldly existence, you are the supreme boat;
Kṛṣṇa himself is the helmsman who brings all to the further shore.
Grant me some vessel that will cause me to reach the end of the ocean of existence.
"Having attained [your] favor, I shall go to Mathurā, the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
O Mother, tell me of whatever course of time there is for the gods, for humans, for the ancestors, for the world of Brahmā, and for that which is beyond it. (11–12)
"Having crossed over that very same terrible and difficult-to-traverse [ocean], I shall go to the abode of Hari.
O Consort of Kamala, grant me such a means as well!
For they meditate upon Your lotus feet from afar, day and night. (13)
"The gods, beginning with Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa, reside upon that chest of yours.
Having heard Uddhava’s words, the lotus-dweller laughed;
wiping away the tears from her eyes with her garment, she spoke to him.
Rādhā said:
O Uddhava, you are asking these questions solely because of Mādhavī’s words.
In this world, the female species is weak; what knowledge, then, can I possibly give to you? (16)
O child, the Blessed Lord Hari knows the pure course of time;
so too do Brahmā, Maheśa, Śeṣa, and the four Vedas themselves.
O son, the virtuous know it somewhat according to the guidance of the Vedas.
Listen, O Kṛṣṇa-faced one, regarding the course of time in Goloka and the Rāsa-maṇḍala (18).
I shall now describe to you that very same course of time which is observed in Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and Brahmaloka at present (19).

By whatever means the wise [ascertain] the course of time—which is certain for humans, ancestors, gods, and the world of Brahmā and so forth; for the external world beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); and for the subterranean realms (pātāla)—which is difficult to overcome.
O best of the wise, listen as I describe how they cross over:
they worship the Lord of the worlds, the death of Death, the Teacher of the universe, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign who is beyond qualities and free from desire. (21–22)
This body falls instantly when separated from that eternal Self; by serving that [Self], one indeed transcends the course of time. And the sun alone takes away the life of all living beings.

O son, behold the four mental sons of Brahmā— Sanaka and the others— who are devotees of the Lord and whose devotion to Him is perfectly firm, apart from the pure devotees of Śrī Hari, the virtuous, and those who possess merit. (24–25)
He [honored] Rudra and the others according to their lineage, as well as his constant kinsmen, the gurus of his guru, children who had not yet been initiated, infants up to five years of age,
and those who were in the interim state— those who were exceedingly robust, smiling, and naked.
[He saw] Vaiṣṇavas purified by meditation on Śrī Kṛṣṇa and purified by sacred fords;
free from anxiety regarding the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and Śāstras, they were full of joy;
day and night, they were constantly devoted to Hari with a spirit of devotion and through the sentiment of love.
And those who were devoid of external worship, yet purified by mental devotion;
the highly fortunate conquerors of death, likewise vanquishers of the serpent of Time;
and Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana.

Those who remember Sanatkumāra in every way obtain the fruit of bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and are liberated from committed sins. Devotion to Hari arises within them, and they attain service to Hari.
Behold Mṛkaṇḍu’s son, the best of the twice-born,
whose lifespan was but ten years; though he blazed intensely with the splendor of Brahman,
through the service of Hari, he subsequently became one who lives until the end of seven kalpas.
Behold Pañcaśikha, Lomaśa, and likewise Āsuri—
devoid of all ritual actions, solely intent on the service of Hari,
possessing a lifespan of a hundred kalpas, and meditating upon the feet of Hari.
Behold Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who is long-lived;
and Hanumān, Bali, Vyāsa, and Aśvatthāman;
as well as Vibhīṣaṇa, Kṛpa, the Brahmin Jāmbavān, and the bear Bhalluka.
And by the meditation on Hari, these are purified and become long-lived.
O Uddhava, among the lords of the Siddhas, the lords of the Munis, and other men,
all those who are purified by the meditation on Hari are long-lived.

Behold Prahlāda among the Daityas, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu; though he was an enemy of Hari and difficult to subdue, he was entirely devoted to the meditation upon Hari. Behold another as well—long-lived, having conquered Time, and beyond counting.

Having obtained birth in Bhārata through the austerity of many lifetimes, those who do not serve that Hari are fools and evildoers. Having abandoned Vāsudeva, a person remains devoted to sense objects. (39–40)
Having abandoned the nectar of immortality, the great fool consumes poison by his own will.
Whose wife is there, whose son, or likewise whose kinsmen?
On this earth, who is a true friend in times of calamity, other than Śrī Kṛṣṇa?
Therefore, the virtuous always worship Kṛṣṇa alone, day and night—He who removes birth, death, old age, and disease; the supreme destroyer of all;
the means for crossing over time; the worship of the Supreme Self. (42–43)
Listen, my child, to the course of time as it pertains to Ānandanandana, the most perfectly complete one, and as it falls within the scope of my knowledge—
concerning men, ancestors, gods, and even Brahmā. (44)

O dear son, I shall tell you the hidden meaning concerning the Nāgas, the Rākṣasas, and others as well; listen attentively. The Great Virāj is the supreme station above all and the support of everything. (45–46)
Behold the atom, which is subtler than everything else, within whose hairs all those things—both the numbered and the unnumbered—are contained;
it is the essence of time and its beginning, the most minute of all, and the supreme object of desire. (47)
The ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) should be known as that which is the final limit of real particulars, being manifold and never conjoined. O King, it is from this that the delusion of unity arises.
Two atoms constitute a minute particle (*aṇu*), and three of those constitute a mote of dust (*trasareṇu*). (48–49)
The wise have stated that three *trasareṇus* constitute a *truṭi*.
A *vedha* consists of exactly one hundred *truṭis*, and likewise, a *lava* consists of three *vedhas*.
A *nimeṣa* consists of three *lavas*, and a *kṣaṇa* consists of three *nimeṣas*.
Five *kāṣṭhās* make one *laghu*, and ten *kāṣṭhās* make one *laghu* [of the next order].
Fifteen *laghus* make one *daṇḍa*; listen now to its measurement.
It is twelve *ardha-palas* in weight and four *catur-aṅgulas* in length. (51–52)

A muhūrta consists of sixty daṇḍas, and a lunar day (tithi) consists of eighty daṇḍas. A prahara is one-eighth of that [day]. This is the definition and measurement. (53) [The time it takes for] a vessel with a hole made by a gold māṣa to be submerged in a prastha of water constitutes one daṇḍa. Two such daṇḍas make a muhūrta.]

A night is said to consist of four watches, and a day likewise consists of four; (54) the measure of a fortnight is proclaimed to be fifteen lunar days (tithis). A month consists of two fortnights, known as the bright (śukla) and the dark (kṛṣṇa). (55)
A season consists of exactly two months, and six of those constitute a year.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, and the cold and dewy seasons—these are the divisions.
Those who know time have determined that the rainy season is to be understood as being of five kinds.
Those who know time understand these as *saṃvatsara*, *pravatsara*, *ilāvatsara*, *anuvatsara*, and this *vatsara*. A year (*abda*) consists of twelve months;
hear its names, O Uddhava. (57–58)
Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādra;
Āśvina, Kārtika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna;
the month of Caitra is to be known as the last, designated as the remainder of the year.
Spring is proclaimed by the pair of months Caitra and Vaiśākha;
summer is celebrated by the two months Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha;
the rainy season occurs in Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, while autumn is in Āśvina and Kārttika.

The winter season (*hemanta*) consists of the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa; the cool season (*śiśira*) consists of Māgha and Phālguna. A year consists of two solstices: the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). The northern course, which is desired, is formed by the six months beginning with Māgha.
The six months beginning with Śrāvaṇa constitute the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
From Māgha until Āṣāḍha, the day indeed increases in length progressively;
from Śrāvaṇa until Pauṣa, the night increases in length.

The bright fortnight is proclaimed to end with the full moon, beginning from the first day (pratipad). The dark fortnight, however, is to be understood as ending with the new moon; this has been determined by those learned in the Vedas.
The second and the third, the fourth and likewise the fifth;
the sixth and the seventh, as well as the eighth and the ninth; the tenth, the eleventh, and also the twelfth and the thirteenth. (66–67)
The fourteenth lunar day and the new moon (kuhū) are recorded as the duration of the day;
likewise, the constellations Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī,
Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and the two Punarvasus.
Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī;
likewise Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā;
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, as well as Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā—these are to be known [as such]. 69–70.
Śravaṇa, Abhijit, and Dhaniṣṭhā are proclaimed;
thereafter Śatabhiṣā is to be known, as well as Pūrvābhādrapadā.
Likewise, Uttarā is to be understood, and Revatī is remembered as the last.
Likewise, the moon has twenty-eight lunar mansions as his wives;
he dwells eternally with them in succession. And in the Vedas it is heard that the moon has twenty-seven lunar mansions as his wives.

Because of the shadow of the Śravaṇa [constellation] during the Abhijit [nakṣatra], it is remembered as the twenty-eighth. Once, in the spring month of Madhu, the Moon took delight day and night constantly with Rohiṇī, his beloved; however, Śravaṇā became angry at this. (74)
Having offered her shadow to the moon, she went to her father’s presence out of fear.
Then, taking her father with her, she performed a ritual division;
by that act, the constellation named Abhijit came into being in ancient times.
Having heard this from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa on Mount Śataśṛṅga, O child, listen as I speak of the asterism that revolves constantly along with the lunar day,
as well as the *yoga* and the *karaṇa*.
Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and Śobhana; Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, and likewise Śūla; Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, and Harṣaṇa. (78–79)
Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva,
Siddhi, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Indra, and likewise Vaidhṛti—
this group of yogas has been proclaimed to you; now hear of the karaṇas.
Bava and Bālava, as well as Kaulava and Taitila;
Gara and Vaṇija, and also Viṣṭi and Śakuni; Catuṣpāt and Nāga, and Kiṃstughna—thus they are proclaimed. (81–82)

For humans, that which is one month is a day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs). Among them, the bright fortnight is proclaimed as their day, and the dark fortnight as their night. For humans, that which is one year is a day and night for the gods (surās).
For them, the day is during the northern course [of the sun] and the night during the southern course.
Seventy-one divine yugas constitute a Manvantara;
the lifespan of a Manu is proclaimed to be the lifespan of Śakra.
Twenty-five thousand and five hundred [yojanas] further,
there is no movement of the sun, following the descent of Śakra.
And those dwelling in the world of Brahmā know [the passage] day and night.
Two *daṇḍas* constitute a human *pala*, and that *pala* [is measured] by the falling of a *śakrapāta*.
Thus, in exactly thirty days, a *dhātu*-month is proclaimed; and a year consists of twelve such months for one whose lifespan is a hundred years. (87–88)
By the very falling of Brahmā, and even by a blink of Śrī Hari,
there is no distinction between day and night in Vaikuṇṭha according to the movement of the Creator;
likewise, it is remembered that the movement of the sun does not exist there, as it is from Goloka.
All the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha do not perceive day and night at all.
Indeed, there is no movement of the moon or the planets there;
nor does the discus revolve according to the will of Hari, as it does among the zodiacal signs.
By day, the world is illuminated by the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
and when Hari has entered his abode, it is devoid of light at night.
Such is the constant passage of time there in the realm of Viṣṇu.
The Lord, the Supreme Self, is the very nature of Time and is formless.
His movement through the moon and sun does not exist even in the seven netherworlds; those dwelling there do not perceive it, nor do they suspect it, day or night. (93–94)
During the day, the jewel on the heads of the serpents shines constantly;
at twilight, there is a blazing fire, and the night is shrouded in darkness.
The inhabitants of that place determine the time by the measure of the copper-colored light.
As it is on earth, so its measurement is proclaimed there.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga), and that is measured by twelve thousand divine years. (96–97)
The Kṛtayuga is defined by those who know time as consisting of four thousand years plus eight hundred divine years;
its total measure is twenty-eight thousand [years].
Seventeen lakhs and three thousand six hundred [years] are declared to be the human measure. O child, those who know time understand that this is called the Tretā age by divine years. (99–100)
The period known as the Tretā-yuga is proclaimed by those who know time to consist of twelve lakhs and ninety-six thousand human years;
it is also said to be two thousand four hundred [years] more.
The Dvāpara age is proclaimed by those who know the times to be one divine year.
Indeed, the Dvāpara age is proclaimed by those who know the times to consist of eight hundred and sixty-four thousand human years. (102–103)
Two hundred and ten thousand divine years—
thus measured, O child, is the Kali Yuga described by the wise. In human reckoning, it consists of four hundred and thirty-two thousand years.
And [the sage] skilled in time reckoning established the *varṣa* (year) in the Kali age.
Together with forty-two hundred thousand and twenty thousand human years, the four ages (*caturyuga*) are clearly defined by those who know time. (105–106)
Thus, my child, I have explained to you the determination of the measurement of time, according to what was heard and according to my knowledge. Go now, my child, to the city of Hari.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of Time," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, [in the section] concerning Nārada’s narration of the lamentation of Rādhā.
Now begins the ninety-seventh chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing Uddhava departing, the beloved of Śrī Hari became deeply distressed.
Rising quickly from her seat with a heart full of anguish,
the virtuous Satī, accompanied by the gopīs and filled with great agitation, swiftly offered him auspicious blessings and likewise placed her hand upon his head.
He presented tender dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, white grain, auspicious flowers,
parched grain, fruit, and likewise leaves and curd;
he also showed a vessel of water and a full pitcher adorned with sprouts.
O best of the twice-born, [this] fruit, along with fragrance, sindhūra, musk, and sandalwood; a flower garland, a lamp, a jewel, and perfume;
as well as gold and silver—[these should be offered by] a virtuous woman who has sons and a husband.
To him, the great saintly woman spoke words that were beneficial, truthful, and auspicious;
she concealed her tearful eyes and, grieving in her heart, spoke as he lay fallen. (6) Rādhikā said:
May there be auspiciousness; may your path be well; may there be constant welfare.
May you obtain knowledge from the abode of Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and become his most beloved.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa and service to Kṛṣṇa are the most excellent boons upon each of the petals.
The fivefold devotion to Hari is the most excellent and superior form of liberation.

(8) Even compared to the state of Brahmā, the state of a god, the state of Indra, the status of an immortal, the attainment of immortality, or the acquisition of supernatural powers, service to Hari is extremely difficult to obtain. (9)
O twice-born one, if a person born in Bhārata attains devotion to Hari through the combined power of many births and austerities, that birth is truly difficult to obtain.
His life is fruitful as he brings his past karma to an end.
One thousand ancestors of one’s own father and mother are certain [to be benefited],
as are hundreds of maternal grandfathers, a brother,
a kinsman, a wife, teachers, disciples, and servants. (11–12)

O child, that action which is the offering to Kṛṣṇa is auspicious; for that action is beautiful and pure because it brings satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa. Action performed according to the prescribed rules with full devotion is the means for fulfilling one's resolve.
That alone is auspicious, blessed, and brings about happiness in the end.
That alone is the vow, that is the penance, that is the truth; likewise, that alone is devotion and worship.
Fasting with that as its sole purpose is the only cause for the state of servitude.
The gift of the entire earth, as well as circumambulating the world,
bathing in all sacred fords, every vow and austerity,
the performance of all sacrifices, and likewise the fruit of all gifts— [all these are attained]. (16)
The study and teaching of all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas;
likewise, the protection of those who are afraid; the imparting of knowledge, which is very difficult to obtain;
the honoring of guests; and the protection of those who have come for refuge. (17–18)
The worship of all the gods, the salutation and the recitation of the mantra,
the feeding of Brahmins and deities preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite,
service to the guru, devotion to one's parents, and the nurturing [of dependents]. (19)
All of this does not equal even a sixteenth part of the service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s servitude.
Therefore, O Uddhava, with great effort worship Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest,
the Supreme Soul, the Lord, who is beyond all material qualities and free from worldly desire.
The eternal, true, supreme Brahman, the Lord beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the most perfect, pure, and the embodiment of grace for His devotees;
He is the witness of the actions of those who perform rituals, yet remains entirely untainted. (22)
He is the nature of light, the supreme cause of all causes;
the essence of all, the Lord of all, the auspicious bestower of all prosperity; the giver of devotion, the giver of service, and the bestower of His own state of innate perfection. (23–24)
Abandoning the notion of kinship and the ill-omened envy that brings misfortune,
joyfully worship Him, the Supreme Bliss, the Delight of the Nandana grove.
In the Kauthumi branch of the Veda, there exists a thousand names of His.
"Even for one named Nandanandana, obstacles are very difficult to overcome in the performance of deeds.
(26) Having heard all this, Uddhava was filled with supreme wonder;
having attained complete knowledge, he became fully enlightened. (27)
Tying his own garment around her neck, he prostrated himself before her like a staff;
binding her feet with the hair of his head again and again, his entire body covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears, he paid homage out of devotion. (28)
Out of love and grief for that separation, O Nārada, she wept loudly.
Rādhā wept out of love for him, and the group of cowherd women wept as well; out of longing, they took hold of Uddhava’s neck and consoled him.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa’s mind unconscious, fainted, yawning, and deprived of consciousness, Rādhikā quickly raised him up;
she restored his senses by placing water upon his lotus-like face. (31)
And Nārada bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, saying, "O child, may you live!
Then Uddhava, having regained consciousness, spoke to him in that great assembly before the weeping gopīs, bestowing the supreme truth.
Uddhava said:
Blessed and glorious is Jambūdvīpa among all the continents, which is so very difficult to attain;
for within it lies Bhāratavarṣa, the most excellent object of desire for all.
Oh, how sacred is the forest of Vṛndāvana in Bhāratavarṣa!
Purified by the dust from the touch of Rādhā’s lotus feet, it is desired even by the gods. Blessed and venerable is this earth, honored throughout the three worlds.
O excellent one,
in former times, for sixty thousand divine years at Puṣkara,
Brahmā performed penance according to the Vedas with devotion, purified by the dust from the lotus feet of Rādhā.
Out of a longing to behold Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa in Goloka,
he did not see Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa in Goloka even in a dream at that time. Then, by way of divine play, he heard a celestial voice which was true in its nature.

"In the sacred land of Bhārata-varṣa, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, during the most delightful Rāsa festival, you shall see [Kṛṣṇa] right there in the circle of the Rāsa dance. You will see him standing firm in the midst of the gods; of this there is no doubt. (39-40)

Having heard this, Brahmā desisted from his asceticism and returned to his own abode. Kṛṣṇa was seen, and he was delighted, his heart’s desire fulfilled. (41) The birth and life of the cowherds and cowherd-maidens have become fruitful;
they behold daily his lotus feet, which are difficult even for Brahmā and others to attain. (42)
The virtuous, the lords of yogis, the lords of sages, the lords of siddhas, and likewise the Vaiṣṇavas, always and eternally serve the proud Rādhikā—
she who is chaste, meritorious, purified by sacred fords, inherently pure, and exceedingly difficult to attain. (43)
That lotus, which is difficult for Brahmā and others to obtain, has become easily accessible;
for its toe-nails have been marked with red lac by Kṛṣṇa himself, the Supreme Soul and Lord of all lords. (44–45)
On Mount Śataśṛṅga, in the Rāsa-maṇḍala of Goloka, Kṛṣṇa himself performed her worship and offered this most rare King of Hymns,
along with handfuls of Pārijāta flowers and fragrant sandalwood paste.
She who offered tender *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) at her lotus-like feet;
she who is the sovereign of thirty thousand crores of *gopīs*,
and the sovereign of those thirty-six companions, is known by the name Rādhikā.
Those who hate, revile, or laugh at the sinful,
and especially at the supreme Goddess Rādhikā, whose life-breath is dearer than Kṛṣṇa’s—
without a doubt, they incur the sin of killing a hundred Brahmins. (49)
And by that sin, they are cooked in Kumbhīpāka and Raurava,
in the most terrible Taptataila, in Dhvānta, Kīṭa, and Yantraka,
for the duration of fourteen Indras, together with seven generations of ancestors.
Thereafter, they are born for a single lifetime in the world;
and due to their sin, they become worms in excrement for a thousand divine years.
They become worms in the wombs of unchaste women, feeding upon their blood and impurities.
"And there are insects with sores that consume pus in that human year," so said the Lotus-born One in the Kāṇva recension of the Veda.
To him who had spoken thus as he was departing, Rādhikā spoke again:
And as he wept, she too wept, distressed by the separation from Kṛṣṇa. Rādhikā said:
"Go, my child, to Madhupurī and inform Mādhava of everything."
"Act with such effort that I may see Govinda.
My life has passed away in vain; go away with your false and wicked hope.
For hope is the supreme suffering, and freedom from hope is the supreme happiness. (55–56)
After reflecting upon Govinda, she became liberated while yet living;
having spoken thus, Rādhikā wept there again most bitterly.
Having prostrated before her as she was weeping, she went to the house of Yaśodā.
O Nārada, when Uddhava had departed, Rādhā fell into a swoon (58).
She repeatedly lost consciousness and became absorbed in meditation upon her bed of lotus filaments and water, situated in the mud, O Sage (59).
Those excellent gopīs, their lotus-eyes filled with tears, placed her there;
by the mere touch of her, the bed was reduced to ashes.
Then, on a smooth spot covered with thick foliage and marked with sandalwood paste, they laid her down.
They placed her back down, distressed by the fever of separation.
The fragrant sandalwood water suddenly became dry;
without Uddhava, that moment became like a hundred ages.
"Alas! O Uddhava, go quickly to Hari and say this:
'Bring back Hari swiftly, the lord of my life!
Thus she spoke, wretched and distressed, her consciousness stolen by the fire of grief.
All the gopīs wept; placing Rādhā upon their own chests, they restored her consciousness and awakened her to her desired object.
Thus ends the [section] concerning the conversation between Rādhā and Uddhava in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrīmad-Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janma-khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
The Ninety-Seventh Chapter.
Then the Ninety-Eighth Chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Uddhava, having bowed to Yaśodā with haste and joy,
went toward the Yamunā, keeping the grove of date-palms (*kharjūraka*) to his left.
Having bathed and eaten right there, he returned again to Mathurā and beheld Govinda standing in seclusion at the foot of a banyan tree.
Even though he was joyful, upon seeing Uddhava weeping, consumed by grief, with tearful eyes and trembling, he spoke to him with a smile. The Blessed Lord said: 3. Śrī Bhagavān said:
"Come, O Uddhava! Good fortune! Rādhā lives, she lives!
And the gopīs, endowed with auspiciousness, live through the fever of separation.
May there be well-being for the cowherd boys, for the calves, and even for the cows."
"How is my mother Yaśodā today, separated from her son?
Tell me truly, O friend, what did she say upon seeing you?
And what did your mother say when addressed by you, or what did she say to me?"
Behold that holy Yamunā bank and the sacred forest of Vṛndāvana, enchanting with its vast, secluded groves and the circle of the Rāsa dance;
delightful with its multitude of bower-huts and beautiful with its pleasure-lake.
The flower garden was in full bloom and crowded with bees. (8) And the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree was seen, lush and verdant, accompanied by children.
The cow-pen was seen, and Gokula was seen, along with the herd of cows. (9)
If that Rādhā is alive, what did she say to me upon seeing you? O friend, tell me all of that; it causes my mind to tremble. What did all the gopīs say, and what did the cowherd boys say?
And what did the elder cowherds say? What did my father’s companions say? What did Rohiṇī, the virtuous mother of Balarāma, say?
And what, O Father, did the other cowherd women, who are dear to their kinsmen, say?
What was eaten, or what unprecedented gift was given by Mātā and Rādhā?
