What kind of very sweet speech was there, and what was their conversation like with the cowherds, the cowherdesses, the children, and even with her own mother? (13)
And what kind of love does Rādhā have for me, O Uddhava—even more than yours?
(14) My mother remembers me, and Rohiṇī remembers me;
and that Rādhā, distressed by separation from my love, remembers me. (15)
The gopīs, the cowherds, and the cowherd boys remember me;
and at the foot of the banyan tree on the Bhāṇḍīra hill, the children play without me. There, the food offered by the brahmin women was eaten by me as if it were nectar. (16)
Together with the young women and children, they beheld that desired place:
the site of Indra’s sacrifice was seen, the excellent Govardhana was seen, and that supreme spot where the cows were rescued by Brahmā was seen. (17–18)
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which were spoken out of grief yet imbued with sweetness,
Uddhava spoke this to the eternal Blessed Lord.
Uddhava said:
O Lord, whatever you have spoken has all been seen exactly as desired;
our life and birth here in this very land of Bhārata have become fruitful.
We have beheld Vṛndāvana, the sacred forest, the essence of Bhārata.
And the essence of that is the most beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala in the land of Vraja.
(21) The excellent Gopīs dwelling in Goloka are the essence of that;
and the supreme Rādhā, the Queen of the Rāsa, is seen as the very essence of them. (22)
In the middle of a grove of plantain trees, in a secluded place frequented by her friends,
upon a bed made of lotus leaves set in mud, moistened with water and smeared with sandalwood paste—
she lay there, utterly despondent and divested of her jeweled ornaments.
Extremely soiled and emaciated, she was covered with white garments;
there she was constantly attended by her female companions with white chowries.
With a slender waist, deprived of food, she would breathe for a moment and then for a moment more.
Does she live for even a moment, or is she tormented by the fever of separation?

O Hari, what is water and what is land? What is night and what is day? (26) Deprived of external knowledge, she meditates upon Your feet; does she not know a man from a beast, or a stranger from a kinsman? (27)
He shines with fame throughout the three worlds; his death shall be the source of that fame.
Even the ignorant and the bandits do not desire the sin of killing a woman.
Go quickly, O Lord of the World, to the desired grove of plantains.
That Rādhā, who is devoted solely to you, does not exist outside the worlds;
she is an exceedingly devoted one, protected always by her Lord, and must never be abandoned.
Indeed, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a devotee superior to Rādhā.
Manmatha was afraid of Śaṅkara, and you were the deity who stood before him;
yet Rādhikā, though burnt by desire, obtained a husband such as you.
Therefore, that action is supreme above all, and it cannot be thwarted by anyone.
The moon, though sweet, burns with its constant rays;
and the wind, though perpetually fragrant, [scorches] her who is now without a protector and utterly humiliated.
She, whose luster was once like the color of molten gold, is now like collyrium.
He whose hair is golden-hued, adorned with exquisite garments and attire;
he who is himself the Ordainer, the supreme lord among the gods, and your devotee.
Lord Śaṅkara, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis, is your devotee.
Sanatkumāra is devoted to you, as is Gaṇeśa, the best among the wise.
(35) And how many kinds of lords of sages on this earth are your devotees? Yet there is no other devotee like Rādhā; no devotee is her equal. (36)
"Rādhā herself is not like the Lakṣmī whom he meditates upon.
"And Hari shall come"—thus was it promised by me in the presence of Rādhā. "Go quickly, O fortunate one; make that very promise meaningful.
Having heard the words of Aḍḍhava, Mādhava laughed and said:
He related what is declared in the Vedas, together with the rules for truth and good vows.
The Blessed Lord said:
"In matters concerning women, at lawful marriages, for the sake of livelihood, or in a life-threatening crisis..."
For the sake of cows or for the sake of Brahmins, a falsehood would not be considered contemptible.
[But] for one who is devoid of accepting that [truth], how can there be hell? How can there be hell?
My devotee goes to Goloka; he certainly does not see hell. (39–40)
"Nevertheless, I shall make your acceptance fruitful;
I will go even in a dream to Gokula, which is distressed by separation.
Having heard this, the highly illustrious Uddhava went home.
In a dream, Hari went to Gokula, which was filled with Vṛndāvana;
having consoled Rādhā in the dream and bestowed upon her most rare knowledge, He delighted her and the gopīs with play as was fitting. (42–43)

Having awakened Yaśodā while she was still sleeping after nursing at her breast, and having likewise awakened the cowherds and the cowherd boys, he departed once again. Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter of the *Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa*, in the *Uttara-bhāga*, in the section concerning Nārada. Chapter 98.
Now begins the ninety-ninth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
In the meantime, Garga went to the hermitage of Vasudeva.
Carrying a staff and an umbrella, with matted hair and blazing with Brahmanic luster;
wearing a white sacred thread, an ascetic always self-restrained, with white teeth and white garments—he was the family priest of the Yadu lineage. (1–2)
Seeing him, Devakī rose up suddenly and prostrated;
Vasudeva, with devotion, offered him a jeweled lion-throne,
as well as the honey-mixture, the wish-fulfilling cow, and garments purified by fire.
Having offered incense, flowers, and garlands, he worshipped with devotion.
He diligently fed him sweetmeats, *paramānna*, cakes, and honey,
and gave him scented betel.
Having bowed mentally to Kṛṣṇa along with Balarāma and having beheld him,
Garga spoke to Vasudeva and the devoted Devakī.
Garga said:
"O Vasudeva, understand this; behold my son together with his army—pure, now at an age appropriate for instruction, and excellent.
Vasudeva said:
"O venerable deity of the Yadus,
perform an auspicious moment that is appropriate for the investiture, pure, and praiseworthy even among the virtuous.
Garga said:
"O Vasudeva, you who are like the god of wealth, send an invitation to all your kinsmen and prepare the provisions with great care;
tomorrow is indeed an auspicious day, and it is fitting that you come here."
The day was considered pure even by the wise, as were the moon and the stars.
(10) Having heard the words of Garga, Vasudeva, who was like a Vasu, dispatched all his kinsmen with auspicious letters. (11)

Accompanied by his retinue, he prepared delightful streams of clarified butter, streams of milk, streams of curd, streams of honey, and streams of molasses; he also prepared heaps of various offerings,
gems, jewels, and gold.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, remembered with devotion various ornaments and garments made of pearls, rubies, and diamonds, as well as the hosts of gods, the lords of sages, the foremost of the Siddhas, and his own devotees within his mind. (13–14)
When an auspicious day arrived, they all assembled:
the lords of sages, kinsmen, gods, and many kings;
as well as celestial maidens, daughters of the *nāgas*, and princesses from every quarter. (15)
Vidyādharīs and Gandharvas arrived with musical instruments;
Brāhmaṇas, mendicants, Bhaṭṭas, ascetics, celibate students, renunciants, Avadhūtas, and yogis also assembled there.
The female relatives of their own kin, the groups of the maternal grandfather’s relatives,
and all the kinsmen of their friends arrived for the auspicious ceremony.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, Aśvatthāman, and the twice-born Kṛpa also came.
The virtuous Dhṛtarāṣṭra arrived together with his wife;
so too did Kuntī, the widow accompanied by her sons, overwhelmed by both joy and grief.
There were also worthy kings and princes born of various lands. (19–20)
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Cyavana, Bharadvāja of great austerity,
Yājñavalkya, Bhīma, Gārgya, and Garga of great austerity;
Vatsa with his son, Dharma, Jaigīṣavya, and Parāśara.
Pulaha, Pulastya, Agastya, and Saubhari;
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
the venerable Sanatkumāra, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha. (22–23)
Turvasa, Angiras, Vyasa, Vyasa’s son Shuka,
Kushika, Kaushika, Rama, Rishyashringa, Vibhandaka,
Shringi, Vamadeva, Gautama, and Gunarnava. (24)
Kratu, Yati, Āruṇi, Śukrācārya, Bṛhaspati,
Aṣṭāvakra, Vāmana, Vālmīki, Pāribhadraka, Paila, Vaiśampāyana, Pracetas, and likewise Purujit. (25–26)
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Madhujit, and Kaśyapa the Prajāpati;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, and Diti, the progenitor of the Daityas;
as well as Sumantu, Subhānu, Kaṇva, and Kātyāyana. (27)
Mārkaṇḍeya, Lomaśa, Kapila, Parāśara,
Pāṇini, Pāriyātra, Pāribhadra, Puṃgava, Saṃvarta, Utathya, Nara, myself, and Nārada as well. (28–29)
Viśvāmitra, Śatānanda, Jābāli, Taitila, and Sāndīpani— the portion of Brahmā and the preceptor of yogis and men of knowledge;
Upamanyu, Gauramukha, Maitreya, and Śrutaśravas.
Kaṭha, Kaca, Karakha, and Bharadvāja, who was a knower of dharma—
these sages, together with their disciples, all went to the hermitage of Vasudeva.
And seeing them, Vasudeva prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
Then, in the meantime, Brahmā arrived with a smile, mounted upon his swan-vehicle;
and Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī, came in a chariot fashioned of jewels.
Nandin himself, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, and Subhadraka were there as well.
Maṇibhadra, Pāribhadra, Kārtikeya, and Gaṇeśvara;
Mahendra with Gajendra, Dharma, Candra, and likewise Ravi; Kubera, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Vahni as well. (34–35)
Yama, the lord of Saṃyaminī; Jayanta and Nalakūbara;
all the planets, the Vasus, and likewise the Rudras with their hosts;
the Ādityas, as well as Śeṣa and various other gods—all arrived.
And Vasudeva, with devotion, prostrated himself upon the ground, saluting him with his head;
he praised the lords of the gods and the deities with supreme devotion,
his head bowed low in reverence and his body covered in horripilation.
Vasudeva said: "The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest—the Creator himself and the protector of the worlds—is in my house. (39)
He is the progenitor and creator of the Vedas, the eternal cause of creation;
the teacher of the gods, the lords of sages, and the masters of the Siddhas.
Even for a moment, his lotus feet are extremely difficult to behold even in a dream.
By the mantra of the remembrance of Śiva, all misfortunes flee;
having crossed over every calamity, a person attains auspiciousness—he who is the foremost among all and the supreme leader of the gods. (41–42)
In the jars, may there be auspiciousness through mantras, devotion, and invocation.
The Lord Gaṇeśa himself is the manifest destroyer of obstacles.
And the Lord Kārttikeya is worshipped by the gods and others.
Mahālakṣmī, the most excellent among the gods, worthy of worship, higher than the highest;
in my home is my mother Pārvatī, the primordial form of the worlds,
whose very nature is all-powerful energy, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti.
She is the supreme among the high and the low, the transcendent one whose nature is the Supreme Brahman;
by worshipping her feet, a man obtains his heart's desire.
And she is present in person within my temple through autumnal beauty and through devotion.

Accompanied by all the gods and their attendants, she who is affectionate toward her devotees, full of compassion, has manifested out of mercy in Bhārata. Blessed am I; I have accomplished my purpose; my life is fruitful.
"Since you have come from the inaccessible place to my home, O Primordial Goddess,"—
in this manner he praised them all to one another in succession.
Then, joyfully tying a cloth around the necks of all the lords of sages and the brahmins, he honored them.
He caused each of them to sit upon an excellent jewel-throne;
he honored them individually and in due order according to the prescribed rites; and he invited Brahmā and the other gods one by one.
With devotion, he honored the groups of sages, the brahmins, and his family priest Garga with gems, corals, jewels, pearls, rubies, and diamonds;
as well as with ornaments, garments, garlands, perfumes, and sandalwood paste.
In the midst of them all, upon a beautiful throne of precious stones,
he installed Gaṇeśa for the sake of worship during the auspicious rite;
[he did so] with water from the seven sacred fords using a golden pitcher.
With cool, scented water joined with flowers and sandalwood— water like that of the celestial Gaṅgā from the Puṣkara lake—
and with pure *pañcāmṛta* and *pañcagavya*, [he should perform the rite] with devotion. (55)
He bathed Heramba with ocean water according to the mantras (56).
O Nārada, he honored him with a garland of *pārijāta* flowers,
as well as with ornaments of precious gems and a garment purified by fire (57).
With perfumes, sandalwood paste, flowers, jeweled garlands, and rings,
she praised the auspicious son of Pārvatī, the lord of all gods,
the destroyer of obstacles, the peaceful, eternal Blessed One.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Consecration of Gaṇeśa during the Initiation of the Blessed One by Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa. Now begins the ninetieth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then there were Aditi, Diti, Devakī, Rohiṇī, Rati,
Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and the devoted Yaśodā;
as well as Lobāmudrā, Arundhatī, Ahalyā, and Tārakā.
Having seen Pārvatī, they departed from the palace with great speed.
Having conversed with one another and embraced her again and again,
and having bowed down, they led her into the palace constructed of jewels.
They seated the Goddess upon a beautiful jewel-throne;
they honored her with garlands, garments, and jeweled ornaments.
And [they offered] a captivating flower from the Pārijāta tree, brought by Indra.
And Devakī, with devotion, placed that lotus-foot upon her head;
she applied a dot of vermilion at the parting of their hair, a mark of sandalwood paste on their foreheads, and scattered musk, saffron, and other fragrances all around them.
He caused them to eat sweet food and gave them well-scented cool water,
as well as excellent and beautiful betel-leaf perfumed with camphor and other fragrances.
He also applied red lac to the nails of their lotus-like feet.
She also cultivated the red hue of saffron with white chowries.
Having honored the goddess Pārvatī, she then duly worshipped the wives of the sages, who were virtuous women possessed of husbands and sons, in their proper order.
The lady of excellent vows worshipped the captivating daughters of kings, gods, and nāgas, as well as the daughters of sages and the daughters of kinsmen;
out of curiosity, she played various kinds of delightful musical instruments.
He performed auspicious rites and fed the Brahmins;
he worshipped Bhairavī, the deity of the village of Mathurā,
as well as Ṣaṣṭhī and Maṅgalacaṇḍikā with the sixteen types of offerings.
Vasudeva’s beloved wife caused him to perform pure, auspicious rites that bring merit and well-being, and she had him recite the Vedas;
she did so with the excellent water of the celestial Gaṅgā and from a golden pitcher.
Devoted to her son, she bathed Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with Balarāma. She then dressed them both in garments, sandalwood paste, and garlands,
and adorned them with captivating ornaments fashioned from the finest jewels.
O Nārada, Kṛṣṇa himself, richly adorned with his mother’s ornaments and accompanied by his army, arrived at the assembly of the gods and the lords of sages.
Seeing him, the charioteer of the worlds, he rose up with great speed.
Brahmā himself, Śambhu, Śeṣa, Dharma, and Bhāskara;
the gods, the sages, Kārttikeya, and Gaṇeśvara—each in turn praised the Supreme Lord individually and in due order. (17–18)
Brahmā said: O Lord, you are ineffable, your form being the grace bestowed upon devotees;
and since even the Vedas are unable to describe you, who here is capable of praising you, O Īśvara? (19)
Mahādeva said: The pervasive Lord, eternally situated within the bodies of embodied beings, remains indeed untainted;
He is the pure witness of the actions of those engaged in ritual acts, Himself remaining the witness of witnesses.
"What can I praise? You are devoid of form, devoid of qualities, and beyond all attributes.
Ananta said:
"O Lord, what indeed do I know of you, the infinite Sovereign, for I am ignorant?"
The cause of infinite millions of cosmic eggs, the deliverer from suffering;
(21) within the pores of the hair and the waters of Mahāviṣṇu, there exist innumerable worlds—variegated and artificial. (22)
The peaceful gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—are your own portions;
likewise, the sacred fords and Bhārata are reflected in your images.
And I myself, abiding within the single cosmic egg, exist in the form of a subtle serpent.
And you have placed [him] upon a tortoise like a mosquito upon a lordly elephant.
There is nothing anywhere in the universe more subtle than the supreme atom;
nor is there anything anywhere equal to the great Viṣṇu in terms of vastness.
You are beyond Mahāviṣṇu, and there is nothing whatsoever beyond you.
O Lord, you are the Great One, more gross than the gross and subtler than the subtle.
Furthermore, O Mahāviṣṇu, you yourself exist as the support in the form of water.
Goloka is indeed the reservoir of water, and you are its bearer in the form of the immobile earth.
The great wind is the support of all beings, taking the form of your inhalation and exhalation.
O Lord, you are eternal, possessing a body for the sake of bestowing grace upon your devotees.
"Even with many more mouths than these, granted by you in the past, I would wish to praise your yoga; yet the divine knowledge was not granted.
The gods said:
If even the infinite Lord were not capable of praising you, who are infinite;
if neither the Creator himself nor Śiva, whose nature is knowledge, were able;
and if Sarasvatī herself had become paralyzed—what can we do but offer our praise? (30)
The lords of sages said:
"If even the Vedas are not able to praise You or to know You, the Lord, then what can we do—being virtuous knowers of the Vedas—to offer Your praise? (31)
This hymn, which brings great merit, was composed by gods and sages.
Whoever, being self-restrained and pure, recites it with devotion at the time of worship,
shall enjoy happiness in this world and attain stainless knowledge.
Having ascended the jewel-vehicle, he goes to Goloka.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Initiation of the Lord" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, within the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janma-khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and first chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having offered praise, the gods and sages ceased their chanting, for Kṛṣṇa was not in their minds; they beheld him in the courtyard, resplendent in his yellow garments.
O Sage, it was like a fresh rain-cloud accompanied by lightning,
and likewise adorned with a row of cranes and a garland of *mālatī* flowers;
upon his skull was sandalwood paste mixed with musk, applied in the shape of a circle.
He is like the moon with its spot, yet beautified by a cloud;
he has two arms, is dark-complexioned and lovely, the beloved of Rādhā, and enchanting.
His face is bright with a slight smile, and his very form is the embodiment of grace toward his devotees.
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets, he was crying in his father’s lap together with Bala. Then, at an auspicious time and a delightful, favorable moment, [he was born]. (5)
When the lords of the ascendant and the seventh house are situated in their respective positions, are aspected by benefic planets,
are not aspected by malefic planets, and are indeed aspected by benefics, one should undertake auspicious undertakings preceded by the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*). (6–7)
And Vasudeva also acted according to the command of the god and the brahmin; having respectfully given a hundred pieces of gold to the brahmin,
he paid homage to the lord of gods, the lords of sages, and the family priest.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Śaṅkara, and Śivā—
this group of six deities— with unbroken grains (akṣata) in the assembly of the gods, he remained self-restrained and offered worship with the sixteen services (upacāras) preceded by devotion.
He performed the consecration of his son with Vedic mantras in the assembly,
having worshipped various deities, the guardians of the quarters, and the nine planets,
and having offered the sixteen mothers with devotion through the five types of ritual service.
Having offered the Vasudhārā rite seven times with clarified butter,
and having bowed to and honored Vasu, the King of Cedi, he departed once more;
having well-performed the Vṛddhi-śrāddha as well as whatever rites pertaining to the gods were required.

Having performed a sacrifice as prescribed in the Vedas, the sage Sāndīpani joyfully bestowed the sacred thread upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, who was standing at the head of Baladeva. He likewise imparted the Gāyatrī mantra to both of them.
And Pārvatī, with the utmost reverence, first gave alms:
a necklace given by her father, fashioned from the essence of diamonds and set in a vessel of priceless gems—pearls, rubies, and diamonds. (15–16)
And she bestowed auspicious blessings with white flowers and *dūrvā* grass. Then Aditi, Diti, the wives of the sages, Devakī,
Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, the joyful Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī [did likewise].
To each one she gave alms adorned with jewels and gold.
There were daughters of gods, daughters of nāgas, and daughters of kings, all devoted to their husbands—lovely women who smiled at their kinsmen with affectionate eyes. (18–19)
Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Pavanānī, Rohiṇī,
Svāhā the wife of Kubera, and Rati, the beloved of Kāma—
each of them gave alms adorned with jewel ornaments.
Having received alms with devotion, the Blessed One, together with his attendants,
gave a portion to Garga and likewise a portion to his own preceptor.
Having completed the Vedic rite, he bestowed the sacrificial fee upon Garga.
He respectfully fed both the gods and the brahmins;
and those who had come to the sacrifice, having bestowed auspicious blessings upon Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva, departed for their homes with joyful hearts. (23)
Nanda, together with his wife, having indeed extinguished the funeral rites for his son’s auspicious deeds,
took Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa onto his lap and kissed their faces;
then Nanda and the devoted Yaśodā wept aloud.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having consoled him, diligently instructed him.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Mother Yaśodā, go joyfully and without haste to your father."
In the ultimate sense, you alone are my mother and nourisher, and you are my father as well.
O dear one, I shall now go with my army to the city of Avanti,
to the abode of the sage Sāndīpani, which I desire for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
Then, after a very long time has passed, a meeting occurs;
desire effects the union, and it also brings about separation.
O Mother, everything—the separation and the reunion of men—is brought about by Time.
Happiness and suffering, joy and sorrow, and the abode of auspiciousness—
this reality, difficult even for yogis to attain, has been bestowed by me.
Nanda, along with Ānanda, will explain all of this to you alone.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds went to the assembly of Vasudeva;
having obtained his permission for a moment, he went to the house of Saṃdīpani.
After greeting Vasudeva and Devakī with humility, [he departed].
Nanda departed with his wife, his heart burning with grief.
Devakī gave to Nanda pearls, gems, gold, rubies, diamonds, as well as fire-purified cloth and jewels. (32–33)
Kṛṣṇa and Vasudeva respectfully gave to Nanda a white horse, a lordly elephant, and an excellent golden chariot.
Following the two of them were the women headed by Devakī, along with the brāhmaṇas.
Vasudeva, as well as Akrūra and Uddhava, departed with joy.
Having reached the vicinity of the Yamunā, they all wept in grief;
then, having conversed with one another, they all returned to their own abodes.
O sage, Kuntī, accompanied by her sons, at the command of Vasudeva,
obtained various jewels and gems and joyfully departed for her heavenly abode.
Vasudeva and Devakī likewise [departed] for the sake of the welfare of their sons.
He respectfully and joyfully bestowed various jewels, gems, garments, gold, and silver,
as well as pearls, rubies, necklaces, and sweet food like nectar,
upon the learned Brahmins.
He diligently caused a great festival to be held, including the recitation of the Vedas, the auspicious chanting of Hari’s names alone, and the feeding of the brāhmaṇas;
he also bestowed appropriate honors upon his kinsmen and relatives.
He adorned [him] with charming jewels, rubies, pearls, and garments.

(41) Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Initiation of the Blessed Lord," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Nārada and the Blessed One.
Chapter One Hundred and Two.
Nārāyaṇa said: Having gone to the house of Sāndīpani with his army, Kṛṣṇa joyfully paid obeisance to his own guru and to his guru’s wife, who was devoted to her husband.
Having accepted the auspicious blessings and given a jewel-gem to Hari,
he spoke appropriately to his preceptor and his wife.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"I shall receive from you the knowledge I desire; it is my wish, O Brahmin. Having determined an auspicious moment, please instruct me as is appropriate.
Saying "Om," the best of sages joyfully honored him.
With the consumption of the madhuparka offering, with a cow, a garment, and sandalwood paste,
he fed him sweet food and offered well-scented betel leaf.
He spoke very pleasant words and praised the Supreme Lord.
Sāndīpani said:
O Supreme Brahman, O Supreme Abode, O Supreme Lord, O Higher than the highest!
You consist of Your own will, are self-luminous, uniquely untainted, and all-powerful.
O sole Lord of devotees, beloved of devotees, whose form is the grace bestowed upon devotees;
O wish-fulfilling tree for the desires of devotees, the life-breath dear to devotees.
You appear in the form of a child through *māyā*, yet you are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa.
O King, through his illusory power (māyā), he has descended upon earth for the sake of removing the world's burden.
Yogis know him thus as the eternal light of Brahman (brahmajyotis),
while multitudes of devotees joyfully meditate upon him within that light.
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, beautiful and dark-complexioned, with all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, smiling and affectionate toward his devotees;
the Lord wearing yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland. (10)
With the waves of his playful side-glances, he mocked the one swooning from the god of love;
likewise, his beautiful lotus-feet were like a palace of liquid lac.
His divine form was enchanting, its limbs illuminated by the Kaustubha gem. (11–12)
With a slight smile and a serene countenance, well-attired and attended by the gods,
he was the God of gods, the Lord of the world, the supreme enchantment of the three realms; possessing the grace of ten million Cupids, he was both desirable and beyond all masters.
Adorned with a multitude of ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels;
the most excellent, the one worthy of being chosen, the bestower of boons, and the desired object of those who grant boons;
the cause of even the four Vedas and of all causes. (14–15)
You have come to this place dear to me by means of your illusory power for the sake of study;
your recitation is for the instruction of the world, as are your dalliance, your departure, and your battle.
[All these belong] to the Lord who delights in his own self and is the most perfect of the perfect. (16)
The wife of the guru said:
"Today my birth has become fruitful, my life has become fruitful;
my devotion to my husband has become fruitful, and this grove of asceticism has become fruitful. (17)

The hand that crushes the grain is fruitful for him by whom the desired food has been given; that hermitage is the supreme sacred site, marked by the footprints of the Lord of Tīrthas. Purified by the dust of your feet, the house and the excellent courtyard [become holy].
Upon seeing your lotus feet, which destroy the cycle of our births—
[we realize that] there was only so much suffering and grief, only so much worldly enjoyment and disease, as well as only so many births, karmas, hunger, thirst, and the like. (19–20)
As long as there is neither the sight nor the worship of your lotus feet—
O Lord, the Death of Death, O Blessed One, the Sovereign of the Creator and the Destroyer!—
have mercy, O Lord of Compassion, O cutter of the delusion of Māyā.
Having spoken thus, with eyes full of tears, she took Hari again onto her lap and,
out of love, made him drink from her own breast, just as Devakī had done.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Mother, why do you praise me, your young son whose mouth is still full of milk?
Go quickly to your desired Goloka with your Lord, leaving behind this material, false, and perishable body. (23)
Having fashioned a stainless body that removes birth, death, and old age—
having spoken thus and studied the four Vedas from the bull among sages,
and having, with supreme devotion, restored within a month his son who had previously died; || 24–25 ||
Three hundred thousand gems, five hundred thousand jewels, four hundred thousand diamonds, five hundred thousand pearls,
two hundred thousand rubies, and garments rare throughout the three worlds. (26)
And she gave to her teacher a necklace bestowed by Durgā, a jewel-encrusted ring for the hand,
ten crores of gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and an ornament for every limb of a woman fashioned from priceless gems.
The sage gave a pair of excellent, fire-purified garments to his beloved wife;
and having given everything to his son along with his wife,
he mounted a chariot of fine jewels and departed for the supreme Goloka.
Having seen that wonderful Hari, he departed for his own abode with joy.
(30) O Nārada, listen thus to the life-story of the God who is devoted to Brahmanas.
Whoever recites this highly meritorious hymn with devotion, (31) [shall attain the supreme goal].
One attains unwavering devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
One whose fame was obscure becomes renowned, and the fool becomes a scholar.
Having obtained happiness in this world, one goes at the end to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Therein, one eternally attains the service of Hari; of this there is no doubt.
(33) Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Hymn by the Sages' Wives," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and third chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, having arrived at Madhupurī and bowed to his father,
the all-pervading Hari, accompanied by his army, remembered Garuḍa at the foot of the banyan tree.
With reverence, he dismissed the desired Viśvakarman and the salt ocean;
he cast off his cowherd attire and assumed the dress of a king.
In that interval, the Discus itself approached Hari.
It is called Sudarśana, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
it is like Hari himself in brilliance, the supreme crusher of enemies, an unfailing weapon among weapons, the most excellent, the highest of the high. (3–4)
Placing the jewel-vehicle (the Garuda) at their head, Garuḍa approached the presence of Hari; Viśvakarman was there with his disciples, and the ocean was likewise trembling.
They all bowed their heads to Hari with devotion.
With a smile and great respect, the Lord carefully addressed them one by one.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O illustrious Ocean, grant me a stretch of land ten yojanas wide for the sake of a city; afterwards, I shall certainly give you something in return.
O Kāra, build a city that is difficult to find in the three worlds—
a place delightful to all and desirable to women,
the supreme fulfillment of the desires of devotees, and equal to Vaikuṇṭha itself. (8)
"O best of birds, O highly fortunate one, remain day and night in the presence of Viśvakarman until he completes Dvārakā— the supreme, desired limit of all heavens. (9–10)
"And O best of discs, remain by my side day and night.
Having said "Om," they all departed except for the disc, O sage.
[He then installed] the very powerful Ugrasena, the auspicious father of Kaṃsa.

He established the king as the ruler of the city of the virtuous Kṣatriyas. And having conquered Jarāsandha and likewise slain the Yavana by means of stratagem, O illustrious one, the Lord [established] the process of creation.
The Blessed Lord said: "A hundred yojanas in extent, the city is most enchanting,
[adorned] with unsurpassed rubies, emeralds, and sapphires."
With emeralds, coral trees, palankas, and syamantakas;
with fragrant substances and gālimas, as well as moonstones and the like;
with sunstones and the like, and with sons fashioned from crystal.
With yellow-colored gems, with dark-green chowries with white tips,
with yellow substances like *gorocanā*, with those shaped like pomegranate seeds,
with those resembling lotus seeds, and with blue ones having the color of a lotus. (16–17)
With jewels that have the appearance of collyrium, as well as brilliant and polished ones;
with those having the hue of white campaka flowers and resembling molten gold;
with those worth hundreds of times the value of ordinary gold, slightly reddish, and most beautiful. (18)
Honored with the heaviest, the most excellent,
and the finest jewels, the hosts of Yakṣas from Himālaya carried away the gems— whatever was desired, wherever it was released, according to the prescribed rule and its proper application. (19–20)
Day and night they shall act, preceded by their emanations,
together with seven hundred thousand yakṣas sent by Kubera,
as well as a hundred thousand vetālas and a hundred thousand kūṣmāṇḍas appointed by Śaṅkara.
"By the Dānavas and Brahmarākṣasas appointed by the Daughter of the Mountain,
perform the divine rite for your sixteen thousand wives,
as well as for the one hundred and eight other women."
The camp was provided with a moat and surrounded by high ramparts;
it possessed twelve halls and was adorned with a lion-gate,
equipped with various wonderful artificial porticos.
Free from forbidden trees and adorned with famous ones;
(25) likewise, the courtyard possessed auspicious marks and was pierced by the moon.
Such was the divine hermitage of the Yadus, as well as that of their servants. (26)
Everywhere there was established the residence of King Ugrasena,
and the hermitage named Sarvatobhadra belonging to Vasudeva, my father.
Viśvakarman said:
O Teacher of the World, tell me which trees are praised and which are forbidden, and which among them bestow good or evil fortune. Also,
tell me for whom a camp established with bones brings auspicious or inauspicious results.
"O Lord, tell me in which direction water is auspicious and in which it is inauspicious.
O Lord of the Gods, what tree bestows good fortune in which direction? And what should be the measurement for houses and courtyards? (29–30)
O Lord of the Gods, where in which direction is the auspicious Kusumodyāna grove and its tree? What is the measurement of the ramparts and the moats?
And what is the measurement of the gates, the houses, and the ramparts?
"O Lord, which wood from which specific tree is recommended for the camp?
Or which woods are inauspicious? You should tell me all of this.
The Blessed One said:
In a hermitage it is a coconut tree, and for householders it bestows wealth.
To the northeast or the east of the camp, there should be a tree that grants sons;
everywhere, this charming king of trees is worthy of auspiciousness.
The mango tree (rasāla) in the east likewise bestows prosperity upon people;
it grants auspiciousness everywhere and brings about divine favor—observe this.
So too do the wood-apple (bilva), the jackfruit (panasa), the citron (jambīra), and the jujube (badarī).
In the east it bestows progeny, and likewise in the south it bestows wealth;
everywhere it bestows prosperity, for by means of it the householder prospers.
There are the Jambū tree, the pomegranate, the plantain, and the Āmrātaka.
In the east it bestows kinsmen, and likewise in the south it bestows friends;
everywhere it bestows auspiciousness, granting wealth, sons, and well-being.
In the south and likewise in the west, the *guvāka* tree bestows joy.
In the northeast, it is indeed a giver of happiness; observe that it is auspicious everywhere.
Everywhere on earth, the *campaka* is pure and likewise a bestower of welfare.
Also, the *alābu*, the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the *āyāmbu*, and the *kiṃśuka* [are likewise beneficial].
The date palm and the karkaṭī gourd also bestow auspiciousness in the camp.
The vāstūka, the wood-apple (bilva), and the eggplant (vārtāka) grant prosperity; the fruit of the creeper is likewise auspicious. It is certain that all these are beneficial everywhere.
Listen to what has been declared as recommended and what is prohibited:
wild trees are forbidden both in the camp and in the city.
The banyan tree (*vaṭa*) is always forbidden in the camp, because of the danger of thieves.
It is renowned in cities and likewise bestows merit upon being seen.
However, the *śālmali* tree is forbidden in camps, cities, and towns;
it constantly brings suffering to rulers at all times. (44–45)
One who is neither prohibited nor renowned in villages and cities,
but whose learning is extremely forbidden, will then constantly bring about suffering.
One should carefully avoid such a person, who is like a *kāra* tree or a tamarind tree.
There would be a loss of wealth by a hundredfold, and the loss of progeny would be certain.
[The practice] is strictly forbidden in the camp and to some extent in the city;
it is not forbidden and is well-known in both villages and cities.
A wise man should avoid one who is forbidden by his learning and intelligence.
Likewise, the *kharjūra* and *gaha* [types of trees] are forbidden within a military camp (*śibira*).
However, those that are well-known are not forbidden in villages and cities.
The trees of chickpeas and other such grains are auspicious;
so too are they in villages, cities, and likewise in military camps.
The sugarcane tree bestows good fortune and is a constant bringer of auspiciousness. (50–51)
The Aśoka, Śirīṣa, and Kadamba trees bestow auspiciousness.
Is there perhaps the auspicious Haridrā, as well as the auspicious Ārdraka?
And is the Harītakī tree, which grants prosperity, present in both villages and cities?
The *vādya* tree always certainly bestows auspiciousness, as does the *āmalakī*.
Likewise, the bones of elephants and horses bring good fortune to those who establish them in their dwellings, just like [the bones] of the noble horse Uccaiḥśravas. (53–54)

It does not bestow auspiciousness upon others; it is the supreme destroyer of causes for monkeys, humans, donkeys, and even cattle, as well as for dogs, jackals, and cats—indeed, it is inauspicious for them all. (55)
For hunters, pigs, and fishermen, it is an auspicious place.
In the northeast, the east, the west, and likewise the north of the camp, water is beneficial; elsewhere, it is indeed inauspicious.
A wise man should not construct a long rectangular hall that is equal in length and breadth within his residence;
such a square-shaped house causes the destruction of wealth for householders. A long rectangular hall measured by two and four [units] is likewise detrimental.
The auspicious void is devoid of [the other elements]; it bestows emptiness upon men.
(59) A door that is two cubits wide and three cubits long brings good fortune to houses, as well as to walls and dwellings. (60)
In the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), nothing should be made either deficient or excessive;
a square camp with a "moon-piercing" (candravedha) layout bestows auspiciousness.
A camp with a "sun-piercing" (sūryavedha) layout brings misfortune, whereas one with a "lucky" (maṅgala) layout bestows prosperity.
The Sūryavedha [tree] grants misfortune, and the courtyard is likewise [inauspicious]. However,
the Bhadrā Tulasī planted within the camp bestows wealth, sons, merit, and devotion to Hari upon men.
Seeing the *tulasī* at dawn, one obtains the fruit of giving gold.
Likewise, the *mālatī*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, *mādhavī*, and *ketakī*;
the *nāgeśvara*, *mallikā*, *kāñcana*, and the auspicious *bakula*.
And Aparājitā is the desired garden for them, bestowing auspiciousness.
To the east and to the south, it likewise bestows auspiciousness; of this there is no doubt.
A householder should not build a house more than sixteen cubits in height.

A wall higher than twenty cubits does not bestow auspiciousness. A wise man should not establish a carpenter, an oil-presser, a goldsmith, or a diamond-cutter at the base of a garden or in the middle of a village.
One should station near the camp a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a virtuous Śūdra, an auspicious astrologer, a Bhaṭṭa, a physician, and a florist. Furthermore, at the site of the camp,
a moat of one hundred cubits in measurement is highly recommended.
Beyond the encampments, there should be a deep moat ten cubits wide, preceded by a causeway, serving as the desired gateway for the trench—
a place inaccessible to the enemy yet easily accessible to one's own friends.
Likewise, [the sight of] *śālmalī*, *tintiḍī*, and *hintāla* trees is inauspicious;
so too is that of *nimba*, *sindhuvāra*, and *badarī*.
[The sight of] *dhattūra*, *vaṭa*, and *eraṇḍa* trees is undesirable. (71–72)
"Among these excesses, one should avoid desiring wood within the camp, as well as trees and those with thunderbolts in their hands; the Earth-god would cast them down.
The Lotus-born One has declared that [such acts] would destroy one's sons, wife, and wealth."
"This was told for the sake of instructing the world, excluding the city of Kurukāṣṭha. "And now, at an auspicious moment, go, my child, as you please.
Having bowed to Hari, Viśvakarman departed along with the bird.
And near the ocean, at the charming foot of a banyan tree,
the bird and the artisan slept there during the night.
Likewise, Garuḍa beheld the beautiful city of Dvāravatī in a dream.
O Sage, whatever instructions had been spoken by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
he beheld all those very characteristics in the city.
And in their dreams, all those artisans saw him laughing.
Buddha saw Garuḍa, other Garuḍas, and birds crying out; Garuḍa and Viśvakarman were ashamed [to see] the exceedingly beautiful city of Dvārakā, extending for a hundred yojanas. (79)

And having conquered the city of Brahmā and others, which was resplendent, covered with splendor that eclipsed the sun, and adorned with jewels. (80) Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Construction of Dvārakā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janma-khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada. (103)
Now begins the one hundred and fourth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
In the meantime, Brahmā, Bhavānī, and Bhava himself—
Ananta, Dharma, Bhāskara, and Hutāśana; Kubera, Varuṇa, Pavana, and likewise Yama;
Mahendra, Candra, and those eleven Rudras.
Other gods, sages, and the seven Vasus,
as well as the Ādityas, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,
came to Dvārakā to behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
Seeing him suddenly approaching the beautiful foot of the banyan tree,
all the deities praised Puruṣottama;
and from the sky, they arrived at the foot of the banyan tree in celestial chariots.
They beheld the beautiful Dvārakā, exceedingly enchanting,
adorned with rows of jewels consisting of pearls, rubies,
and diamonds; it was square on all sides and measured one hundred yojanas.
It was encircled by seven deep moats and provided with nine ramparts; it possessed hundreds of thousands of pleasure-lakes,
enchanting with lotuses and frequented by bees.
It was adorned on all sides with three hundred thousand flower gardens of the *sarvatobhadra* variety,
made fragrant everywhere by breezes carrying the scent of blossoming flowers,
and rendered sweet-smelling by the cool, gentle breeze of sandalwood.
It was beautified by hundreds of millions of coconut trees,
adorned with jackfruit trees four times as numerous as those,
and provided with mango trees four times as many as the jackfruit trees.
O Sage, it was surrounded by *panasa* trees equal to mangoes in size, and beautifully adorned with *tāla* trees equal to mangoes in size;
it was also filled with *aśvattha*, *badarī*, *bilva*, *āmrātaka*, and *vaṭa* trees.
It was adorned with *śālmali*, *jambu*, and *kadamba* trees;
likewise with bamboo, *tintiḍī*, *campaka*, and *bakula*;
and it was filled with *nāgeśvara*, *nāgaraṅga*, *jambīra*, and *dāḍima* trees. (13–14)

It was completely flooded on all sides by dates, arjuna trees, crushed sugarcane, and even golden [trees], as well as by myrobalans, emblic myrobalans, and moon-like [flowers]. It was also filled with śāla, priyāla, hintāla, śirīṣa, and saptaparṇa trees.
It was filled with various other desirable trees, and it was graced by,
endowed with, and overflowing with countless beautiful and exceedingly lofty mansions,
constructed from the finest essence of jewels and adorned with pearls and rubies.
[It was] variegated with rubies and diamonds, provided with excellent jars made of precious gems,
and possessed of desirable, superior flights of stairs constructed of jewels;
it was equipped with firm, solid doors and bolts and crossbars.
It was joined by clusters of pillars made of emeralds,
adorned with various wonderful and diverse paintings,
embellished with mirrors, fine fabrics, and white chowries.
It was adorned with courtyards featuring rubies and other gems as well as sapphires,
and it was provided with pathways and royal roads inlaid with jewels;
it shone like the midday sun of summer, blazing with the luster of precious stones.
Seeing the beautiful city of Dvārakā, adorned with hundreds of thousands of windows and equipped with horse-stables, those gods were filled with wonder. Then the divine,
unborn Lord Balarāma, the wielder of the plow, appeared with a serene countenance.
He remembered the assembly of the Yadu clan headed by Ugrasena,
as well as Vasudeva, Devakī, and the Pāṇḍavas with their mother;
Nanda, Yaśodā, the cowherds, the king of kings, and the foremost of sages.
Together with the best of the Yadus,
Nanda, Yaśodā, the cowherds, and the Pāṇḍavas along with their mother,
as well as the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Vidyādharīs, O Nārada. (25–26)
There were also kinnarīs, dancers, singers, and musicians; mendicants, actors, bards, and astrologers;
kings from various lands, physicians, and other men. (27)
Renunciants, ascetics, the Avadhūtas, and celibate students;
all these sages, preeminent among the Siddhas, arrived together with their disciples—Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana. (28–29)
The blessed Sanatkumāra, the teacher of teachers among the wise,
remained naked for five years together with thirty million disciples;
likewise, the unborn blessed Durvāsā was accompanied by three hundred thousand disciples.
Kaśyapa with a hundred thousand disciples, Vālmīki with three hundred thousand; Gautama with a hundred thousand disciples, Bṛhaspati with a hundred thousand;
Śukra together with thirty million, and Bharadvāja with a hundred thousand.
The venerable and unborn Aṅgiras was with three crores of disciples;
Vasiṣṭha with ten million disciples, and likewise Pracetas with ten million;
Pulastya with three hundred thousand, and Agastya together with ten million.
Pulaha was accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples, as was Kratu;
Atri with thirty million disciples, Bhṛgu with fifty million,
Marīci with thirty million, and Śatānanda with a thousand.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga Vibhāṇḍaka was with three and a half crores of disciples;
likewise, Kātyāyana was with ten million disciples, and Pāpinī with one hundred thousand.
Yājñavalkya was with thousands, and Vyāsa with three crores of disciples.
Garga, the family priest, was accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples;
Gālava by thousands; Saubhari likewise by thousands; Lomaśa by thirty million; and Mārkaṇḍeya by thirty million.
Vāmadeva with ten million, Jaigīṣavya with thirty million, Sāṃdīpani and Devala each with thirty million excellent disciples;
likewise Voḍhu with ten million disciples, and Pañcaśikha with one hundred thousand.
I am Nārāyaṇa, and Nara is my uterine brother.
Viśvāmitra is there with thirty million disciples, Jaratkāru with thirty million, and Āstīka with thirty million. (40–41)
Paraśurāma had three crores, Vatsa had one hundred thousand disciples, Dakṣa had three lakhs of disciples, Kapila had five crores,
Saṃvarta had three lakhs, and likewise Utathya.
Jaimini was there with thousands, and Paila likewise with hundreds of thousands;
Vaiśampāyana was there with thousands of followers,
and the disciple of Vyāsa, who went before them all, was accompanied by hundreds of thousands of disciples.
Śṛṅgin was likewise with hundreds of thousands of disciples, as was Upamanyu;
Gauramukha had thousands, and Kaca, the son of the Guru, had hundreds of thousands. So too were Aśvatthāman, Droṇa, and Kṛpācārya together with their disciples.
Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Śakuni, King Duryodhana,
all the brothers of the king, and all the other monarchs [approached] the Teacher of the World.
The Blessed Lord said:
When the auspicious rite is completed, those who have gathered here—
the gods such as Śiva and Brahmā, the sages, and others— shall depart.
You, however, along with the Yādavas, enter the city of Dvārakā.
"O King, at the hour of Mahendra, my father shall go along with my mothers;
other Yadavas and others as well shall go to the city of Mathurā.
Having heard this, the king became despondent and, overwhelmed by fear, spoke to him: || 48-49 ||
Ugrasena said: "O Vāsudeva, I shall not go again to that ancestral land,
which is pure and supreme among all sacred sites for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors."
If one performs the offering for the ancestors on land belonging to another,
that land is seized by the owner’s ancestors during the śrāddha rite; thus,
the śrāddha for the ancestors becomes fruitless, as does the worship of the gods.
Even a small gift bestowed upon the ancestral site yields fruit;
indeed, the paternal land is always dearer than sons, grandsons, wives, or even one's own life.
Ancestral land is difficult to obtain, and that belonging to one’s father is more venerable than that of one’s mother. (52–53)
That [land] is both true and purifying for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
It bestows sport and grants gifts; however, what is given by another is impure.
One who dies upon ancestral land obtains a fruit equal to that of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
O Hari, the water of the Pitṛkhāta is as pure as the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed there in that pure water, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
There, the libation to the ancestors and the worship of the gods are purifying.
If it is one’s paternal birthplace, one shall obtain double that fruit;
for the wise, land given as a gift is equal to paternal land.
Vāsudeva said:
Wealth is yours; who can prevent your marriage?
That [marriage] is like a paternal pilgrimage site; what pilgrimage site is superior to Dvārakā?
Dvārakā is the best of all pilgrimage sites, granting great merit.
By the mere entry into which the cycle of birth for men is destroyed;
O King, [the merit of] giving gifts at Dvārakā, performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), and worshipping the gods there is four times that of the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords (tīrtha). || 59–60 ||
Go, together with the Brahmins, the sages, and the Yādavas, to the palace of the lord of kings; there, once more, receive him with due respect.
He constantly treats Amarāvatī, the city of Mahendra, with contempt.
Dwell, O King, in Sudharmā and in the realm of Mahendra.
The kings residing in Jambudvīpa, the lords of the circles of royal power,
shall pay tribute to you, just as the gods pay tribute to Mahendra.
May Kubera be surpassed by his wealth and abundance of riches;
may even the Sun-god be surpassed by his splendor, and Mahendra by his prosperity.
The gods have been conquered by battle alone, and the sages have been conquered by merit.
By his asceticism, he was like an ascetic, and by his vows, he was like one bound by vows.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a king equal to Ugrasena,
in whose assembly sat the blessed Baladeva of great strength.
O lord of men, the entire universe is placed upon a single one of his thousands of heads,
like a mustard seed in a winnowing basket.
Indeed, there is no god equal to Ananta in strength, nor any who is more powerful than he.
Because there is no end to his qualities, the wise have declared him to be infinite. (68) The eight highly fortunate Vasus, the Rudras with the exception of Śaṅkara,
the twelve powerful Ādityas, and Mahendra, who is equal to all the gods— (69)
"They are certainly not capable of conquering Ugrasena, the lord of kings.
Having heard Kṛṣṇa's words, the king, with a cheerful countenance,
set out together with the Yādavas from the abode of Mahendra.
The lord of men beheld his own residence in the midst of Dvārakā, blazing with the luster of jewels;
he saw the gateway guarded by thousands of doorkeepers armed with tridents and staffs in their hands, who were stationed there for protection.
And within the camp, at the six gates,
he beheld hundreds of palaces adorned with jewels,
and in the elephant-stable, ten million rutting lordly elephants.
The four yugas, the multitude of elephants, and likewise six times as many elephants;
the mighty horses that mock the horse of the Sun; and the king of lordly elephants, the sovereign of all vehicles—[these he beheld]. (74–75)
O Nārada, he constantly saw Airāvata laughing, and he beheld ten million of the highly desired Uccaiḥśravas horses,
as well as one hundred million donkeys and six times that number of foot soldiers.
There was a construction of five hundred thousand [palaces] made of the finest jewels;
likewise, there were five hundred thousand charioteers, and six times as many horses.
The horse-stable was equal to that, as was the Sudharmā assembly hall.
In that beautiful interior, I beheld her accompanied by hosts of gods and sages;
she was adorned with lovely garments of fire-purified silk and with red woolen cloths,
and graced by beautiful, reddish-brown thrones of precious gems.
Resplendent with the brilliance of streets fashioned from priceless jewels,
and surrounded by hundreds of millions of terrifying *kiṃkara* attendants,
he entered the beautiful assembly hall upon hearing the auspicious sound of the conch shell. (80–81)
Upon seeing the sounding of musical instruments and kettledrums, as well as the Vedic mantras of the sages,
Hari, together with his army, rose up swiftly toward the king.
So too did Brahmā, Maheśvara, Śeṣa, and the foremost among the gods.
All the gods and the sages of great vows rose up;
likewise did the lords of kings and the lords of the Siddhas, led by Vasudeva.
And the mighty Ugrasena sat upon a beautiful throne of jewels.
By the command of Hari, Nārada dwelt there at Mahendra,
as well as by the command of the gods, the preceptors, and Garga too;
with a water-pot filled with the water of the seven sacred fords, O Nārada.
With the syllable "Ja" and Vedic mantras, the consecration of the king was performed.
A pair of garments, pure as fire and captivating to the mind—
which had formerly been given to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, by Varuṇa— was presented to him.
The immensely powerful Baladeva gave him a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, sandalwood paste, jeweled ornaments, and a gem-encrusted parasol;
Brahmā gave him a water-pot, and Maheśvara likewise gave him a trident.
Pārvatī gave him a jewel necklace, and the virtuous Mālatī gave a pearl necklace.
Other gods, sages, lords of kings, and eminent Siddhas likewise gave him wedding gifts, each separately and in due order. (89–90)
Vasudeva gave him an auspicious white chowrie that had formerly been given by Pavana to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
and Nanda gave him the honored Surabhi, the wish-fulfilling cow.
Yaśodā and Devakī joyfully gave him the finest jewel.
Surrounded by seven servants with white chowries,
Akrūra held the umbrella out of devotion and at the command of Hari.
Seated upon a beautiful jewel-throne, he beheld a jeweled mirror; and preceded by Hari, he saw that which is attainable only through great merit, as well as deer.
Then the bards, the bhṛṅgukas, and the brahmins likewise offered hymns of praise.
The gods and likewise the sages bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
Out of devotion, the king gave ten million jewels to the Brahmins,
a hundred jewels to the Bhaṭṭas, and the same amount to the mendicants.
Having consecrated the lord of men, the gods, and the foremost of sages,
and having honored the brahmins, the bhaṭṭas, the mendicants, the twice-born, and the preceptor,
all the Yādavas, filled with joy, returned to their own abodes.
All those who were the attendants of Hari returned to their own abodes.
At dawn, they all came to the Sudharmā assembly hall of Hari;
having offered obeisances to the king of men, they all sat together in the council.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Coronation of Ugrasena and the Entry into Dvārakā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and fifth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, in the land of Vidarbha, there was Bhīṣmaka, the lord of kings of Vidarbha, possessed of great strength and prowess;
he was meritorious, truthful in character, a portion of Nārāyaṇa, and a bestower of all prosperity. (1)
He was most righteous, venerable, and preeminent, and was highly honored.
His daughter was Mahālakṣmī, Rukmiṇī, the best among women;
she was exceedingly beautiful, charming, and the most esteemed among lovely women.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with jewel ornaments,
possessing the luster of molten gold, and blazing with splendor,
she was virtuous; she was of the nature of pure being, truthful in character, and devoted to her husband.
Śāntā, Dāntā, Nitāntā, and she who is endowed with infinite virtues;
Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Candranārī, and Rohiṇī; the wife of Kubera, the wife of Sūrya, Svāhā, Śāntā, and Kalāvatī. (5–6)
Among all other beautiful women, even the most excellent and captivating cannot equal even a sixteenth part of Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka.
Seeing her, the supreme delight of childhood play, the king of kings was struck with wonder.
A young girl, most beautiful, adorning herself like a digit of the moon amidst the clouds;
rich with the splendor of the full autumnal moon, with eyes like autumnal lotuses;
a youthful woman fit for marriage, her auspicious face bowed down with modesty. (8–9)
Having suddenly reflected upon the matter, he who was of righteous character and firm in his vows questioned his daughter, his sons, the brahmins, and the family priests:
"Whom shall I choose as my son-in-law— the boar or the preeminent bridegroom?"

"My daughter Vardhamānā, who is marriageable and captivating, seeks a son of a sage, a son of a god, or the desired son of a lord of kings. Quickly find for her a worthy bridegroom who stands in the bloom of youth. (11–12)
If you make the prince— one who is virtuous in character, true to his word, devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
born of a noble lineage, and established in every excellence— an expert in the science of warfare, [then all will be well]. (14)
If you make the son of a god a great chariot-warrior, worthy of prowess, and steadfast at the forefront of battle;
and likewise, if you make him a god endowed with virtues;
and if you make the son of a sage one who is proficient in the four Vedas.
Having heard the words of the king of men— words that were eloquent, discerning, and thoroughly grounded in the established doctrines— the son of the sage spoke to him.
Śatānanda, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, was the son of Gautama.
The authoritative speaker is wise, virtuous, and the family priest;
he knows all principles on earth and is proficient in all ritual acts.
Śatānanda said:
O Indra among kings, you are a knower of dharma and an expert in the treatises on dharma. Listen as I relate an ancient narrative declared in the Vedas:
Nārāyaṇa himself [descended] upon the earth for the purpose of removing the world's burden.
The son of Vasudeva, the glorious and most perfect Lord;
the ordainer of even the Ordainer, saluted by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa;
whose nature is light, the supreme one, whose form exists for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
And the Supreme Self is beyond the nature of all living beings;
He is untainted, devoid of desire, and the witness of all actions.
O King of kings, [offer] the maiden to Him, the most perfect one.
Having given [this], you shall go to Goloka along with hundreds of ancestors. And by giving away this maiden, you shall obtain liberation in the form of the deity (sārūpya-mukti) in the hereafter;
even in this world, become one worthy of worship by all, the teacher of the Teacher of the Universe.
O Lord, having given all your possessions as the sacrificial fee, and having offered Mahālakṣmī Rukmiṇī,
perform this dedication and bring about the end of rebirth.
O King, the Creator has ordained this relationship, which is approved by all.

"Dispatch the twice-born Kṛṣṇa quickly to the city of Dvārakā. Having swiftly determined an auspicious moment with the consent of everyone, bring back the Supreme Soul, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon His devotees. (26–27)
O King, by the mere sight of that supreme, eternal body which is the cause for following the path of meditation, bring about the destruction of the karma of your own birth.
That which the four Vedas, the virtuous, and the gods do not know— [28] — [that you shall behold].
The lords of the Siddhas, the lords of the Munis, and the gods beginning with Brahmā likewise meditate upon him who is purified by meditation; yet even the yogins do not know him.
Sarasvatī has become stunned, as have the Vedas and whatever scriptures there are. (29–30)
Śeṣa with his thousand mouths, Sadāśiva with his five faces, the four-faced Creator of the world, Kumāra, and likewise Kārttikeya;
as well as the sages and ascetics who are supreme Vaiṣṇava devotees. (31)
He who is beyond the praise of those incapable [of it] and unattainable through meditation even by yogis—O Great King, I am but a child; what can I say of his qualities?
Having heard the words of Śatānanda, the king’s face blossomed with joy.
Rising up with haste, the king gave him an embrace;
he bestowed upon him various gems, gold, garments, and jeweled ornaments. With a face bright with favor, the monarch granted him further gifts.
A preeminent lordly elephant, a horse of the finest breed, and a chariot fashioned of jewels;
a delightful gem-encrusted throne, as well as vast wealth; and auspicious land, rich with all kinds of crops, where rain falls perpetually. (35–36)
"A village that is easily cultivated, worthy of worship, and praised by all"—
in the midst of this, Rukmin, the prince, became enraged;
trembling, joined with unrighteousness, his face and eyes turned red.
Then Rukmin, being unstable, spoke to his brahmin father while standing before all the members of the assembly. (38–39) Rukmin said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, to these beneficial, truthful, and praiseworthy words:
abandon the speech of greedy and angry mendicants, as well as that of dancers, merchants, bards, and even petitioners. (40)
The speech of scribes and monks is always untruthful.
(41) The speech of potters, actors, women-addicts, lustful men, the poor, and fools is always preceded by praise. (42)
O mighty-armed one, having slain Kālayavana, the lord of kings, from afar out of fear, Kṛṣṇa obtained that wealth through a stratagem;
thus Kṛṣṇa became the possessor of Dvārakā by means of the Yavana’s riches.

Out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha alone, I have lived within the ocean for so long. I am capable of slaying even a hundred Jarāsaṃdhas in a mere instant, as if in play; being thus alone, what need is there to mention any other king?
"I am the disciple of Durvāsas and am highly skilled in the science of warfare;
certainly, O Bhīṣmaka, by that very [skill] I am capable of destroying the universe.
Paraśurāma is my equal, and Śiśupāla is also my equal."
"He is a powerful and heroic friend, and he is capable of conquering heaven.
I am able to defeat Mahendra along with his hosts in an instant.
O King, having defeated Jarāsandha in battle—though he is a weakling compared to a yogi—"
Filled with egoism, Kṛṣṇa thinks in his mind that he is a hero:
"If he comes to my village desiring to perform the wedding, I shall certainly send him to the abode of Yama in an instant. (49)
Aha! You accept the daughter of the Vaiśya Nanda and that cowherd who is the manifest paramour of the gopīs, the eater of the remnants of the cowherds' food;
and you accept Rukmiṇī, who is worthy of a god. || 50–51 ||
O Indra among kings, you wish to give by word alone to the brahmin Bhiṅuka; you are devoid of wisdom because of the speech of that weakling.
Let him not be a prince, nor a hero, nor of noble birth, nor pure.
"O King, do not think that he is not a donor, nor wealthy, nor worthy, nor one who has conquered his senses.
Give your daughter to Śiśupāla, O lord of the earth, for he is a son of a great king and has pleased Rudra through his strength. (53–56)
"O King, quickly send invitations by means of letters to the kings born in various lands, to your kinsmen, and to the lords of sages—
from Aṅga, Kaliṅga, Magadha, Saurāṣṭra, and excellent Valkala. (55)
Send the Brahmin to Rāṭa, Varendra, Vaṅga, Gurjarāṭī,
Paṭhera, Mahārāṣṭra, Virāṭa, Mudgala, Muraṅgaka,
Bhallaka, Gallaka, Kharva, and Durga. (56–57)
There were a thousand streams of clarified butter and a thousand streams of honey;
a thousand streams of curd and a thousand streams of milk;
five hundred streams of oil and two hundred thousand streams of molasses.
A hundred heaps of sugar, four times as much of sweet foods;
a hundred heaps of flour made from barley and wheat, and a hundred heaps of flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), with four times as much of other grains. (59–60)
A hundred thousand cows, two hundred thousand deer,
four hundred thousand rabbits, and likewise tortoises;
ten million goats, and for rhinoceroses, four times that amount.
"O King, on this festival day, offer an oblation with devotion to the village deity.
Prepare cooked meat for their food,
and provide a complete array of various side dishes."
Then, having heard those words, the lord of kings, together with his family priest, quickly held counsel with his ministers in a secluded place.
He dispatched a suitable and desired brahmin to Dvārakā.
Having determined an auspicious moment desired by everyone,
the king quickly gathered the necessary materials with clay and,
at the command of his daughter, issued invitations everywhere.
The Brahmin, having reached Sudharmā, which was surrounded by kings and gods,
presented the auspicious letter to King Ugrasena.
With a blossoming face, the king, having heard the highly auspicious message of the letter, [was filled with joy].
With joy, he gave a thousand pieces of gold to the brahmins.
He had drums beaten everywhere in Dvārakā,
and [honored] the gods, sages, kings, as well as his kinsmen and relatives.

The king respectfully fed the Bhaṭṭas and the mendicants, and he had the most beautiful and incomparable marriage procession for Śrī Kṛṣṇa prepared, one that is difficult to find even in the three worlds. (70)

And he caused the foremost and best of the worlds to undertake the procession. At the beautiful and most enchanting Mount Mahendra, Brahmā first went forth seated upon a chariot together with Sāvitrī, accompanied by the delightful Vedic mantras.
The great and joyful Bhava himself was with Bhavānī on the chariot,
as were Śeṣa, the Sun-god, Gaṇeśa, and Kārtikeya;
likewise Mahendra, Candra, Varuṇa, and Pavana.
Kubera, Yama, Vahni, and Īśāna also went with joy.
There were thirty million gods and sixty million sages;
three hundred thousand lords of kings and three hundred thousand white parasols.
King Ugrasena shone like the moon among the stars;
the mighty Baladeva, with a cheerful countenance,
proceeded toward Kuṇḍina in a vehicle fashioned of jewels.
Vasudeva, Uddhava, Nanda, Akrūra, Sātyaki, the cowherds, the lords of the Yādavas, and those of the Lunar dynasty departed;
as did all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, headed by Duryodhana and his brothers. (77–78)
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Phālguna, Nakula,
and Sahadeva— these five Pāṇḍavas set forth in their vehicles.
So too did Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the mighty Aśvatthāman.
Kṛpācārya, Śakuni, and Śalya set forth with joy.
There were thirty million warriors, one billion brāhmaṇas,
and a thousand renunciants, ascetics, and celibate students.
Two thousand who had conquered anger and likewise those who were world-renouncers (avadhūtas),
a thousand blue lotuses, and a thousand flower-makers;
they carried various kinds of perfumes, both variegated and wondrous.
There were a hundred thousand musical instruments and a hundred thousand dancers;
O Nārada, there were likewise a hundred thousand Gandharvas and singers.
In that Kalpa, the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa was present through his devotion alone.
And you alone were in their midst, surrounded by fifty passionate women;
likewise, there were a hundred thousand Vidyādharīs, a hundred thousand Apsarases,
three hundred thousand Kinnaras, and three hundred thousand Gandharvas.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Rukmiṇī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and sixth chapter. Nārāyaṇa said:
In the meantime, the exceedingly powerful Kakudmin arrived.
Having arrived from the world of Brahmā for the sake of obtaining a bride,
he gave away his daughter Revatī— she who possessed perpetual and stable youth,
was enriched with ornaments of priceless jewels, and was difficult to find even in the three worlds. (1–2)
Out of affection, he gave her to Bala, the god Balarāma, according to the prescribed rites in the assembly of the lord of sages and gods;
she had spent twenty-seven yugas of the ages in Satyaloka. || 3 || Having bestowed the maiden according to the ritual injunctions in the presence of the king of sages, [he departed].
He gave three hundred thousand lordly elephants as a dowry to his son-in-law;
ten hundred thousand horses, one hundred thousand chariots,
and also one hundred thousand maidservants adorned with jewels and ornaments.
O moon among kings, he respectfully gave to the powerful Bala a hundred thousand jewels, a hundred thousand gems, ten million pieces of gold,
beautiful fire-purified silken garments, and pearls, rubies, and diamonds;
and he gave his daughter as well.
He went to Kuṇḍina together with them by means of a chariot made of the essence of the finest jewels.
(7) Then, while the auspicious rites were being performed along with their constituent parts, he caused Revatī—the very embodiment of the beauty of Lakṣmī—to enter the bridal chamber. (8)
Devakī, Rohiṇī, Yaśodā the wife of Nanda,
Aditi, Diti, and Śānti, having made their way to the palace,
joyfully fed the brāhmaṇas and gave them wealth.
The beloved wife of Vasudeva caused the auspicious rites to be performed.
Then, O king of kings, the gods, sages, and the royal princes, together with their armies, joyfully reached the city of Kuṇḍina in a mere moment through their divine play.
They all beheld the city, which was exceedingly beautiful,
surrounded by seven deep moats and provided with seven walls as well as hundreds of gates. (12)
The travelers on their excellent journey beheld the outer gate of the city, which had been constructed by Viśvakarman with various jewels and gems;
it was guarded by protectors along with four great chariot-warriors. (13–14)
Rukmi, Śiśupāla, and the mighty Dantavakra;
and Śālva, the best among masters of illusion and an expert in the science of warfare—standing upon his chariot, eager for battle, with various missiles, weapons, and arrows. (15)
Beholding Kṛṣṇa’s army, the prince grew enraged. He spoke words that were harsh, piercing to the ear, and difficult to endure;
he mocked the lords of sages, the gods, and the preeminent seers.
Rukmin said:
"Alas! By whom can the action wrought by Time and Destiny be averted?
What indeed shall I say in the assembly of the lords of the gods? (18)
To seize the maiden Rukmiṇī, who is worthy of the gods and captivating to the mind,
the protector of Nanda’s cattle comes along with the gods and sages—
he who is the manifest paramour of the gopīs and who eats the remnants of the cowherds' food.
There is no exclusion from birth regarding food and sexual intercourse.
(20) Is he indeed the son of a king of kings, or is he the son of a sage?
Vasudeva is a Kṣatriya, yet he ate [the food] in the house of a Vaiśya. (21)
In his childhood, this evil-minded one committed the murder of a woman;
a hunchback died from sexual union with him, and a washerman died because of his clothing.
By killing a lord of kings, this wicked man will certainly incur the sin of murdering a Brahmin.
And in Mathurā, the most righteous Kaṃsa was instantly struck down.
Śālva said:
"O gods, what that was spoken by Rukmin—is there anything untrue in that?"
"Who indeed is this husband of Rukmiṇī, this cowherd of Nanda?
(24) Śiśupāla said: "Aha! What wonder is there on earth, even for the gods such as Brahmā and the rest?"
The lords of sages and the sons of Brahmā arrived at the command of Manu.
Dantavakra said:
"Brahmins are constantly greedy, yet the gods are affectionate toward their devotees."
And how did the sons of Brahmā arrive at the command of Nanda’s son?
Having heard their words, the leader of the host of gods, as well as the assembly of the kings of sages and Lāṅgalin and the others, became enraged.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Rukmiṇī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the section concerning the Birth of Kṛṣṇa, as narrated by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and seventh chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O bull among sages, the exceedingly powerful Baladeva, his eyes yellowed with rage, shattered Rukmin’s chariot with his plow;
having slain the horses and the charioteer, that lord of the world [proceeded].
He went to slay Rukmin, that most wicked man who remained on the ground;
and Rukmin, with ease, warded him off with a net of arrows and employed the serpent-weapon (*nāgāstra*) to bind the Lord Halin.
The wielder of the plow himself neutralized the Naga-weapon with the Garuda-weapon;
and O Sage, Rukmī, out of anger, seized the supreme Pāśupata weapon—
which is unfailing, a crusher of enemies, and possesses a radiance equal to a hundred suns.
On one side, Rukmī was made to yawn by Halin with the yawning-weapon (jṛmbhaṇāstra).
Standing on the ground, Adukrmi was put to sleep by Sthāṇu with the very same sleeping-weapon (nidrāstra).
Seeing him asleep, Śālva discharged hundreds of arrows at him.
He brought down a rain of rocks, a rain of stones, and a rain of water;
he also brought down a rain of blazing embers and a rain of arrows.
But the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) forcibly warded off them all with his divine weapon.
With his mace, he crushed that chariot to pieces in the midst of the battle;
with ease, he slew both the horses and the charioteer.
Then, as he was about to kill him by force out of anger, an incorporeal voice spoke.
"Abandon Śālva, who is to be slain by Kṛṣṇa; what manliness do you have in battle?
For him upon whose head the universe rests as easily as a mustard seed on a winnowing basket.
Having heard that, Baladeva [struck] his head with his plow.
Pained, he reduced [himself] to powder and fell at the head of the battle.
Having seen Śālva’s fall, the mighty Śiśupāla unleashed a rain of arrows upon him, like a downpour of water upon the earth.
Hala crushed his chariot with his plow,
and with an arrow shaped like a half-moon, he effortlessly warded off [the opponent's] shafts.
Śaṅkara himself forbade him from killing him.
"O Balarāma, abandon this foremost of your attendants who is destined for death at Kṛṣṇa's hands," said Hara. He then broke Dantavakra’s tusk with his plow.
Because of that battle with Supravr̥tta, they all laughed at him.
Seeing Bala’s prowess, all the heroes fled;
all those on the bridal procession entered Kuṇḍina.
In the meantime, the great sage Śatānanda was there.
Together with ten million sages, he came before Hari.
He caused him to enter the city, which had a hundred gates and was difficult to assail; it was inaccessible to enemies yet provided happiness to friends.
Daughter-goddesses, daughter-nāgas, and likewise daughter-kings, as well as daughter-sages, arrived with smiles to behold the bridegroom;
all those women gazed [at him] with unblinking eyes. (19)
The moon-crested Lord, smiling, caused [him] to become gracious.
[He beheld] the Supreme Lord seated upon a chariot fashioned from the finest essence of jewels,
the Supreme Self of all, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon devotees.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, adorned with yellow garments,
his entire body sprinkled with sandalwood paste and decorated with a forest garland;
radiant and resplendent, crowded with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and necklaces of gems.
Adorned on his cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings,
he is delighted by the tinkling anklets fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems;
with a smile, he gazes at a jeweled mirror while holding a flute in his hand.
He was served by seven cowherd companions with white whisks;
endowed with fresh youth, his eyes were like autumn lotuses.
His face resembled the full moon of autumn, and he was the bestower of grace upon his devotees. (25)
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, it is truth, eternal, and everlasting.
Purified by sacred fords and purified by its own glory, it is worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
It is a form that brings supreme bliss, with a radiance equal to ten million moons. (26–27)
Unattainable through meditation, difficult to propitiate, supreme, and beyond primordial nature—
he who bears a blade of *dūrvā* grass, a silken thread, a mirror of the finest gems,
and the bright cluster of blossoms from a plantain tree along with a small knife.
Seeing the Lord with his topknot shaped like the three strides, adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers,
and wearing upon his head a crown of blossoms offered by a young woman,
the maidens fainted at the sight of the bridegroom.
"Rukmiṇī’s life is blessed and praiseworthy," they said as desired. The queen, the beloved of Bhīṣmaka, beheld her son-in-law with eyes and face bright with joy, gazing without even a blink. (31)
With a gracious countenance, the king, together with his ministers and his priest,
approached the gods, the Brahmins, and the monarchs, and prostrated before them. He granted them a suitable hermitage, filled with food that was like nectar.
