Day and night he said, "Let it be given! Let it be given!
He spent the night happily with the gods and his kinsmen.
And at dawn, Vasudeva performed his morning rites.
Having bathed, performed the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and other rites, and put on two clean garments,
he performed the auspicious consecration (*adhivāsana*) of Hari with Vedic mantras.
Having worshipped all the *mātṛkās* and all the deities in person, [he proceeded].
Having bestowed a stream of wealth as well as performed the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other rites,
he fed the Brahmins, the gods, and his kinsmen;
he caused musical instruments to be played and had auspicious ceremonies performed.
He had the bridegroom dressed in excellent attire that was highly praised;
he also had a magnificent human carriage prepared. Thus King Bhīṣmaka made all the auspicious preparations suitable for the wedding.
With the assistance of his family priests and Vedic mantras, he performed every rite;
he provided jewels, gems, wealth, pearls, rubies, and diamonds,
as well as foodstuffs, clothing, and unsurpassed offerings.
With joy, he gave [gifts] to the learned Brahmins and to the mendicants;
he caused musical instruments to be played and had auspicious rites performed. He also had Rukmiṇī dressed in beautiful and enchanting attire.
The queens and the wives of the sages performed the rites as was appropriate;
then, when an auspicious moment had arrived, during the supreme exaltation of Mahendra,
at a wedding-favorable *lagna* joined with its presiding deity (*lagnādhipati*).

When the auspicious moment is purified by the aspect of benefic planets and free from the gaze of malefics; when it is a favorable hour in a favorable lunar mansion, with the moon and stars perfectly pure;
and when it is devoid of defects such as planetary piercing (vedha) and free from the presence of needles and other such obstacles.
At such a time, which was worthy of bestowing happiness upon the couple and granting them future bliss,
Hari arrived at the courtyard of Bhīṣmaka along with the gods, sages, brahmins, and priests.
Together with his kinsmen, relatives, father, mother, and kings;
with cowherds, attendants, and charming companions;
and with bards and astrologers who were experts in the knowledge of the science of the stars (jyotiḥśāstra).
With various kinds of musical instruments, as well as dancers and singers,
with practitioners of various crafts and other florists,
and with vidyādharīs, apsarases, and kinnarīs, all arrived in haste.
The gods, sages,
and lords of men all assembled there, eager to witness the wedding;
they provided a site adorned with thousands of plantain pillars decorated with silk threads.
With sprouts of *cambaka*, *candana*, and *rasāla* trees,
and with various kinds of garlands— yellow, red, and white—
and with auspicious jars filled with fruits and sprouts placed all around. (52)
It was adorned with leaves, parched grain, fruits, flowers, and dūrvā grass, anointed with musk-sandalwood and made radiant with saffron;
it was surrounded by sages, brahmins, and even great kings. (53–54)
It was enchanting, furnished with an altar fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems;
it was anointed with smooth sandalwood paste mixed with musk and saffron;
and it was made fragrant by gentle, cool, and scented breezes.
It was ablaze with thousands of jewels emitting brilliant, flickering light;
it was exquisitely perfumed with various kinds of incense and fragrant substances;
and it was adorned with diverse, wonderful, and manifold works of skilled artisans who had performed meritorious deeds.
On every side it was rendered exceedingly beautiful by things worthy of adornment, sweetened by the melodious songs of the Gandharvas,
and by the dances of Vidyādharīs, professional dancers, and skilled artisans. (58)
There, it was adorned with rows of people and motionless paintings;
it was watched by women from concealed doors and windows;
and it was graced by auspicious jars and the loud proclamation of the family priest.
When King Kuśahasta, with his gift of a gift-object,
had cleared the courtyard of the king, the gods, headed by Brahmā,
likewise descended swiftly from their chariots and stood joyfully in the courtyard.
The lords of kings, the lords of the Dānavas, the wise Sanaka and others,
and the blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, accompanied by his foremost attendants—
seeing them, Bhīṣmaka likewise rose up suddenly with speed.
He saluted with his head the gods, the lords of sages, and the kings; then,
having honored them with great respect, he seated them one by one on separate, most beautiful jeweled thrones.
With tears in his eyes and palms joined in reverence, King Bhīṣmaka, filled with devotion, praised them all with piety— Vasudeva and Vāsudeva— with these words: Bhīṣmaka said:
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived;
it has become the severing of the root of karma for tens of millions of births.
You are yourself the creator of the worlds and the bestower of all prosperity.
O Lord, I am not even capable of beholding Your lotus feet in a dream;
yet You, the bestower of the fruits of austerities and the Creator, have appeared in the courtyard of my home.
To those who are self-contented and fulfilled, an inquiry regarding auspicious matters is not desired.
That Lord Śiva, who is not perceived even through meditation by the lords of yogis, the lords of perfected beings, the lords of gods, and the lords of sages— he,
the Lord who is the time of time and the master who is the death of death, dwells in my courtyard. (69)
And Mṛtyuñjaya, the Lord of all, has come within the range of vision of men.
He, upon whose thousands of heads the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings resides,
and whose end cannot be found even in all the Vedas— he, this very one, is now in my courtyard.

He who is led by all desires, whose worship is foremost among all, and who is the most excellent of the hosts of gods—that Gaṇeśa is in my courtyard. (72) The venerable Sanatkumāra, the preeminent among sages and Vaiṣṇavas, the teacher of the wise—he is visibly present in my courtyard. (73)
The sons of Brahmā, as well as his grandsons and great-grandsons born of his lineage—
all of them are blazing today within my house with the splendor of Brahman.
Oh, until the end of the kalpa, my hermitage has become a sacred pilgrimage site!
In whose house the sacred ford is purified by the water used for washing their feet,
those very same holy sites that exist on earth are present in the ocean,
and those holy sites that exist in the ocean are likewise present in the feet of the Brahmins.
As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of a Brahmin,
for that long the ancestors drink water from lotus leaves.
Having partaken of the water from a Brahmin’s feet and having given a sacrificial fee to the Brahmin, [one attains the highest reward].

One certainly obtains the fruit of all baths and all sacred fords (tīrthas). The water from the feet of a brāhmaṇa cuts through calamities, is the root cause for uprooting disease, and bestows happiness and auspiciousness; it is the very essence for human beings. (78–79)
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, no god higher than Mādhava,
no devotee greater than Sanatkumāra, and indeed no tree like the Kalpavṛkṣa;
there is no flower superior to the Pārijāta, and no vow greater than that of Hari’s day (Ekādaśī).
In His worship, there is indeed no object of worship, nor is there any leaf superior to the *tulasī*.
There is no Goddess even greater than *Prakṛti*, nor any support higher than the wind.
Indeed, there is nothing grosser than Mahāviṣṇu, nor anything subtler than an atom.
"There is no one purer than a Brāhmaṇa, nor any higher stage of life (āśrama), nor any sacred ford (tīrtha);
there is no god, nor anyone else superior," so said the Lotus-born One.
He is the Lord who transcends Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti).

He is certainly unattainable through meditation and difficult to propitiate even for yogis. He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and formless (nirākāra), yet he assumes a physical form out of grace toward his devotees. He alone is the God who has appeared visibly before my eyes in my own home. (84–85)
"The lotus-feet of which are meditated upon by the gods, Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa,
and which are difficult even for the Lord of Wealth, Gaṇeśa, and the Sun-god to attain"—
having spoken thus, Bhīṣmaka himself brought Kṛṣṇa before him.
He praised the Supreme Lord with a hymn recited from the Sāmaveda.
Bhīṣmaka said:
"The inner self of all, the witness of all, and indeed entirely unattached."

Some say that you alone are the eternal one whose form is light, the cause of both actions and the causes of those actions; and others call you the Supreme Self, of whom the individual soul is a reflection. (88–89)
Some, with deluded intellects, describe the individual soul as being composed of primordial matter; others, who are awakened and possess subtle insight, maintain that it possesses an eternal body.
Within the light, there is an eternal, ancient form in the shape of a body.
"From where does fire arise, possessing its form, without a Lord?
(91) Having thus offered praise, O Nārada, he sipped water for purification and, remembering Viṣṇu, joyfully offered water for the feet at His lotus-like feet which are worshipped by Padmā. (92)
There he offered the *arghya* consisting of *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and water,
as well as the fragrant *madhuparka* and sandalwood paste for all his limbs—
gifts that had been bestowed by Mahendra as a dowry for this auspicious rite.
And he placed a garland of *pārijāta* flowers around the neck of his son-in-law.
King [Purūravas] performed the formal acceptance (*varaṇa*) of him with devotion, using the priceless jewel-ornaments that had been given by Kubera.
The pair of garments of pure silk that had formerly been given by Agni,
he gave to Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect one;
and the blazing jewel-crown that had been given by Viśvakarman.
The king offered incense, jeweled lamps, and most enchanting food offerings upon the head of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul; he also gave various kinds of flowers and a jeweled throne.
Water from the seven sacred fords (tīrthas) for rinsing the mouth once more,
excellent and beautiful betel leaf well-scented with camphor and other fragrances,
a delightful bed that brings pleasure, and scented water for drinking.
Having performed the formal invitation (*varaṇa*), the king granted him an exemption (*parihāra*).
With palms joined in reverence, the king offered him a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Marriage of Rukmiṇī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa concerning the Birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, within the section on Nārada’s Narratives.
Now begins the one hundred and eighth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: In the meantime, the goddess Mahālakṣmī and Rukmiṇī—
She arrived in the midst of the assembly, which was filled with sages, gods, and others.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, she was adorned with ornaments of gems,
wearing garments as pure as fire, and graced by the weight of her braided hair.
Smiling, that virtuous woman gazed upon the mirror of priceless jewels;
she was adorned with spots of musk and anointed with smooth sandalwood paste.
Her forehead was eternally radiant in its center with a drop of sindūra.
Possessing the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to a hundred moons,
her entire body was anointed with sandalwood and she was adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
she was escorted by seven young princes.
The lords of the gods, the lords of sages, the lords of the perfected ones,

and the foremost of kings beheld the goddess Rukmiṇī, the great Lakṣmī, devoted to her husband. Having performed seven circumambulations and having prostrated before her own husband, that virtuous woman—
He sprinkled her with cool water and with tender leaves of smooth sandalwood.
At that auspicious moment, the beloved of the world sprinkled his beloved, who was tranquil and smiling; the beloved gazed upon his beloved, and the beloved gazed upon the beloved.
Then the goddess of auspicious countenance sat upon her father’s lap,
her face bowed with modesty yet blazing with her own splendor.
The king [offered] Deveśvarī to that most excellent man.
O Nārada, by means of a formal gift accompanied by Vedic mantras, Kṛṣṇa joyfully accepted the goddess, saying "May there be well-being," at the command of Vasudeva;
he was like Bhava accepting Bhavānī. || 10-11 ||
The king gave five hundred thousand pieces of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, who is most perfect;
and having placed the maiden upon his chest, he completed the auspicious rite.
The king wept out of delusion in the assembly of the lord of sages;
having made an offering to him with words of dismissal,
he drenched the blessed maiden with the water from his pair of eyes.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Rukmiṇī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and ninth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
In the meantime, Queen Rukmiṇī’s mother,
accompanied by virtuous women whose husbands and sons were living, arrived joyfully; she performed auspicious rites there, such as the ritual sprinkling of water.
He caused the couple to dwell in a palace constructed of jewels,
(2) richly adorned with various wonderful paintings, decorated with necklaces of diamonds, radiant with pearls, rubies, and gems, and furnished with mirrors. (3)
Right there, Kṛṣṇa beheld Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune;
as well as Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Rati, Rohiṇī, and the virtuous Satī—
the wives of gods, the wives of kings, and the wives of sages, all devoted to their husbands.
Seeing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, standing nearby adorned with jewel ornaments and seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, they rose up;
and he joyfully invited her to sit upon that beautiful gem-studded throne.
The gods and the wives of the sages offered praises to Mādhava there,
with their hands joined in *añjali*, each separately and in due order.
And the queen fed the bride along with her husband.
She gave him betel with camphor and scented water.
There, Durgā presented Kṛṣṇa with an auspicious letter;
by the command of all [the goddesses], she told him, "Read this."
In the assembly of the goddesses, Kṛṣṇa read the letter with a smile:
"Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, the virtuous Rādhikā;
Tulasī, Pṛthivī, Gaṅgā, Arundhatī, Yamunā, and Aditi."
"May Śatarūpā, Sītā, Devahūtī, Menakā,
and these other goddesses bring about the supreme [union] of this couple.
Kṛṣṇa recited this, and they heard it and laughed.
Pārvatī said: "O beloved of Rukmiṇī, look at this mature, beautiful, and charming woman of fresh youth, who gazes at you with a smile.
Śacī said:
"And this young woman, worthy of you and adorned with jewel ornaments,
has long sought you, disregarding another lord.
Sāvitrī said:
Just as the groom, so was the bride joined together by destiny in the past;
the union everywhere between a clever woman and a clever man is auspicious.
Rati said:
"Who on earth would be capable of mocking the Lord?
He is unattainable through meditation and difficult to propitiate; he disregards all other lords. Gāyatrī said:
Just as the bridegroom was, so too was the maiden, while the house of the Bhaiṣmaka was agitated.
Rohiṇī said:
"Tell the truth, O Lord of the World, in this assembly of women who desire you."
"What kind of woman is the beautiful Rādhikā, and what kind of woman is Rukmiṇī?
Sarasvatī said:
"The love that exists for Rādhā is not at all the same as that which exists for Rukmiṇī."
In former times, she was his devoted companion, increasing his joy in all his pastimes.
She is the presiding goddess of the vital breaths; being superior to the five vital breaths, she is Rukmiṇī, Kamalā herself, the supreme deity of all riches. (19–20)
You are the embodiment of all powers of the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa;
you are Durgā, the supreme Nārāyaṇī, and the presiding deity even of the intellect.
You are Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, the goddess who presides over all deities.
I am the presiding deity of knowledge (*vidyādhidevatā*), as are all other various arts and sciences (*kalākalāḥ*).
[This power] does not reside in Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, or the Lord of Day (the Sun);
nor in his devotees, nor in Lakṣmī, nor in Pārvatī, nor even in me.
The kind of serene devotion one has for her is not found toward others;
therefore, among the three worlds, the earth is blessed, and within it, Bhārata is most meritorious.
Therein, Vṛndāvana is blessed, marked by the lotus feet of Rādhā.
"Among all the goddesses, Rādhā alone is truly meritorious.
Having heard this, "She applied smooth red lac to the toenails of Rādhā’s lotus-feet," all the women laughed. (25–26)
All the messengers meditate upon Rādhā, who resides upon the chest [of Kṛṣṇa];
therefore, having offered salutations to Rādhā, they indeed consider her their equal.
(27) Having heard the words of Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, and Satī—
And all the other women in the assembly said, "Excellent!
Lopāmudrā, Anasūyā, Ahalyā, and Arundhatī—
all those wives of sages— impelled the Lord with great enthusiasm.
Then Bhīṣmaka honored the gods, the kings, and the lords of sages according to the prescribed rites and fed them with great respect, saying:
"Eat, O people! Give, give! (30)
A sound arose in the city with the auspicious music of instrumental ensembles.
(31) Then, at dawn, Brahmā, Īśa, Śeṣa, the gods, and likewise the kings, ascended their vehicles in great haste. (32)
King Mahograsena and Vasudeva, filled with haste,
arranged the journey for Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the virtuous Rukmiṇī.
Subhadrā, the mother of Rukmiṇī, placed her daughter upon her own breast.
She wept loudly with her friends and kinsmen, and she spoke thus:
Subhadrā said:
"Where are you going, leaving me behind, my child, your sovereign mother?"
"How shall I live having abandoned you, and how indeed will you live?

O Mahālakṣmī, you who are my daughter in the form of a maiden through your illusory power (māyā), you, being the virtuous beloved of Vāsudeva, are going from my house to the abode of Vasudeva. (35–36)
Having spoken thus, Bhīṣmaka, with eyes full of tears, out of grief drenched the maiden with the waters of his own eyes; and having entrusted the girl to Kṛṣṇa and made that formal relinquishment,
he wept most loudly and intensely.
Queen Rukmiṇī wept, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa too [wept] by means of his illusory power (māyā).
Vasudeva placed his son and his daughter-in-law upon the chariot. In the meantime, the king gave wedding gifts to his son-in-law.
A thousand elephants, six times as many horses,
a thousand female slaves, hundreds upon hundreds of servants,
a thousand gems, and ornaments made of priceless jewels.

And with great respect, he joyfully presented five hundred thousand highly refined gold vessels for water and food, beautifully crafted by Viśvakarman, which were golden and enchanting; and he gave him fragrant cows. (41–42)
A thousand milch cows with their calves,
priceless and beautiful garments purified by fire,
and Vasudeva along with Ugrasena, together with the gods and sages— || 43 ||
With a joyful countenance, he went quickly toward Dvārakā.
Having entered his beautiful city, he caused auspicious rites to be performed and had exquisite,
most enchanting music played.
Devakī, Rohiṇī, the lovely Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda,
as well as Aditi, Diti, and likewise Varakāminī—
having gazed again and again upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the beautiful Rukmiṇī.

He caused him to enter his home and had auspicious rites performed. Having fed the gods, the foremost of sages, the kings, and his kinsmen with the four kinds of food, he also granted them tax exemptions.
With joy, he gave gems and other gifts even to the learned Brahmins;
he fed them as well, and they departed smiling and fully satisfied.
Having thus enjoyed themselves and received wealth, they all went home with delight.
The beloved wife of Vasudeva performed the auspicious rites.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Rukmiṇī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa within the glorious Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, [narrated] by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and tenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
When the auspicious rites, along with all their constituent parts, had thus been completed,
Nanda, together with Yaśodā, approached his two sons.
Yaśodā said:
O Mādhava, you have bestowed knowledge upon my father Nanda;
O child, O ocean of mercy, please show compassion toward me as well, your mother. (2)
O illustrious one, cause of the upholding of the earth, lift me up—
I who am terrified and fallen into the ocean of worldly existence, which is so fearsome.
That primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of illusion, is the boat for crossing the ocean of existence.
"O Compassionate One, you alone are the helmsman for those who have crossed over through devotion.
(4) Having heard these words of Yaśodā, Puruṣottama laughed;
the teacher of even the wise spoke with devotion to his mother. (5)
The Blessed Lord said: O Mother, there is knowledge consisting of yoga, and there is knowledge consisting of sense objects;
but the knowledge consisting of devotion is the most excellent, auspicious, and the cause of my service.
Knowledge is declared to be of five kinds, as agreed upon in all the Vedas. Among these, that which consists of devotion is the supreme; hear now their characteristics.
[The first is] the subduing of hunger, thirst, and so forth, and the purification of one's own mind.
One should perform the purification of the channels (nāḍīs) as well as the piercing of the centers (cakras).
Then, one should meditate upon the Lord conjoined with the Śakti Kuṇḍalinī. Furthermore, there is the subduing of the senses and the abandonment of greed and other such vices.
The six cakras are proclaimed as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and the one called Jñāna.
This is difficult to understand even for women, and especially for the foolish.
O virtuous lady, knowledge consisting of yoga is the desired goal to be accomplished by the perfected ones (siddhas).
Likewise, all beings possess knowledge regarding their own respective domains;
indeed, all the holy ones understand this through my own will.
And for the Siddhas, it consists of accomplishment and is appointed for all ritual actions.
Among the thirty-four [categories], there is likewise the means of attainment and the awakening of the Siddhas.
Knowledge, which consists of liberation, is established as the supreme cause of nirvāṇa.
The devotee desires only that very path of renunciation upon which you have ascended.
And Rādhā will bestow upon you that knowledge which consists of devotion;
having abandoned the human state within her, she will bring about [your] realization.
"The knowledge that was given to Nanda, He will bestow that upon you as well.
Go, O Mother, respectfully to the cowherd settlement of Nanda along with Nanda. Having spoken thus and shown humility, Hari went inside.
Nanda went with Yaśodā to the plantain grove.
There he saw Rādhā asleep, having cast off her ornaments;
she was wearing white garments, fasting, and thin-waisted. (17–18)

She lay upon a lotus leaf resting in the mud, amidst water, and honored with sandalwood paste; her lips were parched, her eyes filled with tears, and she was unconscious, meditating upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (19)

Having abandoned all external cognition, with her mind entirely absorbed in Him, she beheld her beloved with a smile; and in a dream, in the presence of her beloved, she gazed upon his lotus-like face while both laughing and weeping. (20–21)
Constantly attended on all sides by her friends with white chowries,
and protected day and night by hundreds of millions of gopīs who were ever-vigilant and held staffs in their hands, [she beheld] the Goddess.
Seeing her at the seven gates and throughout the surrounding courtyards, Nanda, along with his wife, was filled with wonder;
bowing down like a staff, he prostrated himself with supreme devotion. (23–24)
Having suddenly abandoned sleep, she woke up by the will of the Lord;
in an instant, she regained consciousness, which was enriched by the knowledge of her surroundings.
Seeing the couple before her, the virtuous woman inquired of them with respect.
In that very assembly of friends, Rādhikā spoke thus sweetly:
"Who are you who have arrived here? Tell me, what is your purpose? (26)
I have no cognition of sense-objects; I do not distinguish between a man and a beast.
Listen: whether it be water or land, night or day, woman, man, or eunuch—I do not perceive any such distinction. (27–28)
Having heard Rādhikā’s words, Nanda was filled with wonder;
Yaśodā, becoming afraid, went into the presence of the gopīs who had been conversing.
She sat near her and spoke these pleasing words.
And Nanda sat there, provided with a seat offered by the gopīs.
Yaśodā said:
"O Rādhā, regain your consciousness and protect yourself with great effort."
And you shall see the Lord of Life when the auspicious day arrives.
O Goddess of the Gods, through service to your lotus feet, the entire universe, your own lineage, and the gopīs—who are themselves meritorious—shall become purified by you. (31–32)
The worlds shall sing of you— the auspicious one purified by the sacred ford of your fame—
just as the virtuous, the four Vedas, and the ancient Purāṇas sing of the Primal One.
Know me to be Yaśodā and this Nanda, existing in the form of my intellect.
O daughter of Vṛṣabhāna, O lady of excellent vows, listen to me!
O auspicious one, I have come from the city of Dvārakā, from the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; O virtuous woman, I have been sent to you by Hari.
Listen to this auspicious news and the blessing of the wielder of the mace (Gadābhṛt).
O Goddess, steady your mind; you shall behold that Kṛṣṇa directly.
Now, grant me the realization whose essence is devotion.
We have come into your presence by the instruction of your husband.
O fair-faced one, Hari will come to you in a mere moment;
before long, there shall be the release from Śrīdāman’s curse.

Having heard Yaśodā’s words and received news of the wielder of the mace (Balarāma), Rādhā regained consciousness; by the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s name, all inauspiciousness had been cast far away, and she honored the mother of Kṛṣṇa.
Śāntā spoke sweetly regarding the supreme worldly devotion.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, within the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa*.
Now begins the one hundred and eleventh chapter.
Rādhikā said:
"O virtuous one, he who is the supreme embodiment of knowledge and is worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa, has not granted you knowledge; rather, he has sent me to uproot your pride."
Why do I teach you the true meaning through that very same pretext?
Neither the Vedas nor the wise know its true meaning.
The female species is weak and deluded, intent on ignorance regarding the speaker.
Then, with my consciousness utterly destroyed by the constant separation from him,
what indeed shall I say? Listen as I tell you of the fivefold knowledge that is supreme over all and consists of devotion.
O virtuous one, do not be fearless even by the boon of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
for even in Goloka, a fall may occur for a false yogi.
Therefore, renouncing everything, worship the Supreme Lord.
Abandoning the notion of [him] being your son, behold him as the form of Brahman.
O Yaśodā, having renounced everything that is perishable,
go to the beautiful Vṛndāvana and the meritorious field of Bhārata.
Having performed her bath at the three periods of the day in the pure waters of the Yamunā,
and having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with smooth sandalwood paste, O virtuous lady,
she meditated with a pure mind according to the instructions given by Garga.
Having worshipped that supreme bliss, go joyfully to His abode. O virtuous lady,
having performed deeds that cut away [bondage], always engage in conversation with a Vaiṣṇava along with hundreds of your ancestors.
A devotee would rather choose the cage of the flames of fire, rather dwell upon thorns, or rather consume poison;
[but] association with those devoid of devotion to Hari is not for their destruction. (11)
One who is himself ruined and devoid of devotion causes this [lack of devotion] to increase.
(12) The sprout of the tree of devotion grows through association with devotees and, moreover, by being watered with the nectar of discourse concerning Hari. (13)
Even by a mere fraction of the flame of the lamp of conversation with non-devotees, the sprout of [spiritual life] goes to dryness; yet, through sprinkling [of devotion], it grows again.
Therefore, being vigilant, abandon association with non-devotees.
Just as a man, having seen a black cobra, flees in fear,
so too should one [flee] from the destruction of glory with great effort; [one should instead worship] one's own son as the Lord—
Rāma, Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Mukunda, and Madhusūdana.
"Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, Kaṃsāri, Hare, Vaikuṇṭha, Vāmana"—one should recite or cause others to recite these eleven names;
by doing so, one is liberated from the sins of thousands of millions of births. (17)
The syllable "rā" signifies the universe, and "ma" likewise denotes the Lord.
Since he is the Lord of all universes, he is celebrated as Rāma. He delights with Ramā [Lakṣmī] in everything; therefore, the wise know him as Rāma.

Those who know Rāma understand him to be the place of delight for Ramā; for the letter *rā* signifies Lakṣmī, and the letter *ma* signifies the Lord. The wise proclaim that Rāma is the Lord of Lakṣmī and the ultimate refuge.
Whatever fruit one may obtain from the recollection of a thousand divine names,
that same fruit one certainly obtains merely by the utterance of "Rāma.
The wise know that the word "rāma" signifies both liberation in the form of the deity (sārūpya) and final release (mukti).
That deity who is their refuge is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;

for "nārāḥ" refers to those who have committed sins, and "ayana" is understood as their destination or place of going. Since he is indeed the destination to which they go, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.

By uttering "Nārāyaṇa" even once, a person certainly becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā, despite having committed three hundred sins. For "nāra" signifies liberation, and "ayana" signifies the meritorious, desired knowledge.
Since knowledge arises from these two, he is this Lord Nārāyaṇa;
because there is no end to him in the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the four [Vedas],
and in other scriptures and yogic systems, the wise know him as Ananta (the Infinite).
And *muk* signifies Nirvana, which is synonymous with liberation. That God who bestows that [liberation] is celebrated as Mukunda.
Furthermore, *muk* is a word denoting the essence of devotion and love, as is agreed upon by the Vedas. (27–28)
Because he bestows that [liberation] upon his devotees, he is celebrated as Mukunda;
because he is the slayer of the demon Madhu, he is Madhusūdana—
thus do the wise speak of the Lord, whose meanings are sought as distinct even within the Veda.
*Madhu* refers to the impotent, as well as to honey-wine (*mādhvīka*) and the auspicious or inauspicious results of performed actions. *Madhusūdana* is the destroyer of the deeds of devotees;
he is the one who destroys the sweet honey—the action that is pleasant while being inauspicious in its ultimate transformation—for those who are deluded. (30–31)

For he who performs the slaying (sūdana) is indeed Madhusūdana. The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies "excellent," while *ṇa* denotes "true devotion. The syllable *a* also signifies "giver"; therefore, the wise know him as Kṛṣṇa.
*Kṛṣi* (plowing) exists in supreme bliss, and *ṇa* exists in the act of servitude to Him.
That deity who is the giver of these two is celebrated as Kṛṣṇa. While sin accumulated over ten million births remains, and while one persists in suffering, there is *kṛṣi*. (33–34)
Because he leads his devotees to liberation (*nirvāṇa*), Kṛṣṇa is thus celebrated by that name.
Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting the thousand divine names three times,
a person obtains that same fruit by reciting [the name] "Kṛṣṇa" once.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a name superior to the name of Kṛṣṇa. (36) The knowers of the Vedas understand that the name "Kṛṣṇa" is supreme above all others.
O Gopī, whoever constantly remembers Him who cries out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"—(37)
Just as a lotus rises from the water, he shall uplift [the soul] from hell;
for him whose auspicious name "Kṛṣṇa" proceeds upon his lips,
millions of great sins are instantly reduced to ashes.
The fruit of chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa is superior even to a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Better than those sacrifices is rebirth [in a state of devotion], for there is no rebirth from this [devotion].
It surpasses even hundreds of thousands of all sacrifices and vows. (39–40)
All ritual baths at sacred fords, all austerities and fasts,
thousands of recitations of the Vedas, and a hundred circumambulations of the earth—
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of this chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s name.
From devotion to them, men shall obtain the fruit of heaven for a very long time.
From the self-luminous Lord Hari, who reclines upon the water within all bodies, the state of liberation is surely attained by the man who performs his recitation (japa). 42–43.
All the followers of the Vedas declare that supreme god to be Keśava.
Because he is the enemy of Kaṃsa— who was a source of sin, obstacle, disease, sorrow,
and a demon— he is celebrated as Kaṃsāri, the slayer of Kaṃsa.
In the form of Rudra, he is the eternal destroyer even of all worlds; therefore, Hari is celebrated as such. And she who is the nature of Brahman, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti— || 45-46 ||
She is renowned as Nārāyaṇī, the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu;
she is Mahālakṣmī in her essential form, Sarasvatī, the mother of the Vedas,
Rādhā, Vasuṃdharā, and Gaṅgā— and Mādhava is the Lord of them all.

Worship with devotion the Thief of Butter, who is praised by Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, and others, as well as by Sanaka and the rest through their meditations; he who has not been fully defined even by the Vedas and Purāṇas. (48) Where indeed is milk, where curd or freshly extracted ghee, and where is the desired buttermilk?

Where could there be a thief for them, or where even a bond, within the very root of existence? [49] Neither by yogīs, nor by hosts of Siddhas, nor by lords of sages, nor by multitudes of devotees who have transcended the lotus of worldly existence; neither by yogic powers, nor by those capable of protection—how then has he been bound from within the root of your [existence]? [50]
O Bhārati, worship your son with faith, devotion, praise, and offerings;
and O Sati, constantly meditate with effort upon the Supreme Lord situated within the lotus of your heart.
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever is desired in your mind.
"I shall give everything in this world, even that which is difficult for the gods to obtain.
Yaśodā said: "Unwavering devotion to Hari and service to Him are what I desire."
And what is the etymological derivation of your name? You ought to tell that. Rādhikā said:
May you have unwavering devotion and the rare service of Hari.
"Obtain [your desire] even by my boon; I shall tell you the definitive conclusion.
Long ago, I was seen by Nanda at the foot of the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree, and I spoke to Nanda and restrained that lord of subjects."
I myself am Rādhā, the shadow and the beloved of Rāyaṇa.
Rāyaṇa is a great and foremost attendant (pārṣada) of Śrī Hari, a portion of Him.
And the syllable "Rā" refers to Mahāviṣṇu, whose body hairs are the entire universe.
The word *dhātrī* denotes the sustainer and mother among all living beings and all things.
(57) I am their mother, the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), the Sovereign;
therefore, I was designated as *Rādhā* by Hari and by the wise of old. (58)
Now, due to the curse of Sudāmā, I am the daughter of Vṛṣabhāna;
meanwhile, my separation from Hari shall last for a hundred years.
And Vṛṣabhāna is a great and foremost attendant of Kṛṣṇa.
Kalāvatī, my mother, was the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs. Both I and my mother were born without a womb in Bhārata;
together with you, we shall go again to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Thus I have told you everything; go, O Queen of Vraja, go to Vraja together with your husband, the Lord of Vraja, who is a knower of truth.
For now, you are an obstacle to my meditation.
"O beautiful one, for men as well, there is a great fault in the breaking of meditative absorption.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada, Rādhā, and Yaśodā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma... Mahā... Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the one hundred and twelfth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: O sage, by the command of Vasudeva, Vāsudeva went from Dvārakā to the excellent palace of Rukmiṇī, which was resplendent with jewels.
Resembling pure crystal, fashioned from priceless jewels,
beautiful before and all around, and adorned with various paintings;
[it was] with a pinnacle of priceless jewels, white chowries, and mirrors.
He beheld Queen Rukmiṇī, who was exceedingly fresh in her youth, adorned all around by pure white garments that were cleansed by fire;
she was lying joyfully upon a jeweled couch with a gentle smile. (3–4)
She was a young bride, inexperienced and bashful at her first union,
adorned with ornaments fashioned from priceless gems;
she bore a most beautiful mass of braided hair and was decorated with garlands of *mālatī* flowers.
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, she immediately bowed down to her.
Having obtained her, the Lord of the World rested upon a couch of jewels;
and at an auspicious moment, he took his pleasure with that beautiful Rāmā.
Through the mere experience of pleasure, the virtuous woman attained a state of rapture with joy;
therein was born Kāmadeva, who had been reduced to ashes by Śambhu.
Having slain Śambara, he obtained that virtuous Rati there.
Rati, having given her shadow upon the bed in the abode of Śambara by means of a sign to the god named Māyāvatī, remained as his wife.
Nārada said:
"O highly fortunate one, tell me in detail this auspicious story: by what means did Kāma carry off the Daitya Śambara?
Nārāyaṇa said:
When seven days had passed, the Daitya took the boy from Rukmiṇī’s lying-in chamber and departed swiftly for his own abode.
And the lord of the Daityas, being childless, was filled with great joy upon obtaining the son.
Delighted, he gave [it] to Māyāvatī; the virtuous Māyāvatī was also delighted.
By means of extreme care, she caused Bāraka to grow.
Sarasvatī spoke to her in private, in a secluded place.
Sarasvatī said:
"In the past, your husband was reduced to ashes in the fire of Śiva’s wrath;
he is this very son of Rukmiṇī who has now been carried off by the Daitya."
Furthermore, by means of his illusory power (*māyā*), the Lord of Illusion brought you from the maternity chamber of Rukmiṇī and gave him to you as your husband; he was not your own son.
And that virtuous mother of the world spoke of this at her will.
This Rati is your wife; sport with Rāmā.
You alone are the son of Rukmiṇī, not the Manmatha of any other Daitya.
Without you, the virtuous woman has been constantly weeping like a female osprey.
Having spoken thus, the voice of Brahmā departed for the abode of Brahmā. That handsome one took constant delight in solitude with Rāmā.
Once, two Daityas beheld Manmatha standing in secret, playfully engaging in amorous dalliance with Rāmā.
He beheld Rati, smiling, standing between the smiling [Śiva] and [Kāma], situated upon his chest; she was fainting from passion and longing for sexual union.
Upon seeing her, the Daitya grew enraged and seized an excellent sword.
With sword in hand, he spoke to Kāmadeva and the virtuous Rati.
Śambara said:
"Fie upon you, O great lustful one, a fool who fancies himself a scholar!"

"O virtuous woman! You are the foremost among those who commit great sins; you are intoxicated, have violated your mother, and are devoid of conscience. Shame on you, you wanton, drunken, lustful woman!
Having taken your son into private, you practice lewd pleasure. (22-23)
Having spoken thus, as the Daitya was exerting himself to strike her with his sword,
Manmatha urged Rati toward the one who sought to kill her.
O Brahmin, he fell from afar, unconscious and tormented by his own limbs.
Then, regaining his composure and as if blazing with rage,
he seized the trident given by Śiva with great intensity.
O Sage, that trident possessed the radiance of a hundred suns and was like the fire of universal destruction.
Having seen her, the gods known as Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa arrived;
and Pavana (the Wind-god) diligently whispered into the ear of Kāma:
"O Smara, remember Mahāmāyā, Durgā, the destroyer of difficult passages!"
Having heard the words of Pavana, Manmatha remembered Durgā.
The trident [he had hurled] became a beautiful and captivating garland upon her body.
Then, with joy, Manmatha struck that Daitya with the Brahmāstra.
Taking Rati with him, he went by chariot to the city of Dvārakā;
all the deities departed after personally praising Pārvatī.
Having performed auspicious rites, Rukmiṇī took her son Rati into her arms.
Hari caused a great festival to be held for supreme well-being;
he fed the Brāhmaṇas and worshipped Pārvatī.
Then, Kṛṣṇa, in due order, on an auspicious day prescribed by the Vedas, [prepared for the marriage].
He took the hands of seven beautiful women in marriage:
Kālindī, Satyabhāmā, the virtuous Rājñijitī, Jāmbavatī, and Lakṣmaṇā. He performed their wedding rites.
Together with them, he produced sons in due order. From one wife, ten sons and one daughter were born in succession.
Having slain the Daitya Naraka along with his sons and his lordly king, [he established his reign].
He slew the powerful Daitya Mura at the forefront of the battle.
There he beheld sixteen thousand maidens,
along with hundreds of female companions who were eternally in the prime of youth.
With their faces in full bloom and adorned with jeweled ornaments, Mādhava took the hand of each of them at an auspicious moment;
and together with them, he took his pleasure in due order at those auspicious times. (37–38)
From one [wife], ten sons and one daughter were born in succession; these children of Hari were thus produced separately.
Once, the eminent sage Durvāsas came to the beautiful city of Dvārakā.
He arrived with a playful grace, accompanied by thirty million disciples.
King Mahograsena came along with his son and his family priest;
likewise Vasudeva, Vāsudeva, Akrūra, and Uddhava.
Having performed the sixteen-fold ritual service, they bowed down to that bull among sages;
and he bestowed auspicious blessings upon them individually, O Brahmin,
and at an auspicious moment, he gave him that maiden Ekānaṃśā.
He gave him pearls, rubies, necklaces, and wedding gifts as dowry.
He took delight with Rāmā in a jeweled palace on Mount Mahendra.
He gave him an auspicious hermitage constructed from the finest essence of precious gems.
Once, that best of sages, having reflected within his own mind, [beheld] a learned man,
well-versed in the Purāṇas, lying somewhere on a certain beautiful bed made of jewels with faith.
And in a certain auspicious courtyard during a great festival,
he was seen by Satyabhāmā respectfully offering him betel-leaf;
and in another place, he was served on a couch by Rukmiṇī with chowries.
The Blessed One spoke with equal courtesy everywhere to the sage, who was joyfully lying down in some place with his feet pointed toward the Yamunā.
Seeing that supreme marvel, the two brahmins were struck with wonder.
He praised the Lord of the worlds, who was again dwelling in the palace of Rukmiṇī,
and who was beautiful as he sat in the assembly of the virtuous in the Sudharmā hall.
Durvāsas said:

Victory, victory to you, O Lord of the worlds, Janārdana who has conquered all! You are the soul of all, the Lord of all, the primordial seed of all, the ancient one, devoid of qualities and free from desire. (50) Untainted, stainless, formless, yet possessing a form for the grace of your devotees; eternal in your true nature, yet beyond all forms, both ever-ancient and ever-new. (51)

"O Lord of Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa; O You whose lotus-feet are served by Lakṣmī; O Ineffable Radiance of Brahman; O You whose qualities and form are unknown even to the Vedas; O Supreme Self worthy of honor by the great ether—salutations be unto You!
(52) Having spoken thus with his mind and with the permission of Hari, the lordly brāhmaṇa bowed down and stood right there before Hari. (53)
The Lord of the World spoke to him words that were beneficial, true, and ancient;
knowledge ordained by the Vedas and approved by all the virtuous.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Do not fear, O Brahmin; you possess a portion of Śiva. Do you not know this through your wisdom?
I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds.
I am the Self of all, and without me nothing exists. (55)
When I have entered the bodies of living beings, all powers indeed depart [from them].
(56) Even though I am one in the genus (*jāti*), I am distinct in each individual manifestation (*vyakti*).
Satisfaction belongs only to him who eats, and never to others. (57)
I am the supreme perfection of all living beings, including individual souls, and the very measure of all creatures; yet, in Goloka within the circle of the Rāsa dance, I am the most complete of all.
Due to the curse of Śrīdāmā, Rādhā is currently unable to behold me.

And all [of them] exist in the form of portions (*aṃśa*) and parts (*kalā*) derived from those portions. (59) The portion resides in the palace of Rukmiṇī, while the parts reside in the palaces of the others; likewise, some portion of mine is in one place, and some collection of parts is in another. (60)
"Wherever there are parts of a fraction of a fraction, whether in idols or in embodied beings," having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds entered the interior of his house;
and Durvāsas, abandoning his beloved, departed for the penance grove of Śrī Hari. (61)
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Sage Nārada and Kṛṣṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the one hundred and thirteenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
And Durvāsas, accompanied by his disciples, having left the city of Dvārakā,
went with devotion to Kailāsa to behold the Lord Śaṅkara.
Having gone to Kailāsa, the sage prostrated before Śiva and Śivā.
Bowing down with supreme devotion, pure and accompanied by his disciples, he offered praise.
He related that entire account of Śrī Hari,
as well as the true nature of his own austerity and the state of his mind’s dispassion.
Having heard the words of the Sage, the virtuous Pārvatī smiled and spoke these beneficial and truthful words in the very presence of Śaṅkara himself. (4) Pārvatī said:
"You do not know the true nature of dharma, yet you consider yourself most righteous.
O sage, having abandoned your childless wife, where are you going for penance?
She is young, born of noble lineage, and devoted to her husband. (5)
Having renounced worldly ties, they may become a *saṃnyāsī*, a *brahmacārī*, or a *yati*.

Or, one who goes far away for a long time—whether for trade, travel abroad, to a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), or for asceticism (*tapas*) in order to attain liberation and break the cycle of birth—[is likewise freed]. (6–7)
There is no liberation for him; the transgression of dharma is certain.
Through the curse of his wife, he shall go to hell in the next world, and even in this world, there is the destruction of his fame—so said the Lotus-born One.
"Go to Dvārakā, O brāhmaṇa; protect your own dharma now.
Righteously protect Ekānaṃśā, who is a portion of Me.
[Attain] the lotus-foot [of the Lord], which is earned by the lotus-feet [of devotion] and is most difficult for all to obtain. (9–10)
It has been sung continuously by Śambhu and by the lords of sages, such as Sanaka and others:
"Abandon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and the celestial tree!
O child, where are you going for penance, having abandoned the enchanting nectar? (11)

O Sage, whoever chants the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet even in a dream is liberated from the sins committed in a hundred lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. Whatever [sin] was committed in childhood, in youth, in old age, or in adolescence—
Whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, even a sin reduced to ashes becomes purified upon seeing the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa directly in the land of Bhārata-varṣa;
one becomes instantly worthy of worship and certainly attains liberation while living.
One is immediately liberated from the sin acquired over ten million lifetimes.
For it is from this [source] that all sacred fords are eternally purified;
it is that vow, that austerity, that truth, that merit, and that worship. (15–16)

For this makes fruitful the destruction of one's own birth through its connection with Kṛṣṇa; yet, a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas but is devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa—through association with him and conversation with him, devotion to the Lord perishes. (17)

That brāhmaṇa who eats the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s meal and is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa is purified by the fire and the wind; he is capable of purifying the entire world. O twice-born one, having abandoned Śrī Kṛṣṇa, where are you going to perform penance?
One obtains the fruit of austerities through the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
yet, he in whom devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, does not arise,
is the supreme enemy of his own teacher, for he renders his birth fruitless.

Having heard Pārvatī’s words, Śaṅkara, overwhelmed with love and with all his limbs bristling with horripilation, praised the Supreme Goddess. Durvāsas, having prostrated before the lotus feet of Śiva and Durgā, [did likewise]. || 21–22 ||
Remembering the feet of Kṛṣṇa again and again, he went once more to Dvārakā.
Having arrived there and beheld Hari, he praised the Supreme Lord. Then, having gone to the abode of Ekānaṃśā, he took delight with her.
Out of concern for Yudhiṣṭhira, Kṛṣṇa departed for Hastināpura (24).
Having taken leave of Kuntī, the king, and his brothers, he set out filled with joy.
By means of a stratagem, he slew Jarāsaṃdha as well as Śālva (25).
He performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, which was desired by the lords of sages and the lords of men, according to the prescribed rites and with the appropriate sacrificial fees;
and there at that sacrifice, he slew Śiśupāla and Dantavakra.
As he was excessively reviling the gods and the king in the assembly, his body fell down;
his life-force departed and went to the abode of Hari.
Not seeing the Lord of All there, it returned and praised Mādhava.
Śiśupāla said: "O Mādhava, you are the progenitor of the Vedas and of the Vedāṅgas;
[you are the source] of the gods, the asuras, and of all embodied beings of the material world. (29)
Having brought about a subtle creation, you also effect the differentiation of the kalpas;
through your own Māyā, you yourself become Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Viṣṇu.
You are likewise the Manus, the sages, and the gods who protect the creation.
Even by a mere fraction, a part, the guardians of the quarters and the planets and so forth [are derived from Him].
He Himself is male, He Himself is female, and He Himself is neuter.
He Himself is the cause, He Himself is the effect, and He Himself is both that which is born and that which brings to birth.
The merit and the fault of the machine, as well as the merit and the fault of the operator, have been heard [by me] from the Śruti.
All machines are you, O Bhavānī; everything is established in you.
Forgive the offense of me, your gatekeeper, who am deluded.
"Protect us, protect us from the curse of Brahmā and from evil-mindedness, O Teacher of the World!
Having spoken thus, Jaya and Vijaya then departed joyfully and quickly toward their desired destination, the gateway of Vaikuṇṭha.
All of them were filled with wonder by Śiśupāla’s hymn of praise;
having rendered him utterly overwhelmed, they recognized Kṛṣṇa as the Lord.
Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, he fed the Brahmins.
He incited the war between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas through sowing dissension.
That treasure-house of compassion brought about the removal of the earth’s burden.
Then, by the king’s command, he returned to Dvārakā after having stayed there for a long time.
He restored the sons of a Brahmin woman whose children had died to life;
having brought them back from the place of death, he gave the sons to their mother.
Seeing this, Devakī was delighted and requested her own deceased sons.
Having brought his brothers back from the place where they had died, he gave them to their mother.
He instantly removed the poverty of the brahmin Sudāmā,
who had come from his own home to Dvārakā seeking refuge.

Having eaten a single grain of the broad-beaned rice offered by his devotee, he who is compassionate toward his devotees bestowed upon him the royal fortune of seven generations, which remained unshakable.
And his kingdom became like Amarāvatī, the city of Indra.
Just as the god Dhaneśvara became exceedingly wealthy,
he granted him unwavering devotion to Hari and service that is very difficult to attain,
along with an excellent boon according to his desire in the imperishable Goloka. (43–44)
He took away the *pārijāta* tree as well as Śakra’s very pride;
he caused Satyabhāmā to perform her desired meritorious vow (*puṇyaka-vrata*),
O Sage, and he constantly increased [the performance of] both regular and occasional rites everywhere.
There, at the conclusion of the vow, he gave his own self as a sacrificial fee to the prince;
he fed the Brahmins and joyfully bestowed jewels upon them. He caused Satyabhāmā’s great honor to increase in every respect.
O sage, he constantly increased Rukmiṇī’s extraordinary good fortune, as well as the ever-renewing prosperity of the others,
and the worship of Vaiṣṇavas, gods, and brahmins everywhere,
both regularly and on special occasions.
The Lord bestowed the supreme spiritual knowledge upon Uddhava,
and having cleared away all obstacles through his compassion, that ocean of mercy spoke the Gītā to Arjuna on the field of battle.
The Lord bestowed upon Yudhiṣṭhira the sovereign fortune of the earth;
he worshipped Durgā, the Vaiṣṇavī, and the village deity;
and he caused a splendid sacrifice to be performed, accompanied by ten million oblations.
With various kinds of food offerings and enchanting incense and lamps,
he likewise fed the Brahmins for the pleasure of Pārvatī on the beautiful Raivata mountain, in a palace of priceless jewels.
He worshipped Gaṇeśa, the supreme lord of the gods,
offering five hundred thousand sweet and enchanting laddūs and sesame sweets as a joyful oblation.
He presented to Gaṇeśvara seven hundred thousand sweetmeat balls (*laḍḍuka*) and *svastika* cakes, which were like nectar; a hundred mountain-like heaps of sugar;
and ten hundred thousand ripe plantains and *apūpa* cakes. (55–56)
Delicious milk-rice, lovely and sweet *svastika* cakes, clarified butter, fresh butter, curds, and milk resembling nectar;
incense, lamps, and garlands of desired *pārijāta* flowers. (57)
He gave fragrant sandalwood paste and incense to Vahniśuddhāśuka;
he also caused an auspicious sacrifice to be performed, accompanied by ten million oblations (koṭihoma).
He fed the Brahmins and offered praise to Gaṇeśvara.
There he indeed played ten kinds of musical instruments;
and Sāmba, for the sake of destroying his leprosy, worshipped the Sun.
He also had Sāmba and his mother partake of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya).
Having been honored for a full year with unsurpassed offerings, Bhāskara himself granted a boon and a hymn of praise to Sāmba.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of Gaṇeśa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa within the glorious Brahma [Purāṇa]. 113.
Now begins the one hundred and fourteenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
And Kṛṣṇa’s son Pradyumna possessed great strength and prowess.
His son Aniruddha was also indeed a portion of the Creator.
Once, that Aniruddha, endowed with fresh youth,
was sleeping in secret upon a couch smeared with flowers and sandalwood paste.
In a dream, he beheld a young woman in a garden of blooming flowers;
she was reclining upon a bed of fragrant blossoms, anointed with smooth sandalwood paste, smiling beautifully, lovely, and endowed with fresh youth. (3)
Adorned with ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels,
she was graced by beautiful armlets, bracelets, conch-shaped earrings, and bangles;
her cheeks were made radiant by a pair of jeweled ear-pendants.
Wearing exceedingly fine garments, colored by the tinkling of her golden waist-belt,
with lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit and eyes like autumn lotuses,
she eclipsed the radiance of the autumnal lotus and put to shame ten million moons with her face.
Her rows of teeth were enchanting, as if adorned by strings of pearls;
she bore the weight of her hair in three curls and was decorated with garlands of *mālatī* flowers.
She was anointed with musk, saffron, lac, smooth sandalwood paste, and collyrium.
Resplendent with beautiful cheeks adorned by decorative leaf-patterns,
embellished with a dot of vermilion in the shape of a pomegranate flower,
and radiant with thighs that put to shame the trunks of the plantain trees of Śrī Rāma; (9)
Adorned with a pair of breasts that were exceedingly high and rounded,
she was bent by the weight of her hips; oppressed by the arrows of Kāma,
she was a passionate and desirable woman, gazing with sidelong glances.
Seeing her, who was radiant with lotus-feet stained red with saffron and lac,
and whose breasts were clearly visible as her garment fluttered in the wind,
the son of Kāma had his mind agitated by desire. (12)
He spoke sweet and charming words to her who was intoxicated with desire, exceedingly delicate,
possessing the beautiful hue of a campaka flower, covered in horripilation from passion,
both very mature and newly wedded, and restless in her longing for amorous sport.
Aniruddha said:
"O Goddess, what are you? And what is this Gandharva-like state of yours in the forest, O lovely one? Whose wife are you, whose daughter, or whom do you desire, O beautiful lady? (15)
"O you of incomparable beauty in the three worlds, who captivates the minds of sages!
Tell me, why are you not afraid, being all alone with me?
I am now the grandson of the Lord of the Three Worlds and the son of Kāma. (16)
"O beloved, I am Aniruddha, struck by fresh youth;
I am desirable and full of desire, an expert in the science of love.
I myself am the lord capable of fulfilling the longing of a passionate woman. (17-18)
O beautiful woman, worship me, who am well-attired, of excellent character,
a hero in love, wise in the essence of passion, and fond of the essence of passion—
O beloved, I am the son of Rati, the very essence of delight, intoxicated with joy, and a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor.
A woman who desires love seeks a youth who is free from disease and full of passion.
A clever woman approaches a clever lover out of desire for pleasure.
The union of a clever woman with a clever man is virtuous.
Covering her face with her garment, she who was bashful at their first union gazed at him from the corner of her curved eye and spoke to him. (22) The lovely woman said:
You are a lover, the son of Kāma, now agitated by desire. If you were not fit for a woman of passion, why would you have thought of her?
You are the grandson of the Lord of the Three Worlds, who is inherently self-exalted. (23)
Being yourself worthy and having a worthy son, why did you not perform the marriage at all?
She was wedded as the wife of the sacrifice, virtuous in her holy vows, steadfast, ever-accomplishing, increasing [prosperity], and always a companion. (24–25)
A woman whose husband is hidden is won over by fear, affection, or gifts, yet she remains unsteady; she is not won by policy, nor is she one who follows the Vedas.
She is a supreme stairway to hell and brings infamy both here and in the next world.
A virtuous person born of a noble lineage who is a Vaiṣṇava does not take delight in that [worldly path].
If one was previously deluded, he turns away through association with the virtuous.
This is the way of beings: worldly engagement leads to rebirth, whereas renunciation yields great fruit.
If one who has performed penance is defiled again, having turned back from his vows as a sinner,
he becomes an object of ridicule on earth, like the "cleansing of an elephant.
A virtuous, beautiful, peaceful, and praised lawful wife—
She is devoted to her husband, easy to manage, and always speaks with great affection;
she has delicate limbs, is clever, youthful, and bestows the joys of love.
To abandon such a woman and depart for ascetic penance—how can one call him a Vaiṣṇava? (30–31)
When she has become virtuous, self-controlled, peaceful, and possessed of sons through [the practice of] *jet* (conquest), then all is well;
otherwise, everything would be in vain, and there would be a failure of one's asceticism.
If he is wicked, of a low lineage, or should approach another man's wife, [then it is likewise lost].
He goes to a terrible hell along with his father and seven ancestors.
I am Ūṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa; Bāṇa is the servant of Śaṅkara.
Bāṇa is the conqueror of the three worlds, and Śaṅkara is the Lord of the worlds.
A passionate woman is not independent; she is dependent [on others] throughout the three periods of time.
A wanton woman who is independent is born of a base lineage.
Her father gives her away to a suitable bridegroom.
"A maiden should not solicit a bridegroom; this is the eternal law.
You are worthy and I am worthy; if you desire me, O Lord, then pray to Bāṇa, or to Śambhu, or to the virtuous Pārvatī. (36–37)
Having spoken thus, that virtuous Sundarī vanished from sight.
O Sage, the lover, the son of Kāma, suddenly abandoned his sleep.
Having understood the dream and realized its significance, his inner being was tormented by desire.
He became agitated and restless, not having seen his beloved who was dearer than life.
Abandoning food, sleepless, distracted, and with a wasted frame,
he would stand for a moment, lie down for a moment, and weep in secret.
Seeing their son weeping, Devakī, Rukmiṇī, Rati,
and all the other women spoke to the Lord.
Having heard their words, the slayer of Mura laughed.
And Kṛṣṇa, the knower of all truths, whose mind was full, spoke.
The Blessed Lord said: "The daughter of Bāṇa, afflicted by desire, beheld the pleasure of Śiva and his consort."
Durgā, agitated by the weapon of Madana, obtained a boon;
and Pārvatī revealed a dream to her, and out of curiosity, she made Aniruddha,
my grandson, intoxicated with passion.
"And now, I shall turn that daughter of his, Pramati, into a dream-woman.
Stay here at your ease for no long time; there is no anxiety or mental distress.
Thus did Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of all perfections, console her.
And he showed him a dream of Bāṇa’s daughter, who was full of desire;
that young woman, endowed with fresh youth and adorned with jewel ornaments, lay asleep upon a fine bed strewn with flowers and anointed with sandalwood paste. (46–47)
Lying upon a jeweled couch, she beheld her desired dream in an exceedingly secluded place, within a palace constructed of jewels:
[she saw] one who was dark as a fresh rain-cloud and possessed of extreme youthful vigor. (48)
Possessing the playful grace of ten million Cupids, smiling and most enchanting;
adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and jeweled anklets; and made radiant upon the surface of his cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings. (49–50)
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with yellow garments,
and his chest radiant with a beautiful garland of *mālatī* flowers,
he lay upon a jeweled couch smeared with flowers and sandalwood.

Seeing him, the virtuous woman suddenly went joyfully to his side. Afflicted by the arrows of Kāma, the beloved wife of Kāmadeva’s son, her heart burning with longing, the virtuous woman spoke sweetly.
Ūṣā said:
"Who are you, O handsome suitor? May you be blessed; please accept me, who am afflicted by love—me, who am both mature and newly wedded, and yearning for a fresh union. (54)
"Marry me, who am devoted to you and full of love, by the Gāndharva rite.
Among the eight forms of marriage, the Gāndharva is easily accessible to men.
That deceitful man who, having obtained a beloved and devoted wife, should abandon her—" || 55 ||
Therefore, having uttered a most terrible curse, Mahālakṣmī departed.
The man said: "I am the grandson of Kṛṣṇa and the son of Kāmadeva himself."
"How can I take you, my beloved, without their permission?
Having spoken thus, that man vanished.
Distraught with desire, the beloved did not see her desired lover.

Having abandoned sleep and risen from that very enchanting couch, she became despondent in the midst of her friends; intoxicated and weeping bitterly, she asked those excellent companions with certainty, "What is this? What is this? (59)
The highly yogic Citralekhā spoke and awakened her:

"Awaken your consciousness, O auspicious one! Why do you have such intense fear? Śambhu himself and Śivā are present here in person; while this city is so difficult to overcome, every misfortune flees at the mere remembrance of Śiva."
Everything becomes auspicious everywhere; Śiva alone is the abode of auspiciousness.
Through meditation upon her who destroys misfortune, every difficulty perishes;
she who is the most auspicious among all that is auspicious bestows blessings upon him.
Having heard Citralekhā’s words, Sundarī said nothing;
abandoning both food and sleep, she constantly thought of that man.
Then her friend Citralekhā went and spoke to Bāṇa regarding his beloved.
Having heard the words of Citralekhā regarding Durgā, Śaṅkara, Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and the Guru of Yogins, Satī wept loudly and excessively;
Bāṇa, however, despaired in the presence of Śaṅkara and fell into a swoon.
Śaṅkara, Durgā, Kārttikeya, and Gaṇeśvara laughed.
Gaṇeśvara said:
"He who, deluded by pride and infatuation, certainly inflicts suffering upon another,"
Through the investigation of subtle principles, he attains a fourfold merit.
And having seen the play of Śiva and Śivā, she who was infatuated by desire,
Durgā granted her a boon— a boon indeed very difficult to obtain.
Having gone to him in a dream and intoxicated the son of Samara himself,
the Goddess now stands like one mute at the left side of Śambhu.
And the omniscient Lord Hari, the Sovereign, having understood everything—
In a dream, he showed a well-dressed man to the maiden.
Having seen that well-dressed young man, the young woman felt a supreme desire; yet, out of fear of violating dharma, she turned away from it.
Upon seeing a well-dressed man, an unchaste woman born of a lineage of sin abandons sleep, her own food, her husband, her son, her wealth, and her home;
she forsakes her consciousness, her household duties, her family’s shame, and both families.
One should certainly not abandon a youth who is a hero in love, even if he is extremely low-born. (73) One may eventually abandon one's caste, one's dharma, and even one's life;
therefore, a wise man should always strive with effort to protect his young wife even at the cost of his own life. (74)
One should always guard against women and never trust them; the heart of women is like the edge of a razor, yet their speech is sweet.
Neither the virtuous nor the Vedas and those learned in the Vedas truly know their minds.
"Let Citralekhā, the highly skilled yoginī, go immediately to Dvārakā to capture the heedless Aniruddha by her power. Having heard this, Mahādeva spoke to Gaṇeśa.
"Do not listen; act so that the arrow may accomplish its auspicious purpose.
Citralekhā then went quickly to Hari’s palace in Dvārakā;
she entered it with ease, though it was difficult for all others to penetrate.
Having gathered together Aniruddha, who was asleep, through her yogic power,
she joyfully placed the sleeping boy upon the chariot.
O Sage, having taken the child, that auspicious lady, who travels as fast as thought, departed.
Within a moment, having sounded his conch at Śoṇitapura, he departed;
then, within the hermitage, all the women wept:
"Alas! Where has our dear child gone, the one who carried away Bāṇa and was so beloved as our very life?"
The omniscient Kṛṣṇa, the knower of all truths, having consoled them,
together with Sāmba, Kāma, Bala, the dark-complexioned Satyaki,
and the heroic Uḍa, quickly took the cows and mounted his chariot.
The Lord of Gods will subsequently proceed with the Sudarśana discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, the Padma lotus, and the Kaumodakī mace; likewise, he will go to the city of Śoṇita,
which is protected by Śaṅkara along with his attendants and by Pārvatī.
Then that yoginī, auspicious, meritorious, and honored among women,
a peaceful disciple of Durvāsas who grants success through perfected yoga,
awakened Bāraka as he wept, calling his mother to mind. (85–86)
Having bathed him, she gave him garlands, sandalwood paste, and ornaments;
having dressed the boy in fine attire, she entered the desired inner apartments of the maidens by means of her yogic power, even though they were guarded by sentries.
Seeing Uṣā sleeping there, fasting and with a slender waist,
he quickly awakened her while she was being guarded by her female companions;
and having had Uṣā well-bathed and adorned with garments and ornaments, [he departed].
With garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and auspicious sindūra markings,
he caused a conversation between the two to take place there on Mount Māhendra at an auspicious moment,
in secret and with the consent of his companions.
Seeing her husband, the devoted wife rejoiced, freed from all anxiety.
The son of Smara married her by the Gāndharva rite;
their love became for a long time the source of happiness for both.

Afflicted by love, the son of Smara did not perceive day or night; nor did the mature Uṣā, though newly wedded, cease her longing due to their fresh union. The lustful woman fell into a swoon at the mere touch of the man.
O Brahmin, while this most enchanting union continued constantly in secret for a very long time, the king heard of it from his guard.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Union of Uṣā and Nīruddha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa within the glorious Brahma-mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the one hundred and fifteenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: Then those guards, becoming terrified, approached Bāṇa, the lord.
Having prostrated like a staff before Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and Durgā, the guardians said:
"Alas! This time is wicked and exceedingly difficult to overcome."
The independent young girl, now grown mature, desires a husband.
O Lord, association with the unattached is a cause of suffering for the virtuous;
for men, virtues and faults always arise from association. Citralekhā herself, acting as a messenger, brought a supreme bridegroom.
A hero in battle, a great warrior, a lord of men, and a mighty chariot-fighter—
youthful, free from disease, and more beautiful than even Kandarpa—
he caused him to enjoy [her] and did not perceive day or night.
Now that daughter of yours, Ūṣā, being pregnant,
has become like a glowing coal to both her own family and the family of her husband;
indeed, she has now become a son-in-law or a daughter-in-law to you.
Behold this maiden, exceedingly mature, like a city filled with citizens;
her entire body marked by nail-scratches, dependent on her lover, and fickle;
she is constantly clinging to men and devoted to amorous play in secret.
Smiling, casting side-long glances, and looking with restless eyes—
having heard this, Bāṇa was ashamed and grew enraged there;
though earnestly forbidden by Śambhu, he set his mind on battle.
And he was constantly restrained by Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and likewise by Śivā,
by Bhairavī and Bhadrakālī, by the Yoginīs,
by the eight Bhairavas, and by the eleven Rudras.
By the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *vetālas*, and *brahmarākṣasas*;
by the lords of the *yogīs*, the lords of the *siddhas*, and likewise by the *rudras* such as Caṇḍa and others;
and by Koṭarī and Prāmadevī, as well as by the Mothers (*mātṛs*), for the sake of welfare.
Śaṅkara spoke to Bāṇa, who was foolish yet considered himself wise, words that were beneficial, true, according to the treatises on ethics, and conducive to happiness in the end.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, Bāṇa, I shall relate this ancient story:
in order to remove the burden of the earth, the Lord himself appeared in Bhārata;
having slain all the lords of kings, he now shines resplendent in Dvārakā.
He in whose body hairs all things reside—of him the Lord himself is the garment.
Therefore he is celebrated by the wise as Vāsudeva;
he is the creator of the Creator, the Blessed One, the wielder of the discus, manifest on earth himself. (15–16)

He is the Lord of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others; beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and free from worldly desire (nirīha). His form manifests solely for the grace of his devotees. He is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and the Supreme Self of all embodied beings.
When that [mind] has departed, the living being becomes a corpse, and through it, battle arises.
O deluded one, just as the great space is pierced by weapons, so too are the directions;
likewise, the formless Self, though possessing a body, is [pierced] for the sake of meditation. (18–19)
His son was Aniruddha, possessed of great strength and prowess;
he himself was capable of destroying even the three worlds in an instant.
All the gods and Daityas were powerful and great chariot-warriors.
All of them together are not worth even a sixteenth part of Aniruddha.
(21) Marriage and friendship should exist only between those whose wealth is equal and whose strength is equal, but never between the prosperous and the destitute. (22)
Your father Bali, the very essence of the Daityas and a great chariot-warrior,
was sent to Sutala in an instant by him who is a portion of Hari.

[He meditates] upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Vṛndāvana and the Supreme Soul.

he took from him the maiden Rukmiṇī, who was worthy of the gods.
Satrājit, a servant of the Sun, obtained the Lord of Jewels (the Syamantaka) from the god.
Having slain [his enemies] by means of stratagem, he seized the maiden Maṇikanyā.

Aniruddha said:

By his own karma, he has been reduced to ashes by the very fire of Śiva’s wrath;

Having slain his enemy Śambara and recovered his beloved Satī,
he returned to Dvārakā with the moon and sun as witnesses.
O fool, do you not know Vāsudeva, the Grandfather?

Food prescribed by the Vedas is the eternal [sustenance] for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

And that sacred field of Bhārata came from Goloka.
Filled with joy, he took delight together with those women who were his own wives;

they were the foremost attendants of Hari, equal to Hari in splendor.

By the power of the Lord of Māyā, through his own illusion, [he became] a child for the sake of protecting the cowherds.

"If my son is now such as this,

And Bhadra hurled a spear possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns.

Subhadra then discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon at the forefront of the battle.
Having prostrated, the powerful son of Madana lay down fearlessly;
he brandished his weapon aloft, which possessed a radiance equal to a hundred suns.
That weapon, the cause of the destruction of the universe, vanished into the sky.
When the weapon had vanished, Aniruddha seized a great sword and shattered Bhadraratha’s chariot; he slew the horses and the charioteer,
and with ease struck down Subhadra at the forefront of the battle.
While Subhadrā was being struck, Bāṇa, possessed of great strength and prowess,
discharged a hundred arrows at the forefront of the battle.
The son of Kāma then consumed that multitude of arrows with his fire-arrow.
Bāṇa discharged the Brahmāstra, the cause of creation and destruction;
seeing it, the son of Kāma quickly neutralized it with ease by means of the very Brahmāstra itself, employing the seed-syllable and preceded by the appropriate mantra.

In the battle of yawning, he quickly released that [weapon] at the great chariot-warrior;
Bāṇa became inert and motionless at the front of the fray. He then discharged the sleep-inducing weapon again, and it rendered him fast asleep.
Seeing Bāṇa asleep, Kārttikeya seized an excellent sword and attempted to slay him;

[He struck] the illustrious Aniruddha, the powerful wielder of the bow. And Aniruddha, with an irresistible spear, suddenly shattered Kārtika’s chariot, which was constructed from the finest essence of jewels.
