Aniruddha, for his part, effortlessly [struck him] with a razor-sharp crescent-headed arrow.
He severed Kārtika’s bow with a bhallāstra weapon.
Then Kārtika struck him with a formidable mace. Madana’s son swiftly seized the mace from his hand.
Seizing his spear and intent on slaying Skanda himself,
Aniruddha, out of anger, hurled him far away.
Kārttikeya, however, returned and seized the son of Kāma.
And seizing him with his very hand, he cast him down upon the ground.
Aniruddha, the mighty lord, took up a sword and stood firm;
then Gaṇeśvara brought their conflict to an end at a distance.
Kārtikeya, the son of Smara, went to the house of Ūṣā;
that lord of the Gaṇas went to inform Śambhu of everything.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter [of the Uttarakhaṇḍa] of the glorious Brahma... Mahā... Śrīkṛṣṇajanma... Nārada... Bāṇa... [section]. 116.
Now begins the one hundred and seventeenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Gaṇeśa, having gone to the abode of Śiva and bowed to Maheśvara, [proceeded].
He reported everything in due order, one by one:
the battle between Bāṇa and Aniruddha, as well as the death of Subhadrā,
the battle between Skanda and Aniruddha, and the valor of Aniruddha.
Having heard the words of Gaṇeśa, the Blessed Lord Bhava smiled and spoke in gentle words that were well-guarded and in accordance with the Vedas.
Mahādeva said:
O illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas, listen to my words:
they are beneficial, truthful, the essence of ethics, and conducive to happiness in the end.
Know that the entire multitude of countless universes is the son born from Kṛṣṇa.
Know Kṛṣṇa to be that which is the effect and the cause of all causes.
O Lord of Gaṇas, understand that everything in the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is truly the eternal Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa. (5–6)
In Goloka, [I meditate upon] the two-armed, peaceful, and enchanting Lord, the beloved of Rādhā;
the Supreme Perfection personified, in the form of a child, dressed as a cowherd,
accompanied by the gopīs, the hosts of cowherds, and the wish-fulfilling cows.
In the auspicious, delightful, and beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala of Vṛndāvana,
[he saw Him] wandering with a flute in His hand, worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa,
at the foot of a banyan tree on the mountain-king Śataśṛṅga, which was free from all disturbance.
In the cow-pen near the Bhāṇḍīra tree, upon the pure bank of the Virajā,
he shone, dark as a fresh rain-cloud and adorned with yellow garments,
like a mass of new clouds illuminated by lightning.
Their manifestation indeed occurs in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance;
likewise, they appear in as many forms in the delightful and holy Gokula, in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
All of them are partial expansions (aṃśakalā) of the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Himself.
His desire was most fully realized, yet he had forgotten his own [nature] due to a Brahmin’s curse.
His son Aniruddha, possessed of great strength and prowess,
was dispatched by me into that most terrible great battle, like Skanda himself.
And Bāṇa, having died in battle, was protected by that Skanda.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, in the battle between Skanda and Aniruddha, there was indeed equality.
And all the eight Bhairavas and those eleven Rudras were present.
The eight Vasus, these gods beginning with Śakra,
likewise the twelve Ādityas, and all the lords of the Daityas;
Skanda, the leader of the gods, and Bāṇa together with his hosts.
And all of them together were unable to defeat Aniruddha in battle.
Aniruddha is Brahmā himself; Pradyumna is indeed Kāma;
Baladeva is Śeṣa himself; and Kṛṣṇa is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
All this has been told to you; O Lord of the Gaṇas, protect Bāṇa! You are of auspicious nature and the destroyer of obstacles.
Hari will soon arrive, taking his Sudarśana disc with him.
[He took] that supreme weapon, unfailing and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Battle between Bāṇa and Śiva-Lambodara," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Brahma... Mahā... Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janma-khaṇḍa*, [narrated by] Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and eighteenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having instructed Gaṇeśa, Śambhu went into another chamber;
there, upon a beautiful throne, sat Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune.
Bhairavī, Bhadrakālī, Ugracaṇḍā, and Koṭarī—
having risen up suddenly, they bowed down to the Lord of the World.
Then Gaṇeśa arrived there, as did the heroic Kārtikeya.
Bāṇa, Vīrabhadra, Nandin himself, Sunandaka,
Mahākāla, and the great minister— these are the eight Bhairavas.
Furthermore, there are the lords of the Siddhas, the lords of the Yogins, and those eleven Rudras.
In the meantime, Maṇibhadra arrived there;
standing himself as the doorkeeper at the main gate, he spoke to his lord.
(5) Maṇibhadra said:
And there were innumerable armies of the Yādavas, O Maheśvara;
as well as Baladeva, Pradyumna, Sāmba, and likewise Sātyaki;
King Mahograsena, Bhīma, and Arjuna himself.
Akrūra, Cārudeṣṇa, and Jayanta, the son of Śakra;
and in a most beautiful, supreme chariot fashioned from the essence of jewels,
the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Controller and ordainer of destiny.
Attended by seven companions who were celestial cowherds,
possessing the playful charm of ten million Cupids, and adorned with a forest garland,
he held an incomparable discus whose radiance was equal to ten million suns.
Having placed his mace Kaumodakī and his infallible trident within the chariot,
he also set down the great conch, the cause of the universal dissolution, in the midst of the chariot.
[He was accompanied] by hundreds of thousands of great chariot-warriors and thirty million chariots.
With three crores of lordly elephants and three crores of wrestlers;
with ten billion horses and four times that number of shield-bearers;
with seven times that number of swordsmen and twice that number of archers.
Together with these, he quickly arrived at the city of Śoṇita;
there, like the son of Daśaratha, he surrounded Laṅkā on all sides—
a city a thousand palm trees in height, blazing and radiant with tongues of fire.
And above, it was surrounded by a moat impassable for both asuras and devas;
likewise, it was rained upon by masses of water from the celestial Gaṅgā and the oceans.
There, Garuḍa, the lord of birds, visibly brought about its purification.

Baladeva shattered with his plows a city whose walls, constructed from the finest gems, scraped the very clouds; and the Lord uprooted three hundred thousand gardens and a hundred thousand wrestlers. (16–17)
Having prostrated before the gatekeepers, he entered the great gate.
Upon hearing this, Mahādeva spoke thus in the assembly of the gods:
"Pārvatī, Bhadrakālī, Skanda, and likewise Gaṇapati—"
And the eight Bhairavas, the Rudras, Vīrabhadra, Mahākāla, and Nandin— all these nine generals—
Mahādeva said: (19)
The Lord of Goloka, the Blessed One, the wielder of the discus, has arrived—
he who is capable of shattering the entire flood of the universe in an instant, let alone a city.
By every possible means, all of you must protect Bāṇa with great effort.
"Let Bāṇa go to battle, remembering the supreme Lambodara.
Let Skanda be at Bāṇa’s right and Gaṇeśvara in front;
let the Bhairavas and Rudras be on his left, and Nandin himself with his chariot. (21–22)
Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, and whoever other soldiers there may be;
above, Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Hyagraṇḍā, and Koṭarī—
protect Bāṇa, O illustrious Durgā, destroyer of misfortune!
You are the power of Kṛṣṇa; therefore, you are remembered as Nārāyaṇī.
O Viṣṇu-māyā, Mother of the World, Auspiciousness of all auspicious things!
Protect Bāṇa from the Sudarśana, the unerring essence of the discus.
"Bāṇa is dearer to me than all others, even than Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya.
Place your hand, along with the dust of your lotus-feet, upon Bāṇa’s head.
Having heard these words of Śiva, Durgā, the destroyer of distress, [acted accordingly].
Laughing, she spoke sweetly, truthfully, and in accordance with the occasion.
Pārvatī said: "Whatever there may be of gems and jewels, such as pearls, rubies, and diamonds,"

"O Bāṇa, bestow upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, your entire wealth— your daughter adorned with jewel-ornaments— placing before him Aniruddha, the supreme bridegroom, who is richly adorned with jewel-ornaments. (28–29)
"Rule your kingdom free from obstacles; why wage war against yourself?
When that [Self] has departed, the vital breaths have gone—where then is the living being along with the senses?
I am Power (Śakti), the Mind, Brahmā, and Śiva himself, whose nature is knowledge. (30)
The body falls instantly and becomes a corpse once Śiva has departed;
who indeed can stand in battle against the splendor of your discus, O Śiva?
The Self is not the body nor the ether; pierced by an arrow, how could there be a battle with one's own Self?
And the Supreme Self is the embodiment of grace for all devotees.
Kṛṣṇa is indeed eternal, true, and the most perfect Lord. Gaṇeśa and Kārtikeya, and even you yourself, are subordinate to those two.
Among the servants, Bāṇa is dear; indeed, there is no one dearer than Kṛṣṇa.
In Vaikuṇṭha I am Mahālakṣmī, and in Goloka I am Rādhikā herself. I am Śivā in the world of Śiva, and in the world of Brahmā I am Sarasvatī.

In former times, I was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa; having slain the Daityas, she abandoned her body due to your censure. And I am this daughter of the mountain; we two are one, though appearing as different forms through the division of our manifestations, such as in the battle with Raktabīja.

I am Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas; I am Sītā, the daughter of Janaka; and in Dvāravatī, in Bhārata, I am Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka. Now, by the divine curse of Sudāmā, I have become the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu.
And the lawful wife of Kṛṣṇa [resides] in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana.
What more shall I say? You are the omniscient Lord, Śiva, and the eternal; what ought to be done that is appropriate for the occasion?

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Battle with Bāṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Now begins the one hundred and nineteenth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard Pārvatī’s words, Śiva himself, the Lord of Gaṇeśa,
as well as Kārttikeya and Kālī, offered her praise.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu spoke to the supreme Mother of the worlds.
The Supreme Goddess, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) whose very form is light—
Mahādeva said:
"O Queen of the Gods, everything you have spoken is desired and is declared in all the Vedas."
War with the Supreme Self is improper and laughable.
Let Bāṇa give his daughter, adorned with golden ornaments;
it will bring harmony, fame, and auspiciousness in all undertakings.
When Bāṇa, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, does not give [battle],
turning his back in fear during the fight, he brings dishonor to the Blessed One.
Let Bāṇa go forth, armored and skilled in the science of war.
"And afterwards, O auspicious one, we shall return as those clad in armor.
[6] He spoke to Bāṇa to give her away, but he did not agree.
Durgā sought to enlighten him, yet he did not understand her virtuous words. [7]
In the meantime, the great Dharma and Bali, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, arrived at that very assembly hall of the great Uramā;
the mighty one, having mounted a chariot fashioned from the finest jewels.
He was served by seven radiant Daityas with white chowries;
surrounded by seven hundred thousand lords of the Daityas and being an expert in supreme weapons,
he quickly descended from his chariot and [approached] Gaṇeśa and the auspicious Śivā.
Having prostrated before Kārttikeya, he sat in the assembly.
Upon seeing him from afar, all except Śaṅkara rose up.
Mahādeva, addressing him with kind words, spoke to him.
Mahādeva said:
O Blessed One, you are the bestower of all perfections;
indeed, this meeting with Vaiṣṇavas is the supreme gain.
Even sacred fords become purified merely by the touch of a Vaiṣṇava.
Among all stages of life, the pure Brāhmaṇa is the most honored; yet, if that Brāhmaṇa is a Vaiṣṇava, he is honored even more. Indeed, I do not see anything purer than a Brāhmaṇa who is a Vaiṣṇava.
He is purified by the wind alone, and he is purified by the sacrificial fire;
yet that god fears all the sacred fords as well.
Indeed, no sins remain in his body, just as dry grass and the like do not remain in the fire. (15–16)
Bali said:
O Lord of the World, how can you, the Sovereign, praise your own servant? O Protector, supreme sovereignty, so difficult to attain, has been bestowed by you upon me. (17)
Now, by fate, you have been placed even below all others in Sutala;
yet, O Lord of the Gods, sovereignty was granted to Indra by me because he is my devotee.
You, who possess all forms, assumed the form of Vāmana through you [the Supreme Self], for you are omnipresent.
"Awaken Bāṇa and my supreme son Bhadra, who are as dear to me as my own life-breath. Moreover, a battle with one's own self is censured even among the gods.
Having spoken thus, he bowed his head and prostrated before Śiva.
With his entire body covered in horripilation, his eyes filled with tears, and deeply overwhelmed, he praised the Supreme Lord with a hymn declared in the Sāmaveda,
while constantly meditating upon Him who resides eternally within the most beautiful lotus of the heart. (21)
And having recited the eleven-syllable mantra given by Śukra,
Bali said:
"By the very prayer of Aditi and by the vow of my mother, the goddess..."
O Lord, in former times I was deceived by you in the form of Vāmana.
You devotedly bestowed upon me, your devotee, Mahālakṣmī in the form of prosperity;
and certainly, you gave her from me to your meritorious brother Śakra, who is likewise devoted.
Now this son of mine, Bāṇa, a servant of Śaṅkara,
has been protected from afar by that very friend of devotees;
and he has been nourished by Pārvatī just as a son is nurtured by his mother.
And he forcibly seized that virtuous young maiden.
When he rose up to kill him, he was restrained by Kārttikeya:
"You have come again to kill; you are capable of subduing even my grandson. || 26-27 ||
The state of being equally present everywhere as the self of all is heard in the Śruti;
O Lord of the worlds, how then do you commit such a transgression?
For who on earth can be the protector of one who has been slain by you?
For the splendor of Sudarśana is supreme, resembling ten million suns.
By the weapon of which gods was it ever repelled?
For Sudarśana is indeed the most excellent and best among weapons. (29–30)
Likewise, you are the supreme lord of all the gods;
as you are, so too is Kṛṣṇa, the creator even of the creators.
Viṣṇu is the repository of the quality of goodness (sattva), and Śiva likewise is the refuge of goodness.
He is the self-ordainer, the creator of passion (rajas), the progenitor;
he is the Lord Kālāgnirudra, the cause of the destruction of the universe, and the refuge of darkness (tamas); he is also the great and most excellent among the Rudras. (32–33)
He alone is a portion of Śaṅkara, and the other Rudras are his emanations;
you (Bhava) are among them, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and likewise beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Indeed, he is the Supreme Self of all, whose forms are the syllables *pra* and *ṇa*, and who is Viṣṇu himself.
The mind is Brahmā himself, and Śiva is himself the essence of knowledge. Intellect is the foremost of all powers, the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the sovereign lady.
The individual soul (jīva) is the reflection of one's own self within all embodied beings.
The individual soul is the experiencer of its own actions, and you likewise are their witness.
When you, the god among men, have departed, all follow after you like attendants.
Without you, the body immediately falls lifeless—a corpse that may not be touched by you.

Even though they are Buddhas, they do not know you, for they have been deceived by your illusion (māyā). Those virtuous ones who worship you alone cross over this illusion. Nature (prakṛti), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇā), is indeed Durgā, the eternal power of Viṣṇu.
Supreme is your Māyā, the sovereign Nārāyaṇī, which is difficult to transcend.
In every universe, your portions manifest as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
And he who is the great Virāṭ, the support of all universes—
By means of yoga, he lies upon the water like Viśveśa in Gokula.
He alone is the Blessed One Vāsudeva; you are his supreme deity, celebrated by those who know the ancient lore as Vāsudeva.
By one part you alone are the sun; by one part you alone are the moon;
by one part you are the fire, and by one part you yourself are the wind.
By one part you are Varuṇa, as well as Kubera and Yama.
By one portion you are Mahendra, and by another portion you are Dharma himself.
By yet another portion you are Śeṣa, as well as Īśāna and Nairṛti;
you are the sages, the Manus, and the planets that bestow their fruits.
All living beings, both moving and unmoving, are [born] from a portion of a fraction of Kalākalā.
You are the supreme Brahman, the light, whom yogis always meditate upon. Your devotees revere You, who meditate upon You within their hearts.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, clad in yellow silk garments,
with a face brightened by a gentle smile, the Lord of devotees who is affectionate toward his followers—
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, two-armed, and holding a flute. (47–48)
He had a crest of peacock feathers and was adorned with garlands of jasmine;
he wore armlets and bracelets fashioned from priceless jewels,
and his cheeks were illuminated by a pair of jeweled earrings.
Adorned with a finger-ring of precious gems and graced by tinkling, sweet-sounding anklets;
possessing the grace of ten million Cupids, with eyes like autumn lotuses, a face that puts the autumn full moon to shame, and a radiance equal to ten million moons. (50–51)
He was gazed upon by millions upon millions of smiling gopīs,
served by his companions, attendants, and cowherds with white chowries,
and appearing in the guise of a cowherd boy while resting upon the breast of Rādhā.
Unattainable through meditative absorption, difficult to propitiate, and worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu;
saluted and praised by the lords of the oceans, the lords of sages, and the lords of yogis;
indefinable by the Vedas, supreme, consisting of His own will, and all-pervading. (53–54)
The Lord, who is the grossest of the gross, the subtlest of the subtle, the supreme, the truth, the eternal, the praiseworthy, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
untainted, desireless, and the ancient Blessed One.
Having meditated thus, purified and holding tender *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains in their hands, they were eager to offer water at your lotus-feet, which are worshipped by the goddess Padmā.
The Vedas are unable to praise you, nor is Sarasvatī capable of doing so. (56–57)
Even Śeṣa, the Self-born, Śambhu, Īśvara, Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Mahendra, and Candra are unable to praise him;
nor is Dhaneśa capable of praising him—how much less others whose intellects are dull? (58)
"How can I praise the Supreme, who is beyond qualities, devoid of effort, and without attributes?
"This Asura is ignorant; he is no god. You ought to forgive him.
Having heard those words of Bali, the Lord of the World spoke to him:
The most perfect, glorious Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, said:
"Do not fear, my child; go home to Sutala, which has been protected by me."
By my boon and grace, even your son shall be free from old age and death.
I shall bring about the destruction of the pride of that foolish and arrogant one.
A boon has been granted to Prahlāda, who is devoted and an ascetic.
With a joyful heart, thinking, "Your lineage shall be invincible," I shall grant to your son the supreme knowledge that conquers death.
This desired hymn, composed by you, is proclaimed in the Sāmaveda.
In ancient times, it was likewise bestowed by Brahmā upon Sanatkumāra at the most meritorious and praiseworthy Siddhāśrama during a solar eclipse;
and it was also bestowed by Gaurī upon Gautama on the banks of the Mandākinī.
It was given by the compassionate Śaṅkara to his devoted disciple Brahmā on the banks of the Virajā;
and in former times, it was given to Bhṛgu by the wise Kumāra.
And you shall give it to Bāṇa; Bāṇa will praise me with this.
Having taught this most meritorious hymn from the mouth of his guru—who was chosen and honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste—[he shall do so]. (67–68)
Whoever, having bathed well, recites this daily with devotion at the time of worship, is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
This hymn is the shatterer of calamities and the cause of all prosperity.
It is the warding off of suffering and grief, the boat for crossing the terrible ocean of existence;
it is the destruction of dwelling in the womb, the supreme remover of old age and death; it is the shattering of bonds and diseases, the ornament of devotion.
He has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.

One who observes all vows among vows and is an ascetic among ascetics certainly obtains the fruit of all gifts through the recitation of this hymn. By reciting the hymn one hundred thousand times, men shall attain perfection in the hymn.
If one becomes a reciter of this hymn of accomplishment (*siddhistotra*), he attains all perfections.
In this world he becomes equal to a god, and at the end, he goes to the abode of Hari.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Offered by Bali during the Battle with Bāṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa within the glorious *Brahma... Mahā...* [Purāṇa], as related by Nārada. 119. End of Chapter.
The one hundred and twentieth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: Then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, along with Uddhava and Balarāma, [departed].
Having held an auspicious consultation, he dispatched a messenger to where Śiva,
Gaṇapati, Durgā— the destroyer of distress—
Kārttikeya, Bhadrakālī, Ugracaṇḍā, and Koṭarī were present. (1–2)
Having arrived and bowed down to Gaṇeśa, Śiva, and Śivā, as well as the human beings worthy of honor, the messenger spoke to them appropriately.
The messenger said:
O Maheśvara, Kṛṣṇa is challenging Bāṇa for the sake of battle;
or rather, take Aniruddha and Ūṣā with you and go for refuge.
For he who, being invited to battle, does not go because he is overcome by fear— || 4 ||
He goes to hell in the next world together with his seven ancestors.
(5) Having heard the messenger’s words, Queen Pārvatī herself spoke appropriately in the midst of the assembly in the presence of Śaṅkara. (6)
Pārvatī said:
"Go, O illustrious Bāṇa, taking your daughter;
having given all your possessions as a dowry, seek refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (7)
The Lord of all, the seed, the giver of all prosperity,
the most excellent one to be chosen, the refuge, the compassionate one who is affectionate toward his devotees—
having heard these words of Pārvatī, those lords of the gods spoke to him.
In the midst of the assembly, they constantly praised him, saying, "Blessed! Blessed! (9).
Then this asura Bāṇa, overcome with anger, suddenly rose up;
equipped for battle and bow in hand, he paid obeisance to Śaṅkara and departed. (10)
Though being restrained by all, the mighty one, his eyes bloodshot and trembling,
was clad in armor along with thirty million Daityas—
Kumbhāṇḍa, Kūpakarṇa, Nikumbha, and Kumbha himself.
And these lords of the generals likewise went forth, fully armed:
Unmattabhairava, Saṃhārabhairava,
Asitāṅgabhairava, and Rurubhairava.
Known as Mahābhairava, Kālabhairava,
Pracaṇḍabhairava, and Krodhabhairava—
all of them, fully armored, set forth together with their Śaktis.
The Lord Kālāgnirudra went forth, fully armored, accompanied by the Rudras.
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍināyikā, Caṇḍeśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍī, and Caṇḍakapālikā [also followed]. (15–16)
And all eight heroines set forth, carrying skull-bowls;
Koṭarī, seated upon a jeweled vehicle, and Śoṇitagrāmadevatā also departed, their faces blooming with joy, bearing swords and skull-bowls. (17)
Indrāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Śāntā, Brahmāṇī, and the expounder of Brahman;
Kaumārī, Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī of formidable form, Māheśvarī, Mahāmāyā, Bhairavī, and she of terrifying appearance. (18–19)
And all eight Śaktis, stationed upon their chariots, set forth with joy; Bhadrakālikā, seated in a vehicle made of the finest essence of jewels, also departed.
She was red in color, possessed three eyes, and was terrifying with her flickering tongue.
With tridents, spears, and maces in her hands, and bearing a sword and a skull-bowl, she departed;
and Maheśvara, mounted upon his bull and holding a trident in his hand, set forth; and Skanda, riding upon his peacock vehicle, bow in hand and weapon in grasp, followed.
And so they all proceeded, with the exception of Gaṇeśa and Pārvatī;
and having seen Mahādeva accompanied by these [attendants] and Bhadrakālī,
the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) engaged in appropriate conversation with them.
Bāṇa, having sounded his conch and bowed to the Lord of Pārvatī,
took up his strung bow, which was joined with a divine weapon.
Seeing Bāṇa prepared for battle, Sātyaki, the slayer of enemy heroes, [advanced].
Though forbidden by all of them, Saṃnāhin advanced with joy;
O Nārada, Bāṇa discharged the divine weapon named Añjana, which was unfailing, as radiant as the midday sun in summer, and exceedingly sharp. (26)
Upon seeing the weapon, Sātyaki bowed slightly;
was he not consumed as it proceeded toward the midst of the sky?
Bāṇa discharged the fire-weapon, and Sātyaki countered it with the Vāruṇa weapon.
He extinguished that blazing [missile] which was as tall as a palm tree,
and he cut down the terrible, fierce, and formidable Vāruṇa weapon with ease by means of the Pārjanya weapon. Sātyaki likewise cut it down with effortless playfulness.
Bāṇa hurled the fierce, terrifying, and formidable Pāvana weapon;
but Sātyaki effortlessly cut it down with the Parvata weapon.
Then Bāṇa discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon at the forefront of the battle.
By the training of Arjuna, Sātyaki fell to the ground like a staff;
Bāṇa, the best among those skilled in weapons, discharged the Māheśvara weapon,
but Sātyaki effortlessly severed it with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
And Bāṇa also hurled the Brahmā weapon at the front of the battle.
Satyaki extinguished that Brahmā weapon in an instant;
then Bāṇa, skilled in combat, also hurled the Nāga weapon.
In an instant, Sātyaki withdrew [the weapon] by means of the Gāruḍa [mantra]. He seized Śaṅkara’s most terrible and infallible trident.
Sātyaki praised Durgā, and a garland appeared around his neck.
Then Bāṇa took up with his bow the Pāśupata weapon;
likewise, Sātyaki rendered Bāṇa, along with his own arrow, into a yawn.
Seeing that Bāṇa had been made to yawn, the mighty Kārttikeya [acted].
Kāma effortlessly cut down the crescent moon that had been hurled;
then Skanda cast a mace, radiant as the morning sun,
but Kāma extinguished it with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
And Skanda, acting with haste, discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon. By the instruction of Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff.
Then Skanda hurled his spear, which possessed a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Kāma brought that [weapon] to extinction with the Nārāyaṇa-weapon;
then Kārttikeya hurled the Brahmā-weapon at the front of the battle.
With that Brahmā-weapon as well, Kāma brought it to extinction.
Then, out of anger, he seized the divine Pāśupata weapon, Kārttika.
Madana also rendered him unconscious with the sleep-weapon (nidrāstra).
Seeing Kārttika thus asleep and Bāṇa likewise yawning, [he acted].

In her wrath, Bhadrakālī seized Kāma along with his chariot; and the Mother of the worlds took Bāṇa and Skanda upon her lap and departed from the battlefield to where Pārvatī, the virtuous one, was located.
She awakened Kārttikeya and restored Bāṇa to health.
Suddenly, Kāma, deprived of his chariot, emerged terrified through the path of the nostril and fled to the battlefield.
Then the Yādavas, seeing Kāma together with his chariot, abandoned him;
all those Śaivas present there stood with parched throats, overwhelmed by fear.
Then Bāṇa, again enraged, mounted his chariot out of anger.
And the blessed Kārtikeya returned once more for battle.
Bāṇa, meanwhile, discharged five arrows at the forefront of the fray;
the exceedingly powerful Baladeva cut them down with a crescent-headed shaft.
The wielder of the plow shattered Bāṇa’s chariot with his plow,
and with effortless ease struck down the charioteer and the horses with his mace.
Then the one of great strength [Bali] made an effort to sever the plow-wielder [Balabhadra].
The Lord Kālāgnirudra warded [him] off with ease;
the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), filled with rage, shattered the chariot of Kālāgnirudra,
and with his plow struck down the charioteer and the horses at the head of the battle.
Kālāgnirudra, out of anger, hurled the formidable fever;
all the Yādavas, with the exception of Hari, became overwhelmed by that fever.
Seeing this, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa indeed unleashed the Vaiṣṇava fever.
He hurled that Māheśvara fever at the front of the battle in order to destroy it.
(54) A most terrible battle between the two fevers took place for a moment;
then, driven out by the Vaiṣṇava fever, he fell upon the battlefield.
But he became motionless and again praised Mādhava.
Jvara said:
"O Lord of the World, whose form is the grace bestowed upon devotees, protect my life!"
"You are the Self, the Puruṣa, the Full; your equanimity prevails everywhere.
(56) Having heard the words of Jvara, the fever belonging to Maheśvara withdrew his own fever; terrified, he indeed departed from the battle. (57)
Bāṇa, having returned once more, discharged a thousand arrows purified by mantras, resembling the flames of the fire of universal destruction;
Phālguna effortlessly warded them off with a net of his own shafts.
And Bāṇa hurled a spear, radiant as the summer sun;
but the mighty Savyasācin cut it down with ease.
He [Bāṇa] then seized the Pāśupata weapon, which possessed a brilliance equal to a hundred suns.
Seeing that [missile], which was exceedingly terrible and the cause of the destruction of the universe, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) hurled his own fierce discus.
In the midst of the battle, it severed the thousand arms along with the formidable Pāśupata weapon, and [the demon] fell like a lion from a mountain.
The Pāśupata weapon, which was unfailing and terrible in the world, resembling the crest of the fire of universal destruction, went into the hand of Paśupati.
And with the mass of Bāṇa’s blood, a great river came into being.
Bāṇa fell motionless, pained and deprived of consciousness.
Then the Blessed Mahādeva, the teacher of the world, arrived there;
having come, he wept out of compassion and took Bāṇa to his own chest.
By the falling of Śiva’s tears alone, a lake was formed;
the Lord Karumā-sāgara brought it to life.
Taking his arrows, he went to where the god Janārdana was.
He placed his lotus-like foot, which was honored by the goddess Padmā, upon Bāṇa.
Then Candraśekhara, the Lord of the worlds and Master of devotion, praised him with that hymn composed by Bali,
which is declared in the Vedas.
Hari bestowed upon the wise Bāṇa the knowledge that conquers death;
he placed his lotus-hand upon Bāṇa’s body and made him free from old age and immortal.
Bāṇa, in turn, praised him with devotion through hymns and offerings.
Having brought an excellent maiden adorned with jewel ornaments,
he gave her with devotion to Hari right there in the assembly of the gods.
He also gave five hundred thousand lordly elephants and four times that many horses.
And a thousand maidservants adorned with jewel ornaments;
a thousand wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu), each accompanied by its calf and granting all desires;
and a hundred lakhs of rubies, pearls, and gems.
With his neck bowed in devotion, he gave him a hundred lakhs of enchanting *maṇīndra* diamonds (73),
as well as thousands of water-vessels and bowls fashioned from gold (74).
And Bāṇa, by his own devotion and by the command of Śaṅkara, gave all kinds of excellent, fine garments and cloths purified by fire.
O Nārada, he also gave full vessels of betel leaves and honey.
With devotion, he gave thousands of various boons;
he even offered his daughter at the lotus feet of Hari.
He wept aloud out of his own devotion, and the Lord granted him release.
Having granted him a boon and auspicious blessings as prescribed in the Vedas, Kṛṣṇa departed for the city of Dvārakā with the permission of Śaṅkara.
Having gone there, he took that newly wedded daughter of the high-souled Bāṇa.
Hari himself quickly gave [the child] to Rukmiṇī and Devakī;
he diligently caused a great festival and auspicious rites to be performed,
fed the Brāhmaṇas, and bestowed wealth upon them.
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Battle with Bāṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, as related by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-first chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Kṛṣṇa, residing with his attendants in the Sudharmā assembly hall,
was visited by a brāhmaṇa who blazed with spiritual luster.
Having arrived, he beheld and praised Puruṣottama with devotion.
Calm yet fearful, he spoke sweetly and with humility.
The Brahmin said:
"Śṛgāla, Vāsudeva, Rājeśa, and Maṇḍaleśvara."
Listen attentively to the words he spoke to you.
The jackal said: "In Vaikuṇṭha, I am Vāsudeva, the four-armed Lord of gods."
The Lord of Lakṣmī, the creator of the worlds, and the protector of the creator;
at the request of Brahmā, I have come for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth,
and my journey is directed toward Bhārata-varṣa for that very end.
The son of Vasudeva is a Vaiśya, yet he is arrogant as a Kṣatriya;
he considers himself a devotee of Viṣṇu, yet he is a master of illusion and a deceiver.
Having defeated person after person, the weak by means of the strong.
Having caused them to fight, the great deceiver had those kings slain.
He had Duryodhana, Jarāsandha, and another weak king killed on the earth by the powerful Bhīma, who was but a youth.
By means of his power and through his illusory might, he caused Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and whomever else there was upon the earth—
whosoever was weak, whether famous or obscure— to be slain by Arjuna alone.
By means of his power and through illusion, he caused the death of Śiśupāla,
Dantavakra, and Kaṃsa, who had long been afflicted by disease;
as well as my own son Naraka, and the weak Keśin and Mura.
Alas! He himself suddenly slew him under a pretext and by means of a signal;
for he was a deceiver in righteous battle, a child, and indeed unrighteous.
He killed Pūtanā and Kubjā, and acted as a slayer of women for the sake of a garment.
Though ill-behaved myself, I struck down the remaining washerman who was a deceiver;
having slain the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa,
as well as Madhu and Kaiṭabha, I am the protector of the virtuous.
I alone am indeed Brahmā; I alone am indeed Śiva.
I am Viṣṇu, the protector of the worlds and the destroyer of the wicked. All the Manus and likewise the sages exist through my partial manifestations and portions.
I am Nārāyaṇa himself, devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). Out of shame, compassion, and the thought that you are my friend, I have shown you respect.
O gentle one, what is past is past; now fight with me.
Indeed, through the mouth of my messenger, I hear a very loud proclamation of self-aggrandizement.
For even such [arrogance], subduing is appropriate, as is the striking down of the haughty.
Moreover, the supreme duty of a king is that I am now the ruler of the earth.
"Taking up the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, I shall become four-armed.
I myself will go to Dvārakā with my attendants for battle.
Fight if you so desire; do not seek refuge with me. (19–20)
If he who has come to me for refuge does not go to my protection,
I shall reduce Dvārakā to ashes in an instant,
along with you, your army, your sons, your hosts, and your kinsmen.
I am capable of burning [him] in an instant with ease, even without assistance.

Having defeated Śaṅkara in battle—though he was an ascetic and an old man—and having defeated Śakra, who was afflicted by disease due to a Brahmin’s curse and whose body was marked by female organs; ||| 22–23 ||
You consider yourself a hero, yet you are intoxicated by pride;
for you are conquered by women and have acted in vain for the sake of the *pārijāta* tree. You are a coward, greedy for the womb [of rebirth], and wretchedly dependent on Rādhā and others in Gokula.
"O sage, having spoken thus, 'Now he is like a servant even to Truth and his other wives,' the brahmin remained silent.
But Śukrācārya, along with his attendants, heard this and laughed very loudly."
Having fed and honored the fourfold assembly of brahmins,
he passed the night in sorrow, as if afflicted by a fever caused by the arrows of their words.
At dawn, having mounted his chariot with his retinue, he departed swiftly and joyfully.
With effortless ease, the jackal went to where the king was.
(28) Having heard that news, the deceitful four-armed one himself arrived at Hari’s abode with his retinue for the sake of battle. (29)
And Kṛṣṇa engaged in worldly conversation with the friendliness of a companion; he embraced him, spoke sweet words, and looked upon him with affectionate eyes and a smile.
(30) The king extended an invitation, but Kṛṣṇa did not accept it.
Fearing Kṛṣṇa and casting off all pride upon seeing him, he spoke.
The jackal said:
"Having severed my head with your discus, go very quickly to Dvārakā."
"May this sinful body fall away, for it is impermanent and subject to destruction.
(32) I am Subhadra at your door, as are Jaya and Vijaya.
You know everything, O All-Knowing One; do not delay, O Lord. (33)
"By the curse of Lakṣmī, I have fallen; my period of time has been completed.
At the end of the hundred-year curse, I shall go to your abode.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O friend, strike me first; afterwards I shall fight you.
I know everything; go to Vaikuṇṭha, my child, as you please.
Then Śṛgāla discharged ten arrows toward Mādhava.
Having prostrated themselves, those who were like the very form of Time departed swiftly toward the sky.
(36) The king hurled a mace resembling the crest of the fire of universal destruction;
yet, by the mere touch of Kṛṣṇa’s body, it was shattered in an instant. (37)
He hurled a spear, a club, and likewise an axe;
yet by the mere touch of Kṛṣṇa’s body, they were shattered in an instant.
He also cast a bow and a sword that was as formidable as Death itself.
By the mere touch of Kṛṣṇa’s body, he was shattered in an instant.
Seeing the king disarmed, the treasury of compassion spoke thus:
"Go home and bring your very sharp Mitrāstra."
The jackal said:
"The self is not the ether, nor is it pierced by weapons; what kind of battle is there with oneself?
O cause of the earth’s upholding, rescue me from the ocean of existence!"
O Lord, this ocean of existence is treacherous and its objects are more poisonous than poison itself.
Sever for me the shackles of illusion, the snare of delusion born of my own karma.
You are the master of karmas, their ordainer, and indeed their creator.
He is the giver of auspicious fruits and the bestower of all perfections;
he is the cause of past deeds and is capable of nullifying them.
I am going to your very own Vaikuṇṭha home, which is the seventh door.
Having cast off his mortal body, composed of the five elements,
and having heard the praise and nectar-like words of his friend,
that ocean of compassion wept there on the battlefield out of pity.
There, by the sudden falling of a drop of tears from Kṛṣṇa’s eye,
there came into being the divine Bindu-saras, the supreme and most excellent of holy fords (tīrtha). By the mere touch of its water, a man becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
One is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this.
The Blessed Lord said: "O friend, how is it that you possess such an intellect and a pure mind?"
"And how was such harsh and cruel speech uttered through the messenger?
The jackal said:
"Having been addressed by me in this manner, you have come here out of anger."
"Otherwise, O Lord, your vision would be difficult to obtain even in a dream.
(49) In the meantime, having abandoned her material body through yoga and beholding Kṛṣṇa, she joyfully departed for Vaikuṇṭha by means of a celestial vehicle. (50)
And there, having bowed to his lotus-feet— which were seven *tāla* trees in height, possessed a most brilliant luster, and were worshipped by lotuses with lotuses— he departed.
Having gone to Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa bowed to his father and mother.
Having quickly seen that most wonderful sight, the glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his attendants,
went with a blossoming face toward Dvārakā;
he entered the house of Rukmiṇī, which was perfumed with flowers and sandalwood.
And upon a bed of flowers and sandalwood, he took his pleasure with her at night;
she, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, attained a state of swoon, having placed Kṛṣṇa upon her own breast.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation of Śṛgāla and Vāsudeva," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa*, within the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa*, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-second chapter.
Nārada said:
[Regarding] all those women and Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul...
The blessed one has joyfully related to you the account of the marriage;
however, O illustrious one, the desired narrative of the Syamantaka jewel has not been heard by me, so you ought to explain it to me.
Nārāyaṇa said:
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Moon, having abducted Tārakā, abandoned her on the Yamunā; and the Preceptor (Bṛhaspati) took her as his wife.
Rebuked by her guru, Tārā, though pregnant, was filled with shame; out of that shame and anger, she formerly cursed Candra, who was afflicted by lust. (4) Tārā said:
"O embodied being, whoever beholds you shall become stained by the blemish of worldly existence;
having seen a sinner, he too shall become sinful and defiled.
Having heard this, that Moon [resided] at the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Having performed the Nārāyaṇa penance, he was released from his committed sin.
Seeing him afflicted by the penance and greatly terrified, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person and ocean of compassion, spoke to him out of mercy.
The Blessed One said: "O storehouse of digits, though you are stained, you shall be liberated at all times;
[you shall be] the locus of the curse for Tārakā during the month of Bhādrapada, both in its bright and dark fortnights. (8)
Whoever gazes with desire upon the moon risen on the fourth lunar day,
that stain [of the moon] shall go to him, and he will become stained.
On the white and black [fortnights] of the month of Bhādrapada, the drum is struck by Hari.
On the fourth lunar day, the moon should never be looked at when it has risen.
Having seen this himself, he ought to uphold his own word.
On the fourth day of the month of Bhādrapada, however, the moon indeed became stained with a mark.
I shall describe that form by which he became stained; listen.
For the sake of instructing the world, the Lord released himself from the stain.
Satrājit was a devotee of the Sun, and having performed austerities at Puṣkara, [he attained his station].

He obtained from the Sun himself the Syamantaka, the most excellent of jewels, which constantly yields eight *bhāras* of gold; it is presided over by the Sun-god, and is exceedingly pure and merit-bestowing. (13–14)

Having given Satyabhāmā to Kṛṣṇa out of devotion, the great Satrājit was prepared to give a jewel as a wedding gift to the Great One. But the evil-minded Prasena, oppressed by Time (Death), forbade him. || 15 ||
Taking the jewel, he set out for the holy city of Vārāṇasī.
But on the way, a powerful lion killed him by force,
seized the beautiful jewel, and wore it tied with a thread around his neck.
And the son of the King of Kaliṅga, having been addressed by that Brahmin on account of a most terrible curse, entered the womb of a beast;
[then] the powerful Jāmbavat, a bear, having slain a lion in the forest...
Having taken the jewel, he departed for his own city, which was constructed of gems.
All those in Dvārakā said: "Mādhava has seized the jewel;
we do not know his intention, nor by what means he did so."
Having heard this, the Blessed One set out for the formidable forest by a path marked by the signs of thieves in order to remove the stain;
seeing the dead Prasena, he became sorrowful and beheld the lion.
Seeing that it was devoid of the jewel, Mādhava was despondent.
Knowing everything, the omniscient one went to the bear’s dwelling;
there he saw the weeping boy in the lap of his nurse.
Filled with compassion, the nurse awakened the boy, saying: "O child, take this jewel; for this is indeed your Syamantaka.
The lion killed Prasena, and that lion has been slain by Jāmbavān. (24)
"O Sukumāra, do not weep; for this Syamantaka belongs to you.
Whoever, remembering these auspicious words spoken by the nurse, drinks water, is cleansed of the sin arising from the anger caused by the moon's disappearance as perceived through fate.
"If those who are hypocritical and revilers of the Vedas should look [at this] out of desire,
they will surely become stained with blemish," so said the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Having heard the words of the nurse, Kṛṣṇa took the jewel from the boy.
The nurse, having gone there, spoke to the bear in anger. Jāmbavān, arriving there, bowed down and offered praise;
he gave his daughter, Jāmbavatī, to him, and presented a jewel as a wedding gift.
Having brought the jewel to Dvārakā, he showed it to the Yādavas;
and that Lord became entirely pure and stainless.
This supreme narrative of the jewel has been told to you, my child.
Merely by hearing this chapter, a man becomes free from blemish.
That which was heard from the mouth of the Speaker of Dharma has been recounted here according to the scriptures;
this narrative is very difficult to obtain. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Seizure of the Syamantaka Jewel," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Nārada and [the sages].
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-third chapter.
Nārada said:
The narrative of the worship of Gaṇeśa is rare even among the Purāṇas;
it was heard from the mouth of Brahmā in its general form and in brief.
[It concerns] the majesty of Gaṇapati, the Lord who is worthy of being worshipped by all.
O Vyāsa, I desire to hear from you, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogis: how,
in the past, a great worship was performed for Rādhā and Mādhava by those residing in the three worlds at Siddhāśrama, and how their union occurred there once again in ancient times.
O sage, how was it that Rādhā first performed worship at the beginning of the past century, upon the release of Śrīdāman from his curse,
while the lords of the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others— were present?
While Śeṣa, the lord of nāgas, remained among the great nāgas;
while the lords of kings remained on earth; while the most powerful asuras, the gandharvas, the rākṣasas, and other mighty beings remained [in their respective domains]. (5–6)
O illustrious one, you ought to explain that to me in detail.
Nārāyaṇa said: In the three worlds, the earth is blessed, venerable, meritorious, and virtuous.
Therein lies the auspicious Bhāratavarṣa, which yields the fruits of actions.
It is blessed, glorious, and worthy of worship; and within that land of merit, Bhārata, is Siddhāśrama, a most sacred field that bestows liberation and is auspicious.
The blessed Sanatkumāra became a perfected one (siddha) there;
indeed, the Creator himself, having performed austerities in that very place, became a perfected one.
So too did the lords of yogis, the lords of sages, and the lords of perfected ones such as Kapila and others.
Having performed [these deeds] there, Śatakratu became Mahendra.
O Sage, it was for that reason that the abode of Gaṇeśa, named Siddhāśrama— which is difficult to attain even for all others— is eternally situated right there.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, the gods worship the auspicious image of Gaṇeśa fashioned from priceless jewels;
likewise do the Nāgas, humans, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
The lords of the Siddhas, the lords of the Munis, and the lords of the Yogins, such as Sanaka and others;
Śambhu, the benefactor, arrived there together with Pārvatī, along with his Gaṇas and Kārttikeya; and Brahmā himself, the Lord of Progeny, also came. (14–15)
Then Śeṣa arrived there in haste along with the lords of the nāgas;
all the gods, as well as the Manus and the sages, likewise came there.
All those kings also arrived with joyful hearts for the purpose of offering worship.
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa arrived together with the inhabitants of Dvārakā;
likewise, Nanda came along with the residents of Gokula and with three hundred million gopīs who dwell in Goloka.
Accompanied by her companions, who were as powerful as millions of elephants,
the beautiful Rādhā— the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s very life— arrived;
she, the Queen of the Rāsa dance and one who delights in the divine nectar, came after a hundred years had passed.
Having bathed well, joyful and pure, wearing two washed garments, self-restrained and fasting, she went to the jeweled pavilion;
her lotus-feet were thoroughly washed, and the beloved one was the purifier of the world. (20–21)
Then, desiring to please Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she formed a firm resolve and bathed Heramba with devotion using water from the Gaṅgā;
she also performed meditation according to the Sāmaveda with white flowers.
The divine lady, whose form is intellect, is the mother of the four Vedas and of the worlds,
as well as the supreme progenitor of the wise;
she meditated upon that supreme meditation, which is of the nature of contemplation.
Śarva, the pot-bellied and stout one, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, elephant-faced, fire-colored, single-tusked, and infinite;
the teacher of teachers for the Siddhas, Yogins, and the wise. (25)

The eternal Lord, whose nature is Brahman, the supreme auspiciousness and abode of all blessings, was meditated upon by the lords of sages, the lords of gods, and those known as Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa, as well as by the lords of the Siddhas and the virtuous sages. (26–27)
He who removes all obstacles, who is peaceful, and who bestows all prosperity;
he who is the helmsman for those engaged in action by means of the boat of *māyā* across the ocean of worldly existence;
and he who is solely devoted to the protection of the wretched and the distressed who have come for refuge.
She meditated upon the one whose nature is meditation, the goal to be attained, the Lord of devotion who is kind to his devotees.
(29) Having thus meditated and offered a flower upon her own head, Satī again performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) prescribed in the Vedas for the purification of all her limbs. (30)
Again, having meditated with that very same auspicious meditation,
Rādhā offered a flower at the lotus feet of Lambodara,
[anointing them] with the cool water of seven sacred fords, scented and pure.
She offered water for the feet at her lotus-like feet, which had been worshipped with lotuses and other offerings.
Then the resident of Goloka herself personally offered the *arghya* upon his head with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken grains of rice, white flowers, and fragrant sandalwood water.
Rāsaśvarī herself joyfully placed upon the neck of Gaṇeśa a beautiful garland of pārijāta flowers together with sandalwood.
She also gave him fragrant, smooth sandalwood paste smeared with musk and saffron.
The playful maiden of Vṛndāvana placed [the flowers] upon all his limbs;
and the virtuous Mahāpadmalayā gave him fragrant white flowers, honored with fragrant sandalwood paste, at his lotus feet.
And the beloved of Kṛṣṇa offered to Him, the Lord of the worlds, incense endowed with fragrance and accompanied by pure substances,
as well as a lamp kindled with ghee, which serves to destroy the darkness.
To that Lord of the Gods, she gave the most ancient and eternal [offering]:

various kinds of delightful food-offerings (naivedya), exquisitely sweet and captivating, consisting of the fourfold types—things to be sucked, chewed, licked, and drunk—which were like nectar itself. (38–39)
And there were fruits, well-ripened and difficult to find even in the three worlds,
as well as sweet roots, both cultivated and wild, O Nārada.
There were also those various other things in countless numbers, including cakes made of sesame seeds.
Well-cooked *laḍḍukas*, sweet and flavorful;
and cooked flour-cakes made from barley and wheat flour, delightful, anointed with ghee, and mixed with sugar. (41–42)
Large and beautiful *laḍḍuka* sweets shaped like svastikas,
various kinds of fried foods, unbroken grains mixed with sugar,
a delightful stream of ghee, a stream of milk, and a stream of honey.
A stream of molasses and curds, as well as of milk-rice (pāyasa);
heaps of flour-cakes, svastika-bread, and plantains; and auspicious servings of śāli rice accompanied by sweet side-dishes. (44–45)
The goddess who is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath gave to that Lord of the Gods a magnificent and excellent throne fashioned from priceless jewels;
and she who dwells upon the shining banks gave [these gifts] for the destruction of obstacles.
The dweller of Śataśṛṅga gave to the daughter of the Mountain a beautiful pair of fine garments, priceless and purified by fire; she also gave pure,
sweet honey combined with clarified butter.
The resident of Vṛndāvana gave him madhuparka,
as well as excellent and beautiful betel leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other ingredients;
and the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu gave these to the bestower of all prosperity.
The Queen of Gopas joyfully gave him water for drinking— pure, very white, and well-scented— with the waters of the seven sacred fords; she also gave him a priceless,
rare, and perfectly pure white chowrie.
The Sovereign Primordial Nature (Mūlaprakṛti) offered to that Supreme Lord a magnificent bed,
fashioned from priceless gems— pearls, rubies, and diamonds—
and adorned with flowers and anointed with sandalwood paste. (52)
Adorned all around with a fine white silken garment,
she who rested upon the dark chest of Kṛṣṇa gave [this] to the son of Śiva;
and having given the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) along with her calf, which grants all desires.

Having offered an exceedingly great salutation, Vṛndā presented a handful of flowers with the divine root mantra, radiant and accompanied by its seed-syllable (sabīja). The resident of Kālindī’s banks then performed the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
"Oṃ gaṃ gauṃ to Gaṇapati, the destroyer of obstacles, svāhā.
(56) Thus she recited this sixteen-syllable mantra of Gaṇeśa one thousand times, as well as the excellent *parā* and *salpataru* mantras. (57)
With her neck bowed in devotion, her eyes filled with tears, and her body covered in horripilation, she praised him with supreme devotion through a hymn of Kauthuma.
Rādhikā said:
I praise the one who is higher than the highest, the supreme abode, the supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Sovereign;
the destroyer of obstacles, the peaceful, the nourishing, the beautiful, the infinite,
who is praised by the lords of gods and asuras and by the lords of the Siddhas.
To the sun among the lotuses of the gods, to Gaṇeśa, the refuge of auspiciousness—
this supreme hymn of great merit, which removes obstacles and sorrow;
whoever recites it upon rising in the morning is liberated from all impediments.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Dialogue with Nārada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter.
Nārada said:
Having worshipped Rādhā according to the prescribed rites and having praised her,
the virtuous [Gajendra] gave her ornaments for all her limbs fashioned from priceless jewels.
Having heard Rādhā’s hymn of praise and having seen the worship and the gift, [he was moved].
The peaceful Gaṇeśa spoke sweetly to the peaceful Mother of the Three Worlds.
Gaṇeśa said:
"O auspicious Mother of the World, your worship serves as an instruction for the world."
Abiding upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa, you are of the very nature of Brahman.

(3) The gods, beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa, as well as the lords of sages such as Sanaka and others, meditate upon that which is equal to your lotus feet—[you] who are so difficult to attain. (4)

You are the supreme beloved, dearer than life itself, the presiding goddess of his vital breaths; you are the liberated souls, the devotees, and the lords of perfected beings such as Kapila and others.
Rādhā was fashioned from his left side, and Mādhava from his right side.
Mahālakṣmī, the Mother of the World, was fashioned from your left side.
You are the progenitress of Vasu, the abode of all;
you are the Supreme Sovereign, the primordial Nature (Prakṛti) and the Mistress of the Vedas and of the worlds.
O Mother, all natural things in creation are Your manifestations;
the entire universe consists of effects, while You are the form of the cause.
At the dissolution, when Brahmā falls, that is but a single moment for Hari.

by these powers alone do the vital breaths depart from the Supreme Self after its severance.
Having spoken thus, Rādhikā trembled before the Lord, the Supreme Self.
Having joyfully performed the worship of His feet, He caused Him to sit upon His own seat.
The glorious Lord sat upon a jeweled lion-throne together with Rādhā,
constantly served by seven gopīs with white whisks.
Candanā applied fragrant sandalwood paste to the body of Hari;
the smiling Ratnamālā placed a jeweled necklace upon his neck;
and the virtuous Padmāvatī honored his lotus-like feet with lotuses. (23)
She offered the guest-offering (arghya) consisting of water, dūrvā grass, flowers, and sandalwood paste.
Mālatī placed a garland of jasmine upon the head of Hari,
and the virtuous Campāvatī gave him a basket of campā flowers.
And Pārijātā joyfully gave a *pārijāta* tree to Hari, as well as betel-leaf with camphor and scented, cool water. That Kadambamālā gave him an auspicious garland of *kadamba* flowers. (26)
The very tender Kamalā placed in the hand of Hari a fresh, priceless toy-lotus that served as a mirror for his face,
as well as a beautiful pair of garments formerly given by Varuṇa. (27–28)
Sundarī gave to Hari a vessel of bee-honey, sweet and filled with honey, which shone like actual gorocanā;
and Sudhāmukhī, out of devotion, gave him a vessel of nectar filled with nectar.
And the gopī prepared a bed of flowers, anointed with sandalwood paste,
adorned with a profusion of garlands of unfading mālatī blossoms,
within a most enchanting palace constructed from the finest essence of jewels. (30–31)
Adorned with necklaces of the finest gems, pearls, rubies, and diamonds;
made fragrant by a breeze scented with musk and saffron;
and brilliantly illuminated by hundreds of blazing jewel-lamps. (32)

Having continuously perfumed [the place] with incense composed of various substances, the gopīs, smiling, prepared a bed that was conducive to pleasure; and having seen the couch in private, which was most beautiful and enchanting, [they rejoiced]. (33–34)
Mādhava entered the pleasure-chamber together with Rādhā;
there, on the couch, between the two of them who were afflicted by love, there occurred various kinds of laughter and amorous jesting appropriate for the god of desire. (35)
She gave a garland and fragrant betel nut to Kṛṣṇa; the virtuous woman also placed upon His dark chest sandalwood paste smeared with musk and saffron,
and a beautiful campaka flower upon His crest.
He placed a play-lotus with a thousand petals upon his hand;
casting the flute from his hand, he gave him a jeweled mirror.
He presented before him a fresh flower from the Pārijāta tree.
Smiling, the beloved Rādhikā spoke sweet, secret, and charming words— peaceful, lovely, and captivating— to her lover. (39) Rādhikā said:
O abode of auspiciousness,
O source of all auspiciousness, O auspicious one who bestows auspiciousness—
though an inquiry regarding welfare is fruitless when addressed to you, nevertheless, at this time, a question concerning well-being is appropriate for the occasion.
Even worldly convention is more authoritative than the Vedas; likewise,
O beloved of Rukmiṇī, O Lord of Satyabhāmā, all is well now,
since by Your command the battle with Mahendra was waged as if in sport.
It is heard that he uprooted the *pārijāta* tree from heaven, went to Amarāvatī, and having conquered the gods, gave it to her; furthermore,
by means of that *pārijāta*, he performed a meritorious rite of great virtue.
When the ritual fee was completed, she gave you alone as the object to be won (sādhya) and as her beloved;
how is it that you, who are the insurmountable for Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and even Sādhya himself, have been made "the one to be won" by her?
And yet, among all amorous women, you are afraid of Satyabhāmā!

"O beloved of Jāmbavatī, tell me truly and with certainty: was there excessive love, good fortune, and great respect for Rukmiṇī; and was fear, garlands, and constant praise heard for the blessed Satyā? || 46 ||
Among all those beloved women, for whom do you have the greatest affection?
(47) Among them, who is the supreme connoisseur of love or of every emotion?
Who is devoted to you, clever, fortunate, and exceedingly virtuous? (48)
She is a woman who is truly devoted who protects her husband, and he is a husband who protects his wife.
Beyond mere physical passion, such mutual love between a man and a woman is extremely rare throughout the three worlds.
A refined woman, being virtuous and faithful, recognizes her husband as her own.
A bee, out of greed for honey, runs from afar toward a lotus that knows its virtues, is full of nectar, brave, and always well-behaved during dalliance;
yet the frog does not realize this, and so it places its foot upon its head. (50–51)
The musician knows the essence of the music, but neither the instrument;
the connoisseur knows the taste of milk, but neither the ladle nor the vessel.
Those who enjoy know the pleasure of tasting a fully ripened fruit.

Just as those who are always situated together yet bear no fruit at all [do not perceive it], so too the thirsty do not perceive the taste of the water of good conduct; for neither the pond nor the jar, though situated together, [can provide that taste]. (53–54)
For those who are discerning recognize the supreme, delicious flavor of the rice;
yet, if it remains in one place, it is not like a field or a vessel [to be enjoyed].
One who seeks sandalwood and knows its enjoyment perceives the scent of the sandalwood.
It is not like a donkey carrying a load, nor is it like his water-pot.
(56) That which neither the Vedas, nor Brahmā, Īśāna, and the others, nor yogins, sages, and perfected beings (siddhas) know—how could women know that? (57)
Good fortune, dignity, and love—rare and eternally new—are found among women;
yet they do not remain so for long, becoming as if pulverized in an instant.
O Lord, one who has risen too high surely meets with a fall.
The harming of Vaiṣṇavas is a seed of calamity far removed [from liberation].
And Śrīdāmā, who was devoted to you and compassionate toward devotees, was cursed by me.
Such has been my misfortune, O son, due to the curse of Śrīdāmā.
To whom is the Lord not a kinsman, or who is dear or even disliked by Him?
He is eternally attainable through devotion, and he who is devoted is His Lord.
Thus do the Vedas, the Vedic sages, and the Purāṇas declare.
It is fruitless to say that the Lord Mādhava is to be won over by Rādhā.
Having conquered Śambhu along with his attendants and having severed the arms of Bāṇa,
the grandson of Rukmiṇī brought him back to his capital together with his wife.
"Aho! When you arrived, what did Rukmiṇī say?
Has your mutual love remained equal, or has her respect for you increased?
By the war between the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, the Kurus have been slain by you."
Likewise, where is there any equality between the kings on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas and Arjuna,
the son of Kuntī, who was born directly from Mahendra?
For you alone, standing at the center of the circle of kings, were his charioteer.
What was said by that pure Bhīṣma, the high-souled one,
when he was ashamed before those great ladies?
And how was he seen even by the gods known as Brahmā, Īśa, and Śeṣa?
He was not addressed at all by any of his servants, who were devoted to him like lions;
for he is the Lord who is inexpressible in the four Vedas, in the Purāṇas, and in the Itihāsas, and who transcends primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is devoid of qualities, free from desire, and untainted by all actions;
he is the witness of all deeds and possesses a form for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
He is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Light, the Supreme Lord, and higher than the highest.

And the Supreme Self became the charioteer for all, stationed upon the human chariot. Furthermore, you have enjoyed the company of a hunchbacked woman— an aged Kṣatriya woman who was childless, possessed of an extra limb, and unfit to be touched by a youth.
From the past:
"For what reason was your maternal uncle Kaṃsa slain by you? And having thought, 'He will come,' you went [to him] but did not return. (72–73)
"Having slain all the Yādavas and divided the city of Dvārakā,
the Goddess was restrained by the people from binding you and taking you away.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Rādhikā wept most bitterly.
He suddenly fell into a swoon and became breathless.
The gopīs, standing at the lattice-windows, heard and likewise saw this;
having seen him, they all approached and said to Rādhā, "He is dead."
Taking Rādhikā upon their laps, they all wept loudly and said, "O Hari! O Nṛsiṃha! O Lord! Protect us, protect us! (77) The gopīs said:
"What have you done? What have you done, O Kṛṣṇa? Rādhā is dead before our eyes! Bring Rādhā back to life—blessings be upon you—or else we shall all go to the forest.
Otherwise, all of us women shall inflict the punishment for killing a woman upon you."
O Nārada, having heard the words of the gopīs and of Rādhikā, Mādhava spoke and restored her to life with a glance;
then the goddess Rādhikā, though proud and weeping, arose.
The gopīs awakened her by placing her on their laps again and again.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Listen, O Rādhā; I shall proclaim the supreme spiritual knowledge."
"Having heard which, even a foolish plowman instantly becomes a scholar.
(82) 'By birth I am the Lord of those who have gone [to heaven]; what [is the use] of women such as Rukmiṇī?
I am the manifest form of cause and effect, distinct from Rādhā in each and every way. (83)"
I am the one Self of all beings, inherently composed of light by virtue of my genus; and I exist as an individual within all living creatures, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Furthermore, when one person has eaten, another person is not thereby satisfied.
Even when I, the Self, have departed, one dies while another lives on.
By birth I am of dark form and am myself the most perfect one,
in the holy Goloka, Gokula, and the forest of Vṛndāvana.
The two-armed infant Lord of Rādhā himself, dressed as a cowherd,
is accompanied by cowherds, cowherdesses, and the wish-fulfilling cows (Kāmadhenus).
I, the eternal one, am four-armed in Vaikuṇṭha, existing in a twofold form.
He is the beloved of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, whose form is eternally peaceful.
On earth, he is the lord of the mortal Lakṣmī, while the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī) is the mistress of his mind;
moreover, in Śvetadvīpa and in the abode of Śrī, he is four-armed.

I am the sage Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the eternal Dharma; I am the speaker of Dharma, the most virtuous one, and the promulgator of the path of Dharma. Śānti is the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, most virtuous and devoted to her husband.
In this sacred field of Bhārata, I am her husband;
I am Siddheśa, the bestower of perfection, and I am Kapila himself, the husband of Satī.
O beautiful one, I assume various forms according to different manifestations.
I am eternally four-armed in Dvārāvatī, having Rukmiṇī as my consort;
I am the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, and I am in the auspicious house of Satyabhāmā.
Furthermore, through the manifestation of a multitude of bodies, I am present individually in the palaces of my other wives.
I am the Ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa, the charioteer of this Phālguna;
and that Ṛṣi among men, the son of Dharma, is my powerful portion upon earth. By him, through ascetic penance, I was propitiated at Puṣkara for the office of charioteer.
Just as you, O Goddess Rādhikā, are in Gokula within Goloka,
so too are you Mahālakṣmī in Vaikuṇṭha and Sarasvatī;
you are also the mortal Lakṣmī, the beloved of the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
You are the daughter-in-law of the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) and Peace (Śānti) herself, whose nature is Fortune (Lakṣmī).
You were the beloved wife of Kapila in Bhārata as the virtuous Satī;
you were Sītā in Mithilā, and Draupadī was your shadow, the virtuous one.
In Dvāravatī, you are the great Lakṣmī, the virtuous Rukmiṇī;
and by a portion of yourself, you are the beloved of the five Pāṇḍavas. You were abducted by Rāvaṇa, yet you remain the wife of Rāma.
Just as you, though being one with me through a portion of my shadow, appear in various forms,
so too do I appear in various forms through a portion of my own nature.
Yet I am also the most perfect, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest.
"Thus I have told you all this concerning the internal reality.
O Rādhā, O Supreme Goddess, forgive my offense.
Having heard these words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Rādhikā was deeply satisfied.
And the cowherd women, being thoroughly satisfied, bowed down to the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter [in the Uttara-khaṇḍa] of the Śrī Brahma... Mahā... Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, all the gopīs, greatly delighted with joy, went to their homes after bowing down to Rādhikā, their lord. (1)
That virtuous woman, with her eyes flickering and casting sidelong glances, smiled as she manifested the erotic sentiment of Rādhā, preceded by the sixteen artistic refinements.
And having again offered sandalwood paste and garlands to her Lord, she [continued].
He again made a secret joke and a jest. Having drawn Rādhikā toward him and brought her to his chest, Kṛṣṇa kissed her lips, her chin, and both her cheeks.
Rādhā kissed Kṛṣṇa’s enchanting moon-like face;
she embraced Kṛṣṇa with her arms and drew him to her chest.
She performed the sixteenfold erotic art (śṛṅgāra) as desired and prescribed in the treatises on love.
The Lord, the Sovereign, brought about that which produces delight for both woman and man.
Her entire body was marked by nail-scratches, her lower lip was wounded by his teeth;
her frame was covered in horripilation, she was free from lassitude, and her breasts were small.
Faint from the enjoyment of pleasure, clinging [to him], her consciousness lost,
she remained with only her breath remaining, her eyes sealed in sleep;
a heroine of love, with delicate limbs, she lay upon the breast of her beloved.
In the cold season, her entire body was pleasantly warm; in the summer, she was pleasantly cool.
(9) At the time of love-making, she—possessing full hips and breasts—bestowed pleasure;
and when bent low by the weight of her hips, she was a giver of happiness during their union. (10)
The clever, connoisseur-like, excellent, and lustful woman, having suddenly regained consciousness, heard the sound of the cuckoo.
Upon hearing it, she became utterly terrified; distressed and filled with apprehension for the wretched, [she spoke].
And that supreme Rādhikā, having bound the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest, again and again with her pair of arms and thighs, spoke. (12) Rādhikā said:
"O fortunate one, go to the holy forest of Vṛndāvana, the place of the rāsa dance;
there I shall sport both upon the water and on the land.
Then I shall go again to the beautiful Malaya mountain and its jeweled palace. (13)
"Furthermore, there is another secret that I have not heard from Janaka;
I have a great longing to go there together with you. Through their mutual conversation, the auspicious night passed away.
Even at the time of sunrise, the virtuous woman did not abandon Mādhava;
out of affection, Mādhava awakened her with gentle words.
Then, having performed his morning rites, Hari ascended his chariot.
Together with Rādhā and the gopīs, he whose eyes are like autumn lotuses [resided] in houses thirty million in number, each a yojana in length and breadth,
adorned with blazing mansions constructed from the finest essence of jewels. || 17–18 ||
It had come from Goloka, moving there at the speed of thought and captivating the mind;
it was equipped with a thousand wheels and set in motion by a thousand horses.
It was adorned with thirty million jeweled pillars and resplendent with rows of gems.
It was beautifully adorned with pearls, rubies, and excellent diamond necklaces;
it was decorated with various wonderful paintings, white chowries, mirrors, radiant garments purified by fire, and networks of garlands. (20–21)
With jeweled couches fashioned from precious gems, anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste,
and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of gopīs dressed in identical forms and attire,
the Blessed Lord returned once more to Vṛndāvana by means of that chariot. (22)
Having gone there, he sported at night both on the water and on the land (23).
After indulging in amorous pastimes for a very long time in the forests and groves, he showed Rādhikā everything as if it were all brand new (24).
In Vispandaka, Surasana, and Māhendra; in the Nandana grove, on the lovely peak of Sumeru, and on Mount Gandhamādana;
on every beautiful mountain and in every cave and forest. (25)
In a secluded flower garden, by every river and every stream;
on the delightful sandy banks of the ocean, in the forest of Pārijāta trees,
in the Subhadra and Puṣpabhadrā forests, and at the Nārāyaṇa lake.
In the abode of Pavana, on Malaya and Surālaya, on Trikūṭa, Bhadrakūṭa, Pañcakūṭa, and Sukūṭaka,
as well as in Kāñcanī, which is beloved by the gods.
In every ocean and on every enchanting island,
in excellent and delightful market-towns, and at the meritorious Candrasaras lake,
as well as at Supārśva and Munipārśva, he took delight together with Rādhā.
Returning swiftly once more to the merit-bestowing Jambūdvīpa,
he showed him Dvārakā as well as Mount Raivata.
Having returned again to Gokula, which was crowded with cowherds and herds of cattle—
Having seen that there, he went to the holy Bhāṇḍīra forest in Vṛndāvana.
(32) Hearing of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arrival, Yaśodā and Nanda, as well as the cowherds, cowherd-maidens, and the elders, were tearful-eyed yet free from agitation. (33)
Placing the lordly elephant at their head, the courtesans, actors, and dancers [followed],
as well as a virtuous Brahmin woman accompanied by her husband and sons, and likewise a Brahmin;
just as the gods, having seen Agni, saw Nanda and his mother.
Bālakṛṣṇa Mādhava arrived together with Rādhā.
Madhusūdana, smiling, climbed onto his mother’s lap;
Nanda, along with Yaśodā, kissed his lotus-like face.
Embracing him tightly, she drenched him profusely with tears from her eyes;
and the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa himself drank from Yaśodā’s breast.
Everyone saw him exactly as he appeared when he departed for Mathurā.
With the flute resting in his hand, adorned with jewel ornaments,
appearing like an eleven-year-old youth, beautified by yellow garments,
with a crest of peacock feathers and decorated with garlands of jasmine.
He had Mādhava enter the temple together with Rādhā;
Yaśodā, having performed auspicious rites, fed the brāhmaṇas.
She offered worship to the gopīs and the sages just as ordinary people do.
He joyfully gave to the Brahmins a jewel-gem, coral, and likewise excellent gold; a pearl, a ruby, and a diamond;
as well as a jewel-elephant, a jewel-cow, and a charming jewel-horse.
He gave seats, bowls, and likewise ornaments;
he also gave grains, crops, and garments.
He showed Mādhava, together with Rādhā, who was never seen before.
O Nārada, she also respectfully served sweet foods to the group of cowherd girls;
she caused kettledrums to be sounded and had auspicious rites performed;
and she joyfully fed the gods with delightful offerings.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter [in the Uttara-khaṇḍa] of the Śrī Brahma... Mahā... Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, concerning Nārada’s...
Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Eight.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa issued a challenge and summoned the cowherds;
he himself stayed there at the foot of the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree.
Previously, it was at that very spot that a group of brahmin women had given him food.
The goddess Rādhikā dwelt on the left side of Hari;
on the right was Nanda Gopa together with Yaśodā. To his right was Vṛṣabhānu, and to his left was Kalāvatī.
Other cowherds, as well as cowherdesses, kinsmen, and friends—
Govinda spoke to them with words that were truthful and appropriate for the occasion.
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, Nanda, I shall now speak that which is appropriate for the occasion—
truth, the ultimate reality, and that which brings happiness in the next world.
Behold all this as a delusion, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Like a flash of lightning in water, like a streak across the sky, or like a bubble upon the water—
everything that was told in Mathurā has been revealed without exception.
Then Rādhikā awakened Yaśodā in the plantain grove.
That alone is the supreme truth, the lamp that dispels the darkness of delusion;
abandoning false illusion, remember that highest state, which removes birth, death, old age, and disease, and bestows supreme joy. (8)
It removes the torment of grief and cuts away the very root of karma.
(9) Meditating again and again upon me alone—the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed One, the Eternal—abandoning the notion that I am your son, attain the highest state. (10)
Go quickly to Goloka together with the inhabitants of Gokula,
before the arrival of Kali, which cuts away the very root of karma.
There is no restriction for men or women, nor likewise for the various castes.
In that brahmin, there was no performance of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and so forth, nor the mark of the sacred thread (yajñopavītaka).

The sacrificial cord (yajñasūtra), the sectarian mark (tilaka), and all else were certainly lost. He was intent on sexual intercourse during the day and had desisted from righteous deeds (dharmakarma). (12–13)
