Due to the curse of Kedārakanyā, sacrifices, vows, and even ascetic penances have utterly vanished; indeed, there is no dharma at all. Women wander according to their own will, while husbands remain perpetually under their control. (14)
One should constantly beat him and scold him day and night.
Always attain preeminence over women and their families;
be their master and remain perpetually triumphant over them. (15–16)
In the Kali age, all women will be intent on serving their paramours;
their affection for a paramour will be equal to that for a hundred sons.
They will give him food with the same anger they would show toward a servant.

Smiling and casting sidelong glances, she constantly beheld her paramour with an amrita-like gaze out of desire, yet always looked upon her husband with a poison-like gaze. They always showed great respect and affection toward their paramours and their kinsmen.
She constantly struck her husband with blows from her hand,
and she gave sweet food with faith and devotion to her paramour.
Always dressed in fine attire, she was perpetually intent on serving her lover.
In the Kali age, life is the kinsman and the refuge, and the self is the lover of women.
Hospitality toward guests has vanished, and the service of Viṣṇu has been utterly lost;
likewise, the worship of the ancestors and of the gods has ceased.

A man shall constantly become a hater of Viṣṇu and the Vaiṣṇavas; likewise, those who worship Vāmamantras and members of the four castes devoted to them [shall suffer]. So too shall those who [despise] the Śālagrāma, Tulasī, Kuśa grass, and the water of the Gaṅgā.
A deceitful man, always devoted to the conduct of barbarians, should not touch [it].
It is the cause of all causes, the seed of everything,
the eternal bestower of happiness, liberation, and all prosperity.
Having abandoned me with supreme devotion for the sake of bestowing petty prosperity,
that brahmin shall, through his illusory power, mutter the left-hand mantra which is devoted to the Vedas;
then the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu will cause him to be deceived.
By my command, O Blessed One, you who are difficult for the worlds to overcome,
my image shall remain on earth for ten thousand years of the Kali age;
and for half those years, Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world, shall remain.
As long as there are *tulasī* plants, devotees of Viṣṇu, the Gaṅgā,
and the recitation of the Purāṇas— even if they are few— on this earth, so long shall my own glorification not cease; come to me at the end of this Kali age.

The Kirātas will become uniform in appearance, powerful, and deceitful. (30) All men will abandon service to their parents, service to their teachers, service to gods and Brahmins, and likewise service to guests.
The earth will be devoid of crops due to incessant drought. (31)
A tree devoid of fruit, a river devoid of water,
a Brahmin devoid of the Vedas, a king devoid of strength, and all people devoid of their caste— such a king shall become a barbarian (mleccha). || 32-33 ||
A son may strike his father like a servant, and likewise a disciple may strike his guru;
a wife may strike her husband, and a householder [may strike] like a greedy cock.
All people perish in the Kali age, and at its end, only sinners remain.
Some [perish] from the heat of the suns, and others even by the flood of waters.
O Lord of Vaiśyas, the earth does not perish at the end of the kalpa;
it truly becomes so again at the time of re-creation, for the seed of truth is eternal.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, there appeared a beautiful chariot,
four yojanas wide and five yojanas high,
resembling pure crystal and constructed from the finest essence of precious gems.
It was adorned with clusters of garlands of unfading pārijāta flowers;
it was embellished with ornaments of gems and kaustubha jewels; it possessed a water-pot of priceless jewels, from which hung strings of diamond necklaces. (38–39)
It was embraced by thousands of millions of enchanting palaces;
it possessed two thousand wheels and two thousand horses;
it was covered with fine garments and surrounded by millions of gopīs.
They suddenly beheld him who had come swiftly from Goloka to Vraja.
By Kṛṣṇa’s command, they mounted him and went to the supreme Goloka.
[There were] the goddess Rādhā, Kalāvatī, Dhanyā, and she who was not born from a womb.
O Nārada, all those gopīs from Goloka, who were not born from a womb, as well as all the wives of the Vedas, have come [to this world] in their own bodies;
yet they have all certainly abandoned these perishable bodies.
And Rādhā went to Goloka together with the inhabitants of Gokula.
She beheld the bank of the Virajā, adorned with various jewels;
having crossed it, O Brahmin, she went to Mount Śataśṛṅga.
Studded with various clusters of jewels and adorned by the circle of the rāsa dance,
she then traveled some distance to the holy forest of Vṛndāvana.
There, she beheld the Akṣaya-vata tree, which stood three hundred yojanas high.
Extending for a hundred yojanas and covered with millions of branches,
it was further adorned with masses of large, red-colored fruits;
there, the enchanting Vṛndā dwelt together with thousands of millions of gopīs.
Following her with reverence and a smile, she arrived;
quickly alighting from the chariot, she bowed down to Rādhā.
Having conversed with that Queen of the Rāsa dance, she entered her own abode.
Vṛndā settled her upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne adorned with strings of diamonds,
while she herself remained intent on serving her feet;
she was attended by seven female companions who fanned her with white whisks.
All the gopīs arrived to behold that Supreme Goddess;
having assigned Nanda and the others to their respective places, Rādhā, whose very form is supreme bliss, [entered] with supreme joy. (52)
She set out for her own most delightful residence together with the cowherd girl.
(53) Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Kṛṣṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janma-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
There, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Supreme Master,
immediately granted the liberation of *sāyujya* to the inhabitants of Gokula.
He dwelt for five days at the foot of the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree with the five cowherds.
He beheld the entire Gokula to be in such a state of agitation;
Vṛndāvana forest was likewise unprotected, scattered, and desolate.
Through yoga, a rain of nectar, and his compassion, that treasury of mercy made Vṛndāvana completely full of gopīs and gopas, as well as exceedingly beautiful and enchanting. (3–4)
He consoled the cowherds residing in Gokula and spoke words that were sweet, beneficial, prudent, and rare to find.
Śrī Bhagavān said:
"O friend of the cowherd clans, stay happily and remain steadfast!
Enjoy the most delightful Rāsa-maṇḍala together with your beloved.
From that time forth, [he remained] in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana, the grove of Kṛṣṇa.
And he remained constantly empowered for as long as the moon and sun endure.
In that manner, the Creator of the worlds himself went to Bhāṇḍīra,
as did Śeṣa, Dharma, Bhavānī, and Bhava himself.
Sūrya, Mahendra, Candra, and Agni; Kubera, Varuṇa, Pavana, and likewise Yama;
Īśāna, the gods, and the eight Vasus as well.
All the planets, the Rudras, the sages, and likewise the Manus,
all arrived in haste where the Lord, the Master, was seated.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground, Brahmā himself spoke to him.
O Supreme One, most fully expanded, whose nature is Brahman and whose form is eternal;
O Supreme Light, beyond primordial nature, let there be salutation unto You. (12)
O You who are perfectly anointed, formless yet possessing form through the cause of meditation,
the supreme abode consisting of Your own will— O Supreme Self, homage be unto You!
O Lord, whose nature is all effects, and the cause of all causes!
O Lord of Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa; O Lord of all gods; O Lord of all! ... 14. O Lord of Sarasvatī, Lord of Padmā, Lord of Pārvatī; O Supreme beyond the supreme!
O Lord of Sāvitrī, Lord of Rādhā, Lord of the Rāsa dance! ... 15.
O you who are the primordial source of all, you are everything, as well as the Lord of all; you are the protector of all, the destroyer, and the form of creation.
Blessed and purified by the dust of your lotus feet is the earth.
O Lord, now that you have departed for the supreme state, this world has become empty in your absence.
(17) You leave behind these twenty-five hundred years that have passed and depart for your own abode, leaving me weeping and tormented by separation. (18)
Mahādeva said: "O Lord, having been entreated by Brahmā, you have come to the earth;
having removed the burden of the world, you shall return to your own abode. (19)
In the three worlds, the earth is blessed, for it is instantly purified by being marked with [Your] footprints;
and we, the sages, are blessed, having directly beheld Your lotus feet.
[You are] unattainable through meditation and difficult to propitiate even for those sages whose vital energy is drawn upward.
The Lord who is ours is now on earth as Cākṣuṣa;
he is Vāsu, the abode of all, in whose body-hairs reside the entire universe—
the god Mahāviṣṇu, Vāsudeva, upon the surface of the earth.
That incomparable lotus-foot, which is exceedingly difficult for even the lords of perfected beings to attain despite long asceticism, is the eye for all living creatures.
Ananta said:
O Blessed One, you are indeed infinite; I am merely a tiny fraction of a part.
When the entire universe rests upon the single, minute tortoise, I am like a gnat upon an elephant.
There are countless other Śeṣas and tortoises, whose very nature consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
And you yourself are the Lord of those infinite universes.
O Protector, when will such a fortunate day come for us?
For that Lord who was seen by all living beings in a dream has now been beheld in person.
"O Lord, you are departing for Goloka after having purified the earth,
leaving her protectorless, weeping, and submerged in an ocean of grief.
The gods said:
"The Vedas, as well as Brahmā, Īśāna, and the others, are not able to praise him; how then can we offer praise? Obeisance be unto you! Having spoken thus, those gods departed for the city of Dvārakā.
Filled with joy, they went quickly to behold the Blessed One residing there. Then those cowherds departed for the supreme Goloka;
the earth trembled in fear, and the seven oceans were agitated.
Having abandoned Dvārakā, whose splendor was destroyed due to the curse of the Brahmins,
the Lord of Rādhikā entered the form situated at the foot of the Kadamba tree. All those Yādavas likewise fell in the battle with the Caidyas.
The queens also ascended the funeral pyre and departed together with their husbands.
Arjuna, having returned to his own city, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira;
that king, along with his brothers and his wife, went to heaven.
Having seen the Supreme Lord standing at the foot of the Kadamba tree,
the gods, headed by Brahmā,
bowed down with devotion and praised the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul and Master.
Dark-complexioned and youthful in age, adorned with jewel ornaments;
(35) wearing garments as pure as fire, graced with a forest garland;
exceedingly beautiful, peaceful, the beloved of Lakṣmī, and captivating to the mind. (36)
Seeing his lotus feet, which were joined by the arrows of the hunter and were worshipped by Lakṣmī and others,
he smiled and granted freedom from fear to Brahmā and the other gods.
Having consoled the weeping Earth, who was overwhelmed with love, [he spoke].

He dispatched Vyādha to his own supreme and highest abode. The most wonderful remnant of Bala’s splendor entered Kāma, while that of Pradyumna entered Aniruddha, and that of Aniruddha entered into Brahman.
O Nārada, the goddess Mahālakṣmī, who was born from an improper source (ayoni), and Rukmiṇī went directly to Vaikuṇṭha in their own physical bodies;
Satyabhāmā, whose abode is the lotus, entered the earth.
Queen Jāmbavatī herself entered Pārvatī, the mother of the universe;
and whatever goddesses there were, as well as those who existed on earth in the form of their portions,
they each entered into their respective counterparts individually.
The most wonderful splendor of Sāmba entered Skanda;
likewise, Vasudeva entered Kaśyapa, and Devakī entered Aditi.
Abandoning Rukmiṇī’s palace, he [departed] from the entire city of Dvārakā.
And the ocean, his face and eyes blossoming with joy, received him;
the salt-water sea, having approached, praised Puruṣottama,
yet wept in distress with tearful eyes due to the separation from him.
O Sage, the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Padmāvatī, and likewise the Yamunā; the Godāvarī, Svarṇarekhā, Kāverī, and Narmadā;
the Śarāvatī, Bāhudā, and the merit-bestowing Kṛtamālā.
And they all arrived together and bowed down to the Supreme Lord.
The goddess Jāhnavī, weeping, her eyes filled with tears, exceedingly distressed and trembling from the fever of separation, spoke to the Supreme Lord.
Bhāgīrathī said:
"O Lord, O best of lovers, you are going to the supreme Goloka;
what will our destiny be here in this Kali age?"
The Blessed Lord said: "Remain upon the earth for five thousand years of Kali; whatever sins the sinners offer to you through bathing [in you], [you shall receive them]. (50)
O Jāhnavī, by the touch of those who worship my mantra, [all things] shall be reduced to ashes at that very moment;
indeed, by the mere sight and even by the act of bathing [in you], they shall be so.
For wherever the names of Hari and the Purāṇas exist, [there such power resides].
Having gone there, you shall listen attentively along with these women.
Through the hearing of the Purāṇas and the chanting of the names of Hari,
even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are reduced to ashes.
Just as fires burn dry grass and wood, so too do those very sins of even the most wicked people in this world become reduced to ashes through the embrace of a Vaiṣṇava. (54)
Whatever sacred fords and meritorious sites exist upon the earth, O Jāhnavī,
they reside eternally within the purified bodies of my devotees.
By the dust from the feet of my devotees, the earth is instantly sanctified.
Holy places become instantly purified, and likewise the entire world becomes instantly purified.
Those Brahmins who worship my mantra and partake of the remains of my food constantly meditate upon me alone; they are dear to me and hold more value to me than my own life-breaths.
By the mere touch of that [water], both Vāyu and Pāvaka became purified.
For ten thousand years of the Kali age, there will be devotees of mine on the surface of the earth;
and when those devotees of mine have passed away, they shall become of a single caste.
The earth will become devoid of my devotees, swallowed by the Kali age. In that interval, a four-armed person emerged from the body of Kṛṣṇa there, possessing a splendor equal to a hundred moons.
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and marked with the Śrīvatsa,
he mounted a beautiful chariot and went to the shore of the ocean. And the virtuous daughter of the ocean herself proceeded there in embodied form.
A captivating mortal Lakṣmī was born from the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. When Viṣṇu, the protector of the world and whose nature is pure goodness, departed for Śvetadvīpa, he became twofold in form.
The right portion is two-armed, having the form of a cowherd boy;
he is dark like a fresh rain-cloud, adorned with yellow garments, possessing a face like a lotus-stalk, glorious, smiling, and lotus-eyed. (64–65)
Possessing the beauty of ten million moons and the splendor of ten million Cupids,
the Lord is supreme bliss, most perfectly full.
He is the supreme light, the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, himself devoid of attributes.
And the Supreme Self is the embodiment of grace toward all devotees;
the Lord, the Sovereign, possesses an eternal body and is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Thus do the yogis describe Him as the eternal one whose form is light.
Whom the devotees know as the eternal form within the midst of light;
whom the wise Vedas declare to be the true, eternal, and primordial;
and whom all the gods call the Supreme Lord, consisting of His own will. (69)
All the lords of siddhas and sages describe him as the form of all;
Śaṅkara, the lord of yogis, speaks of him as being inexpressible;
and the Creator himself declares him to be the cause of all causes. (70–71)
Śeṣa spoke of the infinite Lord, whose form is ninefold;
the six systems of logic each have their own desired sixfold form;
the Vaiṣṇavas have one single form, and the Vedas likewise have but one.
Therefore, the Purāṇas are remembered as being of one form, yet divided into nine types.
That which Śaṅkara calls the "Inexpressible" (Anirvacanīya) doctrine,
the wise Vaiśeṣikas call the "Eternal" (Nitya) doctrine.
The Sāṃkhyas call that God the eternal form of light;
the Mīmāṃsakas, the one whose form is all things; the Vedāntins, the cause of all;
Patañjali, the infinite; and the Vedas, the one whose nature is truth. (75)
He is composed of His own will, the Ancient One, and possesses an eternal form for His devotees.
He is this very Lord of Goloka, the Consort of Rādhā, and the Son of Nanda; He who assumes the guise of a cowherd in Gokula and dwells in the sacred forest of Vṛndāvana.

In Vaikuṇṭha, he is himself the four-armed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Mahālakṣmī, whose name is the cause of liberation. By uttering "Nārāyaṇa" even once, a person [is purified] for three hundred kalpas.
O Nārada, he becomes as one who has bathed in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā;
surrounded by his attendants Sunanda, Nanda, and Kumuda,
he bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and is marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Adorned with the Kaustubha, the king of jewels, and a forest garland,
and praised by the gods, he went to his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, by means of a celestial vehicle.
When the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha had departed, the Lord himself, the husband of Rādhā, [remained].
And he produced the supreme sound of the flute, which enchants the three worlds.
O Nārada, the hosts of gods and even the sages fell into a swoon;
they became unconscious through his illusory power, with the sole exception of Pārvatī.
The goddess Pārvatī spoke to the eternal Lord:
"The divine Viṣṇu-māyā is eternal and possesses all forms;
she whose nature is the Supreme Brahman and whose nature is the Supreme Self. (84)
She is both with attributes and without attributes; she is the supreme, consisting of her own will, and is Satī.
Pārvatī said:
"I alone am Rādhikā in form in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance."
O Lord, make Goloka, which is devoid of the *rāsa*, completely full once more.
Ascend the chariot adorned with pearls and rubies and depart;
I am most fully satisfied, remaining upon the surface of your chest.
By your command, I am Mahālakṣmī, going to Vaikuṇṭha;
and Sarasvatī likewise shall be at the left side of Hari.
By your command, I was born from your mind as the Daughter of the Ocean.
"I am Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas;
by a portion of myself, I was present before Brahmā in the past during the Satya Yuga at your command.
There, an abode was established, and the body of the Goddess was maintained therein. (89–90)
The Daityas, beginning with Śumbha, were slain by me with effortless ease;
having destroyed Durga, I am Turgā; in the slaying of Tripura, I am Tripurā;
and having slain Raktabīja, I am the destroyer of Raktabīja.

By your command, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who is the very embodiment of truth, abandoned her body through yoga; and by your command, I am the daughter of the mountain. You have bestowed [these] upon Śaṅkara in the circle of the Rāsa dance in Goloka.
Because I am devotion to Viṣṇu, I am indeed Viṣṇumāyā and Vaiṣṇavī;
because I am the Māyā of Nārāyaṇa, I am remembered as Nārāyaṇī.
I am superior to Kṛṣṇa’s very life-breath, and I am the presiding deity of his life-force.
Rādhikā herself is the mother of both Mahāviṣṇu and Vāsudeva.
By your command, I, who am the embodiment of the fivefold primordial nature (pañcaprakṛti), have become fivefold;
and through my minute portions and sub-portions, I exist as the wives of the gods in every household.
"Go quickly, O illustrious one! There I am, distressed by separation, constantly wandering about in the *rāsa* dance together with the cowherd girls.
Having heard Pārvatī’s words, the Lord of Rasikas smiled.
Having ascended the jewel-chariot, he went to the supreme Goloka.
Pārvatī herself likewise enlightened the host of gods;
the eternal Viṣṇu-māyā was concealed by the sound of her illusory flute. || 98-99 ||
Having uttered the word "Hari," they went to their own homes filled with wonder.
Durgā, together with Śiva, departed for her own city, greatly rejoiced.
Then Rādhā, along with the hosts of gopīs, [saw] Kṛṣṇa approaching.
Accompanying him as he departed, the omniscient lady went along, joyful, her life-breath’s beloved.
Seeing him approaching nearby, the virtuous woman descended from the chariot and,
together with her friends, bowed her head to the Lord of the World.
The cowherds and cowherd girls, joyful with their faces and eyes blossoming,
eager for the arrival of the Lord, sounded their kettledrums.
Having crossed the Virajā river and beheld Rādhā, the Lord of the World—
Quickly alighting from his chariot and taking Rādhikā’s hand,
he wandered through the most beautiful Śataśṛṅga and the Rāsa-maṇḍala;
having seen the holy Akṣayavaṭa, he went to the sacred Vṛndāvana.
Having seen the grove of *tulasī*, he proceeded to the grove of *mālatī*;
leaving behind on his left the groves of *kunda* and *mādhavī*,
Kṛṣṇa made the desired forest of *campaka* trees his right-hand path.
Immediately thereafter, he quickly created a beautiful sandalwood grove.
He beheld before him the most delightful and supreme abode of Rādhikā,
and he dwelt together with Rādhā upon an excellent jeweled throne.

He enjoyed betel-leaf with camphor and scented water; he slept upon a flower-couch adorned with fragrant sandalwood. Immersed in an ocean of aesthetic delight, he took his pleasure together with Rāmā.
Thus everything has been told, exactly as it was heard from the mouth of Dharma. What more do you wish to hear regarding the beautiful ascent to Goloka?
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ascent to Goloka," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Brahma Purāṇa Mahāpurāṇa, [recorded] by Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and thirtieth chapter.
Nārada said: O highly fortunate one, everything that was desired has been heard by me without remainder.
"Is this Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa something unprecedented or is it ancient, and does it grant desired boons?
(1) Now, what shall I do? Tell me that, O Teacher of the World!
Give me your command; I am going to the Himalayas to perform penance. (2)
Nārāyaṇa said:
"In another birth you were the Gandharva Uvabarhaṇa, the husband of five hundred women; now you are the son of Brahmā."
Among them, one virtuous and beautiful woman, having propitiated the supreme Śaṅkara through austerity, obtained her desired boon: that Nārada should be her husband.
And she was the daughter of Sṛñjaya, the sister of Svarṇaṣṭhīvī.
"How can the command of Śaṅkara, 'Perform that marriage,' be rendered in vain?
[For] Sundarī is the most beautiful among the beautiful, tender as a digit of the moon, devoted to her husband, highly blessed, lovely, and sweet-spoken. (5–6)
She was a passionate and desirable woman, eternally in the prime of youth;
yet by whom can the karma written by the Creator in the past be averted? (7) Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
whatever has been done, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced. (8)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa with a grieving heart,
Nārada bowed down and quickly departed for the abode of Sṛñjaya.
Śaunaka said:
O highly fortunate Sūta, ah! What most wonderful thing have you heard?
What is this unprecedented secret, so full of flavor and ancient?
"Now I desire to hear about the marriage of the sage Nārada,
who is beyond the senses and the son of Brahmā, at this present time.
Sūta said:
Having seen the daughter of Sṛñjaya—
a woman of ascetic merit, highly fortunate, and devoted to the vow of Viṣṇu—
Nārada and Mūka went to the beautiful assembly hall of Brahmā, which was surrounded by all the gods.

Having bowed to his father, he, being tranquil, spoke to him of the entire truth. Having heard this auspicious news, Brahmā, the lord of the worlds, with a joyful countenance, attained both his ascetic son and [the fulfillment of his purpose].
In an auspicious moment, accompanied by the gods and a vehicle fashioned from jewels,
he placed his son before him and proceeded to the palace of Sṛñjaya.
Upon hearing that, King Sṛñjaya [welcomed her] who was adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Having taken the beautiful maiden, he joyfully gave her to Nārada.
Having given his entire wealth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), including jewels, pearls, and the like,
he joined his palms in reverence and performed the ritual dismissal (parihāra).
Having entrusted the maiden to Brahmā, the king, the best among yogis, wept loudly and bitterly, crying out, "O child! O child!
"Where are you going, leaving my house empty, O lotus-eyed one? (18)
"Leaving you behind, I am going to the terrible forest, alive yet as good as dead.
Having bowed to her father and likewise to her weeping mother, the weeping maiden,
while she herself was still crying, ascended the chariot of Brahmā.
Having taken his son along with his wife, Dhātṛ, filled with joy,
departed for the world of Brahmā together with the lords of the gods and the sages.
During the auspicious rite accompanied by its constituent parts, he fed the Brahmins.
He caused the drums to be sounded for the gods and the Siddhas as well.
But Nārada, the best of sages, was constrained by his past karma;
O Brahmin, whatever one's destiny from former lives is, it is difficult to overcome—by whom can it be warded off?
On a most beautiful flower-bed, adorned with fragrant sandalwood, he took delight together with Rāmā; day and night passed him by unnoticed.
Having thus performed the marriage, the best of sages withdrew from worldly affairs.
He dwelt at the root of a charming banyan tree in the worlds of Brahmā. There arrived the venerable Sanatkumāra, naked and blazing with the splendor of Brahman, appearing like a child in person.
In age, he is like a five-year-old child even before the creation;
he is unmarried, uninitiated, and devoid of Vedic study and the *saṃdhyā* rites—he who mutters the mantra "Kṛṣṇa," for whom Nārāyaṇa is the preceptor. (27)
And for an infinite number of kalpas, together with his three brothers—
he who was the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, the teacher of teachers among the wise,
and the best of the virtuous— Nārada beheld his brother from afar as he was setting.
Suddenly, he prostrated himself on the ground before him like a staff;
the boy, smiling, spoke to Nārada concerning the supreme truth.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O brother, what are you doing? Is all well with the husband of this young woman? The love between man and woman increases constantly; it is ever-new.
It is a bolt upon the path of knowledge and the door-panel of the gateway to devotion. (31)
It obstructs the path to liberation for a long time and is the cause of bondage;
it is the seed of dwelling in the womb and the supreme cause of hell.
The sinful man, the lowest of men, consumes poison with the notion that it is nectar.
He whose mind dwells upon any object other than the Supreme Nārāyaṇa is deceived by Māyā; having abandoned the nectar of immortality, he would partake of poison.
For all those engaged in ritual action who seek the enjoyment of their fruits, there is no lord other than the Supreme Lord.
"We are the sons of the Creator, and that is the destiny of embodied beings.
(35) "If you have no enjoyment [of worldly life], how did you attain birth as a Gandharva? How are you the son of a maidservant, yet liberated through association with devotees?
Depart for asceticism, O brother; abandon this beloved who is free from disease. (36)
In the most meritorious land of Bhārata-varṣa, worship Mādhava through austerity.
(37) While Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord who bestows His own abode, is present, one who is attached to sense objects and blinded by them is certainly deceived by māyā. (38)
"Accept my mantra, the two syllables 'Kṛṣṇa'—
the essence of all essences, higher than the highest,
found within all the Purāṇas and the four Vedas. (39)
Among the treatises on Dharma and the Tantras, there is no one superior to Manu.
This [text] was given to me by Nārāyaṇa at Puṣkara during a solar eclipse;
having chanted it for countless kalpas, I wander about, honored by all.
Having spoken thus and having caused him to bathe, he gave him the supreme mantra.
Day and night, he recited it with a purified rosary of beads.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings and the mantra upon him, that foremost of Vaiṣṇavas—
He went to Goloka to behold the eternal Lord.
Nārada, however, having reached Manu, who bestows all perfections as a boon,
[attained] unwavering devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which cuts away the bonds of past karma.
Having abandoned his illusory wife, he went to the land of Bhārata for asceticism;
on the bank of the Kṛtamālā river, he beheld the supreme Śaṅkara.
Upon seeing him, the sage suddenly prostrated himself with his head before Śiva.
The Lord of the World, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke to that devotee.
Mahādeva said:
"O Nārada, having seen you, I am pleased by your own splendor."
For embodied beings, the sight of devotees is a truly auspicious day.
Indeed, this union with devotees is the supreme gain for those who possess a body.
He who has beheld a Vaiṣṇava has effectively bathed in all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Moreover, this great mantra, which is very difficult to obtain in all the tantras,
was bestowed by me upon Gaṇeśa and upon Skanda, my own son;
and it was given to me by Kṛṣṇa in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance.
Dharma was given to Brahmā, and Dharma was given to Nārāyaṇa;
Brahmā, in turn, gave it to Sanatkumāra, and by him indeed it was given to you.
Merely by the reception of this mantra, a person becomes Nārāyaṇa.
In this [mantra], there is no deliberation regarding what is timely or untimely, nor what is auspicious or inauspicious;
its *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished by reciting it five hundred thousand times.
A Vaiṣṇava should meditate according to the meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda.
And meditation is the burner of evil and the cutter away of the root of karma.
[One should meditate on] Kṛṣṇa, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, a youth clad in yellow garments,
possessing a beauty equal to a hundred million moons, incomparable and supreme.
Adorned with a multitude of ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste and resplendent with the Kaustubha gem;
with a crest of peacock feathers and decorated with garlands of jasmine.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, he is eternally worshipped by Śiva and others;
he is unattainable through meditation, difficult to propitiate, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
he is the Supreme Self of all, whose very form is for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
I worship that Lord of All, who is beyond the definitions of the Vedas;
having meditated upon that eternal Blessed One through this meditation, worship Him—
the Supreme Bliss, the Truth, the Eternal, and the Highest of the High.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, departed for his own abode.
Having prostrated before that Lord of the World, Nārada went forth to perform austerities.
Recalling Śrī Hari, Nārada abandoned his physical body through the power of yoga.
And [he] is absorbed in the lotus-feet of Hari, whose feet are worshipped by Lakṣmī.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Section on Nārada’s Marriage and Other Matters," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrīmad-Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janma-khaṇḍa.
[Now begins] the one hundred and thirty-first chapter.
Śaunaka said:
I have heard this most extraordinary narrative, supremely wonderful, highly secret and yet more secret, delightful and ever-new.
What is this ineffable, desirable, and heart-stealing thing?
This ancient narrative, so difficult to obtain, has been proclaimed in the Purāṇas.
When will such an auspicious day dawn for us?
That birth is truly fruitful and blessed wherein there is association with Vaiṣṇavas.
It cuts asunder the dwelling in the womb and severs the very root of karma;
it bestows pure service to Hari, increases devotion, and flourishes for the devotees.
The narrative of the birth of Gaṇeśa, which is the cause for uprooting evil through association with the wicked and through false intellect,
is very difficult to find among the Purāṇas.
Furthermore, what supreme and unprecedented account of Tulasī and Rādhikā has been heard?

O highly fortunate one, whatever else is to be kept secret— whether manifest or unmanifest, desired, heard, complete, or captivating— all that has been learned by me. Now, I wish to hear the desired account of the origin of Fire.
"O highly fortunate one, you should explain that to me regarding gold as well.
Sūta said:
"Water alone is the material cause of creation, and fire is its consumer."
In the same way, primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternal, and so too is the Great One (mahat).
Just as the directions and the great ether [are eternal], so too are the sphere of creation, primordial nature, the Great One, and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). (8–9)
Just as sound is a mere subtle element (*tanmātra*), so too is fire;
nevertheless, listen as I describe its origin.
Once, at the time of creation, Brahmā, Ananta, and Maheśvara—
They all went to Śvetadvīpa to see Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World.
Having conversed with one another while seated upon their thrones,
they all spoke in the midst of the assembly before the All-pervading Lord in that most beautiful place.
There, women born from the limbs of Viṣṇu, who are portions of Kamalā,
dance and sing songs of Viṣṇu with melodious voices. 13.
And having beheld their firm hips, their firm orb of breasts,
and their smiling lotus-faces, Brahmā, being deeply desirous,
the Grandfather was unable to restrain his mind. (14)
The powerful one cast down his semen and covered it with his garment out of shame.
O twice-born one, when the music had ceased, that semen, along with the cloth, being heated by the fever of passion, was cast into the Ocean of Milk. (15–16)
Rising from the water, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
the man sat upon the lap of the ashamed Brahmā in his assembly.
In the meantime, [another] rose from the water in haste, filled with rage.
Having bowed to the gods, Varuṇa prepared to lead away the boy.
The boy, weeping out of fear, held Brahmā with both his arms;
O twice-born one, the Creator of the worlds said nothing out of shame. (18–19)
Grasping the boy by the hand, the Lord of Creatures, Varuṇa, drew him toward him in anger; then he hurled him into the midst of the assembly. Thereupon the god Varuṇa fell from afar, being weak.
Alas! By his wrathful gaze, he fell into a swoon as if dead;
then Śaṅkara restored him to consciousness with his nectar-like glance.
Having regained his senses, the Lord of Waters spoke to him there:
Varuṇa said:
"This child born from the water is my desired son;
I shall take him and depart. How could Brahmā strike me? (23)
Brahmā said:
O Viṣṇu, O Maheśvara, this boy has come to me for refuge.
How can I abandon one who is terrified, weeping, and has sought shelter?
That fool who does not protect one who has come for refuge, being distressed and miserable,
is cooked in hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Having heard the words of both, Madhusūdana laughed.
There, the omniscient Lord of All spoke as was appropriate.
The Blessed One said:
"Upon seeing the hips of the lustful woman, the seed of the Creator fell."
Out of modesty, she impelled him into the pure waters of the Ocean of Milk.
Thereupon, he became a child according to dharma, the son of Vidhi;
and in the scripture, he is also considered the secondary son of Varuṇa, known as Kṣetrajña.

Mahādeva said: "Those who know the Vedas understand that the relationship based on learning and biological origin which is prescribed in the Vedas involves equality toward both the disciple and the son. (29)
May Varuṇa grant the mantra and the lore to Bālaka;
he who is the son of Vidhātṛ and the disciple of Varuṇa.
May Viṣṇu grant to the boy the blazing power of combustion.
The fire-god, who had been completely consumed, was extinguished by Varuṇa.
And by the command of Śiva, Viṣṇu gave him his burning power;
Varuṇa gave him a mantra, a vidyā, and a captivating necklace of jewels.

Taking that boy onto his lap, the god kissed him through his illusory power (māyā) and gave him directly to Brahmā, as well as to Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara. Having bowed to Viṣṇu, Brahmā departed, and Śambhu went to his own abode.
The origin of fire has been told; now listen to the origin of gold.
Having beheld Rambhā of the beautiful hips, the god of fire was filled with desire;
his seed fell, and he covered it with his garment out of shame.

And the god of fire, filled with desire upon beholding the beautiful-hipped Rambhā, discharged his seed; he then covered it with his garment out of shame. But the mass of gold, blazing with radiance, cast off the cloth and rose up.
In an instant he caused it to increase, and indeed that Sumeru became so.
The wise call the fire Hiraṇyaretas (the Golden-Wombed).
Thus everything has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Origin of Fire and Gold," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa, in the section concerning Nārada.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-second chapter.
Śaunaka said:
"O Lord of Dharma, I have heard everything without exception from you and from Brahmā.
O highly fortunate one, please relate the Purāṇa once again;
for such a Purāṇa as this has never been heard by me since birth."
"O dear one, neither has such a horse been seen nor heard of.
Sūta said:
"Listen, O highly fortunate one, with attention and self-restraint."
By merely hearing this chapter, one shall obtain the fruit of the Purāṇa.
And the Brahmakhaṇḍa has been narrated, which describes the Supreme Brahman;
it is indeed indefinable, according to the scriptures, for those who [seek it].
With form and without form, with attributes and without attributes, each distinct;
and according to the capacity of those [practitioners], so too is their meditation.
Furthermore, there is a description of Goloka and other realms, presented sequentially and individually.
In that regard, O twice-born one, whatever incidental narratives were employed,
as well as the determination of the various castes and likewise of the mixed castes—
whatever distinguished narrative there was, it was [told] in accordance with the requests of the inquirers. (6–7)
O best of the twice-born, [this work contains] the pastimes of Rādhā and Mādhava, the manifestation of Mahāviṣṇu, and a concise description of all the worlds;
as well as the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada concerning the supreme truth.
The consecration of Nārada and likewise that of the lord of sages;
by the command of Brahmā, Nārada’s journey to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa and his meeting with them there. (9–10)
The conversation between those two and the report to Nārada and others—
O best of the twice-born, the Brahmakhaṇḍa has been told there in due order.
O sage, now listen to the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, which is like a fragment of nectar.
The definition of primordial nature (prakṛti) has been declared, as well as a description of the various natures;
the meditation upon them and their description, beginning with the worship of the elements, have been given.
Likewise, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, and Rādhikā [have been described]. (12–13)
Thus is the conduct of these women, as well as that of others individually;
likewise the narrative of Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī,
the unprecedented account of Rādhikā, and similarly that of Sāvitrī.
The dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī, which grants life like the truth;
the description of the Kṛṇḍas and likewise their characteristics;
the ripening of the fruits of one's lifespan, and the determination of enjoyments. (15–16)
The unprecedented narrative of Rādhikā, which is well-hidden within the Purāṇas;
the most wonderful life-story of King Suyajña;
and the account of Tulasī, which is well-hidden within the Purāṇas—[all these have been told]. (17)
The great battle in the dialogue between Maheśa and Śaṅkhacūḍa;
the conversation between Tulasī and Kṛṣṇa, as well as their union;
the death of Śaṅkhacūḍa, and the liberation of Śrīdāmā from his curse. (18–19)
The attainment of the station of the gods, as well as the destruction of calamities,
the seed of liberation for living beings, and the desired narrative of Gaṅgā;
likewise, the supreme narrative of Manas, which increases great joy.
Thus has been described the utterance of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, as well as other [mantras].
Whatever incidental narration was spoken in accordance with the questions of the interlocutor—that constitutes a section of the *Prakṛti*; now hear of the sections of Gaṇapati. (21–22)
Exceedingly sweet, delightful, and delicious at every step;
well-guarded within the Purāṇas, it is beautiful, ever-new, most rare, and supremely pleasing to the listener. (23)

The supreme sport of Pārvatī and Parameśvara has been proclaimed. First, the birth of Skanda, as well as the interruption of their play, the pleasing of Pārvatī, and likewise the relinquishing of pride. (24–25)
The meritorious vow of Viṣṇu, the supreme account of the Goddess,
the granting of a boon by Hari himself to Pārvatī of excellent vows,
and the vision of Hari appearing in the form of a Brahmin guest.
The manifestation of Gaṇeśa occurred by the grace [of Śiva] in the temple of Śiva;
and in the house of Śiva, there was the sight of the faces of their sons by Pārvatī and Parameśvara, as well as a great festival consisting of supreme bliss. (27–28)
The gods and all others beheld the child—the eternal, unborn, and all-pervading Lord;
the supreme reality whose nature is truth, the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman;
the remover of all obstacles, the peaceful one, and the bestower of all prosperity. (29)
The all-pervading Lord, who bestows the fruits of austerities, silent recitations, sacrifices, and vows;
who is exceedingly desirable and delightful to women;
and who is dearer than life itself to Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord (Śiva).
And [he saw] the Lord, the eternal, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self— the Lord of all, the seed of all, manifest as Nārāyaṇa himself;
by the sight of whom, and likewise by his praise, prostration, and worship—

The lifting up [of the image] during Kārttika, as well as its consecration, is declared to be unachievable through meditation, difficult to attain, and the destroyer of the sins of ten million births.
Likewise, the worship of Gaṇeśa is the destroyer of all obstacles. (33–34)
The battle between Jamadagni and Kārtavīryārjuna, the abduction of Surabhi, as well as the death of the sage;
and the mounting of the funeral pyre by Śukā, the wife devoted to her husband.
The terrible and most dreadful vow made by Bhṛgu;
likewise, O twice-born one, the twenty-one-fold eradication of the Kṣatriyas;
and the dialogue between Gaṇeśa and Paraśurāma, as well as the attainment of knowledge.
The fierce battle between the two, the breaking of Heramba’s tusk,
Durgā’s lamentation and her curse directed at Bhārgava,
the remembrance of Paraśurāma, and the manifestation of Hari.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself enlightened Pārvatī. [39] The description of Śiva’s world, which is most wonderful and desired, was given;
and the great weapon was granted by Śaṅkara to Paraśurāma. [40]
He [received] the mantra and the armor of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
he was granted boons and fearlessness, as well as the bestowal of all prosperity.
He brought about the destruction of kings twenty-one times over.
O Brahmin, the observation of the earth’s burden was undertaken by Bhṛgu.
O best of the twice-born, the section concerning Gaṇapati has thus been narrated in brief, following the sequence of questions and their prior explanations.
Listen with full attention to the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa,
which removes birth, death, old age, and disease, and which grants supreme liberation.
It bestows service to Hari, is pure, most pleasant to hear, and like nectar.
This most excellent narrative called the *Mūṇa* is delightful, delightful, ever-new and ever-fresh. Whatever has not been heard before, it is sweet upon every step.
It is a lamp for all sentient beings and the supreme means of crossing the ocean of existence. (45–46)
It is the crushing of the diseases of karma and its fruits, a rejuvenating elixir,
and the cause for the steps leading to the attainment of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O twice-born one, it contains a description of the fierce quarrel between Śrī Dāma and Rādhā.
The narration of the curse of those two, and then their dismissal;
the birth of Hari on the surface of the earth as requested by Brahmā—
this most wonderful account is told in the Janma-khaṇḍa.
The manifestation of Hari himself in the house of Vasudeva,
and the journey of Hari to Gokula due to fear of the demon Kaṃsa;
Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, [was born] because of the curse of Śrīdāman.
The description of the Supreme Soul’s childhood sports in Gokula is told;
likewise, the destruction of the Daityas and others by Hari is celebrated.
The arrival of Garga is proclaimed, as well as the auspicious first feeding of rice of Lord Hari.
The destruction of Pūtanā and the immediate overturning of the cart;
the binding and liberation by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the breaking of the twin Arjuna trees;
the vision of the three worlds within His mouth, and likewise the stealing of the calf.
Having fashioned a calf and offered praise to Hari,
Nanda, out of fear, suddenly abandoned Gokula and went with Nandana to the holy forest of Vṛndāvana.
The creation of Vṛndāvana has been described as most wonderful;
there, Hari played together with the boys.
Furthermore, the feeding of the Brahmin women with excellent food by Hari has been recounted.
The granting of boons to them and their previous description (57);
likewise, the description of the sacrifices and the theft of the garments;
and the granting of boons to the gopīs performed by Kṛṣṇa himself, O twice-born one (58).
The Kātyāyanī-vrata has been proclaimed, as well as the worship of Śrī Durgā;
and on the bank of the Yamunā, Pārvatī granted a boon to the gopīs.
The eating of palmyra fruits has been declared, along with the crushing of Indra’s night.

The separation and union of Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā, as well as the pastimes of the gopīs, have been described; furthermore, it is proclaimed that Rādhikā was in Kṛṣṇa’s lap, while her shadow remained in the house of Nanda by the illusory power (māyā) of Hari. (60–61)
Having manifested sixteen kinds of amorous passion within the circle of the *rāsa* dance,
Hari vanished from the forest together with Rādhā;
O best of the twice-born, he likewise went to Mount Malaya along with her.
O Sage, there, in that secluded place, the dialogue between Rādhā and Mādhava took place;
the various kinds of liberation attained by the gopīs were also described,
as well as their return once more to the holy forest of Vṛndāvana.
The vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by the gopīs, their expression of joy, and His various kinds of pastimes both in the water and on land are described;
as well as the good fortune of the gopīs, and especially that of Rādhā. (65)
The beautiful, delightful, and ever-new splendor has been described by Vyāsa;
likewise, the vision of the gods residing in the sky and the mental lapses of the goddesses within the circle of the *rāsa* dance have been told. (66–67)
O twice-born one, it has been told how the goddesses took birth through portions [of themselves],
as well as Akrūra’s arrival and the lamentation of the cowherd women;
everything has been related in due order, including likewise the rebuke of Akrūra.
The arrival of Viṣṇu at Mathurā, the grief of the inhabitants of Gokula,
the mass of flames from the fire of Rādhikā’s separation as it appropriately occurred, and likewise the sight of his own root-form by Akrūra on the bank of the Yamunā have been described. (69–70)
The entry into Mathurā has been described, as well as the death of the washerman;
his union with Kubjā and her very liberation;
the propitiation of the weaver and the release of the garland-maker. (71)
The breaking of Śambhu’s bow and likewise the destruction of his elephant;
the entry into the assembly hall and the display of various forms have been proclaimed.
The slaying of Kaṃsa and the lamentation for his kinsmen have also been proclaimed. (72–73)
The performance of his funeral rites according to the rules, as well as those of his father;
the cremation of Nanda, and the most wonderful hymn of praise;
and the conversation between the father and son told in a secluded place. (74)
The All-pervading Lord bestowed the supreme spiritual knowledge upon Nanda.
Furthermore, the departure of the sages and the narrative of Dhanya were recounted by Kumāra; indeed, that which was spoken is very difficult to attain.
The arrival of Uddhava has been described, as well as Rādhā’s secluded abode;
and the auspicious knowledge from their conversation has indeed been told.
[Also mentioned are] Kṛṣṇa’s sacred thread and the gift of learning in the house of Gura.
And the restoration of his dead son was formerly told to that preceptor;
likewise, the subduing of Jarāsandha, the death of the Yavana,
the construction of Dvārakā, and the exertion of Viśvakarman.
The entry into Dvārakā has been described, as well as the consolation of Ugrasena;
likewise, the abduction of Rukmiṇī and the subduing of kings have been told,
as well as his marriage to all those lovely women.
The liberation of Māyāvatī and the death of Śambara;
the release of Śiśupāla during the Rājasūya sacrifice of the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira),
as well as the liberation of Dantavakra and the death of Śālva, O Sage.
The theft of the jewel and the Pārijāta tree from heaven, the war between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, the removal of the earth's burden,
the abduction of Ūṣā, and the lopping off of Bāṇa’s arms have been described.
The hymn of praise by Bala has been proclaimed, as well as the heroic exploit of Aniruddha (84).
The conversation between Rādhā and Yaśodā, which is extremely difficult to obtain, has been proclaimed;
and the most wonderful liberation of the jackal has also been proclaimed (85).
In the course of a pilgrimage to sacred sites, there was likewise the worship of Gaṇeśa;
the vision of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, together with Rādhikā;
the vision of the Goddess Rādhā; and the manifestation of Rādhā’s splendor.
O Śaunaka, [this section contains] the amorous pastimes of Rādhā at the sacred ford, the wandering in secret,
the destruction of the Yadu dynasty by the curse of the Brahmins,
the liberation of the Pāṇḍavas, and Hari’s departure to his own abode. (87–88)
The marriage of Nārada, as well as the origin of Fire and Gold— O highly fortunate one, all this has been declared once again in brief. And the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa consists of four sections.
"O best of sages, what more do you wish to hear beyond this? (90).

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Table of Contents for the Conversation between Nārada and Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Brahma-vaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-third chapter.
Śaunaka said:
My birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived, since I have heard without obstacle this fruit-bearing account from the Brahmavaivarta, which is the cause of liberation. (1)
"O child, O father, grant me fearlessness;
then I shall make a certain request.
Sūta said:
"Abandon your fear, O illustrious one; ask whatever you desire.
I shall tell you everything, even that which is beautiful and secret.
Śaunaka said:
"Now, O son, I wish to hear the definition of the Purāṇas, their number, and also the fruit thereof.
Sūta said:
O Śaunaka, I shall relate to you the extensive Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, the Saṃhitās, and the Pañcarātras exactly as they have been received.
[The topics include] the primary creation (sarga), the secondary creation (pratisarga), the genealogies (vaṃśa), and the periods of the Manvantaras.
O Brahmin, the lineage history (vaṃśānucarita) and the Purāṇa with its five characteristics—
these the wise know to be the definition of the Upapurāṇas.
Now I shall tell you the definition of the great Purāṇas.
The creation and the emission [of beings], their maintenance and protection;
the latent impressions of actions, the livelihoods, and the duties in their proper sequence;
the description of the dissolutions and the exposition of liberation.
The glorification of Hari alone and of the Vedas individually;
the tenfold characteristics of the great ones as they have been proclaimed; and the enumeration of the Purāṇas—learn them from me as I tell you. (9–10)
The Para-Brahma Purāṇa consists of exactly ten thousand verses;
the Pādma is proclaimed to have fifty-five thousand verses;
and the wise know the Vaiṣṇava to consist of twenty-three thousand verses.
The Śaiva Purāṇa is described as having twenty-four thousand verses;
the wise know the Śrīmad Bhāgavata to consist of eighteen thousand verses,
and the Nāradīya is proclaimed to have twenty-five thousand verses.
The learned know the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa to consist of nine thousand verses,
as well as fifteen thousand four hundred. Furthermore, the beautiful Agni Purāṇa has been fully described.
The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of fourteen thousand verses plus an additional five hundred; and the esteemed Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa consists of eighteen thousand verses.
The wise know that this alone is the essence of all the Purāṇas.
The supreme Liṅga Purāṇa consists of eleven thousand verses,
while the Vārāha Purāṇa is proclaimed to have twenty-four thousand.

The Skanda Purāṇa is declared by the virtuous to be the best, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses and an additional one hundred. The Vāmana Purāṇa has ten thousand verses, while the Kaurma has seventeen thousand. (18–19)
The Matsya Purāṇa is declared by the learned to be the fourteenth;
the Gāruḍa is proclaimed to consist of nineteen thousand verses.
Furthermore, the Brahmāṇḍa is proclaimed to consist of twelve thousand verses.
Thus, the enumeration of the Purāṇas is declared to be four hundred thousand [verses]. (21) The wise know that it is exactly thus for the eighteen Purāṇas;
and in this same way, eighteen Upapurāṇas are proclaimed. (22)
The *Itihāsa* and the *Bhārata*, the *Vālmīki* and the *Kāvya*, the fivefold collection of the *Pañcarātras* preceded by the *Kṛṣṇamāhātmya*,
as well as the *Vasiṣṭha*, the *Nāradīya*, the *Kāpila*, and the *Gautamīyaka*.
Furthermore, there is the Sanatkumāra-pañcarātra and the Pañcaka;
the Pañcaka of the [five] companions, endowed with devotion to Kṛṣṇa, as well as those of Brahmā, Śiva, and likewise of Prahlāda. (24–25)
The Saṃhitās of the youth Gautama have been fully proclaimed.
Thus everything has been told to you in due order and individually.
In this same way, there exists a vast scripture for me as well, according to tradition.
In the past, in the circle of the Rāsa dance at Goloka, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself spoke this ancient account to Brahmā, his own devotee;
Brahmā spoke it to Dharma, the most virtuous; and Dharma spoke it to the sage Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa spoke it to Nārada, and Nārada to me, his devotee;
and I, O best of sages, relate that most excellent Purāṇa, the Brahmavaivarta, which is difficult to obtain and longed for. (29)
That which indeed encompasses the entire flood of the world as the supreme self of all living beings—
that is Brahman, the witness-form of the very actions of those who act.
Wherein that Brahman is revealed, there lies its unsurpassed majesty.
Therefore, the wise know this as the *Brahmavaivarta*;
it is a meritorious Purāṇa, auspicious and the bestower of auspiciousness.
It contains secrets that are well-guarded, and within it, there is ever-new beauty.
It bestows devotion to Hari, and it grants the rare state of service to Hari;
it confers happiness and the Supreme Brahman, it is the essence that destroys grief and torment.
Just as the auspicious Gaṅgā among rivers immediately grants liberation, so too is this [work]. (33-34)
Just as Puṣkara is the purest among sacred fords (tīrthas) and Kāśī is the best among cities,
so too is the auspicious Bhārata-varṣa the immediate bestower of liberation among all regions.
As Sumeru is the foremost among mountains and Pārijāta among flowers, [so is this land supreme].
Among leaves, the *tulasī* leaf; among vows, the vow of Ekādaśī;
among trees, the Kalpa tree; and among gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
among the lords of the wise, Mahādeva; and among the lords of yogis, Gaṇeśvara. (36–37)
Among the lords of the Siddhas, Kapila is preeminent, just as the Sun is among the luminous;
the venerable Sanatkumāra is the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas,
just as Rāma is among kings and Lakṣmaṇa among archers.
Among goddesses, she is like Durgā, who is most meritorious;
among those dear to Kṛṣṇa, she is like Rādhā, who is dearer than life itself;
among sovereign ladies, she is like Lakṣmī; and among the learned, she is like Sarasvatī. (39–40)
Likewise, among all the Purāṇas, including the Brahmavaivarta,
there is none more distinguished than this one, which bestows happiness, is sweet, grants great merit,
and is proclaimed as the Purāṇa that shatters all doubts.
In this world, it bestows happiness and grants all forms of prosperity;
it confers auspiciousness and merit, and is the supreme destroyer of obstacles.
It grants service to Hari and bestows great joy in the next world.
The fruit of this is not equal to that of sacrifices, sacred fords, vows, or likewise austerities, nor even to the merit of circumambulating the earth;
indeed, its fruit is superior even to the recitation of all four Vedas.
O son, he who listens to this Purāṇa here with self-restraint shall obtain a virtuous,
learned, and Vaiṣṇava son. And if an unfortunate woman listens to it, she shall obtain good fortune from her husband.

A woman who has borne only stillborn children, one who has given birth to a son that died as a crow (kākavandhyā), and even a sinful woman who is barren—by listening to the Purāṇas, she obtains a son who lives for a long time.
One without a son obtains a son; one without a wife obtains a beloved spouse.
One of obscure fame becomes renowned; a fool becomes a scholar.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one who is bound is released from bondage.
One who is afraid is freed from fear; one who has fallen into calamity is freed from that calamity.
In the midst of a forest, one who is terrified will certainly be liberated from a forest fire.
Sin, leprosy, poverty, disease, and terrible grief—
the meritorious person knows these only by hearing [of them], while the one devoid of merit does not know them at all.

He who, being well-restrained, listens to even half a verse or a quarter of a verse, obtains the merit of giving a hundred thousand cows; of this there is no doubt. He who, having conquered his senses, listens to the *Yuga-purāṇa* at a pure time, [obtains the same merit]. (51–52)
He who hears this with devotion, having offered a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births— whether committed in childhood, youth, old age, or middle age; of this there is no doubt.
Having assumed the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by means of a vehicle fashioned from jewels,
he shall go eternally to Goloka and attain the state of being a servant of Kṛṣṇa.
Even when countless Brahmās pass away, there shall be no falling for him.
Having become an attendant, he performs service for a long time nearby.
Having heard the *Brahmakhaṇḍa*, well-bathed, self-controlled, and pure,
[he offers] milk-rice, flour-cakes, fruit, and betel leaf.
Having fed the reciter, one should give him gold;
likewise, having offered sandalwood, white garlands, and beautiful fine garments to Vāsudeva, these are presented to the reciter. (57–58)
And having heard a section of the *Prakṛti* that is pleasant to hear and like nectar,
one should feed him curd-rice and give him gold. (59)
Having heard this section on Gaṇapati, one who is self-controlled should, for the destruction of obstacles, devoutly offer a beautiful, auspicious cow along with her calf;
as well as a golden sacred thread, a white horse, an umbrella, and a garland. (60)
A svastika-shaped sesame sweetmeat is given to the weaver.
Having heard the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janma Khaṇḍa with devotion, the devotee [should offer] only fully ripened fruits produced in their proper time and place. (61–62)
And one should give to the reciter a supreme jeweled ring,
fine cloth, a garland, and an excellent golden earring;
as well as a garland, a beautiful swing, and well-cooked milk.
One should give one's entire possession as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and certainly perform the hymn of praise;
with the utmost reverence, one should feed a hundred Brahmins,
including an excellent, learned Brahmin who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and well-versed in the scriptures.
One should employ a pure reciter; otherwise, it would be fruitless. [This applies to] a Brāhmaṇa who is averse to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is wicked, or who has not been instructed.
However, he who listens to the Purāṇa endowed with devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa [attains the fruit].
He does not obtain devotion or merit, and he destroys the merit previously performed.
But he who listens to the Purāṇa from one endowed with devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa obtains both devotion and merit; at the end, he goes to the abode of Śrī Hari.
"All this that was heard from the mouth of my guru has been told to you.
O best of Brahmins, grant me leave; I am going to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa. Having seen the assembly of Brahmins, I have come here to pay them homage."
The supreme Brahmavaivarta has been narrated by me at your command.
Salutations be to the Brahmins and to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul; constant salutations to Śiva, to Brahmā, and to Gaṇeśa—salutations, salutations!
Day and night, with devotion of body, mind, and speech, worship the Supreme Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Rādhā, who transcends the three qualities (guṇas).
Salutations to the Goddess Sarasvatī; salutations to the Preceptor of the Purāṇas.
Salutations again and again to Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of all obstacles.
O Śaunaka, having beheld your meritorious feet,
I shall today go to Siddhāśrama, where the Lord Gaṇeśvara resides.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter (133) in the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, in the latter half of the Śrī Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, and the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
This concludes the latter half of the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa from the venerable Śrīmad Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
This concludes the fourth section, the Śrī Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa,
as well as the entire Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa composed by the venerable sage Vyāsa.
